en: The Explanation of the Treasury of Abhidharma with Clarified Meaning (Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā) I
(The First Chapter of the Treasury, titled "Exposition of the Elements") Homage to the one who crushes the hosts of Māra.
He possesses great strength, with wisdom and meditative concentration as his tusks.
I bow my head to that Naga among Teachers, who, having shattered the cage of birth, entered the peaceful forest of nirvāṇa.
Performing the task of a teacher in the world by means of composing a treatise on the ultimate truth,
they call him— the foremost among the wise— the second Buddha.
By him named Vasubandhu, the future kinsman of the ultimate truth for the world,
this *Abhidharmakośa* has been composed as a compendium of the Abhidharma.
This commentary on this jewel of a treatise, extracted from the ocean of the Abhidharmabhāṣya, has been composed by me; it is truly worthy of its name, "Sphuṭārthā" (The Clear Meaning).
The explanation of the meaning of the words which was well-composed by commentators such as Guṇamati and Vasumitra is approved by me; and this meaning has been written down by me accordingly.

Having exposed those interpretations which have deviated from the meaning of the established doctrine (siddhānta) here and there as composed by them, I have provided here a different interpretation according to the truth.
Those who have exerted themselves in the Abhidharmavibhāṣā and the Abhidharmakośa should examine whether this commentary is logical or not.
If this [position] is logical, it should be accepted; otherwise, it must be rejected.
For the intellect of one such as I cannot possibly fail when confronted with an inconsistent matter.
Having paid homage to that Teacher of Reality, who has utterly destroyed all darkness and has lifted the world out of the mire of saṃsāra;
Explaining the meaning of this verse— "I shall proclaim the treatise, the Abhidharmakośa"— the Master says:
"Desiring to compose the treatise, [Vasubandhu] begins his salutation to the Teacher, preceded by a description of his qualities, in order to make known the greatness of his own Teacher."
Desiring to compose— that is, desiring to create— the treatise *Abhidharmakośa*, [the author] refers to his own teacher,
his personal teacher; for that Blessed One is the teacher belonging to the Master (Vasubandhu), because he has entered into that teaching.
Or rather, by that Teacher who is dependent upon great compassion, the entire world has been embraced as his own.
Therefore, for the Master as well—who has been embraced as his own—that Blessed One becomes his own Teacher.
This is for the purpose of making known [the Teacher’s] majesty.

"Great-souledness" (*mahātmatvam*) is "magnanimity" (*māhātmyam*), which is the perfection of accomplishing the welfare of oneself and others; it is for the purpose of making that known and for the purpose of awakening to that.

"Preceded by the proclamation of qualities" (*guṇākhyānapūrvakam*) means preceded by the description of qualities; the meaning is that he undertakes a salutation to him, that is, he pays homage to him.

Since the time [of the composition] has passed, one should have said "he began" (*ārabdhavān*); however, the use of the word in the present tense is intended to show that even now there is the intention to begin the homage, or because the commencement of the homage continues through the succession of disciples. Such usage of words is also observed in the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*).
"Now, the instruction on words.
This word "now" (atha) is employed for the purpose of introducing the subject matter.
If it is argued that the greatness [of the science] is understood through the mere statement of its qualities and not through an act of salutation:
No,
because that [homage] indicates it.
For by means of the homage, his greatness is indicated.
Alternatively, the greatness [of the Buddha] is made known precisely by the description of his qualities, not by the act of salutation.
The commencement of the salutation, however, is for the purpose of generating one's own merit,
or for the purpose of demonstrating conformity with the conduct of the virtuous.
For virtuous people begin their undertaking only after performing worship, praise, and prostration to their chosen deity; this is because it is the practice of the virtuous.
To this we reply: for what purpose is the greatness [of the author] made known there?
It is for the sake of generating reverence toward him.
Furthermore, the generation of reverence is for the sake of listening to that teaching with respect.
Listening with respect is for the sake of gradually generating the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The generation of that [wisdom] is for the sake of abandoning the afflictions.
Furthermore, its ultimate purpose is for the sake of attaining nirvāṇa, which is characterized by the cessation of all suffering; this constitutes the finality of the purpose.

As for the demonstration of the greatness [of the treatise], the Teacher has explicitly stated it as a single purpose because it is the immediate purpose. However, the others could have been inferred, and thus they were not mentioned.
The word "ya" (who/that) is said with reference to the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Although the word "ya" is a general term, it functions as a specific [designation] because it is qualified by what has been previously established.
For example: "Among these Brahmins, he who is fair-complexioned and wears white garments—he is Evasarman."
So it is here as well:
he who has utterly destroyed all darkness in every way has lifted the world out from the mire of saṃsāra.
Regarding the phrase "having paid homage to him," the word "he" (yat) refers to the Blessed One, the Buddha himself.
For no one other than the Buddha could possibly exist as distinguished by such qualities; therefore, he explains it thus.
The word "yaḥ" (he who) refers to the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Regarding the term "buddha," the suffix *kta* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
He is called "awakened" (*buddha*) because of the blossoming of his intellect (*buddhi*).
The meaning is "fully awakened," just as one says "the lotus has blossomed. Alternatively,
the meaning is that he is "awakened" or "fully enlightened" due to the departure of the two-fold sleep of ignorance.

Others say that the term "awakened person" (*prabuddhapuruṣa*) is formed according to the rule for the *karmakartṛ* (the agent as the object), which prescribes the suffix *-ta*. The meaning is that he is "awakened" (*buddha*) because he awakens by himself.
We see no fault even in the application of the suffix *kta* to the word *karman*.
The meaning is that he is known (*buddha*) by other Buddhas—or by others—due to his being endowed with the perfection of all virtues and his being entirely free from all defects.
The inclusion of the second word, *bhagavantam*, is for the purpose of eliminating any lack of respect or any notion of [his] insignificance.
For in the world, it is observed that names without qualifiers are treated with disregard,
such as "Devadatta.
However, the authors of the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā* formulate four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭikā*).
There is a Buddha, but not a Blessed One (Bhagavān).
A Pratyekabuddha may be called "Buddha" because of his self-awakening,
but he is not a Blessed One.
Because the equipment of giving and so forth is not yet complete.
For one who possesses greatness is called "Bhagavān.
There is one who is a Bhagavān but not a Buddha.
A bodhisattva in his final existence possesses both [characteristics], because he has fulfilled the perfections such as generosity and because he has not yet attained full awakening.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, exists in both ways; and there is one who exists in neither way, setting aside these aforementioned modes.
Therefore, "the Buddha, the Blessed One" contains two qualifying attributes.
He is "one by whom darkness has been destroyed" (*hatāndhakāra*), meaning either that darkness has been destroyed by him or that darkness has been destroyed for him.
In the case of a genitive *bahuvrīhi* compound, if one were to say "darkness was destroyed by the path," the path, acting as the agent, would have to be supplied as an ellipsis.
In the case of a third-case *bahuvrīhi*, however, the instrumental "by means of" (*mārgeṇa*) must be supplied.
Another [teacher] says:
the presentation of two analyses is for the purpose of including both meanings of the root *han*—namely, "to strike" and "to go," as in the rule *hana hiṃsāgatyoḥ*.
When the analysis [of the compound] is "her darkness has been destroyed" (*hatam asyāndhakāram*),
then the root *han* is understood in the sense of "going";
the meaning is that "her darkness has gone."
When, however, it is a third-case *bahuvrīhi* compound, then the root *han* is understood in the sense of "striking";
the meaning is: "darkness has been struck by this."
In this way, having first formed a single compound from the two subsequent words, one subsequently forms a locative *tatpuruṣa*:
"one in whom darkness has been destroyed in its entirety" (*sarvahatāndhakāra*). And that being so, the word *hata* does not undergo prior placement here.
One must consider by which rule the seventh-case compound (*saptamīsamāsa*) occurs here.
It is a compound according to the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ*.
The word *hatāndhakāra* is listed among the *śauṇḍādi* group.
Since the *śauṇḍādi* group is established as an open-ended class (*ākṛtigana*), its inclusion therein should be understood;
or else, it follows from the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the locative case" (*saptamī*); or alternatively, the compound is formed by the general rule [Pāṇini 2.1.4].
When *sup* is present [in the rule] *saha supā*, that which ends in a *sup* suffix is compounded with another word ending in a *sup* suffix.

Regarding the phrase "where it is desired," either a *tatpuruṣa* compound whose specific technical definition has not yet been applied should be understood as included in the list beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*, or else [it is understood] by this [rule]. How is it that the darkness (*andhakāra*), having become a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), is connected with "in all" (*sarvasmin*)?
It is true that the darkness is not connected with this [word "all"].
The destruction of darkness, however, is connected with this [Buddha].
For that destruction of darkness through which the Blessed One, by virtue of its possession, has destroyed darkness—
that destruction of darkness of his is to be understood as the support of all.
Just as in the case of "a cheat at dice":
because he possesses the quality characterized by cheating,
that cheat has the dice as his locus.
In this case as well, it should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, we observe that a compound is possible here in another manner as well:
*sarvahatam* means "killed in everything" (*sarvasmin hataṃ*).
"In every way, all [darkness] is destroyed; in every respect, all is destroyed.
Because his darkness is destroyed in every way, or by means of this [knowledge], he is one "by whom darkness is destroyed in every way" (*sarvathā-sarvahatāndhakāra*).
Thus, the word *hata* (destroyed) stands in grammatical apposition with *andhakāra* (darkness). (Abhidh-k-vy 4)
And as for the rule regarding the prior placement [of words],
it means "in every way," that is, by virtue of the disappearance of both afflicted and unafflicted darkness.
This occurs with respect to all objects of knowledge, characterized by the twelve sense bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).
"Everything, everything," O Brahmin—referring precisely to the twelve sense-bases (dvādaśāyatana), according to the statement in the Sūtra.
What here is meant by the word "darkness" (*andhakāra*)? Is it the darkness of the night? No, he says.
Ignorance (ajñāna) should be understood as darkness (andhakāra) because it obstructs the perception of reality.
For the word "darkness" is well-known to denote nocturnal gloom;
it is called "darkness" because it makes people as if blind.
Because it obstructs the perception of the forms of truly existent things such as jars and cloths,
ignorance also receives the name "darkness" due to its similarity to that;
for it obstructs the perception of the true objects, namely the truths of suffering and so forth.
"And that" refers to that ignorance.

"By the attainment of the counteragent" means by the attainment of the noble path (*āryamārga*). It is called the "counteragent" (*pratipakṣa*) because it is the side (*pakṣa*) that opposes the afflictions (*kleśa*), which are the "adverse factors" (*vipakṣa*). Thus, it is so designated because it acts as the side for the purpose of striking down the adverse factors.

Alternatively, knowledge (*jñāna*) is untainted (*anāsrava*) and is the antidote to ignorance (*ajñāna*); by the attainment of that [knowledge], [ignorance] is "destroyed" in the sense that it has been rendered non-manifest through abandonment, because it is of a nature never again to arise with respect to any object of knowledge whatsoever, in every way and at all times.
Therefore, he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavān*).
Since both Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas are worthy of honor, the word "Pratyekabuddha" is placed first [in the compound].
The term "kāmam" expresses permission;
however, it does not mean "in every respect."
Because non-afflicted delusion has been completely eliminated.
But is it not the case that all contaminated things have been abandoned by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas just as they have by a Buddha? Why, then, is this being said?
It is the absolute departure of their afflicted delusion.
For it has been said:
"I do not declare the making of an end to suffering for one who has not directly known and fully understood even a single dharma."
Likewise, [the Buddha said], "I do not declare the making of an end to suffering without having fully understood and abandoned even a single dharma.
Therefore, even for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, that non-afflicted ignorance is indeed abandoned through the abandonment of desire and attachment, just as it is with the eye and other faculties.
Otherwise, there would be no making of an end to suffering for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This is indeed true for the noble ones (*sat*):
their non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) has been abandoned just as their afflicted ignorance has.
However, although it has been abandoned, that [non-afflicted ignorance] still manifests for them, just like the eye and other faculties.
In the case of a Buddha, however, that which has been abandoned does not manifest again.
For this very reason, it is specified as "destroyed" because it is of a nature never to arise again;
otherwise, he would have simply said that it is abandoned in every respect and with regard to all objects of knowledge.

As for those who explain that the cessation of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas occurs through the mere removal of afflicted delusion (*kliṣṭasaṃmoha*), that is a false explanation; it is refuted by the statement "of these, as has been said," and so forth.
For it is thus, in detail: [the text continues].
"Tathā hi" means "because. Alternatively, "tathā" means "not in every respect";
the word "hi" indicates the reason.
"Of these" refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding the "Buddha-qualities," such as the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) and so forth,
and regarding objects that are extremely remote in space and time— that is, objects situated in extremely distant places and at extremely distant times.

And regarding objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which have infinite varieties and whose intrinsic nature is not that of the Buddha-qualities (*abuddhadharma-svabhāva*), there indeed exists non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*); the meaning is that this ignorance actually manifests there.
In that context, "Buddha-qualities" refers to those such as the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and so forth.
Regarding these [qualities], because they are by nature supremely subtle and profound, there is ignorance of them among those other than a Buddha.
As it has been said:

"Śāriputra, do you know the Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), his aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), his aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), his aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and his aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*)?"
Thus was it said by the Elder Śāradvatīputra when questioned by the Blessed One:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
However, those other objects which possess form are aggregations of atoms.
If those [bases] are situated in an extremely remote location;
and even those which are non-informative (avijñapti) or immaterial (arūpin)—
if they too, by virtue of having an extremely remote location as their support, come to be situated in an extremely remote location.
Even regarding those [objects], they possess ignorance because the locations are separated by many world-systems.
Indeed, it is heard that the Elder Maudgalyāyana lacked full knowledge of the location of his own mother, who was born in the Mārīcī world-system, an exceedingly distant place.

Furthermore, even concerning objects belonging to extremely remote past or future times, they certainly experience ignorance because those things are separated by the destruction and manifestation of an immense number of intervening eons.

For it is heard that the Elder Śāriputra rejected a man seeking ordination because he did not perceive any roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*). However, the Blessed One perceived his roots conducive to liberation and said: "I indeed observe a very subtle seed of liberation in him."
"Like gold hidden within a crevice of ore-bearing rock," so it was said;
and that man became a renunciant.
Regarding the phrase "in infinite varieties": it refers to objects that are difficult to comprehend due to their distinctions such as realms, destinies, modes of birth, and rebirths.
Ignorance regarding these indeed exists.
For it has been said:
"The cause of even a single eye on a peacock's tail in all its aspects cannot be known by those who are not omniscient; for the knowledge of that is the power of an omniscient one."
Thus, these are the four causes of ignorance.
Among them, one may apply them as the case may be: in some instances one, in some two, in some three, and in some all four.
"Thus, the perfection of the practice for one's own benefit," and so forth.
Practice for the sake of one's own benefit is "the practice for one's own benefit.
The perfection of the practice for one's own benefit is "the perfection of the practice for one's own benefit"; the meaning is the accomplishment of the fruit.
And this perfection should be understood as having the nature of the perfections of knowledge and abandonment.
The perfection of the practice for the benefit of others should also be considered in the same way.
Others explain it differently.
The practice for one's own benefit is the accomplishment of one's own benefit;
that is to say, the acquisition of what is beneficial for oneself. The perfection of that is the perfection of the practice for one's own benefit.
In this way, the perfection of the practice for the benefit of others should also be explained.
Furthermore, that [practice] has the nature of bringing about the attainment of nirvāṇa, which is the pacification of all suffering.
Thus, it "lifts the world out from the mire of saṃsāra."
Because it is so stated.
*Saṃsāra* means wandering (*saṃsaraṇa*), the state of coming and going (*ājavaṃjavībhāva*), which signifies the succession of births and deaths.
Alternatively, *saṃsāra* refers to the triple world (*traidhātuka*), because sentient beings wander within it.
Samsara is like mud; thus it is called "the mud of samsara" because of its similarity to mud.
Therefore, he says:
"For samsara is like mud, because it is a place where the world becomes attached and because it is difficult to cross."
For in this world, mud is a place of attachment because its nature is to cause one to sink;
for that very reason, it is difficult to cross.
Alternatively, it is difficult to cross because of its instability, or because it must be crossed by relying on another.
For cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is also a locus of attachment because it is moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
It is difficult to cross over precisely because of the agitation caused by views and doubt;
or else, it is difficult to cross over because it must be crossed by relying upon the Buddha.

Therein, the Blessed One, feeling compassion and taking pity upon the world— the realm of sentient beings— which is submerged therein either by way of entering into identity with it or by way of being its aggregate and its parts, and which is without protection and without refuge, extends the hands of the teaching of the True Dharma;
for the teachings of the True Dharma themselves are his hands.
These are their gifts.
The plural number is used because of the great number of those to be rescued.
By means of these, he has uplifted them according to their respective capacities.
Just as in common worldly usage, even when it is not explicitly stated, it is understood that [an action] is performed "according to suitability," because this is how it is observed;
for example, when it is said, "Having summoned the brahmins, he fed them," those who are capable of being fed and are present there— whether in the village or the city— are understood to be meant.
It is understood that he fed those very [brahmins].
Since it is impossible to feed all the brahmins of the entire world,
so too here, it refers to those people who are capable of being uplifted.
"He has indeed rescued that very [person]"—
therefore, he explains "according to their respective capacities" with the words "having paid homage to him."

Because the word *namaḥ* (homage) has as its basis the act of prostration, the term *praṇipatya* (having prostrated) is synonymous with *namaskṛtya* (having paid homage). Furthermore, since in the world prostration is understood to be performed with the head, he says "with the head.

Although homage by speech and mind is not explicitly mentioned here, it is established by implication, because physical action is preceded by verbal expression and mental activity, and because [this context] begins with the proclamation of qualities.
Regarding the word "tasmai" (to him), what kind of dative case is this?
On this point, many commentators are confused.
The teacher Guṇamati and his disciple, the teacher Vasumitra, have stated:
"The dative case occurs in connection with the word *namaḥ*, according to the rule:
'Also when there is connection with *namaḥ*, *svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣaṭ*.
This, however, is incorrect."

When used in conjunction with the word *namaḥ*, that fourth case ending occurs [only] when it is independent (*svatantra*). However, this word *namaḥ* is not independent because it has become the locus of an action (*kriyāspadībhūta*).
For this very reason, it was explained by this same Teacher [Patañjali] in the *Vyākhyā*:

By saying "having bowed to the Sage with one's head," the accusative case is employed as it is characterized by its function [as the object of the action]. Therefore, the dative case is not used in connection with the word *namaḥ*.
Others say that the fourth case-ending has been employed in place of the second; however,
this is merely their own preference,
for there is no grammatical rule (lakṣaṇa) for it.
By what rule, then, is this fourth case [used]?
We explain that this fourth case is characterized as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). How is the designation "recipient" established?
"That which one aims at through an action is the recipient (saṃpradāna). Thus,
the author of the *Cūrṇi* explains the word "action" (*karman*) in two ways.
[There are two types of object: the technical (pāribhāṣika) and the worldly (laukika).

Among these, when the technical object—defined as "that which is most desired by the agent"—is relied upon, then [the rule applies] to that which one intends through what is most desired by the agent.
That [recipient] receives the designation *saṃpradāna*.
Thus, the expression "he gives a cow to the Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇāya gāṃ prayacchati*) is established.
But when worldly action (*karma*) is understood as "activity" (*kriyā*), then that which one intends by means of that activity receives the designation of recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
Thus, this is established:
"He arms himself for battle" and "She lies down for her husband."
The agent intends the battle by means of the act of arming himself;
[he intends] the husband by means of the act of lying down.
Thus, the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) is established for the battle and so forth.
Likewise here as well, the Teacher intends the Instructor by means of the act of salutation.
Therefore, the designation "recipient" (saṃpradāna) applies to the Instructor.
When the designation "recipient" is present, the fourth case ending occurs according to the rule: "The fourth case is used for the recipient."
And having done so, first bowing down to the one who is the foremost among speakers,
the embodiment of valid cognition, and the seeker of the welfare of the world, [one should speak] regarding the treatise.
"Having prostrated to the Teacher, the Sugata, the Protector"—
in this way, the word-forms mentioned in other poetic treatises (*kāvyashāstra*) become well-guided [grammatically].
If, then, only the designation of "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) is intended [for the Teacher],...
Regarding the phrase "having paid homage to the Sage with his head," the accusative case does not apply here.
This is not a fault.
The grammatical cases (kārakas) arise from the speaker's intention to express. When there is the intention to express the object (karman), then the accusative case (dvitīyā) is used.
When there is the intention to express the recipient (saṃpradāna),
then the fourth case (caturthī) applies; thus both [the third and fourth cases] are established,
as in the expression *yathārthaśāstra*.
Thus,
*śāstṛ* is a word derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes.

According to the rule "the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* are added after [roots] such as *śaṃs* and *kṣā* when forming a proper name, and they are without the augment *iṭ*," the form *śāstṛ*, ending in the suffix *tṛn* and lacking the augment *iṭ*, is established.
But is it not the case that one speaks of "teaching" (*śāsti*) with respect to a designation (*saṃjñā*)?
And this is not a designation;
rather, this is indeed a designation.
For perception (saṃjñā) is of two kinds: specific perception and general perception.
Specific perception refers to names such as "Devadatta" or "Yajñadatta. General perception refers to [terms] such as "mother," "father," and so forth.
For *mātṛ* and the others are also prescribed as technical designations (*saṃjñā*) in that context:
*naptṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *bhrātṛ*, *jāmātṛ*, *mātṛ*, *pitṛ*, and *duhitṛ*.
Therefore, just as this term "mother" (*mātṛ*) is the designation for all mothers.
And he is the father of all fathers; likewise, this designation "Teacher" (śāstṛ) applies to all teachers. Yet that Teacher is of two kinds.
It is both non-conformable to reality and conformable to reality.
Pūraṇa and others are non-conformable to reality,
whereas the Tathāgata is conformable to reality.
Therefore, he specifies [the Teacher] as "one who teaches according to reality" (*yathārtha-śāstṛ*), meaning one who teaches without error.
And this qualification is for the purpose of indicating the means for accomplishing the welfare of others.
For this very reason, he says:

"He reveals for him the means for practicing for the benefit of others," and so forth. However, the word *prabhāva* (power) is connected to each [term] individually, as in "by the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*) and by the power of granting boons (*vara-pradāna*)."

The power of supernatural transformation (*ṛddhiprabhāva*) is, for example, Viṣṇu’s manifestation of his universal form (*viśvarūpa*). The power of granting boons (*varapradānaprabhāva*) is, for example, the common saying that Maheśvara bestows a boon.
Alternatively, it may be understood as a copulative compound (*dvandva*) consisting of three members.
These are supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), the granting of boons (*varapradāna*), and majestic power (*prabhāva*).
Majestic power is a specific kind of capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*).
But do not the Buddhas also sometimes display the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) for those to be trained?
This is indeed so;
however, their [action] consists merely in attracting others.

But by means of the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*), through the sequence of cultivating the antidotes to passion and the like, there occurs the crossing over of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
The question "What will he do? arises because the rule governing the suffix -ktvā requires the expectation of another action. Thus: "having paid homage. (Abhidh-k-vy 8)
For the rule regarding the suffix *ktvā* applies when two actions have the same agent and the action denoted by the *ktvā*-suffix occurs at an earlier time.
[Thus, one says] "I shall expound the treatise" (*śāstraṃ pravakṣyāmi*).
A treatise (*śāstra*) is a collection of names that illuminates specific meanings.
If it is argued that a collection is impossible because of momentariness,
we say no;
for we postulate a collection consisting of the forms of the cognitions that apprehend those [moments].
It is called a *śāstra* because it instructs disciples (*śiṣya-śāsanāt*).
The intention [of the question] is: "What is the *śāstra*? What is its name? [The answer is: the *Abhidharmakośa*. (I.2ab)
The etymological derivation of this will be stated later.
Let this matter rest for now.
Since the understanding of the meaning of a whole is preceded by the understanding of the meaning of its parts, we shall first consider the meaning of the parts.
He asks:
"What is this so-called Abhidharma?
Abhidharma is stainless wisdom along with its attendants.
Thus, at the time of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), wisdom (*prajñā*) is primary; therefore, "wisdom" is mentioned in its primary sense. [The term] "immaculate" (*amala*)...
It is untainted (*anāsrava*),
because "taints" (*mala*) is a synonym for "outflows" (*āsrava*).
It is "with its attendants" (*sānucara*).
[She is] together with her retinue. Even though a servant moves about together with the king, he is called "one who follows the king" because he acts in accordance with him.
Likewise here too, although they arise at the same time, those factors that coexist with it are called "concomitants.
Which ones are these?
They are the mind and mental factors, the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), and the factors dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta*) such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth.
But is it not the case that the mind is primary compared to the mental factors?
For these are called "mental factors" because they arise from the mind or exist within the mind.
Therefore, it is wisdom alone that ought to be the retinue of the mind.
But it is not the case that mind [is subordinate] to wisdom, because [mind] is a mental factor; this is indeed so.
Nevertheless, at the time of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), wisdom acts as the sovereign over the entire collection of mental factors.
In certain instances, a particular phenomenon assumes predominance.
For example, at the time of firm conviction, it is called "faith," and so forth.
Regarding the statement "the untainted [state] consists of the five aggregates":
within that collection, the untainted restraint is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Whatever is feeling, that is the aggregate of feeling. Whatever is perception...
That is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
Volition and the rest, as well as birth and so forth, are the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
And here, consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha).
"This, first of all" (*eṣa tāvat*): the word *tāvat* indicates sequence.
"Ultimate" (*pāramārthika*).
The ultimate itself is the "pertaining to the ultimate" (*pāramārthika*).
Alternatively, that which exists in the ultimate is the "pertaining to the ultimate.
Or, that which sports in or moves within the ultimate is the "pertaining to the ultimate."
The conventional [Abhidharma], however, is that which pertains to worldly usage.
Furthermore, it is established here that the wisdom directed toward the attainment of that [ultimate Abhidharma], along with its attendants, is also Abhidharma.

For the sake of attaining that untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*), whatever wisdom there is— whether consisting of hearing, reflection, or cultivation— that is tainted (*sāsravā*), as well as that which is acquired through birth (*upapattipratilambhikā*),
is also the conventional (*sāṃketika*) Abhidharma. Among these, that which arises from the application of hearing is the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī*).
That which arises from the application of rational reflection is that consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*).

That which arises from the application of cultivation is that consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*). That which arises from acquisition at birth is that acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhikā*).

Because he possesses that which is acquired through birth (*upapattipratilambha*), the suffix *ṭhan* is applied according to the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*; thus, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening of the vowel.

The Abhidharma belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) consists of four aggregates—namely, those consisting of hearing, reflection, acquisition through birth, and cultivation—because of the absence of concomitant matter (*anuparivartaka-rūpa*).
However, because the restraint of meditative absorption (dhyānasaṃvara) exists within the realm of form (rūpāvacara), the Abhidharma consists of five aggregates (pañcaskandhaka).
And when it says "the treatise" (śāstra), it is intended to mean the Abhidharmaśāstra.
Regarding that [attainment], there is a difference in interpretation as to whether it is "with its attendants" (*sānucara*) or "without its attendants" (*na sānucara*).
Some maintain that it is "with its attendants" because it consists of a collection of non-mental and non-mental-factor elements.
Thus, they do not follow [the tradition].
Some do follow it because of the possibility of [categories such as] birth and so forth;
for this Abhidharma consists of a single aggregate (skandha).
Or it consists of two aggregates,
and for that [person], birth and so forth exist.
But others explain that "the treatise" refers to the *Jñānaprasthāna*.
That [Abhidharma], which constitutes its body, has six feet:

the Prakaraṇapāda, the Vijñānakāya, the Dharmaskandha, the Prajñaptiśāstra, the Jñānaprasthāna (Hātukāya), and the Saṃgītiparyāya. Therefore, that treatise, together with its followers, is called "conventional Abhidharma" because it leads, through a traditional succession, to the attainment of the ultimate Abhidharma.
For the wisdom acquired at birth follows after the hearing of a treatise and its meaning.

From that arises the wisdom consisting of hearing; from the wisdom consisting of hearing, the wisdom consisting of reflection; from the wisdom consisting of reflection, the contaminated wisdom consisting of cultivation; and from that, the uncontaminated wisdom is born—such is the sequence.
This is what is meant by "this [process]."
The word "that" (*tad*) serves to introduce the statement.

"This" (*ayam*) refers to the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) and conventional (*sāṃketika*) Abhidharma, which is defined as that which maintains its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). [The phrase] "the ultimate dharma" (*paramārthadharma*) [is used].
The object (*artha*) of supreme knowledge (*parama-jñāna*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Alternatively, the supreme object (*parama-artha*) is the ultimate truth, because it is the foremost among all phenomena (*dharma*).
It is both the ultimate truth and a phenomenon; thus, it is the "ultimate-truth-phenomenon" (*paramārtha-dharma*).
Or, it is the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

This refers to specific and general characteristics (*svasāmānyalakṣaṇa*), such as the earth element having the characteristic of solidity, or [the fact that] "it is impermanent, it is suffering," and so forth. Abhidharma is the teaching (*dharma*) that is directed toward—that is, oriented toward—the acquisition, penetration, or realization of that [characteristic]. Thus, it is *abhimukha* (directed toward) *dharma*. Therefore, it is called *Abhidharma*.
The term *kugatiprādayaḥ* [refers to] a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
But surely, by the rule *lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye*, an *avyayībhāva* would result when *abhi* is compounded with a mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
For it is indeed when *abhi* is compounded with a mark that this applies.
In that case, it is an *avyayībhāva* compound.
For example: "moths fly toward the fire" (*abhyagni śalabhāḥ patanti*).
Here, the falling of the moths is characterized by the fire.
Thus, fire is its characteristic;
however, this dharma is not the characteristic of anything else.
What then?
It is the objective.
Because it is directed toward [nirvāṇa] by its very nature,

even the conventional Abhidharma known as the treatise is directed toward nirvāṇa or the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) as a proximate cause (upaniṣad), for the purpose of attaining or illuminating them.
How much more so, then, the ultimate [Abhidharma]? Therefore, by means of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, "Abhidharma" is established.
(I.2cd) Thus, Abhidharma has been explained.
Through its essential nature (*svabhāva*), its classifications, and its etymology (*nirvacana*), the meaning of its constituent parts has been understood.
However, since the meaning of the whole [compound] has not yet been established, he asks about the meaning of the whole:
"In what sense is this treatise the *Abhidharmakośa*? [The answer is: "Because its meaning is contained within this."
Thus,
because that treatise designated as Abhidharma has been mentioned immediately prior, it is included by implication.
In terms of its meaning...
Thus, it is not by way of the letter;
this entry is by way of the meaning.
Not in its entirety.
Therefore, it is an *avyayībhāva* compound meaning "according to what is predominant. [The term] *antarbhūtaḥ* means "included" or "entered."
This treatise of mine serves as a treasury for that meaning;
it is like a storehouse.
In this sense, there is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound.
The *Abhidharmakośa* is the treasury (*kośa*) of the *Abhidharma*.
For that into which a sword enters is its sheath (*kośa*).
Alternatively, that Abhidharma, such as the *Jñānaprasthāna* and others, serves as the basis for this treatise of mine;
for this treatise of mine has been extracted from that Abhidharma of the Sages.
This is understood to mean "in terms of its meaning."
Therefore, that very [Abhidharma] is its "treasury" (kośa).
In this sense, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound:
"that which has the Abhidharma as its treasury" is the *Abhidharmakośa*.
For just as that from which a sword is drawn out is its scabbard,
so this treatise is called the *Abhidharmakośa*.
He indicates that its collective meaning has also been understood.
(I.3) But for what purpose is the instruction of the Abhidharma? What is its utility? This is the sense.
For the composition of a treatise is proper only when it possesses a purpose.
It is not without purpose.
And by whom was this first taught? By whom was this Abhidharma originally expounded?
The intention is that for a treatise taught by a reliable authority (*āpta*), there ought to be a concise summary (*pratyāsa*) of its essential form. The term "first" is a qualification,
because the subsequent teaching [of the *Abhidharmakośa*] is established through the synthesis of the works of the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra and others.
For there is indeed dispute regarding the initial instruction;
"from which," and so forth, means from which cause.
The teacher is the author of the treatise.
He pays respect—that is, he shows reverence—to the *Abhidharmakośa*, the proximate treatise, in order to speak of it and compose it. This is the meaning.

Having thus answered the two questions, he says— expanding on the phrase "the discernment of phenomena" (*dharmāṇāṃ pravicaya*)— to demonstrate that the Abhidharma treatise possesses a purpose and is based on the instruction of an authoritative teacher.
Because, without the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*)— in such forms as "form" and "feeling are impermanent and suffering"—
there is no means for the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The words "another" constitute the ellipsis of the sentence.
By implication, it follows that this alone is the means for the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
For example, when it is said that there is no means for sustaining life without food, it follows by implication that food itself is the means for sustaining life.
It is just like that.
[The author asks: "If there were no subsiding of the afflictions (kleśa), what would happen? To this, he says:
"And by means of the afflictions, this world wanders in the ocean of existence.
By this, he shows that the pacification of the afflictions is something that must necessarily be accomplished.
Existence (*bhava*) and saṃsāra are synonymous. Existence itself is the ocean; thus, it is "the ocean of existence" (*bhavārṇava*).
Because it shares the common characteristic of being a place of immersion, existence is like an ocean.
In this ocean of existence (*bhava*).

The inclusion of the word "here" (*atra*) is for the purpose of negating an existence distinct from the characteristics of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), which have been directly perceived.
Here, the world wanders because it remains in a state of identity with that [existence].
For the designation of a locus is also seen by way of identity (tādātmya), as for example: "The grove stands in the *palāśa* trees because of the non-utility of other trees.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, by indicating that the third case ending has the sense of a cause (*hetu*), the causal meaning is expressed through the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
"And the afflictions cause the world to wander.
"Therefore" is a restatement of the previously mentioned reason;
because it is so.
Therefore, the meaning is that Abhidharma has been indicated.

Since the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is the means for the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and no other phenomenon [serves this purpose], it is the teaching of Abhidharma; thus, it is the connection [to the goal]. For this reason, it was said: "for that cause."
Thus,
that very cause is "the cause of that" (taddhetu); it belongs to that [result], or [is so called] because of that [result].
"Because of that" means:
for the sake of that discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), there is a discernment of phenomena caused by the instruction of the Abhidharma.
The Teacher, the Buddha, taught the Abhidharma so that there might be an investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya).
Precisely for this reason,
for without the teaching of the Abhidharma, a disciple would not be able to investigate phenomena.

The form *udita* is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *vad*, with the semivowel having been vocalized (*saṃprasāraṇa*); it is not derived from the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *ut*, because that would not yield the intended meaning.
"Udita" means "spoken"; "upadiṣṭa" has the same meaning.
Regarding the word "kila": the particle *kila* indicates the intention of another.
This is the opinion of the Abhidharmikas; however, it is not our opinion as Sautrāntikas—this is the sense.
For indeed, authors of the Abhidharma treatises are heard of.
For example, Ārya Kātyāyanīputra is the author of the *Jñānaprasthāna*; Sthavira Vasumitra is the author of the *Prakaraṇapāda*;
and Sthavira Devaśarman is the author of the *Vijñānakāya*.
Ārya Śāriputra was the master of the *Harmaskandha*;
Ārya Maudgalyāyana was the master of the *Prajñaptiśāstra*;
and Pūrṇa was the master of the *Hātukāya*.
Regarding the *Saṃgītiparyāya*, [the master] Mahākauṣṭhila [states]: "What is the meaning of 'Sautrāntika'?
They are those for whom the sūtras are the authority, not the treatises (*śāstra*)."
They are the Sautrāntikas.
If they do not accept the treatises (*śāstra*) as authoritative, how is their arrangement of the Three Baskets established—
namely, the Basket of Sūtras, the Basket of Vinaya, and the Basket of Abhidharma?
For even in the Sūtras, the Abhidharma Piṭaka is recited;
thus, there is no fault in [the statement] that "a monk is one who possesses the three Piṭakas.
For it is specific Sūtras themselves—such as the *Arthaviniścaya* and others—in which the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are described, that bear the designation "Abhidharma."
To dispel this doubt, they say:
"But that was spoken by the Blessed One in a scattered manner," and so forth;
just as [it was] by the Elder Dharmatrāta in the *Udānavarga*.

Phrases such as "Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena" were spoken by the Blessed One in various places in the Sūtras and compiled together in one location according to the needs of those to be trained (*vineya*).

In the same way, the Abhidharma—consisting of the instruction on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)—was also spoken by the Blessed One in various places according to the needs of those to be trained; it was then [compiled] by the Elder Kātyāyanīputra and others in works such as the *Jñānaprasthāna*.
The Vaibhāṣikas say that it has been established by being condensed into a single whole.
They are called Vaibhāṣikas because they sport in or move according to the *Vibhāṣā*,
or because they know the *Vibhāṣā*.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after [the word] *uktha*, etc., due to their being mentioned in the list;
thus, [we have] "dharmas with outflows and without outflows."
Those which possess outflows (āsrava) are "with outflows" (sāsrava).
Those in which outflows do not exist are "without outflows" (anāsrava).
The compound [sāsravānāsrava] means "those with outflows and those without outflows."
It is called a *dharma* because it maintains its own specific and general characteristics.
This is the brief explanation of all *dharmas*.
There are only this many *dharmas*, namely: those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*).
There are no phenomena (dharmas) apart from these.
Therefore, he says "of all phenomena.
"A concise indication" means a summary indication.

The detailed exposition, however, will follow later until the conclusion of the treatise; there are also other concise expositions, such as "conditioned and unconditioned," "material and immaterial," "visible and invisible," and so forth.
For what purpose has this specific concise exposition been stated?
When what has been stated is there no further objection?
Alternatively, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the defiled and purified sides, since that is the aim of the treatise.
For by understanding those two sides, one may abandon the side of defilement and, through practicing the side of purification, attain the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
Conditioned phenomena, excluding the Path,
are "with outflows";
thus they are exclusively conditioned, not unconditioned.
Form and the other [aggregates] produced by causes and conditions are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Are they all [conditioned]? No, he says.
"Devoid of the path" means devoid of the truth of the path.
Since the truth of the path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), [the same] consequence would follow; therefore, he specifies it in this way.
This is what is meant:
with the exception of the truth of the path, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) are with-outflows (sāsrava). But how, then, are they with-outflows?
If only those minds and mental factors that are afflicted by association with the outflows (*āsrava*) were to be "with outflows" (*sāsrava*),

and no others; or, if [they were so] because of arising simultaneously with the outflows, then for a sentient being in whose continuum a defilement is currently active, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) would be "with outflows" according to their occurrence.
It is not for one whose afflictions are not currently active,
nor are external phenomena [the basis]. Rather,
it is those which are the bases of the outflows (āsrava).
Regarding the statement "they are with-outflows" (*sāsrava*):
it would follow that only the six internal sense-bases (*āyatana*) are with-outflows;
or else, those which are the objects (*ālambana*) of the outflows are with-outflows.
The truth of cessation and the truth of the path would also consequently become contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, a higher stage (*ūrdhvā bhūmiḥ*) would be contaminated by the outflows (*āsrava*) that take the higher stages as their objects; therefore, he says:
(Abhidh-k-vy 13)
Because the outflows (āsrava) adhere to them.

Therefore, the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) must be supplied from the preceding context as "therefore they are with-outflows" (*sāsravāḥ*). "They adhere" (*anuśerate*) means that they obtain nourishment;
or it means that they obtain a firm footing.
"Upon the attainment of nourishment or the attainment of stability, those [afflictions] such as attachment increase.
Others explain it thus:
"Just as one reflects, 'This food of mine is conducive,' meaning it becomes wholesome and suitable."
In the same way, passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions] also lie latent (*anuśerate*) within those phenomena;
the meaning is that they become concordant with them.
For contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are produced by karma that is moistened by passion and the other [afflictions].

Because of the statement that "the variety of the world is born of karma," they are called *anuśayas* because they lie latent (*anuśerate*) and attain nourishment (*puṣṭi*) in accordance with their conditions.
Alternatively, they are called *anuśayas* because the conditions (*pratyaya*) adhere to them or function in accordance with them.
Their adherence (*anuśayana*) should be understood as occurring either by way of the object (*ālambana*) or by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).
However, the Master Guṇamati explains it here as follows:
What is the reason that, among all phenomena which serve as objects for the outflows (*āsrava*), only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*)— excluding the Path— are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*)?
To say that "all phenomena are objects for the outflows" is not the doctrine of the Abhidharmikas,
because space (*ākāśa*) and cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) do not serve as objects for the outflows.
For it is taught that there are exactly six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that have the untainted (anāsrava) as their object;
and these have only cessation (nirodha) and the path (mārga) as their objects.
They are false view (mithyādṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), the ignorance associated with those two, and ignorance alone.

Because of the statement that "the six [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path have the untainted as their object," we see that this [previous position] was not well-written.
"Kāmam" means "even though" (yady api).
Alternatively, "kāmam" is a particle meaning "admission" (abhyupagama);
the meaning is that it is indeed admitted that outflows (āsrava) arise even when they have the truths of cessation and the path as their objects.

Regarding the truths of cessation and the path, we shall explain [this] precisely in the exposition of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). [The reason is: "Those [factors] which have the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the higher realms as their objects do not [become objects of the afflictions], because they are not appropriated and because they are opposed [to them]."
Regarding this point:
for when a thing has been appropriated by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are also able to become latent therein.
Just as dust cannot remain on a moist cloth, so too it is not possible for [defilements] to abide in that which is untainted (anāsrava),
nor in a higher stage (bhūmi).

Therefore, those [defilements] do not increase with respect to those [objects], because nirvana and the path are their opposites, and a higher stage is the opposite of lower stages. Thus, the defilements that have these as their objects do not adhere to them.
For this reason as well, they do not find a firm footing within them,
like the soles of feet upon a heated stone.
The untainted [factors] are the Truth of the Path and the threefold unconditioned.
"Since this is established through presumptive proof (*arthāpatti*), it need not be set forth as a formal sūtra"—to such an objection, the teacher Guṇamati first replied:
"This must indeed be stated. What is the reason?"
For the path is twofold: mundane and supramundane.
Therefore, it is stated again for the sake of distinction;
and for this very reason, the Truth of the Path is specifically mentioned here.
That which is well-established is understood through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), not that which is unestablished;
and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is unestablished.
Thus others explain.
This is stated again, even though it is established by presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*), in order to dispel the doubt that there might be a third category.
For just as there are three types of feeling (*vedanā*):
pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
In the same way, phenomena (dharmas) might also be conceived as being either with outflows (sāsrava), without outflows (anāsrava), both with and without outflows,
or neither with nor without outflows.
Therefore, one might doubt whether those things which have been excluded by implication are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), or whether they are both tainted and untainted (*sāsravānāsrava*),
or perhaps neither.
For there is indeed room for the conceptual distinction between that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
How so? First, according to the system of the Vaibhāṣikas:

Defiled [dharmas] are accompanied by latent dispositions (*sānuśaya*) in two ways, whereas non-defiled [dharmas] are so because of the latent dispositions that adhere to them; this is according to the statement [of the Abhidharma].
Thus, those which are the eye and so forth, or external objects such as visible forms and so forth, that are non-defiled.
They are "with outflows" (sāsrava) only by means of those outflows that are currently active as latent tendencies (anuśaya), not by those that are not so active.
When those outflows have been abandoned and are no longer active as latent tendencies, they are not "with outflows.
However, when they are not abandoned—even if they belong to the mental continuum of another—they are indeed "with outflows."
Furthermore, according to the method of the Dārṣṭāntikas, the eye and so forth belonging to the continuum of an Arhat, as well as external objects such as visible forms, are untainted (*anāsrava*),
because they are not a basis for the outflows (*āsrava*).
And yet, they are also tainted (*sāsrava*), because they are not an antidote to the outflows.
There is a doubt that the status of being with-outflow (*sāsrava*) or without-outflow (*anāsrava*) regarding the eye and so forth is conceived only figuratively (*pāryāyika*).
To dispel that doubt, this is said:
"The Truth of the Path and the threefold unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are without-outflow."
Thus [it is said].
"Without exception, these are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), not tainted (*sāsrava*)," is a repetition of what was already stated.
In that case, where should those eyes and so forth belonging to an Arhat be classified by the Vaibhāṣikas?
"Is it on the side of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) or on the side of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
They say: "On the side of the contaminated. [The question is: "How are those things established as contaminated by means of the abandoned outflows (*āsrava*)?
[They are those] in which the outflows adhere (*anuśerate*), have adhered, or will adhere."
These are with-outflows (*sāsrava*).
For even when intending to express a meaning pertaining to the three times, usage in the present tense is observed in common worldly speech; for example: "He who protects the subjects."
"He is a king" means that he who has protected, as well as he who will protect,
is indeed understood to be a king.
Therefore, it is explained in this way:
Alternatively, even if they are not "with outflows" (sāsrava) by virtue of having abandoned those [specific] outflows,
they are nonetheless certainly with outflows by virtue of the immeasurable outflows that have not been abandoned, including even those residing in the mental continua of others.
But surely, because of the very mention of them as a compound— “dharmas with outflows and without outflows”— there would be no possibility of a third category.
No,
because in that case it is possible to employ a collective designation (*ekaśeṣa*),
namely: "the contaminated and the uncontaminated" (*sāsravāś cānāsravāś ca*) or "the contaminated-uncontaminated" (*sāsravānāsravāś ca*).
The term *sāsravānāsravāḥ* is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member) compound.
It is accepted that a *ekaśeṣa* may occur even between dissimilar forms,
as in the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoh*.
Others, however, say:
this is indeed established through presumptive reasoning (arthāpatti);
nevertheless, it is explained in detail for the sake of clarification.

For example, by the very rule "the qualifier [is compounded] frequently with the qualified," everything is established. The detailed elaboration beginning with "words denoting prior time, 'eka' (one), 'sarva' (all), 'jara', 'purāṇa' (old), 'nava' (new), and 'kevala' (exclusive) [are compounded] with a word in the same case" is stated;
this [case] is just like that.
He asks because [the threefold nature of] the unconditioned is not well known: "What is the threefold unconditioned?
The inclusion of the word "threefold" is for the purpose of determining its extent;
for there are some, such as the Vātsīputrīyas, who assert that the unconditioned is only one, namely *nirvāṇa*.

The Vaiśeṣikas maintain that many things, such as atoms and so forth, are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). In order to refute their view, there is this determination of the limit [of unconditioned phenomena]. As for the question, "Which two?"—it refers to these two.
He asks specifically about cessation through deliberation and cessation not through deliberation, but not about space,
because space is well-known in the world.
In that context, "space is non-obstruction": here, "therein" (tatra) is used either for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*) or for introducing a statement (*vākyopanyāsa*).

The etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is that it is called "space" (*ākāśa*) because it provides room (*avakāśa*). Others say it is space because phenomena shine forth intensely (*bhṛśam*) within it; it is also [defined as] non-obstruction (*anāvṛti*).
Non-obstruction.
It is derived either as an agent-noun (*kartṛ-sādhana*) or as an object-noun (*karma-sādhana*).
It is that dharma which does not obstruct other dharmas, nor is it obstructed by others.
That space has non-obstruction as its intrinsic nature.
Because it is not an object of direct perception, it is inferred through the non-obstruction of other phenomena;
it is not, however, merely the absence of obstruction.
And for this very reason, it is explained as follows:
"Where there is the movement of form. This means that which neither obstructs nor is obstructed.
That is space.
Since conditioned factors such as mind and so forth are likewise non-obstructive, they reach space;
yet they do not reach it.
Because they constitute an obstruction for others.
For those possessing supernatural powers (*ṛddhimant*) obstruct the movement of others' minds and mental factors through the power of their own mind and mental factors.
In that case, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) would also be equivalent to space (*ākāśa*), since they do not act as obstructions.
No;

because those two—conjunction and the non-arising of substances—are obstructions by virtue of being the certain preventers of the attainment of conjunction and by virtue of being the preventers of the obstruction to arising.
Alternatively, that which has non-obstruction as its very definition, and no other definition, [is space].
That is space.
Since those two [cessations] have other characteristics, they do not attain the status of space.
In that case, it follows that space is either not omnipresent or impermanent.
Because [the perception] exists when there is an absence of obstruction,
and does not exist when that [obstruction] is present;
for indeed, in the case of walls and such, there is an obstruction of another form.
In this case, because the characteristic of space is absent, it would follow that there is no space at all.
Furthermore, since it comes into existence again once walls and other obstructions are removed, it would follow that it is impermanent.
Yet, it does not follow that it is impermanent.
Even there, space certainly exists because it provides room for walls and other objects.
For if there were no space there, those very walls and other objects could not remain, as they would have no room;
as for the fact that another form cannot remain there [in the same place], that is due to resistance.
That [obstruction] is due to coverings such as walls, not because of the absence of space.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "O Gautama, upon what is the earth established?"
“O Brahmin, the earth is established upon the circle of water. O Gautama, upon what is the circle of water established?
“It is established upon the wind.”
"Venerable Gautama, where is wind established?
"It is established in space.
"Venerable Gautama, where is space established?"
"You overstep, Great Brahmā! You overstep, Great Brahmā!
Space, O Brahmā, is without foundation and without support," and so forth.
Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that space exists.
By specifying "that which is dissociation" (*visaṃyoga*), impermanence-cessation (*anityatā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are both excluded.
For those two cessations do not have the characteristic of dissociation.

Disjunction (*visaṃyoga*) is the state of being dissociated; it is characterized by dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśa*). Alternatively, that phenomenon (*dharma*) which constitutes a definitive obstruction to the attainment of conjunction is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Regarding the phrase "of the noble truths such as suffering," this refers to aspects such as truth and so forth;
what then?
It refers to aspects such as the tranquility and so forth of the higher and lower stages, and the magnificence and so forth [of those stages].

Regarding the phrase "distinction of wisdom" (*prajñāviśe� cessation*): the inclusion of the word "distinction" is for the purpose of including the wisdom of the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) that abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is the cessation to be attained by means of that distinction of wisdom.
"Having performed the elision of the middle term.
This is an extension of the rule for compounds such as *śākapārthiva* (the vegetable-king).
By the intended meaning "kings who are fond of vegetables," there is an elision of the middle term, resulting in *śākapārthivāḥ*.

If *pratisaṃkhyā* were taken to mean only untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom, then cessation attained through the mundane path would not be included, and thus it would result in a definition that is too narrow (*avyāpin*). It is not too narrow;
for every cessation of tainted things within the three realms is attained by means of the untainted [wisdom].
There is no such cessation that is attained by mundane wisdom alone and not by untainted wisdom.
What, then, is the purpose of mundane wisdom?
For whatever cessation is attained by means of the mundane path is indeed attained again by means of the supramundane path; therefore,
in that case, it is only supramundane wisdom that is involved, not mundane wisdom.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is a substantial entity (*dravyasat*), because it is taught among the exposition of the four truths, just like the truth of the path.
"Separately" means individually, that is, distinct.
"For as many substances as there are for conjunction" means:
conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the act of joining;
substances that serve for conjunction are "substances for conjunction" (*saṃyogadravya*).
Alternatively, they are called "conjunctions" (*saṃyoga*) because [the mind and mental factors] are conjoined with them.
Since they are both conjunctions and substances, they are "substances of conjunction.
This amounts to saying that they are "contaminated substances" (*sāsravadrvya*).

For the Blessed One has said that contaminated substance (*sāsrava-dravya*) stands in the place of a pillar, the fetter (*saṃprayoga*) stands in the place of a rope, and the person (*pudgala*) stands in the place of an ox.
"Otherwise" means if [the person] were one and the same.
[The phrase] "the realization of the cessation of all afflictions" (*sarvakleśanirodhasākṣātkriyā*) [is used].
The meaning is: the attainment of the cessation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are to be abandoned through the vision and cultivation of the origin (*samudaya*) and so forth.

"The cultivation of the remaining counteragents would be useless" means that the production of the path of counteragents—which consists of those to be abandoned through the vision and cultivation of the origin and so forth of the remaining afflictions—would be purposeless.
As for what was said— that cessation is without a counterpart— where was this said?
In the Sūtra.
When she was questioned by her former husband, the householder Viśākha, the nun Harmadinnā replied:
"Is cessation, Noble Lady, homogeneous?
"It is non-homogeneous, Venerable Viśākha."
Having perceived the meaning that cessation is without counterpart (*apratisadṛśa*), he asks:
"What is the meaning of this?
For the opponent's intention is that if there were multiplicity, there might be another thing that is its counterpart.
"Nothing is its homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
*Sabhāga-hetu* and *sabhāga* have the same meaning, with the word "cause" (*hetu*) being elided.
For we see people employing single parts of words for whole words, and single parts of sentences for whole sentences.
For example: "Satyabhāmā" is simply "Bhāmā"; "Evadatta" is simply "Datta"; "Enter the rice-gruel," "Enter the porridge. Indeed, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is eternal;
what need has it for a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*)?
The non-homogeneous cause (*asabhāgahetu*) is "non-homogeneous" (*asabhāga*).
It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has no homogeneous [result]" (*nāsti sabhāgo 'sya*). Thus, it does not belong to anything.
It is under discussion that this analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is not the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of any other dharma.
What is the reason? It is accepted that the homogeneous cause exists only among conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena.
In this context, "not homogeneous" (*asabhāga*) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound;
it does not mean that there is nothing whatsoever similar to it.
The meaning is that there is no other cessation (*nirodha*) that is not similar to this cessation.
The other cessation, which is not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā*), is the absolute obstruction of arising.
It is the absolute obstruction of the arising of future phenomena; that is, an absolute and definitive hindrance.
It is "other" [than analytical cessation].
Thus is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
For it is other than the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) mentioned immediately prior. [It is called] "non-analytical" (*apratisaṃkhyayā*).
This negative particle (akāra) functions as a non-implicative negation (prasajyapratiṣedha);
the meaning is that it is not attained through analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā).
Alternatively, it may function as an implicative negation (paryudāsa).

That which is other than analytical discernment and consists in the deficiency of conditions is non-analytical [cessation]. The cessation attained through that is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
[This is] due to the elision of the middle term.
This is incorrect;
for non-existence is indeed the deficiency of conditions.
How is that cessation attained through non-existence? There is no fault here because it is used in a figurative sense.
Alternatively, "non-analytical cessation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) means it is not an analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) is said to be merely the state of being other than analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha);
it does not, however, imply the operation of a deficiency of conditions (pratyayavaikalya).
The inclusion of the term "arising" (utpāda) is for the purpose of excluding cessation through impermanence (anityatānirodha).
Cessation through impermanence (*anityatā-nirodha*) is an absolute obstruction to the persistence of a phenomenon (*dharma-sthiti*), not to its arising.

The inclusion of the term "absolute" (*atyanta*) is for the purpose of excluding the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);
for these indeed obstruct the arising of future mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
But it is not absolute [non-existence], because the state of being an obstacle to that [cognition] is merely temporary.
"As in the case of one whose eye and mind are intent upon a single form," and so forth; "as" (*yathā*) is used to provide an illustration.
It refers to one for whom both the eye and the mind are intent upon a single blue form.
With his eye and mind fixed exclusively on that single form,

all those other forms— other than the blue being perceived, namely other blues, yellows, reds, whites, and so forth; as well as colors and shapes, and all sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles— [do not appear].
"They pass away" means they transcend the present time period and proceed toward the past time period.
"By those having that as their object" [means...].
Those objects just mentioned, such as the blue interval and so forth, are the objective supports (ālambana) of these;
thus, they are "those having that as their objective support" (tadālambanāḥ). Which ones?
The five groups of consciousness:
by means of these, it is not possible for [an object] to arise; this is a derivation based on the state of being (bhāvasādhana).
"For they are not capable," and so forth.
For those five groups of consciousness are not able to grasp a past object, even though it is their own objective support (*ālambana*),
because the five groups of consciousness have only the present as their objective support.
Now, why do [mental states] not arise by taking another present object, such as a different blue color and so forth, as their focal point?
It is simply impossible for this to occur,
because all dharmas are fixed within a fourfold determination.
[This applies] to the cause, the fruit, the basis, and the object.
Whatever is the object of a given consciousness, that alone would be its object.
"It would not be otherwise.
Due to the deficiency of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), those five groups of consciousness do not arise again.
Therefore, he says:
"It is their non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*)," and so forth.
This [cessation] is attained regarding those five groups of consciousness due to the deficiency of conditions, specifically the deficiency of the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

For it is only by means of the four conditions—the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*)—that minds and mental factors arise when they are arising.
If even one of these is lacking, there is no arising.
Others say this is due to the deficiency of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
For at that time, the immediately preceding condition—characterized by mind and mental factors—provides the opportunity for the arising of only that single blue-cognition.
This does not apply to other cognitions, such as those of another blue object and so forth,
because it is impossible for multiple cognitions to arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, this is merely an illustration.

In this way, for all five types of persons who have attained patience (*kṣānti*) and so forth, the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of future aggregates that would otherwise lead to the miserable realms is attained due to the deficiency of conditions, because the conditions for their arising are confronted by opposing conditions. This is how the example should be applied. And it was with reference specifically to this non-analytical cessation that the Blessed One, concerning the person who has entered the stream (*srotaāpanna*), said: "For him, the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) have been ceased."
Thus, for those future phenomena of such a kind, due to the deficiency of conditions,

that phenomenon which constitutes the certain obstruction of their arising in the absence of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is called "cessation not through analytical discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

For it is not logically tenable that there is an absolute non-arising of that [effect] merely due to a deficiency of conditions, because it would follow that it must arise again when conditions of its own kind are present.
For what obstacle could there be to its arising at that time? Thus say the Vaibhāṣikas.
"And here there is a fourfold alternative," and so forth.

Here, in the detailed exposition of the characteristics of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), there is a fourfold alternative, meaning a four-part response to questions.
For what purpose?
It is for the sake of explanation;
namely, that for those contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena which are past, present, or destined to arise,
only analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is obtained because they are contaminated.
Because the arising of past and present [dharmas] has already been accomplished,
and because those subject to arising necessarily exist,
non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) is not obtained.
For non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is characterized by the absolute prevention of arising;
for example, [it applies] to untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) that are subject to non-arising.
Because their arising is absolutely prevented, they possess the nature of non-arising (*anutpatti-dharmatva*).

Consequently, non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) is obtained for them. For example, when one of the paths of the faith-follower (śraddhānusārin) belonging to the six stages— the stages of the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the [four] dhyānas— is manifested, there is non-analytical cessation of the remaining five,
but not analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha), because they are untainted (anāsrava).
For that which is faultless is not subject to abandonment.

The inclusion of the term "having the nature of non-arising" (anutpattidharma) is for the purpose of excluding the past, the present, and those things destined to arise; the inclusion of the term "untainted" (anāsrava) is for the purpose of excluding that which is tainted (sāsrava).
The inclusion of the term "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) is for the purpose of excluding the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
For even the unconditioned, by its very nature, possesses the characteristic of non-arising;
therefore, that qualification is provided so that the [definition] might not apply to it by implication.
For some, the reading is as follows: "of those that are non-arising and untainted" (*anutpattidharmāṇām anāsravāṇām*).
For them, how is it that there is no consequence of including unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)?
The subject here concerns those phenomena for which both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) are possible;
these two cessations do not apply to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
For non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is the absolute obstruction to arising, yet there is no arising of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, the compound *anutpattidharmāṇām* is a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
It refers to those phenomena similar [to conditioned things] which are other than those possessing the nature of arising (*utpattidharma*).
They are of a nature not to arise.
And what things are similar to them?
Only conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta), not unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta).
They say that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) do not involve [the acquisition of] non-possession (*aprasaṅga*).
There are those for whom both exist—namely, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
For example, [this applies to] contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*), and so forth.
Because it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), this analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is attained;
because it is of the nature of non-arising (*anutpattidharman*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is also attained.
When the attainment of these two is intended, it does not necessarily follow that their attainment occurs simultaneously.
For some, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) is attained first, and subsequently non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha).

This is the case, for example, for an Arhat whose eye and mind are occupied with a single visible form; [there occurs] the non-analytical cessation of the five groups of consciousness that have other visible forms and so forth as their objects.
For some, non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) is attained first, and subsequently analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha);
as, for example, with one who has attained receptivity (kṣānti), regarding the states of miserable rebirth (apāyagati).
For some, it occurs simultaneously.

For example, when the antidote to the most intense of the intense afflictions (*kleśa*) arises for one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), both the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of those future intense afflictions are attained simultaneously.
In this same way, it should be applied to other cases as well, according to their possibility.
