For example, regarding uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas that are past, present, or destined to arise:
because it is impossible to obstruct the arising of these past and so forth [dharmas], analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is not obtained for them.
Furthermore, because these are untainted (*anāsrava*), even analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is not obtained for them.
However, since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack arising, there is no non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) for them.
For it was stated previously that non-analytical cessation is the absolute obstruction to arising.
And because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), even analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) does not exist [in that regard].

(I.7) Thus, since there is little to be said regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), having concluded the questions concerning it, he now introduces the preliminary discussion (*upodghāta*), desiring to explain the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
As it was said:
Conditioned phenomena, excluding the Path, are said to be with outflows.
Which are those conditioned phenomena?
Furthermore, those are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).

The word "furthermore" (*punaḥ*) is stated for the purpose of showing another classification; the previous classification was "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*) and "without-outflows" (*anāsrava*), whereas this is a further classification, being separated by the explanation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The mention of "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) once again is for the purpose of excluding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
(Abhidh-k-vy 20) Ta.
Thus [it is said]. The word "that" (tat) refers back to what was previously mentioned. And what are those things previously mentioned?
Those which are excluded are the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena;
those which are not excluded are those whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
Both types are intended here.
How is this understood?
From the statement that those which are with-outflows are the aggregates of clinging, because of the explicit extraction of the "with-outflows" from among the "without-outflows."
That which is the pentad of aggregates, beginning with form, whose characteristics will be explained hereafter.
These should be understood as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Among them, there is mutual inclusion.
The mention of "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth is for the purpose of excluding the aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the rest.
For there are also five other aggregates:

the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*).
The inclusion of the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) is for the purpose of excluding objects such as visible form (*rūpa*).
"Having come together" (*sametya*) and "having arisen together" (*saṃbhūya*) are synonyms. Alternatively, "having come together" means having met and having depended upon one another;
thus he shows the meaning of the prefix *sam-* as "having produced together" (*saṃjanya*).
For it is not produced by a single condition.
Even when there is the absolute minimum of conditions, there are necessarily two conditions.
For mind and mental factors arise from four, while the two meditative attainments arise from three.
Because of the statement, "But others are born from two," it is said to be "like milk."
Because the word *saṃskṛta* ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix, he demonstrates the illustration by means of a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix: "like milk. "Milk" (*dugdha*) means *kṣīra* (cow's milk).
It is logical that what has been drawn out from the udders is called "milk."
As for that which will be milked out,
and that which will not be milked out at all but remains situated within the cow itself—
that is not attained [as] "milk."
And it is said in the world, "This is milk.
Likewise here too, those conditioned phenomena that will be produced and are subject to arising in the future, as well as those that will not be produced and are not subject to arising—
these too are called "conditioned."
Because they belong to that same class, because they possess similarity in their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). "Those very [dharmas] are the time-periods," and so forth.

The entire Abhidharma is the meaning of the Sūtras, the touchstone of the Sūtras, and the commentary on the Sūtras. Thus, even for those factors such as the "time-periods" (*adhvan*) mentioned in the Sūtras—which are here expressed through synonyms such as the aggregates (*skandha*)—this explanation of the time-period is given by referring to the "time-period" as it is commonly understood in the world, based on the states of having gone, going, and about to go.
For it is said in the world: [text continues].

"This path has gone to the village," "this path is going," and "this path will go"—in the same way, here too, the past path is that which has gone, the present is that which is going, and the future is that which will go. Alternatively, they are called "paths" (*adhvan*) because they are consumed (*adyante*) by impermanence; this is the governing definition.
This meaning has been shown with reference to etymological derivation (*nairukta*).

Because they are consumed— that is, devoured— by impermanence, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) things alone are taught by the Blessed One under the term "paths" (*adhvan*), since they are "eaten" (*adyante*) by impermanence.
By the term "basis of discourse" (*kathāvastu*), those very same conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) were taught by the Blessed One.
"Monks, there are these three bases of discourse— neither fourth nor fifth— relying upon which the noble ones engage in discourse when they speak."
Which three? The past subject of discourse, the future subject of discourse, and the present [subject of discourse]. Discourse (*kathā*) means speech (*vākya*), and so forth.

"Speech" (*kathā*) means a sentence, which is to say, sound consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*). Its "object" (*vastu*) means its domain, namely the name (*nāman*). Furthermore, by means of the name, the referent (*artha*) is what is expressed (*abhidheya*).
For it will be stated thus: "Speech operates upon the name;
it illuminates the meaning of the name."

If indeed the "basis of discourse" (*kathāvastu*) is merely a portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), how is it that by the term "basis of discourse" only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are expressed?
To this he says: "But because it includes a basis that possesses meaning, the conditioned is called the 'basis of discourse'.
Otherwise, [as explained] in detail...
If a meaningful entity (*sārthaka-vastu*) were not included, it would contradict the *Prakaraṇapāda* treatise,
which states that "the bases of discourse (*kathāvastūni*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
By what reasoning, then, is a meaningful entity understood?
The object of discourse is twofold: direct and indirect. That which is called the direct object is as follows.
The object exists through a traditional succession;
for that [object] is the object of the name which constitutes its own sphere. Therefore, it too is established as an object.

Why is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) not stated to be a basis of discourse (*kathāvastu*)? Because a name that falls within the time periods (*adhvan*) cannot have a referent (*artha*) in common with that which does not fall within the time periods.
Alternatively, it is because the word *vastu* (basis) is understood here as denoting two meanings: "object" (*viṣaya*) and "cause" (*hetu*).
For that which is both the object of discourse and possesses causes and conditions is a "basis of discourse" (*kathāvastu*).
However, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not a basis of discourse, because it lacks causes and conditions for discourse.
Alternatively, it is because conditioned phenomena of the past and so forth possess such a vast multiplicity of forms that they are suitable for being narrated:
"In such and such a way, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara existed;
and in such and such a way, the Tathāgata Maitreya will exist."
Since it is said that "King Kapphiṇa was thus and so," only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are stated to be the subject matter of discourse, not unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
The "nirvāṇa of all conditioned things" refers to nirvāṇa without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

If this is the case, then since that [nirvāṇa] exists for what is with outflows (*sāsrava*), there is a logical connection between the state of being with outflows and the state of possessing an essence (*sanissāratva*).
But how is it for the truth of the path?

For those who understand the discourse on the Dharma as being like a raft, even the [teachings of] dharmas must be abandoned, let alone non-dharmas; thus, the transcendence of the truth of the path is indeed established. All conditioned phenomena whatsoever possess transcendence.
"Accompanied by a real entity" (*savastuka*) means:
first, the effects reside in this [entity], and subsequently, they arise from it.
The meaning is that "entity" (*vastu*) is the cause.
Since these [factors] possess such an entity, they are called "with-entity" (*savastuka*).
For in the teaching (*pravacana*), the word "entity" is seen to be used in five senses.
Regarding intrinsic nature, the object, that which is to be fettered, the cause, and appropriation: first, concerning intrinsic nature, it is whatever entity has been acquired.
"He is endowed with that object" is understood to mean "by way of that intrinsic nature.
Regarding the object:
what are the phenomena to be known?
He said:
"All phenomena are to be known by means of knowledge according to their actual state and according to their objective support; this is the meaning.
[This applies] to that which is subject to fetters."
Regarding whatever object one is bound by the fetter of attachment,
one is also [bound] by the fetter of aversion toward that same object;
this refers to the cause.
What are phenomena with a basis?
They are all conditioned phenomena.
[This refers to] appropriation.
"Having abandoned the appropriation of fields, houses, shops, wealth, and property, he abstains from them.
Here, the word *vastu* should be understood as denoting a cause; it is a term for a cause. This is indicated by the particle *kila*.
The word *kila* indicates the opinion of another; his own position, however, is indicated by this:
conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) possess a real basis (*savastuka*) and possess intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*).

"But the unconditioned [dharmas] lack a real entity because they exist only as designations" (I.8). Furthermore, "those very conditioned [dharmas]" refers to those previously mentioned as being both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*), as he shows.
"Those which are with outflows are the aggregates of clinging"— in this context, the word "of them" (teṣām) is to be supplied.
"What is established?
He examines that which is implied by the meaning.
The aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) and so forth have been taught in the Sūtras;
therefore, they are explained here.
It has been stated in detail that the entirety of the Abhidharma is the meaning of the Sūtras.
"Arising from that, they are the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*).
The aggregates produced from clinging are the "aggregates of clinging," due to the elision of the middle term.
Just as fire produced from grass is "grass-fire" (*tṛṇāgni*),
and fire produced from chaff is "chaff-fire" (*tuṣāgni*),
others establish that the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) are formed by a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) alone, without omitting the middle term.
And they illustrate it in this way:
just as it is logical that fire [consisting] of grass is called "grass-fire," so it is for those who are reckoned as sentient beings.
Those aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) exist because they have karma, moistened by the afflictions (*kleśa*), as their cause.
But how can external entities be aggregates of clinging?
They too are produced from clinging.
Because it is an established tenet that "the variety of the world is born of karma," or because [the world] is subject to that [karma], like a king's servant.
Just as a person who is subject to a king is called a "king's man," so too the aggregates are subject to the appropriations,
because by their power they proceed toward different objects of perception.
"Or, the appropriations arise from them.
This is merely an explanation of the meaning;
however, the words should be stated as follows:

The aggregates are "aggregates of clinging" (upādānaskandha) because they are the source or the cause for the arising of clingings, just as a tree is the source or the cause for the arising of flowers or fruits. It is like saying "flower-tree" or "fruit-tree."
In the same way,
the aggregates (*skandha*) of an Arhat are also subject to the grasping (*upādāna*) belonging to another continuum, because they produce transformation.
Furthermore, since grasping belonging to other continua can arise from them as well, it is not contradictory for these to be "aggregates of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*).
For the *raṇas* are the afflictions (*kleśa*), because they cause harm to oneself and others.
The meaning is that those which harm both oneself and others are *raṇas*, that is, battles.

In the same way, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are called "strifes" (*raṇa*). This is because they are "underlying tendencies" (*anuśayita*) to them; the meaning is that they have been made to lie latent (*anuśayita*) by, or cultivated (*upasevita*), through those [afflictions].
Alternatively, those [dharmas] are called "possessing latent dispositions" because they have been made to possess latent dispositions by them;
the state of being that is "the state of possessing those latent dispositions.
Therefore [it is said].
Because they are accompanied by those [latent tendencies], or else because those [defilements] have the nature of being latent tendencies therein;
therefore.
The *saraṇas* are like the *sāsravas*.
Whatever explanation was given regarding the state of being *sāsrava*,
that same explanation should be stated for this.
It is called suffering because it is disagreeable to the Noble Ones;
it is disagreeable to the Noble Ones by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). It is called the origin because suffering arises from it.
They describe the aggregates that function as causes as "origination," and the aggregates that function as effects as "suffering.
It is called "the world" (*loka*) because it disintegrates (*lujyate*).
"In this very body, O Rohitāśva, which is but a fathom in height, I declare the world and the origin of the world"—this is the Sūtra.
Furthermore, it was said by the Blessed One himself: "It is broken (*lujyate*) and utterly destroyed (*pralujyate*); therefore it is called the 'world' (*loka*).
The meaning is that it is broken, that is, it perishes.
The word *loka* is not actually taken here;
rather, according to the rules of etymology (*nairukta*), the letter *ga* has been changed to *ka*,
and thus it becomes *loka*.
"View resides in this" means:

because of the statement, "O monks, whoever perceives in terms of a self and what belongs to a self, they perceive these very five aggregates of clinging as a self and as belonging to a self," it follows that the aggregates of clinging are the locus of views.
"Existence" (bhava) refers exclusively to contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma), as indicated by the statement:
"What is existence? It is the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha)."
Furthermore, these terms such as "suffering" (duḥkha) and so forth would also apply to the truth of the path (mārgasatya).
For the truth of the path is indeed suffering by virtue of being the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (saṃskāraduḥkhatā);
moreover, through its status as the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) and others, it gives rise to contaminated entities (sāsrava-vastu).
And it is destroyed.
Furthermore, "it perceives that" means that it exists and arises with respect to that object.
This is not a fault,
for the application of a term depends upon conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

Those factors (*dharmas*) which, by virtue of being the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), are disagreeable to the Noble Ones (*ārya*), painful, and antagonistic— those which are well-known as the producers of that [suffering] and the generators of the nourishment of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
In this beginningless saṃsāra, beings perish and come into existence.
It is precisely regarding these [conditioned phenomena] that the Noble Ones have designated terms such as "suffering" and so forth, not regarding the truth of the path.
Therefore, only those dharmas that are with-outflows (sāsrava) are denoted by terms such as "suffering," and not those that are without-outflows (anāsrava).
For when it is said that "a cow is so called because it goes," not every goer is called a cow.
Therefore, it is well stated that [the truths are] suffering, origin, and so forth.
(I.9ab) Form.
Thus ends the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The word "five" is used for the purpose of excluding the mental faculty (*manaindriya*).
Objects (*artha*) are the sense-objects; they are called "objects" because they are sought after (*aryante*) or known. Furthermore...
The mention of "five" is for the purpose of excluding those objects that belong to the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Their consciousnesses have these as their supports.
Thus [it is said].
The word "that" (tat) refers back to the objects.
"Cognitions of those" (tadvijñānāni) means either cognitions regarding those objects or cognitions belonging to those [objects].
Their supports are the supports of those consciousnesses;
they are the translucent forms (*rūpaprasāda*).
"Those which are both forms and translucent" means "translucent forms.
By this qualification, the mental faculty (*manas*) is excluded;
for the mind, too, is the support for those consciousnesses.

According to the established tenet that "the five [faculties] are co-arisen with them," they are possessed of latent dispositions (*anuśayita*). However, because the mind does not have the nature of form (*rūpa*), this [objection] is refuted.
However, the inclusion of the term "form" (*rūpa*) here is for the purpose of excluding faith (*śraddhā*).
If it is argued that faith is not included because of the qualification "they are the supports of those consciousnesses," we say no.
Because the possibility of that [absurd] consequence arises when a *bahuvrīhi* compound is assumed;
however, when "form" (*rūpa*) is taken [as the object], the assumption of a *bahuvrīhi* is precluded.
For there is no translucent matter (*prasāda*) consisting of form upon which those consciousnesses could be conceived as depending as their support.
The mention of "clarity" (*prasāda*), moreover, is for the purpose of making known a specific kind of clarity that is distinct from the objects grasped by the sense faculties.
For the Vaibhāṣikas indeed assert that the sense faculties are merely specific transformations of the primary elements (*bhūta*).
But it is not so in the Teaching (pravacana).

What then? There are sense-faculties (indriya) distinct from objects such as visible form, which are translucent, beyond the reach of the senses, and to be inferred by their own cognitions; those of which the bases (adhiṣṭhāna), such as the eye and so forth, are seen.
The qualification "the supports of those consciousnesses" is intended to prevent confusion regarding their mutual characteristics.
For if one were to say merely that "the eye and so forth are the translucent forms," [the distinction would not be clear].
Is it the eye, or the ear and so forth, that is the eye?
Since it is specified in this way:
"that translucent matter which is the basis of the consciousness of visible forms."
"That is the eye.
Therefore, there is no confusion of defining characteristics;
for neither the ear nor any other sense faculty is the basis of visual consciousness.
In this way, up to the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) which is the basis for the consciousness of the tangible— that should be called the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*),
as it was stated by the Blessed One.
The intention is that this explanation follows the Sūtra. How so?
"Internal" means that which is the support of consciousness.

For it will be stated that the word "self" (ātman) is used metaphorically for the mind (citta). That which is "with respect to the self" (adhi-ātman) is "internal" (adhyātma); that which is internal is "pertaining to the internal" (ādhyātmika).
When that which has the characteristic of mind (*cittalakṣaṇa*) is to be established as the self (*ātman*), this meaning is expressed by the word "internal" (*ādhyātmika*);
that is to say, it refers to the basis of consciousness (*vijñānāśraya*). Alternatively, the full expression is "those which... and so forth.
Alternatively,
by that word "tat," the sense faculties are intended.
This—that there is "eye-consciousness," "ear-consciousness," and so forth—is well-established in the formal teaching (pravacana).
However, it is not the case that there is "form-consciousness" or "sound-consciousness.
Yet, in common worldly usage, such [expressions] might occasionally occur.
Therefore, this other explanation is adopted.
Thus he says:
"And by doing so, the text of the *Prakaraṇa* is also followed," and so forth.
How can that which is unestablished here be established by means of what is unestablished?
For the eye itself is unestablished;
since that is unestablished, visual consciousness is also unestablished.
How is that established by means of them as its basis?
These five specific types of consciousness are already established.
However, for the sake of distinguishing their mutual differences, we demonstrate them by qualifying them with these [bases], such as the eye and so forth.
This is what is meant:
the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) which is the basis of this first, unique, self-cognizable specific cognition—
that is the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
In this way, up to this point, that translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) which is the basis of this fifth, self-cognizable, specific consciousness is the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
[Objection: This is not a proof of an unestablished [subject] by means of an unestablished [reason].
(I.10) "Form is of two kinds.
The object of the eye is of two types due to the distinction between color and shape.
Since this is well-known in the world, its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not stated; rather, only its classification is explained.
Color is of four kinds, beginning with blue:
blue, red, yellow, and white are the primary colors;
others are their subdivisions, such as the color of clouds and so forth.
Others explain it thus:
"The others are different from that" means that due to specific combinations of the four colors— blue and so forth— even colors such as the hue of a crow's egg arise,
not only those like clouds and the like.
Configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is a specific form.
Furthermore, that very same [configuration] is divided by internal distinctions into twenty types.
Namely, blue, yellow, and so forth.
Shape is of eight kinds, from long to uneven.
The remaining twelve kinds are color; thus, there are twenty types in total.
"And the sky is of a single color" means that which is seen from afar as having the appearance of a wall of lapis lazuli; "vṛtta" means circular.
Circular refers to the shape of a wheel.
Elevated refers to forms such as thick or protruding. Depressed refers to forms that are low-lying or concave.

The statement "where there is the seeing of forms" is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between shadow and darkness; it means that [the distinction] has not been elaborated upon nor analyzed. This is what is investigated here.

If clouds and the like are nothing other than the fourfold distinctions of color such as blue and so forth, and are not distinct from them— just as the colors of a crow’s egg and the like are not mentioned here— then clouds and the like should likewise not be mentioned.
This has not been investigated by the commentators.
However, it can be stated as follows:
because they resemble illusory forms (*māyārūpa*), those clouds and so forth, although consisting of distinctions such as blue and other colors, are mentioned separately.
For indeed, they appear from afar like walls, but when one approaches them, they are no longer seen.
Let it not occur to anyone that this is nothing at all.
Or there is doubt:
"Does this exist,
or is it merely an illusion?"

In order to eliminate the misconception and doubt regarding that [matter], these things such as clouds and so forth are mentioned [to show] that they truly exist and have the nature of the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). They are regions characterized by length and so on.
The meaning is "the location ranging from long to wide.
To the question "What is that location? he says: "It has the nature of bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti)."
For bodily intimation is sometimes long, sometimes short, and sometimes even irregular. But how is it to be understood?
It is that which is bodily action produced by a mind directed toward that object.
However, it should be understood that those things whose intrinsic nature is not bodily action—ranging from "long" to "irregular"—are excluded.
There is [action] in both ways;
this refers to what remains.
That which has been rejected, such as length and so forth,
as well as clouds, smoke, dust, and mist.
(Abhidh-k-vy 26)
For indeed, the determination of length and so forth is observed in the case of blue and other colors.
There is the apprehension of spatial configurations such as long and so on in blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, and darkness.
Therefore, the intention is that these too are included within the third category.
But how can a single substance exist in two ways?
How can a single substance consist of both color and shape?
For it is your established tenet that the form of shape is a distinct substance from the form of color.
Because both are cognized therein;
because color and shape are apprehended therein;
for this root *vid* has the meaning of "cognition," not the meaning of "existence."

The meaning is that this form belongs to the verbal root *vid* with the suffix *luṅ-vikaraṇa*, signifying "is found" (*vidyate*), and not to the verbal root *vid* in the sense of "existence" (*sattā*) with the suffix *śyan-vikaraṇa*.
In that context, knowledge proceeds in both forms.
"A single substance cannot possess both characteristics"—this is the Vaibhāṣika rebuttal.
"In that case, the same consequence would apply to bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) as well," says the Master;
for when bodily intimation is being perceived, the perception of color does not fail to occur.

This is the intention of the Vaibhāṣikas: the apprehension of blue and so forth, or the apprehension of sunlight and light, proceeds independently of shape; however, the apprehension of bodily intimation proceeds independently of color.
However, the apprehension of the remaining form-āyatanas proceeds in dependence upon color and shape.
But this master, who sides with the Sautrāntikas, does not accept this point;
for this apprehension of shape is not visual.
But this [notion of shape] is merely a mental construction.
For shape is simply a particular arrangement of color;
there is no such substance as "shape" that exists in itself.
Because there is no apprehension of shape when there is no apprehension of color.
This will be examined in the section on action (karma) in the Abhidharmakośa.
And [it is] "designated as sentient and non-sentient."
The meaning is that it consists of vocal intimation-sound and that which is distinct from it.
Some read "reckoned as sentient and non-sentient," and this alone is the intended meaning here.

For if the intended meaning were "arising from the continuum of a sentient being or a non-sentient being," then the subsequent explanation— that the sound of vocal intimation is designated as "sentient" while other sounds are designated as "non-sentient"— would be entirely purposeless.
Therefore, the reading *sattvāsattvākhyaś ca* (and [the sound] designated as sentient or non-sentient) should clearly be recited.

"Having as its cause the appropriated great elements (upāttamahābhūtahetuka)" means that the present elements which are inseparable from the sense faculties are "appropriated," while others are "non-appropriated."
"Having appropriated primary elements as its cause" means that its cause consists of appropriated primary elements (*upāttamahābhūtahetuka*). For example, the sound of the hand or the voice,
if what is intended is that which arises from the continuum of a sentient being (*sattvasaṃtānaja*).
For even an externally emanated form in human shape might produce sounds with its hands or its voice.
It should be understood that this has as its cause the great elements (mahābhūta) that are not appropriated (anupātta), because it exists as something separate from the sense faculties (indriya).
And it might speak even human speech by the power of the emanator.
For it will be said:
"When one speaks, all the emanations speak;
when one becomes silent, they all become silent."

And that external, produced sound is included here under the category of "having as its cause the non-appropriated great elements," such as the sound of wind, forest trees, or a river; for the word "such as" (yathā) serves the purpose of providing an illustration.

(Abhidh-k-vy 27) That which is designated as "sentient" (*sattvākhya*) is the sound of vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*); that which is "other" than this is designated as "non-sentient" (*asattvākhya*).
It is called "designated as sentient" because it designates a sentient being.
For it is by means of the sound of vocal intimation that one recognizes, "This is a sentient being.
Excluding that sound of vocal intimation, any other sound—even the sound of a hand—is indeed designated as non-sentient.
How much more so, then, is that which arises from the continuum of a non-sentient being? Thus it is explained.
Thus, that which has appropriated primary elements (*upātta-mahābhūta*) as its cause is both designated as "sentient" (*sattvākhya*) and "non-sentient" (*asattvākhya*).

Furthermore, even sound produced by non-appropriated primary elements (*anupātta-mahābhūta*)—such as the sound of emanations (*nirmita-śabda*), which is of the nature of vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*)—is designated as "sentient.
On the other hand, the sound of one's own hands, or the sound of wind, trees, and so forth, is designated as "non-sentient."
Sound is of four kinds, which, when divided by the distinction between pleasant and unpleasant, becomes eightfold—
just as a single atom of color [is fourfold]. Sound does not exist by depending on two sets of the four primary elements.
Because it is derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*); the sense is that it is like a color-atom (*varṇaparamāṇu*). "Taste is sixfold."
This was said with reference specifically to the six fundamental types [of taste].
However, due to the particular combinations of these six tastes with one another, an extremely great variety of tastes arises.
Indeed, in the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, sixty-three tastes are taught based on the conjunctions of combinations of one, two, three, four, five, and all six [tastes].
"Because of the equality or inequality of the fragrance of the pleasant-smelling and the foul-smelling"—
this means because of the non-intense or intense nature of the fragrance.
In this view, fragrance is held to be of two kinds.
"But the treatise [speaks of] three kinds" means that there is another, a third, which has an equal odor.
Others, however, explain it differently.
"Uniform fragrance" means that it is simply one part of those same two [fragrances]; thus the meaning remains the same, though only the terminology differs.
"Cold" is that which produces a desire for warmth.
This is stated with reference to its occurrence:
that phenomenon which produces heat and desire is the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) called "cold."
Even if one does not perform that [act] during the summer, it should nevertheless be understood as being "cold" because it belongs to that same class;
this is due to the metaphorical application of the effect to the cause.
Hunger (*jighatsā*) is the mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) consisting of the desire to eat.
The cause of that is as follows:
that which is touched by the body-faculty within the stomach is the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) called hunger.

Just as "the arising of Buddhas is happiness" and so forth is said because the arising of a Buddha is the cause of the happiness of higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*) and the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*), so too is that [arising] called happiness.
It is just like that.
In the same way, thirst should also be explained.
Furthermore, the statement that "accumulated [atoms] weigh" is intended to mean that they possess subtle gravity.
Herein is the inference:
clothing and so forth belonging to the realm of form possess weight,
because they exist in a relationship of support and supported.
"Like a jujube fruit in a bowl.
[The phrase] "it is said that there is a supporting factor" (anugrāhakam) contains the word *kila* for the purpose of indicating that this is the opinion of the Vaibhāṣikas.
Our own position, however, is that concentration alone is the factor that assists here;
what is the use of this imagined "cold"?
[This refers to the phrase] "when there is the exclusion of those specific types."
When there is an engagement with the signs of modes such as blue and so forth,
auditory consciousness and the others arise in the same way.
This refers to the various kinds of sound that have been described.

In that regard, sometimes auditory consciousness arises from a single substance when there is a discernment of its specific type; sometimes it arises from many substances when there is no such discernment.
This is as, for example, when one hears a collection of musical sounds consisting of various forms of sound, such as high-pitched and low-pitched tones.
In the same way, the consciousnesses of the nose and tongue should also be applied to their own respective objects.
As for body-consciousness, however, it is "at most fivefold.
How so?
Sometimes it arises from a single substance when there is a delimitation of that particular type;
sometimes from two up to five substances when there is no such delimitation.
And "from one" refers to [qualities] such as smoothness and so forth.
What is the reason for this?
Because qualities such as hardness depend upon another set of four primary elements (*bhūta-catuṣka*).
But [if that were so], then—[as explained] in detail—how could it be?

Just as mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is established as having a general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) for its object by way of grasping the objects of visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses collectively; so too,
since a single visual consciousness grasps those four objects of the four visual consciousnesses— blue, yellow, red, and white— along with many other objects collectively,
it follows that this [single visual consciousness] has a general characteristic for its object.
This is because its objective support (*ālambana*) is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*).
In the same way, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses are also to be applied to their respective objects.
[The phrase] "perceiving the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sense-base" [is used].
One's own characteristic is the *svalakṣaṇa*.
The *svalakṣaṇa* of the sense bases (*āyatana*) is the "sense-base *svalakṣaṇa*," such as being cognizable by visual consciousness and so forth.
Or [it may refer to] being the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth.
In this regard, it is maintained in the *Pravacana* that these five groups of consciousness have specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objects;
it is not maintained, however, that they have the specific characteristic of a substance (*dravyasvalakṣaṇa*) as their object—this is the point under discussion.
The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of substances such as blue and so forth is their being cognizable by visual consciousness and the like through the aspect of blue and so forth,
or the aspect of blue itself.
Since these five groups of consciousness are not asserted to have that [aspect] as their object of the specific characteristic, there is no fault.
Regarding the phrase "when objects are encountered simultaneously":
it is possible for the body-faculty and the tongue-faculty to encounter their respective objects at the same time;
however, the simultaneous arising of two consciousnesses is not possible.
Therefore, he asks:
"Which consciousness arises first?
That one whose object is more intense.
If the object of the body-faculty is more intense, body-consciousness arises first;
if the object of the tongue-faculty is more intense, tongue-consciousness arises first.
However, when the objects are equally attained, they are equal—this is the meaning.
Tongue-consciousness arises first.
Why?
Because the continuum is directed by the desire to eat.
The meaning is that the personal existence (ātmabhāva) is inclined toward the desire for food.
Because of the statement that "first the tongue-consciousness arises," it is implied by the sense of the argument that "subsequently the body-consciousness will arise.
Therefore, this is investigated here.

Is it that the body-object moment which had previously occurred together with the tongue-object moment gives rise to that body-consciousness? Or rather, does it arise in relation to another body-object moment?
He says: "In another [case].
How is it that the restriction of the object (*ālambana-niyama*) is not violated?
This is not a fault.
That consciousness which has that object as its focal point is ceased by non-analytical cessation;
however, another body-consciousness similar to it arises.
Therefore, it is said that it arises after that, by means of a metaphorical attribution of oneness based on the commonality of its genus (*jātisāmānya*).
Since the section concerning the non-informative (*avijñapti*) has, as it were, perished due to being interrupted by manifold elaborations of discourse,
he introduces this [verse] (I.11).
The five sense objects and the manner in which they are apprehended have been explained,
beginning with the statement that sometimes visual consciousness arises from a single substance, and so forth.
In the phrase "the apprehension of them," the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Now, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) must be explained.
Matter consists of the five sense faculties, the five objects, and non-informative matter itself. (Abhidh-k-vy 29)
Only non-informative [action] remains.
It must be explained that this is the occasion for the definition of its characteristics.
[The phrase] "of one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind" [is used].
Some read the commentary in this way. According to this reading, the analysis of the sūtra is as follows: "one who has a distracted mind or no mind at all" is called *vikṣiptācittaka*.
Alternatively, one who has a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) or who lacks a mind (*na asti vā cittaṃ asya*) is "one with a distracted or no-mind" (*vikṣiptācittaka*).
There is the elision of one instance of the word *citta*.
Some read it in this way.
Regarding the term *vikṣiptasya*:
in this reading, one forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the latter two words, and subsequently analyzes it as follows:
"one who is distracted (*vikṣipta*) and one who is without mind (*acittaka*) is 'distracted-and-without-mind' (*vikṣiptācittaka*)."

A "distracted person" (vikṣipta-pudgala) means one whose mind is distracted (vikṣipta-citta). Regarding the phrase "of one whose mind is distracted," this refers to one whose mind is other than that [state], meaning a mind other than an undistracted mind.
For example, the mind that originates a wholesome unmanifest action (avijñapti) is itself wholesome.
One whose mind is other than that has a mind that is either unwholesome or neutral; it is such a person with a distracted mind who is intended here.
However, for unwholesome non-informative action (*avijñapti*), an unwholesome mind is the motivator (*samutthāpaka*).
One whose mind is other than that— possessing either a wholesome or an indeterminate mind—
should also be understood as having a distracted mind. Of such a person:

"Even for one whose mind is otherwise directed," and "even for one who is without mind"— that is, even for one who has entered the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
By the word "even" (*api*), it is understood that this applies even to one whose mind is not distracted and who possesses a mind.

This refers also to a third entity distinct from these two types of persons. That which is "continuity" (anubandha) or "stream" (pravāha) means a phenomenon (dharma) that is endowed with a constant flow.
The "possessor of a stream" (pravāhin) is indicated by means of the "stream" (pravāha), because it is characterized by the stream.
Alternatively, it is called "anubandha" because it follows after (anubadhnāti). Furthermore, the word "stream" (pravāha) is a compound term formed as a bahuvrīhi.
A "stream" (*pravāha*) is a phenomenon (*dharma*) that has set forth (*pravṛtta*) or is preeminent (*prakṛṣṭa*) in its flow (*vāha*).
That alone is being indicated;
it is not the stream itself.
"Wholesome or unwholesome":
this is a restriction meaning "only wholesome or unwholesome";
the sense is that there is no indeterminate [state].
By this, the [acquisition of] the eye and so forth should be understood as refuted.
There is also such a continuous flow of acquisition (*prāpti*);

since that acquisition flows continuously even for one whose mind is distracted or undistracted, and is exclusively wholesome or unwholesome, it is stated [in the sūtra] for the purpose of distinguishing it from that.
"Dependent upon the great elements" means having the great elements as its cause;
just as when it is said that fire exists dependent upon fuel.
It is understood that fire has fuel as its cause. This is because [fuel] functions as the cause for its production and so forth—
namely, through production, reliance, maintenance, support, and nourishment.
The cause of production is because they arise from them.
The cause of reliance is because that which has been produced conforms to the primary elements (*bhūta*), like relying on a teacher and so forth.
The cause of support is because it serves as a foundation, like a wall for a painting.
It is a supporting cause because it is a cause of non-interruption;
it is a nourishing cause because it is a cause of increase.
Based upon which great elements?
Are they the primary elements that serve as the basis, or are they the primary elements that serve as the support?
They say: "They are the primary elements that serve as the basis."
"It is for the purpose of making known its name.
The meaning is that although it has the nature of form and action, it does not inform another like a *vijñapti* (informative action); therefore, it is called "non-informative" (*avijñapti*).
"Even having the nature of form and action" is a dual qualification.
For what purpose?
Because there are entities that have the nature of form alone and do not have the nature of action.
Therefore, it does not cause [the object] to be perceived by another,
just like the eye and other [faculties]. Furthermore, although its intrinsic nature is indeed that of activity, it does not have the intrinsic nature of form.
Even that does not lead to the ultimate;
for example, volition (*cetanā*).
However, that which possesses the nature of both [is different].
It makes another understand that;

for example, informative action (*vijñapti*). For informative action makes another understand the mind that has originated it—whether it be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; gentle, cruel, or neither—as being such.
Therefore, "like a manifest [action]" (*vijñaptivat*) is an application of a dissimilar example (*viparīta-dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the phrase "in brief," however,
the Master shows that form which is non-manifest (*avijñapti-rūpa*) by means of a concise statement for the sake of the students' easy understanding.
Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is wholesome or unwholesome matter produced from informative action (*vijñapti*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This should be applied according to the possibilities:
it is wholesome matter produced from bodily and vocal informative action, which is either comprised within the Prātimokṣa restraint or comprised within neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint.
Furthermore, the unwholesome is comprised within non-restraint as well as that which is comprised within neither restraint nor non-restraint.
That which is produced from meditative concentration, however, is exclusively wholesome.
This is of two kinds.

That which arises from contaminated concentration has the nature of the meditative restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*); that which arises from uncontaminated concentration has the nature of the uncontaminated restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*);
and it also has the nature of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
It should be understood that [unmanifest form] does not have the nature of mind or mental factors.
But would it not follow, then, that manifest form (*vijñapti*) is also unmanifest?
For that too is produced from a preceding manifest form that has become its homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Because of the restriction that it is "only wholesome or unwholesome," there is no over-extension [of the definition] to informative action (*vijñapti*). For informative action can also be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

For this very reason, even though the divine eye and ear are produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they do not entail being non-informative action (*avijñapti*), since they are born of informative action and are matter as karmic maturation (*vipāka-rūpa*).
In this regard, the master Saṃghabhadra refutes this sūtra on the definition of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*):
"It is deficient, it contradicts the treatise, its loss follows, and its reality is undermined;
furthermore, the word 'also' (*api*) is redundant, and the qualificand here remains unqualified."
For "continuity" (*anubandha*) has been explained as a stream (*pravāha*).
And the first moment is not the stream, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, it is not included here by the definition; thus, [the claim] that "unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) is a non-substance because a stream is not a substance" contradicts the treatise (*śāstra*).

Furthermore, for one who is in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), there is no continuity of non-informative form (*avijñapti*) for one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind (*acittaka*); thus, it follows that such non-informative form would not exist, which is a flaw.

If it is argued that this fault does not apply because there is a continuity of it for one whose mind is not distracted, then it follows that both virtuous and non-virtuous informative forms (*vijñapti*) would possess the characteristics of non-informative form; therefore, its true nature as such is logically entailed.
Regarding the phrase "even for one who is without mind" (*acittakasyāpi*), the word "even" (*api*) is redundant because its purpose has already been fulfilled by the preceding [term].
By the phrase "even for one whose mind is distracted" (*vikṣiptacittakasyāpi*), all states involving a mind are indeed included.
What, then, would be another state?
The phrase "the addition of the word *api*" refers to the fact that it would be included by the second occurrence of the word *api*.
Furthermore, with reference to the state of being without mind (*acittaka*), the connection to virtuous non-informative matter (*śubhā avijñapti*) should have been specified;
yet, since it was not specified even in the commentary, the subject remains unspecified.
And this further qualification, "unimpeded matter" (*apratighaṃ rūpam*), remains unspecified.
Thus, because it is corrupted by numerous defects, this definition is not coherent.
To this we reply:

As for what was said— that because the continuum is taught as non-informative (avijñapti), the first moment would not be non-informative— first, he should be asked: what is this so-called "continuum" (pravāha)?
The term "stream" (pravāha) refers to many moments.
If this is so, then even the first moment is established as a stream,
because a stream is defined as many moments beginning from the first moment.
For indeed, the designation "stream" applies to the water flowing out from a well or a pond, starting from the very first particles of water;
thus, there is no lack of pervasiveness in the definition.
Furthermore, when one says "it follows" (*anubadhnāti*), the word *anubandha*—ending in the suffix *-ac*—refers to the substance itself.
At that time, there is not even the slightest suspicion of deficiency.
For this very reason, the fault of deviating from the treatise (*śāstra*) is also avoided.
Furthermore, the term *anubandha*—derived from the sense of "following after" (*anubandhana*)—is used to designate a "stream" (*srotas*).
Nevertheless, there is no fault here, because the context concerns matter (*rūpa*).
However, it is indicated by the term "stream" (*pravāha*) because it exists as a continuous flow.
Furthermore, it is not the case that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is not apprehended even when one is in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).

For although that [non-informative form] does not continue through a continuum that is distracted or devoid of mind, it certainly continues through a continuum that is undistracted and possessed of mind.
However, by virtue of its commonality as a genus of non-informative form, the continuity that exists even for one who is distracted or devoid of mind is called "non-informative form" (avijñapti).
Furthermore, as for what was said:
"If it is argued that this fault does not apply because there is a continuous succession [of the mind] for one whose mind is undistracted," [the response is:
if there is a continuous succession belonging solely to one whose mind is undistracted.
You state that this [unmanifest action] is also unmanifest (*avijñapti*), and thus there is no relinquishing of the unmanifest associated with meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
You further argue that since manifest action (*vijñapti*)—whether wholesome or unwholesome—is likewise [of the nature of non-informative matter], it would follow that it too is unmanifest for you.
However, that is not a fault, because of the restriction [in the definition] that it is "only" wholesome or unwholesome.

For it is possible that informative action (*vijñapti*) may even be neutral (*avyākṛta*); thus, it does not follow as a logical consequence that informative action is non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
Alternatively, this undesirable consequence will not arise because of the attainment of excellence (*prakarṣagati*).
For that which is a continuous succession in its excellence is precisely the non-informative (avijñapti).
And informative action (vijñapti) does not continue in a state of excellence in the same way that non-informative action does.
Because even when there is no cessation of the non-informative [action], its cessation is observed.
As for what was said—
that the word "also" (*api*) is an excessive statement— [it is not so].
That too is stated incorrectly.
For in this sūtra, the word "api" (also/even) is recited only once;
however, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), it is recited twice because its meaning is connected with those two types of persons (*pudgala*).

By using even that single word "api" (also) recited in the Sūtra, the Master, by speaking of that very third type of person— who possesses mind (*sacittaka*)— as having the non-informative (*avijñapti*) as its basis,

thereby indicating that the two types of persons previously mentioned by his own name, namely the distracted (*vikṣipta*) and the one without mind (*acittaka*), share the common nature of having the non-informative as their basis, declares that the non-informative is an entity distinct from informative action (*vijñapti*), mind (*citta*), and mental factors (*caitta*).
For there are only three types of persons: one whose mind is dissimilar to the informative act, one whose mind is similar to the informative act, and one who is without mind.
Among these, the person whose mind is dissimilar to the informative act is intended here as one whose mind is distracted;
for such a person, that vocal and bodily informative act has ceased.
But for one who is without mind (*acittaka*), even the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) have ceased.
In that case, this non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is a distinct entity from both the informative action (*vijñapti*) and the complex of mind and mental factors,
because it is distinguished from these by its nature as a continuous succession.
Showing that very same point, he says:
"Even for one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind. (Abhidh-k-vy 32)
It is not a distinctive feature that non-informative action (avijñapti) occurs for one whose mind is undistracted,
for informative action (vijñapti) also occurs for such a person.
However, the distinctive feature is that it also occurs for one whose mind is distracted.
For that [unmanifest action] has no manifest action;
however, because it is accompanied by non-manifest action, it is distinguished from manifest action.
Likewise, there is no superiority [in the case of unmanifest action], since non-manifest action continues even for one whose mind is distracted.
For even the mind and mental factors do indeed continue to exist for that [state];
however, the distinction is that it continues to exist even for one who is without mind,
because for such a person the mind and mental factors have ceased.
However, because non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) is continuous, it is distinguished from the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Thus, in order to specify this as a distinct entity (*dharmāntara*), the term "even" (*api*) is used to denote both one whose mind is undistracted and one who is either distracted or without mind;
even by that single word "even," the Master has stated that it also applies to one whose mind is undistracted and who possesses a mind (*sacittaka*).
Because it is the third [of the three] states of being.
Otherwise, he would have said "even for one whose mind is not distracted" (*avikṣiptacittakasyāpi*) by means of the word "also" (*api*), or "even for one who possesses a mind" (*sacittakasyāpi*).
It is just as there are three types of people in the world.
One person is wealthy, while the other two possess only wealth.
Having observed them, when one says, "Viṣṇumitra has wealth," the second would likewise say,
"Evadatta and Yajñadatta also have wealth."
By the word *api*, it is meant that Viṣṇumitra also exists.

The meaning is that by the word *api*—which, as it were, has fallen into a state of duality through its connection with Devadatta and Yajñadatta—it is that very Viṣṇumitra who is indicated (*lakṣyate*), and not something additional (*avasṛjyate*).
Therefore, the word *api* here is not at all redundant.
The same should be understood here as well.
Furthermore, regarding what was stated—
that with reference to those without thought, the connection with virtuous non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) must be specified— this is the point.
That too is of no consequence.
This definition was formulated with reference to the category of non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*).
What is intended to be expressed is simply this: that category of non-informative [matter] occurs even for one who is without thought (*acittaka*).
What is the point of this qualification?
Even in your own definition of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), the connection with pure non-informative matter is not qualified with respect to the mindless state (*acittaka*).
It is [present] even when a dissimilar mind has arisen and even when there is an absence of mind (*cittātyaya*).
"Unmanifest form is that which is designated as non-obstructive; for it is accepted as being *avijñapti*.

And it will be explained in the fourth chapter of the *Kośa* that this unmanifest form, which arises from manifest action (*vijñapti*), is exclusively wholesome and can occur even in one who is without thought (*acittaka*).
And as for the statement that "that which is non-obstructive" is without qualification,
we shall demonstrate that later as well.
There are ten [elements] that are with obstruction.
Regarding the phrase "those that possess form":
this is because of the restriction that only ten elements are characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*).
Non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) is recited among the factors of the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).
It will be established as being non-obstructive (apratigha).
Therefore, this definition of the characteristic of non-informative matter belonging to our own [school] is thus free from fault.
Let it be so.
(I.12) "The primary elements are the earth element," and so forth.
The inclusion of the term "element" (*dhātu*) is for the purpose of excluding earth and the other [elements] that consist of color and shape.
They are called "elements" because they uphold their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
They are elements because they uphold hardness and so forth as their own specific characteristics, as well as the derived matter of the eye and so forth.

The eighteen elements (*dhātu*), however, are so called because they maintain their own specific and general characteristics. Alternatively, the meaning of "element" is "lineage" (*gotra*), without regard for the sense of "maintaining.
Furthermore, in the teaching of the six elements, the meaning of "element" is the sense of being a "seed" for renewed existence, insofar as they nourish existence.
Their "greatness" (mahattva) is due to their being gross because they serve as the basis for all other types of derived matter;
the meaning is that they are great by virtue of being the support for all derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
[The phrase] "in those whose activity has become manifest" means:

Those aggregates of earth, water, fire, and air in which the functions— such as supporting and so forth— have arisen from and become manifest through those great elements (mahābhūtas) are called "those whose functions have arisen from them. In them [is the action].
Because these great elements constitute a vast configuration and a grand construction, they extend (tanvanti) what has come to be (bhūtam), and thus they are called "elements" (bhūtāni).
They are fully established through their functions such as supporting and so forth.
The specification of the functions such as supporting (dhṛti) and so forth regarding earth and the other elements is for the purpose of inferring the remaining ones.

For, in the case of earth-substance such as a stone, because the functions of cohesion (saṃgraha), maturation (pakti), expansion (vyūhana), and motion (īraṇa) are observed, the existence of the remaining elements—water, fire, and air—is inferred.
Likewise, in the case of water, because the functions of supporting a boat (nausaṃdhāraṇa), heating (uṣṇatā), and motion (īraṇa) are observed, the existence of earth, fire, and air is inferred.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the existence of earth, water, and wind is established by observing stability, cohesion, and motion within a flame; and the existence of earth, water, and fire is established by observing support, cold, and hot touch within the wind.
Furthermore, "expansion" (*vyūhana*) means either growth or spreading.
Growth (*vṛddhi*) is the production of limbs, such as sprouts, that exceed the body’s prior dimensions due to its connection [with nourishment].
Creeping (*prasarpaṇa*) is the successive production of bodies and so forth in different locations.
Heat (*uṣṇatā*)...
Even when expressing the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*); for example, "heat" (*uṣṇatā*) is simply that which is hot (*uṣṇa*).
[The movement of fire] is like the carrying away of a lamp because it produces [the flame] in another location.
For things that are momentary, there is no movement to another location; wherever they arise, right there they perish. Therefore, it is said thus.
The movement of the stream of primary elements has as its intrinsic nature the production [of them] in another location, because of their momentariness,
like a lamp.
And the primary elements are momentary, because they possess the nature of form,
like a lamp.
And since a lamp is well known to be momentary, it serves as an example.
Its intrinsic nature is manifested by its action;
that is, lightness is distinguished by the action of moving.
That which has mobility as its nature and lightness is the wind element;
the wind element is light and mobile.
But that which is subtle is derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
(I.13) Since the earth element and so forth, as well as earth and so forth, are mentioned in the Teaching (pravacana), he asks [this question].
What, then, is the distinction between these?
It is by way of worldly designation— that is, by way of worldly convention.

Regarding the word *vātyā*: it is a collection (*samūha*) of winds (*vātānām*), hence *vātyā*. By the rule *brāhmaṇādibhyo yañ*, the suffix *yañ* is applied in the sense of a collection; and because it is feminine, the suffix *āp* is added.
For it is said thus in the *Arthavargīyas*.
The *Arthavargīya* sūtras are recited in the *Kṣudraka*;
it is stated in them:
"If he, while desiring," and so forth. Of him.
If, for an embodied being who is desiring and born of his own will...
Desires and sense objects do not come to fulfillment.
They do not succeed.
He is afflicted as if pierced by an arrow; the meaning is that he is oppressed.

In the sutra passage, "Monks, that which is called 'rūpyate' (is afflicted) is so called because it is delimited by the meaning of affliction," the word *rūpyate* is determined to have precisely the meaning of affliction.
It is logical that one who is pierced by an arrow or possessed by desire is afflicted because they experience suffering; but how is *rūpa* (form) afflicted?
Therefore he says:
"the production of transformation.
This means the production of change.
Likewise, since this meaning applies here,
even in the case of the statement "it is perceived as if pierced by a thorn," if the sense "it undergoes modification" is accepted.
The meaning is even more appropriately applied:
"obstruction" (pratighāta) refers to the prevention of another's arising in one's own location.
"In that case, it would follow that the form of an atom is not form.
Why? Because the form of a substantial atom (dravyaparamāṇu) would not qualify as form.
Why?
"Because of being non-material.
The intended meaning is: "because of being non-material while possessing no parts.
This objection is raised against both positions.
In the case of being afflicted and in the case of being obstructed, a substantial atom (*dravyaparamāṇu*) cannot be affected because it lacks parts.
Indeed, there is no such thing as a single, independent form that is an atom.
The use of the term "single" is for the purpose of illustrating the substantial atom.
The meaning is that it exists as something separate, not abiding in a composite.
Such a thing does not exist;
rather, that which abides in a composite is eternal.

Because of such statements as "in the realm of desire, that which is without sound consists of eight substances," it follows that when situated within a composite [body], it is indeed subject to transformation (rūpyate). By implication, this is what is intended.

That form which consists of the substance-atom (*dravyaparamāṇu*) exists as an aggregate (*saṃghāta*); it is thus "formable" (*rūpyate*), meaning it is subject to transformation, obstruction, and resistance. As for the detailed explanation beginning with "the past and future," since the past and future lack spatial location (*adeśatva*), they are not formable, nor are they subject to obstruction or resistance.
"That too," and so forth in detail.
"That too is formed" means by way of having been obstructed and having encountered resistance in the past.
"To be formed" refers to the future that possesses the nature of arising.
By those same two meanings. "Of that same kind" means that which is of the same kind as that which has the nature of arising— that is, the future [phenomenon] which has the nature of not arising—
just like fuel.
That which has been ignited, that which is about to be ignited, and whatever belongs to that same class—
all that is fuel. Furthermore,
that which belongs to the class of fuel is that which, having been intended for the purpose of fuel, will be extinguished in the interim without even reaching the fire.
In that case, non-informative matter (avijñapti) would not be matter (rūpa).
Why?
Because it is non-obstructive (apratigha).
For, by virtue of its non-obstructive nature, it is neither afflicted nor obstructed.
"That too [is] from the manifestation of form," and so forth;
the manifestation (vijñapti) is that which originates the non-manifestation (avijñapti).
Because that [informative action] which possesses resistance is subject to transformation, non-informative action is also transformed.
Just as a shadow moves because the tree that produces it moves, so it is in this case.
"Not because of non-modification.
By this, a fault in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*) is raised. For the opponent has indeed proposed the following thesis:
Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) conforms to the transformations of that which produces it, because it is produced by it,
like the shadow of a tree.
This thesis contradicts a prior admission.
For it has been admitted that even when there is a transformation of the *vijñapti*, there is no transformation of the *avijñapti*.
Thus, for example, when one breaks the *añjali* gesture and forms a *kapota* gesture, it is admitted that the bodily *vijñapti* undergoes transformation, but the *avijñapti* does not.
Therefore, this is not a valid proof.

Furthermore, by the statement, "Or rather, upon the cessation of the manifest (vijñapti), there would be the cessation of the unmanifest (avijñapti)," the reversal of the specific property of the subject (dharmiviśeṣaviparyaya) is also raised against this thesis.
For if it is maintained that the shadow possesses the nature of a tree, it is observed that when the tree ceases, the shadow ceases.
It would be so.
Here, someone objects that this statement, "because there is no transformation," is not correct, and refutes it by saying:
"Indeed, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) does undergo transformation when there is a transformation of informative matter (*vijñapti*)."
"For it is said that when the manifest action (*vijñapti*) is weak, medium, or intense, the non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) likewise becomes weak, medium, or intense.
This is incorrect.
Why?
The arising of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) occurs in this way:
as weak, medium, or intense; but there is no modification [of its nature].
For the transformation (*vikāra*) of a dharma that has already arisen is its arising again in another state;
and that is intended here as "formability" (*rūpaṇa*).
According to others, it is because of the formability of the primary elements (*bhūta*) which serve as its basis (*āśraya*).
The elder master Vasubandhu [states]:
"The mention of 'real' (bhūta) is for the purpose of showing the primary elements as the basis.
Therefore, the other [master] raises an objection."
"If that is so, then the same would apply to visual consciousness and the others," and so forth.
Since the eyes and other bases are subject to transformation (*rūpaṇa*), it follows that those consciousnesses would also be matter (*rūpa*).
To this, [the opponent] replies: "This comparison is unequal."
A certain teacher, a contemporary of the elder Vasubandhu, offers this rebuttal: "For the unmanifested (avijñapti)," and so forth. Shade exists by clinging to and depending upon a tree.
The light [of the gems] is likewise [dependent on them].
These [causes] are merely the conditions for their arising;
the point is that they are not inherently connected [to the result].
The other replies to him:
"This, first of all, is not the Vaibhāṣika position," and so forth.
This is not the Vaibhāṣika position.
According to the Vaibhāṣikas, however, shadow consists of color-atoms that exist depending upon their own four primary elements, and not upon a tree;
likewise, light consists of color-atoms that exist depending upon their own four primary elements, and not upon a gem.
Because they are separate substances.

Thus, since the jewel and the tree do not act as the cause for a substratum, the shadow and the light do not adhere to them in the same way that the great elements (mahābhūta) adhere to a cognition; therefore, there is a lack of commonality between the example and the thing illustrated.
Furthermore, even though they are dependent upon those [jewels and trees], and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, even if it is admitted that this dependence is indirect—
namely, that the shadow rests upon its own constituent elements,
and those elements in turn rest upon the tree.
The light also depends upon its own constituent elements;
however, those elements depend upon the gem,
because they conform to it.
Nevertheless, it is not common [to all].

For it is admitted that even when the great elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as the basis for the non-informative (*avijñapti*) have ceased, that [non-informative] does not cease. Thus, after the first moment, the non-informative belonging to the desire realm is born from past great elements.
This is because it contradicts our established tenet (*siddhānta*).
Therefore, this refutation—
which was stated in detail as "for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is like a shadow to a tree"— is not valid.
"Others, however, offer a rebuttal here," [the author] says.
The Master himself, supporting that view, states:
"The basis has undergone a change."
The meaning is that it is twofold:
some things, such as the eye and so forth, are affected because they possess resistance; others are not affected.
[The objection concerns] the mind. Because of the reversal [of the argument],
the consequence is therefore not the same.
"Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that visual consciousness and the rest would also be 'form' (rūpa), because their bases are subject to transformation (rūpaṇā).
By the statement 'it is form because of transformation,' the meaning is 'because of the transformation of its basis. Regarding this, they raise an objection."
In this way, through such preparation, the non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) that has arisen from informative [action] (*vijñapti*) may indeed possess the nature of matter (*rūpatva*).
But how can that which has arisen from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) possess the nature of matter? It too is matter because it belongs to the same class as that [informative action].
What, then, is this "belonging to that same class"?
The meaning is: "having the great elements as their material cause" (*upādāya*).
This is because those [great elements] serve as the causes for the production and so forth of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).

(I.14ab) "The sense faculties and their objects are those very same [elements]"—this refers to the three types of teachings given by the Blessed One according to the needs of those to be trained: the teachings on the aggregates (*skandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*).
And among these, those phenomena (*dharma*) which are taught within the aggregates...
These very [factors] are taught in the context of the bases (āyatana) and the elements (dhātu);
however, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomena alone are added here.
Furthermore, the entire Abhidharma is an exposition of the Sūtras.
Therefore, this was said:
"The sense faculties and their objects are those very same [elements]," and so forth.

Furthermore, this master, for the sake of brevity, without explicitly stating the characteristics of the aggregates such as sensation, demonstrates by way of conciseness the phenomena that constitute the nature of the aggregate of form within the bases and elements:
namely, the sense faculties, the objects of the sense faculties, and the consciousnesses of the sense faculties.
The qualification "those very [elements]" is intended to exclude other sense faculties and to exclude other objects.

However, in the formal arrangement of the bases (*āyatana*), there are ten bases according to their respective order: the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*), up to the body-base (*kāya-āyatana*) and the tangible-base (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*).

In the classification of the elements (*dhātu*), those same ten elements are the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), the form-element (*rūpadhātu*), and so on, up to the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) and the tangible-object element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*).
(I.14cd, 15) Thus, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and its classification as bases (*āyatana*) and elements have been explained.
However, the classification of the entire aggregate of form as bases and elements has not yet been fully stated.
Since non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) will be explained later,
how can it be said here that "it has already been stated"?
This is an explanation based on the majority.

The meaning is that the establishment of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) is stated by way of its predominance. It is like the designation "a heap of beans" even when a few pea-sized lumps are present among them.
"Experience is threefold. Experience (*anubhava*) means feeling (*anubhūti*), that is, enjoyment (*upabhoga*). Of what?
It belongs to either the mind or the person (pudgala).
And it is of three kinds:
pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
It has the nature of directly realizing the essential form of an object as being free from pleasure, pain, or that which is distinct from both.
Alternatively, it is "experience" (*anubhava*) because by means of it an object is experienced;
or it is "experience" because it experiences.

Others maintain that the experience of contact (*sparśānubhava*) is a specific mental factor (*caitasika-viśeṣa*) that operates in a state free from both the increase and decrease of body and mind, as well as from both of these combined.
The prefix *anu-* signifies a characteristic mark; thus, it means an experience characterized by contact, or rather, an experience having contact as its cause.
That is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
"Consisting of the grasping of signs" means that a sign (*nimitta*) is a specific state of an object, such as blueness and so forth.
Its apprehension is its determination.
It consists of that; it has that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "suffering and so forth," blood and other such things are included.
This is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

If perception were essentially of the nature of discernment (*pariccheda*), then because it would grasp signs (*nimitta*) in conjunction with them, all five groups of consciousness (*vijñāna-kāya*) would be conceptual (*vikalpaka*).
But they are not.
For perception associated with the five sensory consciousnesses is not sharp, whereas that associated with the mental body of consciousness is sharp; therefore, it alone is said to be conceptual.
Thus, there are six groups of perception, just as there are six groups of feeling.
Just as it was explained in detail that "feeling born of eye-contact," so too should it be stated in detail that "perception born of eye-contact.
[This applies] to those other than the four [mental aggregates].

Thus, because the discussion concerns the aggregates (*skandha*), the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) other than the four aggregates— the three already mentioned, beginning with the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) which has been indicated and will be explained— are the aggregate of formative forces (*saṃskāraskandha*).
It is stated in the Sūtra:
"What is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha)? It is the six groups of volition (cetanākāya)."
"Primarily in the act of volitional formation (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*).
Thus, [the mind] is primary in the act of volitional formation, thinking, "May I be thus and so.
This is because of the statement: "Karma is the cause of rebirths."

However, since desire (*chanda*), acquisition (*prāpti*), and so forth follow after volition (*cetanā*)—by way of conforming to its mode and its causal state—they should be understood as belonging to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) alone.
This being the case, it is said that a collection of phenomena (*dharmarāśi*) which is active in the process of conditioning is a "formation.
Others, however, say:
It has been stated that volition (*cetanā*) is primary in the formation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, volition is explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra.

However, because it subsumes all conditioned factors—both associated (*saṃprayukta*) and dissociated (*viprayukta*)—this aggregate alone is designated as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) due to its preeminence.
"Because it is a conditioned aggregate.
By means of a future designation, the five aggregates of the future are called "conditioned," on the grounds that they will perform conditioning.
"Otherwise... and so forth [is the detailed explanation].
If, according to the explanation in the Sūtra, volition alone is intended as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) and not others,

then the remaining mental factors such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth, as well as the factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) such as acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth, would not be included within the aggregates.

This is because they lack the defining characteristics of transformation (*rūpaṇa*) and so forth that characterize the aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and the rest, and thus they cannot be subsumed under them.
And it would be the same regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

Since they would not be included by taking [the aggregates] according to their literal expression in the Sūtra, they would not be included among the aggregates; consequently, they would lack the status of being the truths of suffering and its origin.
Thus, thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) would not occur.
Thorough knowledge is of suffering, and abandonment is of its origin.
