Without higher knowledge (*abhijñā*) by means of the worldly path, and without thorough knowledge by means of the supramundane path.

Alternatively, there is another sūtra which states: "Without having fully understood through the path of seeing and without having fully comprehended through the path of cultivation—thus it is said, 'without having abandoned'—I do not declare that one can bring an end to suffering without having fully comprehended and abandoned even a single dharma. (Abhidh-k-vy 38)
The meaning is that I speak of the cessation of suffering.
But surely, space and analytical cessation are not fully known by means of the supramundane path;
and yet, the end of suffering is desired [to be achieved].
This is because the statement was made with the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) of referring to the basis of affliction (*saṃkleśavastu*).
Furthermore, according to the Sautrāntika view, there is no fault because [the two] exist as mere designations (*prajñaptisat*),
for those two are not the actual bases of affliction.
Why are these two [truths] to be fully known?
In that case, the truths of cessation and the path would also not be objects of affliction, and thus they should not be fully known.
However, because of their connection with the truths of suffering and its origin, their status as objects to be fully known is established.
For it is in this way that yogis investigate:
"What is the cessation of this suffering that has a cause,
and by what means is that cessation attained?"
They also fully comprehend the truths of cessation and the path;
however, because space and analytical cessation have no connection with suffering, they do not fully comprehend those two.
Yet, during the stage of preparation, they cultivate through mundane knowledge even those two in their general form, [realizing] that all phenomena are without self.
Regarding the phrase "designated as the sphere of phenomena and the element of phenomena":
both the sphere (āyatana) and the element (dhātu) constitute the "sphere-element" (āyatanadhātu).
It is both *dharma* and an *āyatana* and a *dhātu*, thus it is the *dharmāyatana-dhātu*.
This is their designation; therefore, these are called the *dharmāyatana-dhātu*.
What are the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations? They are these, together with non-informative matter and the unconditioned.
Thus it is said.
Together with non-informative matter (avijñapti) and together with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomena such as space (ākāśa),
it is called the "sphere of phenomena" (dharmāyatana) in the teaching on the spheres (āyatana).
And in the teaching on the elements,
it is said that the dharma-element consists of seven substances:
unmanifest form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, space, cessation through deliberation, and cessation not through deliberation.
(I.16) "Consciousness is the individual representation" means that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the individual representation, because the context concerns the aggregates.
The prefix *prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
Its meaning is "with respect to each respective object.
"Apprehension" (*upalabdhi*) is the grasping of the mere thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*).
The mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, however, are specific [mental states] whose nature is the apprehension of particulars.
"The six groups of consciousness" refers to the six collections of consciousness.
Furthermore, the six consciousnesses are the mind (*manas*).
Thus,
regarding the six consciousness elements (vijñānadhātu) in their respective order: that which is eye-consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) is the eye-consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu).
In this way, up to whatever is mental consciousness— that is the mental-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu).
However, it should be understood that all these six together constitute the mind-element (manodhātu).
(I.17ab) For that consciousness which has passed away immediately after the six [consciousnesses] is indeed the mind (*manas*).
The genitive case in "of the six" (*ṣaṇṇām*) is used in the sense of selection;
the meaning is that [it occurs] among those very [six] and not elsewhere.
The inclusion of the term "immediately preceding" (anantara) is for the purpose of excluding that which is separated by another consciousness.
For whatever arises immediately after something else, without being interrupted by another consciousness, that is its support (āśraya).
But that which is separated is not its support; rather,
it is the support of another thing from which it is not separated.

For this very reason, even though it has long since passed away, the mind that entered the meditative attainment serves as the basis for the mind of emergence during a state without consciousness (*acittika-avasthā*).
This is because there is no intervention by another consciousness.
The inclusion of the term "past" is for the purpose of excluding the present.
For in that state, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is present as its support;
therefore, it is held to be past. And this very point is what is being stated.
"For the purpose of establishing the sixth basis":
the mention of "consciousness" (vijñāna) is for the purpose of excluding that which has immediately preceded [it], such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth.
For since that which is "mind" (manas) is a designation of a genus (jāti), there is no use of distributive repetition (vīpsā).
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, because the intention is to express the category of substantial entity (*dravyapadārtha*), there is the use of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*):
"Whatever consciousness has just ceased, that is the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
This is explained in detail as "just as that very [same thing]," and so forth.
Just as that very same son receives the designation "father" in relation to another,
and that very same fruit receives the designation "seed" in relation to another,
so too here, that very same visual consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu) and the others receive the designation "mind element" (manodhātu) because it serves as the basis for another.
(I.17cd) There are seventeen elements, or twelve.
Those which are the six consciousness-elements are themselves the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
Furthermore, that which is the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is the same as the six consciousness-elements (*ṣaḍvijñānadhātavaḥ*).
Thus, regarding their mutual inclusion: if the six consciousness-elements are taken, there is no need for the mind-element, and so there are seventeen elements;
if the mind-element is taken, there is no need for the six consciousness-elements, and so there are twelve elements.
"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of establishing the basis of the sixth':

the establishment of the bases for the five consciousness-elements is not accepted [as being established by those elements themselves], because their own respective bases, such as the eye and so forth, already exist."
Since there is no basis for mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is established in order to account for its basis.
By establishing the sixfold set of bases and so forth, there are eighteen elements (*dhātus*).
The sixfold set of bases consists of those beginning with the eye and ending with the mind.
The six supported [elements] are those beginning with eye-consciousness and ending with mind-consciousness;

the six objects are those beginning with form and ending with mental phenomena (*dharma*). However, according to the Yogācāra view, there is also a mind-element (*manodhātu*) that is distinct from the six consciousnesses.
The Tāmraparṇīyas also postulate that the heart-substance (*hṛdayavastu*) is the basis (*āśraya*) for the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*),
and they maintain that this exists even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
For according to them, even in the formless realm, matter (*rūpa*) is intended [to exist].
"Formless" (*ārūpya*) means "slightly" (*īṣat*), as in the word *āpiṅgala* ("slightly tawny").
"The final mind" refers to the moment of the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).
"It will not be mind" means "the mind-element (manodhātu) will not exist," for that [mind] does not exist.
The meaning is that it does not arise.
No;
for even that [mind] exists in the form of the mind (*manas*), and so forth.
This is not so.
Why?
Because even that final moment of consciousness exists as a support by way of being the mind-base (*manas*).
"Due to the deficiency of other causes" means due to the deficiency of the causes consisting of karma and afflictions that lead to rebirth.
"There is no production of a subsequent consciousness" [means that it does not arise].
The intention is that [the consciousness] is not the consciousness that links to a new existence (*punarbhava-pratisaṃdhi-vijñāna*).
This is what is investigated here.
This has been stated:
"The eighteen elements (dhātu) exist because of the establishment of sixfold sets of bases (āśraya), supported [faculties] (āśrita), and objects (ālambana).
First, the sixfold set of supported [faculties] is established.
Regarding the sixfold basis, from the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element:
is a corresponding sixfold set of supports established for this sixfold set of supported [consciousnesses]?
That is, is it the case that the support of the eye-consciousness element is the eye-element, and so on, up to the support of the mind-consciousness element being the mind-element?
He said: "Oṃ.
But when the eye is *tatsabhāga* (non-functional), what is its support?
It belongs to no one.
How then was this said: "The eye-element is the support of the visual-consciousness-element," and so forth?
The eye is precisely that which serves as a basis.
However, that which is not a basis for anything is the "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) eye;
nevertheless, because it belongs to that same class, it is indeed established as the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu).
In this manner, it should be stated for each element up to the body-element (*kāyadhātu*).
As for the mind-element (*manodhātu*), is it the support only of the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*)?
He says: no.
For that [past element] is also accepted as the support for the visual consciousness-element and the others;
thus, it will be stated:
"The support of the last one is past."
"And for the five, it is innate with them.
What, then, was this meant?
"The establishment of the sixth basis is stated in the verse: 'The eighteen elements are taught.
Since that [consciousness] is not the basis for others, there is no establishment of a sixth basis."
This [sixfold set] also serves as the basis for the sixth [consciousness-element], as far as it is possible.
There is also a sixfold set of objects:
the object of the eye-consciousness-element is the form-element, up to the object of the mind-consciousness-element, which is the phenomena-element.
This is now investigated:
Just as for the element of eye-consciousness, all forms (*rūpa*) are its objective support (*ālambana*),
so too is that the element of form (*rūpadhātu*).
In this way, up to the element of body-consciousness, as many tangibles as there are that serve as its object—
that is the element of tangibles. Likewise, for the element of mind-consciousness, as many phenomena as there are that serve as its object— [that is the element of phenomena].
"It is the *dharmadhātu*.
Regarding this, the Elder said:
"The *dharmadhātu* has the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena; the meaning is that it has the intrinsic nature of the eighteen *dhātus*."
How is the establishment of these internal and external elements (dhātu) accomplished?
For it is held that the twelve beginning with the eye are internal, while the six [beginning with visible form] are external.
For if even those were included within the *dharmadhātu*, confusion would result.
The Elder said:
"Their status as internal or external is merely figurative (*pāryāyika*)."
The eye and the other [faculties] are internal because they are the supports of the consciousnesses;
however, they are external because they are objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this.
Because it contradicts the Sūtra.
For it is stated thus in the Sūtra:
"O Bhikṣu, the dharmas are an external sense-field (āyatana), not included among the eleven sense-fields, invisible, and non-obstructive."
Therefore, the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) must be accepted as consisting of seven substances,

because its nature consists of non-informative matter (avijñapti), the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, as well as space, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha), and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha). In that case, however, the explanation of the objective support (ālambana) for the mental consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu) remains incomplete.
Nor is it intended that the explanation of the objects (*ālambana*) of visual consciousness and the others is incomplete.
This is indeed so;

however, because the six [faculties] beginning with the eye are explained as the bases (*āśraya*), while visual consciousness and the others are explained as the supported (*āśrita*), and because the five [objects] beginning with visible form are explained as the objects of the five groups of consciousness, [the explanation is complete].
41) They explain that even though these are objects of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they are not included within the *dharmadhātu*.
In brief, however, it should be understood that this constitutes the inclusion of everything. (I.18)
All things are also subsumed by means of the bases (*āyatana*) and so forth,
but not in brief.
What then?
In detail,
this has been extracted from the threefold teaching and stated in brief:

by means of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the aggregate of form is subsumed, as are the ten bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) whose intrinsic nature consists of the sense faculties and their objects.
Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is a portion of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent element (*dhātu*).
The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is included within the mind-sphere (*manāyatana*).
Furthermore, that very mind-sphere and the seven mental constituent elements (*cittadhātu*) are subsumed therein.

By means of the *dharmadhātu*, the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) are subsumed, as are the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Here, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is subsumed twice;
for example, [it is included both] as the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) and so forth.
The eye faculty is dissociated from the nature of the aggregates such as feeling, the sense bases beginning with the ear, the elements, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
Therefore, this has been said:
the eye faculty is subsumed by the aggregate of form, by the sense base and element of the eye, and by the truths of suffering and origin, because it has those as its intrinsic nature.
"It is not by other aggregates (skandha) and so forth, because it is devoid of their nature.
Here, the large is subsumed within the small,
but the small is not subsumed within the large.
How so?
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is great because it comprises all forms;
the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is small because it is merely a portion of the aggregate of form.
The eye faculty is subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
but the aggregate of form is not subsumed within the eye faculty,
because the aggregate of form exists apart from the eye faculty.
It is just as, for example, the footprint of a bird is subsumed within the footprint of an elephant, but the footprint of an elephant is not subsumed within the footprint of a bird;
it is just like that.
However, that which is equal is mutually included by what is equal;
for example, the eye-faculty is included by the eye-base, and the eye-base is also included by the eye-faculty. This should be understood as the method of the Abhidharma.
"Just as [one wins over] assemblies by means of the articles of attraction. There are four articles of attraction:
generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and consistency of purpose.
The four assemblies are the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. By these, there is a gathering of them;
however, that [gathering] is occasional.
Occasionally, existence is occasional;
sometimes they are given gifts and pleasant words,
yet this is not true integration (saṃgraha).
It has been stated that the conventional [classification] is based on linguistic convention and practical usage,
whereas the classification according to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-saṃgraha*) is ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
(I.19ab) There is a single element (*dhātu*) because of the commonality of genus, object, and consciousness.
Even though the eyes and so forth are twofold, this is stated by implication:
the establishment of the distinction of the elements (dhātu) occurs according to possibility based on differences such as genus (jāti) and so forth.
But it is not due to a difference in their bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
In that regard, there is a mutual difference among the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and the others in terms of genus (*jāti*), object-sphere (*gocara*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*);
whereas for the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) and the others, there is a difference in terms of genus and consciousness.
There is a distinction among the elements of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) regarding their origin and objective sphere (gocara).
For even for mental consciousness (manovijñāna), the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is its unique objective sphere.
The same should be applied to the auditory and olfactory [consciousnesses] as well.
There is a commonality of genus (*jātisāmānya*) for both, because they both have the nature of the auditory faculty (*śrotra*).
There is a commonality of object (*gocarasāmānya*) for both, because they both have sound as their objective domain (*viṣaya*).
There is a commonality of consciousness (*vijñānasāmānya*) for both, because they both serve as the basis for a single auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*).
Therefore, the auditory element (*śrotradhātu*) is indeed one only.
The same should be applied to the olfactory organ as well.
[Objection: In that case, since there would be no other function, it would follow that the two do not arise; therefore, he says:
"But for the sake of beauty, there is the arising of pairs.

Because there would be great deformity from the occurrence of only one eye-socket and ear-base, or only one nostril, there arises one eye-socket and ear-base, and one nostril. Thus, because of the occurrence of these, there is no great deformity.
There would be deformity.
But is it not the case that for camels, cats, owls, and the like, there is no beauty of the physical basis (āśraya-śobhā) even though the pair of eyes and so forth arise?
[Response: With respect to other species, they do not possess the beauty of the physical basis.
However, with respect to its own kind, for one who possesses both eyes and so forth,
there is the beauty of the basis within that specific kind;
for one who does not possess them, there is not.
Regarding the claim that this [explanation] is inconsistent:
this is not to be criticized.
However, the Master Saṃghabhadra has explained the meaning of this sūtra.
"For the sake of beauty" means for the sake of sovereignty;
for it is taught that one who is endowed with sovereignty shines in the world.
And these are the physical bases of those sense-faculties.
For them, there would be mastery over pure seeing, hearing, smelling, and so forth.
For indeed, just as pure seeing occurs through two eyes, it does not occur in the same way through one;
the same applies to the other [senses] as well.
In this way, their status as faculties (indriyatva) would be lost. It is for that reason that this was stated;
the meaning is: "for the sake of clear perception."
In this case as well, it can be argued as follows:
let a single, extensive [entity], which serves as the basis for clear perception, be produced by karma;
what is the use of a division of bases?
In the *Vibhāṣā*, however, these two positions are recorded:
one holds that the arising of the two [eyes] is for the sake of beauty, while the other holds that it is for the sake of manifestation. Enough of this digression.
But is it not the case that the arising of the two sense organs occurs through the power of karma?
Why then is something else stated, namely, "for the sake of beauty and for the sake of manifestation"?
It is precisely through the power of karma that the arising of the two sense organs is said to occur here.
How so?
In this way, based on the perception of distinct parts, sentient beings develop a conceit regarding beauty that has been practiced since beginningless time.

Therefore, through karma preceded by a desire for that [beauty] and preceded by a desire for clear perception, those two sense organs are produced for the sake of beauty and for the sake of manifestation.
(I.20ab) "The aggregates, bases, and elements have the meanings of heap, door of arrival,
and lineage. Respectively, their meanings are heap, door of arrival, and lineage.
These—namely the words *skandha*, *āyatana*, and *dhātu*—have the meanings of "heap," "gate of arrival," and "lineage" (*gotra*), respectively.
What are they? They are the terms *skandha*, *āyatana*, and *dhātu*.
Alternatively, what are the meanings of the words "heap" (rāśi), "gate of arrival" (āyadvāra), and "lineage" (gotra)? They are the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).
Because it is stated in the Sūtra:
"The meaning of 'aggregate' (skandha) is the meaning of 'heap' (rāśi).
That is, whatever is the meaning of a heap.
That is the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha).
He demonstrates this by means of a sutra:
"Whatever form there is—past, future, or present," and so forth.
"Aikadhyam" means "in one way," that is, as a single unit. "Anityatāniruddham" means "ceased through impermanence."
The meaning is that it has ceased by way of impermanence, which is a characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
The mention of "impermanence" is for the purpose of excluding other types of cessation.
For cessation is indeed fivefold.

There are five types of cessation: cessation by characteristic (*lakṣaṇanirodha*), cessation through meditative attainment (*samāpattinirodha*), cessation at birth (*upapattinirodha*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).

If one were to say that past matter is simply "ceased" without qualification, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that this term would also apply to cessation through meditative attainment and the others, since no distinction has been made.
Furthermore, they do not accept that those [cessations] have past objects as their referent.
For the cessation of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-nirodha*) pertains only to future mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*),
and the cessation at birth (*upapatti-nirodha*) pertains to these very same [factors].
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) belongs only to those things that are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) also belongs only to future things that are subject to non-arising.
Therefore, this mention of impermanence (*anityatā*) is for the purpose of including cessation as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The future is that which has not yet arisen;
it has not reached the state of the present.
The present is that which has arisen but not yet ceased.
The mention of "arisen" is for the purpose of distinguishing [it] from the future;
the mention of "not ceased" is for the purpose of distinguishing [it] from the past.
Although the future is not ceased, it is not arisen.
Even though the past has arisen, it is not [yet] ceased.
"Internal" means belonging to one's own continuum;
that is, the eye and so forth, as well as visible form and so forth.
"External and other" means that very same thing belonging to another continuum and not reckoned as a sentient being.
Or, "by way of the sense bases."
The internal [bases] consist of the five beginning with the eye, which fall within one's own or another's continuum,
because of the statement that "there are twelve internal [bases]."
The external is other than form and so forth; it consists of the five objects belonging to the continua of oneself and others, that which is reckoned as non-sentient, and unmanifest form (avijñapti).
This is because they have the nature of external bases (bāhyāyatana).
The gross is with resistance;
its nature consists of an accumulation of atoms.
The subtle is without resistance.
Non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*).
Or it is relative;
that is, by comparison, it may be either gross or subtle.
For example, in relation to a louse, a flea is gross;
in relation to a flea, a louse is subtle.
This being so, that which is resistant is indeed both gross and subtle.
But that which is non-resistant is indeed subtle because it is not accumulated.
[The objection that] "it is unestablished because of its relativity" means that the very same subtle louse becomes gross in comparison to a mote of dust in a sunbeam.
And that very same thing is coarse in relation to a louse, yet subtle; thus, coarseness and subtlety are not fixed, like "this shore" and "the other shore.
For how indeed could the coarse become subtle, and the subtle become coarse?
No; because of the difference in dependence (*apekṣābheda*). "Difference in dependence" means a distinction based on what is depended upon.
Therefore, [the reason] is not unestablished.
That which is coarse in relation to something can never be subtle in relation to that same thing;
the meaning is that it can never be the very same thing that serves as the point of reference.
"Like father and son.
For example: Evadatta’s son is Yajñadatta;
Yajñadatta’s son is Viṣṇumitra.
That Yajñadatta is a father in relation to Viṣṇumitra,
and a son in relation to Evadatta;
yet, despite this relativity, his status as both father and son is not thereby invalidated.
Because of the difference in perspective.
For that same Yajñadatta is not a son in relation to Viṣṇumitra,
nor is he a father in relation to that same Devadatta.
In the same way,
that which is inferior is afflicted, because it is abandoned by the virtuous;
that which is sublime is unafflicted, because it is not defiled by the afflictions.
The distant is the past and the future, because it has departed from the continuum and because it has not yet been reached.
The near is the present, because it is contiguous with the continuum.
This applies likewise up to consciousness.

Whatever feeling there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; far or near—all that, having been gathered together as one and condensed, receives the designation "the aggregate of feeling" (*vedanā-skandha*).
The same should be stated for the [other aggregates] up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Up to the point where everything, when condensed into a single whole, comes to be designated as the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
The pastness and so forth of these [aggregates], such as feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest, are just like that of form (*rūpa*).
However, this is the distinction regarding feeling and the others:
The fourfold group beginning with sensation, which relies upon the five sense faculties, is gross.
Because it is formless, there is no perceived grossness [in the case of the mental faculty].
The mental [sensation] is subtle, because its basis (the mind) is also formless.
"Or by way of the stages":
the coarse and the subtle, such as feeling and so forth.
Coarse feeling is that which belongs to the desire realm.
The subtle belongs to the level of the first dhyāna;
the gross belongs to the level of the first dhyāna;
the subtle belongs to the level of the second dhyāna.

In this way, up to the coarse [perception] belonging to the level of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) and the subtle [perception] belonging to the level of the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
Just as with feeling (vedanā), so it is with perception.
In this same way, it should be stated up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"Venerable sir" (*bhadanta*) refers to the Elder (*sthavira*),
or perhaps to a certain Sautrāntika who bears that name.
But Bhagavadviśeṣa says:
"This [is so] because of the Elder’s nature.
To this, we reply:
If Harmatrāta is one who asserts the existence of the past and the future, then "he" refers neither to a Sautrāntika nor to an Ārṣṭāntika; such is the meaning.
For he will state this later.

The Venerable Dharmatrāta maintains that there is a change of state (*bhāvānyathātva*). He is reported to have said: "When a dharma proceeds through the time-periods (*adhvan*), there is a change of its state, but not a change of its substance (*dravya*)."
This Venerable Master (Bhadanta), who adheres to the Sautrāntika view, is recorded in the *Vibhāṣā* by such phrases as "the Bhadanta says," and so forth.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta is likewise recorded in the *Vibhāṣā* under his own name.
"Bhadanta Harivarman said," and so forth.
By this it is indicated that this Sautrāntika is some other elder monk distinct from Bhadanta Harivarman.
"Grasped by the five faculties" refers to the pentad beginning with form (rūpa).
The other five, beginning with the eye, are subtle;
as are non-informative matter (avijñapti).
[The term] "agreeable" refers to these.
It is called *manaāpa* because one finds pleasure (*āpnoti*) in it; the meaning is "pleasing" (*manojña*).
Furthermore, a re-composition (*punar-sandhi*) should be observed here.

Because of the rule "that which was previously unestablished [is not considered as such]," and because the prefix *ñ-* is included in the sense of "slight," it is "somewhat established"; thus, there is a single long vowel by the rule of homogeneous lengthening (*ekasavarṇadīrghatva*).
"Far away, in a place beyond sight" refers to the location of the support and the location of the basis of the support. That which can be seen is "visible."
That which has a visible location is "visible-location" (dṛśyadeśa), meaning the location that serves as the support for the visible,
or the location that serves as the support for the support of the visible—
just as, for example, a jujube fruit in a bowl.
Or, it is near if it is within the range of the eye and so forth;
conversely, that which is in an invisible location is distant.
It was not stated that "invisible" means "far away.
For even something nearby may not be seen due to its extreme subtlety,
yet it is not considered to be far away.
Because it is located in a visible place.
But for what purpose is it explained in this way by the Bhadanta?
Because the past and so forth have already been expressed by their own respective terms.
Otherwise, there would be the fault of redundancy.
However, their "remoteness" or "proximity" is due to the nature of their bases (*āśraya*).
Since those [factors] such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth are immaterial (*amūrta*), they do not occupy a spatial location; therefore, it should be stated as follows.
Feeling and the other aggregates have their basis invisible in the distance; they have their basis visible nearby. Their coarseness and subtlety are as previously described.
The gross [basis] is that which relies on the five sense-faculties;
the subtle is the mental [basis].
They are called *āyatanas* because they extend (*tanvanti*) the arrival (*āya*), that is, the arising, of the mind and mental factors.
The establishment of all [internal and external] bases (*āyatana*) as such follows from the principle that "consciousness arises in dependence upon a dyad.
This refers to [the dyad existing] either in a single support (*āśraya*) or within a continuum (*saṃtāna*). Here, "support" refers to the body, which is characterized by a collection [of parts].
Or, in the continuum characterized by the flow of mind and so forth, of its own genus. What? [Is it the cause?]

The term "sources" (*ākara*) is the subject under discussion. Because they are homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), the previously arisen eye is the homogeneous cause of the subsequent one; thus, the source is the element (*dhātu*).
For since gold and so forth arise from them, they are the sources (ākara) of those [minerals].
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), however, would not be an element (dhātu).
For the unconditioned is not the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) of another unconditioned thing or of anything else.
In that case, what about the mind and mental factors? What [is their cause]?
"Sources" (*ākara*) is the subject under discussion.

Since consciousness arises in dependence upon a dyad, all elements (*dhātu*) are the conditions for consciousness together with its associated mental factors; they are necessarily the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and thus they are "sources.
This is like the case of a "heap" (*rāśi*) or a "person" (*pudgala*).
The aggregates are conventionally real because they are denotable by the word "heap," like a heap of grain.
Or it is like the person (*pudgala*).

For that person exists as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*), because its intrinsic nature is not apprehended independently of the causes for the designation of form and so forth, just like a heap of grain.
[It is called "person"] in the sense of bearing the burden of activity.
The task itself is the burden;
thus, "the burden of the task. That by which something is carried is "carrying" (*udvahana*).
The bearing of the burden of activity is "kāryabhārodvahaṇa. That part of the body is called a "skandha" (shoulder) in the world.
By this [term] as well, the burden of activity is borne, because of such statements as "the six sense-bases have name-and-form as their condition."
Therefore, the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) is a metaphorical expression, like [the word] "aggregate" applied to a heap.
Alternatively, its meaning is "cutting off" or "limiting.
This is the sense.
"The cutting off of form, up to the cutting off of consciousness"—
this [interpretation] is contrary to the sūtra.
For both of these [terms] have the sense of "cutting off" in the sense of bearing the burden of the task.
"Deviant from the Sūtra" means that which goes beyond the Sūtra.
He explains this in detail with the words "for the Sūtra... and so forth.
"Each individually," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
To the question "How so?", he says:
all this, consisting of the past and so forth, taken one by one—that is, each individual instance—is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Thus, by means of the collection (*samudāya*), the substance that constitutes the collection (*samudāyin*) is expressed.
For the intended meaning is that the "heap" refers to those past and other forms.
It is stated exactly thus in the Sūtra:
"What is the earth element?"
"Head-hairs, body-hairs," and so forth.
Each individual substance, such as a head-hair and so on, is understood to be the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*).
Furthermore, this response can also be stated regarding the positions that [the term "earth"] signifies the sense of bearing a functional burden or the sense of delimiting a portion.
"It is not possible in this way," and so forth,
because of the redundant expression "having condensed them into a single unit. It cannot be understood that each individual [aggregate] is the form aggregate (*rūpaskandha*).
For if this were the intended meaning,
he would have simply said, "All that is the aggregate of form," rather than using the expression, "having condensed them together into a single sense."
Therefore, the teacher’s established position is that the aggregates (*skandha*) exist only as designations (*prajñaptisat*), just like a heap (*rāśi*).

However, it should be understood that when the aggregates are taught, they are presented as having a substantial nature (*dravyasadrūpa*) because they consist of a collection of those [substantial factors].
"The material ones as well," and so forth.
The inclusion of the term "possessing form" (*rūpin*) is for the purpose of distinguishing it from that which is formless.
For the mind-base (*manāyatana*), being formless, maintains the status of a cause even when not aggregated.

Furthermore, the bases of the eye and so forth, though possessing form, function as the gateways for the arising of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) only when they are aggregated, not when they are not aggregated.
Because they possess the characteristic of being a collection, like the aggregates (*skandha*), they would exist as mere designations (*prajñaptisat*).
[This is because] the five groups of consciousness have accumulated bases and objects. [To this, we reply:
No.
"Because each one is the cause of all [the factors] taken together"—
this is not so.
Why?
Because each one individually is a cause when they are complete and assembled;
for these many atoms, such as those of the eye and so forth, possess the status of being causes only when they depend upon one another one by one,
but not when they are uncombined.
For example, when pulling a piece of wood, many pullers individually lack the capacity,

but when they are gathered together and depend upon one another, they possess the capacity. Or, for instance, hairs situated separately are not capable of producing a visual consciousness in one suffering from ophthalmia (taimirika).
But when combined, even though they are not conjoined, they are capable.
Similarly, the atoms of the sense organs such as the eye and the atoms of the objects such as visible form are each individually incapable of producing visual consciousness and so forth;
however, when combined, they are capable.
For the capacity of entities must be understood as being of such a nature;
or rather, it is because they act as cooperative conditions for the object.

If, however, the state of being a door of entry belonged to many [atoms] collectively, then there would be a "basis" (āyatana) consisting of an aggregate, not a basis consisting of a substantial entity (dravya).
If the state of being a gateway for the sense-faculties and their objects were due to their atoms being aggregated, then that would constitute a collective base (*samudāyāyatana*);
it would not be a separate base.
Yet, a separate base is accepted, as evidenced by the Sūtra stating, "There are twelve bases."
And here the following proof applies:

those which are auxiliary causes are not, together with them, atoms that constitute the substance of the aggregate of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) within the nature of a collective base (*samudāyātmaka-āyatana*).
Because it is the cause of visual consciousness,
like the atoms of the composite substance of the sense-base of the eye and the sense-base of form.
Just as the atoms of the composite substance of the sense-base of the eye [are the cause of visual consciousness].
In this manner, the same should be applied up to the atoms that constitute the collection of the body-base (*kāyāyatana*).
However, it is stated in the *Vibhāṣā*:
"By this [statement] as well, he explains that the aggregates (*skandha*) exist only as designations (*prajñaptisat*)."
But this is the distinction:
although those [factors] do not exist as substantial entities, they are nevertheless indicated there by way of metaphorical designation.
The word "but" (tu) serves to express this distinction.
"It depends upon the designation 'aggregate' (skandha-prajñapti)" means that it depends upon the designation "aggregate";
it means that it depends upon the designation "heap" (rāśi).
"A single atom is [the unit] of one element" means it is a portion of any one of the ten material elements, such as the eye and so forth;
likewise, it is a portion of any one of these bases (āyatana) and of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
Why is that? For a term that functions with respect to a whole (*pradeśin*) when a designation (*prajñapti*) is required is not established as referring to a part (*pradeśa*).
Or, if it does not require such a designation...
What?
It refers to the designation of the aggregates (*skandhaprajñapti*).
He said:
"A single atom is one element," and so forth.
Each one of those bases (āyatana) and elements that has been mentioned as being any one of them is also the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
For it is the case that even in a part, there is a figurative designation (upacāra) as if it were the whole.

Even in the case of a single part, such as an atom, there is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) based on [the whole], just as in the case of a particular portion of the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) or the element of form (*rūpadhātu*), or like the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). In this context, the suffix *-vat* is used in the sense of "that which belongs to that," just as when one part of a cloth is burned, it is said, "the cloth is burned."
Just as the word "cloth," though applied to a whole,
is used metaphorically for a part— a single portion of the cloth—
likewise the word "aggregate" (*skandha*), though applied to a collection of past and other forms, is used in that same way.
It is applied even to a single atom by way of metaphorical designation.
Thus, it is only the aggregates (*skandha*) that exist as designations, not the sense bases (*āyatana*) or elements (*dhātu*),
because [the latter] are established as "aggregates" in relation to form and so forth.
But when the compound is analyzed as "the aggregates are indeed forms" (rūpāṇy eva skandhāḥ), then the intended meaning is that the aggregates exist as substantial entities (dravyasat).
This is what is investigated here.

What is the reason here that, although the atoms of the sense faculties and the atoms of the objects are equally mutually dependent for the arising of consciousness, these two are not established as having the status of a single *āyatana*— as is the case with the atoms of the sense faculties alone? Because all the atoms of the eye-faculty and so forth serve as common causes for the arising of their respective consciousnesses.
But the atoms of the object are not like that.
For instance, the atoms of the visual faculty are causes for the arising of a consciousness of a blue object, and they are also causes for the arising of a consciousness of yellow and so forth.
However, atoms of the blue object-sphere are causes only for the arising of their own cognition, not for the arising of cognitions of yellow and so forth;
therefore, because the atoms of the visual faculty do not function in the same manner as the atoms of their object-sphere.
Because they exist in separate locations,
it is not logical to establish the atoms of the eye and visible form as being a single sense-base (*ekāyatana*).
In the same way, it should be stated that up to the atoms of the body-faculty and the tangible, it is not logical to establish them as a single sense-base.
(I.20cd) "Because of the threefold nature of delusion, faculties, and inclinations" means because of the threefold nature of confusion, wisdom, and resolve.
"Three kinds" means "threefold.
Some say that in the expression *traidham*, the suffix *aṇ* is used in its own sense (*svarthe*) to mean "in three ways.
Others say that *traidham* is the state of being threefold, where the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
There is a threefold division of delusion (*moha*), faculties (*indriya*), and inclinations (*ruci*).
"Therefore" means:
by way of grasping at a self as a composite whole (*piṇḍātma-grahaṇa*).
Some, having grasped mental factors as a single aggregate, grasp them as a self,
because the grasping of a self proceeds only when there is grasping of an aggregate.
For their sake, the teaching on the aggregates is given.

For in that [classification], mental factors (*caitta*) are taught as threefold by way of the distinctions of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*). This prevents the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) which thinks, "This is a single lump; there are no distinct mental factors here. Alternatively, this personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is of the nature of a lump.
Some who are deluded think that this self is the feeler, the perceiver, and the volitional agent. For them, there is the teaching on the aggregates (*skandha*).

By means of this, the grasping at a self is countered through the realization that "this mass which has the nature of a self does not exist; rather, it is these mental factors here—feeling, perception, and formations—that arise."
Some [hold] that it is in form alone; this refers to those who are deluded by grasping at a composite self. For them, there is the teaching on the sense bases (*āyatana*).

For in that [classification], form is divided in many ways according to the distinctions of the eye and so forth, whereas mental factors (*caitta*) are grouped together as a single *dharmāyatana*, and the mind (*citta*) as the *manāyatana*.
Thus, some say: "In the case of form and mind..."
It has already been established that they are deluded by grasping at the body as a self.
For them, there is the teaching on the elements (*dhātu*).
In that teaching, form (*rūpa*) is analyzed in many ways according to its divisions, such as the eye and so forth.
The mind is [taught] through the distinction of the elements of eye-consciousness and so forth;
however, mental factors are not, because they are taught solely as the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
By that [teaching], the delusion regarding the grasping of a solid mass of form and mind is countered.
"The faculties as well," and so forth.

There are three types of persons because of having sharp, medium, or dull faculties. Alternatively, there are three types of persons: one who understands through a condensed statement, one who understands through detailed exposition, and one for whom the words are the limit.
In that regard, the teaching on the aggregates (*skandha*) is for those of sharp faculties.
For, because they possess sharp faculties, they are able to understand the division of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) precisely through the division of the aggregates.
As it has been said: "O monk, that which is not you, that phenomenon (*dharma*) is to be abandoned."
"I have understood, Blessed One," he said.
"In what way do you understand the meaning of what was spoken in brief by this monk?
'Form, Venerable Sir, am not I.'"
"That doctrine of mine is to be abandoned," and so forth.
The teaching on the bases (*āyatana*) is for those of middling faculties.

For, because they possess middling faculties, they are able to comprehend the differentiation of the elements (*dhātu*) through a moderate, rather than an overly extensive, classification of the bases.
But it is not by means of a concise classification of the aggregates.
The teaching on the elements is for those of dull faculties;
for, due to their dull faculties, they are unable to comprehend the unanalyzed [teaching] through the power of their own intelligence.
Interest (*ruci*) is also threefold.
The threefold nature of interest arises from the connection with previous practice.
Alternatively, for those whose temperament is dominated by tranquility (*śamatha*), interest is concise.
For those whose practice consists of both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), the inclination is moderate; for those whose practice consists of insight, the inclination is extensive.
(I.21) What, then, is the reason? [This is] the detailed explanation.
But was it not stated that the teaching on the aggregates is for those who are deluded regarding mental factors because they grasp at the self as a composite whole?
True, this was stated; however, it was said that their mental factors have been distinguished [from the aggregates].

But why are feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) alone established as separate aggregates from within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), and not others? What is the reason for this?
It is because of "clinging to sensual desires," and so forth.
Attachment to sensual pleasures and to [wrong] views—
of these two, which are the roots of dispute and consist of clinging— feeling and perception are, respectively, the primary causes.
By the use of the term "primary," it is implied by the sense that ignorance and the other [factors] are non-primary causes.
For householders cling to sensual pleasures by virtue of relishing feeling,
and they cling to views by virtue of perverted perception.
What [do they cling to]?
"They cling" is the governing term.

Those who perceive non-dharma as dharma, dharma as non-dharma, and what is selfless and so forth as having a self, cling to such views as the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Who are they?
Generally, those who have gone forth [into homelessness].
"For one who is greedy for feeling," and so forth;
being attached to feeling and perverted by the four perversions, one undergoes a succession of births in saṃsāra due to the cause of sequential progression.
Four reasons for the sequence of the aggregates will be explained: according to their coarseness, their nature as defilement, their function as a vessel and so forth, and according to their realms.
For form is the most coarse of all because it possesses resistance;
among the formless [aggregates], feeling is the coarsest by virtue of its manifest activity.
For thus do they designate it.
"There is a sensation in my hand; there is a sensation in my foot.
Perception is more gross than consciousness, while formations are more gross than perception; therefore, that which is more gross was mentioned first. This is the first reason.
Alternatively, in this beginningless saṃsāra, men and women are mutually enamored of each other’s forms;
this is due to their craving for the taste of sensation (*vedanā*). That craving arises from a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).
The second [explanation] is that the order follows the process of defilement (*saṃkleśa*): first there is perversion (*viparyāsa*), then the afflictions (*kleśa*), and the mind is defiled by them.

Or else, it is according to the analogy of the vessel and so forth: the aggregates beginning with form (*rūpa*) are like the vessel, the food, the seasoning, the cook, and the eater; this is the third [explanation].
Or, from the perspective of the elements (*dhātu*): the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is characterized by desire;
the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are characterized by feeling (*vedanā*);
and the three formless realms (*ārūpya*) are characterized by perception (*saṃjñā*).
The peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is manifested by formations (*saṃskāra*) alone.

These are the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), and consciousness is established within them; this sequence of the aggregates (*skandha*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the field and the seed—this is the fourth reason.
And for this very reason of the sequence, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are made into separate aggregates.
Because these two [elements] are more gross, are the causes for the sequence of afflictions, serve as food and condiment, and are characterized by those two elements (I.22ab),
they cannot yet be included within these [other elements], because their meaning is incompatible— that is,
because the meanings of "being subject to transformation" (*rūpaṇā*) and so forth are incompatible and impossible [in their case].
Whether it be the intrinsic nature of form up to the intrinsic nature of consciousness, it is impossible to include these within these very five aggregates,
because they do not possess that intrinsic nature;
nor can a sixth aggregate be spoken of.
Why?
Because of the impossibility of an object.
The meaning is: because of the connection with objects such as those of the past and so forth.
But surely, since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are numerous, it would be appropriate to have another "unconditioned aggregate" (*asaṃskṛtaskandha*);
what is the point of [categorizing them] by way of the past and so forth?
This is incorrect, because since unconditioned phenomena lack spatial proximity, they cannot be collected together.
"For the purpose of making known the basis of affliction," and so forth.
It is not a basis of affliction because it is untainted (*anāsrava*);
nor is it a basis of purification because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The intended meaning is that the cause of purification is indeed the basis of purification.

Alternatively, when the "aggregate of form" is mentioned, up to the "aggregate of consciousness" being mentioned, one understands that the aggregate of form, up to the aggregate of consciousness, constitutes both the basis of affliction and the basis of purification.
However, when the "unconditioned aggregate" is mentioned, one does not understand a basis for either affliction or purification; therefore, the term "unconditioned aggregate" is not possible.

For them, this same consequence would apply even to the elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana). For those who speak thus, just as the cessation of a jar is not the jar, so too the cessation of an element is not the element.
If it were said that "the cessation of the sense-bases is not a sense-base," then the unconditioned would not be established as either the dharma-element or the dharma-sense-base.
Furthermore, since the inclusion of all phenomena within the elements and sense-bases is intended, this [position] is incorrect.
(I.22cd) Thus, another classification of the aggregates has been explained.

Furthermore, by the word "again" (*punaḥ*), he shows that this term is introduced with reference to another mode of presentation. [The phrase] "the coarsest of all" (*sarvaudārikam*) [is explained as follows].
Form is coarser than all [the aggregates] beginning with feeling,
because it possesses visibility, resistance, and so forth,
whereas feeling and the others are formless.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).

Feeling (*vedanā*) is coarse because its activity is coarse and its manifestation is coarse; this means [it is compared] with the two, namely formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Perception is gross because it is easily known through the discernment of signs.
Formations are grosser than consciousness because they are characterized by volitional construction, such as the thought, "May I be happy, may I not be suffering."
Consciousness, however, is the most subtle of all, because its characteristic is mere apprehension.
Furthermore, it is logical to present the meaning to those to be trained according to its coarseness; thus is the sequence of the aggregates.
And these [aggregates] arise from greed for the relish of feeling.
And those men and women, through attachment to the relish of sensation (*vedanā*), become mutually enamored of each other's forms.
"Craving for that" means craving for sensation.
"Due to the perversion of perception" means due to the grasping of signs such as permanence and so forth.
For even pleasant feeling is suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned change (*saṃskāra-vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
"The vessel and the food," and so forth.
Form is like a vessel because it is the basis for feeling;
feeling is like food because it is that which is tasted.

Perception (*saṃjñā*) is like a sign (*vyañjana*), because it signifies feeling (*vedanā*) by grasping its characteristic marks; or, perception is like a sign because feeling becomes pleasant through the power of perception.
Volition (*cetanā*) is like a cook, because it prepares and brings about the feeling of maturation (*vipākavedanā*).

"Consciousness is the experiencer because it favors that [body]"— or else, the sequence is according to the analogy of the vessel and so forth; or, as for the detailed explanation, it is according to the realms (*dhātu*).
The strands of sensual pleasure themselves are forms;
by them the desire realm is manifested and intensified.
The meditative absorptions are manifested by feeling.
The first dhyāna is characterized by the faculty of mental joy and the faculty of pleasure;
the second is characterized by the faculty of mental joy;
the third is characterized by the faculty of pleasure.
The fourth dhyāna is characterized by the complete purification of the faculty of equanimity.
The three formless attainments are characterized by perception:
the sphere of infinite space is characterized by the perception of space.
The sphere of infinite consciousness is characterized by the perception of consciousness; the sphere of nothingness is characterized by the perception of nothingness;
the peak of existence is characterized by mere formations alone.
For in that [state], volition projects a lifespan of eighty thousand eons.
As to why consciousness (*vijñāna*) is mentioned last of all, he says: "These are the stations of consciousness," and so forth.
There are four stations of consciousness.
The station of consciousness associated with form is the desire realm;
that associated with feeling is the four meditative absorptions;
and that associated with perception is the three formless realms.
Those [other stations] involve the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and extend up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is established within those four stations of consciousness because it is dependent upon them, is mentioned last of all.
Thus, the sequence of the aggregates (*skandha*) has been explained for the purpose of demonstrating the field and the seed.
For this very reason, there are five aggregates, neither fewer nor more.
The meaning is that, according to reasons such as their relative grossness and so forth, they are neither fewer nor more.
(I.23) They are mentioned first because they have present objects.
Those [cognitions] whose objects are present have clear objects;
and since those with clear objects are easy to understand, they were explained first.
The [senses] have present objects and function subsequently; thus they were explained first.
The mind, however, has unrestricted objects; because its objects are manifold, it is difficult to understand, and it generally functions later.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Some have the present as their object, some have [objects] up to the three times and the non-time.
By the word "up to," it is meant that some have the past as their object, some have the future as their object, and some have the three times as their object.

Just as [it is said] that "all phenomena are without self," the meaning is that there is something whose object is not of the three time periods— that is, its object is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
In this way, the mind has an indefinite object.
And thus it was stated later that this [point] is not easily understood;
for in the world, what is easy to understand is typically taught first.
From the sense-object of derived matter (bhautika-artha), there are four [types].
Thus, the tetrad beginning with the eye has as its objects the derived forms (upādāyarūpa) such as visible form;
therefore,
it was mentioned prior to that [body].
The object of the body [faculty], however, is indefinite:
sometimes it is the primary elements (*bhūta*), sometimes it is derived matter (*bhautika*), if there is a perception of distinctness;
sometimes it is both, if there is no perception of distinctness.
Furthermore, the remainder was stated first according to its application by way of functioning at a distance or more rapidly.
The "remainder" refers to the eye and so forth.

That [remainder] is distinguished from the other [faculties] by way of functioning at a distance or more rapidly—that is, by functioning at a distance, functioning at a greater distance, or functioning more rapidly—and thus two [faculties] are [distinguished] from two.
The meaning is that one [organ] is derived from one [element], and again one [organ] is derived from one [element]; this is how it should be applied.
To explain how, he says:
for the eye and the ear have distant objects; therefore, they were mentioned first among the two, [namely] the nose and the tongue.
Between those two, the eye and the ear, the eye functions at a greater distance;
for even when one sees a river from afar, one does not hear its sound. Therefore, it follows that the eye was mentioned first.
The eye was mentioned before the ear because those two function more rapidly.
Between those two— the nose and the tongue— the nose was mentioned before the tongue.
He asks, "How so? and replies:
"Because one perceives the odor of the food even before it has reached the tongue.
This is what is investigated here.
The nose and the tongue grasp objects through direct contact.
How so?
The odor located in the food is grasped by that nose.
But that which resides in what is inedible is not perceived.
However, in the case of wind, another odor arises, or an odor that has come along with a subtle particle of something edible is perceived;
for no odor is perceived by one who is not breathing.
In that case, one should not say:
"Because the odor of the food is perceived by the tongue even though it has not reached it," referring to that food which exists in the form of a mass.
There is no fault here because [the author] intended to say that [the odor] does not reach the tongue.
For the nose functions so rapidly that it smells an odor even when it has come along with a portion of the food;
the tongue, however, does not taste a flavor that has come along with a portion of the food.
However, it should be understood that because one tastes the flavor only as it accompanies the food lump (*piṇḍabhojya*), its operation is not more rapid.
(I.24) Explaining how this serves as a qualification, he says:
"so that it may be understood that [the faculties] are each [distinct]," and so forth.

It is so that it may be understood that each one of these ten possesses the status of an *āyatana*— the five beginning with the eye by virtue of being subjects (*viṣayin*), and the five beginning with form by virtue of being objects (*viṣaya*)—
and not that they collectively constitute a single *āyatana* called the "form-āyatana" (*rūpāyatana*).
And in that case, there would be no mutual distinction [between them].
If other names are stated for the sake of distinction— namely, "the nine bases" from the eye-base up to the body-base, and "the sound-base" up to the tangible-base—
then why is a separate name not also stated for the form-base?
Therefore, he says:
"That which is not designated as 'eye' and is form, being distinguished by the eye and so forth—that shall be known as the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana). Thus, no other name for it is stated.
It is just as when all the cows have been marked, yet there is one cow that has not been marked; for that one, the very absence of marking constitutes its mark.
It is just like that.
Regarding "due to predominance," the predominance of the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) is established by three reasons:
because it is characterized by deformation through contact with the hands and so forth;
and because it is the basis for indicating location, such as "this is here" or "that is there."
And because this very [aggregate] is recognized by the world as "form" (*rūpa*).
It was stated that one [base], the *dharmāyatana*, was taught solely for the sake of distinction. In what way is it for the sake of distinction?
It is so that it may be understood that each of these twelve is an *āyatana* individually, because they are established as subject and object respectively, and not as a collective whole. Furthermore,

since that which is distinguished by the eye and the other [faculties]— namely, that which does not bear the name "eye" and so forth, but is a *dharma*— is to be known as the *dharmāyatana*, no other name for it is stated.
By the phrase "of feeling and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes perception, mental formations, non-informative matter, and the unconditioned.
Regarding the expression "by way of twenty types":
form is twofold, consisting of twenty varieties.
Because of the scriptural statement, and because it is the object of three types of eyes:
the fleshly eye of those such as ourselves; [the divine eye]; and the eye of wisdom.
The divine eye belongs to the gods;
the noble eye of wisdom is the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the noble ones, which has the four truths as its object.
Therefore, visible form alone is the domain of these three eyes.
The eye and the other [faculties] are not [included].
Therefore,
only that is called the sense-field of visible form (rūpāyatana), and not the others.

(I.25) For those for whom the Buddha’s word has speech as its intrinsic nature— namely, for those Sautrāntikas for whom it has vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) as its intrinsic nature— for them, those [words] are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Because the sense-base of sound is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

"For those for whom it has the nature of name" refers to those belonging to other schools (*nikāyāntarīya*) who maintain that there exists a factor dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) called "name."
These are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*),
because "name" (*nāman*) is subsumed within the aggregate of formations.
However, for the Abhidharmikas, the word of the Buddha is held to have the nature of both [name and phrase].
For it is said in the *Jñānaprasthāna*:
"What is the word of the Buddha?
It is the speech, the utterance, the discourse, the expression, the path of speech, the sound of speech, the vocal action, and the vocal intimation of the Tathāgata."
The word of the Buddha should be stated as either wholesome or indeterminate;
it may be wholesome.
It may be indeterminate. What is wholesome?
It is the speech of a Tathāgata who possesses a wholesome mind as he utters words—namely, that which constitutes vocal intimation.
"What is the indeterminate?
It is the mind of a Tathāgata that is indeterminate," as stated previously.
Furthermore, immediately following that, it is said: "What is this phenomenon called 'the word of the Buddha'?"

The sequential arrangement, sequential placement, and sequential conjunction of the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*)—these eighty thousand aggregates of dharma (*dharmaskandha*) are, according to those Abhidharmikas, subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
There is a scriptural statement: "I have personally received more than eighty thousand aggregates of dharma from the presence of the Blessed One."

Regarding the phrase "eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma," this is the reading found in another school's version of the Sūtra. As for the statement, "one [teacher] says it is the measure of the treatise":
The authority of the treatise is "śāstrapramāṇa. That which has the authority of the treatise as its measure is this "dharmaskandha."
Some say that its extent is that of the treatise itself; and they say that this consists of six thousand [verses].

And that treatise, known as the *Dharmaskandha*, consists of six thousand stanzas according to the measure of its textual extent. However, they say that those eighty thousand *dharmaskandhas* have disappeared, and only this one remains.
"Each individual discourse on the aggregates and so forth"—
the phrase "others say" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Each single discourse concerning the aggregates and so forth constitutes a *dharmaskandha*.
And those aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) are explained as numbering eighty thousand.
Here, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and so forth will be explained.

By the inclusion of the term "and so forth" in the phrase "of the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the absence of conflict (*araṇa*), etc.," the bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*), the paths of action (*karmapatha*), the meditation on the foul (*aśubhabhāvanā*), the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), and others are included.
However, the *dharmaskandha* is described as the antidote to conduct (*caritapratipakṣa*).
The word "however" (*tu*) serves either to refute the previously mentioned position or for the sake of emphasis.
[It is described] according to the distinctions of conduct such as passion, hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), views, doubt, and so forth are included.
Some sentient beings are characterized by passion (rāga-carita); some are characterized by hatred (dveṣa-carita).
Some have deluded conduct;
some have proud conduct;
some have views-based conduct.
Some are characterized by doubt;
some are characterized by passion and hatred;
some are characterized by passion, hatred, and delusion.
Some have an underlying intention of attachment but employ hatred; some have an underlying intention of hatred but employ attachment;
and some manifest artificial attachment while suppressing their hatred.
"Some [assert] that they suppress passion through artificial hatred.
These were spoken by the Blessed One as an antidote to them.
(I.27) "As for those other aggregates, bases, and elements," and so forth.
Those aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) that are not included here must also be explained and subsumed within these very same aggregates, bases, and elements.

Having reflected upon their respective intrinsic natures (svabhāva) as they are established in this treatise, the aggregates should be explained among the aggregates, the bases among the bases, and the elements among the elements.
The aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) is subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
because the aggregate of ethical discipline has as its intrinsic nature the abstention of body and speech.
The remaining [aggregates] are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Since concentration (*samādhi*) and the other factors are mental states (*caitasika*),
"liberation" (*vimukti*) here is intended to mean resolve (*adhimokṣa*).
Furthermore, the "knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimuktijñānadarśana*) is simply a specific form of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because they have non-greed as their intrinsic nature, these eight are included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Which are the eight?
They are the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, and white.
And those [eight] will be shown to have non-greed as their intrinsic nature, as it will be said: "Non-greed is eightfold."
Non-greed (*alobha*) is included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*);
therefore, it is subsumed therein.

However, when accompanied by their attendants (*saparivāra*), they consist of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and are thus included within both the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

What is included? The retinue and accompanying forms of that non-greed consist of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha); the aggregates of feeling and perception (vedanā- and saṃjñā-skandhas); the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), which includes associated factors such as volition (cetanā) and dissociated factors such as birth (jāti).
And the consciousness within this collection is the aggregate of consciousness; thus, they possess the nature of the five aggregates.
As for the ninth and tenth, the totalities (kṛtsna) of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness, they will be explained later.
Likewise, regarding the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), because they have non-attachment as their intrinsic nature, they are included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).

However, those [spheres] together with their attendants, because they consist of five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), are to be explained as before by means of the sense-fields of mind (*manāyatana*) and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
As for the totalities (*kṛtsna*) of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the four beginning with the sphere of infinite space:

the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception, because they consist of four aggregates, are subsumed under the sense-fields of mind and mental objects.
For the aggregate of form does not exist there.
"The five bases of liberation," and so forth, as stated in the Sūtra. (Abhidh-k-vy 54)
There are these five bases of liberation.
What are they? Here, monks, either the Teacher teaches the Dharma, or some other wise fellow-celibate who occupies the position of a teacher.
Just as his teacher, or some other wise fellow-celibate in the position of a guru, teaches him the Dharma,
so too does he come to experience the meaning and experience the Dharma within those teachings.
As he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dharma, joy arises in him.
In one who is gladdened, joy arises;
for one whose mind is joyful, the body becomes tranquil;
with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness.
The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
One whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are and sees things as they truly are.
Understanding and seeing things as they truly are, one becomes disenchanted.
Being weary, one becomes dispassionate;
being dispassionate, one is liberated.
This is the first basis of liberation.
When a monk or a nun abides therein, unestablished mindfulness becomes established;
the unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated;
and the untainted outflows that have not yet been exhausted become exhausted.
And he attains the unsurpassed security of nirvāṇa which he had not yet attained.
Furthermore, monk, it may be that neither the Teacher nor some other wise person in the position of a teacher or a fellow practitioner of the holy life teaches the Dharma;
rather, one recites aloud in detail the teachings as they were heard, as they were taught, and as they were mastered.
To the extent that he recites them aloud in detail— just as they were heard, taught, and mastered—
to that same extent he comes to experience their meaning, as described before.
This is the second base of liberation.
"Abiding therein," as before.
Furthermore, O monk, it may be that neither does a teacher teach the Dharma, nor does some other wise person standing in the position of a guru or a fellow practitioner of the holy life [teach it];
nor does one engage in the detailed recitation of the teachings as they were heard, as they were taught, and as they were mastered.
Moreover, he extensively elucidates for others those teachings as they were heard, as they were taught, and as they were mastered.
To the extent that he extensively elucidates for others those teachings as they were heard, as they were taught, and as they were mastered,
to that same extent he comes to experience the meaning within those teachings, as described previously.
This is the third base of liberation.
"Abiding therein" is as explained previously.
Furthermore, O monk, it is not indeed the Teacher—as before.
Nor does he engage in recitation, nor does he proclaim it to others;
rather, he reflects upon, weighs, and examines those teachings exactly as they were heard, up to the point of how they were mastered.
In whatever manner he reflects upon them, up to examining them, exactly as they were heard, up to how they were mastered—[in that very manner he proceeds].
In whatever way he experiences the meaning within those phenomena, as described before;
this is the fourth base of liberation (*vimuktyāyatana*).
"Abiding in which," and so forth, is as explained previously.
Furthermore, monk, it is not that he [thinks], "The Teacher," as before;
nor does he recite, nor does he proclaim it to others, nor does he reflect upon it.
Rather, by him some auspicious sign of concentration has been well-grasped, well-attended to, well-cultivated, well-practiced, and well-penetrated.

That is to say, whether it be a bloated corpse, or a festering corpse, or a livid corpse, or a mangled corpse, or a bloody corpse, or a worm-infested corpse, or a scattered corpse, or a skeleton, or a chain of bones—
in whatever way he has thoroughly mastered any one of these excellent signs of concentration as previously described,
in that very same way he becomes a penetrator of the meaning within those phenomena, as previously described.
This is the fifth basis of liberation.
"For one established therein" is as explained previously.
It is a specific kind of wisdom that serves as the gateway for liberation.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Together with their attendants, they are subsumed under the spheres of sound, mind, and mental objects.
Because there is the grasping of sound during teaching, recitation, and the exposition to others, the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) exists.
However, since the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*) are present everywhere as the retinue of wisdom (*prajñā*), they are subsumed by all three [categories].
Regarding "of two bases," it is stated in the Sūtra:
There are material beings who are without perception and without discernment;
namely, the gods who are non-percipient beings.
This is the first sphere.
There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, dwell having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Namely, the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the second sphere.
Of these two bases, the non-percipient beings are comprised by ten bases, because the bases of odor and taste are absent there; however,
at the times of their death and rebirth, they do possess the mind base.

Those who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are included within the spheres of mind and mental objects; this is the point under discussion. Because they are formless, even in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*, there are said to be sixty-two elements.
It is said in the Sūtra: The Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"To what extent, Bhadanta, is one a wise person skilled in the elements?"
The Blessed One said: "O wise Ānanda, you know and see the eighteen elements as they truly are."
The eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; and so on, up to the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
Thus, Ānanda, he knows and sees these eighteen elements as they truly are.
He knows and sees the six elements as they truly are:
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
He also knows and sees another six elements as they truly are.

He knows and sees, as they truly are, the six elements: the element of desire, the element of ill-will, the element of harmfulness, the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill-will, and the element of non-harmfulness.
