Furthermore, he knows and sees, as they truly are, another six elements:
the element of pleasure, the element of pain, the element of mental joy, the element of mental grief, the element of equanimity, and the element of ignorance.
One knows and sees the four elements as they truly are:
the element of feeling, the element of perception, the element of mental formations, and the element of consciousness.
One also knows and sees these three elements as they truly are.
The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm—these are the three realms he knows and sees as they truly are. Furthermore, he knows and sees another three realms:
the realm of form, the formless realm, and the realm of cessation.
One also knows and sees three other realms as they truly are:
the past realm, the future realm, and the present realm.
One also knows and sees these three other realms as they truly are.
"The inferior realm, the middling realm, and the sublime realm"—
thus he knows and sees these three other realms as they truly are:
the wholesome realm, the unwholesome realm, and the indeterminate realm.
He also knows and sees three other realms as they truly are:
the realm of those in training (śaikṣa), the realm of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and the realm of neither-training-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa).
He knows and sees both of these realms as they truly are.
"The realm with outflows" and "the realm without outflows.
Furthermore, he knows and sees two other realms as they truly are: the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm.
He knows and sees these two realms as they truly are.
"And to this extent, Ānanda, one becomes a wise person skilled in the elements.
Thus, these connected sentences should each be recited even in the middle [of the text].
However, it should be understood that I have not written them here for fear of prolixity.
The inclusion [of all phenomena] should be understood according to their respective application.
First, as for the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), they are indeed those very same [elements];
thus, they are included within those eighteen elements.
Therein, there are six [elements], beginning with the earth element (pṛthivīdhātu).
Of these, the first four are included within the tangible element (spraṣṭavyadhātu).
The space element (ākāśadhātu) is included within the form element (rūpadhātu), because its intrinsic nature consists of light and darkness.
The consciousness element is included within the seven mental elements.
Regarding the six [elements] beginning with the desire realm, "desire realm" here refers to sensual desire;
and that is a mental factor (caitasika).
Since the elements of malice (*vyāpāda-dhātu*) and so forth are also merely mental factors (*caitasika*),
they are included within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
The six [elements], such as the element of pleasure (*sukha-dhātu*) and so forth, are likewise included in that very same [dharma-element].
Of the four beginning with the feeling element (*vedanā-dhātu*), three are included within the mental-object element (*dharma-dhātu*).
The consciousness element (*vijñāna-dhātu*) is included within the seven consciousness elements.
Of the three beginning with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the desire realm is included within the eighteen elements.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are fourteen [elements], excluding the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are the elements of mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness.
Thus, the inclusion of two of the three—namely, the realm of form and so forth—has been explained.
Within the element of cessation, there is the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
The three elements beginning with the past are each subsumed within the eighteen elements.
As for the three elements beginning with the inferior—namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth—their inclusion has already been explained.

The three beginning with the wholesome—namely, the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral elements—are present in the seven elements consisting of the elements of form, sound, and mental phenomena (dharmadhātu), as well as in the seven elements of consciousness.
The neutral element is present in all eighteen elements.

The three beginning with the element of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa)—namely, the elements of those in training, those beyond training, and neither—are present in two elements: the mind element (manodhātu), the mental phenomena element (dharmadhātu), and the mental consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu).
Regarding the third [category], it is within the eighteen elements (dhātu).
Regarding the first two—the contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) elements—it is within all eighteen elements.
Regarding the second [of those two], it is within the mind element (manodhātu), the mental-object element (dharmadhātu), and the mind-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu).

Regarding the conditioned and unconditioned realms: the former is included within the eighteen realms, while the latter is included within the dharma-realm. Thus, these constitute the sixty-two realms.
(I.28) Regarding the phrase "those which are there" in the *Bahudhātuka*: "The definition of two among these has not been stated.
The definitions of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) and so forth have already been stated as follows: [Abhidh-k-vy 57] these...
They are perfected through their functions of supporting and so forth;
[their characteristics are] hardness, moisture, heat, and motion.
But has not the characteristic of the consciousness-element also been stated?
For it is said: "Consciousness is the individual representation."

It has been correctly stated that the definition of all consciousnesses has been given. However, regarding the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*), it has not yet been analyzed whether what is intended here is only a certain portion of consciousness or the entirety of it.
And unconditioned space has the characteristic already described;
however, it is not the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
For this [space element] must necessarily be distinct from [unconditioned] space.
For it has been stated in another sutra: "O monk, this person consists of six elements.
With this intention, it was said that the definition of the two [types of persons] has not been stated.
Therefore, he says:
In that case, should it be understood that space itself is the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*),
and that all consciousness is the consciousness-element (*vijñānadhātu*)?
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "in the mouth, nose, etc.," the ears and so forth are included.
"Light and darkness, so it is said.
The word "it is said" (kila) is for the purpose of indicating another's opinion.
His own position, however, is understood to be the intention that space is merely the absence of obstructive substance.

"Having night and day as its intrinsic nature" means that it refers to the darkness existing at night and the light characterized by the sun's heat during the day; or else, this designation is made according to the majority of cases (*bāhulika*).

"Agha" is indeed form (rūpa) situated in a heap; "situated in a heap" means situated in an aggregation. It is called "agha" according to etymological rules because it excessively strikes (*hanti*) and is struck (*hanyate*).
The substitution of *a* for the word *atyartha* and the substitution of *gha* for *han* have been made.
"Its vicinity" (*taṭ*) means that which is situated near that wall or similar structure.
The meaning is that it is established in dependence upon that.
In this explanation as well, the word "kila" (it is said) is for the purpose of indicating the Vaibhāṣika interpretation;
however, his own position is stated later.
Therefore it is said: "And that is *agha*.
Because other matter does not encounter resistance there, and because other matter is not resisted within it.
"And the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of another form" refers to that which resides in the meditative collection (*cita*).
In this view, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound:
"it is both evil (*agha*) and a preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*)," thus "evil-preparatory stage" (*aghasāmantaka*).
"Consciousness is with outflows (sāsrava)" is said because consciousness is intended here as the cause of birth.
If it is asked, "Why?",
for this reason he says:
because these six elements are intended [as such].

They are the bases of birth. For it is said: "O monk, this person consists of six elements," and because of the statement that "the descent of the embryo into the mother's womb occurs in dependence upon six elements."
"For these, indeed, from birth... and so forth.
For these are the basis [of life] because they produce, nourish, and cause growth.
Here, the consciousness-element (*vijñānadhātu*) is the producer, because it is the seed for rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*).
The [other] elements are nourishers because they serve as its support;
the space element is a promoter because it provides room. For this very reason, these are designated as "elements" (*dhātu*).
They are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they provide the connection for rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*).
However, untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena are not like this;
they are not the basis for birth because they bring about the cessation of birth.
(I.29) Among these, one is "visible," namely form (*rūpa*). What is this that is called "visibility" (*nidarśana*)?

That specific quality through which connection with a particular distinction allows that object to be demonstrated in such a way— that distinction is called "demonstration" (*nidarśana*). By means of speech, a demonstration is produced for another person's visual consciousness.

It exists together with that [quality of being visible]; thus, among the eighteen elements, only one—the form element (*rūpadhātu*)—is "with visibility" (*sanidarśana*). By this restriction—that only the form element is with visibility—it is implied that the remaining [elements] are "without visibility" (*anidarśana*).
And by this, its preeminence is stated through its quality of being demonstrable (*sanidarśana*);
thus, there is no consequence of the fault of redundancy, because that [preeminence] is thereby established.
Furthermore, these subdivisions, such as being demonstrable and so forth, are for the most part shown exactly as they are taught in the Sūtras.
For it is said in the Sūtra:
"O Bhikṣu, the eye is an internal sense-field (āyatana).
It is a translucent form derived from the four great elements; it is material, invisible, and resistant."
Monk, as before, the body is an internal sense-sphere.
Monk, the mind is an internal sense-sphere, formless, invisible, and non-obstructive.
Monk, visible forms are an external sense-sphere.
Derived from the four great elements, it is material, visible, and resistant.
For sound, O monk, is an external sense base;
derived from the four great elements, it is material, invisible, and resistant.
Up to and including tangible objects, monk, is the external sense base.
It consists of the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, which is invisible and impingent. Mental phenomena, monk, are the external sense base.
"Not included among the eleven bases (āyatana), formless, non-demonstrable, and non-obstructive.
These distinctions of the elements (dhātu) alone are explained until the conclusion of the first chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*,
because they consist of the classification of matter and consciousness.
"The ten material [elements] are with resistance.
The inclusion of the term "material" is for the purpose of excluding that which is non-material.

Forming (rūpaṇa) is form (rūpa). Because these possess it, they are called "possessors of form" (rūpin). "Ten" refers to the five elements beginning with the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) and the five elements that are their respective objects.
How can there be a rejection of the dharmadhātu?
For it can indeed be said that it possesses form,
because non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) exists therein.
By the restriction "only those that are material," their exclusion is established.
For only those elements whose intrinsic nature is exclusively material are to be understood;
however, the dharma-element has both a material and a non-material intrinsic nature.
"The obstruction of the arising of another in its own location," and so forth.
Where there is one resistant object, the arising of a second does not occur there.
Just as when one hand strikes another hand, or [strikes] a stone, the hand is repelled;
the hand does not arise in the place of the hand, nor does the stone arise in the place of the stone.
The stone as well.
In place of those two—the hand and the stone—the stone also does not arise.
It is repelled by the water.
The meaning is that it functions within its own domain, namely water.
The inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) in the phrase "mostly among humans" (*prāyeṇa manuṣyāṇām*) is for the purpose of excluding fishermen and others.
"There is neither" means there is no [functioning] in both [domains].
"Of those destined to die in the womb. "These aspects" means these types.
*Titīlā* refers to *jatūnyaḥ*.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of cats, etc.," there is the inclusion of thieves, humans, tigers, and so forth.
That in which something has its functional activity (*kāritra*).
"That is its domain" means that "human effort" (puruṣakāra) refers to functional activity (kāritra).
The functional activity of the eye, ear, and so forth consists of visual perception, auditory perception, and so on, with respect to visible forms, sounds, and so on.
And that [basis] should be understood as characterized by a specific state of being a support for one's own mind and mental factors;
it is that which is grasped by the mind and mental factors through the application of leaning upon a staff.
That objective referent consists of form and so forth.
This being so, the object of apprehension (*ālambana*) belongs only to the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*).
The objective field (*viṣaya*), however, belongs to the eye and other [senses] as well, not exclusively to the mind and mental factors.
Therefore, it is said: "because it does not function beyond that."
For whatever in the world does not proceed beyond a certain point is obstructed there, such as [a movement] at a piece of wood or a wall;
likewise, the eye and other [senses] do not exercise their activity beyond their respective objects.
But it is the object itself that acts; therefore, it is said that "it is struck" (pratihanyate) therein.
Alternatively, "striking" (pratighāta) here refers to an impact (nipāta), as explained in detail.
In this context, "impact" means falling upon that object.
That which is activity within its own object; the meaning is "function. This refers to the detailed explanation beginning with "here, by way of resistance through obstruction."
Regarding the statement "the ten [realms] are with resistance" (*sapratigha*), it is intended that those ten realms are with resistance by way of "obstructive resistance" (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*).

In this context, since it would follow that mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are also with resistance by virtue of "resistance regarding objects" (*viṣaya-pratighāta*) and "resistance regarding focal points" (*ālambana-pratighāta*), there is a fourfold question; "four-cornered" (*catuṣkoṇa*) means "of four types."
Regarding the term *paścātpādaka*:
if one stands up to answer after having grasped the latter part of the question, he is a *paścātpādaka*. If one does so after having grasped the former part, he is a *pūrvapādaka*.
They are also called "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) because of resistance toward objects; these refer to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
For they are with resistance both through resistance toward objects and through resistance toward focal objects (*ālambana*).
The five sense-faculties are not with resistance through resistance toward focal objects, because they lack a focal object.
"Wherein the mind is about to arise," and so forth; that is, in whichever basis (*āśraya*) and object (*ālambana*) the mind desires to arise.
Obstruction and non-arising can be brought about by others.
By way of internal obstruction.
That very [matter] is "with resistance" (sapratigha). Because it possesses resistance characterized by internal obstruction, it is "with resistance."
Others say that they possess resistance because of the obstruction characterized by the prevention of another's arising in their own location.
What, then, is that?
It has the nature of the five sense-faculties and the five object-domains.
By contrast, that which is non-obstructive (*apratigha*) is intended.

Where it is impossible for others to create an obstruction to the mind (*manas*) as it seeks to arise— just as it is impossible to create an intermediate hindrance to the arising of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) from the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the phenomenon-element (*dharmadhātu*)— [that is non-obstructive].
It cannot be produced by others.
Therefore, it is established that [the mind-element] has the nature of the seven mind-elements and the dharma-element, and is non-obstructive (*apratigha*).
Eight [elements] are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Thus,
the restriction is that these eight are indeed indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
They are called indeterminate because they are not defined as being either wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Those which are distinct from both the wholesome and the unwholesome are precisely what is intended here by "indeterminate" (avyākṛta). It does not refer to the wholesome,
because the wholesome is not defined as indeterminate.
Nor are they unwholesome, because they are not designated as either wholesome or neutral.
This is because wholesome and unwholesome states are designated as such by virtue of their being wholesome or unwholesome.
For the application of words depends upon conventional usage and established linguistic habit.
"Three others":
the term "elements" (dhātavaḥ) is understood from the context.
"Only threefold, not manifold, nor twofold"—this is the restriction.
"Associated with non-attachment and so forth, they are wholesome," and so on in detail.
The seven mental elements associated with non-attachment, non-hatred, non-delusion, modesty (*hrī*), and shame (*apatrāpya*) are wholesome.
Those associated with greed, hatred, delusion, lack of shame, and lack of dread are unwholesome (*akuśala*).
They are called "wholesome" (*kuśala*) because they have descended from, gone toward, or departed from what is contemptible;
or else, wisdom (*prajñā*) is like a sharp blade (*kuśa*), and thus it is "wholesome."
They are called "wholesome" because they take up or grasp [the desirable]; their opposites are "unwholesome.
Others, however, which are not associated with non-greed and so forth, nor with greed and so forth, are "indeterminate."
"The realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)," and so forth.
This refers to that which has been described as having non-attachment and so on as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
as well as feeling and the other mental factors associated with non-attachment and so on.
It is originated by non-greed and so forth, dissociated [from mind],
consisting of acquisition, birth, and so forth,
and unmanifest [form].
The wholesome is fourfold: [the three conditioned phenomena] and the other, which is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
The dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) is unwholesome when it has greed and so forth as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), is associated (*samprayukta*) with them, or is originated (*samuttha*) by them.
Any other is neutral (*avyākṛta*), provided it does not have non-greed and so forth as its intrinsic nature, is not associated with them, or is not originated by them.
Nor is it of the nature of, associated with, or originated from greed and so forth.
[These are] space, analytical cessation,
and their acquisitions, birth, and so on, as applicable.

This is the indeterminate *dharmadhātu*. "The other two are indeterminate" means that, apart from those two *rūpadhātu* and *śabdadhātu* which are originated by wholesome and unwholesome minds, there are other *rūpadhātu* and *śabdadhātu* originated by indeterminate minds, comprised within bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), as well as those not comprised within intimation (*avijñapti*).
(I.30) "All are included in the desire realm" means it is determined that all [of these] are indeed included in the desire realm.
This is because they are included merely within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*),
but not individually in their entirety. Therefore, he says:
Regarding the statement "there are fourteen in the realm of form": it is because those two— namely odor and taste— are substantial food (kavaḍīkārāhāra).
For even odor is a subtle form of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its non-existence;
that is, in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of the element of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), because it is [otherwise] edible food.
Because of the established tenet that "edible food consists of three bases in the desire realm."
"This same consequence would apply to odor and taste as well," means that those two which do not have the nature of food would also exist there.
But there is [utility] for the tangible.
What is it?
Utility as the basis for the sense faculties, as a support, and as clothing.
Others, however, say— namely the Venerable Śrīlāta—
that it is "accompanied by pliancy" (praśrabdhi). This means it is arisen together with pliancy, that is to say, accompanied by bodily serviceability (kāyakarmaṇyatā).
In this regard, the Master, disregarding the opinion of the Venerable Śrīlāta and seeing that the Vaibhāṣika position is open to objection, begins his definitive determination with the words,
"If that is so," and so forth.
By implication, the Vaibhāṣikas have made this very claim.
Odor and taste do not exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), because they serve no purpose,
just like the objects of the female and male faculties.
The Master refutes that position:
"This position is faulty because it is vitiated by the fallacy of contradicting the specific qualification of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparyayāpākṣāla*)."

For the subject (dharmin) designated as odor and taste within the realm of form (rūpadhātu) is intended to possess its own apprehending faculty; yet it follows that such a subject would lack its own apprehending faculty. This is because, just as the objects of the female and male faculties are devoid of their own apprehending faculties due to being purposeless.
Likewise, the object known as odor or taste would also [be perceived].
Furthermore, there is a clear inference by which this contradiction regarding the specific nature of the subject (dharmin) is revealed.
"The faculties of smell and taste do not exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) because their objects would be useless,
just like the male faculty. Thus does a certain proponent of the Vaibhāṣika school respond.
"There is a purpose," and so forth.
Without those two—the faculties of smell and taste—there would be neither the beauty of the body nor vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
By this refutation based on perceptible reality (*dṛṣṭabādha*), he turns back the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*).
For in this case, inference contradicts what is observed.
Why is it said that the faculties of smell and taste exist in the realm of form?
"Because it possesses a purpose,
like the visual faculty.
Thus said the Master.
"If this is the purpose," and so forth.

By showing that the beauty of the support and the act of speaking occur through the physical basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) alone and not through the sense faculty (*indriya*), he demonstrates the unestablished nature of the reason [stated] regarding its having a purpose.
A proponent of a Vaibhāṣika school says:
"Nor is there a base without a faculty," and so forth.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), a base for the olfactory or gustatory faculties that is devoid of a faculty cannot exist,
because it would be a base for a faculty.
"Like the locus of the male faculty.
By this, he establishes the proven fact that [the sense organs] possess a purpose.
The Teacher says:
"It is logical that those [organs] are impossible," and so forth.

It is logical that the basis for the male organ (*puruṣendriya*) is impossible there because it serves no purpose. However, the bases for the olfactory and gustatory organs do serve a purpose, as their purposes are the beautification of the physical support and speech, respectively.
Therefore, its occurrence is logical even without the sense faculty. The proof for this is stated:
in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there exists the physical basis of the nose and tongue faculties, even though they lack the faculties themselves.
"Because it has a purpose,
like the physical basis of the visual faculty.
By this, he establishes that very point regarding the unestablished nature of its having a purpose.

Thus, when a certain proponent of the Vaibhāṣika school who asserts that [the sense organs] have a purpose has been refuted, the Vaibhāṣikas— showing that the objection raised at the outset, namely, "In that case, it would follow that the nose and tongue faculties also do not exist because they are purposeless," is a fallacious refutation—
say: "Even though they are purposeless," and so forth.
Just as for those destined to die in the womb, their birth is purposeless— for they do not have the opportunity to see forms and so forth—
so too, in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the production of the olfactory and gustatory faculties will likewise be purposeless.
Therefore, the faculties of smell and taste do not exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
because they are purposeless,
like the male faculty. Thus, it is demonstrated that "purposelessness" is an inconclusive reason.
The Teacher says:
"It might indeed be purposeless," and so forth. It might be that the production of the sense faculties is purposeless.
But it is not without cause, because conditioned phenomena possess causes.
Furthermore, whoever is free from craving for an object is necessarily also free from craving for the sense faculty.
By this, the absence of a logical reason (*hetu*) is demonstrated. Consequently, the proof is stated as follows:
"The faculties of smell and taste do not exist in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)."

Because it would be without a cause, like a causeless sprout or like the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*). Furthermore, the Master himself raises the following alternative: "Or how could the male faculty itself be produced?"
What is the intended meaning?
[It is this: If the production of the olfactory and gustatory faculties occurs without purpose or even without a cause, then the male faculty would likewise not be produced.
For this is the position of the Vaibhāṣikas.
The continuum of a sentient being in the form realm possesses both the olfactory and gustatory faculties because it is a sentient being possessing form,
just like the continuum of a sentient being belonging to the desire realm.
The Teacher, however, by asking "Why would the male faculty not also be produced?", demonstrates the contradiction of the specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparyaya*) for that position.
The subject (*dharmin*) is the continuum of sentient beings in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), which lacks the male faculty.
Its contradiction is the state of possessing the male faculty.
The Vaibhāṣikas offer this rebuttal:
"Because it causes ugliness.
How so?
The male faculty does not exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), because it would cause ugliness, just as being one-eyed or having a withered hand does.
"Because this [position] is not sublated by inference, our thesis does not undergo reversal.
The intention is that, according to the established tenet of the Naiyāyikas, "if it does not sublate what is perceived [it is valid].
The Teacher says:
Why would it not be beautiful for those whose private parts are enclosed in a sheath? "Vastiguhya" means the private part on the penis; the "vasti" is that by which the male organ is enveloped.
The secret part is the male organ. The sheath is that in which it—the private parts of the bladder—resides. Thus, it is "the private parts of the bladder enclosed in a sheath."
For those whose private organs are thus sheathed, does this not look beautiful? The meaning is that it certainly does look beautiful.
By this, he demonstrates that the claim of its being unseemly is unestablished.
"And it is not by virtue of a purpose that [the male organ] arises," and so forth.
By the Vaibhāṣikas stating that it is "because it causes ugliness," this is effectively asserted through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*):
that the male organ is produced by virtue of a purpose.
And that position is sublated by inference, because it has the flaw of being a reversal of the very nature of the subject (*dharmin*).
How so? It is said:
The male faculty is not something that can be produced by the force of a purpose,
because it is produced by its own causes,
just like one-eyedness or lameness.
The Vaibhāṣikas say:
"In that case, the Sūtra is contradicted," and so forth.
This refers to the position that there exists a continuum of sentient beings in the form realm who lack the olfactory and gustatory faculties.
That [position] is flawed because it contradicts the previous thesis;
for the Blessed One has stated that beings belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) are complete and possess unimpaired faculties.
Because they lack the state of being one-eyed or maimed;
"with unimpaired faculties" means because their eyes and other senses are not deficient.
The Teacher says:
"Those which are there," and so forth.

Since the meaning of the Sūtra is understood as "those who are not deficient in their faculties" with respect to those eyes and other [faculties] that exist there in the form realm (rūpadhātu) but are devoid of the olfactory faculty (ghrāṇendriya) and the rest, there is no contradiction.
However, the Vaibhāṣikas explain it in this way:
"They exist," and so forth in detail.
They indeed exist there in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), namely the faculties of smell and taste, but not the odors and tastes.
For it is by way of the personal existence—that is, by way of one's own continuum—within the six sense bases such as the eye, that craving arises in living beings.
And karma is moistened by that [craving].
Thus, in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), which possesses its causes, the faculties of smell and taste [are present].
And therefore, because they possess causes,
those two indeed exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
just like a sprout and so forth which have causes.
And by this they demonstrate that the proof stated— namely, that "the faculties of smell and taste do not exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) because they lack a cause"— is unestablished;
however, [the absence] of the male faculty is established by way of the touch of sexual intercourse.
What?
It is "the manifestation of craving" that is under discussion.
And beings belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) are free from passion for sexual contact.
Therefore, in that case, there is no karma preceded by craving. Because it is thus without a cause,

it is established that the male faculty does not exist there— just as a sprout and so forth would not exist without a cause— and that in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) there are exactly fourteen elements (*dhātu*).
"Those pertaining to the formless realm," and so forth;
[these are] the mind-element, the mental-object-element, and the mind-consciousness-element.
By the restriction that "only those [dhātus] are included in the formless realm" (ārūpyāpta), it is implied that other dhātus do not exist there.

Since rebirth occurs there for those who are free from passion for form (rūpa-vītarāga), the ten dhātus whose intrinsic nature is form— namely, the five beginning with the eye and the five beginning with visible form— do not exist there either.
And the five consciousness-elements do not exist with those as their bases and objects.

"Those" refers to the eye and so forth, and "form and so forth" refers to the objects; those which have these respectively as their bases and objects are "those having those as their bases and objects."
Because of the absence of the bases— the eye and so forth— and the objects— visible form and so forth— those elements of visual consciousness and the rest are also not present there.
(I.31ab) These three are both with-outflows and without-outflows.
This is a restriction stating that these three alone are both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava);
however, the remaining [dharmas] are with-outflows.
For what purpose is this stated?

Is it not already established that the remaining [dharmas] are with-outflows (*sāsrava*), by virtue of the restriction that "only these three are both with-outflows and without-outflows" (*anāsrava*)?
It is not established.
How so?
Because there is the concern that the remaining [dharmas] might be exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) or exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
To prevent that [misunderstanding], this is stated:
"The remaining ones are exclusively with-outflows" (I.31cd).
For the five consciousness-elements are indeed accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Thus,
the word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to restrict [the preceding] to those with vitarka and vicāra alone.
The final three are of three kinds.
Thus,
the restriction is that only the last three types [of mental factors] possess these three modes; this is excluding *vitarka* and *vicāra*.
Since *vitarka* and *vicāra* have the nature of the associated (*saṃprayuktaka*) factor-element (*dharmadhātu*), there is the risk that they would be included here; therefore, they are excluded.
For *vitarka* will be included within the second category, and *vicāra*, arising from the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), is included within the third category.
However, he will explain that anything other than those is not included within any of the three categories.

These elements, beginning with the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and ending with the associated part of the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*), are accompanied by both applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and in the first *dhyāna*—both its preliminary (*sāmantaka*) and fundamental (*maula*) stages—due to their association with applied and sustained thought.
For this very reason, they are without applied thought (*avitarka*) in the intermediate *dhyāna* (*dhyānāntara*), because of the absence of applied thought there.
They possess investigation alone because they are associated with investigation.

For this very reason, from the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), they are without vitarka and without vicāra due to the absence of those two. Furthermore, the entire unassociated (*asaṃprayukta*) portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) is likewise without vitarka and without vicāra.

According to their respective possibilities, these include the form, mind, and formations dissociated from mind belonging to the three realms, as well as the unconditioned; furthermore, in the intermediate dhyāna, there is no *vicāra* because of the absence of *vitarka*,
and there is no *vicāra* because of the absence of a second *vicāra*.
Investigation (*vicāra*) is not included within these three categories.
First, investigation belonging to the levels of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna is not included in the first category,
namely, that which is "with applied thought (*savitarka*) and with investigation (*savicāra*)."
For that [first dhyāna] can be accompanied by vitarka, but it cannot be accompanied by vicāra because of its association with vicāra.
Nor is it included within the second [dhyāna],
for it is "without vitarka and with vicāra only."
It is not included in the third [dhyāna] either, because of its association with applied thought (*vitarka*) and because of the absence of sustained thought (*vicāra*) in the second [dhyāna].
"Without applied thought (avitarka) and without sustained thought (avicāra)":
for although it is without sustained thought because of the absence of a second sustained thought,
it is not without applied thought because of its association with applied thought.

How is that to be described? To this he says: "It is without investigation (avicāra) and consists of mere initial inquiry (vitarka-mātra). It is "without investigation" because of the absence of a second investigation.
It consists of vitarka alone because of its association with vitarka.
"For this very reason" means that on the level of those states accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, vicāra itself constitutes the fourth type.
"Without investigation and with only initial thought" means that the remaining [mental states] are devoid of both.
The remaining ten material elements (*rūpī dhātu*) have been mentioned.

In response to the doubt as to whether they might be "without applied thought and with sustained thought only" (*avitarkā vicāramātrā*) or "without applied thought and without sustained thought" (*avitarkā avicārā*), it is determined that the remaining ones are indeed devoid of both; thus the meaning is that they are exclusively "without applied thought and without sustained thought.
(I.32) How, then, are they said to be "non-conceptual" (*avikalpaka*)?
Because of the statement, "One endowed with visual consciousness cognizes blue, but does not think 'it is blue,'" it is said that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is of three kinds.
The word "kila" (it is said) is for the purpose of indicating the opinion of another.

His own intention, however, is that *vitarka* is simply a particular kind of volition (*cetanā*) and discernment (*prajñā*); thus, there is no separate dharma called "intrinsic-nature conceptualization" (*svabhāvavikalpa*).
For this reason, he stated in the *Pañcaskandhaka*:
"What is *vitarka*?"
Investigative mental discourse is a specific form of volition and wisdom; it is that coarseness of mind.
What is analysis? It is likewise reflective mental discourse; it is that subtlety of mind.
Volition (*cetanā*) is established as being present in the state of non-investigation, while wisdom (*prajñā*) is established as being present in the state of investigation.
Thus, these [mental factors] possess conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) regarding their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The word "tad" is a particle used for introducing a statement or has the sense of "therefore."
Because conceptualization has a coarse characteristic by its very nature,
intrinsic conceptualization (*svabhāvavikalpa*) is *vitarka*.
Since this exists through association with these five groups of consciousness, they are said to be "with conceptualization."
The other two types of conceptualization—investigative and recollective—do not exist for these;
therefore, they are called "non-conceptual.
This is just as a horse with only one leg is called "legless."
When three feet have been cut off, even though one foot remains, one is called "footless.

In the same way, those with a single conceptualization are said to be "without conceptualization. For that [single conceptualization] is indeed the conceptualization of investigation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).
That mental wisdom which is non-concentrated consists of that derived from hearing and reflection, as well as that acquired at birth.

It is called "mental" (*mānasī*) because it exists in the mind (*manasi*). It is "distracted" (*vyagrā*), meaning its various points of focus (*vividhāgra*) are scattered across diverse objects (*vividhālambana*).
Alternatively, it is "devoid of a primary object" because it repeatedly relies upon different objects of focus.
Why is it called "distracted conceptualization through investigation"?
Because it proceeds by depending upon names with respect to this or that object of focus.
Furthermore, because [the former] involves the analytical investigation that "form and sensation are impermanent, suffering," and so forth,
whereas meditative cultivation consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmayī*) proceeds toward its object without depending on such [investigation],
this [latter] is not called "conceptualization consisting of analytical investigation" (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).
All mindfulness is indeed mental;
it is both concentrated and unconcentrated.
It is said that, being independent [of external objects], it proceeds by taking as its object merely that which has been previously experienced.
What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)?

Its characteristic is "the longing of the mind. However, because that which is associated with the five groups of consciousness does not function as a longing for an object previously experienced, it is not accepted as the conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇavikalpa*).
(I.33) "Seven have an object" is a double restriction:
only seven have an object, and those that have an object are only these seven.
"And half [of the factors] are with an object by way of their intrinsic nature.
This is stated as an exception to what has already been mentioned.
Here too, there is a double restriction:
only half of the dharmas have an object,
and only that which has an object is half of the dharmas.

And because there is the restriction that "only seven [elements] have an object, as does half of the dharma-element," it is therefore established— and thus stated— that the remaining material elements and the portion of the dharma-element that is dissociated are without an object.
For if this were not restricted, this meaning would not be established.
"Nine are non-appropriated" means that nine are exclusively non-appropriated; this is the restriction. "Together with half of the eighth."
"Along with" means up to that point.
And those are eight.

And those seven mind-elements (cittadhātu) and that half of the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) which was stated to have an object (sālambana)— the mention of "eight" is for the purpose of including the entire dharma-element, lest it be understood that only half of the dharma-element is included.
Those eight and sound as the ninth are said to be non-appropriated;
the other nine are of two kinds.
The five beginning with the eye and the four beginning with visible form—excluding sound—these nine are of two kinds only;
that is to say, they are either appropriated (*upātta*) or non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
It does not mean, however, that they are exclusively appropriated.
And for this purpose,
it is further formulated in the Sūtra that "the other nine are twofold."
"Because they conform to one another through benefit and injury.

This means that through the benefit and injury of the eye-element and so forth—characterized by the application of ointment or the striking with a hand, respectively—there occur the benefit and injury of the mind and mental factors.
And through the benefit and injury of the mind and mental factors—characterized by joy and dejection—there occur the benefit and injury of the eye-element and so forth.
Therefore, they are said to be "appropriated" by the mind and mental factors in the sense of being their basis; the meaning is that they have been taken as one's own.
That which in the world is called "sentient" means "possessing life.
(I.34) Tangible objects are of two kinds.
Thus, there is a double restriction:
the tangible alone is of two kinds, and that which is of two kinds is the tangible alone.
The remaining nine material [elements] are derived from the primary elements.
Thus, here too there is a double restriction;
and in the statement "and a portion of the dharma-dhātu is derived matter," here too there is a double restriction.
And because these two are thus determined,
it is established that the remaining seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), excluding non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), are neither of the two [types].
This is because the primary elements (*bhūta*) have been defined by their characteristics, such as the tetrad of solidity and so forth.
Because of the restriction to fourfold categories, the elements of earth, water, fire, and air are the four primary elements (*mahābhūta*) within the tangible element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*).
Smoothness and so forth, as well as the eye and other sense organs therein, are not primary elements.

Furthermore, because of the restriction to the characteristics of hardness and so forth, other phenomena such as the eye and others are not included within the elements of earth, water, fire, and air.
How so? There are four great elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
What is the earth element? It is solidity, and so forth.
"And because they are tangible. This means that those qualities, such as hardness and so forth, are tangibles,
since they are objects of touch.
But color-form and the other [objects] are to be seen, heard, smelled, and tasted.
How is it understood that they are also to be touched? To this he says:
For hardness and the other [characteristics] are not perceived by the eye and the other [faculties].
What then?
They are perceived by the body-faculty alone; therefore, it is understood that these are tangibles.
It might be your thought that color-form (*varṇa*) and so forth are also tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*); therefore, he says:
"Nor are color-form and so forth [perceived] by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
What [is perceived]?"
"They are grasped" is the subject under discussion.
And it has been stated in the Sūtra, and so forth;
it has also been clearly demonstrated in another Sūtra.
"How so?"—this is explained in detail up until this point:

"O Bhikṣu, tangible objects are an external sense-field; they consist of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements, being material, invisible, and offering resistance.
By this, it is clearly demonstrated that the remaining sense-fields, such as the eye and so forth, do not consist of the great elements.
As for what was stated in the Sūtra, and so forth:
the meaning is that which is hard, solid, and of a harsh nature within the fleshy lump of the eye;
they raise this objection because they consider the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) to have the nature of solidity.
This is a designation for the mass of flesh that exists inseparably from it;
that is to say, this statement refers to the physical basis (adhiṣṭhāna) which exists inseparably from the visual faculty (cakṣurindriya).
For indeed, the metaphorical designation "eye" is applied even to the physical basis of the eye.
For this very reason, there is the designation "a lump of flesh.
Otherwise, if it were intended to be the sense faculty itself, one would have simply said "the two eyes. As for the detailed passage: "O monk, this person consists of six elements," and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that because the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra* teaches only the primary elements (*bhūta*) during the stages such as the *kalala*, there is no derivative matter (*bhautika*), he says:
"For the purpose of demonstrating the fundamental substance of a sentient being.
This means precisely for the purpose of demonstrating the fundamental substance of a sentient being.
The four elements, beginning with the earth element, constitute the fundamental sentient being,
because the five bases of contact, such as the eye and so forth, arise from them.
The mind element (*manodhātu*) is also the fundamental sentient being, because the mind-base of contact (*manaḥ-sparśāyatana*) arises from it.
Alternatively, because the four elements beginning with earth serve as the support for derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*),
and because the consciousness element serves as the support for mental factors (*caitasika*), these alone constitute the fundamental sentient being (*mūlasattva*).
How is this known?
Furthermore, because of the mention of the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭsparśāyatana*).
In that very same sutra, it is stated later:
"The six bases of contact," namely, from the eye-base of contact up to the mind-base of contact.

Therefore, it is understood that the statement, "O monk, this person consists of six elements," is for the purpose of demonstrating the fundamental substance of a sentient being, and not because [the person] is merely the primary elements (*bhūta*).
But is it not the case that, although the sense-base of mental contact (*manaḥ-sparśāyatana*) is not distinct from the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), it is nevertheless mentioned again?
In this way, the eye and the other [faculties] might also be said to be non-different from the four elements.
Therefore, the existence of material entities distinct from those [elements] is not established by the repeated mention of the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭsparśāyatana*).
This is not so.
For if the earth element and so forth were themselves the bases of contact (*sparśāyatana*), he would have said simply that "the primary elements (*bhūta*) alone are the bases of contact.
But it is not so.
What then?
From the statement "the eye-sphere of contact up to the mind-sphere of contact," it is understood that the eye and the other [senses] are distinct from the earth element and the others.
The consciousness element (vijñānadhātu), however, is mentioned again in connection with the discussion of the sense bases of contact (sparśāyatana) beginning with the eye.
What is the meaning of "sense base of contact"?
It means the basis (āśraya) for contact, which is a mental factor (caitasika).
"And because it would follow that [the person] is merely a state of mind.
If, O monk, this person consisting of the six elements were to be perceived exactly as it is— as only those primary substances and not other substances dependent upon them—
then this consequence would follow.
Because of the mention of the consciousness-element alone, there follows the undesirable consequence that the mental factors, which depend upon it, are not included.
If it is argued that this is not a fault because such is intended, [we reply: no.
No,
because this position is subject to fault.
For this position is indeed faulty.
Because it would contradict your own established tenet that mental factors (*caitasika*) are nothing other than specific states of mind (*cittaviśeṣa*).
Therefore, he says:
"And it is not logical to accept that the mind itself is the mental factors."
Why?
Because of the scriptural statement: "Perception and feeling are mental factors; this phenomenon is dependent upon the mind.
And here, the formal proof (sādhana) applies as follows.
Perception and feeling are entities distinct from the mind,
because they are taught separately in the exposition of the aggregates,
just like the aggregate of form.
Alternatively, perception and feeling are entities distinct from their own basis,
because they depend upon it;
for whatever depends upon its own basis is an entity distinct from that basis.
It is, for example, like a painting supported by a wall.
Furthermore, because of the statement regarding a mind possessed of attachment and so forth:
"One understands as it really is, 'This is a mind possessed of attachment; this is a mind possessed of attachment.'"
"One understands as it really is a mind free from passion as 'a mind free from passion';
one understands as it really is a mind with hatred as 'a mind with hatred,'" and so forth.
Herein is the proof.
"In a mind with lust" (*sarāgaṃ cittaṃ*) indicates that the mind and lust are distinct entities from one another, because they are designated as being in a state of association (*sahayoga*).
This is like the designation "Caitra has a son," where Caitra and his son are designated as being in a state of association.
"Ten are accumulated" means that these ten alone have the nature of being an accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu*). By this restriction, it is established that the other elements are not accumulated.
(I.35) "It weighs" (*tulayati*): of which verbal root is this the form? For indeed, from the root *tula* meaning "to measure," the form becomes *tolayati*.
This is not a fault.

The forms *tulām karoti* and *tulayati* are accepted as derived from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) verbal root; and in the sense of the object (*karman*), the form *tulya* occurs. These constitute the four external roots.
Thus, form and the other [sensory objects], excluding sound, are designated as "axe" and "wood," respectively.
That which is designated as an axe and so forth cuts; that which is designated as wood and so forth is cut.
This is stated with reference to the possibility of occurrence:
sometimes that which is designated as an axe and so forth is cut,
and that which is designated as wood and so forth also cuts.
"Arising in connection," and so forth.
That which has the nature of arising (*utpāda*) without separation through connection (*saṃbandha*) is "arising in connection.
This means a stream of aggregation (*saṃghāta-srotas*), that is, a continuum (*saṃtāna*) of the aggregation of form and so forth.

The production of a division, which is the generation of a separation, is what constitutes "cutting. For momentary entities, cutting indeed occurs even without an axe or similar tools; however, it is through an axe or such means that the cessation of the continuum occurs.
It is said that an axe and so forth cut.
Due to the power of a specific collection of causes, a specific transformation arises.
In this regard, it is determined that the four elements either cut or are cut.
And because of such a restriction, it is established that other elements are neither [of these two types].
For this very reason, he says:
"The body-faculty and so forth are not cut," and so on in detail.

In this context, although one should have said "the eye-faculty and so forth," why is the expression "the body-faculty and so forth" used? Because the severance of the body-faculty is most manifest; therefore, the faculties are described as being headed by the body-faculty. This refers to the severance of all limbs without exception—that is, the severance of every major and minor limb.
Because of that non-dualization; that is, because of the non-dualization of those [faculties], such as the body-faculty (kāyendriya).
But how is it understood that there is this non-dualization?
Therefore, he says again:
For the sense-faculties do not become twofold, because a severed limb that has been separated from the body is devoid of sense-faculties.
How is this understood?
That a severed limb which has been separated from the body is devoid of sense-faculties.
Because, depending on that [body] and on tangibles and so forth, the cognitions of the body and so forth do not arise.
How then does the cognition of the body arise when the tip of the nose, having been severed, is joined again?
There is no fault here, because the body-faculty arises once more through its connection with the base of the nose.
How is it that here the tails of house-lizards and the like throb even when they have been cut off, if the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is not present there?
It should be understood that this is a transformation of the wind-element (*vāyudhātu*) and is not the activity of the body-faculty;
furthermore, they do not cut [the tail], because of its translucence, like the luster of a jewel.
Just as the luster of a gem does not cut because of its transparency,
so it is with the sense faculties. It is burned and weighed in this same manner.
By the word "thus" (*ity evam*), that same external fourfold set of elements (*dhātu*) is shown to be such [as described].
The transformation of wood and so forth caused by fire is "burning."
And yet, this does not apply to the sense-faculties because of their transparency, like the luster of a jewel.
For they do not undergo transformation like wood or like leather;
what then?
Through connection with that [body], the continuity of the stream is severed.
Furthermore, it is precisely those four elements—acting as the scale—that weigh [the object], and not the sense faculties, because they are likewise translucent (*acchatva*).
However, for the formless elements (*amūrta-dhātu*), because they are indeed formless, the severance of the stream and so forth is impossible.
For them, cutting and so forth are not considered. Why? Because sound is subject to cessation.
What [is it that is not considered]?
It cuts, is cut, burns, or is weighed because it exists as a continuous flow.
The dispute regarding the burner and the weighed object persists hereafter as well; [the Sāṃkhya claims] "sound is not [cut], because it is subject to destruction."
That same set of four elements is both that which burns and that which is weighed.
Fire, alkali, and so forth are "that which burns," because this entire set of four elements is the cause of transformations such as ash.
Salt and so forth are equivalent.
In that case as well, according to the opinion of some, it is because the whole [salt] is the cause of the bending of the scale;
thus, it is the fire element alone that is burned, and weight alone that is weighed.
Only the fire element (*tejodhātu*), when present in flames and the like and having its activity manifested, burns.
This is because we observe that even though the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*) and others possess their own manifested activities, they do not burn.
Furthermore, it is only the derived form (*upādāyarūpa*) of heaviness (*gurutva*) that is considered to have its activity manifested.

Because, even when color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities] are present in a manifest state within light substances such as sunlight, they are observed to be unequal [in their intensity].
(I.36, 37ab) "Five are internal" means:
The mention of "five" is for the purpose of excluding the mind.
The mention of "internal" is for the purpose of excluding visible form and so forth.
This is a restriction: the five internal [bases] are exclusively born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and accumulative (*aupacayika*), and not outflowing (*naiṣyandika*).
Why?
Because there is no outflow (*naiṣyandika*) apart from those [two].
Although that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and that which is accumulative (*aupacayika*) are not outflows, [the others are].
This is because an outflow (niṣyanda) is similar to its cause;
however, those [two] are subsumed solely under the categories of being born of maturation (vipākaja) and being accumulative (aupacayika).
They are not understood as being "outflow-produced" (*naiṣyandika*).
Rather, those which resemble their own causes and are neither born of maturation (*vipākaja*) nor accumulative (*aupacayika*),
these are intended here as "outflow-produced."
And such things as the eye and so forth are not like that;
rather, they are either born of maturation (*vipākaja*) or accumulative (*aupacayika*). Therefore it is said:
"because there is no outflow (*niṣyanda*) apart from those."
How, then, is it known that those [faculties] are not outflowing (*naiṣyandika*)? Because they do not persist after death.
For, unlike visible form and so forth, the eye-element and the others do not continue to exist in one who has died.
"Born from the ripening cause" means:
the cause of the fruit that is ripening is the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*). That which is born from the ripening cause is "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*).
It is due to the elision of the middle term, that is, the elision of the word "cause" (*hetu*), as in the case of "ox-cart" (*goratha*).

Just as a cart yoked with oxen is called an "ox-cart," so too is action (*karman*) that has reached the time of its fruition [called "fruit"]. Alternatively, it refers to action that has attained the time of its result.
The meaning is: existing in the moment immediately following the arising of the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
It is called *vipāka* because it matures; the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the agent being identical with the object (*karmakartṛ*).
"Born from maturation" (*vipākaja*) means born from maturation (*vipāka*).
Since "maturation" (*vipāka*) is simply the process of ripening (*vipakti*),
it is a *ghañ* derivative used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*).
Or let there be, as the detailed explanation states, a metaphorical designation of the fruit upon the cause;
even though its intrinsic nature is not maturation (*vipāka*), the cause characterized by karma is called "maturation" because it produces that [maturation].

"Just as the cause is applied to the fruit," and so forth. These six bases of contact (*sparśāyatana*), beginning with the eye, are "ancient karma" (*paurāṇaṃ karma*). Ancient karma means that which existed in a previous birth, or simply that which is ancient.
Although these bases of contact do not have the nature of ancient karma, they are nevertheless called "ancient karma."
Because it arises from that [cause].
In this context, the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of "the opposite" should be understood as follows:
those things accumulated by means of specific types of food, refinement, sleep, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are called "accumulative" (*aupacayika*).
The word "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is connected with each [term].
Among these, food and sleep are well-known in the world;
"formative activity" (*saṃskāra*) has the nature of anointing the body, bathing, applying oil, and so forth.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is characterized by one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
Accumulation (*upacaya*) is that which is gathered nearby. Those things existing in accumulation are "accumulative" (*aupacayika*), like soldiers.
Or rather, "accumulative" (*aupacayika*) means simply "accumulation" (*upacaya*), as in the case of the term *vainayika* [meaning "discipline" itself],
because a secondary derivative suffix is prescribed here in its own sense.
And some say, "[it is nourished] by celibacy."
Because we observe the physical growth of celibate practitioners whose sense faculties are tranquil;
however, by that [celibacy] there would be merely the absence of injury.
Through non-celibacy, there is the decay of the body.
However, through celibacy (*brahmacarya*), there is no depletion of the body. Therefore he says: by that celibacy there would be merely non-destruction, not growth.
Accumulation, however, occurs through food and so forth alone.
Why, then, does the deterioration of the body occur for some who have gone forth?
That [deterioration] must arise from being joined with the fever of desire and the like.
"Like a protective wall around a rampart.
This means that the continuity of accumulation (*upacaya-saṃtāna*) acts as a protection by surrounding the continuity of maturation (*vipāka-saṃtāna*).
Sound is accumulative (*aupacayika*), because one does not observe excellence of sound in a body that has not undergone accumulation.
"Because it proceeds from desire":
sound proceeds by the desire "May there be sound for me";
it does not proceed without desire.
Furthermore, a phenomenon born of maturation (vipākaja) proceeds even against the will [of the agent].
Therefore, sound is not born of maturation.
And here, the proof is stated:
Sound is not born of maturation,
because it proceeds from volition,
like the mental factor of appropriate attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
As for that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
its activity does not proceed by one's own will,
just as, for example, in the case of the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
"If that is so," and so forth.
By this, he points out the contradiction with his own established tenet (*svasiddhānta*) in the proposition.
"This third succession is one," and so forth.
The primary elements (bhūta) that constitute the nature of the maturation (vipāka) of the path of action consisting in abstention from harsh speech arise in the throat; from these, sound is produced.
According to the second position as well, the primary elements born of maturation arise from the actions themselves.

From those [great elements], there arise the accumulative great elements, either through the accumulation of nutriment or through the accumulation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). From those, there arise the outflowing (*naiṣyandika*) great elements, which are adventitious (*āgantuka*) and distinct from the preceding great elements.
From those, sound arises.
However, with reference to its production through a continuous succession, it is stated that from the abstention from harsh speech, the quality of possessing the voice of Brahmā is produced.
By this, the contradiction of that proposition with one's own established tenet is avoided;
for if it were like sound [produced instantaneously], there would be a conflict with reason.
Sound is said not to be born of maturation because it arises from desire, which contradicts the logic of maturation.
If, like that [sound], bodily sensation also arose from desire, it would not be born of maturation;
however, it does not arise from desire.
What then?
It proceeds even without desire,
like the eye and other sense organs.
Therefore, the intention is that it is logical to say it is "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
What, then, is it like?
It is that which proceeds even without the application of conditions for pleasure or pain.
"Outflowing [dharmas] are those produced by the similar-cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive-cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
This is a restrictive definition meaning that they are produced by the similar-cause and the pervasive-cause alone, and not by the ripening-cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
"Ripening-born [dharmas] are those produced by the ripening-cause."
The restriction is that they are produced by a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), but not produced by a ripening cause alone;
for they are also produced by a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and are thus "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*).
Among those, eight are non-obstructive and are outflowing results (*naiṣyandika*).
It is restricted to being "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) alone.
For these are not "accumulative" (*aupacayika*), because there is no accumulation; the meaning is that they do not have the nature of an accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
"Only three grains":
it is restricted to exactly three grains.
In this regard, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are necessarily inseparable from the sense faculties (*indriya*),
because it is stated that "maturation is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomenon belonging to sentient beings."
However, those that are outflowing (*naiṣyandika*) and accumulative (*aupacayika*) may also be dissociated from the sense faculties (*indriya-vinirbhāgin*).
How, then,
is it known that there are outflowing [atoms] even when they are dissociated from the sense faculties?
Because it is observed to continue even after death;
for those [factors] reckoned as non-sentient are not admitted to be born of maturation (*vipākaja*);
[it is] substantial and singular.
Thus,
there is the restriction that "only one possesses substance.
It is called "substance" (dravya) because of its essentiality (sāratva), that is, because of its indestructibility.
"They exist for one moment without being outflow" means that they are produced by a non-homogeneous cause (*asabhāga-hetu*) for a single moment.
Since there is no preceding moment of the untainted (*anāsrava*), they are momentary; however, the intended meaning here is that they do not perish at another subsequent moment.
Otherwise, because of the restriction that only the final elements are momentary, it would follow as a logical consequence that all other elements are non-momentary.

But how can the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu) exist simultaneously within the complex of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti)?
For the coexistence of two consciousnesses is not admitted.
It is not said that those two exist simultaneously.
What then?
In this case, a single consciousness is established as being twofold in terms of its constituent elements (*dhātu*).
The meaning is that it is described by two names.
Therefore, he explains: "The mind associated with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering is the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu);
the remaining factors co-arising with it are the dharma-element (dharmadhātu)."

In that group of factors consisting of patience (*kṣānti*), the remaining factors other than the mind itself are those co-arising with it; that is, they arise simultaneously with that patience. These are as follows: untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) as form (*rūpa*), and the associated mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.

And for these, possession (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth constitute the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). (I.37cd) "One acquires possession" means that one acquires a possession not previously acquired.
"By means of the visual consciousness element as well, he [does so].
What?
It is understood that "he acquires possession."
By the phrase "separate acquisition," the first and second alternatives are shown;
and also [the phrase] "together."
By this, the third alternative (koṭi) has been shown.
As for the fourth, it is not shown because it is easily understood as being "excluded from those mentioned. And—
Or it is also stated by way of sound:
"not separate" and "not together.
This refers to one who gradually acquires the eye-faculty within the desire realm.
A person situated in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)— whether in the gradual sequence of the embryo (*kalala*, etc. or in the sequence of death—
is associated with what regarding the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*)?
Is it only in the desire realm?
No, it is said;
without distinction, one who is acquiring [the dharma] associated with either the desire realm or the form realm.
In the stages such as the *kalala* and so forth, as well as at the time of death and at the time of "blind" death, one is not possessed of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
This is because that [element] is absent during the stages such as the *kalala* or at the stage of death.
At the stage of the arising of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) or in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one now acquires possession of it through that [eye-element].

But it is not the case that one who was previously unendowed with the visual consciousness element attains such endowment [at that time]. This is because he was already endowed with the past and future wholesome and afflicted [consciousness] at the time of rebirth-linking in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
For this refers to a state of being separated [from the present], and not a state of having already attained or about to attain [it].
"By means of the eye-consciousness element," and so forth.

One who has been reborn in the second dhyāna or above lacks that eye-consciousness element there; having previously not possessed it, he now acquires possession of that eye-consciousness belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, which is by nature unobstructed and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
Thus, he obtains possession of that eye-consciousness element.
But one who was not previously endowed with the eye-element does not acquire its endowment [at that time],
because it is already possessed as if already acquired;
and having fallen from that state, one is reborn below.

One who has fallen from the second dhyāna or higher and is being reborn below—in the first dhyāna or in the desire realm—attains possession of the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) with which they were previously unendowed.
This occurs through the wholesome or afflicted [visual consciousness] of the past and future at the moment of linking existence (*pratisaṃdhi*) in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
However, one does not attain possession of the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*) with which one was previously unendowed.
Because of being both acquired and possessed.
"It may be by both," and so forth.
One who has passed away from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) was previously non-possessed of both the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) and the eye-consciousness-element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu).

At the very moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one acquires possession (*samanvāgama*) of the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)—whether wholesome or afflicted—that is about to arise, even though it is past or future.
This is because those in the intermediate state possess unimpaired faculties.
"Neither" refers to excluding these aforementioned modes.
The meaning is: having abandoned the categories of phenomena mentioned in the three millions.

One who dies in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in that very same realm is not "endowed with" both [the possession and the non-possession] in such a way that he acquires possession; for while there is non-possession there, there is no acquisition of possession.
Furthermore, one born in the second dhyāna or above, who does not manifest eye-consciousness, does not acquire possession of both [the eye-organ and eye-consciousness] when previously lacking it.
How so?
Although he acquires possession of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), he was not previously devoid of the eye-element.
Although one who lacks the visual consciousness element does not acquire its possession (*samanvāgama*), it is because he does not bring it into manifestation.
A sighted person dwelling in the desire realm, through death and the subsequent linking of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), does not simultaneously lack both and acquire their possession,
because he already possesses them.
"One who is endowed with the eye-element is also endowed with the eye-consciousness-element.
By this very sutra, which states "attainment both separately and together," he also formulates this fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
For "acquisition" (lābha) is indeed "attainment" (pratilambha).
However, depending on the speaker's intention, it sometimes refers merely to "possession" (prāpti).
In the first tetrad, attainment is intended; in the second, however, it is mere possession.
"The first alternative," and so forth in detail.
One born in the second or higher dhyānas is necessarily endowed with the eye-element because of the completeness of his faculties;
however, he is not here endowed with the eye-consciousness-element.
Because it does not exist there;
because visual consciousness belonging to the level of the first dhyāna is not being manifested [in that realm];
and because one has either not yet acquired or has lost the eye in the desire realm.
"One whose eye is unobtained or lost" refers to one who has not obtained the eye or whose eye has been lost.
One who has not obtained the eye is in a stage such as the *kalala* (embryonic stage) and so forth;
one whose eye is lost is one whose eye has perished.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), at the moment of linking existence (*antarābhava-pratisandhi*), he is endowed with the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)— which has been acquired and is either wholesome or afflicted—
but not with the visual faculty element (*cakṣurdhātu*), because that [faculty] does not exist [at that stage].
This refers to one who has acquired and not lost the visual faculty.
"One who has obtained and not lost the eye" is one whose eye has been acquired and not lost.
Such a person is endowed with the eye-element and the eye-consciousness-element in the desire realm—both of which were previously acquired and are now present as neutral (avyākṛta).
Furthermore, one born in the first dhyāna is endowed with both of these.
Because that which belongs to its own level necessarily exists there, and because an eye belonging to another level is possible;
and for one born in the second dhyāna or above who is seeing—
this means he is manifesting an eye-consciousness belonging to the level of the first dhyāna.
And he too is necessarily endowed with both of these.
The fourth case is "having set aside these modes," which refers to one reborn in the formless realm (ārūpya).
"They should be inferred according to what is appropriate" means:
he who possesses the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and acquires its possession also possesses the form-element (*rūpadhātu*);
or he who possesses the form-element also possesses the eye-element.
The eye element and the form element may be acquired separately as well as together. First, [the case of] separate acquisition:
There may be one who is endowed with the eye-element but not with the form-element:
namely, one who is gradually acquiring the eye-faculty in the desire realm.
There may be the case of possessing the form element (*rūpadhātu*) but not the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*); this alternative does not exist.
It may also be the case that one who was previously unendowed with both now acquires their possession.
One who, having passed away from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), is reborn in the form realm (rūpadhātu) or the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
[The case] of neither [possessing both] is set aside by excluding these modes.
One who is endowed with the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) is also endowed with the form-element (rūpadhātu); this is the first alternative (pūrvapādaka).
First, one who is endowed with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is also endowed with the form-element (*rūpadhātu*).

However, there may be one who is endowed with the form-element but not with the eye-element—such as those in the embryonic stages of the *kalala* and so forth, or those who have not yet acquired the eye, or those who have lost the eye they previously acquired.
Furthermore, one who, being previously unendowed with the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), acquires its endowment, also acquires the form-element.
Or, whoever who was previously not endowed with the form element (rūpadhātu) attains such endowment, does he also attain endowment with the eye-consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu)?
In that same way, there may be the acquisition of these two either separately or together.
First, regarding the distinction:
there may be possession of the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) without the form element (*rūpadhātu*).
This is the case for one born in the second dhyāna or higher who is bringing eye-consciousness into manifestation.
There may be [the acquisition] of the form element (rūpadhātu) but not of the eye-consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu).
This occurs when one dies from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and is reborn in the second or higher meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
It may also occur simultaneously.
There may be one who, being previously unendowed with both, acquires their possession:
namely, one who dies in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and is reborn in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or in the Brahma-world (brahmaloka).
There may be one who is neither.
Setting aside these cases:
one who is endowed with the eye-consciousness element is also endowed with the form element;
or, one who is endowed with the form element is also endowed with the eye-consciousness element.
The first alternative:
