whoever is endowed with the element of eye-consciousness is also endowed with the element of visible form.
There may, however, be one who is endowed with the element of visible form but not with the element of eye-consciousness.
One born in the second or higher dhyānas who does not manifest visual consciousness [is an example].
Just as this reflection on the acquisition and possession of the eye-consciousness and the form-element has been conducted,
so too should the reflection on the acquisition and possession of the ear-consciousness, the sound-element, and so forth be carried out.
"There may be the separate acquisition of the ear-element and the auditory-consciousness-element, as well as their simultaneous acquisition," and so forth.
(1.38ab) "Twelve are internal.
This is a restriction of both [terms].
By this very restriction, it is established that others, such as form (rūpa) and so forth, are external.
"Internal" (adhyātma) means within the self (ātmani),
or alternatively, that which pertains to the self (ātmānam) is internal.
Those which are internal are *ādhyātmika*.
Or, those that exist within the internal (*adhyātma*) are *ādhyātmika*.

Because it is the basis for the notion of "I," the mind (*citta*) is metaphorically designated as the "self" (*ātman*); thus, proponents of a self (*ātmavādinaḥ*) conceive of the basis of the notion of "I" as being the self.
And because the mind is the basis for the notion of "I," it is metaphorically designated as the "self.
To the question "How so? he says:
"For by means of a well-tamed self, the wise man attains heaven."
Thus it is stated in the verse.
But how is it understood that "mind" is expressed by the word "self"? To this he says:
And it has been stated by the Blessed One elsewhere that there is the taming of the mind. It is said in another verse:
"The taming of the mind is good; a tamed mind brings happiness."
Thus, this is the meaning:
with respect to the self— that which is to be made conscious— or with respect to the mind itself, those dharmas that exist as a basis due to their state of proximity.
Those which exist as internal are the internal;
however, those which exist as objects are the external.
What, then, is this state of proximity by which consciousness conforms to their transformation?
For it is in the eye and other [faculties] that consciousness is observed, not in visible form and the other [objects]. (Abhidh-k-vy 75)
For in this way, the mind is delimited within the region of the body connected to the sense faculties, and not within the region of the objects.
If that is so, then regarding the detailed explanation of the "six consciousness-elements":
here, first of all, the five consciousness-elements are understood as being exclusively present.
Because they are simultaneous with their respective sense-faculties and objects.
For the five groups of consciousness have present objects, and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) is also established here as being only present.
This is because its basis, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), is established as having just passed away in the immediately preceding moment.
For it is precisely due to the difference in time that the element of mind (*manodhātu*) and the element of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*) are established as distinct.
Therefore, they do not qualify as internal.
Indeed, these [mental factors] cannot serve as the support of the mind unless they have attained the state of the mind-element and have attained the state of being past.

"When it is so, they remain those very same things; thus, they do not transcend their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). What is established by this statement? This is what is established by it: [that] they do not transcend their defining characteristic.
Even for those [elements] that are present, there will be the state of being a basis; thus, their status as internal arises by virtue of their future state of being a basis.
Or else, "of the future and the present," and so forth:
that which has the characteristic of the mind-element (manodhātu) in the past time.
The intended meaning is that this [characteristic] certainly exists even in the future and present time-periods (*adhvan*).
For there is no deviation of a characteristic across the time-periods;
the meaning is that there is no abandonment of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
(I.38cd) "That which is designated as 'dharma' is sabhāga.
This is a restrictive determination meaning that what is designated as 'dharma' is exclusively sabhāga.
For whatever object is fixed for a particular consciousness—
just as visible form is the fixed object of visual consciousness, up to mental phenomena being the fixed object of mental consciousness—
if, in that case, that visual consciousness has arisen or is subject to arising.
As long as the mental consciousness has arisen there, or is destined to arise,
that object is said to be "homogeneous" (sabhāga). And [the factors] of that [consciousness], excluding its own nature and its co-existent [factors], are [also homogeneous].
"Free from their own intrinsic nature and from that which co-exists with it" means free from both intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and co-existent factors (*sahabhū*).
All phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are the objective support (*ālambana*) for that consciousness; its own intrinsic nature is not.
Because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself.
Indeed, that very tip of a finger cannot be touched by that same fingertip;
nor can that very edge of a sword be cut by that same sword-edge.
They are not coexistent,
whether associated or dissociated,
because of their extreme proximity.
For eye-salve situated in the eye is not perceived by it.
Furthermore, that moment of consciousness becomes the object (*ālambana*) for another moment of consciousness—
those factors (*dharma*) which were co-existent with its own nature in the preceding moment but were not previously taken as objects.
Since those [dharmas] are also taken as objects, all dharmas become the object of the two moments [of consciousness].
Therefore, the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) is always homogeneous (sabhāga).
For the dharma-element is restricted exclusively to the mind.
And the remaining [dharmas] are "similar-to-that" (tatsabhāga).
By the word "and" (ca), it is meant that they are also "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
It is thus determined that only the remaining [dharmas] are both homogeneous and similar-to-that.

But surely, if it were restricted by the statement that "only the dharma-element is homogeneous (sabhāga)," then it would follow that the remaining elements are not homogeneous, and thus they would be established as both homogeneous and partially homogeneous (tatsabhāga).
They are not so established;
for even if it were the case that they are simply not homogeneous, [they would still not be established as such].
They might, however, be considered as exclusively "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
To prevent this [misconception], the following is undertaken:
"The remaining [elements] are indeed both homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and partially homogeneous (*tatsabhāga*)."

It is not that they are exclusively homogeneous (*sabhāga*), nor are they exclusively non-homogeneous (*tatsabhāga*). One should connect this by stating: "that which does not perform its own function is non-homogeneous."
"And those that are similar to them" (tatsabhāgāḥ). Because they were mentioned immediately prior, it follows that this has been stated.
"One who performs its own function is *sabhāga*.

By the restrictive sense—"only one who does not perform its own function is *tatsabhāga*, or only a *tatsabhāga* is one who does not perform its own function"—it follows by implication that "one who performs its own function is *sabhāga*.
[The phrase] "he saw forms" [is used].
It should be stated that "he saw.
For in this way, both the past of today and the past of yesterday are included;
otherwise, the definition would be non-comprehensive.
Now, this very reading should be understood as merely an illustration;
that which pertains to the present and the past must also be stated.
In this manner, it should be stated for each faculty up to the mind (manas) according to its own activity regarding its respective object.
It must be stated according to its own objective human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
How so?
By means of that ear through which one has heard, hears, or will hear sounds.
Thus it is said that "the ear is homogeneous" (sabhāga), meaning all of it;
"conjoined with consciousness" (vijñānasamāyukta) and "not conjoined" (asamāyukta) means connected with consciousness and disconnected from it.
Is that which is homogeneous for one person's eye [also] so for all?
The term "homogeneous" (sabhāga) continues to apply here, meaning that what is "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) for one is likewise partially homogeneous for all.
The meaning is that whatever is the partially homogeneous eye of one person is the partially homogeneous [eye] for everyone.
"Because of the mention of 'attained' (prāpta)" refers to odors and so forth;
those very [objects] which are grasped by Devadatta when they have reached the sense organs, such as the nose.
They are not grasped by Yajñadatta because they have entered into his own nose and other faculties;
thus, due to their specific (asādhāraṇa) nature, it is logical to extend [the analysis] to them just as in the case of the eye and so forth.
Whatever odor is homogeneous for one [person], it is so for all;
in the same way, its "homogeneous counterpart" (tatsabhāga) should also be described.
But it should not be said that "as with form, so too with odor and the rest.
For there is this possibility: those very same odors and the rest might produce olfactory consciousness and so forth for one person, and yet produce them for others as well.
If those [objects] were to reach the sense faculties, such as the nose, of Evadatta, they would produce consciousness in Evadatta;
or else, if they were to reach the sense faculties of Yajñadatta, they would produce consciousness in Yajñadatta—this is the meaning.
Alternatively, "those very same [objects] belong to others as well."
In that case, they would also produce consciousness in the minute insects and so forth contained therein,
and not only in that very Devadatta to whose olfactory and other sense faculties those odors and so forth have reached.
This is because there is a mutual dependence among the sense faculties, their objects, and the consciousnesses.
Activity occurs through mutual orientation by way of the relationship between the basis, the object, and that which depends upon the basis.
For instance, the sense-element bases (indriya-dhātu) serve as the basis for the consciousness-element bases (vijñāna-dhātu), according to their respective applications;
that is to say, they attend to them.
And they [the sense faculties] relate to the object-elements by way of being their possessors.
Likewise, the object-elements relate to their own respective faculty-elements by way of being objects.
However, they relate to the consciousness-elements by way of being objects or by way of being focal points (*ālambana*).
Likewise, the consciousness elements partake of their own respective sense-faculty elements by way of being their supported entities;
and they partake of the object-elements either by way of being the subject or by way of being the apprehender. Thus, "part" (bhāga) refers to this mutual partaking.
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of a state (*bhāva*).
Alternatively, a "portion" (*bhāga*) is that which partakes in activity (*kāritra*).
The activity of the eye and the other [faculties] consists of seeing and so forth.
The state of being a cognizer belongs to the elements of consciousness;
the state of being their respective objects of focus belongs to the elements of the objects.
The "partaking of activity" (kāritrabhajana) is the partaking in that activity.
The meaning is that he possesses these.
This is merely an illustration; however, the analysis of the compound should be constructed as follows.

They are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) because they exist together with a portion (*bhāga*). Alternatively, their portion is common (*samāna*); thus, these are the homogeneous ones. The substitution of *sa-* for the word *saha* when it has the sense of "common" has been prescribed [by grammatical rule].
Or because they have the same effect as contact. What? It is "homogeneous" that is under discussion.

In this case, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). It is called a "portion" (*bhāga*) because it is divided (*bhajyate*); however, the analysis of the compound is as before.
Contact is a mental factor;
it is the common effect of these—the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness.
Depending upon the eye and visible forms, visual consciousness arises.
Because of the statement, "The coming together of the three is contact," and so forth. As for the detailed explanation of those which are "non-homogeneous" (*asabhāga*):
those other [faculties] such as the eye and so on which are non-homogeneous in this manner.
Of those [elements] that are "homogeneous" (sabhāga) as defined by their previously stated characteristics, those that are "homogeneous," meaning similar,
are "tatsabhāga" (of the same class).
Alternatively, those that are homogeneous with respect to them, or by means of them, are "tatsabhāga."
For here, the word "sabhāga" (homogeneous) is taken in the sense of "equal. Regarding the phrase "to be abandoned by seeing":
"seeing" refers to the initial vision of the truths, which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and comprised of fifteen moments of consciousness.
Cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the repeated seeing of that very same [object];
or, cultivation is mundane concentrated knowledge (*samāhita-jñāna*). Ten [defilements] are to be abandoned by cultivation, as are five.
"The material elements are ten and five, as are their respective consciousness-elements.
But how is it known that these [elements] are precisely those?
Because of the statement, "The last three are of three kinds," it is said that those other than the last three are indeed the fifteen elements (dhātus).
It is determined that these are to be abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
"Of three kinds" means: those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*), those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), and those not to be abandoned (*aheya*).
These very same [factors] are the eighty-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) together with their co-existent factors.

The latent dispositions—such as the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth—which are differentiated by realm, type, and aspect; their co-existent factors, whether associated (saṃprayukta) or dissociated (asaṃprayukta), such as consciousness, feeling, and so forth; their primary characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa); and their acquisitions (prāpti) along with their attendants (sānucara)—[these constitute the eighty-eight].

By that word [“those”], the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth are connected. The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of those latent dispositions and of their co-existent factors are “their acquisitions” (*tatprāptayaḥ*).
Even though they are co-existent with the latent dispositions, [they are so designated].
But not all [possessions].
For some possessions are co-nascent with the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and so forth, being simultaneous with them;
others, however, exist before or after them. Therefore, possession is mentioned separately.
By the inclusion of the phrase "together with their attendants," their acquisitions (*anuprāpti*) and their characteristics (*tallakṣaṇa*) are also subsumed.

"The remaining contaminated [factors] are to be abandoned by cultivation" means that these very same three final realms, which are other than those [factors] to be abandoned by seeing, are the remaining contaminated ones.
These are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Which ones, then?
The ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya), their co-existent factors, and their acquisitions (prāpti), together with their attendants.
Wholesome contaminated [phenomena],
unobscured-neutral conditioned phenomena,
and contaminated non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) together with their attendants.
"Untainted and not to be abandoned" means having the nature of the truth of the path and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
But as for the detailed explanation "is there not also another [category]?"—

the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is included among those things to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), because its nature consists of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) that are non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Furthermore, bodily and vocal action leading to the miserable destinies (*apāya*) has been stated to be abandonable by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is form (*rūpa*).
For this reason, the Vātsīputrīyas raise an objection:
[it must be so] because it is contrary to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).

The state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) does not exist when the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) arises. Furthermore, when there is karma leading to the miserable destinies (*apāyika*), the Noble Path does not arise;
yet, when the Noble Path has arisen, karma leading to the miserable destinies does not arise.
Therefore, they explain that both of these, like the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, are to be abandoned by insight (*darśanaheya*).
Although this has already been stated for the purpose of refuting that [position],
it is stated once more in summary for the sake of easy comprehension.
That which is non-afflicted, nor form, nor born of the sixth [consciousness], is not to be abandoned by vision.
Vision is seeing. That which is non-afflicted—meaning either unobscured-neutral or wholesome—is not to be abandoned by vision.
Form, however, even when afflicted, is not to be abandoned by insight.
That which is not born of the sixth [consciousness], but is born of the five sense faculties— the fivefold consciousness— even if it is afflicted, is not to be abandoned by insight.
But other [states] can indeed be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*), as has been stated:

"And the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) is undefiled-neutral (*akliṣṭa-avyākṛta*), because even those who have severed their roots of virtue (*samucchinnakuśalamūla*) and those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*) still possess it. It is accepted that those who have severed their roots of virtue are not possessed of virtuous factors (*kuśalair dharmair asamanvāgatāḥ*).
However, they are endowed with the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*),
because it is precisely on account of this that they are considered ordinary persons.
Therefore, the state of being an ordinary person is not wholesome.
Nor is that [attainment] defiled,
because even those free from passion possess it;
for it is held that a defiled entity is abandoned by its very nature.
"Severance of attainment" means abandonment.

If that state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were defiled (*kliṣṭa*), then for those who have attained detachment from the world through mundane paths, there would be a severance of its attainment, and thus they would no longer be possessed of it. Yet, it is accepted that they are indeed possessed of it.
For it is held that those who are free from passion in the world are indeed ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
There is no fault in [their being] of one nature as unafflicted and neutral (*akliṣṭavyākṛta*).
The abandonment of desire and lust (*chandarāga*) is held to pertain to the unafflicted.

The meaning is the severance of the possession (*prāpti*) of the afflictions that have that [object] as their objective support; however, the severance of the possession of those [afflictions] belonging to oneself is not intended.
For thus it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, whatever desire and lust there is for form..."
"Abandon that!
In this way, that form of yours becomes abandoned," and so forth.
Therefore, although the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*)—which is undefiled and neutral—is abandoned for them, it still manifests like the eye and other faculties.
Therefore, one is endowed with it.
What, then, is the reason?
Because it is non-defiled and neutral, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is not to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
And because they possess the nature of form (*rūpatva*), he says that bodily and vocal actions [are included].
Because there is no misconception regarding the truths,
and because they are not defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*), the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) does not involve misconceiving the truths such as suffering (*duḥkha*).
The meaning is that it does not proceed in a perverted manner.
Furthermore, because it lacks an objective referent (*anālambakatva*),
even the actions of body and speech do not go astray precisely because they lack an objective referent.
Therefore, both of those are not to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Furthermore, this reason—"because there is no misconception regarding the truths"—should be applied even to that which is not born of the sixth [consciousness].
And because, if it were so, there would follow the consequence of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) during the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

This "cause of accumulation" (*upacayahetu*) is stated specifically for the purpose of precluding the view-eliminated nature of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), because bodily and vocal actions do not [directly] connect with it.
At the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), the acquisition of the state of being an ordinary person is severed;
however, it is not yet destroyed, just like the acquisition of the afflictions to be abandoned by that [receptivity].
For it is stated that "the path, as it is ceasing, abandons its obscuration";
however, in the case of the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering, the acquisition of that [obscuration] is severed.

Because that [attainment] exists, that person would be an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*) during the stage of the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Yet, it cannot be established that he is an ordinary worldling at that stage, because he has realized the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
For what, then, is "ordinariness" (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
The non-attainment of the noble dharmas is the characteristic of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
That non-attainment is reversed by the attainment of the noble dharmas;
therefore, such a person is indeed a noble one (*ārya*).
First, venerable Vaibhāṣikas, you should be asked this:
is that state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) abandoned solely through the attainment of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
It is said: "No."
That state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) belongs to nine stages, ranging from the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Furthermore, it is non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).
It is abandoned at the stage of abandoning the ninth category of afflictions for each respective stage.
For all undefiled but outflowing (sāsrava) states are abandoned precisely in the ninth path of liberation (vimuktimārga).
If this were so, then an noble one (ārya) would be an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) during the state of not yet being free from passion.
This is not the case.
Because the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) has been abandoned.
For from the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), that state is indeed abandoned,
but it is not yet relinquished.

What, then, is the distinction between abandonment (*vihāni*) and relinquishment (*prahāṇa*)? Abandonment is established as the severance of possession (*prāpti*), whereas relinquishment is established as the acquisition of the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*).

Therefore, because of the severance of that acquisition and because of the non-possession of that state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), at that stage one is indeed a noble one (*ārya*) and not an ordinary person; thus, there is no fault in this. (I.40, 41) Furthermore, the eye and a portion of the *dharmadhātu* constitute "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Thus, it is determined that the eye itself— and specifically a portion of the dharma-element— is "view," namely,
the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth.

They are the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of grasping at extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), false view (mithyādṛṣṭi), adherence to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), and adherence to rites and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
For a learner (śaikṣa), it is "untainted" (anāsrava) wisdom; for one beyond learning (aśaikṣa), it is "beyond-learning" (aśaikṣī) wisdom. This is what is intended.
The untainted wisdom of one beyond training is "the wisdom of one beyond training.
It should be stated that this excludes the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising; for he will say:
"The cognition of destruction and non-arising is not vision.

This is explained in detail as "with clouds and without clouds," up to: "the seeing of phenomena by means of views that are defiled or undefiled, mundane or belonging to those in training or beyond training."
That which exists in the world is worldly (*laukikī*).
It is both afflicted (*kliṣṭā*) and unafflicted (*akliṣṭā*), thus [it is] "afflicted and unafflicted.
And this [wisdom] is both afflicted and unafflicted, and it is also worldly.

It is the mundane, whether afflicted or non-afflicted; and it is the mundane, whether afflicted or non-afflicted, as well as that of the learner (*śaikṣī*) and that of the one beyond learning (*aśaikṣī*). Through these—the mundane, whether afflicted or non-afflicted, and those of the learner and the one beyond learning—there is the vision of phenomena (*dharmadarśana*).
To the question "Of what kind? he says:
"Like the perception of forms on a cloudy night and during the day.
This means, for example, the perception of forms on a cloudy night.
Thus, the vision of phenomena through an afflicted worldly view, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
is even more indistinct; the meaning is that it is like the perception of forms on a cloudless night during that very same period.
Thus, the vision of phenomena through an undefiled worldly view is indistinct; this is the meaning. It is like the perception of forms on a cloudy day.
Thus, by means of the vision of one in training (śaikṣa), there is a seeing of phenomena (dharmadarśana) that is clear, yet not excessive,
just like the perception of forms on a cloudless day.
In this way, the vision of phenomena occurs through the vision of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī dṛṣṭi*).
The meaning is that it is exceedingly clear; [it is so called] because of the absence of deliberation (*atīraṇāt*).
Thus, because there is no investigation (*asaṃtīraṇa*).
Investigation, moreover, is the drawing forth of certainty preceded by close contemplation of the object.
For this very reason, it is said "and others as well," and so forth.

For this very reason— because it does not involve investigation (*asaṃtīraṇa*)— other mental wisdom (*mānasī prajñā*), whether afflicted (*kliṣṭā*) and associated with attachment and so forth, or non-afflicted (*akliṣṭā*) such as the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), or even the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛtā*), is not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
As for the phrase "in the sense of perceiving form," the eye is not a "view" by virtue of its being an investigator.
What then? It is for the purpose of observing form;
it is thus shown that wisdom (prajñā), however, functions by way of investigation.
"One who possesses another consciousness" means a person for whom another consciousness is manifest,
that is, one who is occupied with another consciousness.
[Such a person] might see by means of the visual faculty due to the proximity of the object and other conditions.
However, for one who holds the position that visual consciousness sees,
there is no fault, because such consciousness is impossible [independently];
let it be that the consciousness itself, supported by the eye, sees.
Because visual perception exists when that [object] exists and does not exist when it is absent; for it is said,
"Visible form is indeed not seen when it is obstructed"— the word "indeed" (*kila*) indicates the opinion of another school.
"Because it is non-obstructive.
Consciousness, being formless, would see even by passing through walls and the like.
The proponent of consciousness (vijñānavādin) says this.
For visual consciousness does not arise at all when [the object] is obstructed; the intention is that this is because the object has not come into the range of appearance (*anābhāsagatatvāt*).

What then does not arise? The sense is that, because [consciousness] is non-obstructive (*apratighatvāt*), it would arise with respect to an object as if it were not separated by walls and the like, having pierced through those walls and so forth.
"But for one who... [refers to the following].

For me, the Vaibhāṣika, whose position is that "the eye sees," because that eye is characterized by resistance (*sapratighatva*), there is an absence of activity with respect to what is obstructed by walls and the like; for that eye,
there is an absence of the activity of visual perception.
Anticipating the objection that, according to the Vaibhāṣika, consciousness would then reach even what is obstructed, that same Vaibhāṣika replies:
"There is likewise no arising of consciousness.

Just as it is logical that the functioning of the eye is absent when there is an obstruction, so too is the non-arising of consciousness—meaning the absence of the functioning of consciousness—logical, because consciousness functions upon its basis (the sense organ) directed toward the same object.
For if that very object which is obstructed from the eye were to be the object of consciousness,
then it would be logical that consciousness also does not arise.
But for you, the Vijñānavādin, because consciousness is non-obstructive, consciousness would arise even with respect to an obstructed object.
But it does not arise [as a seer].
Therefore, it is established that the eye sees, not consciousness.
When the proponent of consciousness (vijñānavādin) has thus been refuted, the Master, adopting his position, says:
"Is it not the case that the eye has an object that must be reached? and so forth.
Just as the body-faculty has an object that must be reached and does not grasp an object obstructed by a wall or the like due to the resistance of the wall and such, [so too would the eye].
Because it is unable to proceed beyond that point.

Is it then the case that the eye, having reached its object, fails to perceive an object obscured by a wall or the like because it is obstructed by the resistance of the wall and so forth, and thus unable to go beyond it?
This is not tenable.
Therefore, one should not say that the eye does not see what is obstructed because it possesses resistance (sapratighatva).
[If that were so], how is it that things separated by glass, clouds, films, crystal, or water are seen?
How is a form seen when it is screened or obstructed by glass, a layer of clouds, crystal, or water?

For, according to the established tenet, the eye—being characterized by resistance (*sapratighatva*)—should not see what is obstructed by glass and the like, just as it does not see what is obstructed by walls and such; yet it does see it.
This is because there is no obstruction of light in those cases.
For when there is light, the object comes into range of appearance, and thus the arising of consciousness is possible.
Indeed, this is how the cause of consciousness is taught:
the visual faculty must be unimpaired.

The object comes into the range of appearance, and the mental impulse (*manasāra*) produced by it becomes present; therefore, when a form is obstructed by glass or similar substances, visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) indeed arises there. However, where there is an obstruction by walls or the like—which possess a nature unlike that of glass and are characterized by darkness—it does not arise when the object is thus concealed.
What?
It is visual consciousness. Because it has not yet arisen, being obstructed, it does not see.
As for your question, "What indeed does not arise?"—since you have asked for the cause of its non-arising, we say that this is its cause.
Regarding what was stated in the Sūtra, and so forth:
"Having seen forms with the eye, one does not grasp at their signs (nimitta), nor does one grasp at their secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana)," and so on.
Since the eye sees, the intention is that the person sees by means of the eye. The Teacher said:
"By means of that basis"—this is the intended meaning here.
The intended meaning is simply "relying on the eye.
The sense is: "having seen by means of the consciousness which has the eye as its basis."
How is this known? He says:
"Just as one cognizes phenomena with the mind.
This means that by means of the mind—that is, by means of consciousness which serves as the basis—one cognizes.
For the mind that has just passed away does not cognize mental objects (*dharma*).
It is during its present state that consciousness performs its activity;
or rather, the action of the dependent is metaphorically attributed to the support.
The activity of the supported consciousness— namely, seeing— is metaphorically attributed to the supporting eye.
When it is the consciousness that sees, there is the metaphorical expression "the eye sees," just as one says "the benches are shouting."
Just as when men sitting on a platform are shouting, there is the figurative expression that "the platforms are shouting," so it is here.
And as it is stated in the Sūtra, and so forth in detail.
This is also the position of the Vaibhāṣikas:
the eye does not cognize; what then?
"Consciousness cognizes.
Yet it has also been said that "forms are to be cognized by the eye and are desirable.
In this regard, one must necessarily accept that the action of the supported is metaphorically attributed to the support.
"As far as the door for the seeing of forms" means that "door" is like a gateway; the intended sense is that it is the cause and the basis (*āśraya*).
This is the meaning expressed by the phrase "by this scripture, by that basis."
He supports that very point:
"By means of that eye as a door, consciousness sees. Thus, in the act of seeing, the eye is designated as the "door."
"O Brahmin, the eye is merely a gateway for the seeing of forms"—this is what is meant here.
For it is not logical to say "the seeing of forms for the sake of seeing";
the intention here is that this is not logical because it is a non-expressive [redundant] statement.

If "vision" (darśana) is the instrument, it is so called because "one sees by means of it" (*anena dṛśyate*); or, using the *lyuṭ* suffix in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), it is "vision" because "it sees" (*paśyati*).
And the term "for the sake of vision" (*darśanāya*) is derived as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*).
"Vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) means seeing; [the phrase] "for the sake of that seeing" (*darśanāya*).
How is this logical?
Because there is no seeing apart from the eye.
If it is argued that it is "mere observation," no;
because it is not distinct from consciousness, mere observation is indeed consciousness itself.
We see nothing other than this.
However, if "the eye-door" is understood to mean an opening for the seeing and the cognition of forms, then it is appropriate;
just as a certain kind of wisdom is also said to "see."

The word "iti" (thus) is to be supplied here in the phrase "it is also said that it sees. By this presentation, he demonstrates that seeing (*darśana*) and cognition (*vijñāna*) are not different in meaning.
But what is this wisdom (*prajñā*) that is so described?
That which has been described as having vision as its nature;
noble wisdom other than that is of both kinds.
Because it is stated in the Sūtra: "For one who thus knows and thus sees.
By the use of the term "something," it is implied that not all consciousness sees;
for it is specifically visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) that is said to see.
But it is not the case that auditory consciousness and the others [are so];
for what other activity of seeing could there be than that which consists in being a perceiver?
The intention is that its seeing is logical.
"This is not to be questioned," and so forth;
[this applies] if consciousness cognizes.

The same objection arises: one must explain what other act of cognition there could be for consciousness that has become the agent. Furthermore, there is no distinction between the agent and the action;
there is no difference or otherness between the consciousness that is the agent and the action characterized as consciousness.
Furthermore, there occurs the designation of a relationship between an agent and an action,
such as "consciousness cognizes.
In the same way, it should be so here as well.
That "the eye sees" is not to be questioned.
Others hold that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is the seeing;
because it is the basis (*āśraya*) for that [consciousness], it is said that "the eye sees."

Just as it is said that "the bell rings" because it serves as the basis for the sound, [then in what way does consciousness cognize form by serving as its basis? He says: "Because it serves as the basis for consciousness.
This means: because it serves as the basis for visual consciousness.
"That consciousness is conventionally known in the world as 'vision' (*darśana*).
This means that in the world it is conventionally established as "vision," but it is not conventionally established as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). How is this understood? He says:
For when that [eye-consciousness] has arisen, it is said that "form is seen," not that "it is cognized.
The statement "it is also said in the *Vibhāṣā*" intends to convey that this very same meaning is expressed there as well.
"Attained by the eye" means it has come into the range of the eye;
"consciousness," however, [is present] by mere proximity,
which shows that it is not through the mode of being its support (āśraya).
Just as it is said that "the sun makes the day," meaning that the sun is said to make the day by its mere presence,
so too it is said that "consciousness cognizes."
Why?
Because it is established as such in the world.
For this [world] is indeed devoid of activity, and so forth.
"Without activity" means without effort. For by this, he negates an action that is distinct from the agent.
"Mere phenomenon" (dharmamātra) means:
It negates an independent agent.
And by the phrase "merely cause and fruit," it demonstrates that even in the absence of an agent, there exists the causal relationship between cause and fruit.

In this regard, conventional designations are applied according to intention (*chandataḥ*). Whatever thing serves as a basis for worldly discourse (*vyavahārāṅga*), that is here conceptually constructed (*parikalpya*) as having an existent form even though it is non-existent, for the sake of establishing worldly discourse and accomplishing its purpose—such as the formulation of agent and action:
"the eye sees," "consciousness cognizes," and so forth.
One should not become attached to this.

"One should not adhere to the etymological explanations of regions (*janapadanirukti*) such as 'an entity (*bhāva*) is distinct [from its] agent (*bhavitṛ*],' and so forth. In this context, "etymological explanation of a region" refers to speech that is fixed and determined within a particular region.
One should not adhere to that.
Therefore, this is the etymological explanation here;
or rather, one should not assume that every etymological explanation is meaningful.
"And one should not pursue the designations of the world"—
that is, one should not superimpose upon the world such designations as "self" (ātman) or "living being" (jīva).
The meaning is that one should not proceed by means of an unreal attribution, thinking, "The self exists as something distinct from the body and so forth."
Alternatively, one should neither pursue nor overstep the conventional designation (*saṃjñā*) of the world.
The meaning is that one should not conceptualize that "designation does not exist because its referent (*artha*) does not exist.
"Overstepping" (*atisaraṇa*) and "transgressing" (*atikramaṇa*) have the same meaning.
(I.42ab) "By both as well"—
because of the word "also," there is no restriction here that it must be by one alone;
for when both eyes are open, the vision is more perfectly clear.
It is said: "Not from the alteration of one or the other.
This means that when the eyes are half-open and half-closed, if one of the two undergoes an alteration—that is, if that which was open becomes otherwise—[the object is not seen].
That [eye] should be made half-closed or entirely closed;
and that which is half-closed,
if it were made entirely closed or entirely open.
At that time, the vision of two moons does not occur.
Therefore, it is understood that both eyes have a functional role in the arising of this consciousness.
Because they are situated in a location, like visible form (*rūpa*), this is a counter-example (*viparītadṛṣṭānta*).
Just as form (rūpa) undergoes disintegration due to the disintegration of its basis because it is established in a specific location,
it is not so with consciousness (vijñāna).
For consciousness does not undergo disintegration through the disintegration of its basis.
(I.42cd) For it is said that one sees form from a distance. Wherever a form is seen,
the visual faculty that apprehends it does not exist there.
Because it is not perceived there by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
like Devadatta and others who are not present there;
just as, for example, the eye [is not perceived].
The same should be said for the ear as well.
The other replied: "The eye and the ear reach the location of their own objects."
Because it is a sense faculty (*indriya*),
like the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) and so forth.
By this inference, he demonstrates that the reason— namely, "the non-perception of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there"— is unestablished (*asiddha*).
The Teacher says:
"And [this is so] because the sense organs have reached their objects," and so forth.
If it were assumed that the eye and ear reach their objects, then the divine eye and ear would not arise here among humans who practice meditation.
For if the eye and the ear were to perceive form and sound respectively, even when they are located at a great distance or obstructed by walls and the like,
then their divine nature would be possible;
however, that would not be the case if their objects were [only] those with which they come into contact.
Like the nose and so forth.
Just as the divine [faculties] of the nose, tongue, and body would not arise for meditators because their objects must be physically reached, so it is in this case.

By this, he demonstrates that the position [that the sense organs] reach the location of their own objects is flawed by a contradiction regarding the specific nature of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparyayāpākṣālatvam*).
For the eyes and ears are the subjects when their divinity is possible;
the state of lacking such possible divinity is the contradiction regarding their specific nature.
"It reaches [the object]"—this is the fault; because of this fault, it is [established as] being inferential (*anumāna*).
It establishes that its [reaching] is not perceived by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the eye and the ear have objects that are not reached.

"If the eye does not reach its object," and so forth. Since that non-attainment is equal whether the object is nearby, situated at an extreme distance, or obstructed, it follows that seeing would occur in those cases as well.
Is this a proof for the opponent's position or a refutation of it?
If, first of all, the proof is thus rejected as being too far-fetched— that the eye and ear perceive by means of contact because they do not reach [their objects],
like an object situated nearby.
That is not a valid proof, because the reason (hetu) is itself unestablished,
or because it contradicts a prior admission.

Alternatively, it would constitute a refutation (dūṣaṇa), as it would entail the undesirable consequence that the subject (dharmin) characterized as the eye and the ear must be capable of grasping all objects with which they come into contact.
That is not a valid objection, because it is refuted by inference.
To explain how, he says:

having introduced the example of the magnet by way of the question, "How is it that a magnet does not attract all iron that is not in contact with it?", [he shows that] the eye and the ear do not apprehend everything that is not in contact.
The eye and the ear do not apprehend everything that is not in contact [with them], because they lack the capacity to apprehend everything that is not in contact,
like a magnet.
For a magnet attracts iron without reaching it; the meaning is that it draws it toward itself.
Yet it does not attract everything that is unattained.
The eye and the ear are like that.
This is the same even when the object has been reached.
An object that is not too distant is not grasped by the eye or the ear because it is unfit for perception.
It is like a rod of ointment that has been applied.
Alternatively, the eye and the ear do not grasp everything that can be grasped,
due to the inherent nature of the sense faculties.
Like the olfactory faculty and the others.
For the objects of the olfactory faculty and so forth are those that have been reached, yet not all of them, because they do not perceive coexistent odors and the like.
For odors, tastes, and tangibles, which coexist with the nose and the other [faculties], are not grasped by the nose and the others;
for such is the capacity of the sense-faculties.
But as for the mind, it is because it is formless.
The state of being "reached" (prāptatva) would be established for material things alone, and not for immaterial things;
thus, no investigation is made regarding the claim that "the mind has objects it does not reach.
"The other three are otherwise."
The undertaking [of this discussion] is for the purpose of establishing the restriction that "the triad [of nose, tongue, and body] has only reached objects.
Otherwise, it might be suspected that they have both reached and unreached objects.
This is because one who is breathless does not perceive odors.
When the subtle set of four primary elements (bhūtacatuṣka) has reached the nose along with the breath,
its odor is smelled by the nose.
Others maintain that a different odor arises within the air.
They would become mixed, they would become a single entity.
Now, [if it were] by way of a part— what [would happen]?
The phrase "they would touch" carries over [from the previous context].
How is sound produced?
If they do not touch.
The intention is that if there were no impact, the production of sound would not occur.
"For this very reason" refers to the Kashmiris;
for if [the atoms] were to touch one another, [sound would not be produced].
A hand struck against a hand would stick to it, like lac to another piece of lac.
How is it that a collection [of atoms] is not shattered when struck back?
How is it that the aggregate of atoms, which do not touch one another, is not shattered when struck by the hands and so forth?

That very thing is their state of being without interval (*nirantaratva*), namely that there is nothing whatsoever in between; because there is no light or the like in between, their state of being without interval is established.
And that alone is their state of contact (*prāptatva*), not otherwise.
Furthermore, as for the phrase "api khalu": [it means]...
Moreover, this is the meaning:
since aggregates possess parts, they touch; thus there is no fault.

As for the fault that was stated—namely, that "if they were to touch with their entire self, the substances would become intermingled, but if they were to touch by way of one part, it would follow that they have parts"—[that objection does not apply].
"Dependence upon a cause" means:
whatever kind of cause something has,
that is its cause.
He says "depending on whether it is touched or untouched. The phrase "at times" is the elaboration. "Having touch as its cause" means:
That which is touched by another has "touched" as its cause;
likewise, there is that which has "untouched" as its cause.
This refers to when it falls apart.
It is, for example, like dry clay being ground into powder; it is when it reaches such a state. It is, for example, like snow.
For that which was previously subtle later becomes large; it is called an "accumulation" of things that possess accumulation,
just as when two lumps of clay come together.
"It would persist into the subsequent moment," [he says], because it arises through contact. But the Venerable One [says]: "However, when there is no interval, there is the designation 'contact'."
"And the opinion of the Bhadanta should be accepted.
Why should the opinion of the Vaibhāṣikas not be accepted?
Has it not been stated by the Vaibhāṣikas as well in this very way?
That very absence of anything in between is what constitutes their state of being "without interval.
This is indeed so;
however, that statement is made with room for further qualification.
The Vaibhāṣikas, asserting that there is nothing whatsoever in the middle, do not admit light and so forth in the interval;
however, they do not claim that there is no space for the entry of other atoms.
For otherwise, if atoms were separated by intervals, what would obstruct the movement of those possessing motion through the empty spaces between them? This is the completion of the sentence.
And there is this further fault:
aggregates are not something other than atoms, as the Vaibhāṣikas imagine.
Those very atoms that constitute the aggregates are what are touched.
"Just as they are transformed" means that they are indeed aggregates and not single entities.
And "if [it were] of an atom," and so forth.
Desiring to explain the non-establishment of the atom (*paramāṇu*), the Master investigates:

if a distinction of directional parts—such as the eastern side and so forth—is imagined for a single atom, then whether it is in contact with another or not in contact, the consequence follows that it must possess constituent parts (*sāvayavatva*).
If not [such a distinction is imagined], then [the atom cannot be established].
What?
The phrase "distinction of spatial directions" (digbhāgabhedah) continues [to apply].
Thus, there is no undesired consequence even for that which is touched.
Of what?
Of the state of having parts (*sāvayavatva*). Herein is the proof (*sādhana*).
The atom is not partless,
because it possesses distinctions of spatial directions,
like a heap of beans.

The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this [notion] of having distinctions of spatial direction (digbhāgabhedavattva). For such a distinction of spatial direction is postulated only for those things that consist of composite forms (saṃghātarūpa).
And they explain it in this way.

This is the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that those which possess resistance (*sapratigha*) must occupy distinct locations. Lest they appear to occupy the same location due to their existence in immediate proximity (*nairantarya*), their movement is obstructed by their resistance even when there is space between them.
Furthermore, mountains and the like [appear to move] with rapid motion, like a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*).

If it is maintained that only an object equal in size to the self is apprehended, one might ask: how is it that large objects such as mountains appear to be apprehended all at once rather than sequentially? Anticipating this objection, [the author] provides the reasoning for such apprehension with the words "by rapid succession" (*āśuvṛttyā*) and so forth.
Just as the apprehension of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) and the like, though occurring sequentially, appears as if it were simultaneous.
Likewise, the perception of sounds such as those of mountains and rivers occurs through rapid succession;
or rather, it is "of the similar and the dissimilar," as in the case of seeing grapes and other fruits, which are similar [in color].

The intention is that [this occurs] regarding the seeing of things such as the tip of a hair or a mountain, which are unequal [in size]. "By the mere opening [of the eyes]" means not by way of the principle of sequential perception.
"In the same way by the ear," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Sometimes they are smaller, when one hears the sound of a mosquito;
sometimes they are equal, when one hears the sound of someone whose voice has a magnitude equal to that of the atoms of the auditory faculty;
and sometimes they are larger, when one hears the sound of thunderclouds.
"Situated like the flowers of the ajājī plant" means situated like the flowers of black cumin (*kālajīraka*); that is to say, they are situated on a single surface.
"Situated within the *bhūrja*" refers to that which has the color and shape of a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapattra*) inside the ear; because it is like birch-bark, it is called *bhūrja*.
The atoms of the auditory faculty situated within that [cavity] are located inside the skull—
the "skull" here referring to the nasal cavity— and they are arranged like a garland.
"Arranged in a circle in a single row" means they are situated in a uniform line.
Regarding the phrase "said to be the size of a hair-tip," the word "said to" (*kila*) is used for the purpose of indicating that this is based on scriptural authority (*āgama*).
"Unmanifest" means unpermeated.
"It is said that... implies that it would not disintegrate solely through the power of karma;
by the word "it is said" (kila), he indicates his lack of approval [with this view].
"Because they have a composite basis and a composite object" means because they have a composite basis and because they have a composite object.
(I.43cd) "The basis of the last one is past."
The restriction is that it is "only past.
For this very reason it is said:
because the five groups of consciousness have two types of faculties as their support.
They have as their bases the sense-faculties such as the eye and the sense-faculty of the mind.
Therefore, a fourfold alternative (catuḥkoṭika) arises.
The first alternative is "the eye."
The eye serves as the basis for visual consciousness by way of being its support, not by way of being its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
For the eye does not have the nature of mind or mental factors;
rather, it is the minds and mental factors that have arisen—excluding the final ones—that constitute the immediately preceding condition.

And such is the definition of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). The second alternative is the mental factor (*caitasika*) of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) that has just passed away, by virtue of its being the immediately preceding state.
For it is held that there are only six bases for consciousness, from the eye up to the mind, and no others.
The third [category] is the mind that has just passed away,
because it possesses both characteristics.
The fourth consists of those phenomena (dharmas) excluded from what has been mentioned.
The three categories—those dissociated from mind, the unconditioned, and so forth—are excluded.
In this manner, up to the case of body-consciousness, its own faculty should be stated as that which serves as its basis.
This refers to that which functions as the basis for auditory consciousness.
Regarding the statement "it is also [the cause] of that by way of being an immediately preceding condition," there are four alternatives (catuḥkoṭika).
The first alternative is the auditory faculty (śrotra).
The second [category] is the mental factors (caitasika) of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) that have just passed away; the third is the mind (manas) that has just passed away;
the fourth category consists of those phenomena (dharma) excluded from what has been mentioned.
It should also be stated in this way:
"The mental consciousness is the prior member," meaning that which exists as the basis for the mental consciousness.

It is also [the cause] by way of being the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*); thus, "it is his" is the first part of the argument. First, that which exists by way of being the basis (*āśraya*).
"By way of being an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) as well.
That is to say, the mind (*manas*) is necessarily an immediately preceding condition;
it may exist by way of being an immediately preceding condition, but not by way of being a support (*āśraya*).
The mental factor that has just passed away is the nature of the six bases, beginning with the eye, because it belongs to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
"Because it undergoes transformation according to their transformation," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
The modification of those [faculties], such as the eye and so forth, is "their modification" (*tadvikāra*).
The modification resulting from that modification is "modification due to their modification" (*tadvikāravikāra*).
Since these consciousnesses possess this [quality], they are called "those which undergo modification due to their modification" (*tadvikāravikārīṇi vijñānāni*).
The state of being that [is] "changing in accordance with its transformation.
Therefore,
it is determined that the eye and so forth alone are their supports.
"Because they conform to the intensity or dullness of benefit and injury.
The visual consciousnesses and the others conform to the benefit of the eyes and other faculties through collyrium and the like, and to their injury by dust and the like,
because they arise accompanied by pleasure and because they arise accompanied by pain.

They conform respectively to the sharpness and dullness of those [faculties]. Because of the arising of sharpness and dullness, it is understood from this that a transformation of consciousness occurs through a transformation of the eye and other [faculties].
But surely it is observed that when the form is sharp, a sharp visual consciousness arises, and when it is dull, a dull one.
[This refers to] those [faculties], the eye and so forth. Even if the visual consciousness were to conform to the sharpness or dullness of the form, [the argument remains].
However, between the two discordant states of the eye and visible form, visual consciousness conforms only to the state of the eye,
not to the state of the visible form. For instance,
when the eye is benefited and the visible form is impaired, visual consciousness arises without distortion for those who are free from passion toward it and for those who are neutral.
But it does not arise accompanied by suffering.

Furthermore, when form is assisted and not abandoned, yet the eye is impaired by jaundice, by the disease of cataracts, or by an optical disorder, there occurs a mistaken perception of yellow or a vision of floating hairs and the like.
Likewise, when form is vivid but the eye is dulled by old age, a dull visual consciousness arises.
Thus, if the eye is extremely sharp even when the form is dull, a sharp visual consciousness arises.
For instance, by the very nature of its birth, a sharp vulture’s eye gives rise to visual consciousness even with respect to a dull corpse-form, even if it is separated by many *yojanas*.
In this same way, the ear and the other [senses] are to be applied accordingly.
(I.44cd) "Therefore, because it is uncommon" means:
because it is the basis,
and because it is uncommon.
Since the nature of the basis has already been explained, he does not pay further attention to it;
rather, while explaining its exclusivity (asādhāraṇatva), he says: "How is there exclusivity? and so forth.
"Also of another's eye-consciousness" means also of the consciousness belonging to another continuum.
It is designated by those very [terms].
Visual consciousness arises from the eye and so forth, up to mental consciousness;
it does not arise from visible forms and so forth, up to the consciousness of phenomena.
It is just as one speaks of the sound of a drum or a sprout of barley.

Because they are unique [to that specific effect], there is a designation based on those two—the drum and the barley—just as in the world one speaks of a "drum-sound" or a "barley-sprout," but not of a "stick-sound" or a "field-sprout.

For the stick could be the cause of sounds such as those from a kettle-drum (*paṭaha*), and the field could be the cause of sprouts of rice, wheat, and so forth; thus, because they are common [to other effects], no designation is made based on them.
However, the designation is made by means of the two uncommon factors, the drum and the barley;
it should be understood in the same way here as well.
Furthermore, consciousness is like the eye, because both are reckoned as belonging to sentient beings.
Form, however, is also included among non-sentient things.
Visual consciousness is consciousness by means of the eye; this is because the eye serves as its cause.
Visual consciousness is consciousness in the eye;
because consciousness associated with the feelings of pleasure and pain functions through the benefit or injury of the eye.
Visual consciousness is the consciousness belonging to the eye.
Because it proceeds from that [eye] by virtue of its being unique [to it].
"Eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*) means consciousness of the eye;
this is because [the eye] alone possesses the status of owner (*svāmibhāva*) with respect to what is reckoned as a sentient being (*sattvasaṃkhyāta*).
Visual consciousness is "eye-consciousness.
This is because the pleasant or painful feeling associated with it is discerned specifically in relation to the eye.
The same should be applied to the ear and the other sense organs.
Thus, it is appropriate to designate consciousness by means of the eye and so forth, rather than by means of visible form and so forth.
In the same way, this should be applied to one who sees visible forms belonging to their own level or to lower levels with an eye belonging to the third or fourth dhyāna level.
This should be applied specifically to that very person born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
In this way, it should be applied to the eye of the third dhyāna and so forth.

That is to say, for one born in that very first dhyāna who sees with the eye of the third or fourth dhyāna, [the rule] should be applied: "The eye is not lower than the body. (I.45, 46) The eye is not lower than the body.
Thus,
the meaning is "belonging to a lower stage.
It is permitted that [the mind] belongs to its own stage or to a higher stage.
For the body, the eye, and visible forms belong to five levels.
"Body" refers to the physical frame;
these—the body and so forth—belong to five levels.
Those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and those belonging to the stages of the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, because they do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) belongs to two stages:
that of the desire realm and that of the first dhyāna stage.
Because both of those possess applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and because visual consciousness necessarily possesses applied and sustained thought; therefore,
a form of a higher level is not [an object] of the eye.
Form belonging to a higher level does not become the object of the eye,
because form belonging to a higher level is subtle; however,
form belonging to its own level and to lower levels is permitted.
And consciousness.
What?
It is understood from the context that "it does not [arise] above the eye."

For an eye belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) that is of a lower level, there is no visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) belonging to the level of the first dhyāna. It is permitted [to have] a visual consciousness belonging either to its own level or to a lower level.
For an eye of the desire realm, the visual consciousness belongs only to its own level—that is, it is exclusively of the desire realm.
For an eye belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, the visual consciousness is likewise of the level of the first dhyāna alone;
however, a visual consciousness belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) does not belong to it. But was it not stated that [visual consciousness] of a lower level is permitted?
This has been said truly;
however,
when that which belongs to oneself does not exist, it is accepted as belonging to a lower stage.

"Not existing. For when one's own eye belonging to the second, third, or fourth dhyāna does not exist, the visual consciousness is only that which belongs to the level of the first dhyāna— the lower level—
and not that of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), because the latter is extremely inferior.
However, this was stated according to the possibility, namely that [the object] belonging to a lower stage is permitted.
"Of this" refers to the visual consciousness just mentioned.
For the class of visual consciousness, visible form (*rūpa*) is the object from all [stages].
However, it should be applied according to possibility:
for visual consciousness belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), visible form (*rūpa*) belongs only to its own level.
But for visual consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna—which has as its support the eye belonging to the first dhyāna—visible form belonging to its own level and to lower levels is its object.

However, for that which has the eye as its basis belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna, visible form belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna is its object, as well as all [visible form] belonging to the lower levels.
Likewise, up to the eye as its basis belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, visible form belonging to the level of the second dhyāna and that belonging to the lower levels is its object.
Thus, for the class of visual consciousness, visible form becomes its object above, below, and on its own level.
Both form and consciousness belong to the body in every respect.
For a body belonging to the desire realm—that is, the physical frame—there exist forms and consciousnesses belonging to its own level as well as to higher levels.
For a body belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, there exists only consciousness belonging to the level of the first dhyāna.
Visible form, however, belongs to its own level, to higher levels, or to lower levels—just as the eye does with respect to its own support.
For a body belonging to the second dhyāna or higher levels, the visual consciousness belongs only to a lower level; that is to say, it belongs only to the level of the first dhyāna.

However, for a body belonging to the levels of the second or third dhyāna, visible form belongs to its own level, to a higher level, or to a lower level, just as the eye does with respect to its own support.
For a body belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna, visible form belongs only to its own level or to a lower level,
because there is no visible form above that.
Likewise for the ear; as has been said regarding the eye.
The ear is to be explained in the same way. How so? It is said:
wherever in the body one abides, there with the ear one hears sounds.
Are those body, ear, and sound consciousnesses necessarily of the same level (*ekabhūmika*), or can they also belong to different levels?
He replied:
There is a distinction among all [the cases].
For one born in the desire realm who hears his own sounds with his own ear, everything belongs to his own level; in this manner, the text should be explained in detail according to this direction.
However, this is the fixed rule: [it applies] up to that point.

The ear is not lower than the body, nor is sound higher than the ear; its consciousness is not [higher], but its sound and both [the ear and its consciousness] are [present] everywhere throughout the body— this should be applied in detail.
How so?
The ear is not of a lower level than the body.
For the body, the ear, and sound belong to five levels, ranging from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) up to the level of the fourth dhyāna.

Auditory consciousness belongs to two levels: that of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and that of the first dhyāna. In this regard, the ear belongs to the same level as the body, or it may belong to a higher level.
But it does not belong to a lower level. Whatever level the ear belongs to, its object— the sound— belongs either to that same level or to a lower level.
Nor is there sound above [the level of the ear], because it cannot be heard. For a sound belonging to a higher plane can never be heard by an ear belonging to a lower plane.
And as for consciousness...
Above, there is no sound for the ear, just as [there is no sound] for the body.
But for this [ear], sound is [its object] from all sides, and for the body, both [sound and touch] are [objects] from all sides.
The word "for this" refers to the ear-consciousness mentioned immediately prior; sound is its object from all sides—above, below, and on its own level.
And both sound and consciousness of sound occur everywhere for the body; thus,
the mind is indeterminate.
Thus it is said.
For example, the eye or the ear is restricted [in their range] such that the eye or the ear is not lower than the body;
however, the mind is not restricted in this manner.
For this very reason, he says:

"Even though the body belongs to five levels, the mind and so forth belong to all levels. Thus, the mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness belong to all levels, ranging from those of the desire realm up to those of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

For example, if one born in the desire realm, immediately after a mind of the desire realm, produces a mental consciousness that likewise belongs to the desire realm and has mental objects of the desire realm as its focal point.
All [mental consciousnesses] belong to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).

If, at the time of birth or at the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it arises from the level of the first dhyāna up to the level of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as is possible, it likewise produces a mental consciousness belonging to the desire realm; that [consciousness] has the mind (*manas*) as its basis.
The remaining [mental states] belong to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
Now, if one produces that very consciousness right there [in the first dhyāna],
the phenomena (*dharma*) that serve as its objects (*ālambana*) range from those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna up to those belonging to the level of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
The factors [of the path] are therefore excluded from those [levels].
The remaining [details] are as before.
In this manner, one who is reborn in the first dhyāna up to one who is reborn at the peak of existence (bhavāgra) should be described according to the appropriate application.
(I.47) The incidental discussion is concluded. The eye and a portion of the dharma-element are vision (*dṛṣṭi*).
This [preceding discussion] concerns the governing topic (*adhikārika*).
Now, the passage beginning with "When one is situated in a body and sees forms with the eye" is an incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*) digression,
because it has arisen in connection with the subject of seeing (*darśana*).
"The five external [objects] are cognizable by two [types of consciousness].
The mention of "five" is for the purpose of excluding the *dharmadhātu*.
The inclusion of the term "external" is for the purpose of excluding the eye and the other [internal] sense bases.

By the restriction that only the five external [bases] are cognizable by two types of consciousness, it is established that the other thirteen elements are cognizable by a single type of consciousness,
because they are not objects of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses.
"Unconditioned phenomena are eternal.
This is a restrictive determination that only unconditioned phenomena are eternal.
They are eternal because there is no movement through the time periods (*adhvan*).
"Half of the phenomena (*dharma*) are faculties, as well as those twelve which are taught to be internal."
The section on the elements (*dhātu*) is now under discussion. Twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) have been taught in the Sūtra.
Then the brahmin Jātiśroṇa approached the place where the Blessed One was staying.
Having approached, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa said this to the Blessed One: "Master Gautama, it is said: 'the faculties, the faculties.'"
“How many, O Gautama, are the faculties? And by how many are the faculties comprised?
“There are these twenty-two faculties, O Brahmin.”
Which are the twenty-two? They are:

the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, the pleasure faculty, the pain faculty, the mental joy faculty, the mental grief faculty, the equanimity faculty, the faith faculty, the vigor faculty, the mindfulness faculty, the concentration faculty, the wisdom faculty, and the "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" faculty (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*).
The faculty of final knowledge and the faculty of one who has fully known.
These, O Brahmin, are the twenty-two faculties.
To this extent there is a complete enumeration of the faculties.
Then the brahmin Jātiśroṇa, having rejoiced and delighted in the words spoken by the Blessed One, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
"Half of the Dharma" means a portion of the dharmadhātu.
Some read it as *dharmārdham* using the neuter gender; according to their reading, the term *ardhadharma* would imply an equal division.
According to the grammatical rule "ardha [is] neuter," as in the example *ardhapippalī* (half a long pepper).
Now, if the word *ardha*, even when functioning as a neuter gender, is used in the sense of a single part (*ekadeśārtha*), then the compound is formed in this manner.
It is both *dharma* and a half, thus *dharmārdha*;
or, it is a half of the *dharma*, thus *dharmārdha*.
However, the Abhidharmikas do not respect the established arrangement of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Disregarding the logically appropriate establishment of the six sense bases— namely, the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the body and the sense base of the mind— one places the mind faculty immediately after the life faculty because it possesses an object;
for they recite the feeling faculties and so forth immediately thereafter precisely because they possess objects.
"The eleven beginning with the life-faculty" refers to the life-faculty,
the five feeling-faculties, and the [five] beginning with faith.
And "a portion of three" refers to...
Regarding the nine substances consisting of the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the others:
excluding the mental faculty (manaindriya), the other eight substances constitute a portion of the dharma-dhātu;
the five beginning with the eye are designated by their own names.
The five elements beginning with the eye are the five faculties, from the eye faculty up to the body faculty.
Since the female and male faculties are merely portions of the body faculty,
the five elements beginning with the eye constitute seven faculties.
The seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) are the mind-faculty (*manaindriya*).
Thus, the twelve internal elements constitute eight faculties (*indriya*).

Because of the restriction that "only the twelve internal elements and half of the dharma-element are faculties," it is established that the five elements beginning with form (*rūpa*), as well as the portion of the dharma-element other than those, are not faculties.
The first chapter of the Treasury, titled "Exposition of the Elements," in the *Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* composed by Master Yaśomitra. (Abhidh-k-vy 92) [blank] (Abhidh-k-vy 93)
II.
(The Second Chapter of the Treasury, titled "Exposition of the Faculties") (II.1) The faculties have been explained.
Showing the connection and transition between the first and second chapters (*kośasthāna*), he says:
"The faculties (*indriya*) have been explained. This is because [they were explained] at the conclusion of the first chapter.
It has been stated that "half of the dharmas are faculties.
Therefore, the connection is that this [following] follows from that.
What, then, is the meaning of the term "faculty" (indriya)? Since the grammarians have provided a different etymological derivation for the word "faculty," he therefore asks this question.
What, then, is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*)?

The root *idi* is listed [in the Dhatupatha] with the sense of "supreme sovereignty. From that root, the form *indriyāṇi* is to be understood as derived from the analysis: "they exercise supreme sovereignty" (*indanti*).
How so?
[The term] *indrāṇi* is derived from the root *ind*, meaning "to rule," with the suffix *ra* added according to the *uṇādi* rules; thus, *indrāṇi* means "those who rule.
Then, by adding the suffix *gha* in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*), it becomes *indriyāṇi*. Thus, the faculties (*indriya*) are simply the *indrāṇi*.
Alternatively, it is called *indriya* because they exercise power (*indanti*).
However, because of their plurality, the designation is made in the plural: "they exercise power, therefore they are the *indriyas*.
Thus, the word *indanti* undergoes the grammatical substitution (*ādeśa*) to become *indriyam*.
How so?
There is the substitution of *ra* for the sound *ava*, and the substitution of *iy* for the word *ti*.
By this etymological rule, it becomes *indriya*.
For example, regarding the word *kuñjara*:
grammarians derive the word *kuñjara* by means of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), explaining that it is so called because "it has a *kuñja* (a thicket or temple)";
however, etymologists disregard that and establish it through their own method of etymology, stating that "it is a *kuñjara* because of its movement in thickets (*kuñjacāritva*)."
The same should be understood here as well.

For if, according to the grammatical method, *indriya* were derived as "the mark (*liṅga*) of Indra," then the meaning of "sovereignty" (*ādhipatya*) would be lost from the sense of *indriya*, yet that meaning of sovereignty is intended.
Therefore, the etymology of the word *indriya* must be understood in this way:
"because one avoids danger after having seen or heard it.
That is, after seeing a precipice or the like, and after hearing the roar of a tiger or the like.
"By avoiding the dangers such as ravines and the roars of tigers and so forth.
"Of the two together with their associated [factors]" means together with their mental concomitants (*caitasika*).
"And of the seeing of forms and hearing of sounds" [is also included].
