"The eye sees" and "the ear hears," and so forth, is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Vaibhāṣikas.

Therefore, because the eye and the ear are the uncommon causes (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*) for seeing and hearing—which are characterized by their respective specific objects—the two possess sovereignty (*ādhipatya*).
Regarding "beauty of the personal existence (*ātmabhāvaśobhā*)," it is as explained previously.
Because beings such as those who subsist on odors have an unattractive form;
that is to say, because their personal existence (ātmabhāva) is unattractive.
[The phrase] "due to their enjoyment of edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra)" refers to this.
"Because of the enjoyment of that [object] by those [faculties], such as the nose.
How is it that odor (*gandha*) constitutes substantial food (*kavadīkārāhāra*)?
Because it is made into mouthfuls by means of the partitioning of the intake of odor through the two nostrils.
How is it that the tangible is considered edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*)?
Because through the body, tangibles such as bathing and anointing are taken in mouthfuls by means of the partitioning of the openings of the pores of the skin.
Regarding the phrase "it is said of two": [this refers to the fact that the tangible is food for both the body and the mind].
The word *kila* indicates the opinion of another;
his own view will be stated later. Of the two...
Thus, there is a connection with each [term].
"The distinction of sentient beings" refers to female and male;
"female" is one homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Another [teacher] says it is "puruṣa" (person).
There is a distinction between these two.
"Sattvavikalpa" means the difference in the configuration of the breasts and so forth, as well as the alteration in voice and conduct; this is the meaning of "viśeṣa" (particularity).
"Regarding defilement and purification," says another former master;
[it does not refer] to the differentiation and conceptualization of sentient beings,
because for those belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), such conceptualization is established even without the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*).
The intention is that the differentiation of sentient beings is produced by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Regarding the phrase "those who are separated from and deficient in that": they are both separated and deficient, hence "separated-and-deficient" (*viyuktavikalāḥ*).
Those who are devoid of or deficient in those two, the female and male faculties, are "devoid and deficient in them.
Who are they? Eunuchs, impotent persons, and those with both sets of sexual organs.
Those devoid of that [sexual faculty] are eunuchs (ṣaṇḍha) and impotent ones (paṇḍaka).
This is because they lack the female and male faculties.
Furthermore, what is the specific distinction between eunuchs and impotent ones?
The *ṣaṇḍhas* are those who by nature lack the female and male faculties. The *paṇḍakas* are those whose faculties have been impaired by an external cause.
However, in the Vinaya, only five types of *paṇḍakas* are recited.
The natural eunuch,
the jealous eunuch,
and the periodic eunuch.
The fluid-ejaculating paṇḍaka and the castrated paṇḍaka.
Among these, it is the natural-born paṇḍaka (ṣaṇḍha) that is intended here.
For he who lacks the sexual organ by nature is a natural paṇḍaka;
the remaining types of paṇḍakas are intended here.
First of all, it is clear that the *lūna-paṇḍaka* (castrated paṇḍaka) is deficient in his faculties because his faculties have been severed.
As for the *pakṣapaṇḍaka* (intermittent paṇḍaka) and others, however, they are indeed deficient in those faculties due to their lack of functional capacity;
even at times when their faculties possess functional capacity, they are nonetheless established as being deficient in them.
Because that flexibility of the faculties (*indriyakarmaṇyatva*) does not produce a specific pleasure for the person, nor does it produce procreation.
It is precisely to exclude the suspicion that the sense-faculties actually exist [in them] that the term "eunuchs and impotent ones" (*ṣaṇḍhapaṇḍaka*) is recited separately here.
Otherwise, as in the Vinaya, they would have been recited here in the Abhidharma simply as "impotent ones" (*paṇḍaka*).
Those with both sexual organs are deficient in that [faculty].
This is because of the deficiency resulting from the loss of their physical position and because of the deficiency in being a cause for little pleasure.
Others explain it thus:
Those devoid of that [organ] are eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*);
those deficient in it are impotent (*paṇḍaka*), due to a deficiency resulting from external injury.
And those with both sexual organs,
as well as those deficient in them, [are excluded] because of the deficiency of the [proper] location and because of the deficiency of being a cause for little pleasure.
For them, non-restraint and the like do not exist.
Among humans, non-restraint exists, excluding those who are eunuchs, impotent, and hermaphrodites.
However, immediate retribution (ānantarya) is not admitted for eunuchs and others because they provide little assistance [to others] and lack a sense of shame.
A woman or a man whose conduct is dominated by views cuts [the roots of merit].
Because of this statement,
those [faculties] belong to women and men;
therefore, the female and male faculties have sovereignty over defilement.
And [the attainments of] restraint, fruit, and detachment.
Restraint is threefold: the Prātimokṣa restraint, the dhyāna restraint, and the untainted (anāsrava) restraint.
Not even one of these restraints exists, much less all of them.

Because it is stated that "restraint is also likewise," for this very reason, the attainment of the fruits such as stream-entry and so forth, as well as detachment from the realm of desire and so on, are not possible for them.
"But it exists for women and men.
Therefore, even with respect to purification (*vyavadāna*), the female and male faculties possess sovereignty (*ādhipatya*).
[This is] "with respect to the connection to and the maintenance of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*)."
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is established as having predominance in the arising of the homogeneous group (nikāyasabhāga),
in the connection with that homogeneous group,
and in the maintenance of the homogeneous group.
Because it persists beyond that point by the power of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Furthermore, the mind-faculty (*manaindriya*) connects one to renewed existence (*punarbhava*),
because through its defiled state it links one to renewed existence.
What is the distinction between this [mental faculty] and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
The connection of the life-faculty occurs only in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
whereas that of the mental faculty occurs even in the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
And the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) simultaneously effects the connection of the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*).
The mind-faculty (*manaindriya*), however, effects that connection with a future existence even though it belongs to a different time.
This is what is meant by "conforming to mastery."
The world, or the Dharma as it has been described, follows the mastery of the mind.
As it is said in detail: "By the mind this world is led.
This is also stated in a verse:
"The world is led by the mind; the world is dragged along by the mind.
All phenomena follow the power of this single phenomenon, the mind."

"Because passion and the others adhere to them. This means that these [defilements], such as passion, have the habit of adhering to those [feelings]—pleasure and so forth—either by way of their object (*ālambana*) or by way of association (*saṃprayoga*). Thus, these are the "adherents to them," namely passion and the rest.
Its state is the fact of its being a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) therein.
"Therefore" means:
as it has been stated, passion (*rāga*) lies latent (*anuśete*) in pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*).
In the case of painful [feeling], there is hatred; in the case of neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling], there is delusion. For it is by means of these that one is purified.
The meaning is that one is purified by them.
Thus, it has been stated that these [faculties], beginning with faith, possess sovereignty over the purification of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Others, however, maintain that pleasure and the other [feelings] also possess sovereignty over purification (*vyavadāna*).
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that pleasure and the other [feelings] exercise sovereignty not only over defilement (*saṃkleśa*), but also over purification (*vyavadāna*).
Certain Ābhidharmikas say this:

they cite scripture (*āgama*) to show that these [faculties] also possess sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) with respect to purification (*vyavadāna*), because it is stated in the Sūtra: "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated."
Faith has suffering as its proximate cause. Suffering is its proximate cause;
thus, this faith has suffering as its proximate cause.
The meaning is "having suffering as its cause.
When suffering exists, faith arises in someone toward a certain dharma or toward the Three Jewels,
or they desire to go forth into homelessness.
"Six [types of] mental pleasure and so forth are based on renunciation.
This means: six [types of] mental pleasure based on renunciation;
six [types of] mental displeasure based on renunciation.
There are six types of equanimity based on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*).
Renunciation is the path, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Others say it is the departure from the realm—that is, from cyclic existence—or the state of detachment (*vairāgya*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Dependent upon forms cognizable by the eye, there arises mental gladness based on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*), having renunciation as its object"—this is the meaning.
Or, it means "conducive to renunciation."
In this way, up to: depending on the mind and mental objects (*dharmas*), there arises mental joy based on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*).
Likewise, depending on forms cognizable by the eye, there arises mental distress based on renunciation;
and so on, up to the mind.
Likewise, dependent upon forms cognizable by the eye, there arises equanimity based on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*).
This continues in the same way up to the mind.
Someone may experience mental joy (*saumanasya*) thinking, "I shall attain renunciation."
"No one feels dejection thinking, 'I am making no effort toward renunciation.
Rather, some maintain equanimity toward those [objects] such as form through discernment.
(II.2–4) "Others, however, say" refers to the Sautrāntikas.
"Having understood [it], one avoids the poison"— this means that the avoidance of poison is accomplished by consciousness (*vijñāna*),
not by the eye or the ear. This is the intended meaning.
Nor is there any seeing of forms or hearing of sounds other than consciousness.
When examined, no seeing of forms or hearing of sounds is found apart from the act of apprehension;
and since apprehension is nothing other than consciousness itself, it is not something else.
Therefore, the sovereignty that was previously mentioned regarding the arising of visual and auditory consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors—
that alone constitutes it;
the intention is that this is not sovereignty in any other respect.
Regarding the phrase "of the mind, moreover, in the apprehension of all objects":

although this is already established by [the statement] "due to its sovereignty over the apprehension of its own object," the specific mention of the mind "in the apprehension of all objects" is because the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) does not have the nature of all phenomena.
And this has already been explained previously.
[Objection: But surely objects (artha) also exercise sovereignty here, because of the statement that "consciousness arises in dependence upon a dyad."
For "sovereignty" (*ādhipatya*) means superior power (*prabhutva*).
One who is superior is a sovereign (*adhipati*); the state of being that is sovereignty.
It is because [the eye] is the common cause for the perception of all forms.
Because the eye, which is of a single nature, is the instrument for the perception of all forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth;
whereas a form that is of a single nature is not the cause for the perception of all forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
Indeed, a blue form does not become the cause for the perception of a yellow form.
"And because perception conforms to the sharpness or dullness of that [organ]," meaning that perception conforms to the sharpness or dullness of the eye and other sense organs.
For example, when the eye is sharp, its perception is sharp.
"Sluggish, it makes sluggish.
By the word "etcetera," there is the conformity to unpleasant and pleasant sensations.
When the mind is unwholesome, there is the perception of the unwholesome. (Abhidh-k-vy 97)
In the wholesome, there is the wholesome; in that which is with feeling, there is feeling; in that which is without feeling, there is no feeling.
The apprehension of form does not conform to its intensity, dullness, or other such qualities;
therefore, he says:
"because it is the reverse of that."
Therefore, the eyes and so forth possess a superior sovereignty, whereas form and so forth do not.
From the body, the female and male faculties arise.
Here is the proof:
the female and male faculties have the body-faculty as their intrinsic nature,
because they produce tactile consciousness.
It is like the body-faculty (kāyendriya), which has the nature of neither the female nor the male faculty;
it is unlike the visual faculty (cakṣurindriya) by way of dissimilarity.
[The term refers to] those possessing the form, voice, gestures, and intentions of a woman.
This is because there is a reversal between the intentions of women and the intentions of men.
This being so, the female and male faculties have sovereignty over the very conceptualization of sentient beings as female or male.
The life faculty has sovereignty over the persistence within a particular homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).

But it is not like the Vaibhāṣikas [who hold this] regarding the connection with the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), because in that case, the mind alone has sovereignty. [The phrase] "in defilement, [it is the sovereignty] of the feelings" [is used].
In this regard, there is agreement with the Vaibhāṣikas;
for it is said by them, "in detail," that indeed,

by those [faculties] such as faith, the afflictions are suppressed when they have entered the worldly path, and the path is brought forth when they have entered the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so on.
Thus, it has been stated that within the equipment for purification (*vyavadāna-sambhāra*), faith and the other faculties each possess sovereign power (*ādhipatya*).
For there is no final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*) for one whose mind is not liberated.
The faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) refers to the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) such as the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth.
And that very [mind] is liberated through liberation from the afflictions and through liberation of the continuum.
For one who has attained it, there is *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
Therefore, the sovereignty of the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is established with respect to *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
"Regarding the dwelling in happiness in this very life," and so forth. "The seen dharma" (*dṛṣṭadharma*) means the present life; that is the meaning.
A pleasant dwelling is *sukhavihāra*.
A pleasant dwelling in the present life is *dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*. With respect to that, the faculty of one who has already understood (*ājñātāvīndriya*) exercises sovereignty.
"Because of the experience of the joy and bliss of liberation.
Liberation (*vimukti*) is the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Joy (*prīti*) is mental well-being (*saumanasya*).
Bliss is the bliss of pliancy.
The experience of the bliss of joy through liberation is the "experience of the bliss of joy of liberation.
Therefore [it is said].
This is what is meant: the very experience of the joy and bliss of liberation is itself the "dwelling in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Furthermore, it should be added that speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals also possess the status of faculties (*indriya*).
The Sāṃkhyas postulate sense-faculties such as speech that are distinct from the visual faculty and the others.
The speech-faculty is that by which speaking is performed;
the hand-faculty is that by which some object is grasped.
The foot-faculty is that by which walking is performed; the meaning is "strolling.
The anus-faculty is that by which the excretion of feces is performed.
The faculty of the sexual organ (*upasthendriya*) is that distinct from a portion of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) by which a specific pleasure consisting of bliss (*ānanda*) is obtained.
Indeed, it is not necessary to add ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors to the list as faculties,
for it is on the basis of that specific purpose that the Blessed One taught twenty-two faculties.
Because ignorance and the other [links] are not applicable there.
He asks: "What is this meaning? and replies: (Abhidh-k-vy 98)
"The basis of mind is its conceptual differentiation," and so forth;
that is, the basis of mind is the conceptual differentiation of that basis.
Abiding, affliction,
the equipment for purification, and purification.
And this sixfold sense base (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is the fundamental substance of a sentient being,
because all other [factors] are dependent upon it.
For instance, the physical bases of the faculties (*indriyādhiṣṭhāna*) are produced through the predominance of the six faculties.
Or else, it consists of the six sense objects and the groups of consciousness.
This too is accepted as a substantial entity of a sentient being, but it is not the fundamental one;
for the six sense bases do not arise solely through the predominance of their physical supports and so forth.
The accumulation of purification is by means of five [faculties], namely faith and the others.
Purification itself is by means of three,
namely the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the others.
(II.6) Another interpretation:
"The arising of the basis of the process," and so forth.
This is stated with reference to both the side of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and the side of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Engagement is the basis and the arising of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
[The functions are] subsistence and experience.
For liberation as well, there is the basis, which is origination, subsistence, and experience.
And by this much, the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha) is fully accomplished.
The designation of other sense faculties [besides the intellect] would be purposeless. For you as well, the completion of the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is recited;
its beginning is the perception of sound and so forth, and its end is the perception of the distinction between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the person (*puruṣa*).
In this context, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) constitute the basis of the process of existence (*pravṛtti*), as they are the fundamental substance of the sentient being that transmigrates.
Regarding "arising (*utpatti*) is [dependent on] the female and male faculties":
arising (*utpatti*) is so called because it arises from this.
He asks: "Why? He replies: "Because of arising from that. Of what?
Regarding the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): [it arises] directly from the mind and the body faculties, because it originates from those two;
and because the four [faculties] beginning with the eye arise sequentially.
Abiding is by means of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because of the persistence of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Enjoyment is by means of the feelings (*vedanā*) such as pleasure and so forth.
For faith and the others are the basis for cessation (*nivṛtti*).

Because faith and the other faculties constitute their foundation; the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is the source, meaning its initial arising, because it is the first occurrence of the outflow-free (anāsrava) state.
The faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya) is stability, because it constitutes a continuous succession.
"Experience [is associated] with the faculty of one who has already known" means that because of the experience of the joy and bliss of liberation through that [faculty],
there are only this many faculties; thus, the meaning is that ignorance and the other [defilements] are not accepted as being faculties.
For this very reason, their sequence is as follows:

from the eye-faculty up to the faculty of one who has already understood (ājñātāvīndriya). This is because they serve as the basis for engagement and withdrawal; however, speech does not possess the status of a faculty.
Because speech depends upon specific training.
For a newborn infant perceives forms with the eye even without training,
yet does not produce speech in that same way.

Therefore, because it transcends the nature of the sense faculties (*indriya-dharma*), speech cannot be a sense faculty. Rather, this activity of speaking is the function of the tongue-faculty itself as its basis (*jihvendriyādhiṣṭhāna*). (Abhidh-k-vy 99)
And because the hand and foot are not other than grasping and moving.

For it is the hand itself, arising in one way or another and in various places, that is called "grasping"; and it is the foot itself, arising in one way or another and in various places, that is called "moving."
Because there is an absence of action,
and because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself,
the hands and feet do not possess the status of sense organs.

Regarding the phrase "of snakes and so forth": snakes and the like have no hands or feet, yet they possess the acts of grasping and moving; thus, hands and feet do not constitute sense-faculties (*indriya*) for them.
If it is argued that even for those [atoms] there exists a subtle [form],
we say no;
because that is yet to be proven.
The anus, moreover, is not a sense faculty with respect to excretion— that is, the discharge of impurities—
because any heavy substance falls into space through any opening whatsoever, even outside the location of the anus.
Since a heavy substance falls by its own weight, such falling is not produced by a sense faculty.
"And because it is impelled by the wind.
This means that there is an impelling of that heavy, impure substance by the wind.
That action would belong to the wind alone, not to the anal faculty (*pāyvindriya*).
Because it is not perceived as such.
Even the *upastha* (the organ of generation) does not have the status of a sense faculty with respect to pleasure (*ānanda*).

That is to say, the *upastha*, which is postulated as distinct from the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the male and female faculties (*strī-puruṣendriya*), does not possess the nature of a sense faculty in relation to pleasure.
For that [pleasure] is produced by the female and male faculties, which constitute a portion of the body faculty;
such is the meaning of the statement "afflicted pleasure.
The detailed explanation includes [the contact of] the throat, teeth, eyes, eyelids, and finger joints as well.
If it is not accepted that there are exactly this many sense-faculties for the reason already stated, [then one must account for] the throat in swallowing and the teeth in chewing.
The state of being a sense-faculty (*indriyatva*) would follow [absurdly] for the opening and closing of the eyelids, for the joints (*parvan*) in the action of contracting and expanding bone-joints,
or for everything that serves as a cause; such is the detailed argument.

Alternatively, it follows as a consequence that everything which serves as a cause—such as a seed and so forth—would possess the status of a sense-faculty (*indriyatva*) with respect to its own activity, namely the activity of producing its own effect characterized by the sprout and so on; this is the point under discussion.
If, however, the status of a sense-faculty is asserted for whatever possesses human effort (*puruṣakāra*) toward a particular [effect], then [the fault does not apply].
And that previously mentioned cause for restriction is not accepted.
Therefore, it is incorrect that speech and the others possess the status of faculties (*indriya*). In this regard, the detailed explanation begins with "of the eye and so forth."
In this context, "therein" is used as an introductory phrase for the sentence.
As for the statement "the designation has been made":
the eye and the other [faculties] are the translucent forms that serve as the bases for those consciousnesses.
From the body [arise] the female and male faculties.
Consciousness is the specific discernment [of objects].
Regarding the phrase "of the life-faculty" (*jīvitendriyasya*): it refers to that which was stated [in the verse], "Life is vitality; for it is the support of warmth and consciousness."
"Among the mental factors, such as faith and so forth" refers to this specific section [of the text]: "faith, heedfulness, and pliancy."
But has not feeling (vedanā) already been explained, and will it not also be treated among the mental factors (caitta),
as "feeling is experience"?
Because of the statement: "feeling, volition, and perception."
It is true that the general nature of feeling has been stated and will be stated;
however, since the specific classification is what is intended here, it is said that an explanation of pleasure and the other feelings must be provided.

[Objection: In that case, an explanation of the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the others need not be given, because the definition of the mind (manas) has already been stated.
The [classification] of faith and the other mental factors will be treated among the mental concomitants (*caitta*).
Here, that of pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is being treated;
for these as well, it must certainly be done.
Because it must be shown that these have the nature of nine substances (*dravya*).
In this state, these nine substances receive the name "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*);
in this [subsequent] state, they receive the name "the faculty of knowing" (*ājñendriya*); and in this [final] state, they receive the name "the faculty of one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Since this specific distinction of their states must be demonstrated, it is well said that [this applies] to pleasure and so forth, as well as to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the others. [And:
"That which is bodily feeling is disagreeable."
The term "unpleasant" (*asātā*) is used for the purpose of excluding what is pleasant (*sātā*).
The term "bodily" (*kāyikī*) is used for the purpose of excluding what is mental (*mānasī*).
In this context, the "body" (*kāya*) refers to the five [faculties] beginning with the eye, because they consist of an aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
In that context, it is "bodily" (*kāyikī*) because it exists in the body or because it moves together with the body as its basis.
It is the painful sensation (*vedanā*) based on the five sense faculties.
That...
It should be understood as the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). Pleasure (*sukha*) is that which is agreeable (*sāta*).
In this context, the term "faculty" (indriya) is understood to carry over,
as is the term "bodily" (kāyikī),
and [the term] "pleasurable" (sātā).
The inclusion [of the term "pleasure"] is for the purpose of excluding that which is unpleasant.
This is what is meant:
that is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
That which is the beneficial feeling of the five faculties is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the third dhyāna, but it is mental (*caitasī*).

In the third dhyāna, however, even this mental pleasant feeling is established as the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). Why is it that only the mental pleasant feeling is apprehended there, and not the bodily one?
To this he says:
For there is no bodily feeling (*kāyikī vedanā*) there,
because of the absence of the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*).
Why, then, is that [feeling] not the faculty of mental happiness (*saumanasyendriya*) in the third dhyāna?
Therefore he says:
"But in the third dhyāna, because of being free from passion for joy (prīti),
that [feeling] is the faculty of pleasure itself."
It is not the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*).
For it is called "bliss" (*sukha*) because of its continuity;
it is not "joy" (*prīti*), because it does not have the aspect of exhilaration (*asaṃpraharṣākāra*).
For it is said in the Sūtra:
"Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity," and so on in detail, until: "mindful and dwelling in happiness, he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna.
If it is argued that joy (*prīti*) is something other than mental pleasure (*saumanasya*):
Therefore he says:
"For joy (prīti) is mental gladness (saumanasya)," whereas that which is unpleasant (asātā) to the mind is dejection (daurmanasya).
Thus, mental feeling that is afflictive is dejection (*daurmanasya*),
while equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the intermediate state.
The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), however, is that which is neutral feeling; the meaning is that it is neither pleasant nor unpleasant.
"Both-fold" (*ubhayī*): it is "both-fold" because it possesses both parts; the meaning is that it is both bodily (*kāyikī*) and mental (*caitasikī*).
"Because of non-conceptualization" means because of the absence of the conceptualization of discernment (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).
The inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding the joy and bliss born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and those born of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
As for the phrase "not, however, bodily":
bodily pleasure and pain do not arise from conceptualization (*vikalpana*).
He asks, "What is the reason? and replies:
"Because they arise even for Arhats due to the power of objects.
This is because physical pleasure and pain arise even for Arhats—who have abandoned the conceptual constructions of the pleasant and the unpleasant—solely by the power of sensory objects.
Therefore, there is a distinction between those two by way of being faculties (*indriya*).

There is a distinction—that is, a separation—between those two types of pleasure and pain, whether physical or mental, by way of their being faculties: namely, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of mental joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), and the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

Equanimity (*upekṣā*), however, arises by its own nature, without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), and without conceptualization or discernment; it may be either physical or mental, and it is either born of maturation (*vipākaja*) or a result of outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
Therefore, a single faculty is established as the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), because there is no distinction in its nature as a faculty.
Otherwise, it would be "bodily," and so forth;
by another specific mode of experience, it favors bodily pleasure.
And the mental [feeling] is by means of another [organ].
For the bodily [feeling] is stable,
whereas the mental [feeling] is unstable.
Thus, suffering afflicts the bodily through one specific mode of experience, and the mental through another.
This distinction does not apply in the case of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
This conceptual construction characterized by specific intrinsic nature does not exist. Therefore, with respect to equanimity— that is, toward the act of being equanimous—
there is no differentiation because of the absence of conceptualization and the absence of specific intrinsic nature.
Regarding the phrase "the path of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning":
*dṛk* means vision (*darśana*).

The path of seeing (*dṛg-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) constitute the "path of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning. Within these very three paths, there are nine substantial entities (*dravya*) known as mind, pleasure, mental joy, equanimity, faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

These are established as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Depending upon one another, these nine substances receive their respective names. Furthermore, they are said to be "nine" only in relation to other groups [of faculties].

However, there are not nine substances within a single mental complex (*cittakalāpa*), because only one of the faculties—pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*)—is present.

For if that path belongs to the stages of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the fourth dhyāna, or the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, or nothingness; [then it is as stated].
In that case, there is only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*),
not the faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) or mental joy (*saumanasyendriya*),
provided one belongs to the level of the first or second dhyāna.
In that case, it is precisely the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*).
If it belongs to the level of the third dhyāna,
then there is only the faculty of physical pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and nothing else.

"One who has set out to know what is not yet known" means one who has set out to know—that is, to realize—the four truths that were previously unknown; one who has begun with the thought, "I shall come to know.
The faculty belonging to such a person is the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*).
This is an irregular compound (*aluk-samāsa*).
This word *ājñāsyāmi* is a verbal derivative (*ākhyāta-pratirūpaka*).

On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), there is no new [truth] to be fully known; rather, one fully knows that same fourfold truth for the sake of abandoning the remaining latent tendencies—that is, for the sake of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
The faculty of that person who has attained knowledge (*ājña*) is the faculty of one who has known (*ājñendriya*). Alternatively, it is the faculty that is itself knowledge.
On the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), however, the realization "it is known" is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
This is merely an explanation of the meaning.
The grammatical analysis of the word, however, should be performed as follows:
"ājñāta" means "known"; thus, "ājñātāvaḥ" [is derived from that].
The form *āva* is derived from the root *av* with the suffix *ghañ*.
The term *ājñātāvī* contains a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) meaning "one who has that [protection]";
alternatively, it may contain the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*), meaning "one whose nature it is to protect what is known."
"The faculty of one who has become thus" means the faculty of a person who has become thus;
that is to say, of one who has attained full knowledge (ājñātāvin).
(II.9) "The triad is immaculate.
This is a restriction meaning that the triad is indeed exclusively immaculate.

But was this distinction between the untainted (*anāsrava*) and tainted (*sāsrava*) types not already stated in the Exposition of the Elements (*dhātunirdeśa*), where it says: "The untainted is the Truth of the Path"?
Likewise,
because of such statements as: "These three are both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), but the remaining ones are with-outflows," and so forth.
It is true that this variety of types, beginning with "thus," has been stated; however, it was stated in a general form and not in its specific details.

Therefore, it should be understood that for the sake of the student’s easy comprehension, this very variety of types, beginning with "thus," is being stated once again in the form of individual words.

It need not be stated that "nine are twofold," for it is established as "nine are twofold" precisely by the determination that some are exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) and others are contaminated (*sāsrava*).
For if these nine were exclusively uncontaminated, [the statement would be redundant].
They would be listed among the exclusively uncontaminated [factors], such as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and so forth;
likewise, they would be exclusively contaminated.
They would be listed among the exclusively contaminated [factors], such as the material faculties, the life-faculty, suffering, and mental distress.
But it is not so.
Therefore, it is established that there are nine [types] of two kinds.
This is indeed the case.
However, this is stated again— "the nine are twofold"— in order to exclude other opinions;
that is, the nine are indeed twofold.
The outflows are not manifold as some claim; and they cite scripture to establish that [position], beginning with the passage, "For whom these... and so forth.
"In every way, none exist at all.
"In every way" means by way of the distinctions of weak, middling, and superior.
"None" means that even all five do not exist; this is the meaning.
Because of the statement, "I say that he remains on the side of ordinary persons," it is implied by the sense that one who possesses these [characteristics] is a noble one (ārya).
"This is not a proof," says the Master (ācārya), "because it refers to their being untainted (anāsrava).
For, having established the classification of noble persons (āryapudgala), he said, "He for whom these [faculties] exist..."
How so?
"Monks, there are these five faculties. Which five?"
From the sharpness and perfection of these five faculties—from the faculty of faith up to the faculty of wisdom—one becomes an Arhat.
From those that are even more subtle and softer, one becomes a Non-returner (Anāgāmin). From those that are still more subtle and softer, one becomes a Once-returner (Sakṛdāgāmin).
Then, by means of even subtler and softer [faculties], one becomes a once-returner;
then, by means of even subtler and softer [faculties], a stream-enterer;
and then, by means of even subtler and softer [faculties] than those, a follower of the Dharma.
Then, by means of those that are even subtler and more gentle, one follows through faith.

Thus, monks, in dependence upon the perfection of the faculties (indriya-pāramitā), the perfection of the fruits (phala-pāramitā) is known; and in dependence upon the perfection of the fruits, the perfection of the persons (pudgala-pāramitā) is known.
"Whoever lacks all these five faculties in every respect, him I call an outsider, one who stands on the side of the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Having thus established the classification of noble persons (*āryapudgala*), the Blessed One said, "whoever lacks these."
Or, the ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is of two kinds: the internal and the external. The internal one is one whose roots of virtue are not severed, because he is included within the Buddhist fold.
But the outsider has his roots of merit completely severed; for the opposite is true of the former.
For this very reason, the qualification "outsider" is used.
Otherwise, he would have simply said, "I speak of one who stands on the side of ordinary worldlings."
And it is said in the Sūtra:
"Then, not long after his full enlightenment, this thought occurred to the Blessed One:

'The Dharma realized by me is profound, of profound appearance, difficult to see, difficult to understand, beyond the sphere of logic, beyond the reach of reasoning, subtle, precise, and to be experienced by the wise and the learned.'"
And if I were to inform others of it,
and they did not understand it,
that would be a source of vexation for me.
There might be fatigue;
there might be a lack of mental application.
What if I were to dwell alone in the forest, on a slope, devoted to the practice of dwelling in happiness in this very life?
Then, as Brahmā Sahāpati remained in the Brahma-world, this thought occurred to him:
"Alas, this world is perishing!
Alas, this world is being destroyed!"

It is only at certain times, on rare occasions, that Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas appear in the world— just like the flower of the Udumbara tree. And today, the Blessed One’s mind inclines toward dwelling in ease, not toward teaching the Dharma.
"What if I were to go and entreat him?
Then Brahmā Sahāpati, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, [vanished from the Brahma-world and appeared before the Blessed One].
In this very way, Brahmā Sahāpati vanished from the Brahma-world and appeared before the Blessed One.
Then, at that time, Brahmā spoke this verse:
"Formerly, he appeared in Magadha."
For the Dharma is indeed impure and bound by defilement.
Open the door to the deathless; speak the Dharma that is stainless and free from passion.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these two verses:
"O Brahmā, having split asunder the barren soil, this [Dharma] was attained by me with great difficulty.
(Abhidh-k-vy 104)
And this Dharma is not easily understood by those overwhelmed by passion for existence.
Those stained by passion, shrouded by a mass of darkness, will not see the path that is like going against the current— profound and exceedingly difficult to perceive.
Brahmā said:

"Venerable sir, there are beings born in the world and grown up in the world who possess sharp faculties, middling faculties, and even dull faculties—even before the Wheel of Dharma has been set in motion.
Here, "faculties" refers to faith and the others.
Those who were called "capable" (bhavya) are so because it was stated that even before the Wheel of Dharma had been set in motion, there exist those with sharp faculties and so forth;
therefore, faith and the other [faculties] do indeed exist as contaminated (sāsrava).
"From the world with its devas," and so forth.

"I have not yet dwelt extensively with a mind free from perversion, liberated, emerged, detached, and disjoined from this world with its devas, its Māras, and its Brahmās; from this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans"—this is the detailed statement.
And this method of examination does not apply to the untainted (*anāsrava*) states;
for it is not appropriate to speak of the gratification (*āsvāda*), the disadvantage (*ādīnava*), or the escape (*niḥsaraṇa*) of untainted states.
(II.10) "The Arhat," [it is said].
He is a non-returner because his mental continuum is liberated from the afflictions.
He possesses supernormal powers, meaning he has attained the higher knowledges (*abhijñā*).
"Having attained mastery over the mind" means one who is liberated at all times (asamayavimukta). "Requisites for life" means...
It is a requisite for life because it is conducive to it.
"Having given that and made a vow" means having directed one's mind toward that longevity by making a vow.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"May that karma of mine which has maturation as enjoyment become instead maturation as lifespan."
Regarding "the limit of the ultimate":
its characteristic will be stated as "having reached the culmination of increase."
"He generates the thought and speaks the words.
He indicates that one should employ both mind and speech for its accomplishment, for an effect cannot be produced by a single cause alone.
Thus, by this, he demonstrates that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is indeed the maturation (*vipāka*).
"May that karma of mine which has the ripening of wealth instead have the ripening of longevity;
the power of the cultivation of meditative absorption (dhyāna-bhāvanā) is what draws this about."

"The remainder of the maturation ripens" means that through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), one draws forth and experiences the remainder of the maturation of karma from another birth— which was abandoned with its fruit still incomplete due to untimely death.
"Such is for them" refers to those practitioners (*yogins*).
"Born of prior karma, it is the projection of the duration of its stay.
Prior karma is karma performed in a previous birth;
that which is born from that is "born of prior karma."
Stability is the continuous flow of the sense faculties and the great elements.
The time of stability is "sthitikāla.
Its projection is its impelling force (*ākṣepa*).
The "impetus" (*āvedha*) is the duration of its persistence. It is the capacity for the continuity of moments of saṃsāra for that long;
for by it, that duration of persistence is impelled.
Yogis cause the projection of the duration [of existence] produced by prior karma for the sense faculties and the great elements to cease,
and they project a new, adventitious projection born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
(Abhidh-k-vy 105)
"One question arises from another.

Now, regarding the question: "When an Arhat monk sustains the life-formations (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), of what is that life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) the maturation (*vipāka*)?"—from this question arises another: "For what purpose do they sustain the life-formations?"
"For the sake of the welfare of others and for the sake of the endurance of the teaching.
For the sake of the welfare of others are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
for the sake of the endurance of the teaching alone is the disciple.

"And the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) as being like a disease and so forth" means that it is like a disease, a tumor, a thorn, and so on, because of its connection with the three types of suffering (*triduḥkhatā*).
[The questions] "Where? and "Whose? [are asked].
The answer to the question "Where? is: "Among humans, in the three continents.
The answer to the question "Of whom? is: "Of a woman or a man who is an Arhat liberated at all times (asamayavimukta) and who has attained the dhyāna of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭika).
Regarding the phrase "For him," the full explanation is as follows.

And there is mastery over meditative concentration for one who has attained the dhyāna of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*), due to the sharpness of their faculties. Furthermore, the mental continuum is not supported by the afflictions because of the abandonment of the afflictions without remainder.
Although one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) possesses mastery over meditative concentration, [the other qualities are not present].
However, his mental continuum is not supported by the afflictions.
Although the mental continuum of one liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) is indeed not supported by the afflictions, he does not possess mastery over meditative concentration (samādhi).
But for one who is liberated at all times (asamayavimukta), both [possibilities] exist.
Regarding the plural form:
it refers to the statement "the life-formations" (jīvitasaṃskārān).
That is the plural number.
To the question "Why?", he says:
"Of many," and so forth.
This is because of the relinquishing or the sustaining of many life-formations (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) existing within a continuum. For there is no purpose in relinquishing or sustaining a single moment;
rather, the accomplishment of another's task occurs through a continuous flow.
And because even a single moment does not cause affliction.
Nor is it "enduring over time. That which has the nature of persisting over a period of time is "enduring over time," meaning non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*).
Some say that the plural number is used for the purpose of indicating that this life-substance (*āyur-dravya*) does not exist [as a single entity].
This is the position of the Sautrāntikas: that it exists only in many conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*).
Even in a single moment, those conditioned factors are numerous.

That which is designated as "life-span" (āyuḥ) is not a single substantial entity (dravya). Those conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) should be understood as having the nature of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) or the nature of the four aggregates (catuḥskandha).
Otherwise, he would not have mentioned "formations" (*saṃskāra*) at all. Rather, he would have said:
"The Blessed One, having sustained his vitalities (*jīvita*), relinquished his life-span (*āyus*)," for the purpose of making known his mastery over death.
There is mastery over death;
it lasts for exactly three months and no longer. Three months taken together constitute "trimāsa."
*Traimāsyaṃ* means "for exactly three months"; here, the accusative case is used because of the continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) between time and distance.
It does not extend beyond three months, because there is no further work for those to be trained (*vineyakārya*), as the Buddha’s activity culminates with Subhadra.
"For the sake of accomplishing that as well" means for the sake of accomplishing what was promised;
otherwise, it would be mere words.
[This refers to] the remainder of the eon.
"One full kalpa" means a kalpa plus more than a kalpa; that is, a kalpa with an excess.
Regarding "the Māras of the aggregates and death": there are four Māras—the Devaputra-māra, the Kleśa-māra, the Skandha-māra, and the Marana-māra.
There, in the first watch of the night, the Māra of the sons of gods was defeated.
In the second watch, having surveyed with the divine eye, in the third watch the Māra of the afflictions was defeated.
In Vaiśālī, however, having sustained the formative forces of life for three months, he relinquished the formative forces of longevity.
The aggregates were relinquished for the sake of conquering the Māra of the aggregates. Since one must die once those aggregates have been relinquished,
the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that they were sustained for the sake of conquering the Māra of death.
The incidental discussion, which arose from one question to another, is concluded.
Regarding the phrase "twofold and twelve":
it is determined that they are exactly twofold and exactly twelve.
Excluding the last eight—
beginning with faith and ending with the faculty of one who has already understood— and excluding also the faculty of mental grief.
Apart from the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which is exclusively a maturation (*vipāka*), the other twelve faculties are both maturations and non-maturations.

Among them, the seven beginning with the eye-faculty and ending with the male-faculty are accumulative (*aupacayika*) when produced through dreams and so forth, and are thus non-maturations. [The others are] mind, suffering, pleasure, and so forth, as explained in detail.
Those [factors] such as the mind (*manas*) that are wholesome or afflicted are non-resultant (*avipāka*).

Furthermore, those which are neutral (*avyākṛta*) by nature—namely, those pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and those pertaining to emanations (*nairmāṇika*)—are, according to the case, non-resultant.
The phrase "according to the case" (*yathāyogam*) is a qualification.

Because the airyāpathika and other [mental states] are mental in nature, there is the possibility of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*); furthermore, because the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*) and mental joy (*saumanasya*) are not present in certain cases.

In that regard, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the airyāpathika mind-faculty (*manaindriya*) and the associated faculties of mental joy and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are non-resultant (*avipāka*).
Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the airyāpathika mind-faculty is non-resultant.
The faculty of feeling (*vedanendriya*) and that which is associated with it belong to their respective levels.
That which is emanated (*nairmāṇika*) belongs to five levels;
therein, only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is non-retribution (*avipāka*).

The Venerable Anantavarman maintains that those [mental states] pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*), those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and those pertaining to emanations (*nairmāṇika*) are always associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
As for the remaining [faculties], they are maturation (*vipāka*).

Those mental faculties and so forth that are distinct from those whose nature consists of the wholesome, the afflicted, the deportmental, the craft-related, and the emanational are born of maturation; thus, they are "maturation."
It is established that the remaining [faculties] are not maturation (*avipāka*).
Since it is determined that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the twelve beginning with the eye-faculty are [maturation], it is thereby established that the remaining ones are not maturation.
Which, then, are those?
The faculty of mental displeasure (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*), because it is either wholesome or unwholesome.
For it will be stated [later]:
"But that one [faculty] has maturation."
Thus, the group of eight beginning with faith is wholesome.
Thus, non-resultant [phenomena] are those that are not maturation. Maturation is an indeterminate phenomenon (dharma) designated as a sentient being.
(Abhidh-k-vy 107) Thus, because of the absence of the characteristics of maturation (*vipāka*).
By stating that "the faculty of mental displeasure (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not maturation," he demonstrates a contradiction with scripture (*āgama*).
"With reference to experience through association" means:
"experience" (*vedanīya*) refers to feeling (*vedanā*).
Since mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is experienced in this [karma], it is "karma to be experienced as mental distress" (*daurmanasyavedanīya-karman*).
"Also those to be experienced as mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*.

This is the opponent's intention: that because [the term] refers merely to association (*saṃprayoga*), mental pleasure and equanimity—just like mental pain (*daurmanasya*)—would not be considered maturation (*vipāka*).
[The response is: "There is no fault even in [their being] associated, nor is there a fault in [their being] maturation."
That which is to be experienced as mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) in this [life] is "karma to be experienced as mental pleasure" (*saumanasyavedanīya* karma).
Likewise, that karma for which mental pleasure is to be experienced as its maturation (*vipāka*) is "karma to be experienced as mental pleasure.
For, having no other alternative, it must be understood in this very way.

If mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*), when analyzed through reasoning, is not a maturation (*vipāka*), then it must be explained—since there is no other alternative—that this was stated with reference to its being experienced through association (*saṃprayoga-vedanīyatā*).
Therefore, he asks: "What, then, is the reasoning here that mental dissatisfaction is not a maturation?"
Alternatively, this must be understood as follows out of necessity:
in some cases there is "to-be-experienced-through-association" (*saṃprayoga-vedanīyatā*), and in other cases there is "to-be-experienced-as-maturation" (*vipāka-vedanīyatā*).
"You might then say that it would follow [by your logic] that everything is to be experienced through association.
Therefore, having considered this underlying intention, he asks:
what, then, is the reasoning here that mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*)?"
For mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is produced and [is made to arise], and is also pacified, by specific conceptualizations such as thinking about what is undesirable.
Mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) is likewise:
it is produced and pacified by specific conceptualizations such as thinking about what is desirable.
"In that case, for those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*) and so forth.
This is because mental distress (*daurmanasya*) ceases for those who are free from passion and so forth;
however, the eye and other [faculties] which have arisen as maturation (*vipāka*) do not cease for those who are free from passion and so forth.

But mental distress (daurmanasya) is turned away; for it is stated [in the treatise] that one who is free from passion for the desire realm is not possessed of mental distress. This is also said in the Sūtra.

For one who is not free from passion (*avītarāga*), feeling is said to have two arrows: "one experiences bodily suffering and mental distress (*daurmanasya*)," according to the scriptural statement; whereas for one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), it has only one arrow: "one experiences only bodily suffering.
"They also possess mental joy (*saumanasya*)"—this is the full explanation.
What kind of indeterminate mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) as a result of maturation (*vipāka-rūpa*) could there be for those who are free from passion?
Mental pleasure belonging to them is possible only when it is comprised within meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); and because that is wholesome (*kuśala*), it is not a result of maturation.
Therefore, it must be stated:
what kind of mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) is their maturation (*vipāka*)? Let it be whatever kind it may be.
He shows that even though it is not being discerned, it certainly exists.
For that [neutral feeling], there is room for maturation (*vipāka*), but not for mental distress (*daurmanasya*).
Because it never manifests at all—both in the state of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and in the state of non-attainment—it is established that it is not a maturation.
"The mental faculty [is the cause] for both [types of rebirth] and for both [types of action].
This means for both good and bad destinies, and for both wholesome and unwholesome [actions]. "Maturation" is the subject under discussion.
"This which has been relinquished—the life-faculty being the eighth—is the maturation of wholesome karma in a happy rebirth.
In that regard, one might ask: how can the possession of both sexual organs, which is considered unwholesome, be the maturation of wholesome karma?
To this he says: "In a happy rebirth, the possession of both sexual organs occurs through unwholesome karma by way of obtaining that state."
His status has been lost;
therefore, the acquisition of this unwholesome state is a dissociated factor (*viprayukta-dharma*).
However, the intention is that both sexual organs are indeed the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome karma alone.
(II.11) "But that one has fruition" means that this one alone necessarily possesses fruition.
Therefore he says:
"The word *tu* has the sense of *eva* (only/exclusively) and its position is displaced.
This means that its placement is shifted.
For the sequence "that one [is] with fruition" would not be different;
however, it was stated in this way for the sake of conforming to the metrical composition of the verse.
For it is not that it is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
He demonstrates the reasoning for the restriction "only with fruition" (savipākam eva).
For two kinds of entities are held to be without fruition:
the indeterminate (avyākṛta) and the untainted (anāsrava).
Because it is produced by a specific kind of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
and because it is not in a state of meditative concentration (*asamāhita*), it is not untainted (*anāsrava*).
For that which is indeterminate is, like a rotten seed, incapable of yielding a ripened result (*vipāka*).
However, because it is not moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the untainted (*anāsrava*) [mental state] is not capable of yielding maturation (*vipāka*), like a solid seed that has not been moistened.
By process of elimination, it must be either unwholesome (*akuśala*) or wholesome-with-outflows (*kuśala-sāsrava*).
Therefore, mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) necessarily possesses maturation; there is no such thing as mental dissatisfaction that is without maturation.
"Ten are twofold":
this is a restriction meaning that ten are indeed twofold, and they are twofold indeed.
"Twofold" means those with maturation (*savipāka*) and those without maturation (*avipāka*).
"Mind, the other feelings, faith, and so forth. This means: the mind, the other feelings, and faith and the rest. "Feeling" (vitti) refers to sensation (vedanā).
By the mention of "any" (others), that which excludes mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is understood, because mental distress has already been mentioned.
Faith and the others are faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The term "are included" (*gṛhyante*) is understood from the context; "the rest are not maturation" (*avipāka*).
This is because of the restriction [implied] by the previously mentioned [exclusion of] mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and so forth.

It is established that life-force (*jīvita*), the seven material faculties (*rūpendriya*), and the three beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) are not maturation, respectively, because they are neutral (*avyākṛta*) and because they are untainted (*anāsrava*).
(II.12) "The group of eight is wholesome" means that the restriction is made: the group of eight is exclusively wholesome.
"Displeasure is of two kinds":
this is a restriction meaning that displeasure is exclusively of two kinds, and that which is of two kinds is exclusively displeasure.
"Of two kinds" means wholesome and unwholesome.
There is also another twofold division:
wholesome and indeterminate, and unwholesome and indeterminate.
How, then, is this determined— that it is both wholesome and unwholesome? The specific distinction is understood from the explanation.
Alternatively, it has been determined that mental distress (*daurmanasya*) necessarily possesses maturation (*savipāka*).
Therefore, this [distress] alone constitutes the two-fold [category], and nothing else.
Furthermore, there is another feeling (*vitti*).
Thus, there are four types of feeling, excluding mental distress (*daurmanasya*), because that has already been stated.
"In three ways" refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

"Threefold" means of three kinds (*tredhā*). Regarding the forms *dvaidha* and *tridha*, the suffix *dhamuñ* is applied after the words "two" and "three. Furthermore, the word *edhāś* is derived from *tredhā*; thus, the etymological derivation of the term *edhāś* is as follows.
Those associated with non-greed and so forth are wholesome;
those associated with greed and so forth are unwholesome;
other than these, they are indeterminate.
"Another is singlefold":
it is determined that the other [factor], with vitality as the eighth, is indeed singlefold;
the meaning is that it is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
And it is for this purpose that it is formulated once again;
otherwise, it would be possible for it to be exclusively unwholesome, or exclusively wholesome and neutral, or exclusively unwholesome and neutral.
Therefore, it is stated again so that the desired single realm may be established.
That for which the state of being a single element (ekadhātutva) occurs—that comes to be. And what occurs? It is the state of being indeterminate (avyākṛtatva).

(II.13) "Excluding the pure [dharmas] pertaining to the desire realm. This means that by excluding only the pure [dharmas], they pertain to the desire realm; for those [pure dharmas] are indeed non-associated [with any realm].
The meaning is that it does not fall within the [three] realms (*adhātupatita*).
"Included in the realm of form (*rūpāpta*) are the female and male faculties," and so forth.
"Female and male" is *strīpumāṃsau*.
According to the maxim that "the rule regarding the application of a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) is not mandatory," the compound-final suffix is not applied here.
The sensory faculty of those two is the "female-male faculty" (*strīpuruṣendriya*).
"And in 'suffering'" (duḥkhe) means in the faculty whose intrinsic nature is the sensation of suffering; that is to say, suffering and mental distress.
These, along with the female and male faculties, suffering and mental distress, and the immaculate [faculties] persisting here [in the form realm], are excluded.
The remaining sense-faculties belong to the realm of form (*rūpāpta*).
When asked, "Where are they taught?", he shows the Sūtra:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question," and so forth.
The intention here is that according to the Sūtra,
there exists another state of being male,
which belongs to males in the desire realm.
There is a transformation in the shape, voice, and conduct of the breasts and other [female characteristics].
There is no faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) because,
due to the clarity of the physical basis (*āśraya*), that which is born from physical impact does not exist there.
Furthermore, because it is unwholesome, there is no [mental state] born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
The faculty of mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasyendriya*) does not exist because the continuum is moistened by tranquility (*śamatha*);
and because, through the meditative concentration of tranquility, aversion (*pratigha*) has been removed.
There is no harshness within the mental continuum;
therefore, the faculty of mental distress does not exist there,
as well as because of the absence of objects of malice.
Malice (*āghāta*) is anger.
Its object, or domain, is the "basis of malice" (*āghātavastu*). And there are nine bases of malice.
"He has done me harm, he is doing me harm, and he will do me harm"—this is the first triad of objects for malice.

"He has done harm to my friend, he is doing harm to my friend, and he will do harm to my friend"—this is another triad of objects for malice. "He has done good to my enemy, he is doing good to my enemy, and he will do good to my enemy"—this is another triad of objects for malice.
Due to the absence of these nine bases of malice (*āghātavastu*), there is no mental distress (*daurmanasya*) caused by external objects.
This shows that it is not only distress caused by internal causes that does not exist;
for that which is caused by internal causes is precisely that which produces aversion (*pratigha*) within one's own continuum.
And that [non-informative matter] is produced by conditions, namely, that which is produced by the nine bases of malice (*āghātavastu*).
And [it is said]: "and having excluded [it] from pleasure and from the material.
(Abhid-k-vy 110)
By the word "ca" (and), what was previously stated is drawn back [into the context].
Therefore he says:
"Having excluded the female and male faculties, the two types of suffering, and the untainted [faculties]," this [phrase] continues.
"In pleasure" means in the nature of pleasant feeling, namely, the faculties of pleasure and mental joy (*saumanasya*).
The material faculties are the eye and so forth.
(II.14) The three types of feeling are pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The faculty of pleasure is that which belongs to the level of the third dhyāna and is associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśanaheya*).
That is to be abandoned by seeing.
Other than that, everything else therein is with-outflow (sāsrava),
as is that which belongs to the five groups of sensory consciousness in the desire realm.
That which belongs to the level of the first dhyāna and consists of the three groups of consciousness is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
However, the untainted (*anāsrava*) faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is not to be abandoned.
As for the faculty of mental joy (*saumanasya*), that which is associated with what is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) is itself to be abandoned by seeing.
Therefore, whatever else is with-outflow (sāsrava) is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya); that which is without-outflow (anāsrava) is not to be abandoned.
As for the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya), however, it is all-pervading (sarvaga); this is easy to understand.
"Dejection is to be abandoned by both [methods].
One is dejected due to the association with mental distress;
the state of being so is dejection.

The meaning is "mental distress" (*daurmanasya*). For according to the grammatical rule, "the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used when expressing that quality by virtue of whose presence a word is applied to a substance."
That which is associated with what is to be abandoned by seeing is itself to be abandoned by seeing;
other than that, it is to be abandoned by cultivation.
That which is not to be abandoned [by either] does not exist, because it is not in a state of meditative equipoise.
(II.15) "In the realm of desire, two [types of] maturation are obtained at the beginning.
It will be explained that the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is designated as "desire" (*kāma*) because desire is predominant therein.
Among beings born from eggs, from a womb, or from moisture in the desire realm, two faculties that are of the nature of maturation (vipāka) are first acquired at the very beginning:
the body faculty (kāyendriya) and the life faculty (jīvitendriya). Why is this?
Because at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), the mind and the faculty of equanimity are necessarily afflicted (*kliṣṭa*);
for it is stated that "the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is afflicted by all the afflictions belonging to its own level."
And because the eyes and other sense organs do not exist in that state,
the phrase "not by those born spontaneously" (nopapādukaiḥ) is an exception.
Because there is no qualification [to the contrary], it would follow as a logical consequence that even those born by spontaneous generation (*upapāduka*) would likewise obtain exactly those two;
therefore, this is a prohibition.
Are those two not obtained at all by those born by spontaneous generation?
However, not only two are obtained;
therefore he says,
"or six by them."
The full explanation is as follows:
if they are without sexual characteristics;
that is, if they lack the male or female faculties.
"As in the case of those of the first eon" means that, according to the scriptural statement, "In the beginning of the eon, beings existed as possessed of form."

Which six? The five beginning with the eye, and the life-faculty as the sixth. "As among the gods and so forth" means: [as it is said: "There are beings who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, and the life-faculty. This refers to those born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). "And so forth" includes those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), who possess only the mind-faculty and the life-faculty. Furthermore, there are those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, and the life-faculty; these are those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have not yet lost their faculties. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the female faculty, and the life-faculty; these are those born in the desire realm who are females and have not yet lost their faculties. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the male faculty, and the life-faculty; these are those born in the desire realm who are males and have not yet lost their faculties. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, and the life-faculty; these are those born in the desire realm who are both female and male and have not yet lost their faculties. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukhendriya*); these are those born in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the pleasure faculty (*sukhendriya*), and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the first dhyāna who have not yet lost their faculties. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the joy faculty (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the second dhyāna who have not yet lost their faculties. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*), and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the third and fourth dhyānas who have not yet lost their faculties. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the pleasure faculty, the joy faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the first dhyāna who possess the three types of feeling. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the joy faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the second dhyāna who possess two types of feeling. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the third and fourth dhyānas who possess two types of feeling. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the pleasure faculty, the joy faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the first dhyāna who possess all four types of feeling. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the joy faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the second dhyāna who possess three types of feeling. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the third and fourth dhyānas who possess three types of feeling. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the pleasure faculty, the joy faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the first dhyāna who possess all four types of feeling. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the joy faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the second dhyāna who possess three types of feeling. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the third and fourth dhyānas who possess three types of feeling. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the pleasure faculty, the joy faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born in the first dhyāna who possess all four types of feeling. There are also those who possess the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the joy faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the faculty of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; these are those born
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those in the hells and so forth are also included.
These [faculties] are first acquired at the moment of linking (*pratisaṃdhi*) during the state of existence as an intermediate being (*antarābhava*) or at birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
Furthermore, can even those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*) be born by transformation (*upapāduka*)?
The inferior is the arising with both sexual organs;
the superior is the womb of spontaneous birth (*upapāduka*).
The intention of the objection is: "How can there be a conjunction of these two?"
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is designated as "forms" (*rūpāṇi*) because form is predominant therein.
"Because form is predominant" means that forms are translucent and luminous.
Alternatively, the realm of form (rūpadhātu) does not have the qualities of sensual pleasure as its primary characteristic;
rather,
it has mere form as its primary characteristic.
Nor is it characterized primarily by formlessness like the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
It is also stated in the Sūtra;
that is, it is seen thus in the Sūtra as well.
He shows that this is not his own invention alone:
"Those peaceful liberations which, having transcended forms, are formless—
these too are impermanent, unstable, unreliable, and subject to change," and so forth.
"By those who are without sex organs and are of miraculous birth" refers to the beings of the first eon (*prāthamakalpika*).
"And because it is subsequent to meditative attainment" means that the attainment of the form realm (*rūpasamāpatti*) occurs first.
Next is the formless attainment (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Therefore, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is superior to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
both in terms of its rebirth and because it is more preeminent.
Furthermore, because the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is more preeminent than the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) in terms of its rebirth,
and because there the ripening of karma is extremely peaceful for many thousands of eons,
it is therefore superior for that reason as well, and not merely by way of the location of rebirth.
Because it is stated that "the formless realm has no location" (II.16),
one brings [the mind] to cessation while passing away.
Thus,
one dying in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) ceases these very three faculties. This, however, should be understood as having its exceptions.
Because of the statement, "In the wholesome [state], there are five everywhere," there are eight in the realm of form (rūpa).
Thus,
