in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), these same eight [faculties] are to be ceased together with the five beginning with the eye.
Because they die with all their faculties complete at once.
For this very reason it was said:
"For all those born by spontaneous generation (upapāduka) are born and die with all their faculties complete."
"In the realm of desire, ten, nine, or eight":
one who possesses both sexual organs ceases ten faculties,
provided that they possess all five [sensory] faculties intact.
If one possesses a single sexual organ, there are nine; if one lacks a sexual organ, there are eight. However, if one has impaired faculties—such as being blind or deaf—[the count remains as before].
In that case, that faculty must be abandoned.
Furthermore, this exception should be understood to apply only within the entire realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
He states that exception as follows:
"But for those who die gradually, there are four," because they do not cease separately.
The intention is that in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no cessation of these [faculties] without their being mutually separated from one another.
"And five in all cases of the auspicious.
(Abhidh-k-vy 112) This refers to every previously mentioned mode of death.
The exception to the rule that "one who dies in the formless realm ceases [only] life and mind" is as follows:
for indeed, a threefold dying-consciousness is possible.
[The mind at death is] afflicted, neutral, or wholesome.
Regarding these, the procedure for death with an afflicted or neutral mind has been explained according to the general rule.
However, in the case of death with a wholesome mind, five additional factors—faith and the others—must be added.
For these [faculties], beginning with faith, necessarily exist in a wholesome mind.
Therefore, where three are mentioned, there are eight;
where eight are mentioned, there are thirteen.
Where there are ten, there are fifteen;
where there are nine, there are fourteen;
and where there are eight, there are thirteen.
Where there are four, there are nine; this should be calculated in detail.
In the realms of form and formlessness, there is no gradual death.
(II.17) In the section on the faculties (*indriya*), all the characteristics of the faculties are investigated.
Regarding this section on the faculties (*indriya-prakaraṇa*) being composed here,
some explain that all the properties of the faculties, whether as specific states of the faculties or as specific modes of activity, are being investigated.
Others, however, explain [it differently].

In the section on the faculties (*indriya-prakaraṇa*) and the aggregate of faculties (*indriya-skandhaka*), all phenomena pertaining to the faculties—whether as specific states or as specific functions—are investigated.
Therefore, they are also investigated here;
the intention is that this is because of the close connection between them and this treatise.
Regarding "the attainment of the final two fruits is by nine":
attainment is by means of nine faculties.
It is the attainment of the new;
of which?
Of the two final fruits.
In the final existence (*ante bhave*) means in the last [existence].
In the final fruit (*antye phale*) means in the last fruit.
Of those two.
What, then, are the two extremes? They are the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of arhatship.
Just as a staff has two ends.
Thus, among the four fruits arranged in a row, the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of arhatship are at the two ends;
the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning are in the middle.
The attainment of those two end fruits occurs by means of exactly nine faculties.
He asks, "By which nine? and replies:

by the [eight] beginning with faith, excluding the faculty of one who has already fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), together with the faculties of mind (*manas*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Thus, there are nine.
In this regard, the sequence of clear realization (abhisamaya) is as follows:
the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti),
and the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñāna).
The receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding suffering;
the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering;
the receptivity to dharma-knowledge regarding origination.
Dharma-knowledge regarding origination;
receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding origination;
subsequent knowledge regarding origination.
Receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation;
the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation;
receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation.
Subsequent knowledge regarding cessation;
receptivity to the dharma-knowledge regarding the path;
and dharma-knowledge regarding the path.
The receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path,
and the subsequent knowledge of the path—
these sixteen moments are called "clear realization" (abhisamaya).

In that regard, the fifteen moments—from the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering up to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the path—constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This is because of the statement: "The path of seeing consists of those fifteen moments, due to the seeing of what was not previously seen."
And that is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
However, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge 'nvayajñāna*) is the sixteenth [moment], which is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
From that point until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), the entirety of the untainted path (*anāsravo mārgaḥ*) is the path of cultivation.
And that is called the faculty of "having known.
From the knowledge of destruction onwards, the entire untainted path is the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
And that is called the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
In that regard, the fruit of stream-entry (srotaāpattiphala) is attained during the state of the receptivity to subsequent knowledge (mārge 'nvayajñānakṣānti).
Furthermore, the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā) are necessarily present therein,
because that state is wholesome (kuśala).

This [path] consists of the patience of subsequent knowledge regarding the path (*mārge 'nvayajñānakṣānti*), which has the nature of the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) while it is present.
The mental faculty (*manaindriya*) is also associated with it.
Furthermore, the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is necessarily present because this stage has the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) as its basis.

Furthermore, because the *anāgamya* stage is associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), while in this state the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge ’nvayajñāna*) exists as being oriented toward arising with the faculty of perfect knowledge (*ājñendriya*) as its intrinsic nature;

therefore, that fruit is attained by nine faculties: by the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), by the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), by the faculty of perfect knowledge (*ājñendriya*), and by the faculties of mind (*manas*) and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
"For its attainment is by means of both":

its attainment is by means of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), which has the nature of the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), and by means of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which has the nature of the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*).
This is because they are, respectively, the bringer and the support for the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*).

Because it brings about the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) for that attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyogaprāpti*), because it generates it, and because it serves as the support (*saṃniśraya*) for the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
The meaning is "because of being a support.
It is like two people, one of whom expels a thief while the other closes the door.
For just as between two men, by one the thief is expelled, [and by the other the door is closed].
By the second [moment], its door is closed.

Likewise, by the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) is summoned because it brings about the cessation of the possession of afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*);
it is then maintained by the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Because it arises simultaneously with the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*).
Furthermore, the state of Arhatship is attained through the faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), excluding the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
The fruit of Arhatship is obtained during the state of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Faith and the other faculties, as well as the mental faculty (*manaindriya*), are as previously described.

At that stage, the collection of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) constitutes the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*), existing in its nature as the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*).
Furthermore, one of the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity is present.
If arhatship is attained by relying on the third dhyāna, the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is present there; however,
if it is attained by relying on the first or second dhyāna, the faculty of mental joy (saumanasyendriya) is present there.

Now, relying on any one of the stages—the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the fourth dhyāna, or the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)—the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is present therein.

At this stage, however, the aggregate of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*)—which is the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*)—is oriented toward arising with the nature of the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Therefore, that fruit is attained by nine [faculties]: the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), the faculty of mind (*manaindriya*), and any one of the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity.
The explanation that its attainment occurs through both the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is as previously stated.
The elliptical completion of the sentence is: "the attainment of two [results] occurs through seven, eight, or nine [moments]."
"Each one," and so forth.
The attainment of the fruit of once-returning is by means of seven, eight, or nine [paths].
The same applies to the fruit of non-returning.
Explaining that, he says:
"First, as for the fruit of a once-returner, if one who follows the gradual path attains it, he does so by means of the worldly path.
The worldly path has aspects such as [perceiving] the lower realm as peaceful and the higher realm as gross.

Because of the statement that "the aspects such as 'calm' and 'exalted' have the higher and lower [levels] as their respective objects," the yogi here views the higher level as calm, as excellent, and as an escape.
One views the lower [stage] as coarse, as characterized by suffering, and as having thick walls.
Furthermore, this is described as being of four types:
the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*).
In that context, the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) is that from which the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) arises;
furthermore, it is by means of this [path of preparation] that one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) also arises immediately after the uninterrupted path.
It is the support for the attainment of the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*) is a superior path higher than that.
By means of that path, the nine types of afflictions are to be abandoned.

[The nine grades are] the intense-intense, the intense-middling, the intense-weak, the middling-intense, the middling-middling, the middling-weak, the weak-intense, the weak-middling, and the weak-weak.

Now, if an ordinary person abandons the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing and by cultivation by mixing them together, they abandon them having divided them into nine types according to that distinction of weak, middling, intense, and so forth.
By means of the weak-weak paths of uninterrupted transition and liberation, one abandons the most intense (intense-intense) category of affliction.

In this way, up until the point where one abandons the weakest-weak grade of afflictions by means of the strongest-strong paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The Noble One (*ārya*), however, abandons only those afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) by dividing them likewise into nine grades,
because those to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) have already been abandoned previously by means of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The supramundane path of cultivation likewise possesses sixteen aspects,
due to the distinction between the aspects such as impermanence and so forth.
And it also possesses four types, just like that, due to the distinction between the paths of preparation and so on.
Here too, by means of the two weakest-weak paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one abandons the strongest-strong category of afflictions (*kleśa*).
In this manner, up to the point where, by means of the two strongest-strong paths of uninterrupted transition and liberation, one abandons the weakest-weak category of afflictions.
This is a mere indication of the direction regarding the mundane and supramundane paths.
That fruit of once-returning may be obtained either by one who follows the gradual path or by one who is already largely free from passion.
Among these, the "gradualist" is one who, having attained the fruit of stream-entry, subsequently attains the fruit of once-returning in due order.
And who is such a person?
One who is bound by all fetters, or is marked by one type [of defilement] up to five types, provided they are not marked by the sixth type, enters the path of certainty (*niyāma*).
At the sixteenth moment of mind, he becomes a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

For the sake of abandoning one type of defilement to be abandoned by cultivation, up to the sixth type, because he is one whose practice is characterized by tranquility (*śamatha*), he also generates a mundane path.
When the sixth category [of afflictions] has been abandoned, he attains the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).

The attainment of that fruit is by means of seven faculties: the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), the mental faculty (*manaindriya*), and the seventh, the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), because it relies upon the *anāgamya* stage.
Alternatively, if it is by means of the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), its attainment is by means of eight faculties.
By those same [seven] and the eighth, the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*).
For those very seven faculties, beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), receive the designation of the faculty of "having known," because they are untainted (*anāsrava*).

Now, regarding the term "one who has further abandoned passion" (*bhūyovītarāga*): one who, while in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), had previously attenuated six categories [of afflictions] by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), is called "one who has further abandoned passion."
On account of being "largely free from passion" in many ways.
If he attains the fruit of a once-returner,
how does he attain it?
One attains it in the state of the receptivity to subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) on the path according to the previously mentioned sequence of clear realizations (*abhisamaya*).

For that [attainment], it is by means of nine faculties— just as in the case of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*)— namely, faith and the others, excluding the faculty of one who has already fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
The explanation regarding [the attainment] by means of the faculties of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) and mind (*manas*) is as before.
For this person becomes a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) at the sixteenth moment even without having previously attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*).
This applies if one who follows the gradual path attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Here, "gradual" refers to one who, having attained the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of once-returning, attains the fruit of non-returning;
or one who, having become largely free from passion, attains the fruit of non-returning without even having attained the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of once-returning.
And if he attains it by means of the worldly path (*laukika-mārga*).
Its attainment is by means of seven faculties.
This is intended to mean that it is like the attainment of the fruit of once-returning for one who follows the gradual path;
the meaning is that it is by means of the five beginning with faith, as well as the mental faculty and the faculty of equanimity.
Now, by means of the supramundane path, for that [fruit], it is likewise with eight;
the meaning is that it is just as for the fruit of the once-returner, namely, with eight.
The faculty of "I have known" (ājñendriya) becomes the eighth.
Now, regarding the phrase "one who is free from passion" (*vītarāga*):

for one who is free from passion for the desire realm alone by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) when the ninth category [of defilements] has been abandoned, or for one who is free from passion even up to the first dhyāna or even up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanya*), there is the attainment of the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) by means of nine [paths].
Just as it is for the fruit of stream-entry.
For the fruit of stream-entry is attained through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
and since this [fruit] is also attained by the path of seeing alone, there is a similarity.
However, this is the distinction:
there is one of the faculties of pleasure, mental joy, or equanimity, depending on the specific basis.
This is because of the difference in the support.
If one enters the path of certainty (niyāma) by relying on the third dhyāna,
the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is present there.
However, if one relies on the first or second dhyāna, the faculty of mental joy (saumanasyendriya) is present there.
Then, depending on any one of the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), or the fourth dhyāna, the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya) exists therein.
This is the detailed explanation beginning with the words, "when this person follows the gradual sequence" (ānupūrvika).
Even when this practitioner of the gradual path, who has previously attained the prior fruit and possesses sharp faculties,
enters the fundamental dhyāna by means of the mundane path during the ninth path of liberation, he still attains the fruit of non-returning by means of eight faculties;
in that case, the path of liberation is comprised within the fundamental dhyāna.
And therein is the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*).
However, the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) is comprised exclusively within the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*);
if it does not enter [the first dhyāna], then there is only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) therein, and not otherwise.
Its attainment is by means of eight faculties: the five beginning with faith, as well as the mental faculty, the faculty of equanimity, and the faculty of mental pleasure.
And its attainment is by both;
that is, by means of the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation.
This has been explained as being "like the expulsion of a thief and the closing of a door.

Now, regarding the statement "he enters by means of the supramundane [path]," he should be understood as that same gradual practitioner (*ānupūrvika*) who possesses sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), because the context continues.
Its attainment is by means of nine faculties: namely, those very faculties just mentioned, together with the ninth, the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*).
For it is precisely those same faculties that, being untainted (*anāsrava*), receive the designation of the faculty of "having known."
This is what is being questioned here:
why is it stated thus only for one who follows the gradual path (*ānupūrvika*), and not for one who was previously free from passion (*vītarāgapūrvī*)?

For it is not the case that one who was previously free from passion, having generated the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), enters the fundamental first dhyāna at the sixteenth moment of mind.
In that case, it is because there is no regard for what has already been attained.
For one who proceeds by stages (*ānupūrvika*) seeks the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*), since those have not been previously attained.
Therefore, it is possible that he enters directly into the fundamental [dhyāna] itself.

However, one who was previously free from passion (vītarāgapūrvī) has already shown devotion toward the vision of the Four Truths and not toward dhyāna; thus, the intention is that he does not enter the fundamental dhyāna (maula-dhyāna) at that sixteenth moment of mind.
It has been stated that "the attainment of the nine occurs at the two final moments."
That contradicts what was stated in the Abhidharma,
specifically in the *Jñānaprasthāna*:
"By how many faculties does one attain arhatship?"
He said: "By eleven.
The intention is: how is that not contradictory?
"Because of the occurrence of one":
it is the occurrence of only a certain single person (pudgala), not the occurrence of everyone.

For one who, having a dull faculty, might repeatedly fall away and yet attain arhatship through various successive instances of bliss, mental joy, and equanimity based on specific meditative supports— it is with reference to such a person that it was said: "by eleven."
However, there is no possibility of the simultaneous occurrence (*samavadhāna*) of pleasure, mental joy, and equanimity at one time;
this is because mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arise as individual substances (*ekaika-dravya*).
For instance, if a person of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*) were to attain Arhatship by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) or another basis for the faculty of equanimity.
The attainment of that [state] occurs by means of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
From there, one may again fall away.
Then, relying on either the first or the second dhyāna, one may once more attain arhatship.
His attainment of that [state] occurs through the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*).
From there, he may again fall away.
Then, relying upon the third dhyāna, he may once more attain arhatship.
Regarding the statement "its attainment is by means of the faculty of pleasure":
in each case, upon the attainment of that fruit, exactly nine faculties necessarily function.
These are the five beginning with faith, the faculty of one who has known what was to be known, and any one of the faculties of pleasure, mental joy, or equanimity.
It has been stated that when [the fruit] is attained repeatedly, it is by means of eleven [faculties].
How is it that this same consequence does not apply to the non-returner (anāgāmin)?
Why is it stated in that treatise that only the fruit of arhatship is attained by means of eleven?
But it was not stated that the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) [is also lost] in this way.
For one who has fallen away from it never attains it again through the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
This non-returner falls away because of the attainment of the third dhyāna or of the higher stages.
He has fallen away from a higher stage alone;
he is not said to have fallen away from the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
This applies likewise up to [the fruit of arhatship].
From the second dhyāna. But when one has fallen away from the first [dhyāna],
then one is said to have fallen away from the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmiphala).
For the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) is established through the abandonment of the five lower fetters (avarabhāgīya).
And when he has fallen away from detachment from the desire realm,
then the third dhyāna no longer belongs to him.
How, then, could one attain the fruit of a non-returner by means of the faculty of pleasure? To this he says:
"For one who has fallen away from it never attains it by means of the faculty of pleasure."
What [would it attain] by means of the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*)?
For this reason, there is a specific prohibition only against the faculty of physical pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
If one were to enter the fundamental dhyāna at the ninth path of liberation, one would [attain it];
but this is not the case, for one who has fallen away [from it] cannot do so.
He is one of dull faculties;
and whoever has dull faculties is unable to enter the fundamental dhyāna during the ninth path of liberation.
But one with sharp faculties is able [to do so],
because the transformation of the faculties is difficult to accomplish.
This is true.

However, if that person of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*), who has followed the gradual path (*ānupūrvika*), having attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) and subsequently fallen away from it, should undergo a transformation of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*); and having become one of sharp faculties through that transformation of the faculties, should attain the fruit of non-returner by the very same previous sequence— if he were to enter the fundamental [meditative absorption] during the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*),
then his attainment of the fruit of non-returner occurs by means of eight or nine moments.

It should be understood that [the practitioner is endowed] with the five faculties beginning with faith, the faculty of mind, the faculty of equanimity included within the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), and the faculty of mental pleasure (saumanasyendriya) included within the fundamental dhyāna and the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
Furthermore, if one enters the fundamental dhyāna by means of the supramundane [path],
it should be understood that one is endowed with these eight faculties and the faculty of "having known" (ājñendriya) as the ninth.
Therefore, it is well said: for one who has fallen away from that [attainment] never attains it again by means of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
In that case, however, one who was previously free from passion (*vītarāgapūrvī*) would attain it by means of eleven [faculties].
How so?
A person of dull faculties who has attained the third dhyāna may, relying upon that third dhyāna, enter the path of certainty (niyāma).
At the sixteenth moment of mind, he becomes a non-returner (anāgāmin).
That is the attainment of its fruit:

by means of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*).

Having fallen away from that fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), he makes himself one of sharp faculties through the refinement of the faculties (*indriyottāpana*), and attains the fruit of non-returner based precisely on the *anāgamya* stage during the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

The attainment of that fruit for him occurs, as previously described, by means of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*), the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and the mind-faculty (*manaindriya*) as the eighth; and because it is a supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), it also occurs by means of the faculty of "I have known" (*ājñendriya*) as the ninth.
Thus, at two times, that person would attain that fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) by means of eleven faculties.
Then, in order to refute that [objection], he said this:
"And one who was previously free from passion does not fall away,
because his detachment has been attained through two paths."
Furthermore, one who is already free from passion for the sense realm (*kāmavītarāga*) does not fall away once they have entered the path of certainty (*niyāma*) by means of any support.
Why?
Because that freedom from passion—namely, freedom from passion for the sense realm—is attained through both paths.
Because it brings about the attainment of both the mundane and supramundane paths,
the fruit here is twofold: conditioned and unconditioned.
Because it is stated that "the fruit is both conditioned and unconditioned," therein,
that which is unconditioned is the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmiphala), characterized by dissociation (visaṃyoga).
That was previously attained by means of the mundane path; and upon entering the state of certainty (*niyāma*), it is attained once again by means of the supramundane path.
For its attainment is twofold: mundane and supramundane;
therefore, that detachment is stable.
Therefore, one does not fall away from this. But is it not the case that falling away is from the fruit, not from the previous [state]?
"There is also this other reason: because those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing lack a real objective basis (*avastukatva*).
Why has that not been stated here?"—this too must be addressed. Furthermore, another might indeed say this:
Let there be no falling away from the detachment regarding the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing;
however, why would there not be a falling away from the detachment regarding only the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation for one who has fallen away?
For it is through the abandonment of the five lower fetters that the fruit of non-returning is attained.
In that regard, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are to be abandoned by insight (*darśanaheya*).
Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

For one who was previously free from passion, at the end of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), in the sixteenth moment of mind, there occurs through the worldly path (*laukikamārga*) the abandonment of those two; by the power of that [worldly path], there subsequently arises an untainted attainment (*anāsravā prāpti*).
Because the untainted lineages (*anāsravagotra*) have been attained.

For at that stage, both the conditioned non-returner fruit (*anāgāmiphala*), which by nature consists of the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) and is untainted, and the unconditioned [fruit], which is the abandonment of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth, are obtained.
Therefore, this very reason has been stated.
"By the Noble One, because that detachment is attained through two paths.
This means: because the abandonment of sensual desire and so forth is attained through two paths.
(II.18–20) "One who is endowed with equanimity, life-faculty, and mind is necessarily possessed of three."
Thus:

one who is endowed with, possessed of, or necessarily associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*), life-force (*jīvita*), or mind (*manas*), is necessarily possessed of that very triad consisting of the natures of equanimity, life-force, and mind;
for there is no possession of these [factors] apart from one another.
When there is possession for one,
there is also possession for the other two;
by that, the establishment of their possession is made.
But it is not stated for the eye and the other [faculties].
Therefore, he says:
"By the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue," and so forth.
Regarding the statement that one born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is not endowed with the faculties of eye, ear, nose, or tongue, the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) is not mentioned therein.
This is because the sense of "not having acquired or having lost" applies only to the eye and other [faculties] within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and not to the body faculty.
Otherwise, it would simply have been stated that one born in the formless realm is not endowed with the material faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
They are "not yet acquired" during the embryonic stages such as the *kalala* and so forth;
they are "lost" due to their destruction, as in the state of blindness and so forth, or in the case of gradual death.
The qualification "ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are not possessed [of them]" is used for this reason.
Because the Noble One necessarily possesses it;
for there is no abandonment of the untainted pleasure through the transition between stages.
"By means of mental dissatisfaction, one is free from desire for the realm of sensuality."
Whether abiding here or in another realm, whether an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) or an Ārya, one is not possessed [of these]. Regarding "ordinary persons and those established in the fruits":
those established in the fruits refer to stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and the others, because [these qualities] have been abandoned at the conclusion of the clear realization (abhisamaya).
Therefore, they are not endowed with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Those established on the path of seeing (*darśanamārgastha*) are not endowed with the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) because they have not yet attained it.
Those established on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārgastha*) are not endowed with it because it has been abandoned upon the attainment of the fruit.
In states that are not prohibited, one should understand there is possession (*samanvāgama*) as previously described.
Those states which are not prohibited with respect to possession of the faculties such as the eye—
in those states, whichever faculty has been mentioned [is possessed].
The meaning is that one should be understood as being endowed with those various [faculties].

For example, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding the states of not yet having acquired or having lost them, one is endowed with the faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the tongue.
One born in the desire or form realms (*rūpadhātu*) is endowed with the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), and so forth.
"By means of four [factors] and two pleasant bodies. The word "endowed" (yukta) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
And as for the word "necessarily":
if one intends to express the sequence of enumeration, then immediately after that [phrase] "by them," there follows the mention of pleasure and so forth,
namely, "one is endowed with the faculty of pleasure."
With the exception of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) reborn in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), everyone is endowed with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
One is not necessarily endowed with the others;

specifically, one is not endowed with the faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the tongue-faculty when in the formless realm, or in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) during states where they have not yet been acquired or have been lost.
And [it is absent] from the body-faculty in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu);
from the female and male faculties in both the form and formless realms;
and in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) during the states of not yet having acquired them or having lost them.
With the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) in the realms of form and formlessness;
with the faculty of mental pleasure (saumanasyendriya) by an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) born in the third dhyāna;
and with the faculty of mental displeasure (daurmanasyendriya) in the state of being free from passion for the desire realm.

With the five faculties beginning with faith, [it is absent] in the state of one whose roots of merit are severed; with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), in the states of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and one established in the fruit;
and with the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), in the states of an ordinary person, one established in the path of seeing, and one who is no longer in training (*aśaikṣa*).
One who possesses the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) is not endowed with it during the stages of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) or a learner (śaikṣa).
As for the statement, "Whoever possesses the body-faculty (kāyendriya) also possesses four," this refers to one born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) who is endowed with the body-faculty.
There is not necessarily possession by others.

There is non-possession of the eye and so forth in the desire realm during states where they have not been acquired or have been lost. There is also non-possession of the female and male faculties in that same state, as well as in the form realm.
In this very [state], there is non-possession of suffering;
and for an ordinary person born in the fourth dhyāna, there is non-possession of pleasure.
An ordinary person born in the third or fourth dhyāna is also not possessed of mental joy (*saumanasya*).
The non-possession (*asamanvāgama*) with mental distress (*daurmanasya*), faith (*śraddhā*), and the other [faculties] should be stated as before.
One who possesses the eye and so forth possesses five [faculties].
The meaning is "possessing eyes, ears, nose, and tongue.
And "by that" means by that eye.
When the eye exists, the body-faculty necessarily exists,
but not the ear and so forth,
because in the desire realm there is the possibility of their being unobtained or lost.
The deviation regarding the female and male faculties and so forth should be stated as before.
Likewise for the ear, nose, and tongue faculties.
[This applies to] one who possesses the ear faculty.
He necessarily possesses five [faculties]: equanimity, life, mind, body, and that [feeling] itself; thus all cases should be understood accordingly.
And he may also possess mental joy (*saumanasyin*).
What?
It is governed by the statement that one is necessarily endowed with five.
Why has mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) not been included among the eye and the other [faculties]?
Because it is recited in another location.
For if it were included by means of the word "etcetera" (ādi), the arrangement would become confused.
[The question arises: with which faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is one who is born in the second dhyāna but has not yet attained the third endowed?
The faculty of pleasure exists in the desire realm as belonging to the five groups of consciousness;
in the first dhyāna, it belongs to three groups of consciousness;
but in the third dhyāna, it is mental.

Therefore, one born in the second dhyāna is not endowed with the faculty of pleasure belonging to a lower level, because that has been abandoned through the transition to a different level. Nor is he endowed with that belonging to the level of the third dhyāna, because he has not attained it. Thinking thus, [the opponent] raises an objection.
"With what faculty of pleasure is one endowed?
He replied: "With the defiled [faculty] belonging to the level of the third dhyāna."
For it is an established tenet that all beings born in a lower stage are endowed with the defiled [faculties] of a higher stage as long as they have not been abandoned.
The deviation regarding the remaining faculties should be stated as before.
However, one who possesses suffering is endowed with seven.
Thus it is.
For he is one reborn in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Therefore, he necessarily possesses the body-faculty (kāyendriya) and the four feeling-faculties (vedanendriya).
Excluding the faculty of mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*).
In the state of one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), mental dissatisfaction is absent;
however, the faculties of mind (*manas*) and life (*jīvita*) do exist.
Thus, he is necessarily endowed with seven faculties.
However, the variability regarding the remaining faculties should be stated as before.
[This applies to one] who possesses the female faculty and so forth.
"By eight and so forth" means one who possesses the faculties of femininity, masculinity, mental distress, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Because the faculties of life, mind, pleasure, pain, mental ease, and equanimity have already been mentioned,
and because the three beginning with the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) will be discussed later,
it is these eight faculties alone that are being taken up here.
Regarding the statement "one who is endowed with the female faculty": such a person is necessarily reborn in the desire realm because they possess the female faculty;
therefore, they are invariably endowed with eight faculties.
To the question "By which [faculties]? he says: "By those seven, and by the female faculty.
That is, by the seven consisting of the body, life, mind, and the four faculties of sensation, together with the female faculty as the eighth.
Regarding the remaining [faculties], there is no fixed rule,
due to the reasons already stated, such as the possibility of impairment in the case of the eye and so forth.
Just as with the female faculty, the male faculty should also be explained in the same manner.

One who possesses mental distress (*daurmanasya*) but is born in the desire realm and is free from passion for the desires is likewise endowed with those seven [mental factors] and with mental distress.

One who possesses faith (*śraddhā*) but is a sentient being belonging to the three realms is endowed with those five [faculties] beginning with faith—which are invariably present—along with equanimity (*upekṣā*), vitality (*jīvita*), and the mind (*manas*).
Regarding the remaining [possibilities], there is no fixed rule, as previously stated.

Just as it is with one possessed of faith, so it is up to one possessed of wisdom. "The faculty of one who has known" (*ājñātendriya*) means that the faculty exists precisely in one who has known; thus it is the "faculty of one who has known."
The meaning is that it is the faculty of one who has known [the truth] without remainder (*niravaśeṣājñāta*).

For even the faculty of one who has known (*ājñendriya*) is indeed the faculty of one who has known, but it is not [the faculty of one who has known] without remainder because there remains something yet to be abandoned.
Alternatively, by taking a single part of the term, the person who has attained full knowledge (*ājñātāvī*) is called "one who has known" (*ājñāta*).
His faculty is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*).
One who possesses the faculty of one who has already known necessarily possesses eleven [faculties].
A learner (*śaikṣa*) established in the fruit who possesses the faculty of one who has already known exists in all three realms.
How is one born in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realms (ārūpya) endowed with the faculties of pleasure (sukha) and mental joy (saumanasya)?
Because a noble one (ārya) necessarily acquires the faculty of mental joy upon attaining detachment from the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
and the faculty of pleasure upon attaining detachment from the second dhyāna.
And these two are not abandoned even when there is a transition between stages;
for it will be said:
"The wholesome [state] attained through dhyāna is abandoned by both the transition between stages and by falling away."
Likewise for that which pertains to the formless realm. But the noble [attainment] is [lost] through the acquisition of a fruit, through refinement, and through falling away.

Although, even in the attainment of a fruit and the transformation of the faculties (*indriyottāpanā*), those two paths belonging to the state of being a candidate (*pratipannaka-mārga*) and the path of weak faculties are abandoned,
nevertheless, other paths consisting of the nature of abiding in the fruit and possessing sharp faculties are acquired.

Therefore, even when shifting between stages (*bhūmi-saṃcāra*), the Noble One remains endowed with those two— pleasure (*sukha*) and mental joy (*saumanasya*)— which have not been relinquished, even when reborn in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
With the remaining [faculties], as before, there is no fixed rule.
"One endowed with the faculty of 'I shall come to know' (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is possessed of thirteen," and so forth in detail.
A being belonging to the desire realm who is endowed with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) does so because that faculty has arisen within the desire realm itself;
for it is stated that due to a lack of spiritual urgency (asaṃvega), there is a variety here [in the desire realm] and the culmination there [in the form realm].
Therefore, he necessarily possesses the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
He possesses the four feelings, excluding mental grief (*daurmanasya*), because those would deviate from his state of being free from passion (*vītarāga*).
In this context, the word "necessarily" (*avaśyam*) continues to apply.
It is determined that one is necessarily endowed with these thirteen faculties,
but not with only thirteen;
regarding the remaining [faculties], there is no fixed rule.
Because the path of seeing can also occur among those who are blind and so forth.
How could the path of seeing arise when the female and male faculties are deficient?
For it is said that for those who are devoid of or deficient in the female and male faculties, there is no restraint, no attainment of the fruits [of the religious life], and no detachment.
Some, first of all, say: for those who have obtained the vows, there is the attainment of the fruit;
for indeed, through the arising of both sexual organs, there is the abandonment of the Prātimokṣa vow.

It is not because of the deficiency of those [faculties], nor because of death occurring gradually; for even when the female and male faculties have ceased, the arising of the path of seeing occurs for one who has practiced the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Others, however, say:
In this context, the commonality of the person (*pudgala-sāmānya*) is the subject under discussion.

It is not the case that both necessary possession (*samanvāgama*) and its deviation (*vyabhicāra*) are being stated with respect to a single [person] alone by means of the sense faculties (*indriya*).
How so?
This means that one who is endowed with equanimity, life-faculty, and mind is necessarily possessed of these three.
Any person endowed with equanimity— whether born in the desire realm up to being born at the peak of existence— is necessarily possessed of these three.
However, the deviation regarding the eye and other faculties occurs only where possible, not everywhere.
For only someone born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is not endowed with the material sense-faculties;
but this is not the case for one who is born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
In detail, up to: anyone who is not endowed with faith and the other [faculties], such as one whose roots of merit are severed—yet this does not apply to one born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Here too, whoever is endowed with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is necessarily endowed with all these thirteen aforementioned faculties.
However, deviation occurs only in certain cases.
For instance, some are not endowed with the visual faculty, namely those who are blind; others are not endowed with the auditory faculty, namely those who are deaf.
The same applies to the nose and the other [senses]. This extends to the case where a man possesses the female faculty (*strīndriya*) and a woman possesses the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*).
It should be understood exactly thus: for one who is free from passion, [it arises] with mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) of someone.
(II.21) One devoid of the wholesome possesses the minimum of eight [faculties].
Thus, there is one person who is endowed with the fewest of all. Regarding how many "few" he is endowed with, it is said:
One who is devoid of merit is one whose roots of wholesome virtue are completely severed.
And that occurs only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
A woman or a man of speculative temperament (*dṛṣṭicarita*) severs them.
Thus, detachment from sensual desire is not possible here;
therefore, this [being] possesses all five faculties of sensation.
The body-faculty, the life-faculty, and the mind-faculty exist everywhere;
however, the eye-faculty and the others do not,
because they are absent during the state of gradual death and in states such as blindness.

Taking it as "he knows" (*vedayate*), the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Alternatively, taking "knowledge" (*vedanam*) as "vid," the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the Uṇādi rules.
He shows the indicative proof (*jñāpakam*).
Just as "attainment" (*saṃpadana*) is designated as "attainment" (*saṃpad*),
so too the word "formless" (*ārūpya*) is merely a designation that is connected with the word "thus" (*tathā*).
Because they are exclusively wholesome (*ekāntakuśala*), faith and the others are included by the term "wholesome" (*śubha*).
The meaning is that those which are wholesome—being only wholesome and not unwholesome or neutral—are what is intended.
[Objection: This would entail the inclusion of the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others as well.
Those [other factors] are also exclusively wholesome;
therefore, there would be the undesirable consequence of including them [in the definition].
This is not so.
"Because of the context of the eight" means because of the statement: "The one devoid of virtue [is associated] with eight."
By the phrase "with the eight— equanimity, life, mind, and the wholesome"— the exclusion of the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others is established,
because the number eight serves as a limit.
"And because it pertains to the fool.
Here, the fool is the subject.
The fool is of such a nature.
Because of this statement.
Furthermore, one becomes an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) when the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others are absent.
What is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
Because it is stated that there is "non-attainment of the noble dharmas," there is therefore no such contingency regarding those untainted [dharmas].
(II.22) One who possesses both sexual organs is one whose faculties are complete.
For even one who possesses both sexual organs must have a complete set of the eye-faculties and so forth;
thus, one is endowed with nineteen [faculties] and not otherwise.
This applies to one who has attained the faculty of "one who has already known" (ājñātāvīndriya) or either of the other two.
Because it is possessed of passion (*rāgitva*), the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) must be excluded without exception.
Furthermore, because a noble one (*ārya*) necessarily possesses the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) alternately,
[the faculty of one who has already known] is that which is the faculty of "I shall come to know."

That which is the faculty of one who has already known is not the faculty of "I shall come to know"; that which is the faculty of "I shall come to know" is not the faculty of one who has already known.
The detailed classification of the faculties (*indriya*) that arose in connection with the analysis of the elements (*dhātu*) has been stated.
Within the context of the analysis of the eighteen elements—namely, "Of the eighteen elements, how many are faculties and how many are not faculties?"—it is said:
"Half of the *dharma*-element is a faculty, as are those twelve which are known as internal."
Thus [it is said].
The faculties have arrived.
Their classification [is as follows].
"The triad is pure," and so forth, has been stated in detail.
[Now it is asked: "What are these conditioned phenomena? (II.23)
Those which were previously designated as aggregates, elements, and bases—
just as they have distinct characteristics:
that which is affected (rūpyate) is "form" (rūpa).
Experience is feeling (*vedanā*).
The grasping of signs is perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth. They are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) because they possess the quality of arising.
Or rather, are there some that are necessarily co-arising? There are indeed some that are co-arising but not necessarily co-arising.

Just as the visual consciousness and so forth arise simultaneously with the eye and other [faculties], because the eyes and so forth exist as both "homogeneous" (sabhāga) and "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga);
for this very reason, he asks as follows.
"All these phenomena (dharmas) consist of five.
In this way, the inclusion of all phenomena is established by means of the system of the five categories (pañcavastuka).
This is an exposition of phenomena by way of the collection beginning with form (rūpa).
For the sake of easy comprehension:
since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) never arises at all,
no rule regarding simultaneous arising is considered with respect to it.
The most subtle aggregate of form is the atom (*paramāṇu*).
This is the aggregate-atom (*saṃghāta-paramāṇu*), not the substantial-atom (*dravya-paramāṇu*),
for it is that in which there is no distinction between a prior and a posterior part.
That substance which is devoid of all other forms [of matter] is held to be a substance-paramāṇu (dravyaparamāṇu).
Therefore, he specifies that an aggregate (saṃghāta) is a paramāṇu.
In the desire realm, it consists of eight substances when it is without sound.
Thus,
in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), when sound does not arise therein,
it necessarily consists of exactly eight substances (dravya) and not fewer than that.
"Having another faculty" (*aparendriya*) means that which has another faculty (*aparam indriyam*) in it; thus, it is "having another faculty."
The meaning is "possessing the eye and so forth.
For wherever there is the eye or the ear and so forth, there must also be the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), because the functioning of the eye and other faculties is dependent upon it.

Furthermore, these atoms, when accompanied by sound—namely, those consisting of eight substances and so on—are aggregates of atoms; when they arise together with sound, they arise respectively as aggregates consisting of nine, ten, or eleven substances.
That which consists of eight substances becomes nine substances;
that which consists of nine substances [becomes ten].
That which consists of ten substances;
that which consists of ten substances;
that which consists of eleven substances.
For there is also sound that is inseparable from the sense-faculties.
That which cannot be separated from the sense-faculty is the sound inseparable from the sense-faculty.
The meaning is that [the element] exists inseparably from the sense faculties (*indriya*). Some read the root *bhuji* as "to enjoy" (*avinirbhogī*).
How is it that, given the inseparability of the primary elements (*bhūta*), only a certain aggregate is solid, and so forth?
The earth element is solid;
the water element is fluid;
the fire element is hot.
The wind element is motion (*samudīraṇā*).
The intention is that because the primary elements are equal in their presence, their composites must likewise be equal in form.
"That which is most intense therein," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

Whatever substance is characterized by earth and so forth, in whichever aggregate it is most intense and most manifest— manifest not in terms of its substantiality (*dravyataḥ*), but in terms of its influence (*prabhāva*) and capacity (*śakti*)—
therein that [substance] is perceived.
The perception or apprehension of that substance there is its grasping as a composite,
like the touch of needles, cotton, and a bundle of grass.
In this context, "needles" are understood in the world to be made of iron.
The *tūlī* consists of the flowers, roots, and stalks of the *vīraṇa* grass and other such plants;
those which are commonly known in the vernacular as *siṅkā*.
A bundle (*kalāpa*) is a collection of those needles (*sūcī*) and *tūlī* fibers.
Its touch is like the touch of a bundle of needles and cotton;
and there is the perception of it—
that which has arisen through the power of that most intense [element], the primary element (bhūta).

In that context, the suffix *vati* is applied by this rule: "tatra tasyeva" (in that place, as if it were that). This is what is meant: [the suffix *vati* occurs when there is similarity between two things].
Just as when there is an equal presence of bundles of needles and cotton, the touch of the needles alone is clearly perceived because of their sharpness,
whereas that of the cotton is not because of its lack of sharpness;
so too, hardness is perceived only in certain aggregates, such as wood and the like.
In some cases there is fluidity in water;
in some cases heat in fire;
and in some cases motion in air.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the four great elements do not exist here and there in the aggregate;
rather, it is like the taste of barley-flour and salt-powder.
Just as the taste is perceived from barley-flour and salt-powder [when mixed], so too is it here.
Only the taste of salt powder is clearly perceived,
but not the taste of flour powder;
it is the same in this case as well.
"Because of cohesion, support, ripening, and expansion.
Through the function of cohesion, the existence of the water element is inferred in wood and the like;
otherwise, it would fall apart like a handful of dust.
If the water element were not present there,
the existence of the earth element would be known by the function of support for boats and the like in the waters;
the existence of the fire element would be known by the function of heating.
For if that [wind element] did not exist, wood and other such things would not undergo putrefaction.
The existence of the wind element is understood through its action of expansion;
for there would be neither its spreading nor its growth if the wind element were not present therein.
The same should be applied elsewhere as well.
"And when conditions are obtained," and so forth:
this means that when conditions such as fire and the like are obtained, solid substances and others undergo states such as liquefaction.
Because of states such as fluidity and solidity.
For example, when fire is present, there is the melting of solid iron;
by this it is known that the water-element exists within the iron.
Likewise, when a liquid acquires the perception of coldness and so forth, solidity [is present];
by this it is known that the earth element exists therein.
Similarly, heat is perceived through the friction of solid objects.
By this, the existence of the fire element (*tejodhātu*) therein is understood.
In this same way, it should be applied to other cases as well according to their occurrence.
Another [teacher] says that heat is inferred in water due to its excessive coldness; this is the Venerable Śrīlāta.
Since water is perceived as cold, colder, and coldest,
it is known from this that there is an intensification of cold due to the production of various degrees [of intensity] of fire within it;
and by that, it is understood that fire exists therein.
"Even though there is no intermingling," and so forth. The Master refutes that view:

"Just as there is no intermingling—that is, no mixing—with another substance for sound, yet there is an excellence [of intensity] due to a difference in intrinsic nature, such that a sound is sharp, sharper, or sharpest."
The same would apply here as well.

Just as in the case of sensation (*vedanā*), there is no intermingling with any other distinct substance, and thus its excellence occurs through degrees due to a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*);
so it is here too.
The existence of heat is not understood through this [perception].
For those very waters are some cold, some colder, and some coldest;
thus, according to others—the Sautrāntikas—their presence in those [waters] exists by way of their seeds (*bīja*), not by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*).
The meaning is: "by way of seed," "by way of potential," or "by way of capacity. It does not mean by way of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) or by way of substance (*dravya*).

For there exists indeed a manifold potentiality (*śakti*) by which yogins, through specific acts of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), produce elements such as gold-elements, silver-elements, copper-elements, and so forth.
Why is this so? He says:
because of the statement, "In this log of wood there are various elements (dhātu).
For it was in reference to that very point that the Blessed One spoke of the potencies of the elements.

"For there is no room therein for very many substances such as gold and silver in their own form. Thus they challenge the Vaibhāṣikas: "How can color exist in wind? [The answer is: "In the desire realm, it consists of eight substances."
If this is the rule, how can it be determined that there is color in air?
For in no way is color perceived therein.
"This matter is to be accepted on faith, not by means of inference," say the Vaibhāṣikas.
The intention is that this matter should be accepted as having been stated by the supreme authorities (*paramāpta*), and not that the matter is to be established through inference (*anumāna*).
By the phrase "due to association" or "due to the perception of odor," he demonstrates that there is indeed such an inference.
However, odor is perceived in the wind due to its contact with a fragrant substance;
and that odor does not deviate from color.
For wherever there is odor, [there is color].
"In that case, it must possess color.
And here is the statement of the proof:
"Air possesses color, because it possesses odor, like a jasmine flower."
It has been stated that odor and taste are absent in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
because of the statement: "excluding the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness."
Therefore, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) located therein consist of six, seven, or eight substances (*dravyaka*). "Located therein" means existing there.
By "atoms located therein," the composite atoms (*saṃghātaparamāṇu*) are intended.

That which was stated here as consisting of eight substances, being devoid of sense-faculties and lacking sound, consists of six substances there. That which consists of nine substances is [the atom] possessing the body-faculty.
That [atom] consists of seven substances.
That which has another sense faculty as its tenth substance consists of eight substances.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these [atoms] with sound consist of seven, eight, or nine substances.
Because their nature has already been stated, they are not stated again; the meaning is that because they are similar to what has already been explained, they are not formulated as separate sūtras.
What, then, is meant here by "substance is indeed substance," and so forth?
By primary usage, that which is a substance— that is, that which possesses its own specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)— is what is understood as "substance."
Or rather, is it the case that the sense-field (*āyatana*) is a substantial entity (*dravya*)? This is the subject under discussion.
For it can indeed be said that the sense-field is a substantial entity, because the characteristics of both the general and the particular exist therein.
What follows from this?

And what would be the fault in that? This is the meaning: if "substance" is taken to mean substance itself—that is, if the substantial atom (*paramāṇu*) of earth and so forth, characterized by the limit of form (*rūpa*), is taken [as the referent].
This is stated too briefly.
Regarding the phrase "consisting of eight substances" and so forth:

because other substances—namely shape (*saṃsthāna*), heaviness (*gurutva*), lightness (*laghutva*), smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*), roughness (*karkaśatva*), cold (*śīta*), hunger (*jighatsā*), and thirst (*pipāsā*)—may exist in various places according to the circumstances.
And this being the case, that which consists of eight substances would consist of nine substances, up to fourteen substances; thus, the rule of consisting of eight substances is violated.
The same should be applied to those consisting of nine substances and so forth.
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as well, the distinctions regarding the fixed number of six, seven, or eight substances must be stated.

For it must be stated that [the tangible] consists of four substances; because the primary elements (*bhūta*), such as earth and the rest, are also the sense-sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
Because of the statement that "the tangible is of two kinds," therefore, in the desire realm, that which is without sound consists of four substances.

Visible form, odor, taste, and the tangible—these, it should be stated, consist of five substances when accompanied by sound. As for that which serves as the basis: [it consists of the four great elements].
The four beginning with earth;
that which serves as the basis [of the sense organs] consists of visible form,
odor, taste, and a portion of the tangible.
Thus, since shape (saṃsthāna) is included within visible form (rūpa),
and heaviness and so forth are included within the tangible (spraṣṭavya),
this which has been said is not too little.
Nor are they too many,
because the tangible bases (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) that constitute their support have been extracted and taught separately as fourfold.
"Even so, they are more numerous," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
The set of four primary elements that serves as the support for one derived form, such as blue or yellow,
is not the same support for another derived form, such as odor or taste.
What then?

The Vaibhāṣika tenet is that its basis is a completely different set of four primary elements (*bhūtacatuṣka*). In that context, however, "the substance of the genus" means that the genus of the four primary elements is what is intended here.
For whatever is the birth of one set of the four great elements,
other sets of the four great elements do not transcend that;
thus it is said by way of distinction.
In this context, one kind of substance is taken as the substance that serves as the basis;
another kind of substance is taken as the substance that constitutes the sense-field, which serves as that which is based upon it.
And that which serves as the basis is as follows:
"It is grasped by way of its genus.
For the application of words occurs according to one's preference;
however, the actual object must be examined.
Speech proceeds according to one's will or desire, conforming to the methods of both concise and detailed exposition;
however, their meaning must be examined.
Are those [mental factors] necessarily co-arisen in this manner?
They do not exist.
However, the Yogācāra-Cittamātrins describe a fixed rule regarding the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) during the state of aggregation.
How so?
It is said:
there is a composite consisting of a single element, such as a dry lump of clay; there is one consisting of two elements, namely that same lump when it is moist.
There is that which consists of three elements, namely, heat.
There is even that which consists of all elements, namely, a lump of clay that is both moist and hot during the state of moving.
Regarding derived matter as well, whatever derived matter is perceived within a particular aggregate [is included therein].
It should be understood that this exists therein:
there is a composite consisting of a single derived form,
such as light.
There is that which possesses two derived forms of matter (*upādāyarūpa*), such as wind accompanied by sound and odor. There is also that which possesses three derived forms of matter.
It is, for example, like smoke,
because it is produced by a specific quality of visible form, odor, and tangible object.
Furthermore, in this context, the specific quality of the tangible object should be understood as lightness.
It consists of four derived forms,
such as a lump of molasses;
it consists of five derived forms.
For example, that very same [sound] is with sound;
such [cases] as these should also be stated.
(II.24ab) It should be stated for the "remainder," namely, for the mind, mental factors, and the dissociated factors.
"Mind and mental factors necessarily arise together.
That is to say, mind does not arise without mental factors.
Nor is it determined that mental factors do not exist without the mind;
however, it is not the case that every mind necessarily arises simultaneously with all mental factors,
nor that all mental factors necessarily arise simultaneously with every mind.
"Everything by means of the characteristics of the conditioned" means that which is endowed with the characteristics of the conditioned.
All that necessarily arises together with those conditioned characteristics, such as birth and so forth.
What, then, is that? He says:
whatever arises—whether form, mind, mental factors, or factors dissociated from mind.

For the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has already been excluded [from the scope of arising] previously, because of the statement that "the unconditioned does not arise at all. Alternatively, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an option (*vikalpa*).

The distinction is that some [phenomena] arise together with possession (*prāpti*), namely those classified as sentient beings (*sattvasaṃkhyāta*), while others do not, namely those not classified as sentient beings (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*).

Although there is possession of both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), these two do not themselves arise; therefore, they are not included [in this category].
"This undertaking is indeed a rule of simultaneous arising.
What is the reason that there is no acquisition (*prāpti*) for that which is not reckoned as a sentient being?
Because it is common to all sentient beings.

And it should be understood that one who possesses acquisition arises simultaneously with that very acquisition; it does not arise at a prior or subsequent time. (II.24cd) Regarding the phrase "the sphere of movement":
The meaning is "the object of arising.
Regarding the term *mahābhūmikāḥ*:
their greatness (*mahattva*) is due to their presence in all states of mind.
(II.25) "These, it is said" (*ime kila*).
The word "it is said" (*kila*) indicates the opinion of others.
According to his own view (*svamata*), however, desire (*chanda*) and the other factors do not exist in every state of consciousness.
For it has been written by this very master in the *Pañcaskandhaka*:
"What is desire (*chanda*)? It is longing for an intended object."
What is resolve (*adhimokṣa*)? It is the ascertainment of a determined object as being exactly so, and so forth.
Volition (*cetanā*) is the mental formation (*abhisaṃskāra*).
The "movement of the mind" (*cittapraspanda*) means movement as it were; that is, the meaning is "movement.
"Grasping at the signs of objects" (*viṣayanimittagrāha*) means grasping at the specific forms of objects; that is the meaning.
Contact (*sparśa*) is the touching (*spṛṣṭi*) born from the coming together of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness.
It is the touching produced from the conjunction of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness;
it is called "touching" because it is like the act of touching.
Contact (*sparśa*) is that through the conjunction of which the sense-faculties, their objects, and the consciousnesses seem to touch one another.
As for "discernment of phenomena" (*dharmapravicaya*): it is called discernment (*pravicaya*) because it discerns (*pravicinoti*).
Alternatively, it is called "discernment" (*pravicaya*) because by means of it phenomena (*dharmas*) are discerned;
that is to say, phenomena which are as if intermingled are discerned or selected, like flowers.
[The meaning is: "These are with outflows (*sāsrava*); these are without outflows (*anāsrava*)."
"These are material, these are immaterial"—
this discernment of phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ pravicayaḥ*) is the "discernment of phenomena" (*dharmapravicaya*).

Although it should be called "wisdom" (*prajñā*) because it is well-known as such, it is stated as "intellect" (*mati*) in the verse (*kārikā*) for the sake of conforming to the metrical structure of the *śloka*.
Mindfulness is the non-forgetting of the object of focus.
Through its connection with this, the mind does not forget the object,
and it seems as if it speaks of it.
That is mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Mental attention (*manaskāra*) is the orientation of the mind;
it is the turning of the mind toward an object.
The meaning is "ascertainment.

It is mental application (*manaskāra*) because it is the activity (*kāra*) of the mind (*manas*). Alternatively, it is mental application because the mind applies itself (*karoti*), that is, directs itself toward [the object].
Resolute belief (*adhimukti*) is the determination of the qualities of its object; others say it is "liking" (*ruci*);
the Yogācāra masters say it is the retention [of the object] according to one's ascertainment.

"Concentration (*samādhi*) is one-pointedness of mind. "Point" (*agra*) means "object" (*ālambana*); these are synonymous. It is through connection with this that the mind proceeds continuously toward a single object.
That is concentration.
If concentration exists in every state of mind,
for what purpose is effort made regarding the meditative absorptions?
For the sake of accomplishing powerful concentration (*balavatsamādhi*).
How is the existence of ten mental factors (*caitta*) with distinct characteristics understood within a single moment of mind? To this he says:
"For the distinction between mind and mental factors is subtle," and so forth.

This distinction among the mind and mental factors is difficult to perceive even within their continuums, let alone within moments characterized by temporal limits. Even in the case of material medicinal herbs—certain physical substances such as *harītakī* and others that possess many flavors, including the six basic tastes—the flavors perceivable by the sense organs, specifically those perceivable by the gustatory faculty, are difficult to determine and hard to distinguish;
how much more so for those phenomena that are formless, perceivable only by the intellect, and graspable solely by the mental consciousness?
Therefore, the intention is that because they were taught by a reliable authority (*āpta*), they should be accepted exactly as they are. (II.26) "Faith (*śraddhā*) is the clarity of the mind":
the mind, which has been turbid due to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), becomes clear through its connection with faith.
"Like water [becoming clear] through the application of a water-clearing gem," so too is faith the firm conviction regarding the jewels of the Truths and the results of karma; thus say others.
This is an explanation of faith by way of its characteristic (ākāra).

Faith (*śraddhā*) is the firm conviction (*abhisaṃpratyaya*), the thorough acceptance (*abhisaṃpratipatti*), that these four truths, the three jewels, and the wholesome and unwholesome actions along with their desirable and undesirable fruits truly exist.
Heedfulness (*apramāda*) is the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of wholesome dharmas.
Cultivation refers to the nature of acquiring (*pratilambha*) and practicing (*niṣevaṇa*) wholesome dharmas.
Since it is stated that "the cultivation of the conditioned wholesome is called acquisition and practice," how can that [cultivation] be the mental factor named *apramāda* (heedfulness)?
For it is when this [factor] exists that the cultivation of acquisition and practice occurs.
Thus, that heedfulness is characterized by focused attention.
Therefore, he says:
"that which is attentiveness toward them."
This being so, this is a metaphorical designation of "cultivation" applied to the cause of cultivation; thus,
it is called "the protection of the mind," referring to one who protects the mind from factors conducive to affliction.
That is heedfulness (*apramāda*).
It is the workability (*karmaṇyatā*) of the mind; through connection with which the mind becomes workable.
That pliancy of mind (*cittakarmaṇyatā*) means lightness of mind (*cittalāghava*).

But is it not stated in the Sūtra that there is also bodily pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*)? And what is the distinction by which there are two factors of enlightenment (*saṃbodhyaṅga*) consisting of pliancy?
There is physical pliancy and there is mental pliancy.
In that regard, whatever constitutes physical pliancy, that too is the factor of enlightenment called pliancy; it conduces to direct knowledge, to perfect awakening, and to nirvana.
As for that which is mental pliancy (*cittapraśrabdhi*),
that too is the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhisambodhyaṅga*) which conduces to higher knowledge (*abhijñā*), to awakening (*sambodhi*), and to nirvāṇa.
How is it that this [mental pliancy] alone is so designated?
"Pliancy is the serviceability of the mind.
But as for its being "bodily," it is like bodily feeling.
Just as feeling, even when mental, is called "bodily" because it has as its basis a sense faculty composed of an accumulation of atoms, so too should this pliancy be understood.
"How will that be applied to the factors of enlightenment?"—he asks this because the five groups of sensory consciousness are not in a state of meditative concentration (*asamāhita*).
"In that case, then... and so forth.

In that sūtra, it is precisely bodily confidence (*kāya-vaiśāradya*)—characterized by a specific excellence of the primary elements—that constitutes bodily pliancy (*kāya-karmaṇyatā*), and it is infused with joy (*prīti*).
Because of the statement that "for one whose mind is gladdened, pliancy arises," [the opponent asks]:
"How can that [gladness] be a factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga)?
The intention [of the objection] is that it is not logical [to call it a factor of enlightenment] because it constitutes a separate category and because it is associated with outflows (sāsrava).
"Joy, the factors conducive to joy, and the factor of enlightenment that is joy," and so forth.
It is said that the non-Buddhist teachers spoke thus to the disciples of the Blessed One:
"O sirs, the ascetic Gautama says this."
"In this way, monks, having abandoned the five hindrances which are defilements of the mind and weaken wisdom, cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.
We too say this very same thing.
In that regard, what is the distinction between us and the ascetic Gautama concerning the teaching of the Dharma?
To them, the Blessed One taught this:
"Five exist and become ten; ten exist and are established as five."
The Blessed One has stated that ill-will (*pratigha*) and the cause of ill-will, as well as the nine bases of malice (*āghātavastu*), constitute the hindrance of cruelty (*vyāpādanīvaraṇa*).
This is because they are conducive to it.
