Thus, there are seven [bases], which become fourteen.
There are fourteen [factors], yet they are established as seven by way of this distinction: joy and the cause of joy.
This is because they are conducive to that.
Furthermore, intention and exertion do not have wisdom as their intrinsic nature,
because they respectively have discursive thought and vigor as their intrinsic natures;
thus, those two do not have wisdom as their intrinsic nature.
And when the path is formulated as three aggregates— the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom—
it is stated in the exposition of the aggregate of wisdom:
"What is the aggregate of wisdom?"
Right view, right intention, and right effort.
Equanimity is the evenness of mind;
through its conjunction, the mind proceeds evenly, without effortful application.
That is equanimity; it is called equanimity of formations (*saṃskāropekṣā*).
For there are three kinds of equanimity:
equanimity of feeling (*vedanopekṣā*), equanimity of formations (*saṃskāropekṣā*), and immeasurable equanimity (*apramāṇopekṣā*).
But was it not said that their distinction is difficult to know?
For the distinction between mind and mental factors is subtle; as it is stated: "This is difficult to discern even within [mental] continuums," and so forth.
That which is difficult to know is known with difficulty.
For indeed, even that which is difficult to know can be known,
provided it is not contradictory to other factors such as contact (*sparśa*) within a single moment of consciousness (*cittakṣaṇa*).
This, however, is indeed extremely difficult to understand: that there is no contradiction even where there is a contradiction.
The ellipsis of the sentence is that "no contradiction is established between effort (*ābhoga*) and effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*) within a single moment of consciousness.
For it is never observed that two contradictory states, such as pleasure and pain, coexist within a single moment of consciousness.
"Attention elsewhere" means that there is attention toward one object and non-attention toward another; thus, there is no contradiction.
Other instances of this same category will also follow here.
An example of those belonging to different classes is initial inquiry (*vitarka*) and sustained investigation (*vicāra*).
For their definitions are as follows: initial inquiry is coarseness of mind, while sustained investigation is subtlety of mind.
Because of the statement: "Vitarka and vicāra consist in coarseness and subtlety."
However, it will be explained that there is a contradiction between those two within a single moment of consciousness.
Whatever principle applies to that [case] applies to this one as well.
The intention is that these two function alternately.

It will be explained later that "shame" (*hrī*) and "modesty" (*apatrāpya*) follow. "Lack of shame" (*ahrī*) is a lack of respect toward what is blameworthy; "lack of modesty" (*atrapā*) is the failure to see fear [in wrongdoing].
Here, because of the mention of "perversion," it is said that "it consists of wisdom. That non-delusion has wisdom as its intrinsic nature.
And wisdom (*prajñā*) is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*),
because of the statement: "It is intelligence (*mati*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*)."
This is not called merely a "great wholesome ground" (kuśalamahābhūmika);
rather,
it is also a "ground of the unwholesome and so forth" (akuśalādibhūmika).
"Non-harming" (aviheṭhanā) refers to that through the connection with which another is not harmed. It is non-violence (avihiṃsā), the mental factor that is the antidote to violence (vihiṃsā).
"Exertion of the mind" means that which is the exertion of the mind toward wholesome action;
that is vigor.
However, that enthusiasm of the mind toward unwholesome actions and the like is not vigor;
it is indeed laziness.
It is recited in the teaching because its nature is to sink;
for thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"The vigor of those outside [this teaching] is indeed just laziness" (II.27ab).
Regarding "delusion," it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Ignorance is a distinct dharma that is the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*).
It is explained later:
"the factor that is the opposite of cultivation.
He says "the opposite of cultivation" so that there may not be the apprehension of cultivation as a mere absence.
The same should be explained for laziness and the others as well. "Heaviness of body and heaviness of mind" refers to a state that is the opposite of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
"Just as bodily feeling":
just as feeling, although mental, is explained as "bodily" because it relies upon the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*),
so too is torpor (*styāna*) bodily.
Stiffness (*styāna*) associated with the five groups of consciousness is called bodily; excitement (*auddhatya*) is the lack of tranquility of the mind.
It is a mental factor whose function is to provide a basis for excitement such as dancing, singing, and so forth, as well as for amorous dress and ornaments.
And yet, *styāna* (sloth) is not recited here in the Abhidharma.
Thus, the "Beloved of the Gods" (devānāṃ priyaḥ) knows the literal attainment (*prāpti*) but does not know the intended meaning (*iṣṭi*).

Merely on the authority of the textual recitation, the "Beloved of the Gods" understands that ten universal mental factors of defilement (*kleśamahābhūmika*) are attained; he knows only this attainment, but he does not know the intention or desire of the Teachers (*ācārya*).
Who is this so-called "beloved of the gods" (*devānāṃ priya*)?
Some explain that the "beloved of the gods" is one who is upright by nature;
for indeed, one who is not deceitful becomes beloved of the gods.
Others say that "the fool" refers to the "beloved of the gods" (devānāṃ priya). For he who is favored by the lords does not learn through beating;
thus, he becomes a fool.

"Just as non-delusion" means that just as non-delusion is established as a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*) because its intrinsic nature is wisdom (*prajñā*), it is not restricted to being only a wholesome universal mental factor (*kuśalamahābhūmika*). Consequently, it is not included among the wholesome universal mental factors.

Likewise, the five factors beginning with forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) are not restricted to being exclusively among the great ground-factors of affliction (*kleśamahābhūmika*), because they belong to the [ten] universal ground-factors (*mahābhūmika*).
Consequently, these are not recited in the list of the great ground-factors of affliction.
To the question "How so?", he says:
For indeed, afflicted mindfulness itself is forgetfulness;
afflicted concentration itself is distraction, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth," it is meant that afflicted wisdom itself is lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*).

It shows that afflicted attention (*manaskāra*) itself is improper attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), and that afflicted resolve (*adhimukti*) itself is false resolve (*mithyādhimokṣa*). For this very reason, it is said, and so forth.
Since mindfulness and so forth, as well as forgetfulness and so forth, are established in this very way,
they are not distinct from these [mental factors].
For this reason, it is said that there are four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
He asks rhetorically: "Are those which are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) also universal defilement factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*)?
There are four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There may be factors that are universal mental factors but not universal defilement factors.

There may be those that are universal factors of affliction (kleśamahābhūmika) but not universal factors (mahābhūmika). There may be those that are both universal factors and universal factors of affliction. And there may be those that are neither universal factors nor universal factors of affliction.
The third category consists of "mindfulness and so forth," which refers to the five factors previously mentioned, such as lost mindfulness and the rest.
These are indeed both universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and universal defiled mental factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*).
The fourth [alternative] is "setting aside these aspects.

This refers to those factors excluded from what has been mentioned—namely, the mental factors such as the great wholesome ground-factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*) and others, as well as other [factors] such as form (*rūpa*).
Regarding them, there is another fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*).
Distraction (vikṣepa) should be included in the second alternative (koṭi),
but not in the third.
Therefore, it should be stated as follows:
The first category is as before.
The second consists of lack of faith, laziness, ignorance, restlessness, negligence, and distraction.
The third consists of the four beginning with mindfulness.
The meaning is: forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), and false resolve (*mithyādhimokṣa*).
The fourth [member] is as before.
As for what was said—that *styāna* (sloth) is not recited here—[that refers to the specific context].
He replies to them:
"Furthermore, torpor is accepted," and so forth.
[The question is: "If it is not recited, whose fault is it?"
"Is it my fault that this *styāna* was not recited? Or is it the fault of the Abhidharmika?"—
the intention is that "this is the fault of the author of the Abhidharma, not mine."

Because *styāna* (stiffness) is considered to be associated with all afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding the phrase "but they say thus," the Abhidharmikas state therein the reason for the non-mention of *styāna* in that treatise.
"More quickly, it is said.
The word "it is said" (*kila*) indicates a lack of conviction.
For how indeed could a defiled state (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) be conducive to a pure concentration (*śukla-samādhi*)?
For lethargy and excitement are indeed adversaries to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). How, then, could that which is an adversary be conducive [to it]?
For these two never abandon their tendency to coexist.
The meaning is that these two, lethargy and restlessness, never abandon their nature of being co-existent.
Nevertheless, "whatever is predominant for whom"— that is to say, even so, whichever [of the two], whether lethargy or restlessness, is predominant for a particular person.
That person should be understood as one whose temperament is characterized by lethargy (*styāna*) or one whose temperament is characterized by restlessness (*auddhatya*).
For in some mental complexes (*kalāpa*), a certain factor (*dharma*) becomes predominant,
but not so in others, such as those that are wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth.
(II.27cd) "But in the unwholesome [states], there are lack of shame and lack of dread. The word "but" (*tu*) serves either as a distinction or as a restriction.
"Only unwholesome.
(II.28) "Those belonging to the level of limited defilements."
"Parītta" means small.
What is that?
It is mere ignorance.
The meaning is "ignorance alone";
by that, it means "by ignorance alone," and not by any other affliction such as attachment and so forth.
"By that which is to be abandoned by cultivation," not by that which is to be abandoned by insight;
"only by that which belongs to the mental level."
Not by those belonging to the five groups of consciousness.
Because these secondary afflictions, such as anger and the rest, belong exclusively to the level of the mental faculty (*manobhūmika*),
they are therefore called "minor afflictive levels" (*parīttakleśabhūmika*) due to their association with the mind.
For in any collection [of mental factors] such as attachment and the like, ignorance must necessarily be present; thus, attachment and the others are not limited [to specific occasions].
Therefore, those which are present in every state of mind are the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
Those which exist only in the wholesome are the great wholesome-ground factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*).
Those which exist in the afflicted, the obscured-unwholesome, and the unwholesome...
Those are the universal mental factors of defilement (*kleśamahābhūmika*). Those which exist only in the unwholesome are the universal mental factors of the unwholesome (*akuśalamahābhūmika*).
Those [factors] which are associated with a mind conjoined with limited defilements are the factors of the limited defilement-ground (*parīttakleśabhūmika*). However,
their detailed exposition will be provided among the secondary defilements (*upakleśa*).
In the explanation of the latent dispositions (anuśaya), [it is said]:
"Others also are indeterminate" (II.29–31).
These are those which exist at times in a wholesome mind, at times in an unwholesome mind, and at times in an indeterminate mind.
Regarding the phrase "torpor and so forth":

by the word "and so forth" (ādi), secondary afflictions such as discontent, yawning, lethargy, and irregularity of food, as well as the primary afflictions such as attachment and the rest, are included because they are indeterminate.
For these [afflictions] like attachment are not restricted to any one of the five categories.
They are not universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) because they do not exist in every state of mind;
they are not universal wholesome factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*) because they are associated with wholesomeness;
and they are not universal defiled factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*) because they are absent in all defiled states.
For passion does not exist when the mind is possessed of aversion, nor does aversion exist when the mind is possessed of passion.
In this same way, the other afflictions (*kleśa*) should also be explained.
Regarding this, the Master Vasumitra has stated a summary verse:
Applied thought, sustained thought, regret, torpor, hostility, envy, pride, and doubt— these eight are known as the indeterminate [mental factors].
We do not understand this statement regarding the eight fixed factors.
Why are views (*dṛṣṭi*) also not accepted as being unfixed?
For false view does not arise in a mind that is accompanied by resistance (*sapratigha*) or by doubt (*savicikitsa*).

For it is stated that in the case of unwholesome states that are independent (*āveṇika*) or associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-yukta*), there are twenty [mental factors]; and when accompanied by the four afflictions (*kleśa*) such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, or by remorse (*kaukṛtya*), there are twenty-one.
Therefore, we observe that whatever has been stated regarding this [is as follows]:
first, that which belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) is fivefold;
one is wholesome (*kuśala*).
The unwholesome is of two kinds:
that which is unique, associated with ignorance alone, and that which is associated with other afflictions such as attachment.
The indeterminate is also of two kinds.

The obscured-unspecified [mind] is that which is associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). The unobscured-unspecified [mind] consists of those states such as those born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
The state of having done what should not have been done is remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
Dharma is the result of a wrong action;
however, since that [wrong action] is a mental factor (caitasika), it is not connected [to the term "dharma" in this context].
Therefore, he says:
But here, however, [it is said] that the mental factor which has regret as its object—what is its intrinsic nature? He says: it is remorse of the mind (*cetaso vipratisāra*).
If a mental state that has remorse as its object is called "remorse," then other mental factors and mental concomitants associated with it would also incur the designation of "remorse.
They do not so incur it.
Because these [other factors] are not predominant.
For in the state of remorse (*vipratisāra*), the mental factor characterized by regret (*kaukṛtya*) manifests with the aspect of regret;
the other mind and mental factors then conform to that aspect.
For they describe that a particular dharma possesses preeminence within a certain mental complex.
The door to liberation (vimokṣamukha) which has emptiness as its object is called "emptiness" (śūnyatā).
That specific concentration (samādhi), which is a door to liberation having as its object the aggregates (skandhas) devoid of an internal active person (puruṣa), is termed "emptiness."
Non-greed (*alobha*) which takes as its object the impure things such as the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*), the bloated corpse (*vyādhmātaka*), and so forth, is called "the impure" (*aśubhā*).
It is expressed in the feminine gender because it is connected with cultivation (*bhāvanā*);
thus, it is referred to as "the cultivation of the impure" (*aśubhā bhāvanā*).
Likewise here too, the mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) that has remorse as its object is called "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*).
This is an extension of the name from the basis to those who reside upon it,
just as one says, "the entire village has arrived."
A village is a collection of houses situated on a single level.
When the inhabitants have arrived, people say, "The entire village has arrived," and likewise, "The entire country has arrived."
And remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is the basis for regret (*vipratisāra*),
because it is the objective support (*ālambana*) of regret.
Therefore, such an explanation is logical.
Or, it is a metaphorical designation of the cause by the name of the fruit.
The cause is remorse (*kaukṛtya*);
the fruit is regret (*vipratisāra*).
The cause is metaphorically designated by means of that fruit;
the meaning is that the fruit is expressed by a word denoting the cause.
For example: "These six bases of contact are ancient karma."
The six bases of contact, beginning with the eye, are the fruits of ancient karma performed in previous births;
just as [the designation of "self"] is applied to those [bases] according to that karma, so it is here.
If, then, that which has not been done as its object is so called, how can it be "regret" (*kaukṛtya*)?
He raises this objection, considering that what was not done is simply "not done."
"Even when something has not been done, it is designated as 'done'.
Even when an action has not been performed, the word "done" is employed.
To the question "How so?", he says:
Thinking, "That which was not done by me was not well done," he regards it as if it had been done.
Regarding "that which one regrets for not having performed what is wholesome":
when one regrets after failing to perform wholesome acts such as giving, and subsequently becomes remorseful—
that is wholesome.
And having committed what unwholesome act?
It refers to "feeling remorse.
That is, having committed an unwholesome act such as the taking of life and so forth, one feels remorse.
That too is wholesome.
By the opposite, it is unwholesome.
That is, when one regrets having failed to do what is unwholesome and having done what is wholesome.
That which, having committed an evil deed, one later regrets, thinking, "I have not done well;
that was not done," is unwholesome regret (*akuśala-kaukṛtya*).
And that which is wholesome, such as giving and so forth, yet after performing it one later regrets it, thinking, "I have not done well in performing this act of giving and so forth"—
that too is unwholesome. Thus, both of these possess both bases.
This remorse is both wholesome and unwholesome; it has both as its basis according to the method already described.
It is called "unshared" (āveṇika).
The meaning is that it is distinct from passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
And [it applies] when associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*).
(Abhidh-k-vy 134)
The word "and" (ca) serves to draw in [the term] "unwholesome.
View (*dṛṣṭi*) is a particular kind of wisdom (*prajñā*) that belongs specifically to the great ground-factors (*mahābhūmika*);
it is that wisdom which is investigative (*saṃtīrikā*).
That is the view;
and here, that which is unwholesome is intended.
Therefore, he says:
"False view, and so forth," and "twenty-one with remorse" means [the twenty] together with remorse.
The letter *ca* (and) should be understood as having been elided.
In passages such as "by the four afflictions," it should be understood that the completion of the sentence applies to each [affliction] individually.
For the Abhidharmikas maintain that desire and the other afflictions do not associate with one another.
That affliction and the twenty [mental factors] mentioned as being exclusive [to the afflicted mind] make twenty-one.
The ten universal [mental factors], the six universal afflictive [mental factors], the two universal unwholesome [mental factors], and vitarka and vicāra constitute the twenty.
That affliction—namely, attachment, aversion, pride, and doubt—makes twenty-one.
It should be understood that the restriction regarding the action is that there are exactly twenty-one [mental factors].
"By anger and so forth" refers to anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), dissimulation (*śāṭhya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), spite (*pradāsa*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), and avarice (*matsara*).
In a mind associated with these— namely, deceit (*māyā*), intoxication (*mada*), and harmfulness (*hiṃsā*)— there are likewise exactly twenty-one mental factors (*caitasika*).
These are the same as those mentioned previously in the section on the unique (*āveṇika*) [factors].
And that secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) is either anger (*krodha*) up to harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).
When associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*), those previously mentioned [twenty] and that remorse itself make twenty-one;
for remorse is also a secondary affliction.
It is held to be independent.
Briefly stated, it is "unique" (*āveṇika*); this is the detailed explanation.
In an unwholesome mind associated with ignorance alone, and in an unwholesome mind associated with views, there are twenty [mental factors].
However, when associated with other primary or secondary afflictions (*kleśa-upakleśa*), there are twenty-one [mental factors] that are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Regarding "obscured-unspecified" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*): it is that which is obscured by afflictions and is thus unspecified as being either wholesome or unwholesome.
That is the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

However, the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)—which has the nature of that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*), postures (*airyāpathika*), crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and emanations (*nairmāṇika*)—is not covered [by afflictions].
The outsiders (*bahirdeśaka*) maintain that even regret (*kaukṛtya*) is unspecified.
Those who reside outside the region of Kaśmīra are the "outsiders" (bahirdeśaka).
The number "thirteen" is stated by adding remorse (*kaukṛtya*) as a thirteenth [mental factor] in certain cases of non-obscured neutral states.
Because middha is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral in the state of nodding off or in the state of dreaming,
according to the statement in the Śāstra:
"How should middha be described— is it to be called wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral?"
He said:
"It should be stated as wholesome, it should be stated as unwholesome, or it should be stated as indeterminate.
In this regard, there are twenty-two [factors].
In that regard, the detailed explanation is as follows: where it was stated that there are twenty-two mental factors (*caitasika*),
there *middha* (torpor) makes it twenty-three.
The meaning is "that which completes the twenty-three.
Where there are twenty-three, with remorse (*kaukṛtya*) added in some cases,
there that torpor (*middha*) makes it twenty-four.
In this way, up to the point where, according to the opinion of others, there are twelve indeterminate factors (*avyākṛta*), *middha* (torpor) should be stated as the thirteenth.
However, according to the opinion of the outsiders (*bahirdeśaka*), it should be applied that when *kaukṛtya* (remorse) is added, *middha* becomes the fourteenth.
Therefore, [the phrase] "from what has been stated above" refers to this.
Therefore, because of the rule regarding the simultaneous arising of mental factors as previously described,
remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) do not exist in any way whatsoever;
they are neither wholesome nor neutral, let alone unwholesome.
In every respect, there is no torpor or regret;
deceit, pride, and guile are to be excluded.
Guile and deceit exist in the realms of desire and the first dhyāna because of the deception practiced by Brahmā.
Because it is stated that "sloth, restlessness, and pride belong to the three realms," these are excluded [from the list of hindrances],
since they exist there.
All else is exactly the same.
In a wholesome mind, as before, there are twenty-two [mental factors].
In the unshared [unwholesome] and in the obscured-unspecified minds associated with views, there are eighteen, as in the case of the desire realm.

In states associated with attachment (*rāga*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), or other primary afflictions (*kleśa*), as well as in those associated with the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), and arrogance (*mada*), there are nineteen [mental factors].
These [eighteen] plus that specific affliction or secondary affliction constitute the nineteenth in those cases.

In the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states—namely, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*), and those pertaining to magical transformation (*nairmāṇika*)—there are twelve, as previously stated.
"In the intermediate dhyāna, there is also applied thought (*vitarka*).
The word "also" (*ca*) [in the verse] includes remorse (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), and the unwholesome (*akuśala*).
What does it include?
It is understood that "they do not exist.
The remainder is exactly as before, with the exception of applied thought (*vitarka*);
as has been prohibited, they do not exist.
The meaning is that remorse (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), and unwholesome thoughts (*akuśalavitarka*) do not exist.
Regarding the phrase "and investigation (*vicāra*) and deceit (*māyā*) and guile (*śāṭhya*)," it is because of the word "also" (*api*).
While one might have said merely "and investigation," by the addition of the word "also" (*api*) in the expression "and also investigation," there is an increase in the meaning.

It is also understood that there is no deceit or guile (*māyā-śāṭhya*) therein; however, intoxication (*mada*) is not excluded, for it is said that "sloth, restlessness, and intoxication belong to all three realms."
This is because of the force of that statement.
"The remainder is just as before" means that in the wholesome [state], there are twenty [factors] excluding vitarka and vicāra.
In the unique [mental states] associated with views, there are sixteen [factors].
In those associated with afflictions such as attachment, and in those associated with the secondary affliction of pride, there are seventeen:
namely, the ten universal factors and the six universal afflictive factors.
That is a primary affliction (*kleśa*), and that is a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*).
It should be understood that in the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) state, there are only the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
For it is said in detail: "From [the root] *brahman* up to *shāṭhya* (deceit)," and so forth.

In that context, because it is preceded by deceit (*śāṭhya*), hypocrisy (*māyā*) is also included. [The phrase] "not above, due to connection with an assembly" refers to those who possess an assembly.
In order to win over their assemblies, they employ deceit and guile.
Eight assemblies are enumerated:

the assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of brāhmaṇas, the assembly of householders, the assembly of śramaṇas, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā.
Not even one among them exists beyond this; thus, there is an absence of illusion and deceit.
But Brahmā does have an assembly.
Therefore, he says:
For while he was seated in his own assembly, he was asked a question by the monk Aśvajit, who had gone to the Brahma-world:
"Where do these four great elements cease without remainder?
Not knowing—that is, not understanding that the four great elements cease without remainder in the formless realm—he made a delay, interrupting the course of the discussion.
"I am Brahman," and so forth.
Having said "Brahman," he says "Mahābrahman" in order to demonstrate his own superiority over other Brahmās. Īśvara means one whose nature is to rule.
"Maker," "creator," "procreator," and "one who creates" are synonyms, or they may be understood as successive explanations of one another. "Like a father" means being a father;
of whom? [Of all beings.]
"Of phenomena" (bhāvānām).
"This has been stated," and so forth;
that is, whichever stage, whichever mind, and however many mental factors (caitta) there may be.
It has been stated that this is the stage, that is the mind, and those are the mental factors (*caitta*).
Regarding the phrase "prescribed therein," it means prescribed in the treatise (*śāstra*).
Some read the text as "prescribed therein."
And this is precisely the meaning here:
"in regard to qualities and those possessing qualities.
This refers to qualities such as loving-kindness and compassion, whether they pertain to one's own continuum or to the continua of others.
And regarding persons endowed with virtues, who are perfected in conduct, range of activity, reverence, and so forth—
that lack of respect which one does not exercise because of their association [with such qualities] is disrespect (*agauravatā*).
"He has no reverence" means he is irreverent (*agaurava*).
The state of being so is irreverence (*agauravatā*), which is a specific mental factor (*caitasika-viśeṣa*). What is it?
They state two synonyms:
"lack of dependence" (*apratīśatā*) and "not being under the sway of fear" (*abhayavaśavartitā*). One who is desired by a disciple is called *pratīśa*.
He occupies the position of a guru. He has no equal, thus he is "without an equal" (*apratīśa*). The state of being such is "equalitylessness" (*apratīśatā*).
By the expression "state" (*bhāva*), a mental factor (*caitta*) is understood.
Fear (*bhaya*) is a mental factor belonging to the mind.
One who has the habit of being under the sway of fear is called "one who abides under the power of fear" (*bhayavaśavartī*).
Not being under the sway of fear means not being under the sway of the absence of fear; the state of that is "fearlessness" (*abhayavaśavartitā*).
That itself is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*). One who has no shame is "shameless" (*ahrīka*).
The state of that [lack of shame] is *āhrīkya* (shamelessness). Furthermore, it is a mental factor (*dharma*) that is the direct opposite of respect (*gaurava*),
not merely the absence of that [respect].
"Lack of seeing fear in what is blameworthy is *anapatrāpya* (shamelessness). That which is not to be spoken of is *avadya* (blameworthy).
Therefore, he says:"

"Blameworthy" (avadya) refers to that which is censured by the virtuous. In this context, "lack of dread" (anapatrāpya) means the failure to perceive the undesirable consequences within such blameworthy acts.
In the phrase "one fears from this," the word *bhaya* (fear) functions as the source (*apādāna*).
Therefore, by the word *bhaya*, an undesirable result is expressed.
The full expression is "the vision of fearlessness" (*abhayadarśitā*).
If it were done in this way, then "fearlessness" (*abhaya*) would not be [the term].
One whose nature is to see fearlessness is "one who sees fearlessness" (*abhayadarśin*). The state of being that is "the quality of seeing fearlessness" (*abhayadarśitā*).
Wisdom will discern;
for by means of wisdom one sees fearlessness.
Alternatively, it is further analyzed thus: "one whose nature is to see fear" is a "fear-seer."
One who does not see fear is one who sees fearlessness. The state of that is "seeing fearlessness" (*abhayadarśitā*).
By "seeing fearlessness," ignorance (*avidyā*) is to be understood.
For thus, through the connection with ignorance, one does not see fear.
Indeed, there is no seeing at all, as it has been explained in detail.
It is neither wisdom nor ignorance.
What then?
It is that secondary affliction which is the cause of those two— wisdom and ignorance—
that constitutes the perception of fearlessness.
And that is "lack of shame" (*anapatrāpya*).
It is called *apatrāpya* because one feels shame (*apatrapate*) by means of it;
the suffix *-ṇya* is applied in the sense of an instrument according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.

"Not shame" means "lack of shame. Dissatisfied with how these two roots—*hrī*, meaning "modesty," and *trap*, meaning "shame"—which have the same meaning [in their etymological sense] can denote different meanings, others say:
"In relation to oneself," and so forth.
"Even so, how can two dependencies be established simultaneously?
Seeing that even in this position a simultaneous occurrence of two dependencies is impossible, the objector says:
"Even so."
The intention of the word "also" (api) is that this position as well is faulty.
Having considered how shamelessness (āhrīkya) and lack of dread of blame (anapatrāpya) could exist in a single moment of consciousness, he objects:
"How can two dependencies be established simultaneously?"
Indeed, it is not said that one regards both oneself and another simultaneously; such is the detailed explanation.
He shows the occurrence of these two by way of alternation (*paryāyeṇa*).
For in some cases, even for one who regards oneself with regard to faults, shame does not arise.
"Of someone who is dependent upon another," and so forth;
"shame and dread of blame are the reverse," and so on. First, according to the first interpretation:
By this [definition], "lack of shame" (ahrī) is the absence of respect toward faults, while "lack of dread" (atrapā) is the failure to see fear [in committing them].
By the phrase "possessing reverence," and so forth, it is explained that "dread of blame" (apatrāpya) is the perception of fear.
The meaning is that *apatrāpya* is the perception of fear as its cause.
According to the second interpretation, *āhrīkya* is the lack of shame regarding one's faults with respect to oneself, while *apatrāpya* is the lack of shame with respect to others.
By this [interpretation], *hrī* is the feeling of shame regarding one's faults with respect to oneself.
"Modesty (apatrāpya) is in dependence on others.
Even so, the objection and its resolution must be stated in detail as follows: "There are two kinds of dependence.
Some consider love (prema) and respect (gaurava) to be one and the same.
Therefore, in order to demonstrate the distinction between these two, he says:
"Affection is faith.
Affection itself is faith; it is not respect.
But faith itself is not love.
Therefore, he says:
"For love is of two kinds: afflicted and unafflicted," and so forth.
There may be faith that is not love; thus there is a fourfold alternative (catuḥkoṭika).
Regarding the truths of suffering and its origin, there is only faith in the form of conviction (abhisaṃpratyaya), not love, because they are not objects of longing.
There may be love that is not faith.
Craving has the nature of affection (*priyatā*), whereas faith does not have the nature of conviction (*abhisaṃpratyaya*); therefore, faith is not [identical to] love.

Both—faith and love—are present in the truths of cessation and the path; the meaning is that because they consist of both the nature of conviction and the nature of being desirable, these two [truths] possess the essence of both.
"Excluding these two aspects" refers to other mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, as well as the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*).

Having thus established a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) for love (*preman*) and faith (*śraddhā*) that take phenomena (*dharma*) as their object, he now establishes a fourfold alternative for those that take persons (*pudgala*) as their object.
"Regarding persons," and so forth.

In that context, those who dwell together are the co-residents (*sārdhavihārin*), namely the disciples. Those who have gone forth and live in the presence of their teacher are the resident pupils (*antevāsin*).

Regarding those connected to reliance and study— namely, sons and so forth— there may exist affection (*prema*) and respect (*gaurava*), which can be either afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*), as the case may be. However,
respect is not necessarily affection.
Veneration (*gurutva*)— which will be defined below as a form of reverence (*gaurava*) characterized by moral shame (*hrī*)— is not affection (*prema*), because it is the basis for veneration.
Both affection and respect;
the meaning is that it consists of both of these.
"Neither" refers to any other person who, setting aside these modes, is unrelated and devoid of virtue.
In that context, there is neither affection (*prema*) nor respect (*gaurava*).
Affection is a state of endearment preceded by that [respect];
it is affection when endearment is preceded by an appreciation of qualities (*guṇa-saṃbhāvanā*).
Therefore, the Master [Vasubandhu] maintains that faith itself is not love; rather,
shame constitutes gravity.
As it was said: "Shame (hrī) is defined as having reverence, having respect, and being subject to the influence of fear.
That which is shame is itself reverence.
Thus, in this way, love has the characteristic of faith (*śraddhā*).
However, it has been stated that respect (*gaurava*) has the characteristic of shame (*hrī*); this is the distinction between the two. The same applies to reverence (*sapratīśatā*).

In the same way, shame (*hrī*) also [applies] to both phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*). Regarding those instances of faith (*śraddhā*) and shame that have a person as their object, these two do not exist therein; thus, it is the faith and shame having a person as their object that are being discussed, which some consider to be identical.
It has been stated that these two do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), but exist only in the desire and form realms (*kāmarūpadhātu*).
But how can there be a conjunction of these two in a single moment of consciousness?
For it is not logical that the very same moment of consciousness should be both gross and subtle due to such a conjunction, as they are mutually contradictory.

Regarding the word *niṣṭhyūtam*: this form *niṣṭhyūtam* is derived from the root *ṣṭhīv-* preceded by the prefix *nis-* in its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) form; it means "cast out" (*nirastam*).
It does not become too cold, nor does it become too thick;
it does not dissolve too much, nor does it become too fluid;
it is neither too subtle nor too coarse.
The meaning is "in a middling state.
If that is so, then [the phrase] "acting as causes" and so forth follows;
just as water and heat act as the causes for the solidification and the melting of ghee.
But they do not possess that intrinsic nature; that is, they do not have the intrinsic nature of being solidified or melted.

Likewise, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are the causes for the coarseness and subtlety of the mind, but they do not themselves have the intrinsic nature of coarseness and subtlety.
Therefore, it should be stated as follows:
"Vitarka is the cause of coarseness of mind;
vicāra is the cause of subtlety of mind. You might say that there is no fault here because you accept this [definition].
Then he states this further fault:
"And coarseness and subtlety are relative," and so forth.
This is because of the distinctions between levels (*bhūmi*) and types (*prakāra*).
This is due to the distinction of levels (*bhūmi*) and the distinction of types (*prakāra*). First, regarding the distinction of levels:
in comparison with the first dhyāna, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is coarse (*audārika*), because it involves greater effort (*mahābhisaṃskāratara*).
In relation to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the first dhyāna is subtle because it involves less mental effort (*alpa-abhisaṃskāra*) and is thus more tranquil.
Yet that same [first dhyāna] is gross in relation to the second dhyāna.
In this manner, up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), each stage is subtle in relation to the one below it.
Furthermore, even within that same stage, grossness and subtlety are relative according to their different modes.
For example, regarding those three basic modes of the afflictions— weak, medium, and intense— and likewise for the qualities,
from the desire realm up to the peak of existence, the most intense affliction is gross.
"Soft" means subtle.
Regarding the qualities as being the opposite of the afflictions:
thus, through the distinction between levels and types, grossness and subtlety are relative; consequently, grossness and subtlety would exist even up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
And this is undesirable,
because initial inquiry (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) belong to the levels of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna respectively;
furthermore, it is not logical that there should be a difference in their essential nature (*jātibheda*) based merely on coarseness and subtlety.
A difference in genus is maintained between *vitarka* and *vicāra*,
such that *vitarka* is one thing and *vicāra* is another.
Furthermore, it is not logical to maintain that the distinction in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) consists respectively in coarseness and subtlety.
For what reason?
Because feeling and perception, though distinct by nature, possess respectively grossness and subtlety;
yet their difference in intrinsic nature does not consist merely in that grossness and subtlety.
What then?
Their difference in intrinsic nature consists in their having the characteristic of experience and the characteristic of grasping signs;
therefore, these two also do not possess [a single] defining characteristic.
Others, however, say— namely the Sautrāntikas—
that "vocal formations" means those things that originate speech.
"Having applied thought (*vitarkya*) and sustained thought (*vicārya*), one speaks words; not without having applied thought and sustained thought.
This means that by means of applied and sustained thought, one thinks, "I shall speak in such and such a way.
Among these, those which are gross are applied thought.
Those *vitarkas* are the formative factors of speech (*vāk-saṃskāra*).
Their intrinsic nature is illuminated by their function; otherwise, it would not be possible to demonstrate their specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
In this way, those *vicāras* are subtle.
According to this conception, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) exist as a collective form,
yet they also occur successively, because the aggregate of mind and mental factors (*cittacaittakalāpa*) is that which gives rise to speech.
But how is it said that these two are conjoined in a single moment of consciousness?
Therefore, the Vaibhāṣika says:
"And if another factor is gross within a single moment of consciousness," and so forth.
In a single state of mind, *vitarka* is one distinct factor whose intrinsic nature is grossness, while *vicāra* is another whose intrinsic nature is subtlety.
Because they are, respectively, the causes of mental grossness and mental subtlety, they are called "mental grossness" and "mental subtlety.
Alternatively, that which is gross for the mind is "mental grossness."
The state of grossness of mind is "mental grossness.
In the same way, mental subtlety should also be explained; what contradiction is there in this?
There would be no contradiction if there were a difference in the nature of vitarka and vicāra, as there is between feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā).
Feeling is indeed gross, while perception is subtle.
Since there is a difference in their essential natures (*jāti*), there is no contradiction in both grossness and subtlety existing within a single moment of consciousness.

However, when a single nature—whose specific characteristics are not determined and which is grasped by some as a unity—is perceived, the states of mildness and intensity characterized as grossness and subtlety cannot coexist simultaneously.
By implication, it is stated that [the two] do not arise simultaneously.
For instance, feeling (*vedanā*) or any other phenomenon (*dharma*) undergoes states of mildness and intensity in turn;
it does not become manifest in such a way [simultaneously].
What? A difference in genus.
Why?
Because each of the [three] types has both weak and intense degrees,
feeling (vedanā) is indeed coarse or subtle depending on the distinction of relative comparison.
How so?
Feeling is gross in comparison to perception,
but subtle in comparison to form.
Likewise, perception is gross in relation to mental formations,
but subtle in relation to feeling;
or it is just like the case of applied thought and sustained thought.

For according to your own view as well, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) belonging to the desire realm are coarse, while those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna are subtle;
and in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), sustained thought is even more subtle.
Thus, because each class [of phenomena] possesses degrees of mildness and intensity, [the distinction between the stages is established].
It is not thus made manifest.
The meaning is that the distinction between types is not made manifest by way of being weak or intense.
Regarding this, Master Saṃghabhadra says:
Furthermore, grossness and subtlety occur within a single state of mind without contradiction,
because their periods of predominance differ.
For when *vitarka* (applied thought) is active within the complex of mind and mental factors (*cittacaittakalāpa*), [subtlety follows].
At that time, when there is *vicāra*, the mind becomes gross; at that time, when there is *vitarka*,
it becomes subtle.
It is like the designation "one whose temperament is dominated by passion" or "one whose temperament is dominated by delusion.
For even when passion and delusion occur simultaneously, one is designated according to whichever of the two has the more manifest activity—
being called either "one of passionate temperament" or "one of deluded temperament."
The same should be understood here as well.
To this we reply:
in a certain collection [of factors], there occurs for a particular dharma a state of predominant activity.
"But their definitions have not been distinguished.
This is of no consequence.
For has it not been stated that *vitarka* and *vicāra* are characterized by the grossness and subtlety of the mind?
It is true that they were so stated;

however, as for the claim that each of the *jātis* possesses its own grossness and subtlety, and thus ought to be characterized by grossness and subtlety respectively as previously described—this does not satisfy us.
For another teacher, namely the Master [Vasubandhu], holds the view that initial inquiry (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) do not exist together in a single moment of mind.
In this view, the aforementioned fault does not arise.
But what is the distinction between these two, which function as synonyms?
Regarding this, the former masters say:

What is *vitarka*? It is a mental discourse (*manojalpa*) that investigates, based either on volition (*cetanā*) or on wisdom (*prajñā*), occurring respectively in the states of non-investigation and investigation; it is also the coarseness of the mind.
What is *vicāra*?

Alternatively, it is a mental discourse (*manojalpa*) that, depending either on volition (*cetanā*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), consists respectively of the states of non-investigation and investigation; and it is also the subtlety of the mind.
In this view, *vitarka* and *vicāra* are held to be of a single nature, existing as a composite whole, occurring in succession, and distinguished merely by their modes of searching and investigating.
Regarding this, some provide an illustration:
For example, when many jars are standing there, the deliberation made by striking them with the fist to determine which one is solid and which is cracked is *vitarka*.
The final ascertainment at the end, as to how many are cracked or how many are solid, is *vicāra*.
"That is investigation.
[Objection: How then is the first dhyāna said to have five factors, as explained at length?

[Response: Because it is stated in the Sūtra: "Detached from sensual desires, detached from evil and unwholesome states, he, possessing applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), having attained the joy and happiness born of seclusion (*vivekaja*), enters and dwells in the first dhyāna."
It has been stated that [the path] has five members.
How so?
It has been stated that it possesses five members in terms of its stages (bhūmi), not in terms of its moments (kṣaṇa).
The stage of the first dhyāna is sometimes mixed with vitarka and sometimes with vicāra.
Thus, it is said that it possesses five factors with reference to the continuum (*saṃtāna*), not with reference to a single moment; therefore, there is no fault.
This is because one might otherwise falsely imagine some distinction based on something else.

Whether based on reality or unreality, that mental inflation arising from the conceptualization of being superior to others— such as thinking, "I am brave," "I am wealthy," "I am virtuous," or "I am endowed with intelligence"— is the mental factor called pride (*māna*).
Regarding the phrase "the exhaustion of the mind," the word "but" (*tu*) should be understood as having a restrictive sense and as being displaced in its grammatical order.
For this very reason, he said:
"But intoxication belongs to one who is attached precisely to one's own qualities," and so forth;
[it is] "the total occupation of the mind."
That by which the mind, being attached even to its own qualities such as physical beauty or valor, is overwhelmed and suppressed—
that is intoxication (*mada*), which is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of attachment.
Master Saṃghabhadra states that intoxication is the withdrawal from the performance of wholesome dharmas due to the overwhelming of the mind with pride when one is attached to one's own qualities.
"Intoxication (mada) is a specific kind of exultation. This is intended to mean afflicted mental pleasure (kliṣṭa-saumanasya).
The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this.
Because mental joy (*saumanasya*) exists up to the second dhyāna, and intoxication (*mada*) belongs to the three realms; [as it is said:
"sloth, restlessness, and intoxication belong to the three realms."
Because of this statement:
(II.35) "The mental factors (*caitta*) have been explained together with the mind (*citta*) according to their types.
First, the mind has been explained according to its types.

Consciousness is "the individual representation" and so forth, according to the distinctions of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and the categories such as the wholesome (*kuśala*).

The mental factors (*caitta*) are also distinguished by their own-characteristics and their mutual differences, according to the distinctions of the enumeration of the mind, the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the other levels (*bhūmi*).
"Having a single object" means that which is the mind.
"That very mind is that very consciousness"—since this has the same meaning, it is "single-meaning" (*ekārtha*).
However, a difference in etymological derivation is stated:
it is called "mind" (*citta*) because it accumulates (*cinoti*).
The meaning is that it accumulates what is wholesome or unwholesome.
This is established by means of etymological derivation (*nairukta*):
it is called "mind" (*manas*) because it cognizes (*manute*).
Regarding the term *manas*: this form *manas* arises from an *auṇādika* suffix applied to the root *man*.
It is called *vijñāna* because it cognizes (*vijānāti*) an object; here, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent.
It is called *citta* because it is accumulated (*cita*) by wholesome and unwholesome elements (*dhātu*).
This is according to the method of establishing through cultivation, whether by the Sautrāntika view or the Yogācāra view.
The mind (*manas*) is that which serves as the basis (*āśraya*), while consciousness (*vijñāna*) is that which is based upon it; thus, the mind is defined in relation to its status as a support.
For it is the consciousness that has passed away immediately prior to any of the six [consciousnesses].
That is called "mind" (manas) because it grasps objects;
consciousness (vijñāna), however, is dependent upon its support.
Because of the statement that "the arising of consciousness occurs in dependence upon a duality," mind and mental factors have a basis, an object, and an aspect, and they are associated;
the word "and" (ca) serves to draw in [the preceding term] "associated."
For those very things expressed by the term "mind and mental factors" (citta-caitta) are also expressed by the term "having a basis" (sāśraya);
likewise, they are "having an object" (sālambana), "having an aspect" (sākāra), and "associated" (saṃprayukta).
In that context, they are "with a basis" (sāśraya) because they depend on the sense faculties; the meaning is that they depend on the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).
They are "with an object" (sālambana) because they grasp their respective objects.
For indeed, mind and mental factors do not arise without an object (*ālambana*).
They possess an aspect (*sākāra*) because they take on the aspect of that very object;
for by means of that very aspect of the object, they grasp it, and thus they are "with an object" (*sālambana*).
How so?
For consciousness cognizes—that is, perceives—an object that is blue or yellow;
that very same consciousness experiences that object as its objective support (ālambana) through feeling.
Perception delimits;
volition constructs—and so forth.
Alternatively, consciousness grasps that very object in its general form as the state of being perceivable.
Specifically, however, feeling grasps the aspect of being experienced;
perception grasps the aspect of being delimited, and so forth.
They are called "associated" because they are associated equally.
They are "associated" (saṃprayukta) because they are equal and mutually non-disjoined.
This is by way of equality of basis (āśraya), object (ālambana), aspect (ākāra), time (kāla), and substance (dravya).
By whatever basis the mind arises, [the mental factors arise by that same basis].
By that very same basis, feeling, perception, volition, and so forth arise. Likewise, by whatever object the mind [is directed], by that very same [object] feeling and the others [arise].
In whatever mode the mind [arises], in that very same mode do feeling and the other [mental factors] arise.
For if the mind has the aspect of blue, then feeling and the others associated with it arise having precisely the aspect of blue.
At whatever time the mind occurs, at that very same time do feeling and the other factors occur.
And just as a single substance of mind arises— not two or three—
likewise a single substance of feeling arises, not two or three.
Likewise, there are the substances of perception (*saṃjñā*), the substance of volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.
For this reason, he explains that this very last point is difficult to understand:
for just as the mind (*citta*) is one, so too each of the mental factors (*caitta*) is also one.

(II.36) Desiring to speak of the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*), the Master provides an introduction with the following intention: "The mind and mental factors have been explained in detail along with their classifications; now, the dissociated factors, having reached their turn, are being discussed.
Regarding the phrase "in detail along with their classifications": [it means they were explained] together with their extensive divisions.

"Extensive and detailed" refers to the extensive and the detailed. "Together with the extensive and the detailed" means accompanied by both the extensive and the detailed. Alternatively, "extensive detail" means a detailed [explanation] by way of extension.
Together with their detailed classifications, they are "with detailed classifications.
Among those, the mind (*citta*) has first been explained with its detailed classifications as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*),
"discernment" (*prativijñapti*), and the "mind-base" (*manāyatana*).
By such means as this; the mental factors (caitta) are also the experience of feeling (vedanā).
Beginning with these words, up until "the mental factors are fivefold," as explained in detail.
"And the sets of names (nāmakāya) and so forth.
The word "and" (ca) is intended to indicate other such unmentioned dissociated factors (viprayukta).

For it is stated in the Treatise (śāstra): "The schism of the Saṃgha and so forth are accepted as dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta) in terms of substantial entity (dravyataḥ)," and thus there are others of this same class.
Regarding the term "dissociated from mind" (*cittaviprayuktā*), the inclusion of the word "mind" (*citta*) is for the purpose of demonstrating their similarity to mind.
The meaning is that they are dissociated from mind in the same way that mind itself is [dissociated from itself].
Furthermore, what is their similarity to mind?
(Abhidh-k-vy 143) That these [factors] are formless (*arūpin*).
For it is precisely because they possess form (*rūpitva*) that matter (*rūpa*) does not receive the designation "dissociated" (*viprayukta*), even though it is dissociated from consciousness.

Alternatively, the fact that these [factors] are called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*)—that is, their status as "name" (*nāmatva*)—consists in their being of the same genus (*samānajātīyatva*) as the mind (*citta*).
Mental factors (caitta) are also of the same nature as the mind;

however, because they are associated with the mind in terms of having the same object (ālambana), the term "dissociated" (viprayukta) is employed for the purpose of distinguishing them from it. Furthermore, since unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) are also of the same nature as those [mental factors] in being without an object, the term "conditioned" (saṃskāra) is used to exclude them. For this very reason, he says: [Tib.130b]

"These formations (*saṃskāra*) are neither associated with the mind (*citta-saṃprayukta*) nor do they have the nature of matter (*rūpa-svabhāva*); therefore, they are called 'dissociated from the mind' (*citta-viprayukta*).
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
it is used either to introduce a statement or to indicate a restriction.
The word "tāvat" (so much / for that long) refers to sequence.
"Acquisition" (*prāpti*) means obtaining (*lābha*) and possession (*samanvaya*).
"Attainment" (*prāpti*) is the general designation;
"acquisition" (*lābha*) and "possession" (*samanvaya*) are the specific designations.
"Acquisition" (*lābha*) and "attainment" (*pratilambha*) have the same meaning.
"Possession" (*samanvaya*) and "endowment" (*samanvāgama*) are not different in meaning. When "acquisition" (*pratilambha*) is mentioned, endowment is not included;
when "endowment" is mentioned, acquisition is not included.
When "attainment" (prāpti) is mentioned, however, both [types] are included.
For this very reason, he says:
"For attainment is of two kinds."
There is the acquisition of what was previously unobtained or lost,
and the possession of what has been acquired.
"Unobtained and lost" refers to that which was not previously obtained and that which was subsequently lost.
Its acquisition refers to the acquisition of that which was previously unobtained or lost.
Regarding the unobtained, it is, for example, the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

Regarding the lost, it is, for example, the re-acquisition of that which belongs to the desire realm and was abandoned through detachment from desire, either by returning to that realm or through falling away (*parihāṇi*).

And there is possession (*samanvāgama*) in the second and subsequent moments by means of what has been acquired (*pratilabdha*), because of its continued persistence. And that which is acquisition (*pratilambha*), and that which is possession (*samanvāgama*).
That acquisition (*prāpti*) is twofold; the term "acquisition" applies both to obtaining (*pratilambha*) and to possession (*samanvāgama*).
However, when there is no intention to distinguish between them, acquisition, obtaining, and possession are one and the same thing.
For instance, in the first moment, the acquisition of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is held to be its obtaining.
That too is called "possession" (samanvāgama).

An noble person (āryapudgala) abiding in the first moment is said to be possessed of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti). One endowed with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is possessed of thirteen [faculties].
Because of such statements as these.
How is this a definition?
For even when there is a desire to express a distinction, a definition is not properly formulated by means of a synonymous term.
What is acquisition (*prāpti*)? It is that which is attainment (*pratilambha*) and that which is possession (*samanvāgama*).
Even a statement of synonyms may sometimes serve to define a characteristic.
"Agni is the fire that knows all births.
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "What is ignorance?
It is lack of knowledge regarding the past, lack of knowledge regarding the future," and so forth in detail.
"It is established that non-attainment is simply the opposite [of attainment].
The intention is that since it is already established that non-attainment is simply the opposite, this sūtra need not have been composed for this purpose.
From the opposite [of attainment], these three—non-attainment (*aprāpti*), non-acquisition (*apratilambha*), and non-possession (*asamanvāgama*)—are understood.
In the same way, non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is the general designation for both non-acquisition (*apratilambha*) and non-possession (*asamanvāgama*). Therefore, it should be stated as follows:
non-attainment is twofold: the non-acquisition of those things not previously attained.
"Non-possession (*asamanvāgama*) refers to those [dharmas] that have been acquired and then lost.
Alternatively, "non-acquisition" (*apratilambha*) is the initial non-attainment of what has not yet been attained or what has been lost.
"Non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*) refers to the state from the second moment onward with respect to what has not been attained or what has been lost.
"Acquisition and non-acquisition belong to those [dharmas] that fall within one's own continuum.
This restricts [the rule] such that acquisition and non-acquisition of conditioned dharmas belong only to those that fall within one's own continuum.

"Not those belonging to the continua of others" means that acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) do not occur with respect to factors (*dharma*) belonging to the continua of other sentient beings; rather, they occur within one's own continuum— this is the meaning.
Therefore he says:
"For no one is possessed of [dharmas] belonging to another.

Nor [is one possessed] of those not included within a continuum (*asaṃtatipatita*); the meaning is that they are not [possessed] of those not included within the continuum of a sentient being (*asattvasaṃtatipatita*).
Therefore, it is said:
"For no one is possessed of those things reckoned as non-sentient.
Garlands, ornaments, and so forth, as well as forms and other qualities residing in wood, walls, and the like, are reckoned as non-sentient.

The eyes and so forth are reckoned as belonging to sentient beings; likewise, hair and so forth, which are connected to the material sense faculties, should be understood as being reckoned as belonging to sentient beings as well.
This is because they conform to the transformation resulting from the benefit or injury [to those faculties].
For instance, it is observed that through the injury to the material sense faculties, transformations such as graying occur in the hair and other [parts of the body].

The established doctrine is that through the application of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and other such aids, there is the restoration of conditions such as graying hair; thus, it is established that acquisition (*prāpti*) occurs for all things classified as sentient (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*).

Regarding the two types of cessation (*nirodha*), namely analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which are classified as non-sentient (*asattva-saṃkhyāta*), both acquisition and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) likewise occur.

All sentient beings are endowed with non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) according to the deficiency of their respective conditions. This excludes those who abide in the initial moment [of the path], such as those still bound by all fetters.
The "initial moment" refers to the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Those situated therein are those who abide in the first moment.
They are called "possessing all fetters" (sakalabandhana) because they have all fetters;
that is, they have not abandoned any category of affliction.
Those who possess all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) and abide in the first moment [of the path] are "those possessing all fetters abiding in the first moment" (*sakalabandhanādikṣaṇastha*).
These are to be excluded from these [categories], or they are excluded by them; thus, they are "excluded from those possessing all fetters abiding in the first moment.
Who are they?

All noble ones (ārya) are endowed with analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha). However, those noble ones who abide in the first moment [of the path] while still possessing all fetters are not so endowed.
For in that state, the afflictions to be abandoned by patience are being severed, though not yet severed;
their cessation is being attained, though not yet attained;
and the path, while in the process of ceasing, abandons its obscuration.
This is because of the established tenet (*siddhānta*).
However, those Noble Ones who have written down [the truths] in a single manner and so forth are, in that state, endowed with cessation attained through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
From that point onward, in the second and subsequent moments, they are likewise endowed with cessation attained through the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
And some ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are "endowed" [with certain qualities], such as those who have cultivated [the path] to a single stage (*ekaprakāropalikhita*) and so forth.
However, no one is endowed with space (*ākāśa*), because there is no connection [between them].
But there is a connection with the two types of cessation (*nirodha*).
Therefore, there is no acquisition (*prāpti*) of space.
And for that which has no acquisition, there is also no non-acquisition (*aprāpti*); this is the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of the Vaibhāṣikas.
Why is this so?
Because its own nature and its activity are not perceived—just as in the case of visible form and the eye—he asks [the question].
"From the Sūtra":
by this very explanation, the Vaibhāṣika establishes his point.
"Of the ten dharmas of one beyond training," and so forth. There are ten dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):
the eight limbs of the noble path that are beyond training, plus right liberation (*samyagvimukti*) and right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
"From their arising" means from their manifestation. "From acquisition" means from initial attainment. "From possession" means from subsequent attainment.
"One who has abandoned the five factors" means one for whom the five factors have been abandoned.
The five factors are: the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), adherence to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), sensual desire (kāmacchanda), and ill-will (vyāpāda).
It is not tenable that these [five fetters] are abandoned upon the attainment of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).

However, we observe these five factors as being applicable, namely the higher-tier fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*): attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because he possesses an acquisition (*prāpti*) that serves as a substitute for them, even an Arhat who remains in his natural state (*prakṛtistha*) is called a noble one (*ārya*).
And here is the proof:
"Possession exists as a substantial entity (dravyataḥ), because it is mentioned in the Sūtra, just like the substantial entities of the sense-bases (āyatana-dravya). To this, the Master replies:

In that case, it would follow that possession (*samanvāgama*)— even by means of things called "non-sentient" such as the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*), or even by means of other sentient beings such as the woman-treasure (*strīratna*)— would be substantially real (*dravyasat*),
because [the Buddha] spoke thus in the Sūtra.
To explain how this is so, he shows the Sūtra.
"King, as far as the detailed account goes:
monks, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with seven treasures.
These are his seven treasures."

Namely: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh; such is the detailed list.

By stating that the possession of these seven treasures is mentioned in the Sūtra yet does not exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*), [the author] demonstrates the inconclusiveness [of the opponent's reason].
Furthermore, this points out a flaw in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*).
Because it contradicts inference.
How so? It is said:

"The possession of the ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*) does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyasat*), because its nature is that of a possession, like the possession of the seven treasures of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*)."
By this, he subverts the nature of the dharma in his proposition.
"Mastery" means acting according to one's will;
that is, being subject to one's own desire.
In that regard, "mastery" is stated in the *Cakravarti-sūtra*.
On the other hand, "a distinct substance" is stated in the *Aśaikṣa-samanvāgama-sūtra*.
"But what is this 'lack of logical consistency'?

The Vaibhāṣikas ask: "For in the teaching, two kinds of entities are accepted—those that exist substantially (*dravyasat*) and those that exist as designations (*prajñaptisat*); so how is it illogical?
The Master says:
"This is non-connection," and so forth.
In this context, whatever entity exists as a substantial reality must be either apprehended by direct perception or apprehended by inference.
Among these, that which is apprehended by direct perception consists of form, sound, and so on, because they are apprehended by the five sense faculties.
Even some things apprehended by mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*),
because desire, hatred, and so forth are self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*).
On the other hand, the eye, ear, and so forth are apprehended through inference (*anumāna*), because they are to be inferred from the functions of visual consciousness and the rest.
Because when that [entity] exists or does not exist, it [the acquisition] exists or does not exist.
Furthermore, acquisition is neither graspable by direct perception nor graspable by inference, for no faultless inference is observed to establish its existence.
Therefore, it is established that this is untenable because it cannot possess the properties of a substance.
Now the Master, having repeatedly raised that position, refutes it:
"The cause of arising," and so forth.
That which has acquisition (*prāpti*) arises because of the existence of its cause.
There can be no acquisition (*prāpti*) of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because the unconditioned is not something that arises.

Furthermore, there are those factors (*dharma*) not yet acquired, such as the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and so forth; and there are those that have been relinquished through changing levels (*bhūmisaṃcāra*) or through detachment (*vairāgya*).

For example, the non-defiled states belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), as well as those defiled states belonging to higher realms that have been abandoned through the attainment of detachment (*vairāgya*), would— given their departure from those realms or through falling away (*parihāṇi*)— how could they arise again? For they possess no possession (*prāpti*).
Because it is neither produced nor ceased.
And if it has simultaneous acquisition as its cause, what is it?
Their arising is under discussion. That innate acquisition which is now produced is the producer of them.
He said:
"In that case, what is birth (jāti), or what is the 'birth-of-birth' (jātijāti)?
A 'servant' (kiṃkarī) is one whose nature is to serve."
Birth (jāti) produces the characterized phenomenon (lakṣya-dharma);
however, birth-of-birth (jātijāti) produces that characteristic, namely, birth itself.
Therefore, if the arising of the characterized phenomena were said to be caused by acquisition (prāpti), what function would birth have in that case?
Now, regarding the characteristics: their arising would be said to have that [primary characteristic] as its cause. To this, he says:
Or the conceptual construction is that "the birth of birth is a servant.
Alternatively, if it were to be imagined by you in this way:
"Birth produces the phenomenon (dharma)."
Furthermore, it is said that acquisition (*prāpti*) produces birth (*jāti*). To this, it is replied: "What function does the birth-of-birth (*jātijāti*) perform?"
"Indeed, for those with all fetters," and so forth in detail.
Those for whom not even a single type of affliction has been abandoned are "those with all fetters."
Furthermore, there would be no distinction among those who possess all fetters regarding the types of arising of afflictions—whether weak, medium, or intense.
Why?
Because there is no difference in their possession [of the afflictions].

For those whose fetters are incomplete, a distinction in the arising of weak, medium, or intense afflictions might be postulated due to the incompleteness of their acquisitions (*prāpti*); however, this would not apply to those whose fetters are complete, because their acquisitions are equal.
Or rather, it is from that [distinction in acquisitions] that such a difference arises.
Whether due to the cause of repeated practice or from some other reason, that distinction exists:
for some who are bound by all fetters it is intense; for others it is moderate.
For someone, [the affliction] is weak.
Let its arising occur from that very cause of differentiation:
namely, the arising of those afflictions, such as the weak ones and so forth.
"Therefore, possession (*prāpti*) is not a cause of arising.
To this, the Vaibhāṣika says: "And who says such a thing? and so forth.
Acquisition (*prāpti*) is the cause of differentiation. For if acquisition did not exist, [the distinction] regarding those with worldly minds would not hold.
"Worldly" (*laukika*) means that which exists in the world (*loka*).
*Mānasa* means the mind (*manas*).
Those for whom the mundane mind is [present] are these "those with mundane minds" (*laukikamānasa*);
they are noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
There are noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
The mention of "worldly mind" (*laukikamānasa*) serves as a qualification for the noble ones;
for ordinary persons always possess a worldly mind.
Or, even the qualification "ordinary persons" (pṛthagjana) is possible in the state of the attainment of non-perception (āsaṃjñika) or the attainment of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
[The phrase] "of them" refers to those noble ones (ārya) and ordinary persons; here, the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (nirdhāraṇa).
Or [it may be] characterized by a relationship.
The determination is that there would be no fixed establishment of those [factors].
This refers to the established arrangement that has been made.
That is acquisition (*prāpti*).
It is due to the distinction between having abandoned and not having abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*);
those who have abandoned the afflictions are the noble ones (*ārya*).
Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are those whose afflictions (*kleśa*) have not been abandoned; their state of being such is itself the distinction (*viśeṣa*).
Thus, there is a distinction based on whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not abandoned.
Therefore,
this formal arrangement is appropriate.

But surely there are even some ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have abandoned the afflictions (*prahīṇakleśa*). How then is it determined that only noble ones (*ārya*) are those who have abandoned the afflictions?
This was stated precisely because of the expression "complete eradication.
And how is this so?
It is because of this established distinction: "the affliction of these [beings] has been abandoned, while that of these has not been abandoned."

How, then, will that be? This establishment is accomplished through the possession of the afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*), because of the departure or non-departure of that [possession]— that is to say, because of the severance or non-severance of the possession of the afflictions.
Those for whom there is the attainment and departure of that [defilement] are the noble ones (ārya);
those for whom there is no departure [of it] are not.
"Those are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
[Objection: But is it not the case that for some ordinary persons, the possession of afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*) has also been removed? [Response: It has indeed been removed.
But not by means of the supramundane path.

In that case, how is this distinction produced by the supramundane path discerned—that "this acquisition of afflictions has been removed by the supramundane [path]," whereas "this [has been removed] by the mundane"?
It is due to the difference between the acquisitions of dissociation (visaṃyoga-prāpti) that are with-outflows (sāsrava) and those without-outflows (anāsrava).
"This is established through a distinction of the basis (*āśrayaviśeṣāt*).

This determination—that for some afflictions (*kleśa*) have been abandoned while for others they have not—is established through a distinction of the personal existence (*ātmabhāvaviśeṣāt*). Likewise, it is "transformed" (*parāvṛtta*) in that manner.
Likewise, it is "otherwise become.
This refers to those [defilements] to be abandoned by that [path], namely, those to be abandoned by the paths of seeing and cultivation.
It is like a grain of rice burnt by fire.
Just as rice grain scorched by fire becomes seedless,
so too, when the basis (āśraya) has become seedless through the principle already explained, it is said that the afflictions have been abandoned;
or rather, [it is said] because the state of being a seed has been destroyed.
The term "basis" (āśraya) is understood here [from the preceding context].
