Therefore, it can be said that [the defilement] has been abandoned by means of the mundane path (laukika-mārga),
because there is merely a state of impairment of the seed (bīja).

"By the opposite, it is not abandoned" means that the seed has not been burnt away in the basis (*āśraya*), or that its state as a seed has not been impaired. "And that which is not abandoned," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

And he is endowed with that which has not been abandoned— whether it be [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing, belonging to the realm of desire up to the peak of existence, or those to be abandoned by cultivation, belonging to the realm of desire up to the peak of existence— according to the method just described;
and he is likewise endowed with that which has been abandoned, up to the peak of existence.
"One is designated as being endowed with that.
This shows that this is a conventional designation (*prajñapti-dharma*).
"The wholesome [dharmas] are also of two kinds," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that the defiled [dharmas] are of two kinds; or, in the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*), it means "and the wholesome. Regarding the phrase "because of the non-destruction of their seed-nature": [This refers to the fact that] the capacity for those [defiled dharmas] to arise again exists within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), provided that the seeds of those dharmas have not been destroyed by the power of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*). It is because of this non-destruction of the seed-nature that they are said to be "possessed" (*samanvāgata*). Furthermore, since the seeds of all phenomena are contained within the storehouse consciousness, and because the seeds of wholesome and indeterminate phenomena are likewise never destroyed except by the power of the antidote, they too are said to be "possessed. Thus, the term "possession" (*samanvāgama*) is established based on the presence of the seeds of all phenomena within the storehouse consciousness. This concludes the explanation of possession. As for non-possession (*asamanvāgama*), it is the opposite of possession. That is to say, when the seeds of a phenomenon are destroyed by the power of the antidote, or when the seeds of a phenomenon do not exist at all, one is said to be "not possessed" of that phenomenon. For example, when the seeds of the defilements are destroyed by the power of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one is no longer possessed of those defilements. Similarly, when the seeds of a phenomenon do not exist at all—such as in the case of the seeds of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) in a person born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—one is said to be "not possessed" of them. This concludes the explanation of non-possession. Now, regarding the distinction between the possession and non-possession of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*): there is no possession or non-possession of unconditioned phenomena apart from their seeds. Why? Because unconditioned phenomena lack seeds. However, although they lack seeds, there is still possession and non-possession of them. How so? It is because of the presence or absence of the obstruction to their manifestation. Specifically, regarding the two types of unconditioned phenomena—the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*)—when the obstruction to the manifestation of analytical cessation has ceased through the power of wisdom, one is said to be "possessed" of it; otherwise, one is "not possessed. Regarding non-analytical cessation, when the obstruction to its manifestation has ceased due to the absence of the conditions for its arising, one is said to be "possessed" of it; otherwise, one is "not possessed. This concludes the explanation of the distinction between the possession and non-possession of unconditioned phenomena. Now, regarding the distinction between the possession and non-possession of conditioned phenomena: there are two types of conditioned phenomena: those that are manifest (*samudācāra*) and those that are merely seeds (*bījamātra*). Among these, for manifest phenomena, possession and non-possession are determined by whether they are currently present or not. For phenomena that exist only as seeds, possession and non-possession are determined by whether the seeds have been destroyed or not. This concludes the explanation of the distinction between the possession and non-possession of conditioned phenomena. Now, regarding the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*): the factors of enlightenment are of three types: the factors of enlightenment belonging to the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), those belonging to the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those belonging to neither. Among these, for the factors of enlightenment belonging to the stage of training, one is "possessed" of them when they are present or when their seeds have not been destroyed; otherwise, one is "not possessed. For the factors of enlightenment belonging to the stage beyond training, one is "possessed" of them when they are present or when their seeds have not been destroyed; otherwise, one is "not possessed. For the factors of enlightenment belonging to neither, one is "possessed" of them when they are present or when their seeds have not been destroyed; otherwise, one is "not possessed. This concludes the explanation of the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the factors of enlightenment. Now, regarding the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the faculties (*indriya*): the faculties are of two types: those that are material (*rūpin*) and those that are immaterial (*arūpin*). Among these, for material faculties, possession and non-possession are determined by whether they are currently present or not. For immaterial faculties, possession and non-possession are determined by whether the seeds have been destroyed or not. This concludes the explanation of the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the faculties. Now, regarding the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*): the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are of two types: those that are manifest and those that are merely seeds. Among these, for manifest aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, possession and non-possession are determined by whether they are currently present or not. For those that exist only as seeds, possession and non-possession are determined by whether the seeds have been destroyed or not. This concludes the explanation of the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. Now, regarding the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the truths (*satya*): the truths are of two types: the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and the truth of the origin (*samudayasatya*), which are both defiled, and the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) and the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), which are undefiled. Among these, for the defiled truths, possession and non-possession are determined by whether the seeds have been destroyed or not. For the undefiled truths, possession and non-possession are determined by whether they are present or not. This concludes the explanation of the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the truths. Now, regarding the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the paths (*mārga*): the paths are of two types: the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) and the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*). Among these, for the mundane path, possession and non-possession are determined by whether the seeds have been destroyed or not. For the supramundane path, possession and non-possession are determined by whether they are present or not. This concludes the explanation of the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the paths. Now, regarding the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the fruits (*phala*): the fruits are of four types: the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*). Among these, for each fruit, possession and non-possession are determined by whether the seeds of the obstructions to that fruit have been destroyed or not. This concludes the explanation of the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the fruits. Now, regarding the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*): the meditative absorptions are of two types: those with vitarka and vicāra (*savitarkasavicāra*), and those without vitarka but with vicāra (*avitarkavicāramātra*). Among these, for the first type, possession and non-possession are determined by whether they are present or not. For the second type, possession and non-possession are determined by whether the seeds have been destroyed or not. This concludes the explanation of the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the meditative absorptions. Now, regarding the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): the supernormal powers are of five types: the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), the power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), and the power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*). Among these, for the first four, possession and non-possession are determined by whether they are present or not. For the power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, possession and non-possession are determined by whether the seeds of the obstructions to that knowledge have been destroyed or not. This concludes the explanation of the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the supernormal powers. Now, regarding the distinction between the possession and non-possession of the factors of restraint (*saṃvara*): the factors of restraint are
The seed of those wholesome states acquired at birth is "that seed.
The state of being that seed is "the state of that seed" (*tadbījabhāva*).
Of what?
Of the basis.
The non-affliction of its seed-state is "the non-affliction of the seed-state";
therefore [it is so called].
One is "endowed" with them because their seed-state has not been destroyed. With which ones? With those wholesome [states] that arise without effort.
One is said to be "not possessed" [of the roots] due to their impairment.
Who is this? He says: one whose wholesome roots have been completely severed.
"But of that," [it is said].
The impairment of that basis—the state of being the seed of that [defilement]—is to be understood as occurring through wrong view, and not otherwise.
Therefore, he said:

The intention is that there is certainly no absolute eradication of the seed-state of wholesome factors within the continuum, as there is an absolute eradication of the afflictions within the continuum by means of the Noble Path.
"But those which... and so forth;
[this refers to] those which are produced through application (*prāyogika*).
"By those that have arisen" means by those [dharmas] which have been produced. "Their arising" (tad-utpatti) refers to the production of those [dharmas].
"Mastery over their arising" (tad-utpattau vaśitvam) is a specific capacity or power.
Because of its non-obstruction.
Of what?
Of the continuum.
It is called "possession" (samanvāgama). By what? By those wholesome [dharmas] that arise through effort.

Since this is so, therefore, in this context, it is the seed itself— the specific capacity— which remains undiscarded during the state of possession (*samanvāgama*): [the seed] of afflicted phenomena when not destroyed by the Noble Path, and of wholesome phenomena that arise effortlessly when not destroyed by the mundane path or by wrong view.
And it is the seed of wholesome states— which have been cultivated through effort during the time of mastery— that is under discussion;
it receives the designation "possession" (samanvāgama),
but it is not a separate substance.
Regarding that which has been imagined by the Vaibhāṣikas:
what, then, is this so-called "seed"?
He asks this out of a suspicion that it might be a substantial entity (*dravya*).
That name-and-form which is capable of producing a fruit—

that form consisting of the five aggregates which is capable of producing a fruit, whether directly, immediately, through a succession, or from afar— what indeed is this so-called "transformation" (pariṇāma)?
Fearing the Sāṃkhya position of transformation (pariṇāma), he asks: "What is the alteration of the continuum? This refers to arising in a different manner.
And what is this "continuity" (saṃtati)?

Is it such that, as the Sāṃkhyas maintain, there is the appearance of another property upon the cessation of a previous property within a persisting substance, so too there is a transformation of a persisting continuity?
No, it is said.
What then?
They consist of cause and fruit;
"cause and fruit" (hetuphala) means both the cause and the fruit.

"Cause and effect" refers to the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the three time periods that proceed without interruption; these are established as a "continuum" (*saṃtati*). As for the passage beginning with "But where it is said," and so forth:
this refers to where it is stated in the Sūtra.
What is meant by this?
It means that one who is possessed of greed is incapable and unfit to produce the four applications of mindfulness, beginning with the application of mindfulness to the body.
This is so if "seed" is defined as "possession" (*prāpti*).
If the seed were eternal, there would be no arising of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
This is equally true for your own theory of "possession" (*prāpti*), as its arising would likewise not occur;
therefore, both sides must provide an explanation.
In this context, "possession" (samanvāgama) refers to the acquiescence to greed or its non-dispelling.
Acquiescence means approval;
non-dispelling means the lack of pacification.

"In every way, a designated phenomenon (*prajñaptidharma*) is not a substantial phenomenon (*dravyadharma*). This means that in every respect—whether it be a cause of arising, a cause of establishment, a particular basis, or a mental habituation (*adhivāsana*) or non-removal—it is in every way a designated phenomenon; that is, a phenomenon by way of designation (*prajñapti*), conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), or linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). It is not a substantial phenomenon; the meaning is that it is not a phenomenon as a self-nature (*svabhāva*) in terms of substance.

Alternatively, "substantial phenomenon" (*dravyadharma*) means that which is both a substance and a phenomenon; the meaning is that it is not a phenomenon whose intrinsic characteristic exists [as a separate entity] like form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Its negation—that is, the negation of that phenomenon which is a mere designation (*prajñaptidharma*)—is non-possession (*asamanvāgama*).
Master Saṃghabhadra maintains that acquisition (*prāpti*) is the mark for the cognition "this belongs to this" and the cause for the non-loss of phenomena already attained.
The claim that "this is the mark of the knowledge 'this belongs to that'" is unproven.
We maintain that such knowledge arises through a specific basis (*āśrayaviśeṣa*).
Furthermore, if acquisition (*prāpti*) is held to be the cause for the non-loss of dharmas already obtained, [then this objection does not apply].
There would be no abandonment of what has been attained; yet there is such abandonment. Therefore, this [argument] is not a valid reason.
And he refutes that very state of being a seed, defined as a specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*), which was established by the Teacher.
Is this specific capacity something different from the mind, or is it not different from it?
And what follows from this?
If it is a different entity,
then it is established that "attainment" exists;
there is merely a dispute over the name.
If it is not a different thing, then surely you have admitted that the seed of the unwholesome is wholesome,
and the wholesome is [the seed] of the unwholesome.
For who indeed, when heat is not distinct from fire, would determine that heat alone is the burner and not the fire?
For a wholesome seed exists within an unwholesome or neutral mind;
likewise, an unwholesome seed exists within a wholesome or neutral mind.
In the same way, even the seed of the indeterminate exists in both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
and the seed of the contaminated exists in the uncontaminated, while the seed of the uncontaminated exists in the contaminated mind. Thus, the fault of confusion would follow.
To this, we reply:
If it were not a distinct entity, there would be the fault of confusion;
yet that seed must be said to be neither distinct from the mind nor non-distinct from it.
Because it has the nature of being a designation based upon [something else]. Even if it were not a separate entity, there would still be no fault.
For when a wholesome mind has arisen, it would deposit a seed in a subsequent mind within its own continuum, whether that mind is of the same kind or of a different kind.
Therefore, because there is a distinction in the cause, there is a distinction in the effect; thus it is "distinguished.
By that [cause], that mind would arise.
That distinguished mind would arise as capable of performing the function of the wholesome seed.
In this way, even by an unwholesome [mind], a seed would be deposited in a mind of its own continuum, whether of the same class or of a different class.
And that mind, being distinguished by it, would arise as capable of performing the function of the unwholesome seed.
In the same way, even by an indeterminate mind, a seed would be deposited in a mind of its own continuum, whether of the same class or of a different class.

And that [mind] would arise as distinguished by that [perfuming], capable of performing the function of the seeds of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Even an impure (*sāsrava*) mind could deposit a seed in a pure (*anāsrava*) mind, and even a pure mind [could deposit one] in an impure one; thus, as minds arise from other minds, they proceed by mutually depositing seeds and mutually generating one another, through their relationship as the perfumed and the perfumer.
Nor is a specific capacity (śaktiviśeṣa) deposited in an unwholesome mind by a wholesome [mind] such that that unwholesome [mind] would become wholesome,
or that wholesome [mind] would become unwholesome;
for it is merely a specific capacity.
Potency (*śakti*), seed (*bīja*), and latent impression (*vāsanā*)—these have one and the same meaning.
In this way, the latent impressions of the unwholesome and so forth are also to be explained;
likewise, even when a specific potency is infused into the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) by means of the contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Even when an outflow-free [state] bestows a specific capacity upon an outflowing one,
that outflowing state does not thereby become outflow-free, nor does the outflow-free state become outflowing.
This must also be considered by you Vaibhāṣikas:
when an uncontaminated state arises immediately after a contaminated state of mind, or a contaminated state arises immediately after an uncontaminated state of mind,

is the preceding group— whether contaminated or uncontaminated— capable of producing the subsequent group by way of being the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and so forth, or is it incapable?
And what follows from this?
If it lacks capacity, its status as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and so forth would also be lost.
If, on the other hand, it possesses capacity...
Is that capacity (*śakti*) within a contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind itself contaminated or is it uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
Would that mind then serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and so forth for both a contaminated and an uncontaminated subsequent mind?

In that case, would it perform the function of being the immediately preceding condition for the uncontaminated mind by means of the very same capacity by which it performs that function for the contaminated mind?
If it were by that very same power, how could there not be a confusion of the effects of the powers?

Or, if it were by another power— that one [power] producing the state of being an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and so forth for the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the other for the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—
how is it logical for these two powers, which are non-different from that mind, to have distinct natures and produce distinct effects?
If that is acceptable, then for us as well, there will be the persistence of various powers non-different from the mind and a differentiation of effects.

Likewise, since even an untainted (*anāsrava*) mind can exist by way of being the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted minds, one must likewise assert a difference in form between its powers and a differentiation of effects.
Therefore, what was stated—that "would it not follow that you have admitted that the unwholesome is the seed of the wholesome," and so forth—is incorrect.
For it is not the case that the unwholesome, when distinguished by a specific capacity infused by the wholesome, becomes capable of performing the function of being a seed for the unwholesome.
What then? [Tib.137b] It is rather as follows:
It performs only the function of the wholesome seed;
however, by means of a specific capacity produced by its own [wholesome] benefit, that unwholesome [seed] performs its own seed-function.
How then is this stated?
"The unwholesome is the seed of the wholesome. But you might ask: "If that wholesome seed is planted within an unwholesome mind, how is it that it does not become unwholesome?
It is because you do not understand the true meaning of a "seed."

By means of a wholesome mind that is ceasing, an unwholesome mind endowed with a specific capacity is produced in such a way that it will become suitable for its own arising, either directly or through a succession; thus, it is only this specific capacity that is the seed.
There is no such thing as a "seed" existing apart from this.
Because they exist as designations (*prajñapti*).
For this very reason, acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) are said to be conventional truths (*prajñaptisatya*);
however, the Vaibhāṣikas describe them as being substantial truths (*dravyasatya*) alone.
(II.38, 39ab) “For past dharmas, there is also acquisition that is past,” and so forth.
For past dharmas— such as those that are afflicted— the past acquisition, which has arisen and ceased, may be both prior (*agraja*) and simultaneous (*sahaja*).
Even that which arises at a later time:
for those very [dharmas], the future acquisition is unarisen;
the present one is that which arises at a later time and has already arisen and ceased.
For future [dharmas] as well, possession (prāpti) is past when it has arisen and ceased prior [to the dharma];
it is future when it has not yet arisen;
and it is present when it has arisen but not yet ceased.
Likewise, for present [dharmas] as well, there is a past acquisition (*prāpti*) which has arisen and ceased first;
a future one which has not yet arisen;
and a present one which is simultaneous (*sahajā*).
This was stated by taking into account the general category (*jātisāmānya*) of past and so forth;
however, for a single past [dharma], there is not necessarily a threefold acquisition (*prāpti*).
For it is impossible for a maturation-born (*vipākaja*) dharma to have either a future or a past acquisition.
Because of the statement that "the acquisition of the indeterminate is innate" (*sahaja*).
However, if the establishment of acquisition were made for each individual substance, this would be the case only with respect to what is possible.
For afflicted states and for innate wholesome states, past and so forth, their acquisitions (*prāpti*) as past and so forth necessarily exist.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is no past or present acquisition of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) that has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, this general rule (*utsarga*) should be understood as having its exceptions (*sāpavāda*).
Because it is stated that "the acquisition of the indeterminate is innate," however,
for unconditioned phenomena, the acquisition is past once it has arisen and ceased.
That which has not arisen and is yet to come is the future;
that which has arisen but not yet ceased is the present.
This has not been set forth in a formal sutra because it is easily understood.
"Belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, respectively, for those [dharmas] belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
This means that for one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is an acquisition (*prāpti*) belonging to the desire realm for dharmas belonging to the desire realm;
and for that same person, there is an acquisition belonging to the form realm for dharmas belonging to the form realm.

For that same [person], it is of the formless realm (ārūpyāvacarī) with respect to those [dharmas] belonging to the formless realm; and for one born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), it is of the desire realm (kāmāvacarī) with respect to those [dharmas] belonging to the desire realm—
just as, for example, the mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta) is of the desire realm.
For those belonging to the form realm, the acquisition belongs to the form realm;
for those belonging to the formless realm, it belongs to the formless realm.
For one born in the formless realm, the acquisition of factors belonging to that realm is itself of that same realm.

Regarding the statement "the acquisition of non-acquired [dharmas] is fourfold": for those dharmas that are not included within the realms (adhātvāpta)—namely, the conditioned and unconditioned, and the untainted (anāsrava)—their acquisition is of four kinds:
belonging to the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as being untainted.
"In brief" means having combined all those that are not acquired (*anāpta*).
However, individually they are not of four kinds; therefore he says:
Regarding the detailed explanation of "non-analytical cessation" (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) therein:

for one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation of factors belonging to the desire realm and so forth—according to their respective possibilities—is of the desire realm.
For one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the acquisition of non-analytical cessation of factors belonging to the form realm and so forth is of the form realm.

For one reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of [dharmas] belonging to the formless realm and so forth is itself of the formless realm.
For that acquisition is established solely by virtue of the continuum of the sentient being (*sattvasaṃtāna*);
it is not established by virtue of those dharmas for which there is non-analytical cessation.

For if this were the case, the attainment of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) of the truth of the path would be untainted (anāsrava); and the attainment of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) would be both belonging to the realms of form and formlessness and untainted,
but not belonging to the realm of desire.
Because it is not an antidote to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

However, for that which is attained by a path belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), there is an acquisition (*prāpti*) belonging to the form realm; for that which is attained by a path belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), there is an acquisition belonging to the formless realm.
By means of the untainted (*anāsrava*) path, it is untainted.

However, for a noble one (*ārya*), when [disjunction] is attained by means of a path belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), it is both of the realm of form and untainted; and by means of a path belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), it is both of the formless realm and untainted.
Regarding the noble one’s detachment through the mundane path (*laukika*), the acquisitions of disjunction (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) are of two kinds.
Because of the statement:
"The path-truth has only untainted [attainment].
This negates its worldly attainment.
"This, in brief, is fourfold" concludes the meaning already stated— that it consists, in summary, of both that which pertains to the three realms and that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).
"Of those in training" (*śaikṣāṇām*) [refers to the first three].
The dharmas of one in training (śaikṣa) are the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas of one in training;
those of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are the untainted dharmas of one beyond training.
These should be understood as being nothing other than the truth of the path (mārgasatya).
But those other than the learners (śaikṣa) and the non-learners (aśaikṣa) are neither learners nor non-learners.
Even the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomena are held to be neither learners nor non-learners.
Of these, [the following applies]:
Acquisition is threefold, according to the distinction of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth:
that of one in training, that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and that which belongs neither to one in training nor to one beyond training.

"Attained by one who is non-noble" means attained by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). "By that very same [person] when they are a learner" means by that same individual when they have become one in training (*śaikṣa*).
The acquisition of that very analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) attained through the path of training (śaikṣamārga) is of the nature of training;
that attained through the path of no-more-training (aśaikṣamārga) is of the nature of no-more-training.
This refers to that which is attained through the path associated with the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna).
Because the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) is the basis for the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*).
Although that [attainment] is acquired by the diamond-like (*vajropama*) training (*śaikṣa*) [path], because it brings that [dissociation] about;

nevertheless, when speaking of its acquisition, the acquisition of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī prāptiḥ*) would be distinguished from the acquisition of one in training (*śaikṣyāḥ prāpteḥ*). Therefore, it is not said that it belongs to one beyond training by means of that training [path].
"Of that very [cessation] obtained through the noble path, it is untainted (anāsrava).
This means that of that very cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained through the noble path, the acquisition (prāpti) is untainted;
and it is understood that the acquisition of the truth of the path is also untainted.

Is the acquisition (*prāpti*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) attained by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) through the Noble One (*ārya*) contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
He says: "It is both. Why is it not mentioned [in the verse]?
The commentary is incomplete; it will be shown later that,
regarding the worldly noble detachment, there are two kinds of acquisitions of dissociation.
It is not so stated.
It should be understood that only that acquisition which is unmixed (*asaṃkīrṇā*) is what is referred to here.
[This is] because of its weakness (*durbalatvāt*).
Because they lack volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), they are weak.
"The two supernormal knowledges" refers to the supernormal knowledge of the divine eye and the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear.
And excluding the mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*).
What [is it]?
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the neutral (*avyākṛta*) is innate (*sahaja*).
It should be connected [to the previous statement].
For it is because they are powerful, and so forth;
that is, because those [supernormal powers], such as the divine eye and the others, are powerful.
What?
Is acquisition (prāpti) prior, posterior, or simultaneous?
It is because it is accomplished through a specific application (prayoga).
The accomplishment of the superknowledges (abhijñā), such as the divine eye, occurs through a specific application (prayoga).
Its strength consists in the power of that accomplishment achieved through a specific application.
The connection of the meaning is that because of its strength, there is acquisition (prāpti) both prior to and subsequent to [the action], as well as simultaneous;

this applies even to some [actions] belonging to the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), such as that of Viśvakarman, and to those belonging to the sphere of postures (*airyāpathika*), such as that of the Elder Aśvajit.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that for that which has been intensely practiced and thoroughly internalized, there is acquisition (prāpti) both prior to, after, and simultaneously with it.
What [is this]?
[They mean] the acquisition that occurs before, after, and together [with the action].
And regarding "of the obscured form" (*nivṛtasya ca rūpasya*): the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction;
it conjoins [the term] "acquisition is co-nascent" (*prāptiḥ sahajā*).
And that defiled matter should be understood as belonging exclusively to the level of the first dhyāna, specifically as informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*),
because in other levels there is an absence of that which gives rise to it.
"Even by a superior [degree]" is the full statement.
Even by a mind of the highest degree, a manifest action (*vijñapti*) that has been obscured is produced;
yet that very same highest-degree mind of manifest action does not produce a non-manifest action (*avijñapti*).
Therefore, its weakness is established.
Since its weakness is established, its acquisition (*prāpti*) is innate (*sahaja*).
Regarding the "distinction of acquisitions":
for those [dharmas] that are born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and so forth, which are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), the acquisition is innate.
However, the distinction regarding the two supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth is that their acquisition (*prāpti*) occurs before, after, or simultaneously [with the dharma itself].
Regarding the form belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no "prior" acquisition (*agrajā-prāpti*).

That is to say, for the wholesome or unwholesome informative and non-informative form (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*) belonging to the desire realm, an acquisition that arises prior [to the dharma] does not exist in any way whatsoever.
Whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, the meaning is that [the acquisition] does not exist at all in every respect.
However, it exists both as simultaneous (*sahajā*) and as subsequently arisen (*paścātkālajā*), according to possibility.
For example, in the case of the first moment of informative (*vijñapti*) or non-informative (*avijñapti*) action, there is an acquisition that arises simultaneously at the outset.
In the second and subsequent moments, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of that very first moment arises at a later time.
In this same way, it should be understood that for other moments—the second and so forth—there is both a simultaneous (*sahajā*) and a later-arising acquisition.

Since the prior-arising acquisition (*agrajā prāpti*) is denied only for matter belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara-rūpa*), the prior-arising acquisition of the matter of the meditative restraints (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the untainted restraints (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) certainly exists; thus, [the denial] is waived in their case.
(II.40cd, 41) Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Why is this established?
Because if the non-acquisition of the afflictions (*kleśa*) were itself afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), [it would follow that one could not abandon the afflictions].
For one who has abandoned the afflictions, it would not exist, just as the afflictions themselves do not exist.
If it were wholesome, it would not exist for one whose roots of wholesomeness have been severed.
Furthermore, the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena would itself be untainted.
What would follow?
An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) would not exist, because [everyone] would be eternally endowed with the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
By process of elimination, it is established that non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is exclusively unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
For that which is present, there is no non-acquisition of the present. Since the acquisition of a present dharma exists,
it therefore has no non-acquisition that is present.
Because it is impossible for that [non-acquisition] and acquisition to coexist.
However, regarding past and future [dharmas], it is "belonging to the three time periods.

For qualities acquired through application (*prāyogika*) that have not yet been acquired or have been lost, as well as for future [dharmas] such as the eye and so forth, for which there is no acquisition—there is non-acquisition both in the past and in the future.
For, according to the principle of a stream, their non-attainment arises and ceases within the state of the future.
And [this applies] to those [dharmas] belonging to the desire realm and so forth, as well as to the stainless ones;
the word "and" (ca) serves to draw in the phrase "in three ways."
Those who have attained and are not dissociated from the realms such as the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are "attained to the desire realm and so forth" (kāmādyāpta).
The non-possession (aprāpti) of those things attained to the desire realm and so forth, as well as of the untainted (amala), is threefold.
This is because their establishment is by virtue of the basis of rebirth (upapatti-āśraya).
For non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is established as co-existent with its respective dharma;
it is not established by the power of the dharma in the same manner as acquisition (*prāpti*).

Therefore, for one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the non-acquisition of dharmas belonging to the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, belongs to the desire realm.
For one reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), it is of the form realm;
for one reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), it is of the formless realm.

For example, for one reborn in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there is the non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the qualities belonging to the realm of form and the formless realm—both those acquired through application (prāyogika) and those acquired by birth (upapattilābhika)—at the stage when wholesome roots are severed, because of their lack of detachment from those realms.
The non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of unafflicted states, as well as the non-acquisition of untainted (*anāsrava*) states, belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).

Likewise, for one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is the non-acquisition of qualities belonging to the desire realm that have been abandoned through changing levels, as well as the non-acquisition of the preparatory (*prāyogika*) qualities belonging to the form and formless realms; this is due both to the change of level and to being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Similarly, for one born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is the non-acquisition of qualities belonging to the desire and form realms that have been abandoned through changing levels, as well as the non-acquisition of the preparatory qualities belonging to the formless realm; this is likewise solely due to being an ordinary person.
And it should be understood that the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the untainted (*anāsrava*) [dharmas] belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
What is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
By the scriptural reading of the treatise, "the non-obtainment (*alābha*) of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*)," he demonstrates that this non-acquisition lacks the quality of being untainted.
"Of which noble dharmas (āryadharma) is there non-attainment?

The noble dharmas consist of the entire untainted path (anāsravamārga), beginning from the acceptance of the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti). For this very reason he asks thus, because [the sūtra] speaks of them all without distinction.
It is the non-acquisition of all the knowledges of those in training and those beyond training, such as the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering and so forth.
Why?
Because there is no distinction [between them].

If this were the case, then even when the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) regarding suffering has arisen, one would still be a non-noble being (*anārya*), because he would still lack the acquisition of the remaining noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
Therefore, it says this:
"But he [is a noble being] who [possesses them] without [the formal] acquisition."
That which is non-attainment without [prior] attainment is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). "Otherwise, however," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

If it were maintained that being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) consists in the non-possession of other dharmas even when there is possession of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*), then even a Buddha would be a non-noble one, because he does not possess the noble dharmas belonging to the mental continuums of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
However, this undesirable consequence does not arise if one takes "non-possession" alone [as the defining characteristic].
"In that case, the word 'eva' (only) must be read [there].
It means: 'only the non-attainment of the noble dharmas. For even single words can function as exclusives."
The meaning is that even single words [can be used].
For example, "one who drinks water" or "one who drinks air.
It is not meant that he is *only* one who drinks water or *only* one who drinks air.
The meaning of the word "only" (eva) is understood here as well;
that is, it is just like that case.
Alternatively, one who eats only water is called "water-eating" (abbhakṣa).
Just as in the expression "one who eats only air is an air-eater," where the restrictive sense of the particle *eva*— though omitted from the formal statement— is understood,
so too here [the meaning is] "only non-attainment."
"Of the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and its co-arising factors," so says another; this is the detailed explanation.

The non-acquisition (*alābha*) of the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering and of the factors co-arising with it, such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, constitutes the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*).

In this position, although the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering has arisen, there still exists the non-acquisition of the remaining noble dharmas (*āryadharma*); thus, the fault previously mentioned—that one would remain a non-noble (*anārya*)—does not apply.
That is not possible.

If it were so, then at the moment of attaining the fruit, there would be the abandonment of the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and its co-arising factors; thus, upon attaining the fruit, one would become a non-noble (*anārya*). To avoid this fault, he says:
Nor does it follow from their abandonment.
Nor does the consequence of becoming a non-noble (anārya) arise from the abandonment of those [roots] that coexist with patience (*kṣānti*),
because the non-acquisition (*alābha*) of that [state of being a noble] has been utterly destroyed.
Because that non-attainment is absolutely abandoned.
How so?
Because it is utterly destroyed, since it will not arise again within that continuum.
In that case, they belong to the three lineages (*gotra*).
That is, the lineages of the *śrāvaka*, the *pratyekabuddha*, and the *buddha*.
Of which [lineages] is there non-attainment?
"Of all" means:
of those belonging to the lineages (gotra) of the śrāvakas and so forth.
If that is the case, then the same fault remains.
The meaning is that even a Buddha would be a non-noble one (*anārya*) due to not attaining the three lineages (*gotra*).
Furthermore, that same rebuttal applies:
"But he [is not so] because of not having attained [them]," and so forth, as elaborated previously, up to: "just as one who subsists on water or subsists on air."
"In that case, the effort is futile.

This means that the effort made to define "being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*) as the non-acquisition of the receptivities (*kṣānti*) and their co-arising factors— intended to avoid the fault that one would be a non-noble being (*anārya*) because the non-acquisition of the remaining noble dharmas still exists—
would be in vain.
This is undertaken precisely as a rebuttal to the objection raised in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

"The continuum (*saṃtati*) in which the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) have not arisen" means that the continuum in which the noble dharmas have not arisen is "the state of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*).
The meaning is that it is the continuum of the aggregates (skandha-saṃtati) in which the noble path has not yet arisen.
By implication, it is stated that the continuum in which the noble dharmas have arisen is "noble-ness" (āryatva), due to the revolution of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti).
Now, as for this "non-attainment" (aprāpti):
The non-attainment of all dharmas is what is being urged, not merely the attainment of noble dharmas.
As it is said: "Just as..."
This is an illustration:
"Through the acquisition of that, it is abandoned.
Through the acquisition of that noble path (*āryamārga*), that state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), which is characterized by non-possession, is abandoned.
To which realm does that state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) belong?
Some say it belongs to all three realms.
But surely, the non-attainment [of a state] is established by virtue of its basis in logical possibility.
And the nature of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) has non-attainment as its intrinsic nature.
Therefore, for this sentient being belonging to the desire realm, there exists only the state of being a worldling belonging to the desire realm.
It does not belong to the realms of form or formlessness.
Therefore, we see that it is untenable to say that "the threefold world is abandoned" [by it].

Alternatively, if one considers that it has attained the state of non-arising (*anutpattidharmatā*), then the notion that "the threefold world is abandoned by it" is merely a conceptual metaphor (*upacārakalpanā*).
Let it be so;
this [acquisition] is not being denied.
However, there exists the acquisition of only one type of *pṛthagjanatva* (the state of being an ordinary person), namely that belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
We understand that it is abandoned at the stage of the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Furthermore, that [acquisition] is abandoned in the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) during the detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

However, for a noble one (*ārya*) who is being born into the form or formless realms, as well as for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) residing in each respective level, the acquisition does not arise at all due to the power of having attained the noble path (*āryamārga*).

However, it should be understood that their abandonment occurs on each respective stage during the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). Furthermore, "due to the transition between stages" means when, having attained detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one transitions to the first dhyāna.
And at that time, that state of being an ordinary person belonging to the desire realm is abandoned; yet one does not become a noble one (ārya),
because the state of being an ordinary person belonging to the level of the first dhyāna has arisen.
In this way, by moving from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) is abandoned.
Furthermore, when one moves from a higher level to a lower level, it should be stated that the state of being an ordinary person belonging to the higher level is abandoned.
This same principle should be applied to other cases as well.

Just as it has been applied [in the case] that through the attainment of the noble path (*āryamārga*), the non-attainment (*aprāpti*) of the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is abandoned, so too should it be applied that the non-attainment of other dharmas— such as those consisting of hearing and reflection (*śrutacintāmayādika*)— is abandoned.
How so?

First, regarding the factors belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), such as those consisting of hearing and reflection (*śrutacintāmayādi*), non-possession (*aprāpti*) is abandoned through the acquisition of their possession (*prāptilābha*).

Furthermore, for those wholesome factors acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*), the non-possession of one whose wholesome roots have been severed is abandoned through the acquisition [of those roots].
And [non-possession is also abandoned] by means of changing levels (*bhūmisaṃcāra*).
And when this person, having passed away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), migrates by birth into the first dhyāna,
at that time the non-attainment (*aprāpti*) of the aggregates belonging to that level which are included within the [five] destinies (*gati*) is abandoned.
For it will be explained that the destinies are exclusively undefiled-neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*).
It has been stated that the acquisition of the indeterminate is innate.
In this way, the non-acquisition of the acquisitions of the qualities belonging to the level of the first dhyāna that are produced through application is abandoned.
And because of the transition between stages (*bhūmisaṃcāra*).
One is deprived of the aggregates belonging to a higher stage that are comprised within the [five] destinies (*gati*) by virtue of transitioning to that [new] stage.
We perceive this illustration of the explanation of the transition between stages given by some to be unclear in that regard.
The non-attainment of the aggregates belonging to higher stages that are included within the [respective] destinies is not severed solely by the transition between stages;
rather,
it is also severed through the attainment of those [higher stages].
However, let us consider this unambiguous example:

for instance, there exists the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the qualities belonging to the preparatory stages (*prāyogika*) of the second dhyāna and above by a being of the desire realm who has not yet attained them.
If that being, having achieved detachment from the desire realm, is reborn in the first dhyāna...
That non-acquisition of theirs is lost through the transition to another stage;
however, a non-acquisition belonging to the level of the first dhyāna arises for them.
The same should be applied to others as well.
But surely, in this way, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress regarding acquisitions (*prāpti*): for an acquisition, there is an acquisition of that acquisition,
and for that too, another.
If there were another [possession] for that as well, there would be an infinite regress.
"Through mutual conjunction" means that one is possessed of possession by virtue of the connection with the possession-of-possession (*prāptiprāpti*).
The meaning is that one is "endowed" (samanvāgata) by means of the acquisition (prāpti) through the acquisition of acquisition (prāptiprāpti).
"From the arising of acquisition," and so forth:
from the arising of acquisition, one becomes endowed with that dharma or with the mind.
"And one is endowed with the acquisition of acquisition" is what continues [from the previous context].
Because the acquisition of acquisition arises, one becomes endowed with the [primary] acquisition itself. Thus, acquisition functions in both cases.
But since the acquisition of acquisition (prāptiprāpti) occurs in only one place, there is no infinite regress.
Regarding the wholesome and the afflicted:
these two are mentioned because they possess acquisitions that arise both prior to and subsequent to themselves.
For the acquisition (prāpti) of an indeterminate (avyākṛta) dharma is indeed innate (sahajā).
"In the second moment," and so forth:
in the second moment, there are three acquisitions—namely, the acquisition of that dharma, the acquisition of its acquisition, and the acquisition of the acquisition of that acquisition.
For one becomes possessed of those [dharmas] through connection with their acquisitions (*prāpti*).
Since three further secondary acquisitions (*anuprāpti*) arise for the purpose of being possessed of those three primary acquisitions, there are six acquisitions in total.
This refers to the substances (*dravya*) produced in the first and second moments.
Together with the dharma itself, there are nine acquisitions (*prāpti*) for the nine substances; together with the secondary acquisitions (*anuprāpti*), they become eighteen.
This is the detailed explanation regarding the consequence of successive increase.
The increase of each subsequent moment occurs by means of these acquisitions.
Or, there is an increase in the acquisitions (prāpti) in each successive moment. The consequence of that is the consequence of an ever-increasing growth;
by that [consequence].
Due to the consequence of ever-increasing growth,
these acquisitions spread forth;
we shall demonstrate this by way of illustration.

In the fourth moment, there must be possession (*prāpti*) and secondary possession (*anuprāpti*) for the three factors produced in the first moment; furthermore, there must be possession and secondary possession for the six possessions and secondary possessions produced in the second moment, which themselves possess further possession and secondary possession; likewise, there must be possession and secondary possession for the eighteen possessions and secondary possessions produced in the third moment, which again possess further possession and secondary possession—thus [it concerns] those produced in the first, second, and third moments.

There are twenty-seven acquisitions (*prāpti*) together with an equal number of subsequent acquisitions (*anuprāpti*), making fifty-four acquisitions in the fourth moment. However, in the fifth moment, there arise one hundred and sixty-two acquisitions: namely, fifty-four acquisitions and subsequent acquisitions produced in the first, second, and third moments; fifty-four acquisitions and subsequent acquisitions produced in the fourth moment;
and three sets of fifty-four [produced in the fifth moment itself]. Thus, one hundred and sixty-two acquisitions are born.
In this way, the consequence of an ever-increasing progression must be stated.
Regarding the phrase "of the past and future," the present is not mentioned because it is not necessary.
And regarding those "obtained by birth."
In this context, the non-mention of the "preparatory" (prāyogika) [states] is precisely because they are not necessary.
Regarding the phrase "together with their associated and co-existent [factors]," this refers to those factors such as sensation (vedanā) that belong to the same genus (sajāti), and so forth.
[They belong] to those included within the beginningless and endless cycle of saṃsāra, encompassed within that saṃsāra which has no beginning and no end.
They are infinite and immeasurable for even a single living being; how much more so for many?
Since acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise at every moment,
they consist of infinite substances;
that is to say, they consist of infinite acquisition-substances.
(Abhidh-k-vy 157) "What a great festival indeed these acquisitions (prāpti) are!"—
this is a humorous remark.
It means that they are simply not obstructive because they are formless (arūpin), and therefore the acquisitions find space [to exist].
(II.42a) "Homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) is the similarity among sentient beings," and so forth.
Those who possess an equal (*samāna*) portion (*bhāga*), that is, a commonality (*bhajana*), are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
The state of being that is "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*). Alternatively, a common portion or a common sharing is "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*);
that which is homogeneous itself is "homogeneity."
That substance through connection with which one becomes "of a similar class" (sabhāga) is [the *nikāyasabhāga*].
Its meaning is the equality, commonality, or similarity of sentient beings.
The inclusion of the term "sentient beings" (*sattva*) is for the purpose of excluding non-sentient things.
Homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) is the similarity among sentient beings and those factors (*dharma*) reckoned as sentient;
it is not accepted for non-sentient things such as rice, barley, and so forth.
"In the treatise, its designation is 'nikāyasabhāga' (homogeneity of the group).

In treatises such as the *Jñānaprasthāna*, this dissociated mental factor (*cittaviprayukta*) is indicated by the term "nikāyasabhāga. However, here, for the sake of conforming to the requirements of the verse composition, the intention is that it is indicated by the term "sabhāgatā" (homogeneity).
Furthermore, it is both undifferentiated and differentiated.
That which exists in all sentient beings is called "undifferentiated" even though it is distinct for each individual, because of its similarity.
For it is not, as the Vaiśeṣikas hold, a single and eternal entity; rather, it is distinct, such that it exists in some places and does not exist in others. Therefore, he says:
"Furthermore, they are divided," and so forth.
The three realms are those beginning with the desire realm;
the five destinies are those beginning with the hells.
The four modes of birth (yoni) are those born from eggs and so forth. The castes (jāti) are the Brahmins and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), female lay devotees, nuns, those in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and others are included.
"By way of the aggregates, bases, and elements" means the homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) of the aggregate of form, up to the homogeneity of the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).
"Undifferentiated" means...
"Of a general form" means it is a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*);
that is to say, it is a verbal expression (*abhidhāna*).
In this way, the cognitions and designations regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are also to be applied accordingly.

Some read: "If the substance of the homogeneity of the aggregates (*skandhasabhāgatādravya*) were not undifferentiated, then with respect to the aggregates which are distinguished by their mutual differences, there would be no non-differential cognition [of them] as 'aggregate, aggregate,' nor would there be such a designation.
In the same manner, the cognitions and designations regarding the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth are also to be applied; thus some recite.
To them it should be said:

"If [it were] 'homogeneity' (*sabhāgatā*)," and so on in detail, up to: "in the realms that are distinguished by mutual differences, there would be no undifferentiated cognition or designation such as 'one belonging to the desire realm, one belonging to the desire realm. [This is expressed] by means of a fourfold alternative (*catuḥkoṭika*).
It may be that one dies and is reborn, yet neither abandons nor acquires the homogeneity of sentient beings (*sattvasabhāgatā*).
Regarding "the homogeneity of sentient beings": the homogeneity of sentient beings is *sattvasabhāgatā*, characterized by such states as humanity and so forth.
The inclusion of the term "sentient being" (sattva) is for the purpose of qualifying the dharma;
for in this fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika), it is the homogeneity of sentient beings (sattvasabhāgatā) that is intended, not the homogeneity of dharmas (dharmasabhāgatā).
However, what is meant here is not the homogeneity of aspect (ākārasabhāgatā) in the sense of "sentient being, sentient being."

For if that were intended, the third alternative would not be established; because even during the transition between states of existence (*gati-saṃcāra*), that homogeneity of sentient beings (*sattva-sabhāgatā*) remains as it was.
[This refers to the case of] "one being reborn in that very same place."
For example, one who, having passed away from the human realm, is reborn in the human realm itself:
he passes away from the human realm at death and is reborn there again through the linking of a new existence (*pratisaṃdhibandha*).
Yet, he neither abandons nor acquires that human homogeneity (*manuṣyasabhāgatā*), because that human homogeneity remains in its very same state.
The second [case] is "one entering into the determination of correctness" (*niyāma*).

Such a person abandons the generic similarity (*sabhāgatā*) that has the nature of being an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*), and acquires another generic similarity that has the nature of being an noble one (*ārya*).
The third [case] is "due to moving between realms of existence" (*gati-saṃcārāt*).
For example, one who, having passed away from the human realm, is reborn in the divine realm:
just as one passes away from death, so too does one undergo rebirth through the linking of a new existence.
One abandons the homogeneity of sentient beings characterized by the homogeneity of humans.
"And he acquires another [characteristic], namely the characteristic of the assembly of gods.
Regarding the fourth [alternative], "setting aside these modes" means excluding the previously mentioned categories of the nature of the limits (*koṭi*).
For example, it is like an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or a noble one (*ārya*) who has not yet attained anything.

If there were a real entity (*dravya*) called "ordinary-person homogeneity" (*pṛthagjanasabhāgatā*), then what further need would there be for a "state of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*) imagined as having the nature of the non-attainment of the noble dharmas? This is the implied meaning of the sentence. An ordinary person would be distinguished as such by the very homogeneity of an ordinary person, just as a human is distinguished as such by the very homogeneity of a human.

For the Vaibhāṣikas do not conceive of "human-ness" as having a nature distinct from the human homogeneity (*manuṣyasabhāgatā*), unlike [the case of] non-acquisition (*alābha*). And regarding this, the proof is:
"Ordinary-ness (*pṛthagjanatva*) is not something other than its own homogeneity."
Because it is denotable by the condition of its own generic similarity (*sabhāgatā*),
just like "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*).
Furthermore, the world does not perceive *sabhāgatā* at all, because it is formless (*arūpin*).

The world does not see [the eye] as being of the same class with it by means of the eye, because it is formless (*arūpin*), because it lacks form (*arūpavat*), or because its intrinsic nature is formless (*arūpasvabhāva*).
Just as it does not see, so too it does not hear, up to and including it does not touch.
By this, he demonstrates that [the existence of the sense-faculties] is not established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"And one does not determine this by means of wisdom.
By this, he shows that it is not established even by inference.
"And one realizes the non-difference of the birth of sentient beings."
Even if that [homogeneity] exists, how could it have an operation there?
In the cognition of the non-difference of a genus, there is indeed the cognition of the non-difference of the genus;

however, that [cognition] is not produced by a homogeneity imagined as a separate substance, because such an entity is not perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and thus its operation is impossible.
You might say:
"A cognition of a universal cannot exist without a cause;
therefore, that which is the cause of this cognition of a universal [must be the universal itself]."
Regarding the claim that "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) is a distinct substance:
we too maintain that this general cognition is based on a cause;
for that cognition is produced by similarity.
And we maintain that this similarity is not a separate substance. Therefore it is said:
"Furthermore, why is similarity among non-sentient things (*asattvasabhāgatā*) not also accepted? and so forth.
The general cognition "sentient being, sentient being" is not caused by a generic similarity (*sabhāgatā*) that exists as a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*),
because it functions through a general form,
just like the general cognitions of rice, barley, mung beans, black gram, and so forth.
For this cognition of a universal (sāmānyabuddhi) is produced by the similarity within their own kind (svajātisādṛśya), as in the case of rice and barley.
And that similarity within their own kind does not exist as a separate entity (arthāntara) from those things themselves.
"And of those [homogeneous] groups" (tāsāṃ ca sabhāgatānām), and so forth.

Since it is accepted that the homogeneity of sentient beings (*sattva-sabhāgatā*) is one thing, the homogeneity of realms (*dhātu-sabhāgatā*) another, and the homogeneity of destinies (*gati-sabhāgatā*) yet another—such that these homogeneities are mutually distinct—how is it that you establish the designation "homogeneity" for them without distinction, thinking, "This is homogeneity; this is homogeneity"?
How, then, do conventional usage and cognition arise?

If, even in this case, another "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) were to be postulated by means of which there could arise a cognition of a commonality of homogeneity, then this would constitute a counter-position, because it contradicts the previously stated position.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas would be vindicated in this way.
The intended meaning is that they are "blazing" or "established.
For they too are proponents of the category of the universal (*sāmānyapadārtha*). However, this is the distinction of those Vaiśeṣikas.
Even a single [entity] exists in many, like the thread of a garland,
and like a string around a bull's neck—
provided that [the universals] have been explained, since [the author] maintains the doctrine of the category of the universal (sāmānya).
If [the existence of the afterlife] were not illuminated [by scripture], because [the Buddha] propounds specific views such as unity, plurality, permanence, and impermanence;
for it is not the case that the existence of the afterlife and so forth, though imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas, are not thereby established. "If he comes to such a state" means:

By the practice, cultivation, and frequent repetition of taking life, one is reborn in the hells. If one returns to this state and attains the common lot of human beings, one becomes short-lived due to that taking of life; such is the detailed explanation. "Itthaṃ" means of this kind.
The state of being that is "homogeneity" (*itthaṃtva*).

Master Saṃghabhadra maintains that homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) is the cause for the similarity in the configuration, movement, food, and so forth of bodies and sense-faculties, as well as the cause for mutual connection among them.
This [position] has already been refuted by this very [argument].
For we also desire this very thing:
that this homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) is not a separate substance (*dravyāntara*),
because those very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) themselves assume such a state of being a cause.

(II.42bcd) "The state of non-conception (*āsaṃjñika*) is the cessation of mind and mental factors among those who are without conception," and so forth. This [state] belongs to those without conception; thus it is called "the state of non-conception."

Or, existence among those without perception is "non-perception" (*āsaṃjñika*). It is called "cessation" (*nirodha*) because by means of it the mind and mental factors are ceased, or because it causes the mind and mental factors to cease.

That by which the minds and mental factors remaining in the future period are suppressed for a certain duration— that is to say, they do not obtain the opportunity to arise— is the substance called *āsaṃjñika*.
It is like the damming of a river;
the meaning is "like a bridge.
It is like the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntarika).
Just as there are those gods called the Brahmapurohitas, some of whom—namely the Mahābrahmās—reside in a particular region within the intermediate stage of dhyāna;
so too are there those gods called the Bṛhatphalas, in whose region the non-percipient beings (asaṃjñisattvas) reside.
They do not exist in any other level.
The phrase "possessing perception" (*saṃjñin*) should be connected to both the time of birth and the time of death.
Because the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*) occurs through the defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*),
death and birth take place within a state of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
And because of this restriction:
"due to the exhaustion of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of the previous attainment.
This means due to the exhaustion of the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) characterized by the formative forces of the previous attainment.
The meaning is: "because its fruit has been completed.

Others explain it as: "due to the exhaustion of the projection (*āvedha*) of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) from the previous meditative attainment (*samāpatti*)," and "because there is no accumulation of anything new."
The intention is that because of the absence of mind, there is no accumulation of karma.
"Like arrows shot [into the air] when their momentum has been exhausted, [they fall] to the earth"—
the word "arise" (*upapadyante*) is understood from the context.
Previously, this word *pad* had the meaning of "producing";
now, by virtue of its sense, it has the meaning of "going.
The meaning is that they "become" or "go."
The phrase "they go to the earth" is the ellipsis for the sentence, according to others.
The attainment of non-percipient beings, or the attainment that is non-perception, is the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
This much is what is drawn back by the word "likewise" (*tathā*).
Because specific meanings such as "it is a maturation" are not intended [here].
For the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) is indeed indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
whereas it will be stated that this meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).
"The five aggregates are the maturation" means that at the time of death and rebirth, there is the presence of the state of maturation in the mind and mental factors;
for that very reason, one is said to "possess" it.

Precisely because one who has fallen away from it may give rise to it again and be reborn among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), for that very reason, one who possesses it does not enter the path of certainty (*niyāma*).

For by entering the path of certainty itself, a noble one (*ārya*) obtains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of rebirth in the miserable destinies, among the non-percipient beings, as a Great Brahmā, or as a Kaurava, as well as of an eighth existence and so forth.
They regard this [attainment] as if it were a place of downfall.
The meaning is that they view it as if it were a place of misfortune (*apāyasthāna*).
Others say it is like a place of falling from a mountain precipice or the like;
for they enter into that attainment while perceiving it as a means of deliverance (*niḥsaraṇasaṃjñin*).
The meaning is that ordinary persons possess the notion of liberation;
however, the noble ones do not acquire such a perverted notion.
It is "like meditative absorption" (dhyāna).
Because of the attainment of the fourth dhyāna, yogins obtain the fourth dhyāna that was previously obtained in the beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra) throughout the past and future.
Therefore, he asks whether they likewise obtain that [past and future] state;
[the answer is] that others, for their part, do not obtain it either.
Even ordinary persons do not acquire [the meditative attainments] of the past or future, for which they themselves possess mastery;
how much less so the noble ones, for whom these are not their own?
This is so even though [the attainment] is familiar to them.

In beginningless *saṃsāra*, although it has been obtained before, it is acquired [only] in a single time-period (*ekādhvika*), because it is to be accomplished through great formative effort (*mahābhisaṃskāra*)— meaning it is produced through great exertion— and because it is devoid of mind (*acittaka*).
The meaning is that [the restraint] is obtained as belonging to the same time-period (*samānādhvika*).
For example, regarding the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara*:
even though the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara* is of eight kinds, it is obtained at the very moment it is formally undertaken.
Then it is attained;
and its attainment arises at that very moment.
However, by means of that meditative attainment once it has been acquired, one remains possessed of it in the second and subsequent moments, just like the Prātimokṣa restraint.
As long as one does not abandon that attainment, it persists;
its abandonment occurs either through falling away or by shifting to another stage.
Because it is devoid of mental factors (*acaittika*), it is not cultivated as a future state.
For it is a future wholesome mind that is cultivated;
however, this [attainment] is not "without mind," and thus it is not cultivated as a future state in the same way.
(II.44, 45ab) The one called cessation is likewise.
The term "attainment" (samāpatti) carries over [from the previous context].
The word "eva" is used for emphasis.

Just as in the explanation of the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the word "atha" is used to extend the application [of the definition] that "cessation" (nirodha) refers to the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta).
In the same way, here too, in the exposition of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), that very same principle is extended by analogy:

"by means of mental attention preceded by the perception of a peaceful dwelling" (*śāntavihārasaṃjñāpūrvakeṇa manasikāreṇa*). Here, "dwelling" (*vihāra*) refers to a state of abiding, like a dwelling for recreation.
It is a specific kind of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
A peaceful dwelling is a "peaceful abiding" (*śāntavihāra*).
The perception regarding this peaceful abiding is the "perception of peaceful abiding" (*śāntavihārasaṃjñā*).

The phrase "preceded by that" means that it is preceded by the perception of dwelling in peace (*śāntavihārasaṃjñā*); the term *manasikāra* here has the sense of "mental attention" (*manaskāra*), because it is a compound formed with the elision of the case-ending (*aluk*).

For those who perceive this state as a peaceful dwelling, being exhausted by the activity of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedita*), enter this attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) through such mental attention.

However, the meaning of the phrase "preceded by the perception of escape" regarding that attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) is that it is preceded by the perception of liberation (*mokṣasaṃjñā*).
And "to be experienced in a subsequent life" (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*):
a subsequent life (*aparaparyāya*) refers to the third birth and onwards;
it is that which is to be experienced therein.
How so?
If a noble one, having produced the attainment of cessation in the desire realm, were to be reborn in the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*),
for him that [attainment] would be a fulfilling karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*).

However, for one who falls away from that [fruit] and is reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and after some time attains the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*)— whether or not they produce the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)— and is subsequently reborn in the peak of existence, for such a person that [fruit] is to be experienced in a subsequent lifetime (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
This is the case even if they were to attain final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*) from here.
"His [attainment] is not fixed.
"Because of the fear of annihilation" means because of the fear of the annihilation of all personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
For fools tremble at non-rebirth as if at a precipice.
Why does the fear of annihilation not arise regarding the attainment of non-perception?
Because form exists there.
For they enter that attainment after having adhered to the notion of a self (*ātmasaṃjñā*) with respect to form (*rūpa*).

However, in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because it belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyabhūmika*), even form does not exist; thus, seeing the non-existence of every state of personal existence (*sarvātmabhāvabhāva*), they do not venture to enter that attainment.

But is it not the case that in the formless realms there exist factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*), such as the homogeneous character of the group (*nikāyasabhāga*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and so forth?
Why is it that, having formed the notion of a self therein, they do not enter into that state? Because dissociated [factors] are invisible,
and because [the state] is produced by the power of the Noble Path.
But how is it understood that its production occurs by the power of the Noble Path? To this he says:
"Because of the resolute conviction in that [state] of one for whom there is Nirvana in the present life.
Nirvana in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmānirvāṇa*) means Nirvana in the seen birth.
Of that.
"From conviction in that" (*tadadhimuktitaḥ*): "that" refers to the object; conviction in that is *tadadhimukti*.
Therefore, "resolute belief in that" means resolute belief in it. "From resolute belief in that" means from such resolute belief in it.
In this present life, the Noble One resolves upon it, thinking, "This is Nirvana."
Some, however, read it thus:
"Because of his conviction in that [nirvāṇa] which has been seen.
And they explain it in this way.
"Having seen nirvāṇa by means of this" is one who has seen nirvāṇa (*dṛṣṭanirvāṇa*).
The resolute conviction of that noble one toward that [nirvāṇa] is "resolute conviction in that" (*tadadhimukti*).
"From that resolute conviction" means from *tadadhimukti*.
This is what is meant:
the Noble One who has seen Nirvana is the one who is resolved upon it, and no other.
But is it not the case that even an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) has seen Nirvana by means of the worldly path?
An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) does not see *nirvāṇa* directly;
however, he may attain *nirvāṇa*.
For it is not a matter for objection to say that an ordinary person, perceiving a higher stage as peaceful, attains detachment (*vairāgya*), but not [directly perceives] *nirvāṇa*.
"This is obtainable only through application.
