This attainment, like the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), is likewise to be accomplished through great volitional effort (*mahābhisaṃskāra*).
Thus it is.
It is acquired as belonging to a single time period.
How so? He says:
"And that which is past is not obtained."
When one who has fallen away produces that [discipline] again, it is obtained as something entirely new through application (*prayoga*).
This should be explained in detail as being like the *prātimokṣa* restraint.
"By the power of the mind, because of its cultivation":
the meaning is that it is cultivated as something yet to come by the power of the mind.
[It is] obtainable through enlightenment by the Sage.
Thus,
this is an exception to the general rule that [this attainment] is obtainable only through application (*prayoga*),
because that procedure pertains to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
He will state that enlightenment consists of the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.
Therefore he says:
"Simultaneous with the knowledge of destruction," and so forth.
And [the dharmas] with outflows [are abandoned] by the knowledge of destruction.
Thus the Blessed Buddhas attain this.
For the Buddhas, there is nothing that is called "attained through effort" (*prāyogika*).
As it was said by the author of the hymn:
"O Knower of the End of Virtue, you do not possess any wholesome state that is produced through application;
you are bound by mere desire, for you have mastery over wherever you wish.
But how, then, is the Blessed One "liberated in both ways"?
The obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle to meditative attainments (*samāpattyāvaraṇa*) constitute both parts;
one is liberated from these.
One succeeds as if [liberation] had already been produced.
The Blessed One, who is liberated in both ways, accomplishes it as if it were previously manifested before him,
because he has attained mastery over it through the possession of the power that causes its manifestation.
"How much more so, then, that [he attains] it," and so forth.

This is the nature of things (*dharmatā*): that a bodhisattva in his final existence, having become an obtainer of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) and having generated the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by relying on the fourth dhyāna, emerges from that and enters the meditative attainment of the peak of existence.
Then he enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Emerging from that, and again relying upon the fourth dhyāna, he effects the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). From the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), he becomes an unsurpassed, perfectly awakened Buddha (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbuddha*). Thus, according to the Westerners—those who are later than those from the land of Kaśmīra—he produces that [attainment] while still in the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*).
*Netrīpada* is the title of the treatise of the Elder Upagupta. Regarding this, there is the statement:
"It must be said that the Tathāgata, having produced the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), produces the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*)."
"By sixteen [moments] during the clear realization of the truths":
beginning from the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering up to the subsequent knowledge of the path, this refers to sixteen moments of mind.
"And by eighteen [moments] during the detachment from the peak of existence."

For the abandonment of the nine grades of afflictions belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) which are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), there are nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*); thus, by means of eighteen [moments].
These total thirty-four, being sixteen and eighteen respectively.
The afflictions of the lower stages, however, do not need to be abandoned again.

Because the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth have already been abandoned through the worldly path (*laukikamārga*) precisely during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
if this rule holds— that one need not produce an antidote (*pratipakṣa*) for afflictions already abandoned—

then for what purpose does one produce at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*), which is the antidote to those desire-realm afflictions that have already been abandoned?
Because the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is inseparable from that [category of dharma-knowledge];
for it is impossible for the manifestation of the category of subsequent knowledge to occur if the category of dharma-knowledge has not first arisen.
Indeed, this is what constitutes the "subsequent nature" of subsequent knowledge: that it arises after this [dharma-knowledge].
The Westerners say:
"What, moreover, would happen? and so forth.
What fault would there be if one were to manifest, in the interim, a dissimilar mind that is with-outflows (*sāsrava*)? (Abhidh-k-vy 163)
The Vaibhāṣikas say:
"There might be an intention to emerge," and so forth;
that is, there might be a bodhisattva whose intention is to emerge [from meditative absorption].

Others say that one should be skilled in emerging [from meditative absorption]. For the meaning of "intention" (āśaya) is the meaning of "wholesome root" (kuśalamūla). Thus, this is what is being said: [one should be skilled in emerging from absorption so as to cultivate wholesome roots].

Such are the roots of virtue of the bodhisattvas that, once they have become manifest, they do not rise from them until they have attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment while still on that very same seat. The outsiders say:
"It is true that their intention is not to rise, but it is not as you describe it."
However, they explain it as being exactly as before:
namely, the position that [the knowledge of non-arising] is simultaneous with the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna).
(II.45cd) Even though there are many types of distinctions between these two.
One [is] in the final dhyāna; the other [is] elsewhere.
Born from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
One enters the first through the perception of deliverance (*niḥsaraṇa-saṃjñā*), and the other through the desire for abiding (*vihāra-kāmatā*); thus there are many such distinctions between them.
However, these two are equal in one respect.
"Existing with the desire realm as its basis" means "there might be existence in the form realm," and so forth.

Whatever exists as a form-existence (*rūpabhava*), all such existence consists of five aggregates (*pañcavyavacāra*). This constitutes a fourfold alternative (*catuḥkoṭika*). There may be a form-existence that does not consist of the five aggregates: namely, for gods of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) who possess perception (*saṃjñin*) but abide in a dissimilar state of mind (*visabhāgacitta*), or for those who have entered the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or for the gods who are without perception (*asaṃjñideva*).
The existence that occurs when the state of non-perception (āsaṃjñika) has been attained;
there may be an existence consisting of the five aggregates, yet it is not an existence of the form realm (rūpabhava).
It is the existence of sentient beings belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) who abide in a homogeneous state of mind (sabhāgacitta).
There may be existence in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*), and that existence consists of five constituents.

It is the existence of those gods of the form realm who possess perception and abide in a homogeneous state of mind, as well as the existence of those gods without perception when the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) has not yet been attained.
There may also be that which is neither existence in the realm of form nor an existence consisting of five constituents.
The existence of beings belonging to the desire realm who abide in a dissimilar state of mind, as well as those who have entered the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation,
and the existence of the formless realm—
of these, the first category serves as the illustrative example.
Form-existence (*rūpabhava*) is the fivefold aggregate (*skandhapañcaka*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
"Fivefold range" (*pañcavyavacāra*) means the five aggregates;
"range" (*vyavacāra*) is the designation for the aggregates used by the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.
*Vyavacāra* means specific engagement;
the meaning is deception through a change of state.
That which possesses this is *vyavacāra*.
The suffix *ac* (the letter *a*) in [the word *arśas*] has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), according to the rule *arśa-ādibhyo 'c*.
Thus, the meaning is "that which deceives.
Form is like a mass of foam; feeling is like a bubble.
Because of the contradiction [with the sūtra] beginning with those words.

In that case, if the attainment of non-perception were not admitted in the realm of form, it would not have been stated: "of those who have entered the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation."
By this it is understood that the attainment of non-perception belongs to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
Furthermore, even there, there is this distinction;
that is, despite the similarity [to the attainment of cessation], there exists a specific difference.
"Subsequently, in the realm of form (rūpadhātu)" means:

those noble ones who, having produced the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), have subsequently fallen away from it, and having attained meditative absorption (dhyāna), are reborn in the realm of form;
by them, because they have previously fallen away [from that attainment].
By the force of previous practice, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) may be produced in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

However, the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) is produced by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) even for the first time in both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the realm of form; this is the distinction.
Furthermore, there is some falling away (*parihāṇi*).
"This meditative attainment is similar to nirvāṇa;
how, then, could there be falling away from it?"— thinking this impossible, he asks about the Udāyi-sūtra.
This sutra was spoken by the noble Śāriputra; however, because Udāyin acted as an obstacle therein, it is called the "Udāyi Sūtra. How so?
The setting was Śrāvastī.
There, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the monks:
"In this regard, venerable ones, a monk is endowed with ethical discipline, endowed with meditative concentration, and endowed with wisdom."
He repeatedly enters into and emerges from the cessation of perception and feeling.
He understands, as it truly is, that "this state exists.
Yet, he does not attain full realization in this very life, right now.
Nor does this occur at the time of death.
Upon the dissolution of the body, having transcended the gods who subsist on physical food, he is reborn in a certain divine, mind-made body.
Having been reborn there, he repeatedly enters into and emerges from the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāveditanirodha*).

"He understands as it truly is: 'This possibility exists. Now at that time, the Venerable Udāyin was seated and present in that very assembly. Then the Venerable Udāyin said this to the Venerable Śāriputra:"

"It is impossible, venerable Śāriputra, it is out of the question, that a monk who has been reborn in a certain divine mind-made body could repeatedly enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling,
and yet know as it really is that this is possible.
For a second and even a third time, the venerable Udāyin said this to the venerable Śāriputra.
"It is impossible, venerable sir," as before.
Then this thought occurred to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Since this monk has resisted and rejected what I have said even up to three times,
and not a single fellow-practitioner approves of what I have said,
I shall now approach the Blessed One."
Then the Venerable Śāriputra approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the monks.
In this case, venerable ones, a monk is endowed with virtue,
as described previously.
At that time, the venerable Udāyin was there, as described previously.
In this way, for a second and even a third time, the Venerable Udāyin spoke thus to the Venerable Śāriputra,
as before. Then, this thought occurred to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Even before my Teacher, this monk has rejected and protested against what was spoken by me up to three times.
Not a single fellow-practitioner approves of what I have said.
What if I were to remain silent?"
Then the Venerable Śāriputra remained silent.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Udāyin:
"Udāyin, what kind of divine, mind-made body do you perceive?"
"Is it not so that [the self] is merely formless and composed of perception?
"It is so, Venerable Sir.
"In that case, you, being a deluded man who is blind and without eyes, think that you ought to converse on higher Dharma and higher Discipline with the monk Śāriputra, who possesses eyes."
There, having rebuked the venerable Udāyin in his presence, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, you too look on with indifference while the elder monk is being harassed.
O deluded man, has no compassion arisen in you for the elder monk who is being harassed?"
There, having rebuked the venerable Udāyin and the venerable Ānanda in their presence, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"In this case, monks, a monk is endowed with virtue and endowed with concentration," and so on in detail, up to: "he understands as it really is that 'this possibility exists. Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling for the purpose of seclusion.
In this regard, the Venerable Udāyin raised an objection, reflecting that this "mind-made body" (manomaya-kāya) has been described as belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara),
for in that realm there is no form (rūpa),
but only mind (manas) together with its mental associates (saṃprayoga).
Therefore, it is a mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).
His intention is that this meditative attainment does not enter into that [state].
However, for the noble Śāriputra, what is intended is the divine mind-made body belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), because it manifests without depending upon semen and blood.
For this very reason, the Blessed One questioned the Venerable Udāyin: "Udāyin, what kind of divine, mind-made body do you perceive?
Is it not simply one that is formless and consists of perception?"

He replied, "So be it, Venerable Sir. The Blessed One, intending the divine, mind-made body belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) alone, supported the view of the noble Śāriputra and rebuked the venerable Udāyin:

"You, being a deluded man indeed and lacking vision, think that you should converse on the higher Dharma (*abhidharma*) and the higher Discipline (*abhivinaya*) with the monk Śāriputra, who possesses vision."

"There is this possibility" means that he understands, as it truly is, this possibility which consists in the attainment and the emergence from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"While practicing" means while previously [engaged in practice].
"He realizes full knowledge" means he attains the state of an Arhat (*arhattva*).
And this attainment belongs to the peak of existence (*bhāvāgrika*), as explained in detail.
The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) belongs to the peak of existence,
as does the person who possesses it.
His rebirth would occur only at the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), not in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
And it is said in the Sūtra:
"Having been reborn there in the realm of form, he repeatedly enters into and emerges from the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñāveditanirodha)."
Therefore, it is understood that there is falling away from this [attainment].
This is indeed logical for the Vaibhāṣikas;
but how is this so for the Sautrāntikas?
For it is the established tenet of the Sautrāntikas that only an Ārya attains the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), and there is no falling away from the Noble Path (āryamārga).
How then can it be maintained that such an Ārya falls away from the Noble Path belonging to a higher stage?
For them as well, this sūtra is not contradicted.

How so? For whoever, having attained the peak of existence (bhavāgra), enters the path of certainty (niyāma), being an non-returner (anāgāmin), would produce the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
He would fall away from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) and from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
but not from the path,
because the noble path belonging to a higher stage has never been produced [by him].
Having fallen away from that state, he might produce meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and be reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Therefore, while there is falling away from this [state], there is no falling away from the noble path (*āryamārga*); thus, there is no contradiction with our own established tenet (*svasiddhānta*).
These are the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvasamāpatti*).
The four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"Pertaining to the first eon" means pertaining to that which establishes the attainment at the very beginning.
"Because it is determined as being experienced in both ways.
This means that the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is "determined to be experienced" because it is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadya-vedanīya*).
The attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is "experienced in both ways," meaning it is both determined and undetermined as to when it will be experienced.
For non-returners (*anāgāmin*), [the karma] is necessarily to be experienced;
for arhats, it is not necessarily to be experienced, because they attain final nirvana right here.
This is also [the case] from the perspective of its first arising.
Someone first produces the attainment of non-perception among humans;
someone else [produces it] in the form realm.
However, the attainment of cessation is produced only among humans.
But one who has fallen away [from it] does so in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Now, why does one produce this [attainment] only among humans?

An *anāgāmin*, weary of the activity of mental factors such as applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) through the gateway of perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*), produces the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) with the thought: "By means of that state, may I dwell in happiness."

However, a non-returner reborn in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) does not experience such affliction through the activity of mental factors there, because the realm of form is peaceful; thus, he does not produce [the thought of renunciation] for the first time there.
But one who has fallen away from that state produces it due to previous habituation.

Likewise, one reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and specifically one reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), does not produce it for the same reason—that it is peaceful.
Or else, it would entail the consequence of [attaining] nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).

For in that state, form does not exist; if the mind and mental factors were to cease, there would be his final passing away (*parinirvāṇa*) alone, because the dissociated factors (*cittaviprayukta*) lack the capacity to persist by themselves.

Because one remains as an obstacle to the completion of the fruit of karma that is certain to be experienced (*niyatavedanīya*), the possibility of final nirvāṇa (*parinirvāṇa*) does not exist [for such a person].

However, because one enters the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) with the notion of liberation—that is, preceded by a mental attention (*manasikāra*) based on the notion of escape—one enters it for the first time even in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Why, then, are these [so]? [This is] the detailed explanation.

The intention is that since their intrinsic nature consists in the cessation of all mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), both of these attainments (*samāpatti*) should be described as "the cessation of mind and mental factors. [The phrase] "because of the application of those attainments in opposition to them" means that one applies oneself to those two attainments by way of being opposed to perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*).

The preparation for the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is by way of aversion toward perception (*saṃjñā*), as in the detailed passage: "Perception is a disease, perception is a thorn, perception is an abscess; this is peaceful, this is sublime.
The preparation for the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is by way of aversion toward both perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita*).
This is like the expression used for the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
Just as with the term "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*), it is not the case that mental factors (*caitta*) are never known by means of the knowledge of others' minds; nevertheless,
because one initially applies oneself with the thought, "I shall know another's mind," it is called "knowledge of others' minds" and not "knowledge of others' minds and their mental factors."
In the same way, here too, there is such a statement regarding these two attainments (*samāpatti*).

Regarding this, the Vaibhāṣikas and others maintain that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of perception (*saṃjñisamāpatti*), and the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) are indeed without mind (*acittaka*).
The Elder Vasumitra and others, however, maintain that they possess mind (*sacittaka*) in the form of a non-manifest mental consciousness (*aparisphuṭamanovijñāna*).
The Yogācāras maintain that [the seeds] reside within the *ālayavijñāna* together with the mind; such is the difference in their tenets.
Therefore, this is raised:
"How now, from that which has been ceased for a long time," and so forth.
The mention of "ceased for a long time" is for the purpose of excluding that which has ceased immediately prior.
How does [the cognition] arise from that which has ceased immediately prior?
The Vaibhāṣikas ask: "If it is accepted that what has ceased immediately prior exists, why is it not also accepted that what has ceased for a long time exists?"

We do not assert the existence of that which has just ceased; rather, the present mind, having established itself as the causal condition for another mind, ceases while another arises—like the simultaneous lowering and raising of the ends of a balance scale.
Since that [former] mind has ceased and the other mind has arisen, it is said that "one mind arises immediately after the preceding mind has ceased.
This is stated by treating what is proximate to the present as if it were present.
Others, however, say— namely the Sautrāntikas—
"How, then, regarding those born in the formless realm," and so forth.
The word "tāvat" (then/in the first place) indicates a sequential order.
The meaning is that this very point must first be stated as an illustration:
for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is not admitted for form (*rūpa*);
how then does it arise?
Therefore, we say that it arises from the mind alone and not from form;
for these two are mutual seeds:
the seed of the body together with its sense faculties exists in the mind, and the seed of the mind exists in the body together with its sense faculties.
Regarding the phrase "in the *Paripṛcchā*": the *Paripṛcchā* is a treatise composed by the Elder Vasumitra; he states therein:
For he also possesses treatises such as the *Pañcavastuka*;
therefore, [the author] specifies:
"it is his own fault."
What is that fault?
It is the one stated as: "How now [can there be contact] from a mind that has ceased long ago?
[The answer is: "It is the coming together of the three."

According to the opinion of Bhadanta Vasumitra, there would also be no cessation of perception and feeling here [in the intermediate state], because it is the same as for the sense faculties, their objects, and consciousness.
Even though that attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) possesses mind, there is the cessation of perception and feeling therein.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka raises this objection:
[it must be] "born of contact with ignorance" (avidyāsaṃsparśaja).

Contact conjoined with ignorance is "contact associated with ignorance" (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*). That which is born from that is "born of contact associated with ignorance" (*avidyā-saṃsparśaja*). However, this does not apply to the arising of feeling itself.
However, regarding the arising of feeling, contact has not been specified in such a way as "this specific contact is the condition for feeling.
That very Bhadanta Ghoṣaka concludes:
"Therefore, it is without mind."
"How can that which is without mind be a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*)?
It deserves to be a meditative attainment such as the dhyānas and so forth.
For, by means of concentration (*samādhi*), the mind and mental factors are made equal and brought to a state of one-pointedness; thinking thus, he asks. (Abhidh-k-vy 168)

"By means of bringing about the equilibrium of the great elements (*mahābhūta-samatāpādana*). It is called "attainment" (*samāpatti*) because by it the great elements enter into a state of equilibrium.
Thus, this state of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), as well as the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth, possesses the nature of an attainment.
What, then, is the equilibrium of the great elements here?
It is their abiding in a state contrary to the arising of consciousness.
They "enter" (samāpadyante) because they come together (samāgacchanti).
"Samāpatti" is a term derived from the sense of "reaching together" (samāgacchanti tām).
Since yogins also reach together with meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth, meditative absorptions and the like also possess the nature of *samāpatti*.
"In substance" means by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇataḥ*).
Because they obstruct the arising of the mind;
that is, because they prevent the arising of the mind.
No;
it is not by the very mind of attainment alone.
This is not so.
Why?
Because that [state] is obstructed by the very mind of attainment;
the meaning is that it obstructs the arising of the mind.
He explains how that is so with the passage beginning, "For it is the very mind of attainment," and so forth.
That is indeed the mind of attainment itself; it is not a separate substance.
It arises in contradiction with another mind— that is, in contradiction with a future mind—
by which mind there occurs for a period of time not merely a total non-occurrence.
The word "merely" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding a different substance (*dravyāntara*).
Because it brings about a basis that is contrary to that;
that is, because it brings about a mental continuum as its basis which is opposed to the mind.
This refers to that which is merely the non-occurrence [of the mind].
This is designated as "that attainment.

The meaning is that this is a dharma of designation (*prajñaptidharma*) and not a substantial dharma (*dravyadharma*). If it is not a substantial dharma, how can it be designated as "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*)? To this, he says:
And that is merely a non-occurrence;
it did not exist previously, nor does it exist for the yogin who has emerged from it at a later time.
This attainment—whether the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation—is designated as conditioned by way of conventional usage, but not as a substantial entity.
"Or rather," and so forth.
It is the bringing about of the basis itself in such a way, its being established in such a manner;
that is, a particular state.
The meaning is that this [attainment] is called "attainment" because it is produced by an attainment (*samāpatti*).
Furthermore, since that particular state did not exist previously and does not exist later for one who has emerged from it, its being conditioned (*saṃskṛtatva*) is not contradicted.
Alternatively, the reading is *samāpadana*.
The meaning is that because this attainment is a specific state of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), its conditioned nature is established.
The same applies to the "state of non-perception" (*āsaṃjñika*), and so forth;
in that [state], the yogin obtains precisely a mind that is opposed to the activity of the mind among those who are non-percipient.
And that is merely the non-occurrence of the mind and mental factors—this is the completion of the sentence.
The intention is that it is designated as "the state of non-perception" (*āsaṃjñika*), but it does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
(II.46ab) "That which [arises] from heat," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
The activity of heat and consciousness is dependent upon vitality.
Therefore, vitality is said to be the support of heat and consciousness, as it is their cause of persistence.
[Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of their being eternally unceasing.]
Their stream would then follow continuously.
Regarding the "projection of the duration of the stay of the homogeneous class" (*nikāyasabhāga*):
the homogeneous class has already been explained.

Those very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have thus come to be are, by their very nature, the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Their "duration" (*sthiti*) is their continuity (*prabandha*). The "time" of that duration is for as long as they must remain by means of it.
Those very same [moments] are the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) for that duration.
Their "impetus" (*āvedha*) is the establishment of the state of being a cause for the karma of a previous birth at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*).
But what, then, is that cause?
It is a specific capacity (*sāmarthyaviśeṣa*).
For it is the cause of the continuity characterized by the series of moments of the aggregates (*skandhaprabandha*);
for this very reason, it is called the "projection of the duration of existence" (*sthitikālāvedha*).
For that long, because it is characterized by the projection of a continuous stream; "for that long he remains" refers to that homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
It is like the impregnation of the time of ripening for crops.

Just as the impregnation of the time of ripening for crops—which is a specific capacity inherent in the seed—is imparted to the sprout itself, and which, through a succession of moments, becomes the cause of the continuum of the crop until the time of ripening;
so too is this case.
And it is like the duration and range of a discharged arrow.
Just as the "abiding" (*sthiti*) of a discharged arrow— that is, its arising in successive points of space and the continuity of that series—
has a specific time limit (*kāla*), which is its boundary beyond which it does not occur.
Its penetration is the establishment of the cause.
What, then, is this cause? It is a specific capacity produced by the element of wind, which is brought about by an excellence resulting from effort.

For example, just as the momentum (*āvedha*) that determines the duration of flight of a discharged arrow is not a separate substance, so too should this momentum characterized as life-span (*āyus*) be understood.
As for the one who thinks thus— it is the Vaiśeṣika—
who maintains that what is called "disposition" (*saṃskāra*) is a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*).

The specific quality (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*) of earth and the other elements called "impulse" (*saṃskāra*), which is born of action and has action as its cause—also known by the second name "velocity" (*vega*)—arises in an arrow.
By the power of which, that is, by the power of this quality, the arrow continues its motion until it falls.
With respect to that, this [argument of yours] lacks an illustrative example (*adṛṣṭānta*).
"Just as that which is called 'conditioning force' (*saṃskāra*) is a distinct entity (*bhāvāntara*),
so too would life-force (*āyus*) be. With this, the Master refutes that view.
"Of that," and so forth. Of that Vaiśeṣika, because of the oneness of that— that is, the oneness of the conditioned force (*saṃskāra*)—
and because of the absence of obstruction— that is, the absence of an obstruction characterized by the striking against wood and so forth.
What [is the point]?
It is that there would be no possibility of differences in the time of arrival—whether faster, faster still, or fastest—between different locations.
"Faster, faster still, or fastest arrival" (śīghrataratamaprāpti) refers to an arrival that is fast, faster, or fastest.
With what?
With other locations, such as the spatial regions of the ether and so forth.
Its time [is as follows].
Its differentiation;
its impossibility:
a reaching of various locations with speeds that are swift, swifter, and swiftest is not possible.
Furthermore, due to these two previously mentioned reasons, because the formative force (*saṃskāra*) remains undifferentiated, the occurrence of falling is untenable.
Indeed, as long as the formative force exists, the falling of the arrow is not possible;
for it is not accepted that an effect should fail to occur when its cause is present.

If it is argued that there is an obstruction by air—that is, if it is thought that air here acts as an obstruction, and that due to specific obstructions there arises a difference in the duration of reaching [the ground] with varying degrees of speed, and that falling is thus explained—[we reply]: no, because of the statement that "action ceases due to conjunction with a substance possessing touch.

To this it is said: the consequence would be that the arrow falls prematurely; immediately after the disjunction from the bowstring, or even before reaching its destination, the arrow would fall due to conjunction with air.
The meaning is that even if obstructed by the wind, it would not fall toward the front, nor would it ever fall, nor would it fall behind.
For what reason?
Because there is no distinction in the wind.
For just as there is wind nearby, so too is there wind at a distance.
The fourth [cause] is by way of not avoiding what is irregular; that is, by not avoiding irregularities such as overeating and the like.
When the lifespan has been exhausted, the exhaustion of merit lacks the capacity to cause death;
therefore, the third alternative is not applicable.
Consequently, when both are exhausted, death occurs due to the exhaustion of both.

The meaning of "when both have perished" is to be understood as the meaning expressed by the phrase "from the destruction of both. How is it known that death can also occur from the exhaustion of the life-force (*āyus*)?
This is because of their similarity to crops and the like.

For in the case of crops and such things, when the continuity of the seed has been exhausted, even though other conditions such as the field and water are present, the cessation of the series is observed before reaching the time of fruition or the time of ripening,
due to the lack of sufficient potency in the seed.
Moreover, even when there is the projection of a potent seed (*sārabīja*), the cessation of the continuum is observed due to the absence of conditions for its persistence and growth, such as water.
It is also observed [that the continuum ceases] even when there is no projection of a potent seed, nor conditions for its persistence and growth;
that is, when the projection of the seed has come to an end and there is an absence of water.

Moreover, even when the projection of the seed of essence (*sārabīja*) exists and the conditions for its maintenance and growth—such as water and so forth—are present, the cessation of the continuum of crops and the like is observed to be caused by the intervention of mobile beings and other factors.
This is because the impairment [of the crop] occurs through the impairment of its support, since it is dependent upon that continuum.
This is the opinion of the Bahirdeśikas.
Since that life-force (*āyus*) is bound to the continuum of the basis (*āśraya-saṃtati*), it is said to be "bound to the continuum" (*saṃtaty-upanibaddha*).
Even in the view of the Kaśmīris, the meaning is the same;
only the terminology differs.
"With interruption" (*sāntarāya*) means "without interruption" (*nirantarāya*).

Alternatively, "bound to a continuity" (*saṃtatyupanibaddha*) means bound to its own continuity; it exists only as something occurring within a continuum, and does not remain having arisen all at once.
By this scriptural passage, he says, demonstrating that untimely death exists.
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "There are four ways of acquiring a personal existence," and so forth.
Self-intention is killing by oneself;
other-intention is killing by another.
And it should be stated: "Of the Buddhas.
What [is meant]?
Only their own volition proceeds.
Because they are subject to death by their own volition.
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess the nature of not being subject to external assault, and they have attained mastery over the relinquishment of their lifespan.
The inclusion of the word "mostly" (prāyeṇa) is for the purpose of excluding those mentioned in the fourth category, such as hell-beings and those in the intermediate state.
The royal sages (*rājarṣi*) are those who previously were universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and have gone forth into homelessness.

As for the "messenger of the Victor" (*jinadūta*), this refers to anyone dispatched as a messenger by the Blessed Buddha; for example, a certain parrot sent by the Blessed One to Āmrapālī, who was seen by the Licchavis while they were practicing their arts, and even though they covered him with a net of arrows, they were unable to kill him.
For as long as he does not perform the function of a messenger, neither his own volition nor the volition of another takes effect.
This applies to one who has been instructed by the Victor—meaning one who has been designated by the Blessed One [with the words], "He must live for this long.
Dharmila and others are to be understood through the accounts of those who know the previous lives (pūrvayoga).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), others are also to be understood from that very source.
For them, neither self-intention (*ātmasaṃcetanā*) nor the intention of another (*parasaṃcetanā*) operates.
This also applies to those in their final existence (*caramabhavika*) who attain arhatship in that very same life.

Regarding the mother of a Bodhisattva who bears him as her embryo—that is, one who has a Bodhisattva as her embryo—and the mother of a Cakravartin who bears him as her embryo, there is neither self-intention nor intention by another.

If, then, for all those belonging to the realms of form and formlessness there is neither self-intention nor intention by another, why then was it said in the Sūtra, "and so forth"? [This is the full passage.]
And in that case, neither of the two exists.

There, in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there is no noble path belonging to its own level, because of the statement: "As long as there is the attainment of perception, so long is there the penetration of full knowledge.
Nor is there a preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of a higher level, because there is no level above it.
The noble path belonging to another stage refers here to that which belongs to the stage of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Through the manifestation of the noble [path] of nothingness, however, there is the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because of this statement.
"In that case, because of the inclusion of the limit" (paryaṃtagrahaṇāt tarhi):
here, *tarhi* is a particle used when one intends to express a different meaning.
Regarding the phrase "the comprehension of that as the beginning":
the beginning of that limit—the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)—consists of the four dhyānas and the remaining three formless attainments (ārūpyas).
However, the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is not its beginning, because it is dissimilar due to being non-concentrated (asamāhita).
Alternatively, from the perspective of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*) alone constitute that beginning,
because of the statement "the nine successive attainments.
In this context, "confidence in that beginning" means confidence regarding that initial point.
He says that this is seen elsewhere as well.
"In some places" means from the beginning to the end, and so forth; for example, "the gods of the Brahma-body.
By including the gods of the Brahma-body, the Brahmapurohitas and the Mahābrahmās are also included; thus, the first [level of] rebirth in happiness is established.
For example, the Ābhāsvara gods.
Because they include the Ābhāsvaras as their starting point, the Parīttābhas and Apramāṇābhas constitute the second "rebirth in happiness.
Indeed, only three such rebirths in happiness are accepted.
Because it is said that there are three types of rebirths in happiness, consisting of nine levels within the three dhyānas;
for this is the nature of the illustrative example.
This is the practice regarding examples: when even a single instance of that kind is pointed out, it serves as an indicator for all remaining cases.
For example, in the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar," [the term "like a jar"] includes cloth and other such things as well.
Because the word "tadyathā" (for example) denotes an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*),
[the statement] "this is not a conclusion" means that it is without an illustration (*adṛṣṭānta*).
"Human beings and some gods.

Some gods refers to the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and the gods born in the first dhyāna, excluding those who were first produced [at the beginning of the aeon]. Thus, these alone are the sentient beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions;
there are none other than these. Therefore, this word "tadyathā" (for example) is not used here to express an illustration.
Therefore, this [statement] should be understood as being solely for the purpose of illustration.
And since it serves the purpose of illustration, that very point remains established:
"By the mention of the end, there is the comprehension of the beginning."
(II.46cd) "The unconditioned [is] by way of the opposite.
That wherein these do not exist is the unconditioned.

But is it not the case that stability (*sthiti*) exists as a characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? [We reply: There is no stability of the unconditioned that exists as a distinct entity (*dravyāntara*).
And since, in this context, the characteristics of the conditioned are intended to be entities that exist as distinct substances, this objection is not valid.
But is it not the case that "these three," and so forth?
How so?
In the Sūtra it says: "O monks, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned."
Which three?
Monks, for the conditioned, arising is discerned; passing away is also discerned.
"Also the alteration of duration (*sthityanyathātva*).
The Vaibhāṣikas [hold] that a fourth [characteristic] should also be mentioned here. The interlocutor asks: "What is it that has not been stated here?"

"The Vaibhāṣikas say it is duration (sthiti). If that is so, then since this term 'duration' is heard here in the phrase 'the alteration of duration' (sthity-anyathātva), how can it be said that duration is not mentioned?"— such is the intention of the objector.
This is a synonym for aging (*jarā*).
This aging has been described as "the alteration of duration" (*sthity-anyathātva*).
It is just as "arising" (*utpāda*) is a synonym for birth (*jāti*).
And the passing away is the characteristic of impermanence (*anityatā*).
Likewise, the alteration of duration (*sthityanyathātva*) is a synonym for aging (*jarā*).
But why, when there are four characteristics, did the Blessed One speak of only three?
Therefore he says:
"For those phenomena," and so forth.
The characteristics of phenomena—namely birth, aging, and impermanence—have been stated for the purpose of causing those to be trained to feel revulsion.
For the exposition in the Sūtra is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), not definitive (*lākṣaṇika*) as is the case in the Abhidharma.
Furthermore, regarding aging and impermanence [passing] from the present to the past—
the term "transfers" (*saṃcārayati*) continues to apply by way of context.
Old age and impermanence cause [the conditioned factors] to transition from the present time-period to the past time-period.
Why?
Because they weaken them and destroy them.
Aging weakens;
impermanence destroys—so it is said.
But is it not impermanence itself that causes a phenomenon to transition from the present time-period to the past time-period?
It is not old age.
For old age merely weakens the constituent elements (dharma).
Why, then, is it said thus?
Regarding the statement that "aging and impermanence cause [the dharma] to transition from the present to the past," it is said:
even the act of weakening serves precisely for the purpose of that transition between time-periods (*adhvan*).
For there is no movement through the paths for that which has not been weakened; thus, even aging is established as being involved in that movement.
Furthermore, because even the unconditioned exists as the persistence of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is "abiding" (*sthiti*) within its own characteristic.
Existence [is established] by way of duration. Therefore, because existence is due to duration,
that duration is not established as a conditioned characteristic.

The intention of the Blessed One, the Lord of Dharma, is that since duration (sthiti) is similar to the duration characterized by the specific state of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), he did not state a [separate] characteristic for that unconditioned entity, wishing thereby to avoid the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of it being conditioned (saṃskṛta). Others, however, imagine [otherwise].
They say that "stability" (sthiti) is also mentioned in the Sūtra.
By combining stability and aging, and by combining stability and the alteration of stability (sthity-anyathātva), a single characteristic is stated in the Sūtra;
it is not taught as separate items.
Why?
Because it would entail a contradiction with the statement that "these three are the characteristics of the conditioned.
To the question, "What is the purpose [of this discussion] here?", he says:
"For this is the basis of attachment among these," and so forth.

For this "stability" (sthiti) among these [factors] such as birth is the locus of attachment, the place of clinging; the intention is that it is a dharma by which [a thing] stands. The Blessed One showed this stability—like prosperity accompanied by misfortune, or like good fortune accompanied by ill-fortune—in order that there might be non-attachment toward that stability.
"One should not form an attachment to her, because she is bound by impermanence, like prosperity that is actually misfortune"—this is one interpretation.
Others, however, explain:
"One should not be attached to her, because she is bound by old age, like prosperity that is actually misfortune."
For it is through aging, characterized by alteration, that this [conditioned thing] is unified with impermanence, and not by impermanence alone.
Therefore, there are exactly four characteristics of the conditioned.
This is the conclusion for both positions.
(II.47ab) "There must be other [factors] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth.
By the power of birth, a certain conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) is born;
yet birth itself is also conditioned.
Therefore, that [birth] must also have another birth, because it is contradictory for something to operate upon itself,
and because of the established tenet that "everything [possesses] the characteristics of the conditioned."
In the same way, aging and the other [factors] are also to be applied.
Among them, there are birth-of-birth and so forth.
Thus [it is said].
And regarding the phrase "and birth-of-birth and so forth for them," the word "and" (ca) should be understood as being elided.
Now, as for the detailed explanation beginning with "of each one," etc.:
For each individual characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), there would result a "four-characteristic set" (*catur-lakṣaṇī*), which is a collection of four characteristics.
Furthermore, there would be the fault of infinite regress (*aparyavasāna-doṣa*) and the fault of non-termination (*aniṣṭhā-doṣa*),
because those secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) would again entail the occurrence of further birth and so forth.

Because of the consequence that for every arising, for every arising-of-arising, and so on up to cessation, for impermanence, and for the impermanence-of-impermanence [a further secondary characteristic would be required],
these [characteristics] function with respect to eight factors (*dharma*). The use of the masculine gender in the word "they" (*te*) is due to its connection with the word "factors" (*dharmāḥ*).

Those phenomena (*dharma*) whose intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) consist of birth (*jāti*) and so forth, as well as the birth of birth (*jātijāti*) and so forth, function respectively with respect to eight phenomena and one phenomenon.
The functioning of birth and the others occurs with respect to the eight phenomena; the functioning of the birth of birth and the others occurs with respect to a single phenomenon.
The phrase "with self as the ninth" is stated with reference to the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa).
For it is not the case that, according to possibility, the primary elements (bhūta) or derived matter (bhautika), such as acquisition (prāpti) and so forth, do not arise therein.
In the desire realm, [the atom] consists of eight substances when it is without sound.

Because of such statements as, "Everything [is associated] with the characteristics of the conditioned (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa) or with acquisition (prāpti)," and so forth. The detailed explanation begins: "Birth (jāti), excluding itself... and so on.
Because there is a contradiction in [a factor] acting upon itself, it therefore produces eight factors, excluding itself.
Which eight?

It produces that factor—whether it be matter (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*)—as well as its duration (*sthiti*), aging (*jarā*), impermanence (*anityatā*), birth-of-birth (*jātijāti*), duration-of-duration (*sthitisthiti*), aging-of-aging (*jarājarā*), and impermanence-of-impermanence (*anityatānityatā*).
The "birth of birth," however, produces that very same birth.
In the same way, "aging" and "impermanence" should also be applied accordingly.
Aging, excluding itself, causes eight factors to age.
Furthermore, the decay of decay [destroys] that very decay. Impermanence, having separated itself from its own self, destroys eight factors.
Furthermore, the impermanence of impermanence [destroys] that very impermanence.
"This space is being split" means that it is being divided;
space is merely the absence of any resistant substance.
There is no such thing as space;
it cannot be divided, nor is it logical to do so.
In the same way, these non-existent phenomena, such as birth and the rest, cannot be divided, nor is it logical to do so.
Then he says:
"For these do not exist," and so forth.
For these do not exist as substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*) with their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇataḥ*) in the manner in which they are analyzed.
Birth produces eight factors excluding itself; thus they are analyzed in detail, just as in the case of the factors such as form (*rūpa*).
Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), sound and so forth, feeling and so forth, and the eye and so forth are included.

Among these, form, sound, and the rest are first apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized by visual consciousness and the others.
Feeling and the other [mental factors] are also perceived by direct perception (pratyakṣa) because they are self-cognizable (svasaṃvedya).
The eye and the other [faculties], however, are inferred through inference (anumāna) by means of visual consciousness and the others;

for the eye and the rest are the translucent matter (rūpaprasāda) that serves as the support for visual consciousness and so forth, since their presence or absence corresponds to the presence or absence of those [consciousnesses].
Scripture also states: "Having seen forms with the eye," and so forth;
likewise, "having heard sounds with the ear," and so forth in detail; this should be applied similarly to odors and the other objects.
Likewise: "Whatever form there is—past, future, or present," and so forth in detail.

The same should be applied to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] as well. However, the existence of immaterial mental factors such as feeling belonging to another continuum is inferred from the body's transformations, just as one infers [the existence of] one's own [feelings] by observing the changes in one's own body; for one recognizes them through that [observation]. There is also scriptural authority (*āgama*): "Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; simultaneously with it, there arise feeling, perception, and volition," and so forth.
However, birth and the other [characteristics] are not perceived by the sense faculties such as the eye,
nor is there any inference capable of establishing their existence, nor is there any scripture regarding their substantial existence.
As for what was stated in the Sūtra, and so forth:
"Is it not the case that there is this scriptural authority [āgama], which says in detail: 'The arising of the conditioned is also discerned'?
And it has been said by the Blessed One that "the meaning is the refuge."
Monks, there are these four reliances.
What are the four?
The Dharma is the reliance, not the person.
The meaning is the reliance, not the letter; a sūtra of definitive meaning is the reliance,
not one of interpretable meaning.
"Reliance is on knowledge, not on consciousness.
Likewise, one relies on the meaning,
not on the letter.
"What, then, is the meaning of this?
refers to the Sūtra on the Characteristics of the Conditioned (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇasūtra) that has been presented.
He states that meaning:
"For fools are blinded by ignorance," and so forth.
The meaning is that they are attached to the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-prabandha*), being convinced of it as "self" and "belonging to self" and having developed a taste for it.
"Conditionedness" (*saṃskṛtatva*) and "being dependently originated" (*pratītyasamutpannatva*) are synonyms.
That which is produced by conditions having come together and combined is "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
That which has arisen in dependence upon each respective condition is "dependently originated" (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
However, this does not refer to a single moment.
Desiring to illustrate that it is the continuum (*pravāha*) itself that possesses the nature of being conditioned (*saṃskṛtatva*), he says this;
however, it is not the moment (*kṣaṇa*) that possesses the nature of being conditioned.

For the characteristics of arising and so forth—namely, the phenomena characterized by arising, passing away, duration, and alteration—are not perceived in a single moment, because a moment is difficult to discern.
You might say that even if these [characteristics] are not being perceived, they ought to be characteristics; therefore, he says:
"And these, while not being perceived, cannot be characteristics.
For only that which is actually perceived becomes a characteristic.
"Just as [one knows] the presence of water by a crane.
For this very reason, it is said here:
"for this very reason, the word 'is known' (*prajñāyate*) is included in this sutra."
Otherwise, he would have said simply that "the conditioned has arising, passing away, and also the alteration of its duration.

[The term] "characteristics of the conditioned" means "characteristics belonging to that which is conditioned"; the word "conditioned" is repeated in order to ensure the correct apprehension of this meaning.
"Like a crane in water.
This is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): just as a crane is a sign for the existence of water, but it is not a sign for the "waterness" of the water.
Let it not be understood in that way.
What [is the point]?
These characteristics exist for the sake of establishing the existence of a conditioned entity,
or its quality as good or bad, just like the characteristics of a maiden.

Just as the auspicious and inauspicious marks of a maiden are signs that indicate her good or bad fortune respectively, so too [these] would have to be signs indicating the existence, goodness, or badness of a conditioned entity if they were intended in that way.

For if these were held to be signs of the existence or of the goodness and badness of a conditioned thing, one would say simply "these three are the characteristics of the conditioned," and one would not say "the characteristics of the conditioned of the conditioned."
And it has been established. By this, it is known that these are the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
But how can birth (*jāti*) and the others, which do not exist [as separate entities], be established or recognized within the continuum (*pravāha*)?
We do not say that birth and the other [characteristics] do not exist; rather,
we say that they do not exist in the manner in which they are distinguished as having the nature of substantial entities (*dravya*).
"In that case, let it be explained how they exist according to your own view.
To this, he says:
The beginning of the continuum is "arising," and so forth;
cessation is "passing away.
The stopping of the continuum is passing away.
"That very stream continues" means that the stream which continues through the succession of similar moments is called "abiding."
Regarding the phrase "the distinction between the preceding and the succeeding":
it is the distinction of the succeeding moment from the preceding one;
or, the distinction between the preceding and succeeding moments is the "distinction between the preceding and succeeding."

And it was said "having done so" because this was stated with reference to the Venerable Sundarananda’s state of constant mindfulness regarding impermanence, having taken arising and the other [characteristics] as being of the nature of a continuum (*pravāha*).
For his feelings, belonging to that continuum, arise as if known, persist as if known, and reach their exhaustion and termination as if known; they do not belong to individual moments (*kṣaṇa*).
"Because a moment is difficult to discern," and "because it is impossible for a known moment to endure.
Stating this very point in two verses, he says:
Birth is the beginning of the stream;
thus everything has been stated.
But duration is that [stream itself].
Thus,
that very continuity is stability.
"Of that very [continuity]" means this.
Of that very stream. "Its cessation" means the cessation of the continuity.
Regarding the verse beginning "For a phenomenon that is momentary":
indeed, a phenomenon is momentary.
The meaning is that it would perish without stability.
If you think that stability exists, [then...]
And that phenomenon indeed ceases even while its duration exists; it necessarily perishes because of its momentariness,
since there is no cause for its destruction.
Therefore, the conceptualization of that [duration] is futile and purposeless; this is the meaning of "by means of the conceptualization of duration.
For the conceptualization of duration would not be futile if it consisted in the persistence of the second and subsequent moments.
Therefore, duration is nothing other than the stream itself;
for it would be futile to postulate a duration for a dharma that is momentary.
And this being the case, "this [dharma] as well" [is likewise].
The meaning is: "because stability is nothing other than the flow itself.
For there is no non-destruction of a moment that has already arisen.
In this regard, someone might have the following intention:
Because of the existence of duration (*sthiti*), there is the non-destruction for one moment of a dharma that has arisen. For if duration did not exist,
even that single moment would not exist.
No,
because its existence is preceded by causes and conditions,
according to the statement: "When this exists, that comes to be."
If it is argued that "stability (sthiti) sustains [the phenomenon]," this might be the thought: "Stability sustains the phenomenon as it arises from causes and conditions.
If stability did not sustain it, what would happen?
The existence of the phenomenon would not belong to itself.
In that case, duration (*sthiti*) would be a producer rather than a sustainer.
If it is argued that it sustains the continuum (*saṃtāna*), [we reply: no.
It would follow that the designation "abiding" applies to causes and conditions, because causes and conditions are the cause of the continuity [of the stream]. Thus,
it is logical that the mind belongs to the same class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Even though there are many moments of mind within a single homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), they are called "one" because they arise from the same homogeneous class; this is the intended meaning.
And it is appropriate to speak of that mind as being "in one mind."
Otherwise, how could birth, death, and change belong to a single moment of consciousness? Duration (*sthiti*) is the succession of subsequent moments;
the subsequent moment acts as a substitute for the preceding moment because of its similarity.
Therefore, because that preceding moment seems to persist even until now, the subsequent moment is called "duration" (*sthiti*).
But what about when similar [moments] arise?
That is, when similar [moments] arise.
In that case, there would be no dissimilarity;
yet dissimilarity has been described as "alteration of duration" (sthityanyathātva).
Therefore, the intention is that if only similar things were to arise, there would be no alteration of duration, and thus the definition [of conditioned phenomena] would be underinclusive.
"Thrown by one who is strong or weak, thrown by one who is weak"—this is the full expression.
That which is both thrown and not thrown is "thrown and not thrown.
That which is thrown by both the strong and the weak is "thrown by the strong and the weak."
"Thrown and not thrown" refers to that which is thrown by one who is strong or weak; thus, "thrown and not thrown by one who is strong or weak.
What is that? It is the vajra and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), iron, stones, and so forth are included.
Others, however, analyze the compound as follows:
"thrown" (kṣipta) and "not thrown" (akṣipta) constitute "the thrown and the not thrown" (kṣiptākṣiptau).
"Thrown by the strong and the weak" means thrown by those who are strong and those who are weak.
This is a twofold classification of what is simply "thrown.
[The compound] "thrown, not-thrown, thrown by the strong, and thrown by the weak" refers to that which is thrown, that which is not thrown, and that which is thrown by the strong and the weak.
"Vajrādi" means that which has a vajra, etc., as its beginning.
In this context, "vajra, etc. is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), while "thrown by one who is weak due to having thrown an offering" (*kṣiptākṣiptabalidurbalakṣipta*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*).
For such things as that thunderbolt and so forth, there is a falling that is either slow or rapid according to the circumstances:
when it is thrown, its fall is slow;
when it is not thrown, its fall is slower still.
When thrown with little force, there is a swift fall;
when thrown with great force, the fall is even swifter.
That is its duration.
The distinction of time is due to the difference in the duration of falling, whether it be long or quick. "Of those elements" refers to the great elements such as diamond and so forth.

A specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) is a different mode of transformation for that which has been thrown, by which its fall occurs after a long time. Likewise, up to the case of that which is thrown with great force, it is a different mode of transformation, by which its fall occurs more quickly.
This is the establishment of that specific transformation.
It has been established that because a specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) is achieved for that [series], they do not remain without distinction.
"Then [what of] the last one," and so forth;
this refers to the final moment of a sound or a flame from a lamp or the like, at the time when the continuum ceases.
Or, at the time of the nirvana without remainder of an Arhat, because there is no subsequent moment for those six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), there is no duration (*sthiti*).

Due to the absence of duration, there is no alteration of duration (*sthity-anyathātva*); thus, it follows that the establishment of the characteristics [of conditioned phenomena] is not all-pervasive (*avyāpinī*).
That which has been described as "alteration of duration" (sthityanyathātva) refers to the dissimilarity of that very [duration] which exists. For whatever has duration,
there necessarily occurs alteration.

It is said that for that which has no duration, there is no alteration of duration. For it was stated in the Sūtra with reference to the possibility [of these characteristics] that "these three are the characteristics of the conditioned."

Therefore, for the final moment of sound, the flame, and so forth, only production and destruction are intended as their two characteristics; however, for others besides those, there is also the characteristic of the alteration of duration (*sthity-anyathātva*).
Another teacher says:
Even for the final moments of sound, flames, and so forth, there is duration, which is their own abiding;
and there is change in that [duration] relative to the preceding moment.
Therefore, the three characteristics of the conditioned are established for them as well.
How can it be that the very same phenomenon (dharma) is both the characterized object (lakṣya) and its own characteristic (lakṣaṇa)?
Those who perceive a difference between the characterized object and its characteristic— like water and a crane— raise this objection.
Refuting that [position], the Sautrāntikas say:
"How then [can it be said] that these are the marks of a Great Man," and so forth.
The marks of a Great Man are not distinct from the Great Man himself, because they are comprised within the Great Man.

One might say: "A Great Person is not merely characterized by the marks of a Great Person; rather, it is merely a phenomenon (dharma) that comes into being after not having been, and ceases to be after having been. This, however, is without a supporting example.
To this, we reply:
This is exactly the same.

For just as the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa) are called "the Great Man" and are also called "the marks of a Great Man," so too a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛtadharma) is designated as "conditioned" and as a "characteristic of the conditioned" (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa).
For that phenomenon (dharma) is characterized by specific states such as arising and so forth;
and when a state characterized by a continuum (pravāha) is established, then the whole (samudāya) is characterized by its constituent parts (samudāyin).
Just as the collection designated as a "great person" [is defined] by its constituent parts, the marks of a great person;
by this, the marks such as the dewlap and so forth are explained,
as well as those such as hardness and so forth— this is the detailed explanation.
This example is established for both [parties], because it is established by the scriptural tradition (*pravacana*).
For the earth element is defined as solidity,
and there is no solidity other than the earth element.
This should be applied in all cases.
For that very same earth element, when characterized by hardness, is called the characteristic of hardness.

Likewise, this very conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*), when characterized by having not existed and then coming into being, and having existed and then ceasing to be, is called the characteristic of the conditioned.
It is called a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) because it is that by which something is characterized (*lakṣyate*).
And that [characteristic] is not other than that [thing characterized].
This is as explained in detail in the passage beginning with "by upward movement."

For the Vaibhāṣika who maintains the doctrine of momentariness, the upward movement of smoke is nothing other than the smoke itself. That very same smoke, arising continuously in successive locations above, receives the designation "upward movement.
Thus, that upward movement appears as if it were distinct from the smoke.
Furthermore, the upward movement of smoke is not held to be something other [than smoke];
nor is that [movement] different from it.
Nor is that upward movement different from that smoke.
The same principle applies here:
thus, arising, destruction, and alteration appear as if distinct from it;
yet, for that which is conditioned, there exists no other conditioned thing apart from it.

Furthermore, the conditioned nature of conditioned phenomena such as form and so forth is not perceived by one who grasps their intrinsic nature, nor even by one who grasps the intrinsic nature of form and so forth,
as long as their prior non-existence is not known—
that is, as long as the absence of those forms and so forth prior to their arising is not known.
And later:
what? Non-existence.

And as long as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) are not known, and as long as the distinction within the continuum (*saṃtati*) is not known— this being understood [as the context]—
therefore, that [continuum] is not characterized by itself.
Conditionedness is not characterized by that very same conditionedness.
What then? That conditionedness is characterized by prior non-existence and so forth.

For if, while grasping the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and the other [aggregates], one were to grasp them as "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*), then—without knowing their prior non-existence, their subsequent non-existence, and the distinction within the continuum—that [nature] would be characterized by that very [state].
But since one does not know it in this way, it is not characterized by that very [state].
Furthermore, birth and the other [characteristics] do not exist as separate substances (*dravyāntara*) distinct from those very things, such as form.
Because it is stated in detail that "birth is the beginning of the stream," and so forth.
Because these—birth and the other [characteristics]—are co-existent, meaning they arise at the same time;
[the opponent replies: "No, because there is a difference in the time of their activity."
This is not so.
Why?
Because of the difference in the time of their activity (kāritra).
The meaning is: "due to the difference in human effort and time.
Demonstrating this, he says:
"For birth performs its activity while still in the future," and so forth.
Does the future exist as a substantial entity (dravyataḥ) or not?
First, it will be demonstrated that the future itself does not exist as a substantial entity.
The intention [of the author] is: how could a future birth (jāti) perform its activity (kāritra)?
"But even though that exists," [it is said].
Even though birth (*jāti*) exists substantially in the future state, performing its activity (*kāritra*) while in that future condition, how is it established as "future"?
For the established tenet (*siddhānta*) is that what has not yet attained its activity is "future."
That would be contradictory. Therefore, it must be explained how the present [time] is established.
That which has its activity ceased is accepted as past;
and birth is indeed future.
For if that whose activity has ceased were considered past while still in its present state, it would follow that it could not be present; therefore, the definition of the present must be stated.
If it is argued that the present is that whose activity has not yet been completed, then even the past would be present;
for the activity of giving its fruit is admitted to belong to the past as well.
"For when it is thus, [there is] 'stability,' and so forth.
For the functions of stability, decay, and destruction are mutually contradictory.
Indeed, it is not logical to establish that the very same dharma both persists, decays, and perishes.
Its momentariness would be contradicted [if this were so].
First, stability establishes it;
then, decay causes it to decay.
Then impermanence destroys it,
because it persists for three moments;
thus its momentariness is contradicted.
"For this indeed is our 'moment' (kṣaṇa)" means that it is characterized by the completion of what is to be done, and not characterized by perishing immediately after arising.
"Even so," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
It is not logical for things that have arisen simultaneously to exercise their activity sequentially.
Why is this so?
First, duration causes [the thing] to endure.

But at that time, neither does old age cause it to decay, nor does impermanence cause it to perish. Again, by what is its weakness [at first], and later by what is its weakness, such that impermanence destroys this "stability" (sthiti) together with the dharma to which that stability belongs—that is, together with that very dharma?
By that dharma, impermanence destroys it.
"Having accomplished its task, it does not venture to act again, just like birth (*jāti*). Just as birth, having produced that which is to be born, has its power exhausted and does not produce again,
so too does duration (*sthiti*) likewise not establish [the object] again.
"For it is not possible," and so forth.
It is not possible to bring back again that which has already been brought to the state of being present, because that would entail the fallacy of infinite regress.
However, indeed, that which is to be established by duration can certainly be established for an extremely long time.
Because stability has the characteristic of being an obstruction to destruction; those two, namely aging and impermanence, are that very obstruction.
Those two—aging and impermanence—are the obstruction.
By means of which [aging], stability (sthiti) is unable to establish that which is to be established absolutely;
for aging weakens stability, and impermanence (anityatā) destroys what has been weakened. The Master says:
The word "if" applies to everything.
For if those two—aging and impermanence—were more powerful, they would have already occurred at the very time when the activity of abiding was taking place;
for that reason, that abiding is unable to perform its activity.
"When its function has ceased," and so forth.
When the [characteristic of] duration has ceased its function,
then those two— aging and impermanence— also do not remain.
And that [dharma] as well [does not abide].
For their abiding is postulated on the basis of the activity of abiding;
therefore, they too do not abide.
How can aging and impermanence, not remaining [in the same moment], exert their activity toward a substratum (*dharmin*) in which they do not abide?
Furthermore, what is there for those two—aging and impermanence—to accomplish?
For, by virtue of the power of stability (*sthiti*), that phenomenon (*dharma*), as soon as it arose, did not perish.
Since it is being neglected by that state of persistence whose activity has ceased, and is not being maintained, it will certainly not persist;
this very non-persistence is its destruction.
The intention [of the opponent] is: "What, then, is the function of aging and impermanence?"
And it is not logical for that very same thing to have another mode of being.
If it is that very same thing, it cannot be otherwise;
if it is otherwise, it cannot be that very same thing.

For it is observed that when there is a difference between two things, there is a difference between them, as in the case of Devadatta and Yajñadatta. As for the one who says "a member of another school," he refers to the Āryasaṃmatīya.
He considers that the destruction of a jar or similar object is caused by a hammer or such means, for its form persists over a period of time;
however, the mind and mental factors are momentary. Therefore, it is said:

Furthermore, since it is accepted that mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are momentary, their impermanence— due to the fact that they do not depend on a cause for destruction and are inherently perishable— would mean that the characteristics of duration (*sthiti*) and impermanence (*anityatā*) would exercise their functions simultaneously.
Consequently, it would follow that a single mind or mental factor is both simultaneously enduring and destroyed, which is a contradiction in terms.
Thus, this sūtra is well-expounded:
"Monks, these three are the conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.
This is because [the effect] exists when there is a completeness of causes.
And because it does not exist when [the conditions] are absent.
That is to say, because the produced effect exists when there is a completeness of causes and conditions,
and because it does not exist when they are absent.
Not from the genus.
What?
"We perceive its capacity"—this is the subject under discussion.
For even when the totality of causes and conditions is present, that which is to be produced sometimes occurs and sometimes does not.
Regarding this, the Venerable Anantavarman says:
"Just as the eye does not produce visual consciousness without light and the other [conditions]."
Nor is it the case that, because [the phenomenon] arises from that, [birth] is not the cause.
Thus, birth does not produce a phenomenon without causes and conditions;
nor is it the case that, because [the phenomenon] arises from that, [birth] is not the cause.
To this it is replied:
This is not the same.

For the visual faculty has a perceived efficacy, since we observe that visual consciousness does and does not arise in the blind and the non-blind respectively, even when light and other conditions are present.
"But birth is not like this.
For even the intrinsic natures (*prakṛti*) of phenomena are subtle;
that is to say, the intrinsic natures or essential characters of mental factors such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth are subtle because they are difficult to discern.
This is indeed so.
Although some phenomena are not perceived, they are determined by their activity;
however, birth is not determined by its activity in this manner.
For the activity of contact has been definitively established by the Blessed One himself:
