"Whatever constitutes the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, or the aggregate of mental formations—
all that is dependent upon contact," and so forth in detail.
But the thought "it has arisen" would not occur if "arising" did not exist.
The cognition of form with respect to form depends upon its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
however, the cognition that "it has arisen" does not depend upon its specific characteristic.
Because [the cognition of "born"] occurs even with respect to sensation and so forth,
it is determined that this cognition of being born depends upon a substance (dravya) consisting of a genus (jāti) that is a distinct entity.
Furthermore, there would be no use for the genitive case, as in the expression "the arising of form" (rūpasyotpāda).
For the use of the genitive case occurs when there is a difference of substratum (vaiyadhikaraṇya), not when there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
Therefore he says:
"just as 'the form of form'."
This is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Just as, considering that form is not other than form, the use of the genitive case does not occur— such as "the form of form"—
likewise, [if they were identical], there would not be such an expression as "the arising of form."
Therefore, it is understood that this use of the genitive case is based on the cause of birth (*jāti*).
In this manner, [the same] should be stated for everything up to impermanence (*anityatā*), as appropriate.
However, stability itself would not exist if stability were non-existent.
And there would be a genitive expression, "the stability of form," just as one says "the form of form.
However, without aging, there could not even be the expression "it has aged.
And there would be a genitive expression, "the aging of form," just as one says "the form of form."
Likewise, there could not be the very notion "it has perished" if impermanence were non-existent.
Furthermore, there would be no use for the genitive case in the expression "the destruction of form," just as one does not say "the form of form.
Therefore, [the argument] beginning with "In that case... and so forth [is stated].

If universals (*jāti*) and so forth are postulated for the sake of establishing cognitions such as "it has been born" and for the purpose of prescribing the genitive case, then "selflessness" (*anātmatva*) must also be accepted.
For a cognition of selflessness cannot occur without a basis.
Now, if selflessness is held to be a mere conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*), [then the same applies].
The cognition of selflessness has that as its objective cause.
Furthermore, birth and so forth must be accepted as being existent only as designations;
and the cognition of birth and so forth likewise has those as its objective cause.
And the proof for this is as follows:
birth and so forth exist as designations (prajñaptisat),
because they are apprehended in dependence upon that which exists substantially (dravyasat).
"Like non-selfhood. "Existence and so forth" (sattādayaḥ): by the word "and so forth" (ādi), substance-ness, form-ness, pot-ness, and so on are included.
"One form," "two forms," "large," "small," "separate," "conjoined," "divided," "distant," "near," and "existent form"—
for the sake of establishing such cognitions as "this is a substance," "this is form," or "this is a jar," one must also accept number and the other categories imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas.
Furthermore, for the purpose of establishing the use of the genitive case, one must accept [the category of] "conjunction" in the sense of "the conjunction of form."
The mention of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is merely an illustration;
[terms] such as "the disjunction of form" (*rūpasya vibhāgaḥ*) and "priority and posteriority" (*paratvāparatvam*) should also be applied accordingly.
Furthermore, how is this genitive case to be understood in the expression "the intrinsic nature of form" (*rūpasya svabhāvaḥ*)?
For the Vaibhāṣikas do not accept that the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of form is anything other than form itself.
The designation "born" is employed for the purpose of making known the state of having come into being after not having existed— that is, it has been born and has not yet perished.
"Having many conceptual distinctions" means having many varieties due to the distinctions of form, sensation, and so forth.
To specify that [production], they employ the genitive case in the phrase "the production of form," rather than "the production of sensation and so forth," for the purpose of such specification.
It is held that only arising designated as "form" (rūpa) is perceived, and not that designated as "feeling" (vedanā) and so forth.
To illustrate this, they cite the examples:
"the fragrance and other qualities of sandalwood," and "the body of a stone statue."
Even when there is no difference in meaning, the use of the genitive case is employed.
For the Buddhist tenet is that "sandalwood" is merely a collection of odor and so forth;
however, with respect to the Vaiśeṣika tenet, since "sandalwood" is not established [as a distinct entity], another example is presented.
Regarding the expression "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*):
even according to the tenets of the Vaiśeṣikas, there is no state of being a separate entity between the stone statue and its body, and yet the genitive case is employed.
Indeed, such a designation is made by those who postulate a distinct entity.
In the same way, stability (*sthiti*) and the other [characteristics] are also to be understood according to their respective applications.

Therefore, this is merely a designation (*prajñaptimātra*) made for the purpose of making known the state of continuity; it is designated as "stable" (*sthitam*). And that stability, characterized by the state of continuity, possesses many conceptual variations.
To specify that [duration], they employ the genitive case, saying "the duration of form" (*rūpasya sthitiḥ*),
so that it may be understood as the duration belonging specifically to what is designated as "form," and not some other [duration].
Likewise, this [term] "decayed" (*jīrṇam*) is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti-mātra*) made for the purpose of making known the distinction between its prior and subsequent states.
And that aging, characterized by the distinction between earlier and later states, has many varieties.
To specify it, they employ the genitive case in the expression "aging of form" (*rūpasya jarā*),
so that aging may be understood as belonging specifically to what is designated "form," and not something else.
Likewise, this [expression] "it is destroyed" is merely a conventional designation (prajñapti-mātra) made for the purpose of making known the cessation of the continuum.
And that destruction, characterized by the cessation of the continuum, has many conceptual variations.
For the sake of specifying it, they employ the genitive case, saying "the destruction of form."
In this way, destruction would be understood as being nothing other than that which is designated as "form," so that no other [entity] is perceived.
Furthermore, in every case, two examples must be stated, such as:
"the fragrance and so forth of sandalwood" and "the body of a stone statue."

"And as by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)" means that *dharmatā* is the nature of phenomena (*dharmaprakṛti*), the intrinsic being of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva*), or the characteristic mode of phenomena (*dharma-śailī*).
Why is it said that *dharmatā* is the nature of phenomena?
The eye, though perfected, is empty of a self or anything belonging to a self that is permanent, stable, eternal, and subject to no change.
Why is that? Because such is its very nature.

And just as, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), not everything is held to possess birth— such as space and so forth— likewise, by the very nature of things, it must be accepted that not everything is born;
for there is no reason whatsoever [to claim otherwise] in this matter.
That which possesses birth is necessarily conditioned, not unconditioned— this being apart from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Thus, even though birth does not exist [as a separate entity], that which is conditioned alone arises,
not that which is unconditioned.

And just as, among certain things such as form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*) that possess a common genus, the conditions for those are distinct—meaning the conditions for the arising of form are other than the conditions for the arising of sensation and so forth—those distinct conditions are not capable of producing what is distinct from them; that is, they produce something other than those sensations and so forth.
Thus, "other than those" means other than those sensations and so forth.
What is that? It is form;
it belongs to him.

Just as those conditions, such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, are not capable of producing anything other than that [sensation], so too all conditions for form, sensation, and so forth would be incapable of producing unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) such as space (*ākāśa*).
Previously this was stated by way of the restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-niyama*); now it is stated by way of the restriction of capacity (*śakti-niyama*).
"For it is not the case that because there are critics...
and so forth. Just as barley is not left unsown simply because there are wild animals [to eat it]—the meaning being that it is indeed sown—two negations convey the original sense.
Just as sweetmeats are not eaten because flies have landed on them;
rather,
they are indeed eaten.
Likewise, on the grounds that there are no critics, the scriptural tradition of the Abhidharma treatises is being discarded.
Therefore, one must respond to these faults;
when faults are posited by others, a refutation must be provided.
The intention is that the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) must be followed and not abandoned.
(II.48ab) The sets of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are collections of designations, sentences, and syllables.
The collections of designations are the sets of names (*nāmakāya*).
The collections of sentences are the sets of phrases (*padakāya*). The collections of syllables are the sets of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*).
"Designation" (*saṃjñākaraṇa*) is a worldly expression;
"designation" and "name" (*nāmadheya*) are synonyms.
For thus do people speak in the world.

"The making of the designation 'Devadatta'": the making of a designation is "designation-making" (*saṃjñākaraṇa*). That by which a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) called a designation is made—that is, produced—is [what is meant].
Alternatively, "designation" (*saṃjñā*) itself is the instrument, hence "the instrument of designation.
The mention of "designation" is for the purpose of excluding other instruments,
and the mention of "instrument" is for the purpose of qualifying it as a mental factor (*caitasika*).
For if it were said that "name" (*nāman*) is "perception" (*saṃjñā*), then it might be considered a mental factor (*caitasika*).
However, that which is called "making a name" (*saṃjñākaraṇa*) consists of such things as visible form, sound, taste, and odor.
A "sentence" (*vākya*) is a "phrase" (*pada*).
That by which one goes or is understood is a *pada*. Here, however, the term *pada* is taken to mean a word ending in a nominal suffix (*su*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).
Therefore, he says:
As far as the completion of the meaning is concerned, it is as follows:
"Alas, conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and so forth.
By the word "etcetera," it is meant that those things characterized by arising and passing away,
having arisen, indeed cease.
"Their subsiding is happiness," and so forth.
They explain the meaning of this verse in this way.
"Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena"— this is the thesis; they are subject to the nature of arising and passing away.
This is the reason:
because they possess the nature of arising and ceasing, they are determined to be impermanent;
for having arisen, they indeed cease.
This is the illustration:
those things which arise and cease are impermanent,
just like pots and so forth.
And likewise regarding "the formative forces" (*saṃskārāḥ*).
Others, however, explain this as being for the purpose of establishing an unproven reason (*asiddhahetu*).
How is this understood?
That they possess the nature of arising and passing away, because these are seen to arise and then cease.
Others explain it thus:
"Alas, conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are subject to arising and passing away"—these two are stated as synonyms.
He asks "Why? and says: because, having arisen, they cease.
This is the statement of the reason: their subsiding is happiness; for those things which are impermanent are suffering. Therefore...
He directs those to be trained toward the thought, "The subsiding of these is happiness," by means of which the specific distinctions of action, quality, time, and relation are understood.
Those who know the nature of sentences say that a sentence consists of an indeclinable, a noun-case, and an adjective.

For example: "he cooks," "he reads," "he goes"; or "black," "fair," "red"; or "he cooks," "he will cook," "he cooked. Through these, the specific relations between action, quality, and time are understood. That is a word (*pada*).
For they say that the "sentence-meaning" (vākyārtha) is the settling of words, which generally abide in universals, upon a particular.

Thus, it is stated that a *nāman* (name) is that which illuminates the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while a *pada* (word) is that which illuminates the specific relation [of that name] with action and so forth.
A *vyañjana* (phoneme) means a syllable (*akṣara*), which is to say, a letter (*varṇa*).
But it is not only the consonants; the vowels are also intended as producers of phonemes (*vyañjana*).
[Objection: But are not the syllables also the names for the components of writing?
Scripts are those written by humans and others upon leaves and other materials;
their syllables are their names.
Just as there is a cognition of form when the name of a form is grasped, there is a cognition of the script when the syllables are grasped.
Therefore, since a phoneme (*vyañjana*) would also be the name of the components of a script, there is a confusion of definitions.
Consequently, that which was intended— that a phoneme (*akṣara*) is something entirely distinct from a name—
is not tenable.
"It is certainly not [the case] that [the cognition of writing arises] from the parts of the letters," and so forth;
he explains that this is the opposite [of the truth].
As for the claim that "there is a cognition of writing upon the apprehension of the phonemes."
This is because they are conventionally established as having the relationship of signifier and signified, and not because of the existence of that name itself.
Regarding the term *samukti*: from the verbal root *uca*, meaning "to assemble" (*samavāya*), the form *samukti* arises by adding the suffix *ktin*.
That which is the meaning of "inherence" (samavāya) is the meaning of "aggregation" (samukti); "inherence" is the meaning.
"Now, as for 'those [sounds]'—this is the statement of the Sautrāntikas.
'These are not of the nature of speech,' and so forth—this is the statement of the Vaibhāṣikas.
And it is not by mere sound alone."
The meaning is not understood by means of a sound consisting of phonemes.
What then?
Speech operates upon the name.
That [name], as it were, brings about the state of being the very form of the self for speech, and thereby manifests the status of being an object.
Taking up that speech, it manifests the meaning of the word; the sense is that it causes [the meaning] to be understood.
The Sautrāntika says:
"Speech is certainly not mere sound," and so forth.
We do not describe speech as being merely sound.
Speech, however, is simply a certain sound consisting of phonemes;
it is that which has established its limits and fixed its boundaries with respect to objects of meaning.
By this, he demonstrates that a word conveys its meaning by depending upon convention (*saṃketa*),
and not just any word whatsoever;
rather, it is a word for which a convention has been established that conveys the meaning.
And this [illumination] is established from the mere word whose referent is already understood.
And this illumination of meaning is established from a word devoid of a name, which has a referent such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth; this is its meaning.
"If it produces," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
It is maintained that when speech is present, that [name] which is dissociated from thought arises; therefore, it is suspected:
"If it produces [the name], then everything consisting of sound—even the roaring of bulls and the like—will produce a name, since speech has the nature of sound.
If this were the case, even the bellowing of bulls and so forth would produce a name, because speech is defined as having the intrinsic nature of sound.
You might say: "The sound that consists of phonemes (varṇa) and is perceived is indeed distinguished;
it is that very thing which produces the name.
To this, it is replied:
Alternatively, whatever specific sound is intended to be the producer of a name, that very thing will be the illuminator of the object;
however, the intention is that it is not a factor dissociated from thought (*cittaviprayukta*).
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "it illuminates," and so forth:
that factor dissociated from mind arises simultaneously with the sound as it is produced.
If it is maintained that this [dissociated factor] illuminates that [sound] for the purpose of revealing its meaning, then [the following applies].
To this it is replied:
as before, one must state that everything will be manifested as a mere sound (*ghoṣamātra*).
Furthermore, there is indeed no such thing as a collection (*sāmagrya*) of sounds.
That which is a name consisting of multiple syllables involves a conceptual construction of its arising that depends upon multiple sounds; therefore,
it is investigated in this way.
In this world, sounds perish as soon as they are uttered;
therefore, there is no simultaneous existence of them.

Furthermore, it is not logical for a single entity that exists as a substantial reality (*dravyasat*) to arise in parts or fragments, as is imagined in the case of things that exist only nominally (*prajñaptisat*), such as jars or cloths. How, then, could they produce [the sound]?
Speech should produce the name.
When it produces that [name], how does it produce it? This is the meaning of the sentence.
For it is speech existing in the present that produces a name;
yet not all moments of vocal sound exist simultaneously in the present. For when the sound "ra" [in the word] "rūpa" is present, [the other sounds are not].
At that time, the phonemes *ū*, *pa*, and *ā* are future.
When the phoneme *ū* is present,
then the sound *ra* is past.
The *p* and *ā* vowels are future. Likewise, when the *p* and *ā* vowels also become present in succession,
then the others are not present.
In this way, that speech would not produce the name at all.
You might say: "The sound *ra*, while present, produces the first part of that name-form;
the sound *u*, while present, produces the second part; and so on, until the sound *a* produces its fourth part."
That is incorrect, because it is impossible for a single dharma to arise in parts.
This has already been stated.
How, then, does the final moment of informative action (*vijñapti*), depending on those that have passed, produce non-informative action (*avijñapti*)?
At the time of undertaking the Prātimokṣa vows, bodily and vocal informative actions proceed;
yet there is no simultaneity (*sāmagrya*) among them.

Moreover, the final moment of informative action (*vijñapti*), depending upon the preceding moments of past bodily and vocal informative action, produces non-informative action (*avijñapti*) comprised within the Prātimokṣa restraint.
In the same way, the final moment of vocal sound, depending upon the preceding moments of past sound, produces a name (*nāman*).
"If that is so," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Since the name arises from the very last sound, even one who hears only that single [last] sound, or even one who hears only the final sound "rūpa," would still comprehend the meaning;
he too would grasp the referent of the name "rūpa."
Because that [name] arises [only later],
and one does not apprehend it in this way;
therefore, this is incorrect.
"Or rather, it might be conceived thus," and so forth.
Another position is proposed: that speech which appears moment by moment consists of phonemes (*vyañjana*), and that [speech] also appears as those [phonemes]. Speech produces the phoneme.
But as for the claim that the phoneme (vyañjana) produces the name,
here too the same logical consequence applies because of the absence of a collection of phonemes.
How so?
Indeed, there is no simultaneous totality of phonemes (*vyañjana*).
Nor is it logical for a single dharma to arise in parts. Therefore, how could a phoneme that is arising itself produce a name?
Furthermore, how does the final moment of informative action (*vijñapti*), depending upon past moments, produce non-informative action (*avijñapti*)?
In that case, since the name arises only from the final phoneme, even one who hears only that single final sound which produces the phoneme,
or even one who hears only that single final phoneme, would also comprehend the meaning.
This same argument applies to the manifestation of the name through speech.

Indeed, there is no such thing as a totality (*sāmagrya*) of sounds; nor is it logical for a single property to be manifested in parts. Therefore, how could speech, while manifesting [the name], manifest the name itself?
How, then, does the final moment of informative action (*vijñapti*), depending on those that have passed, manifest the non-informative action (*avijñapti*)?
If that were the case, then since the name is manifested by the very last sound, even one who hears only that single sound would understand the meaning.
Furthermore, it might be conceived in this way: speech manifests the phoneme (vyañjana), and the phoneme [in turn] manifests the name (nāman).
In this case as well, the same objection applies because of the impossibility of the collection of phonemes (*vyañjana*).
For one who holds that a name is merely sound and that a name consists of multiple syllables, yet there is no simultaneous collection of those sounds— how does that name convey its meaning?
Because the comprehension of meaning occurs immediately after the recollection of all the syllables,

for this very reason— and by the logic of invariable concomitance— someone indeed comprehends the meaning at the very moment of hearing the first syllable through the power of recollecting the remaining syllables.
Thus, it is not tenable that speech is either the producer or the illuminator of the phoneme (*vyañjana*) as well.
Previously, having assumed that manifestation (*vyañjana*) is either something produced by sound or something manifested by sound, a fault was pointed out.
Now, since nothing distinct from sound is perceived, its status as both produced and manifested is also non-existent; thus, he uproots that very [position].
It is not, however, because of a lack of causal totality (*sāmagrī*) for sounds.
A fault must be stated:
for the comprehension of a phoneme does not depend on multiple sounds.
Furthermore, since speech has the nature of sound, every mere sound would either produce or manifest a phoneme.
Or rather, whatever specific sound is intended as the producer or the manifester of the phoneme (*vyañjana*), that very thing will effect the meaning of the phoneme.
Furthermore, it might be maintained—as in the case of genus (*jāti*) and so forth—that the name is co-nascent with its object; this is the full argument.

Now, if it is conceived that a name is "co-nascent" (*sahaja*), one might think that such objections as whether a name is something produced by speech or something revealed will not arise; with this in mind, the following alternative position is formulated:

just as the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such as birth (*jāti*) are held to be co-nascent with the object itself, and do not exist in the present for an object that is past or future—exactly so it would be if the name were held [to be co-nascent].
The present name of a past or future object would not exist;
consequently, it would be impossible to carry out linguistic usage regarding past and future objects,
for a name that is itself past or future cannot illuminate its object.

Just as past and future speech is incapable of producing or manifesting a name, and because there would be a multiplicity of names, an innate name could not be distinguished. Furthermore, since unconditioned phenomena lack the quality of arising, they would have no innate name; thus, this undesirable consequence must not be accepted—this is the intended meaning.
"Verses based on names" means that a verse is a sentence;
it is "based on names" because it arises when names have appeared.

Therefore, he says that there is room for the statement that "names and sentences exist. In this regard, the detailed explanation is: "A word whose limit is established with respect to objects is a name. A verse (*gāthā*) is a particular arrangement of names, which are words whose nature is to have their limits established by meaning.
The meaning is "a particular arrangement.
Regarding the phrase "like a row": just as a row is a specific configuration of ants and so forth, and no separate substance arises from them [other than that configuration].
It is like that.
A specific arrangement of birds, ants, and so forth existing at the same time is called a "row.
However, there is no such specific arrangement for words that exist sequentially; anticipating the objection that there is thus a disparity between the two cases, a second example is presented.
And "just like the succession of thoughts":
just as there is no succession other than the thoughts that occur in sequence,
so it is in this case.
"The construction of that is purposeless" means that the conceptualization of a distinct referent for names and phrases is devoid of utility;
for not all phenomena are accessible through ratiocination (*tarka*).
Only some things are accessible through reasoning, not all;
for those that have fallen within the range of the Tathāgata’s knowledge are not accessible through reasoning— this is the intended meaning.

(II.48cd) This is introduced with the intention of explaining the distinctions among the factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*). Now, as for the detailed explanation "to which [realms] are they bound":
to which realm are they bound? To what are they bound?
Regarding the question of what is meant by "designated as sentient beings" (*sattvākhya*) and "not designated as sentient beings" (*asattvākhya*):
those belonging to the desire and form realms that are designated as sentient beings are outflowing (*niṣyanda*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The restriction is that they belong only to the desire and form realms, are only designated as sentient beings, are only outflow-results, and are only indeterminate.
However, "they are inexpressible" means that those sets of names and so forth belonging to the formless realm are inexpressible because speech does not exist there.
How is it understood that they exist?
When they are not expressed in words.
Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that these [mental factors] belong only to the realms of desire and form, and not to the formless realm.
And these [sounds] are designated as "sentient" because their nature consists of phonemes and so forth produced by the effort of sentient beings.
Furthermore, whoever manifests them is endowed with them.
Why,
then, does this doubt arise— that there might be a mutual possession of these [factors] by one another?
Because of the designation "this is its name.
Just as the sentient being who sees is endowed with the visual faculty, but not the object seen;
likewise, the illuminator is endowed with those [faculties], but not the illuminated.
They are outflowing (*naiṣyandika*) because they are produced by a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
They are not born of maturation (*vipākaja*) because they proceed from volition (*icchā*).
They are not accumulative (*aupacayika*) because there is no accumulation of formless things.
And they are unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
They are neither wholesome (*kuśala*) nor unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Why?

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even those who have severed their roots of merit (*samucchinnakuśalamūla*) or those who are free from desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmavītarāga*) would still possess those [roots].
For if that were not the case, then when one whose roots of merit are severed manifests wholesome phenomena (*kuśalān dharmān*),
he would at that time be in possession of wholesome phenomena.
In the same way, this should be applied to the manifestation of unwholesome dharmas even for one who is free from passion for sensual desires (*kāmavītarāga*).
Therefore, they are exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*),
because there is no contradiction between the non-obscured and indeterminate and the wholesome or unwholesome.
(II.49) "Likewise, [it is] homogeneous" (*sabhāgatā*).

By the word "likewise," it is extended that homogeneity is likewise a non-obscured neutral (*avyākṛta*) state, which is a natural outflow (*naiṣyandika*) and designated as a sentient being (*sattvākhya*).
This is because it will be stated later as an exception to its inclusion within the three realms (*tridhātvāpta*).
Regarding the phrase "sā tu":
the word *tu* (but/however) serves the purpose of specification.
For homogeneity (sabhāgatā) is distinguished from the group of names (nāmakāya) and the other [factors].
How so? He says:
"It is also a result of maturation (vipāka)."
The meaning is that it is also born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
It is not only outflowing (*naiṣyandika*);
what then?
It is born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
but not accumulative (*aupacayikī*) because there is likewise no accumulation.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) are of two kinds.
By the word "twofold," only the distinctions between acquisitions (*prāpti*) as being non-orientated (*naiṣyandika*) and born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are expressed,
because other distinctions have already been stated.
The same applies to the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The same two divisions should be stated for birth and the other [factors] in exactly this way.
Non-possession (*asamanvāgama*) is non-attainment (*aprāpti*).
That [non-possession] is also non-obscured and indeterminate, yet it is not born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
For even the non-possession of maturation cannot itself be a maturation;
for it is accepted that there is maturation of both the unwholesome and the wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, non-attainment cannot be a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
For whatever phenomenon is preceded by intelligence, consists of volition, or is associated with and originated from it,
that is a cause of maturation.
And since non-possession (*asamanvāgama*) is not produced by an action preceded by conscious intent (*buddhipūrvakakarmakṛta*), it is therefore not born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Regarding these, it has been said that "what remains to be stated has been stated.

This means that what was to be stated and explained regarding these—namely, possession (*prāpti*), the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and non-possession (*asamanvāgama*)—has already been stated and explained.
What, then, is that "remainder"?
It is the state of belonging to a realm (*dhātu*), the designation as pertaining to sentient beings or non-sentient things, and the state of being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
But how is that stated?

First, it has been stated that those [factors] which are obtained belong to a realm, according to the statement: "Those belonging to a particular realm are obtained by one who belongs to that same realm."

The designation "belonging to sentient beings" is stated because of the mention of possession (*samanvāgama*). For there are no possessions of conditioned phenomena that are not reckoned as belonging to sentient beings.
Possession and non-possession apply only to those [phenomena] that fall within one's own continuum.
Because of this statement:
"How are [the dharmas] described as wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral?
As wholesome and so forth for those that are wholesome and so forth."
Because it is so stated.
It has also been declared that the characteristics (lakṣaṇas) are likewise associated with the three realms,
since everything is [associated] with the characteristics of the conditioned (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇas).
Because of this statement,
it is for this very reason that they are said to be designated as both sentient and non-sentient,
since they coexist with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

For this very reason, it is also stated that they possess the qualities of being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. The mental factors (caitta), the two types of restraint (saṃvara), their characteristics, and those that follow the mind (cittānuvartin) [are so called] by virtue of their time, fruit, wholesomeness, and so forth.
Because of this statement,
it is taught that the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) belongs to the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
specifically within the final dhyāna.
Because of this statement,
wholesomeness (*kuśalatā*) is also [termed] "pure" (*śubha*).
Because of this statement, the state of being designated as a sentient being (*sattvākhya*) is likewise established as being experienced only upon rebirth (*upapadyavedya*).
Because of the scriptural statement:
"The attainment of cessation is also said to belong to the formless realm, as it arises from the peak of existence."
Because it is so stated;
moreover, skillfulness is also called "wholesome."
Because it is stated [in the sūtra].
For this very reason, it is also designated as "sentient" (sattvākhya),
because it is wholesome and conditioned (kuśala-saṃskṛta).

The non-possession (asamanvāgama) is said to pertain to the three realms, according to the statement: "And [it pertains to] those belonging to the desire realm and so forth, as well as the untainted (amala)."

It is designated as belonging to sentient beings because of the statement regarding its possession (*samanvāgama*). Its neutral nature (*avyākṛtatā*) is also stated [in the sūtra] as "non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) that is non-defiled and neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*)."
Because of this statement [in the Abhidharmakośavyākhyā, 188],
and because of the remaining two— namely, the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) and the life-faculty (*jīvita*)—
what [is the case]?
The phrase "what was to be said has been said" continues [from the previous context].

Regarding the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*), it has been stated that it belongs to the realm of form (*rūpāpta*), is designated as a sentient being (*sattvākhyā*), is a result of maturation (*vipāka*), and is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Its maturation occurs in the Bṛhatphala heaven.
From this statement,
it is taught that vitality belongs to the three realms;
vitality is life-force (*āyus*).
Because of this statement,
and because life-force (āyus) belongs to the three realms,
it is also said to be designated as a sentient being (sattvākhya).
"Life is maturation," according to the Sūtra;
for maturation belongs exclusively to what is designated as a sentient being.

Because it is stated that "maturation is an indeterminate dharma, designated as a sentient being, and arising from the determinate," for this very reason its state of being unobscured-indeterminate has also been declared.
The view that was to be stated by the Teacher has now been explained.
How was it stated that acquisition (*prāpti*) and the other [conditioned factors] are designated as belonging to sentient beings (*sattvākhya*)?
"Because of the mention of 'possession' (*samanvāgama*)," and so forth.
(II.50) What are these causes (*hetu*) and what are these conditions (*pratyaya*)?
And what is the specific distinction between causes and conditions?
"No one [is the cause]," he said.
For it was thus stated by the Blessed One:
"There are two causes and two conditions for the arising of right view."
Which two?
The voice of another and internal appropriate attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
Cause, condition, source, reason, sign, mark, and proximate cause are synonyms.
The word *upaniṣad*, however, is sometimes used in a secondary sense and sometimes in a primary sense.
For example, as in "the gods are the *sūryopaniṣadaḥ*. Thus, there is the usage of *upāṃśu* (in secret/whispered) and the usage of *upaniṣad*.
If there is no specific distinction [between them], for what purpose are causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*) taught separately?
They are taught with different specific meanings: the teaching of causes is by one [meaning] and the teaching of conditions is by another.
For in the teaching of causes, specific meanings such as being non-obstructive, coexistence, and similarity have been stated.
However, in the exposition of the conditions (*pratyaya*), another specific meaning has been stated by means of [the categories] such as cause (*hetu*) and immediate antecedence (*samanantara*).
Now, in which sutra are the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*) taught?
For all Abhidharma is the meaning of the sutras, the touchstone of the sutras, and the commentary on the sutras.
"That scripture has disappeared," say the Vaibhāṣikas;
for they explain that while the *Ekottarikāgama* formerly contained teachings of the Dharma up to one hundred [items],
it is now seen only up to ten.
Moreover, there are sūtras that express specific causes;
we shall cite them.
"Dependent upon the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises"—this refers to the cause as a causal factor (*kāraṇahetu*).
For this [path] is established by way of being an unobstructed condition for its arising.
These three factors of the path revolve around right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) that arise together with them constitute the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).
For this is established in the sense that they have the single function of revolving one after another.

This person is endowed with both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, up to the point that there exists in him a subtle concomitant root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) which is not yet severed; from this root of goodness, another root of goodness will arise for him.
Thus, this person will possess the qualities of purification in the future; this is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
For this is established for the sake of producing its own fruit from past and present phenomena.
This is called faith rooted in vision, which is associated with the knowledge of having understood.
"That which one cognizes, one discerns"— this refers to the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*),
for it is established by way of the function of having a single object (*ekālambana*).
Whatever bodily action, whatever vocal action, whatever volition, whatever aspiration, and whatever formative factors (saṃskāra) follow from that person or individual who holds wrong view—
all these phenomena lead to what is undesirable, to what is unlovely, to what is unpleasant, and to what is disagreeable. For what reason?
For his view is evil, namely false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); this is the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*).
It is established in this sense that it produces a continuity of both similar and dissimilar afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*).
Here, they experience the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) karma performed in this life, which consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*), having arisen there.
The ripening (*vipāka*) of intentional (*saṃcetanīya*) karma that has been performed and accumulated is the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*).
For this is established by virtue of its projecting a dissimilar fruit (*visadṛśaphala*).
Thus, these six causes are well-known from the Sūtra itself.
The intention is that the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that there are six kinds of causes.
(II.51a) [The first is] "from itself" (*svataḥ*), which means other than...
Thus, the meaning is "other than itself.
Because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself, that which is its own self is not a cause.
All phenomena—both conditioned and unconditioned—are the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
The cause itself is the "reason" (hetu); thus, it is the "efficient cause" (kāraṇahetu).
That which is not designated by a specific name, but is spoken of by grasping its general state of being a cause, is the efficient cause.
For when there are other causes that have been explained with specific designations, that which has not been so specified serves as their qualification and cause;
for example, as it was said regarding the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*).
"Because they exist in a state of non-obstruction with respect to arising.
Since, with respect to arising, other phenomena distinct from themselves exist as non-obstructive factors for those things that possess arising,
they are therefore called the "causal condition" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
"But surely, as for the passage beginning 'those [defilements] of one who does not know' and so forth:
if these do not give rise to knowledge,
then those outflows would have arisen"— this is the meaning of the conditional (lṛṅ) in the full statement.
Therefore it is said:

for this person who does not know—that is, for a person in whom the paths of seeing and cultivation have not yet arisen—those outflows such as attachment and so forth, which are to be abandoned by the paths of seeing and cultivation, would arise.
For this person who knows—that is, for a person in whom the paths of seeing and cultivation have arisen—those [outflows] to be abandoned by them, such as attachment and so forth, do not arise.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
Knowledge—comprised within the paths of seeing and cultivation—acts as an obstacle to their arising;
and it is understood that the light of the sun acts as an obstacle to the arising of the vision of the luminaries.
This being so, how can all phenomena, excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), be the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) of the conditioned?
For, in the arising of outflows (*āsrava*), knowledge is not the efficient cause;
and in the arising of the perception of light, the sunlight is [the cause].
For it should be stated thus:
"In the arising of an outflow (*āsrava*), all phenomena (*dharma*) except for that which has the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) are the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*);
and in the arising of the perception of light, all phenomena except for that which has the nature of the sun and its radiance are the efficient cause."
"Because of the state of non-obstruction for that which is arising.
When the causes and conditions are complete, a phenomenon that occurs immediately thereafter is said to be "arising.
For that which is arising, all phenomena indeed abide in a state of non-obstruction with respect to its production.
It should be understood that this does not apply to everyone.
However, when knowledge is present, those outflows (āsravas) do not arise,
because of the absence of the completeness of conditions due to the non-existence of acquisition (prāpti) and so forth.
It should be understood that even the perception of light does not arise precisely because of a deficiency in the conditions (*pratyaya*).
Therefore, it remains as it is: with the exception of its own nature (*svabhāva*), all phenomena (*dharma*) are the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) of conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*).
This is illustrated by the detailed example: "just as a ruler who does not oppress," and so forth.
With reference to a village headman who causes no harm, people might say,
"We are happy because of our master.
Why would they speak in this way?
Because, although he is capable of causing harm, he does not cause harm— just as, for example, with regard to nirvāṇa and those phenomena that are by nature non-arising.
What [is this]?
How is there the state of being a cause for the arising of all things?

And how is there the state of being a cause for the arising of the formless aggregates (ārūpyaskandha) for those in the hells and so forth—namely, those belonging to the hellish, animal, and other realms?
The mention of "those in the hells and so forth" implies the intention that [the same applies] to humans and others at times, through instruction and the like.
"For even those that do not exist" means: for these things, such as nirvāṇa and so forth, even though they do not exist, are exactly like those that do exist;
that is, just as existing, present things would be incapable of creating an obstacle.

Therefore, these [obstacles] are indistinguishable in creating hindrances to these things—such as nirvāṇa—whether they are non-existent or existent; the meaning is that they are equivalent to non-existence.
"Even when [the obstacle] is incapable," and so forth.
Even when a village headman is unable to cause them harm, the villagers speak in such a way,
saying, "We are made happy by our lord.
The very same illustration applies here as that which was given previously.

Therefore, by this very example, it is established that even things such as *nirvāṇa*, which are incapable of obstructing, possess the status of a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*) because they abide in a state of non-obstruction.
But why is the status of a causal condition attributed to things like *nirvāṇa*, which are equivalent to non-existence,
and not to other non-existent things such as a rabbit’s horn?
Because there is no such instance [of a non-existent being].
For villagers do not say, with respect to a non-existent village headman,
"We have been made happy by our master."
"Nor are we made happy by a rabbit's horn.
This is not to be questioned;
it is merely a general statement.
This was stated with reference to both the primary efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and the non-primary one:
"All [factors] other than itself are the efficient cause."
For that which is the primary producer is the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*);
it remains as a non-obstructive factor to a much greater degree than any other.
It has been established that food is capable of producing the body,
because of the statement: "From the arising of food comes the arising of the body," and because of its connection with the transformation into nutrients and so forth.
"Seeds and so forth [are the causes] of sprouts and so forth.
This means that seeds, sprouts, stalks, nodes, flowers, fruits, and so on, are capable of producing [their respective effects].
As for the detailed elaboration beginning with "But he who objects in this way": [it refers to the following objection].
Thinking that "when a cause exists, the effect must come to be," he objects:
why does the arising of everything not occur simultaneously?
And how is it that one who commits the act of taking life becomes a partaker in that taking of life?
Likewise, why do all [beings] not become partakers of that?
[The answer is: "Not by way of being an agent.
This shows that it does not function as its cause in a primary sense.
Therefore, first of all, the simultaneous arising of everything does not follow,
because [things] do not arise due to the absence of the completeness of conditions (*pratyayasāmagrī*).
Furthermore, there is no engagement in the taking of life, because [the agent] is not a causal factor (*akāraka*).
But he who is the agent indeed becomes a partaker in the taking of life;
thus, wholesome or unwholesome mental consciousness arises.
The mental consciousness is wholesome because it has nirvāṇa as its object.
From a wholesome or unwholesome mental consciousness that has nirvāṇa as its object, visual consciousness arises. Thus it is said.
Thus, by way of succession, because it also serves as a condition for that very nirvāṇa, it possesses efficacy.
Where?
It is understood to be in relation to visual consciousness.
In this way, it should be understood for others as well:
even those such as hell-beings possess the capacity for the arising of the formless aggregates.
How so?
"Alas, these beings such as hell-beings and pretas are supremely afflicted"—from this, a wholesome mental consciousness arises taking hell-beings and others as its object.
Because one who is thus gradually established in ethical discipline applies himself to cultivation, the formless attainments and rebirth therein are achieved.
Thus it is said.
(II.51b-d) "Coexistent are those which are mutual fruits.
The term "cause" is understood to carry over [from the previous definition].
Those factors (*dharma*) that are coexistent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) are those factors which are mutual fruits; the meaning is that they are reciprocal fruits.
It is not stated that "coexistent causes are coexistent [factors]," [because the definition would be redundant].
Why is this?
For there are certain phenomena that are co-existent but not co-existent causes.
For example, derived matter such as blue and so forth is co-existent with the primary elements.
And they are not mutually co-existent causes;
therefore,
they are mutual fruits.
Such is the inclusion of the meaning.
And this definition is incomplete;
therefore, he will say:

Furthermore, even without being mutual fruits, a dharma is the sahabhū-hetu of its secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas), but those [characteristics] are not [the hetu] of it; this must be added as a supplementary rule (upasaṃkhyātavya). And the making of this supplementary rule is for the purpose of demonstrating the status of this as a great treatise (mahāśāstra).
For great treatises such as grammar (vyākaraṇa) are seen to include supplementary rules (sopasaṃkhyāna).
[The phrase] "as if it were already existent" (bhūtavat) [is used].
The suffix *vat* is used in the sense of "just like" (*tadyathārthe*).
And by doing so, it follows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are, as appropriate, co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*).
This is because the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are co-existent causes for the characterized phenomenon (*lakṣya*).
That [conditioned factor] is also [the co-existent cause] of those [others].
Therefore, as appropriate and as possible, every conditioned phenomenon is a co-existent cause of [other] conditioned phenomena, because it possesses characteristics,
and because the characterized and the characteristic stand in a relationship of mutual co-existent causality.
But it is not the case that everything [is the cause] of everything.
Because they are causes by way of being non-coexistent causes (*asahabhūhetu*) through their respective characteristics, there is a selection according to what is appropriate.
And regarding those [characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth, which belong to the mind—

And for those factors associated with the mind, such as volition and so forth, as well as for the dhyāna restraint and the untainted (anāsrava) restraint, there are four dharmas—beginning with birth—which are said to follow the mind.
[They are distinguished] by way of time, fruit, and so forth, and by way of being wholesome and so forth. (Abhidh-k-vy 192) (II.52d)
Thus: by means of time, fruits, and so forth, as well as wholesomeness and so forth—
hence, "by means of time, fruits, and so forth, and wholesomeness and so forth."
"In terms of time, first," and so forth.
These [mental factors] arise together with the mind, persist together with it, and cease together with it; such is their nature.
"By way of having a single arising, abiding, and ceasing.
"Falling into a single time period" means falling into one [of the three] time periods (adhvan).
Its state is that [of being so].
By the fourth [reason], namely, by virtue of falling within the same temporal period (*ekādhvapatitatva*),
they revolve around the mind in terms of time.
They revolve around the mind by way of having a single fruit (*ekaphalatā*), a single maturation (*ekavipākatā*), and a single outflow (*ekaniṣyandatā*).
In this context, "fruit" refers to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*),
because the fruits of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and outflow (*niṣyandaphala*) have been treated separately.
The sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*), however, is not included here because it is common to all.
It is not counted.
Furthermore, this word "one" (eka) refers to being common in number or having a single result, and so forth;
however, the preceding word "one" has the sense of "together," meaning that they arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with the mind.
For in this case, the sense of numerical enumeration is not possible;
for that which is the arising of the mind is not itself [the arising] of those factors that follow the mind.
Or whatever belongs to them,
that belongs to the mind.
Thus, it is by way of ten reasons.
In terms of time, [they are simultaneous] by virtue of arising together, abiding together, ceasing together, and falling within the same temporal period (*adhvan*).
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that by the phrase 'by virtue of arising, abiding, and ceasing together,' it is already stated that they fall within the same temporal period?
It is not entirely stated.
For when the mind has the nature of non-arising, those mental factors that follow it fall into the same time period;
they do not have simultaneous arising and cessation.
Therefore, falling into the same time period is stated as the fourth reason.

It is said that [the fruit] arises by way of ten [factors]: by way of three—namely, through the state of being a single outflow from the ripening of a single fruit—and again by way of three—namely, through the states of being wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
This statement of "by ten" is made with reference to the occurrence of synonyms or to the [different] types.
For ten causes do not exist within a single state of mind.
Indeed, in a wholesome mind, the two causes—unwholesome and neutral—do not exist;
nor do they exist in an unwholesome or neutral mind that is subject to non-arising.

In the case of an indeterminate mind characterized by non-arising, there are four [conditions]: by way of falling within the same time-period, by way of being a single outflow of fruit, and by way of being indeterminate.
However, in the case of one characterized by arising, there are seven: by these same four, plus by way of having a single arising, abiding, and cessation.
It is the same for the untainted (*anāsrava*) as well.
However, having merely removed its neutral character (*avyākṛtatā*), the quality of being wholesome (*kuśalatā*) should be added.

In the case of that which is unwholesome (*akuśala*) or wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*) characterized by the nature of not arising (*anutpattikadharmin*), there are five [factors]: by way of being unwholesome or wholesome respectively, by way of belonging to the same time period (*ekādhvapatitatva*), and by way of having the same fruit, ripening, and outflow (*ekaphalavipākaniṣyandatā*).

But in the case of that same [state] characterized by the nature of arising (*utpattidharmin*), there are eight [factors], namely those same five plus the same arising, abiding, and ceasing (*ekotpādasthitinirodhatā*).
"The most minimal mind" means that among all [minds],
that mind which has the smallest retinue is called the most minimal.
Furthermore, what is that?
It is the non-obscured-neutral mind from the second dhyāna upward.
In that state, applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra) do not exist.
Nor are the wholesome and other universal mental factors [included here];
rather, there are only the ten universal factors themselves.
This refers to their characteristics.
[This applies] to those [dharmas] characterized by the ten great grounds, but not to their secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), because of the latter's remoteness; however,
it does apply to their own secondary characteristics because of their proximity.
Therefore he says:
"And of the eight [factors], their own-characteristics and secondary-characteristics," meaning "excluding their own secondary-characteristics."
The secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) function with respect to the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇas),
but not with respect to the distinguished mind;
for they are inferior to them.
For the mind acts as a king over the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa).
Therefore, the mind is the co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) of the secondary characteristics,
but they are not [the cause] of the mind.
Since the characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*) do have an operation upon the mind, they constitute the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) of the mind.
Others say there are fourteen [characteristics], because,
unlike the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇas*), the primary characteristics do not have an operation upon the dharma itself.
What then?
[They pertain] to the characteristics of a phenomenon (dharma).
Therefore, their status as causes is not accepted as being the phenomenon itself.

In this way, the activity of those characteristics (lakṣaṇas) occurs only with respect to that which is associated [with the mind], and not with respect to the mind itself; thus, they are not the co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) of the mind.
However, others hold the view that since the mind is like a king in relation to them, it is indeed their co-existent cause.
For otherwise, the *Prakaraṇapāda* treatise would be contradicted regarding the forty characteristics of the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
If those were not accepted as being co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) of the mind, then it would contradict what is stated in the *Prakaraṇas*: [text follows].
There are four noble truths, from the truth of suffering up to the truth of the path.

Among these, how many have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not causes of the view of a self-identity? How many are causes of the view of a self-identity but do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause?
When the question is asked: "How many have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are themselves the cause of the view of a self-identity?
How many neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are they the cause of the view of a self-identity? he provides the answer:
"Two neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are they the cause of the view of a self-identity."
The truth of cessation and the truth of the path.
There is a distinction between these two;
there is a detailed classification of the truths of suffering and its origin.
How so?
There may be a truth of suffering that has the view of a self-identity as its cause but is not a cause for the view of a self-identity.
There may also be [a truth of suffering] that has the view of a self-identity as its cause and is also a cause for the view of a self-identity.
There may be that which has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but is not a cause for the view of a self-identity; this constitutes a threefold classification (*trikoṭika*).
There is no second category.
In that regard, [the first category] is that which has the view of a self-identity as its cause, but is not a cause for the view of a self-identity.

Excluding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) that are past and present, and the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) associated with them;

excluding the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśanaprahātavya*) that are past and present, and the truth of suffering associated with them;
and excluding the future truth of suffering associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Excluding the birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and of the factors associated with it, that which remains is the other afflicted truth of suffering.
That which was excluded is both caused by the view of a self-identity and is itself a cause of the view of a self-identity.
Non-afflicted suffering is neither caused by the view of a self-identity nor is it a cause of the view of a self-identity.
"Just as it is with the truth of suffering, so it is with the truth of origination"—this is the text of the *Prakaraṇa*.
We shall explain its meaning:
those ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and others, which are past or present and are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
Those have been established.
The truth of suffering, consisting of sensation and so forth, associated with those ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), has been established.
What, then, has not been established here?

These same ten future latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and their associated factors, such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth—excluding the future truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—constitute [the category].
For that [future truth of suffering] will be set aside, according to the statement:
"and having set aside the future truth of suffering associated with the view of a self-identity."

The birth and other characteristics (*jāti-ādi*) of that attainment are also excluded, with the exception of the birth and other characteristics of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the factors associated with it; for those will be set aside, according to the statement: "having set aside the birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self-identity and the factors associated with it."
Thus, first of all, the future latent disposition (*anuśaya*) and that which is associated with it— excluding what has been set aside—
are called "other afflicted [states] having the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause.
That which has this view of a self-identity as its cause is "having the view of a self-identity as its cause" (*satkāyadṛṣṭihetuka*).

This is because [the view of self-existence] has as its cause both the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), being caused by past and present views of self-existence.
However, it is not itself a cause of the view of self-existence; for a future phenomenon is not established as either a homogeneous cause or a pervasive cause.
Furthermore, neither a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) nor an associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) is possible in this case.
For the view of a self-identity does not exist together with, nor is it associated with, the view of a self-identity;
because there is no second view of a self-identity within a single mental complex (*kalāpa*).
Nor does it exist together with, nor is it associated with, the view of extremes and so forth.
Because they belong to distinct categories:

those dissociated [factors]—namely, the acquisitions (*prāpti*) and the [characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*) of those [dharmas] belonging to the past and present that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*)—are not included [in the established category]. They are other than the established ones and are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
These [subsequent views] are also caused by previously arisen self-view through the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*);
however, they are not the cause of self-view.
Why?
First, acquisitions (*prāpti*)—like the bark of a tree—are not established as universal because they exist outside of their own universal factors.
Furthermore, due to the absence of universality, they are not the universal cause of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Although the universal types of birth (*jāti*) and so forth are indeed accepted as being universal, [they do not function as universal causes for others].
Because of the established tenet that "those which coexist with these [universal factors], excluding acquisition (*prāpti*), are also universal," they are indeed universal;
however, unlike the mind and mental factors, they are not the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) for subsequent minds and mental factors.

Since they are not primary because their function is directed toward their own specific objects (*svalakṣya*), the universal human activity (*sarvatragapuruṣakāra*) does not exist among other minds and mental factors.
However, the establishment of those [factors] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth as "universal" is due to their being universal causes within their own continuum.
Therefore, the meaning of the treatise is understood to be that they are not the cause of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
In that case, why is it not a similar-cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)?
For the establishment of a similar-cause depends also upon human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
Indeed, whatever dharma possesses human effort toward the production of another dharma [is its cause].
That is its homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
And this very point is the proof that the establishment of the homogeneous cause is according to one's preference.
It is also stated thus in the *Vibhāṣā*.

The eye is the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) of the eye; Devadatta’s eye is the homogeneous cause of Devadatta’s eye. The right [eye] is [the cause] of the right, and the left of the left, up to the point that a substance of the eye is the cause of another substance of the eye.
This also applies to external things: barley is [the cause] of barley, and rice of rice.

For if every eye were intended to be the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of every [other] eye—on the grounds that their neutral nature (*avyākṛtatva*) is equal—then such a qualification would not have been stated.
Therefore, it should be understood that it is not the homogeneous cause of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
However, others say:
This commentary is incomplete.
Therefore, it should be understood that those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) such as those of the same class (*sajāti*), as well as the factors (*dharma*) associated with them, have been set aside;
for these are the birth and other characteristics (*jātyādi*) of a factor and its associated factors which function as co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*).

Together with those [universal factors], those dharmas that have arisen previously become either universal causes (*sarvatragahetu*) or homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*). This is because of the established tenet that "those co-existent factors, excluding acquisitions (*prāpti*), which arise together with these [universal factors], are also universal."
For this very reason it was said:
"excluding the birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of those factors associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, some [of these] characteristics, such as birth and so forth, have also been excluded.
Therefore, it should be understood that anything other than this is "not established.
The reasoning here is to be seen;
for such is the reasoning.
From this it should be understood:

those universal [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), whether past or present, and the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) associated with them, such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth— that is what is set aside.
What else is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), excluding [the aforementioned]?
Those universal [defilements] that are future, and the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) associated with them, such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth—
that is what is excluded.
Furthermore, those non-universal [defilements] such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth that belong to the three time periods,
as well as the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all those [factors],
are not included among the set aside.
However, birth and the other [factors] have not been established at all in one position;
yet in another position, some have been established while others have not.

All of this, which has not yet been established [as having arisen], is to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*); by means of the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), it has *satkāyadṛṣṭi* as its cause, because it has the previously arisen *satkāyadṛṣṭi* as its cause.
However, it is not a cause for *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.
Because universal [factors] and their co-existent factors, by virtue of being future, do not function as universal causes;

and because non-universal factors—such as attachment and the like, their co-existent factors such as sensation and the like, and [the secondary characteristics] such as birth and the like—are non-universal in one respect, as are all acquisitions (*prāpti*).

Furthermore, the defiled latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, those to be abandoned through cultivation, along with their associated factors, their originating factors, and the nature of birth and the like, are not included [among the universal causes].
These [defilements] have the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their cause by way of being universal causes (sarvatragahetu);
however, they are not the cause of the view of a self-identity,
because it is impossible for them to be universal causes and because other types of causes are inapplicable.
That which has been set aside—that which has the view of a self-identity as its cause and is itself a cause for the view of a self-identity—is as follows:

those ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering that are past or present, the truth of suffering associated with them, and birth and so forth belonging to other categories;
all these have the prior view of a self-identity as their cause, by way of both the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) and the pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu).
Those [factors] such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and birth (*jāti*), as well as the birth and so forth associated with them,

have that [view of a self-identity] as their cause by way of the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the two previously mentioned causes. Furthermore, those which are associated with the view of a self-identity—

They have that as their cause by way of the associated cause (*saṃprayuktahetu*) and by way of the causes previously mentioned. And they are likewise the cause of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, those universal [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśanaprahātavya*) which are past or present, along with their co-existent factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, and the [factors] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth in another category, [are also its cause].
They have the view of a self-identity as their cause solely by way of the universal cause;
and they are also the cause of the view of a self-identity.
For a previously arisen view of a self-identity is their cause.
And those [factors] previously arisen are [the cause] of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
However, the undefiled truth of suffering— whether wholesome or unobscured-neutral— is neither caused by the view of a self-identity nor is it the cause of the view of a self-identity,
because the five types of causality are possible [only for defiled factors].
For in this context, "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the producing cause (*janaka-hetu*), not the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
because the latter is common to all [phenomena].
Furthermore, there is an inconsistency here regarding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
This is because the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), being obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), is not subject to ripening.
Consequently, that which was stated there—namely, "excluding the birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self-identity and the factors associated with it"—would be contradicted.
For if the factors such as the birth (jāti) and so forth associated with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) were not co-existent causes (sahabhūhetu),
they would not be set aside;
for those which are set aside [are precisely those that are co-existent causes].
They have the view of a self-identity as their cause,
and they are also the cause of the view of a self-identity.
As for those who do not recite the passage beginning with "those associated with that," [their position is as follows].
One must supply the phrase: "How could their *Prakaraṇa* treatise be contradicted?

For they read the text as follows: "Having set aside birth, aging, duration, and impermanence [of the self] from the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), these characteristics function only with respect to those [factors] associated with it."
Not in the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, their intention is that those [factors] are not co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) for it. They too must recite this as follows: [Tib. 182b]...
Since there is a fault if this is not recited in this way, they should therefore recite this further [text]:
"and those associated with it.
For those associated with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) are considered to be "self-like," because they share the same object, function, and so forth.

Therefore, just as these characteristics are co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) with respect to those [mental factors] and their associated states, so too they are with respect to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); such is the intention of the Vaibhāṣikas.
This should be understood in this way according to the sense of the argument.

By the mention of "the view of a self-identity" (satkāyadṛṣṭi), those factors associated with the view of a self-identity are also included, either by the continuation of the context or because they should be understood in that same way.
The phrase "and those associated with it" indicates that this refers to the Kashmiris and not to those from outside the country.
"Coexistent as well is that," namely the mental factors (caitta) and so forth.
For the mental factors and those characteristics are the coexistent cause (sahabhūhetu) of the mind, and they are also coexistent with it.
"The secondary characteristics of a dharma," and so forth.
The birth-of-birth and other [characteristics] of a dharma are co-existent;
yet they are not causes by way of being a co-existent cause because of their remoteness.
For their activity pertains to birth and the other [characteristics], not to the dharma itself.
And these [primary characteristics] are co-existent with one another, as are they and their secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas), because of their activity regarding birth and the others.
They are not causes by way of being a co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu).
But for those [mental factors], the mental state (*dharma*) is their co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*),
because of its predominance.
For it proceeds as if drawing along its entire retinue of attendants, like a king on a journey accompanied by his servants, leading them all with his own train.
And the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) that follow the mind.

The secondary characteristics of those mental factors (caitta)—namely, the dhyāna-restraints and the untainted restraints (anāsrava-saṃvara) that accompany the mind—as well as the secondary characteristics of those [primary] characteristics, likewise arise simultaneously with the mind;
however, they are not causes by way of being simultaneous causes (sahabhū-hetu).
The word *eva* is for the purpose of indicating the meaning.
And those secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇas*) are co-existent with one another,
but they are not causes by way of being a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).

Furthermore, derived matter that possesses resistance (*sapratigha*)—consisting of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and the tangible—is co-existent within atoms composed of eight substances and so forth;
however, it is not a cause by way of being a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).
The inclusion of the term "possessing resistance" is for the purpose of excluding that which lacks resistance (*apratigha*).

For the non-obstructive form of meditative restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), which consist of the nature of the sevenfold non-informative (*avijñapti*) matter, are mutually co-existent.
They are causes by way of being co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). And all [of these] are [coexistent] with the primary elements (*bhūta*).
Derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), whether with resistance (*sapratigha*) or without resistance (*apratigha*), is co-existent with its own primary elements (*bhūta*).
However, it is not a cause by way of being a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).

Furthermore, although co-arising acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise simultaneously with the phenomenon they acquire (*prāptimat*), they are not co-existent causes; this is because acquisitions are produced at both earlier and later times.
"Because they do not exist simultaneously, there is no consequence of [their] being simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*). This is the qualification "simultaneous.
Why? He says:
"Because they have multiple fruits of maturation and outflow.

This is because those [non-acquisitions], together with that which possesses acquisition, do not share a single fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), since they flow separately like the bark-shoots of a tree;
nor do they share a single fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).

Because it is stated that "the two mindless attainments are not projective, nor are acquisitions," and because they do not have a single outflowing fruit; for the acquisitions themselves are the outflowing fruit of the [attainments], since they constitute a separate continuum.
Only those [dharmas] that follow the mind are held to have a single fruit, namely the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*).
This is not the case for acquisitions (*prāpti*), because they do not move together with the mind; they lack the nature of being concomitants (*sahacaraṇaśīla*).
"All this might be so," refers to what was stated in detail regarding how [things] are causes by way of being co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*),
such as seeds and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the sprout, stalk, stem, and so forth are included.
This principle is not observed;
that is to say, the principle characterized by the relationship of cause and effect between two things that have arisen simultaneously is not observed.
For the seed comes first and the sprout later;
the impact comes first and the sound later.
This is just as with a lamp and its light, or a sprout and its shadow.
What?
It continues: "the state of cause and effect.
A lamp arises together with its light.
It is not devoid of radiance.
Even as a sprout arises in the sunlight, its shadow exists simultaneously;
yet the lamp is the cause of the light that arises together with it, and the sprout is the cause of the shadow.
"In the same way.
"First, it must be thoroughly examined," and so forth.
