The opponent's intention is that the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Because the very same previously arisen collection of causes, such as the wick and the oil, is the cause for the arising of the lamp together with its light;
that same collection is the cause for both the lamp and its light.
However, it is not maintained that the lamp is the cause of the light.

Thus, regarding the production of a sprout possessing shadow, it must be stated that the causal complex (sāmagrī) consisting of the seed, moisture, and so forth, which had already arisen previously, is the cause.
"Necessarily" means that when a certain phenomenon exists, another phenomenon necessarily exists; it is not by mere chance.
That is the cause; the other is the effect-characteristic which possesses a cause—this is the meaning. And this applies to coexistent phenomena (*sahabhū-dharma*).

For example, it would be logical that for the four primary elements (*bhūta*), for those [factors] that follow the mind and mental concomitants (*cittacaitta*), and for the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is the existence of all when one exists, and the non-existence of all when one is absent; this applies, first of all, to those that are co-arisen (*sahotpanna*).
In detail, the relationship of cause and effect is accepted among those that are co-arisen.
For example, although the eye arises simultaneously with the visual consciousness, it serves as the cause for its arising.
But how is this mutual [causality]?
For the visual consciousness does not serve as the cause for that eye.
He said:

For this very reason, the meaning is that because existence and non-existence possess those [characteristics], mental factors and so forth are also causes of the mind; for when they exist, the mind exists, and when they do not exist, the mind does not exist.
"In that case, then," and so forth.
If, when one exists, all exist, and when all are absent, one is absent, then there is a mutual relationship of cause and effect.

In the case of [an atom] consisting of eight substances within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), this same consequence would apply even to the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)— which has the nature of visible form, taste, odor, and tangibility— that is invariably concomitant [with the primary elements].
The meaning is that there would be the consequence of their being mutually simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*).
Furthermore, it would follow that derived matter (upādāyarūpa) would be a co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) with the primary elements (bhūta),
as would the mental concomitants (cittānulakṣaṇa) and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa) that follow the mind are also included.
Regarding the phrase "by the mind and so forth":
here too, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), those factors that follow the mind and its secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) are included.
Thus, it says "by the mind and so forth."
Here too, by the word "etc. (ādi), the consequence of mutual causality with those factors that follow the mind is intended.
By that same word "etc.," it should be stated that this same consequence applies to the possessors of acquisitions (prāptimat) together with their co-nascent acquisitions (sahajā prāpti).
This is like the stability of three staffs through their mutual support.
Abiding through mutual strength is "abiding by mutual strength.
The abiding of the three staffs through mutual strength is "the abiding of the three staffs by mutual strength";
it is just like that.
Just as three staffs remain standing through their mutual support,
so too is the relationship of cause and effect established for coexistent factors such as mind and mental concomitants.
"This, however, must first be investigated," and so forth.
This must be examined.
The intention is that this example is not established.
The "force" refers to the three staffs produced simultaneously.
By what power arising simultaneously with them do these staffs remain? Or is their production in such a manner due to the force of a prior causal complex (*sāmagrī*)?

Or rather, is their coexistence simply due to the force of the causal complex characterized by the prior assembly of primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*bhautika*), just as they were established?
In the same way, even subsequently, there is the arising of those things that depend upon one another.
Furthermore, he shows that something else also occurs therein, and it is not merely their mutual strength.
He asks, "What is that? and says:
A string or three rods are fixed [therein];
the meaning is that it is either a peg or a stake.
Or else, the earth itself serves as the support below.
"Of these as well...

means that among these co-existent factors (*sahabhū*), there are also other causes—namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—which function like the "thread" and so forth; thus, the co-existent cause is established.
(II.53, 54ab) "Defiled [dharmas] are [the cause] of defiled [dharmas]" means:
Defiled, unwholesome, and obstructed-indeterminate states possess the nature of being similar causes (sabhāga-hetu) by virtue of their commonality as defiled states.
Therefore, unwholesome states are the similar cause of unwholesome states, and obstructed-indeterminate states are the similar cause of obstructed-indeterminate states.
It is thus shown that unwholesome states are the homogeneous cause of obscured-neutral states,

and obscured-neutral states are the homogeneous cause of unwholesome states; and neutral states are the homogeneous cause of neutral states— meaning, unobscured-neutral states are the homogeneous cause of unobscured-neutral states.
Form is indeterminate, and the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is an indeterminate homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) for the five aggregates.
However, the four aggregates beginning with sensation (vedanā) are not the homogeneous cause of form, because they are distinct [from it].
Indeed, that which is superior is not accepted as the homogeneous cause of that which is inferior.

Because of the statement "of the equal and the superior," wholesome and unwholesome matter, due to its being produced through volitional effort (*abhisaṃskārika*), is both equal and superior; thus, four [moments] serve as its homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
"Kalala is [the homogeneous cause] of the kalala and so forth.

The five embryonic stages—the stages of kalala, arbuda, peśī, ghana, and praśākhā—and the five postnatal stages—the stages of infancy, childhood, youth, middle age, and old age—these ten are the homogeneous causes for the ten stages.
Specifically, the kalala is the cause for another kalala, and so on, up to the stage of old age.
From an *arbuda* up to a *vārddha* of an *arbuda*,
and likewise from an *arbuda* up to a *vārddha* of a *vārddha*—
this should be stated for each homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) by decreasing one by one and omitting one by one.

When, among other similar types within the same homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), specifically from a human birth, only a human birth arises, then all ten stages [of existence] are [the causes] for all ten stages,
including even the stage of old age for the sake of the subsequent stages.
For that state of old age is the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) of the state of old age in that same birth at another moment;
however, it should be understood that the final state is the homogeneous cause even for all ten states, beginning with the kalala, in a subsequent birth.

The same applies even to external things, as detailed in the passage: "Barley is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of barley, not of rice; rice is the homogeneous cause of rice alone, not of barley. By this it is shown that although they are equally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the status of being a homogeneous cause exists only within one's own continuum (*svasaṃtāna*).
He shows that this is because there is no power to produce [a result] within another continuum.

"Past great elements are the cause and the dominant condition for future great elements" means that they are both the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Because they do not exist simultaneously, it is not a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).
For this very reason, and because it is neither mind nor mental factor (*acittacaittatva*), it is not an associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*).
Because it is not universal (*asarvatraga*), it is not a universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*).
Because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is not a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is understood that it is exclusively a similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
If similar [dharmas] are the similar-type cause of similar [dharmas], [then this applies].

In this way, it would follow that even what arises later is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of what arose earlier; likewise, what arises simultaneously would be a cause of what arises simultaneously, and what has not yet arisen would be a cause of what has not yet arisen. Therefore, he says:
Not all of them either;
rather,
those that are born first.
Those born earlier—whether past or present—are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
It follows by implication that those which are future are not a homogeneous cause. Likewise, past [dharmas] are the homogeneous cause of past and present [dharmas].
Those that have arisen previously are past; those that arise later are past. This should be explained by way of distinction.
It has been stated that past and present [dharmas] are the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) of future ones, but future [dharmas] are not the homogeneous cause of future ones.
From this it is understood that there is no future similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). "Never" means that it is never not a cause; this is the point under discussion.
The meaning is "it is precisely the cause.
Therefore, the intention is that the future similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) exists.
"Simultaneous," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
The intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) or purpose (*abhiprāya*) refers to the simultaneous cause (*sahabhūhetu*), the associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*), and the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*).
It is by means of that [intention] that the statement was made.
Therefore, because the statement was made with the intention of referring to the simultaneous, associated, and ripening causes, there is no fault in the assertion that "it is never not a cause."
For this teaching is intended to be based on the majority of cases;
it refers to the final stage.
The meaning is that it has in mind the ultimate state of the future.
His intention is that [the cause] exists even in the three time periods.
"This is not a valid rebuttal for him" means, in detail,
that this is not a valid rebuttal for that proponent.
Why?
Because that dharma, having not been a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) prior to its state of arising, becomes one afterwards;
the meaning is that it is not eternally a homogeneous cause.
Among future states that are to come into existence, one final state is fixed as being a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*);
many others besides it remain unfixed in that regard.
And concerning those, it was stated in general terms that they are not causes.
If this were the case, it would not be a valid rebuttal.
For even in a single state, one could just as well say: "That dharma which is the immediate antecedent (samanantara) of another dharma is not its homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu)."

The meaning is "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*). It is possible through this conceptualization that the factor (*dharma*), at the stage of its arising, becomes fixed in its status as an immediately preceding condition.
Therefore, with reference to that final state, it might be said—by means of this conceptualization—that there is never a case where [a dharma] is not immediately antecedent.
Why, then, did he say:
"if that dharma has not arisen"?
The meaning is that if that dharma is future, it does not become an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The proponent of the final state says:
"For the purpose of showing two aspects," and so forth.
Just as in that case, whatever phenomenon is the cause of another phenomenon, it is not at times not the cause of that phenomenon. He said:
"Never at any time"—
the same should be applied here as well:
whichever phenomenon is the immediate antecedent of another phenomenon.
"Is it ever the case that one dharma is not the immediate antecedent (samanantara) of that [other] dharma?
He replied:
"It should be stated that it is never so."
"If that dharma has not arisen," [it is] "just as it is here, so it is there.
How so?
Whatever dharma is the immediate antecedent (samanantara) of another dharma.
Sometimes that dharma is not the immediate antecedent (samanantara) of that [other] dharma.
He said:
"If that dharma has not yet arisen."
In this way it should be applied there.
How so?
Whatever phenomenon is the cause of another phenomenon.
Sometimes that dharma is not the cause of that dharma.
He said:
"If that dharma has not yet arisen."
The meaning is that if that dharma is future, it does not constitute a cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Regarding this, the Master says:
"If this were so, what benefit [would there be]? and so forth.
Thus, some merit is gained by this "twofold manifestation" (dvimukhasaṃdarśana).

For it is certainly not the case that, in its state of being produced, that dharma becomes a cause or an immediate antecedent (samanantara) in a primary sense; therefore, one might suspect a lack of skill on the part of the author of the treatise in speaking thus with room for objection in certain instances.
In some cases it is without scope; first, that which has scope is as stated: "Whatever dharma is the cause of whatever dharma."
Sometimes that dharma is not the cause of that dharma. He said: "Never."
Having stated that there is never a time when it is not a cause, he further explains:

"In its final state, it is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). If that dharma has not yet arisen, it cannot be an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), as there would be no opportunity for it.
"But that which has arisen is the immediately preceding [condition].
Here, the intended meaning is that having established a definitive point, he then alters it otherwise.
Therefore, this previous resolution alone is correct.
"There is no fault because this was said with the intention of referring to the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*), and the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*).
As for that which was stated [in the sūtra], "...
and so forth—whence does this follow?
It has been stated that what is future is not at all a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
If, then, the future is not at all a similar cause, why was the future view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) set aside?
For that which is set aside—
Thus it has been explained that [the view of a self-identity] is the cause of the view of a self-identity and is itself the cause of the view of a self-identity.
In this regard, how can a future view of a self-identity be the cause of the view of a self-identity?
It cannot first be a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) or an associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*), because it does not exist simultaneously [with its effect].
It is not a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
It is not a causal condition (*kāraṇa-hetu*) because it is not counted as being common.
By process of elimination, it must be either a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) or a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
And in this context, the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) is indeed nothing other than the similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
Therefore, if future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* is not the similar cause of [present] *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, why was it established for the sake of the third category?
The Vaibhāṣika says:

"Excluding the future truth of suffering associated with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi)"— this is how it should be formulated. Only that which is associated with the view of a self-identity should be excluded,
but not the view of a self-identity itself.

For that [feeling] and so forth, by way of the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) or the associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*), has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause and is itself a cause of the view of a self-identity;
it is not, however, by way of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
For the reading is: "this [past factor] is indeed the cause of future *satkāyadṛṣṭi*."
It should not be recited together with the word *tat* (that) which stands later in the sequence.
However, for the purpose of qualifying the associated truth of suffering (*saṃprayukta-duḥkhasatya*), these two words should be recited as a compound:
"associated with future satkāyadṛṣṭi" (*anāgata-satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃprayuktaka*).

Or rather, it should be understood according to the sense (*arthataḥ*) that if the reading were not made in this way, the reading produced by the objection in the Bhāṣya would not be authoritative; such is the intention. How then is the Bhāṣya on the *Prajñapti* to be interpreted, which states: "All dharmas are fixed within the fourfold [categories]"?
Regarding a cause:
whichever phenomenon is the cause of another phenomenon, that phenomenon is never not its cause;
the meaning is that it is a cause throughout all three times.

In this way, regarding that which is fixed with respect to its fruit: for whichever phenomenon there is another phenomenon that is its fruit—such as human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and so forth—that should be applied accordingly.

In this way, regarding that which is fixed with respect to its basis (*āśraya*): for whichever phenomenon, such as visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), there is a phenomenon that is its basis, such as the eye (*cakṣus*) and so forth—that should be applied accordingly.

In this way, regarding that which is fixed with respect to its object (*ālambana*): for whichever phenomenon, such as visual consciousness, there is a phenomenon that is its object, such as visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth—that should be applied accordingly.
The intention of the objector is that because phenomena are fixed with respect to their cause, they constitute a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) throughout all three times.
To show that there is no fault here because [the sūtra] does not intend to refer to every kind of cause, the Vaibhāṣika says:

"In this context, 'cause' refers to the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), but not to the homogeneous cause or the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)."
Because it has not been established in its future state,
it is not a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
This is because there is no ripening for any immovable (*āniñjya*) karma even in another realm of existence (*gati*).
The fruit consists of the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*),
because these two are the fruits of the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*).
This is the opinion of the Vaibhāṣikas.
"That which exists in the future arises.
Therefore, he raises this objection:

"But if that were so, does it not follow—that is, does it not result—that the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), having not previously existed in its future state, becomes a cause in its present state? This is the meaning.
It is indeed accepted that this applies to the state (*avasthā*), not to the substance (*dravya*).
It is accepted that the state of being a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for a homogeneous cause did not exist previously but exists now;
however, it is not the case that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the substance did not exist previously but exists now.
For the causal complex has the state as its fruit, not the substance as its fruit.
Through the causal complex of causes and conditions, the fruit is the present state, not the substance;
because that dharma exists substantially even when it is future.
"But it is not only in the present. The challenger asks:
"What, then, would be the consequence? and so forth.
The Vaibhāṣika says:
"It would be included in the treatise.
This refers to that future homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
And there is no such inclusion;
for it is not stated in that treatise that "future roots of goodness are the homogeneous cause of future roots of goodness."
The challenger says: "For indeed... and so forth. This is the intention of the challenger:
Even though the future exists as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), it is not capable of the activity of grasping or giving a fruit.

For it is only that [cause] which is past or present—and which is capable of the activity of grasping and giving a fruit, as well as the activity of projecting a fruit—that is designated as a homogeneous cause. This is because only such a cause is grasped.
There is no fault in not including a future similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*),
because it lacks the capacity for the activity of grasping or giving a fruit.
Therefore, a future similar cause does exist.
"And yet it is not stated in the treatise.
The Vaibhāṣika says:
"This is not so," and so forth in detail.
This is not tenable.
For a similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) is possessed of its fruit by way of its outflow-fruit (niṣyanda-phala),
and the outflow-fruit belongs to both the similar and the pervasive causes (sarvatraga).
Because it is stated that "the outflow is similar to its cause," and that [similarity] is untenable for what is future.
That [result] as a flow-on result (niṣyandaphala) is untenable.
Why?
Because of the absence of priority and posteriority.
In the future state, it cannot be determined that "this is prior" and "this is posterior" because they are dispersed;
and in the absence of a prior-posterior relationship, it is not logical for one similar thing to be the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of another similar thing.
Now, if it is thought:
Whether it be past or present, that which has arisen is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the future.
Therefore, he says:
"And it is not logical that what has arisen be the outflow of the future."
Just as the past is not the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the present, so too that which has arisen cannot be the outflow of the future. Why is this? He says:

Let there be no fault in the claim that "the fruit does not exist prior to the cause," because it is impossible for the ripened fruit (vipākaphala) to exist either before or simultaneously [with its cause].
Thus, "let there be no fault in the claim that the fruit does not exist prior to the cause" refers to the impossibility of its existence beforehand.
And there is no coexistence in the future state;
for in the present state, a fruit produced simultaneously with the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) is not perceived, as is the case with the coexistent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
Therefore:

Furthermore, because there is no distinction between "prior" and "subsequent" in the future time, it is not logical for a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to exist first and its ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) later, since the future time is disordered. Therefore, like the similar-cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the ripening cause also cannot be established as being in the future.
The Vaibhāṣika says:
This is not so, as it was stated that the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is also like this;
nor is it logical for there to be a mutual state of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
If a similar dharma is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of another,
how could that very same dharma be its outflow (*niṣyanda*) at that very same time?
For a son does not become the father of his own father at that very same time.
But it is not the case that the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is like this.
What [is not the case]? That there would follow, or result, the state of being mutual cause and effect without a temporal sequence of prior and posterior.
Why? Because the cause and the fruit have distinct characteristics (*bhinnalakṣaṇatva*). "Distinct characteristic" means that the cause has a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
its characteristic is either unwholesomeness or being wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, another characteristic of the fruit is that it is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) consists of the unwholesome and the wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava*);
the ripening (*vipāka*) is an indeterminate phenomenon (*dharma*).
Because of this statement.
"Therefore," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

The homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) is established only by way of its state; it is established according to its state. A homogeneous cause exists in the past state and the present state, but not in the future state.
But the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) is established by its characteristic.
Being established by its characteristic as having the aforementioned definition throughout all three times, even a future ripening cause is not excluded nor prohibited.
This is what is investigated here.

Is it because, in the future time, similar phenomena (*sabhāga-dharma*) are so dispersed that it is impossible to determine that "this is the cause" and "this is its outflow-result" (*niṣyanda-phala*)?
For this reason, the future is not established as a similar cause.
Or rather, [is it because] there might be a phenomenon that could be the similar cause of another phenomenon?
That dharma would be its outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) by virtue of its causes and conditions;
therefore, the future similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*) is not established.
This has not been examined by the commentators.
"But as for me, this very former position appears to be correct.
What is this restriction? Is it determined that [the object] must belong to its own level alone?
The intention is that it does not exist otherwise.
However, the path consists of nine stages [of meditation] for one another.
The word "tu" (but/however) serves as a qualification.
By "path," the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) is intended.
This distinguishes the truth of the path from that which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).

For a contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomenon is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) only for those belonging to its own level, not for those belonging to other levels; however, the Path (*mārga*), even when belonging to another level, is a homogeneous cause.
Here, by the mention of "level," both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena are included.
But if one were to take "dhātu" (element) [as the referent], it would follow that this applies only to that which is with-outflows (*sāsrava*); therefore, he says:

although there is an equal distinction of levels (*bhūmibheda*) for both those things that are with-outflows and for the Path (*mārga*), only the Path—spanning nine levels—is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for one another, and not those things that are with-outflows.
Why is this? He says:
For that [path] is adventitious to those stages; it does not fall within their realm (*dhātu*), because it is not appropriated by the cravings belonging to those stages.

Indeed, the cravings belonging to the nine stages—namely, those based on the desire, form, and formless realms—do not appropriate the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas in the way they appropriate the tainted (*sāsrava*) ones. This is because [the untainted path] is to be realized by relying on all nine stages, and thus it is not comprised within those specific stages.
When one then desires *nirvāṇa* or the Path, that is wholesome desire for the Dharma (*dharmacchanda*), not passion (*rāga*), because of the statement: "Because it is to be abandoned."
"Of the same kind" means of the same kind as that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).
If that were the case, it would follow that everything is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for everything.
Therefore, he says:
Regarding the phrase "of the equal and the distinguished":
[it refers to] mutual—
If so, for what purpose is the inclusion [of the term "homogeneous"]?
It is for the sake of [specifying] that there is mutual [causality] between a higher level and a lower level.
Thus, even something belonging to a higher level is a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for things belonging to a lower level that are either equal or superior.
"Even that which belongs to a lower stage [is the homogeneous cause] of those belonging to higher stages.
"For example," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

The receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is the homogeneous cause of that very same receptivity when it is in the future, by virtue of being equal to it.
And [it is a cause] for a superior [state], from the dharma-knowledge of suffering up to the subsequent knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of non-arising;
but not for an inferior one.
For the dharma-knowledge of suffering is not the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of the future dharma-knowledge-receptivity of suffering.
"The paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning [are the homogeneous causes] of three, two, and one [respectively].
This means that the path of seeing is the homogeneous cause of another path of seeing, of the path of cultivation, and of the path of no-more-learning—thus, it is the cause for three.
The path of cultivation is the homogeneous cause of another path of cultivation and of the path of no-more-learning.

It is not [the homogeneous cause] of the path of seeing; thus, for two [paths], the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga) is the homogeneous cause of another path of no-more-learning, but not of the path of seeing or the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga)—thus, it is the homogeneous cause of one.
"In that case also" means:

In that regard, among the paths such as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of those with dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*)— which has the nature of the path of seeing— is [the cause] for the path of those with both dull and sharp faculties that has that same nature;

the path of those with sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) is [the cause] only for the path of those with sharp faculties, and not for the path of those with dull faculties, because of the latter's inferiority.
In this same way, the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga) are to be explained.
To demonstrate that, he says:
"For example," and so forth.
Even for a single person of dull faculties, there are six paths;
for one of naturally sharp faculties, there are three.
Among these, the path of a faith-follower (*śraddhānusārin*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for another path of a faith-follower belonging to its own category.

The path of a follower of the Dharma (dharmānusārin) that belongs to oneself and is in a future state is the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) of six [paths]: its own path when it is of the nature of arising or non-arising as appropriate, and the paths of one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), one liberated by occasion (samayavimukta), and one liberated independent of occasion (asamayavimukta). Furthermore, the path of one liberated through faith is the homogeneous cause of four [paths]: another path of one liberated through faith, and the three other paths—those of one who has attained vision, one liberated by occasion, and one liberated independent of occasion.

The path of one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of two [other paths]: another path of one liberated by occasion and the path of one liberated irrespective of occasion (*asamayavimukta*).

However, the path of one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) is not the cause of the paths of those who follow through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or those who follow through the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), because the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) occurs at an earlier time, and because the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is superior [to it].
The same should be applied elsewhere as well.

The path of the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārimārga*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for three paths: another path of the follower by dharma, and the paths of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and one who is liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*). The path of one who has attained vision is the homogeneous cause for two paths: another path of one who has attained vision, and the path of one who is liberated at any time.
The path of one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) only for another path of one liberated at any time;
it is not, however, the homogeneous cause of the path of one who follows through faith (*śraddhānusārin*).
This is because the path of one who follows through the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) is superior in terms of its faculties (*indriya*).

Nor [is it so] because the path of one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) is superior by way of its faculties (*indriya*); nor because the path of one temporarily liberated (*samayavimukta*) is superior by way of its faculties.

In that case, it would follow that the path of one temporarily liberated is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for the path of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), which is superior by way of its faculties.
It does not obtain [the status of a fruit],
because it is comprised within the path of one beyond training (*aśaikṣamārga*).
For a cause that occurs at a later time cannot have a fruit that occurred at an earlier time.

Furthermore, the path of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for the path of occasional liberation (*samayavimukta*), because it is inferior in terms of the faculties (*indriya*). How so? This is the detailed explanation. How, moreover, can there be a homogeneous cause between the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), or no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) belonging to higher levels—from the second dhyāna up to the level of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)—and those belonging to lower levels?

According to the case, the path belonging to a lower stage—from the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) up to the stage of access (*anāgamya*)—is, as appropriate, either the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, or the path of no-more-learning;
it may be either equal or superior. It must be understood in some way [as such].
Because the lower stage is inferior, both in terms of the faculties and the accumulation of causes. First, regarding the faculties: he is either equal or superior.
On the path of seeing, the path of the follower by faith belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna is equal to that same path of the follower by faith belonging to a lower stage,
because both possess dull faculties.
However, the path of the follower by dharma belonging to a lower stage is superior to that very [path of the follower by faith].
Because of their sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).
Likewise, the path of the follower of Dharma (*dharmānusārimārga*) belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna is equal to the path of the follower of Dharma belonging to a lower level.

In this way, these very paths of the follower of Faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the follower of Dharma, when belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna, are each equal to the paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path beyond training (*aśaikṣamārga*) belonging to lower levels, which are distinguished by differences in level and faculty.
The terms "equal" or "superior" should be applied according to what is possible.

Likewise, on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), a path of one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) belonging to a lower stage is equal to a path of one liberated through faith belonging to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
because both possess dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*).
The path of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) belonging to a lower stage is superior to that very [path],
because of its sharp faculties.
Likewise, the path of occasional liberation (*samayavimukta*) belonging to a lower stage is equal to that very [path].
Because both possess dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*).
For that very person, the path of occasional liberation (*asamayavimukta-mārga*) belonging to a lower stage is superior because of their sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).

In this way, regarding the path of one beyond training (*aśaikṣamārga*) belonging to the level of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it should be applied as appropriate whether the path of a lower level is equal to or superior to it. Following this direction, all levels should be applied. How so? From the perspective of the accumulation of causes: since a path of a lower level may be either equal to or superior to a path of a higher level, this is stated.
In this regard, the phrase "of the paths of seeing and so forth" is the full statement.
By the inclusion of "and so forth," the paths of cultivation and the path of no-more-learning are subsumed.

Compared to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering belonging to a higher stage, the dharma-knowledge of suffering belonging to a lower stage is superior by way of the accumulation of causes.

Even compared to the dharma-knowledge of suffering belonging to a higher stage, the subsequent-knowledge-acceptance (anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti) of a lower stage regarding suffering is superior by way of the accumulation of causes; this continues up to the subsequent-knowledge-acceptance of a lower stage regarding the path compared to the dharma-knowledge of the path belonging to a higher stage. This is because it is accumulated through a greater number of homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu), increasing by one for each successive stage.
The path of cultivation belonging to a lower stage is superior to the path of seeing belonging to a higher stage by way of the accumulation of causes.

For the path of seeing is accumulated through the causes of the path of seeing alone, whereas the path of cultivation is accumulated through the causes of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Furthermore, the path of no-more-learning belonging to a lower stage is superior to the paths of seeing and cultivation belonging to higher stages by way of the accumulation of causes.
Because they are accumulated through causes belonging to the path of seeing and the path of cultivation:
a path of seeing belonging to a lower stage is equal, in terms of the accumulation of its causes, to a path of seeing belonging to a higher stage when considering simultaneous moments.
Likewise, a path of cultivation is equal to a path of cultivation, and a path of no-more-learning is equal to a path of no-more-learning.

Thus, in this way, a certain [path] may be equal in terms of the faculties (*indriya*) but superior in terms of the accumulation of causes (*hetūpacaya*), even though it belongs to a lower stage (*adharabhūmika*).

For example, the paths of the one who follows through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the one liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) belonging to a lower stage are superior to the path of the one who follows through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.
Conversely, a certain [path] may be equal in terms of the accumulation of causes but superior in terms of the faculties.

For example, (Abhidh-k-vy 206) compared to the path of one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna, the path of one who follows by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) belonging to a lower level is superior with respect to its moment;
that is to say, it is distinguished by way of its faculties (*indriya*) and by the accumulation of causes (*hetūpacaya*).

For instance, compared to the path of one who follows by faith belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna, the paths of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and one who is liberated at times (*samayavimukta*) belonging to lower levels are superior.
Furthermore, among the [nine grades] beginning with the soft-soft, each subsequent one is more accumulated by way of its cause.
This excludes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
because the soft-soft grade and so forth do not exist therein.

In that regard, compared to a weak-weak type from a higher level, even a weak-medium type from a lower level— and so on up to a strong-medium from a strong-weak— is equal or superior by way of the accumulation of causes, depending on whether the moments are similar or dissimilar;
for it is accumulated through causes consisting of one additional type at each stage.

As it was stated that the path of the faith-follower (śraddhānusārin) is the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) of six [paths], how can the path of the faith-follower be the homogeneous cause of the path of the Dharma-follower (dharmānusārin),
given that there is no simultaneous manifestation (saṃmukhībhāva) of those two within a single continuum?
To this, he says:
Even though the paths of the follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) and the follower by dharma (dharmānusārin) cannot both exist within a single continuum,
that which has arisen is the cause for that which is yet to come; for "impossibility" here refers to non-manifestation.
But it is not non-existence;
for those of dull faculties possess their own paths of sharp faculties just as they possess paths of dull faculties.

However, the paths of one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) would only become manifest in that continuum if the transformation of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*) were performed.

Therefore, the path of the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) that has arisen is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*)— as appropriate— of the future paths of the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) which are destined not to arise, and of the paths of those who are liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), those liberated at times (*samayavimukta*), and those liberated independent of time (*asamayavimukta*), whether they are destined to arise or not, and whether they are equal or superior. However, Master Vasumitra says:

It is incorrect to say that the arisen path of the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārimārga*) is the cause for the unarisen path of the follower of the Dharma (*dharmānusārimārga*) or the path of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāptamārga*), on the grounds that followers by faith and others, when transforming their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*),
bring the path of the follower of the Dharma and so forth into manifestation.
This is untenable.
For one who follows by faith does not transition between faculties;
however, those such as those liberated through faith may so transition.
These are called "attained through application."
Those produced by application (*prayoga*) are "applied" (*prāyogika*).
The inclusion of the term "applied" is for the purpose of excluding those acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*).
"Belonging to the desire realm and consisting of what is derived from hearing" (*śrutamaya*) [is the definition].
Those who have emerged through hearing the word of the Buddha are those consisting of hearing;
those consisting of reflection are for those consisting of reflection.
[This applies] only to those consisting of reflection, not to those consisting of hearing;
for it is stated that [this occurs] only between those two when they are equal or superior.
"Because of the absence of that which consists of cultivation (bhāvanāmaya)":
since the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is non-concentrated, there are no [wholesome roots] consisting of cultivation.
"Because of the absence of that which consists of reflection (cintāmayābhāvāt)": [this refers to the same reason].
For when they begin to reflect, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) itself arises for them; this is the reason why there is no [wisdom] consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*) for them.
"For them as well" refers to this.
Regarding those consisting of hearing and so forth:

"the weak-weak are [the homogeneous cause] of all" means that the weak-weak [states] are the homogeneous cause of other weak-weak states of equal strength, as well as of the eight other distinct states, such as the weak-medium and so on; thus they are the homogeneous cause of all.
The weak and medium [degrees] of the eight [types of defilements] exclude the weak-weak variety because it is inferior.
This is the principle.

For example, the weak-intense [defilements] are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of the seven [remaining types]; the medium-weak [defilements] are the cause of the six; and so on, until the intense-intense [defilements] are the cause of those of the same kind that are one degree lower than the intense-intense.
This is because each preceding one is set aside due to the inferiority of each subsequent one.
Regarding "wholesome [states] acquired through birth" (*upapatti-pratilambhika*): acquisition by way of birth is "acquisition through birth."
Those who possess this [nature] are those who have acquired it through birth (*upapattipratilambhika*).
Here, the suffix *ṭhan* is applied according to the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*.
All nine types of these are mutually homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*).
[This applies] from the weakest of the weak up to the strongest of the strong.
The strongest of the strong is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of [factors] from the weakest of the weak up to the strongest of the strong;
it is not [the cause] of only those that are equal or superior.
Because it is non-productive (*anābhisaṃskārika*).
For it is not accepted that a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) which is productive has a result inferior [to itself], but this is not the case for one that is non-productive.
"Defiled [dharmas] are also like this.
All nine types are mutual homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) because they do not require effort.
All those that have arisen previously are homogeneous causes for all subsequent [dharmas] belonging to the same level.
In this context, equality and superiority are not required.
These [factors] are, respectively, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of four, three, two, and one.
That which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is the homogeneous cause of the four [types], beginning with that which is born of maturation.
The airyāpathika [mind] belongs only to the three beginning with the airyāpathika;
it does not belong to those born of maturation (vipākaja),
because they are inferior due to being non-volitional (anābhisaṃskārika).
Those belonging to the sphere of craftsmanship (śailpasthānika) are the cause of two: those of the sphere of craftsmanship and those of emanation (nairmāṇika).
Those of emanation are the cause of only those of emanation, and not of the preceding ones.
Because each subsequent [level] is produced through volitional effort (*ābhisaṃskārika*).
Even the mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) is the fruit of the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
Since it is the fruit of the four meditative absorptions—the fruits of the first, second, third, and fourth *dhyānas*—the mind of emanation belonging to the desire realm is of four types.
In that order, it continues: "the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) belongs to four, three, two, and one [respectively].

The fruit of the first dhyāna is the homogeneous cause of four fruits: those of the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas. The fruit of the second dhyāna is the homogeneous cause of three fruits: those of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
The fruit of the third dhyāna is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for two [fruits], namely the fruits of the third and fourth dhyānas.
The fruit of the fourth dhyāna is the homogeneous cause for only one [fruit], namely another fruit of the fourth dhyāna itself.
What, then, is the reasoning by which such a restriction is established? Desiring to point out that reasoning, he says:
The fruit of a higher dhyāna is not [the homogeneous cause] of the fruit of a lower dhyāna; this is the detailed explanation.

Furthermore, the emanation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to the fruit of the fourth dhyāna is not the homogeneous cause of an emanation-mind belonging to the fruit of the first dhyāna, nor of one belonging to the fruit of the second, up to the third dhyāna—all of which belong to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
He asks, "Why? and replies:

For the fruit of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) that is produced through volitional effort (*ābhisaṃskārika*) and accomplished with great exertion cannot be inferior—that is, accomplished without great exertion.
Indeed, by means of a specific kind of effort, the first dhyāna up to the third dhyāna is brought to completion.
The fourth dhyāna is not accomplished by such [effort] alone;
rather,
it is accomplished by a more excellent and specific effort.
Therefore, it is understood that its fruit is produced by a specifically superior effort;
thus, the fruit of a lower dhyāna is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the fruit of a higher dhyāna,
but the fruit of a higher dhyāna is not [the homogeneous cause] for the fruit of a lower dhyāna.
And just as the fruit of the fourth dhyāna has been applied, so too should the fruits of the third and second dhyānas be applied.
For this very reason, they say: [as follows].
The meaning is: because there is no inferior fruit for a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) that is produced through volitional effort (*ābhisaṃskārika*), therefore they say [this].
What do they say? They say: [as follows].
"It may be that [it] has arisen," and so forth.

The untainted *duḥkhe dharmajñāna* (knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering) that has already arisen is not the cause of those untainted *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣāntis* (receptivities to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering) which are of a nature not to arise.
This is because *duḥkhe dharmajñāna* is superior to the *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣāntis* by virtue of its being a product of volitional effort (*abhisaṃskārika*).
For it is thus distinguished: that which arises together with the attainment of dissociation from the afflictions is distinguished;
and what is distinguished is not the cause of what is inferior.

For example, for one who has fallen away from arhatship, the previously arisen path of an adept (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the subsequently arising paths of once-returners and non-returners. [The text continues:
"Could it be that which is restricted to a single continuum (*ekasaṃtānaniyata*) and previously acquired? and so forth.
The future receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) are acquired at the very first moment; they belong to a single continuum.
The dharma-knowledge regarding suffering arises in the second moment;
those [preceding moments] are not its cause,
because the fruit does not exist prior to it.

For the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering arises prior to the receptivities to the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering; this is because the former has already arisen while the latter have not yet arisen.
Or because a future phenomenon (*anāgata-dharma*) is not a similar-cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Future receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) are indeed obtained in immeasurable numbers, but they have not yet arisen.
[The phrase] "it would be previously arisen" (*syāt pūrvotpanna*) is the full statement.

Previously, it was stated that a dharma which has merely been acquired but not yet arisen does not constitute a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), because that which has not arisen cannot be a homogeneous cause.

Now, however, it is asked with greater precision: even if it has previously arisen, can there be a case where it is not a homogeneous cause? [The answer is: "A superior [dharma] is [the cause] of an inferior one."
The meaning is that a superior [state] belongs to one who is inferior.

For example, in the case of one who has fallen away from a higher fruit— whether from the fruit of arhatship, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of once-returning— there is the manifestation of a lower fruit, such as the manifestation of the fruit of non-returning or the manifestation of the fruit of once-returning.
The superior path of arhatship that has arisen previously is not a homogeneous cause for a subsequently arisen fruit of non-returning or a fruit of once-returning,
because it is inferior [to them].

Likewise, for one who has fallen away from the fruit of non-returning, that path of the fruit of non-returning which had arisen previously is not a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for the subsequently arisen fruit of once-returning,
because it is inferior.
"And the acquisition of the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering," and so forth.

The acquisition of the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering that has arisen previously is co-arisen with those moments that arise subsequently—namely, with the subsequent moments beginning from the moment of the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering up until the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path—and with those [factors] co-arisen with [the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path]. Regarding suffering... [Tib.195b]
For those who have attained the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*), [the receptivities] are not homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*).
What is the reason?
Because they are inferior.
And because that [subsequent knowledge] is superior.
But how is there inferiority in those [forbearances] and superiority in that?

For the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) is superior to the forbearance of the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), because it is liberated from the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions to be abandoned by that [forbearance].
And because it has been accumulated by causes to a greater degree.

Therefore, the acquisition of the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) is superior even to the acquisitions of the receptivities to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) that have been accumulated by causes to a greater degree; and those [receptivities] are inferior because they are merely its acquisitions.

Furthermore, the acquisition of the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering is superior to the acquisition of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering arising in the first moment for precisely those two reasons.
Furthermore, that attainment of the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣāntiprāpti*) is inferior.

Therefore, even though they are preceded by it and arise simultaneously with subsequent moments, other attainments of the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering are likewise inferior, despite having accumulated more causes.
Consequently, it is not the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for them.
(II.54cd) "The associated cause, however, consists of mind and mental factors.
The word "however" (*tu*) serves to restrict the meaning and its position is displaced [from its logical place].
"Only mind and mental factors are the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*).
"This being so," and so forth.

If it were stated merely that "only mind and mental factors are the associated cause," then even those [factors] arising at different times would be associated with those arising at different times, and those arising in different continuums would also be associated with those arising in different continuums.
The associated cause (saṃprayuktakahetu) would follow as a consequence;
for they are not different in terms of time or continuum, nor are they anything other than mind and mental factors (cittacaitta).
[If you say they are distinct because they have] the same aspect (ākāra) and object (ālambana), then...

If mind and mental factors have the same aspect, such as the single aspect of blue and so forth, and have the same object, namely the single object of blue and so forth, then they are associated causes (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) and not otherwise.
The intention is that by this, being born at different times and being born from different continuums (*saṃtāna*) are thereby excluded.
Even so, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains.
The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of things produced in different times and different continua being mutually associated causes (*saṃprayuktakahetu*).

For it is indeed possible for minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), even those produced in different times and different continua, to have the same aspect (*ākāra*) and the same object (*ālambana*).
Thus, there would be the undesirable consequence [of association] even for those produced in different continua.
The state of arising at different times is explained as one [instance].
For when many people see the new moon and so forth, their minds and mental factors (citta-caitta) proceed with a single form as their objective support (ālambana).
They have a common basis (samāśraya).
Thus:
they have a common, undivided basis; therefore, they are called "having a common basis" (*samāśraya*).
For if the word *sama* were used in the sense of "equal" (*tulya*), then that same undesirable consequence would follow, because they are equal by virtue of their genus (*jāti*).
"In the sense of mutual fruit," and so forth: just as travelers in a caravan proceed on the road through their mutual strength.

In this way, the mind is the fruit of the mental factors, and the mental factors are also the fruit of the mind; thus, they are mutual fruits. In that sense, they are co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*). "By five" is the full statement.
By means of five equalities.
The meaning is: by means of the equalities of basis, object, aspect, time, and substance.
It is the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) in the sense of having an equal application and in the sense of functioning equally.
Just as those very merchants, traveling along the road by mutual support, have an equal application toward the activity of enjoying food, drink, bathing, bedding, and so forth;
in the same way, there is a state of equal application among these [factors] for one another.
For this very reason, he said:
For indeed, not even one [of them] is dissociated from all [the others].
(II.55ab) "The previously mentioned universal [factors]" refers to those.

And they are "all-pervading" (*sarvaga*) because they go everywhere; that is to say, they are "all-pervading" because they have arisen previously. This means that the all-pervading latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), belonging to their own level, which have arisen previously—whether past or present—are [the causes] of the subsequent defiled states, whether past or present, that are of the nature of afflictions and are associated with or originated by them.
And [we shall] explain that it is the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) for future [dharmas].
(Abhidh-k-vy 210)

"The views to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its cause, as well as doubt, together with the ignorance that is associated with them and that which is unique"— this we shall explain in the fifth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
"By way of being the general cause of afflicted phenomena," and so forth.
This is because this universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) pertains generally only to afflicted phenomena, even across all five categories;
whereas the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), however, pertains to both afflicted and non-afflicted phenomena.
Therefore, it is established separately.
To demonstrate how this [ignorance] serves as the general cause for afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*), he says:
"Because it is also the cause for those belonging to other schools (*nikāyāntarīya*)."
"Indeed, by the power of these.
Indeed, by the power of these universal [defilements], defilements such as attachment (*rāga*) belonging to other classes and arising in other realms of existence are produced.
But what, then, are they?

The categories of defilements to be abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) that belong to other classes become the pervasive causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) for those to be abandoned by seeing the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The categories of defilements to be abandoned by seeing the truth of origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*) that belong to other classes become the pervasive causes for those to be abandoned by seeing the truths of suffering, cessation, and the path, as well as by cultivation.
They go toward and resort to all categories of defilements with respect to their objects (*ālambana*).
They are called "universal" (sarvatraga) because they function as the cause for all categories of afflictions.

For this very reason it was said: "All afflictions are rooted in the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi); they originate from the view of a self-identity; they arise from the view of a self-identity."
Because greed, pride, hostility, and so forth arise by way of the grasping at a self.
[The question is: "Is this also the case for a noble person (āryapudgala)?
For a noble person, all pervasive [defilements] are entirely abandoned, because they are to be abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya).
Furthermore, passion and the other afflictions manifest in those who are still in training (śaikṣa).
Thinking that these passions and so forth do not have universal causes (sarvatraga-hetu) for them, he asks this question: "What are the afflicted phenomena (kliṣṭa-dharma)?"
Because it is not specified otherwise, it is understood that [the maturation] arises in the mental continua of both ordinary persons and noble ones.
Furthermore, the statement "that which is the maturation of the factors to be abandoned by seeing" was said for the purpose of completing the sense of the argument.
This is not an example [of all] conditioned phenomena being indeterminate; rather,
both the obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) are included.

The obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) factors in the desire realm—namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of grasping at extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and the factors associated with or originated from them—as well as the afflicted factors belonging to the form and formless realms.
The inclusion of the term "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) is for the purpose of excluding space and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha).
These are the two supreme unconditioned (paramavyākṛta) eternalities.
Thus, because these two are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),

the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) factors belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) have as their causes only those very [afflicted] factors— such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth— which serve as their homogeneous (*sabhāga*), pervasive (*sarvatraga*), co-arising (*sahabhū*), or associated (*samprayuktaka*) causes, according to the case; they do not have other [afflictions] such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth as their causes.
It is easy to understand that those belonging to the higher stages [are produced] by other causes as well.
The non-obscured-neutral states have non-obscured-neutral states as their homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
As for the unwholesome states, these are the attachment and so forth belonging to the desire realm.
And those [defiled phenomena] have the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth as their pervasive cause (sarvatragahetu). This is the illustration here.

Furthermore, because it is not specified that they are "unwholesome" (akuśala), both those to be abandoned by seeing (darśanaprahātavya) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāprahātavya) are included.
This is the second indicator here.
As for the statement, "That other afflicted truth of suffering," this is the third indicator.
For that other afflicted truth of suffering is understood—without further specification—to include both that which is to be abandoned by vision and that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.

For it has been explained that, by way of the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*), even for noble ones—as well as for ordinary persons—the [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation are caused by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), yet they are not causes of the view of a self-identity.
If this is so, then how is this *Prajñaptibhāṣya* to be interpreted?
For if unwholesome states have neutral (*avyākṛta*) causes as well, and not only unwholesome causes, how is the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* to be reconciled?

It may be so. When an noble person (āryapudgala), falling away from detachment from the desire realm (kāmavairāgya), first brings forth a defiled volition (kliṣṭā cetanā), at the time of that falling away from detachment from the desire realm,
that volition of the noble person has exclusively unwholesome roots (akuśalahetu) by way of both the co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) and the associated cause (saṃprayuktakahetu).
"Because the views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) have been abandoned, they do not have neutral states as their cause.
Thus, the meaning of the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* is perceived.
It is with this intention that he raises the objection.
The Vaibhāṣika says:
"This was stated with reference to a cause that has not been abandoned.

This passage from the *Prajñapti-bhāṣya* was spoken with the intention of referring to, and having in mind, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) when they have not been abandoned.
For the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, which are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*), are the cause of that volition (*cetanā*);
because they have been abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are not mentioned in the *Prajñaptibhāṣya*.
(II.55cd) [The remaining factors] are the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the wholesome-with-outflows (*kuśalasāsrava*).
Unwholesome states are necessarily with-outflows (sāsrava) alone, and thus they are not further specified.
Wholesome states, however, are of two kinds: with-outflows and without-outflows (anāsrava). Therefore, they are specified.
Those [dharmas] which are wholesome and with outflows (*sāsrava*) are the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*), whereas those without outflows (*anāsrava*) are not;
this is because they possess the nature of maturation (*vipāka-dharmatva*).
The meaning is: "because its nature is that of a ripened [result].
"Because of its weakness, like a rotten seed," is the full explanation.
Just as rotten seeds, even when moistened, do not become a cause for the production of a sprout due to their weakness.
Thus, indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena, even when moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), do not become causes for the arising of maturation (*vipāka*) because they are weak.

Untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena, although powerful, do not produce maturation because they are not moistened by craving. Just as dry, potent, and substantial seeds do not produce sprouts when they are not moistened by water.
It is the same in that case:
for some there is a deficiency of their own capacity, while for others there is a deficiency of other auxiliary causes.
To what [realm] is this connected?
In what is it associated?

What is the result associated with? [The result] is not associated; it is produced as something unassociated among the realms such as the desire realm, being untainted (*anāsrava*). There must be a result that is associated.
Not by that which is unassociated,
because its intrinsic nature consists of dharmas associated with the desire realm and so forth.
"But the remaining ones," and so forth.
The unwholesome [dharmas] and the wholesome-with-outflows (sāsrava) are of both kinds; that is to say, they possess both types because they are of a type characterized by powerful moisture.
They bring about maturation (vipāka), just as seeds that are moistened with a core [of vitality] produce a sprout;
it is just like that.

"The cause of maturation," and so forth. If *vipāka* is a noun derived from the root with the suffix *-ghañ* in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*), then it means "maturing" (*vipakti*), and in that case, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

"Of the ripening (*vipāka*)," [it is said] "the cause. Now, if it is understood as "that which ripens by itself," then the suffix *ghañ* has the sense of an object (*karman*). In that case, the ripening itself, being the object, is the cause; thus, it is the "cause of ripening" (*vipākahetu*).
What follows from this? What fault arises from it?
If one adopts the interpretation that "cause of maturation" is a noun-based derivation (*bhāvasādhana*), then it would not follow that "the eye is born of maturation."
For the eye is not born from maturation;
rather,
the meaning is that it is born from the karma that is the cause of maturation.
For a maturation is not a cause.
Alternatively, if "maturation itself is the cause," this is an adoption of the etymological derivation based on the object (*karman*).
Thus, it is established that the eye is "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
For it is precisely karma that ripens as maturation (*vipāka*), because it is said that "maturation ripens.
However, the expression "the maturation of karma" would not be tenable;
for maturation is said to be karma itself, not the process of ripening (*vipakti*).
And here, in the expression "the maturation of karma" (*karmaṇo vipākaḥ*), the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*) is intended, not the sense of an action (*karmasādhana*).
Therefore, the construction "the maturation of karma" would not be possible [if the latter were intended].
It was stated previously that the application [of the term] is valid in both ways.
They are born of maturation and accumulation.
Regarding the statement "five are internal," those produced from the cause of maturation are "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
It is a derivation based on the sense of an action (bhāvasādhana), following the principle of eliding the middle term as in the word *goratha* ("ox-cart").
Alternatively, an action that has reached the time of its fruition is called "maturation" (*vipāka*),
because it "ripens" (*vipacyate*).
Therefore, "born from that" means "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*); this is the adoption of a derivation based on the action (*karmasādhana*).
But since maturation (*vipakti*) itself is the fruit, it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*).
The meaning is that when one intends to express the fruit, it is adopted as a derivation based on the state (*bhāvasādhana*).

Therefore, it is established that "the eye is born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) either through the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopa*) or by adopting the derivation as an object (*karmasādhana*),
since maturation is the result of karma. It is also established [that the eye is born of maturation] by adopting the derivation as an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*).
For the comprehension of words is preceded by the speaker's intention.
"Vipāka" means a dissimilar ripening;
that is to say, a result that is dissimilar to its cause.
For the cause is indeed determinate, whereas the fruit is indeed indeterminate.
However, in the case of the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the others, the ripening is only similar; thus, there is this qualification.
The Abhidharma treatise is explained in this manner; therefore, it is taught with reference to this:
"A single-skeighed retribution cause has a single fruit," and so forth.
In this context, acquisitions (*prāpti*) exist separately from the mind and other factors, like the bark of a tree.
The distinct fruits of these [causes] are described according to the principle of their fulfillment.
That which has a single aggregate (*skandha*) is a "single-aggregate" ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
[This refers to] bodily and vocal actions, as well as their birth-moments (*jāti*) and so forth.

Because vocal action is subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Since the acquisitions (*prāpti*) reside in whichever aggregate [they pertain to], and their birth (*jāti*) and other characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) reside in that very same [aggregate], they constitute a single aggregate.
Furthermore, whatever is the fruit of the acquisitions is precisely the same as the fruit of their birth and other characteristics.
Because it has a common fruit, it is "single-fruited.
A two-aggregate ripening cause is single-fruited;
it consists of bodily and vocal karma along with their birth-characteristics and so forth.

Because bodily and vocal action are subsumed under the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), while their birth-characteristic and so forth are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), they consist of two aggregates.
And they have a single fruit,
because they do not have separate fruits.

The four aggregates constitute a single fruit: wholesome and unwholesome mind and mental factors. These, together with their [characteristics] such as birth and so forth, [constitute that fruit], because those mind and mental factors are, as appropriate, comprised within the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

Furthermore, because birth and the other [factors] are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), a retributive cause consisting of four aggregates has a single fruit, since its fruit is common [to all].

For there is no fruit for the mind that is distinct from the fruit of the mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth; this is because [the latter] are not in a state of meditative composure (*asamāhita*).
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no retributive cause consisting of five aggregates.
For in this case, bodily and vocal action subsumed under the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) does not have the same fruit as the mind and mental factors (cittacaitta),
because they constitute separate groups.
However, the "three-aggregate" (triskaṃdhaka) [karma] exists in all three realms, because the mind and mental factors necessarily share a single fruit.
Because they have, as appropriate, the nature of four aggregates (*catuḥskandhasvabhāvatva*).
"In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is one aggregate," and so forth:
acquisition (*prāpti*) together with its [characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*) is included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); thus, it consists of one aggregate.
In the same way, because it has a common fruit, it is "of one fruit.
Non-percipient attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) should also be described in the same manner, together with its birth and other characteristics,
because informative action (*vijñapti*) is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

And because birth (*jāti*) and the other [characteristics] have the nature of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), a [karma] consisting of two aggregates has one fruit, as previously stated.

When the mind is wholesome but not concentrated (*asamāhita*), there is no concomitant matter (*anuparivarti-rūpa*); therefore, since it is comprised of the aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*) while excluding the aggregate of matter (*rūpaskandha*), it consists of four aggregates.

The *Pañcaskandhaka* [states]: "When the mind is in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*), there is no concomitant form (*anuparivarti-rūpa*), because form that arises following the mind exists only as a single occurrence together with the mind and its mental factors.
The detailed explanation continues: "In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)... and so forth.
In that case, since no form at all exists [therein], the retribution cause consists of either one aggregate or four aggregates.
Regarding "attainment" (prāpti):
therein, together with its own birth-characteristic and so forth, it consists of one aggregate, as previously described.

It is easy to understand that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), together with its own [characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth, constitutes a single aggregate (*skandha*) that is a ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) with a single fruit.
"There is karma," and so forth:
there is karma for which the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the ripening.

The maturation (*vipāka*) of that karma necessarily consists of that life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and those dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth. Since all of this is comprised within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), one single sphere— the sphere of phenomena—
matures as the maturation for that which has the mind-sphere (*manāyatana*) as its basis.
For that [resultant consciousness], there are two bases: the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*).

For within the complex of that mind-base, there are necessarily co-arising factors such as feeling (*vedanā*), as well as the material form that is maturation (*vipāka*), such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth.

Since these factors—feeling and the others, as well as birth and the others—are subsumed under the phenomena-base, those two, the mind-base and the phenomena-base, constitute the maturation that ripens.

In the same way, for one for whom the sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) [is the object of ripening], that tangible must necessarily possess its birth and other characteristics; thus, the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) also ripens.
It is not only the sphere of the tangible; therefore, two spheres ripen for such a person.
For one who possesses the sense-base of the body, there are three [bases]:
that very sense-base of the body, the sense-base of the tangible, and the four primary elements which serve as its support;
for it necessarily depends upon those four primary elements.
And since that [resultant state] must possess birth and so forth, the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) also ripens there as the third.
"In this way," and so on in detail;
thus, for one whose maturation is any one of the spheres of visible form, odor, or taste.
Three of its bases are maturation (*vipāka*).

That very base is either one among the [bases] beginning with visible form (*rūpa*), namely the base of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), which has the nature of the primary elements that serve as its support, or it is the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), which has the nature of the [characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*) arising from that.
This applies to whichever has the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*).
For that [person], there are four [bases].
Namely, that very eye and the body-base (*kāyāyatana*), because their functioning is necessarily bound to the eye and the body;
and the tangible-object-base (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*), as before.
