"Thus, for whomsoever... and so forth.
Thus, for whomsoever one among the ear and the other [senses] is a maturation (*vipāka*), for that person as well, four bases (*āyatana*) are a maturation.
That very same [karma] consists of any one of the sense-bases beginning with the ear, as well as the sense-bases of body, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), as previously described.
"There is that karma," and so forth;
it may consist of five up to eleven sense-bases, according to what is possible.

But the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*) are not maturation (*vipāka*), because the sense base of sound (*śabdāyatana*) has the nature of being non-maturation. Regarding this, Master Vasumitra explains:
It is not tenable that there is karma for which only a single sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) ripens as its maturation (*vipāka*). What is the reason?
Because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the fruit of the projecting karma.
If, first of all, life in the desire realm matures as a result of karmic maturation (*vipāka*),

then in that case the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) necessarily exist during the stages of the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth, before the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have arisen.
But once the six sense-bases have arisen, there must be seven sense-bases.
[The faculties] consist of the six beginning with the eye and the mind-base (*manāyatana*).

In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as well, there must necessarily be seven [faculties], and in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there must necessarily be two: the mind-base and the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*).
This is because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has as its fruit the projection of an entire birth.
Which realm is intended here? We reply: the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
But surely, since the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) there is the fruit of projecting karma, it must necessarily also be accompanied by the mind-base (manāyatana).
Furthermore, it is not the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) alone that ripens as maturation (*vipāka*),
because maturation is characterized by feeling (*vedanā*).
Therefore, feeling must also be present there.
To this it is said: This was stated with reference to momentary arising.
It refers to that moment when, for one born in the formless realm, a mind born of maturation does not manifest.

At that moment, it is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) alone that ripens as maturation (*vipāka*). Since only the life-faculty arises as maturation and the mind-base (*manāyatana*) does not yet manifest, for what reason does another mind-base not exist when that [life-faculty] manifests? This is what is being investigated: that there are two bases for it—the mind-base and the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*).

Thus, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is indeed the maturation (*vipāka*) of the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*). And when the life-faculty matures, the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*) and the others also mature.
It is not that the maturation of other bases is being denied.
The ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) is considered here.
There exists such karma for which only a single sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) ripens, and no other sphere; this much is what is intended to be expressed.
Now, if it is thought that the very same karma which projects the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) also ripens as the mind-base (manāyatana) and so forth—
and not just a single base— then we reply as follows.
Other factors existing there, such as the sense-base of mind (*mana-āyatana*) and so forth, are also the maturation (*vipāka*) of that very same karma, and not of another karma.
What establishes this restriction?
For it is indeed possible that the maturation of a single karma is the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
"The life-faculty belongs to one [person],
while the mind-base and so forth belong to another. You might say this in the same way that the eye-base belongs to a particular person.

Regarding the statement that for such a person there are the sense-bases of the eye, body-tangible objects, and mental phenomena: for one whose eye-base is a maturation, their body-base must necessarily also be so.
Likewise, the mind-base and the others are also the maturation of that very same karma.
That is not so, because the occurrence of one thing is dependent upon another only in certain cases.
For indeed, there is no manifestation of the eye-faculty without the body-faculty.
However, even in the absence of maturation (vipāka), there is the manifestation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) within the mind; therefore, this [position] is unequal.
But the Master Saṃghabhadra says:
"There is karma for which only the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) matures as its maturation."
For one who possesses the life-faculty and the eye-base, there are five [faculties].
The sense bases of the eye, body, visible forms, tangibles, and mental phenomena;
and so on, up to the sense base of the tongue.
For whom there is the sense base of the body...
It has four [objects]:
visible forms, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).

Because it is inseparable from visible form, another school maintains that the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is also the maturation (*vipāka*) of that very same karma which produces the eye.
However, this teacher maintains another position: that the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is not necessarily the maturation (*vipāka*) of that very same karma;
rather, for one who possesses the sphere of body (*kāyāyatana*), there are three [spheres].
"For one who possesses the eye-base, there are four [bases]"—

the intention here is that the life-faculty, the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), and so forth, which are invariably concomitant with one another, are not necessarily the maturation (*vipāka*) of the same single karma.
These two positions have been set down by the authors of the *Vibhāṣā*. Whichever of these two is pleasing to someone, that one is accepted by them.
Enough of this digression.
Now, how is it that for some karma a single *āyatana* ripens as its maturation (*vipāka*), while for others up to eleven? To this he says:
"Because karma has both variegated and non-variegated fruits, like external seeds," and so forth.
The seeds of the lotus, pomegranate, banyan tree, and others have variegated fruits;
for the lotus seed and the rest possess a diversity of forms through their roots, sprouts, stalks, leaves, filaments, anthers, and pericarps.
And trees such as the *nyagrodha*, rich with many trunks, branches, twigs, leaves, shoots, sprouts, flowers, and fruits, are seen acting like clouds;
some have unvariegated fruits,
such as the seeds of barley, wheat, and so forth.
Because they have a single form of fruit,
this is the nature of seeds:
the ripening of a single-moment action that is past matures as a ripening belonging to the three times— past, present, and future.
But it is not the case that for karma belonging to two time periods—namely, the past and the present—the result belongs to only one period, namely, the future;
nor is it the reverse.
That is to say, for karma consisting of many moments, there may be a result consisting of a single moment.

It continues: "Let it not be that the fruit is too small for its cause. Furthermore, maturation does not ripen simultaneously with the action, because the simultaneous (sahabhū) and associated (samprayuktaka) causes operate upon what has arisen together with them.
And because the ripening cause depends upon a ripening that is dissimilar [to itself],
the ripening does not mature immediately after [the cause].
What is the reason?
Because the immediately succeeding moment is drawn forth by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This is because the immediately succeeding moment is drawn forth by the power of the immediately preceding condition, not by the power of the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Even if that immediately preceding condition were itself a ripening cause, this would still be the case.

Because the immediately subsequent moment—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—arises from the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) by way of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Otherwise, it would necessarily be only neutral. Alternatively, the intention is that the immediately subsequent moment, which is by nature not subject to ripening (*avipāka-svabhāva*), is drawn forth by the immediately preceding condition.

For the cause of maturation (*vipākahetu*) depends upon a continuous stream; it is the nature of things that when a stream of mind and mental factors is present, the cause of maturation would yield its maturation once that stream has passed away.
This is the intended meaning.
It has been stated [previously] that, in terms of their actual meaning, the restriction regarding the time periods (*adhvan*) for these [causes] has been established.
The meaning is that it is stated by way of implication, not by its own explicit word.
For speech is of two kinds: that which is expressed by its own term and that which is stated through implication.
How so?
The homogeneous cause consists of similar factors belonging to their own category and level that have arisen previously.
Likewise,
the so-called universal cause consists of the previous universals within their own level for defiled factors.
Because of this statement,
the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) exist only in the past and the present, not in the future.
By the very statement that there is no distinction, it is implied by the sense that the co-existent, associated, and retributive causes belong to all three time periods.
For it is only the similar and pervasive causes that have arisen previously;
this is because of the restriction that "only those two have arisen previously."

Because it is stated that they are mutual fruits, and because their intrinsic nature consists of reflection and so forth, as well as unwholesome states and so forth, their non-inclusion within the [three] time periods is excluded. Thus it is set forth in the Sūtra.
It is made into a thread or a string; it is "sūtryate.
And the reason for this has already been stated.
How was it stated?
For a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is possessed of its fruit by means of its outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
And that is untenable for what is future, because of the absence of priority and posteriority; such is the argument, and so forth.
This is the reason that has been stated regarding the similar cause.
The nature of the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) should also be understood as having the form already described. For the pervasive cause is similar to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
Indeed, the homogeneous cause consists of defiled [dharmas] for [other] defiled [dharmas].
The pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) is also defiled, and it belongs only to defiled phenomena.
However, it has already been stated that this is established as a separate category from the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) because it serves as the general cause for all defiled phenomena.
Like the homogeneous cause, this [pervasive cause] does not exist in the future.
And it is "fruitful" by way of its outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
Its account is exactly like that.
There are three belonging to the three time periods.
Thus,
because of the restriction that "only those belonging to the three times are the three," and "only the three belong to the three times," the efficient cause (kāraṇahetu) is otherwise.
And how else [could it be]?
[It would be impossible for it] to be both "belonging to all time periods" and "liberated from time periods.
For all dharmas other than itself—excluding its own self-nature—are the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Therefore, it is exactly thus and not otherwise.
(II.56cd) Since these two—cause and fruit—are mutually dependent, he asks:
"But what is that fruit for which these are the causes?"
"Conditioned phenomena together with dissociation are the fruit.
This means it is stated that all dharmas, excluding space and analytical cessation, are the fruit.
"If that is so," and so forth.
Since the unconditioned is a fruit, considering that "the unconditioned is a fruit," it must have a cause other than itself;
for there must be a cause of which that unconditioned is the fruit.
And because the unconditioned is a cause, it must have a fruit other than itself;
that fruit for which the unconditioned is the cause belongs to the conditioned—
those two, cause and fruit, pertain to the conditioned.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), characterized by analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), is the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
It has no cause because it is not produced;
yet it is a cause because it exists as a state that does not obstruct the arising of conditioned phenomena.
And no fruit is established for that [unmanifest action],
because it is incapable of receiving or giving a fruit.
For this very reason, it is said in detail that "the six kinds of causes are impossible."

Neither a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) nor an associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*) is possible for this [unconditioned], because it does not co-exist with any dharma and is not associated [with any].
It has no homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu),
because the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is without similarity and because it is impossible for it to belong to the same level (samānabhūmi).
For this very reason, it is not its pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*),
because it is non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).
Nor is it its retribution cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Because the unconditioned has the nature of being non-resultant.
For fruition is a phenomenon that is reckoned as a sentient being and belongs to the realms of existence.
And precisely because it is not produced, these [three] causes do not apply to it.
Precisely because it is unproduced (*anutpādya*), this [dissociation] does not have a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*).
For this very reason it is asked:
"Why is the path (*mārga*) not accepted as the causal condition for dissociation (*visaṃyoga*)?"
Because it is established as being non-obstructive to arising,
and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) does not possess arising; furthermore,
because it does not fall within the temporal periods (adhvan), it does not have causes.
For a cause is established for a dharma that has entered into the temporal paths (adhvan).
Thus, because the six kinds of causes are impossible, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) has no cause;
and because the five kinds of fruits are impossible, the unconditioned has no fruit.
Why?
Because, in general, that which is devoid of the time periods (adhvan) is incapable of receiving or giving a fruit.
For it has been said:
The five [paths of action] existing in the present take up their fruit; two give it forth,
and so forth.
Furthermore, it cannot first be the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
For that is held to be either co-arisen or subsequently arisen;
[however], a conditioned thing that has never existed before is indeed the dominant fruit of a conditioned thing.
Thus,
because that [nature] is non-arisen, it has neither an innate nor a subsequently arisen fruit,
precisely because it is non-arisen.
Nor is it a flow-on result (*niṣyandaphala*).
For a flow-on result is a similar dharma that arises from something that has arisen;
for this very reason, it is not a result of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), because there is no human effort in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
For that which arises or is attained by the power of something is the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) of that [cause].
For this very reason, it is not the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyogaphala).
For dissociation is to be attained solely by the power of the path,
and the path is not unconditioned;
nor, moreover, is it a fruition of maturation.

Because it differs from the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*). For the cause of maturation is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not associated with outflows.
Alternatively, because of the dissimilarity with the five kinds of causes, there is the impossibility of five kinds of fruits; thus, a fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not possible.
If it is not accepted that the Path is the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), then whose fruit would that be?
For a fruit must possess a cause; in what way, or by what manner, could that be its fruit?
He said:
As for what was stated, "Of what, then, is that the fruit?"—it is the fruit of the path.
And as for what was also stated, "Or how is that its fruit?"—the meaning is that it is a fruit because it is obtained through the power of that, namely, the power of the path.
Alternatively, the connection between the words is as follows:
"Of what is that the fruit?
It is the fruit of the path.
Or how is that its fruit?
[Because] it is attained by means of its power. In that case, attainment itself would then be the fruit of the path.
In that very attainment, due to the efficacy of that path, there is no disjunction. What [is not]?
It is understood from the context that this refers to the fruit of the path.
Regarding the phrase "because of incapacity there":
this means that, in that state of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), the path lacks the capacity [to act as its cause].
Therefore, for the time being, the path is not in any way whatsoever the cause of this [dissociation].
Not even one of the six causes serves as the cause for this path.
And its fruit is dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).
The intended meaning is that the fruit to be attained is not something produced.
Some maintain that there are five kinds of causes:

the producer (*kāraka*), the informer (*jñāpaka*), the manifester (*vyañjaka*), the destroyer (*dhvaṃsaka*), and the bringer-about (*prāpaka*). Of these, the producer cause is, for example, the seed of a sprout.
Smoke is the indicator of fire;
a lamp is the manifester of a jar;
a mallet is the destroyer of a jar.
"A chariot is that which brings about the attainment of another place for one who is to be brought there.
Thus, in this way, the path is the bringer of this [attainment], not its generative cause.
It is thus shown that the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*), which is to be attained, is not something produced.
Now, as for the detailed explanation beginning with "if there were no sovereign fruit" (*adhipati-phala*):
if the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) were to have a fruit, it would have to be a sovereign fruit.

Because it is established as its efficient cause (kāraṇahetu), and because of the statement that "those two do not belong to the unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta), that [objection] has also been refuted for him; thus, once this has been determined, the interlocutor asks:
Now, if there is no dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), how can the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) be a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*)?
It is a causal condition by virtue of being non-obstructive to arising;
this is because it is described as having the nature of being non-obstructive to arising.
It is only in relation to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) that this unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is established as a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*);
it is thus shown that it is not [established] in relation to the unconditioned.
Why is its fruit (*phala*) not established in the same way as that of the conditioned? To this he says:
And it has no fruit,
because that which is excluded from the [three] time periods is incapable of receiving or giving a fruit.
For only a dharma comprised within the time periods possesses the capacity to receive and give a fruit, and nothing else does.
For it will be said: "The five [dharmas] existing in the present grasp the fruit; two give it."
"But it has been stated as a synonym that [the self] is the cause.
This means it was stated by way of a synonym, not by its own specific term.
"They too are impermanent" refers to those [elements].
Because of the restriction that "those too are indeed impermanent," it follows by implication that the cause is not permanent.
The same applies to the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*);
just as the causes here have been stated to be impermanent.
In this way, conditions (*pratyaya*) are also said to be exclusively impermanent, because of the statement: "Those which are causes (*hetu*), those which are conditions.
Therefore, it follows that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot be an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
This is because of the restriction [in the sūtra] to "for the sake of arising" (*utpādāya*).
Those causes and those conditions for the arising of form are themselves impermanent;
however, those [conditions] for its non-arising are not.
For conditions are of two kinds:
productive and non-productive.
The object-condition (ālambanapratyaya) is non-productive, because it is merely an object.
For the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) exercises its activity upon a dharma that is in the process of ceasing,
because it is grasped by present mind and mental factors (citta-caitta).
Two causes exercise their activity upon that which is in the process of ceasing.
Because of this statement.
Now, as for the detailed explanation beginning with "causes also":
a cause is both productive and non-productive.
Therefore, there is no prohibition against the unconditioned being a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*), even though it does not produce [an effect], by virtue of its mere state of non-obstruction.
It was stated that the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) is taught in the Sūtra;
namely, in the Sūtra on the "four conditions" (*catasraḥ pratyayatā*).
But it has not been prohibited.
The intention is that there is no fault because it does not contradict the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, many sūtras have disappeared.
Because of the loss of the original recitation (*mūlasaṃgīti*),
the Master does not insist on this point,
for there is no contradiction with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Rather, it is precisely the unconditioned that is being investigated as to whether it exists or not.
"The unconditioned" refers to everything;
it is not merely analytical cessation.
"As with form, sensation, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), perception and the others are included.
Just as sensation is a distinct entity from form, and perception from sensation, and so on up to consciousness being distinct from the formative forces (saṃskāra).
Likewise, there is no unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entity that exists as a distinct thing apart from the five [aggregates] beginning with form (*rūpa*).
Therefore, the Sautrāntikas maintain that the unconditioned is not a substantial entity (*dravya*),
but is merely the absence of the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*).
The meaning is: merely the absence of a substance possessing resistance (*sapratigha*). "Not finding" means not obtaining.

Regarding the cessation of arisen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and birth: through the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), that is, the power of wisdom (*prajñā*), there is the non-arising of further latent dispositions and further birth once those already arisen have ceased.
Thus, it is stated that the cessation of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is the cessation of the truth of origination, the cessation of birth, and the cessation of the truth of suffering.
Furthermore, the mention of both types of cessation is for the purpose of establishing the distinction between nirvana with remainder and nirvana without remainder.
According to the Sautrāntika system, what are these latent dispositions?
And how is there the cessation of their birth through the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*)?
Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is the underlying tendency.
And for whichever underlying tendency there is a path that serves as its antidote, that is analytical discernment.
Together with that [moment], in the first instant, that latent tendency (anuśaya) arises.
By its power, in the second and subsequent instants, there is the cessation of that [tendency].
And by that very power, there is the cessation of future rebirth without further linking (apratisaṃdhika).
It is as follows: "of that which remains of the homogeneous class," and so forth.
The homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) is characterized by being human and so on;
or it is the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), characterized by the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Its remainder arises with that very characteristic.

When there is an intermediate death due to the remainder of one's homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), there is a non-arising of that [remainder] even before the life-span is exhausted, due to a deficiency of conditions;
that is analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).

Furthermore, the deficiency of conditions refers to the incapacity of the final aggregates—known as the state of death—to connect with a new homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), due to the incompleteness of conditions such as the necessary requisites.
Therefore, this is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
This is the nirvāṇa-element with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
The non-arising of suffering is nirvana without remainder. Furthermore, that non-arising of suffering is what is called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
It is not established without discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*),
because the deficiency of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), which is the cause of arising, is produced by discernment;
therefore, this is precisely cessation through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
"By its own cessation" means by its own nature, not through the power of wisdom;
for [the latter] would be absent if [the former] were not destroyed.
Because as long as that underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) has not been destroyed, there is an absence of its analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Regarding the phrase "for those whose obstruction to arising has not been made":
those for whom an obstruction to arising has not been made are "those whose obstruction to arising has not been made" (*akṛtotpattipratibandhāḥ*).
Among those,
that which is the state of being an obstacle to arising—
this is the efficacy of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā*) in this context.
"If, then, it is precisely non-arising," and so forth.
For what is intended by "abandonment" is nirvāṇa;
and if nirvāṇa is said to be the non-arising of only that which is yet to come.
Since that which is past and present has already arisen, there is no non-arising; how then was it stated in the Sūtra:

"They lead to the abandonment of suffering that is past, future, and present"? How is that scriptural passage to be interpreted for one who holds that *nirvāṇa* is a distinct substantial entity (*dravyāntara*)?
Because one attains *nirvāṇa* through the cultivation and so forth of that [path] even with respect to the past and present, this Sūtra is well-expounded.
"By the abandonment of the afflictions having that as their object" means by the abandonment of the afflictions that have past and present suffering as their object.
"Whatever desire and lust for form":
desire (*chanda*) is the longing for an object not yet attained;
lust (*rāga*), however, is the attachment to an object already attained.
In detail, up to "consciousness":
whatever desire and lust there is for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— abandon that.
When desire and attachment are abandoned, in this way that consciousness of yours will be abandoned.
It is the same for suffering belonging to the three time periods as well.
The abandonment of desire and attachment is itself the abandonment of the suffering of form and so forth.
And there occurs the non-arising of that future desire and attachment.
Thus, he shows that the abandonment of suffering belonging even to the three time periods is logical.
"This is the very method" means:

If the reading is "for the sake of abandoning past, future, and present afflictions," the same principle applies there as well: it refers to that desire-attachment toward an affliction, whether it be lust or hatred.
"Abandon that," and so forth.

The meaning is that because the afflictions which take that [object] as their focal point are abandoned, the affliction itself is also abandoned; it is not abandoned by its own nature alone. Thus, the abandonment of afflictions belonging to all three time periods is logically consistent.
Now, as for the detailed explanation beginning with "or else":
existence in a previous birth is *paurvajanmika*;
existence in this birth is *aihajanmika*.
Thus, in this way, the affliction (*kleśa*) belonging to a single moment is excluded.
How is this to be understood?
It is connected with all afflictions of the previous life as well as those of the present life.
But it is not momentary; therefore he says:
"As in the case of the movements of craving," and so forth.
Since this is seen elsewhere as well, it should be understood in this way.
How are the eighteen modes of craving (tṛṣṇāvicarita) to be applied to a single moment in the past time? Therefore, with reference to a past birth, it is said:
"There are eighteen modes of craving.
O monks, when there is the thought 'I am,' there arises the thought 'I am thus.'"
"There is the thought: 'I am thus,' 'I am otherwise,' 'I am existent,' or 'I am non-existent.
The thought occurs to him: 'I shall be';
or the thought occurs to him: 'I shall not be,' 'I shall be such,' 'I shall be thus,' or 'I shall be otherwise.'"
The thought "May I be" occurs to him;
the thoughts "May I be thus," "May I be so," or "May I be otherwise" occur to him;
and the thought "May I exist" occurs to him.
"May I also be thus, may I be so, may I be otherwise"—such thoughts occur to him. This applies up to the present life as well.
Likewise here too, the entire stream of afflictions from previous births and those of the present birth are connected; they are not merely momentary.
Thus, he states the intention regarding what is to be established:
"By those two types of afflictions," and so forth.

By these two types of afflictions—those belonging to a previous birth and those belonging to this birth—a seed-state, characterized as a latent impression (*vāsanā*), has been deposited within this present continuum as a capacity for their future arising.
Through the abandonment of that seed-state, those two types of afflictions also become abandoned.
It is just as it is metaphorically said that karma is exhausted through the exhaustion of its maturation and the experiencing of that maturation;
it is exactly like that.
How, then, is the abandonment of that which is future established?
For the seed-state has not been deposited in the continuum by that [future entity], such that its abandonment would constitute an abandonment. Therefore, he says:
"Furthermore, the abandonment of future suffering or affliction is their absolute non-arising due to the absence of the seed-state."
And the state of being a seed exists by the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*).
For when [the object] has ceased in the past, or is present and facing cessation, effort toward the production of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) is neither meaningful nor purposeful; this is the sense.
"Detachment (*virāga*) is the foremost among them."
The meaning is that the destruction of passion (*rāgakṣaya*) is dispassion (*virāga*), which is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
How can that which is non-existent be worthy of being the foremost among things that are non-existent?
That is to say, how can the non-existent, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dispassion be worthy of being the foremost among non-existent unconditioned things such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like?
He states the reply to this:
"Even non-existence is a certain [kind of thing]," and so forth.
And "of the second" refers to...

Immediately after the second [truth], the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), there is the fulfillment of the third by means of three things: having seen it for oneself through wisdom (*prajñā*), having pointed it out, and having taught it to others.
What might these be?
"What would be the fault? means what would be the disadvantage. "And what more would there be? means what would be the benefit.

Furthermore, regarding the inquiry into its qualities—"What would [the result] be?"—it is said that the Vaibhāṣika position would be upheld. As for what was asked, "What would it be? What would be the fault?", it is replied here as follows:
"But it would be an unreal construction"—
the meaning is that there would be a fault.
"Like form, sensation, and so forth."
"By direct perception," as in the case of the eye and so forth; this means "by inference from its activity."
This has been explained more than once.
"Of the entity" means of the entity consisting of passion and so forth.
"Because of the possibility of the state of cause, effect, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth," relations such as owner and owned, part and whole, and others are included.
For when a thing has ceased, there can be no cause and effect, nor part and whole, and so on.
"Regarding the restriction of its attainment," and so forth.

This refers to the restriction concerning the attainment of that cessation—the restriction that the attainment belongs to this specific cessation alone and not to any other. What is the cause for that restriction of attainment?
For there is no connection whatsoever between cessation and its attainment, because the relationship of cause and effect and so forth is impossible.
"One who has attained nirvana in the present life" means one who abides in nirvana with remainder (sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa).
If it is a non-existence, how could there be its attainment? [The answer is:
"By the attainment of the counteragent," and so forth.
By the attainment of the Noble Path, because one attains a basis that is absolutely opposed to the arising of afflictions and renewed existence, it is said that Nirvana has been attained.
"Being a mere non-existence. The word "mere" (mātra) is for the purpose of excluding it being a separate substance.
"That which indeed belongs to this," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
"Abandonment" up to "non-manifestation" are synonymous terms.
"Non-manifestation" is stated as an example because it is clear;
they show that since there is no manifestation in this, it is "non-manifestation" (*aprādurbhāva*) by way of a locative derivation (*adhikaraṇasādhana*).
The meaning is that "non-appearance" (*aprādurbhūti*) is not a term denoting an entity (*bhāvasādhana*), namely non-appearance itself.
Since the attainment of that [cessation] is postulated— that is, since the abandonment is postulated as attained through a certain path—
it should be accepted that there is a non-appearance of suffering when that path exists or when that attainment has been reached.
What is the use of imagining another nirvana?
"Liberation of that mind" refers to the time of the Blessed One’s nirvana without remainder.
"According to the object, according to the focal point.
The object of conjunction is that wherein one is conjoined with a defilement; those phenomena which possess such an object are "with object," meaning they have a cause.

"Appropriation" (*parigraha*) means that the object of appropriation (*parigrahavastu*) is appropriated; that very object is the "object of appropriation. [The phrase] "because it is mentioned at the end" refers to this. (II.57)
At the end of the *kārikā*, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is mentioned; its fruit is exclusively the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*). The former—
The efficient cause (kāraṇahetu) is mentioned at the beginning of the verse;
its fruit is the dominant fruit (adhipaja-phala).

*Adhipati* means the sovereign (*adhipa*). That which is born from that is "born of the sovereign" (*adhipaja*), meaning the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Some read *pūrvādhipatam* instead of *pūrvasyādhipatam*.
"This is the fruit of the dominant [condition], thus it is 'ādhipata'.

However, one would expect it to be "ādhipatya," because of the exception [stated in the rule]: "The suffix *ṇya* is applied after *diti*, *aditi*, *āditya*, and words that have *patya* as their final member."
(Abhidh-k-vy 222) Now, it might be argued that even in a case of an exception, there is the inclusion of a general rule,
and thus it would possess that nature;
namely, that this very thing constitutes sovereignty (*adhipatya*).
That which is the abiding in the mere state of non-obstruction;
or rather, there is also the state of being a factor (*aṅgībhāva*).
This means that there is also the state of being primary (*pradhānabhāva*) and the state of being a producer (*janakabhāva*).

Thus, by this it is shown that for both types of causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*)—whether it be an agent (*kāraka*) or a non-agent (*upekṣaka*)—there exists a sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*), with the exception of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
For it will be stated:
"The sovereign fruit of a conditioned phenomenon is exclusively a conditioned phenomenon that has not previously existed."
Thus:
"of the ten bases" means from the base of the eye and the base of visible forms, up to the base of the body and the base of tangible objects.
Because of the statement: "Dependent upon the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises; likewise, dependent upon the body and tangible objects, tactile consciousness arises.
And this is indeed a causal cause (*kāraṇahetu*).
For the sense bases such as the eye are not the co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu) and so forth of visual consciousness and the others; indeed, the five types of causes do not occur [between them].
However, for mental consciousness, the mind base (manāyatana) can be its homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) and other such causes.

Since the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) can also arise through causes such as co-existent (sahabhū) and associated (saṃprayuktaka) causes, it is not restricted to being only the efficient cause (kāraṇahetu).
Therefore, it is said that [the efficient cause] applies to ten [bases], and not to twelve.
And this also applies to the actions [that produce] the receptacle world (bhājanaloka).
What?
It is the subject under discussion that there is a state of being a subordinate factor (*aṅgībhāva*) for the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*).
For the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), although produced by wholesome and unwholesome karma, is not admitted to be a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*), even though it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because it is defined as "maturation is that which is designated as a sentient being," this is therefore the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) of that causal condition (kāraṇahetu).
It belongs not only to the eye, but also to the ear and the other [faculties].
What [is it]?
It is that the eye has sovereignty over the arising of visual consciousness only indirectly,
not directly, as is the case with the eye itself.
How is this known? He says:
because the desire to see arises upon hearing [the teaching].
And the intention is that visual consciousness arises when there is a desire to see.
"Such cases are to be applied accordingly.
This means that "because the desire to see arises after having smelled," and so forth, should be applied.
[Furthermore,] the outflow (*niṣyanda*) belongs to the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and omnipresent (*sarvatraga*) [causes].
The term "fruit" (phala) continues [from the previous context].
It is restricted that the outflow fruit (niṣyandaphala) belongs only to the similar cause (sabhāgahetu) and the pervasive cause (sarvatragahetu).
For the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) can also arise immediately after those two.

"Human effort belongs to two" means that the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) alone [belongs] to the co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) and the associated cause (saṃprayuktakahetu); this is the restriction.
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is the "human" (*pauruṣa*); the meaning is "the fruit of human effort.
Because it is not distinct from the state of being a person, human effort is not separate from the state of being a person.
For human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is simply the action of a person; it is not something other than the person.
Indeed, the Buddhists do not maintain that action is distinct from those who possess the action.
Therefore, whatever is the fruit of human effort—
That which belongs to a person alone is called "puruṣa" (human). "The activity of whichever dharma" means the function or the action of whichever dharma.
That is his "human effort" (puruṣakāra); this is the meaning.

Now, one might object: since there is no person (puruṣa) with internal activity, and the "person" is merely a phenomenon (dharma), it would follow that it is a "phenomenon-effort" (dharmakāra) rather than a "human effort.
To this he says: [it is indeed human effort].
For "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) is like the effort of a person;

just as in the world there is the human effort of a person who is conceptually constructed, so too is there the human effort of a dharma. Thus, it is called "human effort" because it is like the effort of a person.
He provides an illustration:
"The *kākajaṅghā* herb," and so forth.
An herb that has the shape of a crow's leg is called *kākajaṅghā*.
If a person is seen who is like a rutting elephant or is a hero, one might say, "That man is a rutting elephant.
What of others?
"Of causes":
this refers to other [types of] causes as well—
namely, the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Except for the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Why? He says:
because the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is either co-arisen or immediately arisen.
For it has been stated that the fruit arising simultaneously belongs to both the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*).
And that is exclusively the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*);
for there is no other fruit that arises simultaneously.
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) arises only immediately after the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*).
For the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), however, it occurs in both ways.
But is the fruit of human effort distinct from the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) or the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*)?
No, it is said.
For that very same fruit receives various names according to its context.
Thus, because it arises similar to its cause, it is called the "outflow fruit" (niṣyandaphala).
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) arises because [the result] originates through the power of that [cause];
and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) arises because it originates by remaining in a state of non-obstruction.
However, it is not a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
What is meant?
It refers to whether it arises simultaneously or immediately after [the cause].
(II.58, 59) Retribution is an indeterminate dharma.
Thus it is in detail.
It is indeed indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Only that which is designated as a sentient being arises from the determinate.
"Evam" (thus) is a restriction.
By "indeterminate" (avyākṛta), the non-obscured indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta) is intended.
That which has "sentient being" as its designation is called "designated as a sentient being."
The meaning is that it arises from the continuum of a sentient being (*sattvasaṃtāna*).
It is "arisen from the determinate" (*vyākṛtodbhava*) because it originates from what is determinate (*vyākṛta*).

However, the accumulative (*aupacayika*) and the outflowing (*naiṣyandika*) do not arise from the determinate (*vyākṛta*). But is it not the case that the accumulation of the sense-faculties and the great elements occurs for one who has entered a particular meditative absorption (*dhyāna-viśeṣa-samāpanna*), and that this too arises from the determinate?
That [result] is a maturation,
and the mind of emanation is likewise; for both are produced from the mind of meditative concentration.
This is not a fault.
In the expression "arising from the determined" (*vyākṛtodbhava*), the word "out" (*ud*) signifies a subsequent time.
That which arises at a later time from a wholesome or unwholesome [action] that has been projected— neither simultaneously nor immediately—
is maturation (*vipāka*). However,
the accumulation born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) arises both together with the concentration and immediately after it.
The transformation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*), however, arises immediately after [the mind that produces it].

Furthermore, since it is intended that the maturation (*vipāka*) belongs to the same level (*samānabhūmika*), both of these [transformation-mind and maturation] can belong to different levels; thus, there is no unwanted consequence regarding maturation.
The outflow (*niṣyanda*) is similar to its cause.
Thus [it is said],
with reference to the similarity between the wholesome, the afflicted, and the unobscured-neutral.

If this were so, then it would follow that an outflowing fruit (niṣyandaphala) which is untainted (anāsrava) arises from a cause that is wholesome but tainted (sāsrava), because of their similarity as being wholesome.
No, because there is an absence of similarity of category (*nikāya*).
For it is held that a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) must belong to the same category.
Not all [dharmas are similar].
Its similarity is by way of level and by way of being afflicted.
That is to say, the similarity of this pervasive cause (sarvatragahetu) is by way of its level and by way of its being afflicted.
With what?
With its own fruit. How so?
First, with respect to the levels (*bhūmi*), the omnipresent cause (*sarvatragahetu*) ranges from the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgrika*).
Its fruit (*phala*) likewise ranges from the desire realm up to the peak of existence.
Furthermore, by virtue of being afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), the omnipresent cause is itself afflicted.
That fruit is also afflicted,
but it does not have similarity by way of its mode, as is the case with the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu).
However, for that [cause] which has similarity even by way of its mode—
That universal cause (sarvatragahetu) which possesses similarity even in terms of its mode (prakāra) with its own fruit is indeed accepted as being a similar cause (sabhāgahetu).
For it becomes a universal cause precisely because of the similarity in terms of its level (bhūmi) and its afflicted nature (kliṣṭatva).
And it is also a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) by virtue of similarity in its mode.
For this very reason, a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) is formulated,
because the third alternative is possible due to its possessing both natures.
The first alternative is: "the non-universal homogeneous cause.
This refers to the homogeneous cause consisting of attachment and so forth;
for that is indeed a homogeneous cause only for the afflictions belonging to its own category.
But it is not a universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*), because its intrinsic nature is non-universal. Regarding the second [type], the universal cause belongs to another category:
the universal [defilements] such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth.

For that is indeed a universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) because its intrinsic nature is universal and because it is the cause of defiled states belonging to other categories. It is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
Because there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for that which is defiled but not of the same category.
The third [alternative] is the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) belonging to the same category;
this refers to the universal [defilements] such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
For it is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of a defilement belonging to the same category, due to its similarity with other defiled states of that same category;
and it is also the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*).

Because it is omnipresent (*sarvatraga*) and because it possesses the nature of being the cause of defiled states belonging to the same category (*ekanaikāyika*), as well as the nature of being an omnipresent cause (*sarvatragahetu*).
The fourth [alternative] is "setting aside these modes";
the meaning is: excluding the types of phenomena described in the three propositions (*trikoṭi*).
For example, afflicted phenomena are not the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of wholesome phenomena because they are dissimilar;
nor are they the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*),
for the same reason and because wholesome phenomena are non-afflicted.
In this same way, wholesome states should be applied to afflicted states.
Afflicted states are also not homogeneous causes for other afflicted states,
nor do they constitute universal causes.
For example, desire and the like are not the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of defiled states belonging to other categories, because they belong to different categories.
Nor are they the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), because desire and the like are not pervasive.
Furthermore, even pervasive factors are neither the homogeneous cause nor the pervasive cause of defiled states belonging to their own category.
If they are future, this should be applied accordingly.
"Disjunction is cessation through wisdom" means that the cessation attained by wisdom is the fruit of disjunction (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
"By that" means for that reason; because "destruction" (kṣaya) is cessation (nirodha), and "wisdom" (dhī) is insight (prajñā).
For that reason, he explains that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is said to be the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*):
"That which arises by the power of [a certain cause]."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
"The power of which" (*yasya balam*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). From whose power it arises...
Whatever is conditioned, that is a fruit.
The meaning is that "born of human effort" (puruṣakāraja) refers to what has arisen from human effort; it is the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala).
He provides an illustration:

for example, the preparatory mind belonging to a lower level— either the desire realm (kāmāvacara) or the first dhyāna level— has as its object a meditative absorption (samādhi) belonging to a higher level, such as the first dhyāna level or the second dhyāna level.
The phrase "result born of human effort" (puruṣakāraja) is the subject under discussion. For a contaminated (sāsrava) phenomenon, an uncontaminated (anāsrava) one may be its result;
for a mind in meditative absorption (dhyānacitta), a mind of emanation (nirmāṇacitta) is precisely that result.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), other cases are also included.

For example, from a death-moment consciousness belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), there arises the first moment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*); such examples of different types are given for the purpose of distinguishing them from the outflow-result (*niṣyandaphala*).
For a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) belonging to a higher level is not the outflow-result of a preparatory mind (*prayogacitta*) belonging to a lower level.
For that which belongs to a different level is not similar to its cause;
nor should it be said that the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) arises from the contaminated (*sāsrava*).

However, not everything that is a flow-on fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) is also a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*). For when something arises by the power of another, being similar to it, belonging to the same level, and occurring immediately after it, [it is both].
That constitutes for him both the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
In this regard, there are four logical possibilities (*catuḥkoṭika*):
there is that which is solely the fruit of human effort and not the outflowing fruit.
As it has been illustrated:
there is a result that is exclusively a flow-on result (*niṣyandaphala*) and not a result of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*);
namely, the result of homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*) and pervasive causes (*sarvatragahetu*) when it is separated [from them].
There is that which possesses both:
the fruit of the immediately preceding [cause] and of the similar and omnipresent causes.
There is that which possesses neither.
For example, the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) arises from the cause of maturation (vipākahetu).
Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) is also accepted as the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala);
yet, because it is eternal, it does not arise by the power of a cause. Therefore, although this was not mentioned in the verse, he now provides a supplementary explanation of it.
However, it must be stated that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) is that which is attained through a certain power. For analytical cessation is attained by the power of analysis;
therefore, it is the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) of analysis.
"Unprecedented," and so forth.
"Unprecedented" means other than what has previously arisen.
What, then, is that?
It is that which arises simultaneously and that which arises subsequently;
for it is not the case that the fruit exists first and the cause later.
Only a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*) is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), not an unconditioned one (*asaṃskṛta*);
it belongs only to the conditioned, not to the unconditioned,
because the latter lacks the capacity to receive or bestow a fruit.
"Of all" means of both the progenitor and the one who remains in a state free from obstacles.
"The fruit of human effort" refers to the result for the agent.
Because of the statement: "That which arises by the power of something is the fruit born of human effort (*puruṣakāra*). (Abhidh-k-vy 226)
"Even for one who is not the agent, there is a sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala).
This is because of the statement that "the sovereign fruit of a conditioned phenomenon is exclusively a conditioned phenomenon that is not its predecessor."
For others, it is exclusively the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
For those who are not artisans but remain in a state of non-obstruction regarding that craft, that craft is exclusively the sovereign fruit and not the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
Thus, there are four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There is that which is only the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and not the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*),
such as the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
There is also that which is only the sovereign fruit and not the fruit of human effort.
For a neutral cause, the fruit is both remote and immediate;
for an agent cause, it is both co-arisen and immediately arisen.
There is that which is neither; namely, space and cessation not through deliberation. (II.60) "The five present [factors] are the fruit."
The restriction is that only those [dharmas] which are present take up their fruit.
"They take up" means that they project [the result] and remain as its cause;
the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is also like this.
Only that which is present receives its fruit, not that which is past or future;
however, it is not stated that this [present cause] necessarily possesses a fruit,
for the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is accepted as a causal condition (kāraṇahetu).
Furthermore, it has no fruit;
and the causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*) is future.
Nor is it possessed of a fruit by means of a dharma that is presently arising prior [to itself].
"Two give," refers to those currently engaged in the activity.
The co-existent and associated causes give their fruit only when they are present. It is indeed logical that they do so when past;
these two are said to possess a fruit by virtue of their outflow-fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
Because it is stated that "the outflow [result] belongs to the similar and the universal [causes]," how then do these two,
while being present, bestow an outflow result?
For their outflow (niṣyanda) is not observed while they are in the present state; therefore he says:
"Because of its production immediately following [them].
What?
It is understood that [the phrase] "they grant the fruit" applies here. And those two [past causes] have also become past,
because of the non-coexistence of cause and fruit.
"But not that very same [action] is given" means "but not that very same fruit is bestowed.
For the verbal form *datta* (given) ends in the dual number.
Because [the action] has already been given away precisely in its present state.
For that which has been brought to the present cannot be brought again.
And when those two [past causes] bestow their fruit, they are past.
At that very moment, they bestow their own fruit;
for the fruit is produced at the very stage of its arising and not at any other time.
It should simply be understood that this fruit is merely obstructed.
"Severing the roots of merit, one abandons those acquisitions at the very last.
Here, the roots of merit are severed gradually.
How so?
False view is of nine types, ranging from the weakest of the weak to the strongest of the strong.

The roots of wholesome merit are likewise of nine types; conversely, by means of the weakest of the weak false views, the strongest of the strong roots of wholesome merit are severed, continuing in this manner up to the strongest of the strong [false views].
By means of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the most subtle of the subtle wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) are completely severed,
just like the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
In that regard, at the final stage, the most subtle of the subtle wholesome roots no longer manifest.
However, the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of those [defilements] that are "weak-weak" (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) are currently active. He abandons those at the very last;
the meaning is that he causes the acquisitions of those acquisitions to cease.
Those acquisitions in their final state— the wholesome homogeneous cause— grasp the fruit;
that is, it performs the grasping of the fruit,
but it does not give its own outflow fruit.
Because there is no other moment of wholesome [mind] to be produced,
this is the second alternative:
one gives but does not receive.

When reconnecting the roots of virtue, those acquisitions (*prāpti*) which one obtains for the very first time— those very acquisitions that one obtains prior to all else— it is the wholesome similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) that yields the fruit.
It produces its own outflow (*niṣyanda*),
but it does not grasp [it], because it has already been grasped previously.
This, however, is the second alternative (*koṭi*) which is faulty.

For at the time of reconnecting the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pratisaṃdhāna), the acquisitions (prāpti) of all nine types of roots of goodness—past, future, and present—are obtained simultaneously. Among those, as for the past acquisitions:
it is logical that this wholesome homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) gives forth its fruit but does not receive it, because it has already been received.
As for those acquisitions (*prāpti*) that are currently present and likewise obtained,
how is that wholesome homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) determined?
It is because it gives its fruit and does not receive one.
For he both receives and gives; since it is not specified otherwise, this second alternative is faulty. Therefore, the Master said:
However, it should be stated thus:
"For one who reconnects [the continuum], those very [acquisitions] are [the cause].
Those very acquisitions (*prāpti*) are the virtuous homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), because they invariably yield their fruit by giving rise to their own outflow-fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
One does not receive because it has already been received;
this is the third alternative.
One both receives and gives the fruit.
"In the remaining states for one whose roots of merit have not been severed" means excluding two states:
that state in which, while severing the roots of merit, one abandons those acquisitions (*prāpti*) last of all.
And in whichever state one reconnects the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), those [roots] which one acquires for the very first time—
just as the wholesome acquisitions (*prāpti*) of people like us receive and give forth fruit—
it should be stated that they are not separated by another moment of a different kind (*visabhāga*).
It should not be said [that it does not exist].

For even when there is an intervention by a moment of a different class (*visabhāga*), it is possible for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), characterized by its acquisition (*prāpti*), to receive and give forth its fruit.
The fourth alternative consists of excluding these aforementioned modes.

For example, when one has fallen away from a higher stage, those acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the wholesome factors belonging to that higher stage do not take up a result as a wholesome similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
because they have already been taken up previously.
It does not give [possession],
because for one who has fallen away from that stage, there is an absence of possession (*prāpti*) of the wholesome roots and dharmas belonging to that stage.
The same should be stated regarding the state when the wholesome roots have been completely severed.
On this point, Ācārya Saṃghabhadra says: What has been stated is not tenable;
rather, it should be stated as follows.
"These very [roots] belong to one who is reconnecting [the roots].
Why?
Because those [roots] which were abandoned last of all do not exist."
That is the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of those very [virtuous roots].
It is that which one first acquires at the very beginning of reconnecting [the roots] after they have been severed.
For even though the continuity of their possession (*prāpti*) had previously ceased, that [reconnection] is indeed their outflow.
Therefore, since it might be asked how the entire *sabhāga-hetu* (homogeneous cause) could be grasped merely by the grasping of its fruit, this very point is stated for that purpose.
Consequently, the original arrangement alone is correct.
Thus, when the textual corruption has been pointed out in both versions, which reading is superior?
In this matter, we consider the reading of the Abhidharma itself to be superior.
But was it not said: "Because they are not specified, the acquisitions (prāpti) obtained at the time of reconnecting with the wholesome, being present, give their fruit and also receive it"?
[Objection: But surely there is the fault that they only give and do not receive.
[Response: This is not a fault.

When it is said, "reconnecting the roots of virtue," this refers to the state when the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the roots of virtue is about to arise, not to their present state; and in that [present] state, there are no acquisitions of the roots of virtue whatsoever.
They exist in the present.
How can it be said that they receive and give forth their fruit?

However, all past acquisitions of the roots of virtue within one's own continuum, having become homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*), indeed give forth their outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) at that very time.
According to the principle of immediate production,
they do not receive [it],
because it has already been received previously.
By this reasoning, we support the very reading of the Abhidharma.
But if the text were not thus qualified, would it not follow that the future acquisitions of the roots of virtue would also be included in the second category?
For they too, at that time, are acquired just like past acquisitions.
This is not a fault.
Because future dharmas lack the status of being homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*), and because it is the homogeneous cause that is under discussion here.
Even so, it should not be said that only acquisitions (*prāpti*) are intended.
Regarding the phrase "that which one first acquires," it should rather have been stated as "those [faculties] which one first acquires."
The meaning is "those wholesome factors" (*kuśalān dharmān*).
For at the moment of reconnecting with the wholesome, the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) are also acquired first,
not merely their acquisitions (*prāpti*).
This is true;
however, this statement is made precisely because acquisitions (*prāpti*) alone are necessary for the reconnection (*pratisaṃdhāna*) of the wholesome.
For the acquisitions of the wholesome necessarily arise during the reconnection of the wholesome, whether by means of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) or even by doubt (*vicikitsā*).
However, they explain that because the mind and mental factors do not arise at the moment of reconnecting with the wholesome due to doubt, it is only their acquisitions (*prāpti*) that arise.
"Of the unwholesome," and so forth:
the unwholesome similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*) is also fourfold.
There is an unwholesome homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) which receives its fruit but does not give it, and so forth.
This is the first alternative (*koṭi*).
It refers to those acquisitions (*prāpti*) which one who is attaining detachment from the desire realm (*kāma-vairāgya*) abandons at the very last moment.
Those unwholesome [factors] are a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) that receives a fruit but does not give one.
How so?
Here, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are of nine types.
The path, too, is of nine types.
Among them, the highest-of-the-high type of affliction is abandoned by the lowest-of-the-low path,
up to the lowest-of-the-low [affliction] being abandoned by the highest-of-the-high path.
Their acquisitions (*prāpti*) are likewise abandoned.
When one attains detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-vairāgya*), one finally abandons the acquisitions of the most weak-weak unwholesome states (*akuśala*).
Those unwholesome states, as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), receive their fruit but do not give it.

The second [case] refers to the acquisitions of unwholesome states that one first obtains when falling away from detachment from the desire realm, because there is no intervening moment of acquisition of unwholesome states.
Those unwholesome [dharmas] are a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); they give forth their fruit but do not receive it. This should be explained as before.
Regarding this, the Master says:
Rather, it should be stated thus:
"They belong to one who is falling away.
That is, those very acquisitions which one abandons last of all when attaining detachment from the desire realm.
For since they have already been received, they do not receive them again;
rather, they simply yield their fruit.
However, in the earlier recension, the second alternative is not possible, as was stated previously.
On this point, the Master Saṃghabhadra refutes [the opponent] in exactly the same manner:
"This is not tenable," for this is identical to what was stated previously.
Everything should be elaborated.
The third case concerns those who are free from passion for the desire realm in their remaining states.
Excluding two states—
namely, these very first and second states as previously described— in the remaining states, it is just as it is for us.
Those acquisitions (prāpti) which are unwholesome (akuśala) constitute the unwholesome homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu); it both receives and gives forth its fruit.
This is the fourth [alternative].
Setting aside these aforementioned aspects—
for example, the acquisitions of unwholesome states belonging to one who is free from passion for the sense realm and subject to falling away—
that unwholesome homogeneous cause does not "take up" a fruit.
Because it was previously accepted,
one does not give it;
for there is no [further] acquisition of it.
"In the same way for the obscured-unspecified [state]" is the full statement.
In this manner, the formulation of the four alternatives (catuḥkoṭika) applies to the obscured-unspecified as well;
it should be applied accordingly according to the attainment of arhatship and the falling away from arhatship.
There is a case of the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) which receives a fruit but does not give one; this is the detailed explanation.
This is the first alternative (*koṭi*).
It refers to those acquisitions (*prāpti*) that one who is attaining Arhatship abandons last of all.
That obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) similar cause (sabhāgahetu) receives a fruit but does not give one,
because there is no other afflicted moment [to follow].
This is the second [case].
When one falls away from arhatship, those [faculties] which one first acquires—
this is what should be stated:
"those very same [faculties] belong to one who is falling away."
For in this way, the granting of the fruit alone is established.
The justification for the previous reading must also be stated according to that very same sequence. Third.
The fourth [alternative] refers to one who is free from passion for the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) in all remaining states.
This is excluding these aforementioned modes.

For example, for one who has attained arhatship, there are the acquisitions (prāpti) of the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) dharmas belonging to the three realms, as applicable. That obscured-unspecified homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) does not take up a fruit,
because it has already been taken up.
It does not give [the fruit], because it has been abandoned.
Regarding the "subsequent member" (paścātpādaka) of the non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta): it is as follows.
The definition of the "consequent member" (paścātpāda) has already been explained, so it will not be stated again.
That which is an unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) both receives and bestows its fruit.
He said:
First, there is one who both gives and also receives,
because the non-obscured neutral [state] remains present until final nirvāṇa.
There may also be one who receives but does not give.

The final aggregates of an Arhat are [unobscured-indeterminate] because, through the relinquishing of all substrates (upadhi), there is an absence of any outflow (niṣyanda) that is unobscured-indeterminate.
However, regarding the restriction of having an object (sālambana), it is said "moment by moment" (kṣaṇaśaḥ).

Previously, the possibility of those without objects was mentioned as a general rule; but by way of the restriction of having an object, the state of being a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) is stated to belong only to mind and mental factors, and this is specified "moment by moment" in relation to subsequent moments.
But the meaning is not that it ceases by being completely exhausted.
"Immediately after a wholesome mind," and so forth:
when one brings forth a defiled or neutral mind immediately after a wholesome mind.
At that time, that wholesome mind receives the fruit because, falling within its own continuum, there will arise a wholesome fruit— either separated [in time] or future—
or else one characterized by non-arising.
It does not give [the fruit].
Because there is no wholesome state whatsoever immediately following it.
For a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is held to be "fruitful" by virtue of its similar fruit.
This is the second [alternative].
"By the reverse" means:
when one brings a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) into manifestation immediately after a defiled or unobscured-neutral mind (*kliṣṭa-anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*),
then that wholesome mind by which the [subsequent] wholesome mind was previously received as its fruit— [that former mind is now the cause].
He gives that, but he does not receive it,
because it has already been received previously.
This is the third [case].
"Immediately after a wholesome mind, there is only a wholesome [mind].
This refers to bringing [the mind] into manifestation.
That preceding wholesome mind receives and gives the second mind as its fruit.
The fourth [case] is because it arises immediately after; that is,
"having set aside these modes."
When one brings forth a defiled or neutral state of mind immediately after a defiled or neutral state of mind,
then that wholesome homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) possessing an object does not take up its fruit,
because it has already been taken up.
One does not give because of the manifestation of a defiled or neutral state of mind.
In this same way, unwholesome states and so forth should also be applied accordingly.
There is an unwholesome homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) with an object that receives its fruit but does not give it; this involves four alternatives (*catuḥkoṭika*).
The first alternative:
immediately after an unwholesome [thought], one brings forth a wholesome or non-obscured-neutral thought.
The second [case] is from the opposite. The third [case] is likewise.
Immediately after a wholesome [state], there is only an unwholesome one.
The fourth [alternative] is setting aside these aforementioned modes.
By the word "etcetera," the obscured-indeterminate and the unobscured-indeterminate should be applied as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
First, regarding the obscured [neutral], there is the first alternative:
immediately after an obscured neutral mind, one brings forth either a wholesome mind or an unobscured neutral mind.
Second, [the second alternative].
By way of reversal,
it is the third:
immediately after a defiled-neutral mind, there arises only a defiled-neutral mind.
The fourth [alternative].
Excluding these modes,
the first category belongs to that which is unobstructed (*anivṛta*).
Immediately after an unobstructed-indeterminate state, one brings forth either a wholesome or an afflicted mind.
Second:
by way of the reverse.
The third [case]:
immediately after an unobscured-neutral state, there arises only an unobscured-neutral state.
The fourth [case].
"Setting aside these modes [of existence],
because it attains the state of being a seed for that"— that is,
because it attains the state of being the cause for that fruit; this is a metaphorical expression according to the system of the Sautrāntikas.
In some manuscripts, this reading does not exist at all,
such as "the water-mandala," and so forth.
The word "yathā" (as) serves to indicate an illustration.
The water mandala is the fruit of the support for the wind mandala.
By the word "up to" (*yāvat*), the golden earth is [the fruit] of the water mandala;
and the fruit of the support for the golden earth is likewise the crops, medicinal herbs, and so forth—this is the governing principle (*adhikāra*).
Starting from the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) of the foul (*aśubhā*) up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*),
the fruit of the application should be applied in the same way for others as well, such as mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
The fruit of the totality is the "totality-fruit.
Regarding the phrase "of the eye and so forth":
by the word "and so forth," the inclusion of the eye, visible form, light, and attention is intended.
Thus, the compound *bhāvanāphalam* means "the fruit of cultivation. As for the phrase "all this," it refers to the detailed explanation.
These four kinds of fruits are included within the fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and sovereign power (*adhipati*).
The fruit of establishment (pratiṣṭhā-phala) is included within the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala),
specifically within the fruits of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) and sovereignty (adhipati-phala) that arise from preparatory application (prayoga).
(II.61, 62ab) "Defiled" (*kliṣṭa*), and so forth: those that are defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*), associated with them, or originated from them are the defiled.
Those born from a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) are the "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*).

The first untainted [dharmas] are the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and those that arise simultaneously with it. From those three—namely, the defiled and so forth—the remaining [dharmas] are the neutral ones, excluding those that are maturation (*vipāka*), which consist of the deportment-related (*airyāpathika*), the artisan-related (*śailpasthānika*), and the emanation-related (*nairmāṇika*).
Furthermore, the wholesome [dharmas] are those excluding the first moment of the untainted.
By the mention of "wholesome" (*kuśala*), both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are included.

In this context, it should be understood that all wholesome factors—beginning with the complex of the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*)—as well as the paths of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the mundane (*laukika*) ones, are [included]; the remaining factors constitute the third category here.
Therefore, he says:
These four types of phenomena— namely, the afflicted, those born of maturation, the remaining [non-defiled worldly], and the first noble [uncontaminated]—
arise respectively from the remaining [causes], excluding maturation, the omnipresent, and those two [the afflicted and the maturation-born], as well as the similar [cause].
Thus:
"maturation" refers to the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Defiled phenomena, excluding the maturation cause, arise from the remaining five causes—the efficient, co-existent, homogeneous, associated, and pervasive—as applicable.
From the causal cause (*kāraṇahetu*), which consists of all phenomena characterized by the exclusion of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
from the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), which consists of the characteristics of one's own collection of factors, mind, and so forth;
and from the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), which consists of the afflicted characteristics within one's own continuum that have arisen previously.
This is because of the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*), which has the characteristic of its own group of mental factors (*svakalāpa-citta*).
This is because they arise from the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) characterized by previously arisen views such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
and not from the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
For the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) is fruitful by means of its ripened fruit (vipāka-phala).
And since defiled phenomena (kliṣṭa-dharma) do not have the nature of ripening, they do not arise from that [cause].
Phenomena born of ripening (vipākaja) arise from exactly five causes, excluding the omnipresent cause (sarvatraga-hetu).
But it is not [the result] of the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*).
This is because those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*),
whereas the definition of the pervasive cause is that it pertains to defiled (*kliṣṭa*) phenomena.
Although [states] born of maturation arise from universal factors such as wrong view and so forth,
they do not arise from them by virtue of being produced from a universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*).
What then?
"From the ripening cause.
"The remaining ones," and so forth,
means that the remaining factors have non-ripening as their intrinsic nature.
There is no ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
And because their intrinsic nature is non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*), there is no omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Therefore, excluding those two—the ripening cause and the omnipresent cause—they arise from the remaining four causes.

The explanation is as before.
