Those two, the first untainted [dharmas], arise from the remaining causes— namely, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*)— according to their respective possibilities, excluding the previously mentioned fruition cause (*vipāka-hetu*) and pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and including the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), which is drawn in by the word "and" (*ca*).
Because uncontaminated phenomena have the nature of being without maturation, they do not possess a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Because they are non-defiled, they do not possess a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Because the Path has not previously arisen, it does not possess a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
For it is not logical that the contaminated supreme mundane dharmas (*agra-dharma*) should be the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for an uncontaminated complex [of factors];
therefore, the mind and mental factors do not arise from them.

Thus, the mention of "mind and mental factors" is for the purpose of establishing the existence of the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*); for acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth, are dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*).

The untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), which has a material nature (*rūpisvabhāva*), should be understood as being among the untainted factors. These dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) and material factors are distinct from the mind and mental states (*citta-caitta*); they include the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and so forth, as well as those comprised within the afflicted, the resultant (*vipākaja*), the remaining [neutral], and the first untainted [factors]. They arise in the same manner as the mind and mental states;
they differ only in that they are devoid of the single associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*).
Because they have the nature of being non-associated, they do not arise from the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*).
How so?

Defiled dharmas, as well as those dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) and material dharmas (*rūpin*), excluding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) and the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*), arise from the remaining four causes.
Those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) arise from exactly four causes, excluding the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) and the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
The remaining [factors] arise from three causes, excluding the maturation cause, the universal cause, and the associated cause.
The first pure (*anāsrava*) factors arise from the two remaining causes, excluding the maturation cause, the universal cause, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the associated cause.
There is nothing produced by a single cause alone,

because the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) are necessarily inseparable. (II.62cd, 63) For a person, birth is not a singular production that occurs without causes and conditions.
It has been stated.
Therefore, immediately after the detailed explanation of the causes, he asks: "What are the conditions?
The category of conditions is called "conditionality" (*pratyayatā*).
The meaning is "a type of condition," just as in the case of "cowness. [This applies to] mind and mental factors.
Thus is the detailed explanation.
Only mind and mental factors are the *samanantara* [condition].
Thus, the restriction [is made] by the inclusion of "not the last," because those that have a superior [as their object] possess immediate succession.
The inclusion of the term "arisen" (utpanna) is for the purpose of excluding the future.
Since this condition is both equal (sama) and immediate (anantara), it is called the "equal-and-immediate condition" (samanantarapratyaya).
The prefix *sam-* has the sense of "equal.
Regarding "of the form belonging to the desire realm":

for one who has undertaken the vows (*saṃvara*), when a contaminated meditative absorption (*sāsrava-dhyāna*) becomes manifest, sometimes both a form of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) belonging to the desire realm and a form of non-informative matter belonging to the form realm arise.
Sometimes, when untainted dhyāna becomes manifest, both the desire-realm [mind] and the untainted [mind] [occur].

However, immediately after a desire-realm mind, a desire-realm mind and a form-realm mind never arise simultaneously; nor do a desire-realm mind and an untainted mind [arise together], for the manifestation of the form realm is not disordered in that way.
"Because of the arising of a second [kind of nutriment]" means because of the arising of a second kind of accumulative nutriment.
For when one has eaten and goes to sleep, or enters into meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Then, that which is born of nutriment, that which is accumulative, and that which is born of sleep, or that which is born of meditative concentration, arises as accumulative.
Why? Because of its arising in smaller or greater measure.
What [is this]?
The subject under discussion is that "form is not an immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*). The Venerable Elder Sautrāntika [states]:
"In wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral states of mind..."
Because it is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra,
there are twenty-two mental factors in a wholesome mind of the desire realm.
In some cases, remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is added.
However, in the case of the unwholesome mind that is independent (*āveṇika*), as well as that associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*), there are twenty [mental factors].
When associated with the four afflictions (*kleśa*) or with anger (*krodha*) and so forth, along with remorse, there are twenty-one.

According to the sequence stated in the verse, "In the obscured [unwholesome] there are eighteen; elsewhere, in the neutral, twelve are held," sometimes twenty-three mental factors arise from many, or twenty-one, eighteen, or twelve when few mental factors arise.
Sometimes many arise from few, and sometimes the reverse.

Furthermore, within the three types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) characterized by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), there is the concentration with both applied and sustained thought; there is that without applied thought but with sustained thought alone;
and there is that with neither applied nor sustained thought.
In these three types of concentration, there is the arising of mental factors (caitta) in varying degrees—some few and some many.
Consequently, even the mind and its mental factors would not be equivalent-and-immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya).
This is because [the rule applies] with respect to a different category (jātyantaram), but not within its own category (svajātim).
There is a greater or lesser arising with respect to a different category (*jātyantara*), but not with respect to its own category.
For in certain moments of mind, there is the occurrence or non-occurrence of vitarka, vicāra, and so forth, which constitute different categories;
yet, feeling (*vedanā*) is never [more] abundant.
For it never happens that in one moment of consciousness there is only one feeling, while in another there are two or three;
however, with respect to matter (*rūpa*), there is the arising of fewer or more [atoms] relative to its own kind (*svajāti*).
But does this apply only to its own kind?
Is feeling the immediate condition for feeling alone?
No, because it lacks the capacity to produce multiple feelings.
The same applies to perception and the other [mental factors].
It is not from the genus [of the mental factors],
nor from feeling, perception, and so forth;
for otherwise, the arising of mental factors in greater or lesser numbers would not be accounted for.
"But those belonging to the same continuum," and so forth.
A mind is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for another mind,
but not for feeling.
Sensation [is the homogeneous cause] of another sensation,
not of the mind; the meaning is that a factor belonging to the same continuum is a homogeneous cause.
Those who play or engage in discourse by way of similarity of continuum are the *sāṃtānasabhāgikas*, certain Abhidharmikas.
[They argue: "If a continuum is the similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for another continuum, then when a defiled state arises immediately after a non-defiled one..."
How is the determination of the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) established in that case? To this he says:
"But when [a mind] immediately follows one that is non-afflicted," and so forth.
They establish that for a subsequent affliction, the previously ceased affliction— separated by another moment— is its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
because it is not interrupted by another mind of a different kind;
however, an interruption by a non-afflicted [mind] is indeed equivalent to no interruption at all.
Because they belong to dissimilar classes,
just as the mind of one who has entered the attainment of cessation is [dissimilar] to the mind of emergence,
due to the lack of intervention by another mind.
Even though it is separated by the substance of the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it is established as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);
it is just like that.
This is because those associated with the three realms (*traidhātuka*) can manifest simultaneously.

Immediately after the acquisition (*prāpti*) of [dharmas] belonging to the desire realm for a noble one (*ārya*) who has not yet become free from passion for the desire realm, acquisitions of [dharmas] unconnected with the three realms arise.
This is because such a person is still possessed of the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the three realms.
In the same way, their birth (*jāti*) and other [characteristics] also arise.

Thus, because they manifest in a state of confusion, even those formations dissociated from mind—such as acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth—are not the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Why? Because [the text says] "future," and so forth;
for only those that have arisen are immediate.
Thus, it was previously stated that only those [dharmas] of the past and present are the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
For this very reason, he asks as follows:
"Because of their disorder."
Because it is disordered, the future is not accepted as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Furthermore, the disorder of the future time-period arises from the absence of priority and posteriority;
that is, because priority and posteriority do not exist [therein].
For it can be said that the present is prior to the future and the past is subsequent to the present,
because they are connected with earlier and later times;
however, the future has no such priority or posteriority.
For this very reason, a present [dharma] is not accepted as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for another present [dharma].
Because there is no priority or posteriority between them, a simultaneous present [dharma] is not accepted as an immediately preceding condition;
because they exist at the same time, there is an absence of priority and posteriority.
"From the inference of the past and the present.
This means from the inference based on both the past and the present.
Demonstrating that there is an inference from the past, he says:
"He sees the past path," and so forth; showing that this is an inference based on the present, he says:
"And this too is of such a kind at present," and so forth.
"He would not know the future limit" means that his omniscience would be lost; this is the intended meaning.
It is that which has become the sign of the fruit, the mark of the fruit.
It is neither a direct realizer nor a direct seer.

It is not accepted as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) because it has not yet arrived, due to the confusion [of the sequence] and the absence of priority and posteriority. To this, he says:
"Why immediately after the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*)? and so forth.
The Vaibhāṣika states the rebuttal:
"For whatever [dharma], arising is dependent upon whatever [other dharma]," and so forth.

That is to say, for whichever dharma—such as the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti)—arising is dependent upon whichever dharma—such as the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma).
It arises immediately after that,
just as sprouts and so forth arise from seeds and so forth;
for the arising of the sprout is dependent upon the seed.
Therefore, it arises immediately after that.
This is likewise the case for stalks and so forth with respect to sprouts and so forth;
even without an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), that is, even in the absence of an immediately preceding condition.
The intention [of using] the word "also" (api) is that when the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) exists, [the mind] arises all the more readily.

Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that while there is no fixed sequential order of duration, there nevertheless exists a fixed rule for its immediate succession. Why [is it said that] these are the final [minds] of an Arhat?
This question arises from the statement "not final" (acarama),
namely, because of the connection with another mind.
Because no other mind follows immediately after it.
The mind is characterized by its status as a basis (*āśrayabhāvaprabhāvita*).

Just as when the eye has arisen and remains in the state of being the basis for visual consciousness, if visual consciousness does not arise due to the deficiency of some other cause, the eye is not at fault therein.
In the same way, even the final mind of an Arhat remains as a basis;
however, because of the deficiency of other causes, another consciousness does not arise, and thus that [final mind] is not at fault.
For its meaning is this: it is not characterized by functional activity (*kāritra*), nor is it characterized by the human effort of production (*janana-puruṣakāra*).
For if that [mental engagement] were produced by the act of arising itself, then that mind would exist only when the effect is actually in the process of arising.
But this is not the case;
therefore, even when the object to be produced is non-existent, that mental engagement certainly occurs.

The equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), however, is defined by its activity: it becomes an equal-and-immediate condition only when there is something to be produced, not when there is nothing.

Therefore, regarding the phenomenon that has been grasped as a fruit by that equal-and-immediate condition, [the intention is]: "Let this phenomenon which has been grasped as a fruit by that equal-and-immediate condition arise."
He cannot be obstructed by any phenomena that lack intelligence, nor by any sentient beings who act with deliberation, such that he would not arise or would not be subject to arising.
"Those phenomena which have the mind as their immediate antecedent," and so forth;
those produced by a mind acting as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) are "those having the mind as their immediate antecedent."
They are "immediately following mind" (*cittasamanantara*) because they are both equal to and immediate to the mind. Alternatively, the mind is the immediate [precedent];
since these have the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) as their cause, they are called "immediately following mind."

However, because they are not separated by another moment, those [mental factors] are continuous with the mind; furthermore, they are "immediately preceded by mind" (*cittasamanantara*). These are the mind and mental factors, as well as the two attainments: the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) is not taught in the treatise as being immediately preceded by mind, because it arises through the power of karma.
"The first alternative," and so forth in detail.
The mind of emergence from meditative attainment is produced by the mind of entry into meditative attainment;
therefore, it is immediately preceded by mind (*cittasamanantara*), but not immediately contiguous with mind (*cittanirantara*).
Because they are separated by the moment of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). This means that the second and subsequent moments of attainment are intended, excluding the first moment.
They are immediately following the mind because they are produced by that as their condition;
they are not, however, without an interval from the mind.
Because they are separated from the first moment and so forth by an appropriate interval,
[the second moment follows]. The second [moment] consists of the birth and other characteristics (*jātyādi*) of the first moment of attainment, which are immediately contiguous with the mind.
Because they are separated by another moment;
however, they are not immediately preceded by mind (*cittasamanantara*),
because their nature is that of being immediately preceded by non-mind (*acittasamanantarasvabhāva*).
For it is intended that only the mind and mental factors, together with the two meditative attainments, are the immediate antecedents of mind;
and during states possessed of mind, there are the birth-moments and so forth.
Since these are not specified, the birth-moments and so forth belong to all of them—mind, mental factors, and the rest.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), all dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) are included, with the exception of the two attainments (*samāpatti*).
These, in the same manner, are immediately preceded by mind (*cittaniraṃtara*) but are not the immediate antecedents of mind (*na cittasamanantara*).
The explanation is as before.
Regarding the state with mind (*sacittikāvasthā*):

when one moment of consciousness arises from a preceding moment of consciousness, then the subsequent minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are both immediately preceded by the preceding mind and uninterrupted by it.
The fourth [alternative]:
the birth and other characteristics of the moments of attainment from the second onward, as well as those of the mind of emergence, are not "immediately preceded by mind" (*cittasamanantara*),
because their intrinsic nature is that of being "not immediately preceded by mind" (*acittasamanantara*).
They are not continuous with the mind,
because they are separated by the moments of the first and subsequent attainments.
Those which are the third and fourth [attainments] are the first and second, and so forth in detail.
The first alternative consists of the first moment of meditative attainment and the state accompanied by mind;
for these are immediately preceded by mind, because they are produced by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
They are not uninterrupted by meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
This is because the first moment of an attainment lacks the nature of being uninterrupted from all other moments of attainment,
and because there is no attainment during the state possessed of mind (*sacittika-avasthā*).
The second [alternative]:
the birth and other characteristics (*jātyādi*) of the moments of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) from the second onward, as well as those of the mind of emergence (*vyutthānacitta*),
are these factors that are immediate after the attainment (*samāpatti-nirantara*) but not immediate after a mind (*citta-samanantara*).
The third [category] consists of the mind emerging from a mindless attainment (*accittikā samāpatti*) and the second and subsequent moments of that attainment.
These are immediately preceded by mind (*cittasamanantara*) and are also immediately followed by the attainment (*samāpattinirantara*).
The fourth [alternative]:
the birth and other characteristics of the first moment of attainment, as well as those in a state possessed of mind—
these factors have neither the mind as their immediate antecedent nor the attainment as their immediate antecedent.
Because its intrinsic nature is immediately following a state without mind,
and because it exists as the final moment of the preceding meditative attainment;
[this refers to] that which is accompanied by association, meaning together with mental factors.
"Because it has such a characteristic" means because it has the characteristic of being an object of cognition (*ālambya-lakṣaṇatva*).
"By way of the restriction of the sense-base (*āyatana*), substance (*dravya*), and moment (*kṣaṇa*)" [is the meaning].
Their determination is by way of their sense-field (āyatana), substance (dravya), and moment (kṣaṇa).
By that very [determination],
those minds and mental factors (cittacaitta) are restricted to their respective objects (ālambana).

To begin with, visual consciousness together with its associated mental factors is restricted to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) as its object, and not to the sense-sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) and so forth.
Thus it is by way of restriction to the sense-spheres (*āyatana-niyama*).

Furthermore, within that sense-sphere, by way of restriction to the substance (*dravya-niyama*), visual consciousness together with its associated mental factors is restricted to apprehending only blue form when the object is blue form.
Not elsewhere, such as in yellow and so forth.
Thus, by way of the restriction of substance (*dravya-niyama*).
Even there, regarding the objective support (*ālambana*) which is the form of blue, it is that momentary instance of the form of blue which serves as the objective support for [the cognition].
It belongs to that very [moment] and not to another;
thus, by way of the restriction of moments.
In the same way, auditory consciousness and its associated mental factors should be applied to the sense-base of sound and so forth as well.
"Is it also by way of restriction of the support?
means: are these minds and mental factors restricted also by way of the restriction of the supports such as the eye and so forth?
He said, "Oṃ. This means "so it is. Even all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), with respect to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because this condition is superior, it is called the "dominant condition" (*adhipatipratyaya*).
This is in comparison to the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) and the others;
for the causal condition consists of the five causes.
Since an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is not possible for [factors] that arise simultaneously, it is not an additional [condition].
Or, regarding "the condition of the additional":
previously, the additional lord was called the sovereign (adhipati).
The compound is *sa pratyayaḥ* (that condition). Now, one who is the lord (*pati*) of what is superior (*adhika*) or more abundant (*bhūyas*) is the dominant factor (*adhipati*).
The compound *adhipatipratyayaḥ* is thus "the dominant condition" (*sa pratyayaḥ*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "All," and so forth.

All—whether conditioned or unconditioned—is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for everything that is conditioned, with the exception of its own self-nature, whether that [conditioned thing] has an object of cognition (*sālambana*) or lacks an object of cognition (*anālambana*).

The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), however, applies only to that which possesses an object, not to that which does not. In the first analysis, the predominance of the condition is shown; in the second, the predominance of that which possesses the condition.
(II.64) "Activity [occurs] while it is ceasing.
This is a restriction meaning "only while it is ceasing."
Because they have mutual results and because they share a common basis, respectively for the co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) and the associated cause (samprayuktakahetu),
"three are being born" [is said].
The restriction "precisely at the moment of arising" is intended;
however, the other two conditions function in the opposite manner.
The previously mentioned immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) relies upon that subsequently mentioned restriction regarding the time of its activity;
the meaning is that it performs its activity while [the dharma] is in the process of arising.
The subsequently mentioned object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) relies upon the previously mentioned restriction regarding the time of its activity.
The meaning is that it performs its activity while in the process of ceasing.
In the same way, those two [perform their activities] by way of the reverse.
The two perform their activity (*kāritra*).
Therefore it is said:
the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) performs its activity toward that which is arising, by way of providing space.
The object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) [operates] when [the object] is ceasing,
because present minds and mental factors grasp what is present;
for it is by way of the sense of "grasping" that the object-condition is established.
Furthermore, past and future minds and mental factors do not grasp an object as something to be apprehended.
This alone is its activity (*kāritra*):

that it persists in every state by way of being non-obstructive. This very persistence is the activity of this dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). Since this is easy to understand, [the text] does not separately explain the dominant condition.
The intention is that the restriction regarding the time of activity has been indicated.
(Abhidh-k-vy 237) (65) "The cause is of two kinds."
Because associated, omnipresent, and ripening causes are impossible [in this case].
"Wholesome factors belonging to the same level" means that,
for the attainment of cessation, the wholesome factors belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) as a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).
The non-percipient attainment (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) also belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna;
it occurs through the power of those [mental factors] belonging to that level.
Its immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the mind of attainment together with its associated mental factors (*sasaṃprayoga*).
Because all moments of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and all moments of the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) are not interrupted by any other state of mind.
"As before" means:
all dharmas, excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Because it is born from the mental formation (*cittābhisaṃskāra*).
This means because it is born from the mental application (*cittābhoga*).
"It is not the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) because it obstructs the arising of the mind."
Because the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the cause for the arising of consciousness.
"But others [arise] from two" means:
The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis and its position is displaced.

Only from two causes—the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)—are other phenomena produced, namely those distinct from mind, mental factors, and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
[These others include] such things as Īśvara, the *puruṣa*, and *pradhāna*.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), time, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth are included. Now, as for the phrase "for this very reason": if God (*īśvara*) or the Person (*puruṣa*) were the sole cause, one must seek the reason why this is so; that is, what is the logical ground (*hetu*) for this position?

The meaning of the sentence in summary is this: by taking a cause other than Īśvara as the basis for establishing that [creation], it becomes accepted [that there is such a cause]. And because of that acceptance, the refutation—that is, the abandonment—of the doctrine that "the single Īśvara or Puruṣa is the cause of the entire world" follows.
[This is stated] because [the world] does not arise from Īśvara and so forth through a sequence and the like.
Thus, entities do not arise from a creator god (īśvara) or similar causes. Why?
"By means of sequence and so forth.
By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of place, time, and other such factors.
Alternatively, it includes the denial of other persons, time, and so on, because [otherwise] there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress due to having multiple causes.
"If indeed there were only one," and so forth.
The meaning is: if God alone, or Mahādeva, or Vāsudeva, or another such as Puruṣa, were the sole cause;
then the entire world would have to come into existence simultaneously, because the cause would be present.
For this is not accepted:
that an effect does not arise even when its cause exists.
Moreover, the sequential arising of entities—such as the embryo (kalala) and so forth, and the sprout and so forth—is observed.
Therefore, it is understood that [the world] is produced from a succession of its own causes, and thus does not have God or any such entity as its cause.
For one who asserts that the world has a single cause such as God, the thesis is seen to be flawed by the specific property characterized by being produced through a sequence of its own causes.
[Objection: "In that case, [the world arises] by the power of His will."
That variation in sequence would arise from the will of the Lord.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Let this entity now come into existence; let this [other] come into existence later."
Thus, the intention of those who hold that God is the cause is that the arising of entities occurs sequentially and that God is the cause.
Regarding the phrase "due to the difference in will," the full explanation is as follows:

because of the difference in the will of God and because of the admission of a single cause, a contradiction with the previous position arises, resulting in a reversal of the nature of the dharma within that position.
"And that too," and so forth.
That diversity of desire would also have to exist simultaneously;
the meaning is that this is because its cause—the Lord, who is the cause of the diversity of desire—is undifferentiated, that is, unitary.
And consequently, that previously mentioned fault—that [the effects] would arise simultaneously—would follow.
Now, if you think: "Īśvara depends upon other distinct causes for their production," therefore this is said:
"And if there is dependence on a difference in other causes," and so forth.
If one accepts that God alone is the cause, that same fault [previously mentioned] applies.
"And if those [other causes] also," and so forth.

Furthermore, if the successive arising of those other causes is also admitted, then since those distinct varieties of causes would themselves require further distinct varieties of causes, there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
There would be the consequence of an endless series: "those [causes] also require further distinct varieties of causes; those [also] require further distinct varieties of causes," and so on.
This is precisely the same logic as that of the Śākyaputrīyas.
One would not have transgressed the principle of the Śākyaputrīyas that "saṃsāra is beginningless. As for the phrase "even if there were simultaneity," the full explanation is as follows:
it might be argued that...
Even if the intentions of the Lord were simultaneous, there would not be simultaneity in the world.
Why?
Because [beings] arise according to their own respective intentions.
If one has the desire, "Let this [desire] arise right now," then that desire arises from that very desire at that very moment. If one has the desire, "Let it arise later," [then it arises later].
Its production from that [cause] occurs subsequently.
And since this subsequent state is of such a nature, its production from that [cause] likewise occurs as a subsequent state;
but that is not so.
Because there is no distinction among them afterwards;
that is, among those desires, there is no distinction whatsoever after [the initial moment],
just as they did not begin at all before.
Likewise, they would not begin later either; or else, just as they begin later,
so too would they have begun previously.
Alternatively, if there were only one creator and no others, there would be no distinction between them;
consequently, it follows that all entities must arise simultaneously, just like the various desires of Īśvara.
Or, if those specific desires depend upon other causes, then the same fault as mentioned before applies.
"He would not be the lord over that" means that He would not be the lord over that pleasure without the means, because of the power of its cause. This is the lordship of the Lord.
If he were to act independently of other causes,
then it would be exactly the same in the case of another [effect];
just as [he is] not the master over pleasure.
In this same way, it is inferred that there is no Lord (īśvara) in the other three worlds as well. And as for the passage beginning "if [he were] the Lord," [it means]:
having created beings in the hells and other realms, [he would have made them] afflicted by many calamities.

"If he should take pleasure in having created a progeny afflicted and oppressed by many various kinds of calamities, misfortunes, diseases, and so forth— 'Homage be to him!'— this is an ironic statement, as is the detailed verse well-sung concerning him.
And this hymn (*sūkta*) was composed by Vyāsa with reference to that Lord, in the *Śatarudrīya*.
"Because he burns away," and so forth;
since he burns away [all things], therefore he is Rudra.
Thus it is in all cases. Regarding "of others":
the manifest human effort exerted by seeds and so forth toward sprouts and so forth would be denied.
"Because the operation of something other than the causes is observed.

For when visual consciousness and so forth arise from the eye, visible form, light, attention, and so on, or when a sprout and so forth arise from the seed, field, water, and so on, no operation of anything else is perceived.

Indeed, just as the operation of the eye and so forth is seen in the arising of visual consciousness and so forth, and the operation of the seed and so forth is seen in the arising of the sprout and so forth.
Because [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists, and does not exist when that [cause] is absent.

It is not observed that, despite the presence of the eye and so forth, or the presence of seeds and so forth, there is an absence of visual consciousness or sprouts and so forth when Īśvara is absent; nor, conversely, is it observed that they exist when he is present.
Since his activity is also understood to be involved in the production of that [effect],
therefore, for those who postulate God as the cause together with other causes based on the observation of His activity, it would be a mere expression of devotion (*bhaktivāda*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and among the auxiliary causes," and so forth.
As for those other auxiliary factors belonging to that Lord—
would He not be the Lord with respect to them as well?
For they indeed operate by their own capacity toward the production of the effect.
The mention of "others" is intended to show that God might be a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) in other cases; thus,
the initial creation is caused by God,
for in this way there would be no denial of perceptible human effort.
Furthermore, since no activity is observed in anything other than the constituent causes, it is not a fault to say that God is the cause of the world;
for even He does not depend on any other cause,
as this initial creation itself does not depend on any other cause.
The Lord alone is the cause, and nothing else. [If this were so,] there would be the consequence of [the Lord] being beginningless, just like the Lord himself.
And this is undesirable; therefore, the Lord (Īśvara) is not the cause.
In the same way, the argument should be applied to the Pradhāna as well, according to the respective [objections]:
the Pradhāna is insentient.
Therefore, having set aside the conceptualization of desire in that regard, the formulation of the remaining prohibitions should be applied:
if there were only a single primary cause,
the entire world would have to come into existence simultaneously.
Furthermore, the sequential arising of entities is observed.
If one were to depend upon a distinction in other causes, then the *pradhāna* alone would not be the cause.

Since those [other causes] would also require a distinction in further causes for their sequential production, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); such is the detailed argument.
Furthermore, by thus maintaining that the world has a single cause, one would be denying the perceptible human effort (puruṣakāra) of other factors.
Moreover, for those who postulate *pradhāna* as the primary cause even alongside other causes, it would be a mere expression of devotion,
since no activity distinct from the causes themselves is observed.
Furthermore, among other auxiliary causes, that [Pradhāna] would be either primary or non-primary. If, on the other hand, the initial creation were caused by Pradhāna,

then since that initial creation— which has the nature of producing Mahat and the rest— is itself characterized as having no beginning, it follows by implication that it too must be beginningless, just like Pradhāna.

For if the *pradhāna* is eternal and the *pradhāna* is the cause of the *mahat*, it is not established that the *pradhāna* exists first and the *mahat* afterwards. Furthermore, since the *pradhāna* has the nature of productivity (*prasavadharmi*), it must function eternally because it is independent of any other cause.
Indeed, once light has illuminated an object, it does not fail to illuminate it again.
For intrinsic nature does not overlook the fulfillment of its purpose.
"Those of unformed intellect" means those whose intellects have not been refined by the treatises on ultimate reality.
(II.66) The primary elements are twofold; they are the cause of that [derived matter].
Thus:

previously arisen primary elements (*bhūta*) are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for subsequently arisen [elements] belonging to their own continuum; being inseparable [from them], they are the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), because [the derived matter] conforms to the primary elements.
The derivative [matter] conforms to the primary elements,
because it undergoes change when they change,
just like the dependence on a teacher and so forth.
Just as a monk relies upon a teacher (*ācārya*), and by the word "etc. (*ādi*) implies that he also depends upon a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), so it is in this case.
The primary elements depend upon the derivative matter.
Such is the detailed explanation of their relationship. It has been declared that these primary elements are the cause of arising for derivative matter, because the latter originates from them.
It is the cause of transformation because it conforms to that [transformation].
It is the cause of support because it acts as a support.
It is the cause of stability because it is the cause of non-interruption.
"It is the cause of increase because it is the cause of nourishment.
"Because it functions without distinction" means that it is also a cause for others by remaining in a state of non-obstruction.
"Mutually following the mind" refers to body and speech.

Bodily action that follows the mind is comprised within the meditative and the untainted restraints (*dhyāna- and anāsrava-saṃvara*); it is threefold, distinguished by the abstinence from taking life, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.

Verbal action that follows the mind is likewise comprised only within the meditative and the untainted restraints; it is fourfold, distinguished by the abstinence from false speech, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter.
Thus, in this way, the sevenfold bodily and vocal karma are mutually co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*).
The abstention from taking life, as derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), is the co-existent cause of the other six;
and those six are likewise the co-existent cause of that [abstention]. This should be applied to all cases accordingly.

"Nothing else" means that all derived matter (upādāyarūpa), such as the eye and so forth— even when included within the Prātimokṣa restraint and the like— is not a simultaneous cause (sahabhūhetu) for one another, because they belong to distinct groups (pṛthakkalāpa).
"Of the similar" (sabhāgasya) [means...]
A wholesome [action] is the cause of a wholesome [result] belonging to one's own continuum; a defiled [action] is the cause of a defiled [result], and so forth.

"Of whichever bodily or vocal action" refers to that which has the nature of informative (*vijñapti*) or non-informative (*avijñapti*) matter, whether it be concentrated (*samāhita*) or unconcentrated (*asamāhita*), as appropriate.
"It is only one," means that the ripening cause alone is the one [to be considered]; this is a restrictive determination because the efficient cause is not counted in that same way.
"Because they consist of distinct sets of factors," meaning that there is no possibility of them being co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) and so forth.
(II.67) "In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is no unwholesome [state]" means:

having attained the first *dhyāna*, which is secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, and which is accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), born of seclusion, and characterized by rapture and bliss (*prītisukha*).
Because of the statement "he dwells" (*viharati*).
In that realm, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is no unwholesome state (*akuśala*).
For that which is born from seclusion from the unwholesome is pure (*śubha*).
That is called discernment.
As is the cause, so is the fruit.
It is understood that even in rebirth there, no unwholesome [state] exists.
In the realms of form and formlessness, all afflictions and secondary afflictions are exclusively obscured (*nivṛta*) because they lack maturation (*avipāka*); they are not unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Regarding the phrase "immediately following," it will be explained later at the end of the verse.
This should be connected here as follows:
"wholesome at the time of attainment.

Immediately after a wholesome preparatory mind belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), a mind belonging to the level of the first dhyāna arises—either that of the threshold (*sāmantaka*) or that of the fundamental (*maula*) state.
"At the time of rebirth-linking, it is obscured.

Immediately after the death-consciousness belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*) obtained at birth, an obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) consciousness of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) arises at the time of rebirth-linking.
The existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is afflicted by all the defilements (*kleśa*) belonging to its own level.
Because of this statement,
"rebirth" (upapatti) here is intended to mean rebirth in the intermediate state (antarābhava).
In the same way, the linking of existence (pratisaṃdhi) in the intermediate state should also be understood as afflicted (kliṣṭa).
It is "distant" by way of four kinds of distance.
Among these, this is the distance of the basis (*āśrayadūratā*):
that no phenomenon whatsoever belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is manifested by means of a basis belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Just as a transformation-mind (nirmāṇacitta) belonging to the desire realm is brought into manifestation by means of a basis (āśraya) belonging to the form realm, so too,
by this remoteness of basis, the formless realms are remote from the desire realm.
This is remoteness of aspect (ākāradūratā).

When the desire realm is not made an object by a mind belonging to the formless realm— just as [the desire realm] is [not made an object] by a mind belonging to the form realm through aspects such as "grossness" and so forth—
that is distance in terms of the object (*ālambana-dūratā*).
Because the desire realm is not taken as an object by a mind belonging to the formless realm, just as it is not taken as an object by a mind belonging to the form realm.
But is it not the case that the form realm also is not taken as an object by a mind belonging to the formless realm?

Because it is stated that "the fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not have the lower realms with outflows as their object," how can it be said that the formless realms are distant from the desire realm alone?
It is true that the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is not apprehended as an object by a fundamental mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).

However, the fourth dhyāna is apprehended as an object by the preparatory mind of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka-citta*) through aspects such as "coarseness" (*audārika*) and so forth.
Therefore, unlike the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the formless realms are not established as being distant from the form realm.
Remoteness by way of being an antidote:
that the formless realms are not the antidote to the desire realm,
just as the form realm is not.

Thus, by way of distance in terms of basis (*āśraya*), object (*ālambana*), aspect (*ākāra*), and antidote (*pratipakṣa*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is also distant from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Therefore, a wholesome state belonging to the formless realm does not arise immediately after a wholesome state belonging to the desire realm.
This applies to both the states of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Immediately after a wholesome preparatory mind of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara-prāyogika-kuśala-citta*), when entering meditative absorption, the state of a learner (*śaikṣa*) that was previously attained arises;
likewise does the state of one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
This refers to one who is oppressed by an afflicted absorption.

For a yogin oppressed by a defiled attainment (*kliṣṭā samāpatti*), a wholesome mind arises even from the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) state, because he resorts to a lower wholesome level (*bhūmi*).
It is better to resort to a lower wholesome level than to an upper defiled one.
[This occurs] from all minds of the form and formless realms.
Because death can occur with a wholesome or neutral mind,
there are therefore four [minds] from that [unwholesome mind]; that is,
from that unwholesome mind, there are only four belonging to its own level.

Because it is impossible for an unwholesome mind to apply itself toward the wholesome states of a higher realm, and because it is not abandoned, the mind that arises at birth in a higher realm does not occur [immediately after it].
"The wholesome [mind] occurs immediately after the mind of transformation" refers to the time of emerging from transformation.
"Therefore, immediately after that, there are eleven.

This means that at the times of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), emergence from that attainment (*tadvyutthāna*), and entering into emanation (*nirmāṇa*), the arising of eleven types of consciousness is possible.
How so?
There are three belonging to its own level and those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
At the time of emergence, it is wholesome (*kuśala*);
at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), the two defiled states (*kliṣṭa*) occur.
The unobstructed-indeterminate mind of emanation,
and the obstructed-indeterminate mind belonging to the formless realm at the time of rebirth-linking.
And it is wholesome at the time of attainment;
it is both that of the learner (śaikṣa) and that of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
However, it is not the unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara).
Because it is necessarily non-afflicted and because it is incompatible with meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and so forth.

For that [attainment] is not obtainable through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), unlike the transformation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) and the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
"Excluding the two defiled [minds] of the desire realm and the unobstructed-neutral [mind] of the formless realm.
A wholesome mind of the form realm does not arise from the two defiled minds of the desire realm,
because those two defiled minds are incapable of serving as its preparation (*prayoga*).
For this very reason, it does not arise from an unobscured-neutral state belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
Furthermore, because there is no linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*) by means of a wholesome state,
one must exclude the two defiled states of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) as well as the states of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

A defiled-neutral mind of the form realm does not arise from the two types of defiled minds of the desire realm; for as long as those [defilements] have not been abandoned, there can be no occurrence of a defiled-neutral mind in the form realm due to the absence of rebirth-linking (pratisaṃdhibandha) in that sphere.
Nor does it arise from the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Because it is impossible to emerge from that subsequent defiled state.
"And those belonging to the desire realm" refers to the three [types of thought].
At the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), there are two defiled [minds]; and for one oppressed by a defiled meditative absorption, there is also a wholesome [mind].
Furthermore, when the defiled [minds] of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) [arise], there is also that of the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
This refers to the time of rebirth-linking.
And at the time of rebirth-linking, the afflicted [minds] belonging to the lower realms [arise].
From the wholesome [mind] of the formless realm, nine arise:
three belonging to its own level; [and six from the other levels].
Wholesome [minds] of the form realm arise at the time of entering and emerging from that meditative attainment, as well as during retrogressive attainment.
Defiled [minds] of lower stages arise at the time of rebirth-linking.
Furthermore, the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) [arise].
"Excluding the wholesome [mind] of the desire realm and the unobscured-neutral [minds] of the desire and form realms.
It is not possible to emerge from that meditative attainment by means of a wholesome mind of the desire realm because it is too remote;
for this very reason, it is also not possible by means of the unobscured-neutral [mind], because it is not sharp.
For this very reason, there is no emergence from [the meditative attainment] by means of the unobscured-indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta) mind of the form realm (rūpāvacara).
Nor is there a linking of rebirth (pratisaṃdhibandha) by these [minds]; thus, they do not arise from that [attainment].
The phrase "immediately after those six" continues to apply here.

"From the wholesome [mind] of the form realm" refers to the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). "And from the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)" [refers to the time of emergence].
At the time of emergence,
wholesome [thought] pertaining to the form realm [arises] for one who has been oppressed by afflicted samādhi.
"Obscured," and so forth.
At the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*),
this refers to the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) states belonging to the desire and form realms, excluding those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
Because one who is not yet free from passion for the lower stages cannot undergo rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*) by means of that [attainment],
and because it is impossible to emerge from it through either the *śaikṣa* or *aśaikṣa* states, it does not arise from them.
These same four [attainments] and the *aśaikṣa* [state] are [the causes].
The three wholesome [minds] of the triple world [arise] at the time of emergence; the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) [arises] during the flow [of the path];
and following the diamond-like concentration (vajropama), there is the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna), which is the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
"Five from the fivefold" means from those immediately mentioned above;
that is, from the wholesome states of the three realms at the time of entering meditative attainment (*samāpatti*),
and also during the flow [of the continuum] immediately following the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Therefore, it says "four," excluding that of the learner (*śaikṣa*). For the state of a learner does not arise from the state of one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
How is it that [the affliction] does not arise at the time of falling away?
Because its arising is interrupted by the arising of afflictions, and because falling away occurs only for one who has already emerged from meditative absorption.
(II.72, 73) It is both acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and acquired by birth (*upapattilābhika*). That which is acquired through application is what is obtained through practice;
it consists of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as applicable in the three realms.

That which is acquired at birth is that whose acquisition arises first at the moment of linking to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
as well as that whose acquisition arises in the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
It consists of [minds] born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and the mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*).
This distinction arises from a difference in cause and karma.
That which is born from a ripening cause is "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*).
That which exists within the postures (*īryāpatha*)—namely, lying down, sitting, standing, and walking—is "pertaining to posture" (*airyāpathika*).
That which exists in the fields of arts and crafts is "pertaining to the arts" (*śailpasthānika*).
The mind that creates emanations is the "emanation-mind" (*nirmāṇacitta*).
That which exists in an emanation or in the act of emanating is "emanated" (*nairmita*) or "pertaining to emanation" (*nairmāṇika*).
That very point is stated:
"Furthermore, they become twenty.
To the question "How so? he says:
"Having divided the wholesome into six types and the unobscured-neutral into seven types":

this means that within the three realms, the wholesome is divided into six types by distinguishing between the acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and that obtained at birth (*upapattipratilaṃbhika*);
and the unobscured-neutral is divided into seven types by distinguishing those belonging to the desire realm and the form realm.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four types: those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and those pertaining to emanations (*nairmāṇika*).
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are three types: those born of maturation, those pertaining to postures, and those pertaining to emanations.
Thus, these thirteen, along with the remaining seven which are undifferentiated, constitute [the eighteen elements].
Namely: the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified of the desire realm;

the obscured-unspecified alone of the form realm; the obscured-unspecified and the unobscured-unspecified of the formless realm; and the mind of one in training and the mind of one beyond training. Thus, there are twenty minds.

"Because of the absence of postures, crafts, and emanations. This means that these three— postures (*īryāpatha*), crafts (*śilpasthāna*), and emanations (*nirmāṇa*)— do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because of the absence of form as an objective support (*ālambana*).
Form, odor, taste, and tangibles are the objective supports for these [mental states].
Among them, the forms of beds, seats, and so forth, as well as the forms of the parts of one's own body, are the objective supports for the state pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*).

For one belonging to the sphere of arts (*śailpasthānika*), there are the forms and so forth of the artistic field; for one belonging to the sphere of emanations (*nairmāṇika*), there are the forms and so forth of the emanation.

Regarding the phrase "but for one belonging to the sphere of arts, even sound," the word "but" (*tu*) serves as a qualification, while the word "even" (*api*) indicates that forms and so forth are also included.
Sound is also its object.
By taking the sound of instruction regarding a craft as its object, one learns that craft through mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Since that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is not mentioned [as an object], it should be understood that all [factors] beginning with visible form (*rūpa*) are objects.
"Only mental consciousnesses" means that the three types beginning with those pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*) have mental consciousness as their intrinsic nature,
because they function through conceptualization and formative activity (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*).
Because it is not verbal, it is indicated that what is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) has the nature of the six consciousnesses.
However, the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*) are "preparatory" (*prāyogika*) in relation to the deportment-based (*airyāpathika*) and the artisan-based (*śailpasthānika*) states;
they are called preparatory because they exist during the stage of preparation for those two.
Because they arise from seeing up to touching [an object],
there is no preliminary application for the maturation; this is because it flows spontaneously through the power of karma.
"Produced by the [mental consciousness] pertaining to postures," and so forth.
There is a mental consciousness produced—that is, generated—by a mental consciousness pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), which has the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as its object.
Others maintain that it has the bases from the eye-base up to the dharma-base as its objects, and that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Thus they demonstrate this:
there is also another unobscured-neutral [state] that is not included among those such as the postures (*airyāpathika*) and so forth.
And it must be understood in exactly this way.

Otherwise, as he will state: "The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses, as well as that which originates informative action (*vijñapti*), when occurring from the second dhyāna upwards, belong to the first [dhyāna] and are non-defiled-neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*)."
"Transformation is by means of one's own level, but speech is by means of a lower [level]," and so forth.
By which of these four are those consciousnesses subsumed?
They are not, first of all, born of maturation (*vipākaja*).

Because for those reborn in higher realms, there is no possibility of maturation belonging to a lower level; and because the *nairyāpathika* (postures) and so forth do not exist, since postures and the like are absent [there].
And where should the mind, which consists of the latencies of ignorance and so forth, be introduced? It has also been stated by the Venerable Anantavarman in his *Vibhāṣāvyākhyāna*:
"There exist indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) consciousnesses distinct from these four.
One should understand that this explanation is incomplete.
"Except for the fruit of supernormal knowledge.

A transformation mind belonging to the desire realm arises immediately after a preparatory mind belonging to the form realm, but not immediately after a preparatory mind belonging to the desire realm.
[The mind] belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*)— namely, the preparatory (*prāyogika*), the learner’s (*śaikṣa*), and the non-learner’s (*aśaikṣa*)—
at the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
[It arises] from its own [category], namely, from the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
It arises from its own two wholesome states and from its two afflicted states.
This is because afflicted states are absent at the time of preparatory application (*prayoga*),
and because the state resulting from application (*prāyogika*) arises in one who is weary of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Not from the non-obscured-unspecified [states], because they are weak and lack volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskārita*).
"From the two belonging to the realm of form" refers to the preparatory (*prāyogika*) and the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*);
that is, from the preparatory and from the afflicted.
And [it arises] from both the learner’s and the non-learner’s [minds] at the time of emergence;
and from a defiled [mind], for one oppressed by a defiled meditative absorption;
and from a defiled [mind] belonging to the realms of form and formlessness.
At the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*).
For death can indeed occur for a mind acquired at birth (*upapattipratilaṃbhika*).
"As before" means as previously stated.
The meaning is: "except for the fruit of superknowledge" (*abhijñāphala*).
For it has been stated that this [fruit] arises immediately after the preparatory stage (*prayogika*) of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
The detailed explanation, beginning with "and from the two of the form realm," is as previously described.
Regarding the phrase "immediately after the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified":
it should be analyzed as "immediately after the unwholesome" and "immediately after the obscured-unspecified.
For because they are equivalent, they are mentioned together.
From the four [minds] of the form realm—
excluding the preparatory and the fruit of supernormal knowledge—
at the time of rebirth-linking.
For one who abides in the preparatory stage (*prāyogika*) or in the fruit of superknowledge (*abhijñāphala*), there is no death;
therefore, those two types of afflicted states do not arise from those two.
However, for one who abides in the remaining [stages], death does occur.
Therefore, those two defiled [minds] arise from them at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*).
In the same way, it should be explained that this also occurs elsewhere, except in the case of the preparatory [mind] (*prāyogika*).
Six [minds] arise from others, excluding the preparatory mind (*prāyogika*) and the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñāphala*),
because they are weak and lack volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāraka*).
A preparatory mind does not arise immediately after these two.

Furthermore, because it arises immediately after the preparatory stage (*prayogika*) of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), the fruit of superknowledge (*abhijñā-phala*) does not arise from those two. Nor does it arise from the defiled states (*kliṣṭa*) of the form and formless realms; this refers to the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*).
"Six immediately after the [mind] pertaining to the arts (śailpasthānika)":

because death is impossible for one situated therein, just as with the [minds] pertaining to postures (airyāpathika) and those born of maturation (vipākaja), here there is no possibility of the defiled [minds] belonging to the realms of form and formlessness; and its own [result] is exclusively the fruit of supernormal knowledge (abhijñāphala).
At the time of the flow [of the meditative state],
there is the form-sphere preparatory [attainment];
and at the emergence from that, there is the form-sphere preparatory [attainment].

For there is no emergence from the fruit of the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) without having entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). That [emergence] also occurs from these same two states: from the flow [of the fruit] and at the time of entering it.
"Regarding wholesome states of the desire realm":
this refers to the time of emergence from meditative absorption.
For it is possible that there may be emergence from absorption even by means of a state acquired at birth, because of its clarity.
Therefore, both types of wholesome [minds] are included.
And "the fruit of supernormal power" refers to the mind of transformation belonging to the desire realm.
[It arises] at the time of attainment as the preparatory mind of the formless realm, and as the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
It does not arise otherwise [as] the minds pertaining to postures (airyāpathika) or those born of maturation (vipākaja),
because those two are weak and lack volitional effort (anabhisaṃskārika).
"By means of the preparatory and the afflicted" refers to the times when one has emerged from meditative absorption or is oppressed by an afflicted attainment.
"The two afflicted states belonging to the desire realm" refers to the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*).
"Except for the fruit of supernormal knowledge (abhijñāphala)" means that the mind of emanation (nirmāṇacitta) arises immediately after a preparatory mind (prāyogika).
"Defiled [mind] belonging to the formless realm" refers to the afflicted mind of the formless sphere.
"At the time of rebirth-linking.
"Wholesome and afflicted" is a compound meaning those which are both wholesome (*kuśala*) and afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).

In the case of the wholesome [mind], it is because of relying on a basis belonging to a lower wholesome stage; however, in the case of the afflicted [mind], it is at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*). "From those belonging to the desire realm," and so forth, means:
at the time of rebirth-linking.
Death does not occur in the states of the preparatory, the artisanal, or the fruits of supernormal knowledge; therefore, it does not arise from them.
"In the defiled [states] of the desire realm" refers to the time of rebirth-linking.
The defiled [mind] belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) also does not arise from this very [state], because its own preparatory [mind] (*prāyogika*) belongs to that same [level].
This is because the mind pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), due to its weakness and lack of volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskārita*), is unfit for preparation.
The same applies to the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Just as it was stated regarding the [minds] belonging to the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*),
so too here, following those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), seven [minds] arise, with the exception of the fruit of superknowledge (*abhijñāphala*).
The meaning of the text is exactly the same.

"Immediately after the fruit of the supernormal knowledges (abhijñā), two [moments] of one's own [realm arise]" means that during emergence from meditative absorption and during the flow [of the subsequent state], those too arise from these two alone.
"At the time of entry and at the time of flow" refers to the preparatory state (*prāyogika*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*),
which occurs at the moment of emergence from meditative absorption.

Thus, the states of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), as well as their own four [types of mind], are clearly wholesome. They are afflicted at the time of relishing (āsvādana).
But it is obscured-unspecified at the time of emergence;
[it arises] "from the preparatory [wholesome mind] of the form realm" at the time of entering meditative attainment.
"Except for that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
The reason will be stated as "because it proceeds weakly and without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
And [except] for those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
At the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*),
there are defiled states belonging to the lower realms;
and at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), there are those belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) and the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
Regarding "the preparatory and the afflicted":
the preparatory [state] arises from the pressure of the afflicted concentration;
the afflicted [state] occurs at the time of rebirth-linking.
Even in the case of a defiled [mind] belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), it occurs only at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*).
The phrase "from those belonging to the desire and form realms" (*kāmāvacara-rūpāvacarebhyaḥ*) is the full statement;
for death can occur while that mind is present.
"Except for the preparatory [mind]" means that because a preparatory mind does not arise immediately after a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
"The three lower defiled [minds]" refers to the three defiled minds of the lower realms.
At the time of rebirth-linking, there are those belonging to two realms.
That which belongs to the desire realm is acquired through birth;
because of its sharpness, this mind of emergence from training can arise from that [state].
He will state the reason as "because of its sharpness.
However, those [minds] acquired at birth in the form and formless realms are not sharp; therefore, they do not occur [in that context].
The mind of one in training (śaikṣa) occurs in the stream, and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) occurs immediately after the diamond-like concentration (vajropama).
"Excluding one of the trainee [states]" means that a trainee state does not arise from a non-trainee state;
therefore, five [states] follow immediately after a non-trainee state.
But it is not six, as in the case of the learner (śaikṣa).
And those five should be explained in the same manner as the learner.

Here are summary verses in the form of aphorisms regarding the twenty states of mind that serve as the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), which were not explicitly formulated in the sūtra.
From the wholesome [mind] acquired through application (*prāyogika*) in the desire realm, ten [minds] arise; from the others, eight.
From the wholesome [minds], eleven arise; from the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), seven. Separately, from fourteen, those two—the functional (*airyāpathika*) and the resultant (*vipākaja*)—arise as eight.

From those seven, six arise from the sphere of the arts (*śailpasthānika*); from that [six], two arise from the emanated (*nairmita*). From these two, this [arises] from the wholesome (*śubha*) applied (*prāyogika*) state in the realm of form (*rūpa*). From these twelve, eight arise from the wholesome effortless (*ayatnaja*) state.
From those five, nine [arise] from the defiled; from those eleven, again, seven [arise] from the resultant and the postures; from those five, two [arise];
and likewise, from the mind that is the fruit of superknowledge, two [arise], and from those two, it [the superknowledge] arises in the same way.

In the formless realm, from the effortful wholesome mind there arise seven; from that same [wholesome mind] when effortless, six arise. From the defiled mind, eight arise; from those eight, ten minds arise. Furthermore, it is taught that from the resultant mind, six minds arise.
That [unwholesome mind] arises immediately after four; six [minds] arise from the learner's mind; and again, that [learner's mind] arises from four.
Five [minds] arise from the non-learner's mind, and that [non-learner's mind] likewise arises immediately after five, because it is engaged in the performance of postures and artistic crafts.
It is under discussion that the preparatory mind (*prāyogika*) does not arise from these [two].
Therefore, because it is impossible, the preparatory mind does not arise immediately after the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).
The intention is that those two are engaged in the performance of other types of formative activity (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*).
Because the *airyāpathika* [consciousness] is engaged in the formation of postures (*īryāpatha*),
since it has the form of walking and so forth;
and the *śailpasthānika* [consciousness] is engaged in the formation of crafts (*śilpa*).

Because it proceeds with such a mode of activity as "I shall do this" and "I shall do that," and because it flows without weak volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), the preparatory (*prāyogika*) mind does not arise immediately after a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
For that which is born of maturation is weak due to its being morally neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Because it is projected by prior karma,
it flows without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāravāhin*) due to its effortless engagement.
Alternatively, it is so called because it proceeds from the formative activity (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*) of postures and crafts.
After the [minds] pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*) and those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*), the preparatory mind (*prāyogika*) does not arise.

Furthermore, because they are weak and proceed without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), the preparatory mind does not arise after the [minds] pertaining to postures, those pertaining to crafts, or those born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
This is because all of these are weak due to their being morally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

And because it proceeds without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), it belongs solely to that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*); or else, it also applies to the states of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), since they lack the volitional effort of preparatory application (*prāyogika-abhisaṃskāra*).
For it is said that those two are characterized by the activity of volitional effort merely through being intent upon other activities.
Alternatively, this is the connection of this very sentence.

Because they are engaged in the performance of postures (*īryāpatha*), crafts (*śilpa*), and formative activities (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*), and because they proceed with weak formative effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), these—namely, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), and those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*)—are not conducive to the preparatory (*prāyogika*) [state]. Therefore, it should be connected [to the previous statement] as follows: "Consequently, the preparatory [state] does not arise immediately after them."
The mind of departure, however, flows without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāravāhin*).
That mind which is other than the stream of preparatory minds (*prāyogikacitta*) is the mind of departure.

For by that [mind], the yogi emerges from that stream because it is the point of entry into it. Since the mind of emergence flows with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*) or flows without effort (*anābhoga*), it is logical that this mind of emergence—which has one of the natures such as being born of maturation (*vipākaja*)—occurs immediately after a mind of application (*prāyogika*).
Thus it is said: "In that case... [Tib. 235b]

If [it is argued that] the preparatory (*prāyogika*) mind does not arise immediately after the resultant (*vipākaja*) and other minds because they are not favorable to it, then in that case, the preparatory mind would also not arise after defiled (*kliṣṭa*) minds, because of their incompatibility.
For the meaning is that a defiled dharma is incompatible with the wholesome; it is not favorable to it because it is its opposite.
"Nevertheless," and so forth.

Even though that [state] is deficient in qualities, nevertheless, for the yogin who is weary of the active manifestation of the afflictions (*kleśa*), the manifestation of the preparatory mind (*prāyogika-citta*) is appropriate because of the thorough knowledge of it—that is, the thorough knowledge of the active manifestation of the afflictions.
For the thorough knowledge of that very thing is indeed the preparatory mind.
"Because of its sharpness":
the innate mind belonging to the desire realm is sharp; it is possible for such a mind to arise as the mind of emergence from the states of those in training (śaikṣa) and so forth.
For this very reason, one who is oppressed by afflicted concentration takes recourse in that [innate mind].
However, because it flows without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), the states of one in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth do not arise from it.
Furthermore, the innate [mind] belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) is not as sharp as that of the desire realm;
therefore, for one oppressed by afflicted concentration (*kliṣṭasamādhi*), it does not serve as a basis for it.
Only that which is produced through application (*prāyogika*) is relied upon.
There is the arising of mental states (*citta*) immediately following one another,
and since these arise by the power of attention (*manaskāra*), attention is thus introduced.
"Three types of mental attention," and so forth.
Mental attention to a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is "mental attention to specific characteristics.
For example: "matter has the characteristic of being subject to transformation (*rūpaṇā*)," and so on.

By the word "etcetera," [it refers to] "feeling is characterized by experience," and so forth. Mental attention to [characteristics] such as impermanence is mental attention to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanaskāra*); it is associated with the sixteen aspects, from "as impermanent" up to "as leading to liberation.
Mental attention through resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanaskāra*) is mental attention directed toward an object through conviction, rather than toward its actual reality.
In the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*), up to the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth—
the word "and so forth" includes the manifestation of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and other qualities— it refers to the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in lightness and other such attributes.
For example, one who possesses great supernormal power and great majesty may even resolve upon a limited perception of earth.
Even an immeasurable perception.
Desiring it, he causes the earth to tremble; such is the detailed explanation.
That which is accompanied by and connected with the foul is "accompanied by the foul."
This is what is meant:
immediately after the mental application of the foul (aśubhā-manaskāra), one cultivates, generates, and produces the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga).

Since the noble path (āryamārga) is indeed the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, this demonstrates that there is the arising of the noble path immediately after the mental application of resolute conviction (adhimukti-manaskāra).
He said:

If one brings the Noble Path into manifestation immediately after the mental application of general characteristics (*sāmānyamanaskāra*) and not after the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanaskāra*),
how is this [scriptural passage] to be interpreted?
"One cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness accompanied by the foul.
Therefore, this is said:
"Having tamed the mind by means of the foul," and so forth.

Having tamed the mind through the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) during the stage of preparation (*prāyogika-avasthā*), until finally, immediately after the general mental attention (*sāmānyamanaskāra*), one brings the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) into manifestation.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra.
The phrase "even immediately after the Noble Path," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
