Others maintain that it is not only after general mental attention (*sāmānyamanaskāra*) that one brings the noble path (*āryamārga*) into manifestation; rather, even after the noble path, one brings precisely general mental attention into manifestation.
"It might be so," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Regarding the phrase "without exertion, etc.":

by the word "etc.," it is meant that when one enters the path of certainty (*niyāmāvakrānti*) based on the three stages— the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the first dhyāna, and the intermediate dhyāna— one would, immediately after those paths, manifest a desire-realm (*kāmadhātu*) universal mental attention (*sāmānyamanaskāra*) consisting of either hearing or reflection, because of its proximity.

Now, regarding the entry into the path of certainty (*niyāmāvakrānti*) by relying on the second dhyāna and so forth—that is, by relying on the second, third, or fourth dhyānas—how is it that immediately after the noble path (*āryamārga*), one does not bring about the general mental application (*sāmānyamanaskāra*)?
The ellipsis of the sentence is: "because it is not possible to manifest [the general mental application] belonging to the desire realm.
Why is this so?
Because it is extremely remote due to being separated by the first dhyāna,
you might say that one brings forth only that which belongs to the level of the second dhyāna and so on.
To this, he says:
"And that which belongs to those stages has not been attained, except for the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

This means that the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) belonging to the stages of the second dhyāna and so forth, or to the stages of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and so forth, had not previously been attained, with the exception of the aids to penetration.
However, the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), which does not fall into any [specific] aspect (*anākārapatita*), had been attained.
But that is not the case.
Therefore, it is pleasing to the Noble One for the sake of emerging [from meditative absorption].
In that case, he will bring into manifestation the general mental attention (sāmānyamanaskāra) conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
Therefore he says:
"And the noble one does not [possess] the aids to penetration," and so forth.
If it is asked, "For what purpose? [the answer follows].
Therefore he says:
"For it is not logical that one who has already attained the fruit should bring its preparatory application (prayoga) into manifestation.

This is because the preparatory application has already achieved its purpose and is inferior; furthermore, the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) constitute the preparatory application for the Noble Path.

"Another of the same kind as this" means that the general mental attention (*sāmānyamanaskāra*), which belongs to the category of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) because it has the [four] truths as its object, undergoes cultivation and is attained at the time of the arising of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*). This is the meaning.
How so?
"Nirvana is peaceful" is a general mental attention (*sāmānyamanaskāra*), because it takes all nirvana as its object.
[The practitioner thinks: "He will bring that into manifestation."

They do not describe this [view] as one that will be manifested immediately after the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), thinking either "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," or "all phenomena are selfless," or "nirvāṇa is peace.
Why? Because these general mental attentions (sāmānyamanaskāra) of a similar nature are cultivated as being bound to the levels conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
"It is not because they lack connection to the uncontaminated path," [it is said].
"Relying on the *anāgamya*," and so forth.
"Belonging to that level" (*tadbhūmika*).
It belongs to the stage of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*),
or to that same stage, or to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Or it belongs to the stage of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), or to the peak of existence, if one has been reborn in the peak of existence.

In the remaining stages, the mind of emergence belongs exclusively to its own stage and not to another stage, because a mind belonging to another stage must be accomplished through preparatory effort.
"It occurs without effort on its own level" means that it is dependent upon preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Of what [is it dependent]?
Regarding the noble path:
it is specified that immediately after the [noble] path, there is also the manifestation of the innate [wholesome states] belonging to the desire realm.
(II.74) When there is defilement in the three realms, there is the acquisition of six, six, and two [types of minds].
Thus,
the explanation is according to their respective order.
When a defiled mind of the desire realm arises, there is the acquisition of six minds.
The meaning is "acquisition.
[This refers to] six [types of knowledge] in the realm of form (rūpāvacara),
and two in the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara).
Therefore he said:
"For [it is] the defiled [mind] of the desire realm," and so forth; "of one who is not endowed with them."
For a person who is not possessed of those six states of mind,
how is it? Here, the reconnection with the wholesome occurs either through right view or through doubt.
If, then, one reconnects [the continuum] through doubt—
when a defiled mind associated with doubt has become manifest and one returns from the form realm or the formless realm to the desire realm— at that time,
in his intermediate state rebirth-linking consciousness which is necessarily defiled, there occurs the acquisition of that wholesome [state] which he had not previously possessed.
"Of the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified," and so forth.

Both the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) belong exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), because of the context and because the obscured [defilement] of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) is mentioned separately.
Of those two—the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified—and of the afflicted [state] of the form realm...
What?
"Acquisition" is the subject under discussion.
To the question "How is there acquisition?", he says:
"And by returning to a realm and by falling away.

When one returns from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), then—at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)—since the mind is necessarily afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), one of the two, the unwholesome (*akuśala*) or the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), becomes manifest; at that time, there is the acquisition (*lābha*) of those two, the unwholesome or the obscured-unspecified.
Because it was previously abandoned, one is not possessed of it; and because of falling away, that is,
when one falls away from detachment from the desire realm.

Then, when a defiled mind of falling away (*parihāṇi*) becomes manifest, there is the acquisition (*lābha*) of those two defiled [minds] for one who was previously not endowed with them; and there is the acquisition of a defiled mind belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) due to returning to that realm,
specifically when one returns from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Then, in this person's mind at the moment of linking to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is necessarily defiled, there is necessarily the acquisition of a previously abandoned defiled state belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), with which he was previously not endowed. This also occurs through falling away (*parihāṇi*), when one falls away from detachment from the realm of form by means of a mind belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).

At that time, there is the acquisition of that afflicted state belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) which has been abandoned through dispassion (*vairāgya*), as one was previously not possessed of it. There is also the acquisition of the afflicted state belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) due to falling away (*parihāṇi*);
namely, when one falls away from dispassion toward the formless realm by means of a mind belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
Then there is the acquisition of that afflicted [state] belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara) for one who was previously not endowed with it;
and of the state of a learner (śaikṣa), by way of falling away— this being the subject under discussion—
when one falls away from arhatship due to a mind belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara).
At that time, there is the acquisition of this mind of one in training (*śaikṣacitta*) by one who was previously not endowed with it.
Thus, first, when a defiled mind belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) has become manifest, the acquisition of six minds by one who was previously not endowed with them has been explained.
When a defiled mind belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) has become manifest, there is the acquisition of six minds by one who was previously not endowed with them.
"Of those belonging to the realm of form," and so forth.

When one returns from the formless realm to the realm of form, at that time, in his intermediate state rebirth-linking consciousness—which is necessarily defiled—there are necessarily three [types of mind] belonging to the realm of form: the wholesome acquired at birth, the defiled, and the unobscured-neutral.
Because of the existence of the attainment of the first [moment] of the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*);
and because of the acquisition of the unobstructed-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind of transformation belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*),
as well as the acquisition of the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
Regarding falling away from arhatship by means of a mind belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), there is the acquisition of that [mind] by one who was previously not endowed with it.
Thus, for a defiled mind of the form realm as well, the acquisition of six [minds] has been stated.
However, regarding a defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), there is the acquisition of two [minds] by one who was previously not endowed with them.

Regarding falling away: for one who falls away from arhatship by means of a mind belonging to the formless realm, it is the defiled [mind] of which a portion has become manifest; and likewise for the [mind] of a trainee (śaikṣa). Regarding the wholesome [mind] of the form realm, there are three [types].
"Wholesome" (*kuśala*) is a designation by way of genus (*jāti*).
In some wholesome state belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), the acquisition (*lābha*) of three [factors] is possible. How so?

First, when a wholesome mind belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) has become manifest, there is the acquisition (*lābha*) of that very same wholesome mind of the form realm for one who was previously not in possession of it.

Furthermore, when a wholesome mind included within the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) has become manifest, there is the acquisition of the two types of unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) emanation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to the desire and form realms for one who was previously not in possession of them.

When the mind of a learner (*śaikṣa*)—specifically the mind of the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*)—is present, there is the acquisition of that very same learner’s nature consisting of the complex of the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering, which was previously not possessed. Furthermore, there is the acquisition of the non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states belonging to the desire and form realms, as well as the wholesome (*kuśala*) state belonging to the formless realm. In which complex does this occur? He says: [it occurs in the complex of the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering].
Through the noble path (*āryamārga*), there is detachment from the realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and form (*rūpadhātu*).
How so? When one effects detachment from desire by means of the noble path belonging to the stage of the threshold (*anāgamya*).

Then, when the learner’s mind (*śaikṣacitta*) comprised within the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) has become manifest, there is the acquisition (*lābha*) of the two unobstructed-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) emanation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to the realms of desire and form, for one who was previously not endowed with them. then, at the moment the learner’s mind of the first category becomes manifest, there is the acquisition of the wholesome (*kuśala*) mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), according to the principle of obtaining what was previously past or future, for one who was previously not endowed with it.
The mention of "attaining the noble path" is for the purpose of excluding the defiled mind (*sāsravacitta*).

As for what was stated,

"of the desire realm," and so forth.

when one becomes detached from the desire realm by means of either the mundane or supramundane path, there is the acquisition of the two types of emanation-mind belonging to the desire and form realms at the ninth path of liberation, for one who was previously not endowed with them.

the four belonging to the desire realm, the three belonging to the form realm, the obscured-unspecified mind of the formless realm, and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*). These nine are acquired, as appropriate, by one who was previously not endowed with them.

remorse, torpor, and unwholesome states do not exist in the first wholesome mind of the desire realm; likewise, applied thought does not exist in the intermediate dhyāna, and sustained thought does not exist beyond that.

Avīci is that [hell] where there is no interval (vīci), no gap, between the beings embraced by the excessively intense flames of fire. Jambūdvīpa is the continent marked by the Jambu tree.

the eight hells, the four continents, the six [classes of gods] beginning with the Cāturmahārājikas mentioned above, and the hungry ghosts and animals as undivided groups—this is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) consisting of twenty places.
Up to the wind mandala; that is, where the water mandala stands below. This is the realm of form (rūpadhātu).

However, through the intermingling of that very highest [level of the fourth dhyāna] with untainted (anāsrava) meditation—divided further into the distinctions of weak, medium, strong, stronger, and strongest—there arise five other distinct abodes.

Among them, [the first] is called Brahma because it has emerged from vast roots of merit (bṛhat-kuśalamūla).

He is "great" because, after attaining the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), he subsequently attains death and rebirth earlier than others, and because of his excellence in dimensions and other qualities.

They are called the "Utmost Radiance" (*ābhāsvara*) because they illuminate all other places.

The pleasure belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmika*) is called "pure" (*śubha*). Because they have no connection to a [lower] level, like a cloud, they are called the Anabhrakas (Cloudless Ones).

Because of the statement, "Together with the beings, through the arising and passing away of those celestial palaces," there is no other level of ground above them; thus they are called the Cloudless (*anabhraka*).
Others say that, like a cloud, there is no connection to the earth above them.
Because they are produced from immovable karma, their birth is from merits; thus they are called the Merit-Born (*puṇyaprasava*).
Because a vast fruit arises for them—the most excellent among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)—which is connected to another station, they are the "Vast Fruit" (*Bṛhatphala*).
Because their dwelling is pure due to being unmixed with ordinary beings, they are the "Pure Abodes" (*Śuddhāvāsa*).
Because they are not surpassed by other Pure Abodes, they are "Unincreased" (*Abṛha*), meaning they do not expand beyond that.

They are called *Atapa* because, due to the attainment of distinguished meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the afflictions (*kleśa*) do not torment them here; or alternatively, because of their virtuous intention (*kalyāṇāśaya*), they do not cause others to suffer, and thus they are *Atapa*.
They are called *sudṛśa* because they see clearly due to their perfectly pure vision;

They are called *akaniṣṭha* because there is no other stage superior to them, and thus they are not the "lowest" (*kaniṣṭha*), being rather the most eminent (*jyeṣṭha*).

"The continuum of mind here depends upon the group-homogeneity (nikāya) and life-force."
By the word "and" (ca), the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), possession (*samanvāgama*), acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth are included.
"Because of weakness" refers to the continuum (*saṃtati*) of a certain [person].
The mental continuum of material beings is weak because the perception of form has not been eliminated; therefore, it does not function without form, but functions by depending upon form.
By what, then, would its strength be achieved?
For what reason does that [wisdom] belonging to the formless realm possess strength? To this he says:
"Because it is born from a distinguished meditative attainment," and so forth.
"Having transcended the perception of form" means that the perception of form has departed.
Therefore, the mental continuum belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpya*), which arises from that [state], also proceeds independently of form.
Therefore, precisely because it is powerful—having been produced by a specific meditative attainment—it will proceed;
the intention is that it does so without depending on anything whatsoever.
"Just as in the case of those possessing form," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Just as for those possessing form, the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) depend upon form;
so too, for those without form, what do they depend upon? This is the meaning of the sentence.
Thus, these two [factors] are mutually dependent.
The homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) proceeds depending upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
and the life-faculty [depends] upon the homogeneous character.
For what reason are these two not mutually dependent?

The intention is: "What is the basis for form? Regarding the phrase "in that case," it means: in that formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), by what means do those two—the group-homogeneity (nikāyasabhāga) and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya)—possess strength?
This is the same in the case of the mental continuum (*cittasaṃtati*).
Since that mental continuum also arises from a particular meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it will not proceed by depending on both;
rather, it will proceed without any support at all.
The phrase "or it is the same regarding mind and mental factors" is the subject under discussion. What, then, is this commonality? It is the state of mutual dependence.
Just as the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) proceeds by depending on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), [so too do mind and mental factors depend upon one another].
And the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) functions depending upon the homogeneous character of the group (nikāyasabhāga).
Likewise, mental factors (caittas) will function depending upon the mind (citta),
and the mind will function depending upon the mental factors.
The postulation of a basis other than that [the mind] is purposeless.
"Of whichever mental continuum," and so forth:
the cause for the projection of the mental continuum is the projecting cause, characterized by karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).
His craving has departed, thus he is "one whose craving has departed" (*vītatṛṣṇa*).
One who is not one whose craving has departed is "one whose craving has not departed" (*avītatṛṣṇa*).
Where?
Regarding form:
because that mental continuum arises together with form, it proceeds in dependence upon form.
This is because the cause is turned away from it.
The meaning is that it is because the cause of projection is turned away from form (*rūpa*).
"Like a diamond-studded bracelet" means a bracelet, ring, or finger-ring joined with a diamond is a "diamond-studded bracelet" (*vajravālaka*).

And [the term] *maricapānaka* [is explained as follows]: just as a drink associated with black pepper (*marica*) is called a "black-pepper drink" (*maricapānaka*), because of the elision of the middle term.
In the same way,
the realm associated with desire is the "desire realm" (*kāmadhātu*), and so forth.
Or, it is that which is subject to transformation (*rūpaṇīya*).
The meaning is "to be oppressed.
And because of its connection with form, it can be oppressed;
the state of being that [absence of oppression] is "formlessness" (ārūpya).
When this [term] has "dhātu" as its subsequent member,
then it is appropriate as "ārūpyadhātu";
however, when the word "ārūpya" is used without a subsequent member, [it refers to the state itself].
For example, [the phrase] "having transcended forms, [there are] formless [states]" (*atikramya rūpāṇy ārūpyāḥ*).

In that case, one should understand *ārūpyāḥ* as being formed by adding a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) in its own sense (*svārthe*), meaning "those which are themselves formless" (*ārūpā eva ārūpyāḥ*).
Alternatively, I see it as "those which are suitable for the formless realm" (*ārūpye sādhavaḥ ārūpyāḥ*).
Or, he establishes [the term] "the realm of desires" (*kāmānāṃ dhātu*) by means of a genitive compound alone, even without the elision of the word *pratisaṃyukta*.
And what is this "realm of desires"?
He says: it is that which holds (*dadhāti*) the desires.
In this way, the form and formless realms (rūpārūpyadhātu) are to be understood.
The realm of forms is the "form-realm" (rūpadhātu),
meaning that which maintains (dadhāti) forms.
The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is that which holds the formless (*ārūpya*).
"Lust associated with physical food and sexual intercourse":
that which is made into morsels is "morsel-food" (*kavaḍīkāra*).
That itself is nutriment; it is the nutriment of physical food. Sexual intercourse is that which exists in sexual union.

"Embracing in pairs" and so forth. "Associated with" (*upasaṃhita*) means connected with or produced by solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) and sexual intercourse (*maithuna*); thus it is "associated with solid food and sexual intercourse. "Lust" (*rāga*) is desire (*kāma*).
It is called "desire" (*kāma*) because one desires by means of it.
How is this understood? He demonstrates that meaning through a verse spoken by the Elder Śāriputra:
"Those things which are called desires... and so forth.
The full account is as follows: It was stated by the Ājīvaka in another verse that a monk who entertains thoughts of sensual desire is a consumer of sensual pleasures.
Thus it was. This was accepted by the Elder.
For the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is indeed threefold.
By means of body, speech, and mind.
In this regard, one who is not yet free from passion does not cease to be a monk even while mentally enjoying sensual pleasures;
however, his moral conduct remains merely impure.
But he who, having transgressed with body or speech the boundary-line of the training rules of the Tathāgata, indulges in sensual pleasures— he,
being an enjoyer of sensual pleasures, ceases to be a monk. Therefore, he states another fault.
"If those are desires," and so forth; if for you...
The various objects such as forms and so forth are sensual desires.
Thus, you have accepted the position that the Teacher is not free from passion;
therefore,
he too will become [one who is not free from passion] for you.
He will become one who enjoys sensual pleasures.
It would follow that even while experiencing those objects with the body, one would still be attached merely by seeing beautiful forms;
yet this is not accepted.
Therefore,
it is established that desire for a person is passion consisting of mental construction (*saṃkalpa*).
"Kecana" means "some. He said,
"No."
He refutes this.
Because phenomena belonging to one realm manifest in another realm, as well as those that do not fall within any realm at all.
For in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), phenomena belonging to the three realms as well as untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena manifest.
In this way, in the form realm (rūpadhātu), a transformation-mind (nirmāṇacitta) belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) indeed operates there;
in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), those belonging to the formless realm and the untainted (anāsrava) minds operate.
Therefore, he negates it by saying "no."
What then?
Those [dharmas] in which the passions of desire, form, and formlessness lie latent (anuśerate).
In those [dharmas] in which the passion of desire lies latent, either by way of the object (ālambana) or by way of association (samprayoga), as the case may be.

Those [defilements] associated with the desire realm are those in which the latent tendencies of attachment to form and the formless are present; those associated with the form and formless realms are, respectively, those in which these two latent tendencies persist.
"This is now that which belongs to the horse-tetherer.
"Horse" (aśva) and "horse-tetherer" (aśvabandha) form "horse-tetherer" (aśvabandha).
Like a horse-tetherer is "horse-tetherer-like" (aśvabandhīya).
Alternatively, regarding this term *aśvabandhīya*, which means "belonging to the horse-keeper":
someone asks, "Whose horse-keeper is this? and the other replies to him.
"Whose horse is this? He asks again: "To whom does this horse belong?"
The other, however, said,
"He is the one who is this horse-tetherer.
Yet neither [of these facts] was known.
And it is like the case of "horse-tether" and "horse":
just as these two are not defined by one another because both are unestablished,
so too here the elements are not established by the passions.
Thus, both [theories]—that there are passions because of the realms (*dhātu*) and that there are passions because of the places—are unestablished.
For the places within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have already been specified:
they are the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and the six classes of celestial beings.
The desire realm consists of twenty places, distinguished by the divisions of the hells and the continents; these are the locations specified within the desire realm.
The attachment that exists toward those places in one who is not free from passion is [the attachment of the desire realm].
That is sensual lust;
likewise for the lusts of the form and formless realms.
For the [respective] locations have already been explained.
Above the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there are seventeen levels, which constitute the form realm (rūpadhātu).
The attachment of one who has not yet abandoned desire for those [realms] is attachment to form (*rūparāga*).
The same applies to the explanation of rebirth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is without location; it is fourfold by way of rebirth.
It is the attachment of one who has not yet abandoned desire for those [realms].
"That is attachment to the formless" means "according to what is appropriate," which refers to the description of the respective locations.
"Attachment to the meditations and the formless realms": attachment to the meditations of both attainment and rebirth is attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*);
likewise for attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).
Regarding the question, "How can there be desire for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*) in a mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*)?"—

how can there be desire for sense-pleasures in a mind of transformation belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*), which is the fruit of meditative absorption (*dhyānaphala*), for those who are free from desire for sense-pleasures, such that it possesses the character of the realm of desire?
For when that [person] is not yet free from desire, [the mind arises].
At that time, the mind of emanation does not manifest.
When the mind of emanation manifests,
then passion does not arise for him.
The meaning is: how is its status as belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacaratva*) established in the absence of desire for sensual pleasure (*kāmarāga*)?
[It is so] because, having heard [of it] and having fallen away [from it], one relishes it.
Having heard of it from another, desire arises in him toward that mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*).
Or, having fallen away from one's own emanation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*).
Regarding "because of relishing that":

having heard that those who meditate in this way create an emanation belonging to the desire realm by means of an emanation-mind belonging to the desire realm, attachment arises with that [emanation] as its object.
And by recollecting what belongs to oneself, attachment arises there.

"By means of a transformation" means that, having seen a captivating transformation, one feels attachment either toward the mind that produced the transformation or toward the mind of the transformer, thinking: "Such is the transformative mind of this person whose transformation is like this."
Or, because of the creation of odors and tastes.
That mind which creates a creation belonging to the desire realm is itself a mind belonging to the desire realm.
Because it is the cause of dharmas belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*),
like a mind that is the cause of a jar;
whereas that which does not belong to the desire realm is not so.
That is not caused by factors belonging to the desire realm;
for example, a mind belonging to the form realm.
For this very reason, he said:
"Because they are not emanated by a mind belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara).
Why, then, are those two—odor and taste—not emanated by a mind belonging to the realm of form?
Because those two, odor and taste, have the nature of edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra).
"And because one born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) is free from passion for it. "Iṣādhāra" means that which holds raindrops the size of a chariot-pole (īṣā).
"There is no interval or gap" indicates continuity;
however, it was not stated whether [this applies] above or below.
Thus, he shows that world-systems are situated only horizontally.
Regarding the phrase "and a portion of the fifth [realm]":
the six gods of the desire realm have been mentioned as belonging to the divine destiny (*devagati*).
The remaining [beings] belong to the realms of form and formlessness;
otherwise, there would be a confusion of the destinies— that is, a mixing of the destinies.
If they were also wholesome or afflicted, there would be a confusion of the destinies (*gati*).
A human being performs karma leading to rebirth in hell, up to and including karma leading to rebirth among the gods.
Thus, from this [it follows] that there may be a human destiny (*manuṣyagati*) as well as a hellish destiny (*narakagati*), up to and including a divine destiny (*devagati*),
because those karmas are included within those respective destinies.

Furthermore, one born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is endowed with the afflictions (kleśa) belonging to the higher realms, as well as with the defiled states belonging to the desire realm that pertain to all states of existence (sarvagatika).
Thus, it would follow that the very same person is simultaneously a human, a hell-being, and so on, up to a god.
Therefore, [the afflictions] are designated as pertaining only to sentient beings (sattvākhya).
Because one goes there by way of a personal existence (ātmabhāva) in accordance with one's karma.
For this very reason it was said:
"They shall go according to their karma, reaping the fruits of merit and evil."
Thus:
they do not have the nature of a receptacle-world,
nor do they have the nature of an intermediate state.
To establish this point, they bring forward a proof, stating at length that it is said in the *Prajñapti*:
"They are with cause and with movement. Here, "cause" refers to karmic existence (*karmabhava*).
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is "going" (*gamana*),
because one goes by means of it;
whereas a realm of rebirth (*gati*) is called a "going" because it is that which is gone to.
Because that cause, which is existence through karma (*karmabhava*), is excluded from those [realms].
This is because wholesome and unwholesome existence through karma is excluded from those destinies (*gati*).
Furthermore, the Kashmiris (*kāśmīraka*) read the Sūtra as follows: "Those who exist in Kaśmīra are the Kashmiris."
The intention is that only they, and no others, recite that *muktaka* sūtra.
"Of the hell-beings," and so forth;
those who are conducive to hell are "hell-beings" (*nāraka*).
"Of these," and so forth.

This refers to the crookednesses of body, speech, and mind—actions arising from guile (*śāṭhya*)—and the defects and impurities (*doṣakaṣāya*), which arise from hatred (*dveṣa*) and attachment (*rāga*).
For this reason as well, the destinies (*gati*) are indeed non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Since it has been stated that "when the maturation (vipāka) has come to pass, one enters the reckoning as a hell-being," the passage from the *Prakaraṇapāda* treatise stating that "all latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere within the destinies" must be resolved.
The meaning is that a rebuttal must be formulated.
Because it would lead to a contradiction.
For if the five types of phenomena were of the nature of the destinies,
then all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) would adhere (*anuśayīran*).
If, however, the destinies were exclusively non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*),
then it should have been stated:
"They are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*) and are universal (*sarvatraga*)."
For conditioned phenomena that are unobscured-neutral are to be abandoned by cultivation alone.
Among these, the universal proclivities (anuśaya) that are to be abandoned by cultivation adhere to them either by way of the object (ālambana) or by way of association (prayoga),
but no others do.
From this it is known that the destinies (*gati*) are not exclusively unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
For the linking-minds (*saṃdhicitta*) of the destinies are of five types. The linking-minds are the entries into the destinies.
Because they are of five types—
namely, those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering up to those to be abandoned by cultivation—
it is logical that all latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere therein.
"Like the inclusion of the vicinity of a village" means like the inclusion of the surrounding area of a village.
"In the five corruptions" (kaṣāya).
There are five corruptions:
the corruption of lifespan, the corruption of afflictions, the corruption of views, the corruption of the eon, and the corruption of sentient beings.
Among these—
The defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) and the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) are mentioned separately.
The meaning is that the defilement of views is stated apart from the defilement of afflictions.
These two are spoken of separately because they concern the categories of householders and renunciants, respectively.
"Regarding the phrase 'for the purpose of making known the cause of the destinies':
since karma is the cause of the destinies,
this same [logical] consequence would apply even to the intermediate state."
In this way, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would also be a destiny (*gati*),
and it would have been mentioned separately for the purpose of making known the movement toward that destiny;
[for they] go to it.
The appropriation of the means for accomplishing karma;
and since it is not logical for this to occur in the intermediate state (antarābhava) alone, it is not a "destination" (gati).
"The formless realms (ārūpya) as well," and so forth.
The formless realms (ārūpya) would not be destinies (gati), because birth occurs in the very same place as death.
For those going to the formless realms die wherever they may be— in a monastery, at the foot of a tree, or even up to the fourth dhyāna level.
"They arise right there" means that, like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it would not be a [true] realm of rebirth (*gati*). "If that is so," then...
Abandoning the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), they resort to another alternative:

because the designation "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*) is given according to its etymological meaning—as that which exists in the interval (*antara*) between two states of existence (*gati*)—the intermediate existence is not itself a state of existence.
Thus say the Vaibhāṣikas.
"As for the phrase 'If that is so,' and so forth:

the intention behind this is that because the word 'maturation' (vipāka) is used in the expression 'when maturation has occurred,' the destiny (gati) must have maturation as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
The other replies:
When the maturation has come to fruition, one is designated as a "hell-being" (nāraka);
however, it was not stated that [the hell-being] is the maturation itself,
nor was it stated that the destiny (gati) has the nature of maturation.
What then?
The destiny (gati) has the nature of both maturation (vipāka) and non-maturation (avipāka).
Therefore, the intention is that destinies can also be wholesome or afflicted.
The Vaibhāṣika, however, says:
"As for what was stated there in detail,
[it means] 'other than those dharmas.'"
The intended meaning is "from those born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
However, what is under discussion here is that [the author] does not intend to exclude other aggregates (*skandha*).
"And these," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Even in the case of the position that they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), there is a twofold division:
those whose intrinsic nature is accumulative (*aupacayika-svabhāva*), and by the word "also" (*api*), those whose intrinsic nature is maturation (*vipāka-svabhāva*).
As it has been said:
"Vipāka is life; there are twelve of two kinds.
However, those that are outflowing (*naiṣyandika*) are not included.
The master Saṃghabhadra maintains that they are exclusively of the nature of maturation (vipāka); he accepts this very position [stated] previously.
They are the six belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) and those belonging to the first dhyāna.
Which are they?
According to the system of the outsiders (Bahirdeśaka), the Brahmakāyikas, the Brahmapurohitas, and the Mahābrahmans—excluding those who were first produced—are [the second station].
According to the system of the Kaśmīris, however, the Brahmakāyikas and the Brahmapurohitas—excluding those who were first produced—are [the second station].
For according to their system, the Mahābrahmans are included within the Brahmapurohitas themselves and do not constitute a separate location.
"Because of having various colors, marks, and shapes.
Color refers to blueness and so forth;
mark refers to clothing, ornaments, and so forth.
Configuration (*saṃsthāna*) refers to length and so forth;
height (*āroha*) is the state of being elevated;
and circumference (*pariṇāha*) is the horizontal measurement.
"Form-body" (*ākṛtivigraha*) means a body characterized by form (*ākṛtilakṣaṇa*).
By specifying it in this way, the "body" of the Vedas and so forth is excluded,
for that is not characterized by form.
Furthermore, "body" (vigraha) means the physical form;
"speech" (vāk) means the utterance of speech.
"How now? and so forth is the detailed explanation.
By returning to the first dhyāna, they abandoned the second; how then did they recollect their former abodes belonging to that level— that is, belonging to the level of the second dhyāna?

First, it cannot be by means of a mind belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, because that [object] is not its domain. Nor can it be by means of a mind belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, because that has not yet been attained.
If it is argued that it has been attained again:
Therefore he says:
"And when it has been obtained," and so forth.
It is logical that the view of clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśadṛṣṭi*), which has Mahābrahmā as its object, belongs exclusively to the level of the first dhyāna.
And that [defilement], having been abandoned through the attainment of the second dhyāna, does not manifest.
If it is argued that [the defilement] belongs to the level of the second dhyāna, we say no.
Because it is impossible for [a defilement] to have a lower level as its object;
for no defilement whatsoever is admitted to have a lower bhūmi as its object.
[The phrase] "those staying in the intermediate state saw" [is used].
While still in the intermediate state, upon seeing that Mahābrahmā, they said,
"We saw this being.
This position, too, is untenable.

For even in that intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is impossible to remain for a long duration because there is no obstruction to rebirth and because it does not depend upon semen and blood. How then could they have this thought: "We saw this being who was long-lived and remained for a long duration"?
The meaning is that the cognition of remaining for a long duration would not be possible.
"Therefore, they remain right there," and so forth.

Remaining on the level of the first dhyāna, they recollect the former history of that Mahābrahmā; at the very moment of their arising, they see that Mahābrahmā, who had arisen previously, remaining for a long duration of time.
And having seen [it], later on, at a subsequent time, the cognition "we have seen" arose for them; this is the completion of the sentence.
But if this were the case, then this [objection] would remain unrefuted.
And this being had such a mental aspiration: "May we also be reborn here.
By means of the innate [knowledge] belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, they recollected that very mental aspiration of Mahābrahmā.
Because they belong to the same level (*samānabhūmika*),
there is no fault in this;
or rather, [it is so] because of hearing [the teaching] from him.
But would this same consequence not also apply to the Śubhakṛtsna gods?
That is, they would be "unified in body but diverse in perception.
How so?
As it has been said:

"For they, being weary of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the fundamental stage (*maulyāṃ bhūmau*), bring into manifestation the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) belonging to the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*)," and so on, as should be explained in detail.
Furthermore, that "they possess a single body and a single perception" will be stated later.
"By that bliss" means by that which belongs to the level of the third dhyāna. "Because it causes the mind to leap up" means because it makes the mind buoyant.
Because it produces exhilaration. "With the bliss of Indra" refers to the second dhyāna,
because it is characterized by the perception of coming and going.
Because those who have recently been reborn have the perception of arrival;
because those who have long been reborn have the perception of departure.
Alternatively, because those who have recently been reborn have the perception of arrival, while those who have long been reborn have the perception of both arrival and departure.
Because they possess the perceptions of being "terrified" and "not terrified," respectively,
due to having been reborn recently or long ago, they are "those with diverse perceptions.
It is not because they possess the perceptions of pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain, as stated by the Vaibhāṣikas.

In the first dhyāna, it is by means of a defiled perception (*saṃjñā*), because it is associated with the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) due to being fixated upon what is not a cause as being a cause. In the second [dhyāna], it is by means of a wholesome perception (*kuśalā saṃjñā*).
Because it is comprised of both the preparatory and the fundamental [dhyānas].
In the third [dhyāna], it is by means of the perception born of maturation;
that is, because of its association with the pleasure born of maturation.
"The three formless [attainments] are as described in the Sūtra":
There are formless beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, thinking "space is infinite," attain and abide in the sphere of infinite space;
namely, the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space.
This is the fifth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, dwell having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "consciousness is infinite. Such as, for example, the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness.
This is the sixth station of consciousness.
There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing at all," attain and dwell in the sphere of nothingness;
such as the gods who have reached the sphere of nothingness.
"This is the seventh station of consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "the five aggregates and four [aggregates] as appropriate":
the three [formless realms] beginning with the sphere of infinite space are associated with four aggregates.
The five aggregates associated with other [realms] are the remainder; that is what is subject to their destruction.
That by which something is broken apart is "destruction" (*paribheda*).
The destruction of that consciousness is "its destruction" (*tat-paribheda*).
That which possesses this [destruction] exists within it; thus, it is "possessing its destruction" (*tat-paribhedavat*).
The remainder refers to the miserable states and so forth. And in the realms of woe, both are absent: there is neither the desire to dwell here nor the desire to go elsewhere.
Those abiding therein have no desire to emerge,
because their activity is not sharp; that is to say, because the activity of the mind and mental factors is sluggish there.
It is reasonable to say that consciousness does not abide when it is weak.
Furthermore, the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) are the nine abodes of beings (*sattvāvāsa*),
as stated in the Sūtra.
There are nine abodes of sentient beings.
What are the nine?
There are sentient beings who possess form, who are diverse in body and diverse in perception.

Namely: humans and certain gods. This is the first abode of beings (*sattvāvāsa*). The second, third, and fourth should also be stated in the same manner as the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
But this is the distinction:
there are material beings who are without perception and without discernment,
such as the gods who are non-percipient beings (asaṃjñisattva).
This is the fifth abode of beings.
Regarding the formless abodes of beings, three should be explained in the same manner as the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

However, the fourth formless [abode] is: "There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), dwell having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)."
Namely, the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is the ninth abode of beings (*sattvāvāsa*).
Are those other than the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) who have reached the fourth dhyāna also abodes of beings, or not?
"No," they say.
"Why was it said thus by the Teacher? Who, then, are the others? They are the states of woe (apāya)."
This has been stated merely by way of illustration.
It should also be said that those not included among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) belong to the fourth dhyāna.
Here too, the same reason that was stated regarding the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) should be stated.
For those staying here, there is no longing to go to the states of woe;
and for those staying there, there is no desire for material things. Thus, the states of woe are not abodes of sentient beings.
Although those dwelling here may have a desire to go to the Bṛhatphala heaven— which is not included among the non-percipient beings—
ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) residing there seek to enter the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*).
Noble ones (*ārya*), however, even when in the Anabhraka or Puṇyaprasava heavens, seek to enter the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) or the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
"And even for the Śuddhāvāsa deities there is a desire to attain parinirvāṇa;
thus, they have no intention of remaining there.
Therefore, those [heavens] are not 'abodes of sentient beings' (sattvāvāsa)," says the Master Saṃghabhadra.
Others, however, explain it differently.
Who are these "others"?
By the specific mention of the "states of woe" (apāya), they maintain that the Teacher accepts the abodes of beings such as the Anabhrakas and so forth [as being outside the realms of rebirth].
They should seek the reasoning [for this]:
"like places of confinement.
Just as places of confinement are not abodes of sentient beings because one dwells there against one's will.
Thus [are described] the states of woe.
(III.7cd, 8ab) "The station of consciousness that approaches form" means:
it is a station of consciousness because consciousness abides within it.
It approaches, thus it is "approaching" (*upagā*).
The meaning is that it moves in the vicinity of consciousness.
It is both form (*rūpa*) and approaching; therefore, it is "form-approaching" (*rūpopagā*).
In this way, it continues up to: "those formations (*saṃskāra*) and that which approaches them (*upagā*) are 'approaching formations' (*saṃskāropagā*).
However, Bhagavadviśeṣa explains:
"The station of consciousness approaching form (*rūpopagā vijñānasthiti*), up to the one approaching formations, is stated according to the system of the Sautrāntikas."
In that context, the station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) is the non-interruption of the continuity of existence.
Form (*rūpa*) is the resort of this station of consciousness; thus, it is "approaching form" (*rūpopagā*).

"Upaga" means that which is approached, in the sense that it is taken as one's own. Thus, up to the point where the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are the approach for this station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*); this is the "approach by formative forces" (*saṃskāropagā*).
Alternatively, craving is the "abiding.
By means of this, consciousness abides,
because the continuity of renewed existence is not cut off.
Thus, the abiding of consciousness is "consciousness-abiding" (*vijñānasthiti*).
It approaches form because of attachment to it, and is therefore "approaching form" (*rūpopagā*).
In the same way, this continues up to "approaching formations" (*saṃskāropagā*).
Furthermore, he criticizes [the Vaibhāṣika position], stating that according to the system of the Vaibhāṣikas, the meaning of "agent" (kāraka) cannot be applied.
To this we reply:
in both of these explanations, a station of consciousness distinct from form and the other [aggregates] has been stated.
For they are indeed the four contaminated aggregates.
Furthermore, the claim that "the inclusion [of all things] occurs through the four alternatives" is entirely refuted; this is another fault.
Therefore, the previous explanation alone is correct.
We describe this as the Vaibhāṣika explanation, though they have not explained it in this way— namely,
that "consciousness abiding" (vijñānasthiti) is so called because it approaches form (rūpa), and so forth. Others, however, explain it differently.
"The station of consciousness that approaches form" means having form as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As it is stated elsewhere:
"Consisting of hardness and rigidity":
the intended meaning is that the sense of "going" (gati) here has the sense of "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva). This is by way of excluding that which remains stationary.
The meaning is that one thing, such as Devadatta and so forth, is the "one who stands" in the world, while another thing, such as a house and so forth, is the "standing" or the place.
It causes consciousness to flow, which means it sets it in motion; this is according to the analogy of the boat and the boatman.
Just as a boatman steers a boat, so it is in this case;
however, the meaning is not that consciousness, having mounted upon consciousness itself, steers it.

In a single continuum, two consciousnesses do not coexist. Although the consciousness of another continuum may arise simultaneously, it does not abide in proximity to the other; therefore, it does not constitute its stability.
Joy is mental gladness (*saumanasya*).
Furthermore, the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) have the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their intrinsic nature; how is this so?
Since the seven stations of consciousness are accepted as having the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature, why is it not accepted that consciousness itself is a station of consciousness?
"If that is so," and so forth.

Without distinction—that is, as a single unified mass—among the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form (*rūpa*) which are comprised within the spheres of rebirth (*upapattyāyatana*), and among those aggregates comprised within the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) of humans and so on; [this refers to] that which is accompanied by delight, accompanied by attachment.
In the context of the arising of consciousness, consciousness itself is intended as a "station of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*) in the teaching on the seven stations of consciousness.
However, individually, each [aggregate] in relation to its respective aggregate— such as form and so forth— becomes a condition for the defilement of consciousness,
because they have approached it by way of being its basis, its associated factors, and its co-existent factors.
It is not merely that consciousness alone is thus;
rather,
it is understood [from the context] that it leads to affliction.
Why?
Because it is impossible for them to have a simultaneous basis (*āśraya*).
Therefore, in the teaching on the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), consciousness alone is not said to be a station, but rather is taught separately.
Thus, with regard to those to be trained (*vineyajana*), the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) are described in one way in one sutra and in another way in another;
therefore, he says:
Moreover, "by way of being a field," and so forth:

the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), which have the nature of form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*), are taught as the field for consciousness.

Consciousness, by way of being a seed—that is, in the form of that which is to be sown—is accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna*) and possessed of craving (*satṛṣṇa*) through the craving belonging to its own level.
It was taught that [the seed] exists entirely within the continuum;
however, the Blessed One did not establish the seed as being the field for the seed,
for in the world a seed is never established as being the field for itself.
"And those phenomena," and so forth.
Those phenomena that coexist with consciousness, such as form and the rest, are even more suitable as the nature of a field.
For in the world, a field is seen to exist simultaneously with the seed;
however, consciousness does not exist simultaneously with consciousness, because they do not occur at the same time.
In that case, it would follow that past and future forms and so forth are not stations of consciousness.
Those [past and future forms] also, according to their respective natures, serve as the stations for past and future consciousnesses.
Therefore, it should be understood that all contaminated (sāsrava) phenomena, such as form and so forth, within their own level constitute stations of consciousness.
This is the detailed explanation of "the first alternative" (prathamā koṭiḥ).
Regarding the phrase "the consciousness within the seven":
because the seven stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) have the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) as their intrinsic nature,
consciousness is included therein.
It is not in the four [aggregates],
because consciousness is not included therein.
[The phrase] "the aggregates excluding consciousness" refers to this.
Even in the states of woe and so forth, consciousness is not included within the four [aggregates].
It is not included among the seven [stations] because consciousness is not grasped there through its differentiation;
for it is said that in the seven [stations], there are the four aggregates.

The four aggregates that were mentioned as being excluded from consciousness within the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) are also included within all four stations of consciousness. Thus, they are included in both; this is the third alternative (*koṭi*).
The fourth [alternative] is: "setting aside these modes.
This refers to the consciousness in the miserable realms, the fourth dhyāna, and the peak of existence, as well as the untainted (anāsrava) phenomena.
And this [consciousness] is that which is divided by the distinctions of the realms of rebirth (gati) and so forth. (III.8cd, 9)
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the receptacle world, the intermediate state, the levels of existence, and so forth are included.
The chorion (*jarāyu*) is that by which the embryo remains enveloped within the mother's womb; those born from it are the "womb-born" (*jarāyuja*).
"Born from the moisture of the elements" means:
they are born from the moisture—characterized by fluidity—of the elements, such as earth and so forth; thus they are "born from the moisture of the elements.
"Unimpaired" means: due to the absence of deficiency in the visual faculty and the other faculties.
They possess unimpaired faculties because they lack such defects as being one-eyed or having wandering vision.
They are endowed with all major limbs, such as hands and feet,
and endowed with all minor members, such as fingers and toes.
They arise all at once, not through a sequence beginning with the *kalala* stage as in the case of those born from eggs and so forth;
for they act effectively (*sādhukāritva*) in their production (*upapādane*), that is, in their birth (*upapattau*).
Because they are born all at once without depending on semen, blood, or other such material causes,
they are called "spontaneously born" (*upapāduka*).
The detailed explanation is that they were born from a female curlew (*krauñcī*), and so forth.
It is said that two merchants whose ship was wrecked reached a female curlew on the shore of the ocean;
from her they were born as the elders Śaila and Upaśaila. Regarding the King of Pañcāla:
Five hundred eggs were born from that great queen.
The king placed them in a chest and set it adrift upon the Ganges.
While bathing with his harem, the Licchavi king saw the chest being carried by the current; he opened it.
In that [egg], five hundred boys were seen and taken hold of.
Māndhātṛ and others are moisture-born (saṃsvedaja).
How so?

It is said that a boil arose on the head of King Upoṣadha. Following its growth, following its ripening, and following its bursting, a boy was born. He is this Māndhātar; thus he is one born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*).
Indeed, two swellings appeared upon the knees of King Māndhātṛ; as they grew, as previously described, they eventually became two boys.
These two were Cāru and Upacāru.
It is said that a swelling appeared on the chest of King Brahmadatta.
Following his growth, as before, until a daughter was born;
she is this very one named Kapotamālinī.
It is also heard that Āmrapālī was born from a plantain trunk.
Regarding the phrase "those of the first aeon":
formerly, sentient beings were like those possessed of form.
Because of this statement: *suparṇī* is Garuḍa.
This is stated in order to establish that hungry ghosts (*preta*) are born from a womb (*jarāyuja*).
"Of the Venerable One," and so forth.
How is it understood that this is for the purpose of establishing birth from a womb (*jarāyuja*)? [It is understood] from the phrase, "having been born as five at night."
Because of the statement.
But surely it is understood that this is for the sake of establishing the state of being spontaneously born (*upapāduka*) all the more clearly.
At night, five...
"By day [I eat] five [mouthfuls], and likewise others [by night]; nevertheless, I have no satisfaction"—
from such a statement.
For satisfaction would come from eating those born from a womb;
it is for the sake of accomplishing [the power over] those born from a womb,
not for the sake of accomplishing [the power over] those of spontaneous birth.
It is not contradictory for five [beings] to be born at once during the night and another five during the day;
for within that duration, their individual existences (*ātmabhāva*) are fully completed.
Furthermore, it is also not contradictory for five to be born sequentially during the night and another five during the day.
"The nature of beings is such, and the ripening of karmas is inconceivable.
Furthermore, because of the fault of having developed an intense desire to kill, there is no satisfaction either.
By the phrase "even though he has attained mastery over rebirth," he demonstrates the application of the force of karma in the case of birth from a womb.
"Regarding how other non-Buddhist teachers (anyatīrthya) speak disparagingly": the "other non-Buddhist teachers" refers to Maskari and others.
As it is stated in the *Nirgrantha-śāstra*: "Venerable sir, who displays supernatural power (*ṛddhi*)?"
"Gautama is a magician.
Likewise, it is said elsewhere concerning the Blessed One himself:
"Only after the passing of a hundred eons does such a magician appear in the world and devour the world with his magic."
The meaning is "he subsists upon.
"Due to the absence of external seeds" means due to the absence of external factors such as semen, blood, or mud. "Pertaining to the basis" (ādhiṣṭhānikīm) [is the meaning].
That which one empowers with the thought, "Let this be thus," is empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
The supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) that has this as its purpose, or that exists therein, is "empowerment-based" (*ādhiṣṭhānikī*).
For those Buddhists who accept this [power], this [proposed] refutation is not tenable.
Which one?
That which was stated:
"for the purpose of enshrining the bodily relics."
"One question arises from another.
Now, for what purpose was the question "Why is he a bodhisattva in his final existence? stated in detail?
And therein it was said:
"For the purpose of establishing the bodily relics," and so forth.
From that question, this further question arises:
"If [it is] for those born spontaneously (*upapāduka*)," and so forth.
The "destruction of the body" (*kāyanidhana*) is the dissolution of the body.
For what purpose are the two qualifiers "supernaturally born *suparṇin*" and "supernaturally born *nāga*"?
Are there also *suparṇins* and *nāgas* who are not supernaturally born?
They say that they exist.
For both *garuḍas* and *nāgas* are of four kinds, according to the distinction of being born from eggs and so forth.
Among them, those who are spontaneously born (*upapāduka*) are the most excellent.
Those born from moisture are the highest;
those born from a womb are intermediate; those born from eggs are the lowest.
Therein, the Suparṇī, being of apparitional birth, seizes all beings—beginning with those of apparitional birth—for the purpose of devouring them.
They explain that the moisture-born produces three—namely, the moisture-born and the others;
the womb-born produces two—the womb-born and the egg-born;
and the egg-born produces only the egg-born.
"As long as he is not dead" means that while he is alive,
that flesh and so forth do not disappear; this is what is being demonstrated.
"But it does not satisfy this one when he is dead" means "it does not satisfy by means of this one who is dead.
According to the rule *tṛpipūrau vibhāṣā*, the optional sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is intended here.
It should be understood that one is not satisfied by eating a corpse, for once it is dead and its mass of flesh has vanished like space, there is no satisfaction.
For those two destinies are the destiny of hell and the destiny of the gods;
and "a portion of the three" refers to these.
[This applies] to the destinies of animals, hungry ghosts, and humans,
because they exist in the interval between destinies—
that is, because they are situated in the intermediate space between two destinies.
But is it not accepted that the destiny (gati) itself is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta)?
Furthermore, the existence at birth (upapattibhava) is invariably afflicted (kliṣṭa),
whereas the existence at death (maraṇabhava) may sometimes be wholesome (kuśala) or afflicted.
There is no motion.
How can it be said that they possess the term "motion" by superimposing it upon them because of being in the interval between two states of motion?
This is not a fault.

Because at that time, the factors belonging to the death-existence (*maraṇabhava*) and birth-existence (*upapattibhava*)—namely, the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) categories such as the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth—which possess the nature of the destinies (*gati*), are present;
and because in the desire and form realms, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) also necessarily exists.
Furthermore, unlike birth-existence, death-existence is not necessarily afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), nor is it necessarily wholesome (*kuśala*).
Therefore, having superimposed the word "motion" upon those [states], it was said: "because they are intermediate between two motions.
Regarding the statement "because *pada* has the meaning of motion," it is recited that *pada* means "to go."
This shows that the word "arisen" (*upapanna*) has the meaning of "having approached" (*upagata*).
It is not the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that is "arisen";
what then?

"Being reborn" means manifestation and completion. Manifestation of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) occurs through projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), while its completion occurs through fulfilling karma (*paripūraka*).
Because both types of karma function throughout every birth;
for it is said: "One [karma] projects one birth, while many [karmas] fulfill it."

Alternatively, that location where there is the manifestation and appearance of the maturation of name-and-form projected by karma, and where the completion of the six sense bases occurs— that location is to be understood [as the intermediate state].

(III.11, 12) "Because of the similarity to the continuity of rice," and so forth. A *saṃtāna* is a continuous succession (*saṃbadhnan tānaḥ*); the continuity of rice is the "rice-continuity" (*vrīhisaṃtāna*).
Due to that similarity, there is no arising of a severed existence from that which it departs to that wherein it is born.
The form of the existence at birth (*upapattibhava-rūpa*) is preceded by the form existing in the continuum during the interval between [deaths and rebirths],
because its intrinsic nature consists of the continuum of the form of its own appropriated [aggregates],
just like the later form in the continuum of a rice plant.
For it is observed that for phenomena existing in a continuum, there is a manifestation in other locations through their arising in those locations without interruption.
This is just as in the case of the continuum of rice.
Indeed, the form of the subsequent stage of the rice continuum departs from one location.
And wherever it arises in another location, it arises preceded by a form that exists within the continuum of the interval between them;
for this is our established doctrine, O proponents of momentariness.
When rice is carried from one village to another,

that rice does not cease to exist in the former village and then, without being produced again in the interval between those villages, emerge in the other village even though it is separated by many yojanas.
What then?
It arises in another village through a sequence of production and cessation in contiguous points of space;
and that has as its intrinsic nature the form of the continuum of its own material cause (*upādāna-rūpa*).
Likewise, the form of the existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava-rūpa*) also arises.

Here, the master Guṇamati, together with his disciple the master Vasumitra— whose minds are conditioned by an attachment to their own school— having set aside the task of exposition, remains intent solely on opposition. We, however, here take care to provide an elucidation of the meaning of the treatise,
not its refutation.
Because it is devoid of essence and for fear of making too much to say.
"One who is destined to become" means one whose nature is to come into being.
"Even though interrupted," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
"From the original object (bimba) comes the reflection (pratibimba) in mirrors and the like.

By stating that in mirrors, water, and so forth, a reflection in the form of a shadow of the face is seen arising as something distinct from the original face, he points out the inconclusiveness [of the opponent's reason] or offers a counter-argument (pratisādhana).
The form of existence at birth (upapattibhava-rūpa) is not preceded by a form existing in an intermediate continuum between that from which one departs and that in which one is born.
Because its intrinsic nature consists of the continuum of the form of its own material cause (*upādāna*).
[The phrase] "like the form of a reflection" means that it is unproven that what is called a "reflection" arises as a distinct entity (*dharmāntara*) altogether.
The Master’s intention is that, solely by the power of the original object (*bimba*), a mistaken cognition in the form of a reflection arises there in the case of hemorrhoids and so forth.
By stating that "there is nothing called a reflection there," he demonstrates the fallacy of the example known as the "unestablished locus" (*dharmyasiddhi*).
Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntatā*).
And this counter-argument is not valid;
moreover, even if it were established,
it would not serve as a valid example because of the lack of parity.

Thus, even though the reflection is established as a substantial entity (*dravyasattva*), because it is not equivalent to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), the reflection is not an illustration; that is, it is not an example.
How, then, is it unestablished?
The word "tāvat" (first/now) indicates sequence.
Demonstrating first the reasoning for its lack of establishment, he says:
"Because two [contradictory things] cannot exist together in one place."
Thus it is said at length.
For in that very place, the location of the mirror, the form of the mirror is seen by one standing to the side, but not the reflection;
and the reflection is seen in that very same place by one standing facing it, but not the form of the mirror.
Furthermore, there is no coexistence of two derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*) in a single location.
What is the reason?
Because their supporting primary elements (*bhūta*) are distinct.
For the substrata of those two are indeed distinct.
There is no room for the substrata of the reflected image-form in a location occupied by the substrata of the mirror-form;
therefore, the coexistence of these two types of derived matter is impossible.
Thus, because two cognitions do not exist simultaneously,
and because two derived forms cannot coexist in one place,
he demonstrates that there is nothing whatsoever [of that nature].
For in whatever place the form of the mirror is seen, the reflection is in that very place,
and not elsewhere.
"What is the fault? he asks.
[The answer is: "And there is no coexistence of two forms in one place," as should be stated as before.
Alternatively,
the meaning of this sūtra, "because two [entities] do not exist together in one place," is as follows.
The sentence is to be supplied as follows: "Because two persons do not see a single form at the same time, a simultaneous perception [of a reflection] is unestablished.
He asks, "How so? and replies:
"By persons situated in different directions—some situated in the northern direction and others situated in the southern direction."
In a single location of water, such as a pond or a lake,

for those forms situated in front of oneself— namely, the forms standing on the upper part of the southern bank facing a person situated in the northern direction, and also the forms standing on the upper part of the northern bank— [the reflection appears] for both of these.
Is a reflection perceived by one another?
Those situated in the northern direction perceive a reflection beneath the southern bank;
likewise, those situated in the southern direction also perceive a reflection beneath the northern bank.
Thus, they are perceived in relation to one another;
however, the meaning of the statement is that both are not perceived simultaneously.
For a reflection on one bank is not perceived by those standing on that same bank, even if they are looking at the water of the pond from all sides.
If it is asked, "What follows from that? he says:
"But it is not the case that for two persons looking at a single form—whether a jar or a cloth—simultaneous seeing does not occur.
The meaning is that it certainly does occur.
But in this case, simultaneous perception does not occur; therefore, the arising of another form there is not logical.
Alternatively, this is the meaning:
in the world, the coexistence of both shadow and sunlight in one place is never observed.
Where there is shade, whether in a pavilion or elsewhere,
there is no heat;
or where there is heat in the open air.
No shadow is found there;
yet, a reflection of the sun is perceived in a mirror situated in the shade.
How is this so?
A reflection of the sun arises in a pond.
And a mirror is placed in a shaded pavilion situated on the bank of that pond. Therein, within the mirror, another reflection of the reflection of the sun situated in the pond arises.
And as for the reflection of the sun in a pond,
it necessarily arises from the sun; therefore,
it must be admitted that its intrinsic nature is heat.
Furthermore, as for that reflection in a mirror,
since it arises from a reflection of the nature of sunlight, this too must necessarily be admitted to have the nature of sunlight.
This being the case, shadow and sunlight would possess a simultaneous nature.
Moreover, since there is no coexistence of shadow and sunlight anywhere else in the world,
the appearance of this reflection there is not logical;
it is like water in a well.
Just as water situated deep within a well is seen,
so too the reflection of the moon is seen right here inside; yet the mirror does not possess a physical substance corresponding to that result.
And that [reflection], while arising there,
arises within the mirror itself;
it would not be perceived elsewhere, such as below.
And yet it is perceived.
Therefore, that [reflection] does not exist at all;
rather, it arises from the totality of conditions characterized by the object, the mirror, and so forth.
Its power is such that such a vision occurs;
for the differentiation of the capacities of phenomena is indeed inconceivable,
as seen in the way iron moves toward a magnet.
It is not as in the case of wood and other materials.
When the moon rises, water is seen to emerge and flow from the moonstone (*candrakānta*),
but this does not occur from charcoal and such things.
Such things as this should be stated:
"Because it is connected to the continuum of the mirror,
the reflection is not part of the continuum of the original object."
Because it is connected with the mirror,
like the form of the mirror;
and because they exist simultaneously.
It is like another form that is simultaneous with the original object (*bimba*).
Thus, while the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) is a continuation of the death-existence (*maraṇa-bhava*),
the reflection is not such a continuation of the original object.
The example of a reflection is not accompanied by the [required] means of proof (*sādhana*).
However, the example of the later form in the continuum of rice is indeed a member of the same continuum as its preceding form.
Therefore, there is no parity between the example and the reflection.
"From the arising of the two," and so forth.
Arising from two is "arising of the two."
The meaning is: from both that object (*bimba*) and the mirror;
that is to say, the reflection arises depending upon that which is the primary cause, such as the mirror.
For a mirror and so forth are the primary cause of a reflection, because it conforms to them.
For example, if a sword is positioned horizontally,
the reflection is also seen to be horizontal and elongated.
If one stands above,
the reflection is likewise seen in that same position.

However, the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) does not arise from two causes in this manner— from the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*) and from another primary cause standing in the place of a mirror.
If it is argued that the external semen and blood are the primary cause,
we say no, because they are insentient.
And because that [intermediate state] does not exist for those born by spontaneous generation (*upapāduka*),
this example is likewise dissimilar.
What is demonstrated by this?
It has been stated that this example is dissimilar (atulya) with respect to the reason characterized as "departing.
How so?
Because [the property] departs from it.
And that wherein it arises— the form of the existence at birth (upapattibhava)— is preceded by the form existing in the intermediate continuum.
This is because its intrinsic nature consists of the continuum of its own appropriated form, which has arisen non-dually.
"Like the subsequent form in the continuum of rice.
This being so, it has been stated that it is impossible to point out an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) in this proof, nor can a counter-proof (*pratisādhana*) be established.
Establishing the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) through scripture, he says:
"And because it is explicitly stated" means that its existence is established by the direct mention of its own name.
"This sutra is not recited by them" means it is not recited by those belonging to other schools (nikāyāntarīya). Why is it not recited?
Because it is not found in those [accepted] Āgamas.
Why is that which is well-known in the Āgamas of other schools not accepted as authoritative?
Because, due to the loss of the original communal recitation (*mūlasaṃgīti*), such [texts] are suspected of having interpolated sūtras.
"Of three conditions" means of three causes. "The mother is healthy" means the mother is free from illness.
A woman who has reached puberty is one who is menstruating.
Both of these constitute the first condition: that the two, being impassioned, come together.
The two engaging in sexual intercourse is the second condition;
and the presence of a gandharva is the third.
And "the dissolution of the aggregates has arrived" refers to the state of death (maraṇabhava).

The five non-returners (pañcānāgāmin) and the seven destinations of the noble persons (saptasatpuruṣagati) will be explained in the section of the *Abhidharmakośa* that provides the exposition of persons (pudgalanirdeśa).
The same applies to those who attain nirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya) and so forth.
