Otherwise, it would follow that there are gods called "those who attain [nirvana] upon rebirth" (*upapadyā*) and so forth.
Regarding the "seven destinations of superior persons" (*sapta satpuruṣagatayaḥ*):
these same five become seven by dividing those who attain nirvana in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) into three types.
Therefore, it is said that three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state are taught according to the distinctions of time and place;
that is, according to the distinction of the extent of time and the distinction of the distance of space, as appropriate.
And on this point, the Sūtra is recited:
The setting was Śrāvastī.
There, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, I shall teach you the seven destinations of superior persons and parinirvāṇa without clinging."
Listen to that and attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak.
What are the seven destinations of superior persons?
Here, a monk practices in this way.
Thinking, "May I not be, may it not be mine; may I not come to be, may it not be mine; whatever exists, whatever has come to be—that I abandon," he attains equanimity.
He is not impassioned by this existence; he is not attached to this existence.
Then, by means of wisdom, one penetrates the higher state of peace,
and that state is realized by him with his own body.
What would be the destiny of a monk who has practiced in this way?
There would be questions such as: "What is rebirth? What is the future state? Monks, it is just as if a small spark from a firebrand were to go out even as it is being produced.
In this very way, a remainder of pride remains for him, being neither abandoned nor fully understood.

Because that remainder of pride has not been abandoned and not fully understood, yet through the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*).
This is declared to be the first destination of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*).
Furthermore, a monk practices in this way:
"May I not be," and so on as before, up to "may there be questioners.
It is just as when iron balls or iron plates, heated by a blazing fire, are struck with an iron hammer and sparks fly up and immediately go out.

In the same way, as previously described, up until the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañca-avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*).
This is the second destination of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*).
Furthermore, a monk practices in this manner.
As before, up to: just as a spark of iron, having flown up, might be extinguished without even falling to the ground;
even so, for him, as before, up to: he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
This is the third destination of a true person.

Furthermore, a monk practices in this way— as previously described— until it is said that just as an iron spark, having flown up, would be extinguished upon the very ground as soon as it falls, even so, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*), he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*).
This is the fourth destination of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*).
Furthermore, a monk who has practiced in this way— as described previously— would be like a spark of iron that, having flown up, falls upon a small amount of grass and wood;
it would produce smoke there and even generate a flame.
Just as that fire, having produced smoke and generated a flame there, would burn up and exhaust that same small amount of grass and wood and then go out for lack of fuel;

even so, through the aforementioned process up to the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), one becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*).
This is the fifth destiny of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*).
Furthermore, a monk who has practiced in this way—as described previously—until: a spark of iron, having flown up, should fall upon a great and vast heap of grass and wood.
There it would produce smoke and even generate a flame.
Having produced smoke there and generated a flame, and having burned that very same great and vast heap of grass and wood until it is exhausted, it would go out for lack of fuel.

In the same way, as previously described, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*).
This is the sixth destiny of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*).
Furthermore, a monk who has practiced in this way— as described previously— [is like] a spark of iron that, having flown up, falls upon a great and vast heap of grass and wood.
Having produced smoke there and generated a flame, and having burned that very great and vast heap of grass and wood, it would burn a village, a portion of a village, a city, and a portion of a city.
It might burn a country, or a region of a country, or a thicket, or a forest, or an island, or a grove.

Having burned a village, and so on up to having burned a grove, it reaches the end of the road or the edge of water, or reaches a patch of earth with little greenery; having consumed everything, being without fuel, it goes out.
In the same way, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), as previously described, one becomes an "Upstreamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
This is declared to be the seventh type of noble person (*satpuruṣa*).
What is *parinirvāṇa* without clinging (*anupādāya*)?
Here, a monk has practiced in this way—as described previously—up until the point where there may be those who ask.

For a monk who has practiced in this way, I do not say that there is a destination in the eastern direction, nor in the southern, nor in the western, nor in the northern, nor above, nor below, nor in the intermediate directions,
nor anywhere else. In this very life, he is free from shadow.
"Parinirvāṇa, having become cooled, having become brahmic"—this is called "parinirvāṇa without clinging.
This refers to what was said: "O monks, I shall teach you the seven destinations of superior persons and parinirvāṇa without clinging."
This is what is meant by that [statement].
Others, however, say— this is the full explanation—
that it refers to the measure of the lifespan.
"Within that interval" means within that interval of the lifespan, while the lifespan is not yet completed;
or, it means within the vicinity of the gods. "Vicinity of the gods" (devasamīpāntare) means near the gods (devānām antikaṃ), close to the gods.
One who abandons the afflictions while on the way to the vicinity of the gods is an "attainer of nirvana in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin).
Furthermore, such a person attains parinirvāṇa either upon reaching the realm (dhātugata).
One who has just been reborn while in the state of the seeds of the afflictions— meaning one whose afflictions are not currently active—
and who attains parinirvāṇa while having reached perception, that is, during the state in which the perception of objects is active.
One who has entered the realm of the elements (dhātu) attains parinirvāṇa after a longer time than this.
Or, one who has entered into discursive thought (vitarka)— that is, one who attains parinirvāṇa during the state of the active manifestation of discursive thought—
this person also attains parinirvāṇa after a longer time than one who has entered into perception (saṃjñā).
Thus, there are three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin), according to the three similes mentioned.
Alternatively, the first is one who, having taken up a new group-homogeneity (nikāyasabhāga), has just been born;
this refers to the person for whom the simile of the "small spark of fire" was given.
The second [type of person] attains parinirvāṇa after having experienced the prosperity of the gods;
it is with reference to him that this simile is given:
"just like an iron spark."
The third [type of person] enters into the communal recitation of the Dharma and enters into the discussion of the Dharma, and then attains parinirvāṇa;
for whom this simile is intended:
just as an iron spark, having flown up, should be extinguished without even falling to the ground.

Thus, it has been established by those belonging to other schools that even without an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one can be an "attainer of parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyī*); and how his threefold division is established through the three similes has likewise been proven.

Once that has been established, this objection might be raised: "If one who enters the communal recitation of the Dharma (*dharmasaṃgīti*) and attains parinirvāṇa is considered an 'one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state' (*antarāparinirvāyī*), then what kind of person would be an 'one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth' (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*)? To this he says:
"Furthermore, the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth attains parinirvāṇa after entering the communal recitation endowed with excellence."
The intention is that through connection with excellence, it comes to have the sense of "arising.
Considering that there might be an opportunity for the objection that "this distinction is not tenable because of the commonality of entering into the communal chanting (saṃgīti)," he speaks again:
"Or rather, it is mostly struck by wind."
The meaning is that he attains parinirvāṇa after having exhausted much of his lifespan. "These, these" and so forth:
all these three, beginning with those who have reached the [final] element (*dhātugata*), are not connected with the analogies of the firebrand (*śakālika*) and the others.
Why?
Because there is no distinction in the movement to a location;
that is, because there is no specific difference in the movement to a location.
For these [three types of Arhats] there is no distinction in their destination or movement,
because they attain parinirvāṇa in that very same place.
However, for the three examples mentioned in the Sūtra, there is a distinction in their destinations.
"These [beings] are not bound by these [fetters].
And "also in the formless realms," and so forth.
Furthermore, if those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth were instead established as those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), [the following would occur].
They would likewise be recited in the formless realms as well,
because one attains parinirvāṇa there within the interval of the lifespan;
yet this is not the case.
Therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is not as follows:
"or at another time for the duration of life," and so forth.
How, then, is this understood?
Since one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state is not taught to exist in the formless realms, he says:
"By means of the dhyānas, there are four sets of ten."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
By means of the four dhyānas, there are four sets of ten regarding the meanings of the sūtras:
one set of ten for the first dhyāna, up to one set of ten for the fourth dhyāna.
Having performed those [calculations],
there are three sets of seven regarding the formless realms (ārūpya).
In the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness, there are three sets of seven.
Of these, there are three [that are not included],
because of the absence of intermediate existence and because of the absence of two [types of rebirth] due to the absence of the three places of rebirth.
Having performed that,
there is a hexad by means of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because there is no further upward flow for those same three,
and having performed that [action], the group becomes complete.
The meaning is "bound. How so?

Here, a monk, by means of certain aspects, certain marks, and certain signs—secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states—experiences the joy and happiness born of seclusion, accompanied by applied and sustained thought.
Having attained and dwelling in the first dhyāna, he does not indeed attend to those aspects, those marks, or those signs; rather,
he attends to whatever is perceived there, whether it belongs to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He attends to those phenomena as a disease;
he attends to them as a boil, as an arrow, as an evil, as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self.
Having attended to those phenomena as a disease, up to having attended to them as non-self, he causes his mind to become weary of, terrified of, and turns away from those phenomena.
Having caused the mind to become weary of, terrified of, and turned away from those phenomena, he directs it toward the deathless element,
[thinking]: "This is peaceful, this is sublime— namely, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nirvana."
Having spoken this very same sutra, there is this distinction:

for one who thus knows and thus sees, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), and the mind is liberated from the influx of existence (*bhavāsrava*) and the influx of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*).

For one who is liberated, the knowledge and vision arises: "I am liberated. "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; I know no further state of existence beyond this."
Having spoken this very sutra, yet one is not liberated;

rather, by that same desire for the Dharma, by that same affection for the Dharma, by that same love for the Dharma, and by that same delight in the Dharma, one becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Indeed, one does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Rather, he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; indeed, he does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth,
but rather one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.
He certainly does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion;
rather, he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion.
He certainly does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion.
Moreover, he becomes one who flows upwards;
indeed, he does not simply become one who flows upwards.
Rather, through that very desire for the Dharma—as previously described—up to that same delight in the Dharma, he is reborn into the fellowship of the Mahābrahmā devas.
He is certainly not reborn in the company of the Mahābrahmā deities;
rather, by that same desire for the Dharma as before, and so on, up to that same delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the company of the Brahmapurohita deities.
He is certainly not reborn in the company of the Brahmapurohita deities either.

Rather, by that very desire for the Dharma— as previously described— up to that very delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the company of the Brahmakāyika gods. Here, a monk, by means of certain aspects, certain marks, and certain signs, through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), through internal clarity and the unification of the mind,
attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by joy and bliss.
He does not indeed attend to those aspects, those marks, or those signs; rather,
he perceives therein— as in the preceding text—
dispassion, cessation, and nirvana.

Having recited this very sutra, for one who thus knows and thus sees, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), from the influx of existence (*bhavāsrava*), and from the influx of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*), as before, up to: "What was to be done has been done; I know there is no further state of existence beyond this. Having recited this very sutra, yet [the mind] is not liberated.
Rather, by that very same desire for the Dharma as before, up to: by that very same delight in the Dharma, he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Yet, he does not indeed become one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Rather, he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth;
indeed, he does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, but rather one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion;
indeed, he does not even become one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.
Rather, he is one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion;
indeed, he is not merely one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion,
but rather he is one who goes upstream.
He does not indeed become one who flows upwards.
Rather, by that same desire for the Dharma, as before, up to that same delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the company of the Ābhāsvara gods.
He does not, however, [merely] become reborn in the company of the Ābhāsvara gods.

Rather, by that very desire for the Dharma, and even by that same delight in the Dharma, one is reborn in the company of the gods of Immeasurable Light (*apramāṇābha*). It is not that one is reborn in the company of the gods of Immeasurable Light;
rather, by that very desire for the Dharma, as before, and even by that same delight in the Dharma, one is reborn in the company of the gods of Limited Light (*parīttābha*).
In this case, a monk, by means of certain aspects, certain marks, and certain signs, dwells having become dispassionate toward joy;
mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences happiness with the body.
That which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous"—he attains and dwells in that third dhyāna.
He does not indeed attend to those aspects, those marks, or those signs, as previously described for all the sūtras;
there is only this distinction regarding their homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāgatā).
Indeed, he does not become one who flows upwards.
Rather, by that same desire for the Dharma, as before, he is reborn among the company of the Śubhakṛtsna gods.
Indeed, he is not reborn among the company of the Śubhakṛtsna gods.
Furthermore, by that very [cause], as before, he is reborn in the fellowship of the Apramāṇaśubha gods.
Or rather, he is not reborn in the fellowship of the Apramāṇaśubha gods;
instead, by that very [cause], as before, he is reborn in the fellowship of the Parīttaśubha gods.

In this case, a monk, by means of certain aspects, certain marks, and certain signs— through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection—
attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
He does not indeed describe those forms or those signs in detail; all the sūtras are to be recited as before.
However, the rebirths among the classes of gods are distinguished:
by that very delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the fellowship of the Bṛhatphala gods.
Indeed, he is not reborn as before in the fellowship of the Puṇyaprasava gods;
indeed, he is not reborn as before in the fellowship of the Anabhraka gods.

Here, a monk, by means of certain aspects, certain marks, and certain signs, through the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and [the non-attention to] perceptions of diversity...
Through non-attention, [thinking] "space is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space.
He does not indeed attend to those aspects, as before;
however, one should not read the phrase "merely that which pertains to form."
Because of the absence of form therein. From "cessation" up to "nirvāṇa"—
having stated this very sūtra, this is the distinction.
As it was said previously regarding "one who knows thus," up to the point of "I know there is no further existence beyond this"—
having spoken only this much, he is not liberated; rather,
by that very desire for the Dharma, up to that very delight in the Dharma, he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*).
He certainly does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth;
rather, by that very [attainment], he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.
Having stated everything up to "he certainly does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion," it continues until "he does not become one who flows upwards."
Rather, as before, by means of that very same delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the company of the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space.

Here, a monk, by means of certain aspects, certain marks, and certain signs, completely transcends the sphere of infinite space and, [perceiving] "consciousness is infinite," attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
He does not indeed perceive those modes (*ākāra*); thus, seven sūtras should be stated just as in the case of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
The only distinction is that he is reborn in the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Furthermore, here a monk, by means of whatever modes, whatever marks (*liṅga*), and whatever signs (*nimitta*), completely transcends the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking: "There is nothing whatsoever," and [attains] the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
He attains and dwells [therein].
He does not indeed perceive those modes [of perception], and so on as before; thus there are seven sūtras.
Furthermore, here a monk, by means of which [factors]—up to: having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, he attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
All the sūtras are to be stated as before, with the single exception of the "one who flows upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

Thus, by means of the four dhyānas, there have been explained four sets of ten meanings of the sūtras, whose intrinsic natures consist of: the application of the mind to the deathless element (*amṛtadhātu*), liberation of the mind, intermediate parinirvāṇa, birth-parinirvāṇa, non-application parinirvāṇa, application parinirvāṇa, upward movement, and rebirth in three places of rebirth.

However, by means of the first three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), there are three sets of seven meanings from the Sūtra, whose intrinsic natures consist of the mental application to the deathless element (*amṛtadhātu*), liberation of mind, and parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, without exertion, with exertion, and ascending upwards to the place of rebirth. By excluding the upward ascent through the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), a set of six is also taught.

Therefore, it is not correct to say that this one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state is "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the interval of the lifespan," for even in the formless realms, death in the intermediate state is possible.

Because of the statement, "Death in the intermediate state occurs with the exception of Kuru," the intermediate existence (antarābhava) is established not only by reasoning but also by scripture; this is the purpose of the word "also" (api).
Regarding "the Māra Dūṣī": at that time, a Māra named Dūṣī struck a disciple of the Tathāgata Krakucchanda named Vidura on the head with his fist;
having been thus provoked, he was immediately cast down by his own body into the great Avīci hell.
The intention [of the statement] is that there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because of the expression "by his very own body.
For he, while still alive, [is seized] by the flames of hell;
that is to say, this Māra, being alive, is embraced by the flames of fire arising from hell, whereby suffering arises from the condition of his own physical body.

It is said that he fell with his very own body; the intention is that he did not remain in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) after failing to complete his lifespan, nor did he reach the state of existence at birth in hell (*narakopapattibhava*).
"Exceedingly intense and complete" means:
they are exceedingly intense due to their association with excellence of field and intention;
they are complete because they have been accumulated.

"One is reborn in the hells immediately thereafter. The intention of the statement "immediately thereafter" is that there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*). [This is expressed by] the phrase "without having gone to another destination."
The intention is that this statement is intended to exclude rebirth in another [existence], not to exclude the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). "Only five" [is the meaning].
If it were interpreted according to the literal expression,
it would follow that one goes to hell only when all five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) have been committed, and not by one or two;
furthermore, from the word "five," it would follow that one is reborn in the hells immediately after the action and again immediately after the subsequent action.
Having performed and accumulated those [actions], one is reborn in the hells immediately thereafter; this means that one does not live for any interval of time [before being reborn].
Who, indeed, would not accept that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is "being reborn"?
For it is described as being in a state distinct [from the states of birth and death].
For the intended meaning is that "one who is being reborn" (*upapadyamāna*) is one who is facing rebirth; we do not say that he has already been reborn (*upapanna*).
Nor do we say that this term *upapadyate* has the sense of "having been reborn."
Therefore, there is no fault in this.
"One whose age has been brought forward," and so forth.
He by whom youth has been brought near to death is "one whose youth has been brought near" (upanītavayāḥ). O twice-born one!...
An address: a certain aged brahmin was addressed [as follows]:
"Indeed, there is not even a garment for you in between."
This is the indicator here:
the intended meaning is that there is no intermediate state (antarābhava).
[It is] provisions for the journey.
"And there is no wholesome food for you" means that you possess no accumulation of merit pertaining to the next world.
"There is no intermediate dwelling among humans" means that for you,
having gone to death, there is no intermediate dwelling among humans;
the intention is that it is as if someone here were [already] established [in another state].
"From the cessation of going" means from the stopping of going.
This is the intended meaning here, as it is described by you.
"The intermediate state exists" does not mean that this is the intention as it is described by me;
rather, "the intermediate state does not exist."
Whence is this?
From what cause does this arise?
This same inquiry applies equally to you as well.
The meaning is that this question is equally applicable to you as well.
"Because of contradiction with the stated sūtras" means because there is no contradiction with the *Dūṣīmāra-sūtra* and others.
This sūtra is not a proof for the non-existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). For it is said that "a proof is a resort when there is no other resort"—
that is, a resort to which there is no other resort.
This is a recourse for those with no other resort.
This is what is meant:
if there is a sūtra that serves as an indicator (jñāpaka).
Or a verse (*gāthā*):
if it illuminates that very same meaning for which it is spoken in order to clarify that meaning.
Nor is there any other distinct entity that is its opposite.
That [intermediate state] is the indicator [of rebirth], having no other possible destination.
(III.13) It has the form of the future existence in the prior period.
Thus:
*aiṣyat* means "it will come. It is so called because its form is like that which existed in a previous time.
It has the form of the future existence in the previous time.
Why?
Because it is projected by a single [karmic] impulse.
Because the future destination and the intermediate state that leads to its attainment are projected by that very same single karma.
"Of dogs and so forth" means of female dogs,
female pigs, and so on.
"Belonging to the five destinies" means one who goes to the five destinies.
If one were to die even while remaining in the womb, his intermediate state (antarābhava) as a hell-being would burn the mother's womb.
For a hell-being is indeed a blazing lamp,
and the intermediate state (antarābhava) has that same form.
"In the prior-time existence as well," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Even hell-beings in the state of the prior-time existence (*pūrvakālabhava*) are not constantly burning when they wander among the secondary hells (*utsada*) such as the Pit of Hot Ashes (*kukūla*);
how much more so, then, those belonging to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
Or, let it be granted that they are burning.
The intermediate state being is a hell-being.
Regarding the phrase "because of the lack of contact within the womb":
because the bodies of those in the intermediate state are translucent, they do not touch one another, and thus there is no burning.
And because of the obstruction by karma.
Since there is no burning due to the obstruction of that karma,
for this very reason, there is no burning of the wombs of dogs and other such animals.
"A hundred koṭis of four-continent worlds were illuminated.

Because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the Bodhisattva is like that of a full-grown youth, possessing the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), he— while remaining in the intermediate state and desiring to enter his mother’s womb— illuminated the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system, regarding it as his own field.
"A white elephant calf"—
if this refers to the form of the future existence prior to birth (aiṣyat-pūrvakālabhava).
Regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*):
why did the Bodhisattva’s mother see such a form as an elephant calf?
That was merely a sign (*nimitta*).
Because that Bodhisattva has long since turned away from rebirth in the animal realm.
From the time he begins to perform the deeds that ripen into the marks [of a Great Man], when a hundred eons remain, from that point on all his miserable destinies are averted.
For example, King Kṛkin saw ten dreams.
"It is merely a sign of a future event.
Ten dreams are recited in the Vinaya.
It is said that King Kṛkin saw ten dreams.
An elephant, having gone out through a window, became stuck by its tail;
a well pursues a thirsty man from behind;
a measure of pearls is obtained for a measure of barley-meal.
Sandalwood is sold for the price of common wood.
Groves rich in flowers and fruit have all their flowers and fruit stolen by those who take what is not given.
Young elephants are used to frighten scent-elephants.
A monkey smeared with filth defiles others;
the consecration of monkeys takes place;
a cloth is pulled by eighteen men.
“A great multitude of people has fallen into mutual destruction through quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute in one place.
This was reported by him to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa,
and it was explained by the Blessed One.
In a future time, there will be a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni.

His disciples, having renounced the world after abandoning their extensive circles of kinsmen and relatives, will give rise to the notion of "home" within the monasteries and form attachments, like elephants whose tails remain caught as they exit through a window.
By the dream of the well, it is indicated that those very disciples will approach brahmins and householders and teach them the Dharma.
This shows that their desire to hear [the Dharma] will not persist.

By the dream of the measure of parched grain (*saktu*), it shows that those very disciples will proclaim the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and so forth, even for the sake of a mere alms-begging of parched grain.

And by the dream of the sandalwood (*candana*), it shows that those very disciples, having failed to cultivate body, morality, and wisdom, will adopt the doctrines of the heretics (*tīrthika*) and equate them with the words of the Buddha.

By the dream of the garden, it is shown that those very disciples, making their dwellings their basis, will repeatedly sell whatever flowers, fruits, or surplus goods belong to the Saṅgha to make a living,
and with that they will entertain householders. By the dream of the young elephant, it is shown that those very disciples will become immoral and of evil character.
This shows that they will expel from their dwellings those monks who are elders, virtuous, and of noble character.

By means of the dream of the monkey smeared with impurity, it indicates that those very disciples who are of evil conduct and wicked nature will treat as "virtuous" those monks who are actually of noble character.
This shows that they will accuse them with false faults.
By the dream of the monkey’s consecration, it shows that those very disciples will perform the neighboring consecration (sāmantikābhiṣeka) in the monasteries;
and it also shows that in the world, eunuchs will exercise sovereign rule.

By the dream of the cloth, he shows that his very teaching will undergo division into eighteen schools, yet the cloth of liberation itself will not be torn asunder. By the dream of the quarrel, he shows that his disciples themselves, through their adherence to specific sects, will fall into mutual dispute.

The summary verse: An elephant, a well, flour, sandalwood, a young elephant, a grove, as well as the consecration of a monkey, an impure monkey, a cloth, and a quarrel— these ten dreams were seen by King Kṛkin.
Because of the predominance of shame (*apatrāpya*), that is, because shame is intense;
"existence at birth" (*upapattibhava*) refers to the very moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*).
Any existence subsequent to that moment of rebirth-linking is "existence during the prior period" (*pūrvakālabhava*).
"If one is reborn among beings possessing form"—
this specific qualification is stated because there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
[This applies] to those of the same class.
Thus,

a hell-being intermediate state being is seen only by other hell-being intermediate state beings; likewise, up to a divine intermediate state being, who is seen only by other divine intermediate state beings.
"Completely pure" means being free from the eleven defects of the divine eye.

Those defects, moreover, are: doubt, lack of mental attention, physical rigidity, sloth and torpor, restlessness, over-exertion of energy, elation, trepidation, perception of diversity, and excessive talkativeness.
The state of being contemplated regarding the objects of knowledge is as stated in the Sūtra.
"Consisting of supernormal knowledge" (abhijñāmaya) means that its nature consists of the cultivation of supernormal knowledges (abhijñā).
Even that which is acquired at birth by gods and others is considered divine,
yet it is not perfectly pure.
"The intermediate state being of the gods," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Others say:
the intermediate state (antarābhava) is not seen only by those of the same class;
what then?

A being in the intermediate state of the gods sees all those in the intermediate states of the gods and so forth, excluding each preceding category in turn— namely, those in the intermediate states of humans, hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings. How so?
One in the intermediate state of a human, setting aside those in the intermediate state of a god, sees those in the intermediate states of humans, hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings.

One in the intermediate state of a hungry ghost, setting aside the two preceding ones—the intermediate states of gods and humans—sees those in the intermediate states of hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings.

In this manner, up to one in the intermediate state of a hell-being, setting aside the preceding ones such as the intermediate state of a god, sees only those in the intermediate state of hell-beings.
Because the destinies (gati) become increasingly inferior one after another;
for this very reason, it is called "gandharva," since it has gone toward the odor (gandha).
The meaning is that he "eats" (bhakṣayati) fragrance; thus he is a *gandharva*. Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, this root *arv* does not function solely in the sense of "going."
What then?
Even if it is for the purpose of eating, there is no fault even if the meaning of "going" (gati) is included;
thus, a *gandharva* is so called because he goes (*arvati*) or moves toward fragrance (*gandha*) in order to eat.
The shortening [of the vowel] is as in the cases of *śakandhu* and *karkandhu*;
it occurs because of the irregular application (*nipātana*) of the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) in words ending in a *kṛt* suffix.
Just as the formation of the single substitute [pararūpa] in *śakandhu* and *karkandhu* is established,
so too here in the case of *gandharva*. It means one who is called "of little power," lacking nobility, and of low birth.
One who rules is a ruler (*īśa*). One who is a minor ruler is a "minor ruler" (*alpeśa*).
One whose designation is "minor ruler" is "known as a minor ruler" (*alpeśākhya*).
By the opposite, one is designated as "greatly powerful.
This is because of belonging to the same homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*);
that is, both the existence of the previous time (*pūrvakālabhava*) and the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) which leads to it belong to that same class.
The two share one and the same homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga); therefore, because they belong to the same homogeneous class,
by the very same life-force karma that projects the lifespan of the prior-time existence (pūrvakālabhava), it also projects the lifespan of the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Otherwise,
if there were a separate projection for that intermediate state lifespan,
then the death-existence would necessarily follow from the exhaustion of that intermediate state lifespan, just as it does for the prior-time existence.
"Therefore, there is no fixed rule," says the Bhadanta.
"Having smelled that odor, they become greedy for the odor and taste," and so forth.

Those small creatures, having smelled that odor and recollecting the taste experienced as accompanying it, become greedy for the odor and taste; and at the time of death, [they produce] a rebirth within the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) of worms.
Having awakened the karma,
and having caused it to face its maturation through that craving for odor and taste, they are born among worms by means of the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Thus, it is precisely at a time when those conditions are abundant [that this occurs].
In a time abundant with the conditions for worms, those karmas conducive to that state—karmas conducive to becoming worms—attain their functional activity toward the production of maturation.
The meaning is that they become oriented toward yielding their maturation.
Indeed, having obtained the necessary collection of conditions and the [proper] time, they bear fruit for embodied beings.
Because of this statement:
not elsewhere,
nor at a time when that is not predominant.
"Not in another" means not in one with a short lifespan.
The appearance of a wheel-turning monarch does not occur below [an age of] eighty thousand years.
Because of this statement.

"For this very reason" means that even though the karmas conducive to becoming a universal monarch (cakravartin) exist, they only occasionally find the opportunity to function in the actualization of their maturation (vipāka).
Because it depends on many conditions;
because it seeks existence; because it desires rebirth;
for it is karma alone that brings about the assembly of conditions.
By the predominance of karma, it is well known that for horses and other animals, sexual intercourse occurs even at times other than the established season.
This is because they are projected by a single karma;
that is, by the very same karma by which the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) of cattle and so forth is projected.
By that very same karma, that intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is projected.
Therefore, this must be explained:
as for what was said—that one who is to be reborn among cattle at another time [projects the intermediate state earlier].
"He is reborn among the gavayas," and so on in detail.
The fact that [an action] projects a single [rebirth] is not lost due to the difference in the species [of animal],
because that karma belongs to a single class.
And because there is the abandonment of another form and configuration belonging to the cow.

For it is observed that the variety of rebirths resulting from karmas fixed for a particular destiny is seen, as in the case of Kalmāṣapāda and others; thus, Master Saṃghabhadra says that this fault does not exist.
"Perverted mind" means that one becomes perverted in mind by means of a thought accompanied either by attachment or by aversion.
Demonstrating this, he says:
"In that regard, of his parents," and so forth.
This refers to the misconduct of the mother and father, characterized by the union of the two sexual organs.
In one who is male, a man—that is, a being in the intermediate state—sexual desire for a woman arises as if toward a wife;
in one who is female, sexual desire for a man arises as if toward a husband. Conversely, aversion arises [toward the other parent].
In one who is male, a masculine hostility arising from envy is produced toward the father, as if toward a rival man;
in one who is female, a feminine hostility is produced toward the mother, as if toward a rival wife.

Being thus perverted by those two perverted states of mind, through the desire for sexual pleasure and the desire for the act of copulation, he clings to that place—the location of the two organs—and remains in that state.
One conceives of oneself as being in the state of sexual union, thinking, "This action is being performed by me.

And when that impure semen and blood have reached the location of the womb—that is, reached the space between the stomach (āmāśaya) and the large intestine (pakvāśaya)—one becomes attached to it; the meaning is that one takes up residence there.
"Facing the back, squatting" refers to the engagement in the act of sexual intercourse and the conceit of selfhood involved in that act. "Being nourished" means increasing.
"These very [elements]" refers to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of semen and blood. "Other primary elements" refers to those distinct from them.
[The aggregates] are distinct from semen and blood.

According to the principle of the cessation of the seed and the arising of the sprout, the seed ceases and the sprout arises in one and the same moment; for destruction and arising are simultaneous, like the downward and upward movements of the ends of a balance scale.
"That which is called *kalala*":
first there is the *kalala*;
from the *kalala* the *arbuda* is born.
Because of such statements as these. And having established it thus, there is this scriptural passage:

"O monk, 'anthill' is a designation for this body—material, gross, composed of the four great elements, nourished by boiled rice and gruel, and produced from the embryo of the impurities of the mother and father."
The *kalala* is indeed the impurity of the mother and father;
the meaning is that it arises from that.
"Kaṭasi" means a cemetery.
"A cemetery;
a drop of blood is appropriated"—
this is the illustrative example.
This is because it has attained the state of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
There are indeed other primary elements (*bhūta*) distinct from the semen and blood,
just as in the case of a leaf-worm.
Just as, in the case of a leaf-insect, other primary elements arise through karma depending upon the primary elements of the leaf;
these [new elements] attain the nature of sense faculties,
whereas the primary elements of the leaf do not.

Because of the great number of those worms, and because the leaf is not seen as a single whole [but as many parts]. How, then, is the scriptural passage—"born from the impure *kalala* of mother and father"—to be interpreted? To this, he says:
Because it was spoken with the intention that [the embryo] arises based upon the impure, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra regarding the *kalala*;
for other primary elements (*bhūta*) arise by depending on the impure.
In this context, "intention" (*abhisandhi*) means the underlying purpose (*abhiprāya*).
Therefore, that statement refers to the *kalala*.
Consequently, there is no contradiction with this sūtra: "born from the impure *kalala* of the mother and father.
This is what is meant.

Based upon the white and red elements (śukla-śoṇita), other primary elements (bhūta) called the embryo (kalala) arise simultaneously with the white and red elements, possessing sense-faculties (sendriya).
Just as, based upon a leaf, the primary elements of a worm arise simultaneously with the leaf and possess sense-faculties;
however, they say that in other cases, it should be explained according to the specific circumstances.

"The masters of Abhidharma say that this should be explained accordingly for the other two modes of birth, namely the moisture-born and the spontaneously born. And in that regard, this application [of the principle] should be seen," so says the Master.
"And coldness in the hells" refers to the time of rebirth in the cold hells.
"In whatever state" means in the state of a butcher of sheep and so forth.

"As if rising from his seat" means because of his movement toward the place of rebirth above.

"Mahākāya-nāḍīvraṇa" (the great-bodied channel-wound) is a term of reproach. It means "a wound in the form of a channel," like a sinus ulcer.
It is fierce and foul-smelling, possessing a most terrible stench.
It is darkness because it is devoid of light. And it is a pool of impurities, being like a pool (palvala) in its nature.
In that [body], which requires constant remediation and whose purification must be performed perpetually,
there is semen belonging to the male and blood belonging to the female.
By lymph, which is characterized as a specific fluid;
and by impurity, it is moistened—that is, thoroughly drenched—on all sides;
and it is decomposed—that is, excessively putrefied.
When it is boiling, putrid, and slimy, they thrust their hands into it; having cut off and severed limb after limb—such as the hands and feet—they pull them out and draw them away.
It is like a fresh wound, full of pain.

Behaving as if his own self were a fresh wound, he is one for whom the self acts like a fresh wound; thus, he is "one whose self acts like a fresh wound" (taruṇavraṇāyamānātmānaṃ), referring to the child. A weapon and caustic are "weapon-and-caustic" (śastrakṣāraṃ).
Behaving toward themselves as if they were weapons and caustic acid— since the touch of these two hands is like weapons and caustic acid— they seize them with those hands and bathe them.
"Because of the following from its increase" means because of the continuous succession of that [increase]. "Its lack of cause" means the lack of cause for the beginning.
And if this [arising] were causeless,
then everything would manifest as being causeless in that very same way.
Yet, the efficacy of seeds and so forth with respect to sprouts and the like is observed.
The capacity of seeds, sprouts, stalks, leaves, and so forth, to produce sprouts, stalks, leaves, and so forth, exists within those [latter] things.
Why?
Because of the specific determination of place and time.
However, it is due to the specific restriction of place and time.

In this regard, the restriction of place is because production occurs only in a location connected with the seed and so forth. The restriction of time is because production occurs immediately after the seed.

The causal capacity of fire and so forth— such as fire, cold, heat, impact, the eye, and so on— with respect to effects produced by maturation, such as cooked food, pleasure, pain, sound, and visual consciousness, is observed to be restricted by place and time. For if manifestation were causeless,

seeds and the like would lack the capacity for production in sprouts and the like, and fire and the like would lack the capacity for production in cooked food and the like, according to the restriction of place and time.
Everything would arise everywhere and at all times;
however, this is not observed. Therefore, there is no manifestation that is without a cause. The doctrine asserting the existence of an eternal cause has already been refuted.
Because of the statement, "Not from a Lord or the like, due to [the impossibility of] succession and so forth" (III.20).
The remaining eight are in the middle.
The members [of dependent origination] are consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, and existence.
Nor does it belong to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara),
because for one belonging to the form realm (rūpāvacara), the members of name-and-form and the six sense bases already exist at the very time of the member of consciousness.

There are not eight members in the middle [existence], because for one belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), the members of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are absent;
as stated in the *Mahānidānaparyāyasūtra*.
"Ānanda, if consciousness were not to descend into the mother's womb, would that name-and-form coagulate into the state of the *kalala*?
No, Venerable Sir," and so forth—that Sūtra is recited.
For the descent into the mother's womb occurs only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Because of the inclusion of the prior and posterior limits together with their results and causes, respectively. This means:
because of the inclusion of the prior limit together with its result, and the inclusion of the posterior limit together with its cause.
In that regard, ignorance and formative forces are the cause with respect to the past;
its results consist of five members,
from consciousness up to feeling.
Birth and old age and death in the future life constitute the fruit.
Its causes are three members: craving, grasping, and becoming.
Thus, it is explained that there are seven members in the past life and five members in the future life.
(III.21–24) Now, what are these [factors] beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*)?
Is it ignorance alone, or rather all the afflictions (*kleśa*), or perhaps the state of the afflictions? Asking this out of doubt, [the author] says: "Because of their association" (*sāhacaryāt*).
Because the afflictions accompany ignorance,
and because they manifest under its influence;
and because those afflictions manifest under the power of ignorance.
Furthermore, that is its conformity [to delusion].
For the manifestation of afflictions occurs in one who is deluded, not in one who is undeluded.
"As in the case of the statement 'the king is coming,'" and so forth.
Just as when it is said, "The king is coming," the arrival of his followers and servants is established by implication;
because of their constant association, they appear along with him by virtue of that connection.
It is just like that.
Thus, by the power of ignorance;
the meaning is that the factor of ignorance is the state of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore it has been said:
"Ignorance is the state of the previous afflictions.
(Abhid-k-vy 285)
But it was not stated that "ignorance" refers to the stage of prior ignorance;
rather, it refers to the stage of meritorious and other types of karma.
The meaning is: the stage of meritorious and non-meritorious karma.

It should be stated as "prior to the arising of the four sense-bases," because the sense-bases of mind and body arise only at the moment of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*); it is for that reason that they are established [as such] at that time.
The meaning is that at the time of the arising of the sense bases such as the eye, the bases of the body and the mind are established. That occurs prior to the coming together of the triad.
That limb of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) [extends] prior to the meeting of the triad; the meaning is: prior to the coming together of the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness.
Contact (*sparśa*) [extends] prior to...
Thus, contact (*sparśa*), which is the coming together of the six sense-faculties, their objects, and consciousnesses, is established as occurring in the state of birth,
because of the existence of the coming together of the complete six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
From what point?
Prior to the capacity for knowledge regarding the causes of pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations.

That person is a child as long as he is not capable of discerning: "This is the cause of a pleasant sensation; this is the cause of a painful sensation; and this is the cause of a neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation."
That state is called contact (*sparśa*).
For instance, an infant might even touch fire without discerning that this is a cause of suffering; yet, when the capacity for such discernment exists, [contact occurs].
"Vitti" means "feeling" (vedanā).
Up to what point?
The state prior to sexual intercourse,
as long as sexual desire has not yet arisen,
is called "feeling."
For that state is characterized by the intensity of feeling,
because one experiences the causes of feeling;
craving belongs to those who are attached to enjoyments and sexual union.
Thus:
regarding enjoyments, characterized by the qualities of sensual desire such as form and so forth,
and regarding sexual intercourse, which is well-known in the world, for a person possessed of passion.
The state in which that passion becomes manifest is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). Regarding the phrase "having entered into seeking," this is a form derived from the verbal root *iṣ*.
That by which an object (*viṣaya*) or the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is grasped is "grasping" (*upādāna*), which consists of the fourfold afflictions (*kleśa*).
That state is called "grasping";
it is the fruit of future existence (*bhava*).
"Thus.
"He" is the designation for one who is running about.
"Having future existence as its fruit" means that its fruit is future existence (*bhava*).
The meaning is that karma leads to renewed existence; that is *bhava*.
Thus:
"it exists by means of this" is *bhava*, a synonym for karma.
[It extends] up to old age and death.
"Up to the knowledge" means up to the member of knowledge (*vedanā*).
Old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) have the four members beginning with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as their intrinsic nature.
For the sake of causing revulsion in those to be trained, the Blessed One spoke of these four members by the term "old age and death."
"O monks, that which is the arising of form is the arising of old age and death; and so on, up to consciousness."
*Momentary* (*kṣaṇika*) means that which exists for a moment (*kṣaṇa*). Alternatively, it is *momentary* because it possesses a moment.
*Prolonged* (*prākarṣika*) means that which plays or acts with intensity (*prakarsa*).
The meaning is "connected with a continuous series.
Likewise, "relating to connection" means connected with the relationship between cause and effect.
Likewise, [it refers to] the "stages."
The meaning is that there are twelve states consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandhika*).
"Co-arising with consciousness" (*vijñānasahabhū*) is the full expression;
here, "form" (*rūpa*) refers to the co-arising informative and non-informative [matter], and so forth.
The triad of aggregates beginning with perception (saṃjñā) is "name" (nāman).
The sense faculties are established upon name-and-form (nāmarūpa),
because the functioning of the sense faculties is dependent upon them.

Or rather, those [elements] are established within the name by way of being its basis. "Contact is the convergence of the six sense bases" means that the engagement of the eye and the other [senses] with their respective objects is "convergence."
But that [contact] exists according to possibility.
It should be understood that whatever [object] has its impact possible at that time, that is the contact of that [consciousness].
The secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) associated with that [craving] are grasping (*upādāna*).
Those secondary afflictions, such as shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), which are associated with that craving, constitute that grasping.
"Arising from that" means arising from that [craving].
It arises from craving;
others say it arises from volition.
"Emergence" is birth, and "ripening" is old age.
It is the impairment of the capacity to project a fruit;
or, with respect to the preceding moment,
it is destruction, which is death.
It is destruction at that very moment.
Others say that "destruction" (bhaṅga) refers to the state of being oriented toward destruction.
It is both momentary and relational, as explained in the *Prakaraṇas*.
How so?
In the *Prakaraṇapāda*, it is asked: "What is dependent origination?
and it is replied: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)."
In that regard, dependent origination is momentary because conditioned phenomena are subject to destruction at every moment;
it is relational because it involves the connection between two moments consisting of cause and fruit;
and it is continuous because it connects three successive births without interruption.
The twelve states consisting of the five aggregates, connected with past, future, and present births, constitute "situational" (*āvasthika*) dependent origination.
The inclusion of the term "uninterrupted" (*niraṃtara*) is for the purpose of establishing the three sections (*trikāṇḍa*).
This very same [dependent origination] is called "prolonged" (*prākarṣika*).
That very same [type of patience] is "pertaining to states" (āvasthika) because it is connected with excellence (prakarṣa);
it is "prolonged" (prākarṣika) because it consists of many moments or many lifetimes.
(III.25ab) "Intentional" (*ābhiprāyika*) means existing in the intention (*abhiprāya*). The meaning is that it was taught in such a way by virtue of the intention of those to be trained (*vineya*).
In the Abhidharma, [dependent origination] is defined technically (*lākṣaṇika*), because it prioritizes its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
For in the *Prakaraṇapāda*, dependent origination is explained as pertaining to both sentient and non-sentient beings,
since it encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) by virtue of their connection to the causality of all conditioned things.
The twelvefold dependent origination was taught as pertaining only to what is designated as "sentient beings," for the purpose of dispelling the delusion of those to be trained.
Therefore, it is said:
"In order to dispel delusion regarding the prior, the posterior, and the intermediate limits."
Thus it is said.
For this very reason, it is called "consisting of three sections" (*trikāṇḍa*).
Here, "section" (*kāṇḍa*) means a part.
"Who indeed was I?"—
whether as a god or a human.
"How indeed was I?"— thus he reflects.

The meaning is: "In what manner? By what reasoning? The detailed explanation is: "Will I exist in the future time?"—that is, "Indeed, will I exist in the future time? (Abhidh-k-vy 287) [Tib.275b] Will I exist in the future time?
Or rather: "Shall I not exist? Who indeed shall I become?
How indeed shall I become?"
"In what manner" means "by what reasoning.
"What indeed is this?"—
thus he investigates the substance of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
"How indeed is this?
means: in what manner, by what reasoning?
He does not ascertain that very substance of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
"Who are the peaceful ones?
"Who are we that exist now?
"What shall we become?"—in this way, he does not determine [these things].
"In the Sūtra, they are given in order" means that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the past (*pūrvānta*),
while birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the future (*aparānta*).
"From consciousness up to existence [are taught] for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the middle [existence]," as it is stated in detail:
"For it has been said thus in the Sūtra itself.
That is to say, it is shown in this very way even in the Sūtra.
He supports his own explanation with a sutra:
"He does not resort to the past limit, thinking, 'Did I indeed exist in past time? and so forth."
He does not run back toward the past,
wondering, "Did I indeed exist in past time?
The meaning is that, through seeing dependent origination as it truly is, he is not thus deluded regarding the past.
By the word "in detail," it means that he does not pursue the future limit;
namely, the elaboration beginning with, "Shall I exist in the future time? Likewise, he does not pursue the middle limit;
namely, the elaboration beginning with, "What indeed is this?"
"Craving, grasping, and becoming as well"—
all these [factors] of craving, grasping, and becoming are for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the future limit (aparānta),
not for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the middle limit (madhya).
As previously taught, [the members of dependent origination range] from consciousness up to existence (*bhava*).
What, then, is the reasoning here? He says:
"For these are the causes of that very [consciousness]."
Because these are the causes of the future limit alone.
(III.26) "Because they are the basis for afflictions and karma" means that the seven members beginning with consciousness are the entities and the foundations for afflictions and karma.
"The fruit is likewise.
Only seven members—the members of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—are the fruits of ignorance and the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Birth and old age and death are the fruits of craving, grasping, and becoming.
"The five that have become causes" refers to ignorance, formations, craving, grasping, and existence;
this is because their intrinsic nature consists of karma and afflictions.
Ignorance, craving, and grasping have the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) have the nature of karma.
This is because the entity [of dependent origination] is divided into five types.
Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling;
and the two aspects of affliction:
craving and grasping.
In the future time, the fruit is summarized by way of a twofold division:
namely, birth and old age and death.
In the past time, the cause is summarized because the afflictions are taught under a single heading.
The meaning is that this is because the afflictions are taught as having ignorance as their primary aspect;
however, in the future time, the fruit is not expanded in this fivefold way,
nor in the past time is the cause expanded in this twofold way.
(III.27) Because it has been demonstrated here by the Blessed One: what [is it]?
From affliction, affliction.
Such is the method regarding the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*) beginning with this;
from that, the entity (*vastu*).
Thus [it is said].
From that, [it arises] from action.
Then again, [it is said]: "the thing."
From that entity, further entities and afflictions arise.
The term "of the object" (*vastunaḥ*) is understood from the context. Here, the particle *iti* is to be supplied after "are born" (*jāyante*).
Thus, it is made known that [the afflictions arise] either from the object or from the afflictions themselves.
Thus, it is observed that an affliction arises from a thing, as in "from feeling [arises] craving.
Likewise, it is observed that an affliction arises from an affliction, as in "from craving [arises] grasping.
Furthermore, ignorance is declared to have the nature of all afflictions belonging to the prior limit [of existence].
Therefore, it is understood that if grasping arises from craving, then [craving] arises from that object;
or else, it is understood that craving arises from that object.
Consequently, it is made known that ignorance, being of the nature of a defilement, arises either from an object or from a defilement.
It has been explained that old age and death are entities whose intrinsic nature consists of four factors.
And here, it is observed that an affliction arises from an entity, as in the statement: "craving has feeling as its condition.
Therefore, it is made known that from that [entity], an affliction will come to be in the future.
In this regard, nothing further needs to be added, since it has already been made known in this way.
But how is it understood that this method has been demonstrated? He says:
because of the statement, "Thus there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering."
For otherwise, what would be its efficacy?
If this aforementioned principle did not exist:
"From affliction, affliction and action arise; from that, the basis; and from that, again [affliction]."
One should say only this: "The entities and the afflictions arise.
One should not say: "Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces, up to: conditioned by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair come into being."
"Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
Origination (*samudaya*) and arising (*utpāda*) are not different in meaning.
Therefore, it is understood that its efficacy consists in elucidating the manner [of origination] as previously described.
It is stated in another sutra that ignorance has improper mental attention as its cause.
This is in the *Sahetu-sapratyaya-sanidāna-sūtra*.
How so?
"O monks, ignorance has a cause, it has a condition, and it has a source. And what, monks, is the cause of ignorance, what is its condition, what is its source?
O monks, improper mental attention is the cause of ignorance, improper mental attention is its condition, and improper mental attention is its source," because of this statement in the Sūtra.

"And improper mental attention has ignorance as its cause. This refers to what is stated in another sutra, because of the statement in that sutra: "Depending on the eye and forms, there arises a turbid mental attention born of delusion."
For what reason is it not mentioned here?
How is it that it does not become another limb of existence (*bhavāṅga*)? To this he says:
"And because it is included within *upādāna*, it is also said to be [present] here."
"That" refers to turbid mental attention (*manaskāra*).
"Here" refers to the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
How was it stated there?
Because it is included within clinging (*upādāna*).
For clinging is the state in which the afflictions (*kleśa*) are active for the sake of obtaining enjoyments;
and therein, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), which is the application of a distorted mind, is said to be included.
Therefore, ignorance is not without a cause,
nor is it necessary to add another link beyond the twelve beginning with ignorance;
furthermore, there is no consequence of an infinite regress, because improper mental attention has ignorance as its cause.
"Thus says another" refers to the Elder Vasubandhu, the preceptor of the teacher Manoratha; he spoke thus.
The teacher said:
"How so? is the detailed question.
How is improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) included within grasping (*upādāna*)? For improper mental attention does not have the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of grasping.
If [it is argued that it is included] by way of association:
if you maintain that improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) is included within grasping (*upādāna*) because it is associated with grasping,

then it follows that this same improper mental attention must also be included within the two members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), namely craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).
For it is also associated with craving and ignorance;
therefore, it should have been stated that it is already included here within ignorance, craving, and grasping.
But one should not say:
"And here too, because it is included within grasping (*upādāna*), it is already stated.
The intention is that such a restriction—that it must necessarily be included within grasping—should not be made.
"And even if there were inclusion.
We say this even while conceding an inclusion that is impossible,
in order to demonstrate how improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) is the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*).
For there is no such statement in the Sūtra. "If, by way of being included," and so forth:
if it is because improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) is included within grasping (*upādāna*).
Therefore, it is made known that improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) is the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, no other member [of the dependent origination] needs to be mentioned,
because that is established by the very mention of grasping (*upādāna*).
In that case, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are also included within grasping (*upādāna*).
Therefore, since those two are also included therein, it would be possible not to treat them as separate members;
for they are established by the very mention of grasping.
And since craving and ignorance have been stated as separate factors [of dependent origination],
this is therefore not a valid rebuttal.
Another, however, says— namely, the Venerable Śrīlāta:
"In another sutra, improper mental attention is stated to be the cause of ignorance.
This refers to the *Sahetu-sapratyaya-sanidāna-sūtra*, which states in detail:
"Monks, ignorance also has a cause, has a condition, and has a source."
"And that too," and so forth.
That improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) was also specified at the time of contact (*sparśa*).
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Dependent upon the eye and forms, there arises a turbid mental attention born of delusion.
This refers to the time of contact, which is the very time of the arising of visual consciousness.
It is called "turbid mental attention" because it functions in an improper manner (*ayoniśas*) or because it is born of delusion.
"Born from delusion, it is called 'born of delusion.
"Feeling born of contact with ignorance":
feeling born from contact associated with ignorance is "feeling born of contact with ignorance."
Wherever there is a feeling born from contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśaja*),
ignorance is necessarily associated (*saṃprayukta*) with it.
For a feeling that is not associated with ignorance does not become a cause for craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Thus, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) occurring at the time of contact is established as the condition for the ignorance that co-exists with feeling (*vedanā*).
This makes it known that ignorance has improper mental attention as its cause;
therefore, ignorance is not without a cause.
Because it has improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) as its cause,
no other member need be added beyond the twelve,
since improper mental attention occurring at the time of contact is established as the condition for the ignorance that co-exists with feeling.
Nor does there follow the consequence of an infinite regress, because that improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) is also said to be born of delusion (*moha*), as it is stated:
"Turbid mental attention is born of delusion."
Thus, this is described as a circle:
from improper mental attention comes ignorance,
and from ignorance comes improper mental attention.
Seeing this rebuttal as likewise faulty, the Master begins a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) in order to manifest that fault.
"In that case, then," and so forth;
namely, that which was stated in detail according to the Sūtra or through reasoning: "Improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) is the cause of ignorance."
"In that case" (*tarhi*) is used when one intends to express a different meaning;
"now" (*idānīm*) is the specific sense according to the Blessed One.
This was stated elsewhere in a sutra, but it must now be explained here in this *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
"It should not be said," says the Venerable Śrīlāta.
When asked, "By what reasoning?
the Venerable Śrīlāta replied:
"Not indeed," and so forth.
Arhats possess sensation,
yet that sensation does not become a condition for craving.
It is understood that feeling accompanied by ignorance (*savidyā*) alone is the condition for craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
And it is the subject at hand that a non-perverted contact (*aviparīta-sparśa*) does not serve as the condition for afflicted feeling (*kliṣṭā vedanā*).
Furthermore, for an Arhat who is free from ignorance (*niravidya*), there is no such thing as perverted contact.
It is understood that contact (*sparśa*) is likewise accompanied by ignorance (*sāvidya*),
since it was stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* to be the condition for sensation (*vedanā*).
Furthermore, it is understood that ignorance is the cause of this contact.
By this reasoning, it is understood from the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* that feeling has contact associated with ignorance as its condition,
and craving has feeling associated with ignorance as its condition;
thus, by the reasoning as stated.

And since that [unwise attention] is also specified at the time of contact, it is established here in detail within this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that unwise attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) is the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Here an objection is raised:

"If, then, by the statement that 'feeling devoid of ignorance does not become a condition for craving,' and so forth, unwise attention is the cause of ignorance and ignorance is the cause of unwise attention through reasoning inherent to itself..."
It is understood that this is the cause.
What is the purpose of relying on another sutra to demonstrate that ignorance (*avidyā*) and improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) are mutual causes for one another?
To this, it is said:
This is true;
however, this is merely a logical inference in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*,
not an explicit statement.
Therefore, since this reasoning is established through explicit statement in another sūtra, the purpose of citing that other sūtra must be understood.
The author of the treatise [objects]: "In this way, an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would result. He asks: "How does an over-extension result? and then says:
It is stated in another sutra that "craving arises dependent on feeling born from contact with ignorance.
However, for an Arhat who is free from ignorance, feeling does not become a condition for craving;
nor does non-perverted contact serve as a condition for afflicted feeling.

Furthermore, since for an Arhat who is free from ignorance there is no perverted contact (*viparīta-sparśa*), by this reasoning it follows that even these two factors called contact and feeling—which are not mentioned here in this *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*—are understood because they have been taught elsewhere; thus, it would follow that these two factors also need not be stated here.
Indeed, they have been taught in another sutra.
If he performs meritorious formations (*saṃskāra*), his consciousness (*vijñāna*) becomes one that leads to merit;
likewise for that which leads to non-merit and that which leads to the imperturbable (*āniñjya*).
However, for an Arhat who is free from ignorance, there is no consciousness leading to merit, nor even consciousness leading to the imperturbable.
This member of conditioned forces (saṃskāra) is also established by reasoning;
thus, it follows that one need not state [its existence] here.
Likewise, it is understood through reasoning that without birth (jāti), aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) do not occur.
"The limb of birth would not need to be mentioned," and such further consequences would follow.
However, the Master states his own view in detail, asserting that "this is indeed not to be questioned."
"How does one go from the next world to this world? and so forth.
In that regard, this world is connected with ignorance and the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
And this world consists of the members of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.
Through craving, grasping, and becoming, one is connected to the next world;
and that next world consists of birth, as well as aging and death.
This is because only this much of the subject matter was intended to be taught here in the Sūtra on Dependent Origination for the sake of those to be trained.
And because this very point has already been stated previously;
for it was said [in the verse]: "In order to dispel delusion regarding the prior, the posterior, and the middle."
This objection is indeed not to be raised; the connection [of the text] extends in detail up to the point: "nor is the exposition incomplete.
For both [categories] consist of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṭadharma*).
All conditioned phenomena belonging to the three time periods are dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
For this very reason, there is no distinction in their being "dependently originated. How, then, can they be called "uncreated"?
They are called "conditioned" by means of a future designation, just as future things are so designated.
The intended meaning is that they are likewise dependently originated.
Regarding the phrase "by volition that is formative," he says "by formative" in order to illuminate the specific characteristic of all volitions.
For it is "formative" (ābhisaṃskārikā) because it brings about maturation;
it is so called because one has willed and directed [the mind] toward it, such as: "I shall become a god," "I shall become a human," and so forth.
Therefore, future conditioned phenomena are so called;
this refutes the intention [of those who claim] that they are not so designated by virtue of their future status.
As for the question, "How is it with the untainted? [the same principle applies].
Those future states that are with outflows (sāsrava) can appropriately be intended in this way;
but as for those future states that are without outflows (anāsrava),
how can they appropriately be intended?
The challenger says:
"They too were willed by a wholesome volition, with the thought: 'May the untainted dharmas be attained.'"
"There would be the same consequence even for nirvāṇa.
This means that nirvāṇa, too, would entail being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). For if it were intended [to be attained], one would have to attain nirvāṇa by means of its acquisition (*prāpti*).
Thus, for this reason, since there is a fault in establishing the conditioned nature (*saṃskṛtatva*) of future phenomena, another method is proposed:
"Because they belong to that same class," and so forth.

Just as, although future matter (*rūpa*) is not yet being affected (*rūpyate*), it is designated as "matter" because it belongs to the same class as matter that is currently being affected; such is the extension of the definition.

Likewise, because they belong to the same category of phenomena as those arisen through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpanna*), future phenomena are also designated as "arisen through dependent origination"; this is the extended application (*atideśa*) to these future factors.
(III.28ab) "Because of the state of being cause and fruit" means that since that very same limb is both the cause and the fruit.
