And this being so, there is no lack of systematic establishment,
as in the case of "this shore" and "the other shore," or as in the case of "cause" and "effect."
Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and that which is dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) are not established as distinct entities, because they are mutually dependent,
like cause and fruit, or like father and son.
In this context, "cause and fruit" refers to...
For example, like the seed, the sprout, and so forth. Just as that in relation to which something is established as the cause is not, in turn, related to it as the effect.
That in relation to which the fruit is established is not that in relation to which the cause is established.
What then?
A cause is established in dependence upon its fruit,
and a fruit is established in dependence upon its cause;
just as one is designated a "father" in dependence upon someone else.
He is not a son in relation to him;
he is a son in relation to whom [he is a father];
he is not a father in relation to him.
What then?
One is a father in relation to that son,
and one is a son in relation to the father.
And that [object] is not indeterminate;
this case is like that.
The word "kila" indicates a sense of incredulity.
The first alternative consists of future phenomena (*dharmas*).

They are "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) because they are the causes of other phenomena, based on the principle that "from this, [something] arises. However, they are not "dependently originated" (*pratītyasamutpanna*), because they have not yet arisen.
The second [alternative] refers to the final moments of an Arhat;
because they have already arisen, and because no further fruit can arise from them.
The third [category] consists of those other than that;
namely, for an Arhat, the past and present dharmas other than the final [moments].
The fourth consists of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas.
Because they lack that fruit and because they are not subject to arising.
Indeed, what are these propositions being stated?
They would be such as: "Dependent origination is situational (āvasthika)," or "there is dependent origination but no dependently originated [phenomena]," and so forth.
Regarding "ignorance concerning the prior limit":
since it is stated that ignorance alone is meant, and not the other aggregates,
therefore ignorance alone is the constituent member (*aṅga*).
He shows that this is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
"Of definitive meaning" means its meaning has been analyzed.
The Sūtra is like the simile of the elephant's footprint.
And there are other things there as well, such as visible forms and so forth;
that is, among those [parts] such as hair and body hair,
it is not merely the earth element alone.
In the same way, here too, the explanation would be according to what is predominant.
Thus, here also in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*,
among the twelve states consisting of the five aggregates, it is wherever something is predominant [that it is so designated].
In that regard, there would be a specific designation for each respective state:
in the state where ignorance is predominant, there would be the designation "ignorance";
in those states where formations and so forth are predominant, there would be the designation of "formations" and so forth.
"And there are other factors there as well, such as form, sensation, and so forth"—
this is the meaning of "for it is not the case there," and so on.
For in that Sūtra, the hair and other [parts] are not indicated by means of the earth element.
"What are hair and so forth? They are the earth element.
[This is stated] because the description of these things, such as hair and so forth, would otherwise be incomplete;
for there are other factors there as well, such as visible form (*rūpa*) and the rest.
Even hair and so forth have the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form (*rūpa*) and other [sensory objects], not merely the intrinsic nature of the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*).
Nevertheless, the earth element is indicated by means of hair and so forth alone.
What is the earth element?
Regarding "hair and body hair":
there is no internal earth element that exists apart from or beyond hair and so forth.
Thus, this is a complete explanation of the earth element.
In the same way here as well, in this sutra, the exposition of ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth, is complete and not incomplete.
Regarding "tears, mucus, and so forth":
tears, mucus, and the like are not recited in that sutra.
Therefore, he shows that the earth element contained therein is not fully accounted for, and thus it remains incomplete.
Or, let it be exactly so, as detailed:
just as there is a remainder of the earth element in tears, snot, and so forth, because they were not mentioned.
In the same way, let there remain a residue of ignorance if it can be demonstrated.
Thinking that it cannot be demonstrated, he employs the word "if.

This is because all such bases of ignorance have been stated, including: ignorance regarding the past, ignorance regarding the future, ignorance regarding the middle [present], ignorance regarding the Buddha, ignorance regarding the Dharma, ignorance regarding the Saṅgha, and so forth.
But as for the inclusion of other categories such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth within ignorance (*avidyā*), on the grounds that "ignorance is the state of the five aggregates"—
for it is not logical that feeling and the rest should themselves be ignorance—
this is what is meant by the "rule of existence and non-existence."
That for which the presence or absence of one thing is determined by the presence or absence of another, respectively, is indeed a member (*aṅga*).

Since the presence of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) occurs when ignorance (*avidyā*) is present, and their absence occurs when it is absent, ignorance alone is the member; not feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.
For when feeling (vedanā) and the other [links] exist, conditioned factors (saṃskāra) do not arise for Arhats—
meaning those which produce the member of consciousness (vijñāna).
Therefore, he says:
And even though the five aggregates exist, the formative forces do not come to be; this is the detailed explanation.
And even though the five aggregates exist in the state of arhatship, consciousness that leads to merit, up to consciousness that leads to the imperturbable, does not come to be.

The meaning is that there is no rebirth-linking consciousness (*pratisaṃdhivijñāna*). It goes to various births, thus it is "approaching" (*upaga*). Consciousness approaching merit is "merit-approaching" (*puṇyopaga*) consciousness.
In this way, it continues up to the attainment of the imperturbable (*āniñjyopaga*).
Likewise, even though the five aggregates exist, in the state free from ignorance (*niravidyāvasthā*), craving, grasping, and so forth do not occur.
Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is exactly as it has been explained.
The meaning is that only those factors previously mentioned, such as ignorance and so forth, are to be understood.
Therefore, other existing aggregates are not conditions for the formative forces and the rest; thus, they are not "limbs.
[This refers to the formula] beginning with "Thus have I heard," and so on.
The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a community of monks consisting of twelve hundred and fifty monks,
and with a great many bodhisattvas. Then the venerable Śāriputra addressed the bodhisattva Maitreya as follows:
Having observed a rice stalk, this sutra was spoken to the monks:
"O monks, whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dharma."
"Whoever sees the Dharma sees the Buddha"— having said this, the Blessed One became silent.
What, then, is the meaning of this sūtra spoken by the Blessed One?
What is dependent origination? What is a phenomenon?
What is a Buddha?
And how is it that by seeing dependent origination one sees the Dharma?
Regarding this, "dependent origination" refers to the formula beginning with "this ignorance," and so forth.
It was with this intention in mind that this was stated in that Sūtra.

"Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this dharmatā remains fixed: the stability of phenomena, the regularity of phenomena, suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, reality, truth, thatness, non-perversion, and non-inversion"—such is the speech of the Blessed One Maitreya.
[If it were the case] that the future is not dependently originated...
As for what was said— that the first alternative consists of future phenomena— this contradicts the Sūtra;
for birth and old age and death would then not be dependently originated.
And it has been said: "Ignorance [extends] up to birth, old age, and death. Now, as for the phrase "or rather," the full explanation is as follows:
Or rather, even the members of birth, old age, and death are accepted as being dependently originated.
Since it must be accepted that for those two [the past and future], there is no establishment of a future time-period,
the division into three sections is disrupted;
for there would be two [sections] each for the prior and posterior limits, and eight in the middle.
Thus [it is said].
"Those of another school" refers to the noble Mahīśāsakas.
[They argue] because arising is a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
This arising which is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) is conceptualized as permanent by those belonging to other schools.
That has been stated to be a characteristic of the conditioned;
for there are these three characteristics of the conditioned.
The arising of the conditioned is discerned, as are its passing away and its alteration while persisting.
The intention is that it is impermanent because it possesses the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*). You might say, however, that even the characteristic itself is permanent.
Therefore, he says:
"And it is not tenable for an eternal distinct entity to be the characteristic of that which is impermanent.
For neither nirvāṇa nor space serves as the characteristic of anything that is impermanent.

For prior to the arising of the characterized object, of what would that [characteristic] be the characteristic? And once the characterized object has perished, of what would it be? Thus, it is not tenable.
"And as for arising," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, that which is called "arising" (utpāda) has the characteristic of being the existence of what was previously non-existent.
According to the Sautrāntika system, the arising of a dharma occurs only at that very moment.
Therefore, according to your own view, what connection could there be between this unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) arising and ignorance (avidyā) and the other factors?

Just as there is a relationship between rice and cooking characterized by agent and action, such that one says "the cooking of rice," there is no relationship between space and form characterized by originator and originated,
by virtue of which one could say "the space of form."
In this way, what connection does this [dependent origination] have with ignorance and the other factors,
such that dependent origination is said to belong to those factors beginning with ignorance?
Furthermore, the meaning of the term would then be something that lacks a connection.
The meaning of the term *pratītyasamutpāda* is "arising having reached conditions" (*pratyayaṃ prāpya samudbhavaḥ*).
How, then, can it be both eternal and yet dependent origination?
[For] the prefix *prati* has the sense of "reaching" (*prāpti*).
The meaning is that it indicates attainment (*prāpti*).
"Iti" means "to go";
this is the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*).
Regarding the phrase "due to a change of meaning":
verbal roots indeed possess multiple meanings.
Furthermore, since the prefix *prati* indicates attainment (*prāpti*), this root *iti*, having abandoned its sense of motion, comes to signify attainment.
The root *pad* has the meaning of "existence. [This is stated as] "the root *pad* is used in the sense of existence.
By that means—that is, by that reason.
Regarding the rule for the suffix *ktvā* in an action occurring at a prior time:
because of the statement that it applies "to two actions having the same agent when one occurs earlier," and because,
according to the Sautrāntika school, no such thing exists prior to its arising.
Nor is there an action without an agent, because an action is established only when there is an agent. And it is said in this regard:
The Teacher sets down this objection of the grammarian in a verse:
"If [the object] 'reaches' or 'attains' prior to its arising..."
Because it does not exist, it is not tenable.
For a non-existent agent performing an action such as bathing is never observed.
(Abhidh-k-vy 295)
If you then think that it performs the action of dependence and the action of origination simultaneously,
the suffix -ktvā is not established in this case.
The suffix *ktvā*. Why? Because it prescribes an action occurring at a prior time.
In the earlier time [of the rule], there was a prescription for the *ktvā* suffix.

Because of the statement "the *ktvā* suffix occurs when two actions have the same agent and the former action is prior in time," the *ktvā* suffix would not be established [in certain cases]. Therefore, it is stated: "upon its re-origination."
If one imagines the arising of what has already arisen, there follows the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
[For] it would arise again and again in the second, third, and subsequent moments, leading to the consequence of no finality (*aniṣṭhā*).
"Or, if it is future," and so forth.
Since the future has not yet attained its own nature (*alabdhātmaka*), how can agency be established for that which is non-existent and has not acquired its own being?
Or else, how can an action be established as one devoid of an agent?
Therefore, in whatever state it arises according to the grammarian who knows words—
He understands me while remaining in that very state.
[The question] "In what state? means:
"What is his state?"—thus, "in what state."
"Future [dharmas] are those facing toward arising.
Not every future dharma arises.
What then?
Facing toward arising;
facing toward production;
meaning that which is about to arise.
Remaining in that very state— that is, in the state immediately facing arising—
it is said to "approach.
"And this is not established," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
This is the grammatical (śābdakīya) determination of the agent and the action according to the Grammarians.
Why?
Because they perceive a difference between the entity (bhūti), which is conceived as the form of the action, and the agent (bhavitṛ), who is conceived as the form of the agent.
Therefore, there is no fallacy in such expressions as "it arises," "it comes into being," and so forth.
And here he says:
he demonstrates the process according to that established tenet.
"Just as that which is non-existent arises," and so forth.
Just as that which is non-existent— that is, an absence, having not yet attained its own nature— arises.
It is likewise when one returns. The meaning is "non-existent"; or else, "existent."

Now, if it is conceived that what has already acquired its own nature arises, then that which has already arisen would arise again; this results in an infinite regress (*aniṣṭhā*). Since even what has already arisen would arise once more, an endless succession would follow, leading to another undesirable consequence.
For, according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, there is arising only of what exists and not of what does not exist; with reference to this, he says:
"or it existed even previously.
The word "or" (vā) signifies an alternative view.
If your position is that what exists arises, then for us as well, what exists arises;
for according to the Vaibhāṣika system, future phenomena exist.
And according to the Sautrāntika system, because the seed— the dharma that produces [the effect]— actually exists,
what is meant by this statement:
"And it does not exist as anything prior to its arising"?
That which arises at a later time depending [on causes].
Or else, if it is the case that only what already exists arises,
then it follows that the jar must already exist by itself, prior to its dependence on the lump of clay and so forth.
Others, however, explain it thus:
"Whether not having reached completion even previously.
Now, let it be so that there is no undesirable consequence.
One maintains that what is non-existent arises;
then that very same [position] persists:
"Just as what is non-existent arises, so too does it pass away."
"One's own position is established," this should be stated as before.

Furthermore, regarding what was said—that the rule for the suffix *ktvā* applies to the earlier of two actions performed by a single agent—he says the following to demonstrate its deviation: "The suffix *ktvā* occurs even when [the actions] are simultaneous."
The full detail [is as follows].
The rule for the suffix *ktvā* is observed even when the action occurs at the same time [as the main verb]. For example:
"Having reached the lamp, the darkness has gone.
Here, the meaning is not that the darkness first reaches the lamp and subsequently goes away or perishes.
What then?
At that very moment, darkness perishes upon encountering the lamp. Now, if it is thought:
"It is immediately after, not simultaneously.
Therefore, this is further stated:
"Or he sleeps with his mouth open."
For he does not first open his mouth—that is, gape—and afterwards lie down.
What then?
It is one who lies down while opening his mouth.
It is said that "he sleeps having opened his mouth.
Now, if it is thought that he first opens his mouth [and then sleeps], [that is not so].
"It lies behind.
To this he says:
"If it is behind, why does it not enter?"
If someone were to lie down after opening their mouth and then closing it, one would not say of them, "He lies down with his mouth open.
Therefore, it is known [that the expression refers to a state of remaining open].
"He who lies down with his mouth open is said to lie down having opened his mouth.
"But others," however, [say].
The Venerable Śrīlāta maintains that *prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
Repetition is the desire to pervade all the various substrates denoted by [the words] with respect to both action and quality;
this *prati* illuminates that [repetition].
Those who are fit for going (itau) are "ityas.
In this context, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "fit for" (*sādhuḥ*). They are those who are fit for going, that is, for perishing.
The meaning is "non-abiding.
The prefix *sam-* indicates the sense of conjunction (*samavāya*). The root *pad-* preceded by *ut-* has the sense of manifestation (*prādurbhāva*).
Because of the transformation of the root-meaning.
"In dependence upon each respective collection" (*tāṃ tāṃ sāmagrīṃ pratīti*) indicates that the prefix *prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the arising through the combination of these perishable things.
Not a single phenomenon arises alone, because there is a rule of simultaneous arising for form and the other [aggregates].
In the desire realm, an atom that is without sound consists of eight substances;
likewise, mind and mental factors necessarily arise together.
"Because of this rule.
"But this is a conceptual construction," and so forth;
such a conceptual construction—that the prefix *prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), and so on—is appropriate only in this very *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
In this context, how will [the expression] "visual consciousness arises depending on the eye and forms" be understood?
For a compound such as *pratītyacakṣūṃṣi* ("depending-eyes") is not possible because the meaning is untenable.
Rather, the meaning understood is that visual consciousness arises having depended upon—that is, having reached—the eye and forms.
Therefore, that objection remains exactly as it was; the statement that "this meaning of the word is not logical" has been explained at length.
How so? For the rule regarding the suffix *ktvā* applies when there is a single agent performing two actions, specifically with respect to the action occurring at the earlier time.
"One eats after having bathed.
And yet, prior to its arising, visual consciousness does not exist—
that which arises at a later time depending upon the eye and visible forms that existed previously.
Nor is there an action without an agent.
He states two synonymous formulations for the sake of emphasis:
when it is stated merely as "when this exists," [the following is understood].
It should be understood that it is not only when ignorance exists that the formative forces come to be; rather, they come to be when something else exists as well,
just as visual consciousness comes to be when the eye exists.
It is not restricted to the meaning "only when the eye exists";
by that, it is understood that "when the visible form also exists.
However, by the second formulation—"from the arising of this, this arises"—it restricts [the meaning] to the first formulation alone.
"From the arising of this very thing, that arises; not from anything else.
Or, it is intended to demonstrate the succession of the members [of dependent origination].
When this member exists— that is, when the member of ignorance exists— this member of formative forces comes to be.
Furthermore, from the arising of this member of formative forces, this member of consciousness arises.
In this same way, the succession of the other factors should also be stated,
or else the succession of births.
Why?
It continues: "He spoke two formulations in order to demonstrate.
The phrase "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is the elaboration.
He spoke two formulations to demonstrate the status of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors as conditions, both directly and through a continuous succession (*saṃtati*).
The phrase "this being present, that comes to be" demonstrates the state of being a direct condition;
"from the arising of this, that arises" demonstrates it through a succession.
In that regard, the direct [condition] occurs when afflicted formative forces arise immediately after ignorance.
But when wholesome states arise through a continuous succession,
ignorance is absent during that wholesome state.
Furthermore:
Ignorance is the direct condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and [it is] the indirect condition for consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the subsequent members.
This is what is meant:

when the member of ignorance exists, the member of the formative forces comes to be; through the arising of this member of the formative forces, this member of consciousness arises—being directly conditioned by ignorance in the case of the latter, and indirectly in the former.
All of this is the opinion of the Master (Ācārya).
Regarding the statement "another says it is for the purpose of negation," this refers to the Elder Vasuvarman.
By means of the first formulation, it is for the purpose of negating the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), [showing that] an entity does not come into being when there is no cause.
The second [verse] is for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of an eternal cause, [showing that] nothing whatsoever arises from an unproduced, eternal source such as *prakṛti* or *puruṣa*.
The Master says:
"But in this conceptualization," and so forth.
The inclusion of the first member [of the compound] is purposeless,
because the refutation of both positions is established by the formula: "When this exists, that comes to be."

By this very formulation, "from the arising of this, that arises," the existence of a cause and the causality of that which has arisen—thereby establishing the refutation of both the doctrines characterized by the absence of a cause and the eternality of a cause—the previous formulation becomes redundant.
[The opponent asks: "In that case, there are some... and so forth.

There are certain proponents who, while maintaining that a self exists as the basis—that is, as the basis for ignorance—imagine the existence, or arising, of the formative forces and so forth, namely the formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, and the rest.

They further imagine that from the arising of ignorance and the other factors—namely ignorance, the formative forces, and so on—there follows the arising of those [subsequent factors], such as the arising of the formative forces and the rest; this is the subject under discussion.

For this reason, in order to set aside—that is, to refute—the conceptual constructions of those disputants, he determined and reiterated this: "From the very arising of which [factor], there is the origination of the aggregates," and so forth.
What does he say? He says: "From the very arising of which [factor]... up to "...there is the origination of the aggregates."
From the very arising of which something arises; when that alone exists, that comes to be,
and not when another self exists.
That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Only when ignorance exists do the formative forces come to be, and not when anything else exists; thus does there arise the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
How so?
With birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
Only when birth exists do aging, death, and so forth come to be;
they do not exist in another self.
Otherwise, if it were merely said that "when this exists, that comes to be," there would be those who might say:
"When the self exists as a basis and ignorance and the other factors exist, the formative forces and so forth come to be.
If, on the other hand, he were to state the second formulation alone— "from the arising of this, that arises"—
even then they would speculate in exactly the same way.
It is true that from the arising of ignorance and the other [links], the formative forces and the rest arise;
however, since the self exists as their substratum,
he determines this by means of two alternative formulations.
From the arising of which, that which arises; when that very thing exists, that comes to be,
and not when something else exists, such as a self that serves as a basis.
"The teachers" refers to the former teachers.
This is for the purpose of making known that [ignorance] has not been abandoned, and for the purpose of making known its arising.
When ignorance exists and has not been abandoned, the formative forces come to be.
He shows by the first formulation that [the factors] are not abandoned.
He shows by the second formulation that they arise precisely from the arising of that [preceding factor].
Thus, as long as birth exists and has not been abandoned, aging, death, and so forth come to be.
They are not abandoned;
rather, they arise precisely because that [moment] arises.
Another [teacher], the Venerable Śrīlāta, says this is for the purpose of demonstrating duration and arising.
To that end, he stated two formulations:
by the first formulation, it is shown that as long as there is a stream of causes, there is a stream of effects;
by the second, it is shown that because of the very arising of the cause, the effect arises.
"But it is concerning origination," means:
when it was introduced with the words, "Monks, I shall teach you dependent origination.
What occasion, what context is there for a statement regarding stability?

By the statement "when this exists, that comes to be," it is described that as long as the stream of causes persists, so long does the stream of effects persist; thus, its meaning is explained as "abiding.
Furthermore, for what purpose would the Blessed One have spoken [the formula] in a different order?
For arising necessarily occurs first.
Subsequently comes duration.
Since duration is dependent upon arising,
it should have been stated previously that "from the arising of this, that arises."
"Subsequently, this being present, that comes to be;
however, it is not thus.
Therefore, this is not the meaning."
"He speaks again. This refers to that same Venerable Śrīlāta.
The Master replies:

"This being so... and so forth. He shows that it would have been more appropriate to state simply, "When this exists, that does not exist," rather than providing a negation of existence in this very context.
And previously [it was stated], "the arising of the effect.
One would have said previously, "from the arising of this,
that arises," because destruction is preceded by arising.

It is stated in the Sūtra: "Conditioned by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come into being. It should be understood that these are subsumed within aging and death themselves, and do not constitute a separate limb.
In this regard, they arise from the transformation of objects—whether categorized as sentient or non-sentient—and from the transformation of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
Discursive thought associated with mental distress is sorrow (*śoka*).
Lamentation (*parideva*) is the incoherent speech arising from sorrow.
Suffering (*duḥkha*) and mental distress (*daurmanasya*) have already been explained.
Despair (*upāyāsa*) is dejection whose momentum has been interrupted.
Others say that despair is the exhaustion preceded by sorrow and lamentation.
"For the fool," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
The foolish worldling [thinks] that there is "mere conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāramātra*).
The inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of negating a self (*ātman*).
By saying "not understanding," he shows unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).

Attached to and established in the view of self and the conceit "I am," one undertakes through the body and so forth—that is, by means of body, speech, and mind—the threefold karma characterized as meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable (*āniñjya*).
Regarding "imperturbable" (*āniñjya*):
*ig* is another verbal root; this is its specific form.
This is the form of the root *ej* (to move), or alternatively, the reading is *ānejyam*. "Merit for the sake of future happiness" means for the sake of happiness in a future birth.
What?
Wholesome karma belonging to the desire realm; [wholesome karma] of the immovable type for the sake of pleasure and neither-pleasure-nor-pain.
Wholesome [action] pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness:
up to the third dhyāna, it is for the sake of pleasure;
above that, it is for the sake of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

"Non-meritorious [action] for the sake of happiness in this life" means that it was performed with regard to happiness in this world, not with regard to happiness in the future. "By the force of the projection of karma" means by the force of the impetus of the aforementioned karma.
It goes to each respective destination, such as the hells and so forth,
by way of the movement of a flame;
just as it is said that a long flame, following along a blade of grass, moves.

Likewise, by means of the continuity of consciousness (*vijñāna-saṃtati*), because of its connection with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it goes to this or that destination (*gati*) even though it is extremely remote in space through that connection with the intermediate state. And having established it thus: if, beginning from the mind of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi-citta*) in the intermediate state—which has the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as its condition—up to the moment of birth (*upapatti-kṣaṇa*), this entire continuity of consciousness of the six groups of consciousness has the formative forces as its condition.
The consciousness intended [there] is established as that very same consciousness.
In the exposition of the limb of consciousness—that is, the exposition of the third limb—[it asks]:
"What is consciousness?"
"The six groups of consciousness.
For otherwise, if the continuity of the six groups of consciousness were not intended,
then "consciousness conditioned by formations" would have been intended as referring only to the mind at rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi-citta*).
In this case, it would not have been stated that there are "six groups of consciousness. Rather, it should have been stated as follows:
"What is consciousness?"
Regarding "mental consciousness":
for at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), the occurrence of the five groups of sensory consciousness is impossible,
because the connection of rebirth is established by mental consciousness alone.
Because it is stated that "severing [the roots of merit], reconnecting them, detachment, decline, death, and rebirth are accepted as belonging to the mental consciousness alone."
"Because it is explained thus in the Vibhaṅga itself":
because it is explained thus in the analysis of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vibhaṅga*) within the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*. What is "name"?
"The four formless aggregates.
What is form?
Whatever is form, and so forth in detail.
As far as this form (*rūpa*) and this name (*nāma*) exist—
both together are called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
"Craving for sensual pleasure" (*kāmatṛṣṇā*) refers to this.
Craving belonging to the desire realm;
craving for form is that which exists in the three meditative absorptions (dhyānas) associated with pleasure.

In the fourth [dhyāna], there is craving for that which is neither painful nor pleasant. "Craving for that which is neither painful nor pleasant" refers to the craving belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara).
"Grasping at desires and so forth. Desires (*kāma*) are so called because they are desired;
qualities (*guṇa*) are so called because they are multiplied.
The qualities of desire are simply desires;
what, then, are they? They are visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
"The sixty-two views" refers to [the section] in the *Brahmajāla* [Sūtra].
Those views are to be understood through the exposition of the *Brahmajālasūtra*.
"The dog-vow, the cow-vow, and so forth" refers to these.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), practices such as the "deer-vow" (mṛgavrata) and others are included.
Regarding the phrase "of the Nirgranthas etc.," by the word "etcetera," the Pāṇḍarabhikṣus and others are included.
The detailed explanation begins with "of the Brahmins," and so forth.

For Brahmins, it is the staff and the deerskin; for the Pāśupatas, it is the matted hair and ashes; for the wandering mendicants (parivrājakas), it is the triple staff and tonsure. By the two uses of the word "and so forth" (ādi), the carrying of skulls and other such practices of the Kāpālikas and others are included.
The undertaking of that [view] is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*).
It is called "doctrine of self" (*ātmavāda*) because the assertion "this is the self" exists therein,
as it has been said.
"Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas perceive [anything] as 'self,' they all perceive only these five aggregates of clinging," and so forth.
Others say that the doctrine of self consists of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
By introducing the word "discourse" (*vāda*) in the phrase "the clinging to the discourse of self (*ātmavādopādāna*)," he demonstrates the purpose [of using that term]: namely,
that it refers to the unlearned, ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
who lacks the wisdom acquired at birth (*upapattilābhikā prajñā*) produced by the latencies of previous practice.
He is a fool who lacks that which is born of scripture; he is unlearned.
One for whom there is no [realization] born of attainment— that is, no realization born of the direct vision of the truths—
is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
This means they have not transcended mere conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
The meaning is that he conforms to them just as they are designated and just as they are conventionally expressed.
"Of them" refers to desire and the other [afflictions].
Regarding "desire and lust" (*chandarāga*): desire (*chanda*) is the longing for objects not yet attained; lust (*rāga*) is [the attachment] toward those already attained.
The desire and attachment toward those [objects], such as sensual pleasures, is grasping; it is not, however, [the objects themselves].
The intention is that those very same [factors] previously mentioned, when distinguished by way of views, constitute the two types of *upādāna* (clinging), together with ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Leading to renewed existence" means having rebirth as its fruit.
"This is here of existence" means that this is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of existence here.
"By way of the descent of consciousness":

through the connection with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is like the movement of a flame, future birth is "birth" (*jāti*); it consists of the five aggregates because its intrinsic nature is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
"Old age and death" are as described in the Sūtra.
What is old age? It is that which is baldness, graying of the hair, and so forth, as described in detail. What is death?
"Whatever is the passing away and decease of those various beings from this or that state," and so forth;
this shows the meaning of "mere," which is to say, devoid of a self.
"Great" means without beginning or end.
"Of the mass of suffering" means of the collection of suffering.
"That very same Vaibhāṣika principle which was stated previously" refers to the fact that the twelve stages consisting of the five aggregates are the twelve links.
(III.28cd) "That which is not knowledge" [is ignorance].
[If it were defined merely as that which is not knowledge,] there would be the undesirable consequence [of over-extension] even to the eye and so forth;
that is, the eye, ear, and other [faculties] would follow as being ignorance.

For those too would not be "ignorance" (avidyā), on the grounds that nothing at all would exist. The meaning is: if ignorance were the mere absence of knowledge (vidyā), it would be a non-entity (adravya).
And this is not tenable because it is taught as being a condition (*pratyaya*). [The phrase] "its opposite" refers to that.
He shows that the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses contradiction; it does not mean "anyone other than a friend," nor does he show that it is merely an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Nor is it the state of being a friend;
this shows that it does not have the sense of non-existence.
And [the phrase] "unrighteousness, lack of purpose, improper action, and so forth" [is used].
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), irrationality, non-conventionality, non-human beings, and so forth are included.
"Being the opposites of dharma and so forth" means being the opposites of dharma, purpose, action, reasoning, convention, human beings, and so forth.
But it is not that any others, such as the eye and so forth, apart from the dharmas and so on, nor is it the non-existence of the dharmas and so on;
the same applies to ignorance, and so forth in detail.
Why is this so?
Because it is taught as being by way of a condition:
"conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces."
Furthermore, it is not logical to teach that anything other than ignorance— such as the eye and so forth— functions as a condition [for the arising of suffering],
because conditioned formations (saṃskāra) still occur in Arhats, nor can non-existence (abhava) be such a condition.
Because things such as a rabbit’s horn lack causal efficacy (*apratyayatva*).
It is said that from "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) up to "yoke" (*yoga*), it is "ignorance" (*avidyā*);
thus, in the sūtras, it is stated as the "fetter of ignorance" up to the "yoke of ignorance."
Furthermore, mere non-existence cannot be such [a thing].
This means that it cannot be the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth.
Nor can the eye and other [faculties] be such, as is the subject under discussion.
And since that [ignorance] has the nature of a view, it is not logical for it to be ignorance;
for view and ignorance are recited separately as fetters and so forth.
What, then, is that which is not a view?
It is that afflicted wisdom which is associated with attachment and so forth; for [it is not considered a separate affliction] because it is already associated with those views.
The meaning is: "because of being associated with ignorance.
And how is view associated with ignorance? Because delusion, characterized by ignorance, is recited among the universal ground of afflictions (kleśamahābhūmi).
Furthermore, all the universal mental factors of affliction (*kleśamahābhūmika*) are associated with the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
Thus, it is understood that ignorance (*avidyā*), which has the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), is associated with views such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, ignorance is not wisdom.
Because two substances of wisdom cannot be associated with one another,
it is said that "wisdom defiled by ignorance does not become purified";
this is the illustrative example.
By this it is shown that ignorance (*avidyā*) is a distinct entity from wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, it is not logical that wisdom itself should be a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) of that very same wisdom;
therefore, in the teaching on the secondary afflictions of wisdom, ignorance is presented as being a distinct entity from wisdom.
Because it is designated as a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*),
just like attachment (*rāga*).
Therefore, he says:
"As for the statement 'it is other than the mind,' and so forth:

'being intermingled, it does not become pure' means that wholesome wisdom arising in a subsequent moment does not become pure when it is being intermingled with afflicted wisdom arising intermittently."
What is meant by "necessarily obsessed by attachment"?
It means being associated with attachment.
But that [mind] is "afflicted" by attachment in such a manner.
It is not by the active manifestation of passion that the mind is impaired,
but by the implantation of its latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
When the practitioner turns away those latent tendencies— that is, that state of functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*)— his mind is liberated.
Thus, afflicted wisdom (*prajñā*) impaired by ignorance (*avidyā*) does not become pure.
Therefore, he demonstrates that there is no fault in both wisdom and ignorance.
For who can prevent one from making such a conceptual construction?
This states that this is merely a conceptual construction independent of scriptural authority.
As for the one who thinks that all afflictions are ignorance,
he is the Venerable Śrīlāta.
He thinks as follows:
"Ignorance" (avidyā) is a general designation for all the afflictions (kleśas).
There is no such thing as ignorance that exists apart from the afflictions such as attachment (rāga) and the rest.
Why does he think this? From a sūtra of the Buddha:
"O Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, because one does not discern and does not discern, it is therefore called ignorance."
Afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) are also of the nature of ignorance because they consist in a perverted apprehension.
"For that [opponent] also, for this very reason," and so forth;
by this very statement of refutation, the Venerable [Vasumitra] is excluded.
The negation applies to that [opponent's] view; this must be supplied as an ellipsis.
How so? He says: for if it were of the nature of all afflictions (*kleśa*), it would not be mentioned separately among the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth.
Among the fetters such as the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) would not be mentioned separately,
because it is not distinct from the remaining fetters.
Just as after stating "attachment is a bond" and "aversion is a bond," one says "delusion is a bond."

Having stated "the latent tendency of sensual desire" and so forth, one would not then separately state "the latent tendency of ignorance," nor "the flood of ignorance" among the floods, nor "the yoke of ignorance" among the yokes.
Why?
Because they do not associate with one another.
For vision does not associate with vision.
Or, passion [is associated] with passion.
Furthermore, ignorance associated with views and so forth has been mentioned;
for, by virtue of being a universal mental factor of defilement (*kleśamahābhūmika*), it is necessarily associated with the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
Furthermore, it would have been stated that the mind is defiled by ignorance alone;

it would not have been stated that "the mind defiled by passion is not liberated," because the fact that it is defiled by passion and so forth is already established by the very statement that it is defiled by ignorance.
Now, if it is thought that it was stated in that way for the sake of qualification—
namely, that "the mind defiled by ignorance characterized by attachment is not liberated"—
then a qualification would also have to be made regarding wisdom (*prajñā*).
"By means of attachment, aversion, or pride"— this is said so that there may not be the undesirable consequence of including all afflictions (*kleśa*).
If it is argued that [only these three] are intended,
then one would not need to apply such a qualification to "mind" (*citta*) either.
It should rather be stated that "the mind defiled by ignorance is not liberated.
For *saṃprakhyāna*, *prajñā*, and *jñāna* have one and the same meaning;
thus, the fault is exactly the same as in the case of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Now, what is the meaning of "non-apprehension" (asaṃprakhyāna)? If it means that which is not apprehension,
then the same [definition] would apply to the eyes and other [faculties] as well.
"In that case, it would be the absence of clear cognition.
If this were so, nothing at all would exist;
and this is not tenable."
Now, as for that other dharma which is the opposite of clear comprehension (*saṃprakhyāna*),
this too is not understood in the same way as ignorance (*avidyā*).
"What is that?
[The answer is: "Even of such a kind," and so forth.
This means that it is of such a kind as being manifested by karma.

Therefore, the intrinsic nature of ignorance (avidyā) is to be understood through its activity (kāritra). There exists a certain factor (dharma) which is the opposite of knowledge (vidyā); this state of being the opposite of knowledge is its activity. For example: "What is the eye? (cakṣuḥ katamat).

"That which is the translucent matter (rūpaprasāda) that is the basis of visual consciousness. But is it not the case that this definition is characterized by its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), namely "translucent matter"?
No.
Because it is not directly perceptible;
and because it is always to be inferred through visual consciousness.
"I am" refers to the state of being composed of the *sattva* element.
The meaning of this is not understood.
That elder has not grasped its intended referent.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntikas describe ignorance as being differentiated by its various modes.
Or pride (*māna*).
"That which is mentioned in the Sūtra," and so forth; the term "of the *mayatās*" refers to the names of the various types of ignorance (*avidyā*) that are distinguished by their modes.
The intention of the Venerable Dharmatrāta is that [this] is because craving and the others are taught separately.
The Master says:
"This *mayatā* does exist."
In the Sūtra, *mayatā* is mentioned.
There, it is expressed in the singular because it refers to a genus;
however, it is indeed ignorance (*avidyā*).
For what reason is this determined to be "ignorance" (avidyā)?
The Venerable Dharmatrāta explains his own intention: [it is because] it is ignorance.
Because this cannot be said to be any other affliction (*kleśa*).
Why can it not be so?
Because craving (*tṛṣṇā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) are mentioned separately.
The Master says:
"But surely it must be another kind of conceit (*māna*"?).
It is other than the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), being one of the six [types of conceit], and that is *mayatā*."
The intention is that it is "not ignorance.
However, when this matter is further investigated, much that must be said arises;
for when this factor of ignorance is further investigated, this extensive treatise comes into being.
As it has been said:
"Therefore, let this matter rest; let it be just this much.
Or rather, there might be another measure.
"But it is not ignorance.
When such an investigation as "Why is this so? is undertaken again, much that must be said arises through the exchange of replies and counter-replies.
Therefore, let this matter rest; the meaning is that there is no need for further deliberation.

(III.30a) Now, regarding "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): immediately after the exposition of the member of ignorance (*avidyā*), the member of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) ought to have been explained.
Following that, the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is presented;
why has this been introduced [here]? For this purpose the Master will say here:
And it has been said, and will be said further,
that "form has been explained in detail."
Regarding the statement, "Form consists of the five sense-faculties, the five objects, and non-informative [matter] alone," the full explanation is:
"by the power of name, faculty, and object."
It is called "name" (*nāma*) because it bends (*namati*) toward objects such as visible forms by virtue of name, by virtue of the sense faculties, and by virtue of the object itself.
To the question, "By virtue of which name?
he asks this because there are two kinds of names.
But the Teacher explains:
"That which in the world is called 'notoriety' (pratīti)," and so forth;
for example, "cow" or "horse."
That which causes the cognition of a collection is,
for example, "form" or "taste.
That which causes the cognition of a single object is [a single word].
This very tetrad of aggregates beginning with sensation is designated by the term "name" (*nāman*).
Because, by the power of that name— and by the power of forming conceptual designations— it inclines toward or proceeds toward objects even when they are not directly perceived,
[thinking], "this is the meaning of this name."
The meaning is that [the mind] inclines toward, or arises with respect to, visible forms and so forth through the power of the sense faculties;
and it also inclines toward names through the power of their referents,
thinking, "This is the name for this referent."
Furthermore, by what reason does this have the nature of a "name"? By what cause does this name, characterized by the act of designating, possess the nature of a name?
It is because that name bends (*namati*) toward those various objects.
Because, with respect to those objects, that which has the characteristic of the four aggregates is "name" (nāma), and it bends toward or directs [the mind] toward them;
therefore, it possesses the nature of name.
It is called "name" (nāma) on the grounds that it bends (namayati).
"Cast off here," and so forth.

At the time of death, when the body has been cast off, the formless aggregates—feeling and the rest—are called "name" (*nāman*) because they bend toward (*namana*) and go toward (*gamana*) another rebirth.
As it has been said:

Indeed, when one has died and passed away, his kinsmen either burn this putrid body with fire, or cast it into water, or bury it in the earth, or it undergoes desiccation, destruction, and total exhaustion by wind and sun. As for that which is further said:
Whether it be called *citta*, or *manas*, or *vijñāna*, when it is cultivated by faith and cultivated by ethical discipline, generosity, learning, and wisdom,
it becomes upward-tending, tending toward excellence, and leading to rebirth in heaven in the future. (III.30b) Thus, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have been explained.

The bases of those consciousnesses are the translucent forms, such as the eye and so forth. And "consciousness" refers to the individual representation [of objects], which is the mind-base (*manāyatana*). This is stated in that [text].

Furthermore, how can there be a conjunction of the mental faculty (*manas*), which has already ceased, with a future phenomenon such as form (*rūpa*) that is about to arise, and with the present mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?
It is the relationship of cause and effect:
the mental consciousness is the effect.
The cause consists of the mental faculty (*manaindriya*) and the phenomena (*dharma*), such as visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth;
or, it means having a single effect.
"Having a single purpose" (*ekakāryārtha*) means having a single function;
that is to say, the state of having a single purpose.
To the question "In what way does it have a single purpose?", he says:
And all three of those—the mind-faculty and so forth—are conducive and favorable for the arising of contact.
Regarding the "Dharma-discourse of the Six-Sets":
it is called "six-set" because there are six sets within it.
Because of the arising of the sixfold sets of internal and external consciousness, contact, feeling, and craving,
it is indicated that there are "six groups of contact.
For if [contact] were not distinct [from the others], then once the sense-faculties, objects, and consciousnesses had been mentioned, the mention of the "groups of contact" would be redundant.
Consequently, the state of being "six groups of six" would be lost.
[This is said] so that feeling and craving do not exist separately from the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
If separate existence were to result from being mentioned separately,
then since feeling (vedanā) and craving (tṛṣṇā) are also mentioned separately from the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
those two— feeling and craving— would also have to exist separately from the sphere of mental objects.
And their separate existence is not admitted,
because they are included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
"This is not a fault," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

"This is not a fault," as has been stated, because there exists—that is, there is—the presence of the *dharmāyatana*, which is distinct from those [two], namely distinct from both feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and which has the nature of perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth.

"And it is not thus," and so on in detail: for you who assert that contact (*sparśa*) is simply the coming together of the three, there would be another triad that is not contact, distinct from the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness that constitutes contact.
The triad of sense-faculties, objects, and consciousnesses exists;
it is this remainder that is intended by the inclusion [of "six"] in this sūtra.
Thus, there are "six groups of contact" (ṣaṭ sparśakāyāḥ), because, for a specific purpose, they are taken as distinct even though they are not separate from the three that constitute contact itself.
Therefore, even though feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are not separate entities, their separate exposition is logical due to the needs of those to be trained (*vineya*).
However, for you who maintain that contact (*sparśa*) is merely the conjunction [of the three], a separate exposition of the "six groups of contact" is not logical for any purpose whatsoever.

Since the expression "six groups of contact" would already imply the triad of sense-faculty, object, and consciousness, it would follow that these are not mentioned at all; consequently, the "Dharma-discourse of the Six Sixes" (*ṣaṭ-ṣaṭko dharma-paryāyaḥ*) could not be established.
But for me, it is established.

Even though there is mention of the sixfold sets of contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there still exists the possibility of a sixfold set consisting of objects—such as the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and so forth—faculties, and consciousnesses distinct from those [three].
Therefore, because of the separate teaching that "there are six groups of contact," it is established that there is a distinct factor (*dharmāntara*) associated with the mind called contact.
Then he might say:
"In this sutra, the sense-faculties and their objects are taught to be devoid of consciousness, because of the statement:
'There are six internal [bases] and six external [bases].'"
Therefore, this [mention of "contact"] would be included here in order to indicate that the remaining triad— the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness— has become contact.
To refute the argument that "there are six groups of contact," this [following passage] is undertaken.
Even if the sense faculty and the object were without consciousness, they would still be "of the same class" (tatsabhāga);
however, consciousness is never without a sense faculty and an object.
For consciousness necessarily involves both the sense faculty and its object.
And that consciousness has already been indicated here by the phrase "the six groups of consciousness.

Therefore, since the faculty, the object, and consciousness have already been specified among these three, the further mention of "contact" (*sparśa*) by means of the expression "six groups of consciousness" would result in redundancy.
Regarding the "six groups of contact":
it is established from this that contact is something other than the mere coming together [of the three].
On this point, the Venerable Śrīlāta says:
"Indeed not," and so forth in detail.
The eye and visible form that have arisen previously are the cause, but not those that arise simultaneously with the consciousness.
Nor does every visual consciousness [arise] from all [objects],
meaning that what arises later [depends on] the previously arisen eye and visible form,
not on those that arise simultaneously.

Therefore, those things which stand in a cause-and-effect relationship— namely consciousness, the sense faculties, and their objects— are established as contact (*sparśa*) in this Sūtra: "The six groups of contact."
Otherwise, this would not have been made known;
nor do they recite it in this way.
*Vai* is a particle (*nipāta*).
The meaning is that they do not indeed recite it in this way.
How, then, do they recite it?
"That which has arisen from the conjunction, the meeting, and the combination of these phenomena."
They recite that "it is contact" (*sa sparśaḥ*).
Or rather, this is a metaphorical designation of the effect for the cause;
that is, in the sense of conjunction, meeting, or coming together—the cause—it is metaphorically designated as "contact," which is the effect.
Just as it is said that the arising of Buddhas is a source of happiness.
"Spreading in an exceedingly vast variety of ways" means that its nature is to spread (*visartum*) by way of an exceedingly vast variety of modes (*atibahuvistaraprakāra*).
"Designation" (*adhivacana*) is said to be "name" (*nāman*). It is called a designation because by means of it something is designated (*adhyucyate*); thus, it is a designation.
Speech operates upon the name.
Because it illuminates the object through the name, the name is called "designation" (*adhivacana*).
It is said that this name is the predominant and frequent object of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) when it is associated with it.
Therefore, it is called "contact through designation" (*adhivacanasaṃsparśa*).
"Contact" (*sparśa*) and "contact through designation" (*saṃsparśa*) have the same meaning.
By means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), one cognizes blue.
The meaning is that one discerns the denotable object.
And "one discerns it as blue" means one discerns: "This is the name for this object."
"One is characterized by its basis (*āśrayaprabhāvita*).
The first is characterized by its basis as "contact with resistance" (*pratighasaṃsparśa*), which is contact having resistance as its basis, or contact that belongs to resistance.
[The second] is "characterized by its object" (*ālambanaprabhāvita*).
Contact with designation (*adhivacanasaṃsparśa*) means contact having designation as its object, or contact within designation.

It is the engagement of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) with objects such as form and so forth, having taken speech as its reference and having determined speech [in relation to those objects].
The five [consciousnesses], beginning with visual consciousness, do not engage with objects by taking speech as their reference.

Therefore, that very designation, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), operates upon speech as "designation. The contact associated with that [consciousness], or the contact belonging to it, is "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*).
And for this reason, this second type of contact is said to be "distinguished by association" (*saṃprayoga-prabhāvita*).
(III.31) "The contacts of knowledge, ignorance, and the other" means: [the contact of knowledge, the contact of ignorance, and the contact of that which is other than these two].
Knowledge, ignorance, and that which is other than both knowledge and ignorance—these are "knowledge, ignorance, and the other.
These very [three] are the contacts of knowledge, ignorance, and the other; thus they are called "contacts of knowledge, ignorance, and the other."
The meaning is: that which is called knowledge (*vidyā*), that which is called ignorance (*avidyā*), and that which is other than these two.
Knowledge is untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*);
ignorance is afflicted non-knowledge (*kliṣṭam ajñānam*).
Neither ignorance nor non-ignorance is that wisdom which is wholesome-with-outflows (*kuśala-sāsrava*) and that which is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
These contacts (*saṃsparśa*) associated with them should be understood respectively.
Furthermore, regarding "contact of ignorance" (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*): [it refers to the contact associated with the aforementioned types of wisdom].
The detailed explanation is as follows: A portion of the contact of ignorance—which is associated with all afflictions—is that which occurs repeatedly and occurs constantly.
By the inclusion of that [portion], two types of contact come into being.
The contacts of ill-will and attachment;
and the three beginning with that which is to be experienced as pleasure.
The experience (*veda*) of pleasure is "pleasure-experience" (*sukhaveda*).

That which is conducive to the experience of pleasure is "pleasure-experiencible" (*sukhavedya*). Alternatively, that in which pleasure is to be experienced is "pleasure-experiencible" (*sukhavedya*).
"Those for which this is the first" refers to the [dharmas] such as those to be experienced as pleasure (*sukhavedya*).
Regarding "because they are conducive to pleasant feeling and so forth": that which is conducive to pleasant feeling is "to-be-experienced-as-pleasant" (*sukhavedanīya*).
The suffix *cha* occurs after [the root] *krī* (to buy) when preceded by a word ending in the locative case.
"It is known" (*vedyate*) means either that it is being known or that it is capable of being known;
by saying "it is known," he shows that the *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of the mere object (*karman*).
He shows that the term "kṛtya" is used in the sense of "that which is capable of being [performed]," according to the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaś ca*.
"These are the sixteen" refers to the six beginning with eye-contact (*cakṣuḥ-saṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥ-saṃsparśa*).

Furthermore, there are sixteen types of contact (*sparśa*): contact of resistance (*pratigha-sparśa*), contact of designation (*adhivacana-sparśa*), contact of knowledge (*vidyā-sparśa*), contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*), contact of neither-knowledge-nor-ignorance (*naiva-vidyā-nāvidyā-sparśa*), contact of malice (*vyāpāda-sparśa*), contact of attachment (*anunaya-sparśa*), and contact to be experienced as pleasure (*sukha-vedanīya*), contact to be experienced as pain (*duḥkha-vedanīya*), and contact to be experienced as neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanīya*).
Contact has been explained; now feeling (*vedanā*) must be discussed.
But has it not also been said that feeling is the experience of feeling?
Now, even that which has already been stated is being restated:
"In that case, this should not be said— namely,
both what has been stated and what is yet to be stated."
"Therefore, I shall not speak," because of the statement that "what has been said and what will be said is other."
There is no fault because this is an indication of the modes.
Previously the characteristic was stated; now the mode is stated.
"For when [birth] has arisen," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
For when the effect (*janya*) has already arisen, the cause (*janaka*) has no capacity [to produce it], because they have arisen simultaneously.
"Not distinct from the proposition" means that this proof is not distinct from the proposition itself.
If a proof that is distinct from the thesis is not accepted,
then— because it would follow that they are mutual producers— what [is the consequence]?
The subject under discussion is how the relationship of producer and produced can be established between two things that arise simultaneously.
By this, the flaw in the thesis is pointed out:
the thesis that "there exists a relationship of producer and produced between two simultaneous things" contradicts one's own prior admission.
"There is no fault because it is accepted.
This shows his prior admission; he means that this is indeed accepted.
"But in the Sūtra this is not accepted. This [definition] is accepted in the Abhidharma:
"Coexistent [causes] are those which are mutual fruits."
Thus [it is said].
However, this is not accepted in the Sūtra.
Demonstrating that, he says:
"Dependent upon eye-contact, feeling born of eye-contact arises.

Having refuted their status as mutual fruits on the basis of the authority of the Sūtra, [the author] says "and it is incorrect because it transgresses the nature of a producer" in order to refute the notion of a simultaneous relationship between cause and effect.
This well-known principle of Janaka is that there is a difference in time;
for example, first the seed and afterwards the sprout, and so forth.
In that case as well, the sense faculty and the object are first, and consciousness is afterwards.
The sense faculty and the object arise in the first moment, while consciousness arises in the second moment. "Just as, then, in the case of a shadow and a sprout"—
what [is the point]?
There is a relationship of produced and producer between two things that arise simultaneously.
For it is precisely when the sprout has arisen that it produces the shadow;
it is not the case that in the first moment the sprout is without a shadow and in the second moment it possesses a shadow.
The same applies to contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
It can also be said that for these two—as well as for the shadow and the sprout—the preceding causal complex (*pūrvasāmagrī*) is the cause.
However, since this point has already been stated in the exposition on the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), it is not repeated here.
"Feeling occurs at a time subsequent to contact," says another, namely the Venerable Śrīlāta.
That very coming together of the three is contact;
it is this state of being produced by that which produces.
"Feeling occurs in the third moment.
The first moment is that of the sense faculty and the object; the second is the moment of the arising of consciousness; and the third is the moment of the arising of feeling.
Thus, it follows that feeling does not occur in every instance of consciousness.
Because there is no feeling in the second moment of consciousness;
nor is every consciousness contact.
In the third moment, which is the moment of feeling, the consciousness is not contact.
In the first and second moments, contact alone is established.
For feeling in the subsequent moment has the preceding contact as its cause.
This which is now called the second moment is of the nature of contact.
In that regard, feeling arises with the preceding contact as its cause—that is, with the consciousness of the first moment as its cause.
Since feeling preceded by that contact also occurs in the subsequent [moment], it follows that feeling would be present in every instance of consciousness;
for all consciousness is contact.
"And those contacts are accompanied by feeling" means "of two [contacts] having different objects," and so forth.
These two have different objects;
they are thus "those having different objects."

The form of the former [moment] is the object of the latter, and sound is the object of the former; since these two have different objects, it is illogical that the contact caused by the former—which has form as its object—should exist in the subsequent contact which has sound as its object.
With the words "how indeed could this be?", he reveals the fault.
Feeling produced from contact having an object of a different class—produced from contact having a specific type of visible form as its object—would have a different object;
it would have sound as its object.
Because the cause is inconsistent, the effect is impossible.
For when feeling produced from a contact having form as its object will be a feeling having form as its object,
then it is logical that feeling in a subsequent contact has the preceding contact as its cause.
But when, from a contact having form as its object, a feeling arises having sound as its object—
In that case, how will this be consistent?
For in the world, an effect is observed to correspond to its cause.

Now, if it is thought that feeling produced from a contact having visible form as its object remains "having visible form as its object" even when associated with a contact having sound as its object—[that cannot be].
Therefore, this was said:
"Or rather, it has an object different from that mind with which it is associated."
Therefore, it has a different object from the mind that takes sound as its object;
since it arises having form as its object, the meaning is that it has the same object as that [mind].
And how is it said that this [consciousness] is associated with that?
For those that are joined equally are "associated" (*saṃprayukta*).
If it is because they have an identical basis (*āśraya*), then how can that which has arisen with the ear as its basis have visible form as its object (*ālambana*)?
How could it not be so?
Because the mind and mental factors function with a single object by virtue of having a common basis.
Therefore, there is a fault in the case of sensation even when it has a different object.
That fault is now demonstrated.
If, first of all, a feeling produced from a contact having visible form as its object were to take another object such as sound as its objective support,
then that contact having visible form as its object could not be designated as "to be experienced as pleasure" up to "to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant."
"But such a designation is logical if it refers to feeling that has a single object.
"Let it be so," and so forth;
if this is the case, then let there be this fault.
At that time.
At what time?
At the time when sound is the object.
Consciousness that has become contact is without feeling.
Therefore, the consciousness that preceded [the one] having sound as its object and which was accompanied by feeling is not contact.
For in this way, it becomes free from fault.
Otherwise, if the consciousness that has arisen previously, together with its feeling, were itself contact (*sparśa*),
then the aforementioned fault would apply— namely, that "feeling has contact as its condition.
Furthermore, there is another reason.
Some consciousness is without feeling,
and some is not contact due to a deficiency of conditions;
for the conditions are deficient, being situated in a state of obstruction.
For not every immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) is capable of producing a consciousness that has become contact (sparśabhūta) with feeling as its condition.
Thus, in this way, for him, a consciousness having a different object is invariably without feeling,
and that which produces it has not become contact.
If, however, immediately after a visual consciousness having form as its object, there arises either another visual consciousness having form as its object or a mental consciousness,
then that [mental consciousness] which has arisen previously along with its feeling is called "contact."
"If this were so" means that the rule regarding the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) would be violated,
because there is a fixed rule for *sparśa* (contact) and *vedanā* (feeling) to occur in alternation.
Regarding the "three stages":
the stage with both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) consists of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna;
the stage without applied thought but with sustained thought alone is the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
Without applied thought and without sustained thought, from the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra),
there is the wholesome level and wholesome phenomena;
likewise, there are the unwholesome and the indeterminate.

The stage of the learner (*śaikṣī bhūmi*) consists of the untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena of one in training. The stage of the non-learner (*aśaikṣī*) consists of the untainted phenomena of one beyond training.
The stage that is neither of the learner nor the non-learner consists of tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) states are not mentioned here because they are not associated with mental factors (caitta). Therefore,
"those which are in this [state]" and so forth is the detailed explanation.
The word "that" (tad) is used to introduce the statement.
"Which" (ya) refers to those mental factors (caitasika). "In this entire stage" (etasyām sarvasyām bhūmau) means in all these levels.
In the stage with vitarka and vicāra,
up to the stage that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner—
those factors such as feeling (vedanā), volition (cetanā), and so forth, as previously described, are the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika).
Those which exist only in the wholesome stage are the great wholesome ground factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth. Those which exist only in the afflicted stage—
These are the universal mental factors of affliction (*kleśamahābhūmika*).
They are precisely those previously mentioned, beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth. Furthermore, they occur according to possibility; such is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, those [factors] such as the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) which arise in a particular [mental state],
they occur in that [state] in succession.
"But not all [mental factors] arise simultaneously," say others.

For example, although feeling (vedanā) exists in all stages (bhūmi), it does not exist simultaneously with perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manaskāra), and so forth.
Likewise, contact [is associated] with feeling and so forth;
likewise, applied thought and so forth [are associated] with the wholesome—such is the beginning of the explanation.
Others, however, explain it as follows:
As it is written in the *Pañcaskandhaka*,
so should this be understood:
namely, what is desire (*chanda*)?
It is the longing for a desired object.
The intention is that there is no desire (*chanda*) for what is not desired.
What is resolve (*adhimokṣa*)?
Ascertainment is the definitive determination of a determined object as being exactly so.
What is mindfulness? It is the non-forgetting of a familiar object.
It is the state of the mind’s directed expression.
What is concentration? It is one-pointedness of the mind upon the object to be examined.
What is wisdom (*prajñā*)?

In this regard, one should consult the *Pañcaskandhaka* treatise, which states: "It is discernment (*pravicaya*) regarding that very [object], whether it is applied correctly or incorrectly, or otherwise," and so forth.
For it is there stated that there are five universal [mental factors].
Feeling, perception, contact, mental attention, and volition—
these five have specific objects.
Likewise, desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and so forth.
The great unwholesome mental factors (akuśalamahābhūmika), however, are not included because they arise incidentally in the recitation;

for they are mentioned in the Sūtras and other texts in the context of the recitation that classifies states as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Thus, they are not included here by virtue of that incidental mention.
The meaning is that they were added later;
they were not recited previously.

In the *Prakaraṇapāda*, four types are recited: the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikā*), the universal wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmikā*), the universal defiled mental factors (*kleśamahābhūmikā*), and the universal minor defiled mental factors (*parīttakleśamahābhūmikā*).
They are said to be "co-arisen," but not "co-arisen with contact.
Since they are not specified otherwise, these factors— feeling and the rest— are co-arisen with one another.
The meaning is that the Sūtra must be explained by adopting the sense that [the mind] is "not through contact" (*na tu sparśena*).

Regarding the phrase "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*maitrīsahagatam*): this word *saha* is not necessarily used only in the sense of simultaneous occurrence; it is also seen in the sense of immediate succession (*samanaṃtara*).

For there is no coexistence of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). This is because loving-kindness is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), whereas the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness is exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, this is not a proof.
"Seen together" (saṃdṛṣṭa) means "arisen simultaneously" (sahotpanna); such is the intended meaning.
For it is said in that very Sūtra:
"Whatever is feeling, whatever is volition, and whatever is perception," and so forth in detail.
In this context, "sūtra" means the meaning [of the scripture].
"That is not understood," and so forth.
First of all, is this a restriction of the objects (*ālambana-niyama*) of these [factors] such as feeling (*vedanā*), that is, a restriction regarding the object?
Does it mean that one intends toward whatever object one feels, and so on, up to the point where consciousness cognizes that very same object?
Or rather, is there a restriction by moment, such that in the very same moment one feels, [one intends]?
Regarding the phrase "as long as one cognizes that very [object]," we say:
this is a restriction concerning the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Therefore, the intention is that there is no contradiction with the Sūtra.
The Teacher says:
"In that very Sūtra, because of the statement regarding the 'conjoined' nature of vitality and heat when they coexist, the restriction to a single moment is established."
"Life-force and heat are conjoined;
these two factors are not disjoined.
By this, it is stated that life-force and heat arise simultaneously.
Because those two lack an objective support (*anālambana*).
Thus, it has been established in this way:
feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) necessarily arise together.
Because it is stated in that Sūtra by means of the expression "intermingled" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).
[The phrase] "like life-force and heat" (*āyuruṣmavat*)—how is that so? This is the detailed explanation.
