How then can consciousness exist when there is no conjunction of the three— sense faculty, object, and consciousness?
Therefore, if consciousness is to exist, their conjunction must necessarily be admitted.
"And for you, contact is the coming together [of the three].
Therefore, this contradicts your position that not every consciousness is contact.
"Or the conjunction is not contact.
Furthermore, it should be understood that a reconnection (*punar-sandhi*) is to be made here;
because the elision of the *s* sound is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*, the *guṇa* substitution does not apply.
The resolution, however, is this: this *nañ* should be understood in the sense of "slight.
Since it is "not unestablished"—that is, slightly established—the *guṇa* substitution occurs because of its established status, resulting in the elision of the *sakāra*.
"Just as [it is said], 'This is that Rāma, the son of Daśaratha,'" so too [is it said],
"There are six applications of mental joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*)," and so forth in detail. Having seen forms with the eye, one applies oneself to those forms that are conducive to mental joy.

Having heard sounds with the ear, one dwells upon those sounds that are conducive to mental pleasure (*saumanasyasthānīya*). In the same way, up to: having cognized mental objects (*dharma*) with the mind, one dwells upon those mental objects that are conducive to mental pleasure.

Likewise, having seen forms with the eye, one dwells upon those that are conducive to mental displeasure (*daurmanasyasthānīya*) and those that are conducive to equanimity (*upekṣāsthānīya*); this should be applied in detail.
"There will be three" because of the threefold nature consisting of mental pleasure (*saumanasya*), mental pain (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). "One" [is said]...
Because it is associated solely with mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). "Six" refers to the distinction between the six objects, beginning with form (*rūpa*).
"Establishment by means of all three as well":

that single substance of feeling which is associated solely with the mental consciousness is divided into three types according to the distinction between the three intrinsic natures of mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and so forth.
Furthermore, each of these is divided into six types according to the distinction of the six objects;
thus, there are eighteen.
If their establishment by way of intrinsic nature were not admitted, the mental applications of joy, sorrow, and equanimity would not exist.
If the establishment of their association were non-existent, they would not even be called "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*).
Furthermore, they would be distinct from the eighteen [categories].

If the establishment of the sixfold objects—form and so forth—as their objective supports were non-existent, there would not be eighteen mental applications, each divided fourfold according to the distinctions of joy (*saumanasya*) and the others.
Therefore, it is established that they are established by all three [factors]. "Having unmixed objects" means having non-composite objects.
The three mental applications to phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) are of both kinds.
Those which have as their object phenomena distinct from the five objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are the mental applications to phenomena with unmixed objects (*asaṃbhinnālambana*).
However, those that take two, three, or even all six objects— form and so forth— as their objective support are called "those with mixed objective supports" (saṃbhinnālambana).
It is said that this refers to the mind (manas).
The word *kila* indicates the opinion of another.

The meaning is that, depending upon—that is, relying upon—the mind, they range over (*upavicaranti*) objects, which is to say, they take them as their objective support (*ālambante*). They "range over" means they set them in motion.
To the question "How so?", he says:

"Because of the mind's repeated investigation (*vicāraṇā*) of objects by the power of feeling (*vedanā*). The meaning of the prefix *upa-* is "repeatedly" (*punaḥ-punaḥ*). Nor is it "investigating" (*upavicārikā*).
The meaning is "without investigation.
"Inappropriateness" means impossibility.
If feeling were based on the mind alone, it would be a mental application (*manopavicāra*).
The pleasure that exists in the third dhyāna is based on the mind alone;
it is not based on the visual faculty or the other [sensory] faculties.
Why is it not included among his mental explorations (*manopavicāra*)? "Because from the beginning," and so forth. "From the beginning" means at the very start.
"Kila" indicates the opinion of others.
In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there is no pleasure belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmika*).
Therefore, that [pleasure] is not a mental application (*manopavicāra*).
Therefore, even subsequently in the third dhyāna, although the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is dependent on the mind, it is not included among the mental explorations (manopavicāra).
This is not the case as with the mental exploration of dissatisfaction (daurmanasyopavicāra), which exists as the counterpart to the mental exploration of joy (saumanasyopavicāra).
In opposition to the mental application of pleasure, there is a mental application of suffering,
because suffering is not based on the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Therefore, in all cases, that [suffering] is not a mental application of pleasure.
"Conducive to mental pleasure" means those which produce mental pleasure.
"Five," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

This was stated in detail— namely, "with the eye, visible forms," and so forth— with the intention (*abhisaṃdhāya*) and having taken into account (*cetasikṛtvā*) that these are produced and generated by the five groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*).
However, these belong to the level of the mental faculty (*manobhūmika*),
such as, for example, the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*).
It is produced by visual consciousness because it previously involved the perception of the livid corpse and so forth;
yet it belongs to the mental level because it is in a state of meditative concentration.
However, as for the phrase "but rather": [it means that]...
This is not to be questioned because of the statement: "having seen forms with the eye... up to having touched tangibles with the body.

For if it had been said: "while seeing forms with the eye, one investigates forms that are a basis for mental pleasure," and so on, up to "while touching tangibles with the body," [then this objection would apply].
An objection might be raised:
"But this was not stated in that way," yet this is not an objection at all.
This is shown by the passage beginning with, "He who, without having seen... and so forth.
Even those who, having heard from another, mentally explore and take as an object [those sounds],
these too are his mental explorations (*manopavicāra*).
"Otherwise, however," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
The mental explorations (*upavicāra*) of visible forms and so forth that have the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) as their object would not exist;
for one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) has not directly perceived the visible forms and so forth belonging to the realm of form.
Furthermore, the mental explorations of odors, tastes, and tangibles that have the desire realm as their object would not exist for one born in the realm of form.
Because odors and so forth are not its objects.
However, it has been stated as it is most clearly evident.
This is because the mental explorations (*manopavicāra*) that have as their objects forms and so forth already directly perceived are more distinct.
Furthermore, even one who, having seen forms, explores the desires associated with them— that too is a mental exploration for him.
It has been stated in such a way that it is not confused.
To the question "And how is it not confused?", he says:
"By way of the differentiation of the sense faculties and their objects" means that it was stated by way of the differentiation of the sense faculties, such as the eye,
and by way of the differentiation of the objects, such as visible form.
Otherwise, there would be confusion, such as [the statement]:
"Having seen forms with the eye, one investigates the desires that are a basis for mental pleasure," and so forth.
[The opponent replies: "There is a restriction regarding the continuum."
Having observed the continuum of a certain sentient being, [he sees] that for this person there is only that which is conducive to mental pleasure,
up to and including that which is conducive to equanimity.
But the object is not restricted. What [is not restricted]? It is the object.
For what reason?
Because that very same object of perception may be a basis for mental pleasure for one person, yet not so for another.
(III.33–35ab) Thus, up to "associated with the formless," how many are associated with the form realm?
Of those, how many have what as their object?
How many are associated with the formless realm?
And among those, how many have what as their object?
All have their own realm as their object within the desire realm.
Thus,
in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu), all eighteen mental explorations (manopavicāra) of those belonging to the desire realm exist;
and that very realm of desire is the object (ālambana) of them all.
The analysis of the compound in the verse "having their own as object" (*svālambana*) is: "their own realm (*svadhātu*) is the object (*ālambana*) of these.
[And it is said: "the material (*rūpin*) has twelve spheres (*gocara*)."
The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is the objective range (*gocara*) for twelve mental explorations (*manopavicāra*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is excluding six explorations of odor and taste;

that is, setting aside the two explorations of mental joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*) which have odor and taste as their objects, the two explorations of mental grief (*daurmanasyopavicāra*) which have odor and taste as their objects, and the two explorations of equanimity (*upekṣopavicāra*) which likewise have those same objects.
Why?
Because in that realm, the form realm (rūpadhātu), those two—odor and taste—are absent.
[This occurs] without the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness.
Because of this statement:
"The answer to the three."
The higher realm, the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), is the object of the three mental applications (upavicāra) of joy, sorrow, and equanimity belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara),
because of the absence of visible forms and so forth there.
In the two [lower] dhyānas, there are twelve.
Because of the absence of the six mental applications of dissatisfaction (*daurmanasyopavicāra*),
its own [sphere] has eight objects.
The object of eight is "eightfold object. This means excluding the four applications of mental attention (*upavicāra*) regarding odor and taste;
that is, excluding the two applications of mental attention with joy and equanimity that have odor as their object, and the two that have taste as their object.
Because those two do not exist there.
"The formless [realms] consist of two" means:
The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is the object of the mental applications (upavicāra) of joy and equanimity belonging to the levels of the first and second dhyānas,
because of the absence of visible forms and so forth [in the formless realm].
Thus, there exist only six mental applications of equanimity, and no others.
There are only mental applications of equanimity (*upekṣopavicāra*) that have as their objects form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).
This is because mental applications of joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*) are absent in both the third and fourth [dhyānas].
However, it should be understood that those two which have odor and taste as their objects there have as their objects the odors and tastes belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).

Regarding the phrase "there are four": this is because the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space takes the fourth dhyāna as its object, and within that [fourth dhyāna], there exist visible form, sound, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharma*).
"For those for whom that has a distinct object" means:

according to the opinion of those masters (*ācārya*), that preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*) has a distinct object—that is, it has separate objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, rather than a collective object.
According to the opinion of some masters, it takes the fourth dhyāna as its object through aspects such as "grossness" (*audārika*) and so on.

According to the opinion of those masters who hold that the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*) has a unified object (*paripiṇḍitālambana*), namely, the five aggregates belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna as its object— for those masters,
there is only one mental application to phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) therein, which has a mixed object.
"One goes upward"— in whose school's view is this?
For those whose position is that there are four "preparatory stages" (sāmanta) for the formless [attainments].
"For indeed, of the fundamental [attainments]," and so forth.
The meaning is that for the fundamental formless attainments (*ārūpya*), a lower realm is not an object; that is, a contaminated (*sāsrava*) thing belonging to a lower stage is not an object.
I shall explain this later.
"The fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not have the lower realms with outflows as their object" (III.35c).
"The first," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

One is endowed with eight [mental factors] belonging to the levels of the first and second dhyānas, and with four belonging to the levels of the third and fourth dhyānas. To the question "Which ones?", he says: "The defiled ones."
Having excluded those [consciousnesses] that have odors and tastes as their objects,
because odors and tastes do not exist there.
How so?
It has been stated that there are twelve applications (upavicāra) in the first and second dhyānas.
This is because the applications of mental pleasure (saumanasya) and equanimity (upekṣā) are established as having the six sense objects as their focal points (ālambana).
Among these, the four afflicted applications of mental pleasure have as their objects those belonging to their own level: visible forms, sounds, tangibles, and mental phenomena (dharma).
Furthermore, there are four afflicted applications of equanimity (*upekṣopavicāra*).
One born in the desire realm who has attained the wholesome states of the form realm is endowed with these.
For one born in a lower stage is indeed endowed with the afflicted states belonging to higher stages.
But not by means of the four specific [mental applications] that have odors and tastes as their objects; for those are undefiled,
and because one has not yet attained the wholesome states belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara).
And because there is no acquisition of undefiled dharmas belonging to the form realm,
one is not endowed with them.
It is also stated that there are exactly six applications of equanimity belonging to the stages of the third and fourth dhyānas.
One is likewise endowed with those among them which are afflicted and have their own stage as their object.
However, those two [faculties] which have odor and taste as their objects are not afflicted;
therefore, by the very same principle stated previously, one is not possessed of them.
"Only by the defiled [mind]" means not by the non-defiled, because of the absence of the wholesome [in that state].
"One who has attained the [attainment] of the form realm," and so forth.

One who is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and has attained a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) included within the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), yet is not free from passion for the desire realm, is endowed with all eighteen [mental factors] belonging to the desire realm, as well as with ten belonging to the level of the first dhyāna. As to how there are ten, he says: The ten belonging to the level of the first dhyāna are: the five sense-faculties (*indriya*), the five objects (*viṣaya*), and the mental faculty (*manas*). Among these, the five sense-faculties and the five objects are present because they are the basis and the object of the wholesome mind of the form realm; the mental faculty is present because it is the support (*āśraya*) for that same wholesome mind. Furthermore, the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is present because it is associated with the wholesome mind of the form realm, and because it is the feeling of the threshold concentration. The formations (*saṃskāra*) are present because they accompany the wholesome mind of the form realm. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is present because it is the very nature of that wholesome mind of the form realm. Thus, there are ten. These are the ten belonging to the level of the first dhyāna. What are the remaining eight? They are the three feelings, the three [unwholesome] roots, the two views, and ignorance. These eight belong to the desire realm. How so? Because they are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Why are they abandoned by the path of seeing? Because they are abandoned by the path of seeing, and because one who is not free from passion for the desire realm is necessarily endowed with them. Therefore, these eight are present. Thus, one who is not free from passion for the desire realm is endowed with all eighteen [factors] belonging to the desire realm. And since the wholesome mind of the form realm is included within the threshold concentration, it is endowed with the ten belonging to the level of the first dhyāna. Thus, one who is not free from passion for the desire realm is endowed with twenty-eight [factors]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "one who is not free from passion" is used to indicate that those who are free from passion are not endowed with the factors belonging to the desire realm. Why? Because they have abandoned them. If one were to ask, "Why is it said 'one who is not free from passion'? it is because one who is free from passion is endowed with the factors belonging to the form realm, whereas one who is not free from passion is endowed with the factors belonging to the desire realm. Therefore, the phrase "one who is not free from passion" is employed to distinguish between the two. Thus, the meaning is established. This concludes the section on the possession of factors. Now, regarding the section on the possession of faculties: how many faculties does one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possess? It is said: one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possesses twenty-two faculties. Why? Because one who is not free from passion for the desire realm is necessarily endowed with the faculty of life, the faculty of mind, the faculty of equanimity, the five faculties of sensation, the five faculties of faith and so forth, the male or female faculty, and the faculties of suffering and grief. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of joy, and the faculty of bodily ease. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the faculty of ignorance, the faculty of wrong view, and the faculty of doubt. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the faculty of the body, the faculty of sight, the faculty of hearing, the faculty of smell, and the faculty of taste. Therefore, one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possesses twenty-two faculties. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "one who is not free from passion" is used to indicate that those who are free from passion do not possess the faculties belonging to the desire realm. Why? Because they have abandoned them. If one were to ask, "Why is it said 'one who is not free from passion'? it is because one who is free from passion possesses the faculties belonging to the form realm, whereas one who is not free from passion possesses the faculties belonging to the desire realm. Therefore, the phrase "one who is not free from passion" is employed to distinguish between the two. Thus, the meaning is established. This concludes the section on the possession of faculties. Now, regarding the section on the possession of the truths: how many truths does one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possess? It is said: one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possesses three truths. Why? Because one who is not free from passion for the desire realm is necessarily endowed with the truth of suffering, the truth of origination, and the truth of the path. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the truth of suffering, because one is bound by the bonds of the desire realm. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the truth of origination, because one is bound by the fetters of the desire realm. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the truth of the path, because one is bound by the obstacles of the desire realm. Therefore, one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possesses three truths. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "one who is not free from passion" is used to indicate that those who are free from passion do not possess the truths belonging to the desire realm. Why? Because they have abandoned them. If one were to ask, "Why is it said 'one who is not free from passion'? it is because one who is free from passion possesses the truths belonging to the form realm, whereas one who is not free from passion possesses the truths belonging to the desire realm. Therefore, the phrase "one who is not free from passion" is employed to distinguish between the two. Thus, the meaning is established. This concludes the section on the possession of the truths. Now, regarding the section on the possession of the aggregates: how many aggregates does one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possess? It is said: one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possesses five aggregates. Why? Because one who is not free from passion for the desire realm is necessarily endowed with the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the aggregate of form, because one is bound by the bonds of the desire realm. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the aggregate of feeling, because one is bound by the fetters of the desire realm. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the aggregate of perception, because one is bound by the obstacles of the desire realm. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the aggregate of formations, because one is bound by the hindrances of the desire realm. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the aggregate of consciousness, because one is bound by the perversions of the desire realm. Therefore, one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possesses five aggregates. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "one who is not free from passion" is used to indicate that those who are free from passion do not possess the aggregates belonging to the desire realm. Why? Because they have abandoned them. If one were to ask, "Why is it said 'one who is not free from passion'? it is because one who is free from passion possesses the aggregates belonging to the form realm, whereas one who is not free from passion possesses the aggregates belonging to the desire realm. Therefore, the phrase "one who is not free from passion" is employed to distinguish between the two. Thus, the meaning is established. This concludes the section on the possession of the aggregates. Now, regarding the section on the possession of the elements: how many elements does one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possess? It is said: one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possesses eighteen elements. Why? Because one who is not free from passion for the desire realm is necessarily endowed with the six elements of the internal bases, the six elements of the external objects, and the six elements of consciousness. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the six elements of the internal bases, because one is bound by the bonds of the desire realm. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the six elements of the external objects, because one is bound by the fetters of the desire realm. Since one is not free from passion for the desire realm, one is necessarily endowed with the six elements of consciousness, because one is bound by the obstacles of the desire realm. Therefore, one who is not free from passion for the desire realm possesses eighteen elements. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "one who is not free from passion" is used to indicate that those who
"Excluding those having odors and tastes as objects among the afflicted mental applications of joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*).
This means that the mental applications of joy do not exist in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), because the preparatory stages are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Therefore, one is endowed with only the four afflicted mental applications of joy that are comprised within the fundamental [dhyāna] and have their own level as their object; however, one is not endowed with those two that have odors and tastes as their objects.
Because there is no acquisition of the non-defiled [states] without the acquisition of the fundamental wholesome [states].
For there is no defiled dhyāna that has a lower stage as its object.
[This occurs] by means of the six applications of equanimity belonging to the stage of the threshold (anāgamya).
Here, because no distinction is specified, one is also endowed with the four afflicted *upekṣopavicāras* included within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
One is also endowed with the six wholesome *upekṣopavicāras* that have the desire realm as their object, as well as those that have their own level as their object.
This is as previously stated regarding those arising from the second, third, fourth dhyānas, and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
How so?

That same person, born in the desire realm and possessing a wholesome mind of the form realm, but not yet free from passion, [is endowed] with eight [minds] belonging to the level of the second dhyāna—
namely, those very ones.
One who has not attained [the higher stages], having set aside those with odor and taste as their objects,
possesses only the four defiled [mental applications] belonging to the levels of the third and fourth dhyānas, having excluded those with odor and taste as their objects.
With one defiled [thought] belonging to the formless realm alone.
By this method, by this path, the remainder should be understood.
How?
One born in the first dhyāna who has not yet attained a wholesome mind belonging to the level of the second dhyāna is endowed with all [mental factors] belonging to the level of the first dhyāna;
with eight afflicted [mental factors] belonging to the level of the second dhyāna;
and with those born of the third and fourth dhyānas and the formless attainments as previously described.

One who possesses a wholesome mind belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, yet has not yet become free from passion for that level, is endowed with all [mental applications] belonging to the level of the first dhyāna;
and with eight belonging to the level of the second dhyāna—
namely, the four afflicted mental applications of joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*).
Excluding those having odor and taste as objects,
[there are] four mental applications of equanimity included in the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna,
and four afflicted [mental applications] belonging to the level of the third dhyāna.
Excluding those having odor and taste as their objects;
likewise, [there are none] with the fourth dhyāna level,
and only one defiled [mind] belonging to the formless realm.
One born in the second dhyāna who has not yet attained a wholesome mind belonging to the level of the third dhyāna is endowed with all [factors] belonging to the level of the second dhyāna.
He is endowed with the four afflicted factors belonging to the level of the third dhyāna.
Those arising from the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms are as previously described.

One who possesses a wholesome mind belonging to the level of the third dhyāna, yet has not yet abandoned passion for that level, is associated with all [mental applications] belonging to the level of the second dhyāna;
and with four afflicted mental applications of equanimity belonging to the level of the third dhyāna, excluding those having odor and taste as their objects;
and with four mental applications of equanimity comprised within the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the third dhyāna.
By those born in the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms, it is as before.
This is the general direction; by this same method, it applies to the third [dhyāna] and so forth as well.

For one born in the dhyānas, possession of the afflicted and wholesome mental applications of equanimity belonging to their own level and to higher levels should be applied according to what is possible.
[The text specifies] "by means of the mental application of equanimity toward phenomena," because the emanation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the desire realm is associated with equanimity.
"Another says" refers to this very author of the treatise.
"For that which [arises] from that," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Whatever person is free from passion for a certain form or other object, he does not mentally attend to that form or object as an objective support.
How does one so attend?
In that regard, one is either attracted,
or repelled,
or remains indifferent without discernment; such is the case.
When one is indifferent without discernment and does not attend [to the object],
it is unwholesome;
therefore, "without discernment" (apratisaṃkhyāya) is used as a qualification.
Therefore, not all [phenomena] are with-outflows (sāsrava);
rather,
they are those that are defiling (sāṃkleśika).
Those that exist within defilement are "defiled" (sāṃkleśika);
they are conducive to defilement.
By means of these mental factors, such as joy (saumanasya) and so forth, the mind ranges over its objects.
As for the statement, "The six constant abidings are the antidotes to these": they are the antidotes to those factors conducive to affliction;
being constant, they are called "constant" (*sātata*).
The abidings (*vihāra*) are specific types of yoga. And they are six.
How so? He says:
Having seen forms with the eye, one does not become glad;
one is not attracted.
One does not become dejected; one is not repelled.
He becomes equanimous; he does not experience [them].
How does he not experience them?
Is it through non-discernment (*apratisaṃkhyā*) or rather through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*)?
To specify this, he says: "possessing mindfulness and clearly comprehending.
The meaning is that one is examining with wisdom associated with mindfulness.
Thus, up to "having cognized mental objects with the mind.
Because of the distinction of the six types of objects, there are six constant [applications].
"For it is not so for an Arhat," and so forth.

An Arhat possesses mundane wholesome mental joy (*saumanasya*) that has as its object conditioned phenomena (*dharma*), the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), or the dharma of realization (*adhigama-dharma*).
For when he brings to manifestation the qualities belonging to the continuum of a Buddha, wholesome mental joy arises in him.
Therefore, it is not logical to exclude this [joy] from him.
To whom, then, does it belong?
It is understood that this prohibition applies to that which is defiled and constitutes a mental application (*manopavicāra*).
Therefore, not all mental factors such as joy (*saumanasya*) and so forth, even if they are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), are mental applications (*upavicāra*).
Regarding this, the Venerable Anantavarman said:
"This is incorrect."
Why?
Because they are taught otherwise in the Sūtra.
For in the Sūtra, the Blessed One did not state that the mental explorations (*upavicāra*) are exclusively defiled (*sāṃkleśika*).
For it is said thus:
"In that regard, monks, those six applications of mental joy— relying upon them and depending upon them."
Abandon these six mental applications of joy. In this regard, monks, as for these six mental applications of equanimity:
Relying upon them and established in them—
those six applications of equanimity— abandon them.
Monks, there are two kinds of equanimity:
that based on diversity and that based on unity.
Of these, monks, that which is equanimity based on unity—
"Relying upon that, abiding in that"—
meaning, "abandon this equanimity which is based on diversity."
It is known from this sutra that the mental applications (*upavicāra*), such as joy (*saumanasya*) and so forth, are not exclusively defiled (*sāṃkleśika*). This,
however, is not a definitive proof.
Even when there is mention of their abandonment, their state of being defiled does not cease;
for even if one mentions the abandonment of one thing as the support for another, the state of being defiled of these mental explorations (*manopavicāra*) does not thereby cease,
because it is otherwise impossible.
Thus he said:
"Relying upon pride, pride itself is to be abandoned.
For pride can never, under any circumstances, be a factor of purification.

Therefore, because afflictions function in mutual opposition and because one [affliction] possesses relative strength in dependence upon another, there is no fault in the statement made in the Sūtra, as it was spoken with a view toward their relative gravity or lightness. Nanda and others serve as examples in this regard.
Therefore, this is indeed so:
that the Blessed One taught the very applications of equanimity as the basis for the abandonment of the applications of equanimity themselves,
based on such statements as, "O monks, there are two kinds of equanimity," and so forth.

But is it not established—according to the Vaibhāṣika school—that these [mental applications] are both defiled and purified, based on the statement that there are thirty-six "words of the Teacher" distinguished by those based on attachment (*gardha*) and those based on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*)?

There is no fault here; for even according to the Master [Vasubandhu], there exist within them states such as mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and so forth, distinct from the mental applications themselves.
"Furthermore, those very same," and so forth.
Those very eighteen applications of mental attention (*upavicāra*) are some based on existence (*bhava*), that is, based on attachment (*adhiṣvaṅga*);
others are based on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*).

*Naiṣkramya* is the state of departing from defilement or from the suffering of *saṃsāra*. Through the distinction between that which relies on craving and that which relies on renunciation, there are two sets of eighteen, making thirty-six "Teacher's Words" (*śāstṛpada*).
Because that distinction—the twofold division of those mental applications (*manopavicāra*)—has been made known and taught by the Teacher, the Buddha, according to the sūtra.
(36, 37) It is established that "afflictions, karma, and bases" are as follows:
the afflictions are three, karma is two, and the bases are seven.
Because of this statement:
"In this way, karmas [are proximate causes] for the arising of maturation.
The term "proximate cause" is what is being referred to.
For even affliction is a cause of maturation; however, that is remote. And those [causes] have already been explained. (III.38)
That which exists here between the state of death and the state of birth is the intermediate existence (antarābhava);
it occurs prior to death and after the moment of birth.
They have been explained by the statement:
"not by independent *paryavasthānas*," namely,
by envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), anger (*krodha*), and hypocrisy (*mrakṣa*).
Their independence [is established] because they do not associate with other afflictions that are free from ignorance;
for ignorance is indeed present everywhere.
There is no lack of independence due to association with that [state].
However, the connection to rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*) is not prevented by shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and other afflictions associated with it.
Even though that state is dull, and so forth, [the details are as explained].
Even though that state of death is characterized by the lack of clarity in the activity of the mind and mental factors,
death and rebirth occur within equanimity because of the dullness of sensation.

However, whichever affliction a person has frequently and continuously practiced and engaged in, at that time of death— when the moment of death is near— that very same affliction arises and manifests, even if it be wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) or the like,
due to the previous momentum (*pūrvāvedha*) and the previous projection (*pūrvākṣepa*).

The meaning is "due to previous habituation. Alternatively, it is because of the impelling force— that is, the projection— of that very affliction which arises at that time, due to its having been previously grasped as a fruit.
"He then approaches" means that because the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu) are not specifically excluded,
all four states of existence (bhava) are present there.
Because of the restriction that there are exactly three in the formless realms and exactly three only in the formless realms.
In these other two realms, however, the fourfold existence (*bhava*) is known [to exist].
(III.39–41) "Because of the absence of outflow" (*niṣyanda*) means because of the absence of urine and excrement.
"Or, [it is] subtle among the subtle.
That is the subtle nutriment among the subtle.
[It refers to] infants who have just been born.
"Creeping creatures and so forth" refers to lice and the like;
by the word "and so forth," those dwelling in the womb are included.
These are beings that subsist on solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Regarding "desire":
this is a restriction meaning that edible food exists only in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
He asks, "Why? and replies:

because those who are free from passion for that [food], namely those who are free from passion for edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), are reborn there in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).
It is called "edible" (*kavaḍīkāra*) because it is swallowed after being made into a bolus—that is, by being formed into a lump and then ingested.

Furthermore, "ingestion by making into mouthfuls" refers to the division of food into morsels through the mouth and nose. When it is stated that all bases of odor, taste, and tangibles are indeed "edible" (*kavaḍīkāra*), one asks:
how can those odors and so forth in shadows, sunlight, flames, and light be considered food?
For there is no ingestion by making them into mouthfuls of the odors and so forth located therein.
"This explanation is indeed based on the majority of cases.
One does not thereby conclude that the odors and so forth belonging to that [realm] possess the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra*);
rather, it is an explanation given according to the majority.
"In the realm of desire, it consists of three bases.
The word "kila" (it is said) indicates that this is the opinion of another school, while his own intention is now being set forth.
"But even those," and so forth in detail.
"But even those which are not ingested, yet bring about maintenance and bring about subsistence in shadows and the like—
those too are subtle food."
It is like bathing and anointing.
Just as bathing and anointing are not consumed by being made into morsels,
so too is food.
"Similarly," [it is said].
"Because there is no benefit for those already liberated by their own faculties."
Because it does not benefit its own faculty— that is, its own sense organ— and because it does not benefit those who are liberated,
namely non-returners and arhats from the desire realm.
The sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is not nutriment.
And as for the sense-sphere of form at the time of ingestion:
it is at that time when the food, having entered within the mouth, is being consumed and has already passed beyond the range of the eye.
At that time, that form-base (rūpāyatana) does not sustain its own faculty— the eye-faculty— nor the great elements belonging to that faculty,
which are the support (āśraya) of those great elements.
How much less could it favor other sense faculties, such as the ear and so forth?
Because they are not their objects; for the sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana) is not an object of the ear and the other [faculties].
"In that case, it will provide benefit when being seen at the time of eating"; to this he says:
"And even when it is being seen," and so forth.
Now, how is this understood?
Even then, the nutriment is the contact to be experienced as pleasant that has that [form] as its object, not the form itself.
Therefore he says:
"Of those who are liberated," and so forth.
If that which is being seen were to perform the function of nutriment,
it would provide benefit even to those who are liberated— non-returners and arhats— who are free from desire for edible food, when they see even very agreeable food.
This would be just as the sense-bases of odor, taste, and tangibles provide benefit to the sense-faculties and the primary elements at the time of ingestion.
Therefore, it is established that contact (sparśa) to be experienced as pleasant, which has that [consciousness] as its object, is nutriment.
In the phrase "contact, volition, and consciousness," the word *vijñā* ends in a short vowel.
"Wisdom" (*prajñā*) means, for example,
