endowed with various types of potencies,
and by means of winds distinguished by many kinds of power.
The meaning is: by means of winds distinguished by manifold types of capacity for producing that [sound]. "By way of non-simultaneity" means: by way of not occurring at the same time.
For when the effect exists, the cause does not persist;
indeed, it is not [the case] for a substance that remains stable.
Of that which consists of form, taste, and so forth.
"Upon the cessation of another property" means upon the cessation of the milk.
"The manifestation of another property" refers to the production of curd;
that very same substratum [remains].
No.

A phenomenon distinct from the properties of milk and so forth—which consist of form and other qualities—is "transformation" (pariṇāma); it is unarisen and undestroyed even while those [properties] arise and perish.
Upon the cessation of the state of milk, there is the state of curd.
"This is that very same thing" means that the milk itself is the curd.
"And this is not so. And this curd is not the milk; it is not as if "this is that very same thing."
As for what was said regarding "by way of transformation" (*pariṇāmena*),
this is not so;
for it is stated that transformation is merely the becoming otherwise (*anyathībhāva*) of that very same substance.
"This is an unprecedented application of words," he says;
the intention is that it is self-contradictory.
For a difference between the preceding and succeeding moments is indeed asserted.
Furthermore, it is observed that for those two things in which there is alteration, there is also difference,
as in the case of Devadatta and Yajñadatta.
Therefore, cause and effect must be distinct from one another.
"Gold and so forth" means gold,
silver, jewels, earth, and so on.
"A height of sixty hundred thousand yojanas" means [sixty times one hundred thousand].
The meaning is that the height is one hundred and sixty thousand *yojanas*.
(52, 53) Regarding "endowed with the eight qualities":
[the water is] cool, clear, light, sweet, soft, and free from foul odors.
"That water does not distress the stomach nor does it irritate the throat"—
this is a verse from the *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*.
However, when measured along the shore of Yugandhara, its circumference becomes threefold.
That inner ocean, when measured along the side of Yugandhara, is threefold;
thus, its length along the side of Yugandhara is two hundred and forty thousand *yojanas*.
On both sides of that [Yugandhara], including the width of the boundary rivers in the other two directions, there are two further eighty-thousands, making three eighty-thousands in total.
It amounts to two hundred and forty thousand [yojanas].
That is, three hundred and twenty-two thousand.
This measurement of the outer ocean has been stated for one direction between Mount Nimindhara and the Cakravāḍa range.
In this case, it should be stated that there are one thousand, two hundred, and eighty-four [beings],
because of their deficiency.
The same should be stated for the other direction.
Thus, when two thousand, five hundred, and seventy-five *yojanas* are added, that foundation becomes filled,
as it was stated:
"horizontally, three thousand, four hundred and fifty."
"And twelve hundred thousand [yojanas] for the circles of water and gold" means that,
according to this enumeration of the four continents, it exceeds [the measurements] as they are arranged.
This is answered as follows:
this is not a fault,
because the water and golden mandalas outside the Cakravāḍa mountains exceed [the inner ones] by this much.
In that case, the four-continent world is not encircled by that Cakravāḍa mountain range;
rather, it is the upper ground that is encircled by it.
It should be understood that the circle of water is not so encircled.
Another says:
Mountains such as Sumeru and others do not possess cliffs that are absolutely sheer and of uniform height.
What then?
According to the principle of the shape of a mountain, their lower portions slightly exceed [the upper ones] because the distinction [between them] is difficult to perceive;
and having stated that they are equal in height and thickness.
Therefore, since those various lower portions extend slightly beyond [the upper parts], they pervade that support—Mount Sumeru and so forth—which consists of the water and golden mandalas;
thus, there is no contradiction.
(III.54–57) "Others," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
There is no basis other than the Bodhisattva’s own body, nor any location other than the site of the Vajra Seat, that is capable of sustaining that diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).
And as for which continent has which shape—
that is directly perceptible.
The diversity of sentient beings arises from the power of their respective lands.
Among the Kirātas and Śabaras dwelling in the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, a fair complexion and a dark complexion are observed. [There are also] the Dehas, Videhas, and Kurus.
Thus,
because the inhabitants are many, the location is also indicated by the plural number.
"One [is surrounded] by rākṣasas."
One of the two, Cāmara or Avaracāmara.
"From the nine mountains" means:
From the nine mountains shaped like insects;
it is called "Jambūdvīpa" by virtue of its governance over that [region],
specifically by virtue of the Jambū tree.
The continent marked by the Jambu tree is Jambudvīpa; or rather, it is so called on account of its fruit, that is,
because of the Jambu tree.
Because it was lost (*lup*), the fruit [of the jambu tree] is also called *jambū*.
The meaning is that Jambudvīpa is so named because it is marked by those fruits. (III.59, 60) It has four ridges (*catuṣ-skandha*).
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is that they have four walls;
others say they have four distinct structures.
"Encircled by iron walls" means surrounded by an enclosure of iron walls.
"Covered with iron" means they are shielded from above by iron.
Others say that their doors are closed with iron;
"burst open" means pervaded [by flames].
"As before" means that when the foot is lifted again, skin, flesh, and blood are produced once more.
[This refers to] the triad beginning with the razor-path.
Thus, there are three: the Path of Razors, the Forest of Sword-leaves, and the Forest of Śālmalī Trees;
and there are black-and-spotted dogs that devour [the beings].
Those within the forest of sword-leaves are the iron-beaked crows;
those within the forest of *śālmalī* trees are likewise [the iron-beaked crows].
*Prāsas* are javelins, *bhindipālas*, and so forth.
They are called *utsadas* because they are places of excessive torment; the prefix *ut-* has the sense of "excessive."
They are called *utsadas* because beings suffer excessively (*adhikaṃ sīdyante*) therein. But how is there an excess of torment? He says: "In the hells," and so forth.
"Another" refers to the Elder Manoratha.
He [interprets] the word "up" (*ut*) as having the sense of "above."

Therefore it was said: "Because they sink into these [places] such as the Pit of Embers (kukūla) and so forth, above the confinement of the hells—that is, above the confinement of the Avīci and other hells—they are therefore called 'supplementary' (utsada). This is another question following from a previous question.
Having asked, "What are the sixteen secondary hells? it is said: the fourth secondary hell is Vaitaraṇī.
In this river, those beings are prevented from reaching either bank by men with swords, spears, and javelins in their hands; even as they go upward, they are steamed and cooked.
Therefore, this further question arises:
"Are those hell-wardens [real beings]? and so forth.
"Like the winds of cosmic evolution" means that just as during the period of evolution, winds move about for the purpose of bringing forth the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
Therefore, those guardians of hell, known as the Yama-rākṣasas, are merely composed of the primary elements and their derivatives.

The meaning is that beings who have committed evil deeds are born as hell-wardens. "Those who [are instructed] by Yama" refers to those who have been instructed by the instruction spoken by Yama in the *Devadūtīya-sūtra*.
Those inhabitants of the realm of King Yama cast those beings into the places of hell;
these are what are called the "Yama-rākṣasas.
They are not, however, those who inflict the tortures of punishment, such as those with swords, spears, and javelins in their hands.
"Now, where is the ripening of that karma?
Where is the ripening of the karma performed by the hell-guardians within the hells?
It is in those very [guardians]," and so forth.
In those hells where there is room for the maturation of the karma of those who have committed the immediate transgressions (ānantarya),
what obstacle could those hell-guardians (naraka-pāla) possibly present?
This is what is meant.
Even for those who commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), there is room within the hells for the extremely great ripening of such immense immediate karma;
how much more so, then, for the hell-wardens (*naraka-pāla*) who, acting as their instruments, cause them to perform those deeds?
This is because a limit has been established and a boundary set with respect to the hell-wardens.
"These [beings] are not to be burned," because they have been produced from specific primary elements (*bhūta-viśeṣa*). Those specific primary elements are brought forth by their respective karmas.
That they are not burned by that fire means that [the names] correspond to the transformations of the body and sound;
the names corresponding to the transformations of the body are Arbuda, Nirbuda, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma.
Because the bodies of the beings there have the forms of bubbles (*arbuda*) and so forth,
their names— *aṭaṭaḥ*, *hahavaḥ*, and *huhuvaḥ*— accord with the transformations of their sounds.
"For this very reason" [is said].
Because it is broad at the bottom like a heap of grain.
"Outside" means not included within [the mountain].
(III.61–63) The fiery [mirror] consists of sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*), and the watery [mirror] consists of moon-crystal (*candrakānta*).
"According to possibility" means that both of those mandalas [function] for the sake of benefit or harm to vision and the other faculties, in accordance with differences of place, time, and state.
This should be applied similarly to other cases as well.

How so? When it is night in Pūrvavideha, then at Jambūdvīpa it is sunset, in Avaragodānīya it is midday, and in Uttarakuru it is sunrise; in this same manner, it should be applied to other cases as well.
"On the ninth day of the latter half of the second month of the rainy season.
There are four months of the rainy season, from Śrāvaṇa up to Kārttika.
And all months begin with the dark fortnight.
Among them, the night increases on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada;
it decreases during the fourth month of the winter season.
The four winter months begin with Mārgaśīrṣa and end with Phālguna.
Among them, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, *nilavaṃlavaṃla* is subtracted.
The second case ending is used here to express the continuous connection between time and action (*kāladhvanoḥ atyantasaṃyoge*).
On the opposite side, a shadow falling causes the disk to appear incomplete,
just as the shadow of a lamp falling upon a pillar does; the closer the pillar becomes, the more so it appears.
In such and such a manner, the pillar is covered by its own shadow.
For when the lamp is far away, the pillar is seen in its entirety;
as it moves somewhat closer, a portion diminishes, until, when it is very near, the pillar exists as if its form has vanished.
It is just like that.
That is the manner of its movement.
Furthermore, through the process of tilting sideways and rising and falling, the lower portion of the lunar disk is diminished.
And they increase upwards; thus say the Yogācāras. "The Cāturmahārājakāyikas" refers to the host (*kāya*) of the Four Great Kings;
those who dwell there are the Cāturmahārājakāyikas.
"Such as the terraces of Mount Sumeru," etc.;
by the word "etc.," Yugandhara and the others are included.
They have intervals of ten thousand [yojanas]. (III.64, 65)
Thus, the meaning is that they are separated by an interval measuring ten thousand yojanas. "Half is implied" means:
Half is occupied.
"The Ever-Intoxicated" (Sadāmada).

Although one should have said "Sadāmattāḥ," it is stated as "Sadāmadāḥ" for the sake of conforming to the metrical structure of the verse, since the meaning is the same. In the fourth [heaven], the four Great Kings themselves reside:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the eastern quarter.
Virūḍhaka is in the south;
Virūpākṣa is in the west;
Vaiśravaṇa is in the north—this sequence is to be understood.
Regarding the statement "the Cāturmahārājika gods":
because the four Great Kings themselves reside on the fourth terrace, they are thus called the Cāturmahārājika gods.
Because he exists among the great kings, he is the most extensive, the greatest (*mahiṣṭha*, *mahattama*).
He is the twenty-thousand-fold direction.
If this is so, how is it that this was said: "And they are equal in height and thickness"?
Their intention is that this was said with reference specifically to the middle portion.
"One and a half" [yojanas].
"Adhyardha" means that one and a half (adhikaṃ ardhaṃ) is in this;
"adhyardhayojana" means that its length is one and a half yojanas.
The word "in height" (*samucchrāyeṇa*) is to be supplied [from the context]. "By a hundred elements" means by a hundred colors.
"Perfection of the arrangement of various jewel-locations" [is the phrase to be understood].
It is endowed with the excellence of various kinds of jewels and the excellence of the arrangement of various locations.
The glories (*śrī*) of all other dwellings—their majesties (*mahimānaḥ*) or greatnesses—are put to shame; that is to say, they cause shame or produce a sense of modesty.
"In length it is two hundred and fifty yojanas;
each side is of this measure, and even the fourth side is of this same measure."
"Subhūmīni" means those whose grounds (*bhūmi*) are beautiful; thus,
"subhūmīni" refers to pleasure gardens.
"In the four directions" means:
"Having four directions" means it has the four cardinal points;
this is an adverbial modifier of the action.
According to the opinion of Bhāguri, the word for "direction" (dik) ends in the vowel *a*.
Thus, it is said that "having traversed twenty *yojanas*,
there are pleasure grounds," meaning that they are separated by twenty *yojanas*.
Regarding "of the Trāyastriṃśas":
those who exist among the thirty-three are the Trāyastriṃśas;
[the phrase refers] to them.
It is the abode of the excellence of sensual delight and the place of the distinction of sensual delight.
It is said with reference to not exceeding the tree:
that fragrance persists without exceeding that *kovidāra* tree.

"Its branches, leaves, and foliage extend for fifty yojanas"—this was said with reference to not exceeding the dimensions of the tree itself; thus it was stated that "the fragrance wafts for fifty yojanas against the wind.
To this, they reply:
"Indeed, there is no such thing as a wind blowing against the wind."
Wherever it arises, right there it perishes;
it does not extend its continuum to another location.
And it has been said that [the fragrance travels] fifty yojanas against the wind. Therefore, this is not a valid resolution;
hence, he stated this other resolution.
"But of that very [fragrance]," and so forth.
What, then, is the reason that here the fragrance blows with the wind for a hundred *yojanas*, but against the wind for fifty, and not beyond that? To this he says:
"Because of an increasingly weaker commencement," and so forth.
Due to being obstructed by a gentle breeze, there is an increasingly weaker commencement;
consequently, that continuity of fragrance is very quickly cut off.
For this reason, it does not travel such a great distance—a measure of a hundred *yojanas*.
Or rather, is it that the wind arises as something perfumed?
Just as in sesame seeds, another scent arises from the scent of flowers, which is distinct and is no longer the floral scent itself—so he says.
If the fragrance of a flower wafts against the wind for fifty yojanas,
then how is it that the Blessed One said, "The fragrance of a flower does not go against the wind"?
The detailed explanation follows.
Root-fragrance refers to musta and other such substances.
"Judging what should and should not be done" means they accept and deliberate upon what ought to be performed and what ought not to be performed.
(III.70ab) "In brief, those for whom a receptacle is recognized."
The vessel is the locus.
Although there are other gods in detail, such as the Krīḍāpramoṣakas, the Prahāsakas, and so forth,
it has therefore been stated in brief.

(III.70cd) "Sexual union by means of coupling" refers to those for whom sexual union occurs through coupling, embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing; thus they are called those whose sexual union consists of coupling, embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing.
For all of them, it occurs through copulation (*samāpatti*).
For all six classes of desire-realm beings, the cessation of burning passion occurs through sexual union.
However, the duration of time [required for this] is stated in the *Prajñapti*:
it is the amount of time required for embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that during that same amount of time, for those inhabitants of the earth-realm and for those of Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin, sexual union occurs respectively.
The phrase "as much as... as much as" is explained in detail as follows:
to the extent that the objects of the senses become increasingly intense at higher and higher levels, passion also becomes increasingly intense.
The meaning is that to that same extent they engage in sexual intercourse. (III.71cd) Furthermore, those four classes of gods are the Cāturmahārājakāyikas up to the Tuṣitas.
"Enjoying as it arises" means that they possess enjoyment [of objects] exactly as they arise; thus, they are "those who enjoy as it arises.
The state of being so is [the quality of enjoying as it arises].
Therefore.
Whatever is created by oneself according to one's wish;
its enjoyment is as previously described.
"Because of enjoying what is created by oneself and by others according to one's wish.
That which is created by oneself and by another;
that which is created by oneself and by another according to one's wish.
The enjoyment of those two is as before.
Some read: "because they enjoy what is created by others according to their wish.
In that reading, the analysis of the compound is as follows.
"Created by others according to one's wish" means created by others as desired. "The enjoyment thereof" is as explained previously.
For the Nirmāṇaratis, it does not succeed in enjoying the pleasures created by others.

Thus, the distinction of the Paranirmitavaśavartins from the Nirmāṇaratis is demonstrated. Furthermore, in this context, the creation of external objects such as forms and so forth should be understood.
By that which is born of seclusion belonging to the level of the first dhyāna,
because of being secluded from the unwholesome;
and by that which is born of concentration belonging to the level of the second dhyāna.
Due to the disappearance of applied and sustained thought.
"By means of joy and bliss" means by means of bliss characterized by joy.
And by means of a happiness devoid of joy; because of the departure of mental gladness,
they dwell in happiness.
"Sukham" (happily) is an adverbial modifier.
It should be examined whether there is rebirth in happiness [in the intermediate dhyāna].
Because of the absence of pleasure, it cannot be said that the intermediate dhyāna is a rebirth in happiness.
Because it is similar to pleasure by virtue of being the maturation of wholesome karma, it cannot be established as a "rebirth in pleasure.
If it is argued that this would lead to the consequence of there being a rebirth in pleasure even in the fourth dhyāna, we say no.
Because there is an absence of pleasure on that level.
Therefore, the meaning is that this must be investigated and thoroughly deliberated upon.
(III.72cd) "The rest are likewise."
Or, by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), the Yāma gods might go to the Tuṣita heaven—
either if they were led there by one possessing supernatural power or by a god residing there.
However, those belonging to the realm of the Four Great Kings who are on the same level go to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
One may see one who has come from a higher rebirth;
that is, one from the same level, not one from a higher level.
"One born in the first dhyāna [does not see] one born in the second dhyāna," and so forth.
"By his will" means by the will of one who has been born in a higher realm.
"Like that which belongs to this world" (ihatyam iva).
"Belonging to this world" (ihatyah) means belonging to this [present] existence; the meaning is "belonging to a lower level."
"One should see it as if it were present here," so say those of other schools.
This "as if it were a tangible object" is merely an illustration;
by this, it should also be understood that "as if it were a sound" applies as well.

Of the four [heavens] belonging to the desire realm, such as the abodes of the Yāmas and so forth. "Doubled successively" means that the abode of the Tuṣitas is twice the size of the abode of the Yāmas, and so on.
"But the fourth is immeasurable.
The intention is that because its palaces are connected to the *atala* and *vāṭaka* [levels] like stars, its immeasurability is possible.
(III.73, 74) There are a thousand Brahma-worlds.
Thus [it is said].
This means [the deities] of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahman [realms],
because they are recognized as such in the world.
"An appendix" (cūlika).
Because it is like a crest upon the great world-system, it is called a "peak" (*cūlika*).
For "origination" (*saṃbhava*) is indeed "evolution" (*vivarta*);
evolution is the unfolding of various [forms].
It is called *vivarta* because various things evolve within it;
*saṃvarta* means the process of dissolution (*saṃvartana*),
or it is called *saṃvarta* because things dissolve within it.
For at that time, sentient beings gather and assemble together in one dhyāna— whether the second, the third, or the fourth.
We shall explain later how it evolves, remains dissolved, dissolves, and remains in equilibrium.
(III.75–77ab) "The inhabitants of Jambudvīpa are four and three and a half cubits in measure" means that their bodies are three and a half cubits in height.
Some, however, have bodies measuring four cubits;
these are those called Pūrva, Godā, and Uttara.
Their names are "Pūrva" (East), "Go" (Cow), and "Uttara" (North);
thus they are called Pūrvagodottarāhvayāḥ.
For them, respectively, the inhabitants of Pūrvavideha are eight cubits in height; those of Godānīya are sixteen cubits in height; and those of Uttarakuru are thirty-two cubits in height.
This is the detailed explanation of the phrase "increasing by a quarter."
Since it will be stated later that "up to one and a half *krośas*," it is understood that "one quarter" refers to a quarter of a *krośa*.
Thus, the body of the gods belonging to the Realm of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*) is merely a fourth part of a *krośa*.

The [height] of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is two pādas; that of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods is up to one and a half krośas. "Doubled and reduced by three yojanas" means that after doubling [the height], three yojanas are to be subtracted.
The body size of the Anabhrakas is two hundred and fifty yojanas.
Regarding the Puṇyaprasavas:
the body size of the Puṇyaprasavas is two hundred and fifty yojanas.
For the Bṛhatphala [deities], it should be calculated as five hundred yojanas.
(III.77cd–80) "Like the kumuda and padma" means: just as here on earth the kumuda flowers close during the day and bloom at night.
The lotuses, however, are the reverse.
Thus, the distinction between day and night is established there by the closing of certain flowers at night and their blooming during the day,
as well as by the singing and silence of the birds.
Night is [indicated] by silence and dawn by chirping;
or conversely, according to the species of bird;
and also by the departure and arrival of sleep.
Night is recognized by the onset of drowsiness;
it is dawn by the departure of drowsiness. Thus, [the distinction] becomes increasingly greater.
Thus,
"twenty more" means that there is an addition of twenty.
Therefore he said:
"Thus, their life-span is, respectively, forty, sixty, and eighty thousand kalpas.
In the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), it is forty [thousand].
In the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), it is sixty; at the peak of existence (bhavāgra), it is eighty. Therefore, below that, it is half of a great eon (mahākalpa), and so forth.
Eighty intermediate kalpas constitute a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
Half of that is forty intermediate kalpas.
When that half of a great kalpa is treated as a full kalpa, its half consists of twenty intermediate kalpas.
That is the measure of the lifespan of the gods of the Brahma-realm (brahmakāyika).
That which was made into half a kalpa— namely, forty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa)—
is the measure of the lifespan of the gods of the Ministers of Brahma (brahmapurohita).
Thus, half of that [lifespan] is the measure of the life-span of Mahābrahmā;
for he is said to have one and a half kalpas, which is a count of sixty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpas).
This refers to Mahābrahmā and the others.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion, in reverse order, of the Brahmapurohitas and the Brahmakāyikas.
This is because of the reference [in the commentary] stating, "half below that," which depends on the description [of the Abhidharma-kośa] beginning with the divine realm of the Parīttābhas.
(III.81–83) "Their lifespan has been stated" refers to those [deities] of the Great Brahmās, the Ministers of Brahmā, and the Retainers of Brahmā;
their lifespans are equal to the lifespans of the gods of the desire realm.
Thus it is said in detail.
That which has been stated as the measure of the lifespan of the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings is one day and night in Saṃjīva.
In this manner, up to what has been stated as the lifespan of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods,
that constitutes one day and night in the Tapana hell,
just as it is for the gods of the desire realm.
Thus.
"Like the gods of the desire realm" means as among the gods of the desire realm.
In that context, the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of "like that.

Thus, by means of a day-and-night of that place, which consists of twelve months, and by their month of thirty such days, and by their year of twelve such months, their lifespan is five hundred divine years of that place, and so forth.
In this same manner, it should be applied accordingly to the others as well.
That which is the measure of the lifespan of the Yāma gods is one day and night in the Saṃghāta great hell.
By that day and night, the measure of lifespan in that [hell] is two thousand years.
In this same manner, it should be applied accordingly to the others as well. "These eight, monks... [and so forth].

"Monks, there are these eight nāgas, great nāgas, who endure for an eon, who support the earth, and who cannot be driven away even by Suparṇin, the king of birds; they experience and even undergo battles between the gods and the asuras. Who, then, are they? [They are:]..."

They are as follows: Nanda the nāga king, Upananda the nāga king, Aśvatarī the nāga king, Mucilinda the nāga king, Manasvin the nāga king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra the nāga king, Mahākāla the nāga king, and Elapattra the nāga king.
"With his topknot tied" means with his crest tied.
(III.84ab) "Of one bound by a single birth" means of one for whom Buddhahood is obstructed by only one more birth.
"Of one in their final existence" means of one in their last birth, by whom Arhatship must be realized in that very same life.
For him, there is no death in the interval until he attains arhatship.

For those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin), there is no death in the interval until they become one resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
This refers to those who possess these [states] as their internal essence.
For the two mothers of a Bodhisattva and a Cakravartin,
there is no death in the interval until those two are born.
"Of such as these" refers to this.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is meant that for those who have entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), as well as for those who have entered the meditative absorptions of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth, there is no death in the interim as long as they do not emerge from that concentration.
(III.85, 86) Twenty-four finger-breadths make one cubit (*hasta*).
At the time of explaining the Abhidharma, that hand of the person by which the determination of the dimensions of the four continents and so forth is established must be understood.

(III.87, 88) Regarding the term "hemantānām" (of the winters): just as the plural form "varṣāḥ" (rains) is well-established even when referring to a single entity, so too should "hemantāḥ" (winters) and "grīṣmāḥ" (summers) be understood.
In the sacred teaching (pravacana), there are only three seasons, not six as in the world.
For the cold season (śiśira) is called winter (hemanta) due to its common characteristic of coldness,
and spring (vasanta) is called summer (grīṣma) due to its common characteristic of heat.
Autumn (*śarat*) is also called the rainy season (*varṣā*) because it shares the common characteristic of rain.
Thus, [the text speaks of] "the winter, summer, and rainy seasons."
For all Buddhists, the first season is winter,
the second is summer,
and the third is the rainy season.
In that context, "adhyardha" means having an additional half; thus it is a month and a half.
When that month and a half had elapsed.
When Mārgaśīrṣa and half of Pauṣa had passed,
and half a month remained—
that is, when half of Pauṣa was still remaining, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
The omission of a night is [recognized] by the wise Buddhists.
"It is cast down" means "it is abandoned.
On this occasion, the *poṣadha* ceremony is performed by the monks on the fourteenth day.
Thus, when the month of Māgha and half of Phālguna have passed, and half a month remains—that is, when the remainder of Phālguna is left—another *ūnarātra* (intercalary day) is subtracted.
Likewise, during the summer months, two further *ūnarātras* are subtracted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha and on the fourteenth day of Āṣāḍha.
During the rainy season as well, two further *ūnarātras* are subtracted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada and on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika.

(III.89–92) Regarding "the dissolution of the realms of existence" (*gatisaṃvartanī*): the five realms of existence, beginning with the hells, dissolve into a single part of the realms of existence, namely the realm of the gods.
The meaning is that they become unified in one place.
And "the destruction of the realms" means that the desire realm is destroyed within the form realm. "The destruction of sentient beings" [is as follows].

When sentient beings themselves undergo dissolution, they become unified within the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), yet at that time the receptacle worlds do not yet undergo dissolution; the meaning is that they have not yet perished.
Regarding the "destruction of the receptacle world":
this refers to when the receptacle worlds themselves are destroyed, but not the sentient beings,
because not even a single sentient being remains there.
"Regarding the phrase 'this world,' and so forth:
this world has remained in a state of expansion for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*),
from the time it emerged until the appearance of beings in the hells."
The meaning is that it should be stated as "completed.
The meaning is that it should be stated as "entered upon," which is to say, the process of dissolution has begun.
In this same way, the dissolution of the animal realm and the dissolution of the hungry ghost realm should also be stated.

When not even a single being remains among the animals, to this extent this world has become dissolved through the dissolution of the animal realm. At that time, for anyone whose karma necessarily to be experienced as an animal still persists, [it will ripen later].

He is cast among the animals in other world-systems. In the same way, the destruction of the hungry ghosts (preta-saṃvartanī) should be applied when [the text says] "among the hungry ghosts," and so on in detail.
[The phrase] "those who associate with humans" refers to those who live together with human beings.
Those whose nature is to associate with humans,
such as cattle, buffalo, and so forth;
this is what is meant by "obtained through the very nature of things" (*dharmatā-pratilambhika*).
The term *dharmatā* refers to a specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) of wholesome factors (*kuśaladharma*) at that time.
That which is obtained by means of this is "obtained through the nature of things" (*dharmatāpratilaṃbhika*).
Regarding the phrase "among humans": [it refers to those who have previously cultivated the path].
The intention is that this applies to the humans of Jambūdvīpa.
In the same way, the destructions of Pūrvavideha and Godānīya are to be applied accordingly. However, the destruction of Uttarakuru should be stated as follows: [text missing].
That time is when humans in Uttarakuru pass away but are no longer reborn there;
when not even a single sentient being remains there,
by that much this world has become dissolved through the dissolution of Uttarakuru.
Why must it be stated in this way, and not like the destruction of Jambudvīpa and so forth? He says:
because there is an absence of detachment (*vairāgya*) in that case.
In that regard, [it is not cultivated] in Uttarakuru because of the absence of detachment (*vairāgya*).
"From this very neighboring region" means from the neighboring region of the four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*).

"In that the karma which projects it has been exhausted" means that the karma which projects the receptacle world— that is, the karma which produces the receptacle world— has been exhausted. "The flame, burning the Brahmā palace, goes forth" means that it proceeds.
And that flame belongs to that very level;
it belongs to the level of the first dhyāna.
Why? He says:
For heterogeneous and dissimilar calamities and afflictions, such as fire and so forth, do not "assail," which means they do not cause torment.
He asks: "If this is so, why is this said?"
Regarding the phrase "and for that very reason," it is explained in detail as follows:
"Because it arises in connection with that," and so forth.
This means that the flame belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) arises in connection with—that is, produced in conjunction with—the flame belonging to the realm of desire (kāmāvacara).
Its state.
Therefore.
Likewise in another [case].

Just as it was stated regarding the destruction by fire (*tejaḥ-saṃvartanī*), so too should it be understood, as applicable, for the other destructions—by water (*apsaṃvartanī*) and by wind (*vāyu-saṃvartanī*). How so?
Having described the destruction beginning with the hells as previously explained, up until this point, this world has been destroyed through the destruction of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃvartanī*).
Then, when the receptacle world has become empty, the innate water element arises;
that which dissolves the receptacle world like salt.
This water element belonging to the desire realm connects with the water element belonging to the level of the first dhyāna.
And that [fire] connects with the level of the second dhyāna.
Furthermore, that water-element, though belonging to three levels, disappears along with its respective receptacle world.
In the same way, it should be stated that in the destruction by wind, a co-emergent wind arises.
How so?

Having stated it as before, up until "the innate wind-element arises," that [wind] gradually scatters and destroys the receptacle world— from the desire realm up to the level of the third dhyāna— like a heap of dust.
...until he disappears along with him.
Desiring to explain the eon of evolution (*vivartakalpa*) in detail, he says:
"For thus the world has evolved," and so forth.
"Tathā" means as it has been described.
"Tadā" refers to the detailed explanation:
when very gentle winds stir in the sky.
From that time onwards, it should be said that this world, having remained dissolved for twenty intermediate kalpas, has now emerged and reached its completion;
it should be said that it has arrived [at the beginning of the new cycle].
The meaning is that this must now be explained.
Regarding the phrase "according to the prescribed order":
everything arises according to the order and the method as previously described.
The sequence is as previously stated: the wind mandala, then the water mandala, then the golden earth, and then Mount Sumeru and the rest.
According to the prescribed method—that is, whatever dimensions have been specified, characterized by length, height, circumference, and shape—all that arises exactly in that manner.
"But first [the world-sphere] is Brahma's," and so forth. The established rule is that what is destroyed last is formed first.
Therefore he said:
"First, however, the Brahma palace arises; then [the others] up to that of the Yāma gods."

By the word "up to" (*yāvat*), it is shown that after the Brahma-palaces, the Paranirmitavaśavartin palaces arise; immediately after those, the Nirmāṇarati palaces; and immediately after those, up to the Yāma palaces.
Then, immediately after the arising of the Yāma palaces, the wind-circle and so forth arise.
This indicates that this refers to the evolution of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) and not the evolution of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
He is called Mahābrahmā because he is born in an empty Brahma-palace;
"other beings" refers to his retinue.
Having passed away from there, they are reborn among the Brahmapurohitas.
"Then from the Ābhāsvara [heavens]":
this means that it has emerged;
the meaning is that the evolution of the world has reached its completion.
"That has approached" means that the state of evolution (vivṛtti) has begun.
"Nineteen intermediate kalpas for those of immeasurable lifespan" [means as follows].

One intermediate kalpa has passed with the completion of the receptacle world, including the celestial palaces of the Brahma-world; thus, nineteen remaining intermediate kalpas pass for humans of immeasurable lifespan until the appearance of beings in the hells.
That period should be understood as having already passed through the state of evolution (*vivartamānāvasthā*).
Once a being has appeared in hell, the state of evolution (*vivṛttāvasthā*) has begun.
This is what is being said:
for those whose lifespan decreases from being immeasurable down to ten years, that constitutes one *vivṛtta-avasthāntara-kalpa* (an intermediate kalpa of the period of evolution).
Therefore, he says:
That is the first intermediate kalpa of those [aeons] that have evolved and are remaining.
After that, there are eighteen periods of increase and decrease.
But from that,
there is indeed one excellence.
The state of having evolved (vivṛttāvasthā) is to be understood as having a duration of twenty intermediate eons (*antarakalpa*).
A *kalpa* has the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as its intrinsic nature;
these very [aggregates] are the time-period (*adhvan*) and the basis of discourse (*kathāvastu*).
"Thus.
"As a detached [verse]" means that it is not included within the four Āgamas.
"The group of eight was forgotten from the middle" means that because eight locations were lost at some point, they were not recited;
therefore, there are fifty-two locations here.
And there ought to be sixty numerical places.
One should oneself create some names for those eight [remaining] places and recite them,
so that the sixty numerical places may be complete.
"Incalculable" means "innumerable.
They are called "incalculable" because they cannot be calculated by means of numbering.
Because of the use of the plural number, even those [entities] not explicitly mentioned are included as derivatives (*taddhita*).
If this is so,
then that which arises from the three incalculable aeons (*asaṃkhyatraya*) [is meant].
If this is so, how can it be said [that they are "countless"]?
This is not a fault.
They are called "asaṃkhyāḥ" (incalculable) because there is no number beyond them; thus, they are "asaṃkhyeyāḥ" (innumerable) eons.
"Immeasurable, immeasurable, and immeasurable"—thus they are called "immeasurables.
There are three of them.
From those three immeasurables, the eons arise.
"Buddhahood arises from three incalculable eons"—
this is how it should be explained.
"Because that is desired.
This means because that benefit for others is desired;
for whatever is desired [is what one strives for].
"That self-interest has been seen" means:
"because of that cause," that is, because of the cause of attachment to a self (*ātmasneha*).
"Having turned away from self-attachment toward them," and so forth.

Having turned away from self-attachment toward those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) belonging to one's own continuum, and having increased the regard characterized by compassion, it is conceivable that for that reason—that is, for the sake of that regard—one endures sufferings;
whereas the middling person [endures] only the cessation of suffering.
The Pratyekabuddha and the Śrāvaka seek only the cessation of suffering, that is, liberation itself; they do not seek worldly happiness.
Why?
Because it is a locus of suffering;
that is, because that worldly pleasure becomes a basis for suffering.
The supreme bodhisattva [exchanges] the sufferings occurring within his own continuum for the happiness of others.
He prays for the welfare of others, both for their worldly prosperity and for their ultimate liberation, which is by nature the absolute cessation of suffering.
Or else, one prays for the happiness of others, both that which pertains to worldly prosperity (*ābhyudayika*) and that which pertains to the ultimate good (*naiḥśreyasika*).
And he prays for the absolute cessation of suffering itself, which is characterized by Buddhahood, belongs to himself, and serves as the means for accomplishing the welfare of others.
Why? He says:
Because he is one who suffers that very suffering.
Because that bodhisattva becomes sorrowful through the sufferings of others,
for this very reason he seeks happiness in two ways.
(III.93) "Below the period of decline," and so forth.
Below a lifespan of one hundred years, the five corruptions (*kaṣāya*) become excessive;
the meaning is that they become intensified.
Even after a hundred years, they are abundant but not exceedingly so, as they were below.
Regarding the "corruption of lifespan" (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*):
*kaṣāya* refers to that which has become dross, inferior, and base.
The corruption of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) is simply the corruption that is lifespan;
likewise for the corruptions of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) and so forth.
[These are listed] in their respective order.
Failure of life occurs through the corruption of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*). Failure of requisites occurs through the corruption of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
Requisites such as grain, flowers, fruits, and medicinal herbs possess diminished flavor, potency, ripening, and efficacy.
For those things either do exist, or they do not exist at all.
Through two [of these], there is the ruin of the side of wholesome qualities.
The ruin of the side of wholesome qualities occurs through the turbidity of afflictions and the turbidity of views.
How so? It says:
"Because of the engagement with devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasures and self-mortification."
Sensual pleasure (*kāmasukha*) itself is the pursuit of sensual pleasure (*kāmasukhallikā*).
Alternatively, the state of being addicted to sensual pleasure, or sensual craving (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), is the pursuit of sensual pleasure, by which one becomes attached to sensual pleasure.
Self-mortification (*ātmaklamatha*) means self-torment (*ātmopatāpa*), that is to say, self-affliction (*ātmapīḍā*).
Devotion to and pursuit of both the indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification;
this is the subject under discussion.
Therefore.
Thus it has been said:
with reference to the pursuit of sensual pleasure or the pursuit of self-mortification, the ruin of the side of wholesome qualities occurs through the two impurities of afflictions and views.
This much, then, is stated without distinction.
Or [between] the two sides of the householders and the renunciants:
for the side of the householders, there is the ruin of the side of wholesome qualities due to the turbidity of the afflictions; for the side of the renunciants, it is due to the turbidity of views.
Respectively, householders are dominated by desire, while those who have gone forth are dominated by views. "By one" refers to the defilement of sentient beings (*sattvakaṣāya*).
For there are two kinds of *pratyekabuddhas*.
Since even Pratyekabuddhas who move in groups were formerly Śrāvakas—
not only those who are like the rhinoceros horn—
it is therefore not contradictory for them to appear even during a period of increase.

For those who have already produced the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) or the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), and who personally realize arhatship when the Buddha's teaching has disappeared— they are "those who move in groups" (*vargacārin*).
And because they have already attained a state of spiritual urgency (*samvega*) at the time of the previous Buddha's appearance, they do not need to be stirred by urgency again.

"Because of the display of their deportment" means because of the display of the deportment of a Pratyekabuddha, that is, the display of the form of meditative concentration in the cross-legged posture.
And it is not the case that those who are noble would undergo painful austerities.
Because at the very moment of seeing the truths, the view of clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned,
and because the practice of arduous asceticism is preceded by that clinging to rules and observances.
Thus, they are said to be "like the rhinoceros horn" (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*).
Just as rhinoceros horns are solitary,
so too do they dwell without associating with householders, renunciants, or other pratyekabuddhas;
thus they are called "those who are like the rhinoceros horn."
"Successive through a hundred kalpas" means that the causes for awakening have been cultivated throughout a hundred kalpas.
For this very reason, he explains:

"Having practiced for a hundred great eons (*mahākalpa*) by applying himself to the accumulations for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), characterized by ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). And the phrase "and it is possible by them," and so forth, follows.
Moreover, even if they have not attained the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),

they are nevertheless able to teach the Dharma by recollecting the instructions of former Buddhas through their knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*). This is because they manifest supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Because [the Buddhas] manifest such things as traveling through space for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
nor is it because sentient beings lack the capacity [to understand],
for the ellipsis of the sentence is "they do not teach the Dharma."
He asks, "Why? and replies with the detailed explanation beginning with "For thus.
Because at that time, those who are free from passion regarding the worldly realms are indeed found to exist.
Therefore, the intention is that even those who have transcended passion through supramundane means could possibly exist.
If these are not the causes for the non-performance of the teaching of the Dharma, then what is the cause? To this he says:
"What then? and so forth.

This means that due to the force of previous practice—specifically the force of practicing non-association—and due to being inclined toward having little eagerness, one has developed a taste for that [state].

Furthermore, in order to avoid the consequence of attracting a following (*gaṇaparikarṣaṇaprasaṅga*), they do not venture to engage others in the grasping of the profound Dharma. For if such engagement were to occur, a following would necessarily be attracted. But why, then, do they avoid the consequence of attracting a following?
Because of the fear of distraction and social contact;
that is, because of the dread of both distraction and social interaction.
Distraction (*vyākṣepa*) is the failure to engage in the intended activity, such as meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Association" (*saṃsarga*) means contact with others.
Furthermore, the fear of distraction and association arises from the force of previous habituation.
(III.94, 95) "This is [stated] according to the *Prajñapti*" refers to the exposition found in the *Prajñaptiśāstra*.
"There are four kinds of wheel-turning kings.
However, in the Sūtra, only the golden wheel-turning king is mentioned because of his preeminence. This is impossible with respect to the present time.
There is no possibility [of their arising] with respect to the future,
because they could arise simultaneously even in the future time; thus,
they are "neither prior nor posterior," meaning that one is not first and the other not later.
What then?
The meaning is "together.
"Equal and equal" is an intensive expression (*vīpsā*).
Alternatively, he is "equal to the equals" (samasama) because he is equal to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are equal toward all sentient beings.
"Of that extent without effort" means that he perceives that many world-systems effortlessly.
"Those of other schools" refers to the Mahāsāṃghikas and so forth. "Not in one place" means not in a single world-system. "The span of a human life" refers to the full duration of a man's lifespan.
The life-span of a person is "puruṣāyuṣam. The phrase "bearing that" continues [from the previous context].
"This faculty" refers to faith and the others.
"Of this member" means "of this condition. "Is this with reference to a single world-system?"— so it is asked.
The intention is that this was said with reference to either a single world-system of four continents or a triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system.
As for the detailed explanation beginning with "And even for a universal monarch," the statement that "it is impossible,
there is no occasion, for two Tathāgatas to arise in the world simultaneously, neither before nor after" does not, by its own words, prohibit their arising in other world-systems.
Because the Tathāgatas are described in that way; just as, for example, universal monarchs (cakravartins) are also described in that same way.
For universal monarchs, too, are described in that manner.
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that two wheel-turning monarchs (cakravartin) should arise in the world simultaneously, neither before nor after the other.
"Common folk" refers to ordinary people;
"human beings," however, refers to those possessed of intelligence.
They bring forth and brandish weapons.
The householder-treasure (gṛhapatiratna) is of the nature of a treasury superintendent;
the counselor-treasure (pariṇāyakaratna) is of the nature of a commander-in-chief.
"Of a kind connected with that":

it is connected with that *cakravartin*. "Leading to the destruction of what is connected with that" means: its dissolution (*saṃvartana*) through connection with that; that which is beneficial for or conducive to that is "leading to the destruction of what is connected with that" (*tatsambaddhasaṃvartanīya*).
By whichever being karma was accumulated, when that wheel-turning monarch has arisen,
it is that very being's own karmas that cause him to arise.
But it is not the case that a sentient being becomes the causal condition for the arising of the wholesome maturation of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that this wholesome maturation belongs to the universal monarch alone.
"More firmly established" means having an unshakable position.
They are more intensely heated, more radiant,
more complete, and of unimpaired form.
This is investigated in connection with the topic of the universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
(III.96) "What indeed [is meant] by 'including the kings'?
He cites the Sūtra in order to demonstrate the point that they were as if belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
"It is said in the Sūtra," and so forth.
Because they possess a visible form, they are "possessed of form" (rūpin). Because they are of miraculous birth, they are "mind-made" (manomaya).
Because they are endowed with hands, feet, fingers, and so forth, they are "endowed with all limbs and parts."
They are "unimpaired" because their sense faculties are complete; they are "possessing unimpaired faculties" because of the absence of being one-eyed, cross-eyed, or otherwise defective;
they are "beautiful" because of their pleasing physical form.
Because their complexion is beautiful, they are "abiding in color" (*varṇasthāyin*).
Because they do not depend on the light of the sun and other sources, they are "self-luminous" (*svayaṃprabha*).
Because they travel through the sky by means of the supernatural power of karma, they are "moving through the atmosphere" (*vihāyasaṅgama*).
Because they do not depend on solid food (kavaḍīkārāhāra), they have joy as their nutriment (prītibhakṣa).
"Joy as their nutriment" and "having joy as their food" are synonyms.
Likewise, they are long-lived and remain for a long duration of time.

"Sweet as honey" means that its flavor has a taste like honey. For sentient beings who have fallen into the state of being swallowed by improper mental attention— which acts like a crocodile— desire itself is the crocodile.
Therefore, its commencement is an "entering" (āveśa).
"For the sake of the evening meal" means for the sake of eating in the afternoon.
"For the sake of a morning meal" means for the purpose of eating in the morning. "Storing up" means accumulation.
By dividing the fields and providing for their livelihood through rice that grows without being ploughed or sown,
the designations "Kṣatriya" and so forth are established according to the method of etymological derivation (*nirukti*). (III.97) [The term] *niryāṇa* [means] departure.
Thus ends [the section].
"Stained by unrighteous passion" means being obsessed with the passion for sexual misconduct.
"Overcome by improper greed" means:
improper greed is the desire to take what belongs to others, whether by theft or by force;
they are overcome by that.
"Enveloped by false dharmas" means those who illuminate perverted dharmas.
"Not knowing their mothers, not knowing their fathers," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is the time of the world's dissolution (*niryāṇakāla*).
Three terminations of an eon are taught:
weapons, disease, and famine.
Do these three terminations occur sequentially for a single eon in which the lifespan is ten years?
Or rather, is it one for each [of the two] in succession? First, some say:
"One for each."
Others, however, say: for one person, these three occur in succession— first famine, immediately after that disease, and immediately after that the sword.
We see, however, that the former position is intended.
"By those very faults" means by unwholesome states such as attachment and so forth.
Non-human beings, such as *piśācas* and others, unleash calamities such as diseases and the like.
Or they take away one's vital energy (*ojas*).
Or, by their power, they corrupt the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and so forth,
whereby incurable diseases manifest in them.
"From which they die; and then," and so forth. "When here."
In Jambudvīpa there is killing by means of weapons;
at that time, in the two continents of Pūrvavideha and Avaragodānīya, malice reaches its peak.
When there is disease here [in Jambudvīpa], [the same occurs in those two].
Then there is weakness for those two;
when there is famine here,
then there is hunger and thirst for those two.
(III.98, 99) The non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthakāra*),
such as Kaṇabhuj and others,
have stated that wind is the seed.
Because of the statement, "being churned by winds distinguished by many kinds of power," it is said that "it is the cause.
The unperished wind belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) is the cause for the wind produced in the first moment at the time of evolution (*vivartakāla*) in the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
"Seeds are brought forth. There are five kinds of seeds, beginning with root-seeds:
root-seeds, joint-seeds, seed-seeds, tip-seeds, and trunk-seeds.
"Even so" means:
even if seeds are brought forth, they do not maintain that sprouts and the like arise from seeds, shoots, joints, and so forth—which are gross entities—as sprouts, stalks, and the like.
For those [seeds and so forth] are their efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*), not their inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
And there must also be inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa).
Therefore, he asks: "What then?"
"From their own constituent parts," and so forth. For example, a whole such as a sprout [arises] from its own constituent parts, such as the sprout;
and those constituent parts of the sprout likewise arise from their own constituent parts.
For these as well, [the production] is from their own [parts] alone, and so on down to the atoms;
except for the mutual approach of the atoms,
there is no capacity whatsoever in seeds and the like for the act of production.
The intention is that their causal capacity is accepted because of the gradual approach of atoms toward the sprout and so forth.
"There would be no restriction" means that there could even be the production of mats and the like from threads and other such materials.
"Because of the restriction of capacity.
Just as there is no lack of restriction for seeds and so forth due to the restriction of their inherent capacities,
it is like the production of sound or of qualities arising from heating.
Just as sound arises from heterogeneous causes such as impact,
yet it does not arise from just any heterogeneous cause such as odor or taste,
because only specific heterogeneous causes like impact possess the capacity to produce it.
Likewise, color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities produced by maturation (*pākaja*) arise from heterogeneous causes such as fire;
yet they do not arise from just any heterogeneous cause, such as the eye,
because only fire and the like possess the capacity to produce them.
The Vaiśeṣika says:
The specific property of color arises from both those of its own class and those of a different class.
First, from those of its own class:
Color, taste, smell, touch, and so forth are preceded by causes and arise from color, taste, smell, touch, and so forth themselves.
Even conjunctions, disjunctions, those produced by heating (*pākaja*), and so on, arise from heterogeneous causes such as action (*karman*) and the like.
Thus, the property of a quality (*guṇadharma*) is not an illustrative example for the property of a substance (*dravyadharma*).
"For they themselves are such," and so forth.
For it is those very *vīraṇa* grasses and the like that, being arranged and situated in such a manner— that is, in the form of a mat and so on—
receive the designation "mat."
Like a row of ants. Just as ants,
when arranged in such a manner, receive the designation "row."
Furthermore, according to your own established doctrine, there is no substance called a "row" (paṅkti) distinct from those [individual components].
How, then, is it understood that those *vīraṇa* grasses and so forth, when arranged in such a manner, receive the designation "mat" (*kaṭa*) and the like,
rather than being substances distinct from them?
Therefore, he says:
because a cloth is not perceived when there is a conjunction with a single thread.

For when one thread that has begun its effect is conjoined with both the eye and touch, according to your view, the cloth must also be in close proximity to those two; thus, this [cloth]— *Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* 341 [Tib. 327a] ...[would necessarily be perceived].*
It might still be perceived in that very same way.
If one were to say,
"Its non-perception is due to an obstruction," [the response would be:]...
Therefore he says:
"For what obstacle could there be then to the perception of a cloth that exists and is present?
The intended meaning is that there is no obstacle.
Therefore, there is no such thing as a "cloth" that exists as a separate substance.
It might be thought:
"The cloth exists in each individual thread by way of a portion, but it does not exist by way of its entire self."
Therefore it is said:
"Because its occurrence is not complete," and so forth.
If the occurrence of the cloth were considered incomplete, then only a portion of the cloth would exist in each individual thread, and not the cloth itself.
If one asks why, it is said in response:
"And the cloth would be a mere collection," as the phrase continues.
It would follow that one part exists in one thread and another part in another, such that the cloth is merely a collection of many parts residing in the threads;
yet this is not accepted.
Furthermore, what part of the cloth is there that is distinct from the threads?
The followers of Kaṇāda should be asked by which part this [cloth] would exist in the yarn that is in contact with the sense organ.
Therefore, even having devised this hypothesis, no cloth other than these [parts] is established. This might be the thought:
The cloth exists even in each individual thread.
However, the perception of the cloth occurs through the contact of the cloth with the sense organ;
the cause [of this perception] is the dependence upon the conjunction of the cloth with multiple substrates.
Therefore, if perception were to be postulated as depending on a conjunction with multiple substrates, then when a mere collection of threads is perceived, the cloth would have to be perceived;
yet it is not so perceived, because the middle parts of the cloth and so forth are not seen.
Now, it might be thought: even at that time, the middle and other parts are not in contact with the sense faculty;
therefore, the perception of a cloth does not occur when there is merely a collection of threads.
To this, the following is said:
"Or rather, never," and so forth.
That is to say, there would never be the perception of a cloth.
Because the middle and rear parts are not in contact with the sense faculty.
Indeed, it is impossible that all those constituent middle and rear parts could simultaneously come into contact with the sense faculty.
If that were the case, this same consequence would apply even to threads and the like, and thus no effect whatsoever would ever be perceived.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "and in the case of successive contact," it means that when the eye or the tactile organ perceives a cloth successively,
there would be no perception of the cloth as a whole.
Because there is no simultaneous conjunction with multiple substrates for the sense organs of sight and touch,
there would likewise be no perception of other parts [of the object] either.
Therefore, and so forth.

Since the cognition of a cloth or the cognition of a mat occurs successively, therefore that cognition— the cognition of a cloth or the cognition of a mat— arises with respect to the parts themselves, namely the parts of the cloth or the parts of the mat, by the power of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
like the circle of a whirling firebrand.
Just as, when a firebrand is moved rapidly so that it appears to arise in various locations, the cognition of a "wheel of fire" (alātacakrabuddhi) occurs;
it is just like that.
And here is the proof for this:
The cloth does not exist as a substantial entity (dravyasat),
because its perception depends upon the perception of its constituent parts,
like a fire-brand wheel (alātacakra).
"In those of different form, genus, and action," and so forth.
This means: in threads of different forms due to distinctions such as blue, yellow, and so on;
and in [threads] of different genera due to distinctions such as *dukūla* silk, cotton, and so on.
Because there is a distinction between upward and downward movement among those with different actions;
and because color and other qualities are impossible for a cloth,
what kind of "form" (rūpa) could exist there— is it a genus (jāti) or an action (kriyā)?
One might think: "Its color and other qualities are variegated.
But if its color and other qualities are thus conceived as being variegated, there would also be the production of heterogeneous effects;
even from threads and vīraṇa grass, a mat could be produced.

That being the case, a contradiction of the specific property of phenomena (dharmaviśeṣaviparyaya) would follow; the meaning is that substances would then come to produce something of an entirely different genus (atyantavijātīya).
Furthermore, on the other side which is not variegated, the cloth—which is variegated on one side—would not be perceived.
Because that [color] is accepted as having a variegated form (*citrarūpa*).
For the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that upon the perception of color, there is the apprehension of the substance which is its substratum.
And they hold that perception occurs when there is magnitude, possession of multiple substances, and color.
Because it is stated that air is not perceived due to the absence of the formation of color (*rūpa-saṃskāra*),
or else there would be the perception of variegated color on a side that is not variegated if the cloth were visible;
for its color is held to be variegated.
"The action is also variegated; this is most extraordinary. It is not tenable that a single substance possesses variegated actions.
For when there is a diversity of actions, a difference among the substances intended to possess those actions is admitted.
"And in the case of the difference between heat and light," and so forth.
In the case of a composite whole characterized as the flame of fire, a difference in touch is observed at its beginning, middle, and end, which are its constituent parts.
And that difference therein consists, respectively, of intensity, mediocrity, and dullness.
For that composite substance consisting of light, those two—color and touch—are not possible.
Indeed, it is not logical for a single composite to possess multiple colors or touches.
Therefore, there is no composite substance distinct from its parts.
Now, it might be thought: if there is no composite whole such as a cloth that is distinct from its parts such as the threads,
because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses.
And since the sensory object is not composed of those parts,
the entire world would be imperceptible;
yet cows and other such things are seen to be perceptible.
Therefore, it is established that a distinct, perceptible entity is produced from atoms that are themselves beyond the senses; to this, it is replied:
"Even though the atoms are beyond the senses," and so forth.
Just as for you Vaiśeṣikas, although they are beyond the senses, when combined they possess the capacity to initiate an effect, whereas individually they do not.
In the same way, for us as well, perceptibility belongs only to atoms in their aggregate state, not when they are separate, even though there exists no "whole" (*avayavin*) as a distinct entity.
Just as the eye and so forth—the eye, visible form, light, and mental attention—are the causes for the arising of visual consciousness only when combined, and not individually;
likewise, although atoms are beyond the reach of the senses, they possess perceptibility when in an aggregate state, but not individually.
Furthermore, for people suffering from ophthalmia, a mass of scattered and unconnected hairs is perceived even though no composite whole has been produced;
yet each individual hair is not so perceived.
For those afflicted with ophthalmia, a single hair—just like an atom—is beyond the reach of the senses.
Therefore, there is no other substance for you apart from these.

Having thus refuted the possessor of parts (avayavin), and desiring to refute that the possessor of qualities (guṇin) is a distinct entity from the qualities such as form (rūpa) and so forth, he says:
"And [it exists] in form and so forth," and so on in detail.
The designation "atom" (paramāṇu) is applied only to form and the other [sensory objects].
When those are destroyed—that is, when form and the others are destroyed—the destruction of the atom is established.
Thus say the Vaiśeṣikas.
For the substance is the atom; moreover, the substance is distinct from visible form and the other [sensory qualities],
because of established doctrinal statements such as "earth possesses visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility."

It is not established that these are distinct, because these elements—earth, water, and fire—and these qualities of theirs, such as visible form, taste, odor, and tangibility, cannot be distinguished by anyone as "these are earth and so forth" and "these are their qualities, namely visible form, taste, odor, and tangibility.
One might say that they are not determined because they are beyond the senses; therefore, he says:
And those [elements], earth and so forth, are asserted to be perceptible by sight and touch.
Regarding the phrase "and when they are burned," and so forth:
the followers of Pailuka maintain that composite substances such as wool and the like are not burned.
This is what is meant: when the previous qualities cease and qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) arise, the substances that serve as their substrates remain in that very same state.
In that case, the cognition of wool and so forth would likewise persist.
And yet it does not exist.
Therefore, because there is no cognition of that substance,
the cognition of it occurs only with respect to form and the other [sensory objects], and not with respect to a substance that is a distinct entity.

For if a substance such as wool were something other than [the qualities] such as form, then it would remain even when those [qualities] have ceased; thus, when the forms and so forth are destroyed by heat through contact with fire, there would still be a cognition of "wool" and so on.
But this is not the case.
Therefore, the cognition of wool and so forth occurs only with respect to the forms and other qualities themselves.
The Vaiśeṣikas say:

"If the jar were merely its color and other qualities, then because different qualities such as those produced by baking would arise from contact with fire, one would not recognize that 'this is that very same jar.
But for one who holds that through baking only the qualities themselves arise and cease while the jar remains in that same state, the recognition of it is logical; therefore, this is said."
Regarding the recognition of a jar upon the arising of that produced by baking:
it is "due to the similarity of shape.
This means due to the similarity of the form and so forth of the color and other qualities.
It is like a row.
Just as for you there exists no substance called a "row" distinct from those ants,
yet, because of the similarity in the arrangement of the preceding row, there occurs the recognition of it in another [row].
"This is that very same line of ants.
He asked:
"How is this understood?"
"Recognition occurs due to the similarity of configuration, and not due to the persistence of the same state.
To this it is replied:
"Because there is no recognition for one who does not perceive the distinguishing mark."
Because the cognition of that [shape] does not occur for one who does not perceive marks such as brokenness, unevenness, or elevation,
it is therefore established that it is due to the generality of shape (*saṃsthānasāmānya*).
"And that," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
And that joy, through its association with pliancy— since pliancy arises from joy—
is like water because it makes the basis (the body) supple through its association with pliancy.
"For this very reason," and so forth.
Because the basis is made supple;
that is, because in that second dhyāna of meditative attainment, all bodily rigidity has departed.
The cessation of the faculty of suffering has been explained;
and through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of suffering.

"Having already attained the fourth dhyāna—which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness—due to the subsiding of both mental joy (*saumanasya*) and mental grief (*daurmanasya*), he dwells therein.
This is because it is free from the eight internal defects (*ādhyātmika-apakṣāla*).
These eight internal defects are initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), and so forth.

This form *ānejyam* belongs to the verbal root *ejṛ*, meaning "to tremble.
However, when the reading is *āniṃjyam*,
then this form should be understood as belonging to a different verbal root, *ing*.
Those belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host are unable to enter the formless realms because they are characterized by insight (vipaśyanā),
whereas the formless realms are characterized by tranquility (śamatha).
Nor can one go elsewhere, to a lower stage,
because one is proceeding toward excellence.
This is according to this sequence.
Immediately after seven destructions by fire as previously described, there occurs one destruction by water.
Again, immediately after seven destructions by fire, there occurs a second destruction by water.
In this manner, it continues until the seventh destruction by water.
When seven [cycles] have thus passed by water, there is again a cycle of seven by fire;
after that, there occurs one destruction by wind.
For what reason? Because, as has been described, the destruction by water occurs after a long duration of time;
and because the destruction by wind occurs after an even longer duration than that, this is said:
"Just as for them," and so forth.

Just as there is a distinction in the duration of the personal existences belonging to the level of the second dhyāna due to the excellence of the attainment of the second dhyāna compared to the first dhyāna:
the lifespan for those born in the first dhyāna is half a great aeon (ardha-mahākalpa),
whereas for those born in the second dhyāna it is two aeons.
The same applies to receptacles as well.
What?
It is a distinction in their duration.
In this way, the distinction of the third dhyāna from the second must also be stated. And having done so [as follows]:

because there are eight cycles of seven destructions by fire, there are fifty-six destructions by fire; seven destructions by water; and one destruction by wind—thus, there are sixty-four destructions in total.
Therefore, what was stated in the *Prajñaptibhāṣya*— that the lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna deities is sixty-four kalpas— is well-said.
Just as...
But above the Parīttābhas, the physical basis [of the deities] doubles and doubles again; thus it has been stated here that the measurement of the bodies of the Śubhakṛtsnas is sixty-four yojanas.
And their lifespan is said to be measured by the size of their bodies,
because of the statement: "But lifespan [is measured] in kalpas according to its own physical basis."
Each single period of destruction constitutes a *mahākalpa*.
For it is by such a duration of time that their lifespan is brought to completion.
This concludes the third treasury-location (*kośasthāna*) in the *Sphuṭārthā*, the commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* composed by Master Yaśomitra.
(Abhidh-k-vy 345) IV. Exposition of Karma (IV.1) [Tib.
1b] Having had doubt aroused by the erroneous views of the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthakara), he asks.
Now, as for the passage beginning with "that which is this," the detail is as follows:
therein, the diversity of sentient beings consists of the distinctions of realms, destinies, modes of birth, and so forth;
the diversity of the receptacle world consists of the distinctions of Mount Meru, the continents, and so forth.
"Of those who perform mixed actions" means those who perform both wholesome and unwholesome deeds.
Now, why is it that their physical bases (āśraya) are not delightful, while their enjoyments (bhoga) are delightful?
And this being so, the enjoyment of sense objects becomes possible.
For if the basis [of existence] were not delightful, for what remedy would there be the enjoyment of sense objects?
[This applies] to those who act without intermixture.
Regarding those belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*):
even the gods of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) who are like those who act without intermixture possess delightful physical bases and objects,
because they perform the two types of karma that cause such delight.
"And having intended" means "I shall do this in such a way.
If it is argued that verbal action is one [type] by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [then...]
Or rather, [it is called] "action" (*karman*) because it is that which is done;
however, the other two do not possess the nature of action.
Action performed by the body, or action belonging to the body, is bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Thus is mental action.
Therefore, action does not exist by way of intrinsic nature.
This is because of three reasons.
By way of basis, by way of intrinsic nature, and by way of origination.
"Of the three" refers to the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Bodily action is so called by way of its basis;
that is, action which has the body as its basis is "bodily action.
Or, verbal action is so called by way of its intrinsic nature.
"Speech alone is action.
This refers to mental action by way of its origination,
because it is originated by the mind.
(IV.2cd–4) “Others say it is ‘motion’” refers to the Vātsīputrīyas.
They maintain that the acquisition of self-nature is immediately followed by destruction.
By the etymological method, the term "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) denotes that which, having acquired its own existence, perishes immediately thereafter;
or else, a moment is the limit of time,
being its own duration.
That which has this [moment] is "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*). Here, the suffix *ṭhan* is applied according to the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*.
This is because that which is conditioned necessarily undergoes cessation.
It has the nature of perishing immediately after arising,
like mind and mental factors;
for the destruction of entities is indeed spontaneous.
"Accidental" (*ākasmika*) means occurring without cause (*ahetuka*); this is the meaning. And the proof for this is:
destruction is without cause.
Because of its non-existence, like an absolute non-entity.
"It is indeed seen in the case of wood and so forth," and so on; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of form (*rūpa*) and other such factors is intended.
"It is observed that destruction occurs through contact with fire.
This demonstrates the flaw in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*), namely that it results in a contradiction with the nature of the property as established by perception.
