For this very reason, he says:
"And there is no means of valid cognition more weighty than what is seen" means that there is no means of valid cognition more authoritative than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The Teacher, demonstrating the others' misconception regarding direct perception, says:
"How, then, do you conceive it?
[The opponent asks. "For the destruction of wood and so forth is not perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa) in the same way as form (rūpa) and other qualities.
Those who maintain the non-momentary theory (akṣaṇikavādin) say this.
"Furthermore, because of their non-perception" means because of the non-perception of those things, such as wood and so forth.
Thus, he demonstrates the establishment [of the object] by means of inference.
The destruction of wood and other such things has conjunction with fire as its cause, because it occurs when that [fire] arrives;
for whenever something occurs upon the arrival of another, that [latter] is its cause.
That has that as its cause;
for example, a sprout is to be produced when a seed is sown.
This, however, must first be carefully considered.
It does not demonstrate necessity;
for it is not the case that whatever destruction occurs upon the arrival of something must have that thing as its cause.
For when there occurs a contact with the wind, the lamp is destroyed.
Yet that destruction is not caused by the contact with the wind;
for, since the momentariness [of all things] is admitted, the destruction of the lamp is held to be spontaneous.
For that lamp, having arisen and then perished, is itself destroyed by its own nature;
it is simply not seen because another [lamp] does not arise due to the obstruction of the wind,
not because of destruction by that [wind].
Likewise, the sound of a bell is held to be momentary.
When the contact with the hand occurs, there is the destruction of the bell's sound;
yet that [destruction] is not caused by it.
For, due to its momentariness, the sound of the bell perishes of its own accord. Because it obstructs another [sound], that other does not arise and thus is not perceived;
it is not by that [obstruction] that the destruction [of the first sound] occurs.
Therefore, this matter is to be established by inference;
the intention is that it is not established by direct perception.
Consequently, this [reason] is inconclusive.
Whatever destruction occurs upon its falling is caused by that [fall].
But what, then, is the inference here?
Regarding this point— namely, that destruction is causeless— what is the inference?
It has already been stated that because non-existence is not an effect,
destruction is causeless.
Because it is not an effect,
like space;
and this [self] is indeed not an effect.
Because its intrinsic nature is non-existence,
like an absolute non-entity;
nothing arises without a cause.
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is that nothing arises without a cause.
"Like arising" is a comparison by way of contrast.
Just as arising, which is characterized by the acquisition of self-nature, is necessarily with cause and not without cause,
so too would its destruction be.
But this is not the case.
How so? It is said:
the destruction of momentary cognitions, sounds, and flames is observed to be spontaneous.
Thus, there follows by means of inference a subversion of the true nature of things:
the destruction of wood and other such objects is accidental,
because destruction is their inherent nature.
"Like the destruction of cognition and so forth. As for the one who thinks thus— it refers to the Vaiśeṣikas—
who hold that a preceding cognition is destroyed by a succeeding cognition that has arisen.
But one cognition is destroyed by a preceding cognition;
the same should be said for sound as well.
He says:
This is not tenable.
Why?
Because two cognitions do not coexist simultaneously.
The meaning is "because they do not exist simultaneously.
For a cause does not destroy that which is to be destroyed if it is non-existent [at the time of destruction].
How is it known that there is no coexistence of two cognitions?
Therefore he says:
"For it is not possible for doubt and certain knowledge to coexist," and so forth.
This is to be personally realized (*svasaṃvedya*).
When there is cognition of doubt, there is no cognition of certainty;
when there is cognition of certainty, [there is no cognition of doubt].
"At that time, there is no cognition of doubt.
In this way, one should apply the principle to the non-coexistence of pleasure and pain, as well as attachment and aversion;
and just as there is no coexistence of two contradictory things.
Thus, there is also a non-coexistence of two cognitions even when they are not contradictory.
"And when," and so forth;
[this means] "even if there were a coexistence."
Nevertheless, the dull intellect and the dull word would not harm those that are sharp,
because they belong to the same class as the weak;
for it is never observed that one belonging to the same class as the weak harms one who is powerful.
But one who is dissimilar may cause harm even if he is weak,
just as water [extinguishes] fire.
This is because there is no cause for the flame to persist.
"The destruction of entities occurs because there is no cause for their continued existence"—
this reason was stated by the Elder Vasubandhu and others;
however, it is untenable.
"For non-existence cannot be a cause. [Objection:
"Or rather, it is by the power of merit and demerit," says the Vaiśeṣika.
To him, he replies:
Nor [is it the case] "of the causes of arising and destruction.
This refers to the non-dharma that is the cause of arising and destruction.
"In each very moment" means in every single moment.
"In the primary moment" means not in a figurative moment;
or alternatively, "the moment itself is the moment."
The meaning is "at every single moment.
The acquisition of activity and the obstruction of activity—that is, both the attainment of activity and the hindrance to activity—cannot occur at every single moment.
How so?

When, upon the arising of a flame, there is a benefit for someone such as Caitra or Maitra, the dharma of that [flame] has acquired its activity and produces it; thus it is a cause of arising (*utpādahetu*). It is also a cause of destruction (*vināśahetu*).
If its destruction benefits it during the state of darkness,
so too does unwholesome action (adharma),
for which there is harm upon the arising of its radiance.
Its non-dharma, having acquired its functional activity, produces that [destruction];
the cause of destruction also inflicts harm upon it during the state of darkness.
Thus, from the acquisition of their activity, the arising of the flames occurs.
And it is not the case that, without obstructing the acquisition of their activity, those very flames are destroyed by those same [two] at that very moment.
It is not logical for both the acquisition and the obstruction of activity to occur in every single moment for the two [the fuel and the flame].
"And this postulation of a cause is possible," and so forth.

The postulation of a cause—that there is a destruction of dharma and adharma—can be made in all cases: in all conditioned things such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), in impermanent things such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest, and in action (*karman*).
Therefore, this [objection] should not be stated.
"The destruction of wood and other things results from contact with fire," and so forth.

Consequently, the momentariness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is established, because merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) do not depend on any other cause for their destruction. Enough of this dispute.

"From that very same [cause] or from one similar to it. This means: if the contact with fire, having removed the blackness of the jar, produces redness, it is then postulated that the same [contact], having removed the redness, produces a deeper redness.
The cause itself would be the destroyer.
Or, if it is assumed that because flames are momentary, one [flame] is the producer of their conjunction and another is the destroyer,
then the destroyer would be no different from the cause.
And all this is not tenable.
Furthermore, even regarding other flames, the Vaiśeṣikas might still imagine a conceptual distinction despite the difference in causes,
because of their momentariness.
Some flames are producers and others are destroyers.
But when a specific transformation produced by heating arises due to contact with the earth and so forth, what kind of conceptual construction could they possibly imagine?
For their alkaline substances and so forth are not momentary;
in that case, the cause itself would be the destroyer.
As for the passage beginning with "water," the full explanation is as follows.
If water is not destroyed even when in contact with fire, then how is it that water being boiled diminishes? This is the intended question.
[The answer is: "It is the fire element (tejodhātu)."
It is the growth inseparable from that [fire],
by the power of which the mass of water becomes increasingly diminished;
thus, from a specific cause arises a specific effect.
It becomes increasingly attenuated until,
having reached a state of extreme attenuation, it finally no longer continues its series.
The meaning is that it performs its function, but does not bring about non-existence.
"Because of their fragility," and so forth.
Because they have the nature of breaking, they perish by themselves; their destruction is not produced by another.
Being existent, as soon as they have arisen—having obtained their self-nature for a single moment—they perish.
"Like a flame of grass":
just as, although a flame of grass is momentary, there is the misconception of motion when it arises uninterruptedly in different locations,
such that one says, "it burns the grass."
"Flames go"—
it is just like that;
and this is the proof.
Entities such as form and so forth arise continuously in another location without having a [prior] mode of going,
because they are momentary, like a flame of grass. [Tib.]
"Shape is bodily intimation"— this is the statement of the Vaibhāṣikas.
"Facing a single direction."
"Ekadiṅmukha" means that which has its face toward a single direction;
in that [direction].
"Bhūyasi" means in the more abundant or greater [portion].
Thus, all [is explained].
When there is more [space] toward the upper direction or a single direction, it is designated as "elevated. When there is more [space] below, it is designated as "depressed."
This is the general principle.
For example, as with a firebrand-circle:
shape does not exist as a substantial entity.
Because it involves the apprehension of color and because it involves the apprehension of shape,
it is like a firebrand wheel (*alātacakra*);
or else, shape is not a substantial entity (*dravya*).
"Because it would involve grasping a different form, and because it would involve grasping a part [of itself], like a heap of grain.
When this is said, the Vaibhāṣika would reply: "In that case, it would follow that there is a grasping of this [self] by means of two [aspects]."
Length and so forth are not apprehended by the body-faculty;
rather,
they are apprehended only in the constituent parts of the tangible.
When [atoms] are thus arranged, there occurs the perception of length and so forth.
Therefore, it does not follow that this [perception] is apprehended by two [senses]; hence this is said:
"Or, just as in the case of the tangible," and so on.

What is the meaning? It is as follows: just as there is the apprehension of length, shortness, and so forth in the tangible, yet shape is not included within the sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
In the same way, let the apprehension of length and so forth be understood as occurring with respect to color (varṇa) as well.
The meaning is that shape (saṃsthāna), being included within the sense-sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana), would not be a separate entity [from color].
Again, the Vaibhāṣika says:
"In that case, it is mere recollection," and so forth.
In that case, regarding the shape, it is merely recollection.
Because of its association with touch— that is, because it exists in concomitance with tactile qualities such as smoothness—
and not because of a direct perception of shape such as "long" and so forth;
just as, for example, upon seeing the color of fire, there arises a recollection of that fire's heat.
Because of association. For instance, having smelled the fragrance of both a flower and a *campaka* tree, there arises a recollection of its color as well,
due to association.
He said:
"It is appropriate here," and so forth.
It is appropriate here because, in the case of fire, there is no deviation between heat and color.
The recollection of one thing by means of another— such as heat by means of the form of fire,
or its color by means of the fragrance of a flower— but not of anything [else] whatsoever; such is the detailed explanation.

But no tangible quality, such as smoothness and so forth, is restricted to any particular shape, such as long and so forth; for in this case, upon touching a tangible object, there would necessarily be a recollection of the shape. For wherever there is the visible form of fire...
In that place, it must exist as heat;
and where there is the fragrance of the *campaka* flower,
there it must exist in that form.
However, it is not the case that wherever there is smoothness or roughness, there must also be length or shortness.
Therefore, while a necessary connection between those [qualities] and heat or color is logical, a necessary recollection of shape does not follow.
Even if there were such a necessary concomitance between the tangible and shape, the recollection of shape would still necessarily occur.
"The recollection of color would also occur necessarily"—this phrase continues [from the previous argument].
Thus, the meaning is that having touched a tangible object, one would necessarily recollect it.
Alternatively, if the recollection of color occurs without necessity, then, like color, the recollection of shape would also occur without necessity.
"In the long, the short;
in the short, the long.
For what reason?
For with respect to color, recollection occurs without fixed order from the tangible;
sometimes one perceives yellow when it is red, and red when it is yellow.
But such is not the case here.
How is it that this is not so? Just as recollection of color does not occur with necessity, so too recollection of shape does not occur with necessity.

What then? It is incorrect to say that while the recollection of color does not occur with necessity, the recollection of shape does occur with necessity; for this recollection of shape [arises] from the tangible.
How, then, does the cognition of "long" or the cognition of "short" arise?
This has already been explained:

when a greater number of colors or tangibles are perceived in a single direction, there arises a conceptual cognition of "long"; when they are fewer, there arises a conceptual cognition of "short. Such cases are to be understood in this manner.
"Or by means of a variegated [object]," and so forth.
Or, by means of a variegated object—consisting of many colors and shapes seen in various ways—many shapes such as long and so on are seen.
Therefore, from the perception of many shapes, it would follow that [the atom] occupies a single location for many shapes.
For wherever there is length,
there also the apprehension of shortness and so forth occurs;
and that is untenable, just as in the case of the phonemes themselves.
For just as color, because it possesses resistance (*sapratighatva*), does not occupy a single location, so too is shape (*saṃsthāna*).
And this being the case, the thesis that "shape exists substantially" becomes a position fraught with fault.
Because it would contradict the specific nature of the subject.
And that [color] does not exist in the atom.
For example, a color such as blue exists in an atom composed of eight substances and so forth.
And yet, such shape as long and so forth does not exist in an atom.
How, then, is it known that shape does not exist in an atom?
Because when a long shape is diminished, the cognition of "long" ceases to exist.
For if one perceives a long staff, the cognition of "long" would not cease even while that very staff is being diminished.
Indeed, once a substance such as blue has been perceived, the cognition of "yellow" does not arise when that substance is being diminished.
But when a long substance is being diminished, there arises the cognition of shortness, not the cognition of length; and it is not logical to say [that the cognition of length persists].
That very same configuration (saṃsthāna) produces the cognition of "long" and so forth, as well as "short" and so forth. Therefore, the entire [argument] that it exists only in many [atoms] follows.
Now, the detailed explanation begins with "If it is thought... and so on.

The intention is that it is precisely the atoms of shape (*saṃsthāna-paramāṇu*) arranged in such a manner—in the sequence of facing a single direction and so forth—that receive the designations "long" and so on. For things that do not have that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), even if arranged in the same way, are not capable of being perceived by that designation. Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of the parts of shape is not established in the same way as that of color (*varṇa*) and the like.
The components of color have well-established intrinsic natures,
because they are perceived as blue and so forth in each individual part;
however, shape-atoms are not perceived in this way as being long and so forth in each individual part.
Therefore, they do not have the nature of length and so forth as commonly established.
However, if it is the case that they do not possess the nature of length and so forth at all,
then they become the causes for the cognition of length and so forth due to a particular arrangement.
Why is it not accepted that atoms of color and so forth, when arranged in a particular configuration, are themselves the causes of the cognition of length and so on?
As for the objection that [the shape] would be non-different from the color itself:
this would be the case if shape were merely the arrangement of color.
If there were no difference in color, there would be no difference in shape, because clay vessels such as bowls and the like are not distinct entities from the clay itself.
[The opponent replies: "But was it not said," and so forth.

Just as the designation "long" and so forth is applied to a color (varṇa) arranged in a particular way; and just as there is the notion of "color" when it faces a single direction, and so forth in detail;
and just as in the case of ants and so forth, and so forth in detail.
And just as ants and the like are of a single form,
yet their row appears different in one location and different in another;
so too is the distinction between wheels and other such things, and so forth.
Likewise, even though there is no difference in color, there would be a difference in shape.
[Objection: "Then, in the dark," and so forth.
For in the dark, those who do not see color nevertheless perceive the length, shortness, circularity, and so on, of posts, persons, elephants, and the like.
"How so? is the completion of the sentence. If, then, shape were not a distinct category from color, they would not perceive it as they do when seeing a color such as blue or yellow.
Likewise, they would not perceive shape either as long or short;
yet they do perceive it at times.
Therefore, shape is a distinct category [of entity].
"Like the conceptualization of a row or an army":

just as, seeing birds or ants indistinctly in the dark, people conceptualize them as "a long row," or just as, seeing elephants and so forth indistinctly in the very same darkness, they conceptualize that "this army is stationed in a circular formation."
It is just like that.
And this is well known to be so:
as has been stated now, even in the absence of a distinct shape, people perceive only the color there indistinctly and form conceptual constructions such as "long" and so forth.
"Sometimes... and so forth in detail.

"With its delimitation not being determined" means that what is seen is merely a collection [of atoms] whose shape is not being determined—an indistinct mass in which blueness and other qualities are not being perceived.
And since there is no sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) apart from color and shape,
just as no other substance is postulated,
so too shape should not be postulated as something distinct from color.
In that context, "bhavantaḥ" means "those venerable ones," according to the rule stating that [the suffix *śas*] is seen after other [stems] as well.
"How do they designate bodily action?"—thinking that the application of bodily action exists because it is a conceptual construct (prajñaptisat), he asks: "What is its basis? namely, the body.
The meaning is that the body is the objective support (*ālambana*).
For that action which is to be performed by the body is the action based upon the body (*kāyādhiṣṭhāna*).
Therefore he said:
"That volition which leads the body here and there" is to be understood according to the circumstances.
Action that has speech as its basis is vocal action;
mental action, however, is the action of the mind,
or action associated with the mind is mental action.
Therefore, it was said, "according to the circumstances.
The detailed explanation is: "because of the absence of informative action (vijñapti). If informative action were not to exist...

Non-informative form (avijñapti) belonging to the desire realm would also not exist; for non-informative form of the desire realm is dependent upon informative form (vijñapti) and does not follow the mind.
And thus, it would not exist in this way.
Great faults follow as consequences.

These include the fault of the non-existence of restraint and non-restraint, the fault of the non-existence of the increase of merit from the seven bases of meritorious action consisting of material things, and so forth—these are the consequences.
Furthermore, there are counter-consequences to these consequences.
The meaning is that these will be its avoidances.
"From what is designated as bodily action" means from that which has the body as its basis.
"Like the non-informative [action] of one in meditative equipoise.
Just as the non-informative [action] of one in meditative equipoise follows the mind, so too would the non-informative [action] characterized by the Prātimokṣa vows and so forth follow the mind.
The Sautrāntikas say: "It will not be thus;
it will not be that which follows after the mind."

The meaning is that, due to a specific state of volition (*cetanā*) that is not in a state of meditative concentration (*asamāhita*), there is a specific projection of that [unmanifest action]; that is, because of the projection of the unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) which is itself not in a state of concentration.

Furthermore, even that manifest action (*vijñapti*) of yours, being present and existing, relies upon—meaning it depends on—the strength or efficacy of the volition that produces the projection of the unmanifest action.
Why?
Because it is insentient and lacking in acuity, it cannot produce that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) without the power of volition (*cetanā*).

Indeed, in the absence of the volition of formal undertaking (*samādāna-cetanā*), an informative action (*vijñapti*) that arises by chance does not produce non-informative action. However, vocal informative action...
Thus [it is said].
The word "but" (tu) serves as a qualification:
vocal intimation is not of the nature of shape in the same way that bodily intimation is.
What then? The meaning is that sound consists of speech (*vāg-ātmaka*) and word (*śabda*) consists of phonemes (*varṇa-ātmaka*).
(Abhidh-k-vy 352)
It has already been stated that non-informative [action] (avijñapti) was mentioned previously;
however, those two were described as informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti).
In that regard, informative [action] has been explained; non-informative [action] must now be explained.
And that has already been explained [in the context of the phrase]:
"of one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind."
Because of the statement:
"That too does not exist as a substance. That non-informative [action] (avijñapti) also does not exist as a substance;
the word "also" (api) indicates that it is not only informative action (vijñapti) that lacks substantial existence.
"Because it is merely the non-performance of what has been undertaken.

Having undertaken [the vow], thinking, "From this day forward, I shall abstain from taking life and so forth," there is, after that point, the mere non-performance of those acts; thus, the Sautrāntikas maintain that it does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
And regarding those past great elements (mahābhūta),
there is no present intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in past things;
this will be demonstrated in the fifth chapter of the Kośa.
How can those [elements] which do not exist be its basis? Therefore, it does not exist substantially. Furthermore, because of the absence of the characteristic of form (*rūpa*);
for "form" has the characteristic of being susceptible to transformation (*rūpyate*).
And because this [unmanifest form] is non-obstructive (*apratigha*), it does not exist;
therefore, it does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
(IV.5ab) It is of three kinds.
The full explanation is as follows:
that which is threefold and stainless is "threefold-stainless-form";
this is its designation.
"Akurvatpatha" means the path of one who does not act himself.
The meaning is: performing an action by having another do it while not doing it oneself.

These are those whose first members are the expression of the three kinds [of form], the expression of the stainless (amala) form, the expression of increase (vṛddhi), and the path of one who does not act.

These are the threefold [points]: the statement regarding the stainless form, the increase, and the non-performance of the path, etc. By the word "etc.," there is the non-mention of "formless" in the passage beginning with "Dharma, O monk."
The statement regarding the Noble Eightfold Path and the statement regarding the bridge of the Prātimokṣa restraint are both included.
This refers to the inclusion of form within form.
Form is subsumed by form alone,
and not by others such as feeling and so forth.
There exists form that is visible and resistant.
That form which is cognizable by visual consciousness is of two kinds:
there is that which is non-demonstrable and resistant,
such as the eye and the other [sense organs].
Furthermore, that consists of the nine bases of form (*rūpāyatana*).
There is form that is non-demonstrable and non-obstructive,
which is cognizable by mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), namely, non-informative form (*avijñaptirūpa*) included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
"Excluding non-informative [matter] (avijñapti)," and so forth.
Apart from non-informative matter, there is no form that is invisible and non-obstructive as stated in the *Rūpasaṃgraha-sūtra*.
Nor is there any untainted (anāsrava) form apart from non-informative matter; the phrase "excluding non-informative matter" continues to apply here.
For it is not logical that one who has attained the truth of the path (mārgasatya) should possess the form of bodily or vocal intimation (vijñapti-rūpa).
Regarding the phrase "by means of the seven material [meritorious actions]":
material basis (upadhi) refers to monasteries, parks, and so forth.
That which arises from material things is "with basis" (*aupadhika*);
because of the absence of such a basis, it is "without basis" (*niraupadhika*). "Constantly" means repeatedly.
"Continuously" means without interruption.
On this point, there is a sutra: The Blessed One was dwelling at Kauśāmbī.
In the Ghoṣira Monastery,
the Venerable Mahācunda approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the venerable Mahācunda said this to the Blessed One:
"Is it possible, Venerable Sir, to designate a basis for meritorious action consisting of material gifts that yields great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great renown?
"It is possible, Cunda," the Blessed One said to him.
Cunda, these seven bases of meritorious action consisting of material things have great fruit, up to being very extensive.
For a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family who is endowed with these, whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, merit constantly and continuously increases;
merit indeed arises.
What are the seven?
Here, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family dedicates a monastery to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions.
This, Cunda, is the first basis of meritorious action consisting of material things, which yields great fruit and is of great extent.

Endowed with which, for a son of good family— or, to speak more extensively, for anyone— merit indeed arises. Furthermore, Cunda, if a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family establishes a monastery in that very same grove,
this is the second basis of meritorious action consisting of material things, which has great fruit and from which merit indeed continues to arise.
Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family provides bedding and seating in that very monastery.
That is to say, they give a couch, a stool, a cushioned seat, a woolen rug, a pillow with an image, or a square bolster.
Cunda, this is the third basis for meritorious action consisting of material things, as before.
Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son or daughter of good family establishes a permanent provision of alms-food in that very monastery as a favorable offering.
Cunda, this is the fourth basis for meritorious action consisting of material things, which has great fruit, as before.
Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family gives a gift to a visitor or to one about to depart.
This, Cunda, is the fifth basis of meritorious action consisting of material things, as described before.
Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family gives a gift to one who is ill or to a caregiver for the sick.

This is the sixth basis of meritorious action consisting of material things, as before. Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son or daughter of good family, during those times that are cold, stormy, windy, or rainy, [provides for the Saṅgha of monks...]
During such occasions as the cold-season festivals up to the rainy-season festivals, he procures and offers to the Saṅgha meals, refreshments, or drinks of gruel, saying:
"May the Noble Ones, having consumed this while their limbs remain dry and their robes remain unsoaked by rain, dwell in comfort.
And this, Cunda, is the seventh basis of meritorious action consisting of material things that yields great fruit.
Merit continues to arise as long as one is engaged in these seven bases of meritorious action consisting of material things.

For a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family who is endowed with these seven bases of meritorious action consisting of material things, it is impossible to grasp the measure of their merit—
whether it be so much merit, or its fruit, or its maturation.
"However, because of the abundance of merit, it is reckoned as a 'great mass of merit' (*mahāpuṇyaskandha*)," and so forth.
For a second time, the venerable Mahācunda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, is it possible to designate a basis for meritorious action that is without material substratum (*niraupadhika*) as having great fruit, up to being very extensive?"
"It is possible, Cunda," the Blessed One said to him.
"Cunda, there are these seven bases of meritorious action that do not involve material substrata (*niraupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*).
For a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family who is endowed with these, whether walking or standing, and so forth in detail, merit indeed continues to arise."
Which seven?
Here, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family hears that the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata is dwelling in dependence upon a certain village or field.
Having heard this, he further attains a sublime, wholesome joy and gladness associated with renunciation.
Cunda, this is the first basis of meritorious action free from worldly attachment, as described before,
wherein merit continues to arise.
Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family hears that a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata is preparing to arrive.
And having heard it, he further attains it, as described before.
Cunda, this is the second basis for meritorious action that is free from worldly attachment.
Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family...
Or he hears that very Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata has set out on the road and has reached that very village or field. Having heard this, he attains [merit], as described before.
Cunda, this is the third basis of meritorious action that is disassociated from material substrates (*niraupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*).
...merit indeed continues to arise.
Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family hears that a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata has arrived at that very village or field.
Having heard this, he or she proceeds as before.
Cunda, this is the fourth basis of meritorious action free from worldly attachment, as described previously,
wherein merit continues to increase.
Furthermore, a faithful son or daughter of good family approaches that very Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata for the purpose of seeing him.
And having seen [them], he attains [realization] as before.
Cunda, this is the fifth basis of meritorious action that is independent of material substratum (*niraupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*).
Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family hears the Dharma from that very Tathāgata or from a disciple of the Tathāgata.
"And having heard it, he further attains it," as before.
Cunda, this is the sixth basis of meritorious action that is not connected with material substrata.
Furthermore, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family hears the Dharma from that very Tathāgata or from a disciple of the Tathāgata.
Having heard it, they go for refuge to the Buddha, go for refuge to the Dharma, and go for refuge to the Saṅgha;
and they undertake the precepts of training.
"Cunda, this is the seventh basis of meritorious action free from substrate (*niraupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*), which has great fruit," and so on as before.
Due to the fear of excessive length, not everything has been written down.
For the informative act of commanding (*ājñāpana-vijñapti*) does not constitute a path of action (*karmapatha*).
Because that action of killing and so forth has not been performed.
It might be thought:
"Once that action has been performed, the path of action will arise from the informative act (*vijñapti*) of commanding it."
Regarding this, it is said:
"And even when that [action] has been performed, because there is no difference in its intrinsic nature.
Even when that action has been performed by another, there is no difference whatsoever in the intrinsic nature of that informative intimation (*ājñāpanavijñapti*).
By which [factor] would there then be a path of action?
Therefore, it is as before:
because there is no difference in its intrinsic nature.

Just as the path of action (karmapatha) was not established previously, so too it is not established afterwards; therefore, one must admit that there exists that which arises at that time, comprised within the path of action.
Thus, it is said to be "not comprised within the eleven bases" (āyatana).

"Excluding the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana)" means that because speech, action, and livelihood cannot exist [there], since those whose intrinsic nature is informative intimation (vijñapti) are simply impossible [in that realm].
As for that which was stated [in the previous passage], "thus," and so forth:
what is the connection of this? Or rather, it may be thought: [what is the purpose of this statement?]
If non-informative action (avijñapti) did not exist, this eightfold path would not exist, because informative action (vijñapti) is impossible therein. Therefore, non-informative action exists.
Regarding that which was stated [in the sūtra], having been explained in detail up to the words "right concentration" (*samyaksamādhi*), for what purpose is it said thus?
And [the phrase] "and previously for him" refers to everything;
the meaning is "prior to the time of the attainment of the path."
The intention is that they are said to be of the nature of informative form (*vijñapti-rūpa*).
The Vaibhāṣikas offer this rebuttal:
"Liberation from passion through the worldly path," and so forth.

This was stated with reference to the state of detachment through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), wherein there exists informative matter (*vijñaptirūpa*) having speech and so forth as its intrinsic nature.
It does not mean, however, that at the time of the [supramundane] path, the non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*) of speech and so forth included therein does not exist.
"Form that is the object of meditative concentration" means the skeleton and so forth, which are the focal objects (*ālambana*) of meditative concentration.
It is "non-obstructive" (*apratigha*) because it does not obstruct space.
That form which obstructs space is characterized by resistance;
by contrast, it is established that what is otherwise is non-resistant.
"How then can that be matter?"— if the intention is that it cannot be manifested as matter,
this is equally true for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Alternatively, it is the same in that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) does not obstruct space.
Regarding the statement "it is untainted (*anāsrava*) in the untainted concentration":
when a practitioner of yoga brings the Path into manifestation, he acquires a corresponding intention (*āśaya*) and a basis (*āśraya*).
It is that which one acquires as untainted ethical discipline (*anāsrava-śīla*) concurrent with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
When this exists, one abides in the state of natural ethical discipline (*prakṛti-śīlatā*).
Alternatively:
Even in the untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative absorption (*samādhi*), those masters maintain that such a kind of form exists.
Others say: "The form of an Arhat and external form. Other masters describe it in this way.
The form of an Arhat, such as the sense-base of the eye and so forth,
as well as external things such as wood and walls—
that is untainted form (anāsrava-rūpa).
Why?
Because it is not a basis for the outflows (*āsrava*).
For neither the form belonging to the continuum of an Arhat nor external form is a basis for the outflows, which are the afflictions (*kleśa*).
If this is so, then as for what was stated without distinction in the Sūtra— "Which are the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena?
Namely, the eye, and so forth, up to visible forms," and so on—
this was called "contaminated" because it is not an antidote (*apratipakṣa*) to the outflows (*āsrava*).
"For it is specific states of mind and mental factors that are the antidotes to the outflows (*āsrava*). "In that case, by way of a distinction," and so forth.

That very same form of an Arhat, as well as external form, is "with outflows" because it is not an antidote to the outflows; it is "without outflows" because it does not serve as a basis for the outflows.
And thus there would be the fault of a confusion of definitions. "Those forms" means those form-āyatanas.
In detail, up to the statement: "Those phenomena which are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and subject to grasping (*sopādānīya*) are the basis for mental barrenness and hypocrisy.
[It is asked: "Are there form-bases (*rūpāyatana*) that are without-outflows (*anāsrava*)? Furthermore, which of those are with-outflows and subject to grasping?
The forms of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
Because they are the basis for the outflows (*āsrava*) and because they are not their antidote.
Which ones are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
Those forms which belong to an Arhat and those that are external [are not objects of clinging],
because they do not serve as a basis for the outflows (āsrava).
For such is the very nature of things (dharmatā).
It is the beginningless power of phenomena.
"Due to a specific quality" means due to a specific quality such as the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), the immeasurables (apramāṇa), and so forth.
"And because of the distinction in favoring [others]" means due to the excellence of the body’s complexion, strength, and so forth.
"Having that as its object," and so on, is the detailed explanation.
Its objective support (ālambana) is that which possesses a recipient. This is the volition of giving (dāna-cetanā) having that as its object.
Mental continuities (saṃtati), permeated by that volition, attain a subtle, specific transformation (pariṇāma-viśeṣa) which serves as the cause for the arising of the fruit.
"How will it be? means "How will it be for the production of a greater fruit?
For in this case, the gifts of the donors are not being consumed.

Because, through the enjoyment [of that gift], for the recipients there arises a specific excellence of qualities and a specific excellence of benefit; and thus, even for donors whose minds are directed elsewhere—as explained in detail—until they become capable [of further merit], or until merit continues to arise.
This is due to the cultivation of volition (*cetanā*) directed toward that object.
Through the repeated cultivation of volition directed toward the Tathāgata and his disciples,
the mental continuities undergo a subtle, specific transformation by which they become capable of producing a much greater fruit in the future.
[It has been stated that] for one who is walking, standing, or waking, [the mental action] is indeed [constantly present]; but how is it so for one who is sleeping? To this he says:
"Even in dreams, those volitions continue to persist.

However, for the Vaibhāṣika who maintains the doctrine of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), there is no informative action (*vijñapti*) in the case of the basisless bases of meritorious activity (*niraupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*).
Merely by hearing it, one attains a noble, wholesome joy and gladness.
In that case, how could there be non-informative action (*avijñapti*)?
For in the listener, both informative action (*vijñapti*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are impossible.
For non-informative action (avijñapti) arises either from informative action (vijñapti) or from meditative concentration (samādhi).
"Even in the case of those involving material objects" (aupadhika), and so forth;
that is, even in the case of gifts such as gardens and the like.
This is due to the repeated practice of volition (*cetanā*) that has that [recipient] as its object (*ālambana*).
"That recipient is the object of this volition" is to be understood as before.
He said:
If it is the case that even regarding material things (*aupadhika*), there is such [a result] through the repeated practice of volition directed toward them as its object,
then what about the Sūtra? [The passage begins with] "the immeasurable concentration of mind" (*apramāṇa-cetaḥsamādhi*) and so forth.
"Associated with loving-kindness and so forth;
it is a specific type of volition.
This shows that even for a donor whose volition has that [recipient] as its object, there is an immeasurable outflow of merit.
Regarding the phrase "at the completion of the fruit of the action":
the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*) is the "action" (*kriyā*);
the fundamental path of action itself is the "fruit" (*phala*); [the phrase refers to] at the completion of that.

"This is the same principle" means that through one's own action, because of the specific harm inflicted upon others, a subtle and specific transformation of the continuum arises in the agent; all of this is due to the metaphorical designation of the cause by the name of the effect.

The specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtatipariṇāmaviśeṣa*) constitutes the path of action (*karmapatha*); thus, the specific transformation of the continuum is the effect, and the path of action is the cause—
that which consists of the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of body and speech.
For that is the path of action characterized by volition (*cetanā*).
In this case, the term "path of action" (*karmapatha*) is applied to the effect [the bodily or vocal act] by metaphorically designating it with the name of its cause [the volition].
Its nature as being bodily or vocal—
But [it arises] from that specific transformation of the continuum (saṃtatipariṇāmaviśeṣa),
because it is the fruit of that action;
that is to say, because it is the fruit of bodily and vocal action.

Just as for the proponents of non-informative action (*avijñaptivādin*), there is "non-informative action" (*avijñapti*). For the Vaibhāṣikas, who are proponents of non-informative action, non-informative action is designated as a "path of action" (*karmapatha*) because the cause is metaphorically attributed to the effect.
"But its status as bodily or vocal is due to being the fruit of those actions.
Showing in another way that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is not a substantial entity (*adravya*), the Venerable One says:
"In the appropriated aggregates," and so forth.
When the aggregates (skandhas) reckoned as a sentient being are present, the killer is touched by the fault of taking life through volition (cetanā) pertaining to the three times.
How so regarding the three times? It is said:
when the thought occurs to him, "I shall kill," "I am killing," and "it has been killed."
Thus, it is stated here that volition alone is karma.
The Master, showing that the Venerable’s opinion is intended in one respect but not intended in another respect, says:
"But not merely this," and so forth.
If someone were to command thus:
"Kill my mother," and once the killer has set out, that person were to think:
"My mother was killed by him"—
for one who harbors such pride, there would be an immediate retributive act (*ānantarya-karman*).
And that is not accepted.
Therefore, the Venerable [Vasubandhu] must state the qualification "killing oneself.
He says that very thing:
"But for one who kills himself," and so forth.
"This much is the manifestation of volition:
'I shall kill,' 'I am killing,' and 'it has been killed'— this is what is appropriate."
"Only that which is appropriate is 'of an appropriate form' (yuktarūpa).
Here, the suffix -rūpa is used in its own primary sense,
as in the case of [the term] *nāmadheya*.
Some explain that "name" (*nāmadheya*) is just like "name" (*nāman*).
It is of a praiseworthy nature, or of a fitting nature;
or, it is "of fitting nature" because its own-being (*svabhāva*) is appropriate.
"In the same way, it is not clearly perceived": just as non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is difficult to comprehend,
so too is this specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtatipariṇāmaviśeṣa*).
"By means of bodily application following from the mind" means by means of a bodily application preceded by the mind.
"Distinct from those two" [means distinct from the mind and the body].
It is distinct from both mind and body.
Regarding the phrase "arisen from an application performed by someone": that by which it is performed is "performed by someone" (*yatkṛta*).
The completion of the action, which is the completion of the path of karma, arises from the application performed by that [agent].
There occurs for that very same agent— a transformation of the continuum (saṃtatipariṇāma) caused by that [action], namely, caused by that application, belonging to that very mind and mental factor.
"The completion of the sentence is: 'There is satisfaction for us.
And because the fruit arises in the future from the continuum of mind and mental factors, it is not the unmanifest [action]."
What is it? It continues: "Is there satisfaction? [This refers to] "because of the absence of informative intimation" (*vijñapti*), and so forth.
The meaning is that because of the absence of the originating phenomenon (samutthāpaka-dharma), there is an absence of the originated phenomenon (samutthāpya-dharma).

This establishes that non-informative matter (avijñapti) does not exist as a substantial entity (dravyataḥ). By the word "etc. (ādi), it is meant that [non-informative matter] is merely the non-performance [of an action] after having made a commitment.
Because it is designated in dependence upon past great elements;
since those [elements] do not exist,
let that very point suffice.
Regarding the phrase "included within the sphere of phenomena" (*dharmāyatanaparyāpanna*):

that which was stated to be the form of the object of concentration (*samādhiviṣayarūpa*) produced for meditators through the power of concentration—that is indeed invisible (*anidarśana*) and non-obstructive (*apratigha*).
Now, please explain this first.
It is recited as *aṅgāprātilomya*. "Come now, tell me," [is the meaning];
others say it means "come here, tell me."
"Therefore, regarding the sign," and so forth.
Since it is thus,
therefore, with respect to the unmanifest [action] which is the sign, there is the metaphorical designation of that which is characterized by the sign (the manifest action).
Because of the metaphorical application of "right" and so forth.
At that time, it is designated as "non-informative";
the meaning is that it is designated by the names right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
"And intention and basis":
intention refers to the intention not to commit killing and so forth,
or the intention of faith and so forth.
The basis is the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
Therefore, by applying the metaphorical designation of the effect to the cause— the intention and the basis—
one establishes the eight limbs of the path after having applied the metaphorical designations of right speech and so forth.
"That is merely non-action" means that it is merely the non-performance of false speech and so forth. To the question "What is that?", he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "That which is this," and so forth:
if a mere non-action were a factor (*aṅga*), how could it be untainted (*anāsrava*)? To this he replies:
"And that is untainted because it is obtained by relying upon the untainted path."
If a mere non-action were a limb, it would likewise not be substantially existent (*adravyasat*). To the question of how there can then be eight limbs, he says:
"For it is not in all cases," and so forth.
"Preceded by a formal rite" means preceded by the formal rite for undertaking the precepts (*śīla*).
If it is argued that one would not be restrained when possessing a different state of mind:
if that volition (*cetanā*) constitutes restraint,
then when one possesses a mind other than that volitional mind, one would not be restrained.
Just as the volition that restrains body and speech does not exist at that very moment [of restraint], so it is not by means of its cultivation; such is the detailed argument. This is not so.

Through the cultivation of that—that is, through the cultivation of the mental continuum—at the time of action, when a thought of taking life or the like has arisen, one remembers: "I have abstained from taking life and so forth. For one whose mindfulness is thus present, by means of that volition which restrains body and speech because of that presence of mindfulness, [abstinence occurs] due to the manifestation of that volition.
The undertaking of that [vow] is for this very purpose.
How so?
By recollecting this promise not to act, one would not commit immoral conduct.
It is so that no one with impaired mindfulness might break the training.
That non-informative action (*avijñapti*), which acts as a dam to obstruct misconduct,
exists at that time.
(IV.5cd) “For it is not that same collection,” and so forth.

It is not the very same collection of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as the earth element and so on—which serve as the basis for informative action—that has a subtle fruit, because its fruit is non-informative action which is invisible and non-obstructive; nor does it have a coarse fruit, because its fruit is informative action which is visible and obstructive.
Therefore, non-informative action arises depending upon entirely different great elements.

(IV.6ab) "The informative act belonging to that time," and so forth. An informative act that exists at a particular time is an "informative act belonging to that time. Likewise, the great elements belonging to that time are [the basis] of that [informative act].
Does non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arise depending on those very same great elements (*mahābhūta*) that arose at the same time as the informative matter (*vijñapti*)?
The answer is: all of it.

All derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)—whether informative or non-informative, whether comprised within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) or the untainted (*anāsrava*), or such things as the eye, the ear, visible form, sound, and so forth—exists by depending on great elements that are strictly simultaneous with it.
The inclusion of the word "mostly" (prāyeṇa) is for the purpose of excluding certain non-informative (avijñapti) actions belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara).
For this very reason, it is said:
"certain [actions] are present or future, having derived from past great elements (mahābhūta)."
Some derived matter exists depending upon past primary elements;
some future derived matter exists depending upon past primary elements.
To demonstrate what kind of derived matter is such as this, he says:
After the first moment, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) belonging to the desire realm arises having the past primary elements as its basis.
At the time of undertaking the restraints (*saṃvara*) and so forth of the desire realm, the non-informative matter arises depending upon the co-nascent great elements (*mahābhūta*).
In the same way, other non-informative matter also arises depending upon those very same [elements].
Because those past great elements exist for it in the sense of being its basis (*āśraya*).
Just as the present great elements are the basis for other derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*), so too are the past ones the basis for this [non-informative matter].
This is because they are, respectively, the causes for its initial arising and its subsequent continuation.
Past great elements serve as the basis in the sense of being the cause of impulsion and the cause of projection;
present great elements of the body serve as the basis in the sense of being the cause of conformity and the cause of support.
"Like a wheel," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Just as the hand's impulse is the cause of the wheel's movement, so is [the storehouse consciousness] the cause of its own activity;
just as the ground is [the support].
Thus is the cause of continuous occurrence. (IV.6cd) Having explained the restriction of time, he asks about the restriction of the stages:
"Now, from where do they arise? and so forth.

"Up to the level of the fourth dhyāna" is said because, in the formless realms (ārūpya), there is an absence of primary elements (bhūta) and derived matter (bhautika). This is because [the formless realms] do not fall within the [material] realms (dhātu).
Because untainted (*anāsrava*) bodily and vocal action is not bound to any realm (*dhātu*).
The intended meaning is that there is no such rule [that it must arise from them].
If so, why does it not arise based on untainted great elements (*mahābhūta*)? To this he says:
"And because there is an absence of untainted (*anāsrava*) great elements (*mahābhūta*).
But what function do the great elements have for this [unmanifest action]? To this he says:
"And because it arises through their power."
The meaning is that [it arises] by the power of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Now, why does its arising not occur through the power of the mind alone?
Because it would follow that it is not derived matter (*anupādāyarūpa*).
(IV.7, 8) Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is non-appropriated (*anaupāttika*), because, being formless (*amūrta*), it cannot serve as a basis for the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*).
And it is also outflowing (*naiṣyandikī*).

Because it is either wholesome or unwholesome, there is no indeterminate non-informative [action], according to the statement: "Non-informative [action] is not born of maturation, nor is it indeterminate."
And because that which is born of maturation (vipākaja) is neutral (avyākṛta), according to the statement: "Maturation is a neutral phenomenon."
It is not accumulative because there is an absence of accumulation;
by process of elimination, it is outflowing.
It is designated as "sentient being."
Because it falls within the continuum of sentient beings. "Born from primary elements that are outflowing and appropriated" means born from great elements that are both outflowing and appropriated.
Because it depends on the motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*) and because it pertains to informative action (*vijñapti*) of an unconcentrated mind (*asamāhita-citta*),
it is not produced from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are accumulative (*aupacayika*) as in dreams or meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
For this very reason, it is also not produced from the great elements that are born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
"Born of concentration," and so forth;
because it is born of both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) concentration.
The non-informative (avijñapti) restraint born of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and the untainted (anāsrava) is called "born of concentration" (samādhija).
It is also said to be "derived from the great elements that are not appropriated" (anupātta-mahābhūtopādāya),
because by the power of the concentrated mind, it conforms to the mind within that body.
For the appropriated great elements continue to exist even in states such as the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), despite the absence of mind.
"Up to frivolous speech" means:
by the word "up to," [it includes] taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
Because the elements are non-different from the mind;
just as the mind that produces them is non-different,
so too the elements that produce it are likewise non-different.
Furthermore, the great elements are not the support of non-informative matter in the sense of being its substratum;
rather,
they are so in the sense of causing it to proceed.
Therefore,
the statement that the stages are non-different is not contradicted.
In the case of the Prātimokṣa restraint, however, they are distinct from one another because it does not follow the mind; the informative [action],
on the other hand, is outflowing.
Because it continues by the force of projection (*ākṣepa*).
"But that which is appropriated is bodily" means that it is not vocal.
For the bodily [action] is appropriated because it exists inseparably from the primary elements that constitute the body, which serve as its basis; but the vocal [action] is not,
because it exists separately from them.
Regarding this, they raise an objection:
"This contradicts the treatise;
for it says as follows:"
Regarding these five precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*),
how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated (*anupātta*)?
He said: "All are unappropriated.

There is no fault in this, because that description was given either with the intention of referring to the training rules characterized by non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), or because such a designation is used for the most part.
"Because it occurs again in succession, this is not the Vaibhāṣika position," because when one shape arises, the other shape does not cease.
How, in detail, is it established that there can be up to two shapes?

Because they provide mutual space for one another. "Because it is pervaded by the primary elements" means that the limb is pervaded by the primary elements which serve as the basis for informative action (*vijñapti*).
Furthermore, if there were no pervasion by the great elements of informative action (*vijñapti*), how could one communicate through an entire limb?
For it cannot be said that such a person communicates by means of only a single part of the body.
"Not with the entire body" means that the great elements which serve as the basis for informative action do not remain pervading that limb;
because the body is porous, there is space for them.
Even when it has pervaded [the body], that limb should not become larger,
because it enters the body through its porosity.
In that case, that limb should not become swollen or heavy.
Because of its subtlety.
(IV.9, 10ab) It is said to be twofold, threefold, and fivefold;
that is volition and what is produced by it.
Because of this statement,
it is said to be twofold: volition is mental action, and from that [volition] arise vocal and bodily actions.
Because of this statement,
it is said to be threefold;
those, however, are informative and non-informative [action].
Thus [it is said].
Because bodily and vocal action are distinguished as being both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*),
and because mental action— which is of the nature of volition (*cetanā*)— is fivefold, it is said to be of five types.
There is no neutral non-informative [action].
It follows by implication that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is exclusively wholesome or unwholesome. "Powerful karma" refers to that which has the characteristic of non-informative action.
"In the realm of desire as well.
By the word "as well" (*api*), which has the sense of "also" (*iti ca*), the term "in the realm of desire" (*kāma*) is drawn forward.
[The phrase] "like the untainted non-informative [matter]" (*anāsravāvijñaptivat*) means: just as there is untainted non-informative matter.
Just as, for instance, there are no untainted (*anāsrava*) great elements (*mahābhūta*) for untainted non-informative matter (*avijñapti*),
yet it arises in dependence upon the great elements belonging to that very level in which one is born when one produces it.
Thus, for the time being, there would be no great elements belonging to the formless realms.
However, when one born in a certain realm produces a formless [attainment],
there will be non-informative matter belonging to the formless realm, derived from the great elements belonging to that same realm.
No,
because it does not fall within the realms (dhātu);
for here there is no similarity.

Because non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that is untainted (*anāsrava*) does not fall within the realms—namely, it belongs neither to the desire, form, nor formless realms—and because it is not appropriated by cravings, its great elements (*mahābhūta*) are neither similar nor dissimilar to those [elements] according to realm or stage. Therefore, the great elements from which it arises are those born in that same place;
however, non-informative matter belonging to the formless realm cannot arise by depending upon great elements belonging to the desire or form realms that are dissimilar to it.
The intended meaning is that [the formless realm] falls within the sphere of the elements (*dhātu*).
Furthermore,
because it is turned away from all form, the formless attainment is not capable of producing form.

However, the untainted meditative attainment belonging to the level of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is sufficient for the arising of form; that is to say, for the arising of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Why?
The intention is that it is because it is turned away from all form.
And how is there a turning away from all form (*rūpa*) in the attainment of the formless (*ārūpya-samāpatti*)? To this he says:
"Because the perception of form has been transcended" (*vibhūta-rūpa-saṃjñatvāt*).
This means: because the perception of form has departed (*vigata-rūpa-saṃjñatvāt*).
"Morality is the antidote to immorality," and so forth.
Immorality belongs to the desire realm because it originates from unwholesome states.
It is logical that morality belonging to the level of the form realm, characterized as non-informative (avijñapti), serves as its antidote.
If it is argued that the same will apply to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara), he says:
"And the formless realms [are distant] from the desire realm," and so forth.
The formless realms are distant from the desire realm by way of the four kinds of distance.
Furthermore, because of its distance, morality included within the formless realm (ārūpya) is not suitable as an antidote to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The four kinds of distance have already been explained previously, so they will not be explained again here.
In this context, the "distance of being an antidote" (pratipakṣadūratā) serves as the illustration.
"Representation exists in the two levels with discursive thought.
This statement is made for the purpose of restriction, meaning that it exists only in those two levels that possess discursive thought.
"One speaks after having applied thought and sustained thought" indicates that bodily and vocal actions are preceded by applied and sustained thought;
it shows that even in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there is no obscured-unwholesome [action],
not only in the stages devoid of sustained thought.
It is thus stated that [the formless realm] exists only in the Brahma-world.
"Above that" means above the Brahma-world.

"Caused by external great elements" refers to the sense-sphere of sound belonging to wind and so forth. This statement is intended primarily to exclude the sound of informative intimation (*vijñapti-śabda*).
But it is not caused solely by external primary elements (mahābhūta).
For even the sound of limbs such as the hand occurs in the second and higher meditative absorptions (dhyāna);
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the treatise (śāstra).
For it is stated in the treatise:
"Who is endowed with the sound-element (śabdadhātu)?
It replies:
One belonging to the realms of desire or form.
Who is not possessed [of these]?
He says:
Regarding the phrase "belonging to the formless realm":
it is not logical for one to be possessed of external things categorized as non-sentient.
Possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession (*aprāpti*) pertain only to those factors included within one's own continuum (*svasaṃtāna*).
Because of this statement,
and for the sake of avoiding this very fault, others say:
"There is informative intimation (*vijñapti*) even in the second and subsequent meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)."
To which stage does it belong?
It belongs to the stage of the first dhyāna.
This is precisely the position of the Vaibhāṣikas.
There is no other alternative.

The consciousnesses of the body, eye, and ear, as well as that which originates informative action, are at that time pervaded [by the mind] when they occur in the second dhyāna and above; furthermore, they are undefiled-neutral.
This is because of the established tenet (*siddhānta*).
If that is so, then there is another position according to which it belongs to the levels of the second dhyāna and above.
To this, he asks: "Is that [attainment] defined (*vyākṛta*) or undefined (*avyākṛta*)?"
It is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*),
but neither wholesome nor afflicted.
For those residing there who engage in mutual conversation and so forth, there arises an unobscured-neutral informative action (*vijñapti*).
For what reason are they neither wholesome nor afflicted? It is said:
"For one who has been reborn in those [higher realms]," and so forth.
For one reborn in the second or higher dhyānas does not bring into manifestation a mind of such a kind—that is, a mind belonging to a lower stage that is either wholesome or afflicted.
It is by means of that mind that one would produce a wholesome or afflicted informative act (*vijñapti*).
As for the reason why, he says:
"Because it is inferior and because it has been abandoned."
One does not bring forth wholesome states belonging to a lower stage because they are inferior;
nor does one bring forth defiled states because they have been abandoned.
By implication, this is what is meant.
One brings to manifestation an indeterminate mind belonging to a lower level;
by means of that, one originates it.
This is what is meant.
"A manifestation belonging to a higher level is produced by a mind belonging to a lower level.
The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this;
for that manifestation belongs specifically to the first dhyāna, because it is originated by a mind belonging to the level of the first dhyāna.
Therefore he says:
"But they explain it as being only prior," and "and that [occurs] in the desire realm."
Furthermore, that obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) mind which is to be abandoned by cultivation does not exist in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
For it is held that in the desire realm, the obscured-unspecified mind is associated only with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of grasping at extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi);
and by such [a mind], informative action (vijñapti) is not produced.
Because it functions inwardly.
(IV.10cd, 11) "By its very nature" means by way of the self. "Because of its supreme security."
Because there is no connection with even a trace of insecurity (*akṣema*).
For that which is wholesome by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*saṃprayoga*), or origination (*samutthāna*) is not said to be "supremely secure" (*paramakṣema*),
because those that are dissociated lack the quality of being wholesome.

Because mental factors (caitta) and so forth that are not associated with the roots of virtue and the like lack the quality of being wholesome, the wholesomeness of those [factors] is established through their association with them.
By the word "and the like" in the phrase "associated with those very roots of virtue and the like," shame (hrī) and dread of blame (apatrāpya) are included.
"Like milk produced from medicinal water": the milk of a cow that has drunk medicinal water is what is produced from medicinal water.
"But as for acquisitions (prāpti)," and so forth. This refers to the acquisitions of wholesome [dharmas] that have been produced by a dissimilar mind (*visabhāgacitta*).
A dissimilar mind is one other than the wholesome [mind].
Regarding the reconnection of the roots of goodness through doubt, those acquisitions (*prāpti*) of wholesome states possess wholesomeness;
however, this is not due to their being ultimate security (*paramārthakṣema*), as is the case with *parinirvāṇa*.

Nor is it virtuous by way of its intrinsic nature, like non-attachment and so forth, because it does not have that as its intrinsic nature; nor is it virtuous by way of association, like feeling and so forth, because it is dissociated;
nor is it virtuous by way of origination, because the mind that originates it is afflicted.
Likewise, in the case of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), the acquisitions of innate wholesome states (*upapattipratilaṃbhikakuśalaprāpti*) must also be discussed.
It remains to be explained how these are wholesome;
the intention is that an effort must be made here [to clarify this].
To this they offer the following rebuttal:
because they are to be originated by wholesome roots, those [wholesome factors] become wholesome already in their future state.
By means of a defiled mind, the obstruction to their acquisition (*prāpti*) is removed.
"It does not attain the state of being wholesome" means:
"by virtue of having the nature of the occurrence of all suffering.
That which has the occurrence of all suffering as its essence—that is, its intrinsic nature—is "that which has the nature of the occurrence of all suffering" (*sarvaduḥkhapravṛttyātmaka*).
By virtue of that state,
in the ultimate sense, saṃsāra is not secure;
it consists of the acquisition of bodily and vocal actions, birth, and so forth.

Bodily and vocal actions have the nature of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*), and are comprised within non-restraint, neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint, and restraint.
Birth and the other [characteristics] have as their nature the characteristics of birth, aging, duration, and impermanence, as well as the non-characteristics.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) pertain to unwholesome [phenomena].
They are to be compared with disease, unwholesome food, medicine, and so forth.
Saṃsāra is to be compared with disease;
the meaning is that saṃsāra is a disease.
Greed and the other [afflictions] are comparable to unwholesome medicine,
because they depend upon association with others for their arising;
those associated with them are comparable to water mixed with unwholesome medicine.
The bodily and vocal actions, the [four] characteristics such as birth, and the acquisitions (prāpti) are comparable to milk produced from drinking unwholesome medicine.
"If that is so," and so forth; if, in the ultimate sense, saṃsāra is unwholesome.
Nothing that is with-outflow (*sāsrava*) will be either indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) or wholesome (*kuśala*), because that which is with-outflow is within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
This was stated from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); thus it is accepted that everything included within *saṃsāra* is unwholesome.
"But with respect to its maturation," and so forth:
that which is not defined with respect to its maturation [is said to be] "this has maturation."
That is called "indeterminate. This is what is meant: that which is with-outflows (sāsrava).
That is unwholesome because it is the ultimate lack of security.
It is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) in the sense that it cannot be defined with respect to its maturation (vipāka).
The same applies to the wholesome as well.
The same applies to the unwholesome.
It should be understood that the wholesome is so called because its maturation is desirable.
"If by virtue of being fully disclosed," and so forth.

With the intention that "only volition (cetanā) possesses the quality of being wholesome or unwholesome," he examines whether bodily and vocal action possess the quality of being wholesome or unwholesome,
[asking]: "Why not the primary elements (mahābhūta)?"
Regarding the state of being wholesome or unwholesome:
for it is by a wholesome or unwholesome mind that bodily and vocal karma, as well as its great elements, are originated.
The Vaibhāṣika says:
For the agent's intention regarding an action is directed toward the action itself, not toward the primary elements, as in "I shall create the primary elements.
What then?
It is "I shall perform this action."
"The great elements do not possess the quality of being wholesome or unwholesome in the same way that karma does. To this, the Master says:
"In the case of the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) of one who is in meditative concentration (*samāhita*), there is no volitional intention (*abhiprāya*)."
"I shall perform an unmanifest [action].
Yet, there is no unconcentrated mind that can originate it,
such that one would form such an intention.
Because they are of a different kind, because they are dissimilar, or because they are not concentrated with respect to the level (*bhūmi*).
How can that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) which is concentrated be wholesome?
The intention is that its wholesomeness would not exist in the same way as that of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Or else, it would follow that even the divine eye and ear would be wholesome.
This is if [you argue] that an unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) is wholesome even without that intention.
Alternatively, this is the connection [of the argument]: [the text says: "Or else..."
If its wholesomeness were due to the power of a dissimilar mind that is not in a state of meditative concentration (*asamāhita*),
then it would follow that the divine eye and ear are also wholesome,
because at the time of their preparatory application (*prayoga*), there can exist the intention for them.
And there is no wholesome [state] in those two, because of the statement: "The supernormal powers of the ear and the eye are indeterminate."

(IV.12–14) Regarding what was stated—that the mind to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) does not give rise to informative action (*vijñapti*)—for those who say this is because the mind to be abandoned by seeing functions inwardly (*antarmukha-pravṛtta*), how is this not in contradiction with what was said by the Blessed One?
This is the meaning of the sentence: "That was said by the Blessed One."
What is that? It is said:
"From that false view," and so forth.

How is it stated that from false view—which is to be abandoned by seeing—false speech, which has the nature of informative intimation (vijñapti), and false action, which likewise has that same nature, arise?
Regarding the phrase "designated as causal and momentary arising":
causal arising (*hetutthāna*) and momentary arising (*tatkṣaṇotthāna*) together constitute "causal and momentary arising" (*hetutatkṣaṇotthāna*).
That which is designated as "arising from the cause and that moment" is called "designated as arising from the cause and that moment. It is so designated.
Thus it is designated.
Alternatively, its designation is "the cause and the arising at that moment," hence it is "designated as the cause and the arising at that moment.
It is made into a designation of the cause and the arising at that moment.
It is designated as "arising from the cause" and "arising at that moment.
Regarding the term *hetu-samutthāna* (arising from the cause): it is called *samutthāna* because one arises by means of it (*anena*).
That which is both the cause and the origination is "causal origination.
Regarding "origination in that moment":
that moment is the moment of action.
Arising at that very moment is "simultaneous arising" (*tatkṣaṇasamutthāna*).
This is because its existence as an arising occurs at that very same moment;
the meaning is that it exists at that very moment of action.
"Because it is an impeller" means because it is a producer.
"What then? and so forth [is the full statement]. It refers to the capacity of that momentary origination (tatkṣaṇasamutthāna) for that action of informative intimation (vijñapanakriyā).
By which it is said that it conforms at that time.
"For by that," and so forth, means:

for without that momentary origination (*tatkṣaṇasamutthāna*), this intimation (*vijñapti*) would not exist—just as in the case of one who is dead—even though it has been projected and produced by the causal origination (*hetusamutthāna*).

For example, suppose someone were to die while having projected the intention, "I shall go to a village. Because he lacks a subsequent motivating mind (*anuvartaka-citta*), the act of going does not take place.
It is just like that.
"In that case, for one who is without mind," and so forth.
If it were not present due to the momentary origination [of the action], then it would be as if the person were dead.
