For someone who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and is being ordained, while performing a bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), since the absorption of cessation is present at that time, he is without mind (*acittaka*).
How, then, can there be a bodily intimation included within that restraint (*saṃvara*) at the moment the formal ritual pronouncement (*karmavācanā*) concludes?
What does it mean for it to arise without the "simultaneous origination" (*tatkṣaṇasamutthāna*) [of a mental state]? This is the sense of the question.
When this contradiction is raised, another solution is resorted to:
"In that case, it is even more manifest.
This is its efficacy: through the arising at that very moment, the informative act (*vijñapti*) of one who possesses mind becomes more distinct.
"That which incites is to be abandoned by insight" means that it is restricted to the understanding that only that which incites is to be abandoned by insight.
But how is it that [the mind] is the initiator? He says:
because it serves as the primary cause, that is, the causal basis, for the applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) which give rise to it;
thus, it is the initiator of informative action (*vijñapti*).
"But it is not the conforming [mind]," and so forth.
That which is the outward-directed mind is the conforming [mind]; its time is the moment of the activity of informative intimation (*vijñapti*).
Because that [subsequent mind] is absent in that [moment].
The meaning is: because of the absence of that initiating [mind] which is to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*). Therefore, that [subsequent mind] is not a follower (*anuvartaka*).
And this is another fault:
"and the form produced by that," and so forth.
If that were something to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), it would follow accordingly.

The proponent asks: "What would follow if bodily and vocal intimation-form (vijñapti-rūpa) originated by that which is to be abandoned by seeing were itself to be abandoned by seeing? It would be like bodily and vocal action originated by a mind to be abandoned by cultivation being itself to be abandoned by cultivation. This is the objection raised by the challenger.
The Vaibhāṣika maintains that the Abhidharma would be contradicted,
because of the statement: "That which is non-afflicted is not to be abandoned by insight, nor is form."
Furthermore, because there is no contradiction between knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

This means that, like the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, that form is not contradicted by knowledge— that is, by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)— and thus is not abandoned.
Since even those who have seen the truths are still possessed of it, there is no form (rūpa) to be abandoned by seeing.
Furthermore, because it is not in contradiction with ignorance (avidyā),
and moreover, form is not in contradiction with ignorance either.

For it is not the case that ignorance does not exist when there is the state of the manifestation of defiled or undefiled form, nor in the continuity of its acquisition; nor is it the case that such form does not exist when ignorance is present.
This is because the untainted path contradicts ignorance, as [the untainted path] does not arise during the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Because upon its arising, in the state of the stream, certain forms of ignorance are abandoned.
Thus, it is not the case that [this ignorance] is like the untainted (anāsrava) in being something not to be abandoned.
And if it is not something not to be abandoned, [it must be abandoned].
Nor is it to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is established that it is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The other says:

This position— that form is not incompatible with knowledge— is yet to be proven. For how can one who maintains that form is to be abandoned by vision accept that there is no incompatibility between form and knowledge?
The Vaibhāṣika says: "Even the primary elements (*bhūta*), etc. in detail.
If that matter (*rūpa*) were originated by a mind to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*), it would itself be [to be] abandoned by seeing.
In that case, even those [factors] that serve as its basis would have to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Why?
Because they are produced by the same mind.
For that very mind by which that form was originated— being abandonable by insight—
it would follow that its constituent elements (*bhūta*) are also [abandonable by insight] by that same [mind].
And yet, it is not possible for them to be so.
Because it is undefiled-neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*),
and because those [factors] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*) are defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
The other says:
It will not be so;
that they would be abandonable by vision.
If one asks how, he says:
Just as [the elements] do not themselves become wholesome or unwholesome;
and just as by whichever wholesome or unwholesome mind a wholesome or unwholesome form is originated, by that very same [mind] its constituent elements (bhūtas) are also originated.
And that matter (rūpa), which has the nature of bodily and vocal action, is wholesome or unwholesome; it is not so with its underlying primary elements (bhūta).
It is just like that.
He then spoke again by way of reversal:
"Or rather, let them be abandoned by vision.
The Vaibhāṣika said:
It cannot be so.
The ellipsis of the sentence is "to be abandoned by vision.
Why?
Because an unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*) phenomenon is not in contradiction with either knowledge (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*).

For an unafflicted phenomenon— namely, the non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the contaminated wholesome (*kuśala-sāsrava*)— is not contradicted by knowledge, which is the uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*),
in the same way that afflicted phenomena are contradicted through the severance of their acquisition (*prāpti*).
However, because the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions that have that [unconditioned] as their object is severed, its contradiction is not denied.
Nor is it contradicted by ignorance,
because [ignorance] is to be abandoned through the severance of acquisition and through the abandonment of the afflictions that take it as their object.
And the elements are unafflicted.
In that regard, what was said— that "or rather, let them be"—
is incorrect.
Thus, the proof here is formulated as follows:
The great elements that serve as the basis for afflicted matter are not to be abandoned by vision,
because they are non-afflicted.
"Just like non-afflicted mental states and mental factors.
Thus, in this way, the Vaibhāṣika maintains that the consciousness to be abandoned by vision is the instigator.
Having thus established the refutation of the objection, he concludes:
"Therefore, [it is] the origination from causes," and so forth.
This refers to what was stated: that from wrong view comes wrong intention, up to wrong action.
Thus, there is no contradiction with that sūtra.
[It says] "both the initiator and the follower," because they function by being directed either inwardly or outwardly.
The restriction that "the group of five, however, is a follower" is due to its being non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*).
Neither is the untainted (*anāsrava*).
It is neither an initiator nor a follower,
because it proceeds inwardly while in a state of meditative concentration.
"Amlāyamānā" means not declining;
this word ends in the suffix *cānaṭ*.
"Whose every tendency is wholesome" means that their mental continuum is exclusively wholesome.
In the Sūtra, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is called a "Nāga."
How so?
Having spoken at length, saying, "O Udāyin, the Tathāgata in this world with its gods and its Māras... and so forth, he said: "He commits no offense by way of body, speech, or mind;
therefore, he is called 'An-āga' (One Without Offense)."
"He does not commit an offense" means he does not commit a transgression.
"By his lack of desire" means that because the mind of this Buddha does not wander—due to its lack of desire—it does not go toward sense objects; for this reason it was said thus.
"Moving about, the Naga is concentrated," and so forth.

While moving among the four modes of conduct, thinking "I am moving," and so on, up to while sitting, thinking "I am sitting"— because his mindfulness is established in this way, he is said to be constantly concentrated (*nityasamāhita*). This is because [his state] proceeds without volitional effort (*nirabhisaṃskāra*).
For the absence of conditioning—that is, of effort—is "without conditioning" (*nirabhisaṃskāra*).
That which carries [the body] without conditioning is "carrying without conditioning" (*nirabhisaṃskāravāhī*). Its state is "the state of carrying without conditioning."
"Therefore" means:
it is not the case that everything to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) is an instigator (*pravartaka*).
This might indeed be so.
If it were intended that everything to be abandoned by seeing (darśana-prahātavya) is a motivator (pravartaka), it would not be the case that everything is so. What then?
Since it is only wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth that motivates informative action (*vijñapti*), and not the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, he says:
"Or rather, one must state a qualification that 'not all' [motivates], such that this kind is a motivator and that kind is not.
This refers to a mind that is unwholesome (*akuśala*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*).
For one who is being ordained, if by some connection their mind is unwholesome or neutral,
the informative act (*vijñapti*) of the Prātimokṣa restraint— such as joining the palms and so forth— would not be wholesome.
This is because the mind that follows it is considered to be unwholesome or neutral.
"As it is the instigator," and so forth.
Just as the mind that acts as the instigator is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*),
so too is the informative action (*vijñapti*) established.
But it is not established as being a motivator in the same way that what is to be abandoned by seeing is;
why?
Because it is intervened upon by that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.
Because that which initiates it—the [view] to be abandoned by seeing—is separated from the initiating [mind] to be abandoned by cultivation.
How so?

For example, having first resolved, "I must make others understand that 'the self exists'," one then [acts] with a mind that produces speech, which is outwardly directed and to be abandoned by cultivation.
With vitarka and vicāra, one utters speech such as "the self exists," and so forth.
Therefore, it is as explained in detail: "according to that which sets [the mind] in motion."

Thus, immediately after a motivating [mind] that is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*), there necessarily arises a motivating [mind] that is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*), whether it be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
And it is by virtue of that [subsequent mind] that the informative action (*vijñapti*) possesses the quality of being wholesome and so forth.
However, it should be stated as follows, and so on in detail.

However, it should be stated as follows: this was said with reference to a causal origination that is "intervened by another," meaning intervened by [factors] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). The meaning is that it was said with reference to an indirect causal origination (*paraṃparā-hetu-samutthāna*).
(IV.15ab) Non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is of three kinds.
The detailed explanation follows.
Having indicated that it is threefold, [it is said]:
"restraint, non-restraint, and that which is other."
He explains:
it is both restraint and it is non-restraint.
It is both restraint and non-restraint; it is that which is both restraint and non-restraint,
and it is the other as well.
The compound *saṃvarasaṃvaretara* is a [dvandva] compound.
(IV.16) It is because [the three types of restraint] have distinct, specific characteristics.
The characteristic of the bhikṣu-vow is distinct [from others], and likewise is the characteristic of the upavāsa-vow up to that point.
For it will be said:
"Because of undertaking the abstention from five, eight, ten, or all things to be avoided."
"Namely, the lay follower (*upāsaka*), one who observes the fast (*upavāsastha*), the novice monk (*śramaṇoddeśa*), and the fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*). However,
if there were eight types [of practitioners], confusion would arise.
For that which is the bhikṣu restraint is itself the bhikṣuṇī restraint, and so forth;
furthermore, there is the śrāmaṇerī and the śikṣamāṇā.
A female novice whose sexual characteristics change becomes a male novice; and a female trainee whose sexual characteristics change likewise becomes a male novice. Why is this not accepted?
When a monk undergoes a change of sexual characteristics (*vyañjana*), he relinquishes the restraint of a monk and acquires the restraint of a nun; therefore, it is said:
"And not upon the change of sexual characteristics," and so forth.
The appearance of the male or female sexual organs does not constitute a cause for the abandonment of a previous vow.
The abandonment of the Prātimokṣa restraint occurs through the renunciation of the training, death,
the arising of both sexual organs, the cutting off of the roots [of merit], or the passing of the night.
Regarding this, the reason that was stated applies here as well:
"Nor is there any cause for the acquisition of a previously unobtained restraint.
As it has been said:
"The one called Prātimokṣa [is acquired] through the communication of others and so forth.
From this it is understood that the bhikṣuṇī restraint is not something other than the bhikṣu restraint.
The same should be stated for the novices (*śrāmaṇera*) and others as well.

Therefore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the four restraints—the nuns’ (*bhikṣuṇī*), the trainee’s (*śikṣamāṇā*), the novice’s (*śrāmaṇera*), and the laywoman’s (*upāsikā*)—is non-different and not other than the three restraints of the monk (*bhikṣu*), the novice, and the layman (*upāsaka*).
"What are those restraints? and so forth is the detailed explanation.
Just as when five other [units] are added to the number five, it becomes ten through the addition of five;
and when five others are added to the number fifteen, it becomes twenty.
It is like the case of a *dīnāra* coin.
Just as a previous dināra becomes a "surplus" (satera) when combined with a second one;

for in the world, someone might say regarding a second dināra purchased for the price of one dināra, or regarding the value of that dināra itself: "I have obtained a surplus of a dināra," having regard to that previous dināra-value as being in excess.
The meaning is: "I have obtained two dīnāras.

Is it the case that these restraints of the lay follower (*upāsaka*), the novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), and the fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) are designated as distinct from one another because of an increase in abstinence (*virati*), such that while the abstinences from killing and so forth remain exactly as they were, there is a further increase through the addition of new abstinences such as those from dancing, singing, and the like?

The meaning is that the *śrāmaṇera* vow is distinct from the *upāsaka* vow, and the *bhikṣu* vow is distinct from the *śrāmaṇera* vow; thus, they are established as distinct from one another due to their connection with specific partial aspects.
Or rather, do they arise entirely separately?
For the *upāsaka*, there are distinct abstinences from killing and so forth.
Then others belong to a novice monk (śrāmaṇera),
and still others to a fully ordained monk (bhikṣu).
Thus, within the single continuum of one monk, there are three abstinences from taking life and so forth.
Thus are the abstentions from taking what is not given,
and so forth.
"In the same way for the rest" means this.
"Abstaining from dancing, singing, and so forth;
from intoxication and negligence" means from high beds and the like, and from drinking intoxicants and the like.
"From many more causes of killing and so forth.
This means that compared to a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) abstains from many more causes of killing and so forth.
For example, eating at improper times (*vikālabhojana*) might become a cause for killing.
Therefore, the novice monk desists;
[the same applies to] the lay follower (*upāsaka*), and so forth—this should be applied accordingly.
And this being the case, if it were not so:

And the meaning is: "If it were not thus. One who renounces—that is, abandons—the bhikṣu restraint would also relinquish all three, beginning with the upāsaka restraint, because both the upāsaka and śrāmaṇera restraints are included within that bhikṣu restraint.
(IV.17) "From the undertaking of abstention" means that he will later state: "Abstention consists of both informative and non-informative [action].
(IV.18) "From the bringing about" means...
The meaning is "because of its counteracting.
For evil karma indeed operates unequally toward sentient beings;
yet that [non-informative action] is also produced by means of both informative action and the mind.

Non-informative action (avijñapti) comprised within the Prātimokṣa restraint is produced by means of informative action (vijñapti), while non-informative action comprised within the meditative (dhyāna) and untainted (anāsrava) restraints is produced by means of the mind;
that is to say, it is produced by means of meditative concentration (samādhi).
Thus, because it is "produced" (kriyate) in this way, it is called "action" (kriyā); this is a derivative noun in the objective sense (karmasādhana).
"Because it is the cause of action.
This means because it is the cause of action.
For one who abides in restraint initiates an action characterized by informative intimation (*vijñapti*) for the purpose of protecting that restraint.
"And because it is the fruit of action" means that it is the fruit of action characterized by informative intimation (*vijñapti*).
How can that which is produced from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) be an action?
Because it is the fruit of volition born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), that too is an action;
or, because the context concerns the Prātimokṣa vows,
mental [actions] are not included therein.
Thus, the Prātimokṣa restraint is designated without distinction;
both the first moment and the subsequent moments are called "Prātimokṣa restraint," yet its essential nature (svabhāva) exists only in the first moment.
To explain that purpose, he says:
furthermore, the first informative and non-informative [actions] are called *prātimokṣa*,
because by means of them there is liberation (*pratimokṣaṇa*) from evil.
By the very first moment, one is liberated from evil;
that is to say, one is cast off and abandoned.
Although the term *pratimokṣa* would be expected, the form *prātimokṣa* is used because the augment (*vṛddhi*) is prescribed for the sake of the word itself.
The meaning is that because the suffix is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*), an increase [of the vowel] is effected;
it is like *vaikṛta* and *vaiśasa*.
Just as *vikṛta* itself is *vaikṛta*.
"Vaiśasa" is indeed slaughter (*viśasana*);
thus, "prātimokṣa" is indeed individual liberation (*pratimokṣa*).
It is also called "prātimokṣa-saṃvara" (the restraint of individual liberation).
It is both *prātimokṣa* and *saṃvara*.
The meaning is that its purpose is the restraint (*saṃvaraṇa*) of body and speech.
It is also called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*).
The meaning is that it is the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*).
In the second and subsequent moments, it is simply the Prātimokṣa restraint (*saṃvara*).
Prātimokṣa restraint is the restraint that belongs to the class of Prātimokṣa, or the restraint born from Prātimokṣa.
It is not the Prātimokṣa,
because evil is not liberated by it;
for it has already been liberated at the very first moment.
(IV.19) Since there is the restriction that "there are exactly eight classes," he asks: "What indeed of the outsiders? and so forth. "Morality of undertaking" (*samādāna-śīla*) is the qualification.
Because of the twofold nature of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
For ethical discipline is indeed twofold: that consisting of formal undertaking (*samādāna-śīla*) and that obtained through the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-pratilaṃbhika*).
In that regard, the morality of undertaking (*samādāna-śīla*) is that which is formally received with the thought,
"I shall not do this and that.

The morality acquired through the nature of things (*dharmatā-pratilambhika*) consists of the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
"Because they are dependent on existence (bhava)" means that even though they seek liberation, they are impaired by wrong views and so forth;
and for some among them, what they consider liberation is merely a particular state of existence.
Their ethical discipline is based solely on worldly existence;
therefore, they possess the morality of formal undertaking, but not the Prātimokṣa restraint.
The preparatory stage (sāmantaka) is also designated here by the term "dhyāna.
This is because both the dhyāna-restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara) and the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) are accepted as existing even in the preparatory stage;
therefore, it is accepted that the preparatory stage of dhyāna is also expressed here by the word "dhyāna."
Because of the word "also," the fundamental [cause] is indeed included as well.
Regarding the statement "in the case of the co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu)":
the mental factors (caitta) and the two types of restraint (saṃvara) are [the co-existent causes] of those.
Regarding this,
"of the three" refers to the Prātimokṣa restraint, the dhyāna restraint, and the uncontaminated (anāsrava) restraint.
"Because it continues even for one whose mind is otherwise or who is without mind," [is said] because of the statement, "even for one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind."
(IV.20ab) The mention of "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*) is because it is the antidote specifically to the immorality belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
[The phrase continues: "in the paths of immediate succession" (*ānantaryamārgeṣu*).
Because they constitute the path of abandonment for those [afflictions]. "Of those that give rise to them" means of those that give rise to misconduct (*dauḥśīlya*).
"Precisely for this reason":
because its establishment occurs only in the uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*),
therefore a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) is formulated.
The first alternative is the meditative restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) excluding the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the threshold stage (*anāgamya*).

This refers to the meditative restraint found in the paths of liberation, preparation, and excellence belonging to the threshold stage, or in the fundamental first dhyāna and so forth, up to the fourth dhyāna, within their respective uninterrupted, liberation, preparation, and excellence paths.
This is meditative restraint, but not the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
Because of that, there is no abandonment of immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*) that give rise to it.
In the second *anāgamya* and the paths of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*), there is the untainted restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*).
This is the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃvara*), because by means of that very [path], immorality and so forth are abandoned.
It is not the meditative restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*) because it is untainted (*anāsrava*).

In the third [fruit] and in the paths of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), there is both tainted restraint and this restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃvara*), because by means of it there is the abandonment of immorality and so forth.
And it is also the meditative restraint, because it is born from tainted meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The fourth is the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara), excluding the uninterrupted path of the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
This is not the meditative restraint because it is untainted;
nor is it the restraint of abandonment, because by means of it there is no abandonment of immorality and so forth.

Furthermore, that untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) which exists in detail within the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), application (*prayoga-mārga*), and excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*) belonging to the stage of the threshold (*anāgamya-bhūmi*) is likewise [included].
It was stated in this way specifically by way of defining restraint;
otherwise, other factors would also have to be mentioned.
Thus, there is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) regarding whether there is untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) but not restraint through abandonment (prahāṇa-saṃvara).
The first alternative is untainted restraint excluding the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) of the threshold stage (anāgamya).

(IV.20cd) The mention of both [terms] is for the purpose of making known that they possess two natures, since both mental restraint (manaḥ-saṃvara) and sense-restraint (indriya-saṃvara) have mindfulness (smṛti) and clear comprehension (saṃprajñāna) as their intrinsic nature.
For the duality is established precisely by the indication of the dual number. But how is it understood that these two alone possess such an intrinsic nature?
From scripture.
It is said that a certain deity spoke to a monk who was directing his senses toward sense-objects:
"O monk, O monk, do not create a wound!"
The monk said, "I shall cover it, O goddess. The goddess said:
"O Bhikṣu, having made a wound as large as a water-jar, with what will you cover it?
The Bhikṣu replied,
"O Devatā, I shall cover it with mindfulness."
"And by means of clear comprehension" (IV.21,
22). "As long as he does not abandon that non-informative [action]" refers to the relinquishing of the training and so forth.
"After the first moment, one is endowed with the past [non-restraint].
This means it was stated that in the first moment, one is endowed only with the present [non-restraint].
"One who possesses the restraint of meditative absorption (dhyāna-saṃvara) is always endowed with the past and the unborn."

Does one who possesses the restraint of meditative absorption (dhyānasaṃvara) belong to the class of ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) or to that of noble ones (ārya)? He says: both, because no distinction has been specified.
He is endowed with past and future non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Of what characteristic?
Since this concerns the restraint of meditative absorption (*dhyānasaṃvara*), it is understood that it is of the characteristic of the restraint of meditative absorption.
"That which was abandoned in another birth"—
this is intended merely to provide an illustration;
for even that which was abandoned in this very life is included.
"But the noble one, in the first [moment], does not possess the past.
The noble one is always endowed with non-informative matter (avijñapti) that is past and unborn.
Of what characteristic is it?
By means of that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
This is because the context concerns the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
For this very reason, he says:
"A noble person (āryapudgala) likewise [possesses] this through the untainted [path].
He shows the meaning of the word "but" (tu) with the words: "But this is the distinction."
And that [phrase] has a displaced word order.

The meaning is that in the first moment—that is, the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti)—one is not endowed with past non-informative matter (avijñapti).
Why?
Because in beginningless *saṃsāra*, the path has not previously been produced.

But is it not the case that at the time of attaining the fruit, or even at the time of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), when the previous path is abandoned, one is no longer held to be endowed with past non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)?
If that is so, then that [first moment] is also the first moment of the path to the fruit.
In this regard, it should be explained that one does not possess past non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) because the path of fruition has not previously arisen.
However, Master Vasumitra offers the following resolution to this objection.
The untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) is the subject under discussion here.
And that is acquired precisely at the time of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Therefore, by means of that [restraint], one is not endowed with the past in the first moment; rather, in the second moment and those following, one is endowed with both the past and the future.
As for the attainment of another path at a higher level,
it is not mentioned there because it possesses a similarity to the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
We do not understand how such a similarity exists here.
Is this stated with the intention that there exists a contaminated restraint (sāsrava-saṃvara),
or rather that there exists an uncontaminated one?
If it is intended that there exists a contaminated one...

Since that [uncontaminated restraint] exists even at the time of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*), the negation "one is not endowed with the past [restraint]" would be untenable.

If, on the other hand, it is intended that the past uncontaminated restraint exists at the time of attaining the fruit, then how can it be said to exist when it has been abandoned? Thus, the intention behind this [statement] must be considered.
"Abiding in the concentrated and noble paths" means both one abiding in the worldly concentrated path and one abiding in the noble path.
"Those abiding in the concentrated and noble paths" means those endowed with the dhyāna-restraint and the untainted (anāsrava) restraint.

And here, one who has mounted the noble path should be understood as "standing on the noble path" by way of analogy with one standing on a boat; just as, for example, whoever has boarded a boat is said to be "standing on the boat."
Thus, one who has mounted the noble path and entered into meditative absorption is "abiding in the noble path.
Otherwise, even one who is merely endowed with the noble path would have to be considered "abiding in the noble path" [by that definition alone].
It would follow that even a noble one (ārya) abiding in the natural state (prakṛtistha) is endowed with the present non-outflowing non-informative matter (avijñapti).
However, another [author], avoiding such an undesirable consequence, explains:
"In this case, a single remainder (ekaśeṣa) is formed."
The concentrated state and the noble path of one who is concentrated are the "concentrated and noble paths.
One who abides in those two is "abiding in the concentrated and noble paths."

Those two are, respectively, endowed with the present non-informative (avijñapti) of the meditative restraint (dhyānasaṃvara) and the non-informative of the untainted restraint (anāsravasaṃvara); however, they are not so when emerged [from meditation].
That is to say, those who have emerged from that path are not endowed with that present [non-informative].
Because it must conform to that [mind],
it is explained in this way.
This is in response to what was raised by the teacher Saṃghabhadra.
How is the present state of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) understood? It is understood precisely from the statement that one "abides in the Noble Path" (*āryamārgastha*).
If it is argued: "This person is indeed absorbed in that [path], so there is no consequence of stating that they possess (*samanvāgama*) it," [we reply:]...
No,
because this concerns meditative absorption (*dhyāna*),
and because there is an absence of informative action (*vijñapti*) therein.
(IV.23ab) One who abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint is called "intermediate" (*madhyastha*).
This refers to one who is neither a monk (*bhikṣu*) and so forth,
nor a fisherman and so forth.
He is neutral. "Comprising the factors of misconduct and the factors of morality" means that misconduct consists of killing living beings and so forth.
The limb of ethical discipline (*śīlāṅga*) consists of abstaining from taking life and so forth.

That which is neither included within restraint (*saṃvara*) nor non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is referred to by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*); by this term, the informative action (*vijñapti*) of activities such as worshipping a stūpa, striking with a tool, or slapping with the palm is included.

(IV.23cd, 24ab) Considering that persons established in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and restraint (*saṃvara*) are respectively established in unwholesome (*akuśala*) and wholesome (*kuśala*) dharmas, one asks—fearing that the opposite might be the case for these two—“What is meant by ‘one who stands in non-restraint’? and so forth.
[The answer is: “These two persist as long as they continue.”
The force of faith and the force of affliction.
"In others, even by the past" means by the past [mind] in the second moment and those following.
(IV.24cd, 25ab) "From the moment after [the first] until its relinquishment.
Whichever [informative action] is relinquished by someone, until that relinquishment, he remains endowed with that past informative action.
How so?
First, the abandonment of informative action (*vijñapti*) characterized by restraint occurs through such acts as the renunciation of the training.
Until that abandonment, one remains endowed with that past informative action.
The abandonment of informative action characterized by non-restraint occurs through the undertaking of restraint and so forth.
Therefore, one is endowed with this until its relinquishment.
Its relinquishment—characterized as being neither restraint nor non-restraint—occurs through the cutting off of the force of faith, afflictions, and so forth.
Therefore, one is endowed with this until its relinquishment.

For whoever is endowed with the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) of restraint and so forth, they are necessarily endowed from the moment after [the first] with a past non-informative action whose nature is that of the fundamental paths of action (*maula-karmapatha*).
However, no one is endowed with a future informative action (*vijñapti*).
Because it does not follow after the mind.
[Objection: "Of the mind as well.
[Response: In that case, let there be no acquisition (*prāpti*) even for the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind.
The meaning is that [the consequence] should not be entailed.
Why? He says:
for representation is insentient because it lacks an objective support (*anālambanatva*).
And it is dependent on others because it is dependent on the mind;
yet the mind is not like this, meaning it is not insentient.
The meaning is that it is not dependent on another.
Why?
Because of the opposite case: since it is produced by a weak, obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) mind, it becomes even weaker.
(IV.25cd) "Because it is comprised within the fundamental [path of action]" means that volition has that as its purpose.
(IV.26) One who is neutral and acts with weak volition is endowed with informative action (*vijñapti*) alone.
Thus [it is said].
The inclusion of the term "neutral" (madhyastha) is for the purpose of excluding those who abide in restraint (saṃvara) or non-restraint (asaṃvara).
For those abiding in restraint or non-restraint are necessarily endowed with both informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti) action.
The mention of "weak volition" (mṛdu-cetanā) is for the purpose of excluding "intense volition" (tīvra-cetanā).
For one performing an informative act (vijñapti) with intense volition would also give rise to non-informative action (avijñapti);
this is even more so in the case of that which is neutral (avyākṛta).

When one performs an indeterminate action with weak volition, even before [the completion of the act], one is endowed with the informative intimation (*vijñapti*) alone and not with the non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*), because the latter has not yet arisen.

For when one performs a wholesome or unwholesome action with weak volition while abiding in neither restraint nor non-restraint, one is endowed with the informative intimation alone; how much more so when performing an indeterminate action, where one is all the more endowed with the informative intimation alone and not with the non-informative intimation.
Because there is no possibility of the arising of non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*).
"Elsewhere," and so forth: elsewhere than from the seven bases of meritorious action consisting of material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*).
And [it refers] to the paths of action, such as killing and so forth;
for in those cases, even while performing what is neutral (*avyākṛta*), one becomes possessed of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
This is because of the statement in the Sūtra: "Whether walking or standing, constantly and continuously... [and so on in detail] ...merit indeed arises."
Even when performing the paths of action such as taking life with a weak intention, one becomes possessed of non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
"By which noble person (*āryapudgala*)" and so forth:
this refers to a noble person who has changed births, at a time when [the new informative action] has not yet been manifested.
In the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*, and upon rebirth in the formless realm (*ārūpya*),
or furthermore, when informative action (*vijñapti*) has been lost— specifically, when one is deprived of the informative action originated by an indeterminate mind—
the acquisition (*prāpti*) of that [informative action] does not continue as a persistent sequence.
Or [it applies] to one who has constructed a stūpa and so forth. Because that object is destroyed,
he at that time abandons even the non-informative (avijñapti), let alone the informative (vijñapti).

In these states, when there is a transition to another birth, a noble person (āryapudgala) is endowed with non-informative action (avijñapti) alone—which is untainted (anāsrava) and acquired in that other birth—and not with informative action (vijñapti).
But does this rule not also apply to an ordinary person (pṛthagjana)? It does indeed apply.
However, the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not mentioned because it is not necessary;

for only one who has attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), has undergone a change of birth, and either has not yet performed an informative act (*vijñapti*) in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) or is devoid of having performed such an act,
can possibly be so [an *asaṃskṛta-dharma*], and no other.
Or [it is so] because the statement was made with reference specifically to beings belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
Alternatively, since the noble person (*āryapudgala*) was mentioned as an illustrative example, by that [example], the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) should also be understood in the same way.
For this very reason...
"One who is neutral and acts with weak volition is endowed with the informative [action] alone"—
this was stated there [in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*], excepting the meritorious bases of action consisting of material gifts (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*) and the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Considering that this statement is incomplete, two alternatives have been formulated as the first and second; the third and fourth, however, are to be applied accordingly.
The third alternative consists of those who abide in restraint, non-restraint, or the intermediate state, performing either wholesome or unwholesome actions with intense volition.

The fourth [alternative] is that by which it has not yet been manifested by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) during a transition to another birth, or having been manifested, it has been lost. (IV.27) "Because of being co-existent" means:
Because the meditative restraint (dhyānasaṃvara) exists together with the mind of meditation (dhyānacitta).
"Another makes known" means he causes [the recipient] to understand.
"Other than the person" means distinct from the individual.
The restraints of the male novices, female novices, laymen, laywomen, and those observing the one-day fast;
by means of entering the path of certainty through the introduction to the Noble Path;
[as in the case] of the group of five, beginning with Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya.
"By the 'Come, monk' formula" refers to the Blessed One’s words: "Come, monk, lead the holy life.
It is said: "When addressed with 'Come' by the Sugata, the Protector, he became shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes.
This was due to Mahākāśyapa’s acceptance of the Teacher.
It is said that whichever image of a deity Mahākāśyapa paid homage to would shatter,
due to his great spiritual power.
Having approached the Blessed One, he did not pay homage, thinking, "Lest there be the destruction of his physical form. Perceiving that intention, the Blessed One rebuked him.
"Pay homage to the Tathāgata, Kāśyapa.
He then paid homage to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, seeing that the Blessed One’s form was unaltered, he accepted the Blessed One as his teacher; thus, this was his full ordination.
"By pleasing [the Buddha] through answering questions, as in the case of Sodāyin.
By answering the questions posed by Sodāyin, the Blessed One was pleased; through that act of pleasing him, he received full ordination (*upasampad*).
"By accepting the weighty rules (*gurudharma*)."
There are eight weighty rules (*gurudharma*).
Full ordination (*upasaṃpad*) and the status of a nun must be received from a monk.
Every half-month, instruction must be received from a monk.
One should not enter the rains retreat in a residence where no monks are present.
At the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), both Saṅghas should perform the invitation by means of three points;
a monk who has fallen into an offense should neither be accused nor reviled.
In the case of an offense against the heavy dharmas, a *mānāpya* penance must be performed for half a month.
A monk who has been ordained even for a single moment is to be venerated by a nun who has been ordained for a hundred years.
Furthermore, a nun must never reprove a monk under any circumstances.
These and others [are the cases].
By accepting these, there is the formal admission (upasaṃpad) for her. [The case] of Dharmadinnā was by means of a messenger.
It is said that while she was still within the inner apartments, she sent a messenger to the Buddha for the sake of going forth.
Regarding the phrase "with a group of five including one who holds the Vinaya":
four monks constitute a *saṃgha*.
In that regard, in the border regions, one is ordained by the fifth proponent of the motion (*jñaptivācaka*). However, in the central regions, one is ordained by the tenth proponent of the motion.
This refers to those who were ordained by the group of the sixty auspicious ones (*ṣaṣṭibhadravarga*).
"Bhadra-varga" means those whose group is auspicious; it refers to the sixty sons of good family. It means [the ordination] conferred upon them by that assembly or multitude.
Full ordination (*upasaṃpad*) is attained through the threefold recitation of the formula for going for refuge, saying "We go for refuge to the Buddha" three times.
For them, it is not necessarily dependent upon a formal informative act (*vijñapti*).
This is the opinion of those masters who uphold the Vinaya.
The Prātimokṣa restraint is not necessarily dependent upon informative action (*vijñapti*), because for those such as the Buddhas, it is not dependent on informative action.
Alternatively, "for them" refers to those for whom there is no informative action during the rite of full ordination (*upasaṃpad*).
(IV.28ab) "Of restraint" (*saṃvṛteḥ*) means of restraint (*saṃvarasya*).
Some maintain that time is an eternal category (*padārtha*) that exists.
Out of apprehension regarding this, he asks:
"What is this dharma called 'time'?
The meaning is: what is the referent of this designation "time"?
"This is a designation for the illumination of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
This means it is a name that makes manifest conditioned phenomena of the past, future, and present.
For example, when one says "past time" up to "present time," it is understood that these refer precisely to conditioned phenomena belonging to the three time periods.
"And because there is no application toward that by means of it":
by means of that dissimilar basis (*āśraya*), there is no application toward that undertaking (*samādāna*);
and because of non-recollection, one does not recollect that undertaking by means of that basis.
The Vaibhāṣika says:
But on what basis is this reasoned in such a way,
as was just stated?
The Master says:
"Because there is no contradiction with reasoning even in the arising of restraint through another.
Here, reasoning is not contradicted.

Just as after the end of one's life, even though there is a formal undertaking (*samādāna*), there is a contradiction with reason regarding the arising of restraint (*saṃvara*) because the basis (*āśraya*) is of a different nature (*visabhāga*), and so forth; likewise, "it does not reach that which has perished at another time" means by virtue of the intention (*āśaya*) for a duration such as a day and night.
Just like non-informative action (*avijñapti*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) also does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
Just as it has been established that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*), so too non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) does not exist substantially;
the intention is that it is not distinct from volition (*cetanā*).
"Intention toward evil action" means the purpose of performing an evil deed. "With its sequel" means together with its latent tendencies (*savāsana*).

The meaning is that non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is a specific volition accompanied by latent tendencies (*savāsana*). Because of this continuous connection, one who possesses it is said to be "one who possesses non-restraint," which means one who is characterized by non-restraint (*asaṃvarika*).
Because that has not been rejected;
because that intention, along with its continuity, has not been set aside.
The meaning is: because it has not been impaired by a volition contrary to it.
(IV.29) "Even after having eaten, he may take [the vow].
The restraint arises precisely at sunrise,
because it is that which arouses the mind characterized by the discipline of formal undertaking (*samādāna-niyama*).
The mention of "having eaten" is for the purpose of clarification.
Regarding the term *kapotaka*:
it is called *kapotaka* because the four fingers, excluding the thumb, are placed in the space between the thumb and the index finger of the other hand.
(IV.30) Morality (*śīla*) is the absence of defeats (*pārājika*) and the absence of formal meetings of the community (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), etc.; it is a vow (*vrata*).
This is the rule.
"Due to the absence of that" means due to the absence of eating at improper times.
"Both would not exist" [refers to this].
"Mindfulness and urgency"— the Master [Vasubandhu], by means of reasoning, refutes in detail the Vaibhāṣika position that these [factors] belong to those [others],

namely, to those very same factors such as right view, the enlightenment factor of the investigation of dharmas, and concentration, which are [respectively] right view, the enlightenment factor of the investigation of dharmas, and concentration.
These very factors, beginning with right view, are considered to be limbs;
that is to say, they are appropriate.
Why?
Because it contradicts reason.
If it were established that the preceding factors, such as right view, are members (*aṅga*) of the subsequent factors,
such as right view, then in this conception, the Noble Path arising in the first moment would not possess eight members.
For in that case, the right view that arose previously would not be a constituent;
thus it would have only seven constituents.
Likewise, among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the final moment would not be a factor of enlightenment.
For there is no other awakening (bodhi) beyond this for which that could be a limb.
If it is thought that it is a limb of a future awakening,
then there would be no future awakening.
In this way, concentration (*samādhi*) is to be applied.
(IV.31ab) "Except for ignorance" means due to the forgetfulness or lack of understanding on the part of either the giver or the recipient.
"Restraint does not arise for one who is doubtful, or whose intention is corrupted, or who seeks refuge without respect"—
this is the summary statement (*uddeśapada*). "Having taken [it]" (*gṛhī*) is the term [to be explained].
"One clad in white garments" is the term of definition;
"man" is [the referent].
"Possessing the male faculty" is the term of general indication (*uddeśapada*); "by means of the male faculty" is the term of its specific explanation (*tannirdeśapada*).

If one does not become an upāsaka without the restraint (saṃvara), then what about that which was stated in the Sūtra: "By this much one becomes an upāsaka"? [That was said with reference to the minimum requirements.]
"How so? is the remainder of the sentence. He says:
"There is no contradiction with the Sūtra in this regard."
[Regarding] the *Mahānāma-sūtra* (IV.31cd):
"The statement, however, is like that for a monk."
The statement regarding the training rules for a lay follower (*upāsaka*) is like that for a monk (*bhikṣu*).

For just as a monk, even though he has already obtained the vows, is made to grasp and be informed of the training rules in their general outlines through a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha-karman*), [with the words]: "From this and from that—from the defeats (*pārājika*) and so forth—your vow [is established]."
"And your fellow religious practitioners will tell you other things as well.
And what about the novice monk?
What [will happen to him]?
The training precepts are undertaken even before the vow has been formally acquired.

For as soon as he has made this commitment: "I, named so-and-so, follow in the renunciation of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Śākyamuni, the Sovereign of the Śākyas who has gone forth;
I renounce the marks of a householder."
"I take up the marks of renunciation. Regard me as a novice (śramaṇoddeśa).
This is repeated in this manner up to three times.
In the same way, the lay follower also goes for refuge to the Buddha;
up to: he goes for refuge to the Saṅgha.
A second time, and a third time as well.
By this [formula], even one who has already obtained the vows is further made to undertake the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) in detail:
"Having abandoned the taking of life, I abstain from the taking of life," and so forth.
Such a person is a "partial practitioner" (*ekadeśakārī*).
He who observes one precept is a partial practitioner; he who observes two is likewise.
One who practices to a great extent is one who observes three or four precepts.
One who practices in full is one who observes all five.
"He who guards even five is said to be one who practices that"—
the meaning is that he is one who practices a single part, up to one who practices in its entirety.

"For the wording of the sutra is not thus" means that the wording of the Mahānāma-sūtra does not state "having abandoned life for as long as one lives," in the manner that the wording of the Mahānāma-sūtra [actually] states.
"To what extent, venerable sir, does one become a lay follower (*upāsaka*)? Mahānāman, when a householder— in detail, as far as saying 'Please accept me as a lay follower'—
says this, to that extent one becomes a lay follower."
"But where this reading occurs" means:
where in another sutra this reading is found:
"for as long as life lasts, having gone for refuge with life-renouncing faith."

Then those individuals who have seen the truths demonstrate, through the sequence of their verified faith (*avetyaprasāda*) and caused by that verified faith, that they would resort to the True Dharma even at the cost of their lives or for the sake of their livelihood, thinking:
"We are incapable of abandoning this Dharma.
However, this is not a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of restraint (*saṃvara*).
The meaning is that the definition is not taught by this sutra.
Furthermore, the phrase "devoid of breath" (prāṇāpeta) is not recited anywhere,
nor even in the Mahānāma-sūtra.
Nor is it found in the *Dṛṣṭasatya-sūtra*.
Who would recite this [text] whose meaning is so unclear?
It is not understood because of the ambiguity arising from the elision of the middle term.
Does "devoid of life" (*prāṇāpeta*) mean devoid of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), or does it mean devoid of the taking of life and so forth? [In either case,] the question itself is not tenable.
As for this question: "To what extent, venerable sir, is a lay follower one who practices in part, up to one who practices in full?"—
this question is not tenable.
"How is there a formal renunciation?
"In this case, Mahānāman, a lay follower (*upāsaka*), having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life.
To this extent, Mahānāman, a lay follower becomes one who practices a single part of the training."
To say that one who abstains from two training rules extensively is a "partial practitioner" (*pradeśakārī*); one who abstains from three or four is a "majority practitioner" (*yadbhūyaskārī*);
and one who abstains from five is a "complete practitioner" (*paripūrṇakārī*)—this explanation is not at all tenable.
This question is appropriate for one who is capable of observing only that many precepts—
whether it be one training rule, two, or more than that.
[It is also appropriate] regarding the fact that a lay follower (*upāsaka*) is designated even without the formal restraint (*saṃvara*).
In the Mahānāma-sūtra,
beginning with the words, "For indeed, Mahānāma, a householder dressed in white," and so forth,
it follows that even for an Arhat, the Prātimokṣa restraint could be weak.
If the mind that motivates it were weak,
[it would be] "intense" for an ordinary person;
if his mind were intense, [it would be] "weak."
"Except for ignorance" refers to that of both the giver and the receiver.
However, due to a lack of respect for those [precepts], one would not be a lay follower (*upāsaka*) without having gone for refuge.
(IV.33) "Those that constitute a Buddha" means the causes for the designation of a Buddha.
For this very reason, he says:
It is because of these [qualities] being predominant that his personal existence (ātmabhāva) is called "Buddha.
For other qualities also reside [in him], though not predominantly.
Or rather, it is by the acquisition of these [qualities] that [he is so called].
"The knowledge of destruction and so forth, together with their retinues.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the knowledge of non-arising and the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣī samyagdṛṣṭi) are included.
By the inclusion of "together with their retinues," the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha) are understood.
"Because there is no difference in the form-body (rūpakāya) before and after"—what does this mean?
It connects with the statement: "one does not go for refuge to the form-body."
Just as the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is during the stage of a bodhisattva, so it is afterwards as well.
"All Buddhas by way of their characteristics" means that this is not stated explicitly [in the sūtra]; such is the intended meaning.

"Because the path is not of different characteristics" means that the worldly path, characterized by the accumulation of merit and knowledge, and the supramundane path, characterized by the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth, are not of different characteristics— that is, they are equal.
This does not refer to the characteristics of lifespan, birth, and so on.
Therefore, all Buddhas have identical characteristics.
They "become a Saṃgha" because they are indivisible;
that is, because they cannot be divided even by the world including the gods with respect to the Path, they become a Saṃgha.
"They exist in their complete form.
Regarding "by way of their characteristics," it should be explained as before.
"He who will be," and so forth.
In that regard, the Blessed One addressed the two merchants Trapusa and Bhallika:
"Come, you two, go for refuge to this Buddha."
"And the Dharma. Go for refuge also to that which will be known as the Saṅgha in the future time.
This was said with reference to the future Saṅgha itself, at a time when the Saṅgha does not yet exist.

How, then, is this not contradicted by the statement that "he goes for refuge to the entire Saṃgha"? [The phrase] "those who will appear before his eyes" means that the Jewel of the Saṃgha will become manifest to those two, Bhallika and Trapuṣa, immediately after the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
The meaning is that he alone will be the one authorized for the purpose of manifesting and elucidating it by way of its qualities.
"Because it has the single characteristic of peace" means the peace which consists in the cessation of the afflictions and suffering belonging to the continuums of both oneself and others.
That which has this characteristic is "having quiescence as its sole characteristic," namely nirvāṇa;
the state of being that [is the meaning].
Therefore.
He goes to the entirety of nirvāṇa by means of the destruction of the basis (*āśraya-vipādana*).
This refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which is the basis of those [factors] belonging to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Because of its destruction and disturbance, those qualities that constitute a Buddha and which depend upon it are also destroyed.
However, the treatise does not say this; such is the detailed explanation.
The Abhidharma treatise does not state it in this way.
It is not the case that the one who sees [the Buddha] is merely the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What then?
Regarding the term "those which bring about a Buddha":
what are these "buddhakārakas"? They are those mundane and supramundane factors that are the causes for Buddhahood and for the designation of a "Buddha. These are called "the Buddhas."
Therefore, since the basis—characterized by the five mundane aggregates—is not denied to be Buddhahood, this objection is indeed untenable.

As for what was said: "If the Buddha is only the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), how can there be an immediate transgression (ānantarya) from shedding the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind?
[The answer is: "Otherwise, however," and so forth.
If the Buddha is the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
and the Saṃgha consists only of the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training,
then when abiding in a mundane state of mind, he would be neither the Buddha nor the Saṃgha.
Why?
Because worldly factors are neither factors of one beyond training nor factors of one in training.
Or else, if only the factors of one in training were the makers of a Buddha, then the physical basis [the body] would not be the Buddha.
It is ethical discipline alone—designated as the "monk's restraint"—that makes one a monk;
it is not the physical basis.
He said: [it is so].
If the Buddha-nature also belongs to the basis (the physical body), why does the treatise state this:

"He who goes for refuge to the Buddha goes for refuge to the dharmas of one beyond training that constitute a Buddha"? By saying this, it restricts [the object of refuge] specifically to the dharmas of one beyond training.
When the Vaibhāṣika had spoken thus, the Master stated the resolution by means of an analogy:
"But as for one who honors a monk," and so forth;
that is, as for one who honors a monk by way of [his] moral discipline (*śīla*).
He honors that morality which makes one a monk;
yet, morality itself is not the monk.
In the same way, he who goes for refuge to the Buddha does so by way of the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
He goes for refuge to those dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that constitute a Buddha;
it is not, however, that the dharmas of one beyond training existing within his own continuum (*svasaṃtānika*) alone are the Buddha.
Therefore, there is no fault in this.
He who goes for refuge to the Buddha goes for refuge to those dharmas beyond training that constitute a Buddha.
(Abhidh-k-vy 379)
"He [possesses] the eighteen unique [qualities]"— the intention is that these are not shared with others.
They have the nature of vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
With reference to the time of formal undertaking: "and the trees of the caityas.
Trees that have been designated as caityas are "caitya-trees."
"Those [people]" means: "for this very reason," because...
Having come to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
Therefore, the meaning is that among the undertakings of all vows—namely, the undertakings of the vows of lay followers (*upāsaka*) and so forth—these [three refuges] serve as the gateway.
Furthermore, it is because [the violation of them] leads to rebirth in the miserable states (*apāya*). (IV.34ab)
And because sexual misconduct is exclusively leading to the states of woe and conduces to the states of woe,
whereas unchastity is not so;
for the restraint of non-action is indeed the commitment to refrain from doing [the act].
The restriction regarding non-action—that is, non-performance—is the absolute commitment to non-action (*akriyā-niyama*). This is the restraint of non-performance (*akaraṇa-saṃvara*);
it is a restraint characterized by non-performance.
The meaning is that it is not a restraint consisting of formal undertaking (*samādānika-saṃvara*).
According to the Sautrāntika system, that [restraint] is merely a particular state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*);
however, according to the Vaibhāṣika system, it is the non-informative (*avijñapti*) constituent of ethical discipline (*śīla-aṅga*).
(IV.34cd) "Those who, being lay followers (*upāsaka*),... and so forth.
Those who, while having already undertaken the five precepts (*pañca-śikṣāpada*), take wives—that is, marry them—do those lay followers obtain restraint (*saṃvara*) even with respect to those women?
The meaning is "previously obtained.
Now, with reference to the case where it has not been obtained,
the Vaibhāṣika says:
"Attained" means that it should not be partial; rather, it refers to abstaining from all improper conduct. "I abstain from sexual misconduct" means that I abstain from improper conduct.
However, the intention is not "I abstain from this course of conduct because it is unapproachable for this continuum.
For this very reason, he says: "But not in this continuum..."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
(IV.35cd) Regarding "faults by prohibition" (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*): [Tib.
40b] it refers to those actions which are designated as faults by the Buddha's explicit prohibition.
Prohibitive offense:
evil arises for one who performs an action forbidden by the Blessed One,
due to a lack of respect for the Blessed One’s teaching.

When the Abhidharmika says, "That is not afflicted [karma] which one drinks having recognized the non-intoxicating measure," the Vinayadharas establish that alcohol is a natural transgression (*prakṛtisāvadya*), saying,
"O Upāli, setting aside the natural transgressions."

The intention is that one should not be treated with an action that is inherently reprehensible (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), but rather one should be treated with an action that is reprehensible by convention (*prajñapti-sāvadya*). Among the Śākyas, the drinking of intoxicants was not permitted even when they were ill.
Therefore, it is understood that this is a natural transgression (*prakṛtisāvadya*).
For if it were a conventional transgression (*prajñaptisāvadya*), it would have been permitted for the sake of attending to sick Śākyans;
yet it is not permitted.
Therefore, that is a natural transgression (*prakṛtisāvadya*).

And this has been said: "By those who designate me as their teacher, who declare 'Śākyamuni is our teacher,' not even a drop of alcohol the size of the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass should be drunk. Thus, because it is a natural transgression, it was prohibited by the Blessed One.

But not because one knows, "This is intoxicating. For even a quantity of liquor as small as the tip of a blade of kusha grass is not intoxicating. And [the phrase] "by the Noble Ones" is the full statement.
Alcohol is a transgression by nature (*prakṛtisāvadya*),
because even Noble Ones (*ārya*) who have passed into other births do not commit it;
this is the proof, just like the killing of living beings and so forth.
And because it is described as a bodily misdeed (*kāyaduścarita*), there is another proof:
liquor is a natural transgression (*prakṛtisāvadya*),
because it is described as a bodily misdeed.
Like the killing of living beings and so forth.
For fourfold bodily misconduct has been taught in the *Nandika-sūtra* and other texts:
taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants.
"Even of that which is prescribed as a general rule," and so forth.
By this, they resolve the contradiction between the preceding and following statements of the Blessed One.
How?
"Venerable Sir," and so forth, is the general statement (*utsarga*) regarding the drinking of intoxicants.
"The drinking of intoxicants was not permitted even for the sick among the Śākyas" is the exception (*apavāda*).
From this, it is understood that the drinking of intoxicants is not permitted even in a state of illness.
Furthermore, the exception is for the purpose of avoiding an undesirable consequence;
for even liquor drunk once might become an addiction.
For it was said by the Blessed One:
For one who rejects these three positions, there is neither satisfaction, nor sufficiency, nor completion.
[The factors are] intoxicants, unchastity, and sloth-torpor.
Why is there an avoidance of [excessive] consequences? He says:
because there is no fixed limit for the quantity that causes intoxication.
For that very same measure becomes intoxicating or non-intoxicating depending on the substance, the time, one's constitution, and the state of the body.
It is for this very reason that the prohibition against drinking even as much as a drop from the tip of a blade of kusha grass is an expression of extreme precaution.
Thus, having considered that [alcohol] is not inherently unwholesome (*prakṛtisāvadya*), the Blessed One stated that it should nevertheless be avoided.
What then?
It has been shown that it is due to the fault of an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅgadoṣa*).
The Noble Ones do not engage in such conduct because they possess a sense of shame (*hrīmattva*).
The five powers of those in training are recited in the Sūtra.
Which five?
They are the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of moral shame, the power of dread of blame, and the power of wisdom.
Therefore, they do not drink because they possess a sense of shame (*hrīmattva*), and not because it is inherently unwholesome (*prakṛtisāvadya*).
If it is due to their sense of shame that they do not commit that transgression, why do they not drink [water] and so forth when it is unknown [to be unwholesome]? To this he says:
And because of that, there is a loss of mindfulness.
For when one drinks intoxicants, the mindfulness regarding what should and should not be done is destroyed.
If this is so, then let them drink only a small amount.
To the extent that mindfulness is lost, for that reason he says: "Even a small amount [of food] is not to be drunk," because there is no fixed rule.
"Like poison":
just as even a small amount of poison may sometimes kill due to the conjunction of time, nature, and potency,
so too does intoxicating liquor cause intoxication.
The mention of misconduct is because it is a basis for negligence; for through intoxication, one fails to avoid unwholesome states and fails to perform wholesome ones.
Regarding the mention of "the basis of negligence" (*pramādasthāna*) here and not in the others:

it is precisely in this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) that there is a mention of the basis of negligence, because of the statement, "Having abandoned the basis of negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, I abstain from the basis of negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants.
There is no mention of the basis of negligence in the other training rules, such as the abstention from taking life and so forth.

Having abandoned the basis for negligence consisting in the taking of life, one says, "I abstain from the basis for negligence consisting in the taking of life. In this case, "basis for negligence" is not recited; rather, it is said, "Having abandoned the taking of life, I abstain from the taking of life."
In this same way, [the prohibitions on] taking what is not given and so forth are to be applied.
Why? He says:
because they are inherently reprehensible (*prakṛtisāvadya*).
Because those training precepts, such as the abstention from taking life and so forth, are inherently reprehensible (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
This is what is meant: one must abstain from drinking intoxicants because it is a basis for negligence (*pramādasthāna*).
"But this is not a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*)," [it is said].
"By excessive indulgence," and so forth.

For it is stated in the *Nandika-sūtra*: "By indulging in, cultivating, and frequently practicing fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, one is reborn in the hells after the dissolution of the body."

The statement that one goes to an evil rebirth through the excessive indulgence in drinking intoxicants is because, through addiction to that— that is, addiction to drinking intoxicants— there is the continuous and incessant occurrence of a succession of unwholesome states. This refers to the occurrence of that succession of unwholesome states.
The "impetus" (*āvedha*) consists in the projection of new karma that leads to the miserable realms and has those realms as its purpose.
From this [impetus],
there is the acquisition of activity for previously accumulated karma at the moment of death, either through the attainment of its functional operation or for the sake of yielding its fruit.
Therefore, it should be connected as follows: "Because of that [cause], either by way of projection or by way of obtaining its activity, there is the designation 'going to an evil rebirth.'"
"Grain liquor" refers to that which is made from rice. "Liquid liquor" refers to [liquor made from] liquids.
It is produced from sugarcane juice and so forth.
"Or those," and so on in detail;
this refers to *surā* and *maireya*, which at times have not yet attained the state of being intoxicants (*madya*).
When they are new;
or sometimes when their state of being fermented has subsided;
or when they have become very old.
Therefore, the mention of "intoxicant" is used;
the intention is that if it is intoxicating, then there is a fault.
"Betel nuts, kodrava grain, and so forth"— by the word "and so forth," flat beans and others are included.
Regarding the drinking of intoxicants, there is no fault even if they do not currently possess intoxicating properties.
"Surā and maireya do not exist [as such]" means that there is a fault in drinking intoxicants that have the nature of *surā* and *maireya*.
This is because they are the basis for all negligence (*pramāda*).

Drinking intoxicants is called a "basis for negligence" because it is the ground, the locus, and the foundation for all forms of negligence, for all lapses of mindfulness, and for unwholesome acts such as taking life, which serve as their causes.
(IV.36) Regarding the phrase "because one [type] is obtained":
this is because [the path of action] is obtained from the fundamental [karmic paths] and so forth, and from those designated as pertaining to sentient beings and non-sentient beings.

The Prātimokṣa restraint is obtained from that; thereafter, the remaining two— the dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) restraints— are obtained from the fundamental, preparatory, and subsequent stages.
From unwholesome actions consisting of the fundamental, the preliminary, and the subsequent stages,

there are obtained— respectively serving as their antidotes— the informative and non-informative acts known as the Prātimokṣa vows, which possess the nature of the fundamental, preliminary, and subsequent stages.
These are directed toward entities designated as sentient or insentient, characterized by having living beings, plants, and so forth, as their objective bases.
And from actions that are reprehensible by nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), such as the taking of life or the destruction of plants and so forth.
Both of these [types of actions] have both [sentient beings and non-sentient things] as their basis;
for even an action reprehensible by nature has both sentient beings as its basis and non-sentient things as its basis.
Proscribed offenses (*prajñaptisāvadya*) also have both a basis in sentient beings (*sattvādhiṣṭhāna*) and a basis in non-sentient things (*asattvādhiṣṭhāna*).

However, one should not understand it in this way: that natural offenses (*prakṛtisāvadya*) have a basis in sentient beings, while proscribed offenses (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*) have a basis in non-sentient things.

In that regard, first, there is that which is naturally unwholesome (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) based on sentient beings, such as the killing of living beings. There is also that which is unwholesome by convention (*prajñapti-sāvadya*) based on sentient beings, such as a monk’s grasping for the hand of a woman and so forth,
as well as sleeping in the same house [as a woman] and so forth.

Taking gold and so forth is a natural offense (prakṛti-sāvadya) based on non-sentient objects. For a monk, cutting leaves and such from trees is a conventional offense (prajñapti-sāvadya) based on non-sentient objects.
Furthermore, there are instructions regarding food and other matters as stated in the Vinaya.
"Because it proceeds with the designation of a sentient being as its basis.
The intended meaning is: "Because it proceeds with the designation of a sentient being as its basis.
For only present phenomena serve as the basis for the designation of a sentient being, not those that are past or future.
Because they are like that which is non-existent;
for this very reason, he says: "Not from the past or the future."
Because they are reckoned as non-sentient beings. But is it not the case that the Prātimokṣa restraint also occurs with respect to the basis for the designation of non-sentient beings?
For there is a statement that it is obtained from those designated as both sentient and non-sentient.
And this too is not prohibited in such a way.
For just as it is said that [the acquisition] is obtained only from present things designated as sentient beings (*sattvākhya*),
so too it must be stated that it is obtained only from present things designated as non-sentient (*asattvākhya*).
For by this statement, he extends [the rule] specifically to that which has the present as its basis.
It does not apply to those [mental states] following upon preparatory effort (*prayoga*),
because in the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhitāvasthā*), there is exclusively the fundamental [meditation] (*maula*).
Furthermore, in the state of non-concentration, there is no restraint;
how much less could there be [restraint] regarding those things prohibited by designation?
This is because there is an absence of formal commitment.
"And from all times" means that because one obtains the vows (*saṃvara*) even of the past and future, just like the mind that co-exists with them;
for this very reason.
Since these restraints (saṃvara) are obtained in the manner described in detail,
a fourfold logical alternative (catuṣkoṭika) is therefore established.

"In detail" means: there exist those aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana) from which the restraints of meditative absorption (dhyāna-saṃvara) and the untainted (anāsrava-saṃvara) are obtained.
It is not the Prātimokṣa restraint. There are those [objects] from which the Prātimokṣa restraint arises, but not the meditative (dhyāna) or the outflow-free (anāsrava) restraints.
There are those from which both are obtained.
There are those.
"From which neither is obtained"—
this is the detailed meaning.
This is the first alternative (koṭi).

The restraint that consists in abstaining from the present preliminary and concluding stages of the paths of action such as taking life, as well as from prohibited offenses such as cutting down trees,
is the *prātimokṣa* restraint;
it pertains to all [three types of persons] and both [types of offenses].
Because of this statement.
However, due to being subsequent to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the meditative restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) do not exist [in that state].
Second.
The restraint from the seven fundamental paths of action—both physical and vocal, such as killing and so forth—pertaining to the past and the future, is what constitutes those two:
the dhyāna-restraint and the untainted (anāsrava) restraint.
[This applies] to the fundamentals at all times.
Because of this statement:
it is not the prātimokṣa restraint,
because [past and future factors] are past and future.
The third [case] is: from present fundamental courses of action (*maula-karmapatha*). Because they are present courses of action, there is the Prātimokṣa restraint (*saṃvara*).

And because they consist of the fundamental paths of action, the dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) restraints [are acquired] from the present. The fourth case— [acquisition] from past and future preparatory and consecutive stages— is not the prātimokṣa restraint, because those [stages] are past and future.

Because they are proximate and subsequent, the meditative (dhyāna) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) restraints do not constitute restraint from those courses of action (karmapatha) existing within one's own continuum; seeing this, he says:
"But it is not the case that at the time of acquiring the restraint, present courses of action exist.
The Master teaches that it should rather be stated: "from those courses of action which have present bases."
Because one desists from an object that cannot possibly exist in the present; therefore,
it is not [desisted] from past or present [objects].
Since these have already arisen, their restraint is not tenable;
for it is impossible to effect the non-arising of things that have already arisen.
However, it is possible [to effect the non-arising] of those that are yet to come.
The intention of the Master [Vasubandhu] is that restraint (*saṃvara*) is appropriate only for those [actual transgressions].
However, when the Vaibhāṣikas speak in that manner, their intention appears to be as follows:
the preliminary, main, and subsequent stages of the Prātimokṣa restraint proceed respectively for the purpose of restraining the preliminary, main, and subsequent stages of killing and so forth.
