"These [defilements] shall not proceed. In effect, these antidotes arise as if obstructing those [defilements]. The preparatory application (prayoga) is as if it were saying to the [defilement]: "I am obstructing you."
"Do not rise.
In this manner, up to:
"When asked about his back, he speaks as if it were his back"—this is how it should be applied.

Likewise, when one obstructs the present aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—which possess the nature of the preliminary, principal, and subsequent stages of the paths of action—one obtains [the restraint] from those present [factors];
this is called the Prātimokṣa restraint.
Therefore, it should not be stated in that manner.
(IV.37) "Someone [obtains it] from all," and so forth. The bhikṣu restraint is obtained from all paths of action; the meaning is that all paths of action are to be avoided.
Someone from four;
that is, other than those.
"Other than those" means other than the bhikṣu restraint.

The restraint of a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) and so forth is obtained from exactly four factors: from the three bodily [actions], such as taking life, and from the one vocal [action], which is false speech—
provided that non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are the causes.
The causes of restraint are held to be twofold:
either non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion as the causes;
or weak, medium, and intense states of mind.
If the first formulation is intended,
then restraint is obtained through all the causes, which have non-attachment and so forth as their intrinsic nature,
because they exist simultaneously in the wholesome motivating mind.
If weak and other grades of mind are accepted as the causes,
[the fruit] is obtained through a single cause,
because they do not exist simultaneously.
"The final alternative" refers to the position [asserting] weak and other [degrees of] causes.
"There is one who abides in restraint," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
It is "restrained toward all sentient beings" because restraint arises when there is a virtuous intention that extends toward all sentient beings.

It is not [restrained] by way of all its constituent parts (*aṅga*), because the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and others do not involve abstention from every single part. Nor is it [restrained] by way of all its causes (*kāraṇa*), because causes such as the weak (*mṛdu*) and so forth cannot exist simultaneously.
The monastic restraint (*bhikṣu-saṃvara*), however, consists of all its constituent parts, because it involves abstention from every aspect.
This refers to one who undertakes the three restraints with a threefold state of mind.

For example: one undertakes the lay follower’s restraint (upāsaka-saṃvara) with a weak mind; the novice monk’s restraint (śrāmaṇera-saṃvara) with a medium mind; and the fully ordained monk’s restraint (bhikṣu-saṃvara) with a superior mind.
"And by all the causes, but not by all the limbs.
This is because each of the vows, such as that of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), has only one cause at a time, such as being weak (*mṛdu*) and so forth.
"Taking [the vow] in that manner" means:
For one who undertakes [the precepts] through the performance of the fivefold restriction.
How [is it said], "from those who are impossible"?
Those who simply cannot be killed.

How is there the acquisition of restraint (*saṃvara*) with respect to those beings who are impossible [to protect]? On this point, the Master states the resolution: "Because of the undertaking [of the vow] with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) not to harm the life of any living being."
Because, with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), one undertakes the restraint (*saṃvara*) through the non-violation of the lives of all sentient beings.
The Vaibhāṣikas also state another answer to this very question:
"If, however, [it were] only toward those who are capable," and so forth.
It would be subject to increase and decrease:
when sentient beings become capable [of restraint], their restraint would accumulate;
when they become incapable, it would diminish.
Because there is mutual transition between those who are capable and those who are incapable—namely, humans and so forth, and gods and so forth.
Gods and others transition into the state of humans and so forth; humans and others transition into the state of gods and so forth.
Seeing that this Vaibhāṣika rebuttal is open to objection, the Master says:
"It will not be thus," and so forth.
That is to say, the restraint will not be characterized by such increase and decrease.
How so?
Just as when grass and other plants arise for the first time,
or when grass and other plants wither away.
Even though restraint (saṃvara) is obtained even from grass and such things, nevertheless there is neither increase nor decrease of that restraint.
Likewise, even when there is a transition between what is possible and what is impossible, there would be no increase or decrease— that is to say, no accumulation or diminution.
"Therefore, restraint is obtained only with respect to those [beings] who are capable [of being harmed]. And this fault would not arise," so say the Vaibhāṣikas.
"It is not for the sake of sentient beings," and so forth.
It is not thus, as has been stated in detail: "just as when there is the production of previously non-existent grass and so on," and so on.
What is the reason? Because sentient beings exist both before and after their migration [to another realm],
whereas grasses, shrubs, creepers, and the like do not exist either before or after.
Therefore, the fault of accumulation and depletion is not averted by the example of grass and so forth.
Thus, only a mere dissimilarity has been stated; it does not serve the purpose of establishing the probandum by means of the probans.
The Teacher, however, says:
"When they have entered final nirvāṇa, they do not exist at all," and so forth.
Therefore, the former reason alone is correct.
"Because it is undertaken with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) not to harm the life of any sentient being.
Therefore, it is established that restraint (*saṃvara*) is obtained from those beings who are capable [of harming] as well as those who are incapable.
If that is so, then if the Prātimokṣa restraint is obtained from all sentient beings...
Because he does not encounter those Buddhas who have previously entered parinirvāṇa, there would be a deficiency in his ethical discipline (*śīla*),
due to the fact that sentient beings are fewer than before.
The Master says:
Because there is no distinction among all Buddhas— whether arisen previously or later— in their bestowing [benefits] upon all sentient beings.
For if they too had not entered final nirvana,
one would have obtained [the merit] from them even now.
"From all paths of action" means from those that are physical and vocal;
for there is no non-restraint (asaṃvara) that is incomplete.
"By the taking of life alone, and not by taking what is not given," and so forth.
"Endowed with only a weak non-restraint" means because it was previously acquired.
But by means of an intense informative act (*vijñapti*) of taking life—
what?—
the phrase "is possessed of" (*samanvāgata*) continues [to apply].
There is no distinction in the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
In this way, it should be applied to the medium and superior degrees as well:
namely, one who acquires non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) with a mind of medium intensity.

Thus, even when depriving a living being of life with an intense state of mind, one is endowed only with a middling non-restraint, but with an intense informative act of taking life. In this way, for one who acts with an intense state of mind up to the point of an intense [intention], one is endowed only with an intense non-restraint.
And by means of an intense informative act of taking life.
It should also be applied in this way:
one who acquires non-restraint with an intense mind.
Even when depriving living beings of life with a mild mind, one becomes endowed with an intense non-restraint (*asaṃvara*);
however, the informative act (*vijñapti*) of taking life is mild, and so forth.
*Nāgabandhas* are elephant-keepers.
"Trappers" (vāgurikāḥ): there is a species of living being called *paṃpā*, known as the "snare-beast" (*vāgura*); those who kill it are trappers.
"In substance, they are those who possess non-restraint (*āsaṃvarika*).
Kings and judges, although not explicitly mentioned here because they exercise authority as administrators of punishment, should be understood as being indeed those who possess non-restraint.
The same should be applied to others as well.
"Those who kill chickens are called *kaurkuṭika*s," and so forth.
Having first explained at length that this is indeed logical, [the author] asks: "How is it appropriate for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) to exist toward all sentient beings?"
The Vaibhāṣika states the rebuttal:
"For [one would also [not kill] one's mother and so forth," and so on in detail.
The Teacher says:
For it is not the case that they are simply those very same persons;
if one were to kill them while knowing "these are my mother and so forth," how could non-restraint (asaṃvara) be appropriate toward those who are not to be killed?
Furthermore, for those who have become noble ones (ārya), there is no possibility of becoming animals again.
Since it is impossible for them to be reborn as sheep and so forth,
how could they possess non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) with respect to those?
Or, if one were to consider future existences— thinking that they will become sheep and so forth— then there would be non-restraint toward their present mother and others.
"Even though those sheep have become their own sons in a future birth, the butchers would not kill them in every way;
thus, there would be no non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) toward those sheep.
The Vaibhāṣika says:
"How indeed could it be [the case] for those wishing to kill? and so forth.
The Teacher says:
"This is the same with respect to one's mother and others," and so forth.
For how indeed could there be non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) toward those mothers and others for butchers and the like, who do not intend to kill those who have become their sons and so forth?
It would be incomplete as a constituent part of the path of action (*karmapatha*),
and it would also be merely partial (*prādeśika*).
Because not even a single factor has been abandoned;
for, due to the application of restrictions regarding sentient beings, place, time, and occasion, there is only partial abstinence,
and the restraint is likewise [partial].
It may be incomplete or partial, except for the eightfold Prātimokṣa restraint mentioned previously.
Why is this? He says:
"Because of the mutual obstruction of mere morality and immorality":
non-restraint obstructs mere morality,
and restraint obstructs mere immorality.
(IV.38) "By those born into that family" means by those born into a family of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
[This occurs] through the field, the taking up [of the object], and the lack of respect.
Thus:
"earnest effort" (*ādarehana*) means the undertaking of action. The compound is [formed as] *kṣetra* (field), *ādāna* (appropriation), and *ādarehana* (earnest effort).
Therefore, non-informative action (avijñapti) arises.
"On the [specific] lunar day," and so forth;
this refers to the meal on that lunar day.
The meaning is "up to a fortnight's meal.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the drawing of mandalas and so forth is included; or, it means "with such care," that is, by way of intense affliction (*tīvrakleśatā*).
The meaning is: "by virtue of intense faith.
Regarding the phrase "because of the arising of an informative act (*vijñapti*) contrary to the undertaking":
this refers to the undertaking [of a vow] such as, "For as long as life lasts, I shall abstain from taking life and so forth."
Because of the arising of a consciousness that is contrary to it.
Thus, by the first cause, there is the abandonment of the *prātimokṣa* restraint.
[The phrase] "due to the abandonment of the basis" means:
Because of the abandonment of that basis upon which the restraint was undertaken—
namely, death—
it is abandoned through this second cause.
"Because of the transformation of the basis" means that the basis by which the restraint was undertaken no longer remains as it was.
"Because of agitation"—
this is the third reason for its abandonment.
"Because of cutting off the root cause."
The causal basis consists of the roots of merit. Through their severance,
that [basis] is abandoned by the fourth cause.
"And because of the projection for exactly that long.
The projection of the fasting restraint (*upavāsasaṃvara*) lasts for one day and night.
Thus, by this fifth cause, there is the relinquishing of that fasting restraint.
"And by the four previously mentioned causes. And "by a cause involving a downfall" means: by these five aforementioned causes and by a cause involving a downfall.
That by which one falls is "falling" (*patanīya*).
It is fourfold: unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*), [lying, stealing, and killing].
Taking what has not been given in the measure previously described;
the killing of a human being;
and false speech concerning superhuman qualities (uttarimanuṣyadharma).
However, the Kashmiris maintain that for one who has fallen into misfortune, it is like wealth and debt;
this is established through both scripture and reasoning.
Of these, the scripture is as follows:
It is stated in the Vinaya:
"If a monk who is of immoral conduct instructs a nun, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
For it is a monk who has committed a *pārājika* offense who is intended here as "one of immoral conduct" (*duḥśīla*),
not one who has not committed a *pārājika*.
This is understood from the statement made by way of contrast, namely that one who remains in their natural state is "virtuous" (*śīlavat*).
"Even though he is of immoral conduct, he still possesses the status of a monk,
because it is said that 'he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense'.
This is also logical, for it is not reasonable that the abandonment of the entire vow should follow from the disturbance of a single part.
"Even for one who has committed a fundamental offense" means even for one who has committed an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*). "Nor indeed any other offense" likewise refers to this.
"Saṃghāvaśeṣa and so forth.
"When it has been made manifest" means when it has been confessed.

Regarding what was said by the Blessed One, [the text continues] in detail up to "defeated": the phrase "how is that? is to be supplied. This was said with reference to the state of being a monk in the ultimate sense (*paramārthabhikṣutva*).
Because one who has committed that offense is incapable of seeing the truth, he does not attain the state of a bhikṣu in the ultimate sense.

The meaning of the statement is that, knowing that even through a fundamental offense (maulyāpatti) the status of a bhikṣu is not destroyed, those with many afflictions—such as Nanda and others—might commit it; thus, there is the "bhikṣu by designation" (saṃjñābhikṣu).

One who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) but whose name is "Bhikṣu" is a "Bhikṣu by profession" (pratijñābhikṣu). One who engages in unchaste conduct and so forth is "one of immoral conduct" (duḥśīla).
"One who begs is a bhikṣu," meaning a mendicant;
or, "one is a bhikṣu because of having shattered the afflictions."
"I am an Arhat. Regarding this matter, it refers to that which was stated by the Blessed One in detail: "He is no longer a monk, he is no longer a śramaṇa," and so forth.
In this sense:
this fifth person, who has received full ordination through the formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha*), is indeed distinct from the four types of monks previously mentioned.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that this was stated with reference to the state of being a monk in the ultimate sense (*paramārthabhikṣutva*)—that too is so.
To this he replies:
Nor was he previously a monk in the ultimate sense,
such that he would later become a non-monk.
Because of the statement, "He is no longer a monk, he is no longer a śramaṇa," [the author] makes a comparison;
one should connect this by understanding that the treatise itself has provided the answer by making the comparison to a palm tree whose head has been cut off.
The meaning is that the question has been answered. The connection is as follows: the consumption of a single mouthful of food [constitutes] the use of sustenance;
the treading upon a single area the size of a heel [constitutes] the use of a dwelling.

"And excluded from all communal enjoyment with the monks by the Teacher" means that he has been excluded by the Buddha from all communal enjoyment with the monks, such as eating in the same row and so forth.
"Destroy the *kāraṇḍavaka*! [is said].
The *kāraṇḍavaka* is a specific kind of grass called "barley" because it has the shape of barley;
it is that which is called *yavadūṣī*.
In the same way, this person is a non-monk who merely has the appearance of a monk (*bhikṣvākṛti*).
*Kaśambaka* is the name for rotten wood.
In this way, that monk has become rotten.
"Expel him from the community of those who possess virtuous conduct," the Blessed One commanded the monks.
"Then, let them drive away the *utplāvī*.

A *utplāvī* is simply a grain of rice that lacks the inner kernel within the husk; likewise, this person is one who lacks the essence of virtue (*śīla-sāra*) while possessing only the outward form of a monk.
"Flow it forth" means "cause it to emerge.
The one who has conquered the path is the learner (śaikṣa) and the one beyond learning (aśaikṣa).
The Buddha is the teacher of the path.
A virtuous monk lives by the path because he lives for the sake of the path.
One who defiles the path is one of immoral conduct.
This is the illustration here:
"burnt wood," and so forth.
Just as that which has been burnt [is no longer wood].
That is not wood;
rather, because it shares the common characteristic of being reduced to nothing more than the mere form of the previous wood,
that which has been burned is called "wood."
Even when a pond has dried up, it is still called a "pond. A "parrot-beak" (*śukanāsā*) is a structure made by a mason on houses and other buildings;
it is called a "parrot-beak" because it has the shape of a parrot's beak.
Thus, this person is called a "śramaṇa" because only the mere commonality of the form of a monk remains.
A rotten seed is called a "seed" even though it is not a seed, because it does not produce a sprout;
likewise, a fire-brand circle is called a "wheel" because only its shape remains.
Because it has the shape of a wheel.
Furthermore, a deceased being, although no longer a living being (*asattva*), is still called a "being" (*sattva*),
because only the mere form of a being remains.
It should be viewed in the same way.
A monk called a *śikṣādattaka* (one granted the training) has committed unchaste conduct with a woman due to excessive passion.

Immediately thereafter, having become filled with remorse, thinking "Alas, a grievous thing has been done by me," he approaches the community of monks and confesses this evil deed, even though not a single thought of concealment has arisen.
"It has been done.
Because he performs disciplinary acts—such as being placed at the end of all the junior monks—by the instruction of the Noble Saṃgha, he is called one "given the training" (śikṣādattaka).
Therefore, if he were indeed not a monk due to his immorality, [this would be inconsistent].
He would not [be so].
For he is not ordained again;
yet he is established as a monk.
"Therefore, one does not cease to be a monk due to immorality.
"We do not say so," and so forth;
we do not say this.
Not everyone becomes one who has committed a defeat (pārājika) merely through the transgression of unchaste conduct;
rather,
it is by means of the intention to conceal it.
Why, then, is he not ordained? The phrase "one who has not abandoned the training" must be supplied [to complete the sense].
This is because he has been corrupted by intense lack of moral shame (*anapatrāpya*).
His mental continuum has been corrupted by intense lack of moral dread (*anapatrāpya*).
Because his continuum has been thus corrupted, he is incapable of the restraint (*saṃvara*);
therefore, the point is that he is not to be ordained again.
But it is certainly not with regard to his status as a monk;
nor is he refused ordination simply because he no longer possesses the status of a monk. For even one who has committed a defeat (pārājika) and has relinquished the training is not ordained.
Because the continuum has been corrupted by intense lack of moral dread.
(IV.41) "Attained through meditative absorption" means:
What is intended is both that which has the nature of form (*rūpasvabhāva*) and that which does not have the nature of form (*arūpasvabhāva*).
For this very reason, he explains [the text] as "all indeed.
[He says] "by two."
Either by way of rebirth or by way of falling away.
Therefore he said, "or by way of rebirth," and so forth.
When being reborn in a higher realm, one abandons the lower;

and when being reborn in a lower realm, one [abandons] that which belongs to the upper stage. Alternatively, through falling away from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), the wholesome state comprised within that attainment is abandoned.
"And by the abandonment of the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) [one abandons] something.
This refers to the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) that were produced during the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), up to the level of patience (kṣānti).
Even in the absence of a change of plane (bhūmisaṃcāra), they are abandoned through the abandonment of the homogeneous class.
When one dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is reborn in that very same place,
for it will be said:
"The Noble One (*ārya*) abandons those [attainments] through the loss of the level (*bhūmi*), but the Non-Noble One (*anārya*) abandons them through death."
Thus,
the "prior path" refers to the path of the candidate (*pratipannaka-mārga*),
which has the nature of the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), uninterruptedness (*ānantarya-mārga*), and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
"Is it the fruit or something superior to the fruit?"—
the subsequent path is the subject under discussion.
For example, if a non-returner (anāgāmin) should fall away from the fruit of non-returning.
Therefore, the higher path leading to the fruit of non-returning is abandoned.
However, if a non-returner attains the second dhyāna and subsequently falls away from it, [the same applies].
That path of his, distinguished by its fruit, belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, is abandoned.
(IV.42ab) "By the power of causes and conditions" means by the power of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).

The meaning is "by the power of another's voice. It says "one obtains either the meditative restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara)," but it is not said that one obtains the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara).
Because that [non-restraint] is abandoned precisely by the prior arising of the restraint of dhyāna.
Regarding "the intention not to act":

even if one abandons weapons and nets out of the intention, "I shall not perform this action," there is no cutting off of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) without the formal undertaking of restraint (*saṃvara*).
It is just as follows: even when the cause of a disease has been avoided, that fully developed disease does not cease without medicine;
it is like that.
This is what is meant.
"When there is a desire to abandon non-restraint, restraint must be undertaken, and not otherwise. Regarding "the acquisition of that":
it refers to the acquisition of non-restraint.
(IV.42cd) How can it be non-informative (*avijñapti*)?
It should be stated that it is also informative (*vijñapti*).
This is because there is an interruption of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the past informative action produced by oneself at that very moment.
However, one should read: "But by means of the cutting off of momentum, undertaking, action, object, life, and roots, it is intermediate.
The meaning is that it is neither restraint nor non-restraint.

Furthermore, even though only the non-informative (avijñapti) is mentioned, one must state the reason for not mentioning the informative (vijñapti); thus it is said: because the informative is not necessary.
For it will be stated thus:
"The unwholesome [karmas] are six; non-informative action is of two kinds; one is of two kinds."
And since the statement regarding informative action (*vijñapti*) is established by the mention of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), that [informative action] is not mentioned.
Others, however, say:

"There is no continuous acquisition (*prāpti*) following an informative action that has ceased and is comprised within neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint; therefore, this cause for abandonment is stated only with respect to non-informative action."

"Like the movement of a potter’s wheel and an arrow. This means that just as the movement of a potter’s wheel and an arrow is projected by a specific formative force (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*), so too [is this movement].
Through its severance, that too is severed;
it is just like that.
"Enough with this undertaking" refers to the words of renunciation.
"Regarding 'one who does not act according to what has been undertaken':
for example, having resolved, 'I shall not eat without first bowing to the Buddha' or 'without having prepared a mandala.'"
For one who consumes [the food] without having performed that [act], that intermediate non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is severed.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "machines, nets, and so forth," weapons, poison, and the like are included.
He begins to utterly sever the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*).

It is shown that it is severed precisely at the stage of beginning the severance of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*), and not at the stage when they have already been severed. (IV.43) [This refers to] wholesome form (*kuśalarūpa*).
Thus [it is said].

The mention of "formless" (arūpa) is because the cutting off of form (rūpaccheda) has already been stated; [the cutting off occurs] through the severance of the roots and through birth in a higher realm.
Thus it is said.
In this context, it should be stated that "some [faculties] are also [defined] by way of dispassion (*vairāgya*)," such as the wholesome faculty of mental displeasure (*daurmanasyendriya*).
"All" refers to that which belongs to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
"The path of abandonment" refers to that which is the path of relinquishment.
The path of seeing and the path of cultivation,
whether mundane or supramundane according to the case;
this [path] is together with its retinue.

This type of secondary affliction (upakleśa), together with its co-existent acquisitions (prāpti) and attendants, is what is referred to by the phrase "of the type of secondary affliction. The inclusion of the term "secondary affliction" is for the purpose of encompassing everything, since even primary afflictions (kleśa) are included under the category of secondary afflictions.
For it is stated in the treatise:
"Whatever are primary afflictions are also secondary afflictions; however, there may be secondary afflictions that are not primary afflictions."
(IV.44, 45) "Based on both," and so forth.
This is because the affliction characterized by the disposition of a woman or a man is excessive,
and because analytical reflection— characterized by the cultivation of its antidote— is incapable [of overcoming it].
Because they lack intense shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*), they possess no restraint (*saṃvara*).
This is because non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) exists as the direct opposite (*pratidvaṃdva*) of restraint; that is, since non-restraint stands in opposition to restraint.
Therefore, where there is restraint,
there alone is non-restraint. The absence of non-restraint in those such as eunuchs and others is the second reason.
"Because of the absence of undertaking and meditative concentration.
Due to the absence of undertaking, there is no *prātimokṣa* restraint;
and due to the absence of meditative concentration, the restraints of meditation (*dhyāna*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) do not exist.
The absence of that [non-restraint], however, is due to dullness and the lack of proficiency in wholesome states;
and because of the absence of the intention to perform evil deeds, there is no non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
It is through connection with which, and by the destruction of which, [it arises].
Through the possession of which sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*), and through the destruction of which sense of shame and dread of blame,
restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) would respectively come to be—
that intense sense of shame and dread of blame does not exist for those belonging to the miserable realms (*āpāyika*).
If there are neither restraint nor non-restraint for those in the miserable realms (apāya),
then how is it that what was stated at length in the Sūtra is to be understood?
How is that so?
The Prātimokṣa restraint belongs only to humans,
not to gods,
because of the absence of spiritual urgency (asaṃvega) among them.

The meditative and uncontaminated restraints, however, arise respectively from causes, actions, dharmas, and cultivation, as applicable; they are both temporary and ultimate, provided that their maturation is desirable. (IV.46ab) "Temporary" and "ultimate" refer to that which has a desirable maturation.
It is secure because it provides protection from suffering at that very time;
it is that which leads to the attainment of nirvana.
Because it provides ultimate protection from suffering, it is secure (*kṣema*);
for one who has attained final nirvāṇa (*parinirvṛta*), there is no suffering at any time.
(IV.46cd, 47) But was it not stated by the Blessed One that the first three meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are "with agitation" (*seṃjita*)?
"That which is here thought and deliberated upon," and so forth—
this is what the Noble Ones call "movement" (*iñjita*) in this context.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the second [type of movement] is indicated.
That which is here an undiminished joy—
this, the Noble Ones call "agitation" (iñjita) in this context.
Even in the third [dhyāna], that which is here "happiness, happiness"— this is the mental application (cetasa ābhoga).
"This is what the Noble Ones call 'the immovable' (*iñjita*) here.

Now, why is it that all wholesome karma belonging to the realms of form (*rūpāvacara*) and formlessness (*ārūpyāvacara*) is said to be "immovable" (*āniñjya*)? He says: "Because it leads to immovable conditions."

The meaning is: "with reference to the path that partakes of conformity to the immovable (āniñjya) and partakes of conformity to the unshakable (akaṃpya). But what is the reason that, although it is actually "moving" due to being accompanied by the defects of concentration (samādhi-sapakṣāla), it is described elsewhere as "immovable"? To this he says:
Because, in those stages, karma does not waver with respect to its maturation;
thus, it is said that it leads to enjoyments and so forth.
"Enjoyment" refers to the excellence of material wealth.
By the word "etcetera," such things as beauty and a melodious voice are included.
"That very [karma]" is the full expression;
that which would ripen among the gods.
Having cultivated extensively that which consists of morality and that which consists of cultivation,
it occurs to him: "O, would that I might be reborn in the company of those who are fortunate among the gods or those who are fortunate among humans!"

"Up until he is reborn there" (IV.48–50). Regarding "the desire realm and the three dhyānas": in the desire realm and the first dhyāna, bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*) and mental joy (*caitasika-saumanasya*) constitute pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*).
In the second dhyāna, mental gladness (*saumanasya*) is the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*);
in the third dhyāna, it is mental pleasure (*caitasika-sukha*).
This is for the purpose of making known that state.
By that word, "suffering" (duḥkha) is intended.
The inclusion of the word "here" (iha) is for the purpose of making known that this suffering exists specifically in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
[The phrase] "together with their equipment" (sasaṃbhāraiḥ) [is used].
"Accumulation" (*saṃbhāra*) is that by which something is gathered or produced;
it is characterized by the sense faculties, their objects, and their bases. Feeling, together with its accumulation, is the fruit.
"Because it is the maturation of the intermediate dhyāna":
when there is the arising of the intermediate dhyāna, it must be experienced as the maturation of the karma of the intermediate dhyāna.
In that state, there is neither pleasant nor painful feeling.
Therefore, its maturation is a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant.
Even below the fourth dhyāna, there exists karma to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Alternatively, in the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), it would not be possible for there to be the experience that is the ripening of some other karma;
for it is not tenable to say that the ripening of karma belonging to the level of the fundamental first dhyāna—which is to be experienced as pleasure—occurs in the intermediate dhyāna.
Because the fundamental [dhyāna] is inferior to the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara) due to its possession of applied thought (savitarka),

it is not [the result] of karma belonging to the desire realm that is to be experienced as suffering, because of the difference in level (bhūmyantara). For this very reason, it is also not [the result] of karma belonging to the levels of the fourth dhyāna and so forth.
Furthermore, because of the absence of passion (*vītarāgatva*),

some maintain that— desiring to avoid this fault— the maturation (*vipāka*) of the karma of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) specifically within the [first] dhyāna itself.
Others maintain that the maturation (*vipāka*) of that karma of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is not feeling at all; rather, it is form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Do they mean that there is no feeling for those born in the intermediate dhyāna?
It exists,
but it does not have the nature of maturation (vipāka).
What then?
"Regarding the term 'outflow' (naiṣyandikī):
on this point, the Master says,
'This [position] contradicts the treatise.'"
Regarding that which was stated:
"The maturation of the karma of the intermediate dhyāna is the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) in the dhyāna itself," and that which was also stated: [the rest of the passage].
"Its maturation is not feeling at all.
Both of these [positions] are contrary to the treatise.
Demonstrating this, he says:
"For it is stated in the treatise," and so forth. "Of action without vitarka" means of the action of the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).

Therefore, because of the restriction that "only mental feeling ripens as the maturation (vipāka) of wholesome non-discursive (avitarka) karma," it is understood that for such karma, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is neither its maturation exclusively within the dhyānas,
nor is it something other than feeling.
For non-discursive karma exists from the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) upward.
"Neither prior nor subsequent" means neither before nor after.
The meaning is "simultaneously.
The form [object] of that which is to be experienced as pleasure refers to the eye and so forth;
the mind and mental factors [are the objects] of that which is to be experienced as suffering.
Those associated with the five groups of consciousness [are neutral], because mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) is not a result of maturation (*avipāka*).
Those associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanīya*) are dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*).
The life-faculty and so forth do not exist elsewhere than in the desire realm, because karma to be experienced as suffering does not exist elsewhere. What, then, is that?
"To be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
"In that case, then," and so forth.
If there exists wholesome karma to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant even below the fourth dhyāna, [then the following applies].

This contradicts the statement that "wholesome [karma] up to the third dhyāna is to be experienced as pleasure," for it is not only wholesome [karma] up to the third dhyāna that is to be experienced as pleasure.
What then?
[The opponent argues: "There is also [karma] to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
This contradicts the statement that "wholesome [karma] has a desirable ripening."
For wholesome [karma] is not only that which has a desirable maturation; there is also wholesome [karma] whose maturation is the opposite of both desirable and undesirable.
This teaching is "predominant" (bāhulika); the meaning is that it is taught in this way by way of what is most frequent.
That which is to be experienced as pleasure is wholesome up to the third dhyāna;
and that which is wholesome has a desirable maturation.
But how is it that [feeling] does not have the nature of feeling? Having observed that pleasure is experienced and not karma, he asks this.
"Conducive to pleasant feeling" (*sukhavedanīya*) means that which is beneficial for pleasant feeling;
the meaning is that it is favorable to the arising of pleasant feeling.
Alternatively, it means that pleasant feeling is to be experienced by this [object].
The meaning is that its ripening is to be experienced as pleasant.
"Like bathing powder" means,
for example, that by which one bathes.
That is a decoction fit for bathing.
Likewise, that karma by which one experiences a pleasant ripening is "to-be-experienced" (vedanīya).
Karma that is to be experienced as the ripening of pleasure is "to-be-experienced-as-pleasure" (*sukha-vedanīya*).
This is because the gerundive suffix (*kṛtya*) may also be used in the sense of the agent.
It is the same for "to-be-experienced-as-pain" (*duḥkha-vedanīya*).
That which is associated with painful feeling is "to be felt as pain"; this should be applied in detail as before.
The same applies to that which is to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
This refers to "to be felt by way of intrinsic nature."
The nature of being felt is characterized by the experience of feeling its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In this way, it should be applied up to "being felt through manifestation" (*saṃmukhībhāvena vedanīyatā*).
[Thus,] there is contact to be felt as pleasant (*sukhavedanīyaḥ sparśaḥ*).

"Conducive to pleasant feeling" means that because there is pleasure to be felt (*vedanīya*) within this [contact], it is "contact conducive to pleasant feeling" (*sukhavedanīya-sparśa*). Regarding "to be felt as an object" (*ālambana-vedanīyatā*): the objects (*viṣaya*) are what are to be felt.
The meaning is that they are to be taken as objects. "Experiencing form, but not experiencing passion for form" means that one experiences form directly.
The meaning is that he does not experience desire for form (*rūparāga*). Alternatively, it means that he does not experience or take form as an object (*ālambate*) through desire.
"To be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*)—this is the sense.
"Visible-in-this-life-experience" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) refers to karma whose characteristic is ripening (*vipāka*) that is to be experienced in the present life; this is the full explanation.
"At which time," and so forth: at which time one experiences (*vedayate*), that is, undergoes (*anubhavati*), a pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*).
At that time, two of his feelings— namely, the painful and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant— have ceased.
(IV.51) "By virtue of its commencement" means by virtue of the commencement of maturation (*vipāka*) in this very life.
"The establishment of its name" means the establishment of the name "to be experienced in the present life.
"For there exists," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
The example of *suvarcalā* refers to action whose fruit is proximate;
barley, wheat, and so forth refer to action whose fruit is remote. The *dārṣṭāntikas* are the *Sautrāntikas*.
For those who describe the first and second alternatives in this way, karma is of eight types:
[karma] to be experienced in the present life is both determinate and indeterminate with respect to its maturation;
and so on, up to [karma] to be experienced indeterminately.
Karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) is both determinate and indeterminate with respect to its maturation (*vipāka*).
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) is likewise both determinate and indeterminate.
Karma to be experienced indeterminately (*aniyatavedanīya*) refers to that which is indeterminate as to whether it will be experienced in the present life or at other times.
That is both determinate and indeterminate;
thus, there are eight types.
(IV.52, 53) It is said that karma may project four types [of births].
The meaning is that one might project fourfold karma—karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth.
How so? He says:
it may be that in the case of the three [actions]—killing, taking what is not given, and false speech—one employs another, while in the case of sexual misconduct, one applies oneself personally.
When those karmas reach completion simultaneously—

where one is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), another in the next birth (*upapadyavedanīya*), another in a subsequent lifetime (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), and yet another is of indefinite timing (*aniyatavedanīya*)—
this applies to both wholesome and unwholesome [karmas] as the case may be.
Where unwholesome [states] arise is only in the desire realm and nowhere else;
yet they exist in all realms of existence (gati).
This is the exception to that general rule:
"In the hells, wholesome [karma] is of three kinds.
The restriction is that it is *only* of three kinds.
In the hells, there is the projection of only three kinds of wholesome karma,
not four kinds,
with the exception of that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
In these hells, because there is an absence of desirable maturation (*iṣṭavipāka*),
the term "wholesome" (*śubha*) is employed for the purpose of excluding the unwholesome.
For it is possible for all four types of unwholesome karma to project rebirth in the hells.
"One who is detached from that is a steadfast fool.
The compound *yadvirakta* is analyzed as "detached from which" (*yataḥ viraktaḥ*).
The inclusion of the term "stable" (*sthira*) is for the purpose of excluding those of a nature subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*),
for such a person may indeed possess karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) in that particular realm.
The inclusion of the term "fool" (*bāla*) is for the purpose of excluding the noble ones (*ārya*).
For an Noble One (ārya), neither karma to be experienced upon rebirth (upapadyavedanīya) nor karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparaparyāyavedanīya) is possible there,
because he is a Non-returner (anāgāmin). Thus,
a Noble One does not create karma to be experienced in other [future] lives.
Nor does one perform [karma] to be experienced in a subsequent life;
nor does one perform [karma] to be experienced upon rebirth—this is the meaning.
Showing the reasoning for this, he says:

For he is not capable of returning again to a lower plane. Indeed, this noble one, who is of a nature not subject to falling away, cannot possibly return from the level where he has become free from passion to a lower or lower-level plane.
But one of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman) is capable [of being reborn there].
For example:
a noble one who has attained the peak of existence (bhavāgra) and is of the nature of falling away, who, having fallen away, would be reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
For him, karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) are also possible, as stated in the Udāyi-sūtra.

"He would perform indeterminate [karma]" means that even a noble one (*ārya*) of the nature of non-retrogression (*aparihāṇadharman*) may perform indeterminate karma to be experienced, as well as karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) in the very place where he has been born.
In that regard, one should act as follows:
"one who is free from passion for either the desire realm or the peak of existence.
This refers to a non-returner (anāgāmin) who is free from passion for the desire realm.
One who is free from passion for the peak of existence is an Arhat.
"Of those two" refers to the desire realm and the peak of existence. We shall explain this later.
"One who has fallen away from the fruit does not die," and so forth;
[this refers to] that which is to be experienced in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
What?
It is both determinate and indeterminate.
That which is determinate has been described as being of eleven kinds.
"Regarding that which is to be experienced in the present life":
this refers to karma that is fixed as to be experienced in the *kalala* stage, up to karma that is fixed as to be experienced in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
And "those ten stages which follow it" refers to the subsequent states.
The meaning is that [the states] are preceded by the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
For this very reason, no other karma to be experienced in the intermediate state has been mentioned.
Karma is of four kinds.

It was not mentioned here that karma is of four types—namely, to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*), to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), and to be experienced indeterminately (*aniyatavedanīya*)—because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is projected by the very same karma that is to be experienced upon rebirth.
Since it has been stated that karma is both determinate and indeterminate, he now says: [IV.55]
"But what kind of karma is determinate?"— this is the full statement.

"One who has attained a specific fruit or attainment" means that one who has attained the fruit of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and one who has attained the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*) are considered to have attained a specific fruit.
The inclusion of the term "distinguished" (viśeṣa) is for the purpose of including the fruits obtained through the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
One who has attained a distinguished meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) is one who has acquired the attainments of cessation (*nirodha*), restraint (*āraṇā*), and loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Here too, the inclusion of the term "distinguished" is for the purpose of distinguishing these from other mundane (*laukika*) meditative absorptions.
"Whether in such a way or otherwise" means:
whether by the thought of merit or by hatred and so forth;
for even a Persian who kills his mother with the thought that it is an act of merit [commits a grave offense].
Or [if one kills] one's father.
Thus, that unwholesome action of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma) becomes determinate; no other [action does so].
That which is the opposite of this—namely, that performed with weak afflictions, with faith, and so forth.
(IV.56) Regarding "due to addressing the Saṅgha as 'women'":
it is said that a certain monk, having been defeated in a legal dispute, addressed the Saṅgha, saying, "You are women."
In that very life, his male characteristics disappeared and female characteristics appeared.
Thus, due to the excellence of the field, this [karma] becomes to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya).
"Due to a particular intention (*āśaya-viśeṣāt*).
Śaṇṭha, seeing that the castration of the oxen was about to be carried out, thought, "I too suffer such impotence," and with a powerful intention, he liberated those oxen from their castration.
In this very life, the male organ appeared to him.
This has become karma to be experienced in the present life due to a particular intention;
that is, because of the complete detachment from that level.
Then, due to absolute detachment from that level, even that karma which was to be experienced in a future life becomes one to be experienced in the present life.
This is as in the case of non-returners and arhats, who perform actions while still in a state of non-detachment [from lower levels];
because they do not return to a lower level and because they attain parinirvāṇa without further grasping.
But not in terms of state (*avasthā*). That which is indeterminate with respect to states such as the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*) and so forth,
is not indeterminate with respect to its maturation (*vipāka*).
Because it is fixed,
that very [karma] becomes to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya). For this very reason, he said:

Furthermore, that which is fixed to ripen in another state, such as the present life (dṛṣṭadharma) and so forth, has its maturation in that very state; for one who possesses such karma, absolute detachment (atyantavairāgya) is impossible.
The meaning is that, because of such karma whose ripening is fixed to another state, it is impossible for a person possessing such karma to ever become detached from that stage.
(IV.57) Since it was stated [above] that this occurs "due to a particular field," he asks:
"What kind of field, then, is it?"
"Of one who has emerged from the state of non-contention (araṇā)," and so forth.
It is the resolute intention (adhyāśaya) or purpose (abhiprāya) that is beneficial toward immeasurable sentient beings through non-contention;
it is accompanied by that.
By means of that which is exceedingly exalted and sharp,
the mental continuum proceeds, permeated and followed by immeasurable merit.
He will explain *araṇā* later on.
Regarding the phrase "the knowledge resulting from prayer and the absence of conflict":
"of one who has emerged from loving-kindness," and so forth.

The resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is: "May happiness arise for immeasurable beings. It is accompanied by that [intention]. "Exceedingly exalted" (*atyudagra*) and so forth is all as explained previously.
"Stainless due to the transformation of the most recent basis (*pratyagrāśrayaparivṛtti*). "Most recent" (*pratyagra*) means brand new,
because it has just emerged.

Through the transformation of the body, which is the immediate basis, the continuum becomes stainless. For these individuals, the fruit of benefits and harms— of assistance and injury, of wholesome and unwholesome deeds— performed toward them is obtained in this very life, in the present existence.
It shows the meaning as "immediate" (*sadyas*),
by treating it as "as if immediate.
As for the phrase "but of the remainder," the full explanation follows.
The remaining path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is that which brings about the fruits of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and non-returner (anāgāmin).
Its nature or its fruit is incomplete; thus, it is "that whose nature and fruit are incomplete.
The state of being such is [the meaning of the term].
Therefore,
because its intrinsic nature and its fruit are incomplete.
What, then, is its complete intrinsic nature and its complete fruit?
The state of being beyond training (*aśaikṣatva*) is the nature of perfection; for that path has the nature of one beyond training,
by which arhatship is attained.
The state of having the fruit fully perfected (*paripūrṇaphalatā*) is also the attainment of the ultimate goal (*arthattva*).
For that path of fruition is "possessed of fruit" by virtue of the three fruits.
Alternatively, the path comprised within the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) has its own nature as fruit fully perfected.
Because the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) has a perfected nature,
it is one whose fruit is perfected, owing to the fact that its fruit is without remainder.
[The phrase] "of those who have emerged from that" refers to this.
For those who have emerged from the remaining paths of cultivation,
they do not become such a field of merit upon emerging from them as those who have emerged from arhatship.
It goes without saying that this applies even more so to those who have emerged from the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).

It should be understood that this distinction was stated because of the abandonment—both with remainder and without remainder—of the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*). This is because that [attainment] necessarily possesses applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*). (IV.58) It is because it necessarily possesses applied thought and sustained thought.
For it is a fixed rule that the five sensory consciousness-elements possess both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*),
and because applied thought and sustained thought do not exist in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) and beyond.
Furthermore, it is not logical for the maturation of an action devoid of vitarka to be a state involving vitarka and vicāra belonging to a lower level;
for its maturation is said to be painful feeling, and so forth.
That is to say, for that unwholesome [action], painful feeling is accepted as the maturation.
Because that has undesirable results.
Furthermore, mental painful feeling is nothing other than mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*),
and it has already been explained that mental dissatisfaction is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
In the Exposition of the Faculties, it is said: "Life is maturation; [the others] are of two kinds, excluding the last twelve and the eight, as well as mental distress."

(IV.59) Not tolerating the statement that "mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*"), he says: "If, then... and so forth. That is to say: if mental dissatisfaction is not a maturation...
As for the fact that there is mental derangement (*cittakṣepa*) among sentient beings: in which mind does it occur, and by what cause?
This is the intended meaning [of the question].
Mental derangement does not occur within the five groups of sensory consciousness,
because they are non-conceptual.
Furthermore, that [derangement] has unwholesome roots as its cause, because it is undesirable.
Therefore, one must experience mental distress as a result of maturation (*vipāka*).

"Because they are non-conceptual" means that the five groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) are non-conceptual because they lack the two types of conceptualization: investigative (*abhinirūpaṇā*) and recollective (*anusmaraṇā*).
And because mental derangement is characterized by unreal conceptualization.
"Or they set fire to the forests": a forest (*dāva*) is a specific region covered with thickets of grass and the like.
"Or by anything else whatsoever" means by undesirable sensation and so forth.
"Of Vasiṣṭhī and others" refers to [the women] beginning with Vasiṣṭhī.
The Blessed One was staying at Mithilā,
in the Mango Grove of Mithilā.
Now at that time, six sons of a brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan had died.
Due to their death, she became naked, insane, and deranged in mind; wandering here and there, she approached the Mango Grove of Mithilā.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated before an assembly of many hundreds of monks, teaching the Dharma.
The Brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan saw the Blessed One from afar.
Upon seeing him, she stood with her body bent in a crouch, feeling deep shame,
and regained her mindfulness.
From afar, the Blessed One beheld the brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan.
Having seen him, he then addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Give the upper robe, Ānanda, to the brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan;
I shall teach her the Dharma."
The Venerable Ānanda gave his upper robe to the brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan.
Then the brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan, having put on the upper robe, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, she bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
To the Brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan who was seated in seclusion, he instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened her with a discourse on the Dharma.
"He gladdens," and so forth.
For fear of excessive length, the entire sūtra has not been written here.
This is the meaning therein: the Blessed One, having delivered a discourse on giving and so on to her...
He taught the four noble truths.
Eventually, she realized the fruit of stream-entry;
having realized it, she departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
At another time, her seventh son passed away. She did not grieve over his death. Seeing her not grieving, her husband said to her:
Previously you were tormented by the death of your sons;
now you are no longer tormented.
Surely your sons have been devoured by you.
"Since you do not grieve," she replied to him,
"thousands of sons and grandsons, and hundreds of assemblies of kinsmen."
"O Brahmin, throughout this long course of time, both I and you have devoured thousands upon thousands of sons and grandsons; there is no measure to those who,
in various successive births, were being devoured by one another."
Who, having known the escape from birth and death in this world, would grieve, burn with anguish, or lament?
Having known that very escape from birth and death, I [do not].
"I do not grieve, I do not suffer, because the teaching of the Buddha has been established"— such statements as these [would be impossible].
How then does it follow that mental feeling (*caitasikī vedanā*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*)?
The ellipsis for the phrase "of that unwholesome karma" is to be supplied.
The "ripening" (vipāka) of the primary elements (mahābhūta) is their disturbance;
ripening (vipāka) means the process of ripening (vipakti).
Therefore, that which is born from that is a mind produced by maturation (*vipākaja*).
For this very reason, it is said that "it is born from the maturation of karma" (*karmavipākaja*), but it is not stated [that the mind itself is karma]. (Abhidh-k-vy 397)
"And that is born of karma.
"And thus this... and so forth.
Because, by means of that which is born of karma, up to the point where the mind proceeds with lost mindfulness.
Therefore, this fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) is appropriate.
In that context, the example is simply: "The defiled mind of one whose mind is deranged is both [deranged and defiled].
For it is not logical that a defiled mind should be a maturation (vipāka).
Because it is stated that "maturation is an indeterminate phenomenon," [the beings] are impelled and oppressed.
And here, the case of the hell-being who laments with a distracted mind should be cited as an example.
It is said that hell-beings become mentally deranged,
except for the Buddha.
Because of his great accumulation of merit, this does not apply to the Buddha.
Likewise, the mind is deranged by an imbalance of the elements,
but not by karma.
What [is the cause]?
The minds of the Noble Ones are disturbed only due to an imbalance of the primary elements.
He asks: what is the reason? He says: [the following].

Because determinate karma ripens even previously, while one is still in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); whereas indeterminate karma does not ripen during the state of an noble one (*ārya*). For this very reason, it is called "indeterminate."
"By the complete transcendence of the five fears": there are five fears—
fear for one's livelihood, fear of ill-repute, fear of timidity before an assembly, fear of death, and fear of an unfortunate rebirth.

In that context, "fear of ill repute" is the fear of infamy; "fear of timidity before an assembly" is shrinking back in a gathering; and "of one who is unpleasing" refers to one who inspires no confidence.
Regarding the action that is not conducive to serene confidence:
because of his direct knowledge of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
[he knows] that "everything contaminated is suffering."
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
all phenomena are non-self," because of his direct knowledge of the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
(IV.60ab) "Because it has a crooked lineage" means because it has a crooked cause; for crookedness is that which is to be proven.
"Because it follows from being a dye" means that just as a decoction (*kaṣāya*) is the cause of dyeing,
so too— precisely because of this similarity— is it said [to be] "belonging to the desire realm" (*kāmāpta*). (IV.60cd, 61) Thus ends the section on the desire realm.
By this, the wholesome is qualified, not the unwholesome,
because the latter necessarily belongs to the realm of desire.
Why is that which belongs to the formless realm (ārūpyāpta) not mentioned?
For that too is not intermingled with the unwholesome;
the meaning is that it is not mixed with it.
"Where, it is said," and so forth.
The word "it is said" (*kila*) indicates the opinion of another school.
Where, it is said, there is an intermediate state being (*antarābhavika*), that is, existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is a maturation (*vipāka*).
The same applies to that which pertains to the state of rebirth (*aupapattibhavika*).

Furthermore, there is the ripening (*vipāka*) of the threefold karma of body, speech, and mind; for bodily and vocal karma subsumed under the meditative restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*) exist even in the second and higher dhyānas.
It is precisely in that context that it is said: "white [karma] has a white ripening."
That too has been stated in another Sūtra:
"There is also karma pertaining to the formless realm that is white with white ripening."
"Just as in the first dhyāna, so it is up to the peak of existence.
By this, he reveals his own intention.
As for why he used the word "it is said" (*kila*):
this is established from the perspective of the continuum (*saṃtāna*).
Since both the wholesome and the unwholesome manifest within a single continuum, the wholesome is thus intermingled with the unwholesome.
"Because they are mutually contradictory": the wholesome is contradicted by the unwholesome,
and the unwholesome by the wholesome.
A dual nature is not tenable.
It is not necessarily the case that the unwholesome is interspersed with the wholesome; such is the detailed explanation.
It may indeed be interspersed, but it is not necessary.
Because in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) there is an absence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that serves as an antidote, unwholesome states (*akuśala*) possess strength;
for this very reason, wholesome states (*kuśala*) are weak.
Thus, in the desire realm, the roots of the wholesome (*kuśalamūla*) are completely severed by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
But it is not by means of right view that wrong view is completely eradicated.
For this term "non-white" is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*);
it is "non-white" because of the absence of white ripening (*vipāka*).
But the meaning is not that it is *not at all* white;
rather, "non-white" (*aśukla*) means that which was called white does not exist.
"In the great emptiness" refers to the *Mahāśūnyatārtha-sūtra*. Furthermore,
the unobscured-unspecified [phenomena] are white.
Because it is non-afflicted.
It is without ripening because it does not fall within the realms;
that is, untainted phenomena do not fall within the realms.
And since maturation (vipāka) falls within the realms (dhātu), therefore untainted karma (anāsrava-karma) has no maturation.
Why? He says:
"Because it is opposed to the process of cyclic existence (pravṛtti)."
For untainted (*anāsrava*) karma obstructs the activity of those phenomena that fall within the realms [of existence], but it does not produce them; thus, it is without ripening (*avipāka*).
[This refers to the statement] "karma for the sake of the destruction of karma. (IV.62, 63)

The repetition of the term "action" (karman) is for the purpose of illuminating this fourth type of action: that which was designated as "there is action," meaning that action, being existent and present, with its intrinsic nature unaltered, conduces to the destruction of action.
Alternatively:
This is an instance of distributive usage (*vīpsā*).
The meaning is that "it leads to the destruction of each and every [type of] karma.
The phrase "in these four," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

The mention of "receptivity to the Dharma" (*dharmakṣānti*) and the mention of the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantaryamārga*) regarding detachment from the desire realm refer to the path of abandoning black karma belonging to the desire realm, because it is the path of abandonment for that [karma].
Since only the untainted (*anāsrava*) path is under discussion here, the mundane (*laukika*) uninterrupted paths, even though they constitute its abandonment, are not included.
Regarding white karma, this occurs during the detachments from the meditative absorptions (*dhyānavairāgya*).
Thus it is said.
It is determined that [the action] is exclusively wholesome,
because there is an absence of the black [action] therein.
The abandonment of afflicted formations occurs through eight [paths];
however, by the ninth, even the wholesome is abandoned.
For there is no abandonment of its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Abandonment is the severance of acquisition (*prāpti*).
This is because even wholesome states that have been abandoned can still manifest;
[they are truly abandoned] through the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that take them as their object.
Because the affliction that has that as its object is abandoned, there is the abandonment of that wholesome state.
And the abandonment of the affliction having that as its object occurs when the ninth category of the affliction having that as its object is abandoned.
Thus, it is precisely the volition of the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) that leads to the destruction of black-and-white karma.
For at that time, when the possession (*prāpti*) of the ninth category of afflictions is severed, the possession of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) arises.
They explain that the possession of dissociation arises for that black-and-white karma, as well as for other unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
The same should be stated regarding the detachment from the four dhyānas.
"By that, it is to be experienced as such.
By that means, by the cause of the fixed determination of the hell-realm (*narakagati-naiyamyakāraṇa*).
"To be experienced as such" (*tadvedanīya*) means to be experienced in hell (*narakavedanīya*).
"Other than that," and so forth.

Therefore, other than the hell-realm, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—specifically in the destinies of humans and so on—the maturation (*vipāka*) of both unwholesome and wholesome karma occurs. By reason of this restriction to those specific destinies, both types of karma to be experienced in the desire realm other than that [hell] are described as "black-and-white" (*kṛṣṇa-śukla*), without making a distinction between them and by mixing them together.
Furthermore, it should not be understood that what is wholesome is both black and white,
nor likewise that what is unwholesome is so as well.
"Because it is unmixed with the wholesome.
For there is no wholesome [state] that is to be abandoned by seeing;
what is not afflicted is not to be abandoned by seeing.
Thus, according to this rule. Here it is objected:
[the mind] belonging to the desire realm...

One must specify that "the black [karma] is to be abandoned by vision" (*dṛggheyaṃ kṛṣṇam*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of stating that even that which is to be abandoned by vision belonging to the realms of form and formlessness has black maturation (*kṛṣṇavipāka*).
It should not be said [that it is neither black nor white]; however, other [karma] born of desire is both black and white.
Thus [it is said].
Because the term "born of desire" (*kāmajam*) functions as a qualifier for both,
that which is born of desire and is to be abandoned by vision (*dṛggheya*) is black (*kṛṣṇa*).
"Other [actions] born of desire are black-and-white," it is said.
"For that... and so forth;
for that [action] belongs to the realm of desire (kāmāvacara) and is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).
Both the wholesome and the unwholesome arise; having mixed those two together, both are said to be "black-and-white," but not each individually.

(IV.65) "The three states of sagehood" (*mauneyāni*). Sagehood (*maunitā*) or the activity of a sage (*munikarma*) is *mauneya*, as in the case of the word *kāpeya*. There are three types of sagehood.
Thus,
this is the silence (mauna) of the Sage (muni).
"One beyond training" (aśaikṣa), and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

The bodily silence of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is bodily action (*kāyakarman*) whose intrinsic nature is non-informative (*avijñapti*). The same applies to vocal silence. Now, why is only the non-informative [action] taken here?
Nor, however, is it informative [action] (vijñapti),
because since informative action is associated with outflows (sāsrava), it is impossible for it to belong to one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Thus, the mind alone is the silence of the mind (manomauna).
Because the rule for the *vṛddhi* suffix applies to the word itself [as a bahuvrīhi].
For the mind (*citta*) is indeed the ultimate sage (*paramārthamuni*).
The reason for this will be stated as "because of the cessation of all conceptual proliferation of the afflictions" (*sarvakleśajalpoparati*).
That [state] is indeed inferred from the non-learner’s (aśaikṣa) actions of body and speech as being "non-learner.
How is the Tathāgata to be inferred?
From the statement in the Sūtra: "By means of tranquil bodily action and tranquil verbal action."
By using the word "kila" (it is said), the Master indicates the Vaibhāṣika position and then states his own view:
"Moreover," and so forth.
[This is] because of the non-existence of mental non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
Since there is no non-informative [action] of the mind, mental action does not have the nature of abstention (*virati*).
And silence (*mauna*) is so called in the sense of abstaining;
*virama* means *virati*.
The intention is that "silence" (mauna) refers to the sense of abstaining from all unwholesome states.
Therefore, it is the mind alone, when abstained from all unwholesome things, that is called silence.
This is because of the cessation of the conceptual proliferation of all afflictions (kleśa).
Because they consist of verbalization regarding false objects, the afflictions are called "discursive speech" (*jalpa*).
Since these have ceased for the Arhat, the Arhat is the ultimate sage (*paramārthamuni*). Regarding the term "purifications" (*śauceyāni*): [it refers to those things which bring about purification].
The state of being pure is *śauceya*;
it means purity (*śauca*).
(Abhidh-k-vy 400)
The inclusion of the term "all" is for the purpose of encompassing both wholesome conduct that is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
[It refers to] "for a limited time" and "permanently."
The removal of the stains of misconduct for that duration is accomplished by the three types of good conduct associated with outflows (*sāsrava*);
it is accomplished completely by that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
For it is said in the Sūtra: "O monks, that which has been abandoned by noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*) is truly abandoned."
This is for the purpose of distinguishing those who are devoted to false silence and false purity.
Those who see purification through mere silence are devoted to false silence. Those who see purification through the mere removal of bodily impurities are devoted to false purity.
Their analysis consists in causing them to fall away from that vision;
for it is stated in the *Saṃcetanīya-sūtra*: "These [actions] are for that purpose. (IV.66)

"Having performed and accumulated intentional karma (*saṃcetanīya-karma*), one is reborn in the hells. And how, monks, is intentional karma performed and accumulated? Here, monks, a certain person intentionally performs and accumulates threefold karma by way of the body, fourfold by way of speech, and threefold by way of the mind. Having spoken thus in detail, he said: [Tib. 61b]
Monks, how is it that a threefold volitional action performed with the mind becomes done and accumulated?
It is when, for example, a certain person here is covetous and possesses a mind of malice.
"Up to wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
Indeed, monks, there is here a certain person who possesses perverted vision," and so forth.

Since no mental action (manaskarma) other than covetousness and the rest is mentioned therein, the Dārṣṭāntikas—meaning a specific subgroup of the Sautrāntikas—hold that covetousness and the others themselves constitute mental action.
But if this were the case, there would be an identity between karma and the afflictions (kleśa).
Covetousness, malice, and wrong view are afflictions;
these very things would then be karma.
Then there would be identity between them.
This is not the case;
for it would follow that some affliction (kleśa) could also be karma.
Because of the statement, "Karma is volition and what is performed after having willed," one might ask: "If that is so, how is the *Saṃcetanīya-sūtra* to be interpreted? To this he says:
"But in the Sūtra... and so forth.

In the Sūtra, however, because volition proceeds by way of those [factors], namely by way of covetousness and so forth, it indicates that volition through those very factors, such as covetousness, in detail:
"O monks, one indeed becomes covetous," and so on.
Otherwise, this would contradict [the Sūtra's statement]: "O monks, I declare that karma is volition, and having willed, [one acts]."
Furthermore, if karma and affliction were identical, there would be a contradiction with the Abhidharma.
The detailed explanation is as follows: "In the absence of the intention to benefit or harm others," and so forth.
If there is no intention regarding the benefit or harm of others, how can right view and wrong view be wholesome and unwholesome respectively?
Therefore, he says:
"Because they are its root.
This means that right view and wrong view are the root—that is, the cause—of the intention to benefit others and the intention to harm others, respectively.
Therefore, those two possess the nature of being wholesome or unwholesome.
(IV.67) "According to what is appropriate" means according to what is possible. To explain how this is so, he says:
"Wholesome [actions] from well-performed deeds, and unwholesome [actions] from ill-performed deeds. And "others that are afflicted" refers to killing, binding, and so forth.
"Because it is not excessively gross.
This means that because that other afflicted [state], which constitutes the preparatory and subsequent stages, is not excessively gross,
and because volition is a portion of mental misconduct.
The term "not included" carries over [from the previous context].
Regarding the phrase "abstinence from intoxicants, giving, sacrifice, and so forth":
by the first word "and so forth" (ādi), abstinence from beating, binding, and the like is included.
By the second [term], bathing, massaging, providing a steady hand, and so forth are included.
Regarding "kind words and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the teaching of the Dharma, explaining the path, and so forth are included.
The phrase "volition is not included" continues [from the previous rule] regarding good mental conduct.
(IV.68) There are six [types of action] that are non-informative (*avijñapti*).
The six [paths of action] are necessarily non-informative;
however, there is no restriction that only the six are non-informative,
because of the absence of primary informative [action].

Because there is no fundamental informative action (*vijñapti*) subsumed under the paths of action; rather, there is only the informative action of commanding, which is subsumed under the preliminary effort (*prayoga*). This is the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of the Vaibhāṣikas.
One [type] is twofold.
Thus.
The undertaking [of this statement] is for the purpose of restriction, meaning that "one [type of death] is indeed of two kinds.
"Death at that time" means:

In the case of death at the time of a formal act (*vijñapti*), there is [both] the informative and the non-informative; however, in the case of death after some interval of time, there is only the non-informative (*avijñapti*).
The seven wholesome [paths of action] are of two kinds.
Thus,
the restriction "only two kinds" is made because the morality of undertaking (samādāna-śīla) is dependent upon informative action (vijñapti).
For ethical discipline (*śīla*) is twofold:

the ethical discipline of undertaking (*samādāna-śīla*), which is the Prātimokṣa restraint, and the ethical discipline of the nature of phenomena (*dharma-tā-śīla*), which consists of the meditative and the untainted restraints (*dhyāna-anāsrava-saṃvara*).
The ethical discipline of undertaking is dependent upon informative action (*vijñapti*).
For that [precept] is indeed received from another;
however, the morality of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā-śīla) does not depend on informative intimation (vijñapti),
because it depends solely upon the mind.
For this very reason, he said:
"Non-informative [action] is born of meditative concentration."

(IV.69abc) "But the preliminary stages are informative action" means that the preparatory applications for the paths of action belonging to the desire realm are necessarily informative action (*vijñapti*).
But it is not necessarily non-informative; for this very reason he says:
"It may or may not be non-informative.
[He adds] "by means of an outburst" (paryavasthānena).
By means of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and so forth. "With thick juice" means with thick velocity.
"One should act in accordance with that" means an action that conforms to, or is similar to, that path of action (*karmapatha*). For example,
even after the living being has died, further striking, cutting open, or tearing away the flesh, and so forth.
There are two words meaning "he destroys.
The meaning of the latter is "the removal of another's skin";
the meaning of the former should be understood as something different.
And "the fulfillment of the fruit":

the fulfillment of the fruit is the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*) resulting from the preliminary application (*prayoga*). For one who applies himself but does not produce the fundamental path of action [does not fulfill the fruit].
It possesses the fruit of its application, but not the fulfillment of the fruit. This is the case for others as well.
For example, suppose here someone, desiring to steal another's property, rises from his bed and takes up a weapon.
He goes to another's house;
he listens to hear whether [the occupant] is asleep or awake;
he touches another's property.
As long as one does not cause [the object] to fall from its place, that is the preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
But at the moment when one causes it to fall from its place, [that is the fundamental path].
In that context, the informative act (*vijñapti*) and the non-informative act (*avijñapti*) of that same moment constitute the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*).
