For one is touched by the fault of taking what is not given through two causes: by way of the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) and by way of the completion of the result (*phala-paripūri*).
The subsequent moments of non-informative act constitute the "consequent" (*pṛṣṭha*).
As long as he divides that property belonging to another,
sells it,
or guards it.
Or rather, even the moments of his informative intimation (*vijñapti*) constitute the "aftermath" (*pṛṣṭha*).
In this same way, it should be applied to the other five [paths of action] as well, according to what is appropriate.
This refers to one who is situated in the state of existence at death (*maraṇabhava*).
It is indeed immortality.
And this is not our established tenet. It is the same as before: for one who has died, there is no fundamental [result], because another basis has arisen.
This is because of the established tenet (siddhānta). Therefore, it should not be said that "he deprives [one of life]."
Because it is impossible [for them to exist] in the state of being separated [from the cause].
However, it should be stated as follows:
when a living being has died, that which is informative (vijñapti) and the non-informative (avijñapti) belonging to that very moment [constitute the path of action].
"This is the fundamental path of action" (syaṃ maulaḥ karmapathaḥ).
And as for this [statement], "And also this...
and so forth—this is how the Vaibhāṣikas have explained the meaning of this scriptural passage.
In this treatise, by the word "preparatory application" (prayoga), the "subsequent action" (pṛṣṭha) is meant.
It is called "preparatory application" because it is like a preparatory application;
the meaning is that it is an action similar to a preparatory application.
There is a contradiction with this meaning.
Why?
Because at that time, the fundamental [mind] itself has not yet ceased.
The intention here is that the fundamental paths of action are established only when the living being has died.
The Vaibhāṣika says:
"Let it be so, in such a way that there is no fault."
"And how is there no fault? asks the Master [Vasubandhu].
The Vaibhāṣika, however, replies:
"In this context, the word 'preparatory effort' (prayoga) refers precisely to the fundamental [action] itself."
Where?
In this question: "Could it be that a living being has been killed, yet the taking of life has not ceased?
In this context, since the "consequent action" (*pṛṣṭha*) is expressed by the term "preparatory effort" (*prayoga*), has this position been entirely abandoned?
And that [karma] has not yet been abandoned.
For both cases are possible:
if the living being exists in the moment immediately following the state of death (maraṇabhava), it is accepted here that the term "preparatory act" (prayoga) refers to the fundamental act (maula).
"But what about that which follows after?
To this, the Teacher says:
"In that case, how can the informative act (*vijñapti*) at that time constitute the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*)."
For once a living being is dead, informative action (*vijñapti*) is ineffective.
Thinking that there is no further killing of one who is already dead by means of that blow of informative action, he asks this;
why does he not ask about non-informative action (*avijñapti*)?
Because this [unmanifest form], due to its being non-demonstrable and non-obstructive, does not constitute what is called a "blow.
When the Vaibhāṣika asks, "And why should it not be so?",
the Master reveals his own intention.
"Because of lack of capacity.
The Vaibhāṣika says that when a living being has died, the capacity of that [action] is no longer observed.
[The opponent asks: "In that case, how can there be an unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) as a fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*) when capacity is absent?"
Since, in this way, non-informative action (avijñapti) constitutes a fundamental path of action (maula-karmapatha) even when there is no capacity [to act],

therefore, at the time of the fulfillment of the fruit of the preliminary effort— that is, at the time of the completion of the fundamental path of action— when the living being is in the state of death, both of those, known as informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti), would be the path of action; such is the meaning of "it would be appropriate."
In this way, it should be applied to other cases as well, according to the circumstances.
For example, one who desires to steal another's property might, for the sake of accomplishing his purpose, take that which belongs to another and perform a sacrifice with that animal;
and he might commit misconduct with the other's wife, using her very [property] for the purpose of effecting that theft.
One should cause a rift between him and his friends through falsehood, slander, harshness, conciliation, and sowing dissension—
those things which might otherwise serve as his protection—
and one should also harbor covetousness for his possessions.
And one should cultivate malice and wrong view toward the owner of that property.
In this same way, [the factors] such as sexual misconduct and so forth should be applied according to their possibility.
This is the general direction.
(IV.69d, 70ab) It is not the case here that all paths of action reach their completion through greed and the other [roots];
nor do they all reach completion through greed alone.
What then?
It is not for all [unwholesome actions] such as sexual misconduct and the rest,
nor even for all [of them] by means of malice.
What then?
[This applies] only to certain [actions] such as taking life and so forth.
Likewise, it is not through delusion in all cases;
what then?
"Of some only" refers specifically to those with wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
"Tryaṃbukas" are *varatās*.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), tigers and others are included.
And as for that which is instigated by wrong view:
thinking "there is no other world," one kills without regard;
this too is born of delusion.
"For the sake of other gains, honors, and fame" means that one takes away the property of another for the purpose of obtaining other gains,
such as a horse-thief.
To take away honor, reputation,
or wealth— this too is stealing born of greed—
as is that which is instigated by wrong view.
That too is taking what is not given, born of delusion,
because delusion is predominant therein;
he approaches his mother for the sake of unchaste conduct.
The phrase "he approaches his sister" continues [from the previous context]. "Sister" (upasvasāraṃ) means a female sibling (bhaginīm);
he approaches one who belongs to the same lineage (upagotrām).
The meaning is "one of the same lineage.
[This refers to] the sacrificer and the one who offers the oblation.
"And those who say... and so forth is the detailed explanation.
The female sex is like a mortar and other such objects.
Just as mortars and the like are common objects of use,
so too is the female folk.
Therefore, there is no fault for those who approach [the preceptor].
False speech and the others arise from greed and from hatred, as previously stated.
False speech, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter arise from greed, either for the sake of another's gain, honor, or fame.
Or for the sake of protecting oneself or one's friends; those born of hatred are for the sake of retaliating against an enemy. It is not [speech] that strikes at a vital point.
It is not associated with derision.
Regarding the phrase "proceeded from wrong view":
this false speech, uttered by one who lacks restraint because of the [view] that there is no other world, is born of delusion.
But as for slander and the others—slander, harsh speech, and idle chatter—they are produced in the same way as false speech.
"And that which... and so forth is the detailed explanation.
And whatever false prattle there is, such as that of the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, and so forth—
that too is frivolous speech born of delusion.
(IV.70cd) And "of that" refers to...
Of one with a wholesome mind. "He enters the various dwellings" means he enters the mandala.
For there are indeed various dwellings within that great boundary-circle (mahāsīmāmaṇḍala).
Regarding the third formal motion (karmavācanā): by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (jñapticaturtha-karman), a novice (śrāmaṇera) is ordained.
In that regard, by means of the motion (*jñapti*), it is said: "The Saṃgha should ordain this person named so-and-so.
The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is expressed [by this].
By means of the formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*), the meaning of the indicative suffix (*laṭ*) is expressed.
"The Saṃgha ordains this person.
In that regard, the formal proclamation (*karmavācana*) is recited three times.
Up until the completion of the third formal proclamation, it should be understood as the preliminary stage (*prayoga*) of the path of action (*karmapatha*).
At its conclusion, however, the informative act (*vijñapti*) or the non-informative act (*avijñapti*) of that very moment constitutes the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*).
Thereafter, until the four requisites (*niśraya*) are announced—

that is, until the four requisites characterized as robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal provisions for the sick— are announced to him who has been ordained according to the prescribed rule.
And it makes known that basis;
the meaning is that it effects an informative intimation (vijñapti) regarding the basis of reliance.
And the non-informative [intimation] continues as long as it persists.
The meaning is: as long as the restraint is not abandoned.
This is the "consequent action" (*pṛṣṭha*). (IV.71, 72ab) Killing, malice, and harsh speech reach completion through hatred.
The restriction "by hatred alone" means that because of the manifestation of a mind intent on abandonment and harshness,
the completion of the taking of life occurs through hatred, due to the manifestation of a mind of abandonment.
However, due to the manifestation of a harsh mind, there is ill-will and harsh speech.
(72cd) They are said to be "stated in four sections";
that is, they are stated in four parts.
How so?
Killing, malice, and harsh speech are completed through hatred; this constitutes one section.
The second [course of action] is the completion of sexual misconduct with another's wife, covetousness, and taking what is not given through greed.
But for wrong view, it is through delusion; thus there is a third [case].
For the remaining [afflictions], it is held that they arise from all three.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
"The bases of enjoyment" means the bases of sense objects.
"Based on name-and-form" means based on the five aggregates.
For "name" refers to the aggregates beginning with sensation, while "form" refers to the aggregate of form.

"Adhiṣṭhāna," "adhikaraṇa," and "viṣaya" are not different in meaning. False speech and the other [vices] have the collection of names (*nāmakāya*) as their basis, because speech operates upon names. (IV.73ab) It is not the fundamental [path of action].
From this prohibition, it is understood that even the *pṛṣṭha* [offering] does not exist,
because the *pṛṣṭha* is preceded by the fundamental [sacrifice];
nor is one touched by the fault of taking life.
The intention is that it is not by means of the fundamental [path];
because another basis has arisen.
The meaning is: "because they arise from a dissimilar basis" (IV.73cd).
For, in terms of their actual purpose, they act as mutual instigators;
however, they do not act as mutual instigators by means of speech.
What then?
It is because of the commitment to commit the act of taking life; that is, by implication, because it shares a single purpose.
(IV.74ab) "Having perceived" means having discerned.
"Without having mistaken another" means that one does not kill another through delusion.
"In the case of the momentary aggregates" [is the meaning].
The intention [of the objection] is: "Since the aggregates (*skandhas*) perish by their own inherent nature (*svarasena*), how can their cessation be brought about by something else?
Vitality (*prāṇa*) is the wind;
it functions in dependence upon the body and the mind.
How does the wind proceed as dependent upon the mind? Because its activity is bound to the mind;
for it does not proceed in one who has entered the attainment of cessation or the attainment of non-perception, nor in one who is dead.
It is also stated in the Śāstra:
"Regarding these inhalations and exhalations, it should be said: do they proceed based upon the body?"
It should be said that they proceed based upon the mind.
It should not be said that they proceed based neither upon the body nor the mind.
It should be said that they proceed based upon both the body and the mind.
He said:
"It should be stated that they proceed based on both body and mind," and so forth;
[the text] says, "it causes even that to fall."
The meaning is that it causes that vital breath (*prāṇa*) to perish.
Because that which has arisen ceases by its own inherent nature, one says that it "causes cessation" by obstructing the arising of what is yet to come,
just as one says, "he extinguishes a lamp."
Or the sound of a bell,
even though it is momentary—
how does he cause that to cease?
Because it prevents the arising of what has not yet arisen.
Or, "life-force" (*jīvitendriya*) is *prāṇa*.
This shows that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is dissociated from thought (*cittaviprayukta*).
To whom does that life belong? To him who, due to its absence, is said to be dead—
that living being who becomes dead through the absence of life.
That [self] does not exist for the Buddhists because they are proponents of selflessness (nairātmyavādin).
For this very reason, he asks: "Of what [is it the owner]?"—employing the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
In the *Pudgalavāda*, within the section on the refutation of the person (*pudgala*), I shall consider this point at the place where it is asked:
"If there is no self (*ātman*), whose is this memory?
What is the purpose of this genitive case?"
Let this general discussion stand for now; such is the intention.
Therefore, it is the body together with its sense faculties that lives;
that life belongs to the body alone when it possesses the sense faculties.
He shows that it is not [the result] of the self. And that very same [self], being devoid of sense faculties, is dead.
"Not preceded by cognition," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

Even from the killing of a living being committed unintentionally, demerit accrues to the agent; just as burning occurs from contact with fire even when it is done unintentionally and without prior awareness.
The Nirgranthas are the naked ascetics.
For those Nirgranthas who speak thus, this undesirable consequence follows: that even without prior awareness, there would be [demerit] from seeing or touching another's wife.
The meaning is that it would entail the consequence of sin.
This is because of the analogy with fire;
and [it applies] to the plucking of the head-hair of a Nirgrantha, that is, to the tearing out of the hair on the head of a Nirgrantha.
Even in the absence of the intention to produce suffering, there would be the consequence of demerit (*adharma*),
as in the case of being burned by fire;
and likewise in the teaching of arduous asceticism (*kaṣṭatapas*).
According to the teacher of the Nirgranthas, there would be the consequence of demerit even when there is no intention;
for they hold that causing suffering to another leads to demerit,
and this applies even in the case of death from cholera caused by that act.
If Nirgranthas die from cholera or indigestion,
there is an unrighteous consequence for the donor— that is, the giver of food—
because their death was caused by that gift of food.

For even the unintentional killing of a living being is a cause of demerit. Furthermore, there would follow the consequence of demerit for both the mother and the one residing in the womb, because they are mutual causes of suffering for one another.
Precisely from that analogy of fire,
and because even the victim is connected to that action—
namely, the connection to the act of taking life.
There would be the consequence of non-dharma; for when there is one to be killed, the act of taking life belongs to the killer,
just as fire burns its own support.
For fire does not merely burn other things;
rather,
it also burns its own fuel, which is its own substratum.
It is the same in that case.
For they do not require a particular state of consciousness [on the part of the agent].
Furthermore, it would follow that there is no unwholesome karma (*adharma*) for one who causes another to commit killing and so forth.

For those who cause another to touch fire, or for one who touches it themselves, there is no burning, because they have accepted the properties of fire [only metaphorically]. This applies even to insentient things such as wood, clods of earth, bamboo, and the like.
If a house collapses, there would be the consequence of sin due to the killing of the living beings situated inside it;
for a particular state of intention is not made the criterion [for moral responsibility].
Nor can this matter be established by a mere example that lacks a logical reason. (IV.74cd) "Except in the case of a confusion of names."
If one intends, "I shall take the property of Devadatta," but takes the property of Yajñadatta instead, there is no intention of theft; thus, it is not considered taking what has not been given.
This refers to that which was accepted at the time of final nirvāṇa.
It is for the purpose of favoring the merit of the donor. For if there were no recipient, a gift to a stūpa would be fruitless due to the absence of one who accepts it.

The *parivartaka* is the property, such as robes and so forth, belonging to a deceased monk. When the formal act has been performed—that is, when the *jñapti-karman* (the motion) has been carried out.
(IV.75ab) In the case of approaching a pregnant woman, there is injury to the fetus.
A woman who has a daughter in the stage of nursing means one who is feeding her breast milk.
For if she engages in unchaste conduct, her milk diminishes;
or else, that milk will not suffice for the nourishment of the child.
"Like the taking of life":
just as when one kills Yajñadatta with the intention "I shall kill Devadatta," it does not constitute the taking of life; so it is in this case.
Others say that sexual misconduct would not occur if one intends to engage with one object but instead enjoys another object;
[this applies] even down to the king.
If there is no other protector whatsoever, then at the very least, and even after all others, that sexual misconduct [is committed] in the presence of the king;
for he must not tolerate it.
(IV.75cd) Or rather, [is it] "capable of understanding"?
For even one who is capable of understanding an object can be said to be "one who understands the object."
"One understands the meaning" is said because it is intended in the state of being separated [from the words],
or because the meaning of a sentence is the object of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
When it is said, "Devadatta is here" or "he is not," the sound is cognized by the auditory faculty (*śrotra*).
Immediately thereafter, however, the collection of the eye and so forth, or Devadatta— the referent of the sentence— is cognized by conceptual mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Therefore, it would follow that only non-informative action (*avijñapti*) constitutes the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*),
because vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti*) ceases simultaneously with auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*).
And it is maintained that the fundamental path of action has the nature of both informative and non-informative [action].
(IV.76) They are like the dead;
therefore, among these, it is called "consent" (*mata*).
Relying on the etymological method (*nairukta*), the Vaibhāṣikas explain [the term *dharma*] as follows:
"They are considered (*matā*) because they are reached (*prāpta*) by their own faculties," says Master Saṃghabhadra.
This continues in detail up to "mental objects (*dharmāḥ*) by means of the mind."
Those odors which have not been smelled by you with the nose; those tastes which have not been tasted with the tongue;
those tangibles which have not been touched with the body.
"Up to those phenomena which have not been cognized by you through the mind.
This is because the designations "seen," "heard," and "cognized" apply respectively to the three objects—visible form, sound, and mental phenomena (dharmas).
Regarding odors and so forth—namely, odor, taste, and the tangible—the designation "sensed" (mata) is understood to apply.

They are designated by the term "cognized" (*mata*). This being so, if it were not accepted that [the objects] such as odor (*gandha*) are called "cognized," it would be because they are excluded from the states of being "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) and so forth.

Because odors and so forth, by virtue of not having the characteristic of form (*arūpalakṣaṇatva*), lie outside the domain of what is seen; and because, by virtue of not having the characteristics of the sound-base or the mental-object-base (*aśabdadharmāyatanalakṣaṇatva*), they lie outside the domains of what is heard or cognized.
Consequently, there would be no conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding odors and so forth, such as "it is seen" up to "it is cognized. This is the logical argument.
Regarding the phrase "among them, it is called 'the opinion'":
the Teacher says,
"First of all, the Sūtra," and so forth.
"Because it has another meaning.
This is because the meaning of the sūtra is indeed something else.
He states the meaning of the sūtra as follows:
And here, "for you" refers to you [the Yogācāra] regarding the sixfold object, such as form and so forth, and regarding the four conventional usages of seeing and so forth—
the conventional usages of what is seen, heard, thought, and cognized.
It will be merely a conventional usage such as "seen" and so forth;
there will be the conventional usage "seen in form," up to "cognized."
The same applies to sounds and the other [objects].

And in this regard, Mālakīmātar, when you have seen the sixfold range of objects, there will be only what has been seen; when you have heard the sixfold range of objects, there will be only what has been heard.
The intention is that this phrase of the Sūtra—“when the mind has cognized, the sixfold object-sphere is merely cognized”—is explained in this way.
For the meaning of the Sūtra is: “Indeed, there will be for you no superimposition of the signs of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
But was it not said by you: “Those forms which have not been seen by the eye”?
But it was not said that they were "not heard" up to "not cognized.
In this way, sounds were simply said to be "not heard," but it was not said that they were "not seen" up to "not cognized."
In this way, it is stated only that "dharmas have not been cognized," and not that "they have not been seen" up to "not been touched.
This is not a fault.
This was stated by the Blessed One as an illustration:
"Just as forms have not been seen," so too they have not been heard.
They should not be said to be "not yet cognized.
The same should be stated regarding sound and the other [objects].
By that very [principle], their definition is expressed.
"That which [is perceived] by the five sense-faculties," and so forth.
That which is directly perceived through the five sense-faculties, such as visible form and the rest, is "seen.
That which has been received from another regarding the sixfold range of objects is "heard."
That which is approved and intended through logical inference is the "view based on logical inference.
This refers to non-erroneous inference,
and it has the six sense objects as its domain.

"The sixth is other than the seen" means that the sixth object is the phenomena (*dharmas*). Excluding the conventional usage of "seen," it is designated by the three conventional usages beginning with "heard."
Therefore, there is no consequence of the absence of conventional usage regarding odors and so forth.
Consequently, this reasoning also— which was stated by the Vaibhāṣikas as "if it were not accepted in this way," and so on— is not a valid reasoning.
Because conventional usage regarding odors and so forth occurs in other ways as well—
namely, that which is directly perceived by the eye,
and not by all five sense faculties.
That which is heard with the ear and that which is received from another—both of these are intended [as "heard"].
That which is individually experienced, such as pleasure and so forth, is by means of an unconcentrated mind;
however, that which is realized is by means of a concentrated mind.
By the mundane alone,
not by the supramundane;
for the mundane pertains to the domain of conventional discourse.
Thus, even according to the Yogācāra system, these six objects are each designated as "seen," "heard," or "cognized" as appropriate.
Because it is precisely "the cognizer," there is no consequence of the absence of conventional usage regarding odors and so forth.
As for the phrase, "one who [cognizes] otherwise by means of the body":
If one conveys a meaning through a bodily gesture,
that too constitutes false speech.
One should exert oneself and strive [to avoid it].
"One should exert oneself by means of speech" means that one should kill another by means of speech.
However, in this case, because the taking of life is bodily in nature, only the bodily non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is included within the fundamental [path of action].
Nor would there be vocal intimation, nor even bodily intimation here;
[it is said that one] "should exert oneself with the body."
In this context, since false speech is vocal in nature, it should be understood that only the vocal non-informative action (avijñapti) is included within the fundamental path of action.
"Or by both types of fault" means by the fault of body and speech.
Through the mental corruption of the sages, there comes to be connection with bodily transgression;
and here, the example of the *poṣadha* shows that there is also connection with verbal transgression.
For at the *poṣadha* ceremony for monks, when the holder of the Vinaya has proclaimed, "Are you all pure in this matter?",
if any monk should not disclose an existing offense,
he would be a liar by his very silence.
How is the path of action established for those two?
How is it that, for those two—the seer and the monk—who do not exert themselves through body or speech, the taking of life and false speech are respectively established as paths of action?
Effort must be made here [to explain this].

The meaning is that the Vaibhāṣikas must perform the meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding this, the Master Saṃghabhadra states: "In terms of actual efficacy, the sages (*ṛṣi*) are those who issue commands."
For having perceived that their intention was evil, being inclined toward the abandonment of sentient beings, non-human beings who were devoted to them exerted themselves physically;
by this means, the paths of action arose for those sages.
How so?
"By means of another's intimation":
for one in such a state, physical and vocal distortions necessarily occur;
moreover, they even utter curses in that manner.
And in that case, there must necessarily be bodily and vocal activity. However, others say:
"In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), not every non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is necessarily dependent upon informative action (*vijñapti*).
This is because the arising of the Prātimokṣa restraint for the group of five and others is possible simultaneously with the very attainment of the fruit."
Thus, some unwholesome [action] of this kind might exist even without a manifest intimation (*vijñapti*).
Since they have previously manifested [the intention], it will necessarily occur in other cases as well.
This has already been stated regarding the sages, even in the case of a false speech during the *poṣadha* ceremony.
If one who is impure should enter the midst of the Saṃgha, sit down,
and assume his proper deportment.
Or whatever else he speaks that is connected with that [unwholesome state], this is his prior informative act (*pūrvavijñapti*). (IV.77,
78ab) All afflicted speech is frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
The triad beginning with false speech is also [unwholesome],
not only other afflicted [speech].
And that very same [afflicted speech] is frivolous chatter.
For when a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a certain quality,
the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote that [quality].
By reason of that, speech characterized by affliction is called frivolous talk (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
For it is through its connection— that is,
through its connection with frivolous talk— that [it is so designated].
That person is one who engages in frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpin*).
Any defiled speech other than the three beginning with false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) is called frivolous chatter; having stated this, he speaks as follows to demonstrate an example.
"Like flattery, song, and dance, and like the words of false treatises.
"One practices flattery" means that, out of a desire for gain and fame, one utters speech that manifests servility.
"Such as lamentation, socializing, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), it refers to any other conversation of those with afflicted minds besides lamentation and socializing,
because of the existence of talk concerning weddings, marriages, and the like.
*Āvāha* is the coming of the girl to the boy’s house;
*vivāha* is the coming of the boy to the girl’s house.
*Āvāha* is the act of entering.
Others say that "marriage" means the taking of a wife.
By the word "and so forth," the conversation of those with lustful minds is included.
"In an uneven or improper manner" means...
The two synonyms consist of a brief statement and a detailed explanation.
"For it is thus," and so forth, means:
because [it is taught] with reference to the five hindrances (*nivaraṇa*).
This was said with reference to sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), which has the nature of craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatṛṣṇā*).
Having abandoned covetousness (*abhidhyā*) regarding the world, he dwells frequently with a mind free from covetousness.

Having abandoned ill-will (*vyāpāda*), sloth and torpor (*styānamiddha*), restlessness and remorse (*auddhatyakaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) regarding the world, he becomes one who has crossed beyond uncertainty.
Having crossed over doubt,
he is free from indecision regarding wholesome dharmas;
having abandoned the five hindrances, and so forth.
From this it is known that all craving belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) is covetousness (*abhidhyā*).
This is because it includes the gross forms of misconduct (*duścarita*);
that is, among the ten unwholesome paths of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*), it comprises whatever constitutes gross misconduct.
That is included,
but not all of it.
It is the same regarding the wholesome factors.
Therefore, not every covetousness is a path of action.
What then? It is that improper longing for the property of others.
According to the opinion of others, that [covetousness] is a path of action (*karmapatha*),
so that covetousness among the *cakravartins* and the inhabitants of Uttarakuru might not be considered a path of action;
for it is not the case that desire-bondage (*tṛṣṇā*) belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is absent there.
And yet, unwholesome courses of action are not admitted therein.
Thus, this [view] is a denial of karma, its fruit, and the noble ones in their entirety.
For it is recited as follows:
There is no gift; there is no sacrifice; there is no oblation.
There is no good conduct;
there is no misconduct;
there is no fruit or ripening of actions consisting of good or misconduct.
There is no this world;
there is no other world;
there is no mother.
There is no father;
there is no spontaneously born being.
"There are no Arhats in the world.
In that regard, [the views] from "there is no giving" up to "there is no misconduct" constitute the negation of karma.
Likewise, the claim that "there is no mother" or "there is no father" is merely a denial of karma;
as is the claim that "there is no fruition or ripening of the results of well-performed or ill-performed actions."
"There is no this world; there is no other world;
likewise, there are no spontaneously born beings"—this is the denial of results.
"There are no Arhats in the world" is the denial of the Noble Ones (*āryāpavādikā*).
Only the beginning has been shown in the verse;
[it refers to] the view of non-existence regarding the wholesome and the unwholesome.
This is because it is merely an illustration.
(IV.79cd) "The paths of action" refers to the paths of the action known as volition (*cetanā*).
To the question "How so?", he says:
For volition is associated with those [unwholesome roots];
being associated with covetousness and the rest, it flows by means of the flow—the movement—of those very factors, covetousness and the rest.
The meaning is "it goes," because it is conditioned in that way by their influence.
This is because [the mind] proceeds under the influence of covetousness and the others, which respectively have the aspects of attachment, aversion, and false judgment.
Volition (cetanā) constructs in accordance with that; the meaning is that it intends.
Therefore, it flows by means of their flow.
And they are "action" (*karman*),
because their intrinsic nature consists of bodily and vocal actions.
Furthermore, they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*) because they are the paths for that which is called action— namely, volition (*cetanā*).

Of the volition that originates them—that is, the volition that originates bodily and vocal action. "Based upon them" means based upon those [actions], such as killing and so forth, because they proceed from them.
This is because the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is established even for things that are not of the same form.
The retention of only one (ekaśeṣa) is desired for words that are identical in form, whether they are identical in meaning or not.
For example: *vṛkṣaś ca vṛkṣaś ca* becomes *vṛkṣau*;
and *vakraṣ ca kuṭilaś ca* becomes *vakrāv*.

In this case, however, since the term *karman* and the term *karmapatha* lack both phonetic similarity and semantic identity, the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is not applicable; for the meaning of "action" (*karman*) and the meaning of "path of action" (*karmapatha*) are distinct.
Nevertheless, the formation of a single remainder is established for words that are dissimilar in their entirety but similar in one part.
The meaning is "it is desired.
For example, as in the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoh*:
*yaṅ* and *yaṅluk* are [the two] *yaṅlukau*.
Regarding the phrase "of those two":
it cannot be said that "yaṅ and luk are yaṅluk," because this [application of] *luk* is undesirable.
But [the formation is] due to partial similarity (*ekadeśasārūpyāt*).

Because of the similarity between *yaṅ*—which is one part of both *yaṅ* and *yaṅluk*—and the single element *yaṅ*, the rule for "single-remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) applies to the two cases of *yaṅ* and *yaṅluk*.
Therefore, by this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), this [formation] is also established.
"Karma and paths of action" means "paths of action.
Subsequently, there is a collective singular remainder (*sarūpaikaśeṣa*):
covetousness is a path of action, and killing and so forth are paths of action; thus, they are called "paths of action."
Alternatively, the construction is as follows:
the paths of action are *karmapathāḥ*. They are both actions (*karman*) and paths of action (*karmapatha*), hence they are called *karmakarmapathāḥ*.
Covetousness and the others are paths of action;
killing and the others are both actions and paths of action.
Thus, they are called "paths of action."
"In the same way, non-covetousness and so forth," and so on in detail.
The wholesome paths of action are to be applied in exactly this manner;
for non-covetousness and the others are indeed the paths of action.
Abstention from taking life and so forth are both action and paths of action.

"Because it is for that purpose," and so forth: because the engagement in those preliminary applications (*prayoga*) is for the sake of the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*), and because the engagement in their subsequent consequences (*pṛṣṭha*) is rooted in the fundamental path of action.
Therefore, those [preparatory actions] are not themselves courses of action (*karmapatha*).
Although it is said that a course of action can also be the preparation for another course of action,
that [latter one] is designated as the course of action because it is the fundamental (*maula*) act.
But it is not because they belong to the preparatory or the subsequent stages,
as was stated previously regarding the inclusion of the coarse [factors].
Thus, the ten paths of action were taught by way of including those that are coarse.
Because of this statement,
those [actions] which are the preliminary (prayoga) and the subsequent (pṛṣṭha) stages are not included.
"And of those," and so forth.
Of those fundamental [actions], through their increase or decrease, there occurs in the world the increase or decrease of internal and external entities;
but this is not the case for the preparatory or subsequent [actions].
Therefore, these alone are the paths of action.
He will explain that their increase or decrease results in the increase or decrease of those [paths].
All of them yield the dominant fruit, the outflow fruit, and the ripening fruit.
Thus it is said here.
Therefore, those [actions] belonging to the preliminary and the subsequent stages are not paths of action (*karmapatha*).
(Abhidh-k-vy 411)
How, then, can these be their courses of action (*karmapatha*)?

For for them, there is no mental action (*manaskarma*) other than covetousness and the rest; nor is there any volition (*cetanā*) such that covetousness and the others would be the paths of that action, and thus be called "courses of action."
"They themselves must be questioned. The answer must be stated by those very people who think in this way.
"But it is possible," and so forth;
he supports that position according to his own view by stating,
"or because they mutually entail one another."
What is the context? It is the question of whether covetousness and the others are paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Covetousness brings about ill-will and wrong view.
And they are "those" (tām). They are also "actions" (karma). And because they are the paths for either one of these actions, they are called "paths of action" (karmapatha).
(IV.80, 81) Desiring to state the point that the roots of the wholesome are severed by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), he provides an introduction:
"All these [are the causes] of the unwholesome," and so forth.
[He specifies: "by one that is excessive and complete."
The meaning is "by the highest of the high.
What, then, is stated in the treatise?
If the severance of the roots of goodness occurs through wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), it does not occur through the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
That which is stated in the treatise—
namely, that "by means of those unwholesome roots one completely cuts off the wholesome roots," and so forth—
refers to those [roots] whose intrinsic nature is greed and the like.
The meaning is that they do not have the nature of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
"Because they are drawn forth by the unwholesome roots," and so forth:
wrong view is drawn forth—that is, brought about—by the intense unwholesome roots, such as greed (*lobha*) and the rest.
Therefore,
because wrong view is brought about by the unwholesome roots,
that karma is taught in relation to those very roots.
Regarding those very unwholesome roots:
it is the teaching of that karma which, through wrong view, completely cuts off the wholesome roots.
How, then, is the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* to be interpreted when it explains that if the wholesome roots belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) are severed,
it is because one is not possessed of those belonging to the form and formless realms?
"Making distant the attainment of that" means,
with reference to that person, making distant the attainment of the [wholesome roots] belonging to the realms of form and formlessness.
This is what is meant by the statement that "the wholesome roots of the three realms have been severed."
And how, moreover, is there the distancing of that attainment?
By bringing about the fact that the continuum is no longer a fit vessel for it;
because that continuum was previously a fit vessel for those attainments.
Because the roots of virtue have been completely severed, one has now been rendered an unfit vessel for their acquisitions;
therefore, the acquisition of those [roots] becomes distant. This is because one has already fallen away from the [wholesome states] acquired through application (*prāyogika*).
The meaning is that he has already fallen away from those preparatory states (*prāyogika*) consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation while still in the "weak-weak" stage;
at that very moment, there is the severance of their acquisition (*prāpti*).
[This occurs] in the state corresponding to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The denial of the cause corresponds to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);
the denial of the fruit corresponds to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This is what is meant.
Both of these false views, which deny cause and effect respectively, function to sever the roots of wholesome merit;
it is not just one alone.
Another position holds that it is only the one that has the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as its object.
By having suffering and its origin as objects;
that is to say, by not having the untainted (anāsrava), nor cessation or the path, as objects. And [it occurs] only by having the homogeneous realm (sabhāgadhātu) as its object.
The meaning is that [the roots of goodness] are severed only by [a view] having the desire realm as its object;
not by one having a different realm as its object, nor by one having the form or formless realms as its object.
With reference to the statement "the roots of goodness are severed," he asks: why? He replies:
"Because it is weak due to being a latent tendency by way of mere association.
That false view which has the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object and that which has a different realm (*visabhāgadhātu*) as its object,
dwells as a latent tendency toward the associated factors merely through association, not by way of its object.
Therefore, it is weak;
for this reason, the roots of goodness are not cut off by it.
However, the Vaibhāṣikas explain it in this way:
"By all [of them]" means:
that which denies the cause and that which denies the fruit;
that which takes a similar realm as its object and that which takes a dissimilar one.
Whether it takes as its object that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) or that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*), by all such [knowledge], the [latent tendencies] are completely severed,
just like those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*).

Just as the afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and so forth— though they consist of nine grades— are abandoned all at once through the vision of the truths of suffering and so forth, in the same way, the nine grades of the roots of wholesome merit are also cut off all at once; these [roots] are like the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
Just as the ninefold affliction is abandoned by means of the ninefold path:
the highest-of-the-high grade of affliction is abandoned by the lowest-of-the-low path, up to the lowest-of-the-low grade of affliction being abandoned by the highest-of-the-high path.
In this way, even by means of the ninefold wrong view, the ninefold roots of goodness are completely severed.

By the weakest-weak wrong view, the strongest-strong category of the roots of goodness is severed; continuing in this manner until, by the strongest-strong wrong view, the weakest-weak category of the roots of goodness is severed.
In this way, this treatise is preserved:
if, as has been stated, those [afflictions] are completely eradicated like the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation— namely,
those that are subtle and very weak.
Regarding the statement, "By which unwholesome roots one completely cuts off the wholesome roots":

the intention is that the cutting off of the wholesome roots is said to occur through the most intense (adhimātra-adhimātra) unwholesome roots, and not through the weakest (mṛdu-mṛdu) ones and so forth.
"If they are gradually severed for him, then... and so forth.
How so?
This was stated with reference to its completion.
This was stated in detail with reference to the completion of the total severance of the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla-samuccheda*).
Although the severance of the [roots] that are "weak-weak" (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) and so forth was not explicitly mentioned, it should be understood by implication.
Therefore, this was said specifically with reference to the completion [of the process].
Because of their cutting off [the roots] without remainder;
for by those nine types of wrong view, there occurs the complete severance of the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*).
For even a single type of them, if not severed, [prevents total destruction].
The ninth category, which is the weakest of the weak, would be the cause for the renewed arising of all nine categories;
therefore, this was stated with reference to their final completion:
"by both."
By both emerging and not emerging.
Because of the abandonment of that [state], there is the abandonment of it;
namely, the restraint that had been undertaken with a mind that was weak-weak.
When that very weak mind, which is associated with very weak roots of wholesome merit, is abandoned—that is, cut off—there occurs the abandonment of that restraint (*saṃvara*).
In this same manner, up to the point where a restraint has been undertaken by means of an extremely intense mind:
through the abandonment of that [mind], there is the abandonment of that [restraint].
"Because the fruit of karma is directly perceived":
when a son of the gods has recently been reborn, three thoughts arise in him:
"From where have I passed away?"
"Where has he been reborn?
By what karma? Because the fruits of karma are thus directly perceived, the roots of merit are not severed among the gods.
It is only in Jambūdvīpa that they are severed.
The intention here is that this is specifically because of his being a dialectician (*tārkika*).
He is endowed with the very minimum of eight faculties: the five faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*), as well as the faculties of body, life, and mind.
This refers exclusively to one whose roots of merit have been severed (*samucchinnakuśalamūla*).
For in him, faith and the other [faculties] have been utterly severed;
and because he is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), the faculties such as "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) do not exist.
Nor do the [physical] faculties such as the eye exist.
In the case of a deficiency [of faculties],
or during the state of gradual death;
likewise for one from Pūrvavideha or Aparagodānīya.
By means of this extension (*atideśa*), he shows that for these two as well, there is the severance of the roots of merit (*kuśalamūlasamuccheda*).
He says: "A woman or a man severs them."
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "woman and man" (*strī pumāṃś ca*) is indicated as being elided.
One who is endowed with the female faculty (*strīndriya*) is necessarily endowed with eight faculties:
with the four faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*), with the three faculties of body, life, and mind (*kāya-jīvita-manaindriya*), and with the female faculty as the eighth.
The intention is that faith and the other [faculties] are subject to deviation during the state when the roots of merit have been severed.
And this very point is contradicted here.
The eye and the other [faculties] are also subject to deviation, as before.
"Of them too" means:
of those aforementioned destroyers as well,
one whose temperament is dominated by craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*) does not destroy [the roots of goodness].
"Because of having a firm, hidden, and evil disposition.
This is a compound meaning one whose disposition—that is, his intention—is firm, hidden, and evil.
"Firm" means stable.
"Hidden" means concealed.
"Evil" means unwholesome.
This is because it belongs to the category of those whose conduct is dominated by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

The meaning is: because they belong to the class of those whose temperament is dominated by craving (*tṛṣṇācarita*). Just as one whose temperament is dominated by craving has a fickle disposition, so too do those such as the *ṣaṇḍha*s.
And it is like those in the miserable realms (*āpāyika*).
Just as those in the miserable realms do not sever the roots of goodness because their afflicted and non-afflicted wisdoms are not firm,
so it is with the eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*) and others.
"Pratisaṃdhitāni" means those which have been made into a rebirth-linking; they are "pratisaṃdhitāni. This is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
Others read "pratisaṃhitāni. [The phrase] "like the attainment of health and strength" means that health comes first.
But in that case, the attainment of power occurs gradually;
it is not so here for one who commits an immediate transgression.
Thus,
it is said that for one who has committed an *ānantarya* [heinous] offense, there is no rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) here.
By implication, this means that for one who has not committed an *ānantarya* offense, rebirth here does occur.
"Abiding in the intermediate state" means abiding in the intermediate state for the purpose of going to hell.
"Facing death" means being oriented toward passing away.
Facing death and passing away from hell.
"By the power of the cause" means by the power of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Because for those [persons], wrong view is pleasing to them by its own power— that is, by the power of their own [reasoning]—
and by the power of another’s voice— that is, by the power of instruction from others.
Because those for whom false views are pleasing [do so] due to the strength of the cause being essential.
Likewise, "he who by his own power" [is explained as follows].
He who [falls] by the power of his own reasoning is one who is passing away;
he who [falls] by the power of another is likewise.
By the power of hearing from another.
He, being reborn...
as for "one whose intention has failed": [it refers to one who has lost the resolve for enlightenment].
One who has perished and been ruined through the manifestation of wrong view reconnects [with existence] in this very life,
in the present birth;
this applies to one who has perished through failure in both intention and application.
One who has fallen away through the manifestation of wrong view and by the commission of an immediate transgression (ānantarya) reconnects [the roots of merit] after the dissolution of the body.
And in this context, the phrase "by one's own power or by the power of another" is simply a synonym for what was stated previously.

Thus, regarding "one who has failed in view" and "one who has failed in both view and conduct," it should be understood that this is merely another way of expressing what was stated immediately prior. [The phrase] "Pūraṇa and the others" refers to this.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), six teachers are included. Namely: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarī Gośālīputra, and so forth.
Saṃjayī Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambala, and Kakuda Kātyāyana.
"The Nirgrantha Jñātiputra"—
these [people] have their roots of merit completely severed because of their nihilism.

They are not fixed in falsehood because they have not committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*). For those who commit an immediate transgression are fixed in falsehood; Ajātaśatru, for example, was fixed in falsehood.
Because he has committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*),
he is not one whose roots of merit are severed,
for he possesses right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Devadatta has both severed his roots of merit and is fixed in falsehood,
because he caused a schism in the Saṅgha and because he, with a malicious mind, drew blood from the Tathāgata.
The fourth category consists of those who exclude these aforementioned characteristics, such as ourselves.

(IV.82) "The manifestation of covetousness and so forth without another [path of action]" means that when any one of covetousness and the others manifests without another path of action such as killing and so forth,
that volition operates together with one path of action.
"By covetousness, or by ill-will, or by wrong view;
or with an unafflicted mind" means one whose mind is wholesome or neutral.
Through the performance of that agent,
when any one of the material [karmas], such as killing and so forth— excluding sexual misconduct— is brought to completion,
the volition (cetanā) exists together with that single [action].
Or it should be stated that this applies to a defiled mind distinct from covetousness and so forth;
for this same rule is also possible in his case, as in the detailed explanation:
"the killing of a living being by one with a mind of malice," and so on.
It occurs together with two [mental factors]: malice and taking life— namely,
in the case of sexual misconduct and frivolous speech.
It occurs together with two:
namely, with covetousness (*abhidhyā*) and sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*);
or with idle chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*) and any one of covetousness and the others.
It is by means of these two alone. This is what is questioned:
that the killing of a living being occurs when the mind is possessed by malice, and the taking of what is not given occurs when one is overcome by covetousness.
Is this said of one who acts by oneself, or rather of one who causes another to act? If it refers to one who acts by oneself:
The qualification "of one with a malevolent mind" and "of one possessed by covetousness" is not appropriate; for in the case of killing, malevolence is necessarily present,
and in the case of taking what is not given, covetousness is necessarily present.
For a qualification is required when there is a possibility of deviation.
Now, regarding one who causes another to act:
it refers to one whose mind possesses any one of covetousness, malice, or wrong view.
It should be stated: "in the case of killing a living being, or in the cases of taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, or frivolous speech.
It is replied: "when one performs them oneself."
But was it not said that the qualification is not tenable?
This is not a fault,
for this is not stated as a qualification.
What then?
This is a description of their essential nature;
it states that malice and covetousness exist there as secondary factors.

Even so, for one whose mind is possessed of covetousness or another such [unwholesome state] while causing those acts of killing and so forth to be committed, it would be possible for the volition to exist together with two [paths of action].
Therefore, that too must be stated.
This indeed must be stated.
This has been stated merely as an illustration, so there is no fault.
Regarding "the simultaneous killing and stealing by one with a malevolent mind":
this refers to cases where the act of stealing is accomplished through the very act of killing.
For in that case, the courses of action consisting of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), killing of living beings (*prāṇivadha*), and taking what is not given (*adattādāna*) occur simultaneously.
"If that is so," and so forth;
if, at the time of seizing another's property, ill-will arises.
In that case, the completion of taking what is not given would not be established by greed alone,
because greed and hatred do not exist simultaneously. The phrase "of one whose mind is not otherwise" is an elaboration [of this point].
That rule should be understood to apply to the completion of taking what is not given only when there is the intention to steal;
through greed, one completes the acts of sexual intercourse with another's wife, covetousness, and taking what is not given.
Thus it is said.
However, for one whose mind is otherwise directed, or who intends to kill, this rule does not apply;
namely, that speaking untruth is [only a transgression] when there is the intention to cause division.
Because it is intended with the purpose of causing division, that very same [false speech] becomes malicious speech (*paiśunya*).
That very same [speech] is frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
For all that is afflicted is frivolous chatter.
According to the established doctrine:
since it is thus intended as a division, that very same harsh speech is slander,
and likewise, it is frivolous chatter.
It occurs together with four [mental factors].
How so? He says:
for in that case, there is one [factor], namely, the mental [consciousness].
Regarding the three vocal [actions]:
in the case of false speech, there may be covetousness or malice;
these are the three vocal [actions].
False speech, slander, and frivolous chatter;
in the case of harsh speech as well, there is one mental [unwholesome root], namely malice,
and three vocal ones.
Harsh speech, slander, and frivolous chatter—
thus there are three by name alone, but not by way of intrinsic nature.
For that very same false speech is called slander and frivolous chatter;
it does not possess three distinct intrinsic natures.
In the same way, harsh speech should also be understood as having three names.
Others, however, explain that there is also a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For the non-informative (*avijñapti*) actions of lying, slander, and frivolous chatter are indeed distinct.
Likewise, the non-informative (avijñapti) actions of harsh speech, malicious speech, and frivolous chatter are distinguished.
Regarding the phrase "of one who has entered into covetousness and so forth," the full explanation is as follows:
it occurs together with four [factors] for one who has entered into covetousness and so forth.
In that regard, the mental [path of action] is one, being any one among covetousness and the others.

Through its application—that is, through the application directed toward covetousness and so forth—at the time of reaching completion, which is the moment of culmination of the other three courses of action such as killing living beings;
in this manner, it should be applied to five, six, or seven [courses of action].
What is volition? How is it so?
First, it occurs with five [paths of action]:
when one who has fallen into covetousness and so forth brings the other four to completion through that preliminary effort (*prayoga*).
Likewise, it occurs with six and seven when one who has fallen into covetousness and so forth brings the other five or six to completion.
It occurs together with eight [paths of action].

This is because, having performed the preliminary effort for six [actions] such as taking life and so forth, one who has fallen into covetousness performs sexual misconduct oneself, and all reach completion simultaneously.
That it occurs together with nine is not the case.
Because the mental paths of action cannot occur simultaneously,
it is not [accomplished] by one, eight, or five.
It does not exist with only a single mental [path of action],
because non-covetousness and non-malice necessarily exist whenever the mind is wholesome.
Nor does volition occur together with a single material path of action that is comprised within a restraint.

Even in a state of afflicted or neutral mind, in the case of the lay follower's vows (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) and so forth, there is necessarily a coexistence of [the abstentions from] killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech;
it is not [a coexistence] of only five.
Furthermore, when the mind is wholesome, there is necessarily a coexistence of the two, namely, non-covetousness and non-malice.
Furthermore, because these four— such as taking life and so forth— which are comprised within the vows, necessarily coexist,
they do not consist of exactly eight.
This is because in the state of being afflicted or neutral, only seven of those comprised within the bhikṣu-vow— namely, the bodily and vocal ones— are possible.
And because nine or ten [mental factors] can occur in a state of wholesome mind (*kuśalacitta*),
it follows by elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that it is said to function together with two or more [of them]. In this regard, "with two" is the detailed explanation.
In that regard, it occurs together with two [factors].
Among the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), non-covetousness (*anabhidhyā*) and non-malice (*avyāpāda*) exist, but right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) does not.
The wisdom (*dhī*) co-arising with the five sensory consciousnesses is not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) because it lacks investigation (*atīraṇāt*).
This is because of the established tenet (*siddhānta*).
Therefore, in this case, it coexists with only two [factors]: non-covetousness (*anabhidhyā*) and non-malice (*avyāpāda*).
And in the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), it coexists with the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Furthermore, the two types of knowledge—knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)—when they are comprised within the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), coexist with only these same two [faculties].
This is because knowledge of destruction and non-arising is not "vision" (*dṛg*); thus, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is absent therein.

The mention of the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) is for the purpose of excluding the sevenfold paths of action— both bodily and vocal— that are of the nature of the untainted restraint (*anāsravasamvara*), which are included within the meditative attainments (*dhyānasamāpatti*) [but not the formless ones].
The mention of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is for the purpose of excluding right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*),
because the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising do not have the nature of right view.

It occurs together with three [paths of action]. This refers to the mental consciousness associated with right view; the ellipsis of the sentence is that there is an absence of the material paths of action.
For in that case, there are only three paths of action, namely non-covetousness (*anabhidhyā*), non-ill will (*avyāpāda*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
The phrase "by four," and so forth,
indicates by the qualification "of one whose mind is unwholesome or neutral" that the mental [paths of action] do not exist [in such a state].
Furthermore, in the undertaking of the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*),
there are only four paths of action (*karmapatha*), characterized by the abstention from taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech;
for the abstentions from drinking intoxicants and so forth are not included within the ten paths of action.
Because the abstention from slander and so forth are included within the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*),
and because of the statement regarding the undertaking of the novice monk’s vow, the undertaking of the one-day fast (*upavāsa*) vow should be understood as having the form already described.
However, in the undertaking of the novice monk’s vow, the third path of action (*karmapatha*) is the abstention from unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*).
And therein, sexual misconduct is indeed included.

Regarding the six wholesome [paths of action] within the five sensory consciousnesses, there are six when one undertakes those [precepts]: namely, by means of those four as previously stated, together with non-covetousness and non-malice, when undertaking the vows of an Upāsaka or a Śrāmaṇera.
Because right view is absent in the five sensory consciousnesses (*vijñāna*),
[the seven paths of action] exist in a wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) only when there is the undertaking of that [vow].

This occurs precisely upon the undertaking of the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), by means of those aforementioned [paths] together with right view as the seventh path of action (*karmapatha*).
For when the mental consciousness is wholesome, right view exists;
however, when one undertakes the monastic vows (bhikṣu-saṃvara) with an unwholesome or neutral mind, it occurs through only the seven material [precepts],
not through the mental ones.
Because it is an unwholesome or neutral state of mind.
It occurs with nine [paths of action] in the case of undertaking them during the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses,
and in the case of undertaking the bhikṣu restraint.
Because right view itself is absent.
Furthermore, in the mental consciousness associated with the knowledge of destruction and non-arising, it occurs together with those same nine [mental factors],
because right view is also absent therein.
"In that very same" means:
in the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) included within the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), which is associated precisely with the knowledge of destruction and non-arising (kṣayānutpādajñāna).
It is [accompanied] by exactly nine [mental factors].
[The unmanifest] is comprised of the seven material [factors] included within the meditative restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*), as well as non-covetousness and non-malice.
It consists of ten [factors] elsewhere;

that is, in wholesome mental consciousness—excluding the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)—only when undertaking the monastic restraint (*bhikṣusaṃvara*).
"And all," and so forth in detail.

Furthermore, all volition (cetanā) that occurs together with the dhyāna and untainted (anāsrava) restraints, and which is associated with the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), [is accompanied] by seven bodily and vocal [actions] comprised within the dhyāna and untainted restraints,
and by three mental [actions].
It exists together with ten.
It has been shown that volition (cetanā) exists only together with the paths of action (karmapatha) comprised within the restraints (saṃvara).
However, it may exist even with one [path of action] that is free from restraint—that is, free from the eightfold restraint.
To the question "How so?", he says: "of another mind.
This refers to a mind other than that which originates the wholesome paths of action, whether they are included within or excluded from that restraint.
The meaning is: "of one whose mind is afflicted or neutral. Regarding the undertaking of the abstention from a single limb:
[this refers to] the abstention from the limb of taking life.
Or, upon undertaking the abstention from taking what is not given,
it occurs together with that single path of action.
It also occurs with five or eight [paths of action].
For a person possessing wholesome mental consciousness, when undertaking two factors, there are three mental [factors] and two material ones simultaneously,
making five.
When undertaking five factors, there are those same [mental factors] together with the five material ones simultaneously.
And by the three mental [actions], thus making eight.
This has been stated as an illustrative example;
therefore, it can also be explained in another way.
When one with a defiled or neutral mind undertakes the five limbs not included within the vows, it occurs together with five [mental factors]. (IV.83,
85) "Because of the absence of objects that cause passion" means that because of the absence of objects that cause passion in hell, covetousness does not exist there in its manifest state.
And because the results of karma are directly perceived, there is no wrong view.
For this very reason,
there is no malicious speech due to the absence of any purpose.
Because they are eternally distinct from one another, because they lack mutual affection and so forth,
and because there is no sense of "mine" or possession, the path of action of covetousness does not manifest in Uttarakuru. Furthermore,
because their mental continuums are gentle and because there is an absence of objects that provoke malice, there is no ill-will.
And because of the absence of evil intention, there is no wrong view.
These three—covetousness and the others—are likewise absent.
This applies even to oneself.
The explanation is that [these do not exist] by way of manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāva*).
Because he lacks an evil intention (*apāpāśaya*), even the six [unwholesome paths of action], such as taking life and so forth, do not exist by way of manifestation.

Because their lifespan is fixed, there is no taking of life; because they lack the possession of material goods and women, respectively, there is no taking what is not given and no sexual misconduct. And because there is no motive, there is no lying, slander, or harsh speech.
[The opponent] asks: "If there is no possession, how can these beings engage in unchaste conduct?"
"Released from restraint" means that they are not comprised within either restraint or non-restraint.
However, one kills [a being] residing in another realm of existence.
Those situated in the destinies of hungry ghosts and so forth;
even gods die from the severing of the head or the midsection. That is to say, even gods die from the severing of the head and from the severing of the midsection.
When it is said that "a god does not kill a god," the intended meaning is that gods are indestructible.
For even when the limbs and members of gods are cut off again and again, they grow back.
Nevertheless, the intention is that there is indeed the killing of gods, because there is no rejoining [of life] after the cutting off of the head, or the cutting off of the middle [of the body].
"Based on which level," and so forth.
There are five levels,
up to and including the level of the fourth dhyāna.
"Belonging to a particular level" means that which has that level as its basis (*yadbhūmyāśraya*).
Untainted ethical discipline (*anāsrava-śīla*) produced by a noble one (*ārya*) is "ceased";
"produced" means it has been brought into the present time.
It has been ceased and brought into the past time.
It may have a basis in one stage, up to a basis in four stages.
By means of that past [state], one becomes possessed of it in the formless realms.
However, it exists as future [dharmas] based on five levels:
based on a support belonging to the desire realm up to a support belonging to the fourth dhyāna;
whether one has been born there or has not been born there.
By relying on that [basis].
"Except for hell-beings and those in Uttarakuru" is because there is an absence of undertaken ethical discipline (*samādāna-śīla*) therein.
"In other cases, it is both ways.
In other cases—namely, among the gods in the desire realm and among humans, excluding those of Uttarakuru—it is both:
they are either free from restraint or comprised within restraint.
The threefold restraint— the Prātimokṣa restraint, the Dhyāna restraint, and the untainted (anāsrava) restraint— should be understood according to their respective applicability.
Regarding the phrase "cultivated, developed, and practiced repeatedly," this refers to the stages of preparation (prayoga), the fundamental (maula), and the subsequent (pṛṣṭha).
What then?
It means that by that [act] one becomes short-lived;
thus he shows that it is a flow-on result (*niṣyandaphala*) because of the brevity of the lifespan.
External entities,
such as medicinal herbs, the earth, and so forth,
possess little vitality and little potency.
"Abounding in thunderbolts and dust": a thunderbolt (*aśani*) is a rain of stones;
dust (*rajas*) is a rain of soil or a rain of alkaline matter.
Because of this, there is the destruction of crops and other plants.
"Covered with dust" means that dust has arisen. "High and low" means uneven, characterized by elevations and depressions.
"Saline and arid lands.
These are both saline and arid;
they refer to external entities as the subject under discussion.
Those stages are intended here as inferior and censurable.
"Having an irregular seasonal transformation" (*viṣamartupariṇāmāḥ*) means that their seasonal transformation is irregular; these are the crops and medicinal herbs.
In whatever season it ought to rain,
there it does not rain; in whatever [season] it ought to be cold, [there it is not].
In that [place], there is no cold. Where heat ought to be, it is not there; this is how it should be applied.
"That is the fruit of maturation" refers to [the result] within the continuum of a sentient being.
"This is the fruit of outflow" refers to that external object;
it is not the fruit of maturation.
Regarding that, "by means of the preliminary application" (prayoga) and so forth:
in hell, one experiences intense suffering by means of the preliminary application of taking life.
For by means of the preliminary application of taking life, the living being who is to be killed undergoes exceedingly intense suffering.
In this case, one becomes short-lived through the fundamental [act],
just as the life-span of that living being who is to be executed is impaired;
such indeed is this.
For the fundamental path of action is momentary, and since there is no painful feeling therein, it is logical to say here that [the retribution] is due to the fundamental [action]. He says:
If it is by means of the preliminary application (*prayoga*) here that one is reborn there [in hell],
why has it been said:
"By the taking of life, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed, one is reborn in the hells"?
Seeing that the meaning of the Sūtra is "by the fundamental [act] of taking life," he asks this.
[The phrase] "including its concomitants" refers to the fact that it is the fundamental act of taking life itself [that is meant].
Its application is its accompaniment.
Since the designation "taking life" is applied to that application, it is stated as "by taking life," and so forth.
This does not transcend these two.
[It consists of] the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) and the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala).
This is because the fruit of maturation occurs within one's own continuum, whereas the dominant fruit occurs elsewhere.
However, it is described in that way [as "dominant"] due to a specific similarity.
However, because of a specific similarity characterized by the interruption of a desired life, the loss of enjoyments, and so forth, it is stated thus:

"If one comes to such a state as the commonality (sabhāgatā) of human beings, one becomes short-lived through the taking of life, and one becomes subject to the loss of enjoyments through taking what is not given," and so on in detail.
For in this case, there is indeed a similarity between the cause and its ripened fruit (vipākaphala).
The same should be stated regarding wholesome [dharmas] as well.
The outflow fruit (niṣyandaphala) does not transcend the two types of fruits;
however, it is described in that way because of a specific similarity.

If one comes to such a state, attaining the commonality of human beings, one becomes long-lived through abstention from taking life, and so forth in detail. [In that case,] vitality has been destroyed.
Vitality (*ojas*) exists in the region of the heart.
In this same way, it should be applied to the others as well.
For by one who commits taking what is not given, suffering is produced for the owner of the object.
An addiction to enjoyments has been created; vitality has been destroyed.
Therefore, there are three kinds of results: from this causing him suffering, from depriving him of enjoyments, and from destroying his vitality.
How is vitality destroyed? By the destruction of its causes and by its impairment through the misfortune of enjoyments.
Therefore it has been said:
"By taking what is not given, there is an abundance of thunderbolts and dust.
By this, the vital energy (*ojas*) of that [place] becomes impaired.
In this way, by approaching another's wife, one causes suffering to arise for the other;
one makes them have a rival wife,
and their vital energy is destroyed.
By that vigor one is designated in the world as "radiant" (*tejasvin*);
for this very reason it was said:
"They are strewn with dust through sexual misconduct."
The same should be applied to the others as well;
this is the general direction.
Everything should be applied by way of the opposite of what is unwholesome.
How so?
By practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the abstention from taking what is not given, one is reborn among the gods.
If one returns to this state and enters the common lot of human beings, one does not suffer the loss of wealth.
Having thus explained in detail [the benefits] through the cultivation and practice of abstaining from sexual misconduct, it continues until:
"one does not become frequently subject to false accusations among the community of humans. Following this same method, everything else should be applied accordingly.
By refraining from taking life, no suffering was produced for another;
he was not killed, nor was his vitality destroyed.
Thus, there are three kinds of fruit.
In this way, by abstaining from taking what is not given, one does not cause suffering to arise for the owner of the wealth, nor does one bring about the ruin of their possessions.
The future [retribution] has been destroyed;
therefore, its fruit is threefold.
By one who abstains from sexual misconduct, suffering is not produced for another.
He was not made to have a rival wife,
nor was his vital energy destroyed;
therefore, he has this threefold fruit.
In this same way, it should be applied elsewhere as well.
(IV.87) "By various views" means by views such as those concerning auspicious ceremonies, omens, lunar days, moments, and constellations.
"By one whose livelihood depends on others":
the causes for the maintenance of the body— robes, alms-food, lodgings, and so forth— are dependent upon others for a monk,
because of the statement, "relying upon alms-food."
For that monk whose livelihood is dependent on others, there may be wrong modes of livelihood, such as hypocrisy.
Flattery,
hinting,
and belittling.
And the desire to secure gain through gain—
these are difficult to purify.
"There are modes of livelihood" refers to the *Śīlaskandhikā*.
The *Śīlaskandhikā* is the name of a section (*nipāta*).
Regarding this, it was said:
"Tridaṇḍin, there are some ascetics and brahmins who, having consumed what is given in faith, dwell devoted to the practice of various speculative views.
For example:"
In elephant combat,
in horse combat,
in chariot combat.
In hand-to-hand combat; in staff-fighting; in fist-fighting.
In the fighting of cranes,
in the fighting of bulls,
in the fighting of buffaloes.
In bullfights, in ramfights, and in cockfights.
In cockfights,
in quail fights,
and in women's fights.
In a battle of men; in a battle of boys;
in a battle of girls.
In the vicinity of Iṭgālava,
at Utsatikā,
on the tip of the banner.
At the vanguard of the army; in the array of the host;
in the drawing out of the ranks.
Some experience great assemblies;
