thus, a śramaṇa abstains from such engagement with various undertakings for the purpose of seeing [spectacles].
For instance, Tridaṇḍin, there are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, having consumed what is given in faith, dwell engaged in the undertaking of listening to various sounds.
Namely:
the sound of an elephant;
the sound of a horse.
In the sound of chariots, in the sound of infantry, in the sound of conch shells.
In the sound of a drum;
in the sound of a kettledrum;
in the sound of dancing.
In the sound of singing;
in the sound of a bed;
in the sound of a snap of the fingers.
In *pāṇisvara* (Abhidh-k-vy 421),
it is adorned with *kuṃbha* and *tūṇīra*,
and possesses variegated syllables.
Some desire to hear stories concerning variegated words and syllables, or those connected with the Lokāyata.
"In this way, a śramaṇa abstains from such engagement with the undertaking of hearing various sounds," and so forth.
[This refers to] the improper enjoyment of sense objects, that is, the incorrect enjoyment of sense objects.
(IV.88, 89) These are the five fruits that were previously mentioned.
The dominant fruit,
the fruit of human effort,
and the concordant fruit.
The fruit of maturation,
the fruit of disjunction,
and the path for the purpose of abandonment.
It is a derivation based on the action (bhāvasādhana).
The path for the sake of abandonment is the "path of abandonment" (prahāṇamārga).
Thus,
it is a derivation based on the instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), meaning "that by which [defilements] are abandoned.
Furthermore, the analysis of the compound is "the path of abandonment" (*prahāṇo mārgaḥ*).
"Subsequent similar dharmas born of concentration.
The inclusion of the term "born of concentration" is for the purpose of excluding those not born of concentration.
The inclusion of the term "similar" is for the purpose of excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*).
"Co-existent" means that therein are both the associated factors, such as feeling and so forth,
and the dissociated factors, such as birth and so forth.
And as for the statement that "that which is future is cultivated":
a future dharma is attained by its power;
therefore, that [attainment] is its fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*). For this very reason, that abandonment is also established as a fruit of human effort.
"It is not only the fruit of dissociation.
Regarding the phrase "excluding those previously arisen," this is because it is not logical for a previously arisen state to be a fruit;
for thus it has been said:
That which is unprecedented (apūrva) is the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) of only that which is conditioned (saṃskṛta),
excluding the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
Because that which is untainted (anāsrava) has no ripening (avipāka).
For its outflow fruit (niṣyandaphala) consists of subsequent similar states born of meditative concentration (samādhi);
its fruit of dissociation (visaṃyogaphala) is dissociation itself, which is that very abandonment (prahāṇa).
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) consists of those factors drawn forth by it,
such as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) and its co-existent factors.
And that which is cultivated as future is also abandonment.
The sovereign fruit consists of all conditioned phenomena other than its own nature, excluding those that have already arisen.
Regarding "whatever is auspicious or inauspicious":
this refers to any other contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma— whether concentrated (*samāhita*) or unconcentrated (*asamāhita*)— besides the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*).
That too is fruitful by way of four fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
Because this is not a path of abandonment (*aprahāṇa-mārga*), it lacks the fruit of dissociation.
For its ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is the desirable or undesirable ripening within its own level.
The outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) consists of subsequent similar dharmas.
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) consists of those dharmas drawn forth by it, whether they are co-existent or immediately subsequent.
The sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) is the remainder, as explained previously.
"Furthermore, the remainder is untainted (anāsrava).
The inclusion of the term "remainder" is for the purpose of excluding the path of abandonment (prahāṇamārga).
Furthermore, how is that so?

The remainder [of the paths] occurs in the paths of preparation (*prayoga*), liberation (*vimukti*), and excellence (*viśeṣa*). Because these are not paths of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), they do not have the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*) as their result.
And because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it does not have a fruition of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
The rest is as before.
And that which is neutral (*avyākṛta*)—namely, both the obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)—is also [not a fruition of maturation].
That too is fruitful by way of three [results].
Because it is the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*), it does not have disjunction (*visaṃyoga*) as its fruit.
And because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it does not have maturation (*vipāka*) as its fruit.
The remainder is exactly as before.
(IV.90) "Four, two, and likewise three for the wholesome"— this is according to their respective order.
How so?
For a wholesome [action], wholesome dharmas are its four fruits;
for that same [wholesome action], unwholesome dharmas are its two fruits.
For that very [action], there are three indeterminate fruits.
This is because the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is excluded,
since maturation itself is indeterminate.
"Two are unwholesome" refers to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
It is not the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
Because wholesome dharmas are not similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for unwholesome ones,
they do not have [unwholesome dharmas] as their fruition result (*vipāka-phala*),
since fruition is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, because unwholesome states are defined in terms of their maturation (vipāka),
they do not have the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyoga-phala) as their result,
owing to their unwholesome nature.
By process of elimination, they are only the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
These two are to be explained as before.
"The four neutral [dharmas]" means:
How can neutral phenomena be the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of an unwholesome [state]?
And why should they not be so? Because they are dissimilar.
For unwholesome factors produced by non-cultivation are indeed dissimilar [to those produced by cultivation],
because they possess both fruition and non-fruition.
This is not a fault.
For unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and non-obscured-unspecified phenomena possess a similarity by virtue of their commonality as afflicted states.
Therefore, it is logical that the outflow fruits of unwholesome phenomena are the obscured-unspecified, and the outflow fruits of obscured-unspecified phenomena are the unwholesome.
Thus he says:
"Regarding the indeterminate," and so forth.
[This refers to] the universal unwholesome [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin,
as well as the [unwholesome] defilements such as attachment that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
It is said that "the unwholesome [dharmas]" are the outflow fruit of the similar-type (*sabhāga*) and universal (*sarvatraga*) [causes], and so forth.
The unwholesome [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering and so forth belong to the five categories.

Regarding the two neutral views— the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)— their outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) consists of these same three [fruits], excluding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visaṃyogaphala*).
(IV.91) For past karma, there are dharmas belonging to the three time periods— past, future, and present.
Each has four fruits,
excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
Because that [result] does not fall within the time periods.
How so? Of past karma, the past ripening—that is, the fruit of ripening—occurs subsequently.
Those drawn forth by it— whether co-arisen and past, or subsequently arisen and immediately past— are the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
With the exception of its own self-nature (*svabhāva*), those that arise together with it and those that arise subsequently, being past, are the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Similar dharmas that arise later and have passed away are the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). A future [dharma] resulting from a past one is the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*),
namely, the future dharma obtained through the power of [the past cause].
That is the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala).
The sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala) is that which is future;
it is its fruit.
The outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) is that which is similar to it and is future.
In this way, the four fruits of that past [action] are also to be applied to present [dharmas]. For the middle [present action] as well, there are future [fruits].
Thus,
for a present [action] as well, future dharmas are four fruits;
the meaning is that these same [four] are [the fruits], excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
Those [results] should also be applied in exactly the same way.
Present dharmas are the two results of a present [cause], namely the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*).
For that which arises simultaneously with it is born by its power; thus it is indeed both the result of human effort and the dominant result.
Because its intrinsic nature is non-dissociation, it is not the fruit of dissociation.
Because there is no sequence of prior and subsequent, it is not the fruit of outflow.
Since maturation depends upon a continuum, a present [dharma] is not the fruit of maturation of a present [cause].
"Excluding the outflow and disjunction fruits":
the future is not the outflow fruit of the future,
because the similar and omnipresent causes do not exist as future states.
Because it is scattered and because it is impossible to determine that "this is its fruit" based on similarity alone,
it is not the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
Because future dissociation does not exist.

However, there may be a fruition of maturation (*vipākaphala*) for the future; for the fruition of maturation of the future—whether it be unwholesome or wholesome-with-outflows—is that which will arise later.
There is also the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).

The "co-nascent" (*sahaja*) is that which arises simultaneously; the "immediately following" (*anantarabhāvin*) is that which arises subsequently. As for the "dominant fruit" (*adhipatiphala*), however, it is easy to understand and thus is not explained again.
(IV.92ab) Dharmas belonging to their own level...
It is not the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*),
because dissociation does not have the nature of being a level (*bhūmi*).
If they are untainted (*anāsrava*), there are three fruits.
Because a third [result], the outflow result (*niṣyandaphala*), is possible;
for it is an established tenet that the path [of cultivation] belongs to nine levels mutually.
(IV.92cd, 93ab) For the karma of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the dharmas of one in training constitute three [fruits].
This is because the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is not of one in training, and the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*) is also not of one in training.
Those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner also have three [fruits].
It does not have the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), because for a learner (*śaikṣa*), there is no maturation.
It is not a flow-on result (*niṣyandaphala*),
because that which is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training is dissimilar to that which is in-training.
However, it is a result of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*).
Because dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) does not have the nature of being either a learner (*śaikṣa*) or a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*),
it is also the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
This is because it is possible for a learner to draw forth that which is neither a learner nor a non-learner.
And the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) certainly exists as well;
thus, three [fruits] are possible.
"But for one beyond training (aśaikṣa)," and so forth in detail.
For one beyond training (aśaikṣa), the dharmas of one in training (śaikṣa) constitute a single dominant fruit (adhipatiphala); they are not a flow-on fruit (niṣyandaphala),
because [the latter] is inferior.
Because of the statement "of the equal and the distinguished," it is not the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala).
Because there is no arising immediately after [that state].
For a state of one in training (śaikṣa) does not arise immediately after a state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
nor does it have the nature of being neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Furthermore, since there is no maturation (*vipāka*) for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is therefore not a fruition of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
For those beyond training, there are three:
the fruition of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), the sovereign fruition (*adhipatiphala*), and the outflowing fruition (*niṣyandaphala*).
Not in the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) nor in the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyogaphala),
because those two do not have the nature of either the learner (śaikṣa) or the non-learner (aśaikṣa);
and that which has the nature of the non-learner [is likewise excluded].
This is now considered here:
"The two [results] that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner are the result of human effort and the dominant result.
This refers to the result of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
Namely:
the phenomena that arise immediately following what has drawn them forth are the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala).
As before.
Because the causes are as previously stated, there are not three fruits.
The same applies to those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The meaning is that there are two fruits: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
"And so forth" refers to those [two].
"Those which are to be abandoned by seeing, and so forth.
"Those" refers to [the afflictions].
Regarding those to be abandoned by seeing and so forth:
"two are to be abandoned by cultivation" means that when emerging from the untainted path, the wholesome states to be abandoned by cultivation are the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
"Like the beginning and the end," and so forth.
"Like the beginning and the end" means as if it were the beginning and the end.
The term "in order" (yathākrama) is mentioned again for the sake of making it known that this applies to the middle as well.
How so?
First, the word "anukrama" (sequence) is employed in the sense of "yathākrama" (according to order).
For the impure, there are two, three, and four [objects] starting from the pure, respectively.
Because of this statement,
it is also applied at the end:
"But for that which is not to be abandoned, those [factors] are respectively one, two, and four."
Thus,
just as the meaning of the sequence has been explained for the beginning and the end,
so too should it be understood for the middle.
For this is the method of abbreviation;
this is the principle of condensation.
Otherwise, indeed...
"In the cases such as 'of the indeterminate there are two or three,' and 'these are the wholesome and so forth,' it must be stated everywhere that [the sequence] is according to order.
(IV.95) Because they arise from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*)."
That which has arisen there is the mental attention that has proceeded by way of what is not the womb, by way of what is improper, through connection with the afflictions.
The state of being that [is] "therefore" (tasmāt). That by which and in what manner one should go.

When a person does not proceed in the manner in which they ought to proceed, that is their improperly performed action (*ayogavihita-karma*). It is also called "deviation from the rule" (*vidhibhraṣṭa*).
By the word "also" (api), it is understood that it is also afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
That which is other than both of these is "neither way";
it is not prescribed by yoga (*na yogavihitaḥ*).
It is not that which is performed improperly.
Furthermore, what else is neutral (*avyākṛta*) action? It is that which is neutral other than [the two types]—that which deviates from the rule and that which does not deviate from the rule.
(IV.96ab) "Birth" is a designation for the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
The intention is that [this applies] to a formation dissociated from mind, but not to birth (*jāti*).
As for the phrase "then what": [it refers to the following].

If a single karma projects only a single birth, then how is it that the statement made by the Elder Niruddha— "I am that [person]" and so forth— is not contradicted? This is the meaning of the sentence.
In another life, he gave alms-food to the Pratyekabuddha Tagaraśikhin. Because of that, he said: "I am that one," and so forth in detail.
"Having brought about" (*nirvartya*) means "having established" (*viṭhapitvā*).
Even though humanity is equal, some possess all their faculties (*sakalendriya*), while others have impaired faculties (*vikalendriya*).
That [objection] is untenable because of the distinction between completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*) and projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*).
Since the eye and the other [faculties] are the fruit of projecting karma,
for it is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) that are projected.
However, it is reasonable to say that color and so forth are the fruit of completing karma;
for even though they are equal in being human, one possesses a [fine] complexion while another does not.
There is no contradiction because, when the conditions that obstruct its arising are avoided, the power of completing karma brings it about;
otherwise, if there were the projection of birth, no one would have impaired faculties.
(IV.96cd) "The other [karma] also has ripening" means:
"Feeling and so forth," because they do not coexist with karma;
that is, because those two attainments (samāpatti) do not exist together with karma known as volition (cetanā).
Nor is it projected by bodily or vocal actions because of the absence of mind;
nor is it projected by acquisitions (*prāpti*), even those associated with maturation (*savipāka*),
because karma does not have multiple fruits.
Even though the acquisitions (*prāpti*) coexist with the karma that projects [rebirth], they do not share the same fruit as it.
For acquisitions, like the outer bark of a tree, remain external [to the core action].
(IV.97) This refers to the "obscuration of karma" (*karmāvaraṇa*).
Karma itself is an obscuration;
affliction itself is an obscuration;
ripening itself is an obscuration.
And regarding the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) that are preparatory for the noble path (āryamārga)—
namely, those such as "heat" (uṣmagata) and so forth—
they are not fixed toward the miserable states (apāya) and the like.
[These are] those fixed [karmas] pertaining to hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
By the word "etcetera," the fixed karma conducive to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the great Brahmā realm (*mahābrahman*) is included.
Furthermore, that which conduces to being a eunuch (*ṣaṇḍha*), a neuter (*paṇḍaka*), or one possessing both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*) must also be mentioned.
Likewise, the actions that determine birth as an egg-born being, a moisture-born being, as a female, or in the eighth existence must be explained.
For noble ones (*āryas*) are not reborn in the hells and other such realms;
they do not enter the egg-born or moisture-born modes of birth.
They will not undergo an eighth existence as a woman,
because they have seven existences at most; thus,
they are "easily discernible."

They are called *sudarśāni* because they are easily seen by others; *sudarśakāni* is simply another term for *sudarśāni*. Likewise, they are called *suprajñeyāni* because they are easily understood by oneself.
They are indeed easy to understand and easy to explain.
The suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). These two [terms] are synonyms.
"Easy to see and easy to understand.
Regarding "by way of the basis":
the basis is the path of action (*karmapatha*).
Of the three immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), the course of action (*karmapatha*) of taking life is the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
For one [of them], the course of action of false speech is the basis.
For the fifth, the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) of taking life is the basis.
Thus, they are easy to see and easy to point out by way of their basis and by way of their fruit.
Because they all have undesirable results; and because of their destination, since they lead to rebirth in the hell realms.
By way of rebirth,
because it is to be experienced upon rebirth;
by way of the person.
A person is well known because of the manifestation of extremely grave afflictions, such as:
"This one is a parricide," up to "This one is one who has shed the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind."
Others, however, explain it as being by way of the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*),
as before.
By way of its fruit:
because it has hell as its fruit. By way of its destiny.
Because it brings about birth in the human realm.
"The immediate [offenses] exist in the three continents."
Because of the scriptural statement;
because of logical reasoning;
and because it is to be experienced precisely upon rebirth.
In terms of the person:
it is a woman or a man, not a *ṣaṇḍha* or a *paṇḍaka*.
Thus, by these five reasons, [the paths] are easy to see and easy to explain.
However, those actions fixed for the miserable states (*apāya*) and so forth are not easy to see or easy to explain by means of these five reasons;
therefore, they were not mentioned.
"Because of the successive bringing forth" means that the obscuration of afflictions brings forth the obscuration of karma,
and the obscuration of karma brings forth undesirable maturation in the miserable realms.
The obscuration of afflictions is the most evil of all;
the obscuration of karma is lighter than that;
and the obscuration of maturation is lighter still.
For the operation of the obstruction of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*) occurs only in the present life,
not in the second [life].
It is through connection with such a phenomenon as the killing of a father that one becomes "immediate" (*ānantarya*).
When expressing that [state], an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used,
as in "immediacy" (*ānantarya*),
just like the term "asceticism" (*śrāmaṇya*).

Just as one becomes a *śramaṇa* through union with that untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), so too, when expressing that state, there is an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). Thus, *śrāmaṇya* is the stainless path.
Thus it is.
Likewise, [it is] not in Uttarakuru. (IV.98) It is not in Uttarakuru.
Because their lifespan is fixed,
because they possess natural morality,
and because the teaching exists there.
"The very reason for the absence of non-restraint is because one's intention is unstable even regarding evil;
and where there is restraint, [there too it is absent]."
In that regard, there is also non-restraint (asaṃvara),
because it exists as its opposite.
Thus is non-restraint.
"It does not occur for eunuchs and others" means "because of the destruction of which."
Because of the destruction and the agitation of that sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*), eunuchs and others would be touched by the immediate [retribution] (*ānantarya*);
however, toward their own mother and father, that [shame and dread] is not intense in them.
Therefore, for them, there is no immediate [retribution].
It is not accepted.
If it is argued that they provide little benefit because they are causes for an incomplete personal existence (*ātmabhāva*),
therefore their [acts] are not accepted as immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*).
Even for men and women who are blind from birth and so forth, there would not be an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) for killing their mother or others.
No;
for what is intended is a deficiency of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva-vaikalya*) that is contrary to the dharma of realization (*adhigama-dharma*).
That deficiency which is contrary to the dharma of realization is what is intended here;
and by that alone is meant a slight degree of affection,
not a deficiency such as being born blind and so forth.
For this very reason, they are not admitted even for animals and hungry ghosts (preta),
precisely because they provide little benefit and lack a sense of shame.
"Like a well-bred horse.
This refers to the fact that for those with sharp intellects, there may be immediate succession [of realization], even among animals and hungry ghosts. "Like a well-bred horse."
It is heard that there was once a certain distinguished horse of noble breed who would not mate with his mother.
Having had his face covered with a cloth, he was led to his mother; later, realizing what had happened, he tore out his own sexual organ.
Thus, a horse of noble breed possesses a sharp intelligence.
The intention is that there would be an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) for this [person].
Even for a human who kills non-human parents, there would not be an immediate transgression;
the meaning is that there simply would not be an immediate transgression.
How so?
Precisely because they feel no shame regarding their meager assistance.

For a non-human being is not capable of performing a benefit corresponding to that of a human; nor does intense shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*) arise in a human toward non-human parents, because affection is slight due to the difference in their respective realms of rebirth (*gati*). (IV.99) "Four bodily actions" means:
The killing of one's mother and so forth;
or one verbal action:
the schism of the Saṃgha.
Three are "taking life," namely,
matricide and so forth;
one is "false speech."
Regarding the schism in the Saṃgha (*saṃghabheda*):
one [aspect] is the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) for taking life.
Why is causing blood to flow from the body of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind not considered taking life? To this he says:
"For Tathāgatas have the nature of being beyond assault" means that they do not have the nature of dying through the assault of others.
[The phrase] "because of the metaphorical application of the fruit to the cause" [is used].
False speech is the cause of the schism in the Saṃgha, which is characterized as being dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*).
This is a metaphorical designation of the fruit upon that cause;
the phenomenon dissociated from the mind is figuratively designated as the fruit.
"Schism in the Saṃgha" means: it is split by this, or that by which [the Saṃgha] is split.
Alternatively, by adopting the sense of the word as an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), false speech is called "schism in the Saṃgha" (*saṃghabheda*);
for it is by means of false speech that the Saṃgha is split. However, one does not adopt the sense of the word as an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*) [to mean] "the act of schism."
(IV.100) "But schism in the Saṃgha is non-harmony. For the Vaibhāṣikas, this exists as a substantial entity (*dravyasattā*) in its primary sense.
Therefore, he says:
Its intrinsic nature is dissociated;
it is a phenomenon that is non-defiled and indeterminate.
"Will that become an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*)?"— the meaning is that it does not become an immediate transgression characterized in such a manner.
Furthermore, the schismatic is not endowed with that dissociated factor (*viprayukta-dharma*).
Therefore, the intention is that this [act] is not an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).

(IV.101) Furthermore, that false speech is co-nascent with the schism of the Saṃgha, or co-nascent with the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*); its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) and non-intimation (*avijñapti*). This is the meaning.
(IV.102) "A monk causes the schism."
Because the Buddha is a monk,
and because the schismatic acts in rivalry with him;
householders, nuns, and so forth are not [schismatics].
Because their basis is not to be accepted,
and that [basis] consists precisely in conduct based on views,
owing to the firmness and secrecy of their underlying intention.

One who has practiced and engaged in the five [wrong views] beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is one whose conduct is dominated by views (*dṛṣṭicarita*). Alternatively, one for whom views constitute their conduct is a "view-conduct" person.
For such a person, through the power of reasoning and refutation, is capable of persuading others to accept another teacher or another path.
"He is not one whose conduct is dominated by craving" because his disposition is unstable with respect to both the sides of affliction and purification.
"Because he is difficult to overcome" means...
"Because he is difficult to overcome;

because he has directly realized the Dharma"— this means that he has attained direct realization (*sākṣātkāritva*) of both the Dharma of scripture (*āgama*) and the Dharma of realization (*adhigama*).
"Not those who have attained receptivity" means not those who have attained the receptivity that is part of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
because they are equivalent to those who have seen the truths.
"He does not dwell there" means that he does not spend that night there. As for the statement "it becomes broken," [the author] asks, "In what way is it broken? and then says:
"Because it obstructs the proceeding of the Path" means because it hinders the proceeding of the Path.
For as long as the Saṃgha has not been reunited, [the obstruction remains].
To that extent, the engagement of the path remains suspended;
it does not mean that the path manifests within the continuum of anyone. This is the meaning.
Because it is the cause for the schism of the wheel (*cakrabheda*).
The schism of the Saṃgha is called the schism of the wheel.
For the Saṃgha must necessarily be divided into two factions. (IV.103)
The meaning is that one must stand on the side of the Buddha and on the side of the schismatic.
For a *saṃgha* consists of four monks;
and since there must be two *saṃghas*, there must be eight monks who are to be divided.
And by means of the ninth schismatic; but "schism of the Saṃgha" refers to something other than a schism of the Wheel (cakrabheda).
The intention here is that there is no immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
This is because it arises from a division of the action (*karmabheda*).
[The term] "distracted" (*vyagra*) means...
"Various opinions" refers to ritual acts such as the *poṣadha* and other formal procedures (*saṃghakarma*) of the Saṃgha.
"By eight or more" means by those [eight] and more.
In this case as well, there must be two Saṅghas;
the schismatic does not consider himself the Teacher, so there must be exactly eight monks, and not nine or more.
(IV.104) "It becomes of a single flavor" means that it becomes undistracted and of a single-minded nature.
In the preceding state, joy and gladness have arisen.
In the west, he became exceedingly agitated in mind and felt a sense of spiritual urgency.
"Before the Arbuda" means that the fault is the Arbuda.
Whether it be a tumor of views (*dṛṣṭyarbuda*) or a tumor of morality (*śīlārbuda*). Here, regarding the tumor of views,
it is as has been stated:
As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken:
those things declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive conditions are not sufficient to constitute an obstruction when they are indulged in.
Likewise, it is said that "that very mind runs on and wanders through cyclic existence," and so forth.
"Moral tumor" refers to immorality (*dauḥśīlya*).
And because [the cycle] is to be reconnected by means of that [immorality].
And by that pair of disciples, it means that [the lineage] is to be reconnected.
Furthermore, every Buddha necessarily has a pair of disciples:
one is the foremost among those possessed of wisdom.
The second [assembly] was of those possessing supernatural powers.
Here, the noble Śāradvatīputra is the foremost among those possessed of wisdom;
the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana is the foremost among those possessing supernatural powers.
"Because of the absence of an opponent" means that since the Blessed One has entered final nirvana, there is no one who could act as an opponent to that schism.
"When the boundary has not been established" means...
Within the boundary of the maṇḍala.
For indeed, within a single boundary, a schism in the Saṃgha occurs due to the performance of separate formal acts (karma).
But is there not a natural boundary (prakṛtisīmā)?
Villages, cities, and so forth do indeed exist as natural boundaries;
however, when a formal boundary (*jñaptisīmā*) has been established, that natural boundary is then set aside.
It should be understood that for her as well, bondage is indeed established,
because it is dependent upon karma— that is,
by whom karma conducive to causing a schism in the community of disciples has been performed.
That schism occurs only for him [the Teacher],
not for anyone else.
It is said that while Śākyamuni was still in the state of a bodhisattva, he caused a schism in the assembly of a rishi who possessed the five superknowledges.
"By whom the Saṃgha was split by Devadatta" (IV.105,
106ab). "Because of being a field of qualities" means because of being the locus of qualities.
Alternatively, a "field of qualities" (*guṇakṣetra*) is a field by virtue of its qualities;
for through the conjunction with qualities, it becomes a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Just as seed sown in a [fertile] field yields a great fruit.
Thus, the seed of merit sown here yields great fruit,
but not elsewhere— that is,
not in cases such as the killing of an ordinary woman.
"Because of the rejection and destruction of the field of benefactors and the field of qualities.

This means that through the rejection— that is, the abandonment— of either the field of benefactors or the field of qualities, there is an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) in cases such as the killing of one's mother or father.
And because of its destruction and disturbance, it constitutes an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*):
namely, from drawing blood with a malicious mind from the body of a Tathāgata,
and also that which is the schism of the Saṃgha.
That too is its destruction.
This is what is meant:
because it is a field of benefit.
And because she is a field of qualities (*guṇakṣetra*):
since the destruction and ruin of that [field] constitutes immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), it occurs only in cases such as matricide and so forth, and not elsewhere.
Furthermore, what if the mother’s sexual characteristics (*vyañjana*) were to change, or likewise the father’s?
"By the change of gender, that motherhood or that fatherhood has been destroyed.

[The opponent argues] that because there is no killing of the mother or no killing of the father, there would be no immediate retribution (*ānantarya*). Anticipating the concern that this might be the case, he asks.
"Born from whose blood":
that of which the birth is from her blood.
"Born from blood"—
the intention is that he is to be regarded as Avalokita in all ritual activities (*sarvakṛtya*),
that is, in all tasks appropriate for a mother.
Because she is like a mother:
she is the nourisher (*āpyāyikā*), the provider of food (*katāhārikā*), and the sustainer who gives breast milk (*stanyadāyikā*).
The *saṃvardhikā* is one who prepares substantial food and so forth.
Others explain that the term *āpyāyikā* means a wet-nurse who provides breast milk.
The nourisher (*poṣikā*) is so called because of the practice of providing coarse food; the rearer (*saṃvardhikā*) is so called because of bathing, massaging, and avoiding uneven ground.
"Hidden beneath the surface of the bed" (*mañcatalāvalīna*).

For example, it should be cited that a son, thinking a man was sleeping on a bed because he had arranged a covering over it, struck him there with a weapon; by that stroke of the weapon, his mother, who was hidden beneath the surface of the bed, was killed.
And likewise, the son of a washerman or dyer, intending "I shall kill a mosquito," kills his father through an action directed at a mosquito.
There are two types of non-informative action (*avijñapti*): the non-informative action of an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) and the non-informative action of mere killing.
However, as for informative action (*vijñapti*), it is only the immediate transgression itself; the meaning is that it is subsumed solely within that and not in anything else.
For that [offense] as well, there is only one:
that called "killing an Arhat.
"Go and speak to Śikhaṇḍin"—thus, in the city of Rauruka, a king named Udrāyaṇa, having consecrated his son named Śikhaṇḍin, went forth into the religious life.
He attained the state of arhatship through renunciation. He arrived in the vicinity of Rauruka,
desiring once again to rule the kingdom.
King Śikhaṇḍin, incited by his ministers, killed his own father. While he was being put to death, he said to the man who was killing him, "Go and tell Śikhaṇḍin," and so forth.
It should be stated that this occurs due to two causes.
"Go and say to Śikhaṇḍin:
'You have committed an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya) through two causes of immediate retribution.
He should then be told:"
"Or it is censured by way of two aspects.
The intention is that because there are two aspects, there is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of two immediate offenses (*ānantarya*).
For indeed, due to the duality of its causes, that immediate offense is more grave.
(IV.106cd) "Because the basis is absolutely opposed to them" means that the basis of one in whom the Noble Path has arisen is opposed to those courses of action.
And here, a single avadāna serves as an illustration.
It is said that a Śākya man named Cheka, out of fear of Virūḍhaka, took refuge in a rugged forest region and adopted the livelihood of a hunter.
While the Blessed One was spending the three-month rains retreat among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, he descended from there and taught the Dharma to Cheka and his family.
Through this, Cheka attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*).
And by his sons, who had already attained their fruits, snares, nets, and the like were previously laid out for the deer.
Even though the deer were being killed through the employment of those means, because they had attained their fruits, they were not touched again by unwholesome paths of action.
(IV.107) The fifth, third, and first [offenses] are the most serious.
This is the sequence for the recitation of the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*):
killing one’s mother, killing one’s father, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and with a malicious mind, drawing blood from a Tathāgata.
The fifth is the drawing of blood from a Tathāgata with a malicious mind.
Among the remaining [four], excluding the schism of the Saṅgha,
the third— killing an Arhat—
is more serious than killing one's mother or father.
First is the killing of one's mother;
that is more grave than the killing of one's father.
Therefore, he says:
"The lightest [offense] is the killing of a father.
Regarding the word "of the rule" (niyamasya):
the meaning is that one must determine that very thing.

With reference to the extent of its maturation, schism in the Saṃgha is said to be a great transgression because it yields maturation for an intermediate kalpa. With reference to the harming of many people, mental punishment is [the greatest].
Because it rendered the Daṇḍaka forest and other regions desolate;
for it is not possible for such a great multitude of people to be brought to ruin by any other physical or vocal action.
With respect to the total eradication of the roots of virtue, wrong view is the most blameworthy.

For no other unwholesome root cuts off the wholesome roots, because it is only opposed to their manifestation; however, it does not do so immediately. (IV.108, 109ab) But it is not [immediately] thereafter.
They are called "similar" (*sabhāga*) to hell because one will necessarily be reborn there due to their resemblance to it,
but not because of immediate rebirth (*anantara-utpatti*) therein; for otherwise, they would simply be "immediate transgressions" (*ānantarya*), according to the opinion of others.

"Even if they occur immediately after [the murder of a Buddha], those acts cannot be *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses because their timing and maturation are not equal. This is the rebuttal of those who hold the first position. [Now follows] the refutation regarding the mother who is an Arhatī.

Killing a Bodhisattva who is destined for enlightenment is similar to the immediate transgression of killing one’s mother. Killing a Śaikṣa is similar to the immediate transgression of killing an Arhat. Killing a father is similar to the immediate transgression of killing one’s father.

The theft of the community’s gateway is similar to the immediate offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha. The destruction of a stūpa is similar to the immediate offense of shedding the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind.
Furthermore, Master Vasumitra states that the theft of the community’s gateway refers specifically to the misappropriation of the inexhaustible endowment (*akṣayanīvī*).
They explain it thus: "It is the theft of the gateway to happiness. That is, the taking away of that which serves for happiness, by means of which the Saṅgha maintains its livelihood.
(IV.109cd) "Because of the transgression of the level of its maturation" means:
"One who has attained patience does not go to the states of woe" means that they have transcended the planes of the states of woe.
"In the same way" refers to this.
Because of the transcendence of the stage of its maturation.
The meaning is that it is exactly as when creditors rise up against a man who is leaving his country.
(Abhidh-k-vy 431)
(IV.110) "Born into a great *sāla* family" means born into a family with a large outer wall (*mahāprākāra*).
This extends from being born into a great *kṣatriya* *sāla* family up to being born into a great *gṛhapati* *sāla* family.
The meaning is "born into a great householder family.

*Kadarthanā* is harassment preceded by great contempt. With respect to those actions of body and speech through the engagement of which suffering and mental distress arise in another, the restraint of those [actions] is called *yantraṇā*.
(IV.111) "Starting from the ninety-first eon" means:
the eon that completes the ninety-one is the "ninety-first";
starting from that.
The householder Aśibaddhaka, a disciple of the Nirgranthas, said to the Blessed One:

"For what purpose, O Gautama, have you set out to the detriment of these families, that in such a time of famine, together with such a great community of monks, you wander for alms as if destroying them like a thunderbolt?
He was then addressed by the Blessed One:
"From now on, village chief, taking up ninety-one eons," and so forth.
He turns away these four faults:
the fault of an evil rebirth, the fault of low birth, the fault of impaired faculties, and the fault of being female.
And he acquires two qualities:
the quality of recollecting past births and the quality of non-retrogression. This is with the exception of a Bodhisattva who is near [to enlightenment].
He who performs the karma that results in the maturation of the marks brings about the trichiliocosm;
by the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings, the trichiliocosm is produced.
The manifestation of a great trichiliocosm:
that is its measure.
Thus, the measure of merit has been stated.
For those [meritorious deeds] whose measure has been thus established, one mark of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa) is produced by a hundred of them;
and so on, up to the thirty-second. Some explain it in this way.

Others explain that because the mental attention directed toward the Buddha (*buddhālambanamanaskāra*) becomes manifest, there are fifty volitions (*cetanā*); and thinking "may I also become thus," there are another fifty— thus there are one hundred merits (*puṇya*).
The desire realm consists of twenty locations;
the form realm, sixteen;
and the formless realm, four.
There are also eight cold hells; thus, the triple world consists of forty-eight varieties.
With that as its object, this bodhisattva’s mind of compassion arises.
Consequently, there arise forty-eight volitions associated with that [compassion].
Immediately after this, a volition directed toward the Buddhas arises.
One volition is: "By him, sentient beings have been liberated from this triple world.
Immediately after that, a second volition arises.
"May I also liberate them in this way"—this is the intention based on oneself (*ātmālambana*).
There are fifty volitions (*cetanā*), and because these manifest twice, there come to be one hundred volitions.
Others say:
The Blessed Buddha’s abstention from taking life is endowed with five reasons.
These five reasons are:
the purification of the fundamental path of action.
Purity of the vicinity,
non-affliction by discursive thoughts,
and being sustained by mindfulness.
And [the volition] consisting in dedication to nirvāṇa. Thus, there are five types of volitions that have those as their objects.
In this way, there are fifty volitions—ten sets of five—having the ten paths of action as their objects.
Because these [three] appear twice, there is a hundredfold volition; this is the "hundredfold merit.

Thinking, "Just as this Blessed One has arisen from the uncommon ten paths of wholesome action, may I too become so," when this is the case, it is established that each [major mark] is born from a hundredfold merit.
(IV.112) *paryupāsayāmāsa*: this is the form of the root *ās* with the suffix *āṃ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). It means "he attended upon" (*paryupāsitavān*).
"Where [it says] 'by the Blessed One,' and so forth:
having performed service by means of pleasant water, bathing, and anointing while he was the potter's son named Prabhāsa, he made his first vow.
At that time, his perfections of patience and ethical discipline were fulfilled. (IV.114, 115)
First, the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) is fulfilled through the mind being free from anger;
the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is fulfilled by not committing misdeeds through body and speech.
"Neither in heaven nor on earth," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
"Whether in heaven or on earth," it is said according to the principle of stating the general scope.
"Neither in this world, nor in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa."
Not in the divine abode of the gods.
Thus it is said.
The explanatory phrases for the purpose of clarifying that are:
"in this world."
In the world of humans;
"the abode of Vaiśravaṇa" refers to the place of the Cāturmahārājika gods.
"Marubhavana" means in the abode of the Maruts; that is to say, in the abode of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
He says this in order to make known that such [a being] does not exist even in other world-systems, including the divine realm or the realm of the Yāmas and so forth.
Neither in the cardinal directions nor in the intermediate directions.
If you still do not believe this, then let him go.
A certain man [traverses] this earth.
The entire [earth], flourishing and inhabited by many beings, together with its mountains and forests.
The intention is that they should personally inspect [the earth] together with its mountains and forests.
And nine aeons were turned back. Because the perfection of vigor was fulfilled through ninety-one aeons by means of that exertion of vigor,
it is therefore said that [the result] was projected during ninety-one aeons.
"Immediately prior to awakening" means immediately prior to awakening characterized by the knowledge of destruction and non-arising. What is the reason?
For one who has fulfilled the perfections attains awakening, not one whose perfections are unfulfilled. (IV.116) "According to what is appropriate" means:
Some are both merit and action;
some are both merit and action;
and some are merit alone.
And action:
some are both merit and a thing;
some are merely a thing.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"That is to say," and so forth.
They are both actions and paths.
The seven courses of action, beginning with the taking of life,
are so called because they possess the nature of karma and because they are the paths of volition (*cetanā*).
However, the three beginning with covetousness (*abhidhyā*) are "paths of action" only in the sense that they are the paths of the karma known as volition.
Bodily and vocal action are of three kinds.
First, it is merit because it has a desirable maturation;
it is action because its intrinsic nature is that of karma.
The object [is meritorious] because the volition that originates it proceeds by taking that as its basis.
The volition that originates it is the volition that gives rise to bodily and vocal action.
It is merit because it has a desirable ripening.
It is an action because it is mental karma;
it is not a substantial entity because it lacks a physical basis.
The feelings and other factors that coexist with it are likewise [mental].
It is merit alone because it has a desirable maturation;
however, it is not the action itself nor its basis,
because they lack those characteristics.
"Consisting of morality":
as before, this should be applied in three ways.
"Loving-kindness is merit."

This should be applied as before. And it is the basis for meritorious action because of the volition associated with that [basis]— that is, the volition associated with loving-kindness— due to its formative activity (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*) and its intentional engagement (*abhisaṃcetana*) by way of loving-kindness and through the power of loving-kindness.

The volition co-arising with that, which is co-arising with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and the morality included within the meditative restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*), constitute merit and action as previously described.
For volition does not proceed by taking as its basis the thought, "I shall initiate meditative restraint";
therefore, there is no basis for action.
The other factors co-arising with it, such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, are merit alone, as previously explained. Thus,
in the case of giving (*dānamaya*), there is merit, action (*kriyā*), and the basis (*vastu*).
Merit, meritorious action,
and the basis for meritorious action.
In the case of that consisting in ethical discipline (*śīlamaya*), there is merit (*puṇya*), action (*kriyā*), and the basis of action (*kriyāvastu*);
thus it is a "basis of meritorious action" (*puṇyakriyāvastu*).
In the case of that consisting in cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*), there is likewise a basis of meritorious action.
It is both merit and action;
thus, "meritorious action-base" (puṇyakriyāvastu) refers to that which is both merit and action.
The retention of only one from among words that share the same form as their constituent parts (*avayava*) is also accepted,
as in the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoh*.

Furthermore, the word *dāna* is formed by adding the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*) to the root *dā*, according to the principle that "that which is given is a gift" (*yad api dīyate tad dānam*).
That by which something is given is called "giving" (dāna);
however, in this context, "giving" is intended to mean that which is wholesome (kuśala).
For the gift, such as clothing and so forth, is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by passion and so forth," anger, envy, and the like are included.
[It is given] "with the desire to honor or to benefit."
Worship is performed toward the *caityas* of those who have attained final nirvāṇa.
It is done by one desiring to benefit the sense faculties and the great elements through that [offering].
"By which collection" refers to the collection of mind and mental factors (*cittacaittakalāpa*).
"Wholesome aggregates" refers to the five aggregates.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) should be understood as bodily and vocal intimation (vijñapti), or even non-intimation (avijñapti).
Furthermore, this suffix -maya is used in the sense of "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva),
not in the sense of "transformation" (vikāra) and so forth.

For example, regarding the phrase "a house made of grass": there is no transformation (*vikāra*) of the grass itself; rather, that [house] was constructed by those very grasses in their untransformed state. Therefore, it is understood that "made of grass" means it has the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of grass.
Even though that [substance] possesses its own inherent nature, the intention is that the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by postulating a state of transformation (*vikāratā*).
Alternatively, the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed by the grammatical rule: "The suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of being made from that material cause (*tatprakṛti*)."
In the same way, this too should be stated: "a vessel made of leaves" (IV.118ab).
With the exception of that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), it is set aside because it serves both purposes.
Because one has completely transcended the level of its maturation;
that is to say, because one has completely transcended the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
For the desire realm is the level of maturation for giving.
(IV.119) "Endowed with qualities such as learning (*śruta*)":
by the word "such as" (*ādi*), it is meant that he is endowed with qualities such as renunciation (*tyāga*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*).
"He gives with reverence (*satkṛtya*) and so forth."
"Respectfully, etc., of this" means "respectful and so forth.
This is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
There are four distinctions in their respective order.
One who gives with respect becomes a recipient of honor.
One who gives with one's own hand gains a taste for sublime enjoyments.
One who gives at the proper time obtains enjoyments when the time is right.
Not from that which is past its time,
such that one would be unable even to consume it;
the donor who gives without harming others obtains enjoyments that cannot be taken away.
(IV.120) And her limbs possess a touch pleasant according to the season:
they are warm when it is cold,
and cool when it is hot.
"In common [places], they are common" (IV.121ab).
And "in cases such as the cold season," etc.;
by the word "etc.," one includes the rainy season, the monsoon, and so forth.
This has been stated according to the Sūtra.

Regarding the phrase "as in the case of mother and father," the meaning should be understood as follows: because of the particularity of their beneficence, benefit and harm done toward them result in great fruit.
"Retribution" (vipāka) is illustrated by examples such as the *Ṛkṣajātaka* and the *Mṛgajātaka*.

Thus, because those who had been benefactors—having entered a cave with the bear and the deer and having rescued them from being carried away by a river by providing the heat of their own bodies or by cooling them—inflicted harm upon them, their limbs fell off immediately.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as the *Kapijātaka* should be cited.
"By giving to one who possesses ethical discipline (*śīlavat*), the maturation (*vipāka*) is a hundred-thousandfold," and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is meant that by giving to one who has entered the path toward the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala-pratipannaka*), the maturation is immeasurable; greater than that is the [maturation] for one who is a stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*), and so on.
"Setting that aside" means:
The bodhisattva’s generosity has just been described;
for it is indeed for the sake of perfect enlightenment and for the benefit of all sentient beings.
The remainder is not analyzed here because it is easy to understand.
Regarding this [verse] beginning with "a gift to one who has not given to me": "a gift to one who has not given to me" means that because he gave to me in the past, this is the third type of gift.
"‘He will give me a gift’ is the fourth.
‘Gifts were previously given by my fathers and grandfathers’ is the fifth.
Giving for the sake of heaven is the sixth."
The seventh is for the sake of fame.
The eighth is the giving for the sake of adorning the mind, up to the attainment of the supreme goal.
Adorning the mind is for the sake of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
For the sake of the equipment of the mind, there are the eight factors of the path as the equipment of the mind;
for that purpose,
for the sake of the equipment of yoga, and for the sake of the foundation of yoga.
The attainment of the supreme goal is the attainment of arhatship or nirvāṇa. Giving for the sake of that attainment,
though consisting of four types, constitutes the eighth [category].
"Because this alone leads to the attainment of nirvāṇa.
This was stated clearly by the Master.
(IV.122) Regarding the "fourfold excellence of the field":

Regarding the question, "In which category [does it fall] among the fields of rebirth (*gati-kṣetra*), the field of suffering (*duḥkha-kṣetra*), the field of benefactors (*upakāri-kṣetra*), or the field of virtues (*guṇa-kṣetra*)?"—

since for this [person] neither the state of being a field of rebirth nor the state of being a field of virtue is possible, he therefore asks. "[He is] the revealer of the even and the uneven" refers to dharma and adharma.

(IV.123) “Because of the establishment of the certainty of maturation” means because of the establishment of the necessity of yielding a definite maturation. “For someone, solely by virtue of the field” [is the meaning].
For example:
killing one's father is more serious than killing an ordinary person;
furthermore, it is because of the specific basis [of the victim] within that very same field [of merit].
It is due to the power of the paths of action.
How so? He says:
because of the taking of the life of one's mother or father, the karma is heavy; however, it is not so heavy for [the taking of] what is not given and so forth.
For the act of stealing the property of one's mother or father does not become as grave as their murder.
This is because such murder is by nature an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*); by the word "etcetera," lying, slander, and so forth are included.
In this same manner, other cases should also be applied accordingly.
For some, it becomes heavy through a particular application, because it remains fixed in its certainty of ripening;
for some, through a particular volition; and for some, through a particular intention.

(IV.124) "Not done unintentionally, nor done impulsively. Alternatively, "not done unintentionally" means not done without prior reflection, such as thinking, "I shall do this"; that is not accumulated (*upacita*).
For that action is indeterminate;
it was not performed impulsively.
Even though it was performed intentionally, it was not done impulsively.
That unwholesome action which was performed through the habitual practice of uttering false speech and so forth— driven by the impulse of the Bhāṣya— is not accumulated (*upacita*).
This applies up to the phrase "by three," namely,
by the three types of misconduct of body, speech, and mind.
"And being without an antidote" means due to the absence of antidotes such as confession and so forth. "Unwholesome and accompanied by unwholesome associates" refers to this.
"One who, having performed [an action], also rejoices in it" means that it is certain to yield its maturation because of the production of a fully developed unwholesome characteristic.
In the same way, wholesome [karma] should also be applied.
How so?
It is that which is performed intentionally, having been deliberately willed.
It does not occur through an action performed unintentionally.
For example,
with an indeterminate mind, one might give a lump of gold while thinking, "I am giving a stone."
That was done, but not accumulated;
for that action is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
It was not performed impulsively.
Just as truthful speech was performed due to the challenge posed by the commentary, that was wholesome but not accumulated.
Some go to a happy destination by means of a single good deed;
some by as many as three.
Someone [proceeds] by means of one path of action;
someone by as many as ten. In that regard, whoever proceeds by a certain number [of paths], [that is what is meant].
As long as that [action] is not completed, the karma performed is not accumulated;
but when it is completed, it is accumulated.
Thus, up to the point of being certain in the yielding of its maturation.
It should be applied according to the possibility. (Abhidh-k-vy 436) (IV.125ab) "For one who still possesses passion toward a *caitya*" is the full statement.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of one's own welfare, the welfare of others, or both," [the author],
not seeing that merit alone follows from relinquishment, says:
Because there is no benefit for anyone at all.
For it is only when there is a recipient that merit consisting of the act of relinquishment is logical.
For in that case, it is appropriate for the recipient to be one who accepts through the favor of joy (*prīty-anugraha*).
"Like loving-kindness and so forth" means not accepting, just as in the case of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
"Like loving-kindness and so forth" (*maitryādivat*) means as in the case of loving-kindness and the others.
Merit arises even when there is no recipient who accepts,
and even in the absence of benefiting others,
because of the strengthening of the power of the roots of virtue and so forth.

For even in the case of the past, such as the Tathāgata Puṇyavati and others, a gift made to a shrine out of devotion constitutes merit. [Objection: In that case, it follows that the act of giving and honoring would be rendered useless.
If merit were to arise from one's own mind alone, then giving and honoring should be performed by the mind alone,
since merit would be obtained from that very source.
This is not so.
Because the devotion that motivates that action is more excellent.
This is not so.
Why?
Because the devotion felt by one who merely contemplates in their mind the giving and honoring of the Blessed One is surpassed by this devotion of one who actually performs the giving and honoring;
for it also sets in motion the actions of body and speech.
For when one contemplates by means of mind alone, devotion does not set in motion the actions of body and speech.
"Just as," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

For example, suppose someone has formed the intention, "I shall kill my enemy"; the bodily and vocal action arising from that—that is, arising from that intention—is performed with the perception of him as an enemy, [thinking], "This enemy is not yet dead."
Thus, by means of this designation, even when that person has died, a much greater demerit arises for one who acts due to the continuity of volition (*cetanā*),
and not merely through an intention devoid of action. For likewise,

even though the Blessed One has passed away and entered final nirvāṇa, for one who performs acts of giving and honor arising from devotion to him— that is, arising from devotion to the Teacher— as if they were following after him, a much greater merit arises.
"Not by mere devotion devoid of action" (IV.125cd).
"In that case, there will be an undesirable fruit in the case of a bad field.
The Nirgranthas maintain that giving to thieves and the like results in an undesirable fruit.
In a good field there is a desirable fruit, whereas in a bad field the opposite occurs; therefore he says:
"Even in a bad field there is a desirable fruit, because of the non-reversal of the fruit and the seed."
Thus,
we do not say that the desired fruit arises from a particular field;
what then?
It is "distinguished" because a desirable fruit does not arise from the seeds of killing and so forth even in a good field.
For even in a bad field, there is a fruit— such as the grape fruit— that arises from its seed, namely the grape seed.
Non-perversion has been observed;
the meaning is that the grapefruit itself is seen to be sweet,
but the neem fruit is not so.
From a neem seed, only a neem fruit arises;
thus it is "bitter.
The seed of the grape is an illustration of the wholesome.
The seed of the neem tree is that of the unwholesome.
(IV.126) Immorality is unwholesome form.
Immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) is form (*rūpa*) characterized by taking life and so forth, which is naturally reprehensible (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
And [it is also that which is] prohibited by the Buddha. (Abhidh-k-vy 437)
Because it is a transgression by designation (*prajñapti-sāvadya*).
However, for one who has undertaken the training (*samātta-śikṣa*), immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) arises from its violation;
that is, for one who has taken up the abstention from it, immorality is produced through disregard for the words of the Blessed One.
By implication,
it is stated that for one who has not undertaken the training, there is no immorality (*duḥśīlya*). However, pure [morality] possesses four qualities.
Thus.
It has four qualities, hence it is "fourfold. By means of immorality as previously described.
By this [statement], "immorality is unwholesome form," [it is shown that it arises] from greed and so forth.
It is not impaired by those active causes of immorality;
the meaning is that it relies on the antidotes to immorality.
It is purified by the fundamental paths of action.

The meaning is that it is unbroken by the fundamental [offenses] such as taking life. "Purified by the preliminary stages" means it is untainted by the preliminary applications (prayoga) of taking life and so forth.
"By discursive thoughts" means by discursive thoughts of sensual desire and so forth.
"Sustained by mindfulness" means...
It is strengthened by the applications of mindfulness of the body and so forth,
or it is sustained by the application of mindfulness of ethical discipline;
this is called "ethical discipline based on aspiration."
Aspiration (*āśāsti*) means longing (*prārthanā*). "That which is produced by craving for existence, enjoyment,
and honor" refers to the craving that exists toward existence, enjoyment, and honor.
The meaning is: that which has been undertaken by her.
"Of those possessing right view" means:
of those who have entered upon the Buddha's teaching.
For those of other sects, [the path] is not conducive to the factors of enlightenment because they possess false views.
However, that which is concentrated is wholesome. (IV.127ab)
The inclusion of the term "concentrated" (*samāhita*) is for the purpose of excluding that which is not concentrated.
The inclusion of the term "wholesome" (*kuśala*) is for the purpose of excluding afflicted meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) associated with the relishing (*āsvādana*) of concentration.
That [state] arises as something resembling wholesome concentration.
"Coexistent with the intrinsic nature of concentration" means that which exists together with the intrinsic nature of concentration.
For that is "concentrated," and so forth.
That wholesome state of meditative concentration causes the mind to dwell [in virtue] exceedingly; it cultivates it. It also causes the unconcentrated mind to dwell [in virtue].
But he shows that it is not so to an excessive degree.
How so? He says:
because the continuum is made to consist of those qualities (guṇas).
Because the continuum of the mind is made to consist of those qualities through the virtues of meditative concentration (samādhi).
Regarding this, he provides an illustration:
"like the perfuming of sesame seeds with flowers."
Just as sesame seeds are perfumed by flowers through being made fragrant with the scent of those flowers, so it is in this case.
This is what is meant: cultivation (bhāvanā) is habitual perfuming (vāsanā);
merit whose intrinsic nature is that [cultivation] is "consisting of cultivation" (bhāvanāmaya).
(IV.127cd) Now, he asks for the meaning by way of completing the sentence: "To what do ethical discipline (*śīla*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) conduce?
[The answer is: "Ethical discipline [conduces] primarily to heaven (*svarga*)."
Ethical discipline (*śīla*) leads primarily to heaven; other [virtues], however, do not lead primarily to heaven.
What else [is this]?
Generosity.
For generosity also leads to heaven;
ethical discipline also leads to dissociation from defilements.
Because ethical discipline is the foundation for calm abiding and special insight;
and because cultivation leads primarily to dissociation,
as it directly brings about dissociation.
Or because it is comprised within the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*).
This is introduced in connection with the bases of meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*):
it is stated in the Sūtra: [IV.128ab]...
There are four types of persons who generate Brahma-merit.
One who establishes a stūpa containing the relics of the Tathāgata on a piece of ground that has not been previously occupied—
this is the first person who generates Brahma-merit.
He dedicates a monastery to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters and establishes a vihāra within that very monastery.
This is the second person who generates Brahma-merit;
he reunites a schismatic Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples.
This is the third person who generates Brahma-merit.

With a mind imbued with loving-kindness—free from enmity, free from rivalry, free from ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having resolved upon, pervaded, and attained one direction;
likewise the second.
In the same way the third,
and in the same way the fourth;
thus, having pervaded and attained this entire world— above, below, across, and everywhere— he dwells.
This is the fourth person who generates Brahma-merit;
this is what was said in order to indicate the measure of the karma that results in the maturation of the [major] marks.
This refers to what was stated, setting aside the Bodhisattva who is close [to enlightenment].
"Up to the point that it is the fruit of enjoyment for all sentient beings," and so forth.
This is "Brahma-merit. It belongs to the Brahmas; thus, it is Brahma-merit.
And here, the Brahmapurohitas are referred to by the word "Brahma.
Why?
Because the lifespan of the Brahmapurohitas is one kalpa.
For the lifespan of the Brahmapurohita gods is said to be one kalpa;
by this karma, one rejoices in the heavens for a kalpa and generates Brahma-merit.
"He rejoices in the heavens for an eon," according to the reading found in another school's recension.
Because it shares this common characteristic with that, it is called "Brahmic merit.
Now, is it not the case that in the desire realm there is no ripening of a wholesome karma for an entire eon?
True; it is not so for a single [karma].
However, there are many non-human spirits (*ātanā*) that share a single basis;
for them, the heavenly fruit ripens sequentially over the duration of an eon,
because after one has passed away, one is reborn again in that very same place.
Others say that the Brahma-realm possesses vast merit.
Regarding "of the sūtras and so forth": [this refers to the following].
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the twelve limbs [of the teaching].
These twelve limbs are: Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Nidāna, Avadāna, Itivṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, Adbhutadharma, and Upadeśa.
[The phrase] "unafflicted teaching" (akliṣṭadeśanā) refers to this.
The meaning is "arisen from an unafflicted mind" (akliṣṭacittasamutthāpita).
Regarding the term *puṇyabhāgīya*: a "portion of merit" (*puṇyabhāga*) is the attainment (*prāpti*) of merit.
The meaning is "the attainment of a desired result. That which is beneficial for that [attainment] is "conducive to merit" (*puṇyabhāgīya*).
For this very reason, it is said that it has a desirable maturation (*vipāka*).
"Conducive to its attainment.
Alternatively, there are three portions:
the meritorious portion, the non-meritorious portion, and the imperturbable portion.
That which is beneficial for that [state] is "conducive to merit" (*puṇyabhāgīya*). Alternatively, one who partakes in merit is "merit-partaking" (*puṇyabhāk*);
that which is conducive to such a merit-partaker is "conducive to merit."
The suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).
Thus, there is "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
Alternatively, there are two portions: the portion of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra-bhāga*) and the portion of liberation (*mokṣa-bhāga*).
In that regard, that which is beneficial for the portion of liberation is "conducive to liberation" (mokṣabhāgīya).
Alternatively, the attainment of liberation is the "portion of liberation."
That which is beneficial for that [attainment]—
meaning conducive to its acquisition— is called "conducive to liberation" (mokṣabhāgīya).
Its definition will be explained later.
In the same way, the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) should also be applied.
We shall explain this later.
From that, the arising of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) occurs.
Thus, in this context, the definition of these [factors] whose intrinsic nature is karma is stated under the heading of karma:
"That which in the world... and so forth. (IV.130)
"Together with its origination" means together with the aggregate of mind and mental factors.
That by which that bodily action is instigated—
namely, that bodily action together with its instigation— is set in motion through application;
it consists of writing and seals.
This is because the effect is metaphorically designated by the cause.
For that bodily action by which writing is written or a seal is carved is what is intended by the term "writing" or "seal" in this treatise.
It is not as it is in the world, for in the world, "writing" (lipi) is intended to be a mark consisting of syllables on books and such,
while a mark consisting of both syllables and non-syllables is called a "seal" (mudrā).
Calculation and poetry are vocal actions (*vākkarman*).
The phrase "set in motion by yoga, together with its origination" continues [to apply here].
They have the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their intrinsic nature.
In the case of writing and sealing, bodily action constitutes the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). In the case of calculation and poetry, vocal action constitutes the aggregate of form.
However, in both cases, the four aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*) constitute the originating factors.
These have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
That which is the mental enumeration of phenomena—
such as "one," "two," "three," and so forth— is number.
The Abhidharmikas maintain that what is performed by speech and not by mind is "counting" (*gaṇanā*).
Furthermore, this number, when taken together with its attendants, has the nature of the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha-svabhāva*).

Following the incidental explanation of the characteristics of scripts and so forth, there is now introduced an exposition of the characteristics of phenomena such as those that are blameworthy (*sāvadya*) and so on.
In the *Dharmaskandhakavibhāṣā*, these synonyms are specified. The connection is that this [work] is closely related to that; another connection is that these synonyms are being presented here.
They are "with fault" (sāvadya) because they proceed with fault, characterized by the afflictions,
due to being shrouded by the afflictions.
They are obscured (*nivṛta*).
For even the afflictions (*kleśa*) are obscured by other associated afflictions,
because they have been extracted [from their roots] or because they have been abandoned by the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
Inferior; defiled.
However, they are to be understood according to their association with afflictions (*kleśa*).
Those that are pure and stainless (*amala*) are wholesome and untainted (*anāsrava*).
They are sublime because they have reached the excellence of purity.
It is established that those other than the inferior and the sublime are the intermediate.
Since it is determined that only the afflicted are inferior and only the pure and stainless are sublime, therefore others are neither inferior.
Those that are not sublime are middling;
those that are conditioned and wholesome are to be cultivated.
Thus,
whether they are with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), they should be cultivated and attended upon without distinction.
By way of superimposing [the notion of] a continuum.
"The remaining ones are not to be cultivated.
Which are the remaining ones?
And those that are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as well as those that are not wholesome (*akuśala*).
This means those that are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
"Because it is not to be practiced" means because it is impossible to perform repeatedly;
others say it is because it is not to be produced.
"And because it is fruitless. For cause and fruit belong to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), but those two do not belong to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"With superior" means possessing excellence.
Unwholesome states are "with superior" in relation to the obscured-unspecified states,
because the obscured-unspecified states lack undesirable maturation.
The obscured-unspecified [dharmas] are surpassed by the unobscured-unspecified conditioned [dharmas],
because the latter are non-afflicted.
They, too, are surpassed by the wholesome-with-outflows, because the wholesome-with-outflows have desirable fruits.
Even those [uncontaminated states] are surpassed by the uncontaminated;
because they are free from afflictions.
Furthermore, even conditioned uncontaminated states are surpassed by the unconditioned.

Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is eternal. Even among the unconditioned, space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) are surpassed by cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), because cessation through deliberation is both virtuous (*kuśala*) and eternal.
Liberation, however, is unsurpassed.
For there is nothing more distinguished than nirvana.
Thus it has been said: "O monks, whatever phenomena there may be, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared to be the foremost among them."
For analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) is superior to all conditioned phenomena because it is eternal;
and because it is wholesome, it is even more superior than the two unconditioned phenomena, namely space (ākāśa) and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha).
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* titled *Sphuṭārthā*, composed by Master Yaśomitra.
(Abhidh-k-vy 441) V. (The Fifth Chapter of the Treasury, titled "Exposition of the Latent Dispositions") (V.1) The variety of the world is born of karma.
Regarding the phrase "it has been said":
this was stated at the beginning of the fourth [chapter].
Therefore, he demonstrates the connection by showing that the presentation of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) follows from this very sequence.
