And those actions, distinguished by the characteristics as previously described, undergo accumulation through the power of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
They arise here with a certainty of maturation; the meaning is that they become fixed for the giving of their ripening result (*vipāka*).
Without the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and in the absence of underlying tendencies, wholesome or unwholesome karmas are not capable of bringing about or producing existence—that is, birth.
For it is not the case that an Arhat lacks indeterminate karmas pertaining to rebirth;
however, due to the absence of underlying tendencies, they are not capable of bringing about rebirth.
For this very reason, their lack of necessity is established.
Furthermore, the word "ca" (and) should be read in the sense of "hi" (for),
because [the afflictions] are not capable of producing existence without the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Therefore, the intended meaning is that [karma] undergoes accumulation by the power of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Others, however, explain these two sentences as follows:
"And those actions undergo accumulation by the power of the latent dispositions."
The meaning is that those actions which have not yet been performed accumulate for the production of renewed existence due to the power of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
For the actions of Arhats do not accumulate for the production of renewed existence.
Furthermore, without the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), those [karmas] are not capable of producing existence;
and even those actions that have been performed are likewise unable to produce existence without the underlying tendencies.
For it is not the case that Arhats lack wholesome and unwholesome actions performed during their stage as ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)—actions that lead to rebirth and are of indefinite result.
Rather, due to the absence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), those actions are incapable of producing further existence.
Thus, the terms have distinct meanings.
This *ca* (and) is used for conjunction.
"The underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the root of existence."
The underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the root of renewed existence (*punarbhava*) or of existence as karma (*karmabhava*).
The intention is that this is because they are the cause for the accumulation and origination thereof.
Thus, it is said that "it makes the root firm."
For attainment (*prāpti*) is the root;
the meaning is that it makes that [root] firm by way of non-interruption.
It establishes the continuity (*saṃtati*).
The meaning is that it establishes a continuous succession of afflictions (*kleśa*).
"It brings about a field" means that it makes the basis (*āśraya*) conducive to its own arising.
"It produces its own outflow" means it generates its own secondary affliction (upakleśa) as an outflow.
For example, attachment (rāga) generates lack of shame (āhrīkya), restlessness (auddhatya), and stinginess (matsara).
Hatred, anger, envy, and so forth.
It "produces the existence of karma" (*karmabhava*);
karma itself is existence, hence "existence of karma."
The meaning is that it produces that [existence] for the sake of the manifestation of renewed existence;
these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are the root of this existence.
This is the demonstration of the meaning:
"he grasps his own equipment.
His own equipment is the improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) that constitutes affliction (*kleśa*).
It grasps that;
the meaning is that it remains as the causal state for that which is yet to come.
It causes delusion regarding the object of focus.
Because it grasps things as they truly are,
or because it confuses through the impairment of the intellect,
it bends the stream of consciousness.
It bends the continuum of consciousness toward an object or toward rebirth,
if it is the root of existence.
This taking up of renewed existence is an illustration of this:
"it causes one to deviate from the side of the wholesome" means it causes one to fall away from the side of the wholesome.
And it radiates for the purpose of binding;
the meaning is that it pervades and extends the function of binding.
How so? He says:
The meaning is: "by way of not transcending the realm" (*dhātvanatikramaṇayogena*) means by way of not passing beyond that realm.
This is what is being stated:
whichever affliction belongs to a particular realm, it does not cause one to transcend that realm.
Another [teacher] says there are sixteen,
adding six to these.
It produces the corruption of the basis (*āśrayadauṣṭhulya*) by bringing about unworkability (*akarmaṇyatā*).
It hates virtues because it is opposed to them;
it provides a foothold for censures by inciting bodily actions that are condemned by the wise;
and it causes one to stray from the true path by turning one toward the service of perverted teachers.

It sows the seeds of various misfortunes because all the calamities of saṃsāra originate from it. And by way of its dominant fruit (*ādhipatya-phala*), it brings about what is undesirable for the world, since external phenomena undergo transformation through its force.
This is also due to the power of passion (*rāga*) over others.
Where there is attachment, other [defilements] such as aversion also lie latent (anuśerate) toward that same object.
The Sūtra states: "From affection, aversion arises; pride and the others arise as well."

And for this very reason, because of the absence of the latent tendency of passion (*rāgānuśaya*), afflictions do not adhere to the untainted (*anāsrava*) or to a dissimilar realm (*visabhāgadhātu*). We shall explain this further below.
For whatever object is appropriated by the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), [afflictions adhere to it].

In that regard, other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are also capable of adhering there, just as dust settles upon a moist cloth; this we shall explain later. Or rather, is it the case that *kāmarāga* itself is the latent disposition?

According to the Vaibhāṣika system, the latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is itself the active outburst (*paryavasthāna*). According to the Vātsīputrīya system, the latent disposition is possession (*prāpti*). According to the Sautrāntika system, it is the seed (*bīja*).
"An escape to the north" means an escape toward the west. It was firmly and thoroughly struck with great force.
"Forcefully" means well and correctly carried away.
"It is abandoned along with its latent tendencies (*sānuśaya*)"—
this is the illustration here.
This is contradictory here.
For in a compound expressing association (*sahayoga-samāsa*), distinctness is observed; for example, "Devadatta with his son" (*saputra* Devadatta).
And this being the case, there would be contradiction with the Sūtra and contradiction with the Abhidharma;
for the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) is associated with three faculties (*indriya*).
"By which three? It is associated with the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), mental ease (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
For it is not logical that what is dissociated, characterized by acquisition (*prāpti*), should be associated with these faculties; thus, [your position] contradicts the treatise.

"With its latent tendency (*sānuśaya*) means with its continuity (*sānubandha*). By this, what is meant is that the continuity of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) is expressed by the term "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, "continuity" refers to its abiding in a state conducive to the arising of other afflictions (*kleśa*).
Alternatively, *anuśaya* means persistence.
"It is abandoned along with its *anuśaya*" means that the affliction (*saṃkleśa*) does not persist further.
Alternatively, the word "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) in the Sūtra is figurative; that which exists in a metaphorical sense is "figurative" (*aupacārika*). Where is it figurative? He says:
in the case of possession (*prāpti*).
The term *anuśaya* (latent tendency) applies primarily to the state of active outburst (*paryavasthāna*),
but it is used figuratively for possession (*prāpti*),
because the latter serves as the cause for the former.
Just as fire is called "suffering" because it is the cause of the sensation of suffering, so it is here. However, in the Abhidharma, the term *anuśaya* is used in its technical, etymological sense.
That which exists in the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) or that which shines by means of the characteristics is "characteristic-based" (*lākṣaṇika*).
He says, "it is characteristic-based," meaning it is precisely the affliction (*kleśa*).
They are called *anuśayas* because they adhere [to the mind] both by way of having an object (*ālambana*) and by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).
Therefore, only those that are associated are *anuśayas*.
Regarding this point, they cite a verse:

Because they defile the mind, because they are obstructions, because they are opposed to what is wholesome, and because the wholesome is observed [to exist], the latent dispositions (anuśaya) here are not dissociated [from the mind].
"Because it causes defilement of the mind. This is its explanation:
because the mind becomes defiled by the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
The mind does not become afflicted by the dissociated [factors],
because they are obstructions;
this is the explanation of that phrase.
"New wholesome [states] do not arise" means that in a mind accompanied by latent dispositions (*sānuśaya*), new wholesome states do not arise,
because they are opposed to the unwholesome.
The explanation of this term is:
"and one falls away from what has arisen.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are opposed to wholesome states.
Because one falls away from the wholesome state that has arisen,
the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are opposed to the wholesome;
therefore, they are not dissociated (*viprayukta*).
Because, with those [factors] being non-existent in the mind, the aforementioned defiled states and so forth are not possible;
however, all this is consistent when they are associated (*saṃprayukta*).
Now, one might think that it would be the same even if they were dissociated (*viprayukta*).
The mind becomes afflicted by the dissociated factors;
new wholesome states do not arise,
and one falls away from those already arisen.
If that were so, the wholesome would never be perceived,
because those dissociated factors are always present.
However, since those dissociated factors exist during a defiled state, a wholesome state, or any other state, the wholesome is indeed perceived.
Therefore,
because the wholesome is also apprehended here, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not dissociated [from it].
Thus it stands. The Teacher said: "This which has been stated by the Vaibhāṣikas is not a proof."
"Because it causes affliction of the mind," and so forth.
For the Vātsīputrīya is one who maintains that the latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is dissociated from the mind.
"All this" refers to [the following].
"Defilement of the mind and so forth. He maintains that it is caused by afflictions alone; the meaning is that it is caused specifically by the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
Furthermore, since the active outburst (*paryavasthāna*) is not always present, the attainment of wholesome states is established.

If one adopts the position that the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) is [itself] sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), then there is no contradiction with the Sūtra stating that "that which is accompanied by a latent tendency is abandoned"; however, it would follow that the latent tendency is dissociated (*viprayukta*).
Therefore he says:
"And the latent disposition (anuśaya) is neither associated nor dissociated.
To the question "How so? he says:
"Because it is not a separate substance" means that the seed,
which consists of potentiality, is not a different entity from passion and the other [afflictions].
This refers to the personal existence as the basis.
"Born of afflictions" means produced by previously arisen afflictions.
"The power to produce afflictions" is the capacity for the arising of afflictions.
Just as the power to produce recollection, which is born from the knowledge of experience, is not a separate substantial entity.
In the same way,

having raised the objection that there must be some distinct substance among the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) that serves as the cause for the production of memory, he presents another illustration:
"And just as in the case of sprouts and so forth," and so on.
And just as the power of sprouts and so forth to produce another rice fruit—which arises from a previously produced rice fruit—is not a separate substance, so it is in this case.
As for the phrase "but that which": [it refers to the following].
The Vātsīputrīya:
If it is maintained that the latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is the affliction (*kleśa*),
then how is it that in the *Ṣaṭṣaṭka-sūtra* the affliction itself is stated to be the latent disposition?
"It is said that for this person there is a latent tendency toward passion (*rāgānuśaya*) in pleasant feeling.
Passion itself is the latent tendency.
For it is said that passion is so designated when it is actually manifesting during the state of pleasant feeling."
But the intention is that this is not its seed.
Because of the statement "it exists," it is not the latent tendency (anuśaya) at that very moment;
rather, this is said to be the latent tendency of attachment itself.
It is not passion itself;
for it is said that "it comes to be.
This means that in that state, the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of the passion arising therein comes to be.
The seed arises;
it is not, however, already arisen.
The intention here is that the state of the seed's own nature (*prakṛti*) is being described.
When, then, does it exist?
The meaning is: when does the latent disposition (anuśaya) exist?
When it is dormant (prasupta).
The meaning is "when it has ceased.
Or, there is a metaphorical application [of the term] to its cause;
that is, the metaphorical application of the term "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) to its cause, namely, passion (*rāga*).
For passion (rāga) is the cause of the latent tendency of passion (rāgānuśaya).
For it has been stated that the latent tendency of passion is the capacity to produce passion born from passion.
Thus, this is what is meant.
In some places the term "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) refers to the seed; in others, it refers to the "outburst" (*paryavasthāna*).
For, for them, attachment to meditative attainments (*samāpatti-rāga*) is generally predominant.
In the dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādanā-saṃprayukta*), their passion (*rāga*) generally prevails.
Since they also possess passion for celestial palaces (*vimāna*) and other such things, the word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*) is included.
Furthermore, that [passion] functions inwardly because it takes the form of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
And such being the case, the notion of "liberation" arises.
To dispel that [notion], the Blessed One taught: "passionate attachment to sensual pleasures," "passionate attachment to existence," and so forth.
This is attachment to existence (*bhava-rāga*).
"This [desire] does not exist in liberation;
rather, the desire for the Dharma is skillful regarding liberation.
However, the Master's opinion is that "existence" (bhava) refers precisely to the personal existence (ātmabhāva).
"Attainment together with its basis" means attainment together with the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
Those who relish [the attainment] relish the personal existence itself.
Not the qualities of sensual pleasure,
because of being free from passion for sensual pleasures.
Therefore, he shows that this passion is called "passion for existence" (bhavarāga) and not "passion for sensual pleasures" (kāmarāga).
(V.3) "Abhidharma" means that it is not [found] in the Sūtras; this is the intended meaning.
(V.4, 5) "Seven are to be abandoned by the vision of the origin."

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) takes as its object the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), which are the result; therefore, it is to be abandoned only by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*).
Likewise, the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is so because it grasps those very same aggregates as being either eternal or subject to annihilation.

The adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) also takes those same aggregates as its object, regarding them as purity, liberation, and the means to deliverance; thus, it is not to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśanaheya*).
In the same way, those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaheya*) should also be applied.
There are eight to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaheya*),
with the addition of the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

One is purified by the path. Because one rejects that [path] and believes in purification through another form of moral conduct and observance (*śīla-vrata*), one is mistaken; therefore, it is to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
For whatever affliction has arisen for the purpose of denying a particular truth, it is abandoned upon the seeing of that truth,
just as the delusion of a snake is abandoned upon seeing that it is a rope.
"By the mere vision of the truths, because of their abandonment"—
the intention is that they are not abandoned through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*),
since for one who has already seen the truths, abandonment occurs subsequently through the practice of the path (*mārgābhyāsa*).
The governing topic here is: "Are these [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*)?
Thus, cultivation (*bhāvanā*) means repeated practice, that is, arising again and again.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is of one type.

Because it is a misconception regarding suffering by way of the aspects of "self" and "mine," it is to be abandoned only by the vision of suffering. The same applies to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);

since this too superimposes the extremes of eternalism or nihilism upon an object conceived as a self, it is a misconception regarding suffering itself and is therefore to be abandoned only by the vision of suffering.
False view is of four kinds.
Because it functions by way of denying the characteristics of the truths such as suffering, it is a misconception regarding all four truths;
thus, it is to be abandoned by the vision of the four truths.
In this way, the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is also of exactly four types.
For it consists in viewing what is inferior as supreme.
Among these, that which has as its object [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, or the path, is itself to be abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, or the path.
The remainder is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*).

Likewise, doubt (*vicikitsā*)—being of the nature of uncertainty regarding everything—is to be abandoned by the vision of all four truths (*catuḥsatyadarśanaheya*), because it is mistaken with respect to all [truths].
The adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is of two kinds.

The apprehension of a cause in non-causes such as Īśvara and so forth proceeds from the perversion [of perceiving] the eternal and the self; thus, it is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-heya*). The perception of a path where there is no path is to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-heya*).
As for what these [perversions] are like: [they are as follows].
The four afflictions beginning with attachment are being examined:
namely, attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance, which were the subjects of the immediately preceding discussion.
And these are to be abandoned by insight.
These [defilements] are difficult to distinguish as being "to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanāheya*),
yet the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth are not considered [in this way],
for they are those which are fundamentally opposed to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

"Those [defilements] which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering," and so on, up to "those which are mistaken regarding the truth of the path are to be abandoned by the vision of the path"— this is easily distinguished.
In this context, "those" refers to attachment and the other [defilements].
The vision of that truth is itself the vision;
those things which are to be abandoned by that vision are their objective support.
Those which have as their objects what is to be abandoned by seeing are themselves to be abandoned by seeing;
these are attachment and the other [afflictions].
The vision of that truth is "the vision thereof" (*taddarśanam*).
Those things to be abandoned by that vision are "to be abandoned by the vision thereof" (*taddarśanaheyāḥ*).
This is what is meant.

Those afflictions such as attachment and so forth that take as their object the afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering up to those to be abandoned by the vision of the path are "to be abandoned by the vision thereof.
It should be stated that they are "those which have as their object what is to be abandoned by the vision of that [specific truth]."
It should not be said that the latent tendency of ignorance also has the four noble truths as its object,
because this is established by the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one of two identical terms).
That which is the truth and those afflictions to be abandoned by vision are their objects; thus,
these are "those whose objects are to be abandoned by vision," and they are "to be abandoned by that vision."

But is it not the case that the pervasive latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*), which is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), also takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the truths such as the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha*)?
This is because it has all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) as its object.
Consequently, it would follow that this [pervasive ignorance] must also be abandonable by the vision of the truths such as the cessation of suffering.
There is no fault.
For although that [defilement] has the five classes [of beings] as its object, it takes those classes as its object by way of the aspect of their origination (*samudaya-rūpākāra*).
Therefore, because it takes them as its object in that manner, it is indeed to be abandoned by the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
In the same way, that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) should also be included.

This being the case, those who explain that "those whose objects are to be abandoned by the vision of this or that" refer to all things to be abandoned by vision (*darśanaheya*), and not merely to attachment (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions].
In explaining those [two points] as well, these same objections and responses must be stated:
because suffering is absent in the realms of form and formlessness, there is an absence of resistance (*pratigha*).
For it is toward painful feeling that resistance underlies (*anuśete*).
And that [affliction] does not exist above;
furthermore, hatred is harsh like a wind-disease,
whereas those beings possess mental continuums made supple by tranquility (śamatha).
And because of the absence of karmic maturation (vipāka). For its maturation is undesirable;
those two realms are devoid of undesirable maturation.
And because of the absence of objects of malice.
For in that state, there are neither external things such as weeds, salt-encrusted soil, or thorns, nor internal afflictions such as fever or epilepsy;
this is because it has arisen from wholesome roots such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and because of the absence of grasping (*parigraha*).

"By way of distinctions of aspect, type, and realm": the distinction of aspect refers to the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) consisting of the views of self and what belongs to self, eternalism and nihilism, and the views of non-existence, inferiority, and superiority.
Such is the classification by way of type: from the category to be abandoned by the vision of suffering up to the category to be abandoned by cultivation.
The classification by way of realm is that which belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
The form realm and the formless realm.
Therein, the latent tendency of attachment is of fifteen kinds by way of its types and its realms.
There is no mutual difference in their aspects (ākāra).
For all attachment has the aspect of clinging;
therefore, it is not established by way of a difference in aspect.

The latent tendency of repugnance (*pratighānuśaya*) is of five kinds according to its different types. There is no mutual difference in their aspects (*ākāra*), because all of them have the aspect of repugnance.
There is also no distinction by way of realm (*dhātu*), because that [pride] is absent in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*). Thus,
through the distinctions of type and realm, the underlying tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*) is of fifteen kinds.
There is no difference in their aspect,
because all of them have the aspect of elevation.
Likewise, ignorance is of fifteen kinds.
It is by those two alone;
there is no difference in their aspect (ākāra),
because everything has the aspect of non-apprehension (asaṃprakhyāna).
Doubt is of twelve kinds; it is by those very [factors] that [it is classified],
not by a difference in its modes.
Because all [of them] have the nature of doubt.
The latent tendency of views (dṛṣṭyanuśaya) is of thirty-six kinds through the distinctions of aspect (ākāra), type (prakāra), and realm (dhātu).
[Thus, these six latent tendencies... [is the detailed explanation].
(V.6) "Those born at the peak of existence are to be destroyed by patience.
The inclusion of the phrase "to be destroyed by patience" is for the purpose of excluding those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation.
The mention of "the highest stage" (bhavāgra) is for the purpose of distinguishing it from other stages;
for there is no mundane path of cultivation that serves as an antidote to the highest stage.
[The phrase] "in the remaining stages" refers to this.

From the desire realm up to the level of the sphere of nothingness. "According to what is appropriate" means that in the desire realm, they are to be abandoned by the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Beyond that, in the remaining stages, there are those to be abandoned by the receptivity to subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*).
These very same [defilements] are to be abandoned by vision for the noble ones (*ārya*), whereas they are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
For the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is of two kinds.
It is both mundane and supramundane;
for it is stated in the treatise:
"The Blessed One’s disciple abandons [defilements] through vision."
An ordinary person abandons [the afflictions] through cultivation;
however, those to be slain by non-forbearance are abandoned by cultivation alone.
The mention of "those not to be killed by impatience" (akṣāntivadhya) is for the purpose of including those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya).
This applies to all stages,
from the desire realm (kāmadhātu) up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
Those latent dispositions (anuśaya) of attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance which, as the case may be, are to be destroyed by patience (*akṣānti*) or destroyed by knowledge (*jñāna*),
are both always to be abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) for both noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*),
by means of either the mundane or supramundane path of cultivation.
But at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), [the abandonment occurs] only by means of the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*),
because there is no mundane path belonging to a higher level.
For indeed, among outsiders (*bāhyaka*), those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) are never abandoned.
Only those [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are suppressed for them;
however, those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) are to be destroyed only by the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*) in all stages (*bhūmi*).
For it is said thus in the *Mahākarmavibhāga-sūtra*:
It has been stated that for those free from passion, there is the manifestation of views that take the desire realm as their object.
"In this case, Ānanda, a certain person abstains from taking life,
up to and including wrong view."
In this world, one who abstains from right conduct,

upon the dissolution of the body after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a miserable destination, a lower realm, or in the hells. Whosoever— whether a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, or an external non-Buddhist ascetic— possessing supernatural power, the divine eye, and knowledge of the minds of others, perceives him in such a way:
It occurs to him:
"There is no good conduct of body, nor is there any ripening of the result of good conduct of body;
there is no good conduct of speech or mind."
"There is no ripening of good conduct of speech and mind," and so forth.
This is a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) that has the desire realm as its object,
because that karma belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).

And because it is precisely there that hell arises. Furthermore, in the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, it is stated that even for those who hold eternalist views regarding the past eons, views that take the desire realm as their object arise even in those who are free from passion.
Those who have developed such views based on recollecting their previous births are the speculators about the past;
many proponents of eternalism are mentioned therein.
We shall show one example of these:
here, a certain ascetic or brahmin, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling,
through the sequence of exertion and the sequence of abandonment.
Through the sequence of cultivation,
through the sequence of frequent practice, and through the sequence of correct mental attention,
one touches that kind of peaceful concentration of mind.
When his mind is thus concentrated, he recollects twenty eons of world-dissolution and evolution.
It occurs to him: "This self and this world are eternal."
Thus, all these proponents of the past who maintain eternalism,
relying upon this view of eternalism on account of themselves and the world, also rely upon the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In this way, the manifestation of views that take the desire realm as their object has been explained.

Likewise, in that very *Brahmajālasūtra*, the manifestation of views belonging to those who speculate about the past (*pūrvāntakalpaka*), some of whom are eternalists (*ekatya-śāśvatika*) and free from passion (*vītarāga*), but which take the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as their object, is described.
How so?
"Monks, there comes a time when this world undergoes dissolution (*saṃvartate*)."
When the world is undergoing dissolution, for the most part sentient beings are reborn in the Ābhāsvara realm of the gods.

There they exist as embodied beings, mind-made, without deficiency, with unimpaired faculties, endowed with all major and minor limbs, beautiful, abiding in a state of radiant color, self-luminous, moving through the sky, feeding on joy, nourished by joy, long-lived, and remaining for a very long time.
Monks, there comes a time when this world evolves.
As the world evolves, an empty Brahmā palace appears in space.

Then, a certain being, through the exhaustion of his lifespan, the exhaustion of his merit, and the exhaustion of his karma, passes away from the Ābhāsvara host of gods and is reborn in that empty Brahmā palace.
There he remains alone, without a second, and without attendants, for a long time and throughout a vast duration.
Then, after that long period has passed, thirst arises in that being and dissatisfaction takes birth:
"Oh, would that other beings too might be reborn here in my company!"
And such was the mental aspiration of that being.

Other beings, through the exhaustion of their lifespan, the exhaustion of their merit, and the exhaustion of their karma, passed away from the Ābhāsvara host of gods and were reborn in the same state of existence as that being.
Then, this thought occurred to that being:
"I am alone, without a second, without an attendant, long-lived, [wishing] that other beings might also be reborn here in my own company"—
such was his mental vow.
And these beings have been reborn here in my own company.
"These beings have been created by me.
I am the lord of these beings, their maker, creator, fashioner, progenitor, and the father of all things.
To those beings as well, it occurs thus:
"We saw this being all alone, without a second, without an attendant, long-lived, and remaining for a long duration of time.
After the passing of that long period, craving arose in this being and dissatisfaction was born:
'O, would that other beings too might be reborn here in my own company!'"
And such was the mental aspiration of this being:
"May we be reborn here in the same state of existence as this being;
may we be created by this being."
"This being is our lord, even as a father to all beings. Then, another being, due to the exhaustion of his lifespan, the exhaustion of his merit, and the exhaustion of his karma,
passes away from that state and comes into this condition, into the common lot of human beings.
As his faculties matured through the process of aging, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron-colored robes, and with perfect faith went forth from the home to the homeless life.
Having gone to the forest or to the foot of a tree, and so on in detail, he attained such a peaceful concentration of mind that,
with his mind thus concentrated, he recollected his former existence.
It occurs to him: "That Brahmā by whom we were created— he is eternal, stable, permanent, and of an unchanging nature."
"But we, who were created by that Brahmā—
we are impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change. In this way, even the desire realm becomes clung to by that view of grasping at extremes.
Therefore, the active manifestation of views that take the desire realm as their object has been explained.

Likewise, in that very same *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, it is stated— referring to those who speculate about the past— that there is the active manifestation of views concerning causeless origination among those who are free from passion, provided these views take the desire realm as their object.
How so?
In the realm of form, there are gods known as the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*). Through the arising of perception, those beings undergo death and fall from that place.
Then, a certain being, having passed away from that state, comes into this condition within the common lot of human beings.
As before, up until he recollects his former existence;
then, it occurs to him:
The self and the world are arisen without cause.
Thus, by this very means, it becomes so:
the self and the world are arisen without cause.
"I existed previously, yet I did not exist; now I have come into being"—thus, the self and the world are produced without cause.

Thus, by taking the self and the world as their object, they also take the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as an object through that wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); this is what is meant by the active manifestation of those views which take the desire realm as their object.
Furthermore, how does the wrong view arise such that the self and the world are [regarded as] produced without cause?
One denies that previously performed wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or unwholesome actions are the cause of oneself or the world; thus one engages in such repudiation.
Anticipating the opportunity for the statement, "For those who are free from passion for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those views will belong to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*)," he says:
"And the desire realm is not the object (*ālambana*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the form realm."
"Because they are free from passion":
these views do not belong to the desire realm;
rather, they are false cognitions.
Thus some offer this rebuttal; however, that is incorrect for them, because [the view] has the nature of that [view].
(Abhidh-k-vy 450)
[If they have fallen away, how then can there be the manifestation of views having desire as their object for those who are free from passion? To this he says:
"At the arising of a view," and so forth. The Vaibhāṣikas say: "Like Devadatta.

Just as Devadatta fell away from his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) because, while the Blessed One was dwelling with a mind inclined toward little concern, he gave rise to an evil desire to lead away the community of monks.
Because it is stated in the Sūtra.
For it is recited in the Sūtra as follows:
"Then, Devadatta, overcome by gain and honor, this kind of evil desire arose in him: 'O, that the Blessed One would relinquish the community of monks to me!'"
"May the Blessed One, while I lead the community of monks, dwell with little concern, devoted to the practice of dwelling in happiness in this very life.
At the mere arising of that thought, Devadatta fell away from that supernatural power; such is the detailed account.
In the same way, they too fell away at the very moment the [wrong] view arose.
(V.7) For the grasping of a self toward those [aggregates] is preceded by this; that is, it is preceded by the notion of a permanent, unitary whole. "All" means...
"Even the fivefold [view] is the view of a self-identity (satkāya)," that is,
with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandha).

For every view that functions with the nature of a perverted perspective is a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, because of its false contemplation.
But others are superimposing views. How is it that the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is a superimposing view?
This explanation is based on the majority of cases.
It says "the noble one" because [defilements] have been abandoned;
that is, because they have been relinquished.
This is because of the inclusion of the verbal root *ohāk*, meaning "to abandon. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) has been omitted.
Thus, the grasping at [the aggregates] beginning with views as being supreme—that is, as being primary—is called "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
The Master Saṃghabhadra maintains that by the use of the word "other" (para), this sense of "excessive" (atiśaya) is obtained.
Regarding the phrase "the view of a cause in what is not a cause," it is said to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya).
And "seeing a path where there is no path" refers to that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path. "Mere morality and observances" refers to [the same].

Even the moral precepts and ascetic observances of the Buddhists lead to the attainment of liberation; however, it is not through those alone, and for this reason, there is the view of others regarding them.
In this context as well, it is said that the word "etc. (*ādi*) is used.
The adherence to rules and observances, etc.,
is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
What is the reason?
For moral conduct and ascetic observances (*śīlavrata*) are comprised within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Therefore, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is used for the purpose of including the other aggregates.
(V.8) Why is this not to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśanaprahātavya*)?
The intended meaning is: "because there is a misconception regarding the cause.
"The attachment to a cause produced by that" means: even that which is produced by the grasping of a permanent, unitary self as the agent.
"It is abandoned by that very [vision] alone" means it is abandoned by the vision of suffering alone.
As for those who, however, perceive the attainment of heaven through such acts as entering water or fire—
Regarding the notion that purity is attained through moral precepts or ascetic observances:
this is not an adherence to a cause produced by those [precepts].
How, then, is it abandoned through the vision of suffering?
"Therefore, this [view] must be abandoned specifically by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya)," such is their intention.
The Vaibhāṣika says:
"That too is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya)," and so forth; the Vaibhāṣikas hold that it is because of being mistaken regarding suffering.
And how, moreover, is one mistaken regarding suffering?
Because of that, one sees purification in the act of going to heaven;
thus the Master explains at length: "it would lead to an over-extension."

Because all those things which have contaminated objects (*sāsravālambana*) and whose nature is not that of [wrong] views (*adṛṣṭisvabhāva*), yet are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and so forth, are mistaken regarding suffering.
For if every contaminated thing were suffering, it would follow that everything would be to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*).
And if that were the case, nothing at all would be to be abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya*) and so forth.
And this other point must also be stated:

what kind of other adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is to be abandoned by the vision of the path? For one must explain that even he who views purification as occurring through the "cow-observance" (*gośīla*) and so forth, up to the attainment of the transcendence of pleasure and pain, [possesses such an adherence].

"Furthermore, since one perceives this [wrong view] as a cause when it is not a cause, it would be recited as 'the adherence to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
The Vaibhāṣika says:
"That which has as its object what is to be abandoned by the vision of the path."
That which takes as its object the eight [afflictions] beginning with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)— which are to be abandoned by the vision of the path—
is the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that is to be abandoned by the vision of the path.
For even this, the Master says, is indeed a misconception regarding suffering.

For the eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya), beginning with false view (mithyādṛṣṭi), which are to be abandoned by the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya), are the objective support (ālambana) for the adherence to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
And because they are associated with outflows (sāsrava), they are comprised within the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya). It is in regard to these that he is mistaken.
The intention is that it would be abandoned solely by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*).
"And for whom," and so forth:
for whichever person there is no Path—that is, for whom there exists a wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) or doubt (*vicikitsā*) having the Path as its object.
That person either views that there is no path to liberation,
or they doubt,
wondering whether the path exists.
Doubting that "it does not exist," how could he rely upon or practice purification through that wrong view, or through this doubt?
For precisely because of his association with wrong view and doubt, there is no practice leading to purification for him.
"Now, another," and so forth.
This means that having referred to—that is, having grasped—another path to liberation imagined by the Sāṃkhyas and others, he says:
"This Buddhist path to liberation does not exist."
"He too" refers to the non-Buddhist (tīrthika). He believes in purification through that very other [means] imagined by the Sāṃkhya and others.
It is not because it is a wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

For that [person], this adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) would not be established as having as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*).
What then?
Furthermore, this is another fault: that it takes as its object only the paths imagined by the Sāṃkhyas and others.
As for the passage beginning with "And whoever," the full explanation is as follows:
and whoever holds wrong views, through a wrong view to be abandoned by the vision of origin and cessation, believes that purity is attained [by such means].
Why is that [clinging to rules and observances] not to be abandoned by the vision of that [truth]?
The meaning is: why is that clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) not to be abandoned by the vision of the origin and cessation [of suffering]?
Therefore, this matter must be examined.
Since this adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) cannot be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*),
nor can it be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*)—
due to faults such as over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and so forth— therefore, this matter must be examined.

The adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is both to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) and to be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*).
Thus, this [statement] has been rendered problematic by the Teacher;
he did not present his own definitive position.
Others say that this was formulated specifically with regard to the Yogācāra view;
for the Yogācāras describe one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*).
For just as these ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), [so too are there others].
The view of a self-identity,
the view of grasping at extremes,
and false view.
Adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Attachment, aversion, and pride.
And [the category] "ignorance" (avidyā).
In the same way, these ten are to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya);
and likewise, ten are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya).
Regarding the ten [afflictions] to be abandoned by the vision of the path:
there are forty that belong to the desire realm and are to be abandoned by vision,
while six are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Improper views consist of the view of a self-identity,
the view of nihilism,
and innate passion.
Hostility,
pride,
and ignorance.
There are forty-six latent tendencies belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Those belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), however, are forty-one; these are the same [forty-six] with the exception of hostility (*pratigha*).
As it is for those of the form realm, so it is for those of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
"Likewise for those belonging to the formless realm. Regarding this, someone states an objection:
"As it was said, there is an over-extension [of the definition], because all [cognitions] that have contaminated objects are mistaken with respect to suffering."
To this we reply: there is no over-extension [of the definition], because the misconception occurs by way of [the aspects of] suffering and so forth.
Even though they have contaminated objects, they are those who are in error regarding the truth of suffering.
Nevertheless, some are mistaken regarding the aspect of suffering,
some regarding the aspect of its origin,
and some are mistaken regarding the aspect of its cessation.
Some are those who have gone astray regarding the path.
Among them, those who have gone astray with respect to suffering by way of the aspect of suffering are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.

And the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is a misconception regarding suffering by way of the door of suffering, because it involves grasping at [things] as permanent and as a self.
Therefore, it is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
As for that which is a misconception regarding the path, it is a misconception within those who are already mistaken about the path.

For example, the Sāṃkhyas, Nirgranthas, and others, having grasped a path imagined by themselves, give rise to the false view that "the Buddhists have no path to liberation. And the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) regards that false view as supreme.
This adherence to rules and observances of theirs is to be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*).
Because it is a misconception regarding what is a mistaken path;
however, there is no adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that would be a misconception by way of the origin (*samudaya*),
nor is there any that would be a misconception regarding what is a mistaken [view] by way of cessation (*nirodha*).
Therefore, the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is to be abandoned specifically by the vision of suffering and the path.
But how is it that one does not fall into error regarding the aspects of origin and cessation?
On this point, the Master Saṃghabhadra says:

The adherence to the practice of the spear-vow (*śūlavrataparāmarśa*) is to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya*) and the cessation (*nirodha*) [of suffering], because such a body cannot logically arise from that [practice].
For it is an attachment to a cause in what is not a cause.
And through the dogmatic adherence to what is not the path as being the path,
there is the body of the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Regarding the false view that denies the origin [of suffering], if one were to dogmatically adhere to purification, would it not follow for him that the perception of birth occurs without cause?
Because in some cases there is no cognition of a cause;
for since suffering and its origin are not distinct in substance,
even the aggregates [of the world] such as God and so forth would be excluded by that [definition].

However, regarding the false view that negates cessation (*nirodhāpavādikā mithyādṛṣṭi*), because of the return to [the notion of] purification, the very conception of a means for cessation is impossible.
How so? Since one holds the view that "there is no cessation," any subsequent conception of a means for it would be futile.
And thus, the structural basis of the "clinging to rules and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is untenable.
Even for one who has abandoned [afflictions] through the vision of the path, such adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) would not be possible.

This is because it is illogical to conceive of a path following the vision [of the truth], thinking "the path does not exist," when one possesses either false view or doubt directed toward the path as its object. For [only one who possesses these] could [hold such a view].
Seeing that there is no path to liberation, or being skeptical, how could one rely on it for purification? Indeed,
it is entirely possible for one who holds a false view that denies the Noble Path to have an attachment to purification,
because they grasp it as being logical.
For another path to liberation has been instilled in his heart;
consequently, he develops a rational conviction in false view, which denies the truly existent path, thinking:
"This is the correct principle—that there is no other path to liberation."
And as for the phrase "he doubts another path to liberation, whether it exists or not":
for the adoption of a means of purification is only logically possible through right reasoning;
yet that other path to liberation has been instilled within his heart.

That [object] is not at all the object of that adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path, because it has as its objective support only what belongs to its own category.
Now, if it is thought that [the object] is also applicable to that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaheya*), [it is not so].
This is due to the power of that conceptualization.
For another [false] state of liberation has been placed within his heart by him;
consequently, he correctly adopts a false view that deprecates truly existing liberation.
"Therefore, this is the same"—
that is not so. For, when that [notion] is set aside by means of the commonality of grasping what is eternally quiescent, it is impossible for an adherence to purity to arise.
For when there is a distinction between the realization of the substantial and the non-substantial, someone seeks the means to liberation;
it is certain that for him there is liberation—this is the conviction.
And for whomsoever there is this certainty of liberation, [liberation is indeed assured].
In that case, there must be the apprehension of eternal tranquility;
otherwise, a longing for it would be untenable.

In this regard, just as here among those who follow the Dharma, even though there is a distinction between the acceptance of Nirvāṇa as a substantial entity and as a non-substantial entity, because of the commonality of apprehending eternal tranquility, the fault lies precisely in the denial of that [Nirvāṇa].
Even for one who has placed some state of liberation within their heart,
the adoption of reasoning is appropriate when refuting [false] notions of liberation, because of the commonality in grasping at what is eternally peaceful.
For precepts, vows, and the like are distinct from the Noble Path by virtue of both their intrinsic nature and their formal characteristics.
However, there is no distinction in the grasping of what is eternally peaceful;
there is no universal [grasping] based on conceptual construction.
Therefore, it is only the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that is to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*) that is possible.
"It is not to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Here, the Abhidharmikas maintain that the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is of two kinds.
Among these, what kind of adherence to rules and observances is established as being abandonable by the vision of suffering?

What kind of [affliction] is to be abandoned by the vision of the path? For even one who believes that purity is attained through the moral conduct of cattle and so forth sees the non-path as the path.

The adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which has as its object the suffering [caused by] rules and observances and the like is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*). That which has as its object a misconception regarding the path (*mārgavipratipatti*) is likewise [to be abandoned through the vision of the path].
That which has the observance of precepts and vows as its object is to be abandoned by the vision of the path;
it is not a misconception regarding the path itself.
It does not cause such affliction as that which has the wrong path as its object;
for that which has precepts, vows, and the like as its object is coarse.
It is not something far-reaching, nor is it of firm resolve; it is to be destroyed by little effort.
Because it is the opposite of that, it is the objective support for the deviation from the path.
(V.9) "From the three views, the four perversions [arise]" means he shows that the perversions have the three views as their intrinsic nature.
"The view of self within the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the perversion of self," [it is said].
The intention is that it is not the view of "mine" (*ātmīyadṛṣṭi*). Another [teacher] says, "the whole [view of a real body]."

The meaning is that all views of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), namely the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the view of what belongs to a self (*ātmīyadṛṣṭi*), constitute the perversion of the self (*ātmaviparyāsa*).
The Vaibhāṣika asks:
How is the view of what belongs to a self a perversion?
For it is not called the "perversion of what belongs to self. And how should it not exist? The opponent asks this.
[The Vaibhāṣika replies: "From the Sūtra on Perversions."
Because of the scriptural statement that "the inversion is to perceive a self in what is non-self," it does not, however, say "possessiveness. Such is indeed the teaching of the Sūtra.
Furthermore, this [view of self] is not something distinct from the view of a self.
How so?
Because one who perceives a self as the ruler over those very five aggregates of clinging perceives what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).
The meaning is that it does not only perceive a self, but also perceives what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).
This very view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is "two-faced":

it has the two faces of "self" and "what belongs to a self," meaning it possesses the two aspects of the conceit of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) and the conceit of "mine" (*mamakāra*), while existing as a single substance.
Now, from this "I" which was mentioned first, there would be another view indicated by the genitive case as "mine.
There would also be [other views] such as "by me" and "for me.
The term "another view" is understood from the context.
Because of the mention of the instrumental case in "mayā" and the mention of the dative case in "mahyam," this [interpretation] is undesirable.
Therefore, it is established that [the word] is "sakala."
Why are the other afflictions not considered perversions?

[They are] those other than the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), namely: the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), attachment (*rāga*), and so forth.
[They are excluded] for three reasons.
The establishment of the perversions occurs through erroneous investigation and superimpositions,
wherein all these causes are present together.
Those [cognitions] are established as perversions;
however, those in which [the factors] are not all present are said not to be perversions.
"Because of taking as an object purity through mere [rules and rituals]" means that because one takes as an object and determines that purity comes through mere morality and ascetic observances,
the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not exclusively perverted.
It is not that moral conduct and ascetic observances are not causes of purification;
rather, they simply do not suffice.
How, then, are they considered to involve superimposition?
Because one superimposes the status of being a cause of purification upon that alone.
If non-investigation is not a perversion, then how is it that it was stated in the Sūtra?
How is that so?
For neither perception nor mind is investigative.
Regarding the "twelve perversions," within the four perversions, each consists of the perversions of perception, mind, and view.
How so? It is said:
"In the impermanent, [the notion of] permanent," and so forth, up to "in the non-self, [the notion of] self.
In suffering, [the notion of] pleasure—these are the three inversions of perception, view, and mind.
"In the impure, [the notion] 'pure'—these are the three.
Up to: in what is not-self, [the notion] 'self'—these are the three.
Among those, eight are to be abandoned by vision.
There are three perversions of perception, mind, and view: [the notion of] permanence in the impermanent.
Furthermore, there are three [perversions]: [the notion of] a self in what is not-self.
And [the notion of] pleasure in suffering is a perversion of view.
Regarding the inversion of view that perceives the impure as pure: there are four such inversions to be abandoned through cultivation. To ask which these are, he says:

And regarding suffering (*duḥkha*), there are the two inversions of perception and mind (*saṃjñā-citta-viparyāsa*) [taking it] as pleasant; and regarding the impure (*aśuci*), there are another two inversions of perception and mind [taking it] as pure— thus, there are four.
"Of a noble one who is not yet free from passion" refers to the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
"The two reversals of that as well" means the same.
Because of the occurrence of the perception of a sentient being and the occurrence of the mind [conceiving] a sentient being,
why are their two corresponding perversions not also accepted?
Why are the perversions of perception and mind that have a sentient being as their object not also accepted?
The intention is: why are the two perversions regarding the self (*ātma-viparyāsa*) not also accepted?
They ask: what is the reason?
For it is not logical that there should be passion for sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) toward a woman or toward oneself without the perception of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*).

Therefore, it follows that these two—namely, the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) and the perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*) which take what is non-self to be self—are also to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
This is to be understood from the very word "in detail" (*vistara*):

namely, that the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*)—consisting in taking what is suffering to be pleasure, what is impure to be pure, and so on up to taking what is non-self to be self—are abandoned [through cultivation].
Therefore, the two perversions (viparyāsa) consist only of perception (saṃjñā) and mind (citta) that arise from views and are associated with views, and not others;
that is to say, they do not exist when dissociated from views.
This is what is meant.
There exists this confusion of perception and thought, but it is not a cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*),
because it does not arise from [wrong] views (*dṛṣṭi*).
He asks "Why? and replies:
"Because it is merely an illusion at that time.
The intended meaning is that at the time of seeing the woman, it is merely an illusion.
Because at that very time, at the very moment of perception, the delusion of the noble ones arises as false cognition,
just like the delusions of a whirling firebrand, a painted yakṣa, or the like.

Just as when a firebrand is whirled rapidly, an illusion arises that it is a wheel for only that duration and not afterwards; and likewise, upon seeing a yakṣa depicted in a painting, an illusion arises that it is a yakṣa for only that duration.
It is just like that.

Because the Noble One contemplates this [state], there arises for a moment the delusion of pleasure and purity, or the delusion of a sentient being; however, this is not a cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*).
For it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, lapses of mindfulness indeed arise for the learned noble disciple, yet they quickly reach their end, exhaustion, and disappearance.
If that confusion of perception and mind is not a misconception (*viparyāsa*), then [what about] what was said by the Elder Ānanda? [This is the full context.]
The noble Vāgīśa said to the Elder Ānanda:
"Because I am overcome by sensual passion, my mind is consumed with fever.
Pray, Gautama, out of compassion for me, speak to me of peace."
The noble Ānanda replied to him:
"Your mind is consumed by the perversion of perceptions;
therefore, abandon that sign which is associated with passion for the beautiful."
Thus it is said.
For he is a stream-enterer (srotaāpanna),
and by this verse, the existence of the perversions (viparyāsa) has been elucidated for him.
"Therefore," and so forth.
Because the doctrine of other schools is contradicted by the Vaibhāṣikas through scripture, and the doctrine of the Vaibhāṣikas is likewise contradicted by those of other schools.
Therefore, others maintain that all eight distortions of perception and mind are unabandoned by one in training (*śaikṣa*).
Some belong to a third category;
they also resolve the contradiction with the Sūtra.
Of which sūtra?
Of this sūtra which has been cited by the Vaibhāṣikas:
"The learned noble disciple," and so forth, in detail, up until "is abandoned."
"And those [errors] regarding the noble truths," and so forth.
Those eight distortions of perception and thought are abandoned through the knowledge of the noble truths—suffering and the rest—exactly as they are;
not without that knowledge of them exactly as they are.
Thus, because of the explanation of the means and the application of those means, there is no contradiction with that Sūtra.

As for what was stated— namely, "This is the noble truth of suffering, this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—
that was not spoken solely with reference to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
What then?
It is also the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
For the path of cultivation, being untainted (*anāsrava*), likewise has precisely the four noble truths as its object.
(V.10) "Due to the difference in activity" means due to the difference in aspect (*ākāra*).
"When no further distinction has been attained" means...

The "distinctive attainments" (*viśeṣa*) are the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena based upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The "attainment of the distinctive" (*viśeṣādhigama*) is the realization or direct manifestation of those. When that has not been attained—that is, when it has not been brought face-to-face—the conceit "I have attained that attainment of the distinctive" is [the pride of overestimation].
"I am virtuous" when one is devoid of virtue;
for one who is not endowed with virtues, the conceit "I am virtuous" is conceit directed toward an erroneous object, namely false conceit (*mithyāmāna*).
What is the specific distinction between false conceit (*mithyāmāna*) and overweening conceit (*abhimāna*)?
The intention regarding a quality that merely resembles a distinguished attainment already acquired is conceit with a basis (*savastuka-abhimāna*).
False conceit (*mithyāmāna*), however, is the thought "I am possessed of qualities" when one is actually devoid of qualities; it is without a basis (*nirvastuka*).
These are the varieties of conceit.

The types of pride (*māna*). It should be stated that there are three varieties of pride: the variety of pride thinking "there is one equal to me," the variety of pride thinking "I am equal," and the variety of pride thinking "I am inferior. These three are based on views (*dṛṣṭi*).

With reference to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), they are said to be "based on views. First there is the view of self, thinking "I"; immediately thereafter follow these [seven] types of pride (*māna*).
Excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride (*māna*), and inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*) occur respectively as follows: "I am superior" is a form of pride based on [wrong] view, which is excessive pride;
"I am equal" is a form of pride based on [wrong] view, which is pride; and "I am inferior" is a form of pride based on [wrong] view, which is inferiority pride.
This second triad is to be understood in reverse order, respectively:
"There is one superior to me," "There is one equal to me," and "There is one inferior to me"—these are the pride based on views (*dṛṣṭisaṃniśrita*), namely *ūnamāna*, *māna*, and *atimāna*.
The third [triad] is: "There is no one superior to me," "There is no one equal to me," and "There is no one inferior to me."
Respectively, pride (māna), excessive pride (atimāna), and inferiority pride (ūnamāna) are based upon [wrong] views.
"Taking up the exposition from the *Prakaraṇa*" refers to the exposition provided in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
Who is this?
It is that which was previously mentioned:
the exposition beginning with "I am superior to the inferior" or "equal to the equal," and so forth.
There may also be the conceit "I am superior" in relation to one who is inferior;
for this is indicated by the definition of conceit as "I am distinguished from the inferior" or "I am equal to [my peer].
Furthermore, this could also be overweening pride (*atimāna*) in relation to an equal.

Because it is defined as having the characteristic of overweening pride (*atimāna*) in thinking, "I am superior to one who is equal," this could also be considered pride-over-pride (*mānātimāna*), since it is in relation to someone superior that one thinks,
"I am superior to one who is superior," according to the definition of the characteristic of pride-over-pride.
The inclusion of the word "all" indicates that the conceit "I am" (asmimāna) is also to be abandoned through cultivation;
it is not only the remaining [afflictions].
The remaining [afflictions] are also to be abandoned through seeing.

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that it is not only the conceit "I am" [that does not manifest]. The phrase "not necessarily" indicates the rule: that which has been abandoned does not necessarily manifest.
For instance, even though faith and so forth, as well as the faculties of torpor, suffering, and the eye and others, have been abandoned, they still manifest.
This is because those [factors] to be abandoned by seeing are inwardly directed.
Furthermore, informative action is instigated solely by attachment, aversion, and delusion, which take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by cultivation.
Only that which is to be abandoned by cultivation is the obsession with killing and so forth;
this is what is meant by "the obsession with killing and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech are included.
That [path of action] is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) because it has as its object those factors (*dharma*) that are to be abandoned by cultivation;
that is to say, considering that its objects are precisely those factors such as sentient beings who are subject to killing and so forth, which are themselves to be abandoned by cultivation.

For although the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the others take phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation as their objects, they are not themselves exclusively abandoned by cultivation; therefore, they are not [themselves] abandoned by cultivation. In that context, "longing" refers to longing for impermanence within the three realms.
Is there also aspiration in that case?
He says: "There is," as it is stated in the Sūtra.
As long as this self lives, remains, persists, and maintains itself,
so long is it accompanied by disease, accompanied by swellings, accompanied by thorns, accompanied by fever, and accompanied by burning sensations.
But when this self is cut off, perishes, and no longer exists—
To this extent, this self is completely and utterly severed.
A portion of the craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) is grasped;
thus, the craving for existence that thinks, "O, may I become Airāvaṇa, the king of elephants," and so forth, does not manifest.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [thoughts] such as "May I be Kuvera" or "May I be a woman" are included.
By the inclusion of the term "limited" (*prādeśa*), it is shown that thoughts such as "May I be Indra" also arise.
It has been stated that even the mental factors (*māna*) are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Because of the statement, "They are abandoned by vision and cultivation," and because [faults such as] pride and the like do not occur in an Ārya.
"Not 'I'.
Previously, the inclusion of those to be abandoned by cultivation was made; [now it is said] that they are destroyed by both vision and cultivation.
The obsession with killing and so forth, as well as the desire for non-existence, are to be abandoned through cultivation; such is the meaning of this passage.
Now, the non-occurrence of pride and the other [afflictions] in a noble one (ārya) is stated:
pride and the others do not arise in a noble one,
because of the thought "I am not."
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of everything up to the craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*).

The meaning is that there is the inclusion of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) such as killing, the craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*), a portion of the craving for existence, and [the remainder] up to the craving for existence itself.
They do not arise and they do not manifest,
because they are nourished by [wrong] views.
Because it is preceded by that and is augmented by it.
The outburst of killing and so forth is nourished by wrong view, because through the habituation of that [wrong view], one denies the fruit of karma.
"Because its back is broken" means that, due to the absence of anything that nourishes it, its back is broken.
Remorse is to be abandoned by cultivation,
because it has as its object those dharmas that are to be abandoned by cultivation. (V.12, 13) [The universal [afflictions]...]
Thus,
they are called "universal" (sarvatraga) because they go everywhere;
the meaning is that they take all five categories as their objects.
Others maintain that they exist as the causal basis for all five classes [of afflictions].
For it will be stated later: "By their power, even the afflictions belonging to other classes arise.
Thus begins the detailed explanation of the eleven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
There are seven views: five beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering;
two views to be abandoned through the vision of the origin—namely, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*);
and two types of doubt (*vicikitsā*), which are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin.
The two types of ignorance are to be abandoned only by the vision of suffering and the origin; they are so in part, not in their entirety.
For those two ignorances are associated with these universal [defilements].
And the two [roots] that are unique (*āveṇikī*).
These same two become universal (*sarvatraga*) when they are associated with [other defilements] such as attachment (*rāga*), but not when they are themselves associated with attachment and so forth.
Thus, there are eleven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are universal.
There are nine latent dispositions (anuśaya) in their entirety;
they are two when considered by way of partiality.
However, by way of the distinction of realms (dhātu), there are thirty-three.
What is the meaning of "exclusive" (āveṇikī)?
They say this:
"Contact" (saṃparka) is called a "braid" (veṇi); that which is not a braid is "non-braid" (aveṇi).
The meaning is "separate existence. For it has been said: "The Blessed One is distinct; the community of monks is distinct.
The intention is that the Blessed One is separate and the community of monks is separate.
It functions uniquely (*āveṇikī*),
meaning it does not coexist with other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
This is because its object of focus (*ālambana*) comprises the entirety of its own realm.
Because these [defilements] take their entire own realm as their object, they are called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*).
As for the question, "What does 'entire' mean? and so forth: [it refers to the inclusion of all levels within that realm].
Who would believe that purity is attained through the entirety of the desire realm?
Or rather, it is implied that one believes the entirety of the desire realm—which is not a cause—to be a cause.
Therefore, the intention is that adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*).
It is not said that they apprehend their own realm— entirely, without remainder, and manifoldly divided by distinctions— all at once; rather, they apprehend all five types simultaneously,
from those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering up to those to be abandoned by cultivation.

"This word 'all' (sarva) should be understood as referring to the totality of modes," is the rebuttal of the Vaibhāṣikas. "As far as the view of self [extends]" means within the five aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandha).

In that regard, craving for a self (*ātmatṛṣṇā*) exists because [the self] is the object of the adherence to a self (*ātmābhiniveśa*). Where there are views of excellence and purity: when there is a view of excellence regarding the object characterized by the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), that is the misapprehension of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
And the view of purification is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). In that context, "longing" has the characteristic of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Regarding this, some read the text as "longing for that" (*tatprārthanā*).
In that regard, "desire for that" means the desire of that person for that object;
and "pride by means of that" means pride by means of that object.
The meaning is that through that [craving], there is elevation (*unnati*).
"This being so" means:
this being the case when craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and pride (*māna*) are universal (*sarvatraga*).

Because they have as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing and by cultivation—just like the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth—these two, characterized by craving and pride, must be abandoned.
By what are they to be abandoned? Are they to be abandoned by seeing, or rather by cultivation? Those which have as their objects what is to be abandoned by seeing [are abandoned by seeing].
Having in mind the rule that "those [defilements] are to be abandoned by seeing," he asks.
Otherwise, just like the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, both of these would necessarily be abandonable only by seeing; what then would there be to ask about?
For it is not the case that the view of a self-identity and so forth do not have as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing and by cultivation.
"And yet, it is not the case that they are not to be abandoned by seeing.
Regarding this, the Master states the resolution:
"Because that which is to be abandoned by cultivation has a mixed object."
If craving and pride were to have only objects that are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), they would themselves be abandoned by insight;
but it is not so.
Therefore, because their objects are mixed, they are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
"Because of the rule of definition that 'the remaining [defilements] are to be abandoned by cultivation' (bhāvanāheya).
Now, as for "or rather" (atha vā):
that same teacher, turning back, speaks again.
"Furthermore, let it be abandoned by seeing.
What [is meant]? It follows that "both of these" is what is being referred to.
He asks, "Why? and replies:
"Because it proceeds by the application of the power of vision.
The application of the power of vision is its efficacy.
That which has the habit of proceeding by means of the application of the power of [right] view is "proceeding by the application of the power of view"; both of those constitute that state.
Therefore.
"Let both of these be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Now the Vaibhāṣika establishes his own position:
"These two are afflictions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*); they do not become afflictions of general characteristics (*sāmānya-kleśa*)."
Therefore, they are not universal. Wherever there is the view of self, there are craving and pride.
