But they do not exist simultaneously with respect to all [objects], because their nature is that of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and afflictions (*kleśa*).
For those two have only a single part as their objective support (*ālambana*).
Therefore, they are not universal.
If they are not universal,
then those two have as their objects that which is to be abandoned by the vision of this or that [truth].
Those two are to be abandoned by seeing that [truth].
It is established that the remaining two are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Sometimes this [defilement] takes a dissimilar realm as its object.
It has not been stated that "sometimes two" or "sometimes three realms. However,
those dwelling in the desire realm sometimes take as their object a dissimilar single form realm or the formless realm.
"Sometimes there are two, namely form and formlessness.
"Because of not grasping [them] as self or belonging to self," because one does not grasp that Brahmā as a self or as something belonging to a self.
Therefore, there is no view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) regarding Brahman as a sentient being.
Furthermore, since the view of grasping at extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) arises from the view of a self-identity,
the view of permanence regarding that Brahman is likewise not a view of grasping at extremes.
What, then, is this view?
It is this view of existence (*sattvadṛṣṭi*) regarding Brahman,
as well as the view of permanence (*nityadṛṣṭi*).
"This is not a view; rather, this is false knowledge.
Because it has an inverted object, this is false knowledge.
For not every wisdom that has an inverted object is accepted as a view.
The perverted wisdom that perceives what is non-self as self is held to be the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
And the view of permanence (*nityadṛṣṭi*) arising from that is the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);
it is nothing other than that.
For that which serves as the basis for the conceit "I" is precisely the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
And in the case of Mahābrahmā, the view of a sentient being does not serve as the basis for the conceit "I."
He said: "Because they are not grasped as self or as belonging to a self.
[And: "The co-existent factors, excluding acquisition (*prāpti*)."
[The same applies to] feeling and the other [skandhas].
However, acquisitions (*prāpti*) are not like this, because they have multiple fruits;
for it has been stated that acquisitions possess multiple fruits—namely, fruition (*vipāka*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*)—as they belong to the possessor of the acquisition (*prāptimat*).
Therefore, the acquisitions (prāpti) of universal dharmas are not established as being universal themselves.
"For this very reason" means that even the co-existent [factors] are established as being universal.
Therefore, a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) is established.
The first alternative consists of the future universal proclivities (anuśaya);
these are so designated because they possess the nature of being universal.
The first [category] is not a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), because a pervasive cause is not established in its future state.
The second consists of those co-arising factors (*sahabhū*) that are past or present;
because these co-arising pervasive factors are past or present, they constitute a pervasive cause.
The pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) do not exist [in the future], because their nature is not that of a latent disposition.
The third and fourth [categories] should be applied accordingly.
From the third [category], the pervasive latent dispositions are those of the past and the present.
The fourth [category], excluding those aforementioned modes,
consists of future [dharmas] that co-arise with them, as well as their acquisitions (*prāpti*) and so forth. These six are the objects of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Thus,
the restriction is that there are exactly six.
Therefore, it is not logical for attachment and the other [afflictions] to have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
"Because passion is not [present] in him due to its being something to be abandoned, nor is hatred because there is no harm [inflicted]," and so forth;
and ignorance [is present] along with those two.
That which is associated with wrong view and doubt,
as well as the unshared ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā), is this single latent tendency of ignorance (avidyānuśaya).
Three [defilements] are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and have the untainted as their object.
Likewise, those to be abandoned by the vision of the path are also these same three; thus, there are six in each stage.
These are the objects for those whose sphere they are.
Those two are cessation and the path.
"Having that as their range" means those for which these are the range; [the word] "of them" refers to those [dharmas].
Respectively, for the three [types of cessation],
there is the cessation of their own level,
which is the cessation of their own level.
The sphere is the object;
it is the path.

However, that which belongs to the category of dharma-knowledge has six levels, while that which belongs to the category of subsequent knowledge has nine levels; these are the objects of the other three latent tendencies (anuśaya) whose domain is the Path.
How so?
These three latent tendencies have cessation as their object and thus pertain to the nine levels.
[These range] from those belonging to the desire realm up to those belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
For those belonging to the desire realm, the object of focus is exclusively the cessation of phenomena belonging to the desire realm.
For those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, the object of focus is exclusively the cessation of phenomena belonging to the level of the first dhyāna.
For those [cognitions] up to the level of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), their object is exclusively the cessation of phenomena belonging to the level of the peak of existence.
However, the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) pertains to six levels:
those belonging to the stages of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four dhyānas.
All of these [factors] belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) are the objects (*ālambana*) of these three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, that which belongs to the side of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) pertains to nine stages (*navabhūmika*):

namely, the stages of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four dhyānas, and the spheres of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
All of these [factors] belonging to the level of the first dhyāna are the objective supports (ālambana) for these three underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
This continues in the same way up to those belonging to the level of the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
Why, then, is only the cessation (nirodha) of its own level the objective support within its range?
He shows the reason why the path—whether consisting of six stages or nine stages—is their object:
"For the path has mutual causality.
How does it have mutual causality?

The path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣya) on six stages serves as the cause for another path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge—whether it belongs to a lower or higher stage, and whether it is equal or superior—as well as for a path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna-pakṣya). That [subsequent knowledge] path, which belongs to nine stages, should also be applied accordingly; this has been explained in detail.
Regarding the statement, "The path of the nine stages is [the object] for each other when they are equal or superior," it follows that,

in this way, for those belonging to the desire realm who take the path as their object, the category of dharma-knowledge belonging to the stage of the *anāgamya* up to the stage of the fourth dhyāna serves as the object.

The path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), whether it belongs to the stage of the *anāgamya* up to the stage of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), is the object of these paths that have the first dhyāna as their object.
This continues up to those belonging to the stage of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

If the false views and so forth belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that have the path as their object also take as their object the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) called cessation and the path, which is the antidote to the form and formless realms.
"For the entire category belonging to the side of dharma-knowledge is mutually causal.

Why is it that those very [afflictions] such as false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth do not take even the path belonging to the side of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) as their object? He says: "Even though dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge... and so on, because dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge are mutually causal.
Subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is not an antidote to the desire realm;
therefore, those [beings of the form and formless realms] do not take it as their object.
Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), however, is an antidote to the desire realm and thus also takes the antidotes to the form and formless realms as its object.
"Then what about dharma-knowledge? and so forth.
Dharma-knowledge, whether regarding cessation or the path, which serves as the antidote to the three realms on the path of cultivation—that [is the subject].

According to this established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the realms of form and formlessness; because of its existence, it will serve as the object (*ālambana*) for the wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth belonging to those levels—that is, those belonging to the levels of form and formlessness.
"Not all of that," and so forth:
that *dharmajñāna* is not the antidote for the entirety of the realms of form and formlessness.
What, then, is the reason?
It is because the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering and its origin, when subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), do not serve as antidotes to these [two realms].
The meaning is that they do not serve as antidotes to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*).
Therefore, the knowledge of those factors (*dharmajñāna*) is not the object of false views and so forth belonging to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpyāvacara*).
Furthermore, it is not the antidote for both realms in their entirety; this is the meaning of the detailed explanation beginning with "nor for both.
That is to say, the knowledge of those factors is not the antidote for the entirety of the realms of form and formlessness.
What is the reason?
Because it is not an antidote to those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing.
Dharma-knowledge regarding cessation or the path belongs to the path of cultivation.
Because of this statement, he provides the conclusion here: "Since there is no first [knowledge], it does not become an object.

This is because, among the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, the two first ones—the dharma-knowledge of suffering and the dharma-knowledge of origin—lack the nature of being antidotes to the form and formless realms as previously described.

Because that *dharmajñāna* lacks the nature of being an antidote (*pratipakṣatva*) with respect to the first [categories] among those belonging to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpyāvacara*), as well as those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*).

Thus, *dharmajñāna* does not become the object (*ālambana*) of the wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth belonging to those levels which take the Path as their object and belong to the realms of form and formlessness.

Therefore, it is established that, excluding those eighteen untainted objects (*anāsravālambana*) belonging to the three realms, the remaining eighty latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have tainted objects (*sāsravālambana*).
"It should not be something to be abandoned" means that it should not be something to be relinquished by the cutting off of its acquisition (*prāpti*).
For example, wholesome desire for the Dharma, which is of the nature of longing and constitutes right view, is not to be relinquished by the cutting off of its acquisition.
In that same way, this [view] would be [non-defiled].
Therefore, it does not have the outflows (āsrava) as its object.
Nor is there hatred, because there is no harm [inflicted].
Thus,
because they transcend the characteristics of the nine bases of malice, there is no hatred toward cessation and the path.
This is because they are pure in accordance with reality.
Purity in the sense of ultimate reality is cessation,
because it is free from the stains of the afflictions.
The path, too, is purity in the ultimate sense, because it is by means of this that one becomes pure in the ultimate sense.
It is not tenable to establish that the grasping at those two as purity is the "clinging to rules and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Furthermore, they are "supreme" because,
being the purity of the true object, those two— the cessation and the path— are supreme.

Furthermore, if the two types of misapprehension (*parāmarśa*) were to have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, they would partake of the characteristic of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), because the untainted states are both pure and supreme. Consequently, they could not be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanaheya*). For misapprehension of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is logically defined as the grasping at what is inferior and what is not supreme as being supreme.
But it is not so for cessation and the path;
for those two, the grasping at them as supreme does not constitute the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
How many [latent tendencies] increase by way of their object?
"How many [proclivities] are [active] solely through association?
"How many [proclivities] are [active] solely through the object? He asks this without restriction because those which procreate through the object [also procreate] through association.
They necessarily adhere by way of association.

However, those which adhere solely by way of association do not adhere by way of object; these are the latent dispositions whose objects are the untainted (*anāsrava*) or those belonging to a different level (*visabhāgabhūmi*).
In this context, the meaning of *anuśaya* is "conformity.
It is not the case that the conditions belonging to that [same] level exist in conformity for the sake of its arising;
nor is it the case that they are favorable to it.
Furthermore, those [states] such as cessation are not conducive to those [defilements] such as wrong view;
it is like dry food not being conducive to one suffering from wind-disorder (*vātika*).
Just as when it is said that "dry food is not conducive to one with a wind-disorder," it is understood that it does not function in accordance with the body's needs.

In the former position, however, it is for the sake of obtaining a foundation, because of the statement: "One does not obtain a foundation in them. "By which dharma" means by feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.
(V.19) "And that does not exist for those two.
And that suffering does not exist for those two, namely the form and formless realms.
Why?
Because there is an absence of causes for harming others.
The cause of harming others consists of malice and so forth;
because of the absence of that.
"This is the foremost of views" means that this is distinguished from other types of views;
the sense is that it is not excessively blameworthy.

The distinction is that liberation is the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the path, whereas annihilation is intended to be causeless; thus, the view of annihilation is faulty due to such a misconception.
"Because of being deluded regarding its own substance" means:

since one grasps the aggregates of appropriation (*upādānaskandha*) included within one's own continuum as a self or belonging to a self, the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is deluded regarding its own substance.
For those very same [beings], the view of grasping at the extremes of eternalism and nihilism is likewise;
and just as those views are,
so too is the ignorance associated with them.
And because they proceed without afflicting others.
What [is the case]?
It is understood from the context that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
For those two [greed and hatred] do not cause any harm to others.
This same consequence would apply to craving for rebirth in heaven (*svargatṛṣṇā*) and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*):

since craving for rebirth in heaven and the conceit "I am" are not in contradiction with giving and the other perfections, and because they involve delusion regarding one's own property and do not engage in harming others, it follows that they too would be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This is not accepted.
Therefore, with the intention that for these reasons the two [views] do not possess an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛtatva*), he presents the opinion of the former masters (*pūrvācārya*),
beginning with "the innate view of a self-identity" (*sahajā satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
"But that which is conceptualized as unwholesome" refers to that which has been conceptualized by those who propound a self, such as Kapila, Ulūka, and others;
it is not indeterminate.
What then? It is unwholesome; this also includes the view of grasping at extremes.
That which is conceptualized by them is also unwholesome; however,
because it is preceded by that [unwholesome state], it is understood to function in the same manner even though it is not explicitly mentioned.
"But the remaining ones here are unwholesome. Regarding the word "here": it refers to this world.
This is for the purpose of including the remaining [defilements] of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
It is established that in the desire realm, the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*), such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).
(V.20) How many are roots of the unwholesome (*akuśalamūla*), and how many are not?
This exclusion is formulated by way of the continued application of the phrase "of these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) are attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), and delusion (*mūḍhi*).
In the desire realm, those [afflictions] which are attachment, aversion, and delusion— all five types of these— are indeed unwholesome roots,
because they are established as the opposites of the wholesome roots.
"Other latent dispositions do not [arise there].
"Delusion" (*mūḍhi*) is a synonym for ignorance (*moha*).
All ignorance, with the exception of that associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), [does not arise there].
How is it that this is not found explicitly stated in the Sūtra? Because the topic is "the foul" (*aśubhā*), and [the term] refers to only one part [of the whole].
For this very reason it is said:
"If that which is unwholesome is accepted as being the root of the unwholesome alone.

Because of the restriction [implied by] the phrase "these alone," it is established that the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), such as false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth, are not unwholesome roots.
(V.20cd, 21) "There are three neutral roots.
Of these very ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
there are three neutral roots.
The mention of "three" is for the purpose of distinguishing [this view] from the opinion of the Westerners (Bahirdeśaka).
It is thus shown that there are exactly three, and not four.
He asks: which are the three? He says:
"That" refers to craving, ignorance, and that [specific] cognition;
it indicates their neutral nature.
Thus, they are called "the neutral roots."
By this term "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) alone, he shows that craving (*tṛṣṇā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and views (*mati*) are specifically qualified.
And here, although views are not by nature afflictions (*kleśa*), they are accepted as an indeterminate root (*avyākṛtamūla*) by the Vaibhāṣikas;
namely, whatever craving is indeterminate.
In the meditations and formless attainments associated with relishing (*āsvādanā-saṃprayukta*), or at the time of rebirth in celestial palaces (*vimāna*) and so forth as appropriate;

whatever ignorance (*avidyā*) there is in the realms of form and formlessness, and in the realm of desire, which is associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).
Likewise, whatever wisdom (*prajñā*) there is that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Finally, even that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it refers to wisdom associated with the minds of maturation, postures, crafts, and emanations, as well as that associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). In the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*), it refers to wisdom associated with all afflictions and associated with [minds] such as those born of maturation, as applicable. This is indeterminate wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "of one whose activity is twofold": *dvaidha* is the state of being twofold; *vṛtti* is the activity within that state of being twofold.
For that [faith], doubt cannot be the root,
because it is unstable due to its dualistic mode of operation.
"By means of the characteristic of elevation" means: the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of elevation;
by that.
It has an upward growth;
therefore, pride cannot be the root,
for roots are firm and have a downward growth.
Because they are fundamentally dissimilar, doubt is not a root; because it is unstable, it is not a root.
It should be stated that pride is not [a root] because it does not function downwardly.
"Those" refers to the indeterminate [factors].
"Indeterminate craving" refers to that which exists in the realms of form and formlessness.
"View" also [exists] in those two realms, and in the realm of desire, it consists of the nature of the view of a self-identity and the view of grasping at extremes.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is associated only with those [afflictions] belonging to that realm;
in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*), it is all [ignorance].
Those who practice higher meditation are characterized by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and pride (*māna*).
One who practices meditation associated with relishing is one who meditates with craving as predominant. One who,
relying on meditation, gives rise to views such as eternalism and so forth [is one who meditates with views as predominant].
He is one who dwells with views as the preeminent factor, and one who dwells with conceit as the preeminent factor;
for by means of that [attainment], he thinks, "I am a master of this meditative absorption, but others are not so."
He is one who meditates with pride as the predominant factor. In that context, "predominant craving" means having craving as the uppermost;
since it is his habit to meditate thus, he is called "one who meditates with craving as the predominant factor."
Alternatively,
"one for whom craving is predominant" (tṛṣṇottara) means one in whom craving is excessive. And "one who meditates" (dhyāyī) refers to one who meditates with craving as the predominant factor.
In this way, there are those who practice meditation dominated by views and those who practice meditation dominated by pride; and these arise through the power of ignorance.
And those three meditators become thus through the power of ignorance and through association with ignorance.
Therefore, ignorance is also an indeterminate root.

Furthermore, for those who have entered meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), these states of the manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa*) are the root—that is, the cause—of indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*).
(Abhidh-k-vy 465) (V.22) He questions [the opponent] by means of a connection with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
"The fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛtavastu*) in the Sūtra," and so forth.
"The world is eternal;
the world is non-eternal," and so forth.
"Why are they [not] indeterminate?
means: why are they not designated as indeterminate things because they are neither wholesome nor unwholesome?
They are not designated as indeterminate entities.
A question to be set aside is an indeterminate one.
That which is not explained— that is, not stated— by way of being set aside is an indeterminate question.
Its basis is the thing (*vastu*); thus, it is an indeterminate thing (*avyākṛtavastu*).
In connection with that, this is introduced:
"For there are four kinds of questions," and so forth.
"Like death, birth, distinction, self, otherness, and so forth.
That is to say: like death, like birth, like distinction, and like self, otherness, and so forth.
The examples for the categorical response (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*) and so forth follow their respective order. "They will die" is the example for death in the case of the categorical response.
"Those with afflictions (*sakleśa*) will be born, not those free from afflictions (*niḥkleśa*)" is the example for birth in the case of the analytical response (*vibhajyavyākaraṇa*).

Regarding the question "With reference to whom do you ask?", this is the example of a specific [person] in the case of answering by way of inquiry (*paripṛcchāvyākaraṇa*). Regarding the question "Is the sentient being other than the aggregates?", this is the example of the self (*ātman*) as something distinct in the case of answering by way of setting aside (*sthāpanīyavyākaraṇa*). Regarding the question "Will all sentient beings die?", this is to be answered categorically (*ekāṃśena vyākartavya*).
As it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, the life of humans is short;
one must go on to the next world;
one must practice what is wholesome."
"There is no such thing as one who is born not to die. And: "Is the sentient being other than the aggregates, or not other? This is to be set aside," as stated by the Blessed One.
"But, O Gautama, does he who acts experience [the result]?
This, Brahmin, is undeclared.
Or does one act and another experience [the result]?"
"This is undeclared, O Brahmin," you say when asked, "Does he who acts experience [the result]? You say, "This is undeclared," when asked, "Does one act and another experience [the result]?"
Therefore, what indeed is the meaning of this statement of yours, venerable Gautama? To say, "He who acts is he who experiences [the result]," O Brahmin, leads to the view of eternalism.
To say, "One acts and another experiences [the result]," leads to the view of annihilationism.
"Having understood these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by means of the middle way. Thus spoke the Venerable Rāma.
This too must be answered categorically.
"Not all will be born.
This is not to be answered categorically alone.
"But as for one who should ask, 'Will all sentient beings die?'"—thus the Teacher [explains] in detail.
But if someone were to ask in this manner: "Will those who are going to die be reborn?", for him there would be an analytical explanation (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*).
Not all will be born;
rather,
those possessed of afflictions will be born.
"They are not free from afflictions.
Therefore, what was stated— that this must be answered categorically by saying "not all will be born"—
is untenable.
The intention is that, for this reason, the example cited by the Vaibhāṣikas is indeed appropriate.
That same Bhadanta Rāma said:
"And among humans, both [conditions] exist."

Inferiority and superiority—since both of these exist relatively, both must be answered categorically. For example, when the question is asked, "Is consciousness an effect or a cause? it is answered categorically:
it is both a cause and an effect, depending on whether one considers it in relation to its cause or its fruit.
In that regard, as for what was said—"Is a human being inferior or superior?"—the response "This must be answered by asking a counter-question: 'With reference to whom do you ask this?
is incorrect.

"Because this question is to be answered categorically (*ekāṃśena*)," the Master [Vasubandhu] thus supports the Vaibhāṣika position by stating that the questioner asks categorically: "Is a human being exclusively inferior, or exclusively superior?"
It is not because of an absolute prediction that one is either inferior or superior;
rather, a qualified prediction is appropriate, [asking]: "With reference to whom do you ask this?
In that regard, it was stated in detail that both [inferiority and superiority] exist only among humans.
That is incorrect.
He himself said all this: that the sentient being is other than the aggregates.
As for that which is to be set aside (*sthāpanīya*), this is the example of the fourfold [unanswered questions] stated according to the system of the Vaibhāṣikas by the Master;
"the Abhidharmikas say" refers to those who recite only the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*.
From the designation of suffering up to the designation of the path—
this is the designation of the four noble truths according to the sūtra.
It is because they are connected with the goal (artha).
The meaning is: "because it is connected with the [underlying] matter.
"This very thing" refers to the question of one who is deceitful;
that is, this very statement regarding a question that is to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇīya*).
The answer by way of counter-question should be understood as being for an insincere questioner who intends to cause vexation.
The Venerable Rāma said:
"When, then... and so forth.
When those two, the deceitful and the honest, do not ask anything at all, but merely entreat him, saying, "Speak the dharmas," then for those two—
the deceitful and the honest— nothing is explained beyond this: that these dharmas, such as form and so forth, exist with their full details and distinctions.
They are merely asked, "Which ones shall I speak of?
How, then, can there be a question regarding these two— the deceitful and the non-deceitful— and how can there be an answer for an Abhidharmika?
"Indeed, he who... and so forth is the detailed explanation of the conduct.
For when one who is ignorant of the way says, "Tell me the path," has he not asked for the path?
The intention is that this [question] is posed precisely by way of a request.

For just as when one says, "Tell me the path," it is implied by that speaker, "Which is the path?"; so too, when one says, "Speak of the dharmas," it is implied by that speaker, "Which are the dharmas?"
Because the answer is given only after having asked a question— having first asked, "Which many dharmas shall I speak of?"— and then answering that very question or those very dharmas;
since the multiplicity of dharmas has thus been explained,
how is it not an answer by way of counter-question (*paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇa*)?
The meaning is that it is a "response by way of inquiry.
In this regard, what was stated— that nothing at all is explained concerning those two, but they are merely inquired about, and so forth, up to "how there is an explanation"—
is incorrect.
The Teacher said:
"From the sūtra itself," and so forth.
For it is explained in this way in the sūtra.
Having established [the matter] through Sanskrit, it is recited:
"Having performed an intentional action (*saṃcetanīyaṃ karma*), what does one experience?
Is it pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure? A question asked in this manner is to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇīya*).
This is due to the distinction between wholesome and other types of intentional action (*saṃcetanīya*).
Having performed a wholesome, contaminated intentional action, one experiences pleasure or neither-pain-nor-pleasure;
having performed an unwholesome intentional action, one experiences pain.
If one were to say, "It is coarse," [referring to] the material;
[if one says] there is no detailed distinction up to "the soul is other than the body"—
by the word "up to" (yāvat), everything [in that series] is to be stated.
The Tathāgata does not exist after death;
the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death;
the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
The soul is that body;
the soul is one thing and the body another. He is conjoined with it by means of that [body] in that [place]. (V.23, 24) He is conjoined with it by means of that [body] in that [place].
The meaning is that it is indeed known that the person (pudgala) is bound by that latent disposition (anuśaya).
And as for "the afflictions with their own specific characteristics" (svalakṣaṇākleśāḥ):
the "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) refers to an object such as that which is to be experienced as pleasure (sukhavedanīya), and so forth.
In that regard, attachment arises by taking as its object only an entity to be experienced as pleasant;
therefore, it is called a "defilement with respect to its own characteristic.
Since arrogance arises when one takes that same entity to be experienced as pleasant as an object, pride (*māna*) is also a defilement with respect to its own characteristic.
Likewise, since hostility arises by taking an object to be experienced as suffering as its basis, hostility is also called a "specifically characterized affliction" (*svalakṣaṇakleśa*).
Furthermore, there are "general afflictions.
Views, doubt, and so forth are general because they are common [to all], or alternatively, they are called general afflictions because they are afflictions in a general sense.
For these arise without distinction toward objects such as those to be experienced as pleasant;
therefore, having arisen by taking that as their object, they are called "universal afflictions" (*sāmānyakleśa*).
[This applies] to those [afflictions] that are past or present.
Thus [it is said]:
"by those belonging to the past and the present.
"In whatever object attachment, aversion, and pride have arisen," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

These [afflictions], such as attachment and the rest, although belonging to the six groups of consciousness, because they are considered without distinction, are— as appropriate— associated with those objects (vastu) in which they have arisen, whether those objects belong to the three time periods and are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering up to being abandoned by cultivation;
and as long as they have not been abandoned,
one is bound to that object by those [afflictions] such as attachment.
Like a bull tied by a rope to a stake:
for these [afflictions], being afflictions with their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), do not necessarily arise in all persons in every respect;
rather, the meaning is that they arise in some [persons] in some [respects].
Therefore,
the qualification "those which have arisen and are not yet abandoned" is applied to that [category].
"Not abandoned" is the qualification.
Because one was previously bound to a certain object by means of those [defilements] such as attachment and so forth;
if those were abandoned, one would not be bound to everything by them.
Because [the object] has been abandoned and is thus free from underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The inclusion of the term "mental" (*mānasa*) means that these [defilements] exist everywhere in their future states as mental factors.
Regarding the phrase "by others in their own stage," this is because the [afflictions] belonging to the five groups of sensory consciousness are established otherwise;
furthermore, this is a qualification of attachment (*rāga*) and hostility (*pratigha*).
Because that which is mental must necessarily be of the nature of mind.
By means of these future [factors], one is bound to each respective category according to its own nature, throughout all three times and across all five aggregates.
For that is not a thing belonging to the outflows (sāsrava).
That which, even by means of a defilement consisting of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), is not possessed of passion through attachment (*rāga*),
nor possessed of hatred through aversion (*dveṣa*), nor possessed of pride through conceit (*māna*).
For immeasurable future [afflictions] such as attachment and so forth arise with all contaminated things as their respective objects.
One is bound to a future object by means of other future attachments and hostilities.
Thus, all minds and mental factors are restricted to their specific objects.
One is bound to those very future entities that possess the nature of arising,
because the five groups of consciousness have the present as their object.
The mention of "attachment and aversion" is a statement regarding pride, because all types of pride are mental in nature.
This is because of the statement: "Those [defilements] to be abandoned by vision are equal to torpor and belong to the level of mental consciousness.
The word "also" (api) indicates that they are not only associated with the mental consciousness, but also with those belonging to the five groups of sensory consciousness.

One is bound to all things belonging to the three times by those [defilements] which have the nature of non-arising (*anutpattidharmin*). For these, having the nature of non-arising, abide only in the future time;
moreover, their objects of perception (*ālambana*) shift.
For the afflictions, together with their associated mental factors, like the *suvarcalā* plant, remain directed toward their objects even when they are of a nature not to arise (*anutpattidharmin*).
This is because those of a nature not to arise do not arise by having taken an object as their support.
Therefore, for some [afflictions], the object is past.
For some it is present; for others it is future.
Indeed, their non-arising does not occur solely because of the non-arising of the object.
What then? It is due to the deficiency of conditions.
For the established tenet is that the causal totality (sāmagrya) has the state [of the effect] as its fruit, not the substance as its fruit.

"But by all the remaining [factors], one is conjoined everywhere" means that one is conjoined— i.e., bound— by the remaining factors such as views (*dṛṣṭi*) and so forth, even when they belong to different realms (*naikāyika*) and even when the object (*vastu*) belongs to all three time periods (*traiyadhvika*) and possesses five aspects.
He asks: "What is the reason?
and replies: "Because they are universal afflictions (*sāmānyakleśa*).
For these indeed can arise in everyone, in every [state].
Because it has the five aggregates of clinging as its object. (V.25) How can one be bound by that [defilement] to that [object]? How [can one be bound] to a past or future entity?
Is one then bound by that past and future latent disposition,
or is one disjoined from it?
Or rather, how are they established as being in the state of not having been abandoned or having been abandoned?
"Because of their connection with the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
Since the characteristics of the conditioned, such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth, function for the sake of the movement of objects among the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
therefore their impermanence is asserted.
"O monks, if form..."—this is the opening reading of this sutra:
"Form, whether past or future, is impermanent; what need is there to mention that which is present?"
Seeing thus, the learned noble disciple is indifferent toward past form;
he does not delight in future form;
and he practices for the sake of revulsion toward, dispassion toward, and the cessation of present form.
Monks, if past form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not be indifferent toward past form.
But since past form does exist,
therefore the learned noble disciple is indifferent toward past form.
If future form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not delight in future form.
But because future form does exist,
therefore the learned noble disciple does not delight in future form.
“Monks, if present form did not exist,” and so forth, [it continues]:
“the learned noble disciple would not be indifferent toward past form.
The meaning is that, because there would be no object, at the time of detachment, the mind of the noble disciple—which is characterized by indifference toward past objects—would not exist.
When past form is relied upon,
then there is attachment to it. "He would have delighted" means he would have craved.
"Monks, if present form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not be practicing for the sake of revulsion toward, dispassion toward, and cessation of present form;
thus this was not said, because [the existence of form] is established for both parties. From duality..."
Thus it was previously shown that this was stated explicitly;
now, however, the distinction is that it is [stated] by implication rather than explicitly.
Mental consciousness would not arise in dependence upon two [conditions].
The distinction is that [the object] has the past and future as its objective support (*ālambana*). Consequently, consciousness itself would not exist due to the absence of an objective support,
because it is held that consciousness exists only when there is something to be cognized (*vijñeya*).
And the proof for this is as follows:
mental consciousness has only that which exists as its object, because its intrinsic nature is that of apprehension.
"As in the case of visual consciousness.
"From the fruit" means: [it is established] from the result.
Past karma, whether virtuous or non-virtuous, possesses its own existing characteristic (svalakṣaṇa),
because it is producing a fruit at the time of ripening,
just like a present dharma.
(V.26) "There is a change in the state of being" means that there is a change in the state of a thing— whether past, future, or present— but not a change in its substantial essence (*dravya*).
The meaning is that there is no alteration in the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and so forth.
For when the future [dharma] enters the present time-period, it abandons its future state and acquires its present state.
Even while present, it is [regarded as] past;
the two examples, "gold" and "milk," are given respectively to demonstrate the alteration of form and the alteration of quality.
For one who maintains that the alteration is of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇānyathika*), conventional usage depends upon the acquisition of the activity of the characteristic.
Therefore he says:
"A dharma, as it proceeds through the time-periods, when past is endowed with the characteristic of the past,
yet is not separated from the characteristics of the future and the present," and so forth in detail.
If the future were separated from the past and the present, then it would follow that the future itself has not arisen, nor has the past. Alternatively,
if the past were separated from the future and the present, [the same consequence would follow].
The future would become the present and the past;
the present would be separated from both the past and the future;

and the future itself would become the present, while the present itself would become the past. For it is by being endowed with a characteristic that has attained its functional activity (*labdhavṛtti*) that a thing is established [as belonging to a particular time].
The meaning is that it is not dissociated from, nor separated from, anything other than that.
For this very reason, he provides an example:
namely, as follows.
A man is attached to one woman but not detached from the rest;
his fixation on passion for that one woman persists,
while regarding the other women there is merely the possession of passion.
"It does not manifest" means that for one who undergoes change of state (*avasthānyathika*), conventional usage is dependent upon the state;
it refers to that state in which that dharma does not perform its activity (*kāritra*).
In that [action], it is said to be future;
in that [time] during which one performs it, it is present.
Having been obstructed in whichever state,
it is designated as "past" upon reaching that state; thus, by reaching various states, one thing is designated as different from another—
namely, as "future" upon reaching the future state, and so on, up to being "past" upon reaching the past state.

"By way of a different state (*avasthāntarataḥ*), not by way of a different substance (*na dravyāntarataḥ*). The meaning is that when it reaches states such as the future, although its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) remains undifferentiated, it is designated solely by terms such as "future.
For this very reason, he provides an illustration.
"As with a single counting-stick," and so forth.
Just as a single small ball, when placed in the column for ones—that is, established in the position of ones—is called "one"; likewise, in the column for hundreds, it is called "one hundred."
It is said that "a thousand" refers to a thousand in the context of a thousand-fold [array]. This is in relation to a different state; however, there is no alteration in its intrinsic nature.
What then?
Due to the distinction of different locations, another designation arises that indicates a numerical difference;
it is said to be "mutual" in relation to what precedes and what follows.
The meaning is that the past, future, and present are designated in dependence upon what precedes and what follows:
the future is so called in dependence on what precedes it, whether that be the past or the present;
and the present is so called in dependence on what precedes it, namely the past, or on what follows it, namely the future.
The designation "past" is made in relation to something else, namely the present or the future.
Thus, the conventional usage of the "proponent of change through difference" (anyathānyathika) depends upon priority and posteriority.
For this very reason, he provides an illustration.
Just as one woman is called both "mother" and "daughter":
depending on her daughter, she is called "mother," and depending on her mother, she is called "daughter."
It is not a separate substance in relation to what precedes and follows;
rather, it should be categorized under the Sāṃkhya position.
This refers to the refutation of that which belongs to the Sāṃkhya position.
That itself is the refutation of that position;
the intention is that the Sāṃkhya position has been refuted.
For the second [position] as well—that of the Venerable Ghoṣaka—a confusion of the time-periods (adhvan) would result.
That which is intended as belonging to the past would also follow as being present and future. How so?

The past, while being endowed with the characteristic of the past, is not dissociated from the characteristics of the future and the present; the meaning is that it is indeed possessed [of them]. Likewise, the future, while being endowed with the characteristic of the future, is not dissociated from the characteristics of the past and the present.
Even though the present [dharma] is endowed with the characteristic of the present, it is not dissociated from the characteristics of the past and the future;
for this reason, because each one is joined with three characteristics, it follows that the past, the future, and the present would all exist simultaneously.
This same logic should be applied to the future and the present as well.
What is the similarity here?
For a person, there is merely possession (*samanvāgama*) with respect to a certain [dharma];
likewise, does a single characteristic exist for a dharma?
For this very reason, these two characteristics do not exist;
since they are cited in such a manner, there is no parity.
Furthermore, even for the fourth proponent, the Venerable Buddhadeva, it would follow that three time periods exist within a single time period.
In a single past time-period (*adhvan*), there exists the distinction between prior and subsequent moments.
Among these, the prior and subsequent moments are the past and the future respectively;
the prior moment is past, and the subsequent is future.
The middle one is the present.
Thus, in the past time, all three times would be obtained.
Therefore, for all of these—
The Vaibhāṣika maintains that the third [alternative] is the correct one. He asks: "In what way is it correct? and replies:
Because its time periods are established by way of their activity;
furthermore, the activity of the eye and so forth consists of seeing and so on.
Form and the other [objects] also have as their activity being the domain of their respective sense-faculties. "If it is thus," and so forth in detail:
if they are established by way of their activity.
What is the activity (*kāritra*) of the "homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) eye?
That which does not perform its own function, characterized by activity, is the homogeneous;
and for that [eye], there is no activity characterized by seeing.
The intention is: how can that [eye] be "present"?
It is because of the "giving and receiving of its fruit.
That eye grasps—that is, projects—its own outflow-fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
And it yields a fruit; it yields the outflow fruit (niṣyandaphala) immediately thereafter,
as well as the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala),
even if it does not perform the function of seeing.
"But it produces another fruit.
Because it possesses both the giving and the grasping of that fruit, it is established as being "present.
[Objection: "In that case, would not past homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) and so forth also [be considered present]?"
By the word "etcetera," the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) and others are included,
because they grant their fruit. Of these, two— the present and the past— grant [their fruit], while one— the past— grants it.
Because of this statement,
there follows the consequence that there is activity;
namely, that activity exists.
Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence that these [causes], such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and others, when past, would be present.
This is because their activity (*kāritra*) exists just as it does in the present, which results in a confusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasaṃkara*).
You might say: "Those [past causes] for which both the grasping of a fruit (*phalaparigraha*) and the giving of a fruit (*phaladāna*) exist [are present]."
Those for whom both are present are "present";
however, those for whom only one of the two is present are not "present."
Therefore, this is said:
"Or [the consequence] of half-functionality.
The word "consequence" (prasaṅga) is understood from the context.
Alternatively, there would be the consequence that they possess only half of their activity;
or else, it follows that those [factors] which are half-present are actually past.
For they are endowed with the characteristic of the past because their activity of grasping the fruit has ceased.
And because they possess the activity of yielding present results, they are endowed with the characteristic of the present.
This is precisely the fault of the confusion of characteristics;
for this is accepted as the definition of the time-periods (adhvan) such as the past and so forth.
That which has ceased its activity is past; that which has not yet attained its activity is future; and that which has attained its activity but has not yet ceased it is present.
(V.27) What is the obstacle?
This word-form is neuter gender.
The meaning is "what is the obstruction?
Others say: "What is its obstacle? thus "what is the obstructed activity" (*kiṃvighnaṃ kāritram*).
If it is argued that there is an incompleteness of conditions (*pratyaya*),
then this might be the case: namely,
that there is an incompleteness of the conditions, such as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and so forth.
Therefore, it is not the case that it does not exercise its activity at all times.
No,
because its eternal existence is admitted.
It is not logical to postulate the non-assembly of conditions,
because you maintain that conditions always exist here, since what exists cannot be destroyed.
"And as for that activity which is called 'past,' and so forth":
when activity is designated as "past," "future," or "present" according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)— based on such statements as "the past is that whose activity has ceased"—
is there yet another activity belonging to that very activity?

Since its state as past and so forth is described [in this way], if it exists, there follows the consequence of infinite regress; if it does not exist, then the state of the activity (kāritra) as future and so forth would depend solely on the existence of its own intrinsic nature (svarūpasattā). In that case, the state of entities (bhāva) as future and so forth will likewise occur [based on their own intrinsic nature].
What is the use of postulating a functional activity?
How is that [dharma] past, and so forth?
Or rather, it is not at all past, and so on in detail.
That which is neither past, nor future, nor present is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); thus, because it is unconditioned, it follows that it exists eternally.
This refers to "activity" (*kāritra*).
To this he asks: "What follows from that?"
Therefore, it should not be said that when a dharma does not perform its activity (kāritra), it is then "future," because this would entail the impossibility of performing an activity.
"This fault might arise," and so forth.

This fault—that there would be an infinite regress of a functional activity having another functional activity, or that [the activity] would result in being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—would indeed occur if the functional activity were something other than the dharma.
However, it is certainly not other than it.
This is not a fault.
[It is] "by that very self," meaning by that which is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the present.
The meaning is "by that.
What was not previously present for this [activity] in its future state?
If [it is argued that] because the activity is non-different [from the phenomenon], it follows that the phenomenon itself did not exist—this is what is being said.
Furthermore, what does "it does not exist later" mean? It means that it does not exist in its past state.
If it were said that the activity does not exist, it would imply that the phenomenon itself does not exist, because there is no difference between the phenomenon and its activity.
If it is not accepted that [something] comes into being after having not existed, the present is not established.
And if it is not accepted that, having come into being, it ceases to exist again, the past time is not established.

However, the future is understood by implication as that which has not yet come into being after having not existed; thus the three times are established, and otherwise they are not. This is the meaning of the statement.
"Because of the impossibility of arising and destruction.
Since [the dharma] exists at all times, arising and destruction are impossible.
Therefore, this claim—that there is no consequence of eternalism because of the connection with the characteristics of the conditioned—is mere words.
"This is an unprecedented application of words" means that this application of words is contradictory in its preceding and succeeding parts, namely,
[the claim] that "it exists at all times" and yet "it is joined with arising and destruction."
"Intrinsic nature exists at all times" means that whatever is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and so forth is held to exist at every moment.
If the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of form and so forth exists at all times, it follows that the state of form and so forth would be eternal.
Therefore, he says:
"And an entity is not held to be eternal."
This being so, it would follow that an entity is certainly different from its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
To this, he says:
"And an entity is not other than its intrinsic nature."
Thus,
because it is merely a matter of his will, this is clearly the activity of the Lord.
There is no logical justification for this. By saying "the past is that which has previously existed," he shows that it does not exist by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
"Future" refers to that which will come to be when a cause exists.
This shows that even though it is non-existent, it is established as such because of the presence of its cause.
It is in this sense that it is said to "exist."
It is because one considers that "it existed in the past" and "it will exist in the future," but it does not, however, exist in this way as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
This is for the purpose of refuting the view that denies cause and effect.
In order to refute the view that denies the cause, it is said, "the past exists. In order to refute the view that denies the fruit, it is said, "the future exists.
Although one could have said "the past was" and "the future will be," the use of the word "exists" (*asti*) is because the term *asti* is an indeclinable particle (*nipāta*).
For a particle has reference to the three times;
it occurs in the sense of the past and also in the sense of the future, as in the detailed example: "there is [was] of the lamp."
Just as people say that there is the prior non-existence of a lamp and there is its posterior non-existence,
yet it does not exist substantially;
and just as one says that [the lamp] has ceased to exist.

People say, "That lamp was not extinguished by me," yet it does not exist because it has ceased despite the application [of effort]. But is it not the case that for the Vaibhāṣika, even that which has ceased exists?

It is true that it exists; however, it does not exist while actually bearing the nature of a lamp. In this way, it is said that the past and future exist, even though they lack substantial existence (*dravyasattva*).
Otherwise, indeed, the past and the future would not be established.
The meaning is that if they were to exist by means of that very same characteristic, then the past and the future would not be established.
As for the passage beginning, "If the past is what has previously existed, then [regarding] the Laguḍaśikhīyakas," and so forth.
The cause for the women [being reborn as such] was due to the Parivrājaka ascetics of Laguḍaśikhīya; and the sūtra spoken by the Buddha at Nālandā is found in the *Saṃyuktāgama*.
The learned ones say that the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana has been killed.
As for the claim that he has not been killed, it is recited in this very sutra:
"The wandering mendicants of Laguḍaśikhīya, though they have committed an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), [have passed beyond it]."
"Those who speak thus that it does not exist," and so forth.
Do those wandering mendicants of the Laguḍaśikhīya school not accept that such an action was previously committed as an *ānantarya* (immediate) offense?
This is what is meant.
They desired that such action had occurred in the past; however, they disagreed regarding that action, asserting that it was not a substantial entity and that no such past action exists.
Since the Blessed One stated in detail that "that action which has passed away exists"— whereby they were mistaken regarding intrinsic nature—
it follows from that detailed explanation that the past exists by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, in that sūtra, when it is said that "that past action exists," this is not stated with the intention that the action itself is what has passed away.
What then? [It refers to the fact that its result persists.]
"Deposited by that" means deposited or entrusted by that former action.

This was said with the intention of referring to the capacity for yielding fruit within that continuum; this is what is meant by "it was said with this underlying purpose. How is this understood? He says:
For otherwise, an action existing in its own nature as past would not be established.

That is to say, that action existing by way of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) would not be established as being "past" while existing by way of a present-characteristic (*pratyutpannalakṣaṇa*);
the intention is that it would be established as being merely present.
When it is stated in detail that "it is deposited therein" (*tadāhitam*), it is established that past karma exists.
And this is so because,
just as the future does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*), so too the past does not exist.
"In the present time," and so forth.
The meaning is that it comes into being by way of a present state after having not existed.
This is not so.
Because the time-period (adhvan) is not a different entity from the existent thing (bhāva).
It is not the case that it is so;
for the present time-period, which is designated as "the eye," is not a different entity from the existent thing.
The meaning is: because it is not a separate substance.
That which is the present time-path is itself existence (*bhāva*).
How then could that very same present [dharma], having not existed within its own self in the past time, come into being?
For it has been said:
"Those very [dharmas] are the paths (adhvan) and the basis of discourse (kathāvastu)."
Thus,
since the eye does not exist as an eye within its own self, it is established that this future eye does not exist.
It is merely an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
The word *mātra* is intended to exclude [the sense of] being a producer (*janakatva*).
The intention is that phenomena (*dharmāḥ*) are the objective support (*ālambana*) because they arise in that form.
As for the phrase "that which is future by the thousands,"...
It is not logical for a cause that has not yet arisen to produce [an effect] even when it is proximate;
how much less so when it will arise after a very long time?
For it is not logical for a cause existing at a later time to be the cause of an effect existing at an earlier time.
"And [it would be] nirvāṇa. For consciousness, once ceased, would not produce [another], because of the cessation of the progression of saṃsāra; such is the intended meaning.
"It has been" and "it will be":
the meaning is that form which existed in the past state and will exist in the future state is the object (*ālambana*).
How is it known that it is apprehended in this way, and not as "it exists"? To this he says: For no one, when recollecting past form or feeling, perceives it as "it exists.
What then?
"One remembers that form as 'it was,' just as it was seen, and likewise the feeling just as it was experienced, by the power of the experience of visual consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "just as indeed," the Master himself explains the reason for this in detail:
the intention is that the past and the future are grasped just like present form.
And if it exists in that very same way as the present does, then it follows that it is the present. Alternatively,
if it does not exist in that way, then it is established that even a non-existent thing can be an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Because its form does not exist as it does in the present,
and because it is something being remembered; thus,
that very [form] is what is dispersed.
That which is present is itself what is dispersed as the past and the future;
no.
"Because that which is scattered is not apprehended"—
this is not tenable,
because that which is scattered is not apprehended.
Because this form, which was previously not scattered, is now scattered, is not apprehended in that way. And if it were the very same [form], as explained in detail:
if the form were a solid mass even in its present state.
In its past and future states, it is divided into atoms; therefore, it is not perceived as it is in the present.
This being the case, the atoms would be eternal because of their persistence in that same state, for those very same [atoms] are what are future, present, and past.
And this being the case, there would result nothing more than the mere aggregation and disintegration of atoms;
yet there would be neither any arising nor any cessation. Thus, the doctrine of the Ājīvikas or other heretics would be accepted. If that were intended, the Sūtra would be cast aside.
Monks, when the eye arises, it does not come from anywhere;
when it ceases, it does not go to any accumulation.
Thus, monks, the eye, having not been, comes to be; and having been, it passes away.
How, then, is this sūtra rejected and contradicted?
Because the statement that "the eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere with its own form" would be subverted;
and the statement that "when ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation" would likewise be subverted.
Because it is accepted that those atoms were scattered and accumulated in past time.
Regarding the phrase "of those not accumulated from atoms":
how can there be a state of being scattered for things such as sensation (*vedanā*), which do not have atoms as their intrinsic nature?
For it is material things (*mūrta*) that possess either a state of being accumulated or a state of being dispersed, not immaterial things (*amūrta*).
Furthermore, those [objects] are remembered exactly as they were produced and experienced;
thus, they are remembered precisely in their present form.
And if they exist exactly as they are now, it follows that they are eternal. On the other hand,
if they do not exist in that form, then it is established that even a non-existent thing can be an object of cognition.
"A thirteenth base (āyatana) would also be an object of cognition (ālambana).
This means that a thirteenth base, which completes the number of thirteen bases,
would be an object of consciousness (vijñāna).
"If it is maintained that [consciousness] has a non-existent object, then that consciousness would either have that [non-existent thing] as its object.
When the Vaibhāṣika had spoken thus, the Master said:
"Then the thirteenth," and so forth.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that this very name is the object;
that is, the name which constitutes the thirteenth base (āyatana) is the objective support.
In that case, it would follow that only the name does not exist,
and not the referent characterized by the absence of a thirteenth sense-base (*āyatana*).
Furthermore, there is one who takes the prior non-existence of a word as his object.
"What is its object?"— this is the completion of the sentence. Thus, regarding the subject at hand, the Vaibhāṣika says:
"Sound alone is the object" is the subject under discussion. "In that case, then," and so forth, says the Master [Vasubandhu].
This refers to one who takes the prior non-existence of sound as his object.
Therefore, it is sound itself that is apprehended by him,
not prior non-existence.
This follows as a consequence.
For one who seeks the absence of sound, it would follow that sound itself must be produced. If it should be thought that this refers to the state of being future:
That which has this prior non-existence is in a future state; it is that which is apprehended by [the cognition]. Therefore, one who seeks the non-existence of sound [apprehends it as such].
"It would not be necessary for him to even utter the word.
To this it is said:
"If [the object] exists, how can there be the cognition that 'it does not exist'?"
While that sound exists, how can there be for it a cognition of non-existence (*nāstibuddhi*) which takes its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) as its object?

If you say, "It is because [the sound] does not exist in the present," then this would be the case: the cognition of non-existence arises by taking as its object the fact that "it does not exist in the present."
No, because of its oneness;
that which is future is precisely that [same thing].
That very thing becomes present;
it is not something other than that.
How is it that, while that very thing is present, the cognition of its non-existence arises?
Or rather, it is its specific distinction (*viśe�șa*).
That is, the specific distinction which arises in the present state subsequent to that [entity] in its future state;
since that specific distinction does not exist while it is in the present, the cognition of it [as such] does not arise.
It arises.
This is the establishment of its existence after having been non-existent;
that is, the existence of that particular quality after it was previously non-existent.
Its establishment is as follows:
"existence and non-existence. Existence refers to the state of being present; non-existence refers to the states of having passed away and not yet arisen.
Thus, both [existence and non-existence] become the object of consciousness.
As for the passage beginning with "If non-existence is the object of consciousness, then...
and so forth, it was said by a Bodhisattva in his final existence.
By the statement, "There is no possibility that I shall know what does not exist in the world," it is shown that [this knowledge] does not have non-existence as its object.
The Master, demonstrating that this Sūtra has another intention, says:
"Others are those with overweening pride," and so forth.
Others, whose meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are impure, possess overweening pride;
even though the radiance—the radiance of the divine eye—is non-existent during the stage of preparatory application, they perceive it as if it were actually present.
"But as for me, I see that there truly exists a manifestation which is the precursor of the divine eye"—this is the intended meaning in that Sūtra.
Why would he have such a deliberation?
When it is established that all cognitions have real objects as their domain, how could there be any deliberation, investigation, or doubt on his part?
That is to say, what was stated at length as "it does not exist in the world" and so forth—
this kind of critical inquiry regarding cognitions is possible only when they have existent and non-existent things as their objects,
and not otherwise.
"What then is the distinction?"—
what indeed is the distinction of the Bodhisattva from others, if they too perceive only an existing appearance and not a non-existing one?
For this is the distinction regarding cognitions when they have both the existent and the non-existent as their objects.
And this being so, it is thus:
cognitions have non-existent objects.
"He will know what exists as existing, and what does not exist as not existing"—this is the illustration for this point.
Since one will seek— that is, know— a real entity as being existent, and a non-real entity as being non-existent, it is established that cognitions have non-existent objects.
Therefore, this [argument] put forward by the Bodhisattva is also not a valid reason.
"Preceded by that" means preceded by karma; [it arises] from a specific transformation of the mental continuum.
"The refutation of the doctrine of a self" [is as follows].
At the conclusion of the treatise, in the refutation of the Vātsīputrīya doctrine:
"In that case, arising is [the state of] coming into being after not having existed.
Since it is established that arising did not exist previously but exists now, the manifestation of what was previously non-existent is proven.
Because origination shares the same status as that which originates.
Now, [the statement] "everything exists" means that if origination also exists, it is not only the cause, but also the future effect— this is the intended meaning.
Now, of what is there efficacy, and where?
Of what cause is there efficacy toward what fruit?
And the cause is as previously stated: arising; and the fruit is that which exists in the future.
"It is the making present," says the Vaibhāṣika. "What, then, is this 'making present'? asks the Master in detail. "It is not arising that is the making present."
Because that exists, he asks this:
"If it is the drawing [of the object] to another location..."
If you think that the drawing of the fruit to another location by means of a cause is its being made present,
we say in response: the ellipsis of the sentence is "the fruit would be eternally present."
It is merely a drawing from one location to another;
nothing new whatsoever is produced. Thus, it follows that [the entity] must be eternal.
And as for the formless factors such as feeling and so forth,
how could there be their drawing toward another location?
The intention is that because they are immaterial and thus do not abide in a location, that [drawing] is not tenable.

And as for that attraction which is designated as "action," its meaning is the establishment of the non-existence of what was previously non-existent, in the sense that "it came into being after not having been. This is the intended sense.
If, on the other hand, it is a qualification of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*):
If you think that its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is distinguished by a cause, then there is a distinction of the fruit by means of that [cause].
To this we reply: it is established that there is coming-into-being after not having been.
It is established that the coming-into-being, the manifestation, of a qualification occurs after it has not existed.
Or the three time periods.
What?
It is governed by the statement that "everything exists."
It has been stated how it exists here:
that which previously existed is the past; that which will exist when the cause is present is the future.
That which has not yet come is the future.
That which, having come into being, has not yet perished is the present.
In this way, the Sarvāstivāda doctrine is established as correct within the Teaching. How is one bound by that, or to what?
How is one bound by that past or future affliction, or to that past or future object? How is there such a connection?
"By means of affliction, due to the existence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) born from that and having that as their cause.
Therefore, "born from that" (*tajja*) means born from that past [affliction].
"Having that as its cause" (*taddhetu*) means the cause of that future [affliction].
That which is both born from that and has that as its cause is "born-from-that-and-having-that-as-its-cause" (*tajjataddhetu*).
The latent tendency (*anuśaya*) that is born-from-that-and-has-that-as-its-cause is the seed;
[the phrase refers to] the state of being that.
It is bound, respectively, by past and future afflictions (*kleśa*).
That past and future object is its objective support (*ālambana*); thus, the affliction which has that as its support is the latent tendency (*anuśaya*).
Because of the existence of that [tendency], one is bound, respectively, to the past and future object.
"Nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*) refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena.
Since there is an established distinction between time periods such as the past and so forth, he speaks [of *dharmatā*] for the purpose of explaining the conventional usage thereof.
"There is a way of explanation," and so forth.
There is a sequence of statements, namely: that which arises.
Having stated that "it ceases," he provides an illustration:
form arises and form ceases, because [the state] is not other than the substance.
One thing arises and another ceases.
One [moment] that is future arises because it is oriented toward arising;
another [moment] that is present ceases because it is oriented toward cessation.
The time period (*adhvan*) also arises, because a phenomenon (*dharma*) that is arising is comprised within the time periods and possesses the nature of the time periods; this is the meaning.
For they [the time periods] are defined as the bases of discourse (*kathāvastu*).
A phenomenon also arises from the form of its appropriation belonging to the temporal period.
Why? He says:
because the future temporal period consists of many moments.
Because from among a multitude of future moments existing as a collection, only a single moment arises, it is therefore said that [an action] "arises from the time period" (*adhvan*).
This was mentioned as an incidental digression.
By all the remaining [factors], however, [the rule applies] everywhere; thus, as an incidental discussion, comes the investigation into the past and the future.
Regarding the passage beginning with "that which has been abandoned," and so forth:
In this context, abandonment (*prahāṇa*) results from the departure of [the state of] attainment;
dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) results from the abandonment of the afflictions that take that as their object,
with reference to the paths of seeing and cultivation.
"When suffering [to be abandoned] by seeing has been abandoned," and so forth;
"previously abandoned," and so forth.
"By all the remaining universal [defilements]" means by those universal [defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
"By the remaining impurities that have those [three] as their objects."
The meaning is: "by means of those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) whose objects and types have been abandoned.
For example, when the highest-of-the-high type has been abandoned, one is still bound by the remaining unabandoned latent dispositions, such as the high-middling and so forth.
Thus, although he is dissociated from that highest-of-the-high category of affliction which has been abandoned, he is nevertheless still bound by those remaining ones.
(V.29–31) They provide a summary commentary (*piṇḍavibhāṣā*). The meaning is that they provide a concise explanation. Who [are they]?
The Vaibhāṣikas [state]: "Sixteen.
This refers to the five types belonging to the desire realm.
There are four types to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, and a fifth to be abandoned through cultivation.
Likewise, up to those belonging to the formless realm, there are five types; thus, there are fifteen.
Together with the untainted (anāsrava), there are sixteen dharmas.
And these phenomena which are to be abandoned by seeing have the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature;
those which are to be abandoned by cultivation [are likewise].
They have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
How so?
Because those feelings are associated with the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that are to be abandoned by vision.
That which is feeling is the aggregate of feeling. Those which are perceptions are the aggregate of perception.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), the volitions (*cetanā*) and so forth associated with them, the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all these mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest, and the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*)— namely, birth, aging, duration, and impermanence— constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
This also includes the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that is associated with these.
That is the aggregate of consciousness.
Thus, those things whose nature consists of the four aggregates are to be abandoned by seeing.
Furthermore, those other contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) are to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).
How so?
All external and internal contaminated form (*rūpa*) is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
