Furthermore, the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), excluding those to be abandoned by seeing the uncontaminated (*anāsravadarśanaprahātavya*), should be understood as having the nature of the five aggregates and being abandonable through cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*).
These sixteen mental states (*citta*) are as follows:

there are five mental states belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), ranging from those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) up to those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*).
Likewise, there are five each for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), plus the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind; thus, there are sixteen minds.
These sixteen categories of phenomena as objects are described [in terms of] how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) exist therein.

One should infer this: in such-and-such a phenomenon, there are so many latent dispositions which, being associated with that mind, adhere to it either by way of the object (*ālambana*) or by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).

"Those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its cause, and by cultivation, are born in the desire realm" means that those [defilements] belonging to the sphere of desire (kāmāvacara) are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana), the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana), and by cultivation (bhāvanā).
This is the classification by way of analysis:

one's own three [realms], those acquired in the single form realm, and the pure. These are the consciousnesses belonging to one's own three realms, those acquired in the single form realm, and the pure ones.
The objects of those [knowledges] are their own three [realms], the one [realm] attained in the form realm, and the pure consciousness.
"First, those belonging to the desire realm," and so forth.
Those belonging to the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of its origin are, respectively, ten and seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
along with their co-existent factors, their acquisitions (*prāpti*), and their attendants.
The four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation, their co-existent factors and acquisitions (*prāpti*) along with their attendants;
all contaminated form (*rūpa*);
and other non-defiled phenomena (*dharma*).
These factors are the objects of five types of consciousness.
To which ones? He says:
"Of three belonging to their own realm, and of those very same [three] [belonging to other realms]."

Of those [defilements] belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-heya), by the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-heya), and by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
How so?

First, those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering are [the causes] of that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, whether it be associated with universal (sarvatraga) or non-universal [defilements].
And [it is the object] of that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśanaprahātavya*) and is associated with the universal [defilements] (*sarvatraga-saṃprayukta*);
and of the wholesome [state] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*);
and of one [type] belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), which is likewise only to be abandoned by cultivation.

They become the objects of five types of consciousness: that of one born in the desire realm who is on the mundane path while taking phenomena of the desire realm as an object; that of one born in the form realm while perceiving the desire realm; and that of the untainted category of dharma-knowledge.
It is not the object of the two minds belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path,

because those two minds have the untainted as their object— specifically taking cessation and the path as their objects— and because those two minds having tainted objects take only that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path as their object.
[It does not take] the afflicted [states] of higher levels as its object,
because it takes those of lower levels as its object;
nor does it take the wholesome [states] belonging to the formless realm as its object.
Because it is distant by way of the four types of distance.
Likewise, those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of origin are [distant] from two types of [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of origin,
and from those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering that are associated with the universal [defilements].
Of the wholesome [state] to be abandoned by cultivation;
of one [type] belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) which is also to be abandoned by cultivation alone;
and of the untainted (anāsrava).
They are the objects of precisely five [consciousnesses].
And the explanation should be made exactly as before.
Those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya) are also the objects of precisely five [consciousnesses].

[It arises] from the two minds associated with universal [defilements] that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, from the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral mind to be abandoned by cultivation as appropriate,
from one [mind] of the form realm which is exclusively to be abandoned by cultivation,
and from the untainted [mind].
It should be stated as before:
"Of one's own [level], the three lower, the one upper, and the pure [dharmas]."

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "one's own" (*svakānām*), "the three lower ones" (*adharāṇāṃ ca trayam*), and "one's own and the three lower ones" (*svakādharatrayaṃ ca*); together with "the one higher" (*ūrdhvaikam*) and "the stainless" (*amalam*).

These are the very same three types of phenomena belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), because they are the subject under discussion—namely, those [phenomena] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
These are the objects of eight minds:

of the three belonging to their own realm—namely, those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, by the vision of origin, and by cultivation—as previously explained; and of the three belonging to the lower realm, which are likewise those same [three].

Among those, there are two minds to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*) which are associated with universal [defilements] (*sarvatraga*) of a different realm; one mind to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) which is either consisting of hearing (*śruta-maya*) or reflection (*cintā-maya*); one mind of the higher realm (*ūrdhva-dhātuka*) to be abandoned by cultivation alone, comprised within the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); and the untainted (*anāsrava*) side of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). (Abhidh-k-vy 480)
"Having as their objects those belonging to the three realms, the three [types], and the untainted.
This means they have as their objects the three types belonging to the three realms and the untainted.
"Those very same" refers to those very [defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-bhāvanā-heya*). "Of those three types" means:

of the four [defilements] belonging to the desire and form realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin and are associated with universal [defilements] of a different realm (*visabhāga-dhātu-sarvatraga*), and of the two [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), as appropriate.
And [it is the object] of the three belonging to its own realm.
Which ones?
Of the two associated with the universal and non-universal [defilements] respectively, and of that which is to be abandoned by cultivation, as well as of the untainted (anāsrava).
They become the objects of ten types of consciousness.
Those [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path have as their domain all [factors] belonging to their own respective levels and above.
The inclusion of the term "all" is for the purpose of encompassing the three realms (*traidhātuka*).
Because of the statement "the objects of their own respective predominance," it is implicitly stated that these are also the objects of those previously mentioned.

Alternatively, "svādhika" means those that are superior to one's own; thus, "the spheres of those that are superior to one's own" (svādhikagocara) refers to the objects of those [faculties] that are superior. Regarding the phrase "of that which is superior":
It belongs to that which is associated with attachment and so forth,
but not to that which is associated with false view and so forth,
because the latter always takes cessation and the path as its objects.

"Of the five previously mentioned" refers to the three belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*)— those to be abandoned by the two categories of universal [defilements] and those associated with them, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*).
[This applies] only to that which belongs to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) and is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*),
as well as to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Those [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*) are also like this.
How is it so? That which is the object of six minds becomes the object of nine and eleven minds.
Those belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path become the objects (*ālambana*) of nine minds.
Those belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) [become the objects] of eleven.
How so?

The factors of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path are objects for three types [of afflictions] belonging to the desire realm: those to be abandoned by the universal [afflictions] associated with different realms, and those to be abandoned by cultivation;
as well as for three types belonging to its own realm: those to be abandoned by the two classes of universal [afflictions], those associated with them, and those to be abandoned by cultivation.
They are also objects for one type belonging to the formless realm: that which is to be abandoned by cultivation and is comprised within the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
And [it is the object] of the untainted [cognition] belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*),
and of that very same additional mind which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaprahātavya*) or by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*).
Thus, these nine each become objects [of cognition].
The factors belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path also each become objects of eleven types of consciousness:
six belonging to the desire and form realms—namely, those associated with the universal [defilements] directed toward other realms and those to be abandoned by cultivation;
and three belonging to its own realm—namely, those associated with the two classes of universal [defilements] and those to be abandoned by cultivation.
And [the objects] of that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, each being additional,
as well as the untainted [factors] belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge—
thus, these become the objects of eleven [cognitions].
"The untainted [phenomena] are the objects of the final three untainted [knowledges] of the three realms" means that the untainted [phenomena] are cessation and so forth.

Among the three realms, those which are the last three— characterized as being abandoned through the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and cultivation— are, as appropriate, the objects of those [three knowledges] and of the untainted [knowledge].
How so?

To begin with, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and the noble path (*āryamārga*) are, as appropriate, the objects of those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*) that are associated with false view, doubt, and ignorance when they have those [two] as their objects, as well as the object of the untainted category of dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anāsrava-dharmajñāna-anvayajñāna-pakṣa*).
However, it should be understood that space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) are the objects only of the non-afflicted mind to be abandoned by cultivation.

However, Ācārya Guṇamati and Vasumitra explain that space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) are the objects of both the afflicted and the unafflicted [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
That is incorrect.
For wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vimati*), and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with them, as well as independent ignorance, [take these as their objects].
Because of the rule that the six [objects] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path have the uncontaminated as their domain,
it is established as the tenet that the defiled mind does not have cultivation as its object.
"Those belonging to the five, eight, ten, and ten consciousnesses as their objects" means:
those belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin and by cultivation are the objects of the five [consciousnesses].
Those belonging to the form realm are the conditions for eight;
those belonging to the formless realm are the conditions for ten;
and the pure [dharmas] are also the conditions for ten alone.
This should be applied according to the previous explanation.
These same sixteen moments of consciousness become thirty-six.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin, which are associated with non-universal [defilements], and those associated with both similar and dissimilar universal [defilements].
Thus, in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin is of three types each.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is the case except for those associated with the universal [defilements] belonging to a different realm or level (*visabhāgadhātubhūmisarvatraga*).

In all three realms, that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path is of two types each, because their objects (*ālambana*) are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
That which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) is also of two kinds, distinguished as afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*).
The untainted (*anāsrava*) is also twofold: the side of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*) and the side of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna-pakṣa*).
[The phrase] "belonging to the desire realm and to be abandoned by cultivation" refers to this.
The faculty of pleasure associated with the five groups of consciousness belongs to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) and is of five types:
that belonging to the level of the first dhyāna consists of the three groups of consciousness.

Summarizing the mental consciousness belonging to the level of the third dhyāna, there are five types according to their respective applications: those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, up to those to be abandoned by cultivation.
The untainted [consciousness] belongs exclusively to the level of the third dhyāna.
As for the four types belonging to the desire realm:
Regarding that which is to be abandoned through the vision and cultivation of suffering, its origin, and the path:
the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) becomes the object (*ālambana*) for those [afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin.

This is because the faculty of pleasure—whether belonging to its own level or a higher level, and comprised within the truths of suffering and its origin—serves as the object for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), false views, and so forth.

Furthermore, for that [mind] to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaheya*) which is associated with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) subsumed under the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) is the object (*ālambana*).

And for the mind associated with attachment (*rāga*) and so forth that is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), the faculty of pleasure belonging to the fivefold group of consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāyika*) is the object.
Thus, that [faculty of pleasure] is the object of this [mind] of four types.
But it does not apply to a mind that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaheya*).
This is because, in that case, false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth have cessation as their object (*ālambana*),
whereas adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and so forth have their own category (*svanikāya*) as their object.
And because the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is absent there, it is said: "except for that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
This refers to the fivefold [defilement] belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
Because there exists a fivefold faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) comprised within the third dhyāna.
Regarding the phrase "of that which is to be abandoned by the vision and cultivation of the Path":

for a mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) that is to be abandoned by the vision of the Path and is associated with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth, the faculty of pleasure comprised within the Path serves as its object (*ālambana*).
And that very same [object] is the focal object (ālambana) of the wholesome mind that is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya).
Furthermore, it becomes the focal object for all untainted (anāsrava) states as well.
In this regard, it is "according to what is possible" (yathāsaṃbhavam).
Because latent dispositions do not adhere to that which is untainted (*anāsrava*),
and because only certain [dispositions] adhere to certain [objects],
it is therefore said "according to possibility" (*yathāsambhavam*).
In that consciousness, there are four categories belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).

Namely, when [consciousness] is associated with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and has the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as its object, all ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) adhere to it either by way of the object (*ālambana*) or by way of association (*saṃprayoga*), according to the case.
The same applies to those [tendencies] to be abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*).
Those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of the path also increase (anuśerate) in that consciousness which has the faculty of pleasure as its object.

For in a consciousness associated with false view and so forth that has the faculty of pleasure belonging to the Path as its object, false views and the like increase by way of association (saṃprayoga).
Furthermore, adherence to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) and the others also increase by way of the object (ālambana).
Therefore, that category [of defilements] also lies latent there;
even the category to be abandoned by cultivation lies latent here,
because of the connection between attachment and the other [defilements] with the faculty of pleasure as their object and with consciousness as their object.
However, the category [of afflictions] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation does not lie latent there,
because there is no consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object.
This is because those belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) have conditioned phenomena as their objects.
The form-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) has five types of objects for the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
It is easy to understand that four categories (*nikāya*) of defilements adhere (*anuśerate*) therein.
But how do those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaprahātavya*), which have conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their object, adhere?
In the third dhyāna, the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and other such defilements are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). They take one another as their objects.
Thus, they increase (*anuśerate*) therein—either through association or by way of object—in the consciousness that has the faculty of pleasure as its object.
There are two categories belonging to the formless realm:
the category of those to be abandoned by the vision of the path and the category of those to be abandoned by cultivation.
When the faculties of pleasure and so forth associated with the path are taken as objects by false view and the like, false views and the rest adhere [to them] through association.
However, adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the others adhere there by way of their object (*ālambana*).
A category [of afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) also adheres;
for a wholesome mind to be abandoned by cultivation takes the Path as its object.
In that regard, the group [of defilements] beginning with attachment lies latent there.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the omnipresent latent dispositions belonging to the formless realm, as well as those associated with wrong view and so forth that take the Path as their object, lie latent in that very consciousness, or in the consciousness associated with them.
This refers specifically to that twelvefold [consciousness].

[This] consciousness, which has the faculty of pleasure as its object, becomes the object of [the following]: the four types of [defilements] belonging to the desire realm—excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation; the five types belonging to the form realm; the two types belonging to the formless realm—those to be abandoned by the vision of the path and by cultivation; and the untainted [consciousness], because of their capacity to take one another as objects.
Furthermore, that consciousness which has the faculty of pleasure as its object becomes the object of two further types of [consciousness] belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara).
To the question "Of which [two]?", it says:
"Of those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin."

For the consciousness associated with the universal [defilements] belonging to the formless realm— which is of two types due to the distinction between those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin— takes as its object a consciousness associated with false view and so forth that is to be abandoned by the vision of the path in the formless realm,
as well as the wholesome [consciousness] of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation which takes the path as its object.

Thus, this fourteen-fold consciousness, which has the faculty of pleasure as its object, has as its objects those [consciousnesses] therein, having added the two types to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin belonging to the formless realm.

Previously, it was stated that only the universal [defilements] belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) adhere to a consciousness that has the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as its object.

However, when that consciousness has as its object the object of the faculty of pleasure, both categories of defilements belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*) adhere to it.

Therefore, in a mind associated with the universal [defilements], those defilements to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin adhere [to it] either through association (*saṃprayoga*) or through the object (*ālambana*), as the case may be.
The remaining [cases] are to be applied as before. By this method, other [instances] are also to be understood; by this path, other [matters] are likewise to be comprehended.
How so?
When the question arises as to how many latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere to that which has the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) as its object, it must be investigated as follows:

the faculty of suffering is of one kind; it belongs to the realm of desire (kāmāvacara) and is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāprahātavya), because it consists of the five groups of sensory consciousness (pañcavijñānakāyika).
In brief, that serves as the object of five kinds of consciousness:
of the three types belonging to the desire realm— namely,
the two types of consciousness associated with universal [defilements] which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin, and the type to be abandoned by cultivation.
And [the consciousness] belonging to the realm of form that is to be abandoned by cultivation,
as well as the untainted [consciousness].
This is the fivefold consciousness that has the faculty of suffering as its object.

In that regard, as far as possible, the three categories belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

For therein, in a mind associated with the universal [defilements] and in that which is to be abandoned by cultivation, the two categories to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin adhere [as latent tendencies] either by way of association (*saṃprayoga*) or by way of object (*ālambana*), as the case may be.
And in that which is to be abandoned by cultivation, the category to be abandoned by cultivation adheres.

One [defilement] of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*). It should be understood that among those, it underlies the mind to be abandoned by cultivation, and the universal [defilements] of the form realm likewise underlie that very same [mind].
In a consciousness that has as its object the object of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhere?
Furthermore, that fivefold consciousness which has the faculty of suffering as its object, of what consciousness is it the object?
It is the object of that very same fivefold [consciousness] through the principle of mutual objectification.

Furthermore, it becomes the object of the desire-sphere [defilements] that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*) and which have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object;
and it becomes the object of the form-sphere [defilements] associated with the pervasive [factors] (*sarvatraga*).

For by means of those [form-sphere defilements], the wholesome [state] of the form-sphere to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), which has the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) as its object, is taken as an object.

It also takes as its object that which belongs to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara), specifically that which is comprised by the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka) and possesses the aspects of coarseness and so forth, having the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) as its objective support.
This constitutes the eightfold consciousness that has as its objective support that which itself has the faculty of suffering as its objective support.
Among these, there are four categories belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara).
Those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, the origin, and the path, and by cultivation;
and the three categories belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara),
which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin, and by cultivation.
It should be understood that one [defilement] belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*),

as well as the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). Regarding the question of how many underlying tendencies adhere to the consciousness that has the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object, this must be investigated.
Furthermore, that consciousness which has the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object is of eleven types:
five types belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Thus, in brief, this constitutes the object of thirteen types of consciousness.
This is because it has the fivefold conditioned objects of the desire realm as its objective support, since those are conditioned.
The same applies to that of the form realm.
However, for that of the formless realm, there are two types: those to be abandoned by the vision of the path and those to be abandoned by cultivation.
And [the consciousness] of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
This is the thirteenfold consciousness that has the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object.
Therein, according to possibility, the five classes belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) have conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their objects.
There are two categories belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
It should be understood that the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) adhere [to them].
Regarding the consciousness that has the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object, how many latent dispositions adhere?

Furthermore, that thirteenfold consciousness which has the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object— of what consciousness is it the object? It is the object of that same thirteenfold consciousness,
and additionally of the two types belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin.
This is the fifteenfold consciousness that has the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object.
In this regard, having added the two [types of consciousness] belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin,
there are those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) which have conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their objects.

The four classes of [defilements] belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara), with the exception of those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodhadarśanaheya), are to be understood as "the latent tendencies (anuśaya) adhere" (anuśerate). By this method, other cases are also to be understood.

(V.32) "Defiled [dharmas] are accompanied by latent dispositions in two ways" means that defiled [dharmas] are accompanied by latent dispositions both through those latent dispositions that are currently active and through those that are not currently active.
Because it is accompanied by that [defilement] and because it exists perpetually.
An undefiled mind can only be understood as "possessing latent tendencies" (*sānuśaya*) in relation to those very latent tendencies,
for it will be stated as follows:
The affliction is to be abandoned because its nature consists of its objective support.
(V.33) Since it is possible for any [affliction] to arise immediately after any other, there is no universal rule of sequence regarding their arising.

"Having set aside the aggregates as suffering" means that for one who clings to a self by thinking "this is not suffering," the view of grasping at a self in feeling and so forth is the antidote to the view that form is the self.
(V.34) "It is not abandoned and not fully understood":
it is not abandoned because its possession has not been severed;
it is not fully understood because its antidote has not arisen.

"Conducive to the outburst of sensual desire" (*kāmarāga-paryavasthānīya*) means: they are called "outbursts" (*paryavasthāna*) because one is overwhelmed by them, just as one is with bathing powders (*snānīya*).
Thus, they are "conducive to the outburst" of sensual desire, meaning they are favorable to it.

Alternatively, the obsession that is sensual desire itself is "sensual-desire-obsession" (*kāmarāga-paryavasthāna*). That which is conducive to it is "conducive to sensual-desire-obsession" (*kāmarāga-paryavasthānīya*).
These, moreover, are the objects such as visible forms and so forth, which have come into range.
The meaning is that they come to assume the form of objects.
And "in that regard, improper mental attention" means that,
with respect to those objects that have appeared, there is a distorted immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Regarding the powers of cause, object, and application:
the power of the cause is that the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) has not been abandoned and is not fully understood for the arising of sensual desire.
The power of the object consists of those objects conducive to the outburst of sensual desire (*kāmarāgaparyavasthānīya*).
And in that regard, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) is the power of application.
In this way, another affliction also arises:
the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*) remains unabandoned and uncomprehended.
Phenomena conducive to the outburst of aversion come into range of appearance, and therein occurs improper mental attention; such is the principle.
(V.35–38) These very [phenomena] are the four attachments.
The bond of desire (*kāmayoga*), the bond of existence (*bhavayoga*), the bond of views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*), and the bond of ignorance (*avidyāyoga*).
[The phrase] "without delusion" is used because the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*) has been mentioned separately.
Together with the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth, which will be mentioned later, there are forty-one entities.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are thirty-one;
these consist of the twelve views (*dṛṣṭi*).
There are five [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering,
two to be abandoned by the vision of origin,
and likewise two to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Three are to be abandoned by the vision of the path;
four are doubts;
five are attachments.
In this way, there are [twenty] forms of hostility and [twenty-one] types of pride.
Thus, including the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), there are forty-one. These are indeed the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
The particle *eva* is for the purpose of excluding the *paryavasthānas* (outbursts). There are twenty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśayas*):
twelve views, four doubts, five attachments, and five prides.

But is it not the case that even there, in those two realms, there are two types of outbursts? [The answer is: In those two, namely the form and formless realms, there are torpor, restlessness, and pride; [these three] exist in all three realms.
Because of this statement:
"Why is that not included here?
[it refers to] those two types of *paryavasthāna*.
"Because of lack of independence.
How is there a lack of independence?
Because it is associated with passion (*rāga*) and so forth, like envy (*īrṣyā*) and the rest, and because it is not associated with ignorance (*avidyā*) alone.
For these two are associated with passion and the other [afflictions],
whereas envy, avarice, regret, anger, and concealment are not;
they are independent.
"Because of association with ignorance alone. "For both of them" means that those belonging to the realms of form and formlessness are also included.
"Directed inwardly" means that they do not have external objects as their primary focus.
And for the very same reason, attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*) was mentioned.
Because it is inward-looking, [the term "formless" (*ārūpya*)] was employed in order to turn away from the notion that it is liberation.
And by this [statement], "the outflow of existence" (*bhavāsrava*) and "the outflow of ignorance" (*avidyāsrava*) are established. Thus,
ignorance is excluded from the two previously mentioned outflows.
Therefore, it is established that even though it pertains to the three realms, it is called the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyāsrava*).
It consists of fifteen substances,
because ignorance in each of the three realms is of five types.
"Of all these" refers to the outflows of desire (*kāmāsrava*) and so forth, as well as to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
For it has been stated that ignorance is the cause of passion and so on.
Whatever miserable states there may be in this world or in the next, all are rooted in ignorance and arise from desire and greed.
"Likewise, the floods (ogha) and yokes (yoga)": the outflows (āsrava) themselves constitute both the floods and the yokes.
Only the views are established separately.
How so? It is explained as follows: the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*) is itself the flood of sensual desire (*kāmaugha*) and the yoke of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*).
Likewise, the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) is itself the flood of existence (*bhavaugha*) and the yoke of existence (*bhavayoga*).
The conjunction with the flood of ignorance (avidyā-ogha-yoga), however, is to be understood exactly as before.
Here, the conjunction with views (dṛṣṭi-yoga) is stated as the fourth;
therefore, he says, "except for views."
Regarding the phrase "it is said that they":
the word *kila* indicates the opinion of another (*paramata*).
However, the intended meaning is appropriate: namely, that the application of views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*) was taught separately for the sake of those to be trained (*vineyajanavaśāt*).
He asks: for what reason are the views (*dṛṣṭi*) not established separately among the outflows (*āsrava*)?
He replies: "Among the outflows, [they are not separate] because they are without companions," and so forth.
For views that lack companionship, there is no conformity to sitting (*āsya-anukūlatā*) nor conformity to remaining still (*avasthāna-anukūlatā*), because of their instability and their acuteness;
the meaning is that they do not conform to sitting.
Although the form *āsa* would have been expected, the form *āsya* occurs by virtue of the rule favored by Āpiśali.
This is what is meant:

because these views, when without companions, are not conducive to abiding, whereas when they have companions they become conducive to abiding; therefore, it is precisely as having companions that they are described among the outflows (*āsrava*).
The meaning is that they are stated by being combined.
To the question "For what purpose?", he says:

since the etymological definition of the *āsravas* (outflows) as "that which causes one to sit" (*āsayaṃti*) will be explained later, the intention is that there must be [a specific sense of] "sitting" (*āsana*) within the *āsravas*.
Thus, in this way, the flood of sensual desire (*kāmaugha*) consists of twenty-nine entities (*dravya*).
Because the twelve views (*dṛṣṭi*) have been removed, it does not consist of forty-one entities as the outflows (*āsrava*) do;
rather, it consists of twenty-nine entities.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Lust, hostility, and pride" refers to everything.
The flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) consists of twenty-eight entities.
The outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) has been stated to consist of fifty-two entities (*dravya*).
From that number, having removed the twenty-four views (*dṛṣṭi*), there remain twenty-eight entities.
Regarding the statement that "attachment (*rāga*) and pride (*māna*) are twenty," the attachments belonging to the two realms (*dvidhātuka*) constitute ten.
The "floods of pride" (*mānaugha*) are also ten, making twenty.
The "flood of views" (*dṛṣṭyaugha*) consists of thirty-six entities.
This is because there are three [types of] views in each of the three realms, and twelve [types of] views [in total].
The flood of ignorance consists of fifteen entities,
as before.
The yokes are like the floods.
The yoke of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*) consists of twenty-nine entities:
fifteen consisting of attachment, aversion, and pride; four consist of doubt; and ten consist of the secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).
The yoke of existence (*bhavayoga*) consists of twenty-eight entities.
There are twenty substances for the yokes of attachment and pride, eight for doubt, and thirty-six for the yoke of views.
There are fifteen substances for the yoke of ignorance;
it consists of the very same [factors] as previously described, together with ignorance.
Thus is the detailed explanation.
What are these "yogas" as they have been described? This is the subject under discussion; therefore, it is now being explained.
The bond of desire (*kāmayoga*) itself, together with ignorance (*avidyā*), is called the clinging to desire (*kāmopādāna*).
Ignorance is included within its respective categories of clinging to desire and clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*),
because of the twofold nature of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
The fourfold division is due to their separate treatment:

namely, clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmopādāna*), clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*), clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*), and clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*).
This is because rules and observances have been extracted from the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*).
From the thirty-six substances of the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*), having extracted the six instances of adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) according to the division of realms,
the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*) consists of thirty substances,

and the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*) consists of six substances— two each in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
"Because it is an adversary to the path":
since liberation is seen to be attained through the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and so forth, the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*) constitutes an adversary to the path.
"And because it deceives both sides," and so on, is the detailed explanation.
The meaning is: "because of deceiving both the householders and those who have gone forth.

Regarding the phrase "by means of fasting and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes such practices as throwing oneself into water or fire, observing silence, and adopting the vows of a hero.
Fasting and so forth are included within [the category of] ascetic vows and observances (*śīlavratasaṃgṛhīta*), as is the avoidance of desired objects.
Regarding "by means of avoiding desired objects":
this refers to the pursuit of purification through such acts as the renunciation of fine flavors, sleeping on the ground, wearing dirt and mud, wandering naked, and plucking out one's hair.
"But ignorance is not the grasper; rather, it is mixed.
This means that ignorance alone does not take up existence (*bhava*).
Why? He says:
"Because it is dull due to having non-apprehension as its characteristic.
The intention is that when mixed, however, it takes up [the aggregates] by virtue of contact with other afflictions. "It is said that these... refers to this.
The word "kila" indicates the opinion of another; by it, one's own position is stated.
However, it was said by the Blessed One in the Sūtra, as explained in detail.
Thus it continues up to the "yoke of views" (*dṛṣṭiyoga*).
How so?
What is the yoke of views?
In detail, up to: whatever attachment to views (*dṛṣṭirāga*), desire for views (*dṛṣṭicchanda*), and affection for views (*dṛṣṭisneha*) he has, as before.
And in other sūtras, desire-attachment (*chandarāga*) is stated to be grasping (*upādāna*).
How so?
What is grasping? It is that which is here desire and lust;
this is the opinion of the Master.
What is meant by this is that here *yoga* is precisely passion (*rāga*),
or else grasping (*upādāna*);
it is not the other afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore it is said: "that which is desire and attachment toward sense-pleasures and so forth" (V.39).
"Subtle," and so forth, in detail.
They are called *anuśayas* because they lie down (*śerate*) as subtle atoms (*aṇavaḥ*);
this is established through etymological derivation (*nairukta*).
(Abhidh-k-vy 488)
"Because its activity is subtle" means because its functioning is subtle.
But how is its activity subtle?
Because they are formless, they are difficult to discern.
By way of their objective support (*ālambana*), they are like a foe seeking a vulnerability or like the venom of a gaze;
by way of association (*saṃprayoga*), they are like the heat of molten iron balls in water or like the venom of touch.
Just as two nurses lie down beside the infant,
so too these [defilements], increasing their own continuum through their objects or through associated states, augment it by means of acquisitions (*prāpti*) and thus remain bound to it.

Others say that they are called *anuśaya* because of their successive recurrence, like a quartan fever or the poison of a rat; and because they persistently adhere [to the person] due to their repeated manifestation, even when one is not applying oneself [to counter them] and even when one is exerting effort to restrain or prevent them. Thus, they are called *anuśayas*.
"They cause one to dwell in saṃsāra" is the etymological derivation (*nairukta*) of *āsrava*;
or else, it has the sense of "dwelling."
"They flow from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell.
By means of the six sense-bases—which are like wounds, namely the sense-bases beginning with the eye—they flow and leak;
they go from the peak of existence as far as the Avīci hell.

Because even for one who is free from passion regarding the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there is the manifestation of *āvicika* afflictions, or because it is possible for one in whom those [afflictions] have arisen to be reborn there.
What are they that flow? They are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
They are called *āsravas* because they flow (*āsravanti*); the suffix *-ac* is applied here.
They are called *oghās* because they carry away (*haranti*).
They are called *yogās* because they bind (*śleṣayanti*).
"They are called 'appropriations' (upādāna) because they grasp," this is the demonstration of the meaning.
This has been stated by the Vaibhāṣikas:
"This form [of the aggregates] is like floods (ogha)."

They carry away and take one to another state of existence or another object of experience; thus they are called *oghāḥ* (floods). They join together and bind one to another state of existence or another object of experience; thus they are called *yogāḥ* (yokes).
They appropriate and seize the continuum of consciousness for rebirth or within the [objects] such as sensual pleasures; thus they are called *upādānāni* (graspings).
"But in this way it would be better," says the Teacher; "in this way, however, it would be more correct.
He asks: "In what way? and replies:
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are called "outflows" (*āsrava*) because by means of them the continuum—the continuum of consciousness—flows or goes toward sense objects;
this is an analysis based on the instrument (*karaṇasādhana*).
With great effort, the mental continuum is led against the current by wholesome dharmas and is turned away from sense objects.
"By the subsiding of those very formations" means by the cessation of those very efforts.
They are called "floods" because of their excessive momentum.
It demonstrates the similarity to a flood (*ogha*),
considering that they are called "floods" because they are like a flood;
[it says] "because they conform to that."
Because they conform to passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions].
For the *yogas* do not manifest intensely.
This shows the distinction between the floods (*ogha*) and the *yogas*.
For those which do not manifest excessively are "yokes" (yoga);
whereas those which manifest excessively are indeed [fetters].
"These are the floods. And how are they the "yokes"? He says:
because of the joining with various sufferings; that is to say, because of the joining with various sufferings such as birth and so forth.
Or, they are called "yogas" because they are constantly associated [with the mind], or because they are constantly joined within the continuum (saṃtati). Therefore, they are called yogas.
"Because of the grasping for sense-pleasures and so forth.
Those by which sense-pleasures and the rest are grasped are the graspings for sense-pleasures and so forth, consisting of desire and attachment.
(Abhidh-k-vy 489) (V.40ab) Those same underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are further said to be divided into five types by way of the classification of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
Those same underlying tendencies are also said to be fourfold by way of the classification into outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth.

Furthermore, they are taught in the Sūtras and the Abhidharma as being fivefold when divided according to the categories of fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
But is it not the case that outbursts such as shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and so forth are taught as distinct from the latent dispositions?
How then can this be said?
"The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) themselves are the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
True, they exist as distinct from them;
however, they are also accepted as non-distinct.
For it will be stated as follows:

"Affliction (*kleśa*) is also an obsession (*paryavasthāna*)," because of the statement in the Sūtra: "One experiences suffering conditioned by the obsession of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-paryavasthāna*)."
(V.40cd–42) In this same way, other [fetters] should also be applied according to their possibility.
The fetters of repugnance (*pratigha*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*) belong to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
The fetters of pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*parāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) belong to all three realms (*traidhātuka*).
The fetter of views consists of three views:
the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The fetter of clinging consists of two views.
[The fetters of] views and the adherence to rules and observances.
For this very reason it is said:
since three views constitute the fetter of views, and two views constitute the fetter of adherence.
For this very reason it is said:
"It may be that [they exist] among those associated with views," and so forth, as the detailed question;
namely, "among those associated with views."
Regarding the sensations and other factors associated with the view of misapprehension (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*):
one is bound by the fetter of attachment (*anunayasaṃyojana*), that is, by passion (*rāga*);
but not by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*), characterized by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
And it is not the case that the latent tendency of views does not underlie there;
nor is it the case that the latent tendency of views does not underlie those factors associated with views.
What then?
It would underlie.
A double negation implies the original state.
He said "it might be," providing a detailed answer to the question.
The qualification "the knowledge of origin has arisen" is for the purpose of demonstrating the abandonment of the universal fetter of views (*sarvatraga-dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).

[The phrase] "the knowledge of cessation has not arisen" is for the purpose of showing the existence of its associated states due to the non-abandonment of the two types of views of grasping (*parāmarśa-dṛṣṭi*).
"Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path," and so forth,
refers to sensation and the other [aggregates].
For one is bound to them by the fetter of attachment (anunaya-saṃyojana), which is to be abandoned either by the vision of cessation or by the vision of the path.
By what kind of object? By that very object,

because attachment arises by taking as its object those dharmas such as feeling which are associated with the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and which are to be abandoned by the path of seeing cessation (*nirodhadarśanamārga*).
Therefore, by virtue of the object, one is bound by that [view];
yet one is not bound by the fetter of views.
Why? He says:
Because that which is universal—having the nature of being abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin—is already abandoned upon the arising of the knowledge of origin;
and because there is no non-universal fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) that has that [origin] as its object or is associated with it.
For although there exists a non-universal fetter of views, which has the nature of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), that is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path.
However, it does not have as its object the factors such as feeling associated with the view of adherence (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*).
This is because it has the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.
Therefore, it is not bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) by way of its object.
Nor is it associated with those [factors] such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth,
because it constitutes a separate category (*pṛthakkalāpa*).
Therefore, even by way of association (*saṃprayoga*), it is not conjoined with them.
And the latent tendency of views (dṛṣṭyanuśaya) adheres to them.
To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says:
"Those very two [types of] grasping-views (parāmarśadṛṣṭi), by way of association (saṃprayoga)."
Adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) or adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) underlie those factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) by way of association (*saṃprayoga*),
because they arise from their own group [of associated factors].
However, the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) does not underlie them there.

Because he stated that for those two [fetters] there is the "fetter of views" (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), when the latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*) are mentioned, it does not follow that all five views are included. However, when the "fetter of views" is mentioned, it should be understood that only the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) are included,
and not the two types of clinging views (*parāmarśa-dṛṣṭi*).
"Immediately after the fetter of views" refers to the two types of grasping views (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*).
The ellipsis of the sentence is: "there are eighteen substances, [namely] three views.
The meaning of the sentence is that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) consist of eighteen numerable substances.
"Exactly eighteen substances" is the subject under discussion.
There are two views that constitute grasping.
How so?
In the desire realm, there are two: the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes.
And these two are held to be abandonable only by the vision of suffering.
False view is of four types:
that which is abandonable by the vision of suffering, up to that which is abandonable by the vision of the path.
Thus, there are six in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Just as there are six in the desire realm, so too in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), making eighteen in total.
These eighteen are precisely the two views of grasping (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*).
How so?

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is of four types, ranging from that to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) up to that to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*). The adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is also to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
And that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path; thus there are two types.
In this way, there are six [afflictions] in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Just as in the desire realm, so it is in the form realm (rūpadhātu) and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Thus, there are exactly eighteen substances;
the remaining views are not so.
This is because of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper.
The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is the grasped;
the fetter of adherence (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) is the grasper.
"From which" means: [from these].
For this reason—
namely, because they are characterized by being exclusively unwholesome and independent—
it has been stated regarding these [factors].
Thus,
among these outbursts such as shamelessness and so forth, envy and avarice are extracted separately.
It has been stated:
"For there is no other *paryavasthāna* (envelopment) of such a kind.
Lack of shame (*anāhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) are also exclusively unwholesome (*ekāntākuśala*).
But it is not independent, because it is associated with afflictions such as attachment (*rāga*).
Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is also independent, because it is associated with ignorance (*avidyā*) alone;
however, it is not exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).
For that [state] is indeed wholesome.
Furthermore, torpor, restlessness, and lethargy are not independent, because they are associated with passion and other [afflictions];
however, they are not exclusively unwholesome.
For those [factors] are also wholesome and indeterminate.
"Where both of these exist" means where there is both absolute unwholesomeness and independence.
The connection is that there is no other *paryavasthāna* (outburst of defilement) of this same kind.
As for the phrase "for whom there are ten":
this refers to the Vaibhāṣika for whom there are ten *paryavasthānas*.
Since both types of anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*) are exclusively unwholesome and independent,
this [previous] refutation does not hold.
What, then, is the correct refutation of that?
On this point, the Master Saṃghabhadra says:
"Because envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) manifest repeatedly, they are established as separate fetters (*saṃyojana*).

For this very reason, even though there are thirty-six fetters in total, it is said: 'O Kauśika, among those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), gods and humans are characterized by the fetters of envy and avarice.'"
For these two afflictions are, preeminently, a bond to a happy rebirth.
Alternatively,
it is because they are the causes for having little power and little wealth, and because they indicate everything [about one's future].
And because they are afflictions belonging to both sides,
stinginess and envy are treated separately.
Thus, even though one has been reborn in a happy realm, one undergoes intense humiliation.
In this context, envy and avarice are the causes;
for one who is called "of little power" and has few enjoyments is considered bound by both of these.
Thus,
the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are of two kinds: those accompanied by distress and those accompanied by joy.
All these are indicated by these two.
The side of the householder is excessively afflicted by these two bases of enjoyment, and the side of the renunciant is likewise afflicted by these two bases of the Dharma.
Or else, the factions of the gods and asuras suffer excessively for the sake of internal division.
For this very reason, it was said by the Blessed One: "Kauśika, gods and humans are fettered by envy and avarice."
Therefore, among the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), these two alone are fetters (*saṃyojana*). (V.43–44) "The lower realm" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In relation to the totality of the three realms, the desire realm is the lower or inferior realm because it is exclusively non-concentrated (*asamāhita*).
Because unwholesome dharmas, rebirths in the miserable states, suffering, and mental distress exist there,
and because of the density of the afflictions,
one cannot transcend the realm of desire by means of these two.
Thus it is said:
because, as long as that [defilement] is not abandoned, one does not transcend the desire realm;
this is due to their similarity to gatekeepers and attendants.
Sensual desire and ill will are similar to gatekeepers;
for like gatekeepers, they do not permit exit from the prison-house of the bonds of the desire realm.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth share the same nature as attendants.
For just as a man, even though he has escaped from prison when the gatekeeper is negligent, is turned back by the gatekeeper’s attendants; so too here [is it] by these [afflictions].
By three [fetters].
Regarding "the inferiority of beings":

one does not transcend the inferiority of beings characterized by the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) due to the fetters of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Due to the two— sensual desire and ill will—
one does not transcend, one does not go beyond, the inferiority of the realms, which has the nature of the desire realm.
For ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are inferior to the noble ones (*ārya*);
and among the realms (*dhātu*), the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is the lowest.
Therefore, other practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*) maintain that these [fetters] are called "factors conducive to the lower" (*avarabhāgīya*).

"Having exhausted [them] through the abandonment of the three fetters" means: through the abandonment, without remainder, of the fetters of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). Thus, the six afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned.
The five views and doubt;
however, attachment and the other [afflictions] are not mentioned because they remain to be discussed later.
This refers to "having set aside three views."
Regarding the views of grasping at extremes, false view, and the esteeming of views:
he says there are only three;
that is, he says there are only the three consisting of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Who said this?
The Blessed One.
For it is recited thus in the Sūtra.
"To what extent, venerable sir, does one become a stream-enterer?
It is, Mahānāman, when a noble disciple understands, as it truly is, that 'this is the noble truth of suffering' and 'this is the origin of suffering.'"
He understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
And his three fetters are abandoned and fully understood.
Namely: the view of a self-identity, the clinging to rules and observances, and doubt.

Through the abandonment of these three fetters, he becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, destined for full enlightenment, with seven births at most; having transmigrated and wandered among gods and humans seven times at most, he will make an end of suffering.
All of this ought to be stated; that is, it would be so. It is said, moreover, that the afflictions are of three kinds.
Those to be abandoned by seeing are the subject under discussion here.

The views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are of one type, because they are to be abandoned by the mere vision of suffering. The misapprehension of precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is of two types.
There are four types: doubt, false view, and the two kinds of adherence.
Among these, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the gateway for those of one type;
therefore, by the mention of the view of a self-identity, the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is also included.
Doubt is the gateway to the four types [of views];
therefore, by mentioning it, there is the inclusion of wrong view and the esteeming of views.
However, the esteeming of precepts and observances is included directly.
As for those [afflictions] such as attachment that are to be abandoned by insight (*darśanaheya*),
it can be said that they too are indeed included because they have that [self-view] as their object;
thus, the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is set in motion by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Because it grasps at the self as being either eternal or subject to annihilation,
the adherence to views is set in motion by the adherence to rules and observances;
it is through this that one believes purity is attained.
Because it is grasped prior to that [view of self].
False view is said to be "initiated by doubt" because,
for one who is in a state of uncertainty, false conviction arises from hearing and reflecting on what is false.

Therefore, because of the mention of the "root," the inclusion of that which arises from the root is established; thus, the views such as the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and so forth should also be understood as having the form already described.
Others, however, say—this refers to the Master himself—how there is a "deviation from the path" (*mārgavibhrama*), to which he replies:
"Because of resorting to another path" (V.45).
By the mention of the "lower-tier fetters" (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), it is implied that there are also [fetters] belonging to other tiers;
thus, this is stated.
"The five higher fetters" (pañcadhaivordhvabhāgīya) is a [category of] fetters (saṃyojana).
(V.46) "Furthermore, they are taught as fivefold through the distinctions of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth.
With this connection, immediately after the exposition of the fetters, there follows the occasion for the exposition of the bonds (*bandhana*), which is another synonym [for them].
"All attachment is a bond.
"All" refers to it in terms of its types and in terms of its realms.
All hatred [is likewise].
What is "all"?
Ignorance (moha) is "all" in terms of its modes; it is "all" in terms of its modes and its realms (dhātu).
It is "all" by way of both its objects (ālambana) and its associations (saṃprayoga).
In pleasant feeling belonging to one's own or another's continuum, attachment underlies it as appropriate.
In painful feeling, hatred [underlies it] precisely through both the object and association.
In neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, delusion [underlies it] precisely through those two.
But surely, attachment and aversion also adhere as latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] according to their respective natures;
why then is it said that only delusion does so? To this he replies:
"Attachment and aversion do not [adhere] in that way."
Attachment and aversion also underlie [the mind],
but not to the same extent as delusion.
For delusion, due to its dullness, lies dormant all the more because it is concordant with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, which is itself dull.
Or, the restriction is due to having one's own continuum as the object.
Because of the capacity for experiencing pleasure and so forth within one's own continuum, the restriction is thus established.
For when there is a pleasant sensation in one's own continuum, attachment arises; when it is painful, aversion; and when it is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, delusion—by way of association.
Others, however, explain it thus:
"Lust and hatred are not like that.
Just as lust underlies a pleasant feeling, hatred does not likewise underlie it.
Furthermore, does hatred also underlie pleasure?
It underlies the pleasure of an enemy by way of its object (*ālambana*).
And just as hatred underlies suffering, so too does it not [underlie] passion (*rāga*).
But does attachment also underlie suffering?
It underlies the suffering of an enemy by way of being its object;
or rather, there is a restriction based on it being an object within one's own continuum.
Alternatively, attachment underlies one's own internal happiness either by way of its object or by way of association,
but not in the happiness of an enemy belonging to another's continuum.
Likewise, aversion underlies one's own internal suffering either by way of its object or by way of association.
It does not [arise] toward the suffering of an enemy belonging to another continuum.
Thus, the restriction is made from the perspective of having one's own continuum as the object.
Attachment underlies pleasant feeling.
"Through the object and association, hatred arises toward that which is painful" (V.46).
"Because it defiles the mind" means because it causes the mind to become afflicted.
"Those other mental factors as well" means those other than the afflictions.
"They are indeed secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
This means they have the nature of being proximate to the primary afflictions (*kleśa*),
or that the primary afflictions exist in proximity to them.

They are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) because they follow the activity of the primary afflictions and because their characteristics are incomplete compared to those of the primary afflictions.
These secondary afflictions are exclusively mental factors (*caitasika*); they are not dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*).
This refers to those enumerated in the *Kṣudravastuka*.
The intention is that those [factors] recited in the *Kṣudravastuka* section of the teaching are not limited to volition (*cetanā*) and so forth alone.

For example: discontent (*aratir*), yawning (*vijṛmbhikā*), mental sluggishness (*cetaso līnatvam*), drowsiness (*tandrī*), inequality in eating (*bhakte ’samata*), perception of diversity (*nānātvasaṃjñā*), lack of attention (*amanasikāraḥ*), bodily rigidity (*kāyadauṣṭhulyam*), contentiousness (*śṛṅgī*), stubbornness (*bhittirīkā*), and lack of gentleness (*anārjavatā*).

Lack of pliancy, non-conformity with one's own nature, discursive thought of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*), discursive thought of ill-will (*vyāpāda-vitarka*), discursive thought of harmfulness (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*), discursive thought concerning relatives (*jñāti-vitarka*), discursive thought concerning one’s native land (*janapada-vitarka*), discursive thought concerning immortality (*amara-vitarka*), discursive thought associated with contempt (*avamanyanā-pratisaṃyukta-vitarka*), discursive thought associated with family prestige (*kulodayatā-pratisaṃyukta-vitarka*), sorrow (*śoka*), suffering (*duḥkha*), mental distress (*daurmanasya*), and despair (*upāyāsa*). [Drowsiness (*tandrī*) means dullness.]

(V.47–49ab) Regarding that, "lack of shame" (*ahrīkya*) and "lack of dread" (*anapatrāpya*) have been explained: "lack of shame" (*ahrī*) is a lack of respect toward what is blameworthy; "lack of dread" (*atrapā*) is the failure to see fear [in wrongdoing].
"Dharma and material goods," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Stinginess (*mātsarya*) is the mind’s grasping that acts as an obstacle to the giving of the Dharma, material goods, or skillful means.
*Matsara* is the mental aspect [of thinking], "Let it not depart from me";
*mātsarya* is simply the state of being *matsara*.
The state of one who is stingy is stinginess (*mātsarya*).
As for remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and lethargy (*styāna*), they have already been explained.
The state of having done what is bad is remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
In this context, however, the mental state (*dharma*) that has that as its object is remorse (*kaukṛtya*); and lethargy (*styāna*) is the unserviceability of body and mind.
If it were merely stated that "torpor (*middha*) is the contraction of the mind," it would over-extend to include meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); therefore, it is specified [as follows].
"Unable to sustain the body" refers to that very same afflicted entanglement (*paryavasthāna*).
And "regret" (*kaukṛtya*) is also [an entanglement].
That which is afflicted torpor is an outburst;
however, that which is wholesome or neutral is not an outburst.
For torpor is held to be of three kinds,
as is remorse;
that which is afflicted [is associated with the afflictions].
That is a state of obsession;
it is not wholesome.
For that is held to be both wholesome and unwholesome.
Malice (*vyāpāda*) is defined as hostility toward sentient beings or non-sentient things that is devoid of the intent to harm (*vihiṃsā*).
Malice is a specific form of hostility directed toward sentient beings.
It is malice when one proceeds with the thought-form: "May these beings be killed, or bound, or destroyed, or meet with calamity through injustice."
Violence (*vihiṃsā*) consists of engaging in activities such as attracting, terrifying, or threatening sentient beings.
Anger (*krodha*) is malice toward sentient or non-sentient objects other than those two;
for example, the mental provocation of a monk who desires to train.
And there is provocation regarding thorns and the like.
This refers, respectively, to those who are known and those who are unknown.
For persons who are concealing their faults and are known by kings and others, concealment (*mrakṣa*) is the outflow of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

"May gain and honor not come to me"—this is the outflow of ignorance regarding the unknown. Not having faith in the fact that one's own actions are one's own property (*karmasvakatā*), one conceals that fault.
One does not confess it before another for the sake of purification. Thus, some say that concealment (*mrakṣa*) is the outflow of both [ignorance and greed].
How is lack of moral dread (*anapatrāpya*) the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of ignorance? Because *atrapā* is the failure to see danger in what is blameworthy.
"Remorse born of doubt" refers to that which is afflicted.
That very [point] is stated because of the context concerning the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*):
"the stains of the afflictions" (*kleśamala*). (V.49cd, 50)
Just as impurities arise from the body, so too do these [defilements] such as *māyā* arise from the afflictions (*kleśa*), like impurities.
It casts forth and impels.
*Mada* has been explained previously.
"Intoxication (*mada*) is the complete exhaustion of the mind of one who is attached to his own qualities.
(Abhidh-k-vy 495)
(V.51) "And that which is associated with what is to be abandoned by seeing [a particular truth]" means: the vision of a particular truth is "seeing of that" (*yaddarśana*).
That which is to be abandoned by such seeing is "to be abandoned by seeing of that" (*yaddarśanaheya*).
That which is associated with it is what is associated with what is to be abandoned by seeing;
that is to be abandoned by seeing that [truth]. It is to be abandoned by the vision of that truth.
What [is this]? It is shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and so forth.
Other than those, they are to be abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
"Other than those" means that envy and the other [defilements] other than shamelessness and so forth are abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
They are not to be abandoned by insight (*darśanaheya*).
Furthermore, these are independent;
the meaning is that they are not dependent on attachment (*rāga*) and the like.
(V.52) "Styāna, auddhatya, and middha are unwholesome or neutral. Because the context concerns the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments), middha is not said to be wholesome;
beyond that, they are neutral.
Thus.
"According to possibility" means as many as are possible beyond the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

Furthermore, these [factors] such as deceit (*māyā*) and guile (*śāṭhya*) consist in the false display of a self. By means of this false display of a self, Mahābrahmā proceeded to deceive the Venerable Aśvajit.
When asked, "O Brahmin, where do these great elements cease without remainder? he, not knowing the answer, made an evasive remark.
He began to deceive him with the illusion that "I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Lord, the Maker, the Fashioner, the Creator, the Originator, the Father of all beings.
Then that Great Brahmā took the Venerable Aśvajit by the hand, led him aside, and having stood apart, spoke as follows.

"Thinking that one should question me while the Tathāgata is present—this is seen as his deceit (*śāṭhya*). For, out of shame before his own assembly, he acted in such a way while concealing his own lack of knowledge.
Thus it is called "deceit," for it is said:
"Remorse, torpor, and unwholesome states do not exist in the first dhyāna; therefore [they are excluded].
This was stated here as well by way of incidental discussion.
"Others are indeterminate because of that" refers to the aforementioned sequence.
"Excluding five" refers to excluding deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), torpor (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and pride (*mada*).
(V.53) By those [terms], all [factors] belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmika*) are indicated— namely, pride (*māna*), torpor (*middha*),
and the independent secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Envy, avarice, and so forth— those which are mentioned among the universal mental factors of affliction (*kleśamahābhūmika*) are precisely lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), and negligence (*pramāda*). Others are not included here, because lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) have already been taken up previously in this very context.
Because delusion (*moha*) is included by the mention of "afflictions" (*kleśa*).
(V.54,55) [It is associated] with the two [feelings] that are pleasant (*sukha*).
(Abhidh-k-vy 496)
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is: by means of the two faculties whose intrinsic natures are pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*).
This is because they function in the form of joy and dejection (*dainya*), respectively.
Attachment exists in the form of joy, and aversion exists in the form of dejection; this is according to their respective order.
Furthermore, because they belong to the level of the six consciousnesses:
since attachment belongs to the level of the five sensory consciousnesses, it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Hatred is associated with the faculty of suffering;
however, because it belongs to the level of mental consciousness, attachment is associated with the faculty of mental pleasure,
and hatred is associated with the faculty of mental pain.
"Of those who perform meritorious deeds and those who perform non-meritorious deeds, respectively.
For those who perform meritorious deeds, wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*),
because they perceive the futility of performing meritorious actions.
For those who commit evil deeds, wrong view is associated with mental pleasure (*saumanasya*),
because they perceive that the evil they have committed has been fruitless.
These are the four views.

[The five views are] the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of ethical discipline and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
How can the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) be associated with mental pleasure (*saumanasya*)? Because one is intensely attached to it.
"Equanimity remains stable" because it is weak during the state of destruction.
Regarding "as many faculties as there are in whichever stage":
these are mental pleasure (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); [specifically] equanimity and mental pleasure arise [in the respective stages].
