It should be understood that in the meditative attainments (*dhyānopapatti*), there is pleasure (*sukha*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and [mental] clarity (*vitarka*);
this applies even to the higher stages (*ūrdhvabhūmi*).
Those belonging to the four groups of consciousness exist only in the first dhyāna;
they belong to the levels of visual, auditory, tactile, and mental consciousness.
For in the first dhyāna, there exists the faculty of pleasure associated with three groups of consciousness.
The faculty of mental pleasure belongs to the class of mental consciousness (*manovijñānakāyika*).
The faculty of equanimity belongs to the four classes of sensory consciousness (*cāturvijñānakāyika*).
Above that, it belongs exclusively to the level of the mind (*manobhūmika*).
In the second dhyāna, there are the faculties of mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
In the third, there are the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity.
In the fourth dhyāna and in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), there is only the faculty of equanimity.
In that state, all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are associated with their respective faculties of feeling (*vedanendriya*).
Because the mental continuum is moistened by tranquility (*śamatha*), there is no formal distinction between the modes of elation or dejection.
Since these [defilements] such as regret (*kaukṛtya*) and so forth function through a mode of dejection, they are not associated with mental pleasure (*saumanasya*).

Because it belongs to the mental level (*manobhūmika*), it is not associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). "By way of being a consequence of greed" means by way of having greed as its cause.
The meaning is "arisen from greed.
Regarding "intoxication [arises] from the two [types of] pleasure":
With pleasure (*sukha*) and mental ease (*saumanasya*). In the third dhyāna, it is with pleasure, because pride (*mada*) is mental in nature.
"Just as in the case of ignorance":
just as there is no prohibition of association between ignorance and any affliction (*kleśa*) or secondary affliction (*upakleśa*),
so it is also with equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Because shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) belong to the great ground of unwholesome states (*akuśalamahābhūmika*); for it is stated that "in the unwholesome [states], there are shamelessness and lack of dread."

And because lethargy and restlessness belong to the great ground of afflictions (*kleśamahābhūmika*), unwholesome and afflicted states of the six groups of consciousness can arise; therefore, their association with all five faculties is possible.
(Abhidh-k-vy 497)
(V.58) Are the sloth, restlessness, and doubt belonging to the three realms included?
Since these belong to the three realms, they are singled out and asked about.
"This alone," and so forth: "O monks, that which is the heap of the unwholesome is namely the five hindrances"—thus those who speak correctly would say.
For what reason?
Because it is stated in detail that these five hindrances (*nivaraṇa*) constitute "this entire, complete mass of unwholesomeness," due to their being exclusively unwholesome;
[it is said] that the hindrances exist in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), and not elsewhere.
The commentary (vṛtti) and the sūtra words form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).

"Hindrances" (*nivaraṇa*) means obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), attainment (*samāpatti*), and so forth. [They are so called] because they share a single adversary, a single nutriment, and a single function.
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is: "Because they have the same function of nourishing the same adversary.
For indeed, even without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), there can be an expression that emphasizes the state (*bhāva*).
Alternatively, "the function of nourishing a single adverse factor" means the function of nourishing one specific adverse factor.
Regarding the word "thence":
the adverse factor is the counteragent.
In this context, for the sake of conforming to the structure of the verse, "counter-position" (*pratipakṣa*) is intended to mean "adverse position" (*vipakṣa*).
This is because an adverse position is defined as a side that is opposed to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
However, in the *Abhidharma*, the "dark side" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is the adverse position, and the "white side" (*śuklapakṣa*) is that which is opposed to it.

It is well known that the "white fortnight" (śuklapakṣa) refers to the opposing side. Regarding "improperity in eating": it is the obstruction of the body caused by eating an excessive amount of food.
"Non-nutriments" is the antidote. [It is the antidote] to the aggregate of wisdom by means of sloth and torpor.
What [is it]?
"Affliction" (vighāta) is the subject under discussion.
"But in this conceptualization," and so forth,
refers to the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha), the aggregate of concentration (samādhiskandha), and the aggregate of wisdom (prajñāskandha).
In the same sequence in which the aggregates (skandhas) are established,
in that very same sequence their opposites, the hindrances (nivaraṇas), are recited: namely,
sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill-will (vyāpāda), restlessness and remorse (auddhatya-kaukṛtya), sloth and torpor (styāna-middha), and doubt (vicikitsā).
It would follow that the hindrance of restlessness-and-remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*) should have been mentioned first,
because the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*) was stated before the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*).
Since this is not the case, the intention [of the author] is that this is not the reason.
What, then, is the reason for this? He says:
"Therefore, in their respective order, the two aggregates of concentration and wisdom are impaired by these two hindrances, namely, sloth-torpor and restlessness-remorse.
How so? He says:

For one engaged in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is fear of sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha*) because they are of a similar nature; likewise, for one engaged in the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), there is fear of restlessness and regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*).
However, other former masters (*pūrvācārya*) explain it otherwise.
"Of one who has gone on his rounds" means of one who is wandering for the sake of alms. "From grasping at signs" means from the apprehension of it as a female form or as the word "female."
Whether one has gone to a monastery, is in seclusion, or is standing, sitting, or walking, those two—
preceded by the grasping of signs regarding pleasant and unpleasant objects, or preceded by pleasant and unpleasant objects themselves—
act as obstacles to calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) respectively.
Lethargy and torpor create an obstacle to *śamatha* because they arise in close proximity to it. Excitement, regret, and doubt create obstacles to *vipaśyanā*.
Avalokita-vrata-sādhana-vidhiḥ The compound *auddhatyakaukṛtya* is first formed as a dvandva expressing a singular collective sense; this, in turn, is further compounded with *vicikitsā*.
Thus, it becomes *auddhatyakaukṛtyavicikitse*, meaning "restlessness-and-regret and doubt.
Furthermore, doubt creates an obstacle even for one who has emerged from meditative absorption at the time of reflecting upon the Dharma.
Others, however, read the text as follows: "Sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
And they explain it in this way.
Stiffness and torpor create an obstacle to calm abiding (śamatha); restlessness and regret create an obstacle to insight (vipaśyanā);
and doubt creates an obstacle for one who has emerged [from meditative absorption] at the time of reflecting on the Dharma.
(V.59) “Of those that are universal in a different realm,” and so forth.

This refers to the universal [afflictions] in a different realm— namely, wrong view and the others— which are divided into two types by virtue of being abandonable through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin.
When an object is fully understood by means of the category of subsequent knowledge of suffering and its origin— that is, by the path having the form and formless realms as its objects—
at that time those [defilements] are not abandoned,
because they have already been abandoned previously by the dharma-knowledge of suffering and the dharma-knowledge of origin, as the case may be.
For those [afflictions] are to be abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) because they belong to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).

Furthermore, when the objects of the views of adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and so forth— which are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgadarśanaprahātavya*) and which have contaminated things as their objects— are themselves abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, then that object, consisting of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth, which has the nature of the truths of suffering and origin, is thoroughly known according to its respective realm (*dhātu*) through the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) or the category of the knowledge of phenomena regarding the truths of suffering and origin.
At that time, they are not abandoned,
because they are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path.
Furthermore, their object is not fully understood in that manner, because it has already been known previously.

The intention [of the objection] is: "How is their abandonment [achieved]? It is not logical that their abandonment results from the full comprehension (*parijñāna*) of the object (*ālambana*). In this regard, through the full comprehension of the object, those [defilements] belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) which have their own realm as their object, as well as those belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and its origin (*samudaya*), are abandoned.

Among these, for one who perceives the object of those [defilements] having a different realm as their object through full comprehension, there is abandonment simultaneously by means of the two receptivities (*kṣānti*) to the subsequent knowledge of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudayānvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), because they both have two realms as their object.

The qualification "having their own level as their object" is for the purpose of excluding those universal [defilements] that pertain to other realms. "Because of the destruction of those objects" means:
The universal [defilements] of the dissimilar realm are the object of these [defilements], such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Those that have them as their object are the universal [defilements] of the similar realm.
Through the destruction—that is, the abandonment—of those [dissimilar universal defilements].
Those universal [defilements] of a different realm are abandoned.
[The abandonment of the universal defilements of a different realm occurs] through the abandonment of their support by way of abandoning their cause;
[it occurs] "through the abandonment of the object" (*ālambanaprahāṇāt*).

Through the abandonment of false views and other afflictions that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, and which have dogmatic adherence to views and so forth as their objects,
those very dogmatic adherences and others that take contaminated phenomena as their objects are also abandoned;
they perish due to the arising of their antidote.
Thus,

he demonstrates that the destruction of those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation occurs solely through the arising of their antidote, and not from the thorough knowledge of the object (*ālambana*) and so forth.
"We shall explain this later."
For he will state here [in verse 60ab] that "the faults are indeed of nine kinds in each stage, and likewise the qualities.
The path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) is the counteragent of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*).
The side that is the adversary of the opposing side is the "counter-side" (pratipakṣa).
A counter-side for the sake of abandonment is an "abandonment-counter-side" (prahāṇapratipakṣa).
For even the path of liberation is a counter-side, but not for the sake of abandonment; therefore, this qualification is made.
It is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) because by means of it [the defilements] are abandoned.
It is both abandonment and an antidote; thus, it is the "antidote of abandonment" (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*).
For example, the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*).
The "counteractive of support" is that which follows after it;
that is, the path which is the path of liberation (vimuktimārga) following after that path of uninterrupted transition (ānantaryamārga).
For that is the support of abandonment, because it maintains the attainment thereof.
It is called a "support" (ādhāra) because by means of it something is supported; that very thing is the antidote, hence it is the "support-antidote" (ādhāra-pratipakṣa).

For example, it is said that following the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) comes the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*); thus it is called [the fruit] because it is attained by that. This is the detailed explanation.
By whichever path—that is, by the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*)—that attainment is reached, the abandonment (*prahāṇa*) is maintained.
The antidote of support (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*) is that which has the nature of not severing the attainment of that [state].
The "antidote of distancing" (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*), and so forth, refers to that by which the acquisition of afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*) is distanced; thus it is called "distancing."
That very counteragent is the counteragent of distancing (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*).
Alternatively, distancing itself is "distancing.
The counteragent for that [distancing] is the counteragent of distancing.
"The path that follows after the path of liberation" means:
that which is the path of liberation is the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*);
the path that follows after that is the subsequent-knowledge-acceptance of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*) and so forth.

He shows that this is the counteragent by way of distancing (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*). Regarding the statement "the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) also," others say that even that first path of liberation is called the counteragent by way of distancing.
For he also distances himself from that acquisition of afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*).

This being the case, it is stated that the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) receives two names: "the counteractive of support" (*ādhārapratipakṣa*) and "the counteractive of distancing" (*dūrībhāvapratipakṣa*).
It is said that one reviles that realm by seeing it as a fault.
The meaning is that by means of aspects such as impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth, one brings about revulsion toward that realm (*dhātu*).

This being the case, it is thereby shown that even that which has suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) as its object— such as the counteragent of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*) and so on— is also a counteragent of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇāpratipakṣa*).
However, the Teacher [Vasubandhu] maintains that this sequence would be correct.
He demonstrates that this sequence is correct because it relies on the analogy of a staircase and because it avoids confusion regarding the definitions [of the paths].
Thus, he states: "The path of preparation has suffering and its origin as its objects."
Only the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*)— namely, the stages beginning with "heat" (*uṣmagata*)— is included here, and not the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) and so forth,
because those are established as the counteragents for abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*) and the like.
Regarding the phrase "all uninterrupted paths" (*sarvānantaryamārga*): this refers to all other uninterrupted paths whatsoever, even those occurring at a later time.
Furthermore, the term "all" applies equally to all paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
The path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*), however, is that which is distinct from these three; it is this that is understood here.
For an affliction cannot be separated [from the mind] by means of mere association (*saṃprayoga*).
Because it is impossible to separate [the dharma] from its own constituent parts.
First of all, a future [dharma] could be separated from its object; however, for that which has already been separated...
Because that object does not arise again by taking that same thing as its objective support (*ālambana*), for this reason.
But how can it be "past," given that it arose by taking that object as its support?
For it is impossible to make an object that has already been supported into something that is no longer supported.
This too is not absolute.
The destruction of the afflictions is held to occur in four ways:
through the thorough knowledge of the object, and through the destruction of that which takes it as its object.
"Because of the abandonment of the object and the arising of the antidote, there is destruction.
Therefore, it is not an absolute rule that [destruction occurs] solely from the full comprehension of the object.
Therefore, this must be stated; that is to say, this must be refuted.
On this point, the Master Saṃghabhadra offers a rebuttal:
"Defilements are to be abandoned by means of their objects."
For it is by the power of thorough knowledge of the object (*ālambana*) that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned.
And the object of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is twofold:
the basis of bondage (*saṃyogavastu*) and the basis of non-bondage (*asaṃyogavastu*).

In that regard, for a person whose mental continuum is not afflicted, there is the acquisition (*prāpti*)—occurring without interruption—of those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) directed toward objects associated with fetters, as well as those not so directed, which have been produced by the power of those [primary] dispositions; these exist as causes and effects of past and future afflictions.

In the same way, one should understand the acquisition of those latent dispositions directed toward objects unassociated with fetters, as well as those not so directed, which arise following upon afflictions directed toward those very objects.
For it serves as the cause for the arising of future [defilements] by way of providing the necessary conditions;
and for those that are past, it serves as the fruit by way of being their outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Moreover, it is opposed to the presence of the attainment of the outflow of the antidote that abandons them.
Because the afflictions are supported by that [object],
the afflictions that have arisen with a certain object cause other afflictions with different objects to arise as well.

When there is the arising of the outflow of the antidote that abandons that object, and when the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those [afflictions] has ceased, those afflictions— even though they still possess that object— are said to be "abandoned" because they have been deprived of their causes and fruits.

Therefore, because when a certain object of affliction (*kleśaviṣaya*) is not fully understood, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of even those afflictions whose objects are different from it— functioning as the cause and fruit of past and future afflictions— proceeds within the continuum according to the nature of the thing itself through the power of the affliction directed toward that object;
for this reason, it is intended that afflictions must be abandoned by means of their objective support (*ālambana*).
But is it not intended that afflictions are also abandoned through the abandonment of their objects and so forth?
Why then is this said: "afflictions are abandoned by the power of the thorough knowledge of the object"?
For those [other modes of abandonment] are also abandoned solely by the power of the thorough knowledge of the Truth of Suffering and the rest.
Because their presence or absence is contingent upon the presence or absence of that [defilement].
For even those which are said to be abandoned through the arising of an antidote are also to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

It should be understood that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned solely through the power of thoroughly knowing the objects of observation, such as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). What was stated previously is merely a formal presentation;
however, the intended meaning appears to be that the afflictions are also abandoned by means of abandoning their objects of observation and so forth.
"Belonging to one's own continuum [is abandoned] through the cutting off of its acquisition," and so forth.
A defilement in one's own continuum is to be said as abandoned through the disappearance of its acquisition;
however, a defilement in another's continuum is not [abandoned] through the cutting off of its acquisition.
Because that [attainment] does not exist within one's own continuum.
What then? It is because of the abandonment of the afflictions belonging to one's own continuum which have that as their object;
the meaning is: because of the severing of the possession (*prāpti*) of the afflictions belonging to one's own continuum which have the afflictions of another's continuum as their object.
All form (*rūpa*)— whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—
as well as non-afflicted phenomena (*dharma*), which are formless (*arūpin*), whether wholesome with outflows (*sāsrava*) or unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*),
should likewise be said to be abandoned through the abandonment of the afflictions belonging to one's own continuum that take them as their objects.
(V.61) "The remoteness of the elements, ethical discipline, locations, and the two time periods is like [that of other things]. Here, the word *iva* ("like") serves as an illustration;
it should be understood in the sense of "for example."
Remoteness by way of difference of characteristics (*vailakṣaṇya-lakṣaṇadūratā*) is as follows:
for example, among the primary elements (*bhūta*).
Since the water element has a characteristic different from the earth element, the water element is remote from the earth element.
Distance by way of opposition is due to being an adversary; for example, immorality is the distance from morality.
Distance by way of spatial separation is due to the separation of location.
For example, spatial distance is like that of one region from the western ocean to the eastern ocean;
temporal distance is like that of two time-periods characterized as past and future.
For that which is past and future is said to be "distant. Where is it so stated?
In the Abhidharma.
For it has been said thus:
"Which phenomena are distant?
Past and future phenomena."
Which are the proximate phenomena? They are the present phenomena and the unconditioned.
"That which is distant" refers to the past and the future;
"and that which is arising" refers to the present.

The meaning is that it is the future which is oriented toward arising. "Not by way of having long since passed or having long since been produced" means that the past is not distant because it has long since passed, nor is the future distant because it will be produced only after a long time.
Even the present is thus reached as being distant.
Due to the plurality of time-periods (*adhvan*), even that which exists as the present is reached as being distant by virtue of its status as the present time-period,
just as the past and future are [distant] by virtue of their status as the past and future time-periods.
"In that case, it is distant because of its lack of activity (*akāritra*). That which has ceased its activity is the past; that which has not yet attained its activity is the future.
Thus, that which is past and future is said to be distant."

How can there be proximity (*antikam*) for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Since it lacks functional activity (*kāritra*), it would not have proximity; yet that [proximity] is accepted. Which are the dharmas that are proximate?
"Present phenomena" and "the unconditioned," according to the reading of the treatise;
[it is said] because that [non-obtainment] exists everywhere.
Because the possession (*prāpti*) of that unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—namely, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*)—arises everywhere.

It would follow, then, that even regarding the past and future, there is the consequence [of proximity]; for since the possession of the past and future wholesome states and so forth can occur everywhere, it follows as a consequence that they too would be "near" (proximate) even in the past and future.
And how could this apply to space?
And how could space be near?
For there is no reaching of it.
[The same applies to] the past and the future in relation to each other.
The meaning is that the future is distant from the past, and the past is distant from the future.
Furthermore, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is [distant] because it is not separated [by anything];
it is not separated by anything whatsoever.
Just as the past and future are [known] by means of the present,
so too is its proximity;
it is likewise.
Even in this conceptualization,
that which immediately precedes or follows the past and future would, because of its proximity to the present, result in both being [simultaneously] present.
Regarding "distant" and "near":
for that [past] is distant from the future because it is separated by the present,
yet it follows that it is near to the present because it is not separated [from it].
In this way, the future [dharmas] should also be understood.
However, it would be more logical [to explain them] thus;
this is the Master’s own opinion.
The future is distant from the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of phenomena.
Why?
Because it has not yet been attained.
Because its own characteristic has not been attained by that which is future;
or alternatively, because that own characteristic has not been attained— that is, has not appeared—
and likewise [has not been attained] by that which is past.
Why is it distant from the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of phenomena? Because it has fallen away from that; for such is the specific characteristic of phenomena.
Therefore, it has fallen away from the past.

For that which has fallen away from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a dharma is what is called "past. (V.62) [The abandonment of defilements occurs] through the arising of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*). Destruction (*kṣaya*).
Thus it has been said.
Therefore, he asks:
"Is it because of proceeding along a specific path? and so forth.
"Distinction of abandonment" (prahāṇaviśeṣa) means that the abandonment is distinguished.
Here, the "counteragent" (pratipakṣa) is intended to be the path of liberation (vimuktimārga).
Because the attainment of dissociation arises simultaneously with that [path], there is no attainment of dissociation in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
since it is oriented toward arising.
For it can also be established that the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*).
Because it shares a single function with the immediate path (*ānantarya-mārga*), which is the primary antidote.
For it has been said: "Indeed, its attainment is by means of both [paths], because [the uninterrupted path] is the bringer and the support for the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*).
Thus, there are four fruits.
The mention of "four" is for the purpose of excluding the realization of eighty-nine fruits,
or alternatively, for the purpose of excluding the realization of the five fruits beginning with human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
Furthermore, the attainment of the fruit is understood specifically as occurring at the stage of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

The transformation of the faculties (*indriya-vivṛddhi*) is the "transformation of the faculties" (*indriya-saṃcāra*) due to the possession of the existence of the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-lābha*).
This demonstration of the meaning is stated as "the transformation of the faculties" for the purpose of refuting the notion that there is an increase in the number of faculties;
for Master Saṃghabhadra maintains that this is already established by the very mention of the attainment of the fruit (*phala-prāpti*).
To this we reply:
it is true that the attainment of the fruit itself is the increase of the faculties.
However, a specific distinction in the attainment of the fruit must be demonstrated—that is, the case where there is the further acquisition of the fruit of dissociation.

Otherwise, even the statement regarding the attainment of the fruit would not need to be made, since that is already established by the very statement of the arising of the counteragent. Enough, then, with this excessive wrangling.
"For some, up to two":
for certain afflictions (*kleśa*), there is the attainment of dissociation at six times;
by the word "up to," it is implied that for some [afflictions], it is at five [times].
For some, it occurs in four;
for some, in three;
for some, in two.
"For some, in two [moments];
for some, in one moment"— this was not stated because the discussion concerns the disjunction that has been reacquired.
For it is possible that one of sharp faculties attains the dissociation from the ninth category of the Peak of Existence at a single time;
however, because that is not a [subsequent] attainment, it is not so described.
In that regard, first, for one of dull faculties, there is the attainment of dissociation at six times.

The acquisition of dissociation occurs at six times: at the time of the arising of the antidote for those [defilements] belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, its origin, and its cessation; at the time of the fruit of stream-entry; at the time of the fruit of once-returning; at the time of the fruit of non-returning; at the time of the fruit of arhatship; and at the time of the transformation of the faculties.
This is stated with reference to what is possible.
For one of dull faculties does not necessarily transform the faculties.

For that very person of dull faculties, there are five occasions: at the time of grasping the path belonging to the realms of form and formlessness that is to be abandoned by the vision of the path; or at the time of the arising of the antidote; or at the time of attaining the fruit; or at the time of attaining the fruit of once-returner; up to the time of transforming the faculties.

Regarding those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya) belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara), there is the attainment of dissociation (visaṃyogalābha) for the five types— ranging from the highest-of-the-high (adhimātrādhimātra) to the middle-of-the-middle— at those same five stages, excluding the time of the fruit of stream-entry (srotaāpattiphala). However, for the sixth type, which is the middle-of-the-soft (madhyamṛdu), it occurs at four stages.
Because the time of the arising of the counteragent and the time of the attainment of the fruit are one and the same; "in that" means in either of those two,
specifically at the time of the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmiphala).
At the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship;
at the time of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*);

and at the time of the arising of the antidote for the seventh and eighth categories of that same [defilement]—whether it be the weak-intense or the weak-middling—at the time of the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmi-phala*), up to the time of the transformation of the faculties: thus, in these four [instances].
In these very moments, there is the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).
This occurs either at the time of the arising of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to that very last, weakest-of-the-weak category, or at the time of attaining the fruit— namely,
at the time of attaining the fruit of Arhatship (*arhattvaphala*).
And at the time of the transition of the faculties—thus, in these three times, there is the attainment of dissociation.

For one who is attaining that very fruit of arhatship, there are nine types of afflictions belonging to the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned by cultivation, ranging from the "intense-intense" (adhimātra-adhimātra) down to the "mild-mild" (mṛdu-mṛdu).
Excluding the final mild-mild type belonging to the peak of existence (bhavāgra), there is the attainment of dissociation for all of them in those same three times.
At the time of the arising of the counteragent, at the time of the fruit of arhatship, and at the time of the transformation of the faculties.
As for its final category of affliction belonging to the formless realm, which is the weakest of the weak:
Because the time of the arising of its antidote and the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship are one and the same.
That is to say, at either the time of the arising of the antidote or the time of the fruit of arhatship— at whichever of these two times the transformation of the faculties occurs—
there is the attainment of disjunction from the defilements.
Thus far, what has been said applies to one of dull faculties.
For one of sharp faculties, however, it should be stated that for some afflictions [the abandonment occurs] at five times, and for others, up to two times.
Excluding the single occasion of the transition of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
For in that case, there is no transition of the faculties at all;
rather, the attainment of dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśavisaṃyoga*) occurs at that very same time.
[This refers to] the weakest-of-the-weak category of that which is to be abandoned by cultivation belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Furthermore, we consider that it should not be said that "there is no further attainment" [of it].
[The phrase] "because the cause is metaphorically designated as the fruit" means:
Abandonment is the fruit; thorough knowledge is the cause, having the nature of cognition. Regarding that abandonment, there is a metaphorical designation of the cause as the fruit:
"abandonment is thorough knowledge."
For example: "These six bases of contact (*sparśāyatana*), which were previously conditioned and intended, are to be understood as past karma.
But who designates abandonment by the term "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*)?
For it is recited thus in the Sūtra itself:
"Monks, I will teach you the phenomena that are to be fully understood,
as well as full understanding itself and the person who possesses full understanding.
What are the phenomena to be fully understood?"
The five aggregates of clinging. What is thorough knowledge? It is the abandonment of desire and lust for these.
The complete transcendence of desire and lust;
this is called "thorough knowledge," and so forth.
(Abhid-k-vy 504)
"The destruction of the first two types of desire and so forth constitutes one [fruit].
This is due to the attainment of untainted dissociation and the impairment of the peak of existence."

Regarding the statement, "Through the eradication of two causes and through the transcendence of the realms, there is full comprehension," the reason for establishing full comprehension will be explained therein. [This refers to] the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*).
The meaning is the abandonment of the outflows (āsrava) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
This indeed is its designation:
the abandonment of the outflows of the form realm (rūpadhātu).
The meaning is the abandonment of the outflows (*āsrava*) pertaining to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Its name is "thorough knowledge of the destruction of attachment to form" (*rūparāgakṣayaparijñā*).

Although this thorough knowledge is established as the abandonment of other afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), such as pride (*māna*) and so forth, that belong to the realm of form.

However, because passion (*rāga*) is predominant therein, the abandonment of the fetter (*saṃyojana*) pertaining to the higher realms is called the "thorough knowledge of the destruction of passion for the form realm" (*rūparāgakṣayaparijñā*).
The so-called "thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters" (*sarvasaṃyojanaparyādānaparijñā*) is a name for the abandonment of all outflows (*āsrava*).
"Thorough knowledge" (parijñā) is taught as being distinct.

"What is to be known" refers to the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of desire for the form realm (*rūpa-rāga-kṣaya-parijñā*), which is the abandonment of those [defilements] belonging to the form realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Regarding those of the formless realm (*ārūpya*), it is the thorough knowledge of the total destruction of all fetters (*sarva-saṃyojana-paryādāna-parijñā*).
This is because it is stated thus.
It is not the case for those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), for what reason?

Why is it that the thorough cognitions (*parijñā*) of those [defilements] belonging to the realms of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) and formlessness (*arūpya-dhātu*) which are to be abandoned by seeing are not taught individually?

Likewise, there are three types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding the abandonment of all those [defilements] belonging to the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), because it is so stated [in the source]. Furthermore, because the remedies (*pratipakṣa*) for those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are dissimilar, it is said: "In this way, on each respective stage (*bhūmi*), there are [remedies] for those belonging to the form realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation..."

There are nine types of antidotes to the nine things to be abandoned: the uncontaminated paths of non-obstruction and liberation belonging to the stages such as the "unrestricted" (*anāgāmya*), and those comprised within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna up to those comprised within the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*).
Furthermore, there are the paths of non-obstruction which serve as the antidotes for those who dwell in the formless realms.
In the path of liberation, there exist, as appropriate, either the lower stages that are free from outflows (*anāsrava*) or,
as appropriate, those included within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher [stages] that possess outflows (*sāsrava*).
Because these are distinct and their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) are dissimilar, they demonstrate a differentiation in thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
The antidotes for those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing are similar:

since those very antidotes, such as the patiences of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and so forth, which belong to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), are also the antidotes for those belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), they are not established as separate thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).

(Abhidh-k-vy 505) (V.64–66) "The thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the abandonment of the [fetters] concordant with the lower portion," and so forth, refers to the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the [fetters] concordant with the lower portion and the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of passion for the form realm (*rūparāga*).
It is the thorough knowledge that all fetters have been completely exhausted.
Since these are the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they are fruits of knowledge;
for there are no patiences (*kṣānti*) on the path of cultivation.
Regarding the statement "how thorough knowledge is the fruit of patience": "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) have the same meaning.
This is because it is stated that "knowledge and thorough knowledge are untainted wisdom" (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
[End of] the forty-fourth fascicle.
Since stainless forbearances are devoid of cognition,
it is also untenable for forbearance to have the nature of cognition;
how then could thorough knowledge be the fruit of forbearance?
The thought is that it would also be improper to apply the name of the cause to the fruit. Here, it is stated: "Because the patiences (kṣāntis) have knowledge as their retinue.
Since these possess knowledge as their retinue, they are said to have knowledge as their retinue.
Acceptance (*kṣānti*) is also [included] within the fruits of knowledge; therefore, the fruit of knowledge is called the "fruit of acceptance.

This is like applying the designation "king" to the king's retinue; for example, because the designation "king" is applied to the king's retinue, what is done by the retinue is also [attributed to the king].
It is like the expression "made by the king.
Regarding the phrase "because they have the same fruit as knowledge": the patiences (kṣāntis) share the same fruit as the knowledges (jñānas).
Since whatever is the fruit of the patiences is precisely the fruit of the knowledges, it is appropriate to regard the fruit of the patiences as being fully known.
Regarding the statement "all [results] belong to the *anāgamya*":

it is because it is possible for the path belonging to the stage of *anāgamya* to abandon the outflows (*āsrava*) that are to be abandoned through seeing and meditation within the three realms; for it is said:
"By the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) *anāgamya*..."
This is because it is stated that "one is free from passion toward all [objects].
These are those whose nature consists in the abandonment of the afflictions within the realms of form and formlessness.

Regarding this, the Vaibhāṣikas say: it consists of the three thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) as previously explained, which are the abandonment of those things to be abandoned by seeing that pertain to the form and formless realms;

and the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of desire for the form realm, which is the abandonment of those things to be abandoned by meditation that pertain to the form realm; and [the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of desire] for those that pertain to the formless realm...
There are five types of thorough knowledge known as "the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters that have been abandoned.

This is because, by relying on the actual state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-svabhāva*), there is the possibility of abandoning the afflictions belonging to the realms of form and formlessness.
However, the abandonment of the afflictions belonging to the desire realm is not the fruit of the actual state of meditative concentration.
The fundamental states of dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*) are not the antidotes to the desire realm;

therefore, although those who are free from passion possess the untainted attainment of disjunction (*visaṃyogaprāpti*), it is said that the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) belonging to the desire realm is not the fruit of the fundamental states of dhyāna, just as the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the abandonment of the factors conducive to the lower realms (*avarabhāgīya*) is not.
According to the system of the Venerable Ghoṣaka, there are eight.

This means that the Venerable Ghoṣaka maintains that even for a person who is free from desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*), the nature of the three thorough cognitions (*parijñā*) regarding the abandonment of those things to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the sensuous sphere is the fruit of the noble path (*āryamārga*).
Why is that? Because one attains the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).

Even when entering the state of certainty (*niyāma*) based on the fundamental dhyānas, one does not see [the defilements] again; thus, the defilements to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), which were previously abandoned by the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), [are now abandoned].

They also attain the uncontaminated attainment of dissociation; since the path of seeing possesses that capacity, just as the abandonments of the path of seeing belonging to the form and formless realms [are established], the thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) of the abandonments of the path of seeing belonging to the desire realm that were previously abandoned are likewise designated as the actual fruit of the dhyānas. Thus they are categorized.

These three thorough knowledges (*parijñā*)— consisting of the abandonment of those things to be abandoned by seeing which belong to the desire realm, together with the previously explained thorough knowledges of the form and formless realms—
constitute the eight thorough knowledges that are the fruit of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
This is the system of the Venerable Ghoṣaka.
The thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) that abandons the [fetters] concordant with the lower portion has only the fruit of the "unprepared" (*anāgāmya*).

This means that one who is not yet free from passion for the desire realm abandons the [fetters] concordant with the lower portion solely through the unprepared stage, and not through the fundamental [dhyānas],
because those have not yet been attained.

Even when one proceeds toward the state of being free from desire, at the time when, by relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one abandons all afflictions belonging to the desire realm through the mundane path during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), that [abandonment] is not the fruit of the actual state of meditative concentration. Furthermore,

the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the abandonment of the factors conducive to the final part [of the path] within the sixteen moments of mind is also established as being based upon the actual state of meditative concentration.
It is not, however, that it is designated as "the fruit of that [path] at that time.
Rather,

because at that stage one also attains the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*)— which is acquired through the mundane path and consists of the abandonment of the factors concordant with the lower realm— that [abandonment] is...
The thorough knowledge of abandonment is established as follows: at that time, having abandoned those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing which were previously abandoned,

and having combined that with the abandonment of the "lower-tier" (avarabhāgīya) defilements previously abandoned, a single thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower-tier defilements is established.
(Abhidh-k-vy 507) Because there exists the reason for combining them— that one becomes detached from a realm and attains a fruit—

therefore, that thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) which consists in the abandonment of the factors concordant with the lower part (*avarabhāgīya*) is established as having the fruit of the "unrestricted" (*anāgamya*) alone.
It is not the fruit of the actual entity (*vastu*).
On this point,
the systems of the Vaibhāṣikas and the Venerable Ghoṣaka are in agreement.
"One should also intentionally observe the distinguished dhyānas" means that even through the untainted (anāsrava) states of the distinguished dhyānas, the afflictions (kleśa) are abandoned;
therefore, [one should observe] the "unrestricted" (anāgāmya).
Only the fruits of the fundamental dhyānas themselves have been explained, not those of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
Therefore, it is stated: "The intermediate dhyāna should also be regarded in the same manner as the [fundamental] dhyānas."

The "distinguished meditative absorption" (dhyānāntara) is so called because it is distinguished by being free from applied thought (*vitarka*), even while remaining within the first dhyāna itself. It is said that "the intermediate dhyāna exists" in reference to the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
The fruit of full comprehension (*parijñā*) is also established for that [attainment] when it is mundane (*laukika*),
because only for a noble one (*ārya*) is the attainment of untainted dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) possible;
and this applies to the three fundamental formless attainments (*maulārūpyatraya*) as well.
Of the untainted [path],
and two of the mundane path.
For the noble one, through the mundane path, there is detachment from the desire realm and the form realm;
for subsequent knowledge as well, there are two [results].
Of that which is comprised within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
In the latter [two], there are two thorough knowledges (*parijñā*): the destruction of attachment to the form realm (*rūparāgakṣaya*) and the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojanaparyādāna*).
For dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), there are three.
Thus [it is said].
This refers to that which is subsumed within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*):
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding cessation or regarding the path on the path of cultivation.
"That is the antidote to the three realms.
Its last three fruits are the thorough knowledge consisting in the abandonment of the lower fetters, the destruction of passion for the form realm, and the total exhaustion of all fetters.
Why is this so? He says:
"Because it is the antidote to those things to be abandoned through cultivation within the three realms.
There are six [paths of seeing] for that category, or five.
Regarding the category (*pakṣa*) of those two— dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)—
six and five [moments] respectively are included by the mention of the "category," which refers to the inclusion of both the receptivities (*kṣānti*) and the knowledges (*jñāna*).
This is precisely what is meant by the phrase "of the dharma-knowledges and receptivities."
This is a compound of *dharmajñānakṣāntīnām* and *dharmajñānām*.

Regarding the *dharmajñānakṣāntis*, the three aforementioned thorough knowledges (*parijñā*)—which have the nature of abandoning what is to be abandoned through seeing in the desire realm—are the fruit.
Regarding the *dharmajñānas*, this refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

For those [knowledges] comprised within the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of its origin, there is one thorough knowledge: the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa-parijñā*).

However, for those comprised within the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, there are all three thorough knowledges: the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters, the thorough knowledge of the destruction of passion for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya-parijñā*), and the thorough knowledge of the total exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-paryādāna-parijñā*).
These are the same as those of the subsequent patiences and knowledges (*anvaya-kṣānti-jñāna*).
[This refers to] the receptivities to subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*).

These consist of the three aforementioned thorough knowledges (*parijñā*), which have the nature of abandoning what is to be abandoned through seeing (*darśanaheya*) in the realms of form and formlessness, plus the two final [thorough knowledges].
(V.67) Why is it that each abandonment is not [counted as a separate thorough knowledge]?

Why is it not accepted that there is the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by the vision of origination, and so on in detail up to the abandonment of the soft-soft category belonging to the peak of existence?
Because of the attainment of the untainted disjunction (anāsrava-viyoga).
The meaning is: "due to the attainment of untainted dissociation.
Regarding the phrase "due to the impairment of the peak of existence":
The meaning is: "by the abandonment of a portion of the peak of existence.
[This occurs] "due to the eradication of two causes."
The meaning is: by means of the abandonment of the two types of universal causes (sarvatragahetu) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin [of suffering].
The thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) consists in that abandonment.
The intention is that, because its abandonment is preeminent due to these reasons, it is established here as "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).

"In other dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges" means in those dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges beginning from the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*) up to the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*).
"Abandonment, however, is the fruit of knowledge" refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);
for that [abandonment] is not the fruit of the receptive patiences (*kṣānti*).
"Because of the transcendence of the realm (dhātu).
The word "and" (ca) is indicated as being elided.
"And because of the transcendence of the realm.
For this very reason, it is explained as "and from the fourth," meaning when one completely transcends the realm.
When one transcends the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm,
the ellipsis is that "then it receives the designation 'thorough knowledge'.
Why?
Because of detachment from the entire realm;
that is, because of detachment from the whole realm,
and not merely because of partial disintegration.
For the intention is that at that time there is a thorough abandonment.
Regarding "the disjunction from both types of conjunction":
conjunction characterized by the afflictions consisting of the apprehended object (*ālambana*) and the apprehending subject (*ālambaka*) is "conjunction of both."
Therefore, dissociation is the dissociation from both types of conjunction.
The Abhidharmikas say that this is the fifth cause.
And by means of this cause, abandonment is called "thorough knowledge" (parijñā).

Regarding the category that has been abandoned— whether it be that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, up to that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path, or that which is to be abandoned by cultivation— if, when that category has been abandoned, one becomes dissociated from other afflictions (*kleśa*) that take it as their object, whether those afflictions are to be abandoned by vision or by cultivation, others say that this is also the fifth cause for the establishment of abandonment as thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
"But that is not other," and so forth.

That conjunction of both, however, is not other [than the cessation of suffering] because of the eradication of both causes— the universal cause (sarvatragahetu) which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and that which is to be abandoned by the vision of origin— and because of the transcendence of the realm (dhātusamatikrama).

For instance, even when those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) have been abandoned, there is as yet no eradication of the two causes as long as the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) to be abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudayadarśanaprahātavya*), which has that as its object, remains unabandoned. Furthermore, even when those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*)—up to eight categories—have been abandoned, there is as yet no transcendence of the realm (*dhātvatikrama*) until the ninth category is also abandoned; therefore, [it is not so].
We reply:
(V.68) "Not by one," and so forth.
First of all, an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is not at all possessed [of this],
because they lack the acquisition of disjunction from the untainted (anāsrava).

An noble one (ārya), moreover, is not possessed of it while abiding on the path of seeing (darśanamārga), up until the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (samudayadharmajñānakṣānti).

By the word "up to" (*yāvat*), it should be understood that one is not yet endowed with the receptivities and knowledges regarding the dharma and subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmānvaya-jñāna-kṣānti-jñāna*), nor with the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), because two causes have not yet been abandoned.

It should be understood that at the stage of the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), one is endowed with one [receptivity], and likewise at the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), one is endowed with that very same one.

In the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvayajñāna*), there are two: by means of the aforementioned single thorough knowledge of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), and by means of the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyāvacara*).
In the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodhadharmajñānakṣānti*), there are likewise only two.
It should be understood that in the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodhadharmajñāna*), there are three.
Up to this point, one established in the path of seeing is endowed with five [parijñās], but not with six, because the sixteenth moment is subsumed under the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Regarding the phrase "with six" in the case of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna):
it is by means of the previously mentioned [five] and the thorough knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇaparijñā) regarding the path of the form and formless realms seen in the path of seeing.
But will he not say later:
"The establishment of the four fruits occurs due to the presence of five causes:
the abandonment of the previous [path], the attainment of another path, and the aggregation of cessations within the fruit"?

Furthermore, there is the attainment of the eight knowledges and the cultivation of the sixteen aspects; thus, while there is a compendium of abandonments, there is no compendium of thorough cognitions— hence there is no contradiction.
"Until one has attained detachment from the desire realm.

By the word "until," it is meant that even when there is the abandonment of the first type of affliction to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), up to the abandonment of the eighth type, one is still endowed with exactly six [faculties].
"Even when one has fallen away from that" means:
For through falling away from detachment from the desire realm, one is separated from that synthesis;
this occurs whether one has previously attained detachment from the desire realm or afterwards—
whether before or after the clear realization (abhisamaya).
How so?

Having become free from passion for the desire realm by means of the mundane path and having entered into the fixed course of rightness (*niyāma*), he is endowed with one thorough knowledge of abandonment pertaining to the lower portion (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa-parijñā*) at the moment of the subsequent cognition of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*).
This is because, upon reaching the sixteenth moment, that noble one becomes an *anāgāmin* (non-returner).
He is not a stream-enterer,
nor a once-returner;
rather, he is recited as a non-returner because of the abandonment of the five lower fetters.

Therefore, by combining the abandonment of those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing with the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīya*), one is endowed with only a single thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters.

Alternatively, after the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one who follows the gradual path and has attained detachment from the desire realm is endowed with only a single thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters;
likewise, one who has attained Arhatship is endowed with only a single [thorough knowledge].
This is because of the synthesis of thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) at that time.

The qualification "even when fallen away by means of the form realm" is for the purpose of excluding the possession of six thorough knowledges upon falling away by means of the desire realm, and for the purpose of excluding the possession of two thorough knowledges upon falling away by means of the formless realm.
"One who has attained detachment from the realm of form (rūpavairāgya) does so by means of two" means that a non-returner (anāgāmī) is one who is free from passion for the realm of form.
Why is there no inclusion based on detachment from the realms (dhātuvairāgya)?
Because there is no attainment of the fruit.

The compendium of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is intended to be based on both causes together— the detachment from a realm (*dhātu-vairāgya*) and the attainment of the fruit (*phala-prāpti*)— and not by either alone, even if one has fallen away [from the fruit].

"By means of an [affliction] belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*)" refers to the fact that when one falls away from Arhatship due to an affliction belonging to the formless realm, one reacquires the two thorough knowledges (*parijñā*)—the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa*) and the destruction of passion for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya*)—which were previously integrated with the attainment of Arhatship.

However, upon falling away through an affliction belonging to the form realm, one would be endowed with only one [thorough knowledge]; and through an affliction belonging to the desire realm, one would be endowed with six. Therefore, the mention of "an outburst belonging to the formless realm" is made.
(V.69ab) "Of the non-returner and the arhat.
Here, the non-returner who is free from passion for the desire realm is intended.
This is because of the statement regarding the possession of two thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) for the non-returner who is free from passion for the form realm.
"Not more" means not in greater number; the intention is that they are like those who enter the stream by way of the gradual path (ānupūrvika-srotāpanna).
It has been explained that this is "by means of two causes.
What is the meaning of "compilation" (*saṃkalana*)? It means establishing [them] as one. And "of those two states" refers to these two conditions.

For those who are free from passion for the desire realm, both of these— detachment from the realms and the attainment of a fruit— exist in the two states of the non-returner and the arhat; thus, it is said that there is a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).

For a non-returner who is free from passion for the realm of form, there is one thorough knowledge consisting in the abandonment of the lower fetters; for an arhat as well, there is one thorough knowledge consisting in the total exhaustion of all fetters.
(V.69cd) "One, two," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
"Someone abandons one" means that they relinquish it.
One [attains] two, another one.
Some have five; some six.
He abandons it, or he attains it.
One person attains one, another two, and another six;
it is not the case that someone attains five.
Therefore, he says:
"Five not":
no one at all obtains five;
such is the method of the meaning of the Sūtra.

The commentary is explained as follows: one who falls away from arhatship abandons a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), namely the thorough knowledge consisting in the total exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-paryādāna-parijñā*), by means of any thought whatsoever.
This is because, when taken collectively, that [thorough knowledge] exists in each and every state of arhatship.

Likewise, a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) who is free from passion for the form realm (*rūpa-vītarāga*) and falls away from detachment from the desire realm abandons only a single thorough knowledge, namely the thorough knowledge consisting in the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa-parijñā*).
He abandons two thorough knowledges:
the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters and the thorough knowledge of the destruction of attachment to the realm of form.
Who is this? He says:
"It is a non-returner who has already become free from passion for the form realm, but is falling away from his detachment from the desire realm.
One who was previously free from passion abandons five [faculties] at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna).
In the sixteenth moment of mind, which is the moment of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
there is indeed the acquisition of the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) consisting in the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*).

For one who has attained the mundane path, through the acquisition of the untainted disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga*), he abandons the five previous thorough knowledges obtained during the fifteen moments.

However, one does not abandon the sixth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), which is the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through the vision of the path pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness.

Rather, because it has been subsumed within the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) due to the attainment of the fruit resulting from detachment from the realm [of desire], it is as if its form has vanished and is therefore not mentioned here.
As for the gradual practitioner (*ānupūrvika*) who was previously not detached, he abandons six [thorough knowledges] by reason of his detachment from the realm of desire.
The thorough knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) regarding those [defilements] of the three realms that are to be abandoned by seeing are likewise acquired. Thus,
someone may acquire one [thorough knowledge].
Excluding the five,
one obtains up to six; that is,
whoever obtains something not previously possessed.
Whether situated on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) or the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), whoever first acquires a full comprehension (*parijñā*) that was not previously acquired,
he acquires that one alone.

For even on the path of cultivation, one who has previously been free from passion (*vītarāga*) acquires at the conclusion of the path of seeing only the single full comprehension of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa-parijñā*).
One who follows the gradual path also obtains that very same [attainment] on the ninth path of liberation regarding detachment from the desire realm.
An Arhat also obtains another [attainment].
One falls away solely from detachment from the formless realm.
He shows that it is not from any other form of detachment (*vairāgya*).

For he obtains both the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) and the thorough knowledge of the destruction of attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*).
Some say there are six cases, namely, one who falls away from the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
The gradual-type non-returner does not undergo retrogression, for there is no retrogression for one who has previously become free from passion,
because that state of freedom from passion is attained by means of both paths.
For this very reason, no one at all obtains five [parijñās] simultaneously.
For if there were falling away for one who was previously free from passion (*vītarāga-pūrvī*),
that same person would have obtained five parijñās at once.
The fifth treasury-location, titled "Exposition of the Latent Dispositions" (*anuśayanirdeśa*), in the *Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* composed by Master Yaśomitra, is completed.

VI (The Sixth Chapter, titled "Instruction on the Persons and the Path") (VI.1) Demonstrating the connection between the fifth and sixth chapters, he introduces this [topic]:
"It has been explained how [the defilements] are abandoned," and so forth.
"One obtains full comprehension according to the abandonment," because of the statement that "the cause is metaphorically designated by the name of the fruit.
And that too...
The abandonment of the afflictions has been declared; how so? He says:
"From the vision and cultivation of the truths":
this is a compound expressed in the singular form.
"From the seeing and from the cultivation of the truths," or "from the cultivation [of the truths].
It has been explained in detail that by reason of the seeing and cultivation of the truths, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are to be abandoned through seeing and to be abandoned through cultivation:
"These ten, seven, seven, and eight, excluding three and two views respectively."
They are abandoned in sequence by the vision of suffering and so forth within the desire realm;
[as stated] in the passage beginning, "four are to be abandoned by cultivation," and so on.

The vision of the truths occurs by means of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and the cultivation of the truths occurs by means of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); therefore, this is said:
"Now, are these two—the paths of seeing and cultivation—untainted (*anāsrava*) or tainted (*sāsrava*)?
The connection is that this introduces the exposition of the paths.
"Because it is the antidote to the three realms" refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
If it were mundane (*laukika*), it would not be the antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Furthermore, it is because of the simultaneous abandonment of the nine categories of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing.

It is not like the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga). For the mundane [path] does not possess this capacity regarding the abandonment of the three realms (traidhātuka) and the abandonment of the various categories (prakāra).

If supramundane [wisdom] has the power to abandon the nine types [of afflictions] all at once, then it would follow that those [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) must also be abandoned all at once by the supramundane [wisdom]. Thus,
it is restricted that abandonment occurs all at once only by the supramundane [wisdom].
But it is not the case that there is abandonment all at once solely by means of the supramundane [path]; therefore, that consequence does not arise.
For the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) are firm because they possess a real objective basis (*savastukatva*).
Consequently, even by means of the supramundane [path], there is no abandonment of these [afflictions] all at once.
"Otherwise, however" means:
if the exposition were not intended to follow the order of realization (*abhisamaya*).
The prior explanation of causes is the explanation of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*). This is because, in the world, causes are perceived first,
as is the case with the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and so forth.
For example, there is a teaching of the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and so forth that conforms to their actual arising. For the application of mindfulness to the body arises first—
either because its object is coarse, or because its activity ranges from the coarse to the subtle, or because it exists as the prior cause and subsequent fruit.

Then follows the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), and then the application of mindfulness to the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*); such is the teaching of these [foundations] in accordance with their arising.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the teaching of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and so forth, is also in accordance with their arising.
"For some, it is conducive to exposition" means it is conducive to demonstration and conducive to comprehension,
as in the case of the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa).
In each of the dark and light fortnights, there is a distinction between what has arisen and what has not arisen.
For that which has arisen is easy to understand, whereas that which has not arisen is not;
or rather, the dark fortnight is easily understood by those beings who are to be trained.
How does one generate desire, exert effort, arouse energy, uplift the mind, and apply oneself to the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen?
One generates desire for the non-arising of those [states] that have not yet arisen, as described previously.
"One generates desire for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen," as before;
"one generates desire for the stability and non-confusion of those that have already arisen," as before.
For there is no fixed rule that one must first generate desire for the abandoning of those [unwholesome states] that have already arisen.
"Later, for the sake of the non-arising of those [dharmas] that have not yet arisen.
What then? Previously, one generates the desire for the sake of the non-arising of those [dharmas] that have not yet arisen.
"And for the sake of abandoning those that have arisen later"—this is the illustrative example.
In this same way, the white side (the path) should also be applied.

However, he shows that because the truths follow the sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), there would be the consequence of teaching the truths of suffering and origin in reverse order—namely, origin first and suffering later—due to the temporal priority and posteriority of cause and effect.
"For that to which one is attached" refers to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
"By which one is oppressed" refers to that very same [truth].
"And from which [one seeks] liberation" means from that very same Truth of Suffering;
that very [Truth] is what is considered first during the stage of application.
Why is this so? He says:
"In the stage of investigation, in the stage of examination, and in the stage conducive to penetration"—this is the meaning. "Having seen the disease," and so forth.
Disease is the analogy for the truth of suffering;
its cause is the truth of origination;
and its cessation is the truth of cessation.
That medicine is a simile for the truth of the path.
This is also the illustration for the truths in the Sūtra, namely,
the *Vyādhyādi-sūtra*.
How so?
A physician who is a remover of arrows, endowed with four qualities, becomes worthy of a king, fit for a king, and is reckoned as a member of the royal entourage.
With which four?
He is skilled regarding illness,
skilled regarding the origination of illness,
and skilled regarding the abandonment of illness.
And he is skilled in ensuring that the disease once abandoned does not arise again in the future.
In the same way, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with four qualities, is called the unsurpassed physician who extracts the arrow.
With which four?
In this regard, monks, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, understands as it truly is: "This is the noble truth of suffering;
this is the origin of suffering;
this is the cessation of suffering."
"One understands, as it truly is, that 'this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
"Due to prior momentum" means due to prior projection.
"Like the unimpeded gallop of a horse on familiar ground.
Just as a horse gallops without obstruction once the ground has been seen, so it is in this case.
Some read "like the running of a horse" (*aśvadhāvanavat*). They explain that *dhāv* is a different verbal root (*prakṛtyantara*),
because the root *iṇ* has the meaning of "awakening" (*bodhana*).
Every verb meaning "to go" also has the sense of "to understand.
By the word "also" in the phrase "even substantially," it is shown that [it also applies] "even nominally.
[The reason is] "because it is not erroneous."
Because that is non-erroneous for both the noble ones and others;
it is suffering alone and not otherwise,
just as these truths are perceived by the noble ones.
They were seen thus:
the truth of suffering as suffering, as impermanent, as empty, and as non-self;
and so on, up to the path as the path, as correct, as practice, and as leading to liberation.
These have not been seen in this way by others who are non-noble;
therefore, these are called the truths of the noble ones, but they are not called the truths of the non-noble ones.
Why?
Because of their perverted view.
For they perceive the truth of suffering through such modes as "suffering is not suffering," and so forth.
By means of [the contemplations] such as "origination as non-origination," and so forth;
"cessation as non-cessation," and so forth;
and "the path as non-path," and so forth.
"Others know it as suffering" means that,
for example, fools are distressed by the truth of cessation, as if they were falling from a precipice because there will be no further rebirth.
But the Noble Ones know [them] as suffering;
thus, the five aggregates of clinging are the two truths for the Noble Ones.
Because of seeing the truth of the origin of suffering without error, there are two noble [factors]:
by virtue of being wholesome and being untainted.
And they are the truths of the noble ones because of their non-erroneous vision.
Thus, by the rule of retaining only one term (*ekaśeṣa*), it becomes "the Noble Truths" (*āryasatyāni*).

(VI.3) When it is said that "a portion of feeling has suffering as its intrinsic nature," this means that a portion of the aggregate of feeling has the intrinsic nature of physical pain (*duḥkha*) and mental distress (*daurmanasya*),
without exception, according to their respective applications.
Thus,
even agreeable things are suffering due to the suffering of change and the suffering of conditioned formations;
disagreeable things are suffering due to the suffering of suffering and the suffering of conditioned formations.
The meaning of "as appropriate" is that those other than these are suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) alone.
They are called "agreeable" (*manaāpa*) because they are pleasing to the mind.
Furthermore, it has been explained here that there is a re-composition of the compound.
"Other than those" means other than the pleasant and the unpleasant.

"The three feelings in their respective order" means that pleasant feeling is the pleasant, painful feeling is the unpleasant, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is neither pleasant nor unpleasant; this is the meaning.
"By virtue of that" means by virtue of feeling (*vedanā*).
Even though visible forms, sounds, and so forth do not have the nature of feeling, they receive designations such as "agreeable" because they are conducive to it.
"Suffering through transformation" means [suffering] through the transformation of impermanence, as it has been said:
"Alas, Caitraratha! Alas, the pond! Alas, Mandākinī! Alas, my beloved!"
"Thus, even while lamenting in distress, the gods fall to the earth"—
this is because [existence] has suffering as its very nature.
The meaning is: "by way of having a nature that causes affliction.
Painful sensation is painful in its arising and painful in its persistence. But does this not imply, by logical necessity, that it is pleasant in its transformation?
And if that were the case, there would be a confusion of definitions.
This is not its definition;
rather, this instruction is for the purpose of disparagement.
Alternatively, let it be exactly as stated here: that which is criticized in a certain form, it is precisely that [form] which is being considered.
It is indeed suffering.
