Just as a pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*), although it is pleasant because its arising and duration are pleasant, is nonetheless reviled as suffering due to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), since it is intended to be reviled;
so too, [all conditioned things] are suffering by virtue of their very nature as conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
The meaning is: "by means of conditioning alone" and "by means of arising alone.
That which is impermanent is suffering.
That which is not fixedly established is suffering;
that which moves and perishes is suffering.
The meaning is that it is suffering;
therefore, it was said:
"because of being conditioned by conditions."
Because it is conditioned by conditions,
it is therefore suffering.
Just as with feeling, so too should the formations that are to be felt be understood.
The suffering of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are to be experienced as pleasant consists in their transformation.
Pleasant conditioned phenomena are pleasant at the time of their arising, pleasant during their duration, and painful through their transformation.
The suffering of conditioned phenomena that are to be experienced as painful consists in their very nature of being experienced as painful.
Formations to be experienced as suffering are suffering by way of their arising and suffering by way of their persistence.
For formations to be experienced as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, their nature as suffering consists in the very fact of being conditioned formations, because they are produced through conditions.
"That which is impermanent is suffering.
Suffering itself is the state of suffering; this is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).

Because of the word "up to" (*yāvat*), it should be stated that transformation itself is suffering, which is the "suffering of transformation" (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); and conditioned phenomena themselves are suffering, which is the "suffering of conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
This alternative formulation is distinguished only by its grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) and not by its meaning;
for that very same meaning must be understood here.
"Because they are not common," and so forth.
Agreeable conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are not common to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).
Therefore, because they are not common [to that], the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) is predicated of them.
And those things that are unpleasant are unique instances of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
Therefore, because they are unique, they are said to be the "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
However, all things—whether pleasant and so forth—are suffering by way of the "suffering of conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), because that [suffering] is all-pervasive.
If all are likewise subject to suffering, why do not all perceive [it] as the suffering of change? To this he says: "Only the Noble Ones perceive that, not others.
How so? This is introduced, and he says everything here.

"If that is so," [it means]: if all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), then it would follow that even the Path (*mārga*) is suffering, because it is conditioned—that is, because it is produced by conditions. For according to the definition, "suffering is that which is disagreeable," the Path is not suffering.
Why is this being said differently?
Previously it was stated that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent because they are produced through conditions; and whatever is impermanent...
"That is suffering.
And since the path is conditioned by causes and conditions, it is impermanent;
therefore, it would follow that it is suffering.
For if repulsiveness alone were intended as the definition of suffering,
then what was previously stated would lack that definition;
yet, if that [previously stated] is indeed the definition of the nature of suffering, [then repulsiveness alone is insufficient].
"This is without characteristics.
This is not a fault. How so?

That which is impermanent and disagreeable to the Noble Ones is suffering; this is the intended meaning here. Furthermore, what is impermanent and disagreeable to the Noble Ones? It is any conditioned thing (sāsrava-vastu) that is subject to outflows.
Why, then, is the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), although likewise impermanent, not disagreeable to the Noble Ones (*ārya*)? To this he says:
"For its arising is not disagreeable to the Noble Ones, because it brings about the destruction of all suffering.
For even when a statement is made without qualification, a specific distinction is observed in common worldly usage.
For example, one is called a "cow" because of its going; yet a buffalo does not become a cow simply because it also goes.
Thus, when the meaning is fixed, the term "cow" applies to a certain thing. Why does it apply?
Because it goes.
In the same way here as well, whatever thing is with-outflows (sāsrava) is disagreeable to the noble ones (ārya).
Why?
"Because of impermanence" means that very thing which has been viewed as suffering;
it is a contaminated entity (*sāsrava-vastu*).
It should be understood that they perceive the cessation of that very [suffering] as peace, and not that of the path;
it is like the designation "a heap of mung beans" even when mung beans are present among them.

Just as when there is a heap of beans (*māṣa*) in which mung beans, lentils, peas, and so forth are also present, it is observed in common usage that it is designated a "heap of beans" because the mung beans and others are few; so it is here.
[This refers to] "by means of the subtle atom of pleasure from sprinkling."
That which is both pleasant and subtle is "subtle pleasure" (*sukhāṇuka*).
Subtle pleasure resulting from sprinkling is "subtle pleasure of sprinkling" (*pariṣekasukhāṇuka*).
It is for this reason that he said, "Indeed, even... (*khalv api*).
The venerable Kumāralāta [states] that it is because [the aggregates] are a continuity of suffering and because they are the cause of suffering.
Pleasure is the cause of suffering because it is associated with karma that is to be experienced as suffering,
and because it is produced by no small amount of sufferings;
for pleasure arises as something produced by exceedingly many sufferings, such as those consisting of service to others and similar tasks.
And because that [pleasure] is desired only when suffering exists;
for it is only when suffering caused by hunger, thirst,
and so forth exists that pleasure produced by food, drink, and so forth is desired.
Not otherwise.
Therefore, for these reasons,
they determine that what is [actually] suffering is pleasure.
"But together with pleasure" (*sahaiva tu sukhena*).
The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of setting aside the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
[The reason is] "because [all conditioned phenomena] have the single flavor of the suffering of conditioned existence" (*saṃskāraduḥkhataikarasatvāt*).
Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have only one mode of suffering (*duḥkhatā*).
How, then, can it be said that [feeling] has the nature of pleasure?
How do they perceive feeling, which does not have the nature of suffering, as being suffering?
"Because it is disagreeable due to impermanence.
The meaning is that because of its impermanence, it is disagreeable; and because it is disagreeable, they view it as suffering.
This is just as in the case of form, perception, and so forth.
Just as they see form, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as suffering,
yet these are not suffering in the same way that painful feeling is.
Because its intrinsic nature is that of an impairment,
or because they possess that as their characteristic.
As for the one who thinks this— it is the Venerable Kumāralāta.
For that venerable one, this would be the aspect of origination (*samudayākāra*) and not the aspect of suffering (*duḥkhākāra*),
because he perceives it as the cause of suffering.
Furthermore, how could the perception of suffering arise for noble non-returners (*anāgāmin*) when they are reborn in the realms of form (*rūpa*) and formlessness (*arūpya*)?
The meaning is that it does not proceed at all.
For those non-returners (anāgāmin), there is no cause for painful feeling—that is, no cause for a painful sensation.
Which ones?
The aggregates belonging to the realms of form and formlessness:
why are they not causes?
Because suffering does not return to those states again.
And for what purpose would the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) have been taught in the Sūtra?
If they perceive even pleasure as suffering because it is a cause of suffering,
then that which was called the "suffering of conditioned formations" refers to that which is impermanent.
"That is suffering.
For what purpose is that [statement]? Because its purpose is established by the very fact of being a cause of suffering.
The proponent of the cause of suffering says:
"If that is so," [it is asked].

If they perceive [things] as suffering because they are impermanent— according to the principle "that which is impermanent is suffering"— and not because they are the cause of suffering, then what is the distinction between the aspect of impermanence and the aspect of suffering?
On this point, the Master says:
"Because it has the nature of arising and passing away," and so forth.
Just as [it is called] suffering because it is contrary [to our desires].
Explaining this accordingly, he says:
"But that which is seen as impermanent becomes disagreeable; thus, the aspect of impermanence draws forth the aspect of suffering.
This is what is meant.
As for what was said— that "whatever is impermanent is suffering"—
it was not stated in this way merely because of the identity of their aspects.
However, for those who perceive that pleasure as impermanent, it becomes disagreeable;
because it is disagreeable, they perceive it as suffering.
"The Ekīyas" refers to the venerable Śrīlāta and others.
"This is the nature of suffering here" means that this is the characteristic of suffering here. Pleasant feeling is to be viewed as suffering.
Furthermore, there is another scriptural passage:
"cold, heat, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth," sourness, sweetness, and the like are included.
They are excessively used, over-consumed,
and used at the wrong time;
for example, cold [foods] in winter and hot [foods] in summer.
"Or by means of equanimity" means by means of the cause of happiness.
The same should be stated regarding the various postures as well.
For it must be stated that those very things, such as beds and so forth, which are desired as causes of pleasure, remain as they are until they reach a state of manifestation; moreover,
this is because the notion of pleasure arises only in response to the alleviation of suffering.
What?
It is the context that "pleasant feeling does not exist," and it concerns the conceptualization of suffering.
What [is the reason]?
Because of the cognition of pleasure;
likewise, there is no such thing as a pleasant feeling.
Explaining that the notion of pleasure is merely the counteracting of suffering, he says:
"For it is not, indeed, pleasure," and so forth.
Explaining this by way of the differentiation of suffering, he says:
"And the fools, regarding the conceptualization of suffering," and so forth.
Carriers of burdens, shifting the load from one shoulder to the other while the burden remains nothing but suffering, give rise to the notion that there is pleasure in the changing of the burden.
And this is precisely the principle, according to the Teacher.
"Sensual pleasure is not dear to the Noble Ones" means that it is undesirable [to them].
"Because it is otherwise undesired" means because it is so by way of other aspects, such as being a basis for negligence (*pramāda*).
Showing that very point, he says:
"For whatever feeling," and so forth.
[It is] "a basis for negligence."
The meaning is: the cause for falling away from the wholesome.
And [it is] that which must be accomplished through great effort and is subject to transformation;
the meaning is that it produces suffering immediately after [the wholesome state], or it produces neither-suffering-nor-happiness.
Or, it means "having fallen into a state of deficiency.
The sense is that it is impermanent and subject to destruction;
however, it is certainly not [deficient] in its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) or form.
For even among the noble ones (*ārya*), there is no disagreement regarding pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) as having the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of being beneficial.

Furthermore, if that pleasant feeling were not intended as beneficial by its own nature, then no one would ever experience attachment (*rāga*) toward that pleasant feeling, just as they do not toward painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*); this is the intended meaning.
"Because [it is] for the sake of dispassion (*vairāgya*).
For this reason—that is, for the sake of dispassion—they should perceive [the body] as faulty even by way of another aspect.
Otherwise, since the absence of passion would be established without effort, the exertion for the sake of dispassion would be useless.
And this statement, "Thus it was said by the Blessed One," is indeed the very wording of the sutra spoken by the Elder Ānanda; for he would have asked thus:
"Whatever is felt..."
Seeing that the statement "whatever is felt here is suffering" was an improper expression, the Elder Ānanda questioned him about that very point;
for he considered it a contradiction to say that "whatever is felt is suffering.
However, had he seen it as an improper expression to say that "there are three feelings," [he would not have asked].
He would have asked exactly this: "With what intention did the Blessed One say that there are three feelings? Is this not a contradiction?
And the Blessed One would have explained it thus: "It was with this intention that I said there are three feelings.
But he did not explain it in that way.
"Ānanda, it was with reference to the impermanence of conditioned phenomena and their subject to change that I said:
'Whatever is felt, all that is here included within suffering.'"
But he did not say that.
Furthermore, because of the mention of the three feelings, there are indeed three feelings by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
However, it was with this intention that I said: "Whatever is felt, that here is suffering. Thus, the Blessed One shows that this statement regarding feeling is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*).
"Whatever is felt here is [of the nature of] suffering" is said with the intention of referring to the transformation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-vipariṇāmatā*).
This is because they possess the quality of transformation and impermanence;
that is, because they possess the quality of transformation and the quality of impermanence.
Furthermore, transformation (*vipariṇāma*) is the state of being otherwise (*anyathātva*).
"Objects of sensual pleasure" (*kāmaguṇa*) is a designation for desirable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
"Upapatti" is also a designation for a desired birth.
Thus, there is a misconception (*viparyāsa*) for one who perceives a rebirth as having little happiness and much suffering, or as having exclusively happiness.
[The phrase] "in accordance with worldly convention" means:
If it is thought that the statement "there are three feelings" is made in conformity with the way the world determines feeling,
that is not the case.
Because of the Blessed One’s statement that this was spoken with a specific intention regarding the fact that all feeling is suffering:

"Ānanda, it was with reference to the impermanence of conditioned phenomena and the transformational nature of conditioned phenomena that I said: 'Whatever is felt, that here is [included in] suffering. Therefore, the statement that there are three types of feeling was not made merely in accordance with worldly convention.
What then?
The intention is that [it is determined] by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇataḥ*). And this is because of the expression "as it really is" (*yathābhūta*).
The statement that there are three feelings was not made merely in conformity with worldly convention.
How so? He says:
"That which is the faculty of pleasure and that which is the faculty of mental joy."
"This feeling is to be seen as pleasant," having been stated in detail;
that which is the faculty of pain and that which is the faculty of mental grief.

"This feeling is painful," namely the faculty of equanimity; "this feeling is neither-painful-nor-pleasant"—having spoken thus in detail, [it is said]: "by whom these five faculties have been seen thus as they really are with right wisdom."
This is the proof here for the actual existence of the three types of feeling:
because [the Buddha taught] "as it truly is," there is an absence of both superimposition and denial.

Furthermore, how could the world determine that painful feeling is of three kinds—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant—given that, by virtue of having suffering as its intrinsic nature, the determination would necessarily be only that it is suffering?
"In weak, intense, and moderate [degrees]," and so forth. Now,

if it is thought that there is a perception of pleasure in weak suffering, a perception of suffering in intense [suffering], and a perception of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure in moderate [suffering],
we say this in reply:
"Because pleasure is also of three kinds," and so forth.
Due to the distinction of weak, medium, and intense, there would be a perception of intense, medium, and weak pleasure in relation to weak, medium, and intense sufferings;
that is to say, there would be a perception of intense, medium, and weak pleasure.
How so?
When suffering is mild, there is the perception of intense pleasure;
when it is moderate, there is the perception of moderate pleasure.
[The claim that] there is a perception of mild pleasure within intense [suffering] is untenable; for it is not logical to have a perception of mild pleasure when suffering is intense.
What is the reason?
That suffering would not be intense at all if there were a perception of mild pleasure therein.
And if there is a perception of intense pleasure within a mild suffering, how can that suffering be considered mild?
For it is not logical that a clearly manifest experience should be mild in such a way.
Observing that the experience of pleasure follows immediately after the neither-painful-nor-pleasant state, he says: "When [pleasure] arises from a specific odor, taste, or tangible object.
For you, the intermediate state of suffering is what constitutes the neither-painful-nor-pleasant state.
It is not of a mild degree.
Therefore, it must be stated:
what kind of suffering has become mild such that the perception of pleasure arises toward it?
For that pleasure arises solely through the power of the object,
either by the power of the immediately preceding condition of mild suffering or by the power of the immediately preceding condition of intense suffering.
Furthermore, if you maintain that there is a perception of pleasure in mild suffering:
"And when that slight suffering has not arisen or has perished":
when that slight suffering has not arisen or has perished,
there would be an even greater perception of pleasure, because of the complete disappearance of suffering.
Because suffering has been eliminated without remainder.
For you would desire the notion of happiness even when suffering has been eliminated only partially; how much more so, then, when it has been eliminated entirely—this is the intended meaning.
The same should be said regarding the manifestation of sensual pleasure. Just as the pleasure born from specific odors, tastes, and tangibles was described,
so too should it be described regarding the manifestation of sensual pleasure.
How so?

When the suffering of passion is slight, there arises the perception of sensual pleasure. If that suffering of passion were not present or had already ceased, there would be even greater sensual pleasure.
"And this is not seen. "And how indeed... and so forth.
How indeed could this be tenable?
"That which is felt mildly" means that which is felt as mild suffering;
it should be stated that what is grasped is an intense experience.
[In this case,] pleasure is grasped.
"Furthermore, in the middle, it is 'unmanifest' (avyakta).
This means that in the middle [degree] of suffering, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is grasped.
The intention is that in mild suffering, it must be unmanifest by virtue of that [feeling].
"And in the three," and so forth.
This is because pleasure is mentioned in the first, second, and third dhyānas;
for it is stated in the Sūtra that "therein is pleasant feeling."
There would be mild suffering.
What is the reason?
Because it is your intention that there is a perception of pleasure in regard to mild suffering.
Because the Sūtra speaks of neither-pain-nor-pleasure in the fourth dhyāna above that and in the formless realms (ārūpya),
there would have to be intermediate suffering.
Why?
Because of your own position that there is "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" feeling in the middle [level] of suffering,
it is therefore not logical to establish the classification of pleasant and other feelings in relation to mild and other degrees of suffering.
For how indeed could there be mild suffering in the lower dhyānas?
Furthermore, it is logical that the middle [feeling] occurs in the higher realms.
As for the passage, "If form, Mahānāman..."—

if form, Mahānāman, were exclusively suffering, and were not pleasant, nor accompanied by pleasure, nor mental ease, nor accompanied by mental ease, nor experienced as pleasure, then its cause would not even be discerned.
Regarding form, there is passion.
Since, therefore, form exists as pleasant and accompanied by pleasure, as stated before, a cause for form is thus discerned, namely, passion.
To the objection that "this is because the cause of pleasure is not established," we reply:
If, for you, pleasure does not exist because the cause of pleasure is not established,
then suffering would also be non-existent because the cause of suffering is not established.
Furthermore, the cause of pleasure is indeed established.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"For [the cause] depends upon a specific basis," and so forth.
For if the object alone were the cause, the cause would indeed be indeterminate.
But the object alone is not the cause;
for the specific nature of the substratum is also a cause. Thus, it is that very same fire.

For example, that very same fire becomes the cause of sweet cooking when the mass of rice grains is in a slightly cooked state, because it is the cause for cooking the desired boiled rice; yet that same fire is the cause of unpalatable cooking [in other states].
The meaning is: "because it is the cause of its burning.
It does not mean, however, that having reached a state of being cooked, it was once the cause of a delicious cooking;
rather, the meaning is that having reached that same state again later, it is no longer the cause of such a delicious cooking.
This is the illustration for the meaning of that aforementioned point of application.
And how is it that [the first three] meditations (*dhyāna*) are not established as causes of pleasure?
For indeed, those very meditations—from the first up to the third—do not become causes of suffering even for those who have entered them for a long period of time.
And regarding the pleasure born of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), for whom would there be a counteraction?
For there is no suffering within the meditative absorptions.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), this also should be stated.
If there were a perception of pleasure in the remedies for suffering,
then, Mahānāman, it would not have been said that "if form were exclusively suffering, and not pleasure, nor accompanied by pleasure," and so forth; rather,
it would have been said that "pleasure itself arises."
That very sensation arises as pleasant;
it is not that a painful sensation is imagined as pleasant,
[but rather] as long as the body remains in such a state.
It is conducive to the arising of pleasure;
for otherwise, if no pleasure born of that other state were to arise until such a bodily state has ceased,
there would subsequently be an even greater perception of pleasure.
"At the end, from what [does it arise]? and so forth is the detailed explanation.
Now, if it is thought: "From what would there be a perception of suffering at the end of drinking, eating, and so on, if its beginning and initial commencement did not exist?
To this we reply:
Due to a specific transformation of the body.
Through the practice of drinking and so forth, a certain specific transformation of the body subsequently arises, such that suffering does not arise during the state in which pleasure is produced,
whereas it does arise at the end.
He asks, "How so?
and replies: "Like the sweetness turning to acidity at the end of wine and other such substances.
Just as wine, milk, and the like undergo such a specific transformation later on.
Just as sourness— that is, acidity— which was previously non-existent in the state of sweetness during the initial stage, arises at the end;
or, for example, how wine and other such substances initially possess sweetness or acidity due to the specific nature of their transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Through a specific transformation produced by medical treatment and medicine, sweetness arises;
and from that very same specific transformation, sourness follows later.
Here, sweetness is an illustration of pleasure.
"Sourness is suffering"—
that which is the truth of the origin is precisely what is being stated here.
Because it is stated that "those which have become causes are the truth of origination," or because in the first chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* it is said:
"Suffering, origination, and the world..."
Because of this statement; for in the Sūtra it is craving alone that is mentioned.
What is the truth of origination?
"That which is craving, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there"—
regarding this, the Vaibhāṣika says:
"Because of its predominance."
Because of the mention of other things as well elsewhere.
Since in another sutra other factors such as karma and ignorance are also mentioned, these others are also the origin (*samudaya*).
In the future life (*abhisaṃparāya*).
"In the future" means in the next world.
Furthermore, it is said elsewhere in a sutra:
"For this reason, monks, there are five kinds of seeds that are unbroken, undamaged, not rotten, not destroyed by wind or sun, fresh, substantial, and well-preserved."
There is the earth element and the water element;
in this way, those seeds attain growth, sprouting, and abundance.
Thus, monks, this simile has been fashioned solely for the purpose of making this matter understood; having introduced this illustration, this was said.

"O monks, 'the five kinds of seeds' is a designation for consciousness accompanied by clinging (*sopādāna-vijñāna*); 'the earth element' is a designation for the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Furthermore, the seed is the cause;
and that which is the cause [is the station]."
That [karma] is the origin (*samudaya*); the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) are also the cause of subsistence (*pratiṣṭhāhetu*).
Therefore—because it is stated that karma and the other factors are also causes—the status of being the truth of origin (*samudayasatya*) is established.

Therefore, it is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*). It is called "intentional" because it exists in the intention, or because it operates by means of the intention; the meaning is that the teaching in the Sūtra was made with reference to a person characterized by craving (*tṛṣṇā*). However, in the Abhidharma, the teaching is "definitional" (*lākṣaṇika*); it is called "definitional" because it exists in the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, the teaching in the Abhidharma is definitional.
"Every contaminated (*sāsrava*) thing is the origin (*samudaya*)," because the five contaminated aggregates (*skandha*) possess the characteristic of being the truth of origin.
That same Vaibhāṣika, wishing to explain that the status of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth as the truth of origin is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), says: "But rather... and so on in detail.
By speaking of the cause of manifestation (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*), the Sūtra stated that the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) is craving (*tṛṣṇā*) alone.
By speaking of the cause of birth and manifestation along with its causes, it stated everything up to karma, craving, and ignorance.
Karma is the cause of birth.
Craving for existences is the cause of actualization.
Furthermore, he states that ignorance is the cause of those two causes—namely, karma and craving.
How is this understood?

In the verse, "the cause of rebirth is karma; the cause of manifestation is craving," it is because of the Sūtra which states, "karma is the cause for rebirth, and craving is the cause for manifestation.
This is because of the statement in another Sūtra.
"With cause and with condition," and so forth;
in this sutra, either sequentially or by way of the succession of causes.
This is the explanation in the verse:
karma, craving, and ignorance are the causes for the formative forces (saṃskāras), such as the eye and so forth, in the future life.
This is what is meant by that statement.
"Karma is the cause for rebirths. This is from that sūtra, or from the *Sahetusapratyayakrama-sūtra*.
"This is the meaning of the verse as follows:
'How, monks, does the eye have a cause, a condition, and a source? And what, monks, is the cause of the eye? What [is its condition]? "
What is the condition? What is the cause?
Monks, for the eye, karma is the cause.
Karma is the condition, karma is the cause.
And karma, monks, also has a cause, a condition, and a cause.
And what, monks, is the cause of karma?
What is the condition?
What is the cause?
Monks, craving is the cause of karma.
Craving is the condition;
craving is the cause.
Monks, craving has a cause, has a condition, and has a source.
And what, monks, is the cause of craving? What is its condition? What is its source?
Monks, craving has ignorance as its cause,
ignorance as its condition,
and ignorance as its source.
"Monks, ignorance also has a cause, has a condition, and has a source.
And what, monks, is the cause of ignorance? What is its condition? What is its source?"
"Monks, improper mental attention is the cause of ignorance;
improper mental attention is its condition;
improper mental attention is its source."
By explaining the nature of the seed and the field, consciousness and the other factors are also described: consciousness is the seed, and its field consists of the aggregates such as sensation;
these too have been declared to be the truth of origination.
It has been established that the teaching in the Sūtra is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), meaning that it is not only craving and so forth [that are the origin];
rather, all suffering possesses the nature of being an origin (*samudaya*) by its very definition (*lākṣaṇika*).
This is according to the distinctions of types such as the various modes of birth (*yoni*) and so on.
By the word "etc. (ādi), the distinctions of types such as birth, female, male, and so forth are understood.
By "without distinction" (abhedeneti) is meant [the lack of distinction] regarding the realms, destinies, modes of birth, and so on.

"Of these two, respectively" means that karma is the cause of rebirth (*upapatti*), while craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the cause of actualization (*abhinirvṛtti*). "Just as a seed," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
A rice seed is the cause for the production of a rice sprout, a barley seed is the cause for the production of a barley sprout, and so forth;
water, however, is [the cause] without distinction,
such as being the cause for the growth of a rice sprout.
The same applies to the sprout of barley and so forth.
Therefore, since those [conditions] are the cause for the mere growth of all sprouts, there is no birth in the absence of craving;
this is the proof here.
Craving is the cause of birth, because its presence or absence results in the presence or absence of birth,
just as a seed is the cause of a sprout.
Explaining the meaning of the phrase "and because of the bending of the continuum," he says:
"And where there is craving," and so forth.
This means: in whatever object, such as form and so on, there is craving.
What is it? It is the mental continuum. Therein, we observe the mental continuum repeatedly inclining [toward that object].
"Therefore, it is likewise even in rebirth.
This means that in rebirth as well, the continuum of consciousness accompanied by craving bends toward [that new existence];
therefore, it inclines toward it.
And we determine that it proceeds toward that which it inclines toward;
and here, the means of accomplishment (sādhana) proceeds.
The mental continuum continues into a future existence because it is accompanied by craving,
just like the objects such as form and so forth.
"Like a limb smeared with dried lentil bath-powder. Here, *masūra* refers to the bath-powder; its application is what is meant by "dried."
"Having a coating of dried lentil powder for bathing" refers to a limb that has been smeared with a coating of dried lentil powder;
it is just like a limb not grasped by a coating of dried lentil powder for bathing.
Thus it is shown that the personal existence [arises] through craving;
this is the reasoning.
"Craving is the cause of production.
(VI.4) In this context, both [truths] are truths; thus, as an incidental discussion on the truths, this is stated:
"like a jar and water."
Thus.
The presentation of two examples is for the purpose of demonstrating two types of division.
And jars and the like are those that divide at the point of contact.
And water and so forth are "dividers of cognition.
This is because it is impossible to extract taste and other qualities from water and such substances by means of a physical process.
Alternatively, conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is of two kinds.

It relies on another convention and relies on another substance. Among these, regarding that which relies on another convention, both differentiation and the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) are possible.
However, in that case which depends upon a distinct substance, only the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is possible, not differentiation (*bheda*).
For it is impossible to effect a separation of parts in an atom composed of eight substances.
"Conventionally existent" means existent by way of worldly convention. "Ultimately existent" means... [existent in the ultimate sense].
"Existent in the ultimate sense" means existent by way of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
In this same manner, feeling and the other [aggregates] are also to be regarded.
Feeling, volition, perception, and so forth should also be regarded as substantially existent.
How so?
Because when one excludes the phenomena of feeling and the rest through the intellect, the intellect still functions with respect to the intrinsic nature of feeling.
Feeling exists as a substantial reality (*dravyasat*).
The same applies to perception, volition, and so forth.
When people say, "There is a jar" and "There is water," they speak the truth.
"It is not false.
This shows the purpose for speaking in terms of conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).
And it has been said:
The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths:
the conventional truth of the world and the truth of the ultimate meaning.
Likewise, there is "ultimate truth" (*paramārthasatya*).
The object (*artha*) of the supreme knowledge (*parama-jñāna*) is the ultimate object (*paramārtha*);
that which is both the ultimate object and truth is ultimate truth, as it is apprehended by another [type of] knowledge, namely, worldly knowledge.
Likewise is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
It is called conventional truth because it is apprehended through convention, through worldly discourse, or through cognition—whether afflicted or unafflicted.
For for the practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*), reality is threefold.
[It is] existent in the ultimate sense and conventionally existent, and substantially existent.
"Substantially existent" means existent by way of substance, that is, existent by way of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
(VI.5) One who abides in conduct...
Thus is the detailed explanation.
Conduct (*vṛtta*) is ethical discipline (*śīla*).
It is the cause for non-attachment, the cause for non-distraction, and the cause for proper behavior.
"Conducive to the vision of the truths" means that one retains and recites whatever has been heard concerning the subject of the vision of the truths;
or one hears the meaning, that is, one cognizes that meaning through the gateway of the ear.
How so?
Demonstrating that the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*) has both as its object, he says:
"Sometimes one draws out the meaning by means of the phrasing."
By means of a name produced from phonemes (*vyañjana*), one draws out the meaning: "This is the meaning of this name. Sometimes one draws out the phonemes by means of the meaning:
"These are the phonemes and name for this expressed meaning"—this is the sense.
For this term *vyañjana* is employed here in the sense of "name" (*nāman*).
It is also stated in the Sūtra:
"having good meaning and good phrasing" (*svarthaṃ suvyañjanam*).
Regarding this conception, the Master explains at length that wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*) would not be established;
for a definition is being stated that is conflated with the characteristics of wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī*) and wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*).
It is not established that it is "unmixed.
Regarding the phrase "born from reasoned contemplation": reasoned contemplation means thorough investigation by means of reasoning.
"Born from that":
because the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed in the sense of a cause (*hetu*),
authoritative speech (*āptavacana*) is the cause of the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*).
In this context, the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed.

Wisdom that has hearing as its cause is "consisting of hearing" (*śrutamayī*). Likewise, reflection that consists of reasoning is "contemplation," which is the cause of wisdom consisting of contemplation (*cintāmayī*).
Because the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed here.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is the cultivation (*bhāvanā*), together with its cause, for that which consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
Here, the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed.
This is because of the grammatical rule *tatprakṛtivacane mayaṭ*, or because of the rule *tasya vikāraḥ*; however,
this "transformation" (*vikāra*) is merely figurative.
Just as there is a modification of "hearing" (*śruta*) in the term *śrutamayī*, another definition must also be added,
because we observe such usage in the world as "the vital breaths consist of food" (*annamaya*) and "cows consist of grass" (*tṛṇamaya*).
(VI.6–8) [This is] because of the removal of association with unwholesome discursive thoughts (*akuśalavitarka*).
The distancing from social contact is that which consists in dwelling in solitude;
therefore, one becomes physically withdrawn.
The distancing from unwholesome discursive thoughts is the avoidance of afflicted discursive thoughts.
Therefore, one is withdrawn by means of the mind.
"Distress regarding what has been obtained that is unexcellent or insufficient" means that distress is mental unease (*daurmanasya*).
Therefore, one is distressed;
the meaning is that one is exhausted.
This is due to its being unexcellent or because it is insufficient.

According to the Master’s view, dissatisfaction (*asaṃtuṣṭi*) is the distress felt over what has already been obtained; whereas great desire (*mahecchatā*) is the longing and craving for what has not yet been obtained, whether it be excellent or abundant. Furthermore, these two [mental factors] belong exclusively to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).
Because its intrinsic nature is unwholesome greed,
the delight in abandonment and cultivation— that is, the delight in cessation and the path—
is not of the nature of contentment.

How is it that this fourth noble lineage (āryavaṃśa) also has non-attachment (alobha) as its intrinsic nature? To this he says: "Because of turning away from attachment to existence and attachment to sensual pleasures.
That is, because of turning away from attachment to existence (bhavarāga).
And because of the turning away from sensual desire. Turning away is non-greed (*alobha*).
[This refers to those] who have abandoned their own livelihoods and occupations.

"From those who have abandoned their own livelihoods and from those who have abandoned their own occupations. In this context, "livelihood" (*vṛtti*) refers to that by which one lives, such as food and drink;
"occupation" (*karmānta*) refers to agriculture, crafts, and so forth.
"Thus, for the sake of existence and non-existence.
The word "thus" (iti) indicates the various modes of existence and non-existence.
Among those, craving regarding the mode of existence is such as: "O, may I become Indra! May I become a universal monarch (cakravartin)! and so forth.
Craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) is also craving for annihilation (*vināśatṛṣṇā*), such as thinking:
"O, may I be cut off! May I not exist after death! and so forth.
(Abhidh-k-vy 526)

(VI.9) "Smṛta" means simply "mindfulness" (*smṛti*). This indicates that the suffix *kta* is prescribed here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). An "entrance" (*avatāra*) is a ford (*tīrtha*), by which one enters [the stream].

"One whose conduct is dominated by passion is extremely close [to it]" means that for one in whom passion arises quickly even with a slight stimulus, he is one whose conduct is dominated by passion and who is very close to it.
One for whom passion is excessive is one whose conduct is excessively characterized by passion (*rāgacarita*).
This is because [such a person] lacks a diverse range of objects.
Because in the case of air, no variety of color or shape is perceived;
because it is not directed outward but inward.
This [meditation] conduces to the cutting off of discursive thought (*vitarka*); this is the subject under discussion.
"Because of the close contemplation of that object" means because of the discernment of the visual object.
In the phrase "having the aspect of the livid corpse and so forth as its focal point," the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the festering corpse and the others.
"Vipaṭumaka" refers to that in which worms have arisen.
There are four kinds of objects of desire (*rāgavastu*), consisting of color, shape, touch, and service. These do not exist [in the formless realm].
"Because it is a mental attention characterized by resolute belief and partiality.
This means because it is a mental attention consisting of resolute belief (*adhimukti*) and because it is a partial mental attention (*prādeśika*).
This mental attention has resolute belief as its primary feature.
And "limited" means that it is not all-pervasive;
for the meditation on the foul does not have the five aggregates as its object,
nor does it have all stages as its object.
What then?
It has as its object a portion of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), because of that state.
The meaning is that by means of the foul (aśubhā) there is no abandonment of the afflictions (kleśa), but rather only their suppression (viṣkaṃbhaṇa).

Because of the statement, "One binds the mind to the parts of one's own body," [the practitioner does not yet focus] on the parts of a woman's body, since at the very time of practice, the causes of passion have been avoided.
"Purifying the bones":
removing the flesh from the bones, one perceives the entire skeleton.
As it has been said:
"If a newly ordained monk, still a learner whose mind has not yet attained [liberation],
desires to destroy passion, he should go to the cemetery."
Then one should see the livid corpse; then one should see the festering corpse;
then one should see the bloated corpse, and even the skeleton.
Herein, briefly stated, the practitioner of yoga engaged in the meditation on the foul is of three types.
There are three types: the beginner, the one who has achieved mastery, and the one who has transcended mental application.

Among these, the beginner practitioner (yogācāra) with a concentrated mind fixes his attention on a single big toe; he perceives that big toe as becoming moist, and through this, he resolves upon [the visualization] of the flesh and so forth, until the entire body becomes a skeleton of bones.
One who has achieved mastery likewise [extends the visualization] up to half a skull.
One whose mental application has transcended likewise holds the mind between the eyebrows up to that point.
However, one with a mind that expands [the object] extends the bones as far as the ocean; one who contracts it is a beginner. Thus, there are three types, beginning with these.

And having established it thus, there arises a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) question, as in the detailed explanation beginning with "of those whose mental application is mastered and unmastered.

The first alternative is the meditation on the foul (aśubhā) of one whose mental application is mastered, which has one's own body as its object; it is "limited" by virtue of the limitation of its object, because the body is small.
It is not [limited] by way of the limitedness of mastery (*vaśitā*), because the mental application has been mastered; that is to say, because the mental application has been transcended.
The second alternative is the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) with the ocean as its limit for one whose mental application is not yet mastered.
It is "limited" (*parītta*) by way of the limitedness of mastery, because the mental application has not been mastered.
It is not limited by way of its object, because its object extends as far as the ocean.
The third alternative is the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) that has one's own body as its object for one whose mental attention is not yet mastered;
it is limited also by way of its object, because the body is small.
It is also not limited by way of mastery because the mental attention has not been conquered.
The fourth alternative is the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) of one whose mental attention has been conquered, which has the ocean as its limit for its object;
it is not limited by way of the limitation of the object, because its object extends as far as the ocean.
Nor [is it] due to a limitation of mastery, because he has conquered mental attention (manaskāra).

(VI.12) "In the preparatory stages (sāmantaka), the intermediate dhyāna, and the [four] dhyānas": this refers to the ten stages, namely, the four preparatory stages, the intermediate dhyāna, the four dhyānas, and the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Because there are four preparatory stages (sāmaṃtaka) of the dhyānas.
For this very reason, it is said that "it has the object as its focal point" (arthālambanā);
because it takes color and shape as its focal points, it has the object as its focal point.
The intention is that it does not have the name as its object.
The intention is that since it is already established by the name itself as having the aspect of the foul (*aśubhākāra*), the meaning of the aspect need not be stated separately in the Sūtra.
"Belonging to which time, it has that time as its object."
Just as with visual consciousness, the past [consciousness] has only the past as its object, and likewise up to the present [consciousness], which has only the present as its object.
This is because it is restricted to its own specific object.
It is not set forth in a formal sutra because it consists of mental attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
"Because of being habitual or non-habitual":
in the beginningless and vast cycle of saṃsāra, it is acquired through detachment because it is habitual;
it is acquired through application because it is non-habitual.
(VI.13) The applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), such as that of the body, have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This is because they function through the support of its power.

Since these—namely, the application of mindfulness of the body and so forth—function by means of the support of the power of that mindfulness, they are called "applications of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*); thus, the entities of the wisdom of the body and so forth are designated as "applications of mindfulness."

In the same way, because it functions by sustaining the power of mindfulness regarding the wisdom of inhalation and exhalation, it is called "mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation" (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
Regarding the phrase "in five stages":
this refers to the three preliminary concentrations (*sāmantaka*), excluding the fourth preliminary concentration.
In the intermediate dhyāna and in the desire realm— thus in five stages. What is the reason?
Because it is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
For in the preliminary stages (*sāmaṃtaka*) and so forth of the first dhyāna, there is the feeling of equanimity;
whereas in the preliminary stage of the fourth dhyāna, although equanimity exists, [the feeling is not exclusively that].
But that [state] is not the ground for inhalation and exhalation.
Now, for what reason is this equanimity determined to be associated with it alone?
To this he says: "Because it is conducive to discursive thought (*vitarka*)."
There is no association with those two— pleasure and pain— with mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), which is the antidote to them and the antidote to discursive thought (*vitarka*).
This is because pleasure and mental joy (*saumanasya*) are obstacles to focused attention, as they are contrary to the application of the mind (*ābhoga*).
And because that mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) is to be accomplished through focused attention (avadhāna), there is no association with those two [vitarka and vicāra].
It is said (kila) that this is because [the latter] are conducive to discursive thought (vitarka).
The word *kila* indicates the opinion of another. Therefore, this alternative position is introduced with the words "But those who [say] regarding the fundamental [stages]," and so forth.
By "another" [is meant the opponent].
Starting from the fourth dhyāna,
it has the desire realm as its basis because of the abundance of vitarka therein.
That which is acquired through application (*prāyogikī*) is due to lack of habituation; that which is acquired through detachment (*vairāgyalābhikī*) is due to habituation.
"Of these phenomena" (*idaṃdharmāṇām*).

"This dharma belongs to these Buddhists" means "those who possess this dharma" (*idamdharman*); the meaning is that they belong specifically to those Buddhists. [The phrase] "due to the absence of instruction" [is used].

For there is instruction in breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) for outsiders, but no instruction in mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*). Furthermore, it is because outsiders lack the realization of subtle phenomena on their own;
that is, since outsiders do not possess the self-realization of subtle phenomena in the absence of instruction.
Furthermore, its subtlety is due to being endowed with six causes.
"Having disregarded the body or the mind" means not being attached to them.
"The distance of a span or a fathom" [is the range].
Due to the connection with beings who are either strong or weak,
it descends as far as the wind-circle below,
and [it extends] upwards to the Vairambha winds.
Because this involves mental attention to reality (*tattvamanasikāra*), it is not tenable [to claim] that this extends as far as the wind-circle and the Vairambha winds.
Such a conceptualization would be appropriate for mental attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanaskāra*).
"Are these beneficial, up to being warm?"—
this should be understood as a mere setting aside (sthāpanā),
because it is merely a setting aside of specific qualities such as being beneficial with respect to a particular part of the body.
"Mind and mental factors are dependent upon that" means that their activity is bound to that.
"In successive roots of virtue" refers to those that follow one after another.
"In the applications of mindfulness, the stages of heat, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "in the path of seeing and so forth," the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is included.
"Purification consisting of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*) are included.
(VI.14) [The inhalation and exhalation] do not exist where there is no body.

In connection with mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), inhalation and exhalation belonging to all stages (*sarvabhūmika*) are explained. For whichever stage the body belongs to— ranging from the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) up to the stage of the third dhyāna— inhalation and exhalation belong to that same stage.
They do not belong to another stage.
"Dependent upon a distinction of body and mind" means that inhalation and exhalation are dependent upon a distinction of the body and dependent upon a distinction of the mind.
He asks, "Why? and replies:
"Because they are absent in those who have gone to the formless realm (ārūpya) or are in the embryonic stages (kalala) and so forth.
Because of the absence of the body, they do not exist for those who have gone to the formless realm.
And for those who have entered the stages of the *kalala*,
*arbuda*, *peśī*, and so forth, [the faculties] do not exist.
This means that because there is no differentiation of the body and no hollow body, they are absent.
And they do not exist for those without consciousness,
because of the absence of consciousness.
They also do not exist for those who have attained the fourth dhyāna.
Because there is no specific state of mind regarding the stages of inhalation and exhalation.
For this very reason, he said:
"If the body is porous," and so forth.

"Because they are distinct from the sense faculties" means because they function separately from the sense faculties. They are not derived from nourishment (*aupacayika*) because they diminish even as the body increases.
Furthermore, because the inhalations and exhalations that have been severed are reconnected, they are not born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
For this reconnection does not exist for material form that is of the nature of maturation; such reconnection does not occur for material forms like the eye and so forth.
However, the reconnection of non-material mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) is not precluded.

"Not by the [minds] pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*) or the emanated (*nairmāṇika*). Since the mind pertaining to deportment and the emanated mind belonging to a lower stage can manifest even for one born in the fourth dhyāna, this is stated in anticipation of such an objection: "There is no discerning [of objects] by means of those two belonging to a lower stage."
(VI.15, 16) "For the sake of accomplishing insight (*vipaśyanā*).
This means for the sake of accomplishing wisdom (*prajñā*).
For even in one who has attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the afflictions (*kleśa*) are not abandoned without wisdom.
Because of the statement that "the afflictions are to be destroyed by knowledge.
But from what [source] is it known that insight (vipaśyanā) is accomplished through the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness?
From the Sūtra.
"Monks, this is the one-way path, namely the foundations of mindfulness.
This is the entire mass of the wholesome, namely the four foundations of mindfulness," according to this statement. [The cultivation of] body-awareness...
Thus, feeling is discernment; their own-nature (*svabhāva*) is precisely their specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
What is this own-nature?
The body consists of the primary elements and their derivatives; feeling consists of experience;
and mind consists of apprehension.
The intrinsic nature of those other than these three is as it pertains to each.
Regarding "the state of suffering (duḥkhatā) of the contaminated (sāsrava)":
this has been explained as suffering characterized by being disagreeable to the Noble Ones (ārya).
It is said that "phenomena are other than the three" with reference to an unmixed classification;
however, under a mixed classification, the body and so forth are also included.
Furthermore, all phenomena—both conditioned and unconditioned—are to be understood in this way.
The application of mindfulness as intrinsic nature is wisdom (*prajñā*),
because this wisdom is established in dependence upon association and its object.
Therefore, it is called a "foundation of mindfulness.
The qualification "consisting of hearing and so forth" [is added].
Since the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and are not obtained by birth (*upapattilabhya*),
why is it said that their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is wisdom (*prajñā*)?
Is there, then, another kind of application of mindfulness?
It is said:
"Others [arise] from association and objective support."
The others, such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth, which are co-existent with it,
are the application of mindfulness by association (saṃsarga-smṛtyupasthāna),
because of their association with the application of mindfulness by intrinsic nature (svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna).

"Because of having that as its object": the foundation of mindfulness of the object (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*) arises from having the foundations of mindfulness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and association (*saṃsarga*) as its objects.
Others read: "That which has those as its objects is the foundation of mindfulness of the object."
They are called "objects" (ālambana) because they are taken as objects.
Which ones? The body, sensations, mind, and phenomena.
This being so, that foundation of mindfulness which has that as its object consists of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-svabhāva*).
And it was said by the Blessed One:
"O monks, 'all phenomena' is a designation for the four foundations of mindfulness."
For by means of that wisdom, one who possesses it becomes "possessed of wisdom. He is made an "anupaśya" (one who observes closely);
he is called an *anupaśya* because he observes closely (*anupaśyati*).
The suffix *śa* is applied according to the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śa*.
Thus, "one who makes a person perceive" is *anupaśyayati*.
However, when [the term] has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the analysis of the compound is as follows.
The instrument for one who observes is "observing.
For by means of that wisdom, the possessor of it—the wise one—is made an observer.
Just as, through connection with wisdom, a person is called "wise" (prājña).

Thus, because one observes through the application of observation (*anupaśyanā-yoga*), one is called an "observer" (*anupaśyin*); from this, it is established that observation is wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, it was said by the Blessed One:
"He dwells observing the body in the body internally, within himself, as one who contemplates the body."
By this it is also known that "contemplation" (anupaśyanā) is wisdom (prajñā). How so? It is established thus: she possesses contemplation.
What is that? It is vision (darśana).
For that which has the characteristic of seeing is the object of observation;
therefore, the person who observes is like a staff.
Thus, it is a locative tatpuruṣa compound.

"One who contemplates the body is a 'body-contemplator' (*kāyānupaśyī*). Even if the suffix *ṇini* were prescribed in the sense that "one whose habit is to contemplate the body" is a "body-contemplator," we observe that this form is established even so.
[The phrase] "due to the predominance of mindfulness" means:
The meaning is "because of the predominance of mindfulness.
It means "because it functions through the application of the power of mindfulness.
The application of power (*balasyādhānam*) is the exertion of strength.
The strengthening of mindfulness is "strengthening of mindfulness" (*smṛtibalādhāna*).
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is that which functions by means of this strengthening of mindfulness;
its state is [the quality of being such].
Therefore,
just as a split in wood is held together by a sharp wedge driven into it,
so too does this wisdom function toward its object through the support of the power of mindfulness.
For if memory holds the object, then wisdom understands it;

thus, because one "establishes" [the mind] by means of memory, wisdom is called a "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*). This is the meaning according to the Vaibhāṣikas, based on the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, whereby the suffix *-lyuṭ* (ana) occurs even in the sense of the agent.
However, the Master [Vasubandhu] maintains that this [other interpretation] is more logical.
This is an instrumental derivation (*karaṇasādhana*). [The statement] "memory is established by means of this" is merely an illustration of the meaning.
The analysis of the compound should be made as follows:
it is called "application" (*upasthāna*) because one applies oneself by means of it;
the application of mindfulness is "mindfulness-application" (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
He explains how mindfulness is established by means of this [wisdom]:
"Because of the verbalizing of what has been seen.
This is because the object is seen exactly as it is by means of wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is expressed in that very way;
the meaning is that it is grasped by means of mindfulness.
Where, then, does it abide?
Regarding the body up to the mental phenomena:

the application of mindfulness with respect to the body is the application of mindfulness of the body; likewise, up to the application of mindfulness with respect to mental phenomena is the application of mindfulness of mental phenomena.
And just as it is for the foundation of mindfulness by way of intrinsic nature,
so it is also for the foundation of mindfulness by way of association;
for in exactly the same way, mindfulness is established upon the body and so forth by means of wisdom.
"In the same way, it is also by those associated with them.

Now, seeing that the instrumental function (*karaṇatva*) of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as stated in the Sūtra is inconsistent, and wishing to express the meaning through another grammatical relation (*kāraka*), he says:
"But where it is said," and so forth.
Just as the arising and passing away of the body have been explained, so too should they be stated for feeling and the other aggregates.
How so?
From the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling;
from the cessation of contact, there is the disappearance of feeling.
From the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of the mind.
From the cessation of various forms, there is the subsiding of the mind.
From the arising of mental attention (*manasikāra*), there is the arising of phenomena (*dharma*);
from the cessation of mental attention, there is the subsiding of phenomena.
In this sutra, the objects of focus themselves—the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena—are the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
This is because mindfulness is established (*upatiṣṭhate*) upon the body and so forth.
Thus, it is shown that the term is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇasādhana*).
It is called an "application" (upasthāna) because mindfulness (smṛti) attends to this [object].
The application of mindfulness is "mindfulness-application" (smṛtyupasthāna).
In the same way, up to: the applications themselves are the objects of mindfulness, thus the analysis is "dharma-applications of mindfulness" (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
If the object (*ālambana*) were not intended here in this sutra as the foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
the Blessed One would not have spoken thus:
"And how, monks, is there the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness?"
"From the arising of nutriment comes the arising of the body; from the cessation of nutriment comes the passing away of the body," and so forth in detail.
For such a statement would be appropriate only if the body and the other [aggregates] were themselves the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Therefore, it is established that the body and so forth are the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) with respect to their objects.
And their names are according to their objects:

for these foundations of mindfulness, beginning with the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the names are established as "foundation of mindfulness of the body" up to "foundation of mindfulness of phenomena" (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) in dependence upon their respective objects.

Because they take as their objects the continuums of self, other, and both, these applications of mindfulness— beginning with the application of mindfulness to the body— are each of three kinds, individually and one by one, due to taking the continuum of another, the continuum of both, and [the continuum of] oneself as their respective objects.
Because it is stated in the Sūtra.
How so?
"He dwells contemplating the body as a body internally."
Ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
As before, "he dwells observing the body externally" means he is ardent, and so forth.
"He dwells observing the body internally and externally" means as before.
Thus, first of all, there are three modes of the application of mindfulness to the body.

The same threefold application should also be applied in detail to the applications of mindfulness to feelings and so forth, according to the passage: "He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings internally," and so on.
This is because the coarse is perceived first.
The body is coarser than the other three because it is cognizable by the six consciousnesses; therefore,
it is perceived first.
Because feeling is coarse in its mode of activity due to two reasons, it is observed immediately after that [consciousness].
Because they are subtle in their movement and thus difficult to discern, mental factors (dharmas) are subtle; therefore, consciousness is observed before them, and mental factors at the end.
And that is sensual desire;
and that [is] of the mind, meaning that longing for sensation,
because those afflictions have not been abandoned.
That is their lack of self-control.
"Respectively" means that the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is the antidote to the perversion of purity.
The foundation of mindfulness of feeling is the antidote to the inversion of pleasure, [based on the realization]:
"Whatever is felt, that here is suffering.
The foundations of mindfulness of mind are the antidotes to the inversion of permanence.
Because the mind changes rapidly, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) serves as the antidote to the misconception of a self (*ātmaviparyāsa*).

This is because, through the analysis of the composite whole, phenomena are seen to lack the activity of a self; thus, based on the etymological definition of "phenomenon" (*dharma*), there is only a phenomenon, devoid of a self.
Or because of seeing that these phenomena exist individually and separately, and that there is no independent self whatsoever.
"The fourth is of both kinds.

The application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) has an unmixed object (*asaṃbhinnālambana*), meaning it has an unmixed objective support (*amiśrālambana*), because it is possible for it to have as its object phenomena distinct from the body, feelings, and mind.
It also has a combined object (*saṃbhinnālambana*),
in that one perceives two, three, or all four [foundations] of the body and so forth together.
If one perceives both the body and sensation, it is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
That is the mixed object.
If one perceives from the body up to the mental objects (dharmas),
that too is likewise.

Furthermore, when one observes the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena all together, that too is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) with a mixed object (*saṃbhinnālambana*). Thus, one abides in the observation of the combined objects. (VI.17)
Thus,
by synthesizing the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, there arises the "heat" stage. (VI.18–20)
Thus is the wholesome root of the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*).
It is so called because it is the prior form,
that is, because it is the first sign.
Or because it possesses its former intrinsic nature.
"Because it is protracted" means because it is continuous.
However, we shall explain their specific distinctions later; thus, it is said here in the seventh chapter [of the Abhidharmakośa] that "substantially, there are sixteen aspects."
If they too are such [as those previously described], then for what purpose are they taught? To this he says:
"But because they are more excellent, there is another name."
Now, as to why they are called "summits" (*mūrdhan*), he says: "Because they are the summits of the fluctuating roots of merit.
This word *mūrdhan* denotes the ultimate limit of excellence.
For thus people in the world say:
"Indeed, his glory has reached its summit.
For two roots of merit are unstable.

Because falling away is possible in the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*), these two are unstable; conversely, because it is impossible in the stages characterized by Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), these two are stable. Among those two [stages], that which is weak—
That which is [the heat] in its highest degree is the summits.
Of the two immovable [levels] as well, that which is weak is patience;
that which is intense is [the highest mundane dharma].
These are the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). For from these there is either a fall or a transcendence. From the summits (*mūrdhan*) there is a fall, which is to say, a regression.
Either there is transgression or the manifestation of patience.
This is because the "summits" (mūrdhan) are unstable;
for in the world, from the summits of trees and such things, there may be either a falling down or a passing beyond.

"Attainment of the higher" is the common characteristic with the Summits (*mūrdhan*). "The initial arrangement of the aspects upon the Truths" means the first introduction of the aspects such as impermanence and so forth upon the Truths.
The meaning is: the setting in motion of those [minds] that have that as their object.
"By others as well" means: by others as well than the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
"Increasing" means making [the practice] more intense through repeated cultivation;
"one who increases" is the detailed explanation.
For a practitioner who is increasing [the roots of goodness], through that increase there is the manifestation of distinguished roots of goodness;
as for "those previously acquired," this refers to the non-manifestation of undistinguished ones.
Why? Because of a lack of respect.
The meaning is: because of a lack of respect due to [perceiving the person as] inferior.
"Because of the superior acceptance of the truths":
in the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata), one accepts and finds pleasure in the truths in a mild degree;
in the stage of "summits" (mūrdhan), [one does so] in a moderate degree.
Immediately following that, patience (*kṣānti*) now arises from the superior acceptance of the truths.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Because of non-retrogression."
Because one does not fall away from *kṣānti*,
whereas it is possible to fall away from the *mūrdhānas*;
in that same way, there are two kinds [of falling away].
Thus it is. The weak and medium levels of *kṣānti* are exactly as the *mūrdhānas* were described.
"In the same way, by means of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna),
because of the forming of aspects (ākaraṇa) regarding the truths"— this is the meaning.
"Of the whole" means:
Regarding all forms of patience (kṣānti), whether distinguished by the divisions of weak, medium, or intense,
the statement is made solely through the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna),
and not by means of any other, such as the application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) and so forth.
Why?
Because of its proximity to the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
For the supreme mundane dharmas are so called because they are proximate to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It consists precisely of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Because of its proximity to the supreme mundane factors (*agradharma*): since the supreme mundane factors—which have the truth of suffering belonging to the desire realm as their object—arise immediately prior [to it], the receptivity (*kṣānti*) likewise has the truth of suffering belonging to the desire realm as its object.
For its similarity [to the supreme mundane factors] is due to its proximity to them.
"Because there is no statement of restriction":
because, unlike the case of supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), there is no statement of a specific restriction regarding the objects of the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages.
For it is by the very determination of [supreme] patience that the fact that these stages—heat and so forth—have the suffering and other [truths] of the three realms as their objects is established.
How so?
Suffering pertaining only to the desire realm is its object.
Thus, this is superior patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*) which has as its object suffering pertaining to the desire realm.

Because of the restriction "only from patience" (*kṣānter eva*), it is established that the others—the levels of heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth—have as their objects the suffering and other truths of the three realms.
Regarding the phrase "when, it is said," and so forth:
when, it is said, [the practitioner contemplates] the antidotes to the form and formless realms, and so on.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of form and formless realms, cessation, origin, and suffering, as well as the antidotes belonging to the desire realm and so forth.

Through the gradual reduction of the aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) of each individual truth— by the reduction of each aspect of a truth and each object of a truth— until only the suffering of the desire realm remains for two moments, this entire process,
starting from the reduction of the aspects of the antidotes for the form and formless realms, constitutes intermediate patience (*madhyā kṣānti*).
How so?

First, one contemplates the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) through these four aspects: as the path, as the correct method, as practice, and as leading to definitive emergence.
Then, one does so through three aspects, omitting one.
Then, having set aside two by means of two;
then, by means of one; then, having set aside the truth of the path.
One contemplates the cessation of the form and formless realms through their own four aspects;
then, having contemplated it through three, two, and finally one aspect, and having set aside the truth of cessation,
one contemplates the truth of origination through its own four aspects.
Having practiced with three, two, and one aspect respectively,
and having discarded them in that same manner,
he practices the truth of suffering with its own aspects, up to one aspect.
Setting aside that as well,
one contemplates the counteragent to the desire realm through its own four aspects, three, two, and one;
setting that aside as well.

In the same manner, having set aside the truths of cessation and origin pertaining to the desire realm by means of the process of diminishing their respective aspects (*ākāra*), one contemplates the truth of suffering pertaining to the desire realm through four aspects;
then through three; and then through two.
Thus, from the commencement of the decrease onwards, all these moments are said to be "medium patience" (madhyā kṣānti).
In the third moment, there is "intense patience" (adhimātrā kṣānti) having that same object. In the fourth moment, the "supreme mundane dharmas" (agradharmās) have that very same object.

However, "mild patience" (mṛdvī kṣānti) should be understood as that which follows immediately after the highest degree of the "summits" (mūrdhan), wherein one attends to the truth of suffering up to the truth of the path belonging to the desire realm,
as well as those belonging to the form and formless realms,
with all their respective aspects (ākāra) without diminution.
Thus, first of all, some explain it as follows:
the reduction of the object of observation (*ālambana*) is preceded by the reduction of the mental aspect (*ākāra*).
Others, however, explain it differently.
"By the gradual reduction of the objects and aspects of each individual truth.
It should not be understood as "by the gradual reduction of the objects and aspects of each individual truth";
rather, what is it?
It should be explained that [this refers to] the reduction of the objects of those aspects belonging to each of the truths, such as the antidotes to the form and formless realms.
They describe "intermediate patience" (*madhyā kṣānti*) as consisting of one hundred and nineteen moments.
The reduction of the mental aspect (*ākāra*).
For when there is a prior reduction of the object (*ālambana*), too many moments of consciousness (*cittakṣaṇa*) would spread forth;
and this is not logical.
For as long as the truths remain present, the abandonment of their aspects is not logical;
however, when the truths have been abandoned,
then the abandonment of their aspects is logical.
This being the case, one first effects the reduction of the objects of the truths, and subsequently the reduction of their aspects (*ākāra*).
For it is not logical to eliminate the objective support (*ālambana*) of a fundamental [state] without having first eliminated its primary object (*viṣaya*).
Eight [categories of] suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—both concentrated and unconcentrated—are thus established.
It is now taught by another method that there are thirty-two aspects of these [truths]. How so?
When one attends to the suffering of the desire realm through four aspects.

In this way, up until the point where one attends to the antidote for those belonging to the realms of form and formlessness through four aspects— this is "mild patience" (mṛdvī kṣāntiḥ). When, however, one attends to the suffering of the desire realm through four aspects, and likewise up until one attends to the antidote for the formations of the desire realm through four aspects,
starting from the moment one abandons the antidote for the formations of the realms of form and formlessness, "medium patience" (madhyā kṣāntiḥ) has begun.
In that regard, there are twenty-eight moments of consciousness when abandoning the antidotes to the realms of form and formlessness;
