twenty-four when abandoning the antidotes to the formations of the desire realm;
and twenty when abandoning the cessation of the formations of the realms of form and formlessness.
In the relinquishing of the cessation pertaining to the desire realm, there are sixteen; in the relinquishing of the origination pertaining to the form and formless realms, twelve;
in the relinquishing of the origination pertaining to the desire realm, eight;
and in the relinquishing of the suffering pertaining to the form and formless realms, four.
He attends to the suffering of the desire realm through four aspects;
thus, there are four aspects for him.
Furthermore, that practitioner of yoga (yogācāra) is of two kinds.
One whose conduct is dominated by views (*dṛṣṭicarita*) and one whose conduct is dominated by craving (*tṛṣṇācarita*). Furthermore,
the one whose conduct is dominated by views is also of two types.
One who is characterized by the view of a self,
and one who is characterized by the view of what belongs to a self.
For whoever is characterized by the view of a self...
He enters into the determination of correctness by way of the aspect of non-self;
but he who is dominated by the view of "mine" enters by way of the aspect of emptiness.
The one who has fallen under the sway of craving is also of two kinds: one who is afflicted by the conceit "I am," and one who is dominated by indolence.
In that regard, he who is afflicted by the conceit "I am" enters the path of certainty (*niyāma*) by means of the aspect of impermanence;
whereas he who is dominated by indolence [enters] by means of the aspect of suffering.

He [contemplates] by way of the aspect of suffering (*duḥkhākāra*). Therein, the practitioner (*yogācāra*) who has habitually practiced the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭicarita*) again brings that suffering belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) to mind through three aspects,
having set aside one aspect.
Then, by means of two aspects— those of non-self and emptiness—
and then he twice brings into manifestation one aspect, that of non-self,
which is similar to the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and the knowledge of the dharma of suffering.
This is the middling patience (*madhyā kṣānti*); thus, there are one hundred and nineteen moments of mind.

Likewise, for one who is resolved upon [the truth] as pertaining to oneself, when one contemplates by means of the two aspects of emptiness and non-self, one brings the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyākāra*) face-to-face twice.
This is his middling patience; thus, there are one hundred and nineteen moments.
Thus, the one whose conduct is dominated by craving is of two types: one who is afflicted by the conceit "I am" and one who is characterized by excessive indolence; these are to be described.
Supreme patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*), however, lasts for only a single moment.
It is associated with either the aspect of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, or non-self, according to the individual's temperament.
Now, for what purpose is this reduction of the objects and aspects of each truth performed?
For previously, while reviling the three realms, he took hold of the entire counteragent as his object.

Subsequently, because the desire realm must first be abandoned and fully understood, he abides specifically in the suffering belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*). This is because the Path is drawn forth by means of its human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
Without a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
because there is no prior untainted state;
for the Truth of the Path is drawn forth by the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
The preeminence of all worldly things is understood to belong to the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
However, all five aggregates (*skandha*) are included because they are taken together with their retinues.

Since the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth belong to the level of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), there exists for them a form aggregate (*rūpaskandha*) characterized by non-informative matter (*avijñapti*); thus, Heat and the others consist of the five aggregates when taken together with their retinues.
"Let it not be for the Noble One.

This means that because [the Noble One] has already attained them, let there not be a manifestation of the "heat" (uṣmagata) and so forth—which constitute the preparatory application for attaining the fruits—for an Noble Person (āryapudgala). Therefore, the acquisitions (prāpti) are not included among the "heat" and so forth;
for it is not logical that a Noble One who has already attained the fruit of the application should again manifest that application.
Regarding "the production of the heat-stage having the three truths as its object":
when producing the heat-stage having suffering, origin, and the path as its objects,
the present application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present.

Because, when not performing a task that arises from effort, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) alone is capable [of doing so] by virtue of having all things as its object;
for the applications of mindfulness to the body and so forth are incapable because they have restricted objects. Thus, the four future [applications of mindfulness] are cultivated.
This is because, through the application of mindfulness, the body, feelings, and so forth—which are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering and the other truths—are also grasped.

Furthermore, since the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding the body and so forth have been previously acquired, all four are cultivated through the arising of their possession (prāpti).
Regarding the object of the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasatya), that same [heat-stage] occurs in both ways;
that is, when the stage of Heat (uṣmagata) is being produced with the Truth of Cessation as its object.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present; that very same one is cultivated as future,
but not the applications of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth.
Because the body and so forth do not exist within the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

Regarding the statement "the aspects (*ākāra*) are similar everywhere": when one cultivates the aspects of the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*), whether it has the three truths as its object or the truth of cessation as its object, only similar aspects are cultivated.
When the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) is the object, only the four aspects of the truth of suffering are cultivated,
not the aspects of the truth of origination (samudayasatya) and so forth.
When the aspects of the truth of origination and so forth are the objects, only the four aspects of the truth of origination and so forth are cultivated.
"Nothing else," and so forth. "Increasing" refers to [the cultivation] based on the three truths as its object.
One of the applications of mindfulness, beginning with that of the body, can be present;
when the object is the truth of cessation, the last one is present.
In both cases, all four future ones are possible.
All sixteen aspects are cultivated.
What is the reason?

Because the lineages have been obtained; that is to say, because the types [of mental states] such as the application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) which have the four truths as their object have become possible through the acquisition of the lineages.
"Regarding the production of the summits," and so forth.
In the production of the summits, in every case, only the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present.
This is because the applications of mindfulness to the body and so forth lack the capacity for such production.
Even when increasing the cultivation with cessation as the object, the final foundation of mindfulness, which is that of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), is present;
for the others are not applicable.
However, when increasing the cultivation with the three truths as objects, any one of the four foundations of mindfulness may be present.
In all cases regarding the future, there are four [aspects],
and all aspects as well;
this is because the lineages (gotra) have been acquired— so it should be understood.

Regarding the patiences (*kṣānti*), "in all cases the last" means that in both the initial production and the increase [of the roots of goodness], the last foundation of mindfulness (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present.
For it has been said thus:
"The increase by means of the dharma through all patience" refers to the fact that among the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*),
the last one is present when the supreme mundane dharmas are being manifested; that is, the last foundation of mindfulness (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present.
The four future [dharmas] are attained as being exclusively of the nature of non-arising (*anutpattidharma*). Their aspects (*ākāra*) are likewise four:
namely, the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
"Because of the absence of others.
This is because there are no supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) that possess aspects such as "origination" and so forth, since [the supreme mundane dharmas] have suffering alone as their object.

If that is so, then just as future applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), such as that of the body, are cultivated during the state of the active manifestation of the supreme mundane dharmas—even though those applications of mindfulness whose nature is different from the supreme mundane dharmas themselves are not currently present—[so too is it here].
If one asks why it is not accepted that the aspects such as the nature, origin, and so forth of the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) are cultivated when they are future, he says again:
"And because of their similarity to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Only the four aspects of suffering (*duḥkha*) are cultivated.
Why?
Because of its similarity to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
For in the path of seeing, there occurs the vision of whichever truth [is being realized].
Only those aspects are cultivated.
For the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) resemble the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
What, then, is their resemblance to the path of seeing? It is due to their close proximity (*anuśleṣāt*).
In the same way, at the very beginning, there is either the state of having the suffering of the desire realm as its object or the state of belonging to the same level.
For it will be said with reference to the path of seeing:
"That belongs to the same level as the supreme mundane dharmas."

Alternatively, the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) serve as the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) for the destruction of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) through the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*);
thus, they share a similarity with the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"For the paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) are indeed similar to the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). (VI.21–23) "The analysis of the types" is the full statement.
This is the grammatical form [derived] from that root *vidh*.
"Certainty" (niścita). This shows the meaning of the word "niḥ. But how is the piercing certain? He says:
Because of the abandonment of doubt through that, one becomes certain; and because of the differentiation of the truths, [one knows]:
"This is suffering," up to "this is the path."
Nirvedha is the noble path (āryamārga).
Its "portion" (bhāga) is a part of the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Because it is beneficial by way of bringing about or drawing forth that [path], the suffix -cha is applied in the sense of "beneficial for that."
Therefore, it is called "conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
It belongs to the stages of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*antara-dhyāna*), and the [four] dhyānas.
That which has the *anāgamya*, the intermediate (*antara*), and the dhyānas as its stages is called "belonging to the stages of the *anāgamya*, the intermediate, and the dhyānas.
It does not extend upward.
The aids to penetration do not exist in the formless realms.
This is because they are attendants of the path of seeing; the meaning is that they are the preparatory stages for the path of seeing.
"Its absence" means that because it takes the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) as its object,
there is an absence of that path of seeing; thus, it is "its absence."
Where?
It follows that "above" is understood;
the meaning is "in the formless realms."
Why?
Because they do not take the desire realm as an object;
for the formless realms do not take the desire realm as an object.
He asks: "What is the purpose of the path of seeing that has the desire realm as its object?
To this, it is said:
"Because that [desire realm] must first be fully understood and abandoned.
This means that because that desire realm, in its aspect as suffering, must first be fully understood,
and in its aspect as origin, it must be abandoned.
And the reason for this is that since that yogin is afflicted by suffering belonging to the desire realm,
he first seeks liberation from it.
For them, there is maturation consisting of the five aggregates in the form realm.
Because those aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) belong to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), if a yogi were to be reborn in the form realm,
then the maturation (*vipāka*) consisting of the five aggregates would be produced for him there;
and these [aids] are indeed "fulfilling" (*paripūrika*) because they produce desirable experience.
They do not project the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*),
because they are characterized by aversion toward existence;
that is, they hate existence through its aspects such as impermanence and so forth.
"The first two" refers to those whose intrinsic nature is the levels of Heat and Summits.
"Based on the desire realm" means they have their support in the desire realm.
(Abhidh-k-vy 538)
Because the realization of the truths occurs only here [in the desire realm] and not in another realm;
for the path of seeing does not exist above, due to a lack of spiritual urgency (*asaṃvega*),
and because of the scriptural authority stating, "The preparation is here, and the culmination is there."
It is explained that [this occurs] in the three continents, excluding Uttarakuru,
because the inhabitants of Uttarakuru possess dull faculties.
Among the gods, it is said, "it manifests."
Among those belonging to the desire realm,
the fourth stage conducive to penetration occurs even among the gods;
it occurs only there and nowhere else.
There are three aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), excluding the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
In this very life, upon the transformation of the female or male faculty (*indriya*), both women and men obtain those based on both supports—that is, those based on the female and male faculties.
For when women have produced these [aids], they bring them into manifestation as being based on the female support when the state of womanhood appears in another birth.
However, when the state of being a male manifests in another birth, they bring to presence those [karmas] that depend upon a male basis.
For it is not the case that for women who have obtained such [karmas], the female state cannot occur in another birth.
Likewise, males also bring to presence those [karmas] that depend upon a female basis when the female state occurs in another birth.

Regarding the state of being male, [the factors] have the male as their basis. Concerning the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), he says: "A woman attains the supreme mundane dharmas based on two bases."
Only a woman attains the supreme mundane dharmas (agradharma) based on both [genders]; a man does not.
For it is thus: having attained them, a woman becomes possessed of those very dharmas at that time by means of her female basis.
And upon the transition to another birth, when there is the manifestation of a male basis in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), that male is endowed with those [faculties] based on a male basis.
But a male acquires only those based on a male basis.
Why? He says:
"Because of the attainment of the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of femininity.

This means that in that birth, femininity does not exist again even in another birth; this is the attainment of its non-analytical cessation. For one who produces the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
He will necessarily produce the path of seeing immediately thereafter; and it is the established tenet that for one who has seen the truths, there is no further manifestation of womanhood.
"Due to the abandonment of the level," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

Whatever stages of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) have been acquired— whether belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna up to the stage of the fourth dhyāna— the Noble One, when abandoning that stage, that is, when abandoning from the first dhyāna up to the fourth, also abandons those [aids] according to their respective stages, from the stage of the first dhyāna up to the stage of the fourth dhyāna;
it is not otherwise, neither through death nor through falling away (*parihāṇi*).
The meaning is "just as an ordinary person. Furthermore, the abandonment of a stage occurs through the transition to another stage;
he shows that it does not occur through the mere fading away of passion (*vairāgya*).
"But the ordinary person," and so forth.

However, the ordinary person abandons the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) solely by abandoning their homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), whether or not there is a transition between stages (*bhūmisaṃcāra*).
For it is thus: when an ordinary person has attained the aids to penetration belonging to a particular stage, [he abandons them by leaving that stage].
Thereafter, when being reborn, one abandons those [attainments] only through death, even when shifting between stages.
However, one who is not free from passion abandons them through death even without shifting between stages,
and is reborn in the desire realm itself.
But it is not so for a noble person (*āryapudgala*), because their continuum of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-saṃtati*) has been strengthened by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
How is it known that only an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) abandons [the faculties] in such a manner?
It is because an ordinary person who has entered the stages of the embryo, such as the *aṇḍa* or *kalala*, is still possessed of the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*).
Because of the statement in the treatise that it is "not by means of bodily action.
But Master Vasumitra explains:
"An ordinary person (pṛthagjana), however, abandons [the path] solely through the relinquishing of the homogeneous class of beings (nikāyasabhāga)."
Regarding the phrase "whether there is or is not a transition between stages":
here, the term "stage" (bhūmi) includes the entirety of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
In this context, when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), having passed away from among the Brahmakāyika gods, is reborn among the Brahmapurohita gods;
Then one abandons it by abandoning the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
But when one passes away from the first dhyāna and is reborn in the second, then one abandons it both by abandoning the level (*bhūmi*) and by abandoning the homogeneous class.
That is incorrect, because those reborn in the Brahma-world lack the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
For it is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that the aids to penetration arise.
Furthermore, it is precisely through falling away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that they abandon the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
This has also been demonstrated by the Master Saṃghabhadra.
But is it not the case that even an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) may possess the aids to penetration belonging to a particular level?
The claim that one who is being reborn after that point would abandon the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is incorrect;
for they have already been abandoned simply by the relinquishing of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
For one situated in the state of death (maranabhava) abandons them;
however, they have already been abandoned by one situated in the intermediate state (antarabhava).
Therefore, for one who is being reborn beyond that point, there exists nothing that he could abandon.
"It is said that [it is lost] by death alone.
Regarding "like the *prātimokṣa* restraint":
just as when the *prātimokṣa* restraint is abandoned and then taken up again, it is acquired as something entirely new (*apūrva*).
Why?
Because it is to be accomplished through effort that is not habitual;
that is, because it is both unhabitual and to be accomplished through effort.

Because, in this beginningless and vast saṃsāra, they have not been cultivated; since they are attendants of the noble path (āryamārga), they are therefore not obtainable through detachment (vairāgya).
Because they must be accomplished through effort,
those previously abandoned are not regained.
This is so when there is a teacher who defines the boundaries.
"Sīmā" means a boundary (*maryādā*). Its "teacher" (*deśika*) is one who teaches it, namely, one who has attained the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*).
When such a person exists, one produces [the vow] beyond what was previously obtained and then lost.
The meaning is that it produces what has not yet been produced.
The meaning is that, in the absence of a teacher who defines the boundaries [of the path], one begins from the very root, starting from the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*).
Furthermore, regarding these two— loss (*vihāni*) and falling away (*parihāṇi*):
loss has been explained by such statements as "the noble one abandons [it] through the abandonment of the stage" (*bhūmityāgāt*).
Because of the statement, "The first two [are lost] also through falling away," falling away is also mentioned;
therefore, he specifies them with the words "these."
The term "hāni" (loss) includes both *vihāni* (falling away from what has been attained) and *parihāṇi* (retrogression), because it encompasses their common form;
however, *parihāṇi* is caused by defects.
The meaning is "produced by afflictions.
It is not necessarily a loss, for that [loss] may also be produced by virtues, not only by defects.
That which is caused by qualities (*guṇakṛtā*) is, for example, the loss of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) upon the arising of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
That which is caused by faults (*doṣakṛtā*), however, is, for example, the loss of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) through wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*),
or the loss of certain factors (*dharma*) by means of the mind at rebirth (*pratisaṃdhicitta*).
Thus, that which is falling away is also loss; however,
that which is loss [is not necessarily falling away].
This is not necessarily a falling away (*parihāṇi*).
For falling away occurs only from specific qualities (*guṇaviśeṣa*). Thus, one attains the state of non-arising (*anutpattidharmatā*). (VI.24)

The meaning is that one attains the analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of those [factors], such as the destinies (*gati*) and so forth. "But that, according to the case" means that [one attains] that state of non-arising (*anutpattidharmatā*).
It continues that one attains [this] in both the weak and the intense levels of patience (kṣānti), as far as possible.
How so?
In the weak level of patience, one attains the state of non-arising (anutpatti-dharmatā) regarding rebirth in the miserable destinies (apāya-gati).
In the case of the superior [degree of non-restraint], there is birth among the egg-born and moisture-born modes of birth;

in the weak [degree], there is birth among the non-percipient beings, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, and the Great Brahmās; and in the superior [degree], there is birth with a body that is a eunuch, a paṇḍaka, or possesses both sexual organs.
In the highest degree [of patience], there is the state of non-arising for births beginning with the eighth,
for births beginning with the ninth,
and for the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing.
(VI.25) "But of that very lineage" means,
according to the Master's opinion, of the Śrāvaka lineage that has been permeated by *kṣānti*.
The intention is that because it has been permeated by *kṣānti*, it is irreversible.
"Even the other three," [it is said].
A pratyekabuddha might even turn back from the stage of *kṣānti* belonging to the lineage of the śrāvakas.
The intention is that they do not plunge into the miserable states (*apāya*) for the sake of others.
Regarding the phrase "because of the immovable and skillful concentration" (*āniñjyapaṭusamādhitvāt*):
concentration is called "immovable" (*āniñjya*) because it is free from the eight faults.
For this very reason, he is "sharp," either because his faculties are refined and keen, or because, according to the opinion of certain Abhidharmikas, there are Pratyekabuddhas other than the Khaḍga.
For those Abhidharmikas who hold that there exists a Pratyekabuddha other than the Khaḍga.
The intention is that even one who has merely produced the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is a group-dwelling *pratyekabuddha*.

There is no prohibition against those of that lineage turning away from the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "summits" (*mūrdhan*), because the restriction applies only to those who are like the rhinoceros horn (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*).
Liberation is attained quickly in three existences. (VI.26)
Thus,
he who attains liberation quickly would produce the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in a single lifetime.
In the second [dhyāna], the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);
in the third, the noble path (*āryamārga*).
However, for one who has accumulated the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in a previous birth, [the noble path arises even in the first dhyāna].

It should be understood that he produces the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and the noble path (*āryamārga*) even within a single lifetime. Regarding the phrase "the sowing of the seed" and so forth: the sowing of the seed is the production of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); the growth of the crop is the arising of the factors conducive to penetration;
and the production of the fruit is the noble path.
"In this nature of phenomena" means in the nature of the teaching; therein,
entry, maturation, and liberation occur.
Entry is by means of the factors conducive to liberation; ripening is by means of the factors conducive to penetration;
and liberation is by means of the noble path.
"Because of being embraced by that vow" means because of being embraced by a mental vow (*manaḥpraṇidhāna*). Furthermore,
a vow is a specific kind of volition (*cetanā*).
"Having given even a single alms-meal" refers to bodily action;
"and having undertaken even a single training rule" refers to vocal action; and both of these are originated by mental action.

Even this small amount, which has the three types of action as its intrinsic nature, projects that which is conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) by virtue of providing the power for the aspiration toward liberation.
"A portion of liberation" (*mokṣabhāga*) means the attainment of liberation; that which is beneficial for that is "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
It is not otherwise, because wisdom (*prajñā*) and world-weariness (*nirveda*) are absent as appropriate to each case.
First, both are absent among the Kurus;
in the miserable realms (*apāya*), there is world-weariness but no wisdom.
Among the gods there is wisdom, but no sense of renunciation;
therefore, [the path] is projected only among humans in the three continents,
and nowhere else.

(VI.27–28) Since the sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) has begun to be explained, the order of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) starts with the statement: "One who is established in conduct and possesses [the wisdom of] hearing and reflection applies himself to cultivation."
In connection with that, there is the presentation of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
"Dharma-patience" (*dharmakṣānti*) is untainted (*anāsrava*);
however, there is also the endurance of the Dharma by means of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Therefore, there is a qualification by way of its outflow:
that for which dharma-knowledge is the outflow is dharma-knowledge-patience (dharmajñānakṣānti).
Dharma-knowledge-receptivity (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) is receptivity for the sake of dharma-knowledge;
it is like a flower-tree or a fruit-tree, just as a tree is called a "flower-tree" for the sake of its flowers,
and a "fruit-tree" for the sake of its fruit.
In the *kārikā*, however, the expression "receptivity to the Dharma" (*dharmakṣānti*) is used by way of mentioning a single part, just as one says "Datta" for "Devadatta.
It was stated that "rightness" (*samyaktva*) is *nirvāṇa*. What, then, is rightness?
"That which, having brought [the path] to its completion, is the abandonment of passion," and so forth.
In that context, "niyama" means "niyāma.
Regarding that state of correctness (*samyaktva*), "niyama" is the state of being certain (*ekāntībhāva*); the form "niyāma" is derived with the suffix *ghañ*.
However, it is called a "restriction" (*niyama*) because the suffix *ap* is optionally applied in the case of the prefix *sam-upa-ni* according to the rule *yama-sam-upa-ni-ṣu ca*.
Its "approach" (*abhigamana*) means its "entry" (*avakramaṇa*).
That is, the approach to—that is, the attainment (*prāpti*)—of that state of exclusivity (*ekāntībhāva*).
That very state is called "entry into the determination of correctness" (*niyāmāvakrānti*) because of the departure from error.
And "in that" refers to the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*).
It is like the arising of a lamp.
The meaning is "like a lamp" and "like birth.
Just as a lamp that has not yet arisen possesses the capacity to destroy darkness,
and birth that has not yet arisen possesses the capacity to produce that which is to be born.

In the same way, it is accepted that the future receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) possesses the capacity to turn back the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*),
and nothing else; thus,
its activity (*kāritra*) consists in the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"By means of the supreme mundane dharmas," says another;
[the phrase] "the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is turned back" is the subject under discussion.
No.
"Because it is of that nature.
This is not tenable—that there should be a turning away from those [states] by means of the worldly supreme dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
Why?
For those too are the dharmas of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
How could one dharma of an ordinary person turn away another dharma of an ordinary person?
There is no fault here, because they are mutually contradictory.
There is no fault here because the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) are not in contradiction with the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). How so?
He says: "Just as... (Abhidh-k-vy 542).
"Like killing an enemy while mounted on his shoulders.

Just as someone might kill an enemy while actually mounted upon that enemy's shoulders, so too, it is said, the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), while mounted upon the shoulder of the enemy that is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), cause that very state of being an ordinary person to be destroyed.
"By both" means that the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is turned back by both the mundane supreme dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) and by patience (*kṣānti*).
To the question "How so?", he says:

"Because of their similarity to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). This means that the worldly supreme dharmas (*laukika-agra-dharma*) have a similarity to the path of uninterrupted transition, and [the stage of] patience (*kṣānti*) has a similarity to the path of liberation.

Just as a defilement is abandoned by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and is indeed already abandoned by the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), so too is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) discarded by the supreme worldly dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),
and thus it is said to be "discarded by receptivity" (*kṣāntyā vihīnam*).
The heading "untainted" (anāsrava) applies everywhere.

Therefore, it is understood that right here [in this context], the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is untainted. That is what is called "the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering" (duḥkhe dharmajñāna).
He shows that in the treatise there is usage by that name because it has all things as its object, since it takes as its object the suffering belonging to the realms of form and formlessness;
and because it is the first knowledge of the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*).
The meaning is: "because of the knowledge of the reality of phenomena such as suffering from the beginning. "Because of being consequent to that" means "because of having that as its cause."
"Because it follows in the same way.

Just as the truth of suffering and so forth was followed and fully understood by means of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) through its aspects such as suffering and so on, in that very same way, this is subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) because it follows the suffering and so forth belonging to the realms of form and formlessness; such is the detailed explanation.

In this way, by means of the sequence of immediate arising, it should be applied in detail that there is "subsequent-knowledge-acceptance" (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) regarding the remaining origin belonging to the form and formless realms.
This refers to those of other schools, such as the noble Dharmaguptas and others,
who maintain that "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*) is spoken of without distinction.
"This realization of the truths consists of sixteen moments of mind.

Thus, there is no distinction between the realization through vision (*darśanābhisamaya*), the realization through the object (*ālambanābhisamaya*), and the realization through the task (*kāryābhisamaya*), as they all consist of these same sixteen moments of mind.
This is what is meant by "realization through vision."
Insight itself is clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Thus, there is clear realization of the object and clear realization of the task.
Clear realization through vision occurs by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*).
For that, O monks, is indeed "seen," because of the statement: "that which is seen by untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*).
Thus, it is established that wisdom itself is vision (*darśana*).
The grasping of the object occurs through the [mental factors] associated with it, such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth;
by the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that it occurs through wisdom (*prajñā*) as well.
This is because the truths are apprehended as objects by the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
The task of whichever truth is that which ought to be performed;
namely, the full comprehension of suffering and the abandonment of its origin.
The realization of cessation and the cultivation of the path occur even through those factors dissociated from them, such as morality, birth, and so forth.
By the word "also" (api), it is implied that [the four functions] are also performed by wisdom (prajñā) and its associated factors.
For it is by means of wisdom—both associated and dissociated—from which those four effects are produced.
By the phrase "by birth and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the other characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and acquisitions (prāpti).
"Regarding suffering, indeed," and so forth.
For when suffering is being seen through wisdom,
there occurs for that practitioner who realizes it the threefold realization of suffering as previously described.
How so? It is said:

the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of origination and the others—that is, of origination, cessation, and the path—consists respectively in abandonment, realization, and cultivation. Abandonment occurs through the severing of the possession (*prāpti*) of afflictions regarding origination; realization occurs through the arising of the possession of cessation.
It is because of the manifestation of the path of cultivation.
"Due to the difference in aspects" means due to the difference in the aspects of each of these, such as suffering and the others.
Furthermore, it is not logical to perceive origination and the other truths through the aspect of suffering,
because their respective aspects and objects are distinct.
Alternatively, a member of another school might assert that all the truths are perceived through the aspect of selflessness.
Since emptiness and selflessness are the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all truths,
it would follow that there would be no vision of the truths as suffering and so forth—
namely, as suffering, origin, cessation, and path.
And this being so, one who asserts that all [factors] are seen by way of the aspect of selflessness would contradict the Sūtra.
For it is stated in the Sūtra, "of the noble disciple," and so forth.

Now, if you think there is no contradiction with the Sūtra because, prior to the stage of clear realization (abhisamaya), during the stage of preparation (prayoga), the noble disciple attends to suffering as suffering—
And so forth.
Therefore, because all [factors] are seen through the aspect of non-self (*anātman*), there is only a single realization (*ekābhisamaya*).
But that is incorrect.

Because it is stated that "the discernment of phenomena is associated with untainted mental attention" (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), and untainted mental attention is not possible during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-avasthā*).
If it is argued that this refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)—as in the detailed passage beginning, "when a noble disciple attends to suffering as suffering"—[we reply: no.
No;
because cultivation follows from seeing.
This is not so.
For just as there was previously the vision of the truths, so too is there subsequently their cultivation;
the meaning is that this constitutes the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

"Because of the attainment of mastery with respect to the remaining [defilements]" means that the attainment of mastery is the acquisition of the capacity for the manifestation of the vision of origin and so forth without further effort;

"However, one must investigate whether there is or is not an emergence from meditative absorption in the interval.
The intention is that, because mastery has been attained over the remaining [attainments], the fault would arise that an emergence occurs during the interval.
And when investigated in either way, there is a contradiction with many sūtras.
And how their contradiction [is resolved] should be heard from the Āgamas,
because it is stated that upon the vision of one [truth], there is the realization of the task regarding the remaining ones.
Because there is this statement:
"For when suffering is being seen, its realization is threefold;
the realization of the origin and so forth is by way of their effect—namely, abandonment, realization, and cultivation. Since we also accept this, there is no fault.
He said:
Even if it is accepted that there is "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*),
this contradicts the sequential clear realization of the truths (*satya*) as taught in the Sūtra.
Therefore it is said:
"But regarding the realization through vision," and so forth;
that is, there are three sūtras accompanied by similes.
It is recited in the *Saṃyuktāgama*.
How so? Anāthapiṇḍada said:
"Venerable sir, is there a gradual realization of the four noble truths, or is it a simultaneous realization?
"Householder, there is a gradual realization of the four noble truths, but not a simultaneous realization."

"Householder, if someone were to say: 'Without having realized the noble truth of suffering, I shall realize the noble truth of its origin,' and so on in detail up to, 'I shall realize the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering'—he should be told:
'Do not speak thus.'"
For what reason?
It is impossible, it is out of the question, that one who has not fully realized the noble truth of suffering will fully realize the noble truth of the origin [of suffering], as before;
indeed, such a thing cannot occur.
"This is possible," as before.
For example, householder, suppose someone were to say: "I shall establish the wall of a gabled house or a hall with a gabled roof without first establishing its foundation;
I shall establish the upper floor without having established the wall."
"Without having established the floor, I shall establish the roof"—
one should be told, "Do not speak thus.

"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that [the gabled hall]... as before.

"Venerable sir, is there a gradual realization of the four noble truths, or is there a simultaneous realization?
The Blessed One said:
"Of the four truths, O monk," as before, up to: "Just as if, O monk, someone were to say: 'Without having ascended the first flight of steps of a four-flight staircase, I shall ascend the second;
without having ascended the second, I shall ascend the third.'"
Thinking, "Without having ascended the third, I shall ascend the fourth," one should be told:
"Do not speak thus."
For what reason?
It is impossible, it is out of the question, that one should ascend the second step of a four-step staircase without having ascended the first step;
likewise, up to the point that one would ascend the fourth without having ascended the third.
Likewise, here too, this possibility does not exist:
that one might see the truth of origination without having seen the truth of suffering, and so forth.
Thus the noble Ānanda said:
"Venerable sir, is there a gradual realization of the four noble truths, or rather, a simultaneous realization? [The answer is] as in the previous sūtra.
To this extent:
"Ānanda, suppose someone were to say, 'I shall ascend to the palace without having first climbed the first step of a four-stepped ladder.
One should tell him, 'Do not speak thus.'"

the mind is like a flash of lightning."
This is contradictory;

for it has not been stated there that "the category of fetters to be abandoned by receptivity" (*kṣānti-prahātavya-saṃyojana-nikāya*) exists, nor that [it belongs] to the receptivities (*kṣānti*), and so forth.
This is not so.
Why?
Because the patiences (kṣānti) have knowledge (jñāna) as their retinue.
Since the patiences (*kṣānti*) are the retinue of knowledge (*jñāna*), the category of fetters (*saṃyojana-nikāya*) that is to be abandoned by patience is said to be abandoned by knowledge.
This is like the designation of something done by the king’s retinue as "done by the king.
Just as some matter accomplished by the king’s retinue receives the designation "done by the king," so too is this case.
In the same way, however, the aggregate of fetters (*saṃyojana*) that is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) is indeed to be abandoned by knowledge (*jñāna*).
In that regard, even the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) has the nature of knowledge;
for it is specifically the path of immediate succession that is primarily engaged in the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the phrase "because of seeing the truths not previously seen": how does the vision of truths not previously seen occur through knowledge?

That [knowledge] also occurs when another truth remains unseen; thus, the knowledge existing in the interval between paths of vision (*darśanamārga*) is itself considered a path of vision with respect to the indirect sequence (*pāraṃparya*).
By means of that [intervening knowledge], one sees as if seeing what was not yet seen.
Alternatively, it is because of seeing what was not previously seen; that is, from the seeing of the unseen.
The fifteen moments constitute the path of seeing (darśanamārga) as long as this person’s seeing of the unseen continues to proceed.
For as long as his moments of seeing the unseen persist, those moments are the path of seeing.
Even though suffering has already been seen by him, the vision of what was previously unseen still proceeds with respect to its origin (*samudaya*); thus he says:
"In the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) itself, at the sixteenth moment"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Now, one might ask: "Does he not see with that [sixteenth moment] what was previously unseen? What is that which was previously unseen? To this he replies:
Regarding "the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path" (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*):
the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path takes as its object the remaining portion of the path belonging to the side of subsequent knowledge, excluding itself.
This is because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself (*svātmani vṛttivirodhāt*).
Therefore it is said:
"One sees the previously unseen receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path.
This refers to the detailed explanation beginning with "reflection upon each truth."
The consideration regarding truth is whether it has been seen or not seen;
it is not, however, whether a particular moment has been seen or not.
Why is that?
That very truth characterized by the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), which was seen in the fifteenth moment, is also seen in the sixteenth; thus,
there is no seeing of a previously unseen truth.

The path of seeing is not established as consisting of sixteen moments. For it is not the case that the truth of the path remains unseen simply because one moment characterized by the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) has not been seen. He provides a worldly illustration:
Just as a field is not considered "unreaped" simply because it has not been cut by a single blade of grass, nor by a single stalk of grain, nor by a sickle that has not yet severed;
what then?
The meaning is that it is indeed reaped.
For instance, some people, out of negligence, say "the field has been harvested by us" even when a single stalk remains uncut.
"Because it is a fruit," and so forth;
by these reasons beginning with "because it is a fruit," he establishes that the sixteenth moment is indeed the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is the sixteenth moment, because it is a conditioned fruit of asceticism (saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala),
like the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala) up to the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala).

Likewise, because it consists of the eight knowledges and sixteen aspects already cultivated, because the path of the candidate has been abandoned, and because it is continuous, the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is indeed like another fruit. For in the sixteenth moment, the eight knowledges are cultivated.
[The knowledges] from dharma-knowledge regarding suffering and subsequent knowledge regarding suffering, up to subsequent knowledge regarding the path—
likewise, the sixteen aspects, beginning with impermanence, are cultivated.
And just as [in the path of cultivation], there is no cultivation of the eight knowledges and sixteen aspects in the path of seeing.
For in that case, only the cultivation of the aspects of similar knowledge occurs as they arise, because of the statement: "The patiences and knowledges are cultivated in the path of seeing."

Furthermore, at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), there is the abandonment of the previous path—that is, the path of the candidate (*pratipannakamārga*). However, on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no abandonment of the previous path.
Moreover, this subsequent knowledge of the path is continuous (*prābandhika*).

Furthermore, since there is no patience (*kṣānti*) or knowledge (*jñāna*) whatsoever on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) that is continuous, for this reason as well, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) belongs to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The opponent objects:
"The path of seeing consists of sixteen moments."
Because it is necessarily non-retrogressive,
like the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and so forth.
This refutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
"This thesis is flawed because it contradicts the very nature of the property (dharma) as established by inference.
Even if one attempts to prove that [the path] is the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), the state of being non-retrogressive follows from this inference.
Having considered this implicit point, he speaks again.
"But there is no falling away," and so forth.
Because the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing is maintained by the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) as its sustaining counteragent (*ādhārapratipakṣa*).
And if there were falling away from that sixteenth moment, which is the path of the fruit, there would be falling away from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*).
And since there is no falling away from the fruit of stream-entry, one does not fall away from it.
The other says:
"Precisely for that reason."
Is this stated solely as a cause for non-retrogression? We also maintain this very point.
"Why is this response formulated as being 'equal to apprehension'?
The Master says:
"If it is argued that for this very reason it is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)."

If you think that it is precisely because the maintenance of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing occurs through the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) that it is therefore the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
that is not so.
Because it would lead to an over-extension of the principle (*atiprasaṅga*).
If the path of seeing were to exist simply because the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) maintains the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing,
then such an over-extension would follow.

Therefore, since all subsequent paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) following that subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) would maintain the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*), the entire [subsequent] path of cultivation would become the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
And this is undesirable;
for you maintain that only the sixteenth moment is the path of seeing.

A moment consisting of seventeen, eighteen, or more [moments] does not arise according to the principle of a continuous stream. That which arises on the second or third day, being of the same nature, is included within the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*);
however, that is not the case here.
For even from that [state], there is no falling away. Thus, it is shown that the reason stated— namely, "the state of being necessarily without falling away"— is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Because that is inconclusive, it is not a valid counter-argument,
nor is it a refutation of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa). Thus he said.

The seven knowledges range from the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering up to the dharma-knowledge regarding the path; why, then, is the eighth—the subsequent knowledge regarding the path—not included in the path of seeing? This is the intended meaning. It is because the seeing is not yet complete.
Seeing becomes complete at the stage of the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*).
Because at that time, all truths have been seen.
Although suffering belonging to the desire realm has been seen when the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering has arisen,
suffering belonging to the form and formless realms and so forth have not yet been seen.
In this way, up until the point when the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path has arisen, the antidote to the realms of form and formlessness has not yet been seen; thus,
the vision remains incomplete and is not yet finalized.
"Because it is intermediate between those two.
This means because it is intermediate between the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
or because it is intermediate between those two types of receptivity (*kṣānti*).
Those seven knowledges (*jñāna*) are also the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The intention is that this is because that yogin still has a desire to see what remains to be seen.
(VI.31cd, 32) The meaning is that previously, by relying on another—that is, by following the meaning as taught by another—he attained realization of the truths such as suffering (*duḥkha*).

By the qualification "previously," it is stated that at the time of cultivation, there is a pursuit of the meaning independent of the instruction of others. Likewise, regarding the term *dharmānusārī*:
the pursuit by means of the teachings (*dharma*) is *dharmānusāra*.
He is called a "follower of the Dharma" (dharmānusārī) because he possesses this [Dharma],
or because it is his nature to follow by means of the Dharmas.
This is because he previously followed the meaning by himself through the Dharmas— the twelvefold teachings such as the Sūtras and so forth.
The explanation is as before,
up to the point where "five types have been abandoned.
By the word "up to" (*yāvat*), it is meant that if one, two, three, four, or five types have been abandoned.
In the same way, those who have entered the path toward the first fruit are said to be like those who are bound by all fetters;
[the others] are so called up to the destruction of the nine [categories of defilements] in the second [fruit].
Thus [it is said].
"In the second" means "for the sake of the second," just as in the expression, "one kills a leopard for its skin."
"Up to the destruction of the ninefold [defilements]" means up to the abandonment of the nine types;
by excluding the abandonment of the nine types, it is effectively stated that if,
for those two persons, beyond that abandonment of five types, six, seven, or eight types have previously been abandoned by the worldly path (*laukikamārga*).
"Those two are those who have entered upon the second fruit.
This is because of the expression "the second," and because of the governing context of "those who have entered upon [the path]," the determination of the meaning of these terms is thus obtained.
"And upwards" refers to those who are free from passion for the first dhyāna,
up to those who are free from passion for the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
However, it is not possible to attain arhatship from the very beginning.
Without first attaining the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), it is impossible to attain arhatship from the very beginning.
Why is this? He says:
because of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya).
For there is no abandonment of the defilements belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Thus, while abiding in the fifteen moments whose nature is the path of seeing, one would have been a candidate for the third fruit from the beginning; however, when the sixteenth moment of mind has arisen, one would become an Arhat from the beginning, rather than a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

For it is precisely through the abandonment of those [defilements] belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) that arhatship is established.
He says:

If there is no abandonment of the defilements belonging to the peak of existence that are to be abandoned by cultivation by means of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), then arhatship would have been impossible from the very beginning.

In that case, one who has attained detachment from the peak of existence (bhavāgra) through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) while still in the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) would be a candidate for that fruit.
While abiding in those [moments], he would be a candidate for the realization of the fruit of arhatship;
however, at the sixteenth moment of mind, he becomes an arhat from the very beginning.
Therefore it is said:
"And because detachment from the peak of existence is impossible beforehand.
For indeed, in the prior state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), detachment from the peak of existence is not possible by means of the worldly path (laukika-mārga).
Because there is no higher stage [beyond the peak of existence],
therefore, from the beginning, one would neither be a candidate for the fruit nor an Arhat.
This is because they are characterized by resolution (*adhimokṣa*) and vision (*dṛṣṭi*), respectively, due to the predominance of faith (*śraddhā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
One is called "resolved through faith" (śraddhādhimukta) because they are characterized by resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) due to a predominance of faith;
that is, one who is liberated with faith as the predominant factor is called "resolved through faith.
It is not, however, that such a person lacks wisdom altogether.
But because it is not manifested by that [faith],
it does not receive that name.
Due to the predominance of wisdom, because it is manifested by view, one is "attained through view" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
But it should not be said, as before, that he lacked faith;
rather, others, relying on the method of etymological interpretation (*nairukta-vidhi*), explain it thus.

One who is liberated from the [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing through the predominance of faith is "one resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*). One who has attained the fruit through the predominance of [right] view is "one who has attained through view" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
(VI.34) Up to those who have destroyed five types [of defilements].
Thus it has been said.
Therefore, he asks: "What, then, is the reason? and so forth.
[The reason is that] a path distinguished by its fruit is not obtained.
The path distinguished from the fruit refers to those who have entered the state of a once-returner and so forth.
The meaning is that the path which serves as the antidote for the first and subsequent categories of defilements to be abandoned through cultivation is not yet cultivated.
This continues until one applies oneself to the attainment of distinction.
As long as one does not apply oneself to the attainment of another fruit for the sake of abandoning the unabandoned afflictions,
one is not called a "candidate" (pratipannaka); it is only when one so applies oneself that one is so designated.
Then, by implication, it is stated that one is a "candidate" (pratipannaka).

For it is the established doctrine (siddhānta) that at that time, there arises an untainted acquisition (anāsravā prāpti) of the previously abandoned defilements, of their antidote not previously obtained, and of that abandonment itself.
This should be understood to apply similarly to other fruits as well.

Because of the statement that "at the sixteenth moment of mind, one is called a stream-enterer (srotaāpanna) alone," and since it is stated that he is a stream-enterer, this should be understood to apply elsewhere as well—
namely, to the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala) and the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).

Even one who has abandoned eight categories [of afflictions] by means of the mundane path is called only a once-returner at the sixteenth moment of mind, and not a candidate for the fruit of non-returning; because there is no attainment of a path superior to the fruit within that very fruit.
In this way, one who is free from passion for the realm of desire—or even higher—is not called a candidate for the fruit of arhatship at the sixteenth moment of mind.
This is because, as stated previously, "in a fruit, [one is not a candidate] for a fruit superior to that fruit.
As for the passage beginning "but one who is free from passion for the third dhyāna," and so forth: [it refers to one who has already attained a higher stage].

It is possible that one who is free from passion for the third dhyāna, relying on a lower stage—either the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), or the first or second dhyāna—enters into the determination of correctness (niyāma).
Such a person necessarily brings into manifestation a path distinguished by its fruit, or one comprised within the third dhyāna;
for it is through this that the untainted faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) comprised within the third dhyāna is obtained.
For there is the possibility that he might bring face-to-face a path distinguished by its fruit,
because his afflictions belonging to the level of the third dhyāna have been abandoned.
Therefore, it is established as a certainty that he necessarily brings face-to-face a path distinguished by its fruit.
Otherwise, if the meaning were that he does not bring [the path] into manifestation,
then he would be one who has been reborn above that [level],
and he would be an *ārya*.

Therefore, above that third dhyāna— whether in the fourth dhyāna or in the formless attainments (ārūpya)— one would not be endowed with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya). For whatever contaminated (sāsrava) faculty of pleasure there is, it has been abandoned through the transition between levels (bhūmi-saṃcāra).

And as for that which is untainted (*anāsrava*), if that too were not present, one would be devoid of both types of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*); yet it has been stated that noble ones (*ārya*) born in the higher realms necessarily possess the faculty of pleasure.

An ordinary person born in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realms is not endowed with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), whereas a noble one (*ārya*) is so endowed; this is because of the scriptural statement.
Furthermore, whoever is endowed with the faculty of mental happiness (*saumanasyendriya*)...
For there is also the statement: "He necessarily possesses the five faculties of equanimity, life, mind, pleasure, and mental happiness," and so forth.
To this we reply:
This position is indeed recorded in the *Vibhāṣā*.
However, that is not perceived as the established position,
because of the statement, "Others say.
For one who has attained the fourth dhyāna and enters the path of certainty (niyāma) by relying on any one of the six stages [of the form realm]— [that is the case].
He becomes endowed with the fruit of non-returning belonging to the six stages— from the stage of the threshold (anāgamya) up to the stage of the fourth dhyāna— at the sixteenth moment of mind,
because he has likewise become free from passion;
this applies to one who has attained the third dhyāna.
He [attains it] by means of that which belongs to five stages,
excluding the stage of the fourth dhyāna.
Likewise for one who has attained the second dhyāna.
It consists of four stages,
excluding those of the third and fourth stages;
this applies to one who is free from passion for the first dhyāna, or who has attained the first dhyāna but not yet the second.
If he attains the fruit of non-returning,
he is endowed with that fruit of non-returning belonging to three levels:
those belonging to the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna, and the first dhyāna.
For they explain that even the very lowest non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is necessarily endowed with the fruit of non-returning pertaining to the three realms.
Therefore, it would be logical to say that the Master stated this [verse] with reference to the other position.
Thus far, [this applies] to those who have largely abandoned desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*). (VI.35ab)

[This applies] to those who have largely abandoned passion and to those who have abandoned passion for the realm of desire. Among them, one who has largely abandoned passion is one for whom seven or eight categories [of afflictions] have previously been abandoned by means of the mundane path.
One for whom the nine types [of afflictions] have been abandoned is one who is free from passion for the desire realm.
This is the classification of persons among those who are largely free from passion.
Because of the statement in the second [chapter], "up to the destruction of the nine," this applies to those who are free from passion for the desire realm.
Because of the statement, "and above [the realm] for one who is detached from desire," it is as follows:
"these [are] in the desire realm."
Up to those who have destroyed five types [of defilements]; in the second [dhyāna], up to the destruction of the nine;
those detached from desire.
Because of this statement:
nine grades of afflictions are taught in the desire realm.
*Celāt* means "from clothing."
"This is the application of an illustration" (*dṛṣṭāntayoga*).
Others say that the "application of an illustration" (*dṛṣṭāntayoga*) means the reasoning of an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntayukti*), or a type of illustration (*dṛṣṭāntaprakāra*).
Thus, by this reasoning or by this method, he indicates that other illustrations should also be stated.
Otherwise, he would have simply said, "this is an illustration.
[The phrase] "in beginningless saṃsāra" means in a saṃsāra that has no beginning.
The intention is that they have been nurtured and increased through a succession of their own causes, and therefore their magnitude is excessive.

This is because those afflictions are uprooted by the severance of their acquisition (*prāpti*). For acquisitions possess the same nature as roots, since afflictions form a continuous series, just like the extraction of the three-fold [humors] from a swelling.
Just as the extraction of the humors such as wind and bile, which have been accumulated over a very long time, occurs through the application of a threefold decoction,
so too does the destruction of the afflictions occur through the Noble Path, even though it is momentary and subtle.
And just as a great darkness is dispelled by a small, momentary lamp.
"In the same way regarding the afflictions" (VI.35cd). "Seven times at most is his birth" means that seven times is the maximum number of births for him.
The meaning is that there is nothing beyond this.
The meaning is that one goes to nirvāṇa by means of that path;
for in the world, one travels by means of a stream.

If [the status of a stream-enterer] were due to the attainment of the first path: if one were a stream-enterer by virtue of attaining the first untainted path, which is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), then even the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka*) would be a stream-enterer.
The meaning is that one might also be a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala-pratipannaka*).

For, in reverse order, starting from the Arhat among the eight types of persons—the candidates for Arhatship and so forth—the candidate for stream-entry is the eighth, whether he be a follower by faith (*śraddhānusārī*) or a follower by dharma (*dharmānusārī*);
since he too has attained the initial path, he too would be a stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*).
If it is argued that [one is called] a stream-enterer because of the attainment of the first fruit: if you think that one is a stream-enterer due to the attainment of a fruit not previously attained,
then even one who has largely abandoned passion would be a stream-enterer.
One who has abandoned six categories of afflictions and becomes a once-returner at the sixteenth moment would also be a stream-enterer,
because he too has attained a fruit not previously obtained.
In this way, one might also be free from passion for the realm of desire;
for him too, that would be the first fruit.
Now, the refutation is stated:
"With reference to one who attains all the fruits" means because of the attainment of the first fruit.
"All fruits" refers to the four [fruits], beginning with the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
One who has the nature of attaining that is "one who attains all fruits" (*sarvaphalaprāpī*). Alternatively, one who possesses the attainment of all fruits is "one who attains all fruits.

With reference to such a person, and intending such a person, one is called a "stream-enterer" (*srotaāpanna*) because of the acquisition of the first fruit—that is, the acquisition of a fruit not previously attained.
"What, then, is the reason? and so forth.
Why is he alone called a *srotaāpanna* (stream-enterer), and not the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka*), since that one also has entered the stream of the noble path?
"Because of the attainment of the paths of the candidates and the fruits," and so forth.
This is because that [attainer] who reaches all the fruits has attained the path of the candidate, which consists of fifteen moments,
as well as the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which is the sixteenth moment.
But by the eighth [moment], one is a candidate for the fruit because the path itself has been attained.
Furthermore, this is due to the attainment of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation;
for by that [eighth moment], precisely that same path of seeing and that same path of cultivation have been attained.
But for the eighth [person], it is only on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
And because of the realization of the entire stream (*sakalasroto'bhisamaya*), this occurs at the moment of the subsequent cognition of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).

For by him the entire stream has been realized, since he perceives even the moment of the receptivity to the subsequent cognition of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*); but this is not the case for the eighth person.
Therefore, for these reasons, only one who has attained all the fruits is called a *srotāpanna*, not the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka*).
For such a designation is used because of reaching excellence;
just as in the world, one who produces light to an excellent degree [is so called].
He is called the sun,
not a firefly;
it is just like that.
"Therefore, others" means other than this present existence. It is like the "skill in the seven points" and the "seven-leafed tree."
Just as it is said in the Sūtra that a monk is "skilled in the seven points" due to the commonality of the number seven.
How so?
Having spoken at length, it says:
And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the seven points?
He understands form as it really is;
he understands the arising of form, the cessation of form, the path leading to the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger in form, and the escape from form as they really are.
In this way, one understands feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are.
One understands the arising of consciousness, and so forth in detail, up to its escape, as they truly are.
Thus, by this method, there are five sets of seven, which makes thirty-five.
One who is skilled attains thirty-five [virtues].
It is like the *saptaparṇa* tree;
just as that tree is called "seven-leaved" because each of its leaflets resembles a seven-leafed cluster, even though it actually possesses many hundreds of leaves.
It is like that. The first example is established within the teaching (*pravacana*), while the second is from the world; this is the purpose for presenting these two examples.
If it is explained that "at most seven times" (*saptakṛtvaḥ parama*) is due to the commonality of the number seven,
then that contradicts what is stated in the Sūtra; therefore, the intention is that this is a misinterpretation.

There is no contradiction in the fact that one does not bring about an eighth existence within a single realm of rebirth. Alternatively, if it were interpreted according to the literal meaning of the words— namely,

"having transmigrated and wandered seven times among gods and humans, one makes an end of suffering"— then because of the mention of only gods and humans, even the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would not exist.
And it is accepted that seven existences are produced within the destinies of gods and humans;
however, the intermediate existences (*antarābhava*) are not counted [among those seven].
For if the seven existences were counted together with the intermediate existences, he would have only four births.
By this statement regarding the undesired consequence, he [the opponent] thereby supports his own explanation that [this applies] "in one destiny.
The other says:
"Even so, [it would apply to] those who flow upwards," and so forth.

If you explain it thus: "one does not bring about an eighth existence within a single realm of rebirth," then how is it that for one who "flows upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), the production of an eighth existence occurs within a single realm of rebirth?
Furthermore, what is the purpose of the qualification "having the peak of existence as the limit" (*bhavāgraparama*)?
Even for one who has Akaniṣṭha as the limit, the production of an eighth existence is possible,
because of the statement: "He is the leaper (pluta), the half-leaper (ardhapluta), the one who dies everywhere (sarvaścyuta), and another who goes to the peak of existence (bhavāgraga)."
And that too must be stated.
However, we perceive the intention to be that the mention of "having the peak of existence as the limit" (bhavāgraparama) is intended to express the excellence of existence (bhava-prakarṣa).
This is because the statement was made with reference specifically to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
And in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there is one destiny— either the human destiny (manuṣyagati) or the divine destiny (devagati)—
in which he does not bring about an eighth existence (aṣṭamabhava).
"But not in the realms of form and formlessness.
What is the proof for this? Is it scripture or reasoning?
"This was said with reference to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The *sūtra* is the scriptural authority (*āgama*);
the reasoning (*yukti*) here is inference (*anumāna*).
Regarding that which was thus questioned by the objector— "What is the scriptural authority (*jñāpaka*) or the reasoning (*yukti*) for this?"—
he [the respondent] replied in turn:
"And here, what is the scriptural authority for [the statement] that [they arise] individually among gods and humans," and so forth.
"Having transmigrated seven times among each of the gods and humans"—
it does not mean seven times among both gods and humans together.
This is what is meant.
One who has seen the truth among humans,
having transmigrated three times among the gods and exactly three times among humans, then returns from the gods and attains parinirvāṇa;
or one who has seen the truth among the gods [attains it in the same manner].
It is exactly so. Having transmigrated three times among humans and three times among gods, he returns from there to the human realm and attains parinirvāṇa.
For it is thus recited: "seven times among gods and humans."
For it is recited in a general form;
the meaning is that it is not recited by specifying each one individually.
Thus, when the Vaibhāṣika position has been placed in a state of doubt, the Master, providing a justification, says:
"But each individual [school], namely the Kāśyapīyas," and so forth.
The Kāśyapīyas belong to another school;
they recite as follows.
"Seven times among the gods, seven times among humans"—
thus the meaning is obtained for each [instance] individually.
Therefore, by this, both [objections] are refuted.

As for what was asked: "What is the scriptural authority or the reasoning here that this was said with reference to the desire realm (kāmadhātu)? And as for what was further asked: "And what is the authority for saying 'seven times each among gods and humans'? [The answer follows: It is because of the statement: "Having been reborn seven times among the gods and seven times among humans, one attains parinirvāṇa. This is the scriptural authority. As for the reasoning: since it is impossible for a single person to undergo seven births among both gods and humans within a single destiny, and since there is no other destiny than these two where one could take seven births, it is established that this refers to the desire realm. Furthermore, because the *sūtra* speaks of "seven times" without specifying a particular destiny, and because the *sūtra* does not state that they are born seven times among gods and seven times among humans, it is understood that this refers to the desire realm. For by grasping each meaning individually, the underlying intention regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is also indicated.
Indeed, it is not logical for there to be wandering among gods and humans seven times over in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*),
because non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who have been born there do not return to the human world.
The logical reasoning is also understood from this very point:
it is only in that specific stage where one is described as having seven births at most that the prohibition of an eighth birth is appropriate, and not elsewhere.
"One should not be attached to this.
And what here is the proof? "It is of that same kind."
That is its mode:
by which, within that much time, due to the necessary ripening of the continuum, one does not bring about an eighth existence,
just like one bitten by a seven-step venomous snake.
Just as one bitten by that seven-step venomous snake dies after having gone seven steps—
neither beyond nor before—
such is the nature of that species of poison.
And it is like a quartan fever. Just as a quartan fever occurs only on the fourth day—
neither before nor after.
That class of diseases is of such a kind;
it is just like that.
"The two lower fetters" refers to this.
Sensual desire and ill will:
these two arise because one has not yet become free from passion for the realm of desire.
As for the five fetters pertaining to the higher realms:
There are two attachments arising from the realms of form and formlessness, as well as restlessness, pride, and delusion;
because of these, one does not attain nirvana before [the eighth life],
nor does one bring about an eighth existence.
"Because seven fetters remain," this is not a valid reason, according to the Master Saṃghabhadra;
for the higher-tier fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*) are not capable of producing birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), since they belong to the higher stages.
However, those who maintain this as a reason reply as follows:
Even though those [defilements] belong to the higher stages,
by virtue of the capacity of their acquisition (*prāpti*), the production of that many existences occurs.
For they are not established as causes of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) even in the higher realms.
"Because of its being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
"Without" (*antareṇa*) means "in the interval" (*antara*) or "within" (*arvāk*).
"Obtained through the very nature of things" (*dharmatā-pratilaṃbhika*).
The meaning is that it is obtained through the power of the path of one beyond training (*aśaikṣamārga*).
For its very nature is that which joins one with the marks of a monk (*bhikṣuliṅga*).
[The term] "one whose nature is not to fall" (*avinipātadharmā*) means...
It is recited in the Sūtra:
