"One who has become a stream-enterer is of a nature not subject to falling into the lower realms, destined for full enlightenment, and having at most seven more births, after wandering and transmigrating seven times among gods and humans, makes an end of suffering.
Why is it so? It says: [because...]
"Because of the non-accumulation of karma leading to that [state]" means:
*vinipāta* (ruin) refers to the miserable destinies (*apāya*), such as the hells and so forth. That which goes to those is "leading to that" (*tadgāmi*).
That which goes toward that is "leading to that.
What is it?
It is karma.
Because that [karma] which has not yet arisen does not accumulate during the state of an Arya;
and because the continuum (saṃtati) lacks the capacity to yield the ripening (vipāka) of what has already accumulated;

and because during the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), the continuum lacks the capacity to yield the ripening of that karma which was accumulated while leading toward that [state], and which is of indefinite ripening (aniyata-vedanīya).
It is said that he is "one whose nature is not to fall into the lower realms.
Such is the transformation of his continuum of aggregates (*skandhasaṃtati*),
in that it remains incapable of yielding the maturation (*vipāka*) of the accumulated karma that would lead to those states.
Why, then, does that continuum of aggregates remain in such a state due to the deficiency in giving its fruit to the accumulated karma that leads there?
To this it is said:
"Because of the perfuming by powerful roots of virtue."
Because this continuum of aggregates has been perfumed and cultivated by powerful roots of virtue;
and how, moreover, is it perfumed by powerful roots of virtue?
Through the purity of application and the purity of intention. Therein, the purity of application consists of the ethical discipline cherished by the noble ones (*āryakānta-śīla*).

"Purity of intention" refers to verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) toward the Buddhas and others. "One would not even produce receptivity (*kṣānti*)" means that one would not even produce forbearance (*kṣamaṇa*).
One should not even give rise to the thought, let alone the actual application; such is the intended meaning.
Or alternatively:
But when an action leading to ruin is present, that person does not even produce the patience characterized by the aids to penetration;
how much less, then, the untainted path?
Just as [the mind] perfumed by powerful roots of merit becomes incapable of yielding the ripening of accumulated unwholesome [actions].
He demonstrates this with a verse:
"Having done even a small [deed], the fool [suffers] all [of it]."
An ignorant person, having committed even a small evil deed, [is led to ruin].
The wise one goes downward to a state of ruin.
Furthermore, even that which is great.
Having committed evil,
one abandons misfortune and the states of woe.
He establishes those two points in their respective order by means of two examples:
even a small amount of iron, when compacted...
Remaining in the form of a solid mass,
it sinks in water because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That very same iron, moreover,
has been fashioned into a bowl.
The great one has been born in the waters.
It floats; it crosses over.
This is due to the quality of that formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*).
Thus, the ignorant person sinks because they have been rendered unworthy by their qualities; the wise person does not, because they have been rendered worthy by their qualities.
This is because, for the latter, there is no further suffering.
Because there is no suffering beyond this suffering that is comprised within another existence,
it is called "the end of suffering" or "the cessation of suffering.
Otherwise, the end of suffering would occur only at the time of death.
But that suffering is accompanied by rebirth;
therefore he says:
"The meaning is that it brings about suffering that is without rebirth."
"How does one bring about nirvāṇa?"— the intention is that because it is eternal, its being brought about is not tenable.
[It is said] "by removing the obstacles to its attainment."

Because it removes the obstacles to the attainment of nirvāṇa. The obstacle to its attainment is either the possession of afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*) or the substrate (*upadhi*); by removing these, one brings about nirvāṇa.
It is just as space is not perceived when a pavilion stands there.
When there is an obstruction to it,
by removing that [obstruction], one says that one "makes space," even though space is eternal.
Therefore he said:

"Just as there are those who say, 'Make the pavilion like space' or 'Bring it down,' so too there is another, namely an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) whose mental continuum is matured, yet not fixed [in destiny]. Because such a person might attain parinirvāṇa right here, or in the intermediate states (*antarābhava*), he is not mentioned [in that specific category]."
(VI.36) "Two or three births": one who has two or three births is a *dvitrijanman*.
Some read it in this way.
Regarding "two or three births" (*dvitrajanma*): *dvitrāṇi* means two or three.
The compound is formed according to the rule *saṃkhyayāvyayāsannādūrādhikasaṃkhyāḥ saṃkhyeye*.
In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the member denoting the number is to be counted (*saṃkhyeya*), the suffix *ḍac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*).
Thus, "one whose other births are two or three" is *dvitrajanmā*.
In the verse, however, there is a reference to "two."
Regarding the abandonment of afflictions and the arising [of the fruit]:
why is this? He says:

when, for a stream-enterer who proceeds gradually, the [afflictions] to be abandoned by seeing have been abandoned, and subsequently one, up to four types of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation have been abandoned.

The acquisition of the untainted faculty (*anāsravendriya*) which serves as the antidote to those [defilements]—namely, the antidote to one, two, three, or more categories of defilements—is not explicitly mentioned in the verse because it is established by implication;
for there is no abandonment of the categories of defilements without an antidote.

Indeed, even when that Noble One abandons the categories of defilements by means of a mundane path (*laukikamārga*), there occurs the acquisition of the untainted faculty which serves as their antidote.
Birth, however, might sometimes be shorter;
that is, if one were to attain parinirvāṇa right here, or having been reborn in the intermediate state (antarābhava). What is the reason?
Because of the possibility [of attaining] what lies beyond;
that is, because of the possibility of attaining the state of a once-returner up to arhatship beyond the fruit of stream-entry. Therefore, this birth is specified.
"One who has two or three births is a *kulaṃkula*.
This is investigated here for the sake of establishing a restriction.
Regarding one who is liberated from one or two types [of defilements],
what is he?
Some say he is a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner.
The mention of "threefold" or "fourfold" is for the purpose of illustration,
or for the purpose of defining a limit, meaning that there are no more than this.
Others say that one who is liberated from one or two types [of fetters] will have five or six births;
they specify this as "liberated from three or four types" because of the inclusion of such distinctions.
This has not been examined by the commentators, and thus it remains to be investigated.
Why is it not [the case that one becomes] a *kulaṃkula* by means of abandoning five types [of defilements]?
The governing topic is: "What is it that makes one a *kulaṃkula*?"
"Upon the abandonment of that," and so forth.
This is because when five types [of afflictions] are abandoned, the sixth type must necessarily also be abandoned.
He asks: "Why? and then says:
For it is not the case that a single type— the sixth— is capable of obstructing the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).
"As in the case of one with a single interval" (*ekavīcika*) is a counter-example (*viparītadṛṣṭānta*).

Just as for the *ekavīcika*, a single type—the ninth—is capable of obstructing the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), it is not so for this stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*) that the sixth type is capable of obstructing the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).
Why is this? He says:
"Because of not transcending the realm (*dhātu*).
For one who has only one interval remaining (*ekavīcika*) transcends the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Therefore, even a single type [of affliction], namely the ninth, is capable of obstructing his fruit, because transcending a realm is difficult to accomplish.
But the once-returner does not transcend the realm;
for him, a single type of affliction—the sixth—is not capable of obstructing the fruit.
[He is reborn] "in that or another divine assembly."
For example, having seen the truths among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, after wandering through two or three families,
one attains parinirvāṇa right there among the Trāyastriṃśa gods or elsewhere.
(Abhidh-k-vy 557) Or he attains parinirvāṇa among the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods or the Yāma gods.
The same should be applied elsewhere as well.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "Because of the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion."
How so?

Because of the abandonment of the three fetters and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion, one becomes a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*). This is because only the weak grades [of these afflictions] remain.
"Soft-strong," "soft-medium," and "soft-weak"—these are so called because only this much remains.
[This refers to one] for whom seven or eight portions of faults have been exhausted. (VI.37)
The "portion of the faults" (*doṣāṃśa*) is a part of the faults, characterized by seven or eight types.
Regarding the phrase "from the sense-faculties" (*indriyataḥ*), the third cause has not been formulated in the Sūtra; it should be explained in that very same way.
"How is this so?"—this is the detailed explanation.
How is it that for this *ekavīcika*, a single type—the ninth—is able to obstruct the fruit, whereas for a *kulaṃkula*, a single type is not able to obstruct the fruit?
It is said:
because of the transcendence of the realm (*dhātvatikrama*).
Because when that ninth category [of afflictions] has been abandoned, one has transcended the desire realm and is no longer reborn there.

Furthermore, since that ninth category, together with its karma, is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) in that very place, it is therefore capable of obstructing the fruit by means of transcending the level of its ripening (*vipāka*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*) fruits.
For it was stated previously that actions stand as obstacles during the three stages; namely,
that action acts as a great obstacle at the attainment of patience (*kṣānti*), non-returning (*anāgāmitā*), and arhatship (*arhattva*).
But here, it should be applied to the afflictions (kleśa).
For this very reason, he says:
"Just as [the sequence] of actions (karman)."
"Thus, the afflictions," and so forth. "Because he is separated by only one birth" refers to that once-returner who has exhausted seven or eight categories [of afflictions].
Because *nirvāṇa* is separated by only one birth;
or because his fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) is separated from him by only one type of affliction (*kleśaprakāra*), he is called "one who has only one interval" (*ekavīcika*).
He is neither a "one who goes from family to family" (*kulaṃkula*) nor a "one who has only one interval" for that long.
Even if one has previously been liberated from three or four types [of defilements] by means of the mundane path, one does not yet become a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner.
Even if one has eliminated seven or eight categories [of defilements], one does not yet become a "one-interval" (ekavīcika) practitioner,
because there is as yet no acquisition of the untainted faculties that serve as their antidotes.
Therefore he says:
"As long as the path distinguished by the fruit has not been brought face-to-face.

But when that which is distinguished by the fruit—namely, its antidote (pratipakṣa) or the antidote to the higher categories—is brought face-to-face, then, because of the acquisition of the untainted faculties (anāsravendriya), [the fruit is attained].
It is stated by implication that one becomes either a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) or a "one-interval" (ekavīcika).
Regarding the phrase "of the five," the full explanation is as follows:
according to the Sūtra, one is called a "non-returner" (anāgāmin) due to the abandonment of the five lower fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana).
Because of the synthesis of abandonments;
that is, because the abandonment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth is established as a single [act], it is said that "two or three [fetters] have previously been abandoned.
This refers to the case where one who is already free from desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmavītarāga*) enters the path of certainty (*niyāma*).
Two [fetters] were previously abandoned by means of the mundane path:
sensual desire and ill will.
This is because the view of a self-identity and the others were not abandoned exhaustively.
Now, regarding one who follows the gradual path:
three [fetters] have previously been abandoned. By what means?

By means of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the misapprehension of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) [are abandoned].
Therefore, it is said that there is the abandonment of all five [fetters] in their entirety.
(VI.38, 39) He is one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, upon rebirth, with effort, or without effort;
he is a non-returner.

Because he attains parinirvāṇa through effort (*saṃskāra*) or without effort (*asaṃskāra*) after having arisen in the intermediate state, he is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state through effort or without effort" (*antarotpanna-saṃskārāsaṃskāra-parinirvṛti*).
As for what was said, "of one who has thus arisen," we do not understand that.
How can there be a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the expression "of this arisen non-returner, there is parinirvāṇa"?
For it is taught that a *bahuvrīhi* occurs when there is a meaning other than that of its own members (*svapadārtha*), not when there is the meaning of its own members.
Therefore, we see the reading here as "evam utpanne 'sya" (thus, when this has arisen).
It appears that the letter *e* was deleted by a scribe;
for with such a reading, this meaning becomes possible.

"Parinirvṛti upon birth" means that for this person, there is parinirvāṇa once birth has arisen; thus he is "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth. Alternatively, if the reading were exactly as it stands [in the compound], it would be explained in this way.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of disregard.
By that [genitive], the compound is thus formed:
"one for whom there is the parinirvāṇa of the birth already arisen" is an *anāgāmin* who has attained parinirvāṇa upon being born; hence, he is called an *utpanna-parinirvṛti-anāgāmin*.
Alternatively, "of what has arisen" (*utpannasya*) refers to the genus (*jāti*) of what has arisen.
The meaning of "of those that have arisen" (*utpannānām*) is the same as the meaning of "of what has arisen."
Therefore, that which is the parinirvāṇa of those [defilements] that have arisen belongs to him; thus he is one who attains parinirvāṇa upon arising (*utpanna-parinirvṛti*).
Now, this is distinct from the mere sense of "parinirvāṇa" itself because it has a different meaning from that of an *anāgāmin*.

Even though the referent of the first member of the compound is not different [from that of the second], they would desire that the word *utpanna*—which is in grammatical apposition with *anāgāmin*—form a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the word *parinirvṛti*.
This would be well-said:
"That same non-returner (anāgāmin) further becomes fivefold."

He concludes that there are five types: one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion, one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion, and one who goes upstream.
This is because their paths are characterized by being "diligent" and "swift.
"Diligent" means possessing vigor, having initiated vigor.
"One who has a carrying path" means one whose path is carrying.
How is the path carrying?
Because it manifests without volitional effort (*abhisaṃskāra*).
He is both "diligent" (*abhiyukta*) and "possessing a swift path" (*vāhimārga*); thus, he is "one who is diligent and possesses a swift path.
Its state is that [quality];
therefore [it is said].
"Having arisen, he soon attains parinirvāṇa;
by means of nirvāṇa with a remainder of substrate.
Because there are two kinds of nirvāṇa, he specifies that he attains parinirvāṇa by means of nirvāṇa with a remainder of substrate.
The meaning is that he effects the destruction of all outflows (*sarvāsravakṣaya*).
He too [attains] through *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

It is not only the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) who attains parinirvāṇa through *nirupadhiśeṣa-parinirvāṇa* after reaching arhatship without completing his lifespan.
Others say that even one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin) is similar to that; [the author replies:
no, because of the lack of mastery over the relinquishing of the life-span.
This is not so; for he too [attains] parinirvāṇa without remainder of substrate (nirupadhiśeṣaparinirvāṇa).
Why?
Because he lacks mastery over the relinquishing of his lifespan (āyurutsarga).
Because he lacks mastery over the relinquishing of his life-span.
But why does he lack mastery in this regard?
Because mastery over the relinquishing of the life-span belongs only to one who has attained the fourth dhyāna of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*).
And that meditation of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭika-dhyāna) is produced only among humans in the three continents.
And he is one who has been reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Does one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state possess mastery over the relinquishing of life-span?
Since he thus attains final nirvana through nirvana without remainder,
he likewise lacks mastery [over his lifespan].
However, there is no such karma for him to remain in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Regarding the question of what kind [of person] an *upapadyaparinirvāyin* is:

therefore, the *antarāparinirvāyin* attains parinirvāṇa quickly, whereas the *upapadyaparinirvāyin*, having remained for the duration of his lifespan, attains parinirvāṇa; thus it is said that the *upapadyaparinirvāyin* alone attains parinirvāṇa through *nirvāṇa with a remainder of substrate* (*sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).
"He is said to be one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion.
The word "it is said" (*kila*) indicates the opinion of the Vaibhāṣikas;
for his own position will be stated later in accordance with the Sūtras.
"Uninterrupted application" means that the application is not discarded due to the momentum of previous application. "With effort" means with exertion.
"Because he is one who exerts effort and possesses a non-flowing path.
This means that because that yogin exerts effort and possesses a non-flowing path,
for this very reason he is established as one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī).
"Without volitional effort" means by way of the opposite of the previous [state],
because the application has been brought to rest.
"Because of the absence of the path that carries application" means because of the absence of application, which is diligence (*vīrya*),
and because of the absence of the path that carries [the result].
Thus, due to the variety of factors such as application (abhiyoga) and so forth, the distinction in parinirvāṇa has been explained.
For one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin), both are present:
application and a swift path (vāhī mārga).
For one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion, there is application,
but not a swift path.
For one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion, however, neither of these two exists.
"Neither exertion nor a swift path" means that there is parinirvāṇa through a path that takes both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena as its object.
"Conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) and "formative force" (*saṃskāra*) have the same meaning.
Thus, "unconditioned" means "without volitional effort.
One who abandons the afflictions by means of a path that takes conditioned phenomena as its object, or by means of a path that takes suffering, origin, and the path as its objects,
is one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyī).
He who [attains parinirvāṇa] by means of having the unconditioned as his object and cessation as his object is one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion;
but that is not correct.
"Because it would lead to an over-extension.
But that is not so.
Why?
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For even in the cases of one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) and one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), since they attain parinirvāṇa through a path that has either conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena as its object, it would follow that each of them would individually be one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*) or without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Consequently, there would be only two types of persons (*pudgala*) situated therein.
"Not five.

This one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī) was previously recited; this one [who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion] is now recited before the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī).
"One who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion" and "one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion"— it is appropriate [to speak] in that very way, as explained in detail;
that is, respectively for those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion and with exertion.

Because the parinirvāṇa of the two types of persons—the one on the path that flows outward and the one on the path that flows inward—is accomplished without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra-sādhya*) for the former, and accomplished with effort (*abhisaṃskāra-sādhya*) for the latter.
To explain how they are accomplished in such a manner, he says:
"By way of attainment without exertion and with exertion, respectively, of that parinirvāṇa."
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "of the two paths, the flowing and the non-flowing":
it is the two paths themselves that are grasped, not a connection between two persons.
This is because the flowing path is accomplished without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), whereas the non-flowing path is accomplished with volitional effort (*abhisaṃskāra*).
This is because of attainment through effortlessness and attainment through effort:
because the former path is manifested without effort,
while the other is attained through effort.
Thus, it is logical that the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin) is mentioned first. He asks:

"If the path of the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion is 'swift' because it is accomplished without exertion, then is the path of the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin) also swift?"
What is the distinction between these two?
To this it is said:
however, for the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, the path is more forceful and more mastered.
One who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion is not superior in this way in terms of the accumulation of causes;
rather, his underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are weaker because they have been exhausted by a more superior path.
This refers to the "one who flows upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
One whose movement is an upward stream is an *ūrdhvasrotas*. Where it is recited as "ūrdhvam," it means "upward from restraint and from the body."
Regarding the forms *ūrdhvaṃdamikaḥ* and *ūrdhvaṃdehikaḥ*,
it should be understood that by virtue of the co-occurrence (*saṃniyoga*) with those suffixes, the word *ūrdhva* is irregularly prescribed (*nipātita*) as ending in the vowel *m*.
Others maintain that there exists an irregular form (*nipāta*) *ūrdhvam*, just as there is the form *ciraṃtanam* derived from the word *cira*.
However, since there is indeed a word *ūrdhva* ending in the vowel *a*, it is not rejected [as a possible reading].
"Because of being mixed or unmixed dhyānas" means because of being mixed or unmixed meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
Because the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dhyāna is mixed with the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Here, having practiced the intermingling of dhyānas (*dhyānavyavakiraṇa*), one falls away from the three dhyānas. Furthermore, the intermingling of dhyānas is preceded by the intermingling of the fourth dhyāna.
The fourth [dhyāna] is mixed first,
according to the statement; for it is the fourth dhyāna alone that is capable of being mixed from the very beginning.
It is nothing other than this:
since there is no rebirth in the first and subsequent meditations for one who has not fallen away from the fourth meditation, it is therefore said,
"fallen away from the three meditations."
And how is one fallen? He says:
"having relished the first dhyāna. [The term] *madhyānimajjanāt* means because of not sinking into the middle, i.e., because of not sinking in the interim.

"Named 'Half-Leaper' (ardhapluta)," and so forth. The syntactical connection of the sentence is as follows: "one who, having bypassed even a single intermediate station, is reborn among the Śuddhāvāsa deities and then enters the Akaniṣṭha heaven. [It is called this] "because it is a locus for views (dṛṣṭisthāna)."
And for the Mahābrahmās who have first been reborn there, it is due to the conceit of being the creator within the Great Brahmā realm,
and because of being the sole creator.
What [is the result]?

A noble one (*ārya*) is not reborn among the Mahābrahmās. For if a powerful noble one were to arise there, there would be a state of dual leadership; yet, sovereignty over that realm is attained through karma that is without rival.

Therefore, it is not accompanied by a rival. "All other stations" refers to the fourteen intermediate stations beginning from the Brahmakāyikas— having passed away from them and traversed through the stations starting with the Brahmapurohitas up to the Sudarśanas— one enters the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
"Because one does not return at all from wherever one has been reborn.
For example, wherever one has been reborn, such as in the first dhyāna.
Because of never returning again to the desire realm;
likewise, because of never returning again to where one has been reborn;
and furthermore, because of never returning again to that first dhyāna.
The state of non-returning is fulfilled because one does not undergo a second birth there.
For he is one who practices tranquility (*śamatha*);
that is, he who has the peak of existence as his limit is one who delights in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, in the formless realms, meditative concentration is exceedingly tranquil;
therefore, he enters the formless realms.
The former, however, was one whose conduct was characterized by insight (vipaśyanā).

He who was described as having Akaniṣṭha as his ultimate limit enters the Pure Abodes, being one who delights in wisdom (*prajñāpriya*). This is the detailed explanation of "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāṇa*).
This has not been definitively settled by the authors of the treatises,

nor has it been prohibited; therefore, because there is no prohibition, we see it as logical that for those who "stream upwards"— whether having the Akaniṣṭha heaven as their limit or the Peak of Existence as their limit— there may be parinirvāṇa after entering either the Akaniṣṭha or the Peak of Existence in the interval [between them].
The meaning is: "We see, however, that it is possible.
Now, since it was stated that [the limit] is either Akaniṣṭha as the highest or Bhavāgra as the highest, he says:

"But the state of having Akaniṣṭha or Bhavāgra as the limit is because there is no further destination beyond them; that is, because there is no going upward from the Akaniṣṭhas or from the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra)."
For example, regarding the stream-enterer (srotaāpanna), there is the limit of seven births at most.
It is not that it is impossible for him to attain parinirvāṇa after having produced two or three more existences; rather, beyond that, he does not produce an eighth existence.
"It is said that at most there are seven [births].

Furthermore, that [non-returner] is of four types; because of the absence of one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), there are not five types. Thus, these are the six non-returners (*anāgāmin*).

The one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion, the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion, the one who goes upstream, and the one who goes to the formless realm.
Counting the sixth [type] as fourfold,
there is the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life.
The meaning is "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmaparinirvāyī*).
Regarding the question "How are these three? and so forth:
another person, not understanding why the three non-returners (*anāgāmin*) were not mentioned by explicitly distinguishing them, asks this.

The Master (Ācārya), seeing that these [categories] have also been stated by implication (*arthāpatti*), explains them as follows: "Of the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) and the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*," meaning "of the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state and the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth";
"and of the third, the one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*")."
Regarding "due to swift, non-swift, or long-term parinirvāṇa by means of three similes":
one who attains parinirvāṇa swiftly, one who attains parinirvāṇa not swiftly, and one who attains parinirvāṇa after a long time should be applied to the three similes as follows:
for example, a small spark from a firebrand might go out at the very moment it is produced.
Thus is the first, who attains parinirvāṇa quickly.
It is just as when iron balls or iron plates, heated by a blazing fire, are struck with an iron hammer; even as an iron spark flies up, it would go out.
Thus is the second, who attains parinirvāṇa not quickly.
It is as follows: "Just like iron balls," and so on as before, up until: "a spark of iron, having flown up, might be extinguished even before it has fallen to the ground.
In this way is the third type, the one who attains parinirvāṇa after a long time.
And since this sutra has been written out in detail previously, it is not written here again.
Regarding the phrase "due to attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, with effort, and without effort":

the connection is that there are nine types of non-returners (anāgāmin) because of the threefold division based on attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, attaining parinirvāṇa with effort, and attaining parinirvāṇa without effort.
One who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth is one who attains parinirvāṇa immediately after being reborn.
But he does not attain parinirvāṇa through either volitional effort or lack of volitional effort.
One who attains parinirvāṇa with effort, however, does not attain parinirvāṇa immediately upon rebirth;
what then?
One attains *parinirvāṇa* through the power of a previous formative effort (*pūrvābhisaṃskāra*) that has not been relaxed by means of further formative effort.

For although such a person possesses a swift path, they attain *parinirvāṇa* through exertion; however, the distinction is that one who attains *parinirvāṇa* upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*) does so without exertion.

Furthermore, one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*) is one whose previous exertion has been relaxed and who attains parinirvāṇa without further exertion; this indeed is the distinction between them.

However, just as both those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*) and without exertion receive the designation "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (*upapadya-parinirvāyī*), [the author], demonstrating this, says:
For all these are "those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin) because they attain parinirvāṇa after being reborn.
"Due to the distinction of the *pluta* and so forth" means due to the distinction between the *pluta*, the *ardhapluta*, and the *sarvacyuta*.

"Or for all three" means that there is a threefold division among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and those who flow upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*), based on whether their parinirvāṇa occurs quickly, not quickly, or after a long time. A certain one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state may be one who attains parinirvāṇa quickly.
Some are those who attain parinirvāṇa without delay;
likewise, there are those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth,
and those who are "stream-winners heading upstream."
And because of this threefold division, there are nine types of non-returners; that same connection should be stated.

Furthermore, regarding their distinctions, and so forth: of those three—namely, the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and the one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
And for each of these nine, there is a further distinction as previously described due to the threefold division:
namely, from the distinction of karma, afflictions, and faculties (*indriya*).
It arises from the distinction of karma, affliction, and faculty.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Of the three," and so forth.

"Manifestation" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); because of having accumulated karma to be experienced upon manifestation, one is an "attainer of parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state."

Because they have accumulated karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*), they are those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*). Because they have accumulated karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), they are those who "flow upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*). Thus, first of all, the distinction between these three is due to their specific types of karma.

Furthermore, because of the manifestation of weak, medium, and intense afflictions (*kleśa*) respectively, the distinction among these very same individuals is due to their specific types of afflictions.
And because their faculties are respectively superior, medium, or inferior, there is a distinction among these very [nine] based on the difference in their faculties.
Among those as well, for each one, there is a distinction according to the case, precisely for that same reason.
This means that even among those nine who are distinct from one another, there is a distinction for each individual.

Therefore, due to the specific differences in karma and so forth, a distinction should be understood according to what is appropriate— not according to the literal order. To explain how this is so, he says:
"Of the first two triads," and so forth; that is,
the triad of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state and the triad of those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
The distinction between these two triads is due to the differences in their afflictions and faculties; that is,
because of the manifestation of weak, medium, and intense afflictions, and because of having intense, medium, and weak faculties, respectively.
But it is not due to a difference in karma; for the karma to be experienced upon arising (*abhinirvṛtti-vedanīya*) is the same for the first triad,
and the karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*) is the same for the second.
Furthermore, there is a distinction based on the specific nature of the karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karma*) belonging to the latter triad;
for the karma to be experienced in a subsequent life of those who attain the "leaper" (*pluta*) and other states is indeed distinct.
Therefore, it is due to the distinction of karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karma*),

and due to the distinction of afflictions and faculties (*kleśa-indriya*). Because the word "and" (*ca*) draws [the former] along, there is a distinction based on the manifestation of weak, medium, or intense afflictions.
And because of the faculties being superior, middling, or weak;
that is, respectively.
These [nine types] exist because of the ninefold nature of the afflictions and the faculties.
These nine non-returners exist because there are nine grades of afflictions and nine grades of faculties; thus,
there are nine non-returners.
Karma is not mentioned because it is not pervasive;
for there is no distinction between the first two triads based on a distinction in karma.
But how, then, do these nine types of afflictions come to be?
In this context, affliction is of three kinds: weak, medium, and intense.
The weak belongs to those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; the medium belongs to those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
The highest [degree] belongs to those who "flow upwards" (ūrdhvasrotas).
Among them, the first, the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin), has the weakest-weak defilements (kleśa);
the second has weak-medium defilements; the third has weak-strong defilements.
Among those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, the first—the one who attains parinirvāṇa immediately upon rebirth—has middling-mild afflictions.
The second—the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion—has middling-middling afflictions.
The third—the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion—has middling-intense afflictions.

Among those who stream upward (*ūrdhvasrotas*), the "leaper" (*pluta*) has the highest degree of weak afflictions (*adhimātra-mṛdu-kleśa*); the "half-leaper" (*ardhapluta*) has the highest degree of medium afflictions (*adhimātra-madhya-kleśa*);
and the one who dies in every place (*sarvasthānacyuta*) has the highest degree of strong afflictions (*adhimātrādhimātra-kleśa*).
How, then, do the faculties (*indriya*) become of nine types?
In the same way, the faculty is also of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior belongs to those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; the middling belongs to those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
Among those who flow upwards from the lower stage,
the first is one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state and possesses superior-superior faculties;
the second possesses superior-middling faculties.
The third has superior-weak faculties.
Among those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, the first—the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth—has medium-superior faculties;
the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion has medium-medium faculties.
The one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion has medium-weak faculties.
Among those who go upstream, the leaper has weak-strong faculties;
the half-leaper has weak-medium faculties.
"One who passes away from all stages is one with the softest-soft faculties.
(VI.41) If so, how is it that seven destinations of the true persons (*satpuruṣagati*) are taught in the Sūtra?
"O monks, I shall teach you the seven destinations of the true persons."
And there is parinirvāṇa without clinging.
All of this sutra has been written in the section concerning the *Gatisūtra*, so it is not written again here.
And in this sutra, the seven destinations of the true persons (*satpuruṣagati*) are taught.
There are three who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, and three who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; these are six destinies. The seventh destiny is the one who flows upwards.
Regarding the term *ūrdhvasravaṇadharma*:
this form of the word ends in a *kṛt* suffix;
thus he shows that this form of the word is intended in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*).
And "upwards" (*ūrdhvam*) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
"Because there is no mention of its subdivisions" means that there is no mention of the subdivisions of that "one who flows upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), such as the "leaper" (*pluta*) and so forth.
For the exposition of the sūtras depends upon the dispositions of those to be trained.
The phrase "other destinies of those in training" means that it does not refer to the destinies of stream-enterers or once-returners.
"Gati," "utpatti," and "saṃparāya" are stated in the Sūtra as synonyms.
"Of them" refers to the non-returners (anāgāmins).
And their "conduct" (vṛtti) exists when there is [past] karma, because they refrain from taking life and so forth.
And there is non-occurrence when it is absent, because of the non-performance of unchaste conduct and so forth.
For unchaste conduct and the like are performed with an unwholesome mind;
however, for those who are free from passion, activity occurs only when karma is present and not when it is absent, because they have abandoned unwholesomeness.
"Nor is there a return" means that once they have been reborn in those various destinies,
there is no further coming back to them from those places; this is the meaning.

But this which has been stated does not exist elsewhere— that is, existence [only] when [the cause] exists, non-existence when it does not exist, and the absence of returning again. This [state] does not exist in the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) or the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
"Of others as well" means of stream-enterers (srotaāpanna) and once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin) as well.
"In a figurative sense" (pāryāyika).
That which exists in a particular manner is "pāryāyika.
The meaning is that it exists in some specific way.
To explain how this is so, he says:
"Because of the attainment of the restraint of absolutely not committing the fivefold evil.

This means: the restraint (*saṃvara*) is the guarding (*saṃvaraṇa*) through non-doing—that is, through the non-performance—of the fivefold evil characterized by killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants;
it is because of the attainment of that [restraint].
For noble ones do not commit these five kinds of evil even in another birth.
This refers to the restraint of non-action,
because the restraint of formal undertaking is not mandatory.
"Generally speaking" means:
because of the absolute abandonment of all unwholesome states to be abandoned by seeing,
and because of the possible abandonment of certain unwholesome states belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
"Of those," and so forth.

But for those whose state of being a true person (*satpuruṣatva*) is not by way of a figurative expression (*niḥparyāyeṇa*), nor through another mode, as is the case with stream-enterers (*srotaāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
What then?
Because of the attainment of the restraint of never again committing any evil whatsoever,
and because of the abandonment of all unwholesome afflictions to be abandoned by seeing,
as well as the abandonment of all nine grades of afflictions belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
The scope of this sūtra concerns those non-returners (anāgāmin) who are noble beings (satpuruṣa).
Because there are "seven destinations of noble beings," the status of being a noble being for others is not denied in a figurative sense.
Furthermore, does this distinction also apply to a non-returner who has undergone a change of birth?
"One who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state," and so forth.

One who is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) after having transmigrated is one who, having attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*) or the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) in the first birth, becomes a non-returner in the second birth.
The qualification "in the desire realm" (*kāme*) is used [to specify].

Because one who has undergone a change of birth in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) sometimes enters the formless realms (ārūpya), yet attains final nirvana (parinirvāṇa) in that very same birth; this is because,
due to the abundance of suffering in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), such a person possesses intense spiritual urgency (saṃvega).
"As for the phrase 'In that case,' and so forth:
Śakra said, 'If, having passed away from here and been reborn among humans, I do not attain parinirvāṇa after reaching arhatship,
[then may I be born] among those gods renowned as the Akaniṣṭhas.'"
"At the end, while I am declining, my rebirth will take place there.

For he is one who has entered the stream (*srotaāpanna*) among the gods, and because of his statement, "Having come to the human realm, I shall attain final nirvana," he would be one whose birth has been turned back.

"At the end" means at the conclusion of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*); "while I am declining" means while I am falling away from arhatship through the loss of non-attainment (*aprāpti-parihāṇi*).
In this regard, since there is an expression of aspiration stating, "I shall be reborn among the Akaniṣṭha [gods]," it is understood that this demonstrates the existence of going to another realm.
How then is it said that a noble one (ārya) who has undergone a change of birth within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) does not go to another realm? Thus the meaning of the Sūtra is seen.
You might say:
"This was said by Śakra because he was ignorant of the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa);
therefore, there is no fault."
If the Blessed One heard this, why did he not prevent him by saying, "Do not speak thus"?
To this it is replied: The Blessed One did not prevent him because [the statement] was to be commended.
The intention is that it should be gladdening because of the desire to abandon the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmaduḥkha*).
Master Saṃghabhadra says it is because it gladdens one who is distressed by the suffering of death and rebirth (*cyuti-nimitta-upapatti-duḥkha*).
[It is also said] because the faculties (*indriya*) have become more fully matured.
The meaning is that it is due to the specific nourishment of the outflow-fruits (*niṣyandaphala*) of the faculties such as wisdom (*prajñā*),
and because of the attainment of a specific basis (*āśrayaviśeṣa*). For one attains a specific basis that is unimpaired and conducive to the manifestation of the Path.

For it is observed that even those with sharp faculties may fall away from their qualities due to a deficiency in their physical basis (*āśraya*). Therefore, because the faculties have become more fully matured through dwelling in another birth, there is no transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), and because one has obtained a superior basis, there is no falling away.
Furthermore, by this very dwelling in another birth, there is no transition to another realm (*dhātu-antara-gamana*), because the Path has not been mastered and thus does not manifest.
Because the path has not been mastered, it does not manifest;
for that reason, a learner (*śaikṣa*) who is not free from passion—namely, a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) or a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*)—does not attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Furthermore, this is because their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not extremely weak.

Because his underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not very weak, he therefore does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*); this is the teacher’s resolution.
As for the resolution of the Vaibhāṣikas, he says:
"Because the realm of desire is difficult to transcend," so say the Vaibhāṣikas.
How so? It is said:
for much must be accomplished by him.

The abandonment of unwholesome and neutral afflictions means that by this [path], the abandonment of the unwholesome afflictions belonging to the desire realm and the neutral afflictions belonging to the form and formless realms must be accomplished.
Furthermore, for a learner (śaikṣa) who is free from passion, there is only the abandonment of the neutral [afflictions].
Thus, there is the attainment of two or three fruits of the ascetic life (śrāmaṇyaphala).
Two or three fruits of asceticism (śrāmaṇyaphala) are to be attained.
By a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), two fruits of asceticism are to be attained:
the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) and the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala).
A stream-enterer must attain three fruits: the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.

One who is already free from passion, however, need only attain the single fruit of arhatship. Furthermore, the transcendence of the three realms must be accomplished by one who is not yet free from passion.
But for one who is free from passion [for the desire realm] yet not free from passion for the form realm— an intermediate-parinirvāyin— there must be a transcending of two realms.
(VI.43) "It is mixed" means it is intermingled,
that is, it is blended.
The meaning is that the fourth dhyāna with outflows (*sāsrava*) is mixed with the two [meditative attainments] without outflows (*anāsrava*).
"Because it is the foremost among the easy paths" means that the four fundamental dhyānas are the easy paths.
Because it is said that the path within the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) is a pleasant practice,
and among those, the fourth dhyāna is supreme because it is free from the eight defects.
Regarding the phrase "it is said that" (*yadā kila*): the word *kila* indicates the opinion of the Vaibhāṣikas;
his own position, however, he will show later.

But the intermingling of moments is impossible; for, in detail, two moments are similar to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), namely the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the tainted (*sāsrava*).
The third is similar to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and thus it is untainted.
Those of dull faculties practice the intermingling [of dhyānas] out of fear of the afflictions;
by the word "and," it is implied that they also practice it for the sake of rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Those of sharp faculties, however, practice the intermingling solely for the sake of rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life.
It is not out of fear of the afflictions (*kleśa*), because for them, falling away (*parihāṇi*) is impossible.
But how is it that they practice the intermingling [of the dhyānas] for the sake of non-falling away out of fear of the afflictions? To this he says:
"By means of distancing the concentration associated with relishing, for the sake of non-falling away"—
that is, "so that I may not fall away from the fruit.
(VI.44ab) "Of five kinds," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
[The faculties are] weak, medium, superior, more superior, and most superior.
Regarding the first [stage], there are three types of minds;
one should state that such is the capacity of that person, and so on for the subsequent stages as well.
Regarding the second [verse], "six":
there are three—[namely] the untainted (*anāsrava*), the tainted (*sāsrava*), and the untainted again;
then there are another three—the untainted, the tainted, and the untainted—thus making six.
In the same way, one should apply [the numbers] as follows: nine in the third, twelve in the fourth, and fifteen in the fifth.
"Of these, respectively" means that the fruits of those mixed cultivations (vyavakīrṇabhāvanā) are, in their respective order, the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).
The fruit of weak cultivation is the Avṛha heaven; likewise, up to the fruit of the most intense cultivation is the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
This is the opinion of the Venerable Śrīlāta, based on the predominance of the faculties such as faith.
That is to say, the fruit of cultivation characterized by a predominance of faith is the Avṛha heaven.
In this way, up to the cultivation in which wisdom predominates, the Akaniṣṭha heaven is the fruit.
(VI.44cd) For whoever is a non-returner—
whether one liberated through faith or one who has attained vision— [attains that fruit].
"Realization by means of the body":
because of the absence of mind, one realizes by means of the body alone.
To the question "How is it realized by the body alone?", he says:
"Because it arises based on the body.
Such is the teacher's own opinion (*svamata*).
[The attainment is established] "by means of the acquisition (*prāpti*) and the direct realization (*jñānasākṣātkriyā*)."
Because at the time of meditative absorption (samādhi), one directly realizes the attainment of a basis conducive to that [state];
and at the time of emergence, one directly realizes the knowledge that experiences it.
For "direct realization" (sākṣātkriyā) means making something manifest to direct perception (pratyakṣīkāra).
The intention is that realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) is appropriate at the stage of attaining the tranquility of the body accompanied by consciousness (*savijñānakakāyaśānti*).

Alternatively, through the attainment of the tranquility of the body accompanied by consciousness, its acquisition is understood to occur at the stage of the tranquility of the body devoid of consciousness (*avijñānakakāyaśānti*).
Regarding the phrase "the eighteen learners" (*aṣṭādaśa śaikṣāḥ*), this refers to the Sūtra.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada asked the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, how many are worthy of offerings?
The Blessed One replied:
"Householder, there are eighteen types of trainees (*śaikṣa*) and nine types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who are worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*).
What are the eighteen trainees? They are: one who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*)."
The stream-enterer;
the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning;
the once-returner.
One who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of non-returning;
a non-returner;
one who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of arhatship.
The follower by faith,
the follower by dharma,
and the one liberated through faith.
One who has attained vision;
one who goes from family to family;
one who has only one interval remaining.
One who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth;
and one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion.
One who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion,
and one who goes upstream—
these, householder, are the eighteen types of those in training (śaikṣa).
What are the nine types of non-learners? They are: those subject to falling away, and those whose nature is volition.
One whose nature is to guard,
one who is stable and unshakable,
and one capable of penetration.
One of unshakable nature;
liberated in mind;
liberated through wisdom.
(Abhidh-k-vy 567) "The one liberated both ways.
Thus, householder, these are the nine non-learners (*aśaikṣa*).
There are three trainings and their fruit.
The three trainings—higher ethics, higher mind, and higher wisdom—are characterized by the Noble Path.
Their fruit is dissociation (visaṃyoga). Indeed, it is by way of these distinctions that the stages of those in training (śaikṣa) are established.
The meaning is: by way of the distinction in training and the distinction in its fruit.
But how is there that distinction? It is because the trainings of the eighteen types of learners (*śaikṣa*) are of various kinds, as is their fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).

Furthermore, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is not [the state of] one in training (*śaikṣa*), because its intrinsic nature is that of a path which does not involve further abandonment.
Nor is it the fruit of training, because its intrinsic nature is that of the fruit of dissociation (*avisaṃyoga-phala*).
Therefore, a distinction of "one in training" is not stated on account of being endowed with that, namely, on account of being endowed with the attainment of cessation.
Just as these eighteen are trainees (*śaikṣa*), so too is he not a non-trainee. In that regard, it is said:

Regarding the statement "there are eighteen learners" (*śaikṣa*) in this Sūtra, for what reason is the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) not mentioned as a learner? It is because [the classification] is stated according to broad categories. There are five who have reached the realm of form (*rūpopaga*).
The other, who goes to the formless realm, is of four kinds:
one who attains nirvana here, one who does so elsewhere,
and so forth.
"But when distinguished in detail," and so forth.

Here, the Master first explains the distinctions among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) according to their faculties, stages, lineages, and so on, for the purpose of demonstrating the method of calculation.
What is the reason?

For when their distinctions are calculated, just as there is a distinction among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) due to differences in faculties and so forth, so it is up to those who "stream upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*); thus I shall easily apply this analogy.
There are four [distinctions] according to the difference in levels (*bhūmi*).
These are the ones who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state. The stages are the four dhyānas, because those non-returners (anāgāmin) who go to the realm of form (rūpadhātu) are intended here.
In that regard, there are four types from the first dhyāna up to the fourth, namely those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) and so forth.
There are six types based on the distinction of spiritual lineages (*gotra*), such as those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and others;

these are: one subject to falling away, one characterized by volition (*cetanādharman*), one characterized by guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), one stable and unshakable (*sthitākampya*), one capable of penetration (*prativedhanābhavya*), and one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*).
There are sixteen [heavens] due to the distinction of different locations:
from the Brahmakāyikas up to the Akaniṣṭhas.
According to the system of the Vaibhāṣikas, Mahābrahmā constitutes a distinct location.
Even according to the system of the outsiders (bahirdeśaka), since one does not arise there [in the intermediate state] when it is a different location, it is not counted.
Thus, there are sixteen types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state due to the distinction of different locations;
there are thirty-six due to the distinction of stages (bhūmi) and degrees of detachment (vairāgya).
Due to the distinction of levels and the distinction of detachment from them, there are thirty-six types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
How is this demonstrated? It is explained in detail: "In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one who is bound by all fetters," and so forth.

In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are nine [types] in the first *dhyāna*: those bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), those who have abandoned one type of passion, up to those who have abandoned eight types of passion. Likewise, there are nine in the second [dhyāna]: from those bound by all fetters up to those who have abandoned eight types of passion.
Similarly, there are nine in the third [dhyāna].
Likewise, "nine in the fourth" means that four groups of nine make thirty-six,
up to one who is free from passion for the eight categories of the fourth dhyāna.
By the word "up to" (yāvat), this detailed meaning is obtained:
one who is free from passion regarding the ninth category of the fourth dhyāna is not mentioned,
because such a person remains fully bound by fetters within the formless realm (ārūpya).
And one who goes to the formless realm is not under consideration here,
because those who go to the realm of form are intended here.
[This is] "due to the connection with the intermediate state."
And this being so, the detailed explanation is: "due to the distinctions of place, lineage, detachment, and faculties.

Because of the distinctions among places, lineages, degrees of detachment, and faculties, there are two thousand five hundred and ninety-two [types] of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin).
To explain how this occurs,
he says: "In one place," namely, in the Brahmā-purohita heaven, there are six lineages (*gotra*) due to the distinctions such as those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and so forth.
The repetition "gotra-gotra" indicates that there are nine types of persons (pudgala),
ranging from one bound by all fetters up to one who is free from passion regarding eight categories [of afflictions] within their own station,
such as the Brahma-purohita heaven.
There are six groups of nine; because of the inclusion of the six lineages and the nine types of persons, there are fifty-four.
There are sixteen such sets of fifty-four, because of the inclusion of sixteen different stages.
"Sixty-four," and so forth.
This refers to eight hundred plus sixty-four.
However, due to the differentiation of the faculties (*indriya*), it is tripled by way of the distinctions of weak, medium, and intense.
Having established it in this way, why would there be twenty-five hundred and ninety-two?
For by that same principle, nine types of persons (pudgala) are established, ranging from those bound by all fetters up to those who have abandoned eight categories of passion.
Demonstrating that principle, he says:
"For one who is free from passion regarding nine categories in a lower dhyāna," and so forth.
For one who is free from passion regarding nine categories in a lower dhyāna—from the first up to the third—is said to be "fully bound" in a higher dhyāna—from the second up to the fourth.
He asks "Why? and replies: "For the sake of equal enumeration," meaning so that there may be nine [levels] in each of the four dhyānas.
Otherwise, there would be an unequal reckoning.
In the first dhyāna, there would be ten [categories], from one who is bound by all fetters up to one who is free from passion regarding nine types [of defilements].
In the second [dhyāna], there would be nine, from one who is free from passion regarding one type up to one who is free from passion regarding nine types.
Thus, there are nine in the third [dhyāna] and eight in the fourth.
This refers to those who have become free from passion regarding one grade up to those who have become free from passion regarding eight grades.

It has already been stated that for one who has become free from passion regarding nine grades, there is the state of being bound by all fetters of the formless realm; this applies likewise up to the case of the "one who flows upwards" (ūrdhvasrotas).
The same applies to those who attain [the fruit] upon rebirth (*upapadya-sābhisaṃskāra*), those who attain it without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), and those who flow upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

Due to the distinctions of station (*sthāna*), lineage (*gotra*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and faculty (*indriya*), there are twenty-five hundred and ninety-two for each; thus, when totaled again according to the fivefold distinctions, there are thirteen thousand and forty fewer non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
However, those who go to the formless realms (*ārūpyaga*) become exceedingly numerous when divided into the four categories beginning with "those who attain rebirth there" (*sahopapadya*).
Since this point is understood by following the same method [as previously explained], it is not written out here.
(VI.45, 46) One who destroys eight parts of the Peak of Existence (*ābhavāgra*).
Thus [it is said]:
"one who destroys eight parts up to the peak of existence" (ābhavāgrāṣṭabhāgakṣid) means one who effects the destruction of the eight categories up to the peak of existence.
This non-returner (anāgāmī) begins from the point of detachment from even a single category of the first dhyāna.
Since one is established as a non-returner through detachment from the realm of desire,
therefore, beyond that, one becomes a candidate for the fruit of arhatship.
Just as a diamond breaks everything.
Thus, because this concentration breaks all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), it is called "diamond-like" (*vajropama*) by virtue of its capacity; for it is like a diamond.
Because it has already broken [some], it does not break everything;

rather, it breaks the eight types of defilements belonging to the three realms—those to be abandoned by seeing and those to be abandoned by cultivation, ranging from those of the desire realm up to those of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
If it does not actually destroy all [the latent dispositions], why is it said to "destroy all the latent dispositions" (*sarvānuśayabhedin*)? To this he replies: "It is capable of destroying all.
The intention is that this was stated with reference to its potentiality (*saṃbhava*).
"Comprehended by the *anāgamya*" and so forth.

Relying upon nine stages—the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*) excluding the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*)—the attainment of arhatship occurs; for this very reason, it is explained in detail as follows:
"There are eight [moments] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) of suffering and its origin."

There are eight [moments of mind]: four associated with the four aspects of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) having the suffering of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as their object, and another four associated with the four aspects of subsequent knowledge having the origin (*samudaya*) of the peak of existence as their object. In the same way, it should be stated that there are eight [moments] associated with the aspects of the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) regarding cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).

According to the established tenet that dharma-knowledge regarding cessation or the path on the path of cultivation is the antidote to the three realms, only those two are presented here; there is no inclusion of the dharma-knowledges of suffering and origin.
"Up to this point" means that by the word "up to," just as there are four [applications of mindfulness] associated with the aspects having the cessation of the first dhyāna as their object,

so too, for each of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the peak of existence, there are to be described four [applications of mindfulness] each having cessation as their object.

Regarding the statement that there are four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), it is not said here that there are four for each individual level because they are associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge that takes the entire path as its object.
Why? It is said:
"Because it takes the entire category of subsequent knowledge as its object."

For the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is undifferentiated, and since the path acts as a mutual cause by way of being an antidote (*pratipakṣabhāva*), it is taken as a whole.
It is not like cessation (*nirodha*); therefore, only the four paths are associated with the aspects (*ākāra*) of subsequent knowledge.
These are thus distinguished by the differences in their aspects, modes of cognition, and objects (*ālambana*).
They are distinguished by the difference in the aspects of cognition (*jñāna-ākāra*) and by the difference in their objects (*ālambana*).
Alternatively, they are distinguished by the threefold difference of cognitions, aspects, and objects.
First, they are distinguished by the difference in the aspects of cognition.

Because of such statements as "by means of the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and its origin," and because of such statements as "even though distinguished by differences in their objects, [they are distinguished] by having the suffering and origin of the peak of existence as their objects."
"Forty-two":
from the beginning, "two eights" makes sixteen.

There are four [moments] having the cessation of the first dhyāna as their object, up to four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path; thus, nine sets of four make thirty-six.
Sixteen and thirty-six make fifty-two.
"Just as they are included in the *anāgamya*" is the full statement.
It is called *anāgamya* because the fundamental dhyāna arises by entering into the *anāgamya*.
In the same manner as the fifty-two diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*) included within the threshold meditation (*anāgamya*) were just described,
exactly in that same manner there are fifty-two included within the intermediate meditation (*dhyānāntara*).
How so?

There are eight associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin pertaining to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), which are comprised within the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
There are eight associated with the aspects of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path.
There are four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation, having the cessation of the first dhyāna as their object.
In this way, there are likewise four [applications of mindfulness] having the cessation of the peak of existence as their object;
and four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path,
because they take the entire category of subsequent knowledge as their object.
These, distinguished by the differences in their aspects of knowledge and their objects, become fifty-two.
Just as there are fifty-two included within the intermediate dhyāna, so too there are fifty-two included within the first dhyāna,
up to fifty-two included within the fourth dhyāna.
"According to their respective order," and so forth.
Twenty-eight [moments] are comprised within the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*);
twenty-four are comprised within the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
There are twenty [mental applications] included within the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Since the noble path (*āryamārga*) does not exist at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), those [applications] included therein do not exist; thus they are not considered. This is because the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is absent among them.
Because there is an absence of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) in those [levels] such as the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*),
and because dharma-knowledge belongs to six levels (*ṣaḍbhūmika*).
Therefore, the eight [mental applications] associated with the aspects of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path do not exist [there].
Furthermore, because there is no subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) that takes the cessation of a lower stage as its object,

those [moments] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*)— which would otherwise take the cessations of the four dhyānas as their objects and number sixteen— do not exist. Thus, there are twenty-eight [moments], having subtracted eight and sixteen from the fifty-two.

How so? There are eight [moments of consciousness] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin pertaining to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), which are subsumed under the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).
There are sixteen [moments] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation, which have the cessations of the sphere of infinite space and the others as their objects.
There are four [moments] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
Thus, these become twenty-eight, distinguished by the differences in their aspects, knowledges, and objects.
In the same way, having removed the four that have the cessation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-nirodha*) as their object, twenty-four are to be applied.

Those included in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) are twenty, having as their objects the cessation (*nirodha*) of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), while excluding yet others.

What, then, is the reason that the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) take as their object only the cessation of their own level or of a higher level, and not that of a lower level as is the case with the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)?
For it is not possible to take the cessation of suffering on a lower level as an object without first taking the suffering of that lower level as an object.
And all that is suffering is exclusively with-outflows (sāsrava). This is the fixed rule:
the fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not have lower realms with-outflows as their object.
This is the reason.
However, because the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) involve a comprehensive observation, there is no prohibition [against them].
For he will say:
"Meditative absorption has a wholesome object that exists.
Now, why do they take only cessation as their object, and not suffering or its origin?
Because he has already become free from passion for the lower stages down to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
For him, only the ninth category belonging to the peak of existence remains to be destroyed by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
However, since it can have the antidote to the lower stages as its object, it is the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) that is intended here.
And that should be understood as being associated with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*),
because those [two] antidotes serve as mutual causes for one another.

Because of the statement, "The path, however, is mutually [the object] of those that are equal and superior across the nine levels," for all subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) has as its object the category of subsequent knowledge belonging to the nine levels.
"But for those... and so forth.

For those Abhidharmikas who maintain that not only the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*), but also the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), has each individual level as its object of opposition (*pratipakṣālambana*), they add twenty-eight more; thus, there are eighty diamond-like concentrations (*vajropamasamādhi*) comprised within the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*).
How so?
Previously, there were four [moments] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), which had as their objects the entire category of subsequent knowledge.
Now, according to the opinion of some, they are also established as having the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to each individual level as their objects.

There are four [moments] comprised within the *anāgamya* stage that have the counteragents of the first dhyāna as their object and are associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).

Likewise, up to those that have the counteragents of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as their object and are associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path—thus there are twenty-eight additional ones.
By adding these twenty-eight additional ones, the fifty-two become eighty.

What, then, is the reason that the four [applications of mindfulness] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), which have as their object the antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), are not counted?
It is said:
there is no untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) included within the peak of existence that serves as an antidote to the peak of existence.
However, there exists [a path] belonging to the level of the first dhyāna,
up to that belonging to the level of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
Therefore, it is said that [the paths] have as their objects only the counteragents (pratipakṣa) to those respective levels.
"They do not have the antidote to the peak of existence as their object.
Others, however, explain:
"But for those who maintain that even the subsequent knowledge of the path has each individual level's antidote as its object."
The intention is that this is just as the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodhānvayajñāna) is accepted.
Among those, there are eight associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin pertaining to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
There are eight associated with the aspects of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path.

There are thirty-two [moments] consisting of four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*) that take the cessation of the first dhyāna as their object, and likewise up to four that take the cessation of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as their object.
Similarly, there are likewise thirty-two associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*). Thus it is calculated.
By adding twenty-eight more, there are eighty diamond-like (vajropama) concentrations included within the category of the "unshakeable" (anāmya).

For among those [original sixty-two], the four that take the entire category of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) as their object and are associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path do not exist [in the case of the Arhat].
However, those that take the antidote to the peak of existence (bhavāgra) as their object arise in their place; therefore, there are eighty diamond-like concentrations.
In this way, up to those included in the fourth dhyāna, how is it so?
By adding twenty-eight more, there are eighty diamond-like concentrations (vajropamasamādhi) included in the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
Just as they are included in the intermediate dhyāna, [so too are those in the other levels].
In this way, there are eighty diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*) for each dhyāna, comprised within the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Regarding the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and so forth— that is,
in the three formless attainments excluding the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*)— there are respectively forty, thirty-two, and twenty-four.
How so?

First, in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one adds to the twenty-eight diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama*) four that are associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) and have as their object the antidote to the sphere of infinite space;
and so on, up to adding four that have as their object the antidote to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
By adding twelve, they become forty.
