Likewise, by adding four that have the counteragent of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) as their object and four that have the counteragent of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as their object to the twenty-four, they become thirty-two.
Similarly, by adding four that have the counteragent of the sphere of nothingness as their object to the twenty, they become twenty-four.
He said:
"But has it not been stated that [the path] has as its object the counteragent to the lower stage,
because of their being mutual causes?"

Now, why are only those [meditative states] included within the sphere of infinite space and so forth that have as their objects the antidotes to their own level and to higher levels described, and not those that have as their objects the antidotes to lower levels? To this it is said:
It has been stated that, without distinction, the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) across the nine stages takes as its object the antidote to the lower stages;
however, it does not take as its object the antidote to the lower stages when that path is comprised within the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and so forth.
What then?
It has as its object only the counteragent belonging to its own level and to the higher levels.
In that regard, subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) takes the lower level as its object in an undifferentiated form,
not in its specific nature.
However, that which has its own level and higher levels as its object exists even in a specific form.
This, however, was the former position established by the Vaibhāṣikas:
that subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) takes the entire category of subsequent knowledge as its object only in a general form.
For thus it was said by the Master Saṃghabhadra: "All subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) has as its object the category of subsequent knowledge pertaining to the nine stages.
However, others explain it in this way:
There are eight associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin pertaining to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
There are four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation, having the cessation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) as their object.
Likewise, up to those having the cessation of the peak of existence as their object, there are four; thus, there are sixteen.

There are also four [moments] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), which have as their objects the antidotes to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Likewise, up to those four which have as their objects the antidotes to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), making sixteen.
These sixteen, together with the eight previously mentioned, constitute the thirty-four [moments].
There are forty diamond-like concentrations (vajropama-samādhi) comprised within the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).
There are thirty-two comprised within the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana),
because the eight that have as their object the antidote to the cessation of the sphere of infinite space have been excluded.
Twenty-four [moments] are included within the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

This is because another eight moments—those which have as their objects the cessation and the counteractive path (*pratipakṣa*) of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*)—are excluded.
For they also designate the counteractive path belonging to a lower stage as the antidote even for the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Furthermore, they become even more numerous due to the distinctions of lineage (*gotra*) and faculties (*indriya*).
How so?
First, there are those eight who were mentioned at the very beginning.
Among those, that which has the suffering of the peak of existence as its object and is associated with the aspect of impermanence is the diamond-like [samādhi].
It is divided into six types due to the division of the six spiritual lineages (gotra).
Thus, for each of the three [knowledges] associated with the aspects of suffering and so forth, there is a sixfold division.
Each of these also has a further division according to the distinction of weak, medium, and sharp faculties.
And just as there is this division for each of them according to lineage (*gotra*) and faculty (*indriya*).

In this way, for each of the four [knowledges] that have the origin belonging to the peak of existence as their object, there is a sixfold division due to the distinction of the six lineages (*gotra*),
and a threefold division due to the distinction of the faculties (*indriya*).
Just as for these eight [knowledges], there is a sixfold and a threefold division respectively according to the distinctions of lineage and faculty.

In this way, for all [knowledges] included within the stage of non-returning (anāgāmi), which are distinguished by differences in their aspects (ākāra) and objects (ālambana), up to those included within the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), there is a distinction based on the difference between spiritual lineages (gotra) and faculties (indriya).
This should be applied according to this method;
or rather, it should be applied in this manner.

In the first case, there are fifty-two included in the stage of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), up to twenty included in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Summing these together, there are three hundred and eighty-four diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Multiplying these by six and then by three, they become six thousand nine hundred and twelve.
In the second case, where there are eighty at the beginning,
up to twenty-four in the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana),
there are five hundred and seventy-six in total when calculated as a single aggregate.
By multiplying by six and then by three according to the distinctions of lineage (gotra) and faculties (indriya),
there are ten thousand three hundred and sixty-eight diamond-like concentrations (vajropama-samādhi).
For this very reason, that is called the "knowledge of destruction" (kṣayajñāna).
He asks, "Why? and replies:
"Because it arises for the first time simultaneously with the attainment of the destruction of all outflows (*āsrava*).
This is because that knowledge arises for the very first time together with the attainment of the destruction of all outflows.
Therefore, it is called "knowledge of destruction" (kṣayajñāna),
either by eliding the middle term or according to etymological rules.
The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of qualifying the specific knowledge of those such as the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
The inclusion of the word "first" (*prathamataḥ*) is for the purpose of qualifying the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) and so forth.
For the application of words occurs in dependence upon conventional designation (*saṃketa*).
For this very reason, he is [called] "he" (sa).
Because his own purpose is fully accomplished,
and because he is worthy of performing the welfare of others, he is an Arhat.
The meaning is: because of being fit for performing the welfare of others;
and because of being worthy of worship by all those still possessed of passion (*sarāga*).
"Those possessed of passion" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*); he is an *arhat* because he is worthy of the worship of all of them.
"It is established.
What is established?
He says: "The other seven previously mentioned persons are those in training (śaikṣa)."
Three who abide in the fruits and four who are entering toward them have been mentioned.

Since it is determined that "this one alone is an adept" (aśaikṣa), it is established that noble ones other than this are those in training (śaikṣas). By what [criterion] are they "those in training"?

For what reason are those seven persons called "learners" (*śaikṣa*)? It is said: because they have the habit of constantly training for the sake of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). They are called learners because training (*śikṣā*) is their habit (*śīla*).
It is *śīla*.
According to the grammatical rule *chattrādibhyo ṇaḥ*, [the suffix -ṇa is applied]. Where are they those whose nature is to train?
Regarding the three trainings: what are the three trainings?
They are higher training in ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*), higher training in mind (*adhicitta*), and higher training in wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
"What is their intrinsic nature? he asks.
"They, moreover, have the intrinsic nature of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Training in ethical discipline is *adhiśīla*; likewise, up to training in wisdom is *adhiprajñā*."
The term *avyayībhāva* compound is formed according to the rule *avyayaṃ vibhaktau*.

He explains that because there is no distinction between the acts of training and the nature of one's character and so forth, "the trainings" refers to the very nature of one's character (*śīla*) and the like.
[Otherwise,] even an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) would be considered a "trainee" (*śaikṣa*).
It is not the case that even an ordinary person trains in the precepts taught in the Vinaya;
for they lack knowledge of the truths as they truly are.
This is not so.
Why?
Because of the lack of discernment and non-comprehension of the truths, such as suffering and the rest, as they truly are.
For that, O monks, is indeed "seen" because of the statement: "that which is seen by noble wisdom.
Thus, in the Sūtra, after explaining in detail the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla*) or the training in higher mind (*adhicitta*), it asks:
"What is the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*)?"
One understands, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of suffering," "this is the origin of suffering," and "this is the cessation of suffering."
"This is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
This is because of the wisdom that perceives the truths as they truly are,
and because one has trained therein, in the precepts and so forth.
Furthermore, because of training again in that regard,

although a noble one (ārya) may relinquish something due to the abandonment of the *prātimokṣa* vows or due to falling away from the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, he does not relinquish everything.

For it is never the case that a noble one (ārya) lacks the three trainings. An "ordinary" noble one refers to the state of non-concentration (asamāhitāvasthā), which is the natural condition (prakṛti) of sentient beings.
One who stays there— the noble one engaged in activities such as wandering for alms—
is not "one whose nature is training";
the intended meaning is that he would not be a *śaikṣa* (learner).
"By way of intention" means by way of desire (*chanda*). It is like a traveler who has already set out on his journey.
A "traveler" is one who is going along a road.
Even when stationary, one is called a "traveler" because one has not abandoned the intention to go;
it is just like that.
And because of the accompaniment of acquisition (*prāpty-anuṣaṅga*).
For even in one who abides in their natural state (*prakṛtistha*), the acquisitions of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are still present.
Therefore, even one abiding in their natural state is not one whose nature is devoid of training (*aśikṣaṇa-śīla*).
In connection with the explanation and praise of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), this is said:
"Now, what are the dharmas of those in training? and so forth.
The untainted (anāsrava) dharmas of one in training have a conditioned (saṃskṛta) nature.
In this way, the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) belong to one beyond training.
Why is nirvāṇa not [considered] belonging to one in training (śaikṣa)? The intention is: because it is that which has been attained by one in training.
"Because even an *aśaikṣa* and an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) are endowed with that [nirvāṇa].
An ordinary person is also endowed with nirvāṇa attained through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
Thus, he is the first "one who has entered the path" (*pratipannaka*).
"One who stands on the path of seeing.
"Of the remaining," and so forth:

this refers to the remaining candidates for the fruits—the candidates for the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship—because they are not distinct from those established in the three fruits.
Because they are not distinct from those established in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning;
the meaning is that those who have entered the path toward the fruit of once-returning and so forth are not other than those who are stream-enterers and so forth.
This is stated with reference to the sequential attainment [of the fruits].
Regarding the attainment of the four fruits in successive order, it is said:
"In substance, there are five. However, there may also be those who have already abandoned attachment to the lower realms and to the desire realm.
One who has further become free from passion has destroyed six categories [of afflictions].
One who is free from passion regarding the desire realm has destroyed nine categories.
In the path of seeing—that is, during the state of the path of seeing—they would respectively be candidates for the fruit of once-returner and non-returner.
And they are not stream-enterers or once-returners;
rather,
they are distinct from those.
And this being so, there are seven [persons] in substance:

the three who have entered upon the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning, and the four who abide in the fruits; it should be understood that the one who has entered upon the fruit of arhatship is not distinct from the one who abides in the fruit of non-returning.
"For the path of cultivation has been stated to be twofold" means that the path of cultivation is twofold, according to the statement: "But that which is called the path of seeing is untainted."

"Because it is underlain by those afflictions (*kleśa-anuśayitatvāt*)," because the affliction belonging to that level underlies that worldly path (*laukika-mārga*) by way of being its object (*ālambana*).
With the words "For whichever affliction... and so forth, he demonstrates an example based on similarity and dissimilarity (*sādharmya-vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
[The meaning is: whichever path belongs to a particular level...
It is not an antidote to the afflictions of that level,
because it is underlain by those very afflictions,
just like other non-concentrated phenomena belonging to that same level.

By way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya), however, it is like the path of preparation for a higher stage (upari-sāmantaka-mārga), or like the untainted [path] (anāsrava), or like the path of counteraction (pratipakṣa-mārga).
It is said that "detachment is also achieved by means of the mundane [path]" (laukikena api vairāgyam); this refers to the path of preparation for a higher stage.

"Also by the supramundane" means by the untainted (*anāsrava*) path belonging to its own level or a lower level that serves as its antidote. Noble detachment [is achieved] by the mundane [path]. (VI.47cd)
Thus,
for example, in the case of a stream-enterer who practices tranquility (*śamatha*),

as he proceeds toward detachment by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), for each stage [of the path], both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) acquisitions of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) arise.
"Relying on dhyāna" means that because a learner (śaikṣa) transforms his faculties by relying on the six stages,
but not on the formless [attainments].
Because it is stated that "the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) relies on nine stages, whereas the one in training (śaikṣa) relies on six," he therefore says:
"He who, relying on a dhyāna, transforms his faculties."
Because he abandons the entire previous path— due to the abandonment of the previously acquired paths of the formless realm (ārūpya) that are comprised of dull faculties—
and because he attains the path of the solitary fruit, namely, the attainment of the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) which is of the nature of sharp faculties;
thus, having abandoned the inferior fruit, he attains the fruit while increasing it.
Because of this statement,

one would be non-endowed with the dissociation from the afflictions of the higher stages— that is, the dissociation from the afflictions belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara). And this is another fault.

And when that dissociation from the afflictions of the higher stages has been abandoned, one would become possessed of those afflictions belonging to the higher stages. However, as in the case of one who is half-liberated from the peak of existence (bhavāgra) or one born in the higher realms, there is no such possession; thus, "half-liberated" means liberated by half.
One who is half-liberated from the peak of existence is "half-liberated from the peak of existence" (*bhavāgrārdhavimukta*).
One who is born above is "born above" (*ūrdhvajāta*).
One who is both half-liberated from the peak of existence and born above is "half-liberated from the peak of existence and born above" (*bhavāgrārdhavimuktordhvajāta*).
"Like those two" means:
like one who is half-liberated from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) and one who has been born above it.
The completion of the sentence is: "He possesses them."
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of excluding the previously mentioned fault.
Explaining that meaning, he says:
"In its absence," and so forth.

Even though that person lacks a worldly attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*), there would be no possession (*samanvāgama*) of those afflictions (*kleśa*), just as in the case of one who is liberated from half of the categories of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*); this is the full explanation.
For such a person, there is indeed no worldly attainment of dissociation from half of the categories of the peak of existence.
Because there is no mundane path that serves as an antidote to those [defilements],

and because the supramundane attainment of dissociation from them— which would have been relinquished through the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) while relying on meditative absorption (*dhyāna*)—
is not again possessed by those types of defilements belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), so you maintain.
It would be the same for this person.
For example, it is like an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has been born above the level of the first dhyāna, having been reborn in the second dhyāna or higher,
due to the abandonment of the possession of dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the desire realm.
Wholesome [dharmas] acquired through dhyāna are abandoned through the transition of levels and through falling away, due to the attainment of dissociation belonging to the level of the first dhyāna.
In that way, because of the rule that [defilements] belonging to the formless realm are abandoned,
it is accepted that there is no further possession (samanvāgama) of those defilements belonging to the desire realm.
The same would apply to this person (pudgala) as well.

The term "ordinary person" (pṛthagjana) is used because for a noble one (ārya) who attains detachment from the desire realm or from the realms above it by means of a worldly path, there occurs both a worldly and a supramundane acquisition of dissociation from the afflictions (kleśa).

In that regard, the worldly attainment of dissociation from the afflictions belonging to the desire realm is abandoned by one born in a stage above the level of the first dhyāna through the transition of levels (*bhūmi-saṃcāra*), but not the supramundane attainment. However, for the noble one (*ārya*), [the abandonment occurs] through the acquisition of a fruit, the intensification [of faculties], or falling away.
This is because of the rule of relinquishment.
And when that supramundane [attainment] exists, even for a noble one (ārya) born above the first dhyāna, it is no longer possible to be possessed of those [defilements].
However, this is not the case for an ordinary person (pṛthagjana); thus, the term "ordinary person" is employed.
Therefore, this is not a proof.
As for what was stated [in verse VI.48]: "Because, when [the path] is abandoned, there is no longer possession of the afflictions," [this applies] to all cases.
Thus [it is said].
From its own level, the levels above, and the levels below,
because it is both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
(VI.49) "Because of the commonality of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
This means that the faculty of equanimity is identical in both the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the fourth dhyāna and so forth, as well as in their preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
"A certain person is unable" refers to one who possesses dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*).
"Because the transition of the faculties is difficult.

This is because it is difficult for the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) or the faculty of mental happiness (*saumanasyendriya*) to arise immediately after the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Since both the fundamental (*maula*) and the preparatory (*sāmantaka*) stages share the commonality of the faculty of equanimity, for what purpose does one manifest the final path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) from the fundamental stage itself?
It does not arise from the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*),
because of the high esteem for the level free from passion;
nor from a lower level, because one is already free from passion there.
Or, because detachment from the lower realm has already been achieved by means of its preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*).
"Proceeding with the aspects of the truths" means proceeding with the aspects such as impermanence and so forth.
(VI.50) "According to possibility" means: some say that if one views a lower stage as coarse, one views the higher stage as its opposite, namely, as peaceful.
Others explain it thus: [the text continues].
The aspects such as "peaceful" and so forth sometimes characterize [the object] by means of even a single aspect;
it is not necessarily by all of them together.
This is because of their coarseness.
"Coarse" means from the perspective of coarseness.
It is coarse because of its lack of tranquility.
How is the lower stage lacking in tranquility?
Because of the greater degree of intense effort (*mahābhisaṃskāra*).
This lower state, together with its path, requires great effort and is accomplished through exertion. This higher state, together with its path, likewise requires great effort.
Because this [effort] exceeds those two, it is "with greater exertion" (*mahābhisaṃskāratara*).
Its state is that;
therefore [it is so called].
"Khila" means difficult to break through. Because it is a contemptible obstruction (*khila*), it is "duḥkhila"; thus, it is [so called] by virtue of being difficult to break through.
To the question, "In what way is a lower stage not sublime (*apraṇīta*)? he says:
"Because it is adverse due to having a greater degree of *dauṣṭhulya*.

*Dauṣṭhulya* means the unserviceability (*akarmaṇyatā*) of body and mind, that is to say, their conformity to the afflictions (*kleśa*). [The term] "having much *dauṣṭhulya*" refers to that which possesses this [quality].
It is full of many corruptions.
This lower state, together with its path, is also full of many corruptions.
This higher state, together with its path, is also full of many corruptions.
Because this [state] possesses these two to a superior degree, it is "more heavily burdened with corruption" (*bahudauṣṭhulyatara*).
Due to that state,
it is called "having thick walls" (*sthūlabhittikata*).
By way of being like a thick wall;
because one does not escape from that very level by means of that very level, for one does not emerge from that specific level through that same level.
It is like not escaping from a wall.
Just as there is no escape from that very same wall because one is obstructed by the space occupied by it.
"By way of their opposite":

because there is little effort (*alpa-abhisaṃskāra*), because there is a state of non-aversion due to having very little corruption (*dausthulya*), and because one escapes from that stage by means of that [higher] stage, there are respectively the aspects of "peaceful," "excellent," and "escape.
(VI.51) The incidental discussion is concluded.
This must be stated:
that which occurs immediately after the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) must be stated.
However, as a secondary consequence, there is an exposition of the characteristics of the mundane paths of uninterrupted activity and liberation.
If one is immovable, then after the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna), there is the thought of non-arising (anutpādamati);
that is,
the knowledge that there is nothing further to be done.
Therefore, at that time, this [knowledge] does not arise for him.
Because there is the possibility of falling away— that is, because there is room for the arising of afflictions— the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) does not arise for him.
What is the reason?
Because falling away is possible;
for it is possible for him to fall away.
Furthermore, for one who possesses the knowledge of non-arising, there is no falling away.
For it is by means of that [knowledge] that one becomes a śramaṇa. (VI.52)
One becomes a śramaṇa through association with the state of a śramaṇa, just as a cloth is called "white" through association with whiteness.
One is a śramaṇa because one pacifies the afflictions (kleśas).
"Because they are its outflow fruits (*niṣyandaphala*) and fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).

This means that, as appropriate, the paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states are the outflow fruits and fruits of human effort of that asceticism (*śrāmaṇya*) characterized by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
The paths of liberation are both its outflow fruit and its fruit of human effort.
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) things are only the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala).
For whatever arises by the power of something, that fruit is born of human effort;
and whatever is obtained by the power of something, that too is considered the fruit of human effort.
(VI.53) "If that is so, then... and so forth. The meaning of the sentence is:

just as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is made for the ordinary person Pāṇini regarding his own teaching, so too a supplementary rule must be formulated for the omniscient Buddha. This is the sense of the statement.

"The abandonment of the previous path," and so forth. This means the abandonment of the previous path occurs through the relinquishing of the path of the candidate (*pratipannaka-mārga*), and the attainment of a path not previously possessed occurs through the acquisition of the path of fruition (*phala-mārga*).
"Because of the acquisition of a single attainment for all":

at the time of attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), a single attainment comprised within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is obtained for all [abandonments], namely, the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*).

Likewise, at the time of attaining the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), a single attainment comprised within the fruit of once-returning is obtained for all [abandonments], namely, the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing and the abandonment of the six types of what is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation.
The same should be applied to the fruits of non-returner and arhatship as well.
Regarding "the fourfold dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges":
because of the distinction between the [four] truths, there are four types of dharma-knowledges and likewise four types of subsequent knowledges. (Abhidh-k-vy 578)
The simultaneous attainment of the eight knowledges. (VI.54) The two fruits obtained by means of the worldly path are the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning.
For that [abandonment] can also be attained by means of a mundane path.
How, then, is it appropriate for it to be the fruit of *śrāmaṇya*, which is characterized by the untainted (*anāsrava*) path?
Furthermore, abandonment is also the fruit of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
By the word "also" (*api*), the abandonment that is the fruit of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is also included.

For both types of abandonment, a single acquisition (*prāpti*) is obtained, whether it is comprised within the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) or the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).

Therefore, due to its connection with the abandonment that is the fruit of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) fruit of once-returning or the fruit of non-returning constitutes the fruit of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
Regarding the phrase "the abandonment of the three fetters":
the abandonment of the three fetters occurs through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

As for the partial abandonment of the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—their abandonment likewise occurs solely through the path of seeing.
Regarding that abandonment being the fruit of once-returning and non-returning: what is the reason for its inclusion?
From this it is known that the Blessed One spoke thus because of the mixing with abandonment.
[The phrase] "due to falling away by the power of that" [is used].

Regarding the statement that "in the case of noble detachment through the mundane [path], the acquisitions of dissociation are twofold": therein, that abandonment which was attained by means of the mundane path is maintained by the untainted acquisition of dissociation.
The meaning is that it necessarily remains present through its connection with that acquisition.
"One does not die having fallen from the fruit.
For in the absence of that [fruit], death would occur for one who has fallen away, just as it does for a worldly person.
"By its power" means by the power of the acquisition of untainted dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*).

That very same untainted attainment produced by the present mundane path, as well as the future eightfold noble path being attained through mundane power, are established as the conditioned fruit of asceticism (*saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*),
and this is not contradictory;
however, in the Sūtra, the unconditioned fruit of asceticism (*asaṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*) is what is proclaimed.
Because of its predominance,
it should be understood here that the term also includes the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*) consists in the carrying away (*vāhana*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
He is called a *brāhmaṇa* because he has driven away (*vāhita*) manifold kinds of evil and unwholesome states (*dharma*).
The state of being that (*tadbhāva*) is *brāhmaṇya*, which is the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). To the question "How is it the Wheel of Brahmā? he says:
But it is the "Brahma-wheel" because it is turned by Brahmā;
since it was set in motion by Brahmā,
it is therefore called the Brahma-wheel.
"Because of his union with unsurpassed brahminhood" means because of his union with the unsurpassed untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
This is the example stated by Jīvaka: "For this Blessed One is indeed Brahmā."
"By means of swift movement and so forth, and by means of spokes and so forth.
This means: by means of swift movement and the like, and by means of spokes and the like.
"Because of its swift movement," and so forth.
This explains the similarity between the path and the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*).
Just as the wheel-treasure moves swiftly, [so does the path].
Thus is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is called "swift" because it realizes the truths through fifteen moments of mind,
owing to its progressive abandonment [of the afflictions].
Just as one leaves one place and moves to another place,

so too this [path] abandons the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and moves toward the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) by way of its manifestation; or rather, because it abandons one truth and moves toward another.
Because of conquering what is unconquered and dwelling in what is conquered.
Just as one conquers unconquered villages, market towns, and so forth,
and dwells in those already conquered.

Thus, by means of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), one conquers the afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that have not yet been conquered, through the severance of their acquisition (*prāpti*).
And by means of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), one dwells in those [afflictions] already conquered,
because of the simultaneous arising of the acquisition of dissociation from the afflictions.
And because of rising and falling:
just as it rises in one place and falls in another,
so too does this [process] occur through the repeated manifestation of the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Or, it arises accordingly by taking as its objects the truths such as suffering and the realms such as desire;
it arises by taking the form and formless realms as its objects,
and it descends by taking the desire realm as its object.
"Right view," and so forth in detail.

Here, having established oneself in ethical discipline (*śīla*), one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*); from the attainment of concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) is cultivated according to reality. Therefore, right speech, right action, and right livelihood occupy the position of the hub.
This is because right view and the other [limbs] function in dependence upon them; thus, ethical discipline is considered the foundation.
Concentration is like the hub, because it holds the others together;
right view and the other factors are like the spokes,
because they proceed from here and there like spokes.
From where does this [come]?
Is this the Vaibhāṣikas' own opinion—that the path of seeing is the wheel of Dharma—or is it from scripture? [The answer is: "It was set in motion upon its arising."
Because it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Wheel of Dharma was set in motion at the arising of the Path of Seeing.
How so?
The Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
There, the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
"Monks, regarding these dharmas unheard of before, as I applied my mind thoroughly, the eye arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and insight arose: 'This is the noble truth of suffering.
This is the origin of suffering."
"This is the cessation of suffering;
this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
As he applied wise attention to these teachings unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose.

"Indeed, that noble truth of suffering must be fully understood by me through direct knowledge"—when he applied wise attention to these teachings not heard before, vision arose, as described previously.

"Indeed, that noble truth of the origin of suffering must be abandoned by me through direct knowledge"—regarding these teachings not heard before, as described previously. "Indeed, that noble truth of the cessation of suffering must be realized by me through direct knowledge"—regarding these teachings not heard before, as described previously.

"Indeed, that noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is to be cultivated by me through direct knowledge"—regarding these dharmas unheard of before, as previously described. "Indeed, that noble truth of suffering has been fully understood by me through direct knowledge"—regarding these dharmas unheard of before, as previously described.
"Indeed, that noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned by me through direct knowledge"—regarding these dharmas unheard of before, as previously described.
"Indeed, that noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized by me through direct knowledge," regarding these dharmas unheard of before, as previously described.

"Furthermore, that noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering has been cultivated by me through direct knowledge," regarding these dharmas unheard of before, as previously described.
And, O monks, as long as this threefold revolution and twelvefold aspect regarding these four noble truths had not arisen for me as vision... [it did not arise].
Neither knowledge, nor science, nor wisdom had arisen [in me].

I had not yet dwelt extensively with a mind free from perversion, liberated, emerged, detached, and disjoined from this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and from this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods, humans, and asuras.

“Monks, I did not yet claim to have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. But when, monks, regarding these four noble truths, the eye arose in me in this way— three turns and twelve aspects— and likewise the knowledge, the wisdom, the understanding, the light,
and the intelligence arose, then, from that time on, I dwelt much detached from this world with its gods, and with a mind free from perversion.”
Then I realized, "I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose in the Venerable Kauṇḍinya and in eighty thousand deities.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Kauṇḍinya.
"Kauṇḍinya, have you understood the Dharma?
"I have understood it, Blessed One.
"Kauṇḍinya, have you understood the Dharma?"
"It is understood by me, O Sugata.
"The Dharma has been understood by the Venerable Kauṇḍinya," thus did the terrestrial yakṣas raise their voices and proclaim this cry:
"Friends, the Blessed One has set in motion the Wheel of Dharma at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana—a wheel that has three turnings and twelve aspects."
"Never before set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma, for the benefit of many beings," and so forth. Thus,
when the path of seeing had arisen in the noble Kauṇḍinya, it was said by the deities that "the Wheel of Dharma has been set in motion by the Blessed One," according to the statement in the Sūtra.
It is understood that the path of seeing is the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*).
How is it "threefold-turning" (*triparivarta*), and so forth?
"This is suffering, the truth of the noble ones"—this is the first turning.
"Indeed, that must be fully understood"—this is the second [turning].
"Indeed, that has been fully understood"—this is the third.
Thus, these are the three turnings.
In each single revolution, four aspects arise: "This is suffering"—in this regard, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose.
Furthermore, regarding "it is to be fully understood," there are again four;
and regarding "it has been fully understood," there are yet again four.
Thus, these are the twelve aspects.
Among them, untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*) is called the "eye" because its object is directly perceived;
it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because it is free from doubt.
It is *vidyā* because its object is reality;
it is *buddhi* because of its purity,
according to the etymological derivation that "pure intellect is *buddhi*."

Furthermore, the vision of the truths by outsiders (*bāhyaka*) is not an antidote to wrong views, doubt, and ignorance, and it is *sāsrava* (with outflows); therefore, the mention of "eye" and so forth is for the purpose of distinguishing [the noble vision] from that.
Moreover, among the three turnings, the first vision is the eye;
the subsequent investigation of what has been seen is knowledge (*jñāna*).
It is "knowledge" (*vidyā*) by virtue of its extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*),
because it grasps whatever exists;
it is "wisdom" (*buddhi*) by virtue of its mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
Because of the realization of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtārthāvabodha*).
Furthermore, he says "eye" (*cakṣus*) in order to exclude inferential knowledge (*ānumānika-jñāna*) regarding phenomena not previously heard;
and he says "knowledge" (*jñāna*) in order to exclude knowledge based on resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika-jñāna*).
"Knowledge" (*vidyā*) is for the purpose of negating conceited knowledge;
"awakening" (*buddhi*) is for the purpose of negating that which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). Thus it is said:
"In each truth, it is so."
"This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; that indeed must be abandoned;
that indeed has been abandoned"—these are the three turnings.
In each individual turn, "the eye arose, knowledge, science, and awakening"—these are the twelve aspects.
This should be applied similarly to the truths of cessation and the path as well.
He said:
If each truth were indeed thus, there would result three revolutions and twelve aspects, or twelve revolutions and forty-eight aspects.
Why, then, is it said that [the wheel of Dharma] has "three revolutions and twelve aspects"?
Therefore it is said:
"Because of the commonality of three sets of twelve, it is described as having three turnings and twelve aspects,
just like the teaching on the two [bases] and the skill in the seven stations."
It is like the teaching on duality, and like the teaching on skill in the seven points.
For example, after having explained it in detail, [the Buddha] said: "In that case, monk, I shall teach you duality; listen to it, and attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak."
What is the dyad?
It is the eye and visible forms, up to the mind and mental phenomena.
Just as it is called "the dyad" here because of its similarity to a pair.
Thus, due to the commonality of the three triads and the twelve [factors], it is said to have three turnings and twelve aspects.
And just as a monk skilled in the seven points understands form as it truly is,
he understands the arising of form.
The cessation of form;
the practice leading to the cessation of form;
and the gratification and the danger regarding form.
"And he understands the escape as it truly is.
A monk skilled in these seven points, examining the three kinds of objects, will quickly understand the end of suffering in this Dharma and Vinaya.
This is because each of the aggregates possesses the same nature of skill in the seven points.
Thus, here too, because of the commonality of the three sets of twelve, it is said to have "three turnings and twelve aspects. And by these, as detailed in the full explanation:
by these turnings, as specified in the Sūtra, the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning are shown respectively.

Beginning with "This is the noble truth of suffering" and continuing up to "This is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering," the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is shown.

Then, beginning with "That noble truth of suffering must be fully known through direct knowledge (*abhijñā*)" and continuing up to "That noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering must be cultivated through direct knowledge," the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is shown.

Starting from "That noble truth of suffering has been fully known through direct knowledge" up to "That noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering has been cultivated through direct knowledge," the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) is thus shown.
Regarding this, the Master says:
"If it is thus," and so forth.
If, by these revolutions (*parivarta*), the paths of seeing and so on are shown according to their respective order,
then the path of seeing alone is not characterized by three revolutions and twelve aspects.
What then?
It is a single revolution with four aspects.
How is this path of seeing established as the Wheel of Dharma?
The intention is that in the absence of the three turnings, there would be an absence of similarity to a wheel, and thus it would not be appropriate to call it a "wheel.
Therefore, that very exposition of the Dharma (*dharmaparyāya*) is the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*);
that very sutra is the Wheel of Dharma.
Because of the illumination of the Wheel of Dharma,
it is appropriate that it has three turnings and twelve aspects,
since it illuminates their meaning.
Regarding "from the three turnings":
the first turning is from "suffering" up to "the path";
the second is from "to be fully known" up to "to be cultivated."
The third [turning] consists in [the thought]: "It has been fully known... up to... it has been cultivated.
This is because of the threefold treatment of the four truths.
Regarding the essential nature of the truths—suffering, origin, cessation, and path—there is one mode of treatment for each, consisting of four aspects.

The second mode of activity consists of four aspects regarding the act of thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) in its form as a task to be performed: "that which is to be thoroughly known, that which is to be abandoned, that which is to be realized, and that which is to be cultivated.
The third mode of activity consists of four aspects regarding the acts of thorough knowledge and so forth once they are completed: "thoroughly known, abandoned, realized, and cultivated."
It consists of twelve aspects. Of what?
Of that dharma-discourse.
"Setting in motion" means proceeding into the mental continuum of others; it is the impelling [of the teaching] into the continua of those to be trained.
How does it proceed?
By making the meaning known.
Alternatively, the entire Noble Path— the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning— is the Wheel of Dharma,
because it proceeds through the mental continuums of those to be trained;
for it is called a "wheel" (cakra) on account of its proceeding (kramaṇa).

If the entire Noble Path is the Wheel of Dharma, how is it that it is said to have been set in motion for the noble Ājñātakauṇḍinya upon the mere arising of the path of seeing? To this, it is replied:
That [wheel], however, was set in motion within the mental continuum of another—specifically, within the continuum of the noble Kauṇḍinya.
Because it began to turn by means of the arising of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and because it was turned for the first time, it is called "set in motion" (*pravartita*).
The prefix *pra-* is used here in the sense of the initial action.
It is as in the expression, "the rice has been eaten.
But why is there no attainment for the third [dhyāna]?
Because one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) would enter the path of certainty (*niyāma*).
The intention [of the objection] is: why should the attainment of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) not occur at the sixteenth moment of mind? The response is stated:
"For there is no path of seeing (dṛkpatha) above [the realm of desire]."
Thus it is said: "Because of the absence of hearing.
This means that in the formless realms (ārūpya), only the enlightenment of a disciple (śrāvakabodhi) could possibly exist.
Because self-arisen awakening is impossible [without causes],
and because the realization of a śrāvaka does not occur without the voice of another; furthermore, because it does not take the lower realms as its object.
"Root wholesome formless attainments do not have lower realms with outflows as their object.
This is because the path of seeing must necessarily have the three realms as its cognitive object.
"He does not exist there.
*Vidhāna* means "arrangement" (*vidhā*), which is to say "means" (*upāya*).
One whose nature (*dharma*) or intrinsic character (*svabhāva*) is that of falling away is called "one of the nature of falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*).

One of the nature of volition (cetanādharmā) is one whose nature is to take his own life. One of the nature of guarding (anurakṣaṇādharmā) is one who is able to guard that liberation. One who is steadfast and unshakable (sthitākaṃpya) is one who remains established in that liberation.
In that [state], he is unshakable;
he is one capable of penetration;
he is one capable of transforming his faculties.
One whose nature is unshakable is called "of unshakable nature" because his nature is unshakable and irreversible.
He is of two kinds: one who is sharp-facultied by nature.
And one who possesses sharp faculties through the transformation of the faculties.
The restriction "only five are born from those resolved through faith" is intended to be definitive.
The meaning is that these have arisen having become those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
This amounts to saying that they are preceded by resolution through faith.
However, the sixth [type of noble person] can also exist otherwise; thus it was explained as being occasional (*sāmayikī*).
That which arises from conditions characterized by time, requisites, health, a specific location, and so forth, is "temporary" (sāmayikī).
And it is "lovely" (kāntā). The "lovely" is the liberation of the mind (cetovimukti).
Why is it called "beloved" (*kāntā*)?
Because it must be constantly protected.
For in the world, that which is beloved is seen to require constant protection.
It is also said in the Sūtra:

"Suppose, for example, that the kinsmen of a one-eyed man should consider his single eye to be something that must be protected well and thoroughly, thinking: 'Let no cold, nor heat, nor dust or grit fall upon his eye; lest even this one eye of his, which has not yet perished, should also perish.'"
In the same way, for an Arhat liberated by occasion (samayavimukta), this Dharma is to be guarded, cherished, and sustained.
Therefore, such an Arhat liberated by occasion considers that he must guard it well and thoroughly, thinking:
"May I not fall away from this Dharma."
"He does not fall away from that" means:
"like a jar of ghee.
Just as a jar filled with ghee is called a "jar of ghee."
This is due to the elision of the middle word *pūrṇa*.
Or, for example, a jar that is intended for ghee is called a "ghee-jar" (*ghṛtaghaṭa*), meaning a jar into which ghee will be poured;
by the elision of the word *apekṣa*, it becomes "ghee-jar."

In the same way here as well, because the intermediate word *apekṣā* (dependence) has been elided, they are called "those liberated by dependence on time" (*samayavimukta*) because they are both dependent on time (*samaya-apekṣā*) and liberated (*vimukta*).
Furthermore, it has been stated that "time" refers to such things as [favorable] requisites (*upakaraṇa*). He asks: "How is it that they cannot be disturbed? and thus he says:
Regarding "by way of non-retrogression":
it means either by way of temporary liberation or ultimate liberation.
By way of temporary liberation, one is "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*).
The meaning is that "liberation at all times" (asamayavimukti) results from being liberated absolutely.
How is this so? He says:
because of the possibility or impossibility of falling away (parihāṇi).
Because falling away is possible, one is called "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*) due to liberation after a period of time;
because falling away is impossible, one is called "not liberated by occasion" (*asamayavimukta*) due to ultimate liberation.
And he is a follower of one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Thus,
when one who is still in training (śaikṣa) transforms his faculties,
he attains the state of one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Now, if he is by nature of sharp faculties, he is indeed one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) at the sixteenth moment of mind.
Therefore, such a person of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*) is said to have previously been one who had attained vision.
However, this refers to one who transforms his faculties while in the state of arhatship.
It should be understood that this one of immovable nature was not previously one who had attained through vision.
(VI.59cd) Some, however, belong to the lineage of those whose nature is volition from the very beginning.
One of a nature subject to regression is not mentioned because such a person has not undergone refinement;
it was stated that some belong to that lineage from the very beginning.

In that case, what is this so-called "lineage of those subject to falling away" (*parihāṇadharman-gotra*) up to the "lineage of those of immovable nature" (*akopyadharman-gotra*)? They have not specified the lineage of those subject to falling away and so forth.
Regarding this, some explain that the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) are the lineage;
for such virtuous roots belong to a certain person.
One who is of the nature to fall away, up to one who is of an immovable nature.
Others, however, say that the lineage (*gotra*) is the distinction of the faculties (*indriya-bheda*) starting from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
The Sautrāntikas, moreover, explain that the lineage is the seed (*bīja*) and the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the mind.

In the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and in the state of a learner (*śaikṣa*), when the seed of the nature of falling away exists as the cause, one is called "one belonging to the lineage of those subject to falling away.
Likewise, in the state of a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), because of the attainment of the activity of that seed, one is called "one subject to falling away.
This applies in the same way up to "one of immovable nature" (*akopyadharman*).
In this regard, the detailed explanation begins with "one of a nature subject to falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*).
One who is capable of falling away is "one of a nature subject to falling away.
If one were to say only this much:
And one should not say that there is no such thing as the "nature of volition" (cetanādharma) and so forth;
for all four of these, beginning with the nature of volition, are capable of falling away, and thus any one of them would be of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman).
There is no fifth [nature] other than those.
Therefore, distinguishing this one as being distinct from them by calling him "the fifth," he says that he does not possess qualities such as volition (*cetanā*).

Furthermore, since the four beginning with those of the nature of volition (*cetanā-dharma*) do not possess the quality of falling away (*parihāṇa-dharmaka*), it follows from the very description of the specific characteristics of each one that the following must be stated:

one of the nature of volition is capable of intending [to fall away], but is not one of the nature of guarding (*anurakṣaṇā-dharma*), up to and including one incapable of penetration (*prativedhanā-bhavya*).
Thus, one whose nature is to guard [the attainment] does not [fall away] except through a powerful condition for falling away.
The intention is that if there were a powerful condition for falling away, he would fall away.
By this mention of a "powerful condition," he distinguishes this person from the previously mentioned one who has the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
For one of a nature subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) falls away even through a weak condition for falling away.
Furthermore, the conditions for falling away are as stated in the Sūtra:
"There are five causes and five conditions that lead to the falling away of an Arhat who is liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*)."
Which five?
He is intent on his work;
he is intent on talk.
He becomes involved in legal disputes;
he is devoted to the practice of long journeys;
and he is afflicted by chronic diseases.
By the phrase "even without guarding," he distinguishes [this type] from one whose nature is to guard;
for the latter would not fall away only if he were guarding, whereas this one does not fall away even without guarding.
Even without guarding that fruit, he is capable of remaining in that fruit;
he is not capable of falling away from that fruit,
nor is he capable of increasing it by attaining the state of being incapable of penetration (*prativedhanābhavyatā*).
"Without application and without vigor.
By this, it is stated by implication:
"If one were to apply oneself, one would be capable"; thus, this [category] is distinguished from the "incapable of penetration" (*prativedhanābhavya*).
For he is capable of penetrating it even without strenuous effort.
"The first two," and so forth:
one of a nature subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) is deficient in constant and respectful application (*sātatyasatkṛtyaprayoga*).
One whose nature is volitional (*cetanādharmā*) is also deficient in continuous application (*sātatyaprayoga*);
moreover, he is specifically deficient in respectful application (*satkṛtyaprayoga*). This is the distinction between these two.
By the phrase "but one of dull faculties," [the author] distinguishes him from the sixth type.
For the sixth [type of person] possesses sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).
Indeed, the distinction between these two is made by way of their faculties, not by way of their application (*prayoga*).
And having established it thus, the detailed explanation follows.
Since this is not necessarily the case, the intention is that there are six types of Arhats in the realms of form and formlessness as well, and not only in the realm of desire; specifically,
there are two types of "steadfast" (sthitākampya) Arhats in the realms of form and formlessness, and one other.

And the second is one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*). First of all, one who is stable and unshakable (*sthitākaṃpya*) may have a fixed inclination, but would not be one who exerts effort toward the capacity for penetration (*prativedhanābhavyatā*). One who is stable and unshakable in the desire realm does not attain the capacity for penetration.
Furthermore, because there is no powerful condition for falling away in the realms of form and formlessness, he does not fall away from his state;
nor do his faculties undergo transformation. Thus, he remains there as one belonging to the lineage of the "steadfast and immovable" (sthitākaṃpya).
Because of the possession of unshakable liberation, one also becomes of unshakable nature (*akopyadharman*).
Thus, there are only these two;
there are no others besides them.

In the realms of form and formlessness, there are three [types of persons], because of the absence of falling away (*parihāṇi*), the volition for suicide (*cetana*), and the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*). First of all, the one subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) does not exist there,
because of the absence of falling away.
There is also no one of the nature of guarding (*anurakṣaṇā-dharman*), because there is no possibility of guarding due to the absence of falling away (*parihāṇi*).
For this very reason, since there is no transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), there is also no one who is capable of penetration (*prativedhanā-bhavya*).
And so it has been said:
"He, as well as one born in the higher realms, is not subject to the shifting of faculties or to falling away."
And because in that state there is neither volition regarding oneself nor volition regarding others, one does not possess the quality of volition (*cetanā-dharma*).
(VI.60ab) Regarding the four beginning with the quality of volition:
these are the one whose nature is to guard volition (*cetanā-anurakṣaṇā-dharma*), the steadfast (*sthita-akaṃpya*), and the one capable of penetration (*prativedhanā-bhavya*).
For one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) does not fall away further from his own lineage (*gotra*),
because that lineage is unconditioned (*akṛtrima*).
[This refers to] the five types beginning with those of the nature of falling away.
Because even for one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), falling away from the fruit is possible;
since the fruit is adventitious (*āgantuka*),
it does not [occur] from the previous [nature].
Thus,
because of the lineage and because of the fruit,
he does not fall away from that; therefore, he is an Arhat.
He asks "Why? and replies:
"Because it has been made firm by both the path of those in training (śaikṣa) and the path of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This refers to that lineage (gotra) which exists during the stage of one in training.
That [path] was cultivated by means of the path of training (śaikṣa-mārga) and was cultivated again in the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-avasthā).
Because it has been made firm by those two, that Arhat does not fall away from it.
But how is it for one in training (*śaikṣa*)? He says:
because it has been made firm by both the mundane and supramundane [paths], the one in training does not fall away from the first lineage (*gotra*).
That which is his own first lineage was previously cultivated by means of the mundane path.
And because it has been cultivated again by means of the path of training (śaikṣamārga),
one does not fall away from it.
Regarding this, someone says:
As it is said:
"Whichever is one's original lineage (*gotra*),
from that one does not fall away, because it has been made firm by the paths of both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)."
This is not a valid reason,
because even one who possesses the nature of volition (*cetanā-dharman*) and has reached refinement may fall away from that lineage (*gotra*).
That lineage is made firm by both the paths of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Falling away does not occur.
Therefore, that lineage itself is of such a nature that one does not fall away from the first [attainment],
but one may fall away from that which has been brought to refinement through heating (*uttāpanā*).

As for what was also said— that a learner (*śaikṣa*) does not fall away because [the path] has been made firm by both the mundane and supramundane [paths]— this too is not a valid reason, because it would entail the undesirable consequence that a stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*) could fall away.
For the fruit of stream-entry is certainly not made firm by a mundane path.
"Effort must be made in this regard.
Here we shall demonstrate the intention of the Master by which he spoke thus.
How so?
As for what was said— that one of the nature of volition who has reached refinement falls away from that lineage—
that is incorrect.

For that lineage characterized by the nature of volition (*cetanā-dharma-gotra*), which was cultivated during the stage of training (*śaikṣāvasthā*) and further cultivated— and thus strengthened— during the stage of no-more-training (*aśaikṣāvasthā*),
does not fall away even when one falls away from that state of arhatship;
for it has become primary during the stage of training.
And it has been stated by Ācārya Saṃghabhadra: "He who, having attained another lineage (gotra) during the stage of a learner (śaikṣa), attains arhatship—he too abandons that path;
yet he does not fail to remain in the very lineage reached through refinement (uttāpanā)."

As for the lineage of those whose nature is volitional (*cetanādharmagotra*), which has been attained only now in the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣāvasthā*) and was not attained in the stage of training (*śaikṣāvasthā*): one who falls away from that [lineage] does indeed fall away,
because it has not been made firm through both of those stages.
Thus, this is not a valid reason.

Furthermore, as for what was said— that a trainee (*śaikṣa*) would not fall away because he has been made firm by both the mundane and supramundane paths— this too is not a valid reason, because it would entail the undesirable consequence that a stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*) could fall away.
For it is not the case that the fruit of stream-entry has been made firm by either the mundane or the supramundane;
that too was stated through a lack of understanding.
That lineage is said to be the cause.
It is not with respect to the fruit;
for in that regard, another cause will be stated by which one does not fall away from the first fruit.
Indeed, there is no fruit whatsoever that is attained simultaneously by both the mundane and the supramundane paths.
Rather, it is the lineage (*gotra*) that is made firm by both the mundane and supramundane paths,

because it has been cultivated either in this life through the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, or in future lives through the path of abandonment, or by other mundane or supramundane paths during the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*).
As for that which is acquired later through refinement (*uttāpanā*):
since the adventitious lineage (*āgantuka-gotra*) is attained only subsequently and not in both states, one may fall away from it.
Having explained the lineage, the fruit is now explained.
And for whomsoever there is a first fruit, such is the detailed explanation.
For this very reason, there is no falling away from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
This is because if the fruit of stream-entry is attained, it necessarily occurs first.
However, regarding the fruits of once-returner and non-returner, they sometimes occur first if one is already largely detached from passion or entirely detached from passion;
and sometimes they do not occur first if one follows the gradual path.
In that case, whichever fruit occurs first—whether it be the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.
One does not fall away from that [fruit].
However, one may fall away from what follows— the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship— from those.
And having established it thus:
that one does not fall away from whichever lineage or fruit was first attained by him.
Respectively, there are five, six, and seven types.
For one of the nature of guarding (*anurakṣaṇā-dharman*), there are five types:

attaining parinirvāṇa while remaining in that state, the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), falling away and returning to the lineage of the nature of volition (*cetanā-dharman*), and returning to the lineage of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇa-dharman*).
For one who is steadfast (sthitākaṃpya), there are six types:
those same five, with the addition of the sixth being the returning to the lineage of the nature of guarding (anurakṣaṇādharmagotra).
For one capable of penetration (prativedhanābhavya), there are seven types.
And these same six, plus the seventh, which is the returning to the lineage of one who is stable (sthitākaṃpya), constitute [the seven lineages].
Whichever was one's original lineage during the stage of a learner (śaikṣa), that person, having become a learner, [remains in it].
The word "again" (*punar*) is supplied to complete the sentence.
It remains in that very [state] and not in another;
for otherwise, due to the acquisition of a specific lineage (*gotra*), that lineage would become distinct from the lineage belonging to the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*).
Therefore, because of the attainment of a distinguished lineage, there can only be progress for this person;
there is no falling away. How so?

For example, one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), having attained the state of incapacity for penetration (*prativedhābhavyatā*) through the sharpening of the faculties (*indriyottāpanā*) while in the stage of arhatship,
falls away from that arhatship.
Having become a trainee (*śaikṣa*), even when falling away from that very lineage (*gotra*), he does not remain in the lineage of the "steadfast" (*sthitākaṃpya*).
In reverse order, this continues until the lineage of one whose nature is not to lose [attainment] (*acetanādharmagotra*).
What then?
One remains precisely within the lineage of one whose nature is to fall away (*parihāṇadharmagotra*).
"Otherwise" means if one were to remain in another lineage (*gotra*).
"Because of obtaining a specific lineage" means because of obtaining a lineage superior to the lineage of those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
Therefore, when one falls away from arhatship, one necessarily falls away from the lineage as well, even through the refinement of the faculties (*indriyottāpana*).
What, then, is the reason that there is no falling away from the first fruit?

Whichever fruit is one's first—whether it be the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning—it is because the defilements to be abandoned by seeing lack a real object and lack a basis; this is the meaning.
"For these proceed with the self as their basis," and so forth.
These [defilements] to be abandoned by vision proceed by means of the self as their basis.
Why? He says:
Because it is rooted in the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
For it is by the power of the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*) that those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) manifest.
And it has been said: "Furthermore, whatever various types of views exist in the world..."

These [views] have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their root, originate from the view of a self-identity, are of the same nature as the view of a self-identity, and arise from the view of a self-identity.
Since that self does not exist, there is no falling away (*parihāṇi*) because they lack a real objective basis;
this is because they take the [four] truths as their object.
Because the truths are grasped as permanent and so forth.
And which affliction is not like this?
For even attachment and the rest, though to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), have false objects (*vitathālambana*).
Because they take the truths and other realities as their objects through the aspects of purity, pleasure, permanence, and self,
they superimpose a non-existent selfhood [upon them].
As it has been said:

"O monks, whoever perceives 'self' or 'belonging to self,' they perceive only these five aggregates of clinging as self and as belonging to self. And based upon that [perception], there arise the views of grasping at extremes and so forth."
They proceed based on the premise of a self,
[asserting] either that "the self is eternal" or that "it is subject to annihilation."
There is no self;
this alone is the foremost,
this alone is purity.

Those [afflictions] that proceed in such modes as "does this exist" or "does this not exist," which are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), are said to be "without a real object" (*avastuka*).
The meaning is that they are said to be "without a basis" (*niradhiṣṭhāna*);
it does not mean, however, that there is even a trace of a self (*ātman*) or the like.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of "one's own" (*ātmīya*) or the inclusion of "Īśvara" and so forth.
"Specifically determined" means characterized as pleasant, unpleasant, and so on.
For passion (*rāga*) which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), the object is a pleasant thing characterized by the beauty of hair, teeth, and so forth.
For aversion (*pratigha*), it is the disagreeable, characterized by its impurity and so forth;
for pride (*māna*) as well, it is the agreeable; and for ignorance (*avidyā*), it is those same two [objects] that are somewhat delusive.
However, for the [afflictions] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*), it is not characterized by a self (*ātman*) and so forth.

However, for those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing, there is no specific entity whatsoever characterized as "self" or "mine," other than the attachment and so forth that take those [aggregates] as their objects;
therefore, they are said to be without a real basis (*avastuka*).
Therefore, the meaning is that they are not said to have specific objects.
Furthermore, the Master explains in detail:

"In the case of a noble one who is still in training (*śaikṣa*), when he is not reflecting or investigating, an affliction arises due to the loss of mindfulness and the association with afflicted mindfulness."
It consists of passion and so forth.
It does not arise for one who is reflecting.
Just as the perception of a snake in a rope arises for someone who is not reflecting due to a lapse of mindfulness, [so too does it arise for one who is not reflecting].
It is not for one who is reflecting [on them].
It is the same with the view of self and so forth.
This includes the grasping at extreme views and so forth.
What, then, is the reason?
It is because it is not logical for views such as the view of a self to arise in one who is not closely examining [the object].
Because it is investigative.
Of what? Of the afflictions such as the view of a self and so forth.
Therefore, because there is no further contemplation (*anupanidhyāna*), it is not logical for a noble one (*ārya*) to give rise to views such as the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Since there is no cause for falling away, there is no falling away from the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*);
likewise, there is none even from the state of arhatship.
By the word "also" (api), he indicates that there is no falling away not only from the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing, but also from Arhatship itself.
However, falling away from the two fruits other than the first—that is, from the fruits of Once-returner and Non-returner—is possible;
the intention is that this is because their attainment can occur through the mundane path (laukika-mārga).
And the Teacher supports this very principle, stating:
"O monks, that which has been abandoned is indeed abandoned.
That alone is what is abandoned.
That which is abandoned by noble wisdom does not arise again;
however, that which is abandoned by mundane [wisdom] does.
The intention is that it arises again.
The second phrase of the sutra, "and for the trainee, heedfulness," serves as the proof that there is no falling away from arhatship.
And this is its meaning: "I declare heedfulness as the cause and the practice for the trainee; heedfulness must be practiced by the trainee."

But surely, even for one in training (śaikṣa), there is abandonment by means of noble wisdom (āryā prajñā). How then can it be taught that he has something yet to be done through diligence (apramādakaraṇīya)? Because there remains another fruit (phala) to be attained by him that has not yet been attained.
And there is for him an abandonment belonging to the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
Here, a Vaibhāṣika might say: "Because of the statement in the Sūtra, 'Ānanda, I declare that gain and honor are obstacles even for an Arhat,' there is falling away (*parihāṇi*) even for an Arhat.

To this, it is said: "Even for an Arhat," and so on at length, until: "In this Sūtra, falling away is taught only from the state of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*)."
How so?
In this regard, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Ānanda, I declare that even for an Arhat, gain and honor are obstacles."
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, did you say this:
'Ānanda, I declare that even for an Arhat, gain and honor are an obstacle'?"
The Blessed One said: "Indeed not, Ānanda, for the sake of attaining what has not been attained, nor for the sake of realizing what has not been realized."
It is for the sake of realizing that which has not yet been realized.
However, regarding those four higher mental states of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) that he has attained,
I declare that he may fall away from one or another of them.
But as for that unshakable liberation of mind which he has realized with his own body while dwelling alone, secluded, heedful, ardent,
and resolute— of that, I do not say there is any possibility of falling away by any means whatsoever.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should train yourself in this way:
"I shall overcome gain and honor, and my mind shall not remain completely consumed by gain and honor.
In this way, Ānanda, you should train yourself.
If the Vaibhāṣika were to say:
"Because of the qualification 'unshakable' (akopya), there is falling away from that which is occasional (sāmayikī)," he replies:
If it is argued that there is [falling away] from that which is occasional (*sāmayikī*),
we also say this:
there is falling away from that which is occasional.
But that must be examined; indeed, that occasional liberation (sāmayikī vimukti) must be examined.
How so? He says:
Is there such a thing as occasional liberation in the state of arhatship?

Or rather, are the mundane meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) themselves the occasional liberation (*sāmayikī vimukti*)? Why is this doubt raised? He says: "For the fundamental meditative concentration (*maulo dhyānasamādhiḥ*)."
Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) itself is *samādhi*; thus it is "meditative concentration-samādhi.

The mention of the fundamental meditations (*mauladhyāna*) is because they are the foremost among the easy paths of practice (*sukhapratipad*), and because [the fruit] manifests at the appropriate time (*samaya*).
Because it manifests at certain times characterized by silence and so forth,
it is called "occasional liberation" (*samāyikī vimukti*).
Furthermore, because it must be sought again and again, it is called "beloved" (*kāntā*).
The meaning is that it is "desirable" (kānta) because it is to be sought after in each successive falling away;
"because it is to be relished," according to another, namely Bhadanta Rāma.
The intention is that it is "desirable" because it is associated with outflows (sāsrava), due to its connection with dhyāna that is conjoined with relishing (āsvādana).
"But the liberation of arhatship," and so forth.
Arhatship itself is the liberation; thus it is "the liberation of arhatship.
This is because it is eternally present through its connection with attainment (*prāpti*).
By the phrase "it is not appropriate [to call it] occasional," he shows that the liberation of arhatship is the opposite of occasional liberation.
By the phrase "because it is not to be sought again, it is not 'beloved'," he shows that in the reversal of "beloved," the liberation of arhatship is not beloved.
The meaning is: because it exists as something eternally present, it is not to be sought; therefore, it is not "beloved."
"Only from those pertaining to the higher mind.
Those which exist in the higher mind (*adhicetasi*) are the "pertaining to the higher mind" (*ādhicaitasika*) pleasant abidings in this very life;
it is only from these that [they arise].
"For what purpose would he have spoken of falling away?

Because of the statement: "Those mental states of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) that have been attained—from among these, I declare that there may be falling away from any one of them."
If there were the possibility of falling away from arhatship characterized by occasional liberation,
for what purpose would he have spoken of falling away only from those [three lower fruits]?
The meaning is that he would not have spoken of falling away only from those.
"Due to the loss of mastery" means due to the loss of mastery over the manifestation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
He is one whose nature is not subject to decline.
In the Sūtra, one who is of the nature not to fall away (aparihāṇadharman) is recited as distinct from one who is of the unshakable nature (akopyadharman).
