Having explained the eighteen learners (śaikṣa) in detail, it asks:
"Which are the nine non-learners (aśaikṣa)?"
One of a nature subject to decline;
one of a nature not subject to decline;
one of a nature characterized by volition.
One whose nature is to guard,
one who is steadfast and unshakable,
and one capable of penetration.
One of immovable nature;
one liberated by wisdom;
one liberated in both ways.
These are called the nine types of trainees (*śaikṣa*).
One who falls away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) is one of a nature subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
One who does not fall away from that very state is one of non-falling nature (*aparihāṇadharman*).
In the same way, those of the nature of volition (*cetanādharman*) and the others should also be applied accordingly.
How so?
One who, out of fear of falling away from meditative concentration, exerts volition toward himself is one of the nature of volition.
One who somehow protects a particular excellence is one whose nature is to protect;
he is one who remains established in that very excellence.
Therefore, even without guarding it, he is not shaken;
he is one who remains unshakable.
He is one who penetrates [the truth] by means of another.
The meaning is that he produces a specific excellence of qualities.
He is one capable of penetration (*prativedhanābhavya*),
who does not become angry and does not fall away from those qualities already produced.
"He is one of immovable nature (akopyadharmā).
What is the distinction?

[The author] asks this because he does not perceive any distinction, given that all three—beginning with those of non-falling nature (aparihāṇadharman)—are characterized by the quality of non-retrogression.
"One who has not undergone refinement" means that he is of sharp faculties by nature;
the meaning is that he has not attained the refinement of his faculties.
"Therefore, he is not shaken" means "therefore,
because of that specific quality.
This specific quality is what is being characterized.
The Master presents his own view.
If a Vaibhāṣika were to say, "But surely the Venerable Gautika fell away from arhatship," this refutation is undertaken.
"The Venerable Gautika," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
"One who has become a trainee" means that he is not yet an Arhat.
"Wielding a weapon" means carrying a weapon.
Because he was indifferent toward both body and life, he attained arhatship at the very moment of death;
that is to say, after the stroke of the weapon.
And he passed into final nirvāṇa by that very same blow of the weapon.
"And in the *Daśottara*": that is, in the sūtra named the *Daśottara*. He asks, "What is stated [there]? and says:
One dharma is to be produced. Which one? It is said: "The timely, pleasant liberation of mind."
The intention is that this is the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*). One single dharma is to be realized. Which one? He says:
"The unshakable liberation of mind" refers to arhatship; this is the intended meaning.

For, because it is mentioned separately from arhatship characterized by unshakable liberation, the intended meaning is that the "liberation of mind through desirelessness" was not stated to have arhatship as its intrinsic nature.
Seeing an opportunity for the Vaibhāṣika position that the Arhatship is mentioned separately because it is of two types, he speaks again:
"And if Arhatship," and so forth.
That is to say, if Arhatship itself were the occasional, pleasant liberation of mind.

For what reason would he not have stated the twofold grasping of arhatship in that very same Daśaka, rather than in another sūtra, as follows: "One dharma is to be realized: the unshakable liberation of mind"?
The meaning is that he would not have said [it]. For he would have said:
"One single dharma is to be realized: liberation of mind."
One might say that arhatship is of two kinds;
therefore, it is stated through a distinction of terminology:
"one is to be produced" and "the second is to be realized."
To this we reply: nowhere has it been stated that arhatship is something to be produced. What, then, [has been stated]?
"It is to be realized"—
thus it is stated in various sūtras.
Even granting this for the sake of argument, we shall speak further.
And it should be produced as comprised within the faculty of dull senses (*mṛdvindriya*).
What is indicated, what is stated by this indication?
If, first of all, it is indicated that it is possible to produce it; [then so be it].
Because of the rule that the suffix *liṅ* is used after the root *śak* to form a *kṛtya* derivative,
there is also another [attainment] of Arhatship comprised within those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).
And if that were the case, it would have been stated thus in the Sūtra.
One single dharma is to be produced:
namely, the liberation of the mind (cetovimukti).
Thus, it is made known that it is worthy of being produced.
Because the suffix -tṛc is prescribed by the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaś ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.169) to denote fitness,
the state of arhatship (*arhattva*) that is even more worthy— namely, that which is comprised within those of sharp faculties—
is intended here; for the meaning is that it is truly worthy (*suṣṭhu*) to be produced because of its immovability (*akopyatva*).

"How then? and so forth. The intention is that if occasional liberation constitutes arhatship, then it is logical to say that an arhat is "liberated by occasion" (samayavimukta) because of being endowed with that [occasional liberation].
"The manifestation of meditative concentration (samādhi) depends upon specific conditions (samaya).
This is because his concentration—whether it be with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava)—depends on conditions characterized by health, a particular location, and so forth.
It is also stated in the Abhidharma, as follows in detail: [text omitted].
"The latent tendency of sensual desire is not abandoned"—this is one example.
And this is another example:
"and there is improper mental attention toward that."
If it is argued that such is the case for the arising of a complete [defilement]: it might be thought that the arising of a defilement whose causes are complete occurs in this manner,
whereas the arising of a defilement whose causes are incomplete occurs solely through the power of the object.
That is incorrect.
Why? He says:
"Or rather, of what thing that has its causes incomplete could there be arising?"
Of what is there production?
For there is the production of that whose causes are incomplete;
for whatever collection of causes and conditions is established for the production of an effect [is required].
Being deficient in even one part of that [set], it does not serve for its production.

For example, the collection of the eye, visible form, light, and attention is well-known to be the cause for the production of visual consciousness; yet, if it is deficient in any one of those other factors, it does not serve for its production.
Therefore, this is nothing at all.
"Of that form" means of that kind,
or else, of that intrinsic nature.
Now, if the counter-argument is that [the affliction] has not arisen, [it is said] "in its seed-nature" (*tadbījadharmatāyām*).
This means in the essential nature of the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśabījasvabhāva*).
If that [nature] has not been extracted—that is, if it has not been uprooted—how can one be one whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*)?
You might say, "He does not exist.
To this he says:
"Or how can one whose outflows are not exhausted be an Arhat?"
"Practicing in this way" means practicing with mindfulness, because mindfulness is mentioned immediately thereafter.
To refute the statement "he is a learner" (śaikṣa), that same proponent of falling away says:
For he was indeed indicated there as being an Arhat.
How was he indicated? He says:
"For a long time," and so forth.
For those who maintain that there is no falling away (aparihāṇivādin), there might be this opportunity for an objection:
"This mind of the trainee (śaikṣa) is said to be inclined toward seclusion, up to being slanted toward nirvāṇa.
To refute this, the proponent of falling away (parihāṇivādin) speaks again.
For this power of an Arhat is stated elsewhere in the Sūtra.
How so?
"Venerable sir, how many powers does an Arhat monk whose outflows are exhausted possess?"
"Śāriputra, for a long time the mind of an Arhat monk has been inclined toward seclusion, even leaning toward Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, he has viewed sensual pleasures as being like a pit of glowing embers.

Thus, for one who knows sensual pleasures and sees sensual pleasures, whatever desire for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, and so forth, up to attachment to sensual pleasures may arise regarding those sensual pleasures—"
"In that regard, his mind does not remain overwhelmed," and so forth.
Furthermore, because of the expressions "become cooled" (*śītībhūta*) and "become calmed" (*vāntībhūta*),
it is indicated in that very *Aṅgārakarṣūpama-sūtra* that it is only the Arhat who possesses these qualities.
"This is indeed so.

As for what was stated in the Simile of the Pit of Coals— that it was indicated that one is an Arhat only as long as the course [of conduct] has not been thoroughly penetrated— [that remains the case].
The practice of wandering for alms and so forth.
Since this statement was made specifically with reference to the stage of a trainee (*śaikṣa*), there is no fault.
This is what has been said.
"Sometimes, due to a lapse of mindfulness, evil and unwholesome thoughts arise"—
this was said with reference to those in training (śaikṣa), not to the state of arhatship.
As for what was said regarding "longing for seclusion for a long time," [it refers to that].
This is possible even for one in training (śaikṣa), but it occurs in a superior degree for an Arhat; such is the distinction.
Furthermore, as it has been said: "it has become cooled and has become free from the heat of those dharmas conducive to the outflows (sāsrava)."

That too is possible with reference to the stage of one in training (śaikṣāvasthā), because it is described as the state of being cooled (*śītībhāva*) regarding those factors conducive to outflows (*āsrava-sthānīya-dharma*) belonging to the desire realm.
And since it is likewise described with reference to the stage of arhatship, there is no fault; such is the intention of the Master (Ācārya).
(VI.60cd) It is not the path of seeing because preparatory application is impossible.
The path of seeing consists of fifteen moments;
within that, there is no opportunity for preparatory application regarding the transformation of the faculties.
Does someone transform their faculties while in the state of an ordinary person?
Does one transform the faculties by means of a path that falls under aspects such as impermanence? Or does one transform the faculties by means of a path with aspects such as coarseness?
Or rather, by means of a path with aspects such as tranquility?

We see that because it is not specified, it is possible in both ways; for the Master will indicate this meaning by the qualification "of the noble ones" [in the statement]: "For there is no transformation of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) for the noble ones by means of a path with outflows (sāsrava-mārga)."

Having formed the intention for practice, thinking, "May my faculties indeed become sharp," one should understand that one transforms the faculties through the sequence of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), whether it be the mundane or the supramundane path.
The mention of the "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) here refers to someone in the state of being liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
This is because the context concerns those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
However, it should be understood that even one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) undergoes the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
(VI.61) How can there be falling away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*) for one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*)?

Because his faculties are sharp, it is impossible for him to fall away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life; how much less so from unshakable liberation? Anticipating this impossibility, he asks:
"For a Buddha, there is only falling away from enjoyment."
Because he is occupied with the work of training disciples, he does not enjoy the dwellings in happiness in the present life;
that is to say, he does not bring them into manifestation. And this is what is meant by "falling away from what has not yet been attained."
For one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), there is both that loss through the cessation of enjoyment (*upabhogaparihāṇi*) due to some distraction,
and loss through non-attainment (*aprāptiparihāṇi*) because of failing to attain the qualities of a specific type of person (*pudgalaviśeṣadharma*).

This is because even one of immovable nature might fail to attain certain qualities, such as those at the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*) and so forth, belonging to the great śrāvakas like the noble Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
Furthermore, one does not attain certain qualities of the self-awakened ones (svayaṃbhū).
Even the great śrāvakas do not attain certain distinguished qualities of the self-awakened ones, and so forth.
Regarding "another arhat," this refers to those of dull faculties, such as those subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman), who also possess the falling away from what has already been attained.
Because of the word "also," it follows that the aforementioned types of falling away (*parihāṇi*) also exist.

[Objection: Since it is stated that there is falling away from enjoyment (*upabhoga-parihāṇi*) for one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), there is a contradiction with the Sūtra, namely that which was said: [the Sūtra states that for an Arhat there is no falling away].

The contradiction with that sūtra— which begins, "There are these four," and continues in detail until, "Therefore, I declare that there may be falling away from one or another of them"— is thus resolved.

When it is stated that the liberation of all six types of Arhats is "unshakable" (*akopyā*), the Vaibhāṣika might ask: "If the untainted liberation (*anāsravā vimukti*) of every Arhat is indeed unshakable,
why is only the one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*) established as being of an unshakable nature (*akopyadharman*), and not the others?"
Therefore, this is said:
"The untainted liberation of everyone is unshakable.
This is true.
The establishment of the one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*) has been explained as it is. However,

some who possess dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*) may fall away from the pleasant dwellings in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) due to the fault of distraction caused by gain and honor, because of their loss of mastery (*vaśitva*).
Someone does not fall away;
he who possesses sharp faculties is established as one of immovable nature.

Furthermore, since it is precisely because one with dull faculties— not sharp faculties— falls away from the pleasant dwellings in this present life due to the fault of distraction by gain and honor, this objection is not to be raised.
How so?
An advocate of non-retrogression [claims] that there is no retrogression from the pleasant abiding in the present life for one of immovable nature.
Alternatively, this is another connection [to the following].
It was previously stated that for one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), there is no falling away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
And in the Sūtra: "He whose liberation is immovable..."
The falling away from his dwelling in happiness in the present life has been stated.
Since this was stated without qualification, it is therefore said:
"For everyone, untainted liberation is unshakable."

The intention is that one is not established as being of immovable nature (akopyadharman) by that [very same reason]. For this very reason it is said: "But the establishment of the immovable-natured one has been explained according to how it is.
Therefore, this is not to be questioned.
Regarding what was stated based on the Sūtra— namely, how one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*) can fall away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*)—
the term "slow" (*dhandha*) means dull-witted (*manda*). Otherwise, it would be a cause for lack of confidence (*anāśvāsika*).

If one who has fallen away from arhatship were to be born again, [it would be like this]: "But when the holy life has been well-practiced and this path well-cultivated, one is content at the end of life, just as one is upon the departure of a disease"—this is the consolation. [The fear] that such a thing might not happen is improper; for that which is characterized by unchaste conduct and so forth is like a hero’s stumbling, but not his falling.
Just as a hero, upon tripping, does not fall because he maintains himself through his own strength,
so too a noble one (ārya), even if fallen from a fruit, does not die without having attained that fruit.
The mention of a "hero" is used because of his lack of agitation.
Others say he is "powerful" and a "hero.
To the question of how [the path] is cultivated, he says:
because it has been made firm by both the paths of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*). However, the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) is in every case one and the same.
Regarding the penetration of the unshakable state and the attainment of vision:
it is not by means of that which is with outflows (sāsrava), because what is intended here is the transformation of the noble faculties (āryendriya-saṃcāra).

Otherwise, it would contradict the fact that someone transforms their faculties while in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). This is because such transformation cannot occur elsewhere, for the transformation of faculties is held to be desired only out of fear of falling away (*parihāṇi*).
He states that there is no falling away (parihāṇi) elsewhere except among the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) and in the form and formless realms (rūpārūpyadhātu).
A noble one (ārya) born in the higher realms neither transforms his faculties (indriya-saṃcāra),
nor does he fall away in any way whatsoever.
The reason for this has already been stated:
because the faculties have become more fully matured through dwelling for a period of time,
and because of the attainment of a specific basis.

Now, why is there no falling away among the gods of the desire realm? Those who previously, being repelled even by sublime sense objects, necessarily saw the truths— how could they fall away by taking those very same objects as their basis?
The intention is that they necessarily possess sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).
"The one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) relies on nine" is because it is possible for its fruit to be comprised within the nine stages (*bhūmi*).
"The fruit and that which is distinguished by the fruit.
The "fruit" is the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).

That which is "distinguished by the fruit" refers to the first dhyāna and so forth, characterized by the paths of preparation (*prayoga*), uninterruptedness (*ānantarya*), liberation (*vimukti*), and excellence (*viśeṣa*) for the sake of abandonment.
One attains only the path of the fruit;
it is comprised solely of detachment from the desire realm.
Furthermore, the fruit of the non-returner is not comprised within the formless realm.
Because of the statement in the Sūtra that one is a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) due to the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*),
and because the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) does not exist there;
it has already been explained that its absence [in that realm] is due to its not having the desire realm as its object.
(VI.65ab) "And the one of immovable nature is twofold.
Because it is so stated in the Sūtra, there are two Buddhas who are merely distinctions within the immovable [arhat].
Thus,
the one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*) is divided into three types according to the distinction of weak, medium, and sharp faculties.
For the disciple of immovable nature possesses sharp-weak faculties.
A Pratyekabuddha possesses superior-middling faculties;
a Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses superior-superior faculties.
This is due to the distinction of the nine types of faculties, beginning with the weakest-of-the-weak.
One of the nature of falling away has the softest-soft faculties, up to the Blessed One who has the sharpest-sharpest faculties.
(VI.65cd, 66ab) There are seven [types of noble persons], because both the Pratyekabuddha and the Samyaksambuddha are included within those liberated in both ways.
"Already previously," and so forth.

This means that already previously, while in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), having heard from another through reliance on another, one [cultivates] the dharmas such as the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);
subsequently, one applies oneself to their meanings.
The meaning is: "by means of practicing reflection and cultivation.

Likewise, previously, while still in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), by means of wisdom (*prajñā*) and in accordance with the Dharma of the twelvefold scriptural teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), one follows for oneself such factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and so forth; thus, through the practice of reflection and cultivation, one applies oneself to the [true] meanings.
Thus, by way of their application, they become followers by faith (śraddhānusārin) and followers by dharma (dharmānusārin).
"By the predominance of faith-resolution and wisdom" means by the predominance of faith-resolution and by the predominance of wisdom.
Resolute conviction through faith is "resolute conviction by faith.
Due to the predominance of that [faith], there is dullness of faculties;
due to the predominance of wisdom, there is sharpness of faculties.
"By way of liberation" means:
by way of liberation from the afflictions (*kleśa*); that is, one who is liberated from the afflictions through wisdom (*prajñā*) is, for that reason, called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*).
"By way of liberation through meditative attainment" (*samāpatti-vimukti*) means: [liberation through the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling].
[They differ] by way of attainment and by way of liberation.
In that regard, "by way of faculty," and so forth,
refers to how these followers by faith (śraddhānusārin) are enumerated.
We shall demonstrate this according to the text.
From the perspective of the faculties, there are three,
because of being of weak, medium, and superior faculties.

In this regard, however, it should be understood as follows: although all those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) possess dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*), nevertheless, because they exist according to degrees of intensity, they are further divided into three types: those with dull, medium, and sharp faculties (*mṛdu-madhya-adhimātra-indriya*).
There are five by way of lineage (*gotra*).
How so?
There are five, beginning with one of the lineage of those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) up to one of the lineage of those capable of penetration (*prativedhanābhavya*).
Furthermore, due to the distinctions of lineage (*gotra*) and faculty (*indriya*), each one of these fifteen becomes fifteenfold from the perspective of the path (*mārga*).
How so? It is said: "Those abiding in the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the seven knowledges (*jñāna*)."
The path of seeing consists of fifteen moments:
eight patiences (*kṣānti*),
from the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering up to the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path.
There are seven knowledges:
from the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering up to the dharma-knowledge regarding the path.
This is because the subsequent knowledge regarding the path is included within the path of cultivation.
Eight and seven make fifteen;
thus, those situated there become fifteen.
In this way, for these [practitioners] who are divided into fifteen types by way of the path, each one is further divided into seventy-three by way of detachment (*vairāgya*).
How so?
First, there is one [type of person] in the desire realm who is bound by all fetters;
then, there are nine [types] resulting from detachment from the desire realm.
One who is free from passion regarding one category [of defilement], up to one who is free from passion regarding nine categories.
In this manner, up to the detachment from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there are nine [types].
However, it is not possible for there to be nine [types] based on detachment from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because there is no worldly path that serves as an antidote to the peak of existence (bhavāgra),
these eight groups of nine constitute seventy-two.
Together with the previously mentioned "fully bound" state, they become seventy-three.
Furthermore, these are each divided into seventy-three according to their degrees of detachment (*vairāgya*).
Each is ninefold according to their basis (*āśraya*).
How so? He says:
"Born in the three continents and the six classes of gods.
The three continents exclude Uttarakuru,
because the Path does not exist in Uttarakuru.
There are six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara). This is because above that level, the path of seeing (darśanamārga) does not exist.
They are those born among them.
Each of these consists of nine qualities.
When they are combined according to the faculties (*indriya*), spiritual lineage (*gotra*), path (*mārga*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and basis (*āśraya*),
the summary is stated as follows:

"These many" are recorded in the commentary (*vṛtti*). In this way, other individuals (*pudgala*) as well— beginning with those who follow the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) and so forth— are to be enumerated according to their possible existence.
Just as those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) are enumerated according to their faculties (*indriya*), lineage (*gotra*), path (*mārga*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and basis (*āśraya*),
so too are they to be enumerated as possible. However,
for those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and those liberated at any time (*samayavimukta*), there is no distinction of lineage.

However, for those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), there is also a distinction of lineage (*gotra*); thus, it is said "according to possibility.
In that regard, according to their faculties (*indriya*), there are three types of followers of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
In terms of lineage (*gotra*), they are one and the same, so there is no distinction.
In terms of the path (*mārga*), there are fifteen: those established in the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the seven knowledges (*jñāna*).
In terms of detachment (*vairāgya*), there are seventy-three.
One who is bound by all fetters [attains nine]. From detachment from the desire realm, there are nine;
likewise up to detachment from the sphere of nothingness.
There are nine by way of basis:
those born in the three continents and the six classes of gods.
Thus, they are totaled according to faculties, paths, degrees of detachment, and bases.
They amount to twenty-nine thousand,
five hundred and sixty-five.
Thus, from the perspective of the faculties, there are three types of those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
From the perspective of lineage (*gotra*), there are five for each;
from the perspective of detachment (*vairāgya*), there are seventy-three for each, as before;
and from the perspective of the basis (*āśraya*), there are nine.
"Born in the three continents and the six classes of gods.
Thus, when combined according to faculties (*indriya*), lineage (*gotra*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and basis (*āśraya*),
they amount to nine thousand.
And eight hundred and fifty-five.
One who abides solely in the fruit, having attained sixteen moments of mind, is the subject under discussion.
At that time, those with dull and sharp faculties are respectively the one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and the one attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Because this [distinction] is intended here.
However, Bhagavadviśeṣa says: "From the perspective of the path, there are nine."
"Because he is situated on the path of cultivation"—
we do not understand with what intention this was said.
If this were the intended meaning:
From the perspective of the path, there are nine [attainments] for each stage (*bhūmi*).
From the perspective of detachment (*vairāgya*), there are seventy-three; thus, the same meaning would be demonstrated.
This is because they are not distinct from that.
That would be logical,
for that alone would constitute their measure.
Alternatively, if their number were established as nine because they abide in the nine-level untainted path of cultivation, [that too would be problematic].
That being the case, that measure would be multiplied by nine once more;
and thus there would be eighty-eight thousand of them.
And six hundred,
and ninety-five; thus it should be stated for the subsequent cases as well,
provided that the one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) is included up to the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi).
It should be calculated otherwise:
from the perspective of the faculties, there are three types of those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta);
from the perspective of the lineages (gotra), there are five for each.

By way of detachment (*vairāgya*), there are eighty-one: this is by adding eight more to the seventy-three for those who are free from passion regarding the eight categories [of afflictions] at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
By way of basis (*āśraya*), there are twenty-nine.
How so? In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are nine places of rebirth.

In the realm of form (rūpadhātu) there are sixteen abodes, and there are four formless [abodes]. Thus, when totaled according to faculties (indriya), lineage (gotra), detachment (vairāgya), and basis (āśraya), they amount to thirty-five thousand.
And there are two hundred and thirty-five;
for one who has attained through vision, there is no distinction of lineage.
When condensed according to the faculties, the states of detachment, and the bases, they amount to one thousand nine hundred and seventy-one.
If, however, one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) is included up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*),
then they should be enumerated in this way:
they are totaled according to their faculties (*indriya*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and bases (*āśraya*).
This amounts to seven thousand forty-seven.
Since the *kāyasākṣin* is included within the categories of the *śraddhādhimukta* and the *dṛṣṭiprāpta*, they are not counted separately.
However, if they were to be counted, there would be three according to their faculties (*indriya*).
If he is one liberated through faith, he is a body-witness; in terms of lineage, there are five types.
If he is one who has attained vision, there is no distinction of lineage.
In terms of the path, there is likewise no distinction between the two.
Because they have transcended passion for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there is no distinction even in terms of detachment (*vairāgya*).
Even though at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) one may be detached from all fetters, or detached from one type up to eight types [of afflictions],
there is indeed a distinction in terms of the path (*mārga*) or detachment (*vairāgya*).
But bodily witnesshood (*kāyasākṣitva*) is not produced by detachment from the path;
therefore, no distinction based on that is established for him.
Or rather, there is a manifold distinction according to the basis (*āśraya*).
"Because it has its basis in the desire realm up to its basis in the peak of existence"—this is the distinction made by the Blessed One.
How can one who is a body-witness (kāyasākṣin) have as their basis the sphere of infinite space and so forth?
We consider this [following] to be logical.
In terms of their bases, there are twenty-five:
nine places of rebirth in the desire realm and sixteen places in the form realm.
For it is there that a noble one would produce the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
However, in the case of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who has become a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) through connection with the attainment of cessation produced based on the desire or form realms,
[the distinction is made] merely by virtue of his possession (*samanvāgama*) of that attainment.
Even later, the state of being a body-witness (*kāyasākṣitva*) based on the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) would be accepted.
It should be understood that the Peak of Existence would then be the twenty-sixth basis.
Thus, having reckoned [the categories] according to the faculties (*indriya*), lineages (*gotra*), and bases (*āśraya*), they are to be counted.
There is also a distinction for those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*).
In terms of faculties (*indriya*), there are three types of those liberated by wisdom.
In terms of spiritual lineage (*gotra*), there are five.
If they are those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*),
then there is no distinction if they are those liberated independently of occasion (*asamayavimukta*).
In this same way, the case of one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) should also be applied.
(VI.66cd) "Because of being liberated from the obscuration of the afflictions and the obscuration to liberation through the powers of wisdom and meditative concentration.
This means that by the power of wisdom one is liberated from the obscuration of the afflictions,
and by the power of meditative concentration one is liberated from the obscuration to liberation.
Furthermore, the eight liberations will be explained in detail as: "one possessing form sees forms," and so forth.
In that context, "the obscuration of afflictions" (kleśāvaraṇa) means that the afflictions themselves are the obscuration.
"Obstruction to liberation" means the obstruction to the liberations.
Furthermore, that is the unserviceability of body and mind.
"Because by which one is unable to produce the liberations. (VI.67) "But he who, having abandoned the five afflictions here...
refers to the five lower-tier fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīyasaṃyojana*) mentioned, beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
“Of unshakeable nature” (ahāryadharma) means one whose nature is not subject to decline (aparihāṇidharma).
“Only by way of the fruit,” and so forth:
because he is one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), there is no perfection by way of the faculties (indriya).
Because he is not a body-witness, there is no perfection in terms of meditative attainment;
however, because he is a non-returner, there is perfection in terms of the fruit.
[The perfection] is due to the faculties alone.
Because he has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), there is perfection in terms of the faculties (*indriya*).

However, because he is not free from passion (*avītarāga*), there is no perfection in terms of the fruit (*phala*) nor in terms of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), since the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) and [the higher] attainments are absent. In this same way, it should be applied to others as well, according to what is possible.
"Only by way of attainment.
This means that perfection exists only by way of attainment, and not by way of faculties or fruits; this is not the case.
Why?
For there is no attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) without the attainment of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).

And [the statement] that there is fullness by way of attainment and faculty even without the fruit is also not the case; for fullness occurs precisely through attainment and faculty, and not through the fruit.
Because the attainment of cessation does not exist for one who has not attained the fruit of a non-returner.
"By way of faculties and by way of attainment" means by way of having sharp faculties and by way of having obtained the attainment of cessation.
"Only by way of the faculties," and so forth. Because of the statement "of one liberated at any time," his perfection is by way of the faculties.
Because of the statement "of one liberated by wisdom," his perfection does not consist in meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
For it is said that one who has attained the cessation attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is "liberated by wisdom."
"Only by way of attainment" means that because of the statement "of one liberated by occasion," this person does not possess perfection by way of the faculties.

Because of the statement "of one liberated in both ways," his perfection is by way of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). One who has attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is called "liberated in both ways."
By means of both the faculties and the meditative attainments, what [is attained]?
Perfection.

He shows that [the one liberated at all times] is so by way of the faculties because of being liberated independently of time (*asamayavimukta*), and by way of meditative attainments because of being liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
(VI.68) The path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) is that by which one abandons the hindrances;
this is because there exists a path of non-abandonment.
There exists that path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) by which one does not abandon the hindrance,
as in the case of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) and so forth.
[It refers to] that which is first liberated from the hindrance to be abandoned by it.

That which is liberated from the obstruction to be abandoned by the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is [the path of liberation]. The qualification "for the first time" is used because in the third and subsequent moments, a path of that same kind is considered to be the path of distinction (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
And for this very reason he says:
"The path of distinction is that path which is other than these.
The meaning is: other than the path of preparation and so forth.

Furthermore, if one were not to say "at first," but were instead to say only "the path of liberation is that which is liberated from the obstructions to be abandoned by it," then it would follow that all paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and so forth arising subsequent to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) would be liberated from the obstructions to be abandoned by that [dharma-knowledge].
All [paths] would then be paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). And this is undesirable,
because it would entail that even the uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) and so forth are paths of liberation.

Therefore, that which first arises when one is liberated from the obstructions to be abandoned by the path of immediate succession— such as the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti)— and so forth, namely the category [of afflictions] to be abandoned by seeing suffering up to those to be abandoned by cultivation; that is [the path of liberation].
That is the path of liberation;
no other [path] is so called, even though it is free from the obstructions to be abandoned by it.
This refers to any [path] other than these three, beginning with the path of preparation.

That is the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*). One should understand that those untainted moments (*anāsrava-kṣaṇa*) of the same nature as that, beginning with the seventeenth and following after the sixteenth moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), have the path of distinction as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In the same way, other knowledge of liberation (*vimuktijñāna*)—
namely, that which is protracted, such as the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth—
should also be discussed.

And whatever path there is for dwelling in happiness in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-vihāra*) or for the production of distinguished qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*), that too is indeed the path of distinction (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
It has been stated that the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) is that from which the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises;
therefore, it is understood that the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) constitute the path of preparation.
But as for the path beginning with patience (*kṣānti*) that proceeds in reverse order,
it must be stated in what it is included.
He says:
It is indeed included within the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
However, this [stage] is a distant path of preparation; this is its distinction from the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
Furthermore, because it was intended as an illustration, the Master mentioned only the proximate path of preparation.
For this is the path to nirvāṇa; because one goes to it by means of it, just as in the world that by which one travels is called a path.
It is recognized as the path. And by means of this, nirvana is gone to—that is, attained.
Therefore, he shows that it is called the "path."
"Or, it is that by which one searches. The verbal root *mārg* is recited in the sense of "searching";
its form *mārga* is derived from that root with the suffix *ghañ*.
"That by which nirvāṇa is sought is the path.
[Question: How can the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the paths of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*) be considered "paths"?
For nirvāṇa is not attained by those two;

the intention is that since the capacity for its attainment resides only in the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), it does not reside in those two [the paths of liberation].
This is because they are of the same kind [as those paths] but are of a higher degree.
Furthermore, they belong to the same category as the path of abandonment because of their similarity in terms of object, aspect, and being untainted (*anāsrava*).
They are also more intense due to the accumulation of causes;
for just as the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) has the four truths as its object, possesses sixteen aspects, and is untainted.
The same applies to the paths of liberation and the paths of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*).
However, they are distinguished from that [preceding path] precisely by being more superior (*adhimātrataratva*),
because they attain each subsequent stage.
"Or because of entering into the state without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa).
This means that since each subsequent path is attained through both the path of liberation (vimuktimārga) and the path of distinction (viśeṣamārga), these two possess the nature of being paths.
Or rather, because by means of those two one enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
That is to say, upon their arising, there is entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Others, however, explain it in this way:
Because they lead to successive attainments, there is entry into the state without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
Therefore, these two possess the nature of the path (*mārgatva*).
[This is] because they bring about the realization of *nirvāṇa*. (VI.69)
The meaning is that by means of this one attains *nirvāṇa*. Likewise, the pleasant path is also of two kinds:
there is a pleasant path with sluggish direct knowledge.

Regarding the statement "there is [a path] that is pleasant and characterized by swift superknowledge": it is because it proceeds without effort due to the possession of the factors (*aṅga*) and the equilibrium of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). Thus, there is possession by way of the factors; and there is the equality of calm abiding and insight.
There is the integration of the factors and the equilibrium of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Through these two, there is effortless progression; therefore, it is a pleasant path of practice (*sukhā pratipat*).

Because the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are embraced by the [eight] factors and are balanced through both calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā), they proceed without effort; and for this reason, it is called the "pleasant path" (sukhā pratipad).
"Because they do not possess all the factors," and so forth.
Because they do not possess all the factors—the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the formless attainments (ārūpya)—they proceed with effort.
Furthermore, due to the possible deficiency of either calm abiding (śamatha) or insight (vipaśyanā), they proceed with effort.
Because of a deficiency in calm abiding (*śamatha*), the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) proceed according to their natural flow.
Because of a deficiency in insight (*vipaśyanā*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) proceed with effort;
this is due to the presence of those [deficiencies].
Those [stages], such as the *anāgamya*, are the difficult path (*duḥkhā pratipad*). "Slow direct knowledge" (*dhandhābhijñā*) means:
"there is slow direct knowledge in this."
"Slow direct knowledge" (*dhandhābhijñā*) means dull wisdom (*mandaprajñā*).

"Quick direct knowledge" (*kṣiprābhijñā*) means sharp wisdom (*tīkṣṇaprajñā*). This is called "slow direct knowledge" because it is the direct knowledge belonging to a person who is slow and dull-witted.
He shows that this is also established by means of a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound.
In the same way, it should be applied as "the supernormal knowledge of a swift and sharp individual is 'swift supernormal knowledge'.
(VI.70) There are four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The foundations of mindfulness regarding the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena are as previously described.
There are four right efforts:
one generates the will for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen.
He exerts himself;
he arouses vigor;
he uplifts the mind.
He exerts himself.
He generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states, as before.
He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, as before.

He generates desire for the stabilization, non-confusion, cultivation to fulfillment, increase, growth, expansion, and realization through knowledge of wholesome states that have already arisen; as before.
These are the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
The first is the base of psychic power endowed with the concentration of desire and the formative forces of abandonment (*chandasamādhiprahāṇasaṃskārasamanvāgata-ṛddhipāda*).

In this way, there is the basis of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) endowed with the formative forces of abandonment (prahāṇasaṃskāra), consisting of energy, mind, and investigation, along with concentration.
"Bases of psychic power" means the causes of psychic power (ṛddhi).
There are five faculties (indriya).
The faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The five powers:
the powers of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The seven factors of enlightenment:
the factors of enlightenment of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Mindfulness itself as a factor of enlightenment is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness.
In this way, up to: equanimity itself is a factor of enlightenment, namely the enlightenment-factor of equanimity.
[Then there is] the noble eightfold path:
right view.
Right intention,
right speech,
and right action.
Right livelihood,
right effort,
and right mindfulness.
"Right concentration" means because of the abandonment of ignorance without remainder;
that is, because of the abandonment of all ignorance pertaining to the three realms.
Therefore, both [types of wisdom] constitute awakening (*bodhi*).
By this, he demonstrates that the wisdom of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) is not established as awakening.
Furthermore, it is according to their respective order.
And because, through those two, there is the realization, in accordance with reality, that what was to be done for one's own sake has been accomplished and need not be done again;

and because, through the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), there is the realization, in accordance with reality, that [the task] is finished—that knowledge of destruction is awakening (*bodhi*).
One understands, in accordance with reality: "Suffering has been fully known by me."
He understands, as it truly is: "Origination has been abandoned by me," "Cessation has been realized by me," and "The path has been cultivated by me."

By means of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), one realizes as it truly is: "There is nothing further to be done. [The path has been cultivated by me; it need not be cultivated again. That knowledge of non-arising is also awakening (*bodhi*).
"Suffering has been fully understood by me; it need not be understood again."
Thus he understands it as it truly is:
"My origin has been abandoned and need not be abandoned again;
my cessation has been realized and need not be realized again."
"One knows according to reality: 'The path has been cultivated by me; it is not to be cultivated again.
By the statement 'Suffering has been fully understood by me,' the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) is indicated.
By the statement 'It is not to be fully understood again,' the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) is indicated."
Thus, both [of these] demonstrate the person of sharp faculties; in this way, everything is to be understood.

Having thus established the meaning of the individual components—that awakening (*bodhi*) consists of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)—he speaks, establishing the meaning of the whole:
"Because of its conformity thereto."
"However, its factors are thirty-seven. "Anuloma" means favorable to that awakening; thus, it is "tadanuloma" (favorable to that).
Their state is conformity with that;
therefore,
from that conformity, they are the factors conducive to enlightenment.
They are called "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*) because they are conducive to and favorable toward enlightenment.

In the teaching, thirty-seven [factors] are enumerated, beginning with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). [It is said that] these consist of ten substances (*dravya*). (VI.71) They are ten substances.
According to the opinion of some; for he will state that, according to the Vaibhāṣikas, there are eleven [factors] because bodily and vocal actions are not distinct [from the mental factors].
For wisdom (*prajñā*) is indeed the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthiti*).
Thus,
the meaning is that wisdom (*prajñā*) is the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
because mindfulness is established by means of it.
For it is said in the Sūtra:
"Contemplating the body in the body," and so forth;
vigor is called the right exertions (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Thus it is said:
"For one generates desire, exerts effort, for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen."
"Exerts energy" refers to all [the bases of psychic power].
The bases of psychic power are concentrations.

Because it is said that one cultivates the basis of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) endowed with the formative forces of abandonment (prahāṇasaṃskāra) and concentration through desire (chanda-samādhi); furthermore, how are all these formative forces of abandonment [enumerated] here in the Sūtra? They are as follows: the desire of one who has become thus; [and so forth].
Whatever effort there is,
whatever faith there is,
whatever pliancy there is.
That which is mindfulness, that which is clear comprehension, and that which is volition.
And equanimity—
these are called the formative forces of abandonment.
"The faculties, first of all," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Regarding those factors whose nature consists of the faculties and powers— namely, the five substances of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—
it is wisdom alone that constitutes the four foundations of mindfulness and that which is the factor-of-enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena among the factors of enlightenment.
And that which is right view among the factors of the path is not a separate substance;
it is simply energy, which constitutes the four right efforts.
That which is the factor of enlightenment of energy among the factors of enlightenment, that which is right effort among the factors of the path,
and also concentration itself— these are the four bases of psychic power.
Regarding that which is the factor of enlightenment of concentration among the factors of enlightenment,
and that which is right concentration among the factors of the path—
what remains that does not have the nature of the faculty of wisdom and so forth?
Among the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), the factors of joy, tranquility, and equanimity remain.
Among the factors of the path (mārgāṅga), there is right intention (samyaksaṃkalpa) and the three factors of ethical discipline (śīlāṅga).
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—
these are ten entities:
namely, the five beginning with faith.
And there are five [factors] beginning with the awakening factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*).
Since the three factors of ethical discipline (*śīlāṅga*) have the nature of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), they are established as a single substance.
Thus, according to the Vaibhāṣikas, there are eleven substances.
Because bodily and vocal actions are not distinct [from their respective aggregates], they are considered two substances.
Thus, depending on the intended meaning, there is no fault in either of the two positions.
However, if one considers them according to their primary mode of existence, there are as many substances as exist in that collection.
They would be counted as such; however, those ten substances [would not suffice], because the forms of concentrated informative action (*samāhita-vijñapti-rūpa*) consist of seven substances.
Therefore, it should be stated that there are sixteen substances.
(VI.72) By mentioning the primary [factors],
it is thus stated that the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth have wisdom (*prajñā*) and the others as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

However, all qualities acquired through application (*prāyogika-guṇa*), whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanāmaya*), are, as appropriate, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Furthermore, their predominance is due to the fact that others function by means of their power; it is not, however, that those others do not exist.
Since the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) have wisdom (prajñā) as their primary factor, the term "wisdom" is used here.
But it is not wisdom alone that is the application of mindfulness.
What then?
Wisdom, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, joy, pliancy, equanimity, right intention, and so forth are also [the applications of mindfulness].
The inclusion of the term "preparatory" (*prāyogika*) is for the purpose of excluding faith and the other [faculties] that are acquired by birth (*upapattilabhya*).

Likewise, it should be explained in detail that the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) have vigor as their primary factor, while the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) have concentration as their primary factor.
On what basis is it said that the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are concentrations (*samādhi*)? From the Sūtra.
For it is said: "Monks, by making desire (*chanda*) the dominant factor, a monk attains concentration."
Thus, this becomes his concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*).
Monks, by making zeal (*vīrya*) and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) the dominant factors, a monk attains concentration;
this becomes his concentration of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-samādhi*).

"Therefore, body, speech, and mind are properly exerted. They are "exerted" (*pradhīyante*) because they are sustained, restrained, or sometimes set in motion by this [mind]; thus it is called "the exertion" (*pradhāna*). It is "because it is established upon that."
Because supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), characterized by the perfection of all qualities, is established in that concentration (*samādhi*).
Since the basis (*pāda*) of supernatural power is its foundation, it is called a "basis of supernatural power" (*ṛddhipāda*).
However, as for those who say that concentration itself is supernatural power:
The "bases" (pāda) are faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
[According to those Vaibhāṣikas who maintain that] "faith, mind, energy, and investigation" [are the bases],
it follows that for them there would be thirteen factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣa).
Due to the addition of zeal (*chanda*) and mind (*citta*), they are included among the eleven;
however, vigor (*vīrya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are not added here,
because they are already subsumed within the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) and the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
"He becomes manifold," and so forth;
having become manifold, he becomes one again. This is his manifestation.
He experiences concealment through the vision of knowledge.
He passes through walls and through ramparts with his body without being obstructed,
just as if in open space.
He performs the act of emerging from and sinking into the earth as if in water;
he moves upon water with a current that does not break.
Just as on the earth,
he travels through the air cross-legged,
just like a winged bird.
Furthermore, he even touches and strokes with his hand these two moons, so powerful and so majestic;
he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.
This is called supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
What are the bases of psychic power? They are the concentration of desire and the concentration of energy.
Concentration of mind;
concentration of investigation.
These are called the bases of psychic power.
Such is the characteristic of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, meditative concentration itself is not *rudhira*.
Regarding this, the Master Saṃghabhadra says:
This is not a fault on their part;
for they maintain that the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
and that psychic power (*ṛddhi*) itself is also [concentration].
However, desire and the others are mentioned in order to indicate that meditative concentration (samādhi) has four aspects.

For one kind of concentration becomes predominant during the stage of the application of the roots of virtue, while another becomes predominant during the stage of the perfection of the roots of virtue.
In this context, the former is the basis of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), while the latter is supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) itself.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the Sūtras regarding these [terms].
The fruit of the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) is expressed by the word "psychic power" (ṛddhi),
just as the fruit of thorough knowledge (parijñā) is designated by that same term, and so forth.
This is because of the distinction between the weak and the intense.
The faculties (*indriya*) are weak, while the powers (*bala*) are superior.
He states the reason for how there is this distinction between weak and superior:
"Because of being suppressible and non-suppressible."

The faculties (*indriya*) are suppressed by their opposites—namely, lack of faith, laziness, loss of mindfulness, distraction, and lack of clear comprehension—due to their intermittent occurrence; however, the powers (*bala*) are not [suppressed] in this way.
These have been explained again in relation to the stages of the beginner (*ādikarmika*) and the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). (VI.73)
(Abhidh-k-vy 603) Thus, these five stages have been described:
cultivation and vision.
Regarding "two states":
within the seven states, there are seven groups [of verses] in their respective order.
They are manifested, established, or made predominant.
In the stage of a beginner, they are the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);
in the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*), they are the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*).
The bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are at the stage of the summits (mūrdhan);
the faculties (indriya) are at the stage of patience (kṣānti);
and the powers (bala) are at the stage of the supreme mundane dharmas (laukikāgradharma).
The factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) pertain to the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
while the noble eightfold path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga) pertains to the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga). Thus,
the intensification of vigor (vīryasaṃvardhana) is the cause for attaining excellence.
Therefore, the right efforts (samyakpradhāna) are associated with the levels of heat (uṣmagata), because they constitute the entry into the roots of virtue that are not subject to decline.
Regarding the "summits" (mūrdhan): [the same applies].
The entry into wholesome roots conducive to non-retrogression occurs from the stage of the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*),
because of the scriptural statement: "One who has attained the Summits does not sever the roots."
It is called "entry" (praveśa) because one enters by means of these [factors].
For non-retrogression occurs during the stages of patience (kṣānti); such is their state.
The concentrations become the basis for success;
thus, the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are established at the stages of the summits (mūrdhan).
This is because there is no further falling away, and so forth.
Because there is no further falling away from the stages of patience (*kṣānti*),
whereas falling away is possible only from the first two [stages],
therefore faith and the other faculties have attained sovereignty.
Because of that state, the faculties (indriya) are established within the stages of receptivity (kṣānti),
because they cannot be crushed by the afflictions;
for they are not overwhelmed by the afflictions.
In that state, because the afflictions do not manifest,
or because one cannot be crushed by other worldly factors;
alternatively, because one cannot be crushed by other worldly factors, the faculties beginning with faith are designated as "powers" in the stage of the supreme mundane dharmas.
"Because of its proximity to enlightenment" means because of its proximity to the knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*).
For the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is indeed proximate to the knowledge of destruction and non-arising.
The path of seeing, however, is distant because it is separated by the intervening path of cultivation.
[It is said to be] "determined by going" (*gamanaprabhāvita*); for in the world, a path is determined by the act of going.
It is called a "path" (*mārga*) because one goes by means of it, or because it itself goes;
for in common worldly usage, one says, "This road goes to Pāṭaliputra."
The path of seeing is preeminently characterized by rapid progress, whereas the path of cultivation is not.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Because of its swift movement."
One who possesses that [path] also proceeds swiftly by means of it;
however, by means of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one proceeds over a long period of time because of its protracted nature due to the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmi*).
"Others, however, say..."—thus says the Master (Vasubandhu).
This is with the intention that "we and others" [are meant].
Just as the Vaibhāṣikas present a different sequence,
so too do they describe the succession of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) without breaking that [sequence].
This is because the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) pertain to the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
"Of many kinds" is the elaboration:
the object is of many types due to the distinctions of form (rūpa) and so forth.
And because of the distinctions such as blue and so forth.
"Scattering" (vyāseka) upon that [object] is distraction (vikṣepa).
These [mental states] have the nature of spreading out through scattering toward various kinds of objects.
The cognitions (buddhi) spread out, dispersing across many kinds of objects;
the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are for the purpose of restraining them.
"Based on attachment" means based on craving (tṛṣṇā).
"Of memories and intentions regarding desire" means "of memories and intentions regarding objects previously experienced," or alternatively, "of intentions regarding sensual pleasures.
"By the power of that" [is the meaning].
The meaning is: "by the power of the four foundations of mindfulness.
"For the accomplishment of the fourfold task" means that the fourfold task consists in the abandoning of arisen evil and unwholesome states.
The non-arising of those [dharmas] that have not yet arisen;
likewise, the arising of wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen;
and the maintenance and so forth of those that have already arisen.
"Then, from the purification of concentration":
after those right efforts (samyakpradhāna), the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are cultivated through the purification of concentration.
They are "the sovereign factors for supramundane dharmas."
They should be understood as being predominant because they bring about that [result];
these very things are the faculties when the activity of their opposites has been conquered.
They become powers (*balāni*) when the manifestation of faithlessness and so forth has been conquered.
For during the stage of the faculties (*indriyāvasthā*), the manifestation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is still possible.
Because the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) is prolonged. Regarding the "limbs of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*) in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*):
this is because enlightenment (*bodhi*) is defined as untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*).
"The path-factors of both" refers to the paths of seeing and cultivation.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"For it has been said," and so forth in detail.
"The fulfillment through cultivation" means the fulfillment of cultivation; the Noble Eightfold Path attains this.
As that [Path] proceeds, the four foundations of mindfulness bring about the fulfillment of cultivation.
When he requests the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*),
it is understood from the statement "they reach the fulfillment of cultivation" that the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) also exists on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
For indeed, cultivation does not reach fulfillment on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
What then? It refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Furthermore, it has been stated that "the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are established for both [paths].
By stating that this is a designation for the four noble truths, he indicates the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"Setting out by the path as it was come" is explained at length up to "this is a designation for the path," thereby demonstrating the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Setting out by the path as it was come—that is, as it was attained—up to enlightenment (*bodhi*).
Thus, in this way, the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are established both in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and in the path of cultivation.
Therefore, for both [the Śrāvaka and the Bodhisattva], the Noble Eightfold Path must be sought.
(VI.74) Thus, the sequence is established:
first the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and afterwards the Noble Eightfold Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
"The factors of enlightenment and the factors of the path are untainted.
This is a restriction meaning they are exclusively untainted.
The others are of two kinds.
Thus [it is said]:
from the foundations of mindfulness up to the powers (VI.75). Because they are to be carried by strength.
Because it must be brought face-to-face through strength and vigor,
there is an absence of joy (*prīti*) in the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
Joy gladdens a mind that is easily accessible.
"Not the other," because it is accompanied by apprehension regarding the lower stage;
that is, it is apprehensive with respect to falling away.
And for this reason, there is an absence of joy (*prīti*) therein;
for when there is apprehension, the mind does not rejoice.
[The phrase] "excluding volition" (*saṃkalpavarjyāḥ*) means:
Volition (*saṃkalpa*) is applied thought (*vitarka*).
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), they are devoid of the factors of enlightenment and the path (*bodhimārgāṅga*).
How can there be the application of mindfulness to the body at the peak of existence?
For the body does not exist there.
Indeed, the application of mindfulness to the body is wisdom that has the body as its object.
Furthermore, the Peak of Existence does not take the Desire Realm or the Form Realm as its object,
because of the established tenet that the fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not have lower contaminated realms as their sphere of activity.
This has not been written by any commentator.
Therefore, we shall establish this here:
what is the intrinsic nature of the body?
It has been stated that they are "derivative of the primary elements" (*bhautikatva*).
This means that the body consists of both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*).
In that regard, if wisdom (*prajñā*) were to have as its object only the primary elements, only the derivatives, or both together; [it would not be the contemplation of the body].
That would be precisely the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), wholesome contaminated wisdom (*kuśalasāsravā prajñā*) takes the path as its object—whether by way of "the path" or by way of "the principle"—because it has the uncontaminated restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*) and the path as its object.
For it is not accepted that the fundamental wholesome formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) have contaminated phenomena as their objects.
But they do not have the untainted dharmas as their object.
Therefore, it should be understood that this here is the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

(VI.77, 78) There are four kinds of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*): verified clarity regarding the Buddha, verified clarity regarding the Dharma, verified clarity regarding the Saṅgha, and the precepts dear to the Noble Ones (*āryakāntāni śīlāni*).
In that regard, because the Truth of Suffering and the others are phenomena (*dharma*) by nature and do not have the Buddha or the Saṅgha as their intrinsic nature,

one who realizes and perceives the three truths in due order attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) regarding the Dharma and the untainted precepts dear to the Noble Ones; but one does not [yet] attain verified clarity regarding the Buddha or the Saṅgha.
Because the Truth of Suffering and the others are phenomena (*dharma*),
and because they do not have the nature of the Buddha or the Sangha;
just as one who realizes the Truth of the Path attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) toward the Buddha and his community of disciples (*śrāvakasaṃgha*).
Because the truth of the path has the nature of the Buddha and the Saṃgha,
what is intended here by the term "dharma"?
There are many dharmas, such as "wholesome dharmas" and so forth.
Now, what is this "dharma" intended here?
It is that which was stated: "one attains verified clarity regarding the dharma. Alternatively, it refers to the Jewel of the Buddha and the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Therefore, this too should be intended here as the jewel of the Dharma.
For this is said to be the intrinsic nature of the Three Jewels:
"He [the Buddha] is the one who possesses the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) that constitute the Buddha, and both [types of dharmas] that constitute the Saṅgha."
And [the verse says], "he who goes for refuge to the three refuges, including nirvāṇa.
Therefore, one asks: is this intended to be the dharma that is nirvāṇa? Thus he inquires.
"What is this *dharma* intended here?
[The answer is: "Dharma is the three truths," and so forth.
The truths of suffering, origin, and cessation;
and the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) of a bodhisattva during the stage of training (*śaikṣāvasthā*);
and the path characterized by both training and no-more-training (*śaikṣāśaikṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of a pratyekabuddha—these are the dharmas intended here.
Therefore, "all four as well," and so forth.
Even while realizing the truth of the path, one also realizes the Dharma characterized by the paths of the Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Consequently, it is said that for one who realizes all four truths, there is the attainment of verified clarity regarding the Dharma.
The path of the Buddha and the Saṃgha is not called "Dharma" [in this context].
This is because, through the realization (*abhisamaya*) of that [path], one attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) regarding the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
But how can there be a simultaneous manifestation of the three verified clarities—characterized by faith—in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, through the realization of the Truth of the Path?
There is no fault, for that very same [faith] receives three names depending on the distinction of its basis;
or alternatively, while the verified clarity regarding the Dharma exists in the present,
the three future ones are cultivated.
Therefore, it is said that upon the clear realization of the Path, there is also [clear confidence] regarding the Buddha and his Saṅgha.

If the establishment of the clear confidences (*avetyaprasāda*) were based on their respective foundations, then the clear confidence in the Dharma would have to be mentioned first; for this reason, he says:
However, their sequence is according to how one who has emerged from meditative absorption brings them into manifestation;
that is, because they function as the physician, the medicine, and the attendant, respectively.
The Blessed One is like a physician, for according to the Sūtra he is the unsurpassed healer who extracts the arrow [of suffering]; and because he is the teacher of the medicine of the Dharma.
The Dharma is like medicine, because it is the remedy for the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, because it brings about the attainment of the health of nirvāṇa, the Saṃgha is like an attendant; for through mutual service, one attains the health of nirvāṇa. "Purity of ethical discipline produced by clarity of mind" refers to three kinds of clarity of mind.
"The Blessed One is indeed a perfectly awakened Buddha. His Dharma and Discipline are well-proclaimed. His community of disciples has practiced the path correctly."
By him, clarity regarding ethical discipline (*śīlaprasāda*) was produced. Ethical discipline itself is the clarity;
or, the clarity of ethical discipline—its state of being untainted (*anāsravatva*)—is clarity regarding ethical discipline.
After the three clarities (*prasāda*), the fourth, the clarity regarding ethical discipline (*śīlaprasāda*), has been mentioned.
Why? It is said:
for one who is thus clarified [in thought], this practice occurs in detail, beginning with "The Blessed One is indeed a perfectly awakened Buddha."
The meaning is "the practice of ethical discipline beloved by the noble ones.
Alternatively, it is because it is like the state of health.
Why is confidence in ethical discipline mentioned last?
In the sequence of the physician, the medicine, the attendant, and health;
or like the guide, the path, the caravan leader, and the vehicle.
What [is it]?
The phrase "the fourth was stated previously" is understood as the governing topic.
The Blessed One is the embodiment of the teacher;
the Dharma is the embodiment of the path.
The Saṅgha is like a caravan leader;
the virtues beloved by the Noble Ones are like a vehicle.
They are called "beloved by the Noble Ones" because they are dear to and conducive to the progress of the Noble Ones.
(VI.79, 80) "By eight.
A learner (*śaikṣa*) is endowed with eight factors.
With which eight?
[This refers to] the right view of one in training, up to the right concentration of one in training.
One who is beyond training (aśaikṣa) is endowed with ten factors.
With which ten?

By means of the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī samyagdṛṣṭi*) up to the right concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣaḥ samyaksamādhi*), the right liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī samyagvimukti*), and the right knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣaṃ samyagjñāna*).
It is "characterized by liberation and the individual internal knowledge thereof" (*vimuktitatpratyātmajñānābhyāṃ prabhāvita*):
in that liberation, there is individual internal knowledge; that is "the individual internal knowledge thereof. [The compound] is "liberation and the individual internal knowledge thereof."

It is liberation and the personally realized knowledge thereof. It is characterized by these two: by liberation from the afflictions and by the personally realized knowledge of that liberation from the afflictions.
"I am liberated from the afflictions"—this is what is manifested.
The meaning is that it is brought to excellence.
That very statement regarding liberation and the statement regarding the knowledge of liberation belong to that same person who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
"It is not logical for one in training (śaikṣa) [to possess it]" means that resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) is conditioned liberation (saṃskṛtā vimuktiḥ).
This is because the meaning of the verbal root is the same, and because the factors (aṅga) are conditioned.
Just as right view and the other [factors of the path] are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
so too liberation (*vimukti*) is understood to be exclusively conditioned, not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is because they are of a different nature and dissimilar.
Two liberations are taught in the Sūtra: "Through the fading away of passion, there is liberation of mind;
through the fading away of ignorance, there is liberation by wisdom."

The meaning is that it consists of liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*) and liberation by wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*). That same thing is also the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), as well as the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*).
The aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation,
and the knowledge and vision of liberation— these are to be understood here.
As for what was said in the Sūtra:
"O Vyāghrabodhyāyanas, there are these four supreme purities. Which four?"
The preeminence of purity of ethical discipline, the preeminence of purity of concentration,
and the preeminence of purity of view.
Having explained at length that "the preeminence of the purity of liberation" is also [a factor], he said:
"And what, Vyāghrabodhyāyana, is the preeminence of the purity of liberation?
It is whatever desire and vigor... and so forth.
