"Vyāghrabodhyāyanas" is in the plural because there are many of them.
"Preeminent in the purity of liberation" means...
The purification of liberation is "liberation-purification" (*vimuktipariśuddhi*).
That which is primary for it is "the primary [state] of vigor for liberation-purification" (*vīryavimuktipariśuddhipradhāna*).
Thus, in this context, there are three questions regarding that which is primary for liberation-purification.
In this regard, O monk, here the mind becomes dispassionate and liberated from passion; it becomes dispassionate and liberated from hatred;
it becomes dispassionate and liberated from delusion.
Liberation has been explained.
Thus, [it is for] the fulfillment of the aggregate of liberation that is incomplete,
or for the maintenance of that which is already fulfilled.
The purity of liberation is described as having the characteristic of fulfillment and assistance.
That which is desire and vigor is explained at length as the primary factor.
Since liberation from passion and the like is abandonment, liberation is thus defined in the Sūtra by such characteristics; it is not [defined as] resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Therefore, liberation is not merely resolute conviction (adhimokṣa).
What then?

It is another teacher’s view that liberation is the stainlessness of the mind—the state of being free from outflows (anāsrava)—which is not a different entity [from the mind itself], like the clarity of the surface of clarified butter, once passion and the other defilements have been removed by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).
(VI.81ab) "Because it is an obstacle to its arising.
This means because it is an obstacle to the arising of that mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
For the possession of afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*) is indeed the obstacle.
As for that which "does not arise":
it refers to that which is future and does not occur immediately after the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), namely, either the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) itself,
or the mundane [state] within the very continuum of one beyond training.
As for that which is fixed regarding its arising,
it is precisely that which has been stated:
namely, the future [dharma] that is oriented toward production.
That very point is stated in the treatise: "it is liberated.
The intention is that it is easily discernible by virtue of its being in the process of liberation.
"Precisely from that" refers to the obscuration to arising.
Precisely for that reason, because of the attainment of afflictions (*kleśa*),
and because of the obstruction to their arising— this very [reason] must be stated here.
This is provided that one accepts that even the mundane [states] within the continuum of an *aśaikṣa* are liberated.
Even for one in training (śaikṣa), worldly [attainment] arises.
Why, then, is it accepted that he is not liberated? To this, he says:
"It is not such," and so forth.
That mundane [attainment] of one in training (śaikṣa) is accompanied by the acquisition (prāpti) of afflictions;
however, the mundane [attainment] of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) does not become thus, and therefore there is no similarity.
(VI.81cd) "In the process of ceasing" means facing cessation.
"Obstruction to that" refers to the obstruction to the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣacitta*).
As for the unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛtavimukti*) mentioned in the Treatise or right here [in this text]:
The unconditioned is the abandonment of the afflictions;
and these are what are called the three realms.
Where is it stated? In the Sūtras or even in the Śāstras:
"Dispassion is the complete destruction of attachment."
Thus it is said when there is a desire to express distinction.
But when there is a desire to express non-distinction, it is simply "detachment" (virāga).
That is also called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*), as well as "cessation" (*nirodha*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the thing" (*vastunaḥ*):
Regarding contaminated form and so forth,
there are four alternatives.
There may be a case where one becomes weary [of it] but does not become dispassionate.
There may be one who becomes dispassionate but does not feel revulsion;
there may be one who experiences both; and there may be one who experiences neither.
"One becomes weary through the patiences and knowledges regarding suffering and its cause.
By this, he demonstrates that weariness has the objective entity as its cause.
"One becomes dispassionate through all those by which one abandons" thus indicates dispassion (*virāga*) as having the act of abandonment (*prahāṇa*) as its cause.
In this way, the fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) is established.
Having thus determined the causes of world-weariness (*nirveda*) and detachment (*virāga*), [the application] should be made.
The intention is that by this, the fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) is established. How so? He says:
"It is indeed subject to revulsion," and so forth.

It is indeed subject to revulsion by means of the patiences (*kṣānti*) regarding suffering and its origin, and by the knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin, because they have the objects of revulsion as their objective support (*ālambana*).
For suffering and its origin are the two things that constitute the objects of revulsion.
One does not become dispassionate;
for by the statement "not abandoning the afflictions," the activity of abandonment is impossible [at that stage].
Indeed, one becomes dispassionate through the patiences (*kṣānti*) regarding cessation and the path within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one does not become weary because the activity of abandoning occurs through the knowledges of cessation and the path while one is abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because it has objects of joy as its focal point;

for nirvana and the path are indeed the objects of joy that serve as its focal points. "Abandoning the afflictions through both of these" means that one becomes weary of and detached from [suffering] by means of the previous patiences and knowledges regarding suffering and its origin.
How?
One becomes weary because one takes the objects of weariness as one's focal point.
"One becomes dispassionate" means that because of the statement "abandoning the afflictions," there is the actual existence of the activity of abandonment.
It is "neither" [of the two] because, by the subsequent [phrases], one does not abandon the afflictions.
And one does not become weary, nor does one become dispassionate.
Because one takes as an object of focus a basis for joy through the subsequent patiences and knowledges regarding cessation and the path, one does not become weary.
By the statement "not abandoning the afflictions," because there is an absence of the act of abandonment, one does not become dispassionate.
It is said: it was specified in the first and fourth alternatives that one does not abandon the afflictions.
Who does not abandon which afflictions? In this regard, the detailed explanation begins with "one who is free from passion.
Therein, it is for the purpose of introducing the subject matter.
One who is free from passion for the realm of desire up to the sphere of nothingness,
while seeing and realizing the truths,

does not abandon the afflictions by means of the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*), the knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), or the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena.
Because they have already been abandoned previously by the mundane path of cultivation (*laukika-bhāvanāmārga*),
only the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) arises.
However, it is by means of the receptivities to subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) that one necessarily abandons the afflictions.
For there is no detachment from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*). However,
by means of certain cognitions belonging to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—

namely, the preparatory, liberation, and special paths, as well as the uninterrupted paths— one does not abandon the afflictions during certain states such as the transformation of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
Which ones remain?
It is established that one abandons the afflictions by means of the paths of immediate succession other than those.
Thus ends the sixth treasury-location in the *Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* composed by Master Yaśomitra.
(Abhidh-k-vy 610) Blank (Abhidh-k-vy 611) VII. The Seventh Chapter of the Treasury, titled "Exposition of Knowledge" (Jñānanirdeśa).
(VII.1) Immediately following the sixth treasury-location (kośasthāna), in order to demonstrate the connection in introducing the seventh, he says:
"The receptivities (kṣānti) and the knowledges (jñāna) are also taught," and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "the dharma-patience (dharmakṣānti) is untainted after the mundane supreme dharmas (laukikāgradharma)," eight patiences have been mentioned therein.
Following that, there is the dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) regarding the suffering of the desire realm (kāmaduḥkha) in that very same [sphere].
Furthermore,
in this context, "thus" refers to the knowledges;
if [it is] the knowledge of destruction or the vision of one beyond training.
In this context, "right view" refers to that very [view];
and in the passage "that itself is the two liberations, knowledge, and awakening as previously described," it refers to "right knowledge."
Or rather, all of this has been stated right here at the conclusion of the sixth chapter of the *Kośasthāna*:

"One becomes weary through the patiences and knowledges regarding suffering and its cause; one becomes dispassionate through all [of them]; and one abandons [the defilements] by means of those [patiences and knowledges]."
Thus [it is said].
Or rather, this is introduced by way of its connection with the treatise (*śāstra*),
for in the treatise the patiences (*kṣānti*) are also taught.
The knowledges (*jñāna*) consist of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Since this [treatise] is undertaken for the purpose of explaining them, he asks:
"But why are the receptivities (*kṣānti*) not knowledge? and so forth.
"Stainless patiences are knowledge.
Because of the restriction that "only the stainless patiences are not knowledge," it follows that the contaminated patiences are said to be knowledge.
For that is held to be conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "of what is to be abandoned by it":
because the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*), which is to be abandoned by the [patience] (*kṣānti*), has not yet been abandoned.
For in those states, the latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is indeed abandoned;
yet it is not [considered] abandoned because its state has been altered.
Furthermore, knowledge is held to be definitive.
It is not indeterminate;
thus, the patiences (kṣānti) are not cognitions (jñāna).
Furthermore, the patiences arise in the form of forbearance (kṣamaṇa).
They explain that [the path of seeing] is not knowledge because it does not exist in the form of a definitive certainty (*niścaya*).

While it would have been sufficient to say simply "because the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) has not been abandoned," for what purpose is the qualification "of that which is to be abandoned by it" (*tat-praheya*) added?

For in the second moment, the latent tendency of doubt to be abandoned by the first receptivity (*kṣānti*) becomes abandoned; thus, one might otherwise understand that only the first receptivity is not knowledge.
But this is not the case for other patiences (kṣānti).
Therefore, the qualification "of that which is to be abandoned by it" is used;
or rather, it is for the purpose of establishing that the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkhadharmajñāna) and so forth are indeed forms of knowledge (jñāna).

If it were stated merely that [it is so] "because the latent tendency of doubt has not been abandoned," then [the same would apply to] "because its nature is investigation" (saṃtīraṇātmakatvāt). This means that its intrinsic nature is close examination (upanidhyāna).
"Because its intention is without investigation and without searching.
That which has no investigation (*saṃtīraṇa*) is "without investigation" (*asaṃtīraṇa*).
An intention (*āśaya*) directed toward searching is the "intention for searching" (*parimārgaṇāśaya*).
"He has no intention of searching" means he is without the intention of searching (*aparimārgaṇāśaya*).
That which is without investigation (*asaṃtīraṇa*) and without the intention of searching is "without investigation and without the intention of searching" (*asaṃtīraṇāparimārgaṇāśaya*);
its state is [the quality of being so].
Therefore,
the meaning is that the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) are not views (dṛṣṭi),
as long as this person has not yet accomplished what was to be done.
To that extent, one contemplates and investigates the truths of suffering and so forth with a resolute intention (*āśaya*) through the aforementioned aspects such as impermanence and so on.

However, for one who has accomplished what was to be done, there occurs by means of those two [wisdoms] a mere subsequent reflection (*pratyavekṣaṇa-mātra*) upon the Noble Truths of suffering and so forth exactly as they have been seen: "Suffering has been fully known by me; it is not to be known again.
Therefore, those two do not have the nature of views (*dṛṣṭi-svabhāva*).
"Noble wisdom other than that is of both kinds" refers to everything from the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering up to the subsequent knowledge regarding the path.
That [wisdom] is engaged in contemplation and has abandoned doubt regarding its object;
"other" refers to mundane wisdom.
The restriction is that all of that is indeed knowledge;
the meaning is that there is no such thing as wisdom (prajñā) which is not knowledge (jñāna).
What, then, is this wisdom?

It is that which belongs to the five groups of consciousness—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—as well as that which is mental, including that which is associated with afflictions whose nature is view, and that which is unobscured-neutral.
Furthermore, it includes that which has the nature of view itself and that which is wholesome and mental.
What does that become?
He says: "And the six [types of] seeing."
This sixfold mundane wisdom is [proper] view; the others are not view,
because of the restriction that there are only these six.
What, then, is the other?
It is that which was previously mentioned as mundane.
But this [supramundane] knowledge is both this [mundane] and something else.
And this sixfold wisdom, which has the nature of views,
as well as the other previously mentioned [wisdom], is called "knowledge" (jñāna).
For this very reason:
The word "and" (ca) is recited [in the verse] as "and six views" (dṛśaś ca ṣaḍ iti),
because these six are called both cognitions (jñāna) and views (dṛṣṭi).
(VII.2, 3) By means of ten knowledges (*jñāna*). Which ones?

By the knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), the path (*mārga*), destruction (*kṣaya*), and non-arising (*anutpāda*). This undertaking is for the purpose of restriction, [showing that] there are exactly ten knowledges.
Because these—such as the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda*) and the knowledge of persons (*pudgalajñāna*)—are included within these very [categories].
In brief, however, there are only two: the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The qualification "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) is used for this reason.
Conventional cognition takes as its object conventional entities such as pots and cloths;
however, it sometimes also grasps their specific and general characteristics.
Thus it is called "conventional."
That which exists in the conventional is the conventional;
even the untainted, when summarized, [is included therein].
Knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are twofold;
for the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) and the others are included within these two alone.
As for the object (*ālambana*), it is according to what is possible.
Whatever is the object of perception for something, that belongs to it;
for sound is not the object of visual consciousness.
"Because they have that as their object" means because they have suffering and so forth as their objects.
These [are] of four kinds. (VII.4)
Thus, these same two— dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge— are fourfold due to the distinction of their objects, such as suffering and so forth.
When they do not have the nature of [wrong] views, they are called the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.
Furthermore, those two arise first;
that is to say, when the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising have first arisen, they become the subsequent knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of its cause.
The meaning is that they necessarily have suffering and its origin as their objects.
Why? He says:
because they take the aggregates belonging to the peak of existence as their objects by way of the aspects of suffering and its origin.
For it is the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) itself that is abandoned last of all for him.
Therefore, highly valuing liberation from that by which he is oppressed and by which he is bound, he immediately takes as his object the Peak of Existence once it has been destroyed.

And since that [Peak of Existence] is suffering and its origin, he takes the Peak of Existence as his object through the aspects of suffering and origin. Because those two—the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)—which first arise, necessarily [arise] with the aspects of suffering...

One takes as an object the aggregates belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) by means of the aspects of origination (*samudaya*), such as impermanence and so forth, or by means of the aspects of cause (*hetu*) and so forth.
However, when they have not yet arisen for the first time, those two [knowledges] also take the other truths as their objects; this is what is meant by implication.
Immediately after the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) arises.
Immediately after that comes the knowledge of non-arising; therefore, he asks:
"Does the diamond-like concentration also have the same object as those two?
By "those two," the meaning is "as they first arose."

Just as the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) have a single object (*ekālambana*), the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is: is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) also [like] them in having a single object?
If it has suffering and its origin as its object, what then?
The possibility [of it] being "single-object" (*ekālambana*) is that it takes both of those as its object;
however, if it takes cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*) as its object, it is not single-object,
because those two necessarily have the aggregates belonging to the peak of existence (*bhāvāgrika-skandha*) as their object.
For just as the poison of one who has been struck by a poisoned arrow, having pervaded all the limbs of the deceased, remains at the very site of the wound at the time of death and nowhere else;
in the same way, the knowledge of this yogi remains only within the very aggregates belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) that are to be abandoned.
(Abhidh-k-vy 614)
(VII.5, 6) "The knower of another's mind [arises] from four" means that it is comprised solely within those four, beginning with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
It does not [arise] from the knowledge of suffering and so forth,
because its aspect is different.
For untainted knowledge of others' minds has exclusively the aspect of the path, since it is a knowledge of the path.

As for that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it has a mundane aspect (*laukikākāra*), such as "with passion" (*sarāga*) or "free from passion" (*vigatarāga*), and so forth. This refers to the path of one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*).

Respectively, one does not know the path of one who has attained through vision by means of the path of one resolved through faith; nor does one know the path of one liberated at all times by means of the path of one liberated occasionally; for the lower [path] does not know the higher.
One does not know the path of an Arhat by means of the path of a Non-returner.
One does not know the path of a Pratyekabuddha by means of the path of an Arhat, and so forth.
This is because those two have as their objective support the antidotes to the desire realm and the higher realms, respectively.
Regarding those two— the category of dharma-knowledge and the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)—
there is a fixed rule: the antidote to the desire realm is the object of the category of dharma-knowledge,
while the antidote to the higher realms is the object of the category of subsequent knowledge.
There is no knowledge of another's mind (*paracittajñāna*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because the path of seeing is devoid of such functional activity.

This statement is made with respect to what is possible—that is, regarding the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma concerning suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*).

For it is sometimes possible, through the power of preparatory application (*prayoga*), to know the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge concerning suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge concerning suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*).
And the eighth is the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvayajñāna*).

Having known the two moments belonging to the category of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), one makes the application (*prayoga*) thinking, "I shall know the mind belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge. Thus, one brings about the eighth [moment], the subsequent knowledge of origin.
"Because of the mildness of the application" means because of its smallness of application.
For the Śrāvaka, that mind of another which has as its object the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) must be accomplished through great preparatory effort (mahā-prayoga).
Therefore, by the time he begins the preparation for it,
this [Śrāvaka] has already reached the sixteenth moment of mind.
He does not know the intermediate [moments].
He knows only these three: the first, the second, and the fifteenth.
How so?

Having known the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*), and having performed another preparatory application (*prayogāntara*), one knows the fifteenth moment, which is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*).
(VII.7) How does one know it in this way by means of untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) alone?
Because the untainted [knowledges] have the aspects (*ākāra*) of suffering and so forth.
And because this [subsequent knowledge] has such aspects as "this suffering of mine has been fully understood" and so forth, he asks:

"The distinction between those two is due to the distinction of that. By means of the distinction of that conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) obtained subsequent to [the supramundane knowledge], one knows: "Suffering has been fully understood by me," up to "the path has been cultivated by me."

"I have fully understood suffering; it is not to be understood again," and so on, up to "I have cultivated the path; it is not to be cultivated again"—knowing thus, the distinction between those two untainted knowledges, the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), has been made known and demonstrated in the treatise.
For this very reason, it is said: "based upon that."
"Taking that as its basis" means having made that the precursor, or having placed that before oneself;
the intention is that a distinction between those two non-conceptual [knowledges] is inferred from their outflow.
One knows in this same way even by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
There exists an untainted aspect (*anāsrava-ākāra*) distinct from the sixteen aspects.
Others maintain that one knows in this way by means of that very [untainted aspect].

If, according to the statement in the *Śāstra*—“that which, based upon that, is knowledge and vision”—the untainted knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*) is called the fruit of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), such as the full comprehension of suffering (*duḥkha-parijñāna*).
As for what is said:
"The cognition of destruction and non-arising is not vision;
it is not seeing."
That is contradictory.
Therefore he says:
"But the mention of 'seeing' is due to an objection to the Bhāṣya."
Regarding this statement in the treatise that "knowledge is vision," it arises from an objection raised in the commentary.
For in the context of the knowledge of suffering and so forth, it is recited as "knowledge, vision, science, intellect, and awakening."
This recitation of those who recite that [text] follows by implication from its wording.
However, for them, the knowledge of destruction and non-arising does not have the nature of vision (*darśana*);
the meaning is that it does not have the nature of a view (*dṛṣṭi*).
"Or because of its functioning through direct perception.
This means that the functioning of these two cognitions is direct perception;
thus, this is "functioning through direct perception."
Because it has that nature,
there is the mention of "seeing" and "speaking" for these two;
for in these two types of knowledge, the mode of operation is not indirect (parokṣa), as it is in the case of inferential or scriptural knowledge.
And vision is held to be a direct mode of operation,
such as visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Because of its similarity to that, these two types of knowledge are also called "vision."
Therefore it has been said:
"Precisely because it functions as direct perception (pratyakṣa), it is stated in the treatise that whatever is knowledge is also vision."
However, there may be vision that is not knowledge: namely, the eight patiences (kṣānti) occurring at the end of the clear realizations (ābhisamayāntika).
What is meant by this is that these two are accepted as being "vision" (darśana), but not as "view" (dṛṣṭi).

In this context, among those ten knowledges (*jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is itself conventional knowledge by virtue of its inclusion within its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, it is one part—that is, one portion—of the single knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
For of that [knowledge of others' minds], which is both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*), only the portion that is with-outflows is conventional knowledge.
"An outflow-free portion" means that among the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) is one knowledge, namely dharma-knowledge itself;
and it is a portion of seven [knowledges], namely: the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, the path, others' minds, destruction, and non-arising.
How so?
For the knowledge of suffering has the nature of both dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*);
that which is its portion consisting of dharma-knowledge [is what is meant].
That is dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
Likewise, for the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*) up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), which have the nature of dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*),
that portion which is dharma-knowledge is dharma-knowledge.
But it does not include the portion of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

As for the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), which has as its intrinsic nature the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge, path knowledge, and conventional knowledge, the portion that is knowledge of phenomena is simply "knowledge of phenomena.
Likewise, subsequent knowledge is exclusively subsequent knowledge itself.
And it is a portion of the seven;
that which is the portion of those very same [knowledges], such as the knowledge of suffering and so forth, belonging to subsequent knowledge—
that is to be understood as "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna).
The knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) is one among the ten knowledges;
it is precisely that which is the knowledge of suffering.

It also constitutes a portion of four knowledges: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
For these four, beginning with dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), have the four truths as their objects.
That portion among them which has the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) as its object is knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna).
There is no other part.
In this same way, the knowledge of origin and the knowledge of cessation should each be applied accordingly:
one single knowledge is either the knowledge of origin or the knowledge of cessation.

And a portion of the four—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)—which has either origination (*samudaya*) or cessation (*nirodha*) as its object, constitutes the knowledge of origination and the knowledge of cessation.
Among the ten knowledges, the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is one single knowledge; it is precisely that knowledge of the path itself.
And there is a portion for five [knowledges]:

the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
These five are knowledges of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and have the nature of the knowledge of the path.
That which is the portion of these [knowledges] consisting of the knowledge of the path is the knowledge of the path, and not the other;
the knowledge of others' minds is one among the ten knowledges.

And a portion of four—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)—constitutes these four knowledges.
For these four knowledges have as their intrinsic nature both the knowledge of another's mind and the knowledge of one's own mind.
That which among them is the portion of the knowledge of another's mind [is what is being discussed].
That is the knowledge of others' minds;
it is not the other.
Among the ten knowledges, the knowledge of destruction is one knowledge; by way of inclusion of its own nature, it is precisely that knowledge of destruction.
And six parts belong to the knowledges of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
The knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of a knowledge having such aspects as "suffering has been fully understood by me.
Among these, that which has the suffering and so forth of the desire realm as its object [is the knowledge of phenomena].
That which has as its object the suffering and so forth belonging to the realms of form and formlessness is included within the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
That which has as its object [the suffering and so forth] of those same realms is included within subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
That which has each [of the truths], such as suffering, as its respective object, constitutes the knowledge of suffering up to the knowledge of the path.
Among these, that portion which possesses such a characteristic is [the specific type of knowledge].
That is the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and no other;
it is said to be a portion of six knowledges.
Likewise, among the ten knowledges, the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) is one single knowledge, which is that very knowledge of non-arising itself.

And the "portion" (*bhaga*) of the six—namely, the portions of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—is that which has as its outflow (*niṣyanda*) such modes [of cognition] as, "Suffering has been fully known by me; it is not to be known again," and so forth.
That is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
That which has as its object the suffering and so forth belonging to the realms of form and formlessness is subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*);
it is not the other part.
It is said that this is a portion of the six [consciousnesses].
(VII.8) "Because of its aspect, its mode of aspect, and its object."
The aspect and the object-sphere constitute "aspect and object-sphere. The aspect alone constitutes "aspect and object-sphere. The aspect of the aspect constitutes "aspect-aspect-object-sphere."
Therefore,
conventional knowledge is [defined] by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"By way of its intrinsic nature" means through its own essential nature (*svabhāvena*).
It is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Why? He says:
because it is not knowledge of the ultimate truth (*aparamārthajñānatvāt*).
Dharma-knowledge is the antidote to the desire realm; subsequent knowledge is the antidote to the higher realms. For it is said thus in the treatise:
What is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
It is the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) regarding the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) associated with the desire realm;
it is the untainted knowledge regarding the cause of the conditioned factors associated with the desire realm.

The untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of the conditioned phenomena associated with the desire realm, and the untainted knowledge regarding the path for the abandonment of the conditioned phenomena associated with the desire realm—
this is called dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
Furthermore, it is also that which is untainted within dharma-knowledge and on the stage of dharma-knowledge.
This is called dharma-knowledge.
What is subsequent knowledge?
It is the untainted knowledge regarding the conditioned phenomena associated with the realms of form and formlessness.
The untainted knowledge regarding the cause of the formations associated with the realms of form and formlessness;
the untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of the formations associated with the realms of form and formlessness;
and the untainted knowledge regarding the path for the abandonment of the formations associated with the realms of form and formlessness.
This is called subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Furthermore, whatever untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) exists within subsequent knowledge and on the stage of subsequent knowledge,
this is called subsequent knowledge.
Regarding the statement "the knowledges of suffering and its origin are [identical] in terms of their aspects":

this is so only in terms of their aspects, not in terms of their objects, because there is no distinction between those two insofar as they both have the five aggregates of clinging as their characteristic.
For it is said thus in the Śāstra:
What is the knowledge of suffering?
It is the untainted knowledge that arises for one who attends to the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
This is called the knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of origination?
It is the untainted knowledge that arises when one attends to the tainted, causal [phenomena] as being caused, originating, produced, and conditioned.
This is called the knowledge of origination.
"By way of aspect and object, there are the knowledges of cessation and the path.
Thus, the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path are established both by way of their aspects and by way of their objects.
For it is said in the Śāstra:
What is the knowledge of cessation? It is the untainted knowledge of one who attends to cessation as cessation, as peace, as excellence, and as renunciation.
This is called the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
What is the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
It is the untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) of one who attends to the path as the path, as the correct method, as practice, and as leading to liberation.
This is called the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
The inclusion of the term "initially" (*prathamataḥ*) is for the purpose of distinguishing it from the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*),
for that too arises within the mental continuum of one who has accomplished what was to be done.
"Because it has all uncontaminated [dharmas] as its cause.

With reference to the ten knowledges that have first arisen, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) has all uncontaminated [dharmas] as its cause by way of being a similar-cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
However, the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) does not have all uncontaminated [dharmas] as its cause.
For the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is not its cause, because it is superior.
(VII.9) This is because the whole [antidote] is the antidote for the whole;

that is, the entire *dharmajñāna*—comprising both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation and having the four noble truths as its object—is the antidote for the entirety of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which consists of five categories subsumed under what is to be abandoned by seeing and by cultivation.
Considering that it is an antidote (*pratipakṣa*), it is said that dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) is the antidote specifically for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
However, there is also the possibility that dharma-knowledge is an antidote for the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*) as well.
What is that dharma-knowledge?
That which is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding cessation and the path:
for cessation and the path do not fall within the realms (*adhātu*). Even though they are lower, they are established as not being inferior.
However, when [the knowledge] pertains to the origin of suffering belonging to a lower stage and is inferior,
one should understand that such a dharma-knowledge, having that as its object, is not the antidote to the form and formless realms.
This applies to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The inclusion [of these defilements] refers to those belonging to the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*), because they are to be destroyed by the receptivities to subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*).

Why, then, does subsequent knowledge—which is comprised within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and has cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as its objects—not serve as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to all three realms?
Because the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) has already been conquered [by it].
By the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) alone, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is conquered beforehand.
Subsequently, subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) arises.
Therefore, because the desire realm has already been conquered, that [subsequent knowledge] is not the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the desire realm.
However, dharma-knowledge is appropriately the antidote for the form and formless realms because they have not yet been conquered.

Through the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path alone is there the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation belonging to the three realms, and not through the two preceding ones,
because of their lack of similarity in being peaceful and leading to liberation.

For there is no distinction whatsoever between the cessation or the counteragent of the formations belonging to the desire realm and the cessation or the counteragent of the formations belonging to the form and formless realms;

for every cessation is wholesome, unconditioned, and the path is conducive to liberation. "Subsequent" (*anvaya*) means that which follows (*anveti*); thus, it is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
(VII.10–12ab) "In every way" means that it is also included within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
"Those [previously mentioned]" refers to what follows.
We shall explain those aspects, such as impermanence and so forth, further on,
in the context of the sixteen aspects of the stages beginning with "heat" (*uṣmagata*),
because of the grasping of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and so forth.
Because of the grasping of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the grasping of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [forms] such as "eat," "stand," and "go" are included;
for these do not have the aspect of specific characteristics.
What then?
They have exactly these aspects.
However, both [of them]...
"It is both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava).
As for the passage beginning "What then," the intention is that there is a simultaneous apprehension of both passion (rāga) and the mind (citta).
Furthermore, the Sūtra is recited thus:
"One understands a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust' according to reality;
one understands a mind free from lust as 'a mind free from lust' according to reality."
Just as one knows with correct wisdom that [the mind] is with passion or free from passion,

so too one knows with correct wisdom that it is with hatred or free from hatred, with delusion or free from delusion, contracted or distracted, sunken or exerted, agitated or not agitated, unpeaceful, cultivated, unliberated, or liberated.
"Like the simultaneous grasping of a garment and a stain.
Just as there is no simultaneous grasping of a garment and a stain, so it is in this case.
How so?
Just as when a cognition arises with the determined form "cloth," it does not at that time apprehend dirt; and when a cognition arises with the determined form "dirt," [it does not apprehend cloth].
At that time, one does not grasp the garment.
There is "intimate attachment" (*saṃsṛṣṭa-sarāgatā*) and "associated attachment" (*saṃyukta-sarāgatā*). Intimate attachment arises from mental association (*saṃprayoga*).
Some say that it is "associated with attachment" because it is followed by the acquisition of attachment;
others say it is so because it has attachment as its latent object (*anuśaya*).
[The phrase] "by both" refers to these two reasons.
Namely, by way of being associated with passion (*saṃsṛṣṭa-sarāgatā*) and by way of being conjoined with passion (*saṃprayukta-sarāgatā*).
Other than those, it is "with outflows" (*sāsrava*);
that is, whatever is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), or mundane wholesome (*kuśala*).
Because it is accompanied by passion through that conjunction, it is "with passion.
Thus, both of these are said to be "with passion.
He said:
Furthermore, what is the reason that, according to the opinion of some, the antidote to attachment is called "free from attachment" (*vigatarāga*)?
For they say:
if that which is dissociated from attachment were [simply] "free from attachment," then even that which is associated with other afflictions would be so.
It may also be associated with hatred and so forth.
It may be free from attachment;
for that too is either dissociated from attachment or even associated with it.
Furthermore, in the Sūtra, that which is associated with hatred and so forth is not described as "free from passion," because of such statements as "possessing hatred" and "possessing delusion.
However, for those [who hold] that "free from passion" refers to the antidote to passion, [it is consistent].
This is not a fault for them,
because that which is the antidote to attachment is not associated with hatred and the like.
"If that is so," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
If a mind associated with attachment is "with attachment," then the antidote to attachment is "free from attachment.
That which is not its antidote— that is, not the antidote to a mind with attachment—
is an unafflicted mind, namely, an unobscured-neutral mind.
It is not "with lust" because it is not associated with lust;
nor is it "free from lust" because lust is not its antidote.
"And so forth" refers to this.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the same logical application should be extended to [the cases of] "with hatred" (*sadveṣa*) and "with delusion" (*samoha*).
How so?
In this Sūtra, however, a mind associated with hatred is "with hatred," while that which is the antidote to hatred is "free from hatred."
For if that which is not associated with hatred were "free from hatred," it would follow—
according to some— that it must be associated with other afflictions.
If that were the case, then a non-afflicted mind that is not the antidote to hatred would be neither "with hatred" nor "free from hatred."
Thus, a mind that is deluded should be called "with delusion," and one free from delusion "without delusion.
Therefore, a mind associated with attachment (*rāga*) should also be understood here as "with attachment" (*sarāga*).
According to others, because of the word "also" (*api*), it should also be understood as being "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) with attachment.
The Abhidharmikas [hold that] it continues in this manner up to "with delusion" and "free from delusion.
Therefore, in this Sūtra, it must be accepted that "with hatred" is due to being associated with hatred, and "with delusion" is likewise due to being associated with delusion.
"Due to the contraction of the focal object":
a wholesome mind is not associated with distraction;
therefore, there is a contraction of that [mind] toward its focal object.
It may be both contracted (*saṃkṣipta*) and distracted (*vikṣipta*),
due to its association with afflicted torpor (*kliṣṭa-middha*).
Torpor is of two kinds.
[The mind is] both afflicted and non-afflicted.
For that very same mind, when associated with torpor, would be "withdrawn," while as afflicted, it would be "distracted";
thus, there is the fault of confusion.
"And there is contradiction with the treatise.
How so? [The text] states:
"One understands the contracted mind as it truly is," as explained at length in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
For them, first of all, subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) cannot have a contracted mind as its object;
because there is no state of torpor (*middha*) above the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and because subsequent knowledge does not take the desire realm as its object.
Furthermore, path knowledge (*mārgajñāna*) also cannot have a contracted mind as its object.
For the knowledge of the path has the path as its object,
and a mind comprised within the path is not associated with torpor;
therefore, it should have been stated that such knowledge consists of two knowledges.
Namely, dharma-knowledge and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
However, for those who explain that a contracted mind is wholesome because of its contraction toward the object (*ālambana*),
these two faults do not occur.
Since that [state] is not associated with non-afflicted *middha* (torpor), it does not fall under the categories of "contracted" (*saṃkṣipta*) or "distracted" (*vikṣipta*).
Nor is there any contradiction with the treatise.
It is established that wholesome mind—whether comprised within the three realms or not—is "contracted," and that the knowledge thereof consists of the four knowledges (*jñāna*).
Untainted knowledge that takes as its object wholesome states of mind belonging to the realms of form and formlessness is subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is also that which takes as its object the wholesome states subsumed under the Path. This is because it is practiced by those with limited purification.
The meaning is: because it is practiced by those with few roots of merit.
"Because of the opposite of that" means:
because it is practiced by those with great purification.

The relative smallness or largeness of the factors from the roots up to the powers should be understood as limited or extensive respectively, according to the smallness or largeness of each individual root.
How so? It is said:
for that which is afflicted has its roots in two unwholesome roots—namely, delusion (moha)—and either greed (lobha) or hatred (dveṣa).
Because these two do not coexist within a single complex (*kalāpa*).
A wholesome [state] is associated with the three—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—because these are never found apart from one another.
This is because there is no cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of future states of that same kind.
Because there is no acquisition of the cultivation of future factors belonging to the afflicted class, it follows by logical principle that only wholesome conditioned phenomena are to be cultivated.
Furthermore, it is accompanied by three aggregates— the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations—
but not by the aggregate of consciousness.
Because there is no second consciousness within a single bundle (*kalāpa*),
and because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself by means of itself;
however, the wholesome [mind] has a great retinue, because of the existence of the cultivation of future states belonging to that same category.
And it is accompanied by four aggregates:
by those three beginning with feeling,
and by the aggregate of form comprised within the meditative and uncontaminated restraints, because of the impossibility of their following the mind.
"Furthermore, that which is afflicted is indeed weak.
But is not wholesome [mind] also weak, since the five aggregates of the wholesome are eradicated by a single moment of wrong view?
No, for that is not cut off absolutely, because it is reconnected again.

"By means of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti), however, there is the absolute eradication of the ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya); therefore, [it is said] 'also for that reason'—the word 'also' implies 'also for the reason previously stated.
'Because it is their antidote' means because it is the antidote to restlessness (auddhatya)."
Thus, there is that which is unquiet and that which is quiet.
The unquiet is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) because it is associated with restlessness (*auddhatya*).
The quiet is wholesome (*kuśala*) because it is its antidote. Thus, by virtue of being associated or dissociated from the afflictions (*kleśa*), it becomes either unquiet or quiet.
"Concentrated [wholesome states] are wholesome because they are its antidote" means because they are the antidote to distraction.
"By way of the cultivation of acquisition and the cultivation of practice" means...
The acquisition (*pratilambha*) of what was not previously obtained is [the first] cultivation;
its manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāva*) is the repeated practice (*niṣevaṇa*).
These two alone constitute the two types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Because those two have not been cultivated, it is "uncultivated.
For that which is afflicted is not cultivated as a future state in the manner of the wholesome;
nor is it fit for repeated practice because of its inferiority.
Regarding the statement, "The cultivation of the beautiful is called acquisition and practice":
by those two means "by acquisition and practice" is the meaning.
"Because it is not liberated by way of intrinsic nature or by way of the continuum.
It is not liberated by way of liberation through intrinsic nature because of its association with the afflictions;
nor is it liberated by way of liberation through the continuum because, even though the afflictions in the continuum have been exhausted, there is no non-arising [of them].
It is wholesome because it is dissociated from the afflictions (*kleśa*). It is liberated because it arises within a continuum in which the afflictions have been exhausted.
It is accompanied by sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha*).
"Associated with sloth and torpor, internally accompanied by suppression"—
this very point he concludes by stating that [the mind] is not endowed with insight (*vipaśyanā*).
He provides the explanation for "distracted" (*anuvikṣipta*) as "followed by a diffusion" (*anuvisṛta*).
"Because it is not asserted that a defiled state accompanied by torpor (*middha*) is distracted (*vikṣipta*).
On what grounds is distraction not asserted here?
Is it that distraction is not asserted because it does not exist in a defiled mind accompanied by torpor?
Or rather, even though distraction exists here,
it is not asserted because it has been established as being precisely the same as concentration;
thus they explain it in both ways.
Some explain as follows: for that which is defiled other than the defiled state associated with *middha* (torpor) is asserted to be "distracted" (*vikṣipta*).
However, that which is accompanied by torpor is "withdrawn" without distinction, whether it be afflicted or non-afflicted.
Others, moreover, explain it as that which is associated with torpor.
That [mind] is indeed concentrated (*saṃkṣipta*) and not distracted (*vikṣipta*).
However, that which is dispersed among sense objects is precisely what is called "distracted. Therefore, in this context, regarding a mind associated with torpor (*middha*):
"It is not admitted" means that it is better to contradict the treatise;
the intention is that the Abhidharma treatise was not spoken by the Buddha.

"Because they are stated to have an undifferentiated characteristic. This means that all of those [states] from the distracted up to the unliberated have been described as afflicted; thus, the characteristic of being afflicted belongs to these states beginning with the distracted and ending with the unliberated.
Furthermore, "afflictedness" (kliṣṭatva) is association with the universal mental factors of affliction (kleśamahābhūmika).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because the characteristics of the "contracted" (saṃkṣipta), "distracted" (pragṛhīta), and so forth are stated without distinction, no specific difference in meaning has been expressed.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the "exalted" (mahadgata), "unagitated" (anuddhata), "calmed" (vyupaśānta), "concentrated" (samāhita), "cultivated" (bhāvita), and "liberated" (vimukta) states are included.
Their wholesomeness is undifferentiated.
What, then, is this wholesomeness?
It is association with the universal wholesome mental factors (kuśalamahābhūmika).
"It was indeed not said," and so forth.
*Vai* is a particle.
"Not not said"—these two negations mean that it was indeed said.
What has been stated?
It is the specific meaning of the words;
thus he says.

Even though distracted states (*vikṣipta*) and others are equal in their general state of being afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), because one perceives specific defects in each of them—such as saying, "this afflicted mind is *vikṣipta* due to its association with distraction; it is *līna* due to its association with laziness; it is *uddhata* due to its association with restlessness"—the distinction in meaning is indeed expressed through the perception of these specific defects. Likewise, even for wholesome states such as the "contracted" (*saṃkṣipta*) and so forth, because one perceives specific qualities in each, the distinction in meaning is likewise expressed in detail, such as saying, "this wholesome mind is *saṃkṣipta*, [or] *pragṛhīta*," and so on.
"Because the contradiction with the Sūtra has not been resolved.
For in the Sūtra, the "contracted" state is said to be accompanied by *styāna* (sloth) and *middha* (torpor);
that which is afflicted through the conjunction with *styāna* and associated with *middha*.
Therefore, that [definition] is too narrow and not correct,
because *styāna* (sloth) belongs to the category of the universal mental factors of defilement (*kleśamahābhūmika*).
And as for the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "if," and so forth...

If, according to your interpretation, the Blessed One had intended in the Sūtra that what is "sluggish" (līna) is itself "agitated" (uddhata), then the separate mention of sluggishness and agitation would not have been stated.
Why is this so? He says:

At whatever time the mind is sluggish (*līna*), associated with laziness (*kausīdya*), or apprehensive of sluggishness— that is, apprehending that "this [mind] will become sluggish"— at such a time, there would not be this fixed rule that it is the wrong time for the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment consisting of serenity (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
And it should be stated thus:
"At that time, it is also the wrong time for the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment consisting of investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy.
What is the reason?
For that very same mind, when it is sluggish, would be considered agitated. Likewise, at whatever time the mind is agitated or apprehensive of agitation,
there would be no such rule as "this is not the time for the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment consisting of investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy."
And it should be stated thus:
"At that time, it is also the wrong time for the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment consisting of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
What is the reason?
For that very same agitated mind might be considered "sunk";
or else, it would have to be stated without distinction:
at whatever time the mind is sunk, or suspected of being sunk, or when it is agitated, or suspected of being agitated.
At that time, it is not the proper occasion for the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment consisting of tranquility, concentration, equanimity, investigation of phenomena, vigor, and joy.
The factor of mindfulness is not mentioned because mindfulness is omnipresent;
furthermore, since both [factors] are established even when not explicitly stated in either case of mind.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "I indeed declare mindfulness to be omnipresent.
How, then, is it understood that the Vaibhāṣika maintains that what is exactly the same as being sluggish is also what is agitated?
A sunken mind is afflicted because it is associated with laziness;
an excited mind is afflicted because it is associated with restlessness—so it is said.
But what, then, is the meaning here of "the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment being practiced separately"?

Is it that sometimes there is only the cultivation of serenity (*praśrabdhi*) and so forth, but not the cultivation of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and so forth; and sometimes there is only the cultivation of the investigation of phenomena and so forth, but not the cultivation of serenity and so forth? Thus, the cultivation would be fragmented.
The cultivation of these is held to be mental attention (*manasikāra*), not their actual manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāva*).
Mental attention means taking them as an object (*ālambanīkaraṇa*).
When the mind is sunken, it is the wrong time for taking pliancy and so forth as an object, meaning for applying effort toward them.
And when the mind is agitated, it is the wrong time for the investigation of phenomena and so forth.
However, their actual manifestation is not what is intended by "cultivation."
At that time, pliancy and the other [factors] are not to be brought into manifestation;
rather, the investigation of phenomena and the others are to be brought into manifestation. Or else, the investigation of phenomena and the others are not to be brought into manifestation.
"But serenity and the others must be cultivated" means that here, as the detailed explanation goes, laziness is predominant while excitement exists in a subordinate state.
Where laziness is excessive, excitement, however, functions in a suppressed manner.
That which is characterized by excessive restlessness (*auddhatya*) and subdued laxity (*kausīdya*) is "restless" (*uddhata*).
Thus, because of this distinction between these two, there is no contradiction in the separate mention of them in the Sūtra.
However, since they coexist—existing simultaneously within a single complex (kalāpa)—we say that "that which is sunken is the very same as that which is excited.
"Sunken" refers to what is afflicted by association with laziness (kausīdya).
"Agitated [mind] is afflicted because of its association with agitation.
To this the Master says: "This is intentional; however, such is not the intention in the Sūtra."
That which is excessive in laziness is "sunk," and that which is excessive in restlessness is "agitated.
For this reason, it is said: "At whatever time the mind is sunk," and so forth; however, it does not specify it as "excessive in laziness" or "excessive in restlessness."
As for what was said— that every mind associated with attachment is "with attachment"—
how was this stated?
In that context, a mind associated with attachment is "with attachment" in two ways.

Because it is stated that "whatever else is with-outflows (sāsrava) is associated with passion" (saṃyoga-sarāga), and because it is further stated that "in this context, a mind is to be understood as 'with passion' even by virtue of being conjoined with passion," it follows that even a mind of one in training (śaikṣa), though without-outflows (anāsrava), would result in being "with passion."
Because passion still remains within the continuum of one in training (śaikṣa).
If it is argued that it is the object of passion— that is, whatever is the objective support (ālambana) of passion— then...
That [mind] is "with lust" (sarāga) because it is conjoined with lust.

Even the tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) of an Arhat would have to be grasped as "with lust" by one who knows another's mind or possesses the knowledge of others' minds, on the grounds that it is conjoined with lust since it serves as an object for the lust of another.
Now, if it is thought that such a mind is not taken as an object by lust...
To this it is replied:
"Or how is that [object] associated with outflows (sāsrava)? If it is argued that it is because it has the general afflictions as its object, [we respond: no.

Now, if it is thought that because it is the object (*ālambana*) of the universal afflictions— view, doubt, and ignorance— it is therefore *sāsrava* (with-outflows), even so, one would have to include the delusion (*moha*). For an Arhat’s *sāsrava* mind would [otherwise] be included, since it has delusion as its object.
Delusion (*moha*) is also a universal affliction (*sāmānyakleśa*).
Furthermore, the mind of an Arhat can become the object (*ālambana*) of another's delusion;
however, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) does not take possession (*prāpti*) as its object.

Since knowledge of another’s mind is held to have the mind and mental factors as its object, it is not "with attachment" (sarāga) by virtue of being conjoined with attachment through association with the acquisition of attachment; nor is it "with attachment" by virtue of having that [other person's] mind or the attachment [within it] as its object.
The word "that" refers to that mind belonging to another which is apprehended by the knowledge of others' minds; it is expressed by the pronoun "tat.
[It has that as its object.]
That [desire] has that mind as its object; desire has that mind as its object.
Since this knowledge of others' minds has that [desire] as its object, it becomes "that which has desire having that mind as its object as its object.
For the knowledge of others' minds does not take such desire as its object because of its remoteness.
For the knowledge of another's mind has each individual substance as its object.

Furthermore, the knowledge of another's mind does not grasp the object of that [other] mind. This is because it is stated that such knowledge is independent of both the mental aspect (*ākāra*) and the object (*ālambana*).
And because of the statement, "one knows this mind as being with passion," for that reason also, a mind is not "with passion" due to its conjunction with passion;
rather, it is "free from passion" when it is not associated [with it].
The intended meaning is: "even though the acquisition of passion (*rāga*) exists.
With reference to that—that is, the departure from the acquisition of passion and so forth—it was said;

he shows that it was said with reference [to the acquisition] and not to actual conjunction (*saṃprayoga*), when it says: "one whose nature is not to return to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)."
The intention is that this is because of the demonstration of detachment from the three realms.
[Objection: "But was it not said," and so forth. Where was it said?

But here, in the Sūtra, it is stated at length: "For if a mind unassociated with attachment were 'free from attachment,' then even a mind associated with other afflictions would be free from attachment.
This is said with this underlying intention: that because it is dissociated from attachment, it is "free from attachment," even though it is associated with other afflictions.
If this were so, then a mind associated with hatred or delusion, and so forth, would likewise be [free from those].
It should not be said [that it is free from attachment]; therefore, he says:
"But that is not free from attachment," and so forth.
For that mind associated with hatred and the like is not grasped as being "free from attachment" simply because it is [temporarily] free from attachment.
What then?
[It is] "with hatred," "with delusion," and so forth, because it is distinguished by its association with hatred and the like.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the terms mentioned in the sūtra—such as "contracted" (*saṃkṣipta*) and "distracted" (*vikṣipta*)—are included here.
"Otherwise, however," and so forth.
If one were to cognize that "it is attached to this object"—namely, to form (*rūpa*) and so on—then it would also have form as its objective support (*ālambana*).
And if that were the case, it would not be knowledge of another's mind, because it would have form as its objective support.
Furthermore, for one who perceives another's mind along with its object, it would follow that there is a perception of its own nature.
For if the perception of another's mind together with its object were intended, then one's own self would be grasped by the knowledge of another's mind;
for it is indeed possible that the knower of another's mind perceives the very mind of the person whose mind he knows.
That [person], too, would take the mind of that knower of others' minds as his own object.
Consequently, because of the thorough knowledge of the very object of his own [cognition], that knower of others' minds would take his own mind as the object.
And this is not possible.
"That very same object is grasped by that very same mind.
"And all," and so forth. The analysis of the compound is as follows:

its object consists of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a substance, the minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), those that are present, those belonging to the continua of others, those associated with the realms of desire and form, and those that are unassociated. This is the breakdown of the compound.
The mention of "substance" (dravya) is for the purpose of excluding that which exists conventionally (saṃvṛtisat).
The mention of "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) is for the purpose of precluding the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
The mention of "mind and mental factors" (cittacaitta) is for the purpose of distinguishing them from form and so forth.
The mention of "present" is for the purpose of distinguishing [them] from the past and the future.
The mention of "another's continuum" is for the purpose of excluding one's own continuum.
The mention of "associated with the desire and form realms" and "unassociated" is for the purpose of negating association with the formless realm.

"Excluded from the path of seeing" means that one abiding in the path of seeing does not bring the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) into manifestation; therefore, it is not included within the path of seeing.
For the path of seeing does not have as its object a mind and mental factors that are interrupted.
The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is apprehended;
the meaning is that it is comprised within the path of cultivation.
It is dissociated from emptiness and the signless (animitta).
It is dissociated from both the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and the concentration on the signless (*ānimitta-samādhi*).
The concentration on emptiness is associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*);
the concentration on the signless is associated with the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
Nor is it the knowledge of others' minds;
nor does it constitute the knowledge of suffering or the knowledge of the cessation of suffering, because of the difference in their aspects (ākāra) and objects (ālambana).
Therefore, it is said to be dissociated from those two.
By implication, it is stated that it can be associated with the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).

"Comprised within the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising" means that it is not comprised within the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
The meaning is that [the knowledge of others' minds] does not have the nature of the knowledge of destruction or non-arising.
What is the reason?
The knowledge of others' minds has as its intention the investigation and searching for the specific characteristics of substantial entities (*dravyasvalakṣaṇa*).
Nor is it included within either the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*),
for it is excluded from the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*),
since that [knowledge] constitutes the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*).

And the knowledge of others' minds [is included] in the path of liberation and the path of distinction. They are called "ultimate" (pāramārthika) because they relate to the ultimate (paramārtha), even though they partake of the conventional; that is, they either have the ultimate as their object or they operate by means of the ultimate.
Because those two partake of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Since these two partake of the conventional,
the aspects of emptiness and selflessness do not exist [therein].
But how do these two relate to conventional truth?
[They do so] respectively: "Birth is exhausted for me" and "I know no further existence beyond this."
How is it that these [conventional expressions] have such aspects while being untainted?
It is by means of subsequent conventional usage through the power of that [untainted knowledge].
The completion of the sentence is: "by another knowledge."
Because the conventional cognitions (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) arising in the wake of those [supramundane cognitions] proceed with such aspects (*ākāra*),
they are said to "partake of the conventional" (*saṃvṛtibhajana*) by way of being their outflow (*niṣyanda*).
However, the intended meaning is that they do not partake of the conventional in a primary sense (*mukhyavṛttyā*).
And because they proceed as if adhering to the view of self through their natural outflow (*niṣyanda*),
for that reason, it is said that they are associated with exactly fourteen aspects, excluding the aspects of emptiness and non-self.
(VII.12) "Unassociated" means untainted (*anāsrava*).
"Impermanent" means "from the perspective of impermanence.
For this suffix *tasi* is employed here in its own sense (*svārthe*).
This suffix is to be understood in this same way everywhere.
Alternatively, even without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), there can be an expression that emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*).
Thus, "impermanence" (*anityatā*) refers to the state of being impermanent by way of an impermanent form.
This should be applied similarly in other cases as well.
"There is this possibility; there is this reality.
These two aspects as well are untainted (*anāsrava*). "There is this possibility" means "there is this characteristic."
The meaning is that "this thing exists" is the reason.
"One should understand through what is prescribed by yoga" means one should understand without error.

"This is not its meaning," and so forth. "Of this" refers either to the sentence as a whole or to two of its words. If the view were that "there is this possibility, there is this connection—that one might understand [the object] as impermanent and so on"—then [it would be correct]. However, [this is not the case]. "There is this possibility, there is this fact" means: "there is this occurrence, there is this logical conjunction, that one might understand it as impermanent and so forth. If such were the intention, [it would be acceptable]. But it is not. Therefore, the meaning is as previously stated. Furthermore, "there is this possibility" means: "there is this potentiality for understanding it as impermanent and so forth. "There is this fact" means: "there is this actual occurrence of understanding it as impermanent and so forth. Alternatively, "there is this possibility" means: "there is this potentiality for understanding it as impermanent and so forth. "There is this fact" means: "there is this actual occurrence of understanding it as impermanent and so forth. This is not so,

Because two words are not stated in the sentence otherwise. "By that which is to be abandoned by seeing" means by the mode of seeing.
"As self" and "as belonging to self" means with a mind associated with the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). "As annihilated" or "as eternal" [means the same].
By means of the view of grasping at extremes;
by means of false view, [which consists of] regarding things as causeless, as resulting from no action, and through denial;
and by means of the adherence to views, [which regards them] as foremost, supreme, distinguished, and absolute.

"By way of purity, liberation, and deliverance" refers to the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). "By way of doubt, uncertainty, and hesitation" refers to skeptical doubt (*vicikitsā*). "One might become attached" refers to passion (*rāga*).
"He might hate" means through hatred;
"he might think [highly of himself]" means through pride;
"he might be deluded" means through delusion.
"One should understand it as being produced by non-application.

But it is not so.

(VII.13) "Seven substances" means:
The four aspects of suffering exist as distinct entities.
However, since each of the aspects beginning with origination consists of a single entity, there are seven;
for that which is the aspect of cause is the same [as the aspect of origination].
That very same [truth] is origination, source, and condition; these are merely synonyms and not different in meaning, just as Śakra, Indra, and Purandara are.
Likewise, cessation itself is peace, excellence, and escape; thus, they are one single aspect.
The path itself is the principle (*nyāya*), the practice (*pratipad*), and the means of deliverance (*nairyāṇika*); thus, these constitute a single aspect.
This is what is meant:
practitioners should individually bring the four aspects of suffering (*duḥkhākāra*) into manifestation.
The opinion of some is that there is only one [mental application] for each of the aspects such as the cause (*hetu*) and so forth.

The Vaibhāṣikas, however, explain that there are sixteen in substance, because all the aspects— such as origin (*samudaya*) and the rest— must be brought face-to-face individually, just like the aspect of suffering (*duḥkha*).
For they say that the mental aspects (ākāra) have wisdom (prajñā) as their intrinsic nature.
"Because of dependence on conditions," and so forth.
That which has a fixed existence is not impermanent because of its dependence on conditions; the meaning is that its birth is bound to conditions.
"Because its nature is affliction" means because its nature is oppression. "By the opposite side" means...
The meaning is "by way of the counter-position" (*pratipakṣeṇa*). This is because a position that is opposed is called the "counter-position" (*vipakṣa*).
[He states] "the cause by virtue of its possessing the nature of a seed."
It shows that the cause has reached a state of excellence, like the primary seed.
Here, the word *yoga* means "method" (*nyāya*). Thus, it is said:
"The origin [is so called] by way of its manifestation."
He shows the proximity of the cause:
because it arises immediately after that moment,
thinking "it originates from this," it is called "source" (*prabhava*) by way of continuous connection (*prabandha-yogena*).
He shows non-interruption by way of continuity,
like the sequence of seed, sprout, stalk, stem, and so forth.
It is called a "condition" (pratyaya) in the sense of bringing about production.
It shows that [the effect] arises from many factors, such as causes and so forth.
For example, a jar is produced from many things such as a lump of clay and a staff;
it is just like that.
"Because of the extinguishing of the fire" means because of the extinguishing of the fires of passion, hatred, and delusion.
"Because of being free from affliction" means...
The meaning is "because of being free from suffering.
"Because of being devoid of all defects" means because of being liberated from all causes of suffering.
It is called the "path" (*pratipad*) in the sense of proceeding toward *nirvāṇa*, because it is conjoined with yoga, conjoined with logical proof, or conjoined with skillful means; or else,
it is so called in the sense of correct practice.
It is called the "path" (*pratipad*) because one proceeds toward *nirvāṇa* by means of it.
It is "leading to deliverance" (*nairyāṇika*) because it is capable of bringing about ultimate deliverance.
"Because it is not ultimate, it is impermanent.
Previously, it was stated that it is impermanent due to the absence of existence prior to its arising; now, he shows that it is so due to the absence of existence following its destruction.
"Because it has become an imposition" means because it has become a burden;
for that person is broken by suffering which has become a burden.
The meaning is "it is overcome.
Regarding the phrase "because of not acting according to one's will":
one whose nature it is to act out of desire is a "kāmakārin" (one who acts according to their will).
It does not act according to its own will; because it lacks such volition, it is non-self. This meaning has also been stated in the Sūtra.
Monks, if form were the self,
form would not lead to affliction for the self;

and one would be able to exercise power over form, saying, "Let form be thus, let it not be thus," because of the accepted etymological definition that "the self is that which acts according to its will."
