"By way of the method of coming [is meant] 'cause' (*hetu*). For *hi* means "to go"; it is called a cause because [the effect] goes forth from it.
The meaning is that [the effect] arises from this.
"By way of emerging" means that it is as if emerging from the future time-path.
"By way of spreading" means...
By way of continuity.
It is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*) in the sense of being a point of reliance.
The intended meaning is that it is the primary factor in the act of production.

"Non-connection [results] from the cessation of connection" means that because of the cessation of the preceding suffering, there is the cessation of connection with the subsequent [suffering]; this is the meaning of "cessation" (*nirodha*).
Because it is free from the three characteristics of the conditioned;
because it is free from arising, ceasing, and alteration;
and because it is the supreme consolation, being the ultimate security through the eradication of all suffering.
It is called "the path" (*pratipad*) in the sense that it does not obstruct or contradict the city of *nirvāṇa*.
Because by means of this [path] the city of *nirvāṇa* is neither obstructed nor contradicted,
but rather is actually reached (*pratipadyate*), it is therefore called "the path."
It is so called because one practices by means of it.
"Rooted in desire" (chandamūlaka) means having desire as their cause (chandahetuka).
In this context, "desire" (*chanda*) is a synonym for craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
"Arising from desire" means originating from desire.
"Of the nature of desire" means "having desire as their condition. The word "origin" (*prabhava*) should simply be recited later.
The phrase "by the Abhidharmikas" is to be supplied to the sentence.
The intention is that one must indeed follow the Sūtra.
[The Sūtra speaks of suffering] from the perspective of cause (*hetu*) and from the perspective of origin (*samudaya*).
"By way of condition and by way of origin.
But what is the distinction between these terms, which are like poetic meters?
"I am" is the desire for self-existence without differentiation.

The first [type of desire] is the longing for self-existence (*ātmabhāva-cchanda*), which, without determining a single substance among the five appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*) as a whole, takes as its object— either without differentiation or by way of the objects of self-existence belonging to the three times— the present entity of self-existence characterized by other modes, thinking "I am. The second is the longing for mere rebirth without differentiation, thinking "May I be," which is a longing for rebirth in general and not for a specific form.
"May I be thus":
the third is the desire for renewed existence in its specific variety, thinking "May I be of this kind. The fourth is the desire for the connection of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*).
Rebirth-linking itself is bondage;
or, bondage resulting from rebirth-linking is "rebirth-linking bondage.
In that context, the fourth [factor] is desire, which is aspiration.
Or, as is under discussion, the fourth [member] is the desire for the formative activity of karma (*karmābhisaṃskāracchanda*).
Alternatively, it is the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of karma;
therein lies the desire.
"Thinking, 'I shall give a gift in such and such a manner.
Furthermore, explaining how those desires are denoted by terms such as "root" and so forth, he says:
"In that regard, the first," and so on.
The "original cause" (*ādikāraṇa*) is either the beginning that is a cause, or the cause at the beginning.
Because of that state, they have their root in desire (*chandamūlaka*).
For the word "root" (*mūla*) has the sense of "cause" (*hetu*).
"Like the seed of a fruit":
just as the seed is the primary cause and the remote cause of a fruit,
so too is this initial craving the [cause] of suffering.
"Because of its origination by means of that":

because of the origination of renewed existence (*punarbhava*) by means of that second craving, there is the production of the fruit through a succession of moments, just as the production of a sprout and so forth leads to the arising of a fruit.
Just as the production of a sprout and so forth in succession constitutes the origination of the fruit.
In the same way,
the third aspiration is "May I be thus," which means having that as the condition for suffering of a similar kind.

The intention is that whichever kind of desire for renewed existence there is, a condition for that same kind of suffering can arise; because it possesses a specific form, a result that is itself of a specific nature is produced.
This is just as the field, water, manure, and so forth are [the conditions] for a fruit.
A *pāṣi* is dried cow dung.
By the word "etcetera," wind, sunlight, and so forth are included.
For from that as well, there is the attainment of the fruit.
Potency (*vīrya*) refers to being cold in potency or hot in potency.
Ripening (*vipāka*) refers to having a hot transformation or a sweet transformation.
Power (*prabhāva*) is a specific capacity.
For example, although their acidity is equal, the juice of the *bījapūraka* fruit generates bile, whereas the juice of the *āmalaka* fruit pacifies it.

"From that very [desire] arises that" means: from that very desire for the connection of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*), there arises—that is, there is the production—of that which is characterized as renewed existence (*punarbhava*).
It is like the end of the flower for the fruit;
just as the end of the flower is the source of the fruit,
so it is in this case.

In this context, the fourth craving is the direct cause of renewed existence (*punarbhava*), while the preceding three are causes by way of succession. Now, as for the detailed explanation beginning with "And if... [the following applies].

Regarding the discursive investigations of craving (*tṛṣṇā-vicarita*), there are two groups of five and two groups of four; there are four types of desire (*chanda*) which occur in their respective order.
The first type of desire has five aspects;
the second also has five aspects.
The third is of four kinds;
the fourth is also of four kinds. How so?
"Monks, when there is the view of a self based on the notion 'I am,' there occurs the thought 'I am thus,' and there occurs the thought 'I am of such a kind.
The meaning is that through association with that [view], one generates craving.
'I am thus' means exactly as before and not otherwise."
"Otherwise than this I am" means seeing [oneself] in another way through the appearance of complexion, eloquence, and so forth.
"I am existent" occurs;
by the opposite, "I am non-existent. This is the first [type of] desire for self-existence, which is fivefold when not distinguished.
"I shall exist" occurs in the form of eternalism;
"I shall not exist" in the form of annihilationism.
"I shall exist thus," and so forth, is to be explained in detail as previously stated.

Thus, this desire for rebirth in five ways without distinction is the second. The thought "May I be" occurs to him; the thoughts "May I be thus," "May I be in such a way," and "May I be otherwise" occur to him—this desire for rebirth in four ways with distinction is the third.

Furthermore, there arises for him the thought "May I be," as well as "May I be thus," "May I be in this way," and "May I be otherwise. This fourth [craving] is the desire for the fourfold connection of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi-bandha*).
Among these, the first is the root cause because it is the primary cause of suffering; this should be applied in detail as before.
It is called a "path" (*pratipad*) because it is specifically determined.
The path is that which leads with certainty.
But how is it specifically determined?
Because one goes to that [goal] by means of this very [path].
"As it has been said," and so forth.
Regarding "those whose conduct is characterized by the views of permanence, pleasure, selfhood, and a self":
for these individuals, their conduct consists of the views that [things] are permanent, pleasant, belonging to a self, and a self.
These are persons whose conduct is characterized by the views of permanence, pleasure, selfhood, and what belongs to a self.
As their antidotes, there are, in due order, the aspects of impermanence and so forth.
For those whose conduct is characterized by the view of causelessness—the notion that "there is no cause"—the aspect of causality serves as the antidote.
The aspect of origination (*samudaya-ākāra*) is for those whose conduct is based on the view of a single cause, namely that the Lord (*īśvara*) or primordial matter (*pradhāna*) is the sole cause;
[it shows] that origination is a cause, not a single cause.
The aspect of production (*prabhava-ākāra*) is for those whose conduct is based on the view of transformation (*pariṇāma-dṛṣṭi*), [namely] that an entity undergoes transformation.
This is an initial arising;
it is not that something previously existing undergoes transformation.
For those whose conduct is characterized by the view that this world was created by an intelligent agent, this is the mode of perception regarding conditions.
This world was not created by the intellect of a Lord (īśvara).
What then?
Depending upon this or that [cause], this or that comes to be.
For the word *prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
Therefore, it is made known that the world is produced by multiple conditions.
However, it would be more logical [to understand it] in this way.
This is the Sautrāntika view:
"ākāras" are the modes of grasping the object.
[The author] demonstrates that this is a derivation according to etymological rules (*nairukta*), taking the word "ālambana" (object) and the syllable "kāra" from the word "prakāra" (mode).
And when the remaining syllables have been elided, the form *ākāra* arises.
This being so, it is established that wisdom (*prajñā*) also possesses an aspect (*sākārā*). [It is also] "possessing an object" (*sālambā*).
The word-form *ālamba* ends in the vowel *ā*.
Alternatively, it is *ālamba* ending in the suffix *ghañ*.
Those which exist together with an *ālamba*, whether it be masculine (*ālambena*) or feminine (*ālambayā*), are called *sālamba*.
The meaning is that they possess an object (*sālambana*).

Regarding the phrase "the distinction between wholesome and so forth" (*kuśalādibheda*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the unwholesome (*akuśala*), the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the levels (*bhūmi*), and the bases (*āśraya*).

Because it occurs at the beginning of the verse, it is called "the first" (*ādya*); here, he explains that it is not the "first treatise. For in the treatise, the knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*) is recited as the first.
"That which is called dharma exists in six [stages]" because it has as its object the suffering and so forth belonging to the desire realm.
And in the three formless realms, there exists only subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) comprised within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Thus, it is likewise sixfold.
Because it is possible for the knowledge of suffering and the others to have the nature of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
As for the statement that [the knowledge of dharma] is not manifested in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*),
it is indeed logical that the knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*) is not manifested in the formless realm.
Because the formless realms do not take the suffering and so forth of the desire realm as their object.
But why is it not manifested in the realm of form?
Some say:
Dharma-knowledge is primarily for the purpose of reviling the desire realm.
Furthermore, for one who has been reborn in the form realm, dharma-knowledge does not arise in order to revile the desire realm,
because that [knowledge] has already been abandoned through the attainment of detachment and the transition to a different level.

However, one born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), even if free from passion for it, brings that [knowledge] into manifestation, because their birth in the desire realm still has a remainder. For this reason, dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) is not brought into manifestation in the form realm (rūpadhātu).
But the Master Saṃghabhadra says:
Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) is manifested only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
not in the form or formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*).
This is because the minds that enter into and emerge from those meditative attainments exist only in the desire realm.
Or [it is because] there is no basis that accompanies it.
For the basis of the morality that accompanies the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) consists only of the primary elements belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*),
because it acts as an obstacle to the acquisition of the afflictions that give rise to immorality.
Because they are antidotes,
and because those [defilements] do not exist there, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) has its basis exclusively in the desire realm.

(VII.16) It was stated in the exposition of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that the single knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) is the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
"Phenomena (dharmas) are other than body, sensation, and mind. Regarding "the other four knowledges are the foundations of mindfulness":

the knowledges of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, path, destruction, and non-arising possess the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness.
For the knowledge of suffering sometimes has the body as its object, and sometimes it has everything up to mental phenomena (dharmas) as its object;
the same applies to the knowledge of origin.
Path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*) is also that application of mindfulness to the body which has the untainted restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*) as its object. The rest is easy to understand.
(VII.17) "Except for subsequent knowledge" (*anyatrānvayajñānāt*).
If dharma-knowledge were to take uncontaminated knowledge as its object, it would necessarily take only the category of dharma-knowledge as its object.
Likewise, there is a rule that subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) would take only the category of subsequent knowledge as its object.

In that regard, for dharma-knowledge which constitutes the path-knowledge, other instances of dharma-knowledge, as well as the knowledges beginning with the knowledge of suffering and ending with the knowledge of non-arising, can serve as its objects.
However, for that which consists of the knowledge of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) can be its object;
and for that which consists of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds can be its object. Thus, nine knowledges are its objects.
In the same way, subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) should also be applied [in this manner].
For path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*) as well, there are exactly nine types, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
This is because path-knowledge does not take conventional knowledge as its object.
Because of the restriction regarding the objects of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*),
two [knowledges]— conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)—
are included within the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) has the nine untainted knowledges as its object. That which is tainted (*sāsrava*) can have conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds as its object.

Since the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) have the nature of the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) and so forth, all ten knowledges serve as their objects.
(VII.18, 19) "Due to the distinction between the associated (*saṃprayukta*) and the dissociated (*viprayukta*)" means that the associated [factors] are mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*).
Thus [it is said].
The dissociated factors are acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth.
They are divided into the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The wholesome is analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha), because it is the ultimate security.
The two indeterminate [factors] are space and non-analytical cessation.
"The four belonging to the desire realm and the untainted" refers to these.
Due to the distinction between associated and dissociated [factors],
there are six belonging to the realms of form, formlessness, and the untainted (anāsrava),
each being divided into associated and dissociated types.
Those belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness are also six due to that same distinction.
There are two untainted [factors].
Thus, there are those associated with the realms of desire and form, as well as the untainted.

This is because all mind and mental factors belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara), as well as all dissociated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra) and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), are not objects of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
Regarding the phrase "excluding the neutral unconditioned":

since the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) have the four noble truths as their objects, and the neutral unconditioned is distinct from those [truths], it is excluded.
(VII.20) Could one know all phenomena with a single cognition? It could not. How is this known?
From the Sūtra:
"In this regard, O Gautama, while we were seated together and assembled in the assembly hall, a conversation of this kind arose among us:
'It is said that the śramaṇa Gautama has spoken thus.'"
"There is no ascetic or brahmin who could know all at once or see all.
"This is true, sir Gautama; I remember you speaking thus."
Moreover, there is no such person— whether a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa—
who will know or see everything all at once;
this is because of the distinction between the subject and the object, and so forth.
Because of the distinction between the subject and the object;
for that which is the subject cannot be its own object.
Because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself;
for indeed, that very edge of a sword cannot be cut by that same edge.
Therefore, by means of that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not grasped.
Nor are the co-arising mental factors (caitta) grasped by it,
because they share the same object;
for whatever is the object of that conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), [that alone is what is grasped].
That same [principle] applies to associated [factors].
And if those associated factors were to be grasped, they would have their own intrinsic nature as their object,
because they share a single object with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
And this is not logical;
therefore, they are not perceived by it because of extreme proximity.
By that [definition], even those factors that are co-existent but dissociated are not included, just as one does not perceive the collyrium or the applicator-stick when looking at the eye.
And "that" refers to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
"Because its object is a distinct level.
This is because conventional cognition belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) consisting of cultivation takes as its object only a specific level—
either the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or the first dhyāna, up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
What is the reason?
Because the paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take the lower and higher stages as their objects respectively;
thus, they have the aspects of "calm" and so forth, and "gross" and so forth, with the higher and lower stages as their respective domains.
Because of this statement:
if that [path] were to have all stages as its object,
there would be detachment from all [stages] simultaneously.
For the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*) as well, only a certain stage (*bhūmi*) serves as the object (*ālambana*), according to what is possible.
How so?
For that which is comprised within the path of preparation of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) has the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as its object.
For one for whom the other two realms do not exist, the desire realm is not an object of perception.
For one for whom the other two realms exist,
the desire realm is not an object of perception.

In the cultivation of the meditations on the foul (*aśubha*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and so forth, for the purpose of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa*), the object of focus for that which is comprised within the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*) is exclusively the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); it is not the other two realms.
(VII.21, 22) One who is still subject to passion (*rāgin*) is endowed with one knowledge in the first untainted moment (*anāsravakṣaṇa*).
Thus,

because one who possesses patience (*kṣānti*) does not possess knowledge (*jñāna*), and is not even endowed with any other untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledge, the term "one who has passion" (*rāgin*) is used.
For it is because one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) is also endowed with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Regarding the second [moment], it is said that "by three":
that very same dharma-knowledge of suffering is called both "dharma-knowledge" and "knowledge of suffering."
When the designation "two" is applied due to a difference in names, one is endowed with three:
namely, dharma-knowledge, suffering-knowledge, and conventional knowledge.
In the four [stages]...

Thus, during the moment of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding suffering, and during the moments of the dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*) regarding origin, cessation, and the path— just as previously in the case of the receptivities (*kṣānti*), because there is no possession [of them]— in the moment of the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering, it is only the subsequent [knowledge] that increases.
It is not the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
because it has already been previously possessed.
At the moment of the knowledge of phenomena regarding the origin (*samudayadharmajñāna*), only the knowledge of the origin (*samudayajñāna*) increases.
They do not increase during the moments of dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
because one has already been endowed with them from the very beginning.

Likewise, it should be stated that during the two moments of dharma-knowledge regarding cessation and the path, they increase only during the moments of the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
But one who is free from passion (vītarāga) possesses [this knowledge] everywhere by means of the superior knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).

From the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti) up to the moment of the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (mārge dharmajñānakṣaṇa), he is also endowed with the knowledge of others' minds;
it should be understood that he is endowed with those aforementioned knowledges as well.

But regarding the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) on the path, one who is not yet free from passion (*avītarāga*) is endowed with those same seven; however, one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) is endowed with eight, namely,
those seven plus the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

However, since it is easily understood that only an Arhat is endowed with the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising, it need not be set forth in the Sūtra for that purpose; this is how it should be understood. (VII.23, 24) As for the phrase "those that have arisen are cultivated": [it refers to the cultivation of those factors already produced].
In this context, two kinds of cultivation are intended:
cultivation by acquisition and cultivation by practice.
Cultivation by acquisition is by way of attainment; cultivation by practice is by way of manifestation.
"Those that have arisen are cultivated" means that whichever [moments] have arisen, those very ones are cultivated.
For example, when the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) has arisen, a future receptivity of the same kind is cultivated.
"The aspects of that are four" means that the four aspects of impermanence and so forth are the aspects of patience (*kṣānti*), because they share the same nature;
others are not.
Thus, when the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering has arisen, that very same [knowledge] is cultivated in its future state;
only its four aspects undergo cultivation.
The same should be applied to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkhānvaya-jñāna-kṣānti) and so forth.
It is precisely the cultivation of the aspects of similar knowledge.
Why is it that the cultivation of similar knowledge and the cultivation of similar aspects occur only on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and not on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
There is no inquiry regarding the patiences (*kṣānti*),
because they do not exist on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Alternatively, an inquiry concerning them should indeed be made.
This is because they also possess homogeneous cultivation (*sabhāga-bhāvanā*).
For when the receptivity to suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) has arisen, the aspects of the receptivities to origin and so forth do not become cultivated.
However, the inquiry concerning knowledge (*jñāna*)—and not the inquiry concerning receptivity—is for the purpose of providing a mere illustration.
"Because the lineages have not been acquired" means because the homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*) have not been acquired. How so?

When the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) has arisen, the lineage of that [receptivity] and the lineages of its four aspects (*ākāra*) are obtained;
however, this is not the case for the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*) and so forth.
What, then, is the reason that when each individual aspect among the aspects such as impermanence (*anitya*) becomes manifest, the lineages of the remaining aspects are obtained?
Because they proceed toward cultivation due to their commonality through having an identical object of focus; thus,
the lineages (gotra) of all [of them] become attained.

Thus, when the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering has arisen, up until the time the subsequent-knowledge-receptivity regarding the path has arisen, the lineages of those [four truths] and their respective aspects are acquired;
therefore, it is precisely that which undergoes cultivation, and nothing else.

However, on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because all cognitions—both homogeneous and heterogeneous—as well as their respective aspects, become manifest, the causes for all of them are acquired.
Future mental states, characterized by that [object] and having the form of cognition, undergo cultivation;
and the conventional [knowledge] along with the three subsequent knowledges are likewise previously unobtained.
"Not in the dharma-knowledges, because there is no complete realization of the truths.
For at that time, suffering belonging to the realms of form and formlessness has not been fully understood, its origin has not been abandoned, and its cessation has not been realized.
This is because the path has not previously been realized by means of the worldly path.
Previously, by means of the worldly path (*laukikamārga*) within the beginningless cycle of existence (*anādigatisaṃsāra*), suffering, its origin, and its cessation were realized;
however, the path was never realized through conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) by way of the aspects of "the path" and so forth.
Therefore, at the conclusion of the realization (*abhisamaya*) of each of the three [truths], there is cultivation [of the path].
It proceeds;
it does not [proceed] during the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
However, it is not possible to cultivate the entire path [at once].
The meaning is "in order to bring [it] face-to-face.
At that time, even the origin (*samudaya*) has not been entirely abandoned;
that is to say, the portion to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), as well as by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, all suffering within the three realms has already been fully understood because it is that which must be fully understood; therefore, it is only with regard to the origin [of suffering] that an objection is raised: "it is to be abandoned by the vision of that truth.
This means it is to be abandoned by the vision of the truth of the origin.
"Because it has many lineages (*gotra*).
Lineage is the specific distinction within the general continuity of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva-saṃtati*).
Since this path possesses those many lineages, it is called "having many lineages."
The lineage of the pratyekabuddha is distinct from the lineage of the śrāvaka;
likewise is the lineage of the Buddha.
Furthermore, the lineage of the śrāvaka itself is mutually diverse.

Due to the distinction between weak, intense, and so forth, only one of those [antidotes] is cultivated—that is, brought into manifestation—as the antidote for what is to be abandoned by seeing; this is the meaning.
It is not the path [as a whole].
It can be cultivated in its entirety because it is an attendant of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is the attendant of the path of seeing.
Therefore, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is cultivated only at the conclusion of the three truths [of suffering, origin, and cessation],
and not at the conclusion of the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), because that belongs to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Since it is yet to be accomplished, it does not serve as a proof.
This point to be proven is that [this] is exclusively a retinue of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and not also a retinue of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
For we maintain that it is indeed also a retinue of the path of cultivation.

"Having truth as its object is more distinguished" means that whatever was previously mundane during the stage of seeing is indeed surpassed by this [subsequent] mundane [wisdom]; such is the intended meaning.
"Acquisition of the basis capable of bringing that into manifestation" means:
the acquisition of the basis capable of bringing that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) into manifestation;
this alone constitutes its acquisition.
It is not something distinct [from the lineage].
When the lineage is attained, that which belongs to the lineage is attained;
the lineage is the cause capable of producing that [result].
In that context, "belonging to that state" refers to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

What is meant is this: when one acquires a basis (*āśraya*) capable of bringing that [knowledge] into manifestation, then that [conventional knowledge] also becomes acquired as it arises by means of that same basis.
Now, why do the Vaibhāṣikas not accept it in this way?
That [knowledge] is to be attained through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
How, then, could it become manifest on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
Furthermore, there is no opportunity for its arising during the path of seeing; therefore, they describe it as being of a nature that does not arise (*anutpattidharmaka*).
Thus, it continues in detail up to "belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna.
If it belongs to the stage of the first dhyāna, then that which belongs to three stages is cultivated:
that belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna, that belonging to the stage of the *anāgamya*, and that belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
If that which belongs to the intermediate dhyāna stage is cultivated, it pertains to four stages:

that belonging to the intermediate dhyāna stage and those belonging to the first dhyāna stage and so forth, as previously mentioned. Likewise, if that belonging to the second dhyāna stage is cultivated, it pertains to five stages:
from that belonging to the second dhyāna stage down to that belonging to the desire realm.
If it belongs to the level of the third dhyāna, then that which belongs to six levels is cultivated—
ranging from the level of the third dhyāna down to the desire realm (kāmāvacara).
If it belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna, then that which belongs to seven levels is cultivated.
It belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna,
up to and including the desire realm (kāmāvacara).
Since one [type] has been specifically enumerated, it is established that the remainder consists of four.

Because of the double restriction—"only the last [member] in cessation" and "cessation is only the last"—it is established that the remainder consists of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that is cultivated when suffering has been realized:
that consists of the four foundations of mindfulness, because suffering has as its intrinsic nature the body and so forth.
The same should be stated regarding origination (*samudaya*):
that it is precisely the aspect of that [truth].
When suffering has been realized (*abhisamita*), the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that is cultivated [arises].
Each of those has the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The same should be stated for [the truths of] origin and cessation.
Its object of focus is that very same [truth].
Because that aspect has that as its object.
"Acquired through application" means it is not obtained by birth.

"Having the nature of four or five aggregates" means that the [karma] belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) has the nature of four aggregates because of the absence of concomitant form (*anuparivartaka-rūpa*).
That is to say, its nature consists of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

However, those belonging to the higher stages consist of five intrinsic natures, because they have as their intrinsic nature the aggregate of form characterized by the restraint of meditative absorption (*dhyānasaṃvara*).
(VII.25, 26) "Two knowledges are present" refers to the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Because the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) has the nature of both of those.
"The six future ones" refers to the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and so forth.
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is not cultivated,
because it has been previously obtained; for he will say that what has been previously obtained is not cultivated.
Thus it is said.
There is no knowledge of others' minds because one has not yet abandoned desire.
Beyond that, there is cultivation of seven [knowledges].
From the abandonment of one type up to the abandonment of eight types;
"until he becomes free from passion" means until he has abandoned nine types.

In this interval, while the paths of preparation, uninterruptedness, liberation, and excellence are being cultivated, seven knowledges are cultivated. If it is a worldly [path], the knowledges beginning with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) are cultivated, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
If the path of cultivation has the aspect of the peaceful and so forth, or the sublime and so forth, then conventional knowledge is present;
[it is] one of the four knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
namely, any one of the knowledges of phenomena regarding suffering, origin, cessation, or the path.
Because subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*) are not antidotes to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), [the path] is not any one of the subsequent knowledges.
And regarding "among the five superknowledges" (*abhijñā*): this excludes the superknowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*).
"Of the four subsequent knowledges" refers to the subsequent knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
"And of the two dharma-knowledges" refers to the same.
Because the two [knowledges] having cessation and the path as their objects are associated with being antidotes to the three realms,
conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is not cultivated [in that context], since it is not an antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
However, when detachment from the seven stages occurs, even when supramundane [knowledge] is being cultivated, conventional knowledge is also cultivated.
For even conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) serves as an antidote to that category of afflictions;
it is not only supramundane knowledge (*lokottara*). Therefore, conventional knowledge of that same kind is also cultivated therein.
However, in the penetration of the unshakable [state], there is no such conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) that has become the nature of the antidote;
therefore, it is not cultivated therein.
In that context, the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) is the seventh.
Because one abides in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) is cultivated therein;

however, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is not, for one who abides in the path of uninterrupted transition is not yet one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*). And it is for one of immovable nature that the knowledge of non-arising is cultivated.
In the eight paths of liberation during the detachment from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), only seven knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated.
How, then, is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) cultivated?
The knowledge of others' minds is prohibited in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), but not in the path of liberation.

Therefore, when one type [of affliction] has been abandoned, up to eight types having been abandoned, a knowledge of others' minds that is distinguished from the previous knowledge of others' minds is cultivated.
Such a noble person (āryapudgala), having emerged from that path, would bring it into manifestation.
For it is held that a distinction in the knowledge of others' minds arises from a distinction in the mental continuum (saṃtāna).
For both—the one with attachment and the one free from attachment—there is cultivation in the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
However, in the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), there is cultivation for those two alone;
that is, for both the one with attachment and the one free from attachment, there is also the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Regarding the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), for what reason is there dispute?
Some hold that because of its similarity to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it should be cultivated therein just like the [knowledge] at the conclusion of clear realization (*ābhisamayāntika*).
Others hold that there is no clear realization [therein], yet there is a similarity to the path of seeing; such is the dispute.

(VII.28–30) "The cultivation of the six is as before" refers to the knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
It does not include conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), because it resembles the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
What is the similarity here with the path of seeing?
It is the attainment of the fruit;
just as the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning is attained by means of the path of seeing.

In this way, through this path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) as well, when a trainee (*śaikṣa*) refines their trainee-faculties (*śaikṣendriya*), the conditioned states comprised of sharp faculties—such as the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*) and so forth—are attained.
And just as there is no cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) during the state of the path of immediate succession on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), so it is here too.
Thus, due to its similarity to the path of seeing, there is no cultivation of conventional knowledge on the path of immediate succession.
"Likewise.
This refers to the knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Here too, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is not cultivated, because it is not an antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
The knowledge of others' minds does not exist in any uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), because it is excluded from them.
What, then, remains? This is the detailed explanation. How is it that the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) in the process of becoming detached from the desire realm is what remains?
Because of the statement: "On the path of cultivation with attachment, there are seven cultivations above that.
The remaining paths of liberation (vimuktimārga) occur during the detachment from the seven stages, the superknowledges (abhijñā), and the mixed cultivation (vyavakīrṇabhāvanā).

Because it is stated: "In the paths of uninterrupted activity during the mastery of the seven stages, the acquisition of the supernormal knowledges, the attainment of the immovable, and the mixed cultivation."
Likewise, for one who proceeds toward immovability (*akopyatā*),
there is also the cultivation of ten [knowledges] in the final path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), according to the statement;
thus, eight paths of liberation remain as the remainder.

Furthermore, all the paths of preparation and the paths of distinction belonging to an anāgāmin who is free from passion are included among those [cultivated], because they are not mentioned separately in the context of their cultivation.
As for what was stated regarding the learner (*śaikṣa*)— namely, that "in the remaining cases, there is the cultivation of eight"— it applies here as well.
But how, when it is thus not specified, is the understanding of the distinction obtained?
Because for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), there is necessarily the application of the cultivation of nine or ten knowledges.
For this very reason, he says: "Furthermore, for one beyond training, [it concerns] the supernormal powers (abhijñā) and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇabhāvanā*), the dhyānas, and so forth is intended.

Regarding those paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*), liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and excellence (*viśeṣamārga*) that exist during the realization of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and during mixed cultivation—
if one is liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), nine knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated therein.
Excluding the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
If one is of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), then by adding those same ten,
there are eight or nine.

For one who is liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), there are eight; for one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), there are nine, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), because that is excluded from its paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
However, in the case of the two—namely, the path of superknowledge (*abhijñā*) and the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*)—[it is not excluded].
Regarding the paths of liberation for the supernormal knowledges of the divine ear and eye:
because it is stated that "the supernormal knowledges of the ear and eye are neutral," their respective paths of liberation are also neutral.
Furthermore, there is no cultivation of future states for an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharma.
However, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is detachment from the desire realm and the first three dhyānas;
the fourth dhyāna is not included.
Because at the final path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) during the detachment from the fourth dhyāna,
there is the attainment of the fundamental sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*);
and yet, there exists no knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) that is comprised within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because it is to be accomplished through an object that transcends form (*rūpa*).

Regarding the phrase "in the production of the qualities such as the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), the three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*)," the analysis of the compound is as follows:
the paths of preparation, the paths of liberation of the three supernormal knowledges, and the production of the qualities such as the immeasurables.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of qualities such as the liberations (vimokṣa) and the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).
The phrase "the production of qualities such as the immeasurables" includes the stages of the dhyānas for the purpose of excluding the preparatory stages (sāmantaka).
For in those cases, there is no knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

The three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) are the supernormal knowledge of the sphere of psychic power (*ṛddhiviṣayābhijñā*), the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛtyabhijñā*), and the supernormal knowledge of the mental states of others (*cetaḥparyāyābhijñā*).

And these exist in the final paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) regarding detachment from the desire realm and the three dhyānas, as well as in the paths of liberation of the three supernormal knowledges belonging to the stages of the dhyānas.

Furthermore, regarding the realization of qualities such as the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated as a future attainment within the very paths of preparation (*prayoga*), liberation (*vimukti*), and excellence (*viśeṣamārga*) belonging to the stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Moreover, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) that is subsumed therein is cultivated specifically in its distinguished form.
One who has attained those specific qualities would bring [that knowledge] into manifestation,
except for the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), such as the "heat" (*ūṣmagata*) stage and so forth;
for within those stages conducive to penetration, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is not cultivated.
He asks: "What is the reason?
and replies: "Because it is an attendant of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Just as the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is not cultivated on the path of seeing, [so too is it not cultivated here].
The intention is that it is likewise not cultivated even in its retinue.
"Elsewhere," and so forth:

for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), elsewhere—namely, upon the acquisition of a path not previously attained—there is the acquisition of the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), uninterruptedness (*ānantarya-mārga*), and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), excluding the final path of liberation in the detachment from desire and the first three dhyānas.
In that case, when there is the attainment of a path not previously attained elsewhere, only future conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated.

Knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is not; likewise, in the attainments of the uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) during the realization of qualities such as the three supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the bases of power (*pramāṇa*), when there is the attainment of a path not previously attained elsewhere, only future conventional knowledge is cultivated.
In the paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*), there is no knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), because it is not their antidote.
(VII.31, 32) Now, in which path does it occur? In the mundane (*laukika*) or the supramundane (*lokottara*)? It occurs in whichever level (*bhūmi*) the path belongs to.
It is either with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*), beginning from the *anāgamya* stage.
And as for "the level which one first attains":
the meaning is that it belongs to whichever level—from the first *dhyāna* up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*)—one first attains through the process of detachment (*vairāgya*).

How so? If, by relying on the stage of the *anāgamya*, one attains the first *dhyāna* through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) due to detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one acquires both that which belongs to the *anāgamya* stage, having the nature of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*), and that which belongs to the stage of the first *dhyāna*, having the nature of the fundamental stage (*maula*).
In the ninth path of liberation, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated.
Thus, by relying on the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna, one attains detachment from the first dhyāna and acquires the second dhyāna.
In the same manner, both that which is comprised within the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna and that which is comprised within the fundamental (*maula*) second dhyāna are cultivated.

In this way, it should be applied in detail up to the point where, by relying on the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains the peak of existence through detachment from the sphere of nothingness.
Even when one attains the first dhyāna through detachment from the desire realm by relying on the untainted (anāsrava) preparatory stage (anāgamya),
then likewise that conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is cultivated.

Even when one attains the first *dhyāna*—which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and free from passion (*vairāgya*)—by relying on the basis of the fundamental stage of the first *dhyāna*, at that time one also attains conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) comprised within the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second *dhyāna*.
This conventional knowledge serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the first category of the first *dhyāna*, up to its ninth category;
for it is that very stage which is attained for the first time at that moment.
However, in the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)—even though it is comprised within the fundamental second dhyāna—is cultivated as a future state.

In this same manner, the cultivation of conventional knowledge should be applied in reliance upon the stages of the untainted intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), up to and including the stage of the untainted sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
(Abhidh-k-vy 638)
"Regarding 'for the sake of detachment from which': for the sake of detachment from whichever stage; that is its attainment."
The acquisition of whichever stage is "acquisition of that"; in both cases there—
And from that,
faith is cultivated.
"Untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
He explains how this is so by means of the commentary:
"For even for the sake of detachment from a particular level (*yadbhūmi-vairāgyāya*),"—the word "even" (*api*) implies that it is not only [knowledge] belonging to that level (*yadbhūmika*).
The path is also twofold:
mundane and supramundane.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "the path of preparation, etc.," there is the inclusion of the paths of uninterruptedness, liberation, and excellence.
And as for the stage which one attains through detachment:
the untainted [dharmas] belonging to that stage or to lower stages undergo cultivation with respect to the higher stages.
For example, relying on the second untainted dhyāna, one effects detachment from the third dhyāna.
The path belonging to that level—the level of the second dhyāna—brings about the cultivation of untainted knowledge belonging to that same level.

Furthermore, regarding the level from which one effects detachment, namely the third level, untainted knowledge belonging to that level—that is, belonging to the level of the third dhyāna—is brought to cultivation in the ninth path of liberation.
An untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledge belonging to a lower stage—whether belonging to the first dhyāna stage or the *anāgamya* stage—is cultivated.
For even that which belongs to a lower stage, such as the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and so forth, is cultivated because it is of the same nature [as the knowledge being attained].
Now, however, one may effect detachment from the second dhyāna by relying upon the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the third dhyāna.

In that regard, during the eight paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), because that preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) is contaminated (*sāsrava*), the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) knowledge belonging to that level does not undergo cultivation; this is because it does not exist there. However, the uncontaminated knowledge of a similar type belonging to lower levels—namely, that belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the first dhyāna, and the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*)—does undergo cultivation.
It proceeds toward cultivation.
In this same way, it should be applied elsewhere as well; this is the general direction.
And the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) is with outflows (*sāsrava*).

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and [those] without outflows" (*anāsravāś ca*) indicates that those qualities which one, having become an Arhat, would manifest are, at that stage, with outflows (*sāsrava*);
they undergo cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding "the immeasurables, the liberations, and so forth":
by the word "and so forth," the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and others are included.
[They are said to] "breathe out," as it were, through their similarity to a basket.
A basket that has been bound and compressed with a rope is said to "heave" when the rope is cut;
it is called "heaving" because it is designated by a figurative term.
This is because of the similarity to a basket that seems to breathe when its rope is cut.
Just as that basket, which was bound and compressed by a rope, seems to breathe when the rope is severed,

so too the aforementioned qualities such as the meditation on the foul (*aśubha*) seem to breathe as they will proceed within the continuum of one who is no longer subject to outflows (*aśaikṣa*), due to the severing of the rope of the acquisition of afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*) by means of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Because inhalation is a property of living beings, it is metaphorical.
Why? He says:
"for one who has attained sovereignty over his own mind," and so on for all [the following].
The *rājādhirāja* is the king superior to all other kings;
the state of being that is *ādhirājya*.
There is sovereignty (*adhirājya*) over one's own mind because of the departure from subjection to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The meaning is "sovereignty over one's own mind.

For an Arhat who has attained that state, all wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharmas*) undergo cultivation as their virtues proceed to meet him, like subjects coming to welcome a king with offerings (*prābhṛta*) such as garments and the like. This is similar to how, upon the attainment of supreme sovereignty, the territories and provinces of a certain overlord come to him with offerings of clothing and so forth.

Just as when one goes out to meet someone, so too, when the rope of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions is severed, the qualities—as if breathing a sigh of relief—attain their own acquisition; the meaning is that the acquisition of those qualities arises with even greater intensity.

In the desire realm, upon the attainment of Arhatship, the meditations on the foul (*aśubha*) and so forth, consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, belonging to the three realms, proceed toward cultivation according to their possibility.
However, in the attainment of Arhatship within the form and formless realms, they belong respectively to two realms and one realm.

This should likewise be understood according to the levels (bhūmi): it should be known that for one born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), upon attaining Arhatship, those [paths and fruits] belong exclusively to that level.
"Whatever is obtained," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
That which was previously lost and is now obtained again— that is, brought into manifestation— pertains to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). That future [state] is not cultivated,
because it has already been abandoned once it was cultivated within cyclic existence.

The Master shows that whatever among the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and so forth, is not habituated in *saṃsāra* but is distinguished and conducive to the untainted (*anāsrava*), when that [state] becomes manifest, a future state of the same kind— distinguished— is cultivated.
The Master Saṃghabhadra also explains this very point.
That which was previously obtained is not cultivated.
That which was obtained and then lost, and is obtained again, is not cultivated.
By implication, it is understood that what is obtained for the first time is what is cultivated.
Because it is brought face-to-face through effort.
For the path that has not yet been relaxed is brought face-to-face by means of effort;
because its momentum is powerful, it proceeds toward cultivation in the future.
However, that which has previously been calmed manifests without effort.

Because it has been cultivated as calm and because its fruit has already been bestowed upon one who has accomplished what was to be done, it is devoid of momentum; thus, it is not cultivated for the sake of its future manifestation.
That which is future is produced through effort.
The intended meaning is that "it is cultivated.

This being the case, regarding what was stated at length—"conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) first," etc.—Master Vasumitra has written here: "Only that which belongs to the continuum of an Ārya is taken [into account], because it is not habituated to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)."
Regarding this, it is said that the Vaibhāṣikas say:
"This is not so.
Why?"
Because that [attainment] becomes as if unobtained due to having been relinquished;
therefore, even in the case of obtaining again that which was previously cultivated and then abandoned, cultivation indeed occurs.
How can it be "previously unobtained" when it has already been obtained before?
"For such a thing has never been established in the world before.
Others, however, explain:
"This was said with reference to this single birth, not to another birth."
That which was lost and is obtained again in this very same lifetime is not cultivated,
because it has already been cultivated and then relinquished.
However, that which is obtained in another birth is what is cultivated;
it is not obtained [in this life] because its cultivation has been forgotten.
(VII.33) "For cultivation is fourfold.
Cultivation as acquisition (*pratilambhabhāvanā*) means that acquisition itself is cultivation;
the meaning is that the very attainment of what has not yet arisen is cultivation.
Thus, it should be stated that cultivation itself, counteraction itself, and complete removal itself constitute "cultivation. What is cultivation?
And what, up to and including, is complete removal?
Cultivation (*niṣevaṇa*) means bringing [the antidote] into presence again and again; it is the path that serves as the antidote, as stated in the Sūtra:
"one whose body is cultivated, one whose mind is cultivated.
The meaning is: one whose body and mind have had their antidotes cultivated.
Furthermore, the antidote to the body is the path for the sake of detachment from the four dhyānas.
For it has been said: "A monk is called one who has cultivated the body, cultivated the mind, and cultivated ethical discipline.
How does one become one who has cultivated the body?
He is free from passion for the body, free from longing, free from thirst, free from affection, and free from attachment.
Alternatively, according to scripture, that which is the path of immediate succession for the destruction of passion for form is what becomes "free from passion" by means of this [path].
Expulsion (*vinirdhāvana*) is the severing of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of afflictions.
For future [dharmas], it is one:
namely, cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
"For present [dharmas], both" refers to the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha*) and the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa*). "In that way, thus," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

Since it was stated without distinction that the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha*) and practice (*niṣevaṇa*) pertain to all conditioned wholesome (*kuśala-saṃskṛta*) phenomena— both those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*)—

and since it was also stated without distinction that the cultivation of counteraction (*pratipakṣa*) and elimination (*vinirdhāvana*) pertain to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena— both afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*)—
therefore, in this manner, there are four types of cultivation for wholesome phenomena with outflows.

For those [dharmas] which are wholesome, there are the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*); and because they are contaminated (*sāsrava*), there are also the cultivation of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of expulsion (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*).

What, then, of those conditioned dharmas that are neither wholesome nor contaminated, as well as those that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and those that are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*)?

Regarding how many types of cultivation (bhāvanā) they possess, it is said: for those that are untainted (anāsrava), there are two—namely, the cultivation of acquisition (pratilambha-bhāvanā) and the cultivation of practice (niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā).
This also applies to those that are afflicted (kliṣṭa) and neutral (avyākṛta).
Are there two kinds of cultivation? Namely, the cultivation of the antidote and the cultivation of expulsion.
Regarding the faculties, it is the former.

The meaning is that it is the cultivation of restraint (*saṃvara-bhāvanā*) regarding the eye and the other [senses]. "Of the body, the subsequent" refers to the cultivation of analytical discernment (*vibhāvanā-bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, he demonstrates those two types of cultivation in their proper order by means of scripture:
"These six faculties," and so forth.
Moreover, that restraint of the faculties has been stated to have mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*saṃprajñāna*) as its intrinsic nature.
The cultivation of elimination (*vibhāvanā*) is also the expulsion of afflictions that have the body as their object.
"But those," and so forth:

however, those two—the cultivation of restraint and the cultivation of elimination—are included within the cultivation of the antidote and the cultivation of expulsion, respectively; thus, there is no contradiction in saying that both are included within both.

(VII.34ab) "In general, for all" means that at the moment of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), the cultivation of qualities is said to belong to Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Samyaksambuddhas alike;
and those [qualities] are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the knowledge of destruction.
Because of this statement:
"The ten powers," and so forth.
These eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika), beginning with the powers and ending with great compassion (mahākaruṇā), are established by the Vaibhāṣikas.
Some describe eighteen other unshared qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) distinct from [the ten] powers and so forth, as follows:
the Tathāgata has no lapse of conduct.
There is no sound; there is no fluidity;
there is no perception of diversity.
There is no neutral mind;
there is no equanimity that is not preceded by discernment;
and there is no obstructed knowledge and vision regarding the past.
There is no obstructed knowledge and vision regarding the future;
there is no obstructed knowledge and vision regarding the present.
All bodily action follows after knowledge.
All vocal action follows after knowledge;
all mental action follows after knowledge.
There is no loss of zeal.
There is no loss of vigor;
there is no loss of mindfulness;
there is no loss of meditative concentration.
"There is no loss of wisdom;
there is no loss of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
In this context, "chattering" (*ravita*) refers to acting impulsively.
Fluidity is the intention for play.
The perception of diversity is the perception of diversity arising from attachment, aversion, and delusion toward objects that are pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
The remainder is easy to understand.
The ten powers:
the power of knowing what is possible and impossible;
the power of knowing the ripening of karma.
The power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments;
the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties;
and the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations.
The power of knowledge of the various elements;
the power of knowledge of the paths leading everywhere;
the power of knowledge of recollecting past abodes.
The power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth, and the power of knowledge regarding the destruction of the outflows. But the Sūtra says: "O Venerable Ones, there are ten powers of a Tathāgata."
What are the ten? Here, venerable ones, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, what is possible as possible, and what is impossible as impossible.
This is the first power of a Tathāgata.
Endowed with this power, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, claims the noble place of the bull, turns the Brahma-wheel,
and roars the true lion’s roar in the assembly.

Furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the undertaking of karmic actions pertaining to the past, future, and present— in terms of their basis, cause, object, and maturation— just as, venerable ones, the Tathāgata [understands] as previously described, up to understanding them as they truly are in terms of their maturation.
This is the second power of the Tathāgata.
By means of this power— as previously described—

furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the defilement, purification, establishment, and cleansing of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti).

Venerable ones, that the Tathāgata [knows] as before. Furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the degrees of the faculties of other beings and other individuals. Venerable ones, that the Tathāgata [knows] as before.
This is the fourth power of a Tathāgata;
by means of which power, as before, [he acts].
Furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, that the world has various modes of liberation and manifold modes of liberation.
Venerable ones, that the Tathāgata [knows] as before— this is the fifth power of a Tathāgata.
By means of which power, and so forth, as before.
Furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the world of manifold elements and many elements.
Venerable ones, that which the Tathāgata [knows] as previously described— this is the sixth power of a Tathāgata.
"By which power" is as before.
Furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the path leading to all destinations.
That the Tathāgata, venerable ones, [understands this] is as before.
This is the seventh power of a Tathāgata;
by means of this power, it is as described previously.
Furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold previous existences.
That is to say, he recollects one birth, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, and even many eons of dissolution and evolution. "Those beings were named such-and-such;

there I was, with such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a long life, such a duration, and such a limit to my lifespan—and I was that very person."
"From that place he passed away and was reborn there; from there he passed away and was reborn here.
In this way, with its specific modes, its causes, and its details, he recollects his manifold previous existences.
Venerable ones, when the Tathāgata [recalls] as described before...
This is the eighth power of a Tathāgata.
By means of this power— as previously described—
furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, sees beings passing away and being reborn, beautiful and ugly.

He understands, as it truly is, those beings who are weak, inferior, or superior, those going to a good destination or even to a bad destination, according to their karma: "These venerable ones were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech and mind;

they were revilers of the noble ones, holders of wrong views, and because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on wrong view, with that as cause and that as condition, upon the breakup of the body after death, they have fallen into a state of misery, a bad destination, or ruin."

Furthermore, these venerable beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech and mind, not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, and because of undertaking actions and dharmas based on right view—

with that as cause and that as condition— upon the dissolution of the body, they are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world among the gods. Venerable ones, this is what the Tathāgata [knows], as before.

This is the ninth power of the Tathāgata. By means of this power— as previously described— furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the outflows, having himself realized, witnessed, and attained in this very life the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, dwells therein.
He declares: "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; I know no further state of existence beyond this.
Venerable ones, that which the Tathāgata [knows] as before—this is the tenth power of a Tathāgata.
"By which power" is as explained previously.

(VII.34cd–36) Regarding "ten cognitions with respect to the possible and the impossible": the possible (*sthāna*) and the impossible (*asthāna*) constitute "the possible and the impossible" (*sthānāsthāna*).
In this context, "power of knowledge" (*jñānabala*) means that knowledge itself is the power;
its meaning is that it has the nature of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).
How so?

Briefly stated, the possible and the impossible consist of the conditioned and the unconditioned; furthermore, that which is conditioned is to be divided into eight types, based on the distinction between the associated and dissociated factors belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as those that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Likewise, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) should be divided into two types,
by way of the distinction between the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Among these, all ten phenomena are the object of the power of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The meaning is that its activity extends across all ten dharmas.
For dharma-knowledge, there are five:
the four belonging to the desire realm and the untainted [realms], and the wholesome unconditioned [dharma].
For subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), there are seven:
the six belonging to the realms of form, formlessness, and the untainted (*anāsrava*), and the wholesome unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
For the knowledges of suffering and origin, there are six: those belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
For the knowledge of cessation, there is one [object], which is exclusively the wholesome unconditioned.
For the knowledge of the path, there are two, both untainted.
For the knowledge of others' minds, there are three.

The associated [factors] belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, and those that are untainted (anāsrava) are the objects of the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna). These consist of nine categories of phenomena,
excluding the neutral (avyākṛta) unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Having established this, the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible consists of ten knowledges (*jñāna*).
But how, then, are the ten factors said to be "the possible and the impossible"?
Possibility is the possible; impossibility is the impossible.
Alternatively, it is impossible and there is no occasion that a woman should bring about the state of Buddhahood; it is possible, however, that a man should do so.
It is impossible and there is no occasion that a woman should bring about the state of Brahmā.
"It is possible for this person [to attain it]," and likewise, "it is possible that there is the cessation of suffering.
In this way, the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*) should be understood as proceeding through such modes.
"Eight are the fruits of karma.
This is because contaminated karma and its maturation are subsumed under the truths of suffering and its origin.
Knowledge of cessation and knowledge of the path do not [belong to these].
Therefore, there can be eight other knowledges that have those as their objects,
[as stated] in the detailed explanation beginning with "in the resolute beliefs regarding the dhyānas, etc., and the faculties."
"Meditative absorption and so forth" (dhyānādayaḥ) means those things for which meditative absorption is the first; namely, the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
There are four meditative absorptions and eight liberations.
The three concentrations are emptiness and so forth. The two attainments are the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation.
The nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling;
the faculties as sense organs;
and the mental factors of resolute conviction.
The compound *dhyānādayaś cākṣāṇi cādhimokṣāś ca* is a dvandva (copulative) compound.
Within these, there are nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*). How is this so?

Because the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth are distinguished as being associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) or free from outflows (*anāsrava*), and as being either associated (*saṃprayukta*) or dissociated (*viprayukta*), nine knowledges (*jñāna*) can have them as their objects.
However, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) does not [have them as its object].

This is because they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). For them, the knowledge of cessation does not exist; however, for those [unconditioned phenomena], it does exist. But for those [meditative absorptions and so forth], the knowledge of cessation does not exist, because they are conditioned.
Regarding the faculties as well, such as faith and the rest:
that knowledge of what is predominant and non-predominant, through the distinction of weak, medium, and superior faculties, is the power of knowing the superior and inferior [faculties].

Even among those [factors] which are divided by the distinction between being with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*), nine knowledges (*jñāna*) are possible, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
Preferences for [objects such as] primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth constitute various inclinations (*adhimukti*).
These, moreover, are both with and without outflows and belong to the three realms, because they take those [objects] as their focal points, excluding the knowledge of cessation.
Thus is the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātujñānabala*).
For in this context, the master Saṃghabhadra maintains that an "element" (*dhātu*) is a disposition (*āśaya*) arisen from the latencies (*vāsanā*) of previous practice;
furthermore, these are simply those specific mental states and mental factors (*cittacaitta*).

In the same way, for those [paths] distinguished by the division into contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), there are nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); this should be applied as before.
Regarding the phrase "in the paths" (*pratipatsu*), the full explanation is as follows:
here there are many paths leading to the hells and so forth.
The path leading to hell, up to the path leading to the gods,
and the path leading to cessation.
Among these, those paths which lead to hell and so forth [are the paths of unwholesome action].
That is the cause;
for it is by means of them that one proceeds,
and the path is indeed called "the proceeding."
Therefore, disjunction is attained by it.
But how is cessation [attained]? That too is the path.
It is so called because one practices it; or rather, the fruit of the practice is called "the practice" (pratipad).
For this very reason, he says:
If it is held that "the practice is accompanied by its fruit," for here the cause is intended as the practice leading everywhere;
for thus they explain.
Regarding the power of knowledge of the path leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*):
the meaning is "leading to the origin of the view of a real body" (*satkāya*).
In this context, the "real body" (*satkāya*) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ*).
In this context, "origination" (samudaya) is intended to mean "arising" (utpāda), because of the statement: "Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
The cessation of the view of a self-identity (satkāyanirodha) is dissociation (visaṃyoga).
Because it has the nature of going everywhere, it is "all-pervading" (*sarvatragāminī*); and because it is a practice (*pratipad*), it is "the all-pervading practice.
That is knowledge, and that itself is power;
thus, it is the "power of the knowledge of the all-pervading practice."
Therefore, these ten knowledges (*jñāna*) should be applied.
If the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) itself is the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*),
it is the knowledge regarding the destruction— that is, the cessation— of the outflows.
The meaning is that knowledge has the cessation of the outflows (*āsrava-nirodha*) as its object.
This being so, there are six types of knowledge,
because the very category of the knowledge of cessation is differentiated by the distinctions of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and so forth.

Now, regarding the phrase "one whose continuum has exhausted the outflows" (kṣīṇāsravasaṃtāna): the meaning is that the knowledge which exists when the outflows have been exhausted is "the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows" (āsravakṣayajñāna).
