In the mental continuum of one whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*), all knowledges (*jñāna*) are active; thus, there are ten knowledges.

"Except for the non-arising of a Buddha elsewhere" means that except for Jambūdvīpa, there is no arising of a Buddha; the intention is that the ten powers (*bala*) have their basis in a male of Jambūdvīpa, because they arise based on a Buddha.
That very tenfold knowledge is not called the "power" (bala) of another;
for although others also possess this, it is not a power because it is obstructed.
However, that which is unobstructed [is indeed a power].
The intention is that this is the unique power (*āveṇika-bala*).
"The rejection of a person seeking ordination," and so forth: "seeking ordination" (*pravrajana-prekṣa*) means one who looks toward, or seeks, the going forth (*pravrajyā*).

The rejection of that man who was seeking to go forth is "the rejection of the man seeking to go forth. That is the illustration, showing how the knowledge of another might be obstructed. It is said that the noble Śāriputra, while examining the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) of a certain man seeking to go forth, did not perceive them; thus he rejected him and did not ordain him.
This is the meaning.
However, the Blessed One saw him and ordained him;
and concerning him, when questioned by the monks, the Blessed One said:
This very karma was performed by him,
whereby he attained arhatship;
for karmas do not ripen within the earth element.
"Not in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element;
rather, it is only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases," and so forth.
And this has also been said:
For I perceive his own subtle seed of liberation,
like gold hidden within a cleft in a mineral-bearing rock.

Thus, "ignorance regarding [the stages] from birth up to the limit" (upapattyādiparyantājñāna) means that by the word "etc. (ādi), ignorance regarding [the stages] up to the limit of death (cyutiparyantājñāna) is included.
(VII.37) "The strength of Nārāyaṇa. This is the designation for strength: "Nārāyaṇa."
And he who possesses that strength is also called Nārāyaṇa,
just like Cāṇūra and Mahānagna.
"Bhadanta" refers to the Elder Dārṣṭāntika.
"Otherwise" means if bodily power is not accepted as being like mental power.
He would not be capable of enduring the infinite power of knowledge;
the meaning is that the Blessed One would not be one who possesses the quality of endurance.
It was stated previously that "others [reside] in the joints," which introduces the specific types of bone-joints.
"Like a nāga-knot," and so forth.
Buddhas have joints like a nāga-knot;
a nāga-noose is a nāga-knot.
The joints of the Pratyekabuddhas are like chains; the joints of the Cakravartins are like spikes. [There are] ten more...

"The strength of the seven beginning with the elephant" means: the seven beginning with the elephant— namely, the elephant (*hastin*), the scent-elephant (*gandhahastin*), the great athlete (*mahānagna*), Praskaṇḍin, Varāṅga, Cāṇūra, and Nārāyaṇa— their strength is ten times greater [than the preceding], or superior by ten.
To the question "How so?", he says:
The strength of ten ordinary elephants— that is, common elephants—
is equal to the strength of one *gandhahastin* (fragrant elephant).
Thus, the strength of ten *gandhahastins* is the strength of one *mahānagna*; and so on, until the strength of ten *cāṇūras*.
That is the strength of a single Nārāyaṇa.
It is a mountain of tenfold increasing progression;
by a tenfold increasing progression, it is called the strength of half-Nārāyaṇa.
Proceeding in the same manner from the beginning, the strength of the ten Praskandins is half-Nārāyaṇa; twice that is Nārāyaṇa.
However, the Master [Vasubandhu] maintains that it is more logical in the way [the second position] is;
he thus supports the very first position.
Otherwise, he would not be able to endure the power of infinite knowledge; that is precisely the reason.
Furthermore, otherwise, the throwing of Devadatta’s dead elephant’s thumb over seven walls and moats would not have occurred.
Thus, it is indeed a specific transformation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
This demonstrates that this power (*bala*) has the specific nature of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) themselves and is not derived matter (*bhautika*).
It is distinct from the seven types of derived matter.
Others maintain that the derived matter called "power" is indeed something other than the previously mentioned qualities such as smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*) and so forth.
(VII.38ab) "Just as in the sūtra":
"Śāriputra, there are these four grounds of self-confidence of the Tathāgata.

Endowed with these grounds of self-confidence, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, claims his noble, preeminent position and turns the sublime wheel of Brahmā in the assembly correctly."
He roars the lion’s roar.
What are the four?

"While I am truly a perfectly awakened Buddha (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), let no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa challenge me with regard to these dharmas on the grounds that 'these dharmas have not been fully realized by him,' in accordance with the Dharma."
I would cause [others] to remember it.
In this regard, I do not perceive even a sign.
And thus, not perceiving a sign, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained intrepidity; I claim the noble, bull-like position, the state of a Brahma.
I set the wheel in motion;
I roar the lion’s roar correctly in the assembly.
This is the first ground of self-confidence.
"Alas, although I am one whose outflows are exhausted, these outflows have not been abandoned"—if anyone should say this to me, as before, up to: "I roar the perfect lion’s roar in the assembly.
This is the second ground of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*).

Furthermore, regarding those things which I have declared to be obstructive factors for my disciples, should anyone say that they are not sufficient to constitute an obstruction for one who indulges in them, [I claim] of this as before.
This is the third ground of self-confidence.
Furthermore, regarding that path of mine which has been proclaimed for the disciples— noble, leading to liberation, leading to penetration,

and which leads out for one who practices it toward the complete destruction of suffering and the making of an end to suffering— if anyone were to say, "It does not lead out," [as stated] previously, this is the fourth ground of self-confidence.
As with the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible, so it is in detail.

Just as the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible consists of ten knowledges and is comprised within all stages, so too is this fearlessness: "When I am a perfectly awakened Buddha, [there is no basis for anyone in the world to legitimately challenge me]."
In the same way, one should apply this by making a tenfold classification of the dharmas.

Just as the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*) consists of six or ten knowledges and is comprised within the ten stages, so too for the second ground of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), namely, "I am one whose outflows are destroyed"— here also, one should apply it by making a tenfold classification of the dharmas, [resulting in] six or ten knowledges.

Just as the power of knowledge regarding one’s own karma consists of eight knowledges—excluding the knowledges of cessation and the path—and is comprised of all stages; likewise, the third ground of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) is that which was stated by me in detail: "Whatever I have declared to the disciples as obstacles.
Here too, having made the same distinction among phenomena, it is only those things comprised within the truths of suffering and its origin that constitute obstacles.
It should be understood that there are eight knowledges (*jñāna*), as they are not comprised within the truths of cessation and the path.

Just as the power of knowledge regarding the path leading everywhere consists of ten or nine knowledges and is comprised of all stages (*bhūmi*), so too is this fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*): "The path which has been declared by me for the deliverance of the disciples."

In this case as well, it should be understood that there are ten knowledges (*jñāna*) when including the paths with and without outflows (*sāsrava-anāsrava-mārga*) along with their fruits, or nine when excluding the fruits. For fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) is indeed the state of being without dread.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that one becomes fearless by means of these knowledges; therefore, the knowledges themselves are the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*). The Master, however, says: "But it is the self-confidence produced by knowledge."
It is not merely knowledge.
Alternatively, all of this is indeed the word of the Teacher;
for fearlessness is indeed *vaiśāradya*.
For thus, the mental factor that is the antidote to that fear is itself a mental factor;
and fear, too, is a mental factor. And by means of these knowledges acting as causes, one becomes fearless.
How then is it that knowledge itself is fearlessness?
It is logical that fearlessness is produced by knowledge, not that knowledge itself is fearlessness.
As stated in the Sūtra: "O monks, there are these three foundations of mindfulness."
Those which the Noble One practices;
those which the Noble One, while practicing, is worthy of instructing a community.
What are the three?
Here, monks, the Teacher teaches the Dharma to his disciples out of compassion, being merciful, desiring their welfare, seeking their benefit, and feeling pity for them, saying:
"This is for your benefit; this is for your happiness; this is for your benefit and happiness."
My disciples listen to me; they lend an ear;
they apply their minds to understanding.
They practice in accordance with the Dharma and its secondary rules;
they do not act in transgression of the Teacher’s instruction.
Therefore, the Tathāgata feels no delight, no mental pleasure, and no elation of heart.
The Tathāgata dwells therein equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
This is the first application of mindfulness,
which the Noble One cultivates.
That which, when practiced by a noble one, entitles him to instruct the community.
Furthermore, the Teacher teaches the Dharma as before;
yet his disciples do not wish to listen.
They do not lend an ear;
they do not establish a mind intent on understanding;
they do not practice in accordance with the Dharma.
They proceed by transgressing the Teacher’s instruction;
yet because of that, the Tathāgata feels no resentment, no impatience, no lack of confidence, and no displeasure of mind.
In that regard, the Tathāgata dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
This is the second foundation of mindfulness,
which the Noble One cultivates;
cultivating which, the Noble One is worthy to instruct the community.
Furthermore, monks, as long as it concerns the Teaching, the Tathāgata feels neither delight nor gladness, nor any elation of mind;
he feels no resentment, no impatience, no lack of confidence, nor any dissatisfaction of mind.
The Tathāgata dwells there equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
This is the third application of mindfulness,
which the Noble One cultivates;
cultivating which, the Noble One is worthy of instructing the assembly.
"Mindfulness and clear comprehension":
this shows that it has both as its intrinsic nature.
This is because of the statement, "mindful and clearly comprehending. As for the detailed explanation beginning with "even when [it concerns] a Śrāvaka":

it refers to when even a Śrāvaka whose afflictions have been diminished is dealing with disciples who wish to listen, those who do not wish to listen, and both—those who wish to listen and those who do not.
There is no delight, no compliance, nor any malice or hatred.
Why, then, are these called the unique, uncommon Buddha-qualities?
"Abandonment together with the latent predispositions (*savāsanaprahāṇa*).
This means because of the abandonment of joy and so forth along with their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
But what, for the Śrāvakas, is this so-called "latent predisposition"?

For whatever specific affliction one has previously practiced, the particular capacity within the mind that causes transformations in the movements of body and speech produced by that [affliction] is called a "latent impression" (*vāsanā*).
The Venerable Anantavarman maintains that a latent impression is a specific state of the mind that is morally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
"Or rather," the Master explains at length:
"He whose disciples are the disciples of the Buddha, the Blessed One, and not those of another.
What is the reason?"

Whether toward one who desires to hear, one who does not desire to hear, or toward both those who desire to hear and those who do not, for that very disciple, there is the non-arising of those [emotions];
namely, the non-arising of joy and malice.
This is established as a marvel and a wonder.
The meaning is that it does not belong to any other disciple.
(VII.39) "For otherwise," and so forth, means:
if it were not of the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), it would be of the nature of non-hatred (*adveṣa*), like compassion (*karuṇā*).
It would not be established as having all sentient beings as its object;
the meaning is that it would not be established as having the sentient beings of the three realms as its object,
just as compassion does not have the sentient beings of the three realms as its object.
What then?
It has beings of the desire realm as its object.
The intention is that this would be established precisely because it has suffering beings as its object.
And it follows that [compassion] would not be established as having the aspect of the three types of suffering (*triduḥkhatā*), just as [ordinary] compassion is.

Just as ordinary compassion has only the aspect of suffering (*duḥkhatā*) and does not have the aspect of the three sufferings— the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*)— so too [this [compassion] would not be].
And it is accepted that its aspect is the three types of suffering;
therefore, its intrinsic nature is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Demonstrating the reason why it is designated by the term "great" (*mahat*), he says:
"Why is this? and so forth.
"Because of the equipment" means because of the full attainment of the great equipment of merit and gnosis;
that is, because of the full attainment of the great equipment of merit.
The meaning is: "because of the attainment of the equipment of great gnosis.
In that context, the equipment of great merit consists of three perfections:
the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience.
The accumulation of great gnosis (*mahājñānasaṃbhāra*) is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The perfections of vigor (*vīrya*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), however, function in two ways because they operate in both [accumulations].

For without vigor, generosity is not bestowed, ethical discipline is not undertaken, and patience is not cultivated; thus, vigor constitutes a portion of the accumulation of great merit (*mahāpuṇyasaṃbhāra*).
Likewise, since wisdom does not arise without vigor, it partakes in the great accumulation of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*).

Similarly, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) belonging to the category of cultivating the four immeasurables, such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), partakes in the great accumulation of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*).

Meditative concentration belonging to the category of cultivating the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*), such as the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), partakes in the great accumulation of knowledge.

Thus, because it arises from the two accumulations of great merit and wisdom and results in liberation, this compassion is "great," hence it is called *mahākaruṇā*. In terms of its aspect (*ākāra*), it takes on the three types of suffering;
for it perceives through all three forms of suffering, and not merely through the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) as ordinary compassion does.
By way of its object, it has as its object the sentient beings of the three realms;
for it takes as its object sentient beings born in the three realms, and not only those born in the desire realm as is the case with compassion (*karuṇā*).
However, sentient beings of the desire realm are its sphere of activity (*gocara*).
Because of this statement:
"By way of equality, because it functions equally toward all sentient beings.
For it functions equally toward all sentient beings included within the three realms by way of the aspect of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

For this reason also it is called "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*). This is because there is nothing more intense than it; that is, because it is sharper by virtue of having wisdom (*prajñā*) as its intrinsic nature.
For just as one feels compassion through that [compassion], one does not feel compassion in the same way through [ordinary] compassion;
this is the distinction, the specific difference.

"Because their intrinsic natures are non-hatred and non-delusion," means that, respectively, compassion has non-hatred as its intrinsic nature, and great compassion has non-delusion as its intrinsic nature.
"Because it has the aspect of one and three types of suffering":
because compassion has the aspect of one type of suffering,
and great compassion has the aspect of three types of suffering.
Thus, in both cases, [the principles] should be applied everywhere according to their respective order.
This is because [compassion and great compassion] belong to the levels of the four dhyānas and the fourth dhyāna respectively.
Compassion belongs to the level of the four dhyānas.
Because the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) are included by the mention of "the first dhyāna," it was stated that [compassion] belongs to six levels.

However, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) belongs exclusively to the level of the fourth dhyāna, because only that [level], through its flexibility for all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), is capable of producing it.
This is because it arises from the mental continua of Buddhas, whereas [ordinary compassion] arises from the continua of Śrāvakas and others.
By the word "etcetera," the Pratyekabuddhas and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are included.
Because it is obtained through detachment from the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) and the peak of existence (bhavāgra),
compassion is that which is obtained through detachment from the realm of desire.
Great compassion is obtained through detachment from the summit of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Regarding the phrase "by way of not protecting and protecting":
the meaning is that by means of ordinary compassion, Śrāvakas and others merely feel compassion themselves; they simply become weary with pity.
They do not protect [beings] from the fear of saṃsāra.
But the Blessed One, feeling compassion through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), protects them from the great fear of saṃsāra,
because he exercises incomparable compassion.
One feels compassion unequally through ordinary compassion (*karuṇā*),
because one feels compassion only for those who are suffering.
But one feels compassion equally through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), because one feels compassion for all sentient beings alike.

(VII.40) "By the complete attainment of the prior accumulations of merit and wisdom" means by the attainment [of the result] through the accumulation of merit in previous births and through the previously mentioned accumulation of wisdom.
"By the perfect accomplishment of the Dharma-body" means...
The *dharmakāya* is the continuum of the accumulation of untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*),
or it is the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*).
And [it is attained] through the practice for the benefit of others (*arthacaryā*).
Wealth is the cause of heaven and liberation for the world; the accomplishment of that wealth is the practice of benefiting others (*arthacaryā*).
For the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of all Buddhas, which is the cause for the welfare of others, is indeed equal.
"At the proper time" applies to every [instance].
How so?
According to whether the lifespan of beings is long or short at a given time, Buddhas appear with a long or short lifespan respectively.
Furthermore, in accordance with what is appropriate, they appear as kṣatriyas in a world that honors the kṣatriya caste.
The Brahmins are those who honor the Brahmins;
and at the proper time, they are those belonging to the Kāśyapa lineage and so forth,
as well as those belonging to the Gautama lineage and so forth.

Likewise, in a world of small dimensions, they are of small dimensions; in a world of non-small dimensions, they are of non-small dimensions. This refers to the perfection of causes, characterized by the accumulation of merit and knowledge.
The perfection of the fruit, characterized by the *dharmakāya*; the perfection of benefit, characterized by the conduct for the sake of the world;
and the cultivation of the accumulations of all qualities and primordial wisdoms.
The qualities have the five perfections as their intrinsic nature, and the various types of knowledge have the perfection of wisdom as their intrinsic nature;
the "provision" refers to the accumulation of those qualities and knowledges.
Its practice is repeated application.
Practice over a long period of time means for three incalculable great aeons (*mahākalpa*). Continuous practice means without interruption.
Practice with reverence means practicing with intense devotion.
Regarding the fourfold perfection of the fruit:
through the complete accomplishment of the *dharmakāya*, there arise the four perfections of knowledge and so forth; these too are established as the perfections of the fruit.
He will state that the perfection of knowledge is fourfold;
likewise, he will state that the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of power, and the perfection of the form-body are each fourfold.
That itself will be their explanation.
The perfection of the fourfold assistance. How so? It says:
the perfection of ultimate liberation from the suffering of the three miserable realms and of saṃsāra.
The three miserable destinies, beginning with the hells, and cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*);
the suffering of these two;
and the ultimate liberation from that [suffering].
"That very perfection" means the perfection of establishing [beings] in the three vehicles and the happy migrations; "in the three vehicles" refers to the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth.
And establishing them in a happy rebirth— this indeed is perfection; or rather, this is the perfection of the fourfold assistance.
"Uninstructed knowledge" is for the purpose of self-awakening;
"knowledge of all things" is for the purpose of awakening to the specific characteristics of all things without exception;
and "knowledge in every way."
In the sense of awakening to all modes [of existence];

"effortless knowledge" means in the sense of awakening through mere intention; "the abandonment of all afflictions" means the eradication of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation within the three realms; "absolute abandonment" means non-retrogression;
and "abandonment together with the latent tendencies."
Due to the absence of further connection [to afflictions].
"The abandonment of all obstacles to meditative attainments" refers to the one liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
"The perfection of mastery over the creation, transformation, and sustaining of external objects."
In this context, *nirmāṇa* (emanation) is the production of external objects that have not existed before.
*Pariṇāma* (transformation) is the bringing about of stones and such things into the state of gold and so forth.
*Adhiṣṭhāna* (sustaining) is the maintenance [of something] for a long duration.
The perfection of mastery over the relinquishing and the sustaining of life-span is called "the perfection of mastery over the relinquishing and the sustaining of life-span.
"Obstructed," and so forth,
refers to traveling through obstructions, traveling through space, and traveling very far with great speed.
The term "from a Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇāt*) is an *ekaśeṣa* compound [meaning "from one or many Brahmins"]. It is the inclusion of many within a small space;
that is, the inclusion of many things, such as elephants and so forth, within a single atom (*paramāṇu*).
"And that" refers to the ability to travel swiftly to very distant places through obstructed space, and the entry into small or large [spaces].
This should be construed as "the perfection of mastery over those two.
"Various" means of many kinds; "intrinsic" means natural.
What are the marvelous qualities?
They should be construed as "the perfection of those."
This is the natural law of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones: as they walk, the low ground becomes level and the high ground becomes low.
That which was low becomes high;
the blind regain their sight.
"The deaf [lack] hearing;
the insane [lack] mindfulness"—in this way, everything should be followed according to the sūtra.
"Perfection of characteristics" (lakṣaṇasaṃpad).
The perfection of the thirty-two marks of a great man, such as the *ūrṇā* (the hair-tuft between the eyebrows) and the *uṣṇīṣa* (the cranial protuberance).
"Perfection of the secondary characteristics" refers to the perfection of the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), such as rounded fingers and copper-colored, elevated nails.
The strength of Nārāyaṇa is endowed with power.
Because his bones have the essence of a diamond, they are "diamond-essence bones.
Because his body has bones with the essence of a diamond, he is "one whose body has diamond-essence bones."
Its state;
its perfection—
that is, the perfection of having a body with bones as hard as adamant.
This is the summary, the concise version.
Whatever noble persons, having conceived faith, have praised, do praise, or will praise the Buddha, the Blessed One,
they all do so by means of this very threefold perfection.
If his life were to last for many incalculable eons (*anekāsaṃkhyeyakalpa*),
and if the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were to sustain it accordingly,
then they would be capable of knowing and speaking of that entire extent of his greatness.
The intention is that this is because [the qualities] are exceedingly numerous due to having infinite distinctions.
And thus, "to such an extent" (*evaṃ ca tāvat*) is the detailed explanation.
The compound *guṇāś ca jñānāni ca prabhāvaś ca upakāraś ca* is a dvandva (copulative compound).
Furthermore, "infinite" and "wondrous" form a karmadhāraya compound.
These alone are the great jewels; the Tathāgatas are the mines of these jewels.

Moreover, foolish ordinary persons (bāla-pṛthagjana), their resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) and interest destroyed by the poverty of their own qualities— which serves as the basis for inference— do not even show respect to the Buddha, nor do they pay honor to the Buddha,
even by means of mere faith; that is to say, they do so without any realization.
"Of those with indeterminate fruition.
The intention is that this is because those with determinate fruition cannot be bypassed.
That which belongs to the gods is "divine," occurring among the gods.
"Because its fruit is unfailing, excellent, swift, and final.
It has an unfailing fruit because it exists with a certainty of yielding its result.
It has a desirable fruit because its fruit consists of divine objects.
It has an excellent fruit because its fruit is abundant;
it has a swift fruit because its fruit is to be experienced in the present life and so forth;
it has a final fruit because its ultimate fruit is nirvāṇa.
Because of that state, the Tathāgatas are called the unsurpassed field of merit. "Services" refers to beneficial acts such as worship and the like.
(VII.41) "According to what is appropriate" means according to what is possible.
Some qualities of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are shared with the Śrāvakas, such as *araṇā* (the absence of conflict), *praṇidhijñāna* (knowledge resulting from resolve), and so forth.
Some [attainments], such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), are shared with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and others are included.
(VII.42) No one’s passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), or pride (*māna*) arises with those as its object.
Therefore, by avoiding being seen and so forth by him,

and in whatever way he has realized it— having emerged from the concentration of non-affliction (*araṇā-samādhi*)— thinking, "Upon seeing me, passion will arise in this person, hatred in that one, pride in another,
or lack of faith in yet another," he remains attentive even after emerging from that concentration.

Regarding the specific method for protecting the minds of others, the meaning to be understood is that by the mere power of the arising of that concentration of non-affliction (*araṇā-samādhi*), afflictions do not arise in others.
"To cause conflict" (*raṇayati*) means "to cause affliction.
Furthermore, because the fourth dhyāna is the foremost among the paths of easy practice (*sukha-pratipad*), non-affliction belongs specifically to that level.
It does not belong to other dhyāna stages, because falling away is possible; that is, one is unable to avoid it. The afflictions have a real objective basis (*savastuka*).
Which are the afflictions such as attachment that are to be abandoned by cultivation?
Those afflictions that lack a real objective basis are to be abandoned by insight.
Because they are universal (*sarvatraga*) due to having their own entire level as an object, they also have the mental continua of others as objects;
thus, the universal [defilements] cannot be avoided.
(VII.43) However, that [state] has everything as its object.
Thus:
"it takes everything as its object" means it has everything as its objective support (*sarvālambana*);
or, "everything is its object" means it has everything as its objective support.
It does not have the afflictions alone as its object, as is the case with the araṇā;
rather, the meaning is that it also has form and so forth as its objects.
However, the formless realms (ārūpya) are not directly known by the knowledge resulting from resolve (praṇidhijñāna).
What is the reason?
Because the knowledge resulting from resolve belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
And he will say: "The supernormal knowledges have as their objects the spheres of one's own lower levels.
(Abhidh-k-vy 652)
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*) is like a supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
This is because of the distinction between its outflow (*niṣyanda*) and its mode of activity (*carita*).
In that regard, its outflow is extreme subtlety;
its conduct is dwelling in the formless attainments. Thus, it is inferred by means of its effects.
And by this, it is demonstrated that [the cause] belongs to the effect.
For those who have fallen away from that state and for those who have attained its meditative absorption, both of these are directly perceived.
Furthermore, the illustration of the farmer is given here.
Just as a farmer understands the seed by means of the fruit,
or the fruit by means of the seed;
or just as a farmer knows that in such a field there will be grain with such a kind of fruit.
Just as one, seeing grain, infers the field, thinking,
"His field is like this," so too, seeing a being of peaceful appearance, one infers: "This one has passed away from the formless realm."
"And one will be reborn in the formless realms"— this statement [of the Vaibhāṣikas] indicates that others possess knowledge of the formless realms by means of this [text].
The intention is that there is indeed nothing that is not within the range of the Buddhas.
"Preceded by a vow" means preceded by an application of the mind;
the meaning is: having made a vow and having applied the mind.
"To the extent that it is the object of that samādhi" means that he knows as much as is the domain of a śrāvaka.

"And for a pratyekabuddha, up to his own domain," and so forth. (VII.43–45) Regarding "the analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmapratisaṃvid*): here, "phenomena" refers to the Dharma as teaching.
For the word *dharma* has many meanings.

For example: "O monks, I shall teach you the Dharma; I shall proclaim the holy life (*brahmacarya*) that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its own meaning and its own phrasing, entirely complete, pure, and purified."
Herein, the Dharma of teaching is [indicated].
What is the Dharma?
It is the Noble Eightfold Path; herein, the Dharma of practice is [indicated].
Likewise, regarding the instruction "one should go for refuge to the Dharma," here the Dharma as result refers to *nirvāṇa* and so forth.
"Irreversible" means that it is impossible to turn back.
The phrase "the state of having an unshakable nature and a human basis" is connected to these same two meanings by the word "likewise" (*tathā*),
because the objects of focus (*ālambana*) and so forth have been mentioned separately.
This refers to the capacity for "speaking appropriately and eloquently."
"Appropriate" means connected with the meaning; "liberated" means unattached. One who speaks what is both appropriate and liberated is called "one who speaks appropriately and liberately."
The state of that. In that [state],
namely, in the state of being one who speaks appropriately and eloquently.

One who has mastery over concentration is "master of concentration. The clear manifestation and non-forgetfulness of one who is master of concentration is "the clear manifestation of the master of concentration."
In that regard, the distinction is that irreversible knowledge is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
How so?
The analytical knowledge of eloquence has nine knowledges as its intrinsic nature.
That [knowledge] which has speech as its object has the nature of the knowledge of suffering, origin, dharma, subsequent, destruction, non-arising, and conventional knowledge.
That which has the path as its object...

Summarized, it has the nature of nine knowledges—namely, the knowledge of the path, subsequent knowledge, the knowledge of destruction, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of others' minds, and conventional knowledge—excluding the knowledge of cessation.
If "all phenomena" (sarvadharma) is the meaning [of the term *dharmanirukti*], then there are ten knowledges;
for there is no phenomenon that does not exist [within them].
That which does not become an object of the ten knowledges as appropriate is [the ultimate] meaning, if that meaning is nirvāṇa; it is the six knowledges,
because the knowledge of cessation has the nature of the five [knowledges] beginning with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
"Because it has as its object the collection of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, and speech.
For untainted knowledge of suffering and so forth does not take a portion of suffering or a portion of origination as its object by way of the aspect of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇākāra*).
What then?
[They contemplate] the five aggregates of clinging by way of their general characteristics;
therefore, they have conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) as their intrinsic nature.
[The phrase] "because of the absence of the sets of names (*nāmakāya*) above" [is used].
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid).
And wherever there are sets of names (nāmakāya), there also are sets of phrases (padakāya) and sets of phonemes (vyañjanakāya); this is the same principle.
By the statement regarding the existence of the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), the non-existence of the collections of phrases and phonemes (*padavyañjanakāya*) is established.
"Because of the absence of applied thought (*vitarka*) above" refers to the second dhyāna and those beyond it.

The Sūtra states, "Having applied thought (*vitarkya*) and sustained thought (*vicārya*), one speaks words. This indicates that these analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) have names and so forth as their objects even for one who has entered meditative absorption (*samāpanna*). Furthermore, even for one who has emerged from absorption, they have names and so forth as their objects through the irreversible knowledges obtained subsequent to that state.
Moreover, the actual speaking occurs precisely by means of those subsequent knowledges.
"Designation such as 'woman,' 'man,' and so forth.
By the word "and so forth," there is an inclusion of time, grammatical factors (*kāraka*), and the like.
Furthermore, "designation" (*adhivacana*) is a synonym (*paryāya*).
Alternatively, "designation" (adhivacana) is the verbal expression referring to that [object]. "In its non-attachment" means:
in the non-attachment to that designation, or to those words and phonemes.
For this very reason, their sequence is established.
Since the comprehension of meaning follows the words and phonemes,
and since there is unimpededness regarding the designations for singular, dual, plural, feminine, masculine, and so forth, the sequence is established on that basis.

Therefore, [the definitions] such as "matter" (rūpa) and so forth; by the word "and so forth," [definitions] such as "it cognizes, thus it is consciousness" (vijñāna) and "it accumulates, thus it is mind" (citta) are included.

"Successive eloquence" refers to *pratibhāna* according to the *Vādanyāya*. "In due order" means that for the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), calculation is the preliminary practice (*pūrvaprayoga*).
The analytical knowledge of meaning is the word of the Buddha;
the analytical knowledge of expression is the science of grammar;
and the analytical knowledge of eloquence is the science of logic.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that it is indeed the word of the Buddha.
That [word] is of six kinds. (VII.46)
A portion of the fourth dhyāna consists of *araṇā*; a portion consists of *praṇidhijñāna*;
and a portion consists of the three *pratisaṃvid*s.
A certain [type] distinct from that is merely the "ultimate limit" (prāntakoṭika).
Regarding the "three analytical knowledges" (pratisaṃvid):
this excludes the analytical knowledge of language (niruktipratisaṃvid), because discursive thought (vitarka) is absent therein.
Its arousal occurs through [the state] accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
How then is this stated without qualification? "These six are the ultimate limits" (prāntakoṭika).
Thus it is said.
These are called the analytical knowledges of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). Their attainment is by means of that power, but they themselves do not belong to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
What then?
The meaning is that it belongs to the levels of the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
it is adapted to all levels.
Thus,
the meaning is "conducive to all stages. It is that for which the limit (koṭi) has gone beyond (pragata) its end.
*Prānta* means having reached the end (*anta*). That which has an extreme limit (*koṭi*) is *prāntakoṭika*.
It is like the "fourfold limit" (*catuṣkoṭika*).
Just as the fourfold alternative consists of a question of four types, so it is here.
(Abhidh-k-vy 654)
(VII.47–50) "The sphere of supernormal power," and so forth. There are six higher knowledges (*abhijñā*):

the higher knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the sphere of supernormal power; the higher knowledge of the realization of the divine ear; the higher knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the thoughts of others; the higher knowledge of the realization of the recollection of former abodes; the higher knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth; and the higher knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
And there is a sutra on this point:

"In this case, a monk experiences various kinds of supernormal powers (*ṛddhiviṣaya*). Having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one. The detailed text for this should be seen as written here under the heading of the "bases of supernormal power" (*ṛddhipāda*).
This is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the domain of miraculous powers.
Here, a monk, with the divine ear—purified and surpassing that of humans—hears both kinds of sounds, human and non-human, whether they are far or near.
This is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the divine ear.

"Here, a monk sees beings with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans"— this is a long passage as found in the Sūtras, up to where it says, "this is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the divine eye.
"Here, a monk recollects his manifold past abodes"— this is a long passage as found in the Sūtras.
This is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the cognition that recollects past lives.
Here, a monk understands, as it truly is, the thoughts and reflections, the mental and intellectual states, of other beings and other individuals.
He understands, as it truly is, a mind possessed by passion as "a mind possessed by passion."

He understands as it really is a mind free from passion as "a mind free from passion. He understands as it really is a mind with hatred as "with hatred," a mind free from hatred as "free from hatred," a mind with delusion as "with delusion," a mind free from delusion as "free from delusion," a distracted mind as "distracted," a concentrated mind as "concentrated," a sunken mind as "sunken," an uplifted mind as "uplifted," an agitated mind as "agitated," an unagitated mind as "unagitated," an unpacified mind as "unpacified," a pacified mind as "pacified," a composed mind as "composed," an uncomposed mind as "uncomposed," an uncultivated mind as "uncultivated," a cultivated mind as "cultivated," and an unliberated mind as "an unliberated mind. He understands this as it really is.
He understands, as it truly is, "the mind is liberated; the mind is liberated.
This is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the penetration of others' minds.
Here, a monk understands, as it truly is, "this is the noble truth of suffering."
"This is the origin of suffering;
this is the cessation of suffering;
this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—thus he understands it as it truly is.
For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire;
the mind is liberated from the influx of existence and the influx of ignorance.
For one who is liberated, the knowledge and vision arises: "I am liberated."

"Birth is exhausted for me; I shall not undergo further existence beyond this"—this is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).
Supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The domain of supernormal power (ṛddhiviṣaya) consists of emanation (nirmāṇa) and movement (gamana).
Knowledge regarding this domain of supernormal power is the realization (sākṣātkriyā), that is, its manifestation (saṃmukhībhāva).
The supernormal knowledge of the realization of the sphere of psychic power;
the divine ear; and the knowledge therein.
The realization of that is the realization of the knowledge of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-jñāna*).
"Succession of mind" (*cetaḥparyāya*) refers to its specific distinction;
that is, [knowing] it as "attached," "hating," or "deluded," or else [knowing] the sequence [of mental states].
Sometimes it is characterized by attachment, sometimes by aversion, and sometimes by delusion.
In that regard, there is knowledge;
its direct realization is [the goal].
Past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) are like the aggregates (*skandha*).
The recollection of them is the knowledge regarding them; the realization of that [knowledge] is its direct manifestation (*sākṣātkriyā*).
"Death and rebirth" refers to passing away (*cyuti*) and being born (*upapāda*). Knowledge of these two is the "knowledge of death and rebirth.
Its direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) is [the supernormal knowledge].
The destruction of the outflows;
therein lies knowledge;
the supernormal power of its realization—these terms are to be connected respectively.
"Like the fruit of asceticism (śrāmaṇyaphala).
Just as the conditioned fruit of asceticism has the nature of the path of liberation (vimuktimārga),
so too is this.
"Five knowledges regarding the mind" refers to the supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) that consists of the discernment of the mental states (cetaḥparyāya) of others.
The meaning is that it has the nature of the five knowledges (*jñāna*).

This is because uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*) can be a knowledge of others' minds that is either a dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), a subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), or a path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*), while contaminated knowledge of others' minds (*sāsrava-paracittajñāna*) can be either conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) or knowledge of others' minds.
"Just as the power" means, for example, the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*).
If it is argued that the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) has the destruction of the outflows as its object,

then there are six knowledges; for the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) is designated by the names of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Furthermore, because it is possible for conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) to have cessation (*nirodha*) as its object.

If it is argued that the knowledge which exists when the outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted is that knowledge [of exhaustion], because it occurs within the continuum of one whose outflows are exhausted; [we reply: no.
There are ten knowledges (*jñāna*).
Because all ten knowledges exist within the continuum of one whose outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted,
the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) that has the destruction of the outflows as its object is likewise [of this nature].
If it is the supernormal knowledge consisting in the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows,
there are six knowledges;
it is like that.
When there is the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya), whatever supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) exists— if that consists of the ten knowledges (jñāna)—
it is like that.
"Even this belongs to all stages"—
this meaning is obtained by that very statement, "just as power [belongs to all stages]."
And because it is determined that there are exactly five [factors] in each of the four dhyānas.
Therefore, it is understood from this sixth [statement] as well that these supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) belong to all stages (*sarvabhūmika*).
First of all, three do not exist:
namely, the supernormal knowledge of psychic power (*ṛddhi*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), and the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Why?
Because they have form as their object.
For the formless realms do not have form as their object.
"Because the perception of form has been transcended" means that it is accomplished by way of the gateway of form;
the meaning is that it is accomplished through the path that takes form as its object.
In such a form, the mind becomes such; yet, for those in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), form is not an object of perception.
Furthermore, there is no recollection of past lives (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛti*) [in the formless realms], because it is accomplished through the recollection of successive stages of existence.
This is because they accomplish it by recollecting the various successive states of their own selves.
Furthermore, phenomena belonging to the desire realm are not the objects of the formless [attainments]. For it will be said:
"The fundamental wholesome formless states do not have the lower contaminated realms as their sphere."
Thus,
because those other states of the self belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) serve as its object at the time of production, it does not belong to that level (*tadbhūmika*).
Furthermore, this is because [the mind] takes place, lineage, and so forth as its objects.
Having passed away from there as well, he was reborn there.
For it is said in the Sūtra:
"Those beings are named such-and-such."

"I was there, having such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a long life, such a duration of stay, and such a limit to my lifespan. Having passed away from there, I was reborn in another place; passing away from there as well, I was reborn in yet another; and passing away from there, I was reborn here"—thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.

Furthermore, because the formless realms do not have places, lineages, and so forth as their objects, nor do they have lower levels as their objects—for this reason as well, they do not belong to the level of the formless realm.
How is it that the knowledge of others' minds is accomplished by means of a "gateway of form" (*rūpatīrtha*)? To this he says:
"For one who desires to know another's mind," and so forth.
"Applying oneself" means performing an application of the mind.
"Having grasped the sign" means...
The meaning is: having discerned the mode of the mind.
"In reverse order" means that he brings to mind the other successive states of that very same mind as they have just ceased, proceeding in the opposite direction.
"Even skipping over [births], there is recollection.
Even skipping or bypassing one or two births, there is recollection.
How is there recollection of the Śuddhāvāsa deities?
If memory is only of what has been previously experienced,
then there is no coming here for those of the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) because they are non-returners (anāgāmin);
therefore, they have had no experience here.
Nor does it exist there,
because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are not born there;
for [the knowledge] has been experienced through hearing.
For he has heard that the gods called Śuddhāvāsas are of such a nature.
Indeed, experience is twofold: the experience of seeing and the experience of hearing.
"Arising by means of taking another's continuum as its basis" refers to the knowledge of recollecting former abodes (pūrvenivāsānusmṛtijñāna) comprised within the meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
And by that [knowledge], one does not grasp a mind belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara).
And how, moreover, is there production by means of taking hold of another’s continuum?
It is by grasping the signs from the mental consciousness of another that has just ceased, and so forth.
[This refers to] "of others."

Those who have not fallen away from the formless realms (ārūpya) produce [the knowledge] solely by means of their own mental continuum, because the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pūrvenivāsānusmṛtijñāna) is easy for them to accomplish. This refers to the supernormal powers (ṛddhi) and so forth.

Regarding the three supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) of miraculous power (ṛddhi), the divine ear (divyaśrotra), and the divine eye (divyacakṣus), their respective preliminary applications are as follows: for miraculous power, the mental application of lightness;
for the divine ear, the mental application of sound;
and for the divine eye, the mental application of light.

The question "How are these obtained? concerns their acquisition (*prāpti*). However, as for their manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāva*), both those that are familiar (*ucita*) and those that are unfamiliar (*anucita*) occur solely through application (*prayoga*). Regarding the phrase "the unfamiliar through application": [this refers to those not previously cultivated].
Those which are specific and have not been produced previously are all produced through application;
and those which are obtained through detachment.
And regarding those [transformations] that occur through application:
of all of them,
with the exception of sound— because it is discontinuous, sound is not created [by transformation].
For it will be stated:
"The external emanation belonging to the desire realm consists of four sense-bases."
(Abhidh-k-vy 657) "How then? and so forth.

If the supernormal power of the divine eye (*cakṣur-abhijñā*) has the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) as its object, how then [can one say] by means of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyuty-upapāda-jñāna*]: "Alas, these venerable beings are possessed of misconduct of body," and so on?
The possession of vocal and mental karma is not apprehended by visual consciousness.
By the word "etcetera," wrong view is included.
It is not that [possession].
One does not know that [object], such as the possession of vocal and mental karma, by means of that visual cognition.
By what, then, does one know it? He says: "But that is the knowledge which is the retinue of the supernormal power (abhijñā)."
The meaning is that it is mental.
Regarding "the remaining":
the supernormal knowledge of recollecting former abodes and the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows have the four foundations of mindfulness as their intrinsic nature.
How so?

The supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) has the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as its intrinsic nature because it consists of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*).
Even though it consists of six knowledges, the future applications of mindfulness regarding the body, feelings, and mind are also cultivated.
How, then, are those two established as belonging to the levels of the four dhyānas?
For there exists no visual cognition or auditory cognition belonging to the levels of the second dhyāna and above,
because they are associated with visual and auditory consciousness.
And because those two do not exist in the second and subsequent dhyānas; for he will say:
"The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses, as well as that which originates informative action (*vijñapti*)."
"In the second [moment] and so forth, that is attained by the first," means "by virtue of the basis," and so forth.
By virtue of the basis of the eye and the ear, the two cognitions [visual and auditory] also belong to the levels of the four dhyānas.
Thus, the eye and the ear are established as belonging to the levels of the four dhyānas.
This teaching is either based on what is predominant or on what is most frequent.
That which exists in the primary [state] is "primary" (*prādhānika*).
Likewise for "abundant" (*bāhulika*).
The wholesome superknowledges (*abhijñā*) are of primary importance.
Therefore, with reference to that,
the designation "wholesome supernormal knowledge" (*kuśalā prajñābhijñā*) is made.
Alternatively, supernormal knowledges are for the most part wholesome.
Therefore, the designation is as follows:
it is like the designation "a heap of beans" even when mung beans and other grains are present [within it].
This is because [the designation] excludes [all others] from the beginning of the prior limit and so forth. (VII.51)
Up to this point, as follows in order:
Bhagavadviśeṣa and the others say that one dispels delusion regarding the past limit by means of the recollection of former abodes.

By means of the supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth, one eliminates delusion regarding the intermediate state; by means of the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, one eliminates delusion regarding the future limit,
thinking, "I know that there is no further existence beyond this."
This is the intention of those commentators:
the sequence of the time-periods (adhvan) is past, present, and future;
therefore, the understanding of the meaning is as follows.
But the Master Saṃghabhadra explains:
"Because it turns back [the mind] from the prior limit and so forth.
For the supernormal knowledge of former abodes (pūrvenivāsābhijñā) dispels delusion regarding the prior limit."

The supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādābhijñā*) removes delusion regarding the future limit; the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) removes delusion regarding the middle [present].

For this reason, only these three possess the nature of true knowledge (*vidyā*), because spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) arises from seeing the misfortunes of oneself and others through the former two.
The third [verse] refers to others who are likewise agitated, because they have understood the reality of things as they truly are. What is to be understood here?
(Abhidh-k-vy 658) We consider the explanation of the Master Saṃghabhadra alone to be the most appropriate.
The intention of the Master [Vasubandhu] also appears to be exactly the same.
For, having stated that there are three realizations—namely, the realization of the knowledge of former abodes, of death and rebirth, and of the destruction of the outflows—he said:
For these [three knowledges] dispel delusion regarding the past, the future, and the middle [present], respectively.
But how is it known that there are exactly three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and three sciences (*vidyā*)?
Because it has been stated thus.

The realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives belonging to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is a clear knowledge (*vidyā*); the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth belonging to one beyond training is a clear knowledge; and the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) belonging to one beyond training is a clear knowledge. This is because the establishment of the three clear knowledges is based precisely on the Sūtra.
For it is said thus:
"One who possesses the Tripiṭaka is one who possesses the three knowledges (trividyā).
This refers to the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣī vidyā).
The intention is that this is because they are untainted (*anāsrava*).

The supernormal knowledges of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsa*) and of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda*) are neither of those belonging to the learner (*śaikṣa*) nor of those belonging to the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), because they are tainted (*sāsrava*).
(VII.52) The three miracles (*prātihārya*) are, respectively, as follows.
The supernormal knowledge of the domain of psychic power is the miracle of psychic power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*).
The supernormal knowledge of the diversity of minds is the miracle of mind-reading (*ādeśanāprātihārya*), [expressed as]:
"Such is your mind."
The supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) is the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanaprātihārya*).
This means teaching according to reality (*yathābhūta*).
This is because the two prefixes *pra-* and *ati* carry the senses of "initial action" and "intensity," respectively.
The prefix *pra-* has the sense of "commencement of an action," as in "this action has been begun by him.
And the prefix *ati-* has the sense of "intensity," as in "he has gone beyond."
This is what is meant:

they are called "miracles" (prātihārya) because by means of them they captivate the minds of those to be converted (*vineya*) most intensely from the very beginning. [The phrase] "of those who are hostile or indifferent" refers to those whose minds are either obstructed or neutral.

This is stated by relying on the method of etymological interpretation (*nairukta*); it should be applied according to the rule: "the addition of a phoneme (*varṇāgama*) and the transposition of a phoneme (*varṇaviparyaya*)," because [this etymology] is unerring.
Thus [it is said].
"Because it is immediately followed by the destruction of the afflictions" (VII.53, 54).
"It succeeds" means:
The meaning is that it is accomplished.
"By means of the resolve toward what is near regarding what is distant" means:
that which is produced by resolve is "resolute" (*ādhimokṣikī*).
That which is distant, one resolves upon as being near; because of arriving there quickly through that resolution, it is called "resolute" (*ādhimokṣikī*).
It consists of the four external sense bases.
Thus, nothing internal is created; for if such an internal creation were to occur, it would entail the absurd consequence of the manifestation of a previously non-existent sentient being.
"Connected with one's own or another's body" means:
that which one's own self acts as a lion or acts as an elephant is connected with one's own body.
That which is emanated externally from oneself, such as a lion or an elephant, is connected with another's body.
It is likewise twofold in that same manner.
Connected with one's own or another's body.
Thus it is in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Just as one born in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) creates two kinds of emanations (*nirmāṇa*).
It belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
Each of these is again twofold—connected with one's own body or another's body—thus making four types.
In this way, one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) also creates four kinds of emanations.
In brief, emanation (*nirmāṇa*) is of eight kinds.
It is not a possession (*samanvāgama*), like clothing or ornaments.

For example, although clothing and ornaments are connected to one's own body, there is no possession [of them] because they are not reckoned as sentient beings, or because they are not connected to the bases of the sense faculties (*indriyādhiṣṭhāna*).
In the same way,
"two bases" refers to the base of visible forms and the base of tangible objects.
There is no sense-sphere of odor or taste;
the intention is that these are absent because of the lack of possession (*samanvāgama*).
There is no sense-sphere of sound because it has been cut off.
Others say it is because it is produced by an external impact; the intended meaning is that it is adventitious.
(VII.55–58) The fruit of the second dhyāna consists of three [types of sensation].
And two belonging to a lower stage, as well as one belonging to its own stage—
thus four or five are to be applied.
There are four belonging to the stage of the third dhyāna.
[The fruits] of the lower stages consist of three [knowledges] belonging to those lower stages and one belonging to its own stage.
The fruits of the fourth dhyāna and so forth consist of five belonging to the lower stages, four belonging to their own stages, and one belonging to its own stage; such is the detailed explanation.
The emanation that is the fruit of the second dhyāna, which is created by an emanator,
is superior in terms of range to the emanation-fruit belonging to the level of the first dhyāna— that is, to the fruit of the first dhyāna.
That emanation which is the fruit of the second dhyāna reaches the level of the second dhyāna.
However, that which is the fruit of the first dhyāna does not go there; rather, it goes only to the level of the first dhyāna itself. Thus, it is distinguished by the distinction of its destination.
In this way, the fruit of the third dhyāna and so forth should be applied accordingly.
"Acquisition is like that of the dhyānas" means that, as with the fundamental dhyānas, the acquisition of the emanation-minds occurs through the attainment of detachment (*vairāgya*).

At the moment of the manifestation of the mind of emanation, that which is initial arises from the pure [dhyāna].

"From the transformation-mind also, the pure [meditation]" means that upon emerging from the transformation-mind, there is the transformation-mind itself in the flow.

"Abiding in the fruit of concentration" means abiding in a mind that is a transformation produced by concentration (*samādhi-nirmāṇacitta*). "But belonging to a higher stage" means belonging to the stages of the second dhyāna and above.
It is spoken by means of that which belongs to the level of the first dhyāna.
This is because, in the higher stages—the second dhyāna and so forth—there is an absence of the mind characterized by vitarka and vicāra that originates informative action (vijñapti).

"Because, having empowered it, one proceeds otherwise.
Having created an emanation by means of the mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*), one then empowers it with the desire for it to remain, thinking, "Let this endure."

For the continuum follows the prior intention;
for previously he established in his mind: "I shall create an emanation, I shall sustain it, and I shall cause it to speak."
Because the possibility of an empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) exists in two states, he asks:
"Is the empowerment [possible] only while one is alive? and so forth.

The meaning is: "by means of the resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) of the noble Mahākāśyapa. As for the phrase "the threefold [mind] born of rebirth": it refers to that which arises from birth.
For sometimes gods and others create other beings for the sake of benefiting them,

And the emanation (nirmāṇa) created by gods and others, which pertains to oneself and others, consists of nine bases (navāyatana).

Because it lacks the base of sound and possesses the base of form (rūpāyatana).
Because non-sound [factors] such as the sense-base of the eye and the sense-base of visible form exist therein;

How is it known that a created being (nirmita) is without mind? From the treatise (śāstra).
For it says thus:
Should that which is emanated by him be said to consist of the four great elements, or should it be said not to consist of the four great elements?

It should be said that it possesses derived matter, not that it does not possess derived matter.
He said:
It should be said that it possesses derived matter.

He replied:
"It exists by the power of the creator's mind.
If, then, a [body] consisting of nine sense bases (*navāyatanika*) is created,

Since the sense faculties are reckoned as belonging to sentient beings,
he therefore says:
"Because they are inseparable from the sense faculties."

Because a transformation (nirmāṇa) connected to one’s own or another’s body, consisting of visible form, taste, and tangible objects, exists inseparably from the five sense-faculties such as the eye, it is said to consist of nine bases (navāyatanika).
However, it is the established tenet that a sense-faculty itself is not created [by transformation].
Furthermore, when one creates that very same [body] as connected with both one's own and another's body, it consists of only four bases (*āyatana*).
This refers, for example, to [the bodies of] Māndhātṛ and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
This is stated as an illustration of supernatural power born of karma (*karmajā ṛddhi*).
(VII.59) "Are these truly divine?"— the intention here is to ask whether this word "divine" (*divya*) is used in its primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*), or rather in a figurative sense (*aupacārika*).

"Just as in the case of the Bodhisattva, the Wheel-turning King, and the Householder-treasure.

is also acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilabdha*).
For whom is the divine eye acquired at birth?

not for those of the formless realm.

Because there is no distinction between one's own and another's mental continuum,

This is because such a personal existence (ātmabhāva) has not been acquired, as is the case with beings belonging to the realms of desire and form.
Alternatively, none of the superknowledges (abhijñā) exist [there],
because such a physical basis (ātmabhāva) has not been fully realized, as is the case with beings belonging to the desire and form realms.
It is not as if they were exclusively wholesome, like the fruit of meditative cultivation (bhāvanāphala).

"Those situated in other realms always know.
By means of those two—the knowledge of others' minds and the recollection of past lives—those situated in the realms of the gods and so forth always know.
Because it is not afflicted by painful sensations.
For humans, it is not acquired through birth.

Among humans, these aforementioned qualities—such as supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and so forth—exist as those acquired through detachment (*vairāgya-lābhika*), or those produced by reasoning, spells, herbs, or ritual action (*tarka-vidyauṣadha-karma-kṛta*).
However, they do not exist as those acquired through birth (*upapatti-lābhika*).
As for the statement that some are "naturally remembering their former births" (*prakṛti-jātismara*): [this refers to those cases].

The state of being naturally born with the memory of former births (*jātismara*) occurs through the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), and that [recollection] exists at the moment of rebirth.
How so?
The intention is that this [memory] is not something acquired merely by birth (*utpattilābhika*).
He said:
"This [power] of theirs arises from a specific karma.
It is produced by a specific karma of those bodhisattvas.
That which is called "acquired at birth" (upapattilābhika) is that which is obtained naturally by all at the very moment of birth, and not that which belongs only to some after the time of birth,
such as the flight through the air of birds.
Therefore, this [distinction] among them arises from a specific difference in karma.
To explain how this is so, he says: "For it is threefold," and so forth.
The fruit of cultivation is as previously described.
That which is obtained by birth belongs to gods and others;
that which is born of karma belongs to those bodhisattvas.

VIII (The Eighth Chapter of the Treasury, titled "Exposition of the Attainments") (VIII.1, 2).
Showing the connection in introducing the eighth chapter immediately after the seventh, he says:
"By way of the section on knowledge," and so forth.

By way of the section on knowledge—that is, by way of the ten types of knowledge—a description has been made of those things consisting of knowledge and having the nature of knowledge, such as the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) and the superknowledges (*abhijñā*). However, a description must now be given for those of a different nature, such as meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and so forth.
Because they are the basis of all qualities, it is certainly true that even the formless realms (*ārūpya*) serve as a basis for qualities.
They are not the basis for all qualities;
however, the meditative absorptions (dhyānas) are the basis for all qualities.
Thus, the meditative absorptions are of two kinds.
The meaning is that these are meditations on effects and meditations on causes.
"Pure one-pointedness" means:
The one-pointedness of virtuous states of mind.
"Without distinction" means that this applies to all characteristics as well.
Therefore, he states this definition:
"Because they have meditative concentration as their intrinsic nature. The phrase "of the dhyānas" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Alternatively, "without distinction" refers to the inclusion of meditative concentration alone; however, "with distinction," it consists of the five aggregates along with their attendants.
Thus [ends the discussion of] the aggregate of non-informative form.
"Having a single object" means that the minds have the quality of having a single object.

Furthermore, what is the reason that, although mental factors (*caitta*) also have a single object (*ekālambana*), it is said that "minds (*citta*) have a single object," rather than saying "mind and mental factors have a single object"? It is because of their predominance (*prādhānya*); thus, it is the minds themselves that have a single object, which is called concentration (*samādhi*).
Because it is a particular state [of mind], like a variegated teacher.
The Vaibhāṣika says:
"The concentrations are not the minds themselves."
That dharma by which those [mental states] proceed one-pointedly and are concentrated is concentration (*samādhi*).
It is just as, according to the Vaiśeṣika system, a cloth is called "white" because of its connection with the quality of whiteness.
That very quality of this [mind] is called its "whiteness" (*śauklya*).
It is like that.
But is it not the case that, because of momentariness, every state of mind is one-pointed?
Why is it said that "the factor by which those [mental states] proceed one-pointedly is concentration"?
If you argue that for the second [moment], it is because of that [first moment] there is no distraction; [we reply: no.

If this were the case—that for the second moment of mind there is non-distraction from that concentration—[the question would be] "in which object? [and the answer would be] "there is no distraction in this object. In that case, since it would be associated [with the object], concentration would be redundant.
Regarding that first moment of mind associated with concentration:
if it were already associated [with concentration], then concentration would be useless.
This is because, on that basis, concentration would not perform its function in that [first] moment, but would perform it in the second.

Furthermore, for the very same reason that concentration (samādhi) is intended to have the characteristic of one-pointedness, why is it not accepted that thoughts themselves possess a single object? The intention is: what is the use of a concentration that exists as a separate entity?
No,
because concentration is weak.
It does not follow that every state of mind would possess one-pointedness simply because concentration exists as a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*).
That mind which is associated with weak concentration does not become one-pointed; however,
that which is associated with strong [concentration] does.
"That mind is one-pointed.
Even though concentration (*samādhi*) is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*), it does not follow that all minds would necessarily be one-pointed.
"The minds themselves," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Concentration is simply the one-pointedness of minds; it is not a separate entity.
For it is said, "the training in higher mind.
What is the training in higher mind?
"All" refers to the four dhyānas.
Thus, it has been stated that the four dhyānas alone are primarily characterized by the purification of the mind.
This sūtra was written in this regard: "The bases of psychic power are concentrations."
For just as the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) is ethical discipline itself and not something other than it,
so too the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) is wisdom itself.
There is nothing other than that [mind] for it.
Likewise, the training in higher mind is the mind itself; there is nothing other than that [mind].
The meaning is that there is no meditative concentration (samādhi) apart from the mind.
For training in higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā) is held to be meditative concentration.
And as it is said in this very sutra: "the preeminence of the purity of ethical discipline" and "the preeminence of the purity of liberation."
Purity of ethical discipline is not other than ethical discipline itself;
likewise, purity of view and purity of liberation are not other than the view and liberation themselves.
In the same way, purity of mind is also not other than the mind itself.
For the purification of the mind is indeed the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) characterized by the four dhyānas.
"In that case, then" means:
if the dhyānas have meditative concentration as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would follow that all forms of concentration are dhyānas.
There would also follow the consequence that wholesome, afflicted, and neutral concentrations are [also] dhyānas,
because concentration is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*).
This is not so.
"Endowed with excellence," and so forth. This is not so; for the name "dhyāna" is applied to a concentration endowed with excellence, just as in the case of the sun.
For example, only that which produces light to the highest degree is called the "light-maker" (bhāskara),
not a firefly or similar objects.
It is like that.
"For he," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

For that concentration (samādhi) endowed with the factors is called "carrying in yoke" (*yuganaddhavāhī*), because it proceeds like a chariot drawn by two horses yoked together—namely, calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).

Because of that state, it is said in the Sūtra that there is "dwelling in happiness in the present life" and that this is "the pleasant path. It is precisely the meditative concentration (samādhi) endowed with its constituent factors [that constitutes these].
And the phrase "it is said to be a pleasant practice" continues [from the previous context].
Because it is pleasant, they meditate all the more by means of it.
[Objection: How can there be the state of being a dhyāna for that which is afflicted?

If meditative concentration (*samādhi*) associated with the factors of wholesomeness is *dhyāna*, then how can that which is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*)—specifically, that which is not associated with relish (*āsvādana*)—be consistent with being *dhyāna*? This is the completion of the sentence. *Dhyāna* is of three kinds.
Because of the statement that [the dhyāna] is associated with relishing (*āsvādanā*), pure (*śuddhaka*), or untainted (*anāsrava*).
"Due to false contemplation" (*mithyopanidhyānāt*) means:
The meaning is "due to false deliberation.
Regarding the "over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*):
there would be the consequence that even a mind obsessed by sensual desire (*kāmarāga-paryavasthita*) [would constitute wrong view], because it too involves false contemplation.
No;
"it is only similar to that," and so forth.
This is not so, because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

For the designation "defiled meditation" (kliṣṭa-dhyāna) is applied only to that which is similar [to pure meditation], not to that which is excessively different from it, just like a rotten seed. For example,
something that is not a seed, such as a stone, which is utterly distinct from the class to which seeds belong, is not called a "rotten seed."

It is that very same kind of seed which has become impaired;
it is precisely with respect to that that the designation "rotten seed" is applied.
And it has been stated that there are also unwholesome meditative absorptions (*akuśala-dhyāna*).
"Overcome by sensual desire, having made the obsession of sensual desire an interval, he meditates, he intensely meditates," and so forth.

"Like smoke and fire.
Just as when one says, "There is smoke here," fire is also implied by the mention of smoke due to their constant association;
for smoke does not exist without fire.
And it is precisely because of this inseparable connection that smoke is considered more important;
for wherever there is smoke, there is fire.
But it is not the case that wherever there is fire,
there is smoke;
for in the case of iron balls, charcoal, and the like, only fire is perceived.
It is not smoke.
Furthermore, because it is more venerable, smoke is placed first, as in the case of Vāsudeva and Arjuna.
