Otherwise, even in a *dvandva* compound, the word "fire" (*agni*) would have been placed first according to the rule "in a *dvandva* [the term denoting the more venerable comes first]."
How, moreover, is it that by way of concomitance, investigation (vicāra) accompanied by joy and bliss does not exist without initial thought (vitarka)?
Just as the investigation of the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara) is not accompanied by joy and bliss, and is thus without vitarka.
This investigation is not [general] in this way; for this investigation is qualified,
being recited together with joy and bliss.
"Endowed with investigation, joy,
and bliss" means that the first dhyāna is associated with investigation, as well as with joy and bliss.
If, on the other hand, the Sūtra were composed as "possessing applied thought, joy, and bliss," what fault would there be?
It is simply not possible to do so,
because [the factors] are excluded one by one from the preceding ones.
Thus he will say:
"The second dhyāna is devoid of applied thought (vitarka). In that case, the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara) would also result in being the second dhyāna.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the exposition of the first dhyāna, four factors were stated by him in this sequence.
"Having attained and dwelling in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, and characterized by the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
In that context, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and samādhi exist in the first dhyāna.
Together with vitarka, which is mentioned first of all, it is said to have five factors (pañcāṅga) by means of these four factors.
The second, moreover, is described as follows:
"Having attained and dwelling in the second dhyāna, which is without vitarka and without vicāra, born of concentration, and characterized by joy and bliss.
Among these four [dhyānas], it is devoid of the preceding member, namely the characteristic of vicāra.
The third [dhyāna] is also described in this way:
"Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity," and so on in detail, up to "dwelling in happiness.
Thus, having attained the third dhyāna, he dwells therein.
It is devoid of another limb characterized by joy (*prīti*).
Furthermore, the fourth [dhyāna] is described as follows:

"Through the abandoning of pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth in detail, until: he dwells, having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddha*)."
Since even the factor of pleasure is absent and only concentration remains here alone, for this very reason the Sūtra states that it is "possessed of investigation, joy, and pleasure."
(VIII.2–4) And their rebirths have also been explained, because of the statement: "The formless realm is without location; it is fourfold by way of rebirth."
"Because of the absence of concomitant form" means because of the absence of the meditative (dhyāna) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) restraints;
[this refers to] seclusion (viveka).
Thus it is said.
"Viveka" (discernment) is that by which one discerns;
[it refers to] the path by which [one discerns].
Whether by means of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) or even by the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), because they share the same function.
"By way of proceeding toward detachment" (*vairāgyagamanāt*) means by way of proceeding toward turning away from that [defilement].
Regarding the phrase "those called having overcome the perception of form":
one for whom the perception of form has been overcome is "one who has overcome the perception of form."

"Those whose designation is 'having transcended the perception of form' are called *vibhūtarūpasaṃjñākhyāḥ*. First, this [point] is to be established," [referring to] those belonging to other schools (*nikāyāntarīyāḥ*).
The Vaibhāṣikas say: "If it were so, it would indeed be so.
Regarding the term *āpiṅgala*: just as one who is slightly tawny is called *āpiṅgala*.
Thus, the formless [realms] possess only slight form.
How, in the absence of that [form], could there be the restraints of body and speech belonging to those [realms]?

Furthermore, in the absence of a primary element (bhūta) belonging to the formless realm, it is not logical for there to be a derivative material form (samvarabhautika) belonging to the formless realm.
If it is argued that it is like the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*),
then this might be the case:
just as there are no untainted primary elements (*anāsrava-bhūta*).
Furthermore, there exists untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) which is derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).
Likewise, in this case as well, there would not be any primary elements (*bhūta*) belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
Alternatively, there might be a formless-realm restraint that is derived matter.
And that is not so;
because there exist contaminated primary elements (sāsrava-bhūta), there are indeed contaminated primary elements,
and these would exist in the formless realms (ārūpya).

However, untainted (anāsrava) primary elements do not exist. Therefore, it should not be imagined that the untainted restraint arises by depending upon the tainted (sāsrava) [elements] belonging to the place where it is produced, because they are not equivalent.
The negation of form in meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) has also been stated.
By this very negation of form in the state of rebirth, the negation of form in meditative attainment is likewise stated;
no further effort need be exerted here.
How so?
If it were merely the restraint of body and speech,
how could there be restraint of those [actions] in the absence of [the underlying] things?
And it is not logical for there to be a derivative element when the primary element is absent.
If it is argued that this is like the case of the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*),
we say no.
"Because of the existence of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) primary elements (*bhūta*).
This is because of the statement, "by completely transcending perceptions of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*).
Others say that the negation of those [elements] is also stated in regard to the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Thus, it has been shown that there is no form (rūpa) in the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) nor in the formless rebirths (ārūpyopapatti).
If it is argued that this is because [form] is extremely minute (parimāṇālpatva), then [the response is as follows]:
"There exists form (rūpa) no larger than an atom;
therefore, they are held to be 'slightly formed' (īṣadrūpa).
This implies that even among aquatic organisms, because they are minute and their forms are invisible, the same consequence would follow—that is to say, the consequence of being "formless" (ārūpya).
If it is argued that they are called "formless" (ārūpya) because of the transparency of form,
then this would also apply to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and to those belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
For those belonging to the intermediate state and the form realm (rūpāvacara) move without obstruction even through mountains made of diamond because of their transparency;

thus, it would follow that they belong to the formless realm (ārūpya). This is not so, because there is a distinction between their birth and meditative attainment (samāpatti), just as in the case of the attainments themselves.
For just as the attainments of the sphere of infinite space and so forth are most distinguished,
so too must their distinction in rebirth be accepted as being increasingly more transparent.
Therefore, just like the attainments, the distinction in rebirth is also increasingly more transparent.
That alone would be formless (*ārūpya*).
And if the form of rebirth in the formless realm is called "formless" because it is not perceived by the sense-faculties of a lower level due to its extreme subtlety,
then the same would apply to the form of rebirth in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and so forth.
This is the possibility: even for that which has the form of arising through meditative absorption (*dhyāna-upapatti*), there is no perception by means of a faculty belonging to a lower stage.
How so?
There is no perception of what belongs to the second stage by means of a faculty belonging to the first stage of meditation.
In this way, up to the point that form belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna is not perceived by a faculty belonging to the level of the third dhyāna,
because that which belongs to a higher level is more transparent.
Thus, since the form of rebirth in a dhyāna is not perceived by a faculty of a lower level, what distinction is there in that case?

In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), because they are even more transparent than those [in the form realm], although they are similar, only those are accepted as being "formless" (ārūpya) and not those belonging to the form realm (rūpāvacara).
Therefore, there is no form (rūpa) there.
Now, it might be thought that the designations of the two realms are according to their literal meaning (anvartha).
The desire realm is characterized by the qualities of sensual pleasure;
the form realm is characterized by form.
However, the designation for the formless realm is not based on its literal meaning.
What then? It is arbitrary.
What is the reasoning here?
The designations for the two realms are according to their literal meaning.
"Not in the formless realm" (nārūpyadhātāv iti).
Having refuted [the existence of matter] through reasoning, [the author] now wards off any lingering doubt by relying on scripture (āgama) that there is no matter in the formless realm.
To establish the presence of matter there, he provides the detailed explanation beginning with "vitality and heat" (āyur-uṣmaṇoḥ).
If it is argued that "the existence of form (*rūpa*) in the formless realms (*ārūpya*) is established," this phrase should be applied to each [of the following points].
How so? If it is argued that the existence of form is established because of the statement that life-force (*āyus*) and heat (*ūṣman*) are conjoined (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).
In this regard, it might be argued that it is stated in the Sūtra:
"Venerable Kauṣṭhila, that which is vitality and that which is heat—these two dharmas are conjoined;
they are not disjoined," and so forth.
Therefore, since life-force exists there, heat must also exist;
and thus it is established that heat is form (*rūpa*).
This is because name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are said to be mutually dependent, like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
If it is argued that the existence of form in the formless realms is established [by scripture],
it is stated in a Sūtra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, it is as if two bundles of reeds were standing upright in the air."
These two, being mutually dependent, would remain standing by relying upon one another.
If someone were to remove one of them,
the second would fall.
If one were to remove the second, the one would fall. In this way, Venerable Śāriputra, name and form are mutually dependent.

"If it is argued that the existence of form (*rūpa*) in the formless realms (*ārūpya*) is established because [the sūtra] states in detail that they 'stand supported by one another,' based on the statement that 'name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) has consciousness as its condition' (*vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam*)."

It is stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*: "At the moment of the establishment of the formless [attainments], there is name-and-form conditioned by consciousness. From this statement, it is established that there is form (*rūpa*) within the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
The phrase "other than form," and so forth, follows.
It is said in the Sūtra:
"O monks, consciousness abides by approaching form;
thus it has form as its object and is established upon form."
"Monks, if anyone were to say:
'Apart from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, I declare the coming or going [of a self],' that would be merely a matter of words for him."
If it is argued that form exists in the formless realms (ārūpya) on the basis of this scripture as well,
that is not so, because it must be further examined.
Or rather, "all"?
That which belongs to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
This is the intended meaning here.
This was said with reference specifically to the lifespan of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
For it has been said:
"When these—vitality (*āyus*), heat (*ūṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—abandon the body..."
"Then, cast aside, it lies like a piece of wood, devoid of consciousness.
Furthermore, there is no body in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
How much less, then, could there be the destruction of the body?
For although the body exists in the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
the destruction of the body is not perceived there.
Furthermore, as for that which was stated regarding the mutual dependence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),
it appears to have been said with reference only to those belonging to the realms of desire and form (*kāmarūpāvacara*).
For mutual dependence is possible only when both [name and form] are present.
Regarding the statement, "name-and-form has consciousness as its condition" (*vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam*):
in this genitive *bahuvrīhi* compound, "name-and-form has consciousness as its condition" means that consciousness is its condition.

Here, does every kind of consciousness—from that conditioned by formations belonging to the desire realm up to that conditioned by formations belonging to the formless realm—serve as the condition for name-and-form?
Or rather, is it that all name-and-form (nāmarūpa) has consciousness as its condition?

We say that name-and-form has consciousness as its condition; thus, it is determined that consciousness is the condition for all name-and-form, but it is not determined that all consciousness is the condition for name-and-form.
Some consciousness is the condition for name alone, namely that which has the formations belonging to the formless realm as its condition;
some is the condition for name-and-form, namely that which has the formations belonging to the desire and form realms as its condition.
This is what is meant.
Consciousness is indeed the condition for this name-and-form;
however, it is not the condition for this name-and-form once it has already arisen as a whole.
This is stated with reference to its origination.
For in the case of those born by spontaneous generation (*upapāduka*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise directly with consciousness as their condition;
there is no "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). Indeed, the five aggregates in the state where the six sense bases have not yet been fully formed are designated as "name-and-form.
And the Sūtra illuminates this very point.

"Ānanda, if consciousness were not to descend into the mother’s womb, would that name-and-form coagulate into the state of an embryo (kalala)?— No, Venerable Sir. Ānanda, if consciousness, having descended, were to depart immediately, would that name-and-form be made known as suchness?"— No, Venerable Sir.
"No, Venerable Sir.
Ānanda, if the consciousness of a young boy or a young girl were to be cut off, destroyed, and cease to exist, would that name-and-form still attain growth and expansion?
"No, Venerable Sir."
Therefore, by this method as well, it should be understood:
that name-and-form has consciousness as its condition,
and consciousness has name-and-form as its condition, and so forth in detail.
What is meant here by the negation of coming and going, which occurs through the negation of all these [factors] beginning with form?

In that context, "coming" (*āgati*) is birth in this world from a previous world by means of the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). "Going" (*gati*) is, conversely, birth in another world from this world by means of the continuity of the intermediate state.
Or rather, is it by means of even one [of them], such as form (rūpa) or any other?
We say:
its negation occurs through the absence of all [of them].
If it is argued that no deliberation is required because the statement is made without distinction, this thought might occur: "This scriptural statement is made without distinction;

however, by the scriptural statement beginning with 'Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, life' and continuing in detail up to 'consciousness remains supported by form,' it is specified as either the life-force of the desire realm or the form realm."
It was said with a specific intention (*saṃdhāya*) that, as long as all those [factors] such as form (*rūpa*) are absent, there is the negation of that [consciousness].
To this it is replied: there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [consciousness] exists.

For, because of the statement made without qualification— that even external heat cannot exist apart from life— it is not specified that "O Kauṣṭhila, that which is life and that which is internal heat," and so forth.
Furthermore, because of the statement made without qualification, it would follow that even external matter, such as wood or walls, which is reckoned as non-sentient, is dependent upon consciousness.
"And as in the case of the four stations of consciousness," and so forth.
Just as, because of your statement regarding the four stations of consciousness without qualification, you maintain the existence of form (*rūpa*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
so too, because of your statement regarding the fourfold food, it would follow that there is edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) in the realms of form and formlessness.
For thus the Sūtra is recited:
"There are four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, and for the assistance of those seeking rebirth.
What are the four?"
Edible food is gross and subtle;
contact is the second;
mental volition is the third.
"Consciousness is the fourth nutriment.
Since the four nutriments are thus taught for the purpose of the maintenance of sentient beings without distinction,

and because they are not specified as belonging only to those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it follows that for you there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) existing even in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).
"Having transgressed," and so forth.
In this regard, it might occur to one belonging to another school:
"There is an exception to this general rule."
Because of the statement, "having transcended the gods who subsist on edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra)";
because of the distinction made in the Udāyi-sūtra and others, stating that "having transcended the gods who subsist on edible food, one is reborn in a certain divine mind-made body (manomayakāya)";
and because of the mention of "joy as food" (prītyāhāra).
Monks, there comes a time when this world undergoes dissolution.

When the world is dissolving, for the most part, sentient beings are reborn in the Ābhāsvara divine host. There they exist as beings with form, mind-made, without deficiency, with unimpaired faculties, endowed with all limbs and minor parts, beautiful, abiding in a state of radiant color, self-luminous, moving through the sky, feeding on joy, and having joy as their sustenance.
There is no such consequence for edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) because of statements in sūtras such as, "Those of long life remain for a long duration," and so forth.
If that is the case, then there would likewise be no consequence for form (*rūpa*) in the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
What is the reason? Because of an exception [to the rule].
How so?
One sūtra states as an exception that "the formless [attainments] are the escape from forms.
A second [sūtra] states that "those peaceful liberations which, having transcended forms, are formless."
"There are beings who are formless" is the third.
"By completely transcending perceptions of form" is the fourth.
For there is indeed form.

If there were form (*rūpa*) in the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and rebirths (*upapatti*), then since one would necessarily perceive one's own form when form exists, the statement "by the complete transcendence of perceptions of form" (*sarvaśo rūpasaṃjñānāṃ samatikramāt*) would not have been spoken. Yet,
it was indeed spoken.
For this reason as well, there is no form there.
"Coarse," and so forth.
In this regard, it might be argued as follows:
This was said with reference to the coarse form belonging to the lower stages,
as in the detailed passage beginning, "Those liberations which are peaceful.
To this, we reply:
The same applies to edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
How so?

By saying "having transcended the gods who subsist on edible food," this was said with reference to the coarse edible food belonging to the lower realms, and not to the subtle edible food belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
If they are called "formless" (*ārūpya*) because they are an escape from the coarse form of the lower realms,
then it would follow that the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are also formless, since they too are an escape from the lower realms.
How so?

The first dhyāna is the departure from the coarse form of the desire realm; likewise, each subsequent dhyāna is the departure from the coarser forms of the levels below, up to the fourth dhyāna. [If this were the case,] there would be the undesirable consequence that these are not formless (ārūpya).
And why is it not said that they are an "exit from sensation" and so forth?
If the formless realms (*ārūpya*) are so called because they are an exit from the coarseness of the lower stages— even though they possess form belonging to their own stage—
then why are the formless realms not called "without sensation" because they are an exit from sensation and the rest?
Even when there is feeling belonging to its own level—
by the word "etcetera," why are [the other factors] up to consciousness not mentioned?
[That is to say,] even when there is consciousness belonging to its own level.
What is the reason?
Because of the departure from the sensations and so forth of the lower stages.
The meaning is: because of the departure from the coarse sensations and so forth of the lower stages.
But they have transcended the entire category of form (*rūpajāti*).

Whatever category of form there may be— whether gross or subtle, internal or external— the formless states (*ārūpya*) have transcended all of that, both in terms of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and rebirth (*upapatti*).
In both meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and rebirth (*upapatti*), the formless realms (*ārūpya*) do not transcend the genus of feeling (*vedanā-jāti*) nor all feelings (*vedanā*) themselves,
because there exists neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), everything up to consciousness (*vijñāna*) is to be stated.
Therefore, the departure from forms has been taught,
but not the departure from feeling and so forth.
Consequently, for us who maintain this position, this undesirable consequence does not arise.
Because it is an escape from the sensations and so forth of the lower stages.
[The opponent asks: "And why is escape from sensation and so forth not mentioned?
He replies:
If the formless realms (*ārūpya*) are the escape from forms (*rūpa*), then how is it that the formless realm is the escape from the existence of form (*rūpabhava*)?
For it has been stated in the Sūtra: "I do not say that existence is the escape from existence.
How, then, can there be an escape from the existence of form by means of the formless existence?
However, the statement that existence is not an escape from existence is because one does not escape from that very existence by means of that same existence;
it is stated thus because one does not escape from that specific existence by means of that specific existence,
and because it is neither universal nor ultimate liberation.
It is not a complete escape. For the existence of the form realm (*rūpabhava*) is not the escape from the existence of the desire realm (*kāmabhava*);
rather, by that [existence of the form realm], there is also an escape from the existence of the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*).
And by that [formless attainment], there is no ultimate escape from existence in the desire realm,
because one returns [to it].
Likewise, there is an escape from existence in the form realm by means of existence in the formless realm.
It is not [an escape] from existence in the desire realm;
nor is there an absolute escape from existences in the form realm by means of existence in the formless realm.
Thus it has been stated how [existence] proceeds.
"The mental continuum depends here upon the group-homogeneity and the life-faculty," and so forth. The word "three" (*traya*) is used in the masculine gender.
This is because they are connected with the term "formless" (ārūpya).
Regarding the phrase "due to such application":

this shows that at the time of application, space and so forth serve as the objects of focus (ālambana), whereas at other times, other phenomena (dharmas) may also serve as objects of focus according to the circumstances.
"But because of dullness, it is neither percipient nor non-percipient.
Why is the fourth formless realm not called "percipient"?
Nor is it "without perception" (asaṃjñin),
because of its dullness.
By the word "but" (tu), it should be understood that its form is internally included [within the category of non-perception].
For the very reason that this fourth formless attainment is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
that same reason is stated:
"because of its dullness."
The preparatory application (prayoga) for this is thus indicated by the assignment of a name according to its literal meaning.
For this very reason, he says:
Even though there too it is applied in this way, and so forth:
"perception is a tumor; like a tumor, it is a tumor.
This continues up to "it is an arrow."
"Non-perception is delusion.
The meaning is that the absence of perception is indeed the cause of delusion.
The intention is that it is "cool" because of the complete cessation of perception.
What is this? It is this which is peaceful, this which is sublime.
To this he replies:
"Namely, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is intended here is the dullness of perception.
Here it must be asked:
why, however, is that [object] grasped by them in such a way? "By them" means by those who have attained those [meditative absorptions].
"Thus" refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
"Is grasped in this way" means that it is grasped as "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus, when there is an inquiry regarding a compound term, this must necessarily be stated.
Because perceptions are subtle, it is called the "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"; this is precisely what was stated [above].
The fundamental substances of meditative attainments are the primary ones. (VIII.5, 6)
The intention is that their branches do not perish.
To the question of how there are seven [types] of three kinds, he says: "associated with relishing, pure, and untainted."
The notion that "the untainted does not exist" arises from a dullness of perception; because one relishes [that state],
one has emerged from it.
From the pure [attainment].
That by which one relishes it is that into which one has entered.
It is not associated with relishing (*āsvādanā*).
Just as a fourfold army is not a separate entity from its constituent parts, so too the five-factored dhyāna is not a separate entity; thus he shows his own position.
"Joy and so forth" refers to the previously mentioned joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
And internal serenity;
thus the second [dhyāna] has four factors.
In the third, there are five: equanimity, and so forth.
Here, equanimity regarding mental formations is intended.
It is that joy characterized by effortlessness.
Mindfulness is the non-forgetting of the sign of equanimity.
Clear comprehension is the state of being clearly aware regarding the non-forgetting of mindfulness. In the fourth [dhyāna], there is the purity of equanimity;
the purity of equanimity is "equanimity-purity."
Because of the departure from the defects of the lower stages,
the eight defects are diminished;
thus there is the complete purity of mindfulness.
“Belonging to the first dhyāna” means existing in the first dhyāna.
For this very reason it is said: [as follows].
Because internal serenity and the other factors increase in the second dhyāna and those that follow.
How so?
There is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
It may be in the first dhyāna but not in the second;
it may be in the second but not in the first;
it may be in both.
It may be that neither [possesses it].
In this way, all the factors of meditative absorption (dhyānāṅga) are to be applied to one another.
How so?
Those factors which exist in the first dhyāna also exist in the third;
this constitutes a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
The first category consists of applied thought, sustained thought, joy, and bliss.
The second consists of equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and bliss.
The third is meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The fourth alternative consists of those factors excluded from what has been mentioned above.
Those factors which are present in the first dhyāna are also present in the fourth.
There are four alternatives.
The first alternative consists of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*).
The second alternative consists of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*) and the purity of equanimity (*upekṣā-pariśuddhi*).
And the purification of mindfulness is the third [limb].
The third is concentration (*samādhi*).
The fourth consists of those factors not mentioned [among the first three], which are the limbs present in the second dhyāna.
In the third [dhyāna] as well, those [factors] exist.
There is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
The first alternative consists of internal serenity, joy, and bliss.
The second [dhyāna] consists of equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and bliss;
the third is concentration;
the fourth consists of those factors not mentioned [in the preceding].
Regarding those factors that exist in the second dhyāna,
do they also exist in the fourth? There are four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
The first alternative consists of internal serenity, joy, and bliss. The second consists of its constituent factors, excluding concentration. The third is concentration itself.
The fourth [category] consists of those factors (dharmas) excluded from what has been stated.
Those members which exist in the third dhyāna also exist in the fourth;
this constitutes a fourfold logical alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
The first alternative consists of the factors of that [dhyāna] excluding concentration.
The second is likewise.
The third is concentration alone.
The fourth category consists of those phenomena (dharmas) excluded from what has been mentioned.
This is what is called "belonging to a single sphere" (ekāvacara).
Why, then, is pleasure (sukha) said to be a distinct entity (dravyāntara) in the third dhyāna?
How is it said?
Having explained in detail that "these are the eighteen factors of dhyāna," he says again:
"In name alone, it is thus."
Substantially, there are ten and one;
thus, substantially, these become eleven.
There are five factors belonging to the first dhyāna.
In the second, internal clarity increases;
in the third, according to the statement, there are equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and bliss.
"Due to the connection with the faculty of pleasure" means because of the occurrence of the faculty of pleasure.
For there is no mental faculty of pleasure at all in any of the three dhyānas.
What then?
It is precisely bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*) that is established as a constituent member,
because it arises during the intervals between states of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
This is indeed the position of the Dārṣṭāntikas;
for according to them, the faculty of pleasure does not belong to only two levels,
but rather to the levels of the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
What then? The faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) exists even on four levels:
from the desire realm (kāmāvacara) up to the level of the third dhyāna.
For this very reason, it was said by the Bhadanta Sautrāntika in the *Vibhāṣā*:
"The visual consciousness and the others are drawn upward from below by the Ābhidharmikas, as if by a waterwheel.
Thus, this is what he accepts.
Since visual consciousness and the others can also belong to the levels of the second dhyāna and above, this reading— "mental" (*caitasika*)— is an interpolation. This refers to the reading "mental."
And because it is stated in its own words, "he experiences pleasure with the body.
Thus it was said in the description of the third dhyāna:
"Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending."
And he experiences pleasure with the body.
That which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindful, and abiding in happiness," having attained the third dhyāna—he dwells therein.
For if that [pleasure] were mental, how could it be experienced with the body?
"By means of the mind and the body": having spoken thus with reference to the collection [of the five aggregates] as "the mind," what is the purpose [of this]?
The intention is that one should rather say: "He experiences pleasure with the mind" and "He experiences pleasure with the body.
Furthermore, this is because pleasure is not mentioned in the fourth dhyāna, even though there is an abundance of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) therein.
In the fourth dhyāna, the bliss of pliancy (praśrabdhi-sukha) becomes even greater and more abundant.
This is because the fourth dhyāna possesses a higher degree of pliancy than the other dhyānas.
Despite this abundance, there is no mention of "bliss" [as a distinct factor].
In the fourth dhyāna, bliss is not mentioned;
because that bliss is not spoken of,
it is understood that what is referred to as "bliss" in the third dhyāna is exclusively the bliss of sensation.
The intention is that [pliancy] is not mentioned there because there is no pleasant feeling in the fourth [dhyāna].
If it is argued that pliancy favorable to pleasant feeling is what constitutes pleasure,
this might be the opinion.
In the first and second dhyānas,
there is pliancy (praśrabdhi) that is conducive to pleasant feeling (sukhavedanā).
Having stated that these two constitute "pleasure," it is not mentioned in the fourth dhyāna because the pliancy there is not conducive to pleasant feeling.
If this is so, why is the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*) not mentioned in the third [dhyāna]?
For the pliancy of the third dhyāna is also conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
Why, then, is the pleasure of pliancy not stated there?
For in that case, you have established that it is the pleasure of feeling (*vedanāsukha*) itself,
not the pleasure of serenity (*praśrabdhisukha*),
because of the twofold recitation of "pleasure."
If it is argued that this is because [it] is impaired by equanimity (*upekṣā*), the following might be thought:
in the third dhyāna, equanimity has the characteristic of pliancy (*karmanya*).
"It is not said that serenity (*praśrabdhi*) is impaired by that [suffering].
No;
for it is through equanimity (*upekṣā*) alone that its increase occurs.
This is not so;
rather, it is through equanimity alone that there is an increase in the bliss of pliancy in that third dhyāna.
For it is not logical that an increase should occur by means of a cause that is itself a source of affliction.
How is it that its increase occurs through equanimity alone? To this he says:
"Because of its distinction from the former two.
That is, because of its distinction from the former two, namely, the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of the first and second dhyānas.
The pliancy of the third dhyāna is superior because the third dhyāna is superior to the two preceding ones.
"At which time," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
At the time when a noble disciple, having personally realized with his body the joy born of seclusion, attains it and dwells therein,
five qualities are abandoned by him at that time,
and five qualities reach the fulfillment of their cultivation.
[The factors are] internal serenity, joy, tranquility, bliss, and concentration.
If tranquility and bliss were not distinct, how could there be five of them?
Furthermore, if they were indeed distinct entities, it would be established that bliss is exclusively bodily in all three dhyānas.
"How can there be body-consciousness for one who has entered meditative absorption?
To this it is replied:

because of the pervading of the body and its inflation by a wind—produced by a specific concentration—that is termed "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*), which is to be experienced as pleasure or is conducive to the feeling of pleasure.
What [is the objection]? That body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna) indeed occurs.
If it is argued that this leads to a loss of meditative concentration (samādhi) due to outward distraction:

If one should think that because of the arising of body-consciousness there is outward distraction— that is, distraction toward external objects— and thus a falling away from meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
[the answer is] no.
[This is because it is] "born of meditative concentration," and so forth.
"This will not be so.
Why?
Because it means [the sensation] born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), produced within the body, and not produced externally.

The meaning is that because bodily pleasure—that is, the felt pleasure associated with body-consciousness—is conducive to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is no falling away from concentration on account of it.
No;
for this very reason.
One would not have emerged [from meditative absorption] at the time of body-consciousness.
For this very reason, the meaning is that it is "conducive to concentration" (*samādhyanukūla*).
The intention is that concentration re-establishes itself immediately after its manifestation.

Because a tangible object belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) cannot be apprehended by a body-consciousness belonging to the realm of desire (kāmāvacara), this body-consciousness belongs to the realm of form and not to the realm of desire.
For this very reason, the pleasure associated with it cannot be established as a factor of meditative absorption (dhyānāṅga).
This is because [such pleasure] arises from the knowledge of pliancy (praśrabdhi-jñāna).

A [mental consciousness] belonging to the form realm [arises] with a body-consciousness belonging to the desire realm and with the body-faculty, through the empowerment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
For that body-faculty, having entered that state for one who is concentrated,
becomes the basis for a body-consciousness of a higher level.
"Even in the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Even the tangible object characterized by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) which has that as its object—both the tangible and the body-consciousness—could be untainted.
He asks: "What is the reason? and says:
If it is thought that "let it be that some members are with-outflows (sāsrava) and some are without-outflows (anāsrava)," if one should think thus, [the answer is] no,
because the factor of enlightenment of physical pliancy (kāyika-praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) is taught [as being exclusively without-outflows].

That which is bodily pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*)—that too is the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhisambodhyaṅga*), which conduces to higher knowledge (*abhijñā*), to awakening (*sambodhi*), and to nirvāṇa.

And that which is mental pliancy (*cittapraśrabdhi*)—up to the point that it is said: "even the tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*) [when they function as] the factor of enlightenment conduce to higher knowledge, to awakening, and to nirvāṇa."
Regarding the statement that "the tangible and body-consciousness are accepted as being untainted" because they are factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga):
if it is argued that this is because they are conducive to the factors of enlightenment,
then the following response may be made.
Because bodily pliancy is conducive to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), it is metaphorically designated as a "factor of enlightenment," but it is not [itself] a factor of enlightenment.
Its state of being untainted (*anāsravatva*) [is what makes it so].
It may be so.

Because they are conducive to the state of being untainted (*anāsrava*), those tangible objects and body-consciousness are metaphorically designated as "untainted," but they are not actually untainted.
Thus, these two are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
"Contaminated phenomena" (*sāsravā dharmāḥ*), and so forth. What are contaminated phenomena?

If one should think that this contradicts the Sūtra which states: "As far as the eye, as far as forms, as far as eye-consciousness; as far as the body, as far as tangibles, as far as body-consciousness."
That is not so, because the statement was made with reference to other tangible objects and body-consciousnesses.
That is, it was made with reference to tangible objects distinct from that [specific] pliancy, and to body-consciousnesses distinct from that [specific] body-consciousness.
"And it is not untainted," and so forth.

[The objection: "But if the untainted were established as being untainted, would it not follow that some members [of the path] would be tainted and some untainted?"—if one should think that this is a fault.
Because that tangible object and its corresponding body-consciousness are with-outflows (*sāsrava*), whereas the other is without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
To this, it is said:
"What fault is there in their not being simultaneous?
When a contaminated factor is active, at that time an uncontaminated factor is not active.
When a factor is untainted, it is not at that time tainted; thus there is no fault here,
because of the non-coexistence of pleasure and joy.
If it is argued that the first dhyāna cannot possess five factors because of the non-coexistence and non-simultaneity of bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*) and mental joy (*mānasa-prīti*),
and if one should think thus:
That is not a fault.
Why?
Because it is taught with reference to possibility, as in the case of applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra).
Just as "the first dhyāna is with applied thought and sustained thought" is stated as a synonym for the occurrence of applied and sustained thought,
so too there is no fault in this [teaching] regarding pleasure and joy, since they are taught according to their possible occurrence.
If it is argued that this remains to be proven:
It is to be proven that applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) occur alternately.
He says:
It is established.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Because of the contradiction between applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
This is because if there is coarseness of mind, [it is incompatible with *vicāra*].
There is no subtlety.
If there were subtlety,
there would be no coarseness.
Because of their mutual contradiction, vitarka and vicāra cannot occur simultaneously.
This is also because of the statement regarding their defects.

Furthermore, since grossness and subtlety are relative—due to differences in levels (bhūmi) and types (prakāra)—it would follow that vitarka and vicāra would exist even up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra), and so forth.
Some read the text as "doṣāvacanāc ca" (and because no fault is mentioned). The meaning is that by this specific restriction (*asmavadhānena*), no fault whatsoever is stated.
[The phrase] "by the removal of two, three, or four factors" refers to this.
The second dhyāna is established by the removal of two factors,
because of the absence of vitarka and vicāra therein.
The third dhyāna is established by the removal of three factors.
In that state, there is even no joy (*prīti*).
The establishment of the fourth dhyāna is by means of the removal of four factors;
therein, there is even no pleasure (*sukha*).
But it has not been stated that perception (*saṃjñā*) and the others are factors (*aṅga*).
For there is no diminution of perception and the rest in the other meditations (*dhyāna*);
for what reason, then, are only five [mental factors] designated as factors?
If this meaning is not intended—
that is, if the status of being a limb belongs to only five because they are beneficial— then that is not correct.
Because mindfulness and wisdom are more beneficial than applied thought and sustained thought;
for it is not held that applied thought and sustained thought are as beneficial as mindfulness and wisdom.
Because for one whose mindfulness is well-established and who understands things as they truly are, there is an absence of lethargy, excitement, and so forth.
Therefore, this should be investigated.
By stating that "this should be investigated through the examination of the *Yogācārabhūmi*," the Master directs the student's curiosity toward it.
And here, this summary of the meaning should be observed:
with reference to what, moreover, are vitarka and the others alone established as factors (aṅga), even though other dharmas exist? It is by means of just those [factors].
Because the limbs based on the counteragent, the benefit, and both of these are fully completed [in the form realm],
there is no formal establishment of limbs in the formless realms,
owing to the single flavor of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Thus it is said, by taking up the factor of the counteragent, by taking up the factor of the benefit,
and by taking up the factor that is the basis for both.
In the first dhyāna, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are the factors of counteraction,
because through them there is the abandonment of thoughts of sensual desire, ill-will, and cruelty;
joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) are the factors of benefit.
When the adverse factors have been countered by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one attains the joy and bliss born of seclusion from them;
thus, one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is the limb that serves as the basis for both.
This is because the activity of applied thought and the others proceeds by the power of that basis.

Likewise, in the second dhyāna, internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is the factor that serves as the antidote, because it acts as the counteragent to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) are the remaining factors, as previously described.
In the third dhyāna, equanimity (upekṣā), mindfulness (smṛti), and clear comprehension (saṃprajanya) are the factors that serve as antidotes,
because they counteract joy (prīti).
As for the remaining factors— bliss (sukha) and one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā)— they are to be understood respectively as before.

In the fourth dhyāna, the purity of equanimity and the purity of mindfulness are the factors of the antidote, because by means of these two, pleasure is countered within the dhyānas. The feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant is the factor of the benefit.
"One-pointedness of mind is the limb that serves as the basis for both. Faith is clarity (*prasāda*): faith itself is clarity, thus it is 'faith-clarity' (*śraddhā-prasāda*)."
"How can there be the status of being a mental factor (*caitasika*) when there is no separate substantial entity?
[This refers to] applied thought (*vitarka*) and so forth.
For even a particular state of the mind indeed becomes a mental factor.
Because they exist within the mind:
the state of mental discourse that seeks is *vitarka* (applied thought);
the state of mental discourse that examines is *vicāra* (sustained thought).
According to the Venerable Viśeṣa, *vitarka* is the state of the mind that gives rise to speech; *vicāra* is the state other than that;
and *samādhi* is the state of non-distraction.
"The state of the mind flowing in tranquility is internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
Indeed, it is not tenable that pleasure (*sukha*) in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) is mental well-being (*saumanasya*),
even though they possess the same nature of being mental and having the feeling of pleasure as their essence.
Why is mental gladness (*saumanasya*) not called pleasure (*sukha*)? There is a reason for this:
for this joy (*prīti*) is not tranquilized.
For by that [feeling], even a concentrated mind is made to appear as if distracted, as if uplifted, as if agitated with joy and laughter, and as if deranged; yet when it becomes tranquil,
then the sensation of a similar kind belonging to another stage is called "pleasure."
(VIII.10) "Because it is not separated from afflictions" means because it is not separated from the afflictions belonging to that level.
"Because it is turbid with afflictions" [is the meaning].
The meaning is: because of being unpurified by the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Because of being distracted by afflicted pleasure" means because of being distracted by afflicted pleasure.
Mindfulness and clear comprehension do not exist because of being defiled by afflictions; that is,
because of being defiled by the afflictions belonging to that level.
There is no complete purification of equanimity and mindfulness,
because these two belong to the great ground of wholesome factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*).
For tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are recited among the wholesome universal mental factors.
Because it is stated: "Faith, heedfulness, pliancy, equanimity, shame, dread, the two roots, non-harming, and vigor are always wholesome."
But do these two [attainments] also occur in the defiled meditative absorptions according to the former position?
They do not occur; thus he says:
"Why was this not stated?"
Because they are established even without being explicitly mentioned.
Others hold that since the two factors of the great wholesome ground—pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are not included [in the list], those two certainly do exist.
Regarding the phrase "in the breaths":
Inhalation and exhalation.
The dual number is used here for the purpose of showing their duality.
This is because they cannot be shaken by applied thought, sustained thought, joy, or pleasure.
Just as the three preceding meditations are shaken by vitarka and so forth:
the first meditation is shaken by vitarka and vicāra;
the second is shaken by prīti.
The third is shaken by pleasure. But the fourth is not shaken by these in such a way,
just as a lamp in a windless place is not shaken by the wind.
Others say that it is stated in the Sūtra as "it is like that" because it is free from the eight defects; thus,
the first [dhyāna] is attained.
Thus,
it is comprised within the first dhyāna,
like the mind of emanation.
Just as creators who desire to produce an emanation belonging to a particular level must bring into manifestation an emanation-mind belonging to that same level, so it is here:
[the higher mind] is not wholesome because it is inferior.
For that wholesome state belonging to the level of the first dhyāna is inferior and base compared to those belonging to the level of the second dhyāna;
therefore, they do not bring it into manifestation.
Indeed, it is for a specific purpose that they bring the state belonging to the level of the first dhyāna into manifestation.
It is not out of great respect.
Furthermore, that wholesome [action] has a ripening result,
yet since they do not desire that ripening, they do not exert effort in bringing a wholesome mind into manifestation.
(VIII.14) "By means of detachment and by way of rebirth," or "either by means of detachment or by way of rebirth."
The word "or" (*vā*) is used here as an elided reference.
Either through detachment from a lower stage (*adhobhūmi*), one who was previously not in possession of it attains pure (*śuddhaka*) dhyāna or formless attainment (*ārūpya*);
or, through detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one attains the first [dhyāna] in its pure form, which is of three types, excluding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
In this way, up to the point of detachment from the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), one attains the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
Alternatively, through rebirth in a lower plane,
one attains it when being reborn from a higher level into a lower plane.
"Except for the Peak of Existence.
Its acquisition occurs only through detachment from the lower stages.
It is called "conducive to penetration" by way of its preparatory application.
That attainment is not produced by the arising of detachment.
Regarding "it is conducive to decline even through falling away":
one who falls away from the state conducive to stability attains that which is conducive to decline.
Therefore it is said:
because even one who has fallen away obtains that which pertains to falling away (*hānabhāgīya*).
In this way, the same should be applied to both through falling away and through rebirth (*upapatti*).
How so?
There may be a case where one attains pure [dhyāna] through falling away and abandons it through falling away;
there may be a case where one attains pure dhyāna through rebirth and abandons it through rebirth.
He said: "It may be so. [The other] asked: "How so? He replied:

"The first dhyāna conducive to decline" refers to the Brahma-world (brahmaloka), which constitutes the first dhyāna consisting of three levels; this is because of the statement that one is "reborn specifically in the Brahma-world."
It is abandoned through detachment from the Brahma-world.

Because, through detachment from the first dhyāna, the dhyāna belonging to the category of decline (*hānabhāgīya*) is abandoned— due to its conformity with the afflictions— just like the afflictions belonging to that level.
Therefore, it is said that [the path] is abandoned through detachment from the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*).
Thus, first, the answer to the first question has been explained.
One acquires [it] through falling away from detachment from the Brahma-world.
If one falls away through a loss of detachment from the Brahma-world, one again acquires that [state] conducive to decline (dhānabhāgīya),
just like the afflictions belonging to that level.
It is abandoned through a loss of detachment from the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
When one falls away from detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
then the pure [attainment] (*śuddhaka*) is relinquished;
being reborn above, in the Brahma-world, one acquires it again.
One being reborn in the Brahma-world from the second dhyāna or higher acquires the *hānabhāgīya* [state] just like the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to that level.
Therefore, one who is being reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) abandons it;
that is, one who is being reborn in the desire realm from that Brahma-world abandons it.
Regarding the statement "it is also [attained] through the transformation of the faculties as either *śaikṣa* or *aśaikṣa*":

one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhāvimukta*) attains the state of a *śaikṣa* upon reaching the stage of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). One who is liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) also attains the state of an *aśaikṣa* upon penetrating the immovable nature (*akopyaprativedha*).
Not necessarily.
This is because one who follows the gradual path does not obtain it.
That is to say, if one who follows the gradual path enters the fixed course of rightness (niyāma) by relying on the preparatory stage (anāgamya), one does not obtain it.
(VIII.15, 16) "Pure and uncontaminated [minds] belonging to their own level" refers to those at the time of emergence and during the continuous flow [of meditation].
"And those belonging to the levels of the second and third dhyānas" refers to the same.
In the mixed and unmixed conformable attainments (*anuloma-samāpatti*) and in the leaping attainment (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*),
there are seven [attainments] belonging to their own level, which are both pure (*śuddhaka*) and untainted (*anāsrava*).
As before, there are also those belonging to the levels of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
The same applies to the attainment in reverse order (*pratiloma-samāpatti*).
At the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there is only the pure (*śuddhaka*) [meditation], because of the absence of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
It has been stated that the untainted does not exist there due to its dullness (*māndya*).
However, in the case of the forward-order attainment (*anuloma-samāpatti*), that [state] occurs at the time of emergence (*vyutthāna*).

This applies to those belonging to the levels of the third, fourth, and first dhyānas, during the times of unmixed, mixed, forward-order, reverse-order, and leaping attainments (*vyutkrānta-samāpatti*).
There are four belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
These exist at those very same times.
There are three because of the absence of the untainted (*anāsrava*) state.
In this way, ten substances are to be applied immediately after any other dhyāna or ārūpya.
For example, immediately after the third dhyāna, there are ten:
two belonging to its own level, namely the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
There are four belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana),
and likewise four belonging to the levels of the first and second dhyānas; thus,
immediately after the fourth dhyāna, there are ten.
There are two belonging to its own level: the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
There are four belonging to the levels of the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness.
And there are four belonging to the levels of the second and third dhyānas.
Immediately after the sphere of infinite space, there are ten:
two belonging to its own level,
and four belonging to the levels of the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness.
Four [moments] belonging to the levels of the third and fourth dhyānas arise; thus, there are ten.
"And immediately after the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)," and so forth—this is what is being explained.

Because the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) have as their objects both higher and lower stages, there is the possibility of such a consequence; therefore, it is said that "it has a lower basis and object.
This is because that *dharmajñāna* has a lower basis—namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—and a lower object—namely, the suffering and so forth of the desire realm.
Because it has a lower level as its basis and object, one does not enter the formless attainments immediately after the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
The remainder is exactly as in the case of the untainted (*anāsrava*):
both the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted arise belonging to their own level.
"And from a higher level down to the third lower level" means:
"having made a vow," and so forth.
If someone were to fall asleep after forming such a thought as, "I must wake up at midnight, at the rising of the moon, or at the setting of the moon."
Because he follows his previous intention, he awakens at that very time due to the continuity [of his mental stream]. Just as he fell asleep having made such a vow,
his awakening occurs at the intended time.
It is just like that.
"In no way does it arise" means that it arises neither as belonging to its own level nor as belonging to a lower level.
This was said with reference to the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Immediately after both the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), only an afflicted state belonging to its own level arises, not one belonging to another level.
How so?
Likewise, from the pure, one may also attain the defiled of its own level.
From the defiled, one attains its own pure and defiled; thus it is.
However, at the time of death:
In the state of death (*maraṇabhava*). "From the pure [attainment] acquired at birth," and so forth: this refers to that wholesome, concentrated state acquired at birth within the dhyānas of rebirth.
That too is called "pure dhyāna. Therefore, this is said: "But at the time of death..."
Thus it is explained in detail.
What is the reason? Because the state of existence at death (*maraṇabhava*) is not in a state of meditative concentration (*asamāhita*).
For at that time, there is no pure meditative absorption (*samāpatti-dhyāna*).
Therefore, a defiled [mind] belonging to all levels arises;
this means that a defiled, non-concentrated mind of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi-citta*) arises belonging to its own level, a lower level, or a higher level.
It belongs to a higher stage,
because when defilement exists, rebirth there is impossible.
(Abhidh-k-vy 680)
"Except for that which pertains to the distinguished stage" means that there is no higher level beyond this.
Therefore, "the untainted arises from that" refers to arising from the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Regarding the terms *hānabhāgīya* and *sthitibhāgīya*: *hānabhāgīya* refers to the time of the continuous flow [of the meditative state],
while *sthitibhāgīya* refers to the time of proceeding toward excellence.
"Except for that which partakes in decline.

This is because for one who is declining from [the state] partaking in distinction, since they have not abandoned the state partaking in stability, it is logical that only that very same [state] arises.
"That alone is one."
That very same aid to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is [practiced] by way of a continuous flow (VIII.19).
"Drawn forth" means in sequence;
that is, in both forward and reverse order.
(VIII.20) “Is prescribed” means “is performed,” or alternatively, “is established.
What is the reason?
Because of its inferiority. [It is said: "Because of the manifestation of the noble state of nothingness."
It is noble and untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because of the manifestation— that is, the becoming present— of the untainted sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
the abandonment of the outflows (*āsrava*) occurs for one born at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
The word "tu" (but) indicates an exception.
"Because of its own absence" means because of the absence of the untainted path belonging to the Peak of Existence.
"And because of the cultivation of that":
because of the cultivation of that untainted sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), due to its proximity.
"Because the stages are delimited by craving" (VIII.21).
Because it underlies that very level upon which it exists,
that level is delimited by it.
Otherwise, its status as a "higher" level would not be established, just like other distinct locations within a single level.
For this very reason, even though there is a vertical arrangement, the fact that the three groups of three and the group of eight belong to a single level is established,
because of the intermingling of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
"It would follow that it is not untainted because it would entail being wholesome.
For the aspiration for that [higher realm] is indeed wholesome desire for the Dharma (*dharmacchanda*).
The fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not have the lower tainted realms as their object.
Thus [it is said].

The mention of the "fundamental" [attainments] is for the purpose of excluding the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*). For the preparatory stages of the formless realm take as their object the lower, contaminated level.
The inclusion of the term "wholesome" (*kuśala*) is for the purpose of excluding those [formless attainments] associated with relishing (*āsvādanā-saṃprayukta*),
and also for the purpose of including both types of the wholesome.

For if only "the formless [attainments]" (*ārūpyāḥ*) were stated, it might be assumed that the fundamental formless attainments associated with relishing are not objects of the lower defiled [stages].
The formless [attainments] (*ārūpya*) would thus be understood as being exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
The mention of "formless" is for the purpose of excluding the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*),
for even the fundamental meditative absorptions can have tainted lower-level entities as their objects.
Because the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) involve universal observation,
the term "with outflows" (sāsrava) is used for the purpose of excluding those that are without outflows (anāsrava).
For it is possible for untainted (anāsrava) factors of a lower stage to serve as objects of focus for the fundamental wholesome factors of the formless absorptions (ārūpya).
The mention of "lower" is for the purpose of qualifying the "upper," because there is the possibility of taking a contaminated object belonging to a higher stage as an object.
However, having taken up the point that the uncontaminated is the object, he shows [this] by saying, "the entire category of subsequent knowledge."
The term "all" includes those belonging to the nine stages, even though they are distinguished by differences such as faculty (*indriya*) and lineage (*gotra*).

By the inclusion of the word "side" (*pakṣa*) in the phrase "the side of subsequent knowledge" (*anvayajñāna-pakṣa*), the receptivities to subsequent knowledge of suffering and so forth (*duḥkhādyanvayajñānakṣānti*), as well as their co-arising factors, are included;
it does not include the side of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*).
Because it is remote due to having the suffering of the desire realm and so forth as its object,
there is no cessation of a lower stage;
for that would entail the consequence of grasping [the cessation] of a lower stage.
This has been explained previously:
"The afflictions are abandoned by means of the untainted [path]. (VIII.22)
Of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya), that which is untainted (anāsrava) exists;
by means of that, according to its possibility, the afflictions (kleśa) are abandoned. By which untainted [state]? By the fundamental (maula) [untainted state].
For it will be stated that "by the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) as well.
This refers to the fact that defilements are abandoned by means of the pure (śuddhaka) preparatory stage, which functions as an exception (apavāda).
"How much less so by the defiled [path]"—the intention is that the abandonment of afflictions is simply not possible through a defiled path.
What is the reason that afflictions are not abandoned by the pure [path]? He says:
"Because of being free from passion, not [by] the lower," and so forth.
Because one is free from passion for the lower stage, the defilements of the lower stage are not abandoned by means of the pure [meditation]; how much less so by means of the afflicted [meditation]?
Because it is not an antidote to that very [state], it does not exist within its own level—
from that same first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Since it is not an antidote to that, it is "not an antidote to that" (tadapratipakṣa).
That is its nature.
Therefore,
because they are not the antidotes to those [afflictions], the afflictions of one's own level are not abandoned.
For there is no escape from existence by means of existence.
Because they are more distinguished, it is not "above";
that is, the afflictions of a higher level are not abandoned by the pure [attainment] of a lower level.
Because the afflictions are more distinguished [intense],
and it is not logical for the abandonment of distinguished [afflictions] to rely upon something inferior;
thus, by this reasoning, even the *śuddhaka* [attainments] do not abandon the afflictions.
How much less so by a defiled [mind]—this is established.
By the word "also" in the phrase "by the pure also," it is meant that it is also by the untainted (anāsrava).
However, this was stated according to what is possible.
For this very reason it is said:
"Because it is the antidote to the lower stage.
For the afflictions belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) are abandoned by means of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna.
Those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna [are abandoned] by the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna;

likewise, up to those belonging to the level of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), which are abandoned by the preparatory stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
This refers to that by means of which one enters into them. (VIII.22)
By means of which neighboring [stages] is there entry into those fundamental dhyānas and formless attainments? Are they also of three kinds?
Yes, due to the distinctions such as being associated with relish (*āsvādana*) and so forth.
And likewise, there is feeling within them:
in the first two dhyānas there is joy (prīti),
and in the third there is pleasure (sukha).
It was stated that the fourth [dhyāna] is characterized by equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Is it the same in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*)?
And why are they associated with the faculty of equanimity? Because they are brought about through effort (*yatnavāhyatvāt*).
The path that proceeds without volitional effort (*anābhisaṃskāravāhī*) is associated with joy and bliss (*prītisukha*).
However, those preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) proceed with effort and are thus accompanied by volitional effort; therefore, they are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Furthermore, because the agitation regarding the lower stages has not yet subsided, there is no association with joy and bliss.
For this reason also, they are associated with the faculty of equanimity;
and because they are paths to detachment,
they are not associated with relish.
For if they were associated with relishing (*āsvādana*), there would be no path of detachment (*vairāgyamārga*).
Indeed, a path associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*) does not lead to the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Alternatively, the connection [of the text] is as follows.

And they are associated with the faculty of equanimity because they must be brought about through effort, and because they are paths to dispassion due to the non-disappearance of aversion toward the lower stages; thus, for these two reasons, they are not associated with relish.
The remainder should be explained as before.

"Even though the connection [to rebirth] occurs by means of the preparatory mind (sāmantaka-citta)": this is the established doctrine that in all eight meditations and formless attainments, for whichever state there is a preparatory stage, the connection to rebirth occurs by means of that specific preparatory mind, which is afflicted and non-concentrated.
Therefore, this is said:
"Even though by means of the mind of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*)," and so forth.
This refers to the fact that even the *anāgamya* [stage] may be associated with relishing (*āsvādana*).
Because the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage] is sharp.
For just as it can be untainted (*anāsrava*), so too can it be associated with relish (*āsvādana*); this is the intended meaning.
"Because it is a primary rival [to the first dhyāna] and because the arising of relishing is present," says the Master Saṃghabhadra.

(VIII.23) "Because it is a specific type of dhyāna": the meaning is that this very same primary first dhyāna, being distinguished by the departure of applied thought (*vitarka*), is called the "intermediate dhyāna" (*dhyānāntara*).
"Because there is no distinction" means that just as there is a distinction in the first dhyāna—
wherein in some cases there are both *vitarka* and *vicāra*— [so it is here].
In some cases, there is only investigation (*vicāra*).
It is not so in the second [dhyāna] and those following.
Therefore, "the intermediate dhyāna" (*dhyānāntara*) is not established within the [other] dhyānas.
Therefore, it is called "the difficult path of practice.
Indeed, it is because it proceeds with effortful conditioning (*saṃskāra*).
It is because only applied thought (*vitarka*) is prohibited.
Because of the statement, "The intermediate dhyāna is without vitarka," the concentration that has that as its object is called the signless (*ānimitta*). (VIII.24, 25)
In the signless [liberation], the state is signless.
Regarding the "ten aspects":
there are two aspects, namely impermanence and suffering.
The aspect of origin consists of four [factors] and the aspect of the path consists of four; thus, these are the ten aspects.
"Due to revulsion toward impermanence, suffering, and their cause" means: from impermanence, from suffering, and from its cause.
And because of the agitation arising from the cause of that suffering and its origin,
what [is there]?
It is the wishless.
The meaning is "one who has not performed the preparatory refinement" (*akṛtasaṃskāra*).
This is because the path must necessarily be abandoned, as it is like a raft;
a "raft" (*kola*) refers to a small boat (*uḍupa*).
That which has a raft as its simile is "raft-like";
it refers to the path.
Its state is "the condition of being raft-like."
By that [analogy],
the necessity of abandoning the path— likened to a raft— is established;
therefore, the subject under discussion is the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
For just as one crossing a river by relying on a raft does not remain fixed upon the raft—
since it must necessarily be abandoned—
so too, having relied upon the path, one does not remain fixed upon the path.
Because that must necessarily be abandoned.
"Its aspect" means its ten aspects as previously described.
"Because it is oriented toward transcending that.
This means because it is oriented toward transcending that path.
By this, he shows that this [path] must necessarily be abandoned.
That one is oriented toward transcending impermanence, suffering, and their causes is understood even without being explicitly stated.
However, there is no agitation through emptiness and selflessness;
that is, the practitioner does not experience agitation by means of the aspects of emptiness and non-self.
For although the truth of suffering is characterized by the aspects of emptiness and non-self,
one does not experience revulsion toward that suffering because of those two.
Why is that?
Because it is common with nirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa, too, has the characteristic of being empty and selfless;
for emptiness and selflessness are indeed the characteristic of all phenomena (sarvadharma). (Abhidh-k-vy 683)
Nor is there agitation toward *nirvāṇa* because of those two;
therefore, the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) does not have that as its aspect.
"The worldly ones are in eleven" means:
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and in the dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
"Where there is the path" refers to those stages excluding the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the desire realm and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
"Because it is the door to liberation. This shows that the meaning of *mukha* is the meaning of "door.
"Because its objective support is emptiness and so forth, it has that name [of 'entrance']. (VIII.25, 26)
Because it takes emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness as its objects,
it is named "emptiness of emptiness" and "wishlessness of wishlessness."
And as "the signless within the signless," and also as "emptiness" and "impermanence."
According to their respective order:

for emptiness-emptiness takes as its object the emptiness-concentration of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) by way of the aspect of emptiness, thinking "this is not mine," and not by way of the aspect of selflessness.

He asked: "What is the reason here that the emptiness-of-emptiness samādhi has only the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyatākāra*), and not also the aspect of selflessness (*anātmākāra*), as is the case with [the basic] emptiness?"
To this it is replied: because it is to be produced following upon emptiness that has proceeded with the aspect of emptiness.
He said:

But for what reason does its arising occur subsequent to emptiness that has proceeded with the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyatākāra*), and not subsequent to emptiness that has proceeded with the aspect of selflessness (*anātmākāra*)?
To this it is said:
because it is conducive to its arising.

For that very concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), which proceeds with the aspect of emptiness, remains in conformity with the arising of his concentration on the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi*). It is not the aspect of selflessness (*anātman*).
For the vision of selflessness does not cause such agitation as the vision of emptiness does.
For even when states of existence are seen as being without self, there is still attachment to cyclic existence because of the absence of the vision of emptiness.
It is just as a traveler feels joy even from seeing another traveler with whom he has no connection,
whereas one who is alone feels no joy because of that solitude.
In the same way. "By way of the aspect of impermanence" refers to among the ten aspects.
"Not as suffering," and so forth.
They do not take it in the aspect of suffering because that which is untainted (anāsrava) does not have that characteristic;
for it is by virtue of being disagreeable to the noble ones (ārya) that something is considered suffering.

The meaning is that [the untainted] is not [contemplated] through the aspects (ākāra) of cause, origin, production, or condition, because the untainted does not possess those characteristics; that is to say, the untainted does not have the characteristics of origin and so forth.
It is not [contemplated] through the aspects of the path because it is to be abandoned;
for that concentration of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is to be discarded, whereas the aspects of the path do not consist of the nature of discarding.
Therefore, one does not take that samādhi as an object by way of the aspects of the path;
however, since there is no connection whatsoever with the aspects of cessation,
it is not contemplated by means of them.
By process of elimination, it is only by way of the aspect of impermanence.
"Incalculable and inexhaustible" means non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
The signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) takes as its object the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
[perceiving] "This is peaceful because it is peaceful.
How is there non-analytical cessation for that?
For one who has emerged from the signless concentration of an adept (aśaikṣa), if those subsequent moments— both the contaminated ones that pass by and the other uncontaminated ones—
were not to have arisen.
The moments of the signless (*ānimitta*) belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) may have arisen.

At the time of the arising of those [moments], whether they are contaminated (*sāsrava*) or other uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states, the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of those moments of the signless belonging to those beyond training is obtained due to the deficiency of conditions (*pratyayavaikalyāt*).
It takes that non-analytical cessation as its object by way of the aspect of peace.
Because there is no analytical cessation for that which is untainted,
it does not take analytical cessation as its object.
