But why is there no analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) for that which is untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Because it is not disagreeable.
For whatever is disagreeable to the Noble Ones [is subject to such cessation].
Therefore, they strive for the sake of dissociation from that conjunction;
and dissociation is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Consequently, there is no analytical cessation of that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, because there is no analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) for the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
and because non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) stands as its adversary,
he who desires to disparage that [concentration] by means of praising it takes precisely that non-analytical cessation as his object.
For it is observed in the world that by capturing an enemy, harm is inflicted upon the enemy's wife.
[The path is not cultivated] through the aspects of cessation (*nirodha*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*);
cessation is common to all.
"Not cessation" means the state of being that;
therefore.
Because it is common to both impermanence and cessation, this non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) is not characterized by the aspect of cessation (nirodhākāra).
Otherwise, it would not be apprehended as distinguished by the aspect of tranquility (śāntākāra).
For if it were characterized by the aspect of cessation, that non-analytical cessation would be tainted by nothing other than the cessation of impermanence.
The intention is that by criticizing that [signless concentration], the signless concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) would be criticized;
however, this is not done by way of its "excellent" aspect (*praṇītākāra*),
because apratisaṃkhyānirodha is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
For that which is sublime is wholesome, not indeterminate;
therefore, one does not take it as an object under the aspect of sublimity.
Furthermore, this is because apratisaṃkhyānirodha is not a state of dissociation.
One does not take that as an object by way of the aspect of "emergence.
For the separation from affliction is intended as the emergence from affliction;
since there is no emergence from cyclic existence through non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).

For even though non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) exists, for certain wholesome and unwholesome factors, there is still association with them because their possession (prāpti) has not been severed.
Regarding the phrase "because of hating the Noble Path" (āryamārgadveṣitvāt):
how does one hate it?
Because of its aversion to those [objects] through aspects such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "Of the immovable one" means of one whose nature is immovable (*akopyadharman*).
Because he possesses sharp faculties, he has the capacity to produce them, whereas another Arhat does not.

In order to turn away from those other meditative absorptions— the meditations on emptiness and so forth belonging to the Aśaikṣas— which serve as a basis for attachment because they consist in dwelling in happiness in the present life, they enter into different meditative absorptions.
(VIII.27, 28) “In detail”: there is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to dwelling in happiness in the present life.
There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the knowledge and vision of the superknowledge of the divine eye.
There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated repeatedly, leads to the differentiation of wisdom.
There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated repeatedly, leads to the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*). This is the Sūtra.
In that context, "practiced" refers to the cultivation of repeated practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).
It has been cultivated by means of the abandonment of opposing factors;
it has been practiced extensively by means of distancing oneself from opposing factors.
He said:
It has been stated that [this] conduces to the knowledge and vision of the superknowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñājñānadarśana*).
Yet, this is not the cultivation of the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) for the superknowledge of the divine eye.
To this, it is replied:
This is a metaphorical designation of the cause by the name of the fruit.
Since the supernormal power of the divine eye is the fruit of the cause that is the cultivation of meditative concentration,
there is a metaphorical designation of the cause within that fruit.
"The cultivation of concentration for the sake of knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, for those who hold this position:
"The cognition of the path of liberation is sixfold."

Thus, the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) are indeed mental paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) comprised within meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). This is not at all a point of contention, because those paths of liberation are characterized by meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
However, it should be understood that the former position alone is that of those who contemplate the Abhidharmakośa;
for the consciousnesses of the divine eye and divine ear are intended as supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*),
since they are the first of them.
"Even mutually," because it was stated as being merely by way of illustration.
It is not necessarily for the sake of dwelling in happiness in future lives.
The future life is the next world (*saṃparāya*). A pleasant dwelling therein does not necessarily result from this [present practice].
Why is this? He says:
because those who have fallen away from the first dhyāna are reborn in higher realms, such as the second dhyāna and so forth.
And for those who have attained final nirvāṇa,
because there is no dwelling in happiness in future lives,
it is "for the sake of knowledge and vision."
The compound is "for the sake of knowledge and for the sake of vision.
In this context, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

"Vision" (*darśana*) is non-conceptual wisdom associated with visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), arising from such conceptualizations as, "These beings, sirs, are possessed of misconduct of body," and so forth.
"Belonging to the three realms and untainted (*anāsrava*).

Those belonging to the three realms include the [meditation on] the foul, mindfulness of breathing, absence of strife (*araṇā*), knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and so forth.
The untainted ones include the bliss of liberation, the leap-concentration (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*), the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*), and so forth.

In this context, however, because they are associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of "cultivation of concentration" for those qualities belonging to the preparatory stage (*prāyogika*).
"For the sake of the differentiation of wisdom" means for the purpose of drawing forth excellence in wisdom (*prajñā*).

"It is said that this instruction of the Dharma by the Blessed One is 'conducive to oneself' (ātmopanāyikā). 'Conducive to oneself' means 'teaching for oneself. For the Bodhisattva, having gone forth to examine the end of his actions, produced the first dhyāna at the foot of the Jambu tree.
And at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having defeated Māra the Son of Heaven, he produced the divine eye during the first watch of the night."

Having beheld with that divine eye sentient beings situated in the perilous states of death and rebirth, he brought forth the meditative absorptions, liberations, and attainments during the middle watch of the night in order to protect them.
These qualities resulting from his preparatory application arise for the sake of the differentiation of wisdom.

Then, in the third watch, relying upon the fourth dhyāna and entering the path of certainty (*niyāma*), he brought about the abandonment of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) by means of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
And because the teaching of the Dharma is thus presented by way of one's own example,
for this reason it occurs only in the fourth [dhyāna].
It is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama*) which occurs at the end.
Thus.
(VIII.29–31) "Because it has immeasurable sentient beings as its object":
this is the reason for applying the designation "immeasurable."
"According to their respective order":
for those with an abundance of ill-will, loving-kindness is for the sake of abandoning it;
for those with an abundance of cruelty, compassion is for the sake of abandoning it.

For those with an abundance of aversion, sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is for the sake of abandoning it; for those with an abundance of sensual desire and ill-will, equanimity (*upekṣā*) is for the sake of abandoning them.
[One might ask: what is the distinction regarding their being antidotes to sensual desire?
Because of an abundance of sensual desire, there is reflection;
because of attachment to one's mother, father, children, and kinsmen, there is equanimity,
just as toward unrelated persons.
"In the same way these" means that equanimity (upekṣā) is intended [as the antidote].
"Because it is drawn out by greed" means that malice (vyāpāda) is drawn out by greed.
Therefore, the intention is that it partakes of the nature of the antidote to greed.

As for the statement "it is appropriate because it has the nature of both," the meaning is that it is appropriate to have both the nature of non-greed (*alobha*) and the nature of non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
What is the reason?
Because it is the antidote to both attachment and aversion.
Therefore, however, one should not understand that a single dharma possesses the intrinsic nature of both.
What then?
The term "equanimity" (upekṣā) applies to non-attachment (alobha) and non-hatred (adveṣa), as in the thought:
"Oh, how happy these beings are!"
The intention is: "May they be so.
"Alas, beings are suffering!
means the intention is: "May those who are suffering be liberated from suffering."
For it will be explained as follows:
since afflictions and secondary afflictions such as malice are removed,
it is therefore said to be their antidote.

To show how this is so, he says: there exist three [immeasurables], beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), belonging to the level of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and to the level of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), which resemble the fundamental immeasurables (*maula-pramāṇa*).
They are similar to the fundamental ones because of the similarity in their application (*prayoga*), object (*ālambana*), aspect (*ākāra*), and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Having suppressed those afflictions by means of those three immeasurables, one abandons them through the paths of abandonment.
Loving-kindness is for the sake of abandoning ill-will in those who abound in it; [the remaining immeasurable is practiced] because of equanimity.
The meaning is that he is neither enticed by partiality nor repelled by it.
"To those who lack faith," and so forth,
means to those who do not possess happiness.
How is it that there is no perversion because of the resolve that "there is happiness"?
It is because of the intention that "may they be [happy]";
that is, because of the intention that "may they be happy."
The intention is that there is no perversion.
Or, it is because the underlying disposition (*āśaya*) is non-perverted.

"Disposition" refers to wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*), namely those mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitta*) together with their attendants, which consist of the thought: "Oh, may sentient beings be happy!"
Because this intention is non-erroneous, it does not become erroneous.
But how is the intention non-erroneous? He says:
"because of the cognition of resolute belief."
The cognition of resolve is the "cognition of resolve.
Therefore,
because one cognizes that resolve exactly as it is.
One discerns that "this mental attention is based on resolute conviction," and that it is "unwholesome" because of its erroneous apprehension.
No, because it is wholesome.
This is not so.
Why?
Because it is a root of virtue (kuśalamūla). But how is it a root of virtue? He says:
Because they are the antidotes to ill-will and so forth:

loving-kindness (*maitrī*), having non-hatred as its intrinsic nature, is the antidote to ill-will (*vyāpāda*). Furthermore, because it has the aspect of removing suffering, compassion (*karuṇā*) becomes the antidote to cruelty (*vihiṃsā*), which has the aspect of inflicting suffering.
Sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is the antidote to [ill-will] because it is of the nature of mental gladness (*saumanasya*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*), moreover, is the antidote to sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) due to its state of neutrality (*mādhyasthya*).
Thus, [the phrase refers to] those [mental states] which have them as their objects.
The meaning is: "having as their object sentient beings belonging to the desire realm.
By means of the container, that which is contained within the container is shown;
the meaning is that by means of the location, the world of sentient beings residing in that location is shown.
"By including both the concentrated (*samāhita*) and unconcentrated (*asamāhita*), as well as the fundamental (*maula*) and preparatory (*prayoga*) stages.

The reason for stating that all three belong to six and fifteen levels (*bhūmi*) respectively is because they exist accordingly. In this context, the unconcentrated state refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The preparatory stages (*prayoga*) are the neighboring stages (*sāmantaka*); this should be applied according to what is possible.

When the six levels are established, the *anāgamya* is also accepted as a neighboring stage; thus, the neighboring stages, being of the nature of preparation (*prayoga*), are included. What, then, are the fundamental stages (*maula*)?
"Because they belong to the level of the fundamental dhyānas" means because they belong to the level of the fundamental pure (śuddhaka) dhyānas.
For it was stated previously that afflictions are not abandoned by means of the fundamental pure dhyānas.
Because they consist of mental attention directed toward resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manaskāra*), the afflictions (*kleśa*) are not abandoned by them;
for the abandonment of afflictions occurs through mental attention directed toward reality (*tattva-manaskāra*).
Furthermore, because they take sentient beings as their object (*sattvālambana*), there is no abandonment by means of them.
For it is the established tenet that the abandonment of the afflictions occurs through mental attention to the general characteristics of phenomena (*dharmasāmānyalakṣaṇamanaskāra*).
If so, how is it [attained]? He says:
"But by means of its application," and so forth.
Because ill-will and so forth are suppressed through the practice of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables],
it is said that they are their antidotes;
that is, it is stated that they are the antidotes to ill-will and the rest.
The meaning is that they are the abandonments by way of suppression (*viṣkambhaṇaprahāṇa*).

And [it is said] "because of the removal of what has been abandoned" because the afflictions and secondary afflictions, such as malice (*vyāpāda*), are removed by the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), whether mundane or supramundane.
Therefore, their nature as antidotes has been stated.
To show how this is so, he says:
"Those belonging to the level of the desire realm and those belonging to the level of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*)."
Furthermore, there exist three [states], beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which resemble the fundamental immeasurables (*maulāpramāṇa*).

Because they resemble the fundamental ones in terms of their preparatory application (*prayoga*), objective referent (*ālambana*), mental aspect (*ākāra*), and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are similar to the fundamental ones.
Having suppressed those afflictions by means of these three immeasurables, one abandons them through the paths of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), that is, the uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*).

"Even when powerful conditions are encountered" means that even when powerful conditions such as malice (vyāpāda) and so forth are encountered, one remains unassailable by those afflictions (kleśa) in terms of their actual manifestation.
"Supreme" means:
toward the side of friends; for indeed, loving-kindness is easy to practice toward a supreme friend.
"It radiates" means it pervades;
[this is] because of the manifestation of the fruit of former merit.

By observing the fruit of former merit, one who perceives virtues can regard even a person whose roots of goodness are severed as follows: "Merit was performed by this person, by which he possesses such excellence of form and so forth.
And regarding a Pratyekabuddha, one who perceives faults might think: "Surely non-merit was performed by this person, by which he has such deficiency of form and so forth.
Furthermore, resolving that "may they be liberated from suffering," one applies oneself to compassion (*karuṇā*).

Thinking, "May they indeed rejoice," one applies oneself to sympathetic joy (*muditā*) while resolving [upon it]. One is not yet "endowed with sympathetic joy" because there is an absence of mental gladness (*saumanasya*) in the third and fourth [dhyānas].
(VIII.32–34) "The eight liberations" is as stated in the Sūtra.
How so? There are eight liberations.
Which are the eight?
"One possessing form sees forms"—this is the first liberation.
"Being internally percipient of the formless, one sees forms externally"—this is the second liberation.
"Having personally realized the beautiful liberation with the body and having attained it, one dwells therein"—this is the third liberation.

By completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] "space is infinite, space is infinite," one dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space,
just like the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space.
This is the fourth liberation.

Furthermore, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, [thinking] "consciousness is infinite, consciousness is infinite," one dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness,
just like the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness.
This is the fifth liberation.
Furthermore, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing at all," one attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness,
just as the gods who have reached the sphere of nothingness.
This is the sixth liberation.
Furthermore, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, he dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
just like the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the seventh liberation.
Furthermore, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one dwells having personally realized the cessation of perception with the body and attained it.
This is the eighth liberation.
"Having form, one perceives forms": having contemplated forms within oneself, one also perceives forms externally,
because one takes the livid corpse and so forth as objects of focus.
"The method [of meditation] should be understood as being like that of the foul (aśubha).
This should be applied in detail, as appropriate, beginning with the antidote for those with excessive passion, such as passion for beauty and so forth.
"The foul is non-greed, belonging to ten stages, having the visible objects of the desire realm as its object, and arising in humans."
"Respectively":
the liberation belonging to the level of the first dhyāna is the antidote to the passion for color-form (*varṇarāga*) of the desire realm;
the liberation belonging to the level of the second dhyāna is the antidote to the passion for color-form belonging to the level of the first dhyāna as well.
Furthermore, these two should be understood as counteragents through distancing (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*). He asks:
"How is it known that there is no passion for color (*varṇarāga*) in the second and subsequent dhyānas?"
Because of the absence of visual consciousness. For whoever is detached from a particular object is necessarily also detached from the consciousness that apprehends it.
And since visual consciousness and the others do not exist in the second and subsequent dhyānas,
it is established that they are free from passion for color-form (*varṇa-vītarāga*). [This applies to] the pure formless [attainments].
Thus [are] the pure and the untainted.
(Abhidh-k-vy 689) There are also others that are non-concentrated.
This is said with reference to the mind and mental factors born of maturation (*vipākaja*) within the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
However, according to the former position, it shows that the formless states are indeed non-concentrated (*asamāhita*) precisely during the state of the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*).
Furthermore, even the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) receive the designation "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).
"How much more so for those born there?"—this is the meaning of the word "api" (even).
"Not in the path of immediate succession," and so forth; because they are called "liberations" (vimokṣa) due to their turning away from the lower stages.
Therefore, the paths of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) do not receive the designation "liberation" (vimokṣa),
because they have a lower object;
however, the paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) do receive it.
Because it has the upper realms as its object.
But cessation is an attainment;
"the eighth" is the completion of the sentence.
"Because of turning away from perception and feeling":
liberation arises from turning away from perception and from turning away from feeling;
or alternatively, liberation arises from turning away from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
It is called "liberation" (vimokṣa) because it liberates one from the hindrances to meditative attainment (*samāpatti-āvaraṇa*).
It is called "liberation" because it turns away from those hindrances to meditative attainment.

In this context, the "hindrance to meditative attainment" refers to that hindrance due to which there is unworkability of mind (*cittākarmaṇyatā*), such that even those who are free from passion for the three realms (*traidhātuka-vītarāga*) cannot produce even the first fundamental dhyāna (*maula-dhyāna*).
"According to the case" means that for two [of the meditations], the object is unattractive form, such as a livid corpse and so forth;
for the third, the object is attractive form.
"And its cause and cessation" refers to the origin and the cessation of that suffering. And "the entire category of subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna) is included.
The meaning is that [the object] belongs to the levels above, below, or its own level.
And regarding "apratisaṃkhyānirodha" (cessation not through deliberation):
it should be stated that apratisaṃkhyānirodha is also the object of the formless liberations (ārūpyavimokṣa).

But those which are formless have as their objects the suffering and so forth belonging to their own level, to the higher levels, and to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), because of the statement: "those which are formless [have as their objects] the suffering and so forth of the category of subsequent knowledge, of the higher levels, and of their own level."
He asked: "But which non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) is their object?
To this it is said:
They take as their object the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

And these [concentrations] exist in eleven levels—excluding the seven preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*): namely, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four dhyānas, and the eight formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Thus, by including this supplementary enumeration, the definition of a treatise (*śāstra*) is demonstrated.
And as for "space belongs to one," it must be stated that the object of the liberation of the sphere of infinite space is [space],
because there is an absence of attachment to the colors belonging to the level of the second dhyāna.
The meaning is that there is an absence of the passion for color belonging to the level of the second dhyāna which ought to be countered.
That absence [of such passion] is due to the absence of bodily consciousness and because [the second dhyāna] is shaken by the essence of pleasure (*sukhamaṇḍa*).
It is the essence of bliss;
the meaning is that it is the bliss situated above all other blisses.
Because of being stirred by that—that is, because of being shaken by it.
The liberation is not established in the third dhyāna.
If there is no attachment to color belonging to the level of the third dhyāna, why does one produce the beautiful liberation?
Therefore he says: "In order to gladden a mental continuum that has become sluggish through the meditation on the foul, or for the sake of inquiry.
Regarding the phrase "of the liberations, etc.," the word "etc. includes the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth.
It is for the purpose of distancing the afflictions,
because [the meditative absorptions] such as the liberations serve as the antidotes that distance them;
and it is also for the purpose of attaining mastery over meditative attainments.
And that mastery over meditative attainments serves for the production of qualities such as the absence of strife (araṇa),
as well as for noble supernatural power (ṛddhi).
What [is it for]?
"For the sake of accomplishment" is the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, that [accomplishment] consists of the transformation of objects, the sustaining of power, the relinquishing of life, and so forth.
Among these, "transformation of objects" refers to:
Whatever object one resolves upon in a certain way,
it becomes exactly so;
just as clay is transformed into gold.

Likewise, through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), there is the stabilization of a firm object; [this occurs] by thinking, "May this remain for such a length of time. Similarly, there is the relinquishing of one's lifespan. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the entry of Mount Sumeru into an atom and other such [miracles] mentioned in the Sūtras are to be understood.
Why is direct realization (sākṣātkaraṇa) mentioned only for the third and eighth [liberations], and not for the others?
How is direct realization mentioned for the third?
"Having personally realized with the body the beautiful liberation and having attained it, one dwells therein.
This applies to the eighth [liberation] as well:
"Having personally realized with the body the cessation of perception and feeling and having attained it, one dwells therein."
In this context, "having realized" means having made manifest through direct perception.
"Having attained and dwelling" means having entered that meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and dwelling therein.
To this, it is said:
Because the third liberation is superior to the first and second liberations;
due to the complete abandonment of the obscurations to the liberations from form and through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), the realization of the third is said to occur.
Likewise, it is because the eighth [liberation] is also superior.
It is said that realization occurs through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) by means of the complete abandonment of the obstructions to the formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*).
Furthermore, it is because [the fourth dhyāna] abides at the limit of the realms and stages (*dhātubhūmiparyanta*);
for the fourth dhyāna abides at the limit of the stages of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
The peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is also situated at the limit of the stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Thus, "the superior" refers to the detailed explanation beginning with:
"Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are superior—whether beautiful or ugly"—up to "this is the second sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)."
"Being percipient of the formless internally, it is exactly thus.
How so?
Being percipient of the formless internally, one sees forms externally that are limited, beautiful or ugly—as before—up to "this is the third sphere of mastery."
Likewise, one who is internally percipient of the formless perceives external forms that are extensive, beautiful or ugly; as before, up to: this is the third sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Likewise, one who is internally percipient of the formless perceives [external forms] that are extensive, beautiful or ugly; as before, up to: this is the fourth sphere of mastery. These are the four.
Furthermore, being precisely percipient of the formless, one perceives blue, yellow, red, and white.
How so?

Being without the perception of internal forms, one sees external forms that are blue, blue in color, appearing blue, and shining with blue light—just like an *umakā* flower or a fine cloth from Vārāṇasī that is blue, blue in color, appearing blue, and shining with blue light. Having indeed mastered those forms...
He knows and sees having overcome [them]. He possesses such a perception; this is the fifth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Internally perceiving no form, he sees external forms that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster.
For example, like a *karṇikāra* flower or a Benares cloth that is yellow—this is the detailed description.
This is the sixth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Being internally percipient of the formless, one sees forms that are red, of red color, appearing red, and radiant with red light.
For example, like a *baṃdhūka* flower, or like a fine cloth from Vārāṇasī that is red—this is the detailed description.
This is the seventh sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.
For example: "like the star Uśanas, or like a fine Benares cloth, pure white," and so forth.
This is the eighth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
These four, together with the four at the summit (*mūrdhaka*), constitute the eight.
"The first two are like the first liberation.
This means that just as the first liberation is "one possessing form who sees forms," [so too are these two].
Seeing forms within oneself, one sees forms externally; such is the case with the first two spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
For in those two, while seeing forms within oneself, one sees them externally.
For it is recited thus:
"Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited," and so forth;
the second [meditative attainment] is likewise.
However, this is the distinction: one sees external forms as superior.

Furthermore, just as the first liberation belongs to the level of the first dhyāna, serves as the antidote to attachment to the colors of the desire realm, and has the form-sphere (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire realm as its object, so too should these two first spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) be understood.
"Two are like the second" means that just as the second liberation is characterized by one who, being internally percipient of the formless, sees forms externally, so too are these two.
The third and fourth spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) have such characteristics.
For they are recited as follows:
"Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited"—this is recited as the third.
The fourth is recited as: "Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms as vast.

Furthermore, just as the second liberation belongs to the level of the second dhyāna, serves as the antidote to attachment to the colors belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, and has as its object the forms of the desire realm, so too do the third and fourth spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Furthermore, the others are like the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*).

Just as the pure liberation belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna and has as its object the sphere of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*) that is agreeable and belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
Likewise, there are the spheres of mastery over blue, yellow, red, and white;
however, here only the four colors are taken separately.
Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of the beautiful liberation is non-greed (*alobha*).

The same applies to these as well. Just as this pure liberation (śubho vimokṣaḥ), by virtue of including its retinue, has the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) as its intrinsic nature, so too should those [other liberations] be understood.
"By them, there is merely liberation" means that there is no overcoming of the object.
To the question, "And how is there an overcoming of the object by the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)?", he says:
"Because of resolve according to one's wish" means that they resolve upon blue, yellow, and so forth as they wish—
such as [resolving] "in one moment it is blue, in another moment it is yellow," and so on.
Or because of the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding something pleasant in what is unpleasant, such as a livid corpse (*vinīlaka*), and because of the non-arising of afflictions (*kleśa*):
even when one perceives an object that is defiled as beautiful, the afflictions do not arise; thus, by means of those spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), there is mastery over the object.

(VIII.36) "Because of the continuous and total pervasion" means: because of the continuous pervasion—that is, the encompassing—of the entire earth and so forth, they are called the "totality bases" (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
"The form base belonging to the desire realm" refers to...
Earth is said to be color and shape according to worldly convention;
likewise, water, fire, and air are also [earth] because of the statement, "the element itself."
"Regarding wind, there is only the sphere of the tangible"—
this is the view of those who do not accept the sphere of visible form within wind.
They say:
"In the case of air, the object of focus is the extension of the tangible.
Regarding the phrase "pertaining to the entry into the liberations":
the entries themselves are what is meant by "pertaining to the entry."
This is because the rule for the increase of the vowel (*vṛddhi*) applies to its own meaning;
or else, they are so called because they exist at the point of entry, since each subsequent one is more distinguished than the preceding.
Because the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are superior and more distinguished than the liberations (vimokṣa),
and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are superior and more distinguished than the spheres of mastery;
this is what is meant.

Having produced the liberations (vimokṣa), one produces the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana). Having produced the spheres of mastery, one produces the totalities (kṛtsnāyatana). This is said with the exception of the liberation of cessation (nirodhavimokṣa).
Because it belongs exclusively to the continuum of an Ārya.
(VIII.37) "Because of being practiced or unpracticed":
those that are practiced are obtained through the attainment of detachment (*vairāgya*).
The unaccustomed [states] are those acquired through application.
"The rest," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
What, then, remains?
The first three liberations, the eight bases of mastery,
and the eight bases of totality.
This [attainment] has only the human state as its basis.
For what reason?
Because it is produced through the power of instruction.
Because there is no teaching [of such things] elsewhere, such as among the gods and so forth.
(VIII.38) How is it that the production of the specific formless attainments and dhyānas occurs in the form and formless realms?
[It occurs] in whichever level within the formless realm or the form realm one has been reborn.
That which is formless (*ārūpya*) and meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) above that is superior to it; thus, they are called the "distinctions of formless absorption.
How can there be such a distinction of formless absorption without instruction?
Since the remainder has its basis solely in human beings,
and it has been stated that [this knowledge] is produced through the power of instruction,
it was asked in connection with this point.
"How [is it] in the realms of form and formlessness? and so forth.
"Because of weak causes, and because of practice that is proximate and frequent" means:
because of practice that is both proximate and frequent.
How so?
Suppose someone enters a formless attainment (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and, having fallen away from it, is reborn immediately thereafter in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Due to the superior strength of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) characterized by the formless attainment, that person will give rise to a formless attainment while in the realm of form.
Also due to repeated practice (*abhīkṣṇābhyāsa*).
If someone, having repeatedly entered an attainment of the formless realm (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and subsequently fallen away from it, is reborn in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*),

an attainment of the formless realm arises for him even in the realm of form because of the superior strength of that homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) characterized by the attainment of the formless realm.

In the same way, for one who has fallen away from the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) and is reborn in the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana), there is likewise the production of those attainments.
The same applies to one reborn in a realm above that,
and also through the power of karma.
Because for one born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) has become present,
the continuum (*saṃtati*) remains established in a state conducive to detachment from that realm.
For it is not possible for one who is not yet free from passion for the lower realms to be reborn above in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Thus, for one born in the formless realms in the sphere of infinite space, by the power of karma—
because the ripening of karma to be experienced in a subsequent life, belonging to a higher level, namely the level of the sphere of infinite consciousness, has become present—
the continuum remains established in a manner conducive to detachment from that [lower level].
For it is not possible for one who has not yet abandoned passion for a lower level to be reborn in a higher one.
And by means of these two— namely, the power of causes and the power of karma—
how is it that the second and subsequent dhyānas are produced within the first and other dhyānas?
And by the power of the cause, that is, from near or repeated practice;
and by the power of karma, namely that of a higher stage—this should be applied in detail.
And also "by way of the nature of things" (dharmatā).
What is meant by "dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena)?
First, some Sautrāntikas say:

it is the conformity, the natural state, and the intrinsic nature that exists for these very same phenomena when their activity has become manifest, which—due to the predominance of prior meditative impressions (*vāsanā*)—conduces to the arising of meditation even without instruction when such meditation is produced.
This is the meaning.
Some Vaibhāṣikas also say:
the production of meditative absorption is the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) resulting from a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) belonging to a previous birth.
"Without that instruction, there is no other source for the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)" means that the wholesome factors (kuśala-dharma) have attained a manifest activity.
In this context, the meaning is that during the period of world-destruction (saṃvartanī-kāla), the wholesome paths of action (karmapatha) [attain such activity].
Their "activity" (*vṛtti*) is the functional efficacy (*kāritra*) of those very dharmas.
They are called "those whose activity is manifest" (*udbhūtavṛttayaḥ*) because their activity is arisen and preeminent; the state of being so is "the condition of having manifest activity."
Therefore,
this is what is meant:

because those wholesome states attain their own nature through excellence, and because they attain their own nature in a manner conducive to the arising of that [meditation], meditation arises from another source even without instruction, provided there exists a prior latent impression (*vāsanā*) of meditation.

(VIII.39) "These are such categories of phenomena" means that the categories of contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena— such as their realms (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), objects (*ālambana*), and aspects (*ākāra*)— are according to their respective applications. Furthermore,
"those who uphold them" refers to those who speak of them and those who practice them.
Of that True Dharma, which consists of scripture and realization, those who respectively proclaim the scripture are its preservers;
and those who practice the realization are its preservers as well.
"These are its sustainers.
"In this way, regarding realization.
"Its duration is one thousand years."
"But for a much longer time regarding the scripture" means even beyond a thousand years.
We consider this very position to be the logical one.
(VIII.40) "That which is this," and so forth.
That which has been stated here in the Abhidharma characterized by the *Abhidharmakośa*— what is it?
This very Abhidharma of the treatise, characterized by the *Jñānaprasthāna* and so forth, has been taught; therefore, this is said:
"established according to the system of the Kaśmīra Vaibhāṣikas," and so on in detail.
Those who exist in Kaśmīra are the Kāśmīras.
It has been explained that those who sport with the Vibhāṣā are the Vaibhāṣikas.
There are Kāśmīras who are not Vaibhāṣikas.
Those who are experts in the Vinaya and so forth are the Sautrāntikas, such as the Bhadantas and others.
There are Vaibhāṣikas who are not from Kaśmīra;
those Vaibhāṣikas who are from outside [Kaśmīra]—this is the qualification of both.
The Abhidharma established according to their system has for the most part been taught by me here.
By implication, this is what is meant.
Whatever has been wrongly grasped— whether by the system of the Kaśmīra Vaibhāṣikas or by another system— even though it was taught as established by another [non-Buddhist] doctrine.
Therefore, in this statement,
there is no fault on our part.
This is not a fault.
Why? It says:
"In the system of the true Dharma, the sages are the authority."

Thus, in the exposition of the principle (*nīti*) of the True Dharma, characterized by scripture (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*), the Sages— the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Sons of the Buddha such as the Venerable Śāradvatīputra and others— are the authority; that is to say, they are the trustworthy ones (*āpta*) regarding the awakening to all phenomena in all their aspects.
(VIII.41–43) “When the Teacher, the eye of the world, has closed his eyes”:
when the Blessed One, who had become the eye of the world and the one who reveals the path and the non-path, has entered final nirvāṇa.
By this, he shows that the world has become blind.
"And when the witness-people have mostly passed away":

a witness (*sākṣin*) is one who sees directly; the Blessed One is the witness who knows the path and the non-path. Those who have realized the truth and have become companions to the Blessed One constitute the "witness-people. When they have perished through his final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*).
Blinded by ignorance,
they have not seen reality; they are unrestrained and unchecked.
Due to being a dogmatist through one's own [views] and [relying on] fallacious reasoning—
Since you have entered the teaching of the Blessed One, both in its letter and its spirit...
It has been thrown into confusion,
for when the Self-Existent One had himself attained supreme peace.
This second verse is presented as the reason for the meaning stated in the preceding verse: "For when the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddha have entered parinirvāṇa..."
In this world left without a protector, due to the causes for the disappearance of the Teaching,
such as [wrong] views and so forth.
By impurities and unrestrained defects acting at will.
According to one's desire in this world.
It is practiced now, at this very moment.
This is a derivation based on the state of being (*bhāva-sādhana*);
and thus,
when the vital breath has reached the throat in this manner—
The meaning is "as if the vital breath has reached the throat.
Having understood that, as well as the time for [overcoming] the impurities, [one should act].
"Having understood the faults, those seeking liberation must not be negligent"—
this is the derivation based on the accomplishment of the state (*bhāvasādhana*).
(Abhidh-k-vy 696) [blank] (Abhidh-k-vy 697) IX (The Determination of the Person)
Is it indeed that there is no liberation elsewhere than this?
Because of the statement, "Those seeking liberation must not be negligent," this alone is the means to liberation.
"There is no other means to liberation than this.
By this, the Teacher has effectively stated that those who desire liberation must not be negligent. The challenger asks:
"What indeed follows from this?"—this is the detailed inquiry.
To this it is replied: "It does not exist."
He asks, "For what reason? and replies:
"Because they are settled in a false view of self.
The heterodox teachers (kutīrthya) are settled in a false view of self; thus, they are those who are settled in a false view of self.
That is its nature.
Therefore,
there is no liberation elsewhere.
This same point was also stated by the author of the hymn:
"As long as the mind possesses egoism, the continuity of birth does not come to rest;
nor does egoism move away from the heart as long as the view of a self persists."
Since there is no other teacher in the world who propounds selflessness, there is no path to the method of peace other than your doctrine.
And the proof for this is as follows:
Kapila, Ulūka, and others do not possess liberation,
because they are settled in false views of a self.
Like a person who has not seen reality.
And as it has been said: "The afflictions arise from the grasping at a self.

Furthermore, "whatever various speculative views there are among certain recluses and brahmins in this world, all of them are rooted in the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)," and so forth in detail.
And when the view of a self exists, the afflictions such as self-attachment and so forth arise.
This designation "self" refers only to the continuum of the aggregates (*skandha-saṃtāna*).
The meaning is that the designation "self" is a mere conceptual construct (*ātma-prajñapti*).
The meaning is that [the self] is not imagined as another denotable object distinct from the continuum of the aggregates (skandhas).
Why is this so? He says:
"Because of the absence of direct perception and inference."
The intention is that because perception and inference do not exist [for them], they have no existence.
Scripture is not mentioned separately because it is included within inference. For them, perception is apprehension.
"Direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is a qualification of apprehension (*upalabdhi*).
"Direct perception" means that apprehension is direct; that is, apprehension by way of direct perception.
Alternatively, "direct perception" is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it is "apprehension" because one apprehends by means of it.
"When there is no obstacle" means:
when there is no impediment to perception— such as being too near or too far—
in relation to those six objects.

Of the sense-bases of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects; of the sense-base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) characterized by feeling and so forth, which is the object of yogis and transcends scripture and conceptual construction;
and of the mind—what [is it]?
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is apprehension.
For the mind (*manas*), having just ceased, is known by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arising immediately thereafter—

such as [knowing] "it is lustful," "it is hateful," "it is associated with pleasure," or "it is associated with pain," and so forth— according to others, because of its self-cognizability (*svasaṃvedyatā*).
This direct perception (pratyakṣa) is of two kinds: that which pertains to the object (grāhya) and that which pertains to the subject (grāhaka).
And there is inference (anumāna), and so forth;
[it is that] wherein direct perception does not operate.
In that regard, its apprehension is by means of inference,
as in the case of the five sense faculties— namely,
the eye faculty and so forth.
When the causes such as the field, water, and so forth are present,
it is observed that in the absence of another cause characterized as the seed, the effect called the sprout is absent;
and when that seed is present, the rebirth of the sprout is observed once again.
"For example, as in the case of a sprout" is the presentation of the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Having thus presented the illustration, he says, showing the point illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*):
"Or, while it has actually reached the range of appearance," and so forth.
Even when the object, such as form, is present and directly encountered, and when the mental attention arising from it— the cause— is also present,
the absence of the apprehension of the object, namely visual consciousness and so forth, is observed; and then again, its presence is observed.
He shows "of whom" according to their respective order:
it is the absence of those who are blind, deaf, and so forth,
and the presence of those who are not blind, deaf, and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) and others—whether impaired or unimpaired—are included.
Therefore, even in those cases, the absence or presence of some other cause that has not yet manifested its form is determined respectively [as non-existence or existence].
If one asks, "What then is that? he says:
And that other cause which is required is the sense faculty;
the intention is that this refers to the eye and so forth.
And the proof for this is as follows:

that which produces its own effect when accompanied by other causes is an entity characterized by the object and mental attention, which is recognized as the producer of the five groups of consciousness.
Because it produces its own effect only at certain times; that which produces its own effect only at certain times is a producer of its own effect when accompanied by other causes.
For example, soil and water that produce a sprout:
indeed, soil and water, when accompanied by other causes characterized by the seed, produce their own distinct effect only at certain times,
because they bring about the sprout only during the state in which the seed exists.
And because it produces its own effect during the state of the existence of the seed,
such is that entity characterized by the object and mental attention;
for in states such as those of one who is not blind or deaf, it becomes the producer of its own effect, which is characterized by the group of the five consciousnesses.
Furthermore, it does not produce [its effect] during states such as blindness or deafness.
Therefore, this [organ] produces its own effect only when accompanied by other causes;
thus, it is called a "sense-faculty" (indriya).
How is it determined that "this is a faculty"?
For all that is determined here is merely that there exists some other cause;
it is not determined that "this is a faculty."
This is indeed established.
Because it has been determined by the knowledge resulting from the great seer’s aspiration, the sense faculties such as the eye do indeed exist as the causes of visual consciousness and so forth;
furthermore, this is because there is no dispute among anyone on this point.
And thus, because it does not exist as a self, he concludes that "the self does not exist.
For in this way, the proof has been stated according to its actual meaning:
"The self does not exist."
Because it is not perceived by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
like an absolute non-entity; thus,
there is an inference.
If it is argued that the reason is therefore established, we say no; for that [reason] is itself something to be explained.
If indeed that exists,
let it be stated;
one should not object by claiming that this reason is unestablished merely on the basis of words.
As for the passage beginning "the Vātsīputrīyas," and so forth:
the Vātsīputrīyas are the noble Sāṃmitīyas.
By this, he demonstrates that the reason—characterized by being settled upon a false view of self—is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
For liberation is not denied by the Vātsīputrīyas, since they are Buddhists.
Alternatively, he shows by this [statement] that "there is no self" that this position is flawed because it contradicts their previous position.
"For the Vātsīputrīya school is our own faction.
"This must first be examined," he says;
the intention is that there is no fault in this, because in that school the person (*pudgala*) is considered to exist as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*).
When asked whether this [entity] exists substantially (*dravyataḥ*) or as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptitaḥ*), the Master replied:
"If it is a distinct entity like form (*rūpa*) and so forth, then it exists substantially.
That is to say, if it is intended that [the entity] is a distinct entity from sound and so forth, just as form and so forth are [distinct entities].
One comes to accept that the person (pudgala) exists as a substantial entity (dravyataḥ).
Form has a characteristic distinct from sound, and so forth.
If it were a collection like milk and the like, it would exist only as a designation (prajñaptitaḥ).
Just as a house of milk, an army, and so forth are not accepted as being entities distinct from [their respective] visible forms, tastes, odors, and tangibles;
nor are they distinct from grass, wood, bricks, and so forth, or from elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth.
What then?
If you say that it is merely the collection of those very [elements], then the person (pudgala) is accepted as being merely a designation (prajñapti).
For there is no entity whatsoever that exists apart from form and the rest, or from grass and the rest, or from elephants and the rest, such as "milk," "house," or "army."
What follows from this? What fault arises from this? This is the meaning.

If, first of all, the position that [the person] exists substantially (*dravyataḥ*) is adopted, then that person must be declared to be other than the aggregates (*skandha*), because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is distinct and its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is distinct.
It is not merely the collection of the aggregates,
like the aggregates in relation to one another;
for example, the aggregate of feeling is distinct from the aggregate of form and so forth, because its defining characteristic is different.
In this way, the person (pudgala) would be distinct from the aggregates (skandhas),
because the person has characteristics other than those of the form-aggregate and so forth;
furthermore, its cause must be stated.
If the intention is that it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
or if it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
then there follows the consequence of falling into the views of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
Therefore, because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the Vātsīputrīyas fall into the view of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, it would be purposeless;
for what effect do rain and sun have upon space? Their fruit exists only in leather.
If it is like a hide, it is impermanent;
if it is like space, the fruit is non-existent—
this is the meaning.
"This is a deception of the blind, its meaning not yet clarified. It is "blind" as it were, like one who is blind.
Why?
Because its meaning is not disclosed— that is, its meaning is not manifested—
[therefore] "having taken the aggregates as an object" means having grasped them.
Just as the designation "milk" occurs by taking and depending upon [the components] such as form and so forth.
There is no milk apart from [the elements] such as form (*rūpa*).
Likewise, if the designation "person" (*pudgala*) were [applied] in that way, it would follow that the person is non-existent; this is the meaning.
[The phrase] "in dependence upon the aggregates" (*skandhān pratītya*)...
If [it is argued that] "having depended upon" or "having reached" the aggregates [is the meaning], that same fault remains;

the sense is that the designation of a person (*pudgalaprajñapti*) would apply to those very aggregates themselves. Alternatively, the aggregates are the condition for the designation of a person, not the person itself.
But if the person (*pudgala*) likewise exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*),
that same fault remains:
just as fire is designated in dependence upon fuel.
The person (pudgala) exists as a substantial reality;
it is neither different nor non-different [from its constituents],
because it is designated in dependence upon its own basis of appropriation (upādāna).

For that entity which, being designated in dependence upon its own [constituent] material cause, is neither different nor non-different from it—that is a substantial reality (*dravyasat*), just like fire; such is the intention of the Vātsīputrīyas.
And for this very reason, he says:
"If it were another," and so forth in detail;
this demonstrates either a contradiction with worldly consensus or a contradiction with one's own established tenets.
[He says] "because it would follow that [the self] is eternal."
Like the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because it would entail the consequence of annihilation (*ucchedaprasaṅga*).
Like the aggregates (*skandha*).
"Unignited wood and so forth are the fuel," and so on.
By this, he demonstrates that the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For it is precisely the distinctness (*anyatva*) of fire and fuel that is intended.
Therefore, it is said that "it is ignited and burned by that.
By that fire,
that fuel is ignited.
The meaning is that it blazes; it is burned, that is, reduced to ashes,
because it brings about a transformation in the continuum.
The meaning is "because it produces ashes and heat.
Others say that "it is kindled" (*idhyate*) and "it is burned" (*dahyate*) are synonyms.
And both of these consist of eight substances (*aṣṭadravyaka*).
Both the fuel and the fire consist of eight substances:
the four great elements and the four derived forms, from visible form up to the tangible.
In the desire realm, that which is without sound consists of eight substances.
This is because of the established tenet [of the Sautrāntikas].
"Because they occur at different times" means that the fuel comes first and the fire comes later.
Furthermore, difference is observed between seeds and sprouts which exist at different times; consequently, [the self] would also be impermanent,
because impermanence is seen in things such as form that possess an origin.
"In that very same [instance], such as wood and so forth, it is 'ablaze'" refers to the aggregate characterized by both [aspects]. Furthermore,
the distinctness of those two is established because of the difference in their characteristics.
Thus, for these two—fire and fuel—which possess such characteristics, their distinctness is established by the difference in their characteristics.
This is because the earth element and the others have different characteristics;
for indeed, distinctness is observed among things with different characteristics, such as form, sensation, and so forth.
"But the meaning of 'derived' (upādāya) must be stated.
The intention is that [the effect] is not something other [than its cause].
For that [effect] is not the cause of that [cause].
For that fuel, characterized by the three primary elements, cannot logically be the cause of that fire characterized by heat,
because they are co-nascent.
It is like the left and right horns of a cow.
Nor is it [the basis] for that designation; that is, not for the designation "fire."
If it means "basis" (āśraya), the meaning is "having taken up fuel" or "relying upon fuel. Alternatively, it may mean "coexistence" (sahabhāva).
The meaning is simultaneous arising.
The meaning is that fuel is not grasped as being co-existent.
[If it were so grasped,] they would result in being co-existent with their own substratum.
The meaning is that they attain [the state of] being the basis and being co-existent.
The Vātsīputrīyas clearly assert a distinctness from the aggregates (skandha).
"The absence of that" refers to this.
"In the absence of the aggregates" means "because it has the nature of other elements," that is,
because it has the nature of the earth element and so forth.
"Anything else as well" means that it is not only heat itself that is hot;
rather, other things such as earth and so forth, when in contact with a blazing fire, are also established as being hot.
Therefore, there is no fault in its being something else.
The same applies to this [person] as well. Consequently, it would be "inexpressible," which would result in the abandonment of that [former] position.
"Wood and so forth" refers to wood, grass, cow dung, and the like.
"Inexpressible" refers to the *pudgala*.
Because it is undifferentiated, it possesses a neuter gender;
thus, as in the example "What has been born to you?",
it follows that nothing need be said.
Regarding the statement "the knowable is fivefold," how then should it be stated? He says:
"Indeed, that [unconditioned] should not be called the fifth among the past and so forth, nor should it be called non-fifth.
"The same applies to form," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
The designation of form (rūpa) must also be explained.
Since it is perceived when the eye and so forth exist, form is designated in dependence upon those eyes and so forth.
"Discerns" (prativibhāvayati) means "perceives" (upalakṣayati).
Because it has that as its material cause (*upādāna*).
However, it should not be said whether it is "forms" (*rūpa*) or "not forms," because it does not possess the characteristics of those and because it is inexpressible (*avaktavya*).
In this way, up to "whether it is dharma or not," one discerns both milk and water;
these are two examples.
Therefore, it should be stated as follows:
if one perceives milk in dependence upon forms cognizable by the eye, then milk should be said to be cognizable by the eye;
however, it should not be so stated.
Whether they are forms or not— all of this must be stated in the same way:
if one perceives water in dependence upon forms cognizable by the eye.
Water should be said to be cognizable by the eye;
however, it should not be said to be either "forms" or "not forms"— this applies to everything.
Lest there be the undesirable consequence that milk and water would each possess four [sensory objects],
if one were to say "visible forms," or even if one were to say "tangible objects," it would follow that either the milk or the water would possess four [sensory objects].
The meaning is that one obtains milk or water in four ways.
Since sound is adventitious, it is not relevant here.
Therefore, just as form and the other [sensory constituents] alone, when combined and assembled, are designated as "milk" or "water," [so too are they designated as such].
Thus, it is established that the aggregates alone, taken together, are designated as the "person" (pudgala).
[The opponent argues: "Forms are the cause for the apprehension of the person; therefore, one who apprehends forms apprehends the person.
What is the difference between these two positions?
In the first position, the causality of forms is under consideration; in the second, however, it is not their causality.
What then?
Regarding the statement, "The person is perceived in dependence upon forms":
if it is accepted that forms are the cause [of that perception],
then that person must not be said to be something other than those forms.
In that case, this consequence follows for you:
"Form as well," and so forth.
Just as forms are the cause for the apprehension of a person (pudgala), yet it cannot be said that the person is other than them.
Light, the eye, and mental attention are also causes for the perception of form.
Therefore, you must not say that this form is something other than those factors such as light,
because they are the causes for its perception.
Because those factors such as light are the causes for the perception of form,
it follows that the person (*pudgala*) has a nature non-different from form,
since it is perceived by that very same single perception.
Like another form (*rūpāntara*).
Or rather, its designation (*prajñapti*) is in the very form itself.
The phrase "it follows that it is a designation of a person (*pudgala*)" is understood to carry over.
Why?
For that very reason.
And this is form, and so forth, in detail.
If apprehension were one and the same for both form and the person, a distinction between them would not be possible.
Yet, if it is not distinguished in this way, one cannot say,
"this is form" and "this is the person."
How can both be asserted?
For only form itself should be asserted,
because of the existence of its perception.
In this same way, it should be stated up to the dharmas. How so? As it is said:

"What is the meaning of this statement: 'Depending on sounds cognizable by the auditory faculty, one discerns a person'? Does it mean that sounds are the cause for the apprehension of a person, or rather that while apprehending sounds, one apprehends a person?
If, first of all, sounds are the cause for the apprehension of a person..."
And it should not be said that it is something other than those [causes].
If that is so, then sound also should not be said to be something other than light, the auditory faculty, and attention,
because these are the causes for its perception.
Now, when perceiving sounds, does one perceive the person by means of that very same perception,
or by means of another?
If, by that very [reasoning], the person (pudgala) were to result in having an identical nature with the sound, or if the sound itself were its designation,
then how could it be distinguished that "this is the sound" and "this is the person"?
If it is not determined in this way,
how is it fully understood that "sound exists" and "the person (pudgala) also exists"?

For its existence is known by virtue of its apprehension. Following this same direction, [this principle] should be applied to all factors (dharmas) up to the point of saying "yellow as opposed to blue."
When blue is perceived through discernment, yellow is not perceived at that time; however,
it is perceived later.
It is perceived by means of a perception other [than that of the object itself]. And it is recognized that yellow is other than blue;
likewise, the person (pudgala) is perceived by means of a perception other [than that of the aggregates].
It follows that [the self] would be other than form (*rūpa*).
In the same way, one moment must be cited as being other than the subsequent moment;
and so it should be stated for all factors (*dharma*) up to the end.
How so?
Furthermore, because it is perceived at a different time by means of another [perception], it follows that the sound is different,
just as the sound of a clay drum is different from the sound of a kettle-drum.
And from one moment as if to another moment;
just as it was previously stated:
"as yellow from blue, so from one moment to another moment."
The distinctness [of things] has already been demonstrated by their being perceived at different times, whether the objects have distinct characteristics or non-distinct characteristics.
Now, the phrase "in another way" should be applied in detail up to the case of the *dharmas*.
He says: "like form (*rūpa*) and the person (*pudgala*)," and so forth.

If one were to say that just as the identity or difference between form (*rūpa*) and the person (*pudgala*) is inexpressible, so too the identity or difference between their respective perceptions (*upalabdhi*) is inexpressible—then, by that logic, even the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) would become inexpressible; for this very perception characterized by the conditioned would also be inexpressible.
This would constitute a deviation from established doctrine (*siddhāntabheda*).
This established tenet— that the person (*pudgala*) alone is inexpressible—
is contradicted by the view that even the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inexpressible.
"And if this... and so forth.
If it were as you say, then one should not have said, "Are these forms such-and-such or not? Rather, why did the Blessed One say, "Form is non-self," up to "Consciousness is non-self"?
By speaking thus, it is shown that the person (*pudgala*) must indeed be expressible and not inexpressible;
[this is] "like sound and so forth."
The person (pudgala) is not perceived by means of the consciousness of form, because it does not serve as its objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
just like sound.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), one should here apply [the qualities] such as "possessing odor" (*gandhavat*) and "possessing taste" (*rasavat*).
In this same way, its non-perception by the consciousnesses of the ear and so forth must be stated.
This is the general direction.

By this presentation, it should be understood that the fault of a proposition involving a contradiction regarding the specific nature of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparyayapratijñādoṣa*) is being exposed.
"In dependence upon a dyad" means in dependence upon a dyad, but not in dependence upon a triad.
Therefore, this is contrary to the sūtra.
"The eye, O monk, is the cause," and so forth.
A cause (*hetu*) is an immediate condition (*pratyaya*).
But the remote [condition] is the condition alone. Others maintain that the cause is the producer, whereas the condition is merely the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Others say that these two are synonyms.
[If so,] there follows the undesirable consequence of the position that the person (pudgala) is something other than form (rūpa),
because it is cognizable by auditory consciousness, just like sound.
Likewise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the thesis that the person (pudgala) is other than sound,
because it is cognizable by visual consciousness, just like visible form.
In this same manner, the argument should be applied to other cases as well.
It follows as a consequence that the person (pudgala) is something other than form and sound,
because it is cognizable by the olfactory consciousness,
just like odor.
This is the direction [of the argument] regarding "a yojana each.
Because of the statement that they "experience their respective spheres of activity," it is implied that they experience them by means of a person (*pudgala*).
And the mind is their point of reliance.
This was stated as a secondary point;
it is not the primary example.
Nevertheless, the meaning is that since the mind is the resort of these sense-faculties, the sense-faculties serve as causes for the arising of consciousness in dependence upon it.
Or rather, the person (*pudgala*) is not an object.
If the Sūtra is taken as authoritative, then what [follows]? To this he says:
If it is not an object:
if it is not the object of any consciousness, then it is not cognizable.
Consequently, your own established tenet that "the cognizable is fivefold" would be contradicted.

If, on the basis of such scriptural statements, it is established as authoritative that the five [faculties] beginning with the eye do not experience the range and object of one another— that is, their non-deviation from their own respective objects— then, given this non-deviation from their own objects, the person (*pudgala*) cannot be cognized by visual consciousness and the others.
This being so, it follows that the mental faculty (*manaindriya*) would also be non-deviant.
For it is stated at length in the Sūtra: "These six faculties have different spheres of activity.
[For example: Six living beings—a dog, a bird, a jackal, a crocodile, a snake, and a monkey—were bound together by someone, tied with a knot in the middle, and released.
They each desire their own respective range of objects, because they long for villages, open spaces, cemeteries, water’s edge, anthills, and forests.
In the very same way, these six sense faculties each desire their own respective range of objects.
Thus, this is merely an illustration.
Now, even though there is a scriptural statement [to the contrary], there is a deviation regarding the mind-faculty (*manaindriya*).
Likewise, there is a deviation regarding the other faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
And if there were deviation, the person would become cognizable by visual consciousness and the others.
To this we say:
"Not there," and so forth.
In that regard, in the *Ṣaṭprāṇakopama-sūtra*, it is not stated that the eye and so forth are faculties (*indriya*) by virtue of being faculties [in the technical sense]. What is the reason?
Because it is impossible for the five faculties, such as the eye, to have a desire for seeing and so forth.

Because for these [objects], such as visible form, there is no possibility of desiring to see, hear, and so forth, due to their nature as matter (*rūpa-svabhāva*); and because for their respective consciousnesses—
the visual consciousness and the others— there is likewise no possibility of desiring to see and so forth.
Why is it that the desire for seeing, hearing, and so forth is not possible for these [senses]?
Because they are non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*).
However, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) induced by their predominance is called a "sense-faculty" (*indriya*) in the sense that it is *like* a sense-faculty.
How is it known that this [consciousness] is drawn forth by the predominance of those [senses]?
For if visual consciousness and the rest were not produced through the doors of the eye and so forth,
how else could conceptual mental consciousness be produced?
From this it is known that [it is] "drawn forth by the predominance of that.
That mental consciousness, having become the sense faculties such as the eye, desires its own respective objective spheres, such as visible form and so forth.
And as for that which is "exclusive," and so forth:
it does not at all desire the objects of the other [faculties], such as the eye and so on, which are brought forward through the sovereignty of the mind.
What then?
It takes as its object only its own sphere, namely the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana) alone;
therefore, this fault does not apply.
As for what was said—that if this were so, it would follow that the mental faculty (manaindriya) also lacks deviation—[that objection is refuted].
The person is not [to be known].
What [is not]?
That it is to be directly known and fully understood.
Therefore, this person (pudgala) is not even something to be cognized (vijñeya).
But has it not been stated that, by implication, it is neither to be directly known (abhijñeya) nor to be fully understood (parijñeya)?
It was not stated, however, that the object (artha) is to be cognized.
Therefore he says:
"Because wisdom (*prajñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) have the same object.
For even the eye and so forth are objects of consciousness (*vijñeya*).
It is not only to be directly known (*abhijñeya*) but also to be fully understood (*parijñeya*). "By means of the non-self" means by means of the eye and eye-consciousness.
And it is said that a sūtra of definitive meaning (nītārtha) is a point of reliance:
"Monks, there are these four points of reliance. What are the four?"
The Dharma is the refuge, not the person;
the meaning is the refuge, not the letter;
a sūtra of definitive meaning is the refuge, not one of interpretable meaning.
"Reliance is on knowledge, not on consciousness.

"Not having fallen into [the trap of] designation" means that one is attached to that very thing for which the designation "self" was made for the sake of conventional usage, thinking "this is the self."
"There is no sentient being or self here.
This is the example given here:
that a person (pudgala) is not perceived.
And this [is also the case];
"not even that exists" is likewise an illustrative example.
There is not even one who is capable of practicing emptiness.
From the view of a self up to the view of a living being—this is the first disadvantage, which is no different [from others].
"By the non-Buddhists"—this is the second.
The third is that he has entered upon a wrong path.
The fourth is that his mind does not enter into emptiness, nor does it even resolve upon it.
The fifth is that his noble qualities do not become purified.
"In that case, the Buddha is not their teacher.
This is said with the intention that the word of the Buddha is not an authority for them.
"Indeed, this is not the word of the Buddha," he says.
The intention is that these sūtras were interpolated by someone.
"In all other schools" refers to such schools as the Tāmraparṇīyas.
It neither contradicts the sūtra nor contradicts another sūtra.
And it does not contradict other sūtras;
nor does it subvert the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), that is, the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*):
namely, that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are without self (*anātman*).
Furthermore, these do not have the nature of a self, nor does a self exist within them;
thus, all phenomena are without self (*anātman*).
"Depending on a duality" means:
"The eye and forms, up to the mind and mental objects"—
[neither a person nor phenomena].
Regarding the statement "the self is not the aggregates, bases, or elements," it was previously said that one should not say "it is form" or "it is not form."
That which is removed or cast aside is other than the self;
therefore, all [notions] regarding the self are indeed grasping at a self.
He shows that there is nothing other than this.
"If it is so," and so forth.
If it is these very five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) that they have recollected, do recollect, or will recollect— and not a person (*pudgala*)—
then why did he say, "I was possessed of form (*rūpavān*) in past time"?

By the statement "I," it is shown that the person (pudgala) is being denoted. "Those who recollect [the self] in these various ways"— this is the ellipsis to be supplied for the phrase "they recollect thus."
In this case, the very absence of the reading would be the refuge.
For if the reading "I" (aham) were present, there would be the consequence of embracing the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); such is the meaning.
Indeed, the view of a self-identity is taught as having twenty points.
One regards form as the self;
the self as possessing form;
