or form as belonging to the self.
One should state "the self is in form," and so on up to "in consciousness. This is like a heap or a stream;
that is, like a heap and like a stream.
By the word "etc. (ādi), drinks and so forth are included.
A "heap" (rāśi) refers to many things gathered together in a single moment; a "stream" (dhārā) refers to many things gathered together over many moments.

By means of the analogy of a heap, he shows the designation of a person (*pudgalaprajñapti*) among many phenomena; by means of the analogy of a stream, [he shows] how this is understood: that when there is multiplicity, the designation of a person occurs within the flow of the aggregates (*skandha*), such as form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth.
This is the capacity of the continuum (*saṃtati*) called "Buddha."
It is said: when, by mere attention, non-erroneous knowledge arises regarding whatever is desired, but not [merely] regarding a person.
This is what is stated.
Because of the mention of the past and so forth; and those which have passed away...
Thus ends the detailed exposition.
Therefore, it is only the continuum of the aggregates (*skandha-saṃtāna*) that is designated as "Buddha," and not a person (*pudgala*).
"O monks, I shall teach you the burden," and so forth.
"O monks, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the carrier of the burden.
Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak."
What is the burden? It is the five aggregates of clinging. What is the taking up of the burden?
Craving leads to renewed existence; it is accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there.
What is the laying down of the burden?

It is the complete abandonment, relinquishment, exhaustion, disappearance, destruction, fading away, and cessation of this very craving that leads to renewed existence, which is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there.
Quiescence is cessation. Who is the bearer of the burden?
It should be said: "It is the person (pudgala).
That venerable one who has such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such a long life, such a duration of stay, and such a lifespan.
"One who carries the burden" (bhārahāra) means a bearer of the burden;
the intended meaning is the person (pudgala). This is the analysis of the compound. This is the illustrative example.
For this very reason he says:

"Indeed, the burden itself is not the bearer of the burden. This is because it would follow that even the taking up of the burden—characterized as previously described—would not be included among the aggregates (skandhas).
Otherwise, it would follow that the person (pudgala), like a burden, would not be included within the aggregates (skandha);
yet this is not accepted.
Therefore, the person is not an entity distinct from the aggregates, just as the taking up of the burden is not.
Having stated all this in detail, including the phrase "and for this very reason," one must say that it cannot be otherwise.

If the *pudgala* were a substantial entity (*dravyasat*), then in that Sūtra it would have been stated simply: "Which *pudgala* is the bearer of the burden? In that case, the opponent would not have been able to analyze it further.
"He who is that venerable one," and so forth, up to "until the end of his life.

The intention is that this further qualification is for the purpose of understanding the person as a conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*). But how is it known that he is indeed a conceptual existence?
Let it not be understood otherwise—that the person (*pudgala*) is either eternal or inexpressible as a substantially real entity.
"Of the aggregates" (*skandhānām*), and so forth:
therein, those aggregates which lead to affliction are the causes of suffering.
They are called "beings" (bhāva) because they are those who are oppressed; those who follow after them are called "bearers of the burden" (bhārahāra).
"Because of being spontaneously born (upapāduka)" means because of performing [the action] well in the process of arising.
"Because the person (pudgala) is not included among the truths" [is the meaning].

Because the person (*pudgala*), as it is conceptually imagined, is not included among the truths such as suffering and so forth— since the person is not itself suffering, nor [the origin, cessation, or] the path— therefore,
this false view that denies the person is not to be abandoned by the vision of the truths.
For whatever view is mistaken regarding whichever truth, that view is abandoned through the vision of that truth.
Likewise, because the person is not included within the truths of suffering and its origin, [the view of a self] is also not to be abandoned by cultivation.

For a defilement to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) takes as its object only a thing (*vastu*) to be abandoned by cultivation—namely, either suffering (*duḥkha*) or its origin (*samudaya*). Thus, it is logical that such [a view] is abandoned by cultivation.
However, the person (*pudgala*) is not included within those two; therefore, that [view regarding the person] is not abandoned by cultivation.
Alternatively, since a view is never abandoned by cultivation, it is not something to be abandoned by cultivation.
It is like a single sesame seed or a single grain of rice, and like a single heap or a singular expression.
Just as one speaks of "a single sesame seed" or "a single grain of rice" even though they consist of eight substances,
so too one speaks of "one heap" or "the singular."
In the same way, [the claim] that "the person (pudgala) is one" [is untenable].
Because it is admitted that it possesses origination (*utpattimat*);
by the statement "it arises," its possession of origination is admitted.
And therefore, you must say that it is "conditioned" because of the appropriation of another aggregate (*skandha*).
The intended meaning is that its state of being conditioned would not be established [otherwise].
For just as one is called "born a sacrificer" due to the acquisition of knowledge,
yet he is not born in the sense of having come into existence,
so too should everything be applied accordingly.
"But no agent is perceived," and so forth.
An agent of the action is not perceived.
Of what sort is he?
He said:

"That which casts off these aggregates of this life and abandons them, and links with and takes up other aggregates of the next life— that is what is called 'substantially existent' and 'persistently abiding'."
"Except for the conventional designation of phenomena"—thus he spoke by way of the definition of dependent origination, namely: "when this exists.
"I do not say, Phālguna, that there is one who appropriates. If I were to say, "there is one who appropriates," [it would be so].
In this regard, you may think: "Who, O Venerable One, takes up the appropriation?
Therefore, there is no appropriator of the aggregates, nor is there any one who casts them off.
And for him [the question] is likewise.
The meaning is that there is simply a new arising at every moment.
By means of such arguments as "If [it were] a person (pudgala), that is unestablished," he demonstrates the lack of proof for the example.
"Body, knowledge, and characteristic.
Knowledge and characteristic together constitute "knowledge-characteristic.
Body and knowledge-characteristic together constitute "body-knowledge-characteristic."
Just as in the case of those two— the body and the mark of knowledge—
so too it follows that the aggregates and the person are distinct,
just as the body is distinct from the knowledge that is acquired and from its mark.
The intention is that the person (pudgala) is distinct from the aggregates (skandha), which are the objects of appropriation, because [the person] is the appropriator.
The intention is that "it has grown old" and "it is diseased" refers to another body altogether, since there is a difference at every moment due to the persistence of changing states.
In this regard, he demonstrates that the example—"one who was born has grown old," or "one who was born has become diseased"—is unestablished (asiddha).
Now, it might be argued that while the body remains constant, there is the disappearance of one state and the appearance of another state.
But that is not so, for the Sāṃkhya theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) was already refuted in the previous chapter (*kośasthāna*).
How so?
For that very substratum (dharmī) does not exist,
such that one could imagine a conceptual differentiation of other properties (dharmāntara-vikalpa) belonging to it while it remains stable.
And to say "this is exactly that" is a truly unprecedented mode of expression.
"The primary elements are four and matter is one.
What is matter?
It begins with "the four great elements," and so forth.
"The fault is merely partial" means that this statement regarding the fault applies to only one side;
"the position of the *bhūtamātrikas*" means the position of the Elder Buddhadeva, not our own position.
"Nevertheless, however... [means as follows].
Even in the view that there are only the primary elements (*bhūtamātrika*), form is not other than the primary elements.

Even in the view that there are only the primary elements, just as form is not other than the primary elements, it follows that the person (*pudgala*) is not other than the aggregates (*skandha*); thus, the intention is that one would be abandoning one's own established tenet (*svasiddhānta*).
Why was it said by the Blessed One: "That life-principle..."?
"Whether that body is [the self] or something else was not explained"—this is their intention.
[They ask: "If the designation 'person' (pudgala) is applied to the aggregates (skandha), why was it not stated that the body itself is the living being (jīva)?"
"By the predecessors alone" means by the Elder Nāgasena and others. "Excessive talkers" means those who engage in much idle chatter.
The other says:
If the person (pudgala) is not to be described [as either existent or non-existent], why was it not stated that it simply does not exist?
And he is incapable of understanding such a teaching.
The meaning is that he is unfit for the teaching of selflessness.
"Previously deluded in this way" means by means of delusion accompanied by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The intention is that he would fall into even greater delusion, meaning he would give rise to another view accompanied by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
For this very reason, it says:
"I had a self; now it no longer exists for me."
And it is said here:
the Venerable Kumāralāta [states],
"and because of the non-piercing by the fangs of [wrong] views."
The full account is as follows:
view itself is the fang; by means of it, [one suffers] piercing.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach by means of dependence.
The Dharma is selflessness, which serves as its antidote;
and it is also in consideration of the failure of karmic actions.
With regard to the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*),
they teach otherwise, as if demonstrating the existence of a person (*pudgala*),
like a tigress carrying off her cub.
Thus,
just as a tigress carries away her own cub with a grip of her teeth that is not too harsh— thinking,
"May his body not be wounded by my fangs"— so it is here.
Nor does he remove it with an excessively loose grip on the teeth, lest there be a fall or dropping of it in this matter;
the meaning is that he removes it with a perfectly appropriate grip.
Others read "he removes" (apaharati) as "he removes from another place," meaning he takes it away.
Showing the cause for seeing things in such a way, he says:
"The existence of a self," and so forth.

If someone were to maintain the existence of a self, [one would say: "No, that is not so. Why? Because it has been said: "The view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the grasping of the five aggregates as 'I' and 'mine'. Therefore, since the self does not exist, how could there be a view of a self? For it is only when something exists that its apprehension occurs. Thus, because the self does not exist, the view of a self does not exist either. Consequently, how can one be said to "possess" it? Furthermore, if one were to possess the view of a self, one would necessarily possess all afflictions (*kleśa*). This is because the view of a self is the root of all afflictions. And if one possessed all afflictions, one would never be liberated from saṃsāra. However, this is not the case; therefore, the self does not exist. If it is argued that the self exists because it is the object of the notion of "I," we reply: no, because that notion is based on the aggregates. It is with respect to the aggregates that the notion of "I" arises, just as the notion of a "chariot" arises with respect to the parts of a chariot. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be perceived by the eye, etc., or it would be perceived by the mind. If it were perceived by the eye, etc., it would follow that it is material (*rūpin*), like color-form (*rūpa*). But it is not perceived by the eye, etc. Nor is it perceived by the mind, because the mind does not perceive its own nature. Moreover, if the self were perceived by the mind, it would be impermanent, like cognition (*buddhi*). But the self is held to be permanent. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would have to be either different from or identical to the aggregates. If it were different, it would be perceived separately from the aggregates, like a pot is perceived separately from cloth. But it is not so perceived. If it were identical, it would be impermanent, like the aggregates. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the agent of action or the experiencer of the result. If it were the agent, it would follow that the agent and the experiencer are different, which contradicts the principle that the doer of the deed is the same as the enjoyer of the fruit. If it were the experiencer, it would follow that the self is subject to change, like pleasure and pain. But the self is held to be unchanging. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either eternal or non-eternal. If it were eternal, it would be inactive, like space (*ākāśa*). If it were non-eternal, it would be subject to arising and ceasing, like a lamp. But the self is held to be neither. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the cause of the aggregates or the effect of the aggregates. If it were the cause, it would be prior to the aggregates, like a seed is prior to the sprout. But nothing is perceived prior to the aggregates. If it were the effect, it would be posterior to the aggregates, like a sprout is posterior to the seed. But nothing is perceived posterior to the aggregates. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the owner of the aggregates or the owned by the aggregates. If it were the owner, it would be distinct from the aggregates, like a master is distinct from his servants. But it is not perceived as distinct. If it were the owned, it would be subject to change, like a cow is subject to change. But the self is held to be unchanging. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the knower or the known. If it were the knower, it would be impermanent, like cognition. If it were the known, it would be insentient, like a pot. But the self is held to be both sentient and permanent. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the same as the body or different from the body. If it were the same, it would be destroyed at death, like the body. If it were different, it would be perceived separately from the body, like a cloth is perceived separately from a jar. But it is not so perceived. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the cause of the body or the effect of the body. If it were the cause, it would be prior to the body, like clay is prior to a pot. But nothing is perceived prior to the body. If it were the effect, it would be posterior to the body, like a pot is posterior to clay. But nothing is perceived posterior to the body. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the creator of the world or the created by the world. If it were the creator, it would be independent, like a potter. But the self is not seen to be independent. If it were the created, it would be subject to destruction, like a pot. But the self is held to be indestructible. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the soul (*jīva*) or the body (*śarīra*). If it were the soul, it would be distinct from the body, like a bird is distinct from its nest. But it is not so perceived. If it were the body, it would be subject to change, like the body itself. But the self is held to be unchanging. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the enjoyer or the enjoyed. If it were the enjoyer, it would be distinct from the objects of enjoyment, like a king is distinct from his subjects. But it is not so perceived. If it were the enjoyed, it would be insentient, like food. But the self is held to be sentient. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the perceiver or the perceived. If it were the perceiver, it would be impermanent, like the eye. If it were the perceived, it would be insentient, like color-form. But the self is held to be both. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the agent of merit or the agent of demerit. If it were the agent of merit, it would be virtuous, like a donor. If it were the agent of demerit, it would be non-virtuous, like a thief. But the self is held to be neither. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the cause of consciousness or the effect of consciousness. If it were the cause, it would be prior to consciousness, like the sense-faculties are prior to consciousness. But nothing is perceived prior to consciousness. If it were the effect, it would be posterior to consciousness, like the visual cognition is posterior to the eye. But nothing is perceived posterior to consciousness. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the support of consciousness or the supported by consciousness. If it were the support, it would be distinct from consciousness, like a wall is distinct from a painting. But it is not so perceived. If it were the supported, it would be impermanent, like the painting. But the self is held to be permanent. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the object of the notion of "I" or the subject of the notion of "I. If it were the object, it would be external, like a pot. If it were the subject, it would be impermanent, like the mind. But the self is held to be internal and permanent. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the same as the five aggregates or different from them. If it were the same, it would be impermanent, like the aggregates. If it were different, it would be perceived separately from the aggregates, like a horse is perceived separately from a cow. But it is not so perceived. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the cause of birth or the effect of birth. If it were the cause, it would be prior to birth, like the seed is prior to the sprout. But nothing is perceived prior to birth. If it were the effect, it would be posterior to birth, like the sprout is posterior to the seed. But nothing is perceived posterior to birth. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the cause of death or the effect of death. If it were the cause, it would be prior to death, like the life-force is prior to death. But nothing is perceived prior to death. If it were the effect, it would be posterior to death, like the corpse is posterior to death. But nothing is perceived posterior to death. Therefore, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the self existed, it would be either the cause of saṃsā
He is pierced by the fang of views, characterized by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
There would be a person to be trained who,
not having attained the conventional mode of existence,
does not understand the conventional designation of phenomena.
The ruin of the cub of virtue— that is, of wholesome karma— which has become like a tigress's cub.
One should say: "There is no fruit of action. This is merely conventional designation (*prājñaptika*).
Thus, existence within designation is merely designated.
Fearing that someone might grasp that even the conventionally existent person does not exist,
he did not say that it does not exist.
"But if it exists, why did he not say 'it exists'?
[The question is: if the person (*pudgala*) exists in an ultimate sense (*bhūtārthena*), for what reason did the Blessed One not say, "the person exists"?
For there is no fault in the statement "form exists," because it does indeed exist.
This is like the case of the Nirgrantha’s disciple and the sparrow.
A Nirgrantha disciple, having caught a live sparrow, questioned the Blessed One about it.
"Does this sparrow live or not?
His intention was this: if the ascetic Gautama were to declare, "It lives," he would kill it by squeezing it and show it [to him] dead.
If, however, the Blessed One were to declare, "He is dead," he would show him as being very much alive. His intention was: "How might the world come to know that this man is ignorant?"
However, the Blessed One, having understood his intention, did not provide a definitive answer;
rather, he stated only: "Whether this [being] lives or not depends entirely upon your own mind.
In the same way, this [matter] was not definitively answered.
For this tetrad has the same meaning as that one.
This tetrad—"the world is eternal," "the world is non-eternal"—has the same meaning as the tetrad "the world is finite," "the world is infinite.
If this is so, how can there be fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛtavastu*)?
"The world is eternal" is the first tetrad. "It is finite" is the second tetrad.
"The Tathāgata exists [after death]" is the third tetrad.
"The soul is that body" and "the soul is one thing and the body another"—this constitutes two dyads.
There are three tetrads and one dyad; thus, there are fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛtavastu*).
Even though they are established as being of the nature of synonyms, their number remains fourteen, so there is no fault.
"It is you yourself who ask this. Regarding that which you asked— whether [the world] is finite—
how so?
By the question, "Will the entire world depart by means of this path? it is asked whether [the world] is finite or non-eternal.
Or, by the question, "Is it one part of the world? it is asked whether it is both finite and infinite, and both eternal and non-eternal.
[The Buddha] answered that the person exists while living.

The intention is that [the Buddha] provides a definitive answer regarding the person (pudgala) as something existing, though it is inexpressible in terms of being either identical to or different from [the aggregates].
"Because it would entail the fault of eternalism" is the statement of the Vātsīputrīyas.
"Then why does he provide this answer? is the detailed statement of the Master (Ācārya).
The suffix *aṇ* in the word "sarvajña" (omniscient) is an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), just as in the word "yauvana" (youth).
It should not be said whether he sees or does not see;
the meaning is that it is not to be said whether he sees or does not see.
"Let it be made gradually and inexpressible," meaning that it should not be stated whether the Blessed One is omniscient or not.
The inclusion of the term "gradually" is for the purpose of avoiding provocation among those who follow the Śākya son (the Buddhists).
"From the perspective of reality, from the perspective of abiding.
This means "by way of its mode of abiding.
It is called "a basis for views."
The intention is that the basis for wrong view has been stated.
The Teacher says:
"Even 'it exists' is stated to be a basis for [wrong] view."
The meaning is that it has been stated to be the locus of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). This position has already been answered; and how so?
Because it has been rejected.
For it was rejected by the Blessed One in the Sūtra itself, in detail, up to the words, "these are without example.
This explanation of others begins with the question, "On what basis [is this said]? and so forth.
But showing how [the self] transmigrates according to his own view, he says:
"Just as a momentary fire," and so forth.
Fire is well known to be momentary;
yet it is said to "move" by means of a continuity of arisings in successive locations.
In the same way, the collection of aggregates designated as a "sentient being," which is fueled by craving and grasping, [is said to move].
"Craving is its appropriation," thus it is "one whose appropriation is craving. Although momentary, it transmigrates by way of a continuum.
"The Teacher named Sunetra."
In the *Saptasūryodayasūtra*, it is stated that this very Blessed One was once a seer named Sunetra.
[The phrase] "because of the otherness of the aggregates" means that because they are momentary, there is otherness; this is the intended meaning.
It demonstrates a single continuum (*ekasaṃtānatā*).
Since Sunetra was indeed the Buddha’s own continuum,
there is thus a metaphorical designation of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*) in saying, "I am he."
Just as one might say, "This is that very same fire which was previously seen coming while burning," it is said to be "that very same" by way of the continuity of the stream; so it is in this case.
"This would be their view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
This would mean that for these Tathāgatas, there would be a view of a self-existent body characterized by the notions of "self" and "mine.
[This refers to those] whose bonds are embraced by an even firmer attachment to self and mine.
When there is the view of a self and the view of what belongs to a self, there arises attachment to the self and attachment to what belongs to the self.
Thus, considering that passion (*rāga*) is a bond, for those whose bonds have been made firm, liberation would become remote;
the intended meaning is that it would not occur at all.

The intention is that for some, such as the Vātsīputrīyas, there is the grasping at a person (*pudgala*); for others, such as those with a Madhyamaka mind, there is the grasping at universal non-existence.
"From a particular state of mind (cittaviśeṣa) that follows upon the perception of the object of memory.

The object of memory (smṛter viṣaya) is an experienced thing. A "particular state of mind following upon the perception of the object of memory" is a specific mental state for which the cause is the perception (saṃjñā) directed toward that object.
It is only a certain [portion of] the mind, not the whole; this is the meaning.
Therefore, there occurs either recollection or recognition.
When both qualifications have been stated in this way, he asks: "From what kind of mental distinction?
He replies:
"Directed toward that," and so forth.
In that [object] which is to be remembered, there is an application of attention; thus, it is "having that as its application.

A particular state of mind (*cittaviśeṣa*) is said to possess that application, similarity, connection, perception, and so forth, because those—namely, perception and the rest—which are similar to it and connected with it, exist within it.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of aspiration, connection, repeated practice, and so on.
"Distinction of the basis," "sorrow," and "distraction" are the first among these, hence they are called "the distinction of the basis, sorrow, distraction, and so forth.
A particular state of mind whose power is unhindered by these is what is thus demonstrated by this [verse].
Therefore, memory arises from such a specific state of mind.
This is what is meant:
for one who possesses mental application (*ābhoga*), if mental application is directed toward that [object].
[Recollection] occurs for one who possesses the notion of similarity and so forth, where recollection arises from similarity;
for one who possesses the notion of a relation and so forth, where recollection arises even without similarity, such as from the sight of smoke and so forth;

and for one who possesses the basis of a formal resolve, practice, and so forth, where there is a resolve that "it should be recollected at this time," or the practice regarding that which is to be recollected, and so forth.
"Because its power is not impaired by specific conditions of the basis (*āśrayaviśeṣa*) and so forth.
This refers to impairment by a specific condition of the basis characterized by disease, by grief, by distraction due to other tasks,
and by those things included by the word "and so forth," such as karma, spells (*vidyā*), and the like.

"Even such a person," and so forth; the meaning is that even one who possesses the mental application (*ābhoga*) up to the perception (*saṃjñā*) [of the object], and whose power (*prabhāva*) is unimpaired, is "not of that lineage" (*atadanvaya*).
The meaning is "consequent upon the perception of an object that is not remembered. To cultivate means to produce.
"Of another kind" means as follows.
One who possesses non-attention toward that object, up to and including [the absence of] perception, or one whose power is unimpaired;
or [it arises] from a specific state of mind in another person.
No.
"Because of the lack of connection" means that there is no connection between the minds of Devadatta and Yajñadatta due to their not being in a cause-and-effect relationship.
Just as there is a connection between two minds belonging to a single continuum because they stand in a cause-and-effect relationship.
The relationship between the minds of Devadatta and Yajñadatta is not like this;
by this, he demonstrates the lack of similarity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*).
In that regard, if the opponent states the following proof:
The memory-consciousness does not remember an object experienced by the consciousness that experienced Devadatta’s experience, because it is other [than it],
like Yajñadatta’s consciousness.
That is not a valid proof, because the reason itself is unestablished and because the prima facie position is flawed due to contradiction with direct perception.
Now, this refutation might be raised against the thesis that the mind which experiences Devadatta and the mind which recollects it are distinct.
That is not a valid refutation, because a contradiction with perceived fact (*dṛṣṭabādha*) cannot constitute a fault [in this case].
For even in your own established doctrine, the mind of recollection remembers an object that was experienced by the mind of Devadatta’s experience.
Nor do we say that one thing seen by a different consciousness is remembered by another.
The intention is that one does not remember anything else whatsoever.
The meaning is that a mind of recollection arises as something entirely distinct from the mind of perception,
because its cause exists— just as a sprout arises from an existing seed.
And recognition arises from memory alone.
When memory is present, there is recognition:
"This is that very same thing which was seen by me"—this [recognition] is due to memory.
Regarding the phrase "If that is so":
if it is only a particular state of mind (*cittaviśeṣa*) that remembers, then how is it that one says "Caitra remembers"? This is the sentence to be supplied (*vākyādhyāhāra*).
"And that too belongs to him," and so forth.

That too—namely, the continuum of the collection of conditioned factors (saṃskāra) designated as "Caitra"—is considered the causal basis for the production of change and the production in another location of that which is called a "cow. This refers to its state of being the cause for the arising of change and the arising in another place.
What is it that is called "master"? It is not the person (pudgala).
The intention is that this conventional usage depends upon the relationship between cause and effect; it does not depend upon a person (pudgala). Therefore, he says:
"But no one at all," and so forth; likewise, "Who cognizes? and so forth.
Since the self does not exist, who is it that thus cognizes?
What is the meaning of "it cognizes"?
It grasps the object by means of consciousness. Is that grasping something other than consciousness?
In that case, consciousness performs [the action]. That which performs it has already been explained.
The causes of consciousness are the sense faculties, objects, and mental attention.
Therefore, it should not be called "a particular state of mind," because it is associated with other causes such as the sense faculties.
For this very reason it is said: "according to what is appropriate"—this is the distinction.
As for the statement that "Caitra cognizes," it is spoken from the perspective of the view of existence (*bhavadṛṣṭi*) with respect to that continuum (*saṃtāna*) called Caitra.
If there is no self, to whom does this consciousness belong?
For what purpose is this genitive case used?
It is used in the sense of ownership.
Just as it has been explained in detail—who is the master of what—up until: "Furthermore, where is consciousness to be employed such that its master is sought?
It is to be employed toward the object to be cognized.
For what purpose is it to be employed?"
For the sake of understanding:
"Oh, how well-spoken are the words of those who have grown up in happiness!
For indeed, that very thing should be employed for its own purpose."
And how should it be applied?
Is it by way of production, or by way of dispatching?
Because the movement of consciousness is impossible, it is by way of production.
"In that case, the cause alone is the master," and so on in detail, up to: "For whatever is the cause of consciousness, that belongs to it alone;
and as for that which is designated as 'Caitra,' and so on in detail, up to: even there, apart from the state of being a cause, there is no state of being a master.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [it refers to the question]: "Who experiences? Whose is the sensation?"
"Who perceives? Whose is the perception? and so forth—this is the general direction [of the argument]. This also applies to one who says:
"Because an entity depends upon an agent," says the grammarian. "It must exist"—
the intention is that it must exist as a cognizer, namely, as a person (pudgala).
"Like the designation 'going' for that which goes.
Just as there is the verbal designation "goes" in expressions such as "the flame goes" or "the sound goes," just as there is the act of going belonging to the flame or to the sound.
In this way, "Devadatta goes" and "the going of Devadatta" are established;
by means of this analogy, it is understood that "Devadatta" [is the agent].
This is because [the designation] acquires its own nature through similarity.
Because the effect acquires its nature through similarity to its cause. "Even though it does nothing" means even though it does not perform any physical motion (*parispanda*).
"Having that form" means having the form of an object such as blue.
"Because of being the cause in consciousness" [is the meaning].
Consciousness is the cause of subsequent consciousness.
Therefore, because it arises as subsequent consciousness, it is said that "it cognizes.
This is because the term for an agent is applied to the cause.
This is because the cause functions as the agent.
For example, since the bell is the cause of the sound, one says "the bell rings";
it is just like that.
Regarding "lamp":
the term "lamp" is applied metaphorically to the continuum of flames,
treating it as if it were a single entity.
Just as a lamp, arising in successive locations as a continuous series,
is said to "go" to various places,
so too, within the continuum of mental states, the term "consciousness" is used figuratively.
Considering it as if it were one:
that consciousness, which is of the nature of a continuum, is said to "cognize" each respective object as it arises with respect to various objects.
The intended meaning is that it cognizes by means of the continuum—that is, through the arising of consciousness.
Or, as it is said in detail: "Just as form comes to be," and so forth.

Just as for that which comes to be (*bhavitṛ*), there is no difference in meaning from its being (*bhāva*); and for that which arises (*janitr*), from its arising (*jāti*); and for that which abides (*sthātṛ*), from its abiding (*sthiti*).
So it would be in the case of consciousness (*vijñāna*) as well.
The cognizer is not distinct from consciousness because of the existence of consciousness;
for no entity separate [from it] is perceived,
or else because of following the Vaiśeṣika Sūtras.
"Not from the self" means:
if consciousness were not produced from the self, then because there would be no distinction in the characteristic of consciousness, only a consciousness of that same kind would be produced.
However, the intention is that if it were from the self, then a specific cognition would be produced due to a specific intention of that [self].
And not by a fixed order.
Why is it that they do not arise according to a fixed order?
For they also arise without a fixed order; for instance, immediately after the cognition of a cow, there arises the cognition of a woman.
From the cognition of a woman, there arises the cognition of a buffalo.
Why does the cognition of a cow not arise immediately thereafter,
as in the case of a sprout, a stalk, a leaf, and so forth?
From the sprout, only the stalk arises, not the leaf and so forth;
from the stalk, only the leaf arises, not the flower and so forth, nor the sprout and so forth.
It is just like that.
"Of those absorbed in meditation according to their desire" means:

of those who are absorbed in meditation that is sufficient, complete, and according to their wish. "In the arising of a similar body and mind" means: in the arising of a body and a mind that are similar [to the previous ones].
"Arising by itself" means that it does not arise through the intervention of another; this is the intended meaning.
Thus, by this [explanation], the question "Why does it not always arise as exactly similar? has been answered.
That is the dismissal [of the objection].
As for what was asked— that there is no fixed rule of sequence— he says this in order to demonstrate it.
For the sequence of minds is indeed fixed;
this is precisely what is accepted [by us].
"Due to the distinction of lineage" means due to the distinction of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
"From the woman's mind," and so forth.

From the woman's mind—that is, from the mind having the woman as its object—immediately thereafter, there arises in the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) or another virtuous person a thought directed toward the loathesomeness of that woman's body; "that body" refers to the body of that woman. If such a thought should arise, [the result follows].
Or it is the mind directed toward her husband, sons, and so forth.
Her husband, sons, and so forth—
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), daughters and others are included.
The mind that has that as its object is the mind directed toward her husband, son, and so forth;
or it is one of those [other minds] which arises immediately after that woman’s mind. Then, again at another time, through the transformation of the continuum, the woman’s mind arises once more.

Subsequently, that female mind which has arisen becomes capable of producing a mind that reviles her own body, or produces a mind that reviles the body of that woman, or produces a mind directed toward her husband, children, and so forth.
Why is this? He says:
Regarding the phrase "because it has that lineage" (*tadgotratvāt*):
that which has as its lineage (*gotra*) or seed (*bīja*) the mind that reviles that body, or the mind [directed toward] his wife, sons, and so forth, is "of that lineage.
The state of being that is "the nature of that mind" (*cittasya bhāvaḥ*).
Therefore, the intended meaning is "because it belongs to that same class. Otherwise— that is, if it does not belong to that lineage— it would be different.
Furthermore, "by way of succession," and so forth, means not simultaneously, but by way of succession:

from a woman's mind, there arises a mind of revulsion toward her body; from that, a mind directed toward her husband; from that, a mind directed toward her son; from that, a mind directed toward her daughter; and from that very same [mind], a mind directed toward her utensils and so forth arises.

Then, from among the mental states that have arisen immediately after the female mind, that very same mental state arises which is more abundant in its stream, more intense in its power, or more proximate to the mental state about to be produced. This is because the cultivation of that [specific state] is stronger; that is, because the cultivation of that which is more abundant, more intense, or more proximate possesses greater force.
"Elsewhere," and so forth.

"Occurring at that time" means pertaining to that time; it refers to a specific bodily condition and a specific external condition present at that moment. "Other than that" means apart from those two.
For that alone is logically consistent for which a bodily or external object arises as a condition;
that indeed is the stronger.
That cultivation which is described as belonging to what is more frequent, more intense, or more proximate is the stronger cultivation.
"Why does it not always bear fruit? For that mind does not cease.
Being thus questioned by the other, he replied:
"Because its characteristic is the alteration of its state while persisting."
That which has "alteration of duration" as its characteristic is called "having alteration of duration as its characteristic.
This is because of the existence of that [characteristic];
and of that very alteration, which is a characteristic of the conditioned.

The connection of the meaning is as follows: because it is conducive to the arising of the fruit of another cultivation—that is, to the arising of another mind which is the fruit of a different cultivation—it does not always bear that very same fruit.
For thus they say, namely the Elder Rāhula: "in every aspect."
Thus, in every respect,
as many [as there are] in a peacock's eye.
The various modes such as color and configuration;
these are their causes.
This is its cause by which there is such color, such configuration, and such smoothness;
it is not to be known through such modes as these.
It cannot be known by whom?
By those who are not omniscient.
By the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others.
For that knowledge is the power of omniscience;
for that knowledge is the power of the All-Knowing One.
The intention is that by this [explanation], that cause is known.

"Previously, of such varieties of mind" means that even the cause of material form (*rūpa*) cannot be known in every respect; how much more so, then, for those things that are immaterial (*arūpin*)? This is the meaning.
"One of the other sectarians" refers to the Vaiśeṣika.

If it is argued that [the mind arises] because it depends on a specific conjunction with the mind, the following might be thought: although the arising of the mind equally originates from the self, the self at certain times depends upon a specific conjunction with the mind.
Therefore, it is not the case that a mind of exactly the same kind arises eternally, nor does it arise according to a fixed sequence like a sprout, a stalk, and a leaf.
This is not so, because the conjunction with another [cause] is not established.
This is not so.
Why?
Because a conjunction other than those two—the self and the mind—is unestablished.
For no such entity as "conjunction" (saṃyoga) is established for us.
[The phrase] "and of the two conjoined things," etc., applies even if conjunction were admitted; [the full passage is] "and of the two conjoined things," etc.
"Of two pieces of wood well-known in the world, or of any others whatsoever.
The meaning is: "because they are delimited," that is, because they are seen to occupy a delimited space.
And regarding the explanation of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*): [the text continues].
Because the definition of conjunction is specified in the Vaiśeṣika treatise, what follows from that? It would entail the consequence of the self being limited;
it would entail the consequence of its occupying a delimited space.
Where there is the self, there is no mind; where there is the mind, [there is no self].
"There is no self therein.
By this, the reversal of the specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparyaya*) of this thesis is demonstrated through inference, scripture, and logical necessity.
[The opponent's position is: "Conjunction with the mind belongs to the self."
The self is the subject (dharmin). Its specific property (viśeṣa) is omnipresence;
its opposite is non-omnipresence.
"Because it would follow that the self moves as the mind moves.
From that definition— that conjunction is the attainment [of one thing] preceded by the non-attainment [of another]— it follows that as the mind moves from one part of the body to another,
the self likewise moves and departs from those respective locations.
For example, whichever region of the earth a person traverses,
from that very place the heat recedes;
and this being so, its lack of activity (niḥkriyatva) is contradicted.
That very same fault of the proposition applies; or rather, it results in the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) regarding destruction.
The term "consequence" (prasaṅga) is understood to carry over.
And as for [the phrase] "of the self":
wherever the mind wanders,
there the self perishes.
And this is precisely the fault in the thesis here, because it would entail the cessation of the self's permanence.
If it is argued that [the self] is conjoined with a specific location, [we reply: no.
It might be thought that there is a conjunction of the mind with a region of the self,
or a conjunction of the self with the mind in a particular region of the body where the mind is situated.
The mind does not conjoin with that portion of the self;
rather, it conjoins with another portion on its other side.
Therefore, even though conjunction is preceded by non-attainment, the mind conjoins with a portion of the self that was previously unattained.
That is not so,
because it is impossible for that very [self] to be a part of itself;
for there are no other parts belonging to the self.
Nor is it logical that the self itself should be a location for the self. Or, even granting that there is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*), as explained in detail:
even having accepted such a conjunction, since [the mind] is unchanging, how could there be a specific distinction in the conjunction when the mind is undifferentiated?
How does the conjunction become qualified?
Since it has been stated thus: "because it depends on a specific conjunction with the mind.
If it is argued that it is because it depends on a specific cognition (*buddhi*), [then we reply:]...
That very point is challenged above: "How is there a distinction in cognition?
Why does such a mind not always arise in this same way, given that the self (*ātman*) is without distinction?
For it is accepted that a distinction in the effect arises from a distinction in the cause, as in the case of the sounds of a conch, a drum, and so forth.

If it is argued that [cognition arises] from the contact of the self and the mind depending on a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*), the following might be thought: even though the self and the mind are eternal and unchanging, a specific cognition arises from the contact of the self and the mind depending on a specific mental impression.
This is what is being said.

From a specific *saṃskāra*, characterized by a specific cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there arises a specific conjunction of the self and the mind; from that specific [conjunction], there arises a specific cognition. To this, we reply:
"Let it be from mind alone," and so forth.
This is the intention of the Master here:
that there is no dispute regarding the existence of mind including its internal states (*sāntarbhava*), and that there is no dispute between me and you regarding the existence of mind.

There is also a specific conditioning (*saṃskāra*) characterized by a specific cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which we designate as "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*) or "seed" (*bīja*). The difference, however, lies in whether it is a distinct entity or not.
Therefore, let the specific cognition arise from that very mind itself, in dependence upon that specific conditioning.
"Is it by means of a self or by means of its conjunction [with the self] as imagined?
"Not at all," and so forth in detail.
A certain deceitful physician, while giving medicine to a certain sick person, thought:
This medicine is easily obtained,
and it is known to this sick person along with his attendants;
by means of this medicine, the illness of this sick person will be alleviated.
Thinking, "If others likewise disregard me in this way, then I shall gain no profit," he consecrated that [object] with the mantra "Phūḥ svāhā! Phūḥ svāhā! and showed it to the people.
"By this mantra, this medicine is accomplished.
In that case, just as the quack physician’s utterances of "phūḥ" and "svāhā" have no efficacy in accomplishing the action of the medicine,
the efficacy belongs solely to the medicine itself.
Thus, the self has no capacity for the arising of specific states of cognition; rather, the capacity belongs to the mind alone.
If it is argued that these two [cognition and its specific states] can only occur when a self exists:
It might be thought:
"Since those two, conditioned factors and consciousness, arise only when a self exists, therefore the self exists."
To this we say: it is mere words; there is no reasoning here whatsoever.
If it is argued that "it is the substratum," [we reply: no.
It might be thought:
"The two have the self as their support.
But how can one thing be the support of another?
An illustration is sought by way of its basis. Showing that it is improper for this to serve as its basis, he says:
"For those [are not... and so forth.
These two are the conditioned factors (saṃskāra) and the mind (citta).
It is like a painting and a jujube fruit;
just as a painting is supported by a wall and a jujube fruit is placed in a bowl.
By the word "etcetera," [it refers to] food in a vessel and so forth.
Those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the mind are not at all to be placed within that self, nor are they to be supported by it.
Nor is it logical that it [the self] should have a support like a wall or a bowl;
nor is it logical that the self itself should be a support like a wall or a bowl.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), vessels and the like are included.
He asks: "What is the reason? and replies:
"Because of the faults of being obstructive and being separate.

This means because of the fault of being obstructive (*sapratighatva*) and because of the fault of being distinct entities (*pṛthagbhāva*), which would entail the consequence of [atoms] possessing resistance and the consequence of existing as spatially discrete units.
Just as in the case of a variegated jujube fruit and its wall, or a bowl and its container, both resistance and conjunction are observed in the relationship between the supported and the support;
so too would this be for these [atoms]. And this is undesirable.
Therefore, it does not have a non-self as its basis.
Just as there is no earth other than its odor and so forth, so too there is no self other than cognition and so forth.
(Abhidh-k-vy 717) For what virtuous person indeed would maintain that earth is something other than odor and the rest?

For when it is asked, "What is earth?", it is not possible to point out anything other than visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility, in the way that visible form is shown to be other than odor and the rest.
If earth is not other than odor and the rest...
How is this designation "fragrance and so forth in the earth" possible?
For a designation of one thing by means of another is observed,
as in "Caitra’s blanket."
Therefore it is said:
"But the designation," and so forth.
"For the sake of distinction" means for the sake of distinguishing it from water and the other elements.
He explains how this is so with the passage beginning "For it is those very... and so forth.
In the phrase "for it is those very," the particle *eva* (very/only) serves to exclude any other substance of earth apart from them.
These are indeed the odors and so forth; they are designated by those names, namely "earth," so that they may be understood as such.
The connection is that the designation is for the purpose of specification;
"not others" means not those called water and so forth.
The meaning is that those other than what are called "earth" should be understood [as distinct].
It is like the designation of a "body" for a wooden statue;
just as a wooden statue is designated as having a "body."
This is for the purpose of distinguishing it from others, such as those made of clay;
yet the body of a wooden statue is not something other [than wood].
In this case as well, there would be such a designation.
And earth is not something other than smell and the rest.
"Depending on a particular conditioning factor" refers to the contact between the self and the mind.
"For that which is the strongest" [refers to the specific causal efficiency].
It is a specific conditioning force (*saṃskāraviśeṣa*).
By means of it, there is an obstruction of other specific conditioning forces.
Regarding that very [force], the Teacher’s statement is: "Why does this most powerful [force] not always produce its fruit?"
He further said:
"Whatever is the principle for this— whatever is the principle for the conditioning factor (*saṃskāra*), whether it be its destruction or its obstruction—
let that same principle apply to cultivation (*bhāvanā*) insofar as it consists of a seed."
But the self is postulated as being purposeless and devoid of utility;
for that postulation would have to be for the sake of the formative forces (saṃskāra). And whatever is the effect of those formative forces—
"It is performed by cultivation alone.
This refers to the detailed explanation beginning with "of mindfulness and so forth.
It might be thought:

Since memory, mental formations, desire, aversion, and so forth belong to the category of qualities (*guṇa*), and since that category of quality necessarily depends upon a substance (*dravya*)—as taught in the definition: "A substance is that which is the substratum of qualities and possesses qualities"—and since no other substratum such as earth and the like is suitable for these [mental factors] due to reasons such as their being imperceptible to others; [therefore, they must depend on the mind].
Therefore, that which is their substratum is the self;
hence, the self exists.
No; because it is unestablished.
This is not so.
Why?
Because it is not established that memory and the other [mental factors] are categories of quality (guṇa-padārtha). [The opponent says:
"It is a substance that exists."
That which exists by way of its own characteristic is a substance (*dravya*).
There are six substances that constitute the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
The five aggregates, beginning with the aggregate of form, the fruits of asceticism, and the unconditioned as the sixth— these constitute six entities.
Nor do these [fruits] consist of mindfulness and so forth.

For the meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*) has already been examined. As it was explained in detail: "What is the basis of what? For those [elements] are not things to be supported (*ādhārya*), like a painting or jujube fruits [in a bowl]."
"These types" refers to types such as fair-complexioned and so forth.
The "I-notions" (ahaṃkarāḥ) are directed toward the aggregates [with the thought] "this is I.
However, they are not the "I-notion" (ahaṃkāra).
The meaning is that they are not a cognition (pratyaya) having the form "I" (*aham*).
But this brings us back to the very same point: for what purpose is this genitive case used? It is used in the sense of ownership (*svāmin*).
Just as one asks, "Who is the owner of what?"— for example,
Caitra is the owner of the cow— one asks how he is her owner.
For it is because he is dependent upon her that there is his employment of her for carrying loads, plowing, and so forth.

Furthermore, where else could the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) be employed such that its master must be sought? It is to be employed toward the object that is to be made an "I. For what purpose is it to be employed?
"For the sake of egoism.
"Ah, how well said by those raised in comfort!
For indeed, that very thing must be employed for that purpose."
And how is it to be applied?
Is it by way of production, or by way of dispatching?
Because the movement of the notion of "I" (ahaṃkāra) is impossible [in the case of the other], it is by way of production.
In that case, it follows that the cause alone is the master and the fruit alone is the property,
because the cause exercises sovereignty over the fruit.
And by the fruit, the cause is characterized as possessing that [fruit].
That which is the very cause of this ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*),
it is precisely that [cause] of which this [ego-grasping] is the effect.
The example "the tree is in bloom" applies to that philosophical system where a composite whole (avayavin) consisting of the tree is not accepted— that is,
where the production of a body composed of the four great elements of a different genus is not desired. However, it applies to those systems where such a composite whole of the tree does exist.
In this regard, the second example is "a forest that has borne fruit. For there is no such thing as a "forest" that exists in itself.
Just as a forest in which fruit has arisen is said to be "fruit-bearing," so too,
when pleasure or pain arises in a basis characterized by the six sense bases, that [basis] is said to be "possessing pleasure" or "possessing pain."
"Thus it has been said":
just as the basis (*āśraya*) was stated to be the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*),
so too the eyes and the other [senses] are the bases because they undergo transformation in accordance with the transformation of that [consciousness].
Thus it is said.
Now, it is understood that you are citing the *Pañcaskandhaka*;
he alone is the agent.
That very agent, characterized by the five aggregates,
is not the self;
thus our position is established.
Showing that even there [in the body] there is no independence, he says:
"And this action is threefold," and so forth.
The activity of the body is dependent upon the mind, because bodily action is set in motion by the mind.
The activity of the mind with respect to the body is also dependent upon its own causes,
because it is dependent on mental factors (dharma), attention (manaskāra), and so forth.
Likewise, the activity of that very cause of the mind is dependent upon its own causes.
There is no independence whatsoever for the body, the mind, the cause of the mind, or anything else;
for all phenomena are dependent upon conditions.
Indeed, the mind and mental factors arise from four conditions, while the two meditative attainments arise from three.

For it is stated that "others, however, are born from two [causes]. Furthermore, since it is admitted that even the self, when independent, is not the cause for the arising of specific cognitions and so forth, its independence is not established.
Therefore, it is not characterized in this way.
[The opponent says: "The agent is independent. [The author replies: If that is so, then he simply calls him the "agent."
However, that which is the primary cause of something is called its "agent," because [the effect] arises in dependence upon that which is predominant.
Even in this way, he is not logically established as an agent;
the meaning is that he is not logically established even by way of being a primary cause.
Demonstrating his lack of causality, he says:
"For from mindfulness arises desire," and so forth. Mindfulness arises with respect to an object previously remembered;
from mindfulness arises desire, which is the wish to act.
Vitarka arises from desire; it is a specific type of volition characterized by formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*), or, according to the system of the Yogācāras, a specific type of wisdom (*prajñā*).
However, according to the system of the Vaibhāṣikas, it is characterized by the conceptualization of investigation (*abhirūpaṇa-vikalpa*).
From applied thought (*vitarka*) comes effort, which is vigor (*vīrya*).
From effort comes wind.
From that wind comes action, characterized by arising in another location.
What does the self do here?
Because [action] is denied in the case of consciousness;
it is simply perception itself.
That very thing is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
And the capacity of a self (*ātman*) with respect to consciousness has been refuted.
Let it be from the mind (*citta*) itself, depending upon specific formative forces (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*).

For no capacity whatsoever is perceived in the self, just as the "phūḥ" and "svāhā" cries of a quack physician are of no avail when the medicinal treatment has already succeeded. As it has been said: [End of quote].
Because they undergo change when that [consciousness] changes, the eyes and so forth are its supports.
"Supported by that" means supported by the self.
This line of reasoning has already been answered.
For instance, what could be the support for what?
Indeed, they are not things to be supported like a painting or jujube fruits [in a vessel].
Nor is it logical for that [consciousness] to have a support like a wall or a vessel;
because of faults such as its being subject to resistance (*pratighātitva*), it cannot indeed be a support in that way.
"How then?"—this is the detailed explanation.
"For that is deposited by that" means that the capacity is deposited by that seed. "As it was said" refers to what was stated by the Elder Rāhula.
"That which is heavy and that which is proximate," and so forth;
there are four types of karma within a single continuum.
Weighty, near, habitual, and previously performed—among these four, the weighty karma ripens first; thus it ripens before the other three.
Among the near, habitual, and previously performed, the near ripens first; thus it ripens before the other two.
Between actions that have been habitually practiced and those performed previously, that which was habitually practiced ripens first;
in the absence of these, karma performed in a previous life that is to be experienced in a subsequent lifetime (aparaparyāyavedanīya) ripens.
This refers to non-defiled [actions].
[This refers to] the wholesome [dharmas] and the unobscured-neutral ones.
"Arising from a specific state of softening" (viklittiviśeṣaja): softening (viklitti) is a subtle transformation of the fruit resulting from its connection with earth and water.
Its specific quality is that very same [element] when it is extremely intensified. From that, a particular modification is produced.
Therefore, another fruit arises.
Showing from what kind of specific transformation this occurs, he says:
For that which brings about the sprout of a particular kind of reality therein is its seed;
it is the seed of that sprout.

There is no other kind of primary element (*bhūtaprakāra*). The meaning is that the state of the primary elements while in the form of a prior seed is not [the same as] the state of the primary elements [in their manifest form].
However, this is said by way of a future designation (*bhavinyā saṃjñayā*).

Just as there is a designation by means of a future name, as in "he cooks rice" or "he grinds flour," so too the preceding continuum, while still in the state of an unmoistened seed, is designated as a "seed" by means of this future name. Or, [it is so called] because of its similarity.
It is similar to a specific transformation of the primary elements (*bhūta*) produced from a specific state of moisture.
Because that preceding continuum is so designated, it is called a "seed.
The detailed explanation here is the same as that.

If a wholesome, contaminated transformation of the mind arises from the specific condition of hearing the true Dharma and appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), or if an unwholesome transformation of the mind arises from the specific condition of hearing what is not the true Dharma and inappropriate mental attention, then from that, another ripening (*vipāka*) arises.
"It is not otherwise"—this is the same [point].
Just as one fruit does not arise from a fruit itself;
what then?
Because of a specific transformation.
Thus, it is not from one ripening alone that another ripening arises;
what then?
"It arises from a particular modification of the mind"—
this is the same [point]. It is like saying, "the filament is red in the fruit."
Within the fruit is the filament,
wherein the sour juice of the citron remains;
and that [juice] is not something other than it.
The filament is not red; therefore, from that aforementioned filament, another [red] filament is not produced.
What then?
The meaning is that only a natural, non-red filament is produced.
This is the illustration here:

just as from the fruit of a citron flower dyed with lac juice, which has red filaments, another red filament does not subsequently arise; so too, from a maturation born of karma, another maturation does not subsequently arise.
And it is said in this regard:
"For this mind, accompanied by infinite seeds, proceeds as a continuum. Each respective seed attains nourishment when its own specific condition arises within the mind."
That [seed], having found its nourishment in a tree, becomes fruit-bearing in due time;
for it is like the color in the citron flower, which resides elsewhere, in its filament.
It is said again:
"When the cotton seed and the flower of the citron tree are dyed with lac,
the cotton filament is born red."
When that stage has ceased, through the continuity of the cultivated sequence,
and when the action itself has ceased, the arising of the fruit occurs from that cultivation.
Thus,
"karma" refers to everything; [it is] its cultivation.
The cultivation of karma; of that cultivation.
But the attainment of activity is the attainment of your conduct; from that [arises] gain.
Because it attains its activity through that [cause], it is the fruit. (Abhidh-k-vy 721)
Thus, this tetrad is necessarily [attained] by one other than a Buddha through chance.
The śrāvaka and others do not understand in every way and in all aspects.
What is meant by implication is this: the Buddha alone knows all that in every way.
"Thus, this" and so forth is the full statement.

Having observed— that is, having seen— this nature of the Buddhas' teaching (*pravacanadharmatā*), which is pure and irreproachable by way of the path of reason (*hetumārga*), that is, by means of a well-established logical path.
The non-Buddhists are blind because they lack the vision of things as they truly are. A base view is a "wrong view" (kudṛṣṭi).
And her "practices" are the practices of false views (*kudṛṣṭi*).

Those who possess these various practices of false views are called "those of diverse practices of false views"; the meaning is that they have either failed to understand or have wrongly understood the cause of heaven and liberation.

Having discarded—that is, having abandoned—the doctrine and philosophical system (*darśana*) of such non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*) as Kapila, Ulūka, and others, [the wise] go from saṃsāra to nirvāṇa; this is the ellipsis to be supplied for the sentence.

Who are those beings who possess the eye of wisdom? They are the noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*). Alternatively, the meaning is that they go toward and practice that very nature of the teaching (*pravacana-dharmatā*).
Furthermore, in this context, the nature of the teaching refers either to selflessness (*nairātmya*) or to the instruction of the Buddha.

the teaching (*pravacana*) consists of the twelvefold collection of scriptures, such as the Sūtras and so forth;
its true nature (*dharmatā*) is its well-expounded character (*svākhyātatā*), because it is endowed with logical reasoning (*yukti*).
And there is an inclination toward *nirvāṇa* because of the illumination of *nirvāṇa*.

Nirvāṇa itself is the city; thus, "the city of nirvāṇa" [means] that there is a single path to it, meaning that there is no other path than this one path to the city of nirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata himself is the sun; because he illuminates the profound Dharma, the Tathāgata has become like the sun.
His very words are the rays; she is radiant and luminous with them, thus "radiant with the rays of the Tathāgata-sun’s words.
She is "carried by thousands of noble ones" because she has been brought forth by thousands of Āryas.
"Even though it is revealed": although this very selflessness (*nirātmatā*)— which leads exclusively to the city of Nirvāṇa and is radiant with the rays of the words of the Tathāgata-sun—

is revealed, the one with weak vision— whether a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) or even a Vātsīputrīya— does not perceive it, because of the absence of the clear eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*) or because their eyes are shrouded by the film of the sheath of ignorance (*avidyā*).
And here, three qualities of the path are described:
namely, its being a single way (*ekāyanatā*), because it leads to the intended destination;
and its being accompanied by light (*sālokatā*), because one proceeds without fear.
And it possesses the quality of being traversed by those who follow after, because stumps, thorns, and the like have been completely crushed out;
by virtue of which one travels with ease.
This [path of selflessness] is to be viewed as analogous to that.
And for four reasons the path does not exist: because sentient beings are shrouded in darkness; and even though it has been illuminated by the sun, because they have not set it in motion.
Even when carried by many people, it is not seen because it is obstructed; even when unobstructed, it is not seen by the observer because of his weak eyesight.
Thus, only one cause for the non-perception of this path has been stated here among those [factors].
For this path is not seen due solely to the defect of the seer,
and not due to a defect in the path.
Therefore, it should be understood that it is because this person has dull vision that he does not see it.

Just as someone, thinking that poison by its own power spreads excessively through all the limbs and members of the body once it has reached the site of a wound, makes an incision at that wound-site so that "how indeed might this [poison] spread?"— in the same way, for those of great intelligence, the objects of the senses are like the site of the poison because they spread by their own inherent power.

This [work], which is like a casket containing the various meanings of the Abhidharma, has been explained by me...

May the bees that are the wise attend upon this lotus of the treatise, which has blossomed by the rays of the sun that are my explanations; it was brought forth from the womb of the wonder of nectar for those whose thirst has been produced.
Having studied all the treatises and being renowned for his scholarship, Yaśomitra— who was dissatisfied with other commentaries— composed this commentary.
Thus, this commentary on the scriptures of the supreme truth has been composed by Devarūpa, who is like a god, for the illustrious Lord of Speech.
The eighth treasury-location (kośasthāna) is completed in the *Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* composed by Ācārya Yaśomitra.
